Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 1 (part 1 of 3):

The discussion of the interpretation of the words of God, may His praise be exalted: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: The interpreters of the Qur'an (tarajimat al-Qur'an: its exegetes, as has passed above) differed concerning the interpretation of the words of God, may His remembrance be exalted, "Alif Lam Mim." Some of them said: it is one of the names of the Qur'an.

Mention of those who said that:

225 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words "Alif Lam Mim," he said: It is one of the names of the Qur'an.

226 - Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim al-Amili narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah Musa ibn Mas'ud narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, he said: "Alif Lam Mim," a name of the names of the Qur'an.

227 - Al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Dawud narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, he said: "Alif Lam Mim," a name of the names of the Qur'an.

Others said: it is openings (fawatih) with which God opens the Qur'an.

Mention of those who said that:

187 - Harun ibn Idris al-Asamm al-Kufi narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad al-Muharibi narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, he said: "Alif Lam Mim," openings with which God opens the Qur'an.

229 - Ahmad ibn Hazim al-Ghifari narrated to us, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mujahid, he said: "Alif Lam Mim," openings.

230 - Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Adam, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, he said: "Alif Lam Mim," and "Ha Mim," and "Alif Lam Mis," and "Sad," are openings with which God opened [the Qur'an].

231 - Al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same as the report of Harun ibn Idris.

Others said: it is the name of the surah.

Mention of those who said that:

232 - Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Wahb informed us, saying: I asked 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam concerning God's words "Alif Lam Mim, that is the Book," and "Alif Lam Mim, the revelation," and "Alif Lam Ra, these are..." He said: My father said: they are only names of the surahs.

Others said: it is the Greatest Name of God.

Mention of those who said that:

233 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, saying: I asked al-Suddi concerning "Ha Mim," "Ta Sin Mim," and "Alif Lam Mim," and he said: Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the Greatest Name of God.

234 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Nu'man narrated to me, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Isma'il al-Suddi, from Murrah al-Hamdani, he said: 'Abd Allah said, and he mentioned something similar.

235 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj narrated to us, from 'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa, from Isma'il, from al-Sha'bi, he said: The openings of the surahs are from the names of God.

Others said: it is an oath which God swore by, and it is one of His names.

Mention of those who said that:

236 - Yahya ibn 'Uthman ibn Salih al-Sahmi narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: It is an oath which God swore by, and it is one of the names of God.

237 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us, saying: Khalid al-Hadhdha' narrated to us, from 'Ikrimah, he said: "Alif Lam Mim," an oath.

Others said: it is disjointed letters, of names and verbs, each letter of which has a meaning different from the meaning of the other letter.

Mention of those who said that:

238 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us; and Sufyan ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Shurayk, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Abu al-Duha, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Alif Lam Mim," he said: I am God, the All-Knowing.

239 - I was told on the authority of Abu 'Ubayd, saying: Abu al-Yaqzan narrated to us, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, he said concerning His words "Alif Lam Mim": I am God, the All-Knowing.

240 - Musa ibn Harun al-Hamdani narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad al-Qannad narrated to us, saying: Asbat ibn Nasr narrated to us, from Isma'il al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Alif Lam Mim." He said: As for "Alif Lam Mim," it is a letter derived from the letters of the names of God, may His praise be exalted.

241 - Muhammad ibn Mu'ammar narrated to us, saying: 'Abbas ibn Ziyad al-Bahili narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words "Alif Lam Mim" and "Ha Mim" and "Nun," he said: a disjointed name.

Others said: they are letters of an arbitrary alphabet (hija' mawdu').

Mention of those who said that:

242 - I was told on the authority of Mansur ibn Abi Nuwayrah, saying: Abu Sa'id al-Mu'addib narrated to us, from Khusayf, from Mujahid, he said: The openings of all the surahs, "Qaf," "Sad," "Ha Mim," "Ta Sin Mim," "Alif Lam Ra," and other than these, are an arbitrary alphabet.

Others said: they are letters, each of which includes various different meanings.

Mention of those who said that:

243 - Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim al-Tabari narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far al-Razi, saying: My father narrated to me, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, concerning God's words, may His remembrance be exalted, "Alif Lam Mim," he said: These letters, of the twenty-nine letters, around which all tongues revolve. There is not a letter among them except that it is the key to one of His names, and there is not a letter among them except that it is in His blessings and His trials, and there is not a letter among them except that it is in the term and lifespans of a people. 'Isa ibn Maryam said: "And wonderful, they speak of His names, and live by His provision, so how do they disbelieve?" He said: The Alif is the key to His name "Allah," the Lam is the key to His name "Latif," and the Mim is the key to His name "Majid." The Alif is the blessings of God, the Lam is His kindness, and the Mim is His glory. The Alif is a year, the Lam is thirty years, and the Mim is forty years.

244 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi' with similar.

Others said: they are letters from the reckoning of al-jummal (the abjad numerical system). We disliked mentioning the one from whom this was related, since the one who transmitted it is not relied upon in his narration and report. The report with the like of this has already passed from al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

Others said: the Book has a secret, and the secret of the Qur'an is its openings.

* *

As for the grammarians (ahl al-'arabiyyah), they differed concerning the meaning of that. Some of them said: they are letters from the letters of the alphabet, and the mention of those mentioned among them at the beginnings of the surahs has sufficed from mentioning the remainder, which completes the twenty-eight letters; just as the one who reports, concerning someone whom he reports to be among the twenty-eight letters of the alphabet, has sufficed with mentioning "a b t th" from mentioning the rest of their letters, which complete the twenty-eight. He said: And for this reason "dhalika al-Kitab" was raised, because the meaning of the speech is: Alif, Lam, Mim are among the disjointed letters; "that is the Book" which I have sent down to you, collected, there is no doubt in it.

If someone says: But "a b t th" has become like a name among the letters of the alphabet, just as "al-Hamd" was the name of the opening of the Book.

It is said to him: Since it is permissible for a speaker to say: "my son is in t z," and it is known by his saying that, if he said it, that he intends to report about his son that he is among the disjointed letters, it is known by that that "a b t th" is not a name for them, even if it is more prominent in mention than the rest of them. He said: The difference in mentioning the letters of the alphabet in the openings of the surahs was made: they are mentioned at their beginnings differently, and their mention when mentioned by their beginnings, which are "a b t th," in agreement, so as to distinguish the report about them when intended, by mentioning what is mentioned of them differently, indicating connected speech; and when intended, by mentioning what is mentioned of them in agreement, indicating the disjointed letters themselves. They cited, to permit the saying of the speaker "my son is in t z" and the like, of the report about him that he is among the letters of the alphabet, and that this from his speech in clarification stands in place of his saying "my son is in a b t th," the verse of a certain rajiz from the Banu Asad:

When I saw her affair in its cutting... and she was lying in falsehood and denial... I took from her by locks of the braids of the white-haired ones... and my pouring and drawing with her did not cease, until blood covering the head rose.

He claimed that he intended by that a report about the woman that she is in "abi jad," so he placed his saying "when I saw her affair in my ..." in place of his report about her that she is in "abi jad," since that was from his speech, indicating to its hearer what his saying "when I saw her affair in abi jad" indicates to him.

Others said: the openings of the surahs were begun with that so that it would open the hearing of the polytheists to listen to it, when they had agreed to turn away from the Qur'an; so that when they listened to it, the composed part of it would be recited to them.

Some of them said: the letters that are the openings of the surahs are letters with which God opens His speech.

If it is said: Can there be in the Qur'an something that has no meaning?

It is said: The meaning of this is that He opened with them to make known that the surah before it has ended, and that He has begun another; He made this a sign of the separation between them. This is in the speech of the Arabs: a man recites poetry and says:

"Bal, and a town whose people are not of its inhabitants..."

And says:

"No, bal, what stirred sorrows and longing, it has longed."

"Bal" is not from the verse, nor counted in its meter, but by it he cuts off one speech and begins another.

Abu Ja'far said: For each of the sayings that those we described have said, there is a known aspect.

As for those who said "Alif Lam Mim" is one of the names of the Qur'an, their saying has two aspects:

One: that they intended "Alif Lam Mim" to be a name for the Qur'an, just as al-Furqan is a name for it. If the speaker's meaning is so, then the interpretation of his saying "Alif Lam Mim, that is the Book" is in the sense of an oath, as if he said: "By the Qur'an, this is the Book, there is no doubt in it."

The other of them: that they intended that it is a name of the surah by which it is known, just as all things are known by their names which are signs by which they are known, so the hearer understands from the speaker who says: "Today I recited 'Alif Lam Mis' and 'Nun'," which of the surahs of the Qur'an he recited, just as he understands, when he says: "Today I met 'Amr and Zayd," and they are both known to be Zayd and 'Amr, who among the people he met.

And if the meaning of that becomes unclear to someone who says: How can that be so, when the likes of "Alif Lam Mim" and "Alif Lam Ra" in the Qur'an are many surahs? Names are signs only when they distinguish individuals; but if they are not distinguishing, they are not signs.

It is said: Names, even though they have become, because many people share one of them, non-distinguishing except through other meanings added to them, such as attributing the named one to his father, or describing him, or his attribute, by which he is distinguished from others of their kind, nevertheless they were established at the outset for distinction, undoubtedly. Then, when sharing occurs, distinguishing meanings between the two named are needed. So it is with the names of the surahs. Each name, in the saying of the speaker of this view, was made a sign for the surah named by it. When the surah named by it shares it with other surahs of the Qur'an, the one reporting about one surah needs to add to its name, by which it is named, what distinguishes for the hearer the report about it from others, such as an attribute, a description, or otherwise. So the reporter about himself says he recited the surah of al-Baqarah, when naming it by its name which is "Alif Lam Mim": "I recited 'Alif Lam Mim al-Baqarah'," and in Al 'Imran: "I recited 'Alif Lam Mim Al 'Imran'," and "Alif Lam Mim, that is the Book," and "Alif Lam Mim, God, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting." Just as if he intended to report about two men, each named "Amr," except that one of them is Tamimi and the other Azdi, he would have to say to whoever he intends to inform about them: "I met 'Amr al-Tamimi and 'Amr al-Azdi," since he does not distinguish them from others who share their names except by their lineage thus. So it is with that in the saying of whoever interpreted the disjointed letters as names of the surahs.

As for those who said: they are openings with which God, may He be mighty and majestic, opens His speech, they directed their interpretation toward the meaning we related from the grammarians we related from, that he said: these are indicators of the ending of one surah and the beginning of another, and a sign of the separation between them, just as "bal" was placed at the beginning of a qasidah as an indication of a beginning in it and the ending of another before it, as we mentioned from the Arabs when they want to begin reciting a qasidah, they say:

"Bal, what stirred sorrows and longing, it has longed."

"Bal" is not from the verse, nor included in its meter, but by it he indicates the cutting of one speech and the beginning of another.

As for those who said: these are disjointed letters, some of which are from the names of God, may He be mighty and majestic, and some of which are from His attributes, and each letter of them has a meaning other than the meaning of the other letter, they aimed in their interpretation toward the like of the saying of the poet:

"We said to her: Stop for us. She said: Qaf... do not think that we have forgotten the galloping."

By his saying "qalat qaf" he means: she said: I have stopped (waqaftu). By showing the qaf from "waqaftu," she indicated her intent of the completion of the word which is "waqaftu." So they turned his saying "Alif Lam Mim" and what is like it toward this meaning. Some of them said: the Alif is the alif of "ana" (I), the Lam is the lam of "Allah," and the Mim is the mim of "a'lam" (I know), and each letter of them indicates a complete word. They said: so the sum of these disjointed letters, when with each letter is manifested the completion of the letters of the word: "ana Allahu a'lam" (I am God, the All-Knowing). They said: and likewise all that is in the openings of the surahs of the Qur'an is on this meaning and by this interpretation. They said: And it is widespread and evident in the speech of the Arabs that a speaker among them may reduce letters from a word when there is in what remains an indication of what was omitted from it, and may add to it what is not of it, when the addition does not confuse its meaning for its hearer, like their omission in the diminutive form (tarkhim) of "Harith" of the thaa', so they say: "Ya Har," and from "Malik" the kaf, so they say: "Ya Mal." And as for what is like that, and like the saying of their rajiz:

**Commentary of al-Ṭabarī (Jāmiʿ al-Bayān) on Sūrah 2, Verse 1 (part 2 of 3)**

Mā lil-ẓalīm ʿāl? Kayfa lā yā ... yanqudh ʿanhu jilduhu idhā yā [[Sharḥ shawāhid al-Shāfiyah: 267. ʿāl: a curse against him, from the saying "ʿāl ʿawlahu," meaning his mother bereaved him, and it was shortened. The "yā" in the first line seems to be what he intended to say as "yanqudu ʿanhu..." and then he paused, then returned saying "yanqudu," and the "yā" in the last line means: "idhā yaʿduu hādhā al-ʿadū" (when this enemy runs).]]

It is as if he intended to say: "idhā yafʿal kadhā wa kadhā" (when he does such and such), so he suffices with the yāʾ of "yafʿal," and as another of them said:

*Bi-l-khayri khayrātin wa in shaarran fā*
He means: *fa-sharran*.

*Wa lā urīdu l-sharra illā an tā* [[Sībawayh 2:62; al-Kāmil 1:240; al-Muwashshaḥ: 120; Sharḥ shawāhid al-Shāfiyah: 262, and he attributed it on p. 264 to al-Qaym ibn Aws.]]
He means: *illā an tashāʾa* (except that you will), so he suffices with the tāʾ and the fāʾ in both words, from the rest of their letters. And what resembles this of the evidences is more than a book can contain.

**245.** As Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to me, he said: Ibn ʿUlayyah narrated to us, from Ayyūb and Ibn ʿAwn, from Muḥammad, who said: When Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah died, ʿAbdah said to me: "I do not see it except as a coming fitnah (strife), so flee from your property and join your family." I said: "What do you command me?" He said: "It is more beloved to me for you to [lie down]..." — Ayyūb and Ibn ʿAwn said, pointing with his hand under his right cheek, describing lying down — "...until you see a matter you recognize." [[The report 245: Muḥammad is Ibn Sīrīn. As for ʿAbdah, I have not been certain who he is, nor have I preferred one identification. Rather I almost am certain that this is a distortion, and the correct form is "ʿUbaydah," with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, a kasrah on the baʾ, and a ṭāʾ marbūṭah at the end. He is ʿUbaydah ibn ʿAmr (or Ibn Qays) al-Salmānī, one of the major Successors (tābiʿūn), of the generation of the Companions. He embraced Islam before the death of the Prophet (ﷺ) but did not meet him. Ibn Sīrīn was among the most frequent narrators from him. He is biographed in al-Tahdhīb, in Ibn Saʿd 6:62–64, and in Ibn Abī Ḥātim 3/1/91. As for Yazīd, he is Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiyah ibn Abī Sufyān, who died in the year 64. His saying "Qāla Ayyūb..." means that he gestured.]]

Abū Jaʿfar said: He means by "tā" [lying down], so he suffices with the tāʾ from *tadtajiʿ* (lies down). And as another said regarding addition in speech, in the manner I described:

*Aqūlu idh kharrat ʿalā l-kalkāli... yā nāqatī mā julti min majālī* [[al-Lisān (k-l-l); Mushkil al-Qurʾān: 235. Al-kalkal: the chest of a camel and others.]]
He means: *al-kalkal*.

And as another said:

*Inna shaklī wa in shaklaki shattā... fa-lzamī l-khuṣṣa wa-khfiḍī tabayyiḍī* [[al-Lisān (b-y-ḍ) (kh-f-ḍ); Mushkil al-Qurʾān: 234. He says it to his wife. Al-khuṣṣ: a tent made of reeds. His saying "ukhfiḍī" from al-khafḍ: it is ease and softness of living. He says to her: We are two who differ, so keep to your house and live in ease and softness, and the softness of life will increase your whiteness and blessing. As for me, travel is my habit; it tires me and makes me lean.]]

So he added a *ḍād* (the letter ḍ), and it is not in the word.

They said: Likewise, what is lacking from the full letters of each word of these words, which we mentioned are the complements of the letters of *Alif-Lām-Mīm* and its counterparts, is the same as what is lacking from the speech which we related from the Arabs in their poetry and speech.

As for those who said: each letter of *Alif-Lām-Mīm* and its counterparts indicates various meanings — like what we mentioned from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas — they directed this toward the same as what the one who said it is an interpretation of "Anā Allāhu aʿlam" (I am Allah, the Most Knowing) was directed toward, in that each letter of it is part of the letters of a complete word, which is sufficient by its indication of its completeness from mentioning its completion — even though they opposed him regarding each letter of that: whether it is from the word that the first group's speakers claimed it to be from, or from something else. So they said: Rather, the *alif* of *alif-lām-mīm* is from various words, which indicate the meanings of all of that and its completeness. They said: Each letter of that was singled out, and shortened from the full letters of the word, because if all the letters of the word were made apparent, the word which is made apparent — of which these separated letters are a part — would indicate only one meaning, not two meanings or more. They said: Since there would be no indication in that, if all of it were made apparent, except for its meaning which is one meaning, and Allah, mighty is His praise, intended by each letter of them to indicate many meanings of one thing — it is not permissible except that the letter which indicates those meanings be singled out, so that those addressed by it may know that Allah, mighty and majestic, did not intend the aim of one meaning and an indication of one thing by what He addressed them with, and that He only intended by it an indication of many things. They said: So the *alif* of *alif-lām-mīm* requires many meanings, among them the completion of the name of the Lord which is "Allah," and the completion of the name of the blessings of Allah which are the bounties of Allah, and an indication of a people's term that it is a year, when the *alif* in the *jummal* (abjad) reckoning is one. And the *lām* requires the completion of the name of Allah which is *Laṭīf* (the Subtle), and the completion of the name of His grace which is *luṭf* (kindness), and an indication of a people's term that it is thirty years. And the *mīm* requires the completion of the name of Allah which is *Majīd* (the Glorious), and the completion of the name of His greatness which is *majd* (glory), and an indication of a people's term that it is forty years. So the meaning of the speech — in the interpretation of the speaker of the first saying — is that Allah, mighty is His praise, opened His speech by describing Himself as the Knowing, to whom nothing is hidden, and made that a method for His servants to follow at the beginning of their sermons, their letters, and their important affairs, and a trial from Him for them, so that they may deserve by it great reward in the abode of recompense; just as He opened with *al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn* (﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾), and *al-ḥamdu lillāhi alladhī khalaqa l-samāwāti wa l-arḍ* (﴿All praise is due to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾) [Sūrat al-Anʿām: 1], and what resembles that of the sūrahs whose openings He made praise of Himself; and just as He made the openings of some of them the magnifying of Himself and its exaltation by glorification, as He said, mighty is His praise: *subḥāna lladhī asrā bi-ʿabdihi laylan* (﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾) [Sūrat al-Isrāʾ: 1], and what resembles that from the rest of the sūrahs of the Qurʾān, in which He made the openings of some of them the praising of Himself, and the openings of some of them its glorifying, and the openings of some of them its magnifying and its declaring Himself free of imperfection. So likewise He made the openings of the other sūrahs whose beginnings are some letters of the alphabet, praises of Himself: sometimes by knowledge, sometimes by justice and fairness, and sometimes by bounty and benevolence, in brevity and concision, then the relating of matters after that.

According to this interpretation, it is necessary that *alif, lām, mīm* be in the nominative position, some of them raised by others, apart from His saying *dhālika l-kitāb* (﴿That is the Book﴾), and *dhālika l-kitāb* would be a predicate of a subject, cut off from the meaning of *alif-lām-mīm*. And likewise *dhālika*, in the interpretation of the speaker of this second saying, is raised by some of it, though its meaning differs from the meaning of the speech of the speaker of the first saying.

As for those who said: they are letters from the letters of *ḥisāb al-jummal* (abjad numerology), and not other meanings contrary to that, they said: We do not know any meaning for the separated letters that is understood except *ḥisāb al-jummal* and the spelling-out of the saying "alif-lām-mīm." They said: It is not permissible that Allah, mighty is His praise, address His servants except with what they understand and comprehend from Him. Since that is so — and His saying *alif-lām-mīm* has no comprehensible aspect toward which it is directed except one of the two aspects we mentioned — one of its two aspects is invalidated, namely that it is intended as the spelling-out of "alif-lām-mīm" — it is established and confirmed that the second aspect is intended by it, which is *ḥisāb al-jummal*; because the saying of the speaker "alif-lām-mīm" cannot be followed in speech by *dhālika l-kitāb*, due to the impossibility of the meaning of the speech and its departure from what is intelligible, if *dhālika l-kitāb* followed "alif-lām-mīm."

They also argued for their saying with what:

**246.** Muḥammad ibn Ḥumayd al-Rāzī narrated it to us, he said: Salamah ibn al-Faḍl narrated to us, he said: Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq narrated to me, he said: al-Kalbī narrated to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Riʾāb, who said: Abū Yāsir ibn Akhṭab passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while he was reciting the opening of Sūrat al-Baqarah: ﴿Alif-Lām-Mīm. That is the Book; there is no doubt in it﴾. So he came to his brother Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab of the Jews and said: "Do you know, by Allah [[thus in the printed and the manuscript: "taʿlamūna," and the text of Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, Sīrat Ibn Hishām 2:194, has "taʿlamū," with a doubled lām, meaning "iʿlamū" (know). It is frequent in the Sīrah of Ibn Hishām and others.]], I have indeed heard Muḥammad reciting, in what Allah, mighty and majestic, sent down to him: ﴿Alif-Lām-Mīm. That is the Book﴾." They said: "Did you hear it yourself?" He said: "Yes!" He said: So Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab walked with those men of the Jews to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they said: "O Muḥammad, has it not been mentioned to us that you recite in what has been sent down to you: 'Alif-Lām-Mīm, that is the Book'?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yes!" They said: "Did Gabriel bring this to you from Allah?" [[What is in Sīrat Ibn Hishām is: "Did Gabriel bring it to you from Allah?"]] He said: "Yes!" They said: "Indeed Allah, mighty is His praise, sent prophets before you, and we do not know that He clarified to any of them what the duration of his reign was, and the lifespan of his community other than you!" [[In the printed edition, and in all the other books that transmitted the report from al-Ṭabarī: "mā ajal" (what the term was).]] Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab then turned to those who were with him and said to them: "The alif is one, the lām is thirty, and the mīm is forty — so this is seventy-one years. Will you enter the religion of a prophet whose reign and the lifespan of his community is only seventy-one years?" [[In the printed edition: "qāla, fa-qāla lahum: a-tadkhulūn..." and "ajal ummatihi," and the correction is from the manuscript and Ibn Hishām. Al-akl (with a ḍammah then a sukūn): provision. It is said: he is great in akl in the world, meaning wide in provision, and it is the portion of the world, as if it is eaten. And what is meant by it is the span of life that people live in the world eating what Allah has provided them. So it is said of the dead: his akl has ended, meaning his life has come to an end.]] Then he turned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Muḥammad, is there with this something else?" He said: "Yes!" He said: "What?" He said: "Alif-Lām-Mīm-Ṣād." He said: "This is heavier and longer: the alif is one, the lām is thirty, the mīm is forty, and the ṣād is ninety, so this is one hundred and sixty-one years. Is there with this, O Muḥammad, something else?" He said: "Yes!" He said: "What?" He said: "Alif-Lām-Rāʾ." He said: "This, by Allah, is heavier and longer. The alif is one, the lām is thirty, and the rāʾ is two hundred, so this is two hundred and thirty-one years." He said: "Is there with this something else, O Muḥammad?" He said: "Yes: Alif-Lām-Mīm-Rāʾ." He said: "This, by Allah, is heavier and longer. The alif is one, the lām is thirty, the mīm is forty, and the rāʾ is two hundred, so this is two hundred and seventy-one years." Then he said: "Your matter has been confused for us, O Muḥammad, until we do not know: have you been given little or much?" Then they left him. Abū Yāsir said to his brother Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab and to those of the rabbis with him: "What makes you know? Perhaps all of this has been gathered for Muḥammad: seventy-one, and one hundred and sixty-one, and two hundred and thirty-one, and two hundred and seventy-one — so that is seven hundred and thirty-four years!" They said: "His matter has become confused for us!" And they claim that these verses were revealed concerning them: ﴿He it is who sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are clear (muḥkamāt) — they are the foundation of the Book — and others that are allegorical (mutashābihāt)﴾ [[Ḥadīth 246: This is a weak report in its chain. Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq narrated it with this weak chain and with other weak chains:

It was narrated in the Sīrah, which was refined by ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Hishām the grammarian of Basra, who narrated it from Ziyād ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Bakkāʾī from Ibn Isḥāq, and it became known and famous as "Sīrat Ibn Hishām." This Ibn Hishām is trustworthy (thiqah); Ibn Yūnus and others declared him trustworthy; he died in the year 218. His teacher Ziyād al-Bakkāʾī is trustworthy, one of the teachers of Aḥmad. "al-Bakkāʾī," with a fatḥah on the bāʾ and a shaddah on the kāf, is a nisbah to "al-Bakkāʾ," which is Rabīʿah ibn ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿah.

Ibn Hishām said (2:194–195; 2:35–37 of al-Rawḍ al-Unuf, the commentary on the Sīrah): Ibn Isḥāq said: Among those about whom the Qurʾān was specifically revealed were some of the rabbis and disbelieving Jews, who used to question him and test him, to confuse truth with falsehood — as was related to me from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās and Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Riʾāb: that Abū Yāsir ibn Akhṭab passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)... "

This is a weak chain: Ibn Isḥāq left out its narrator, so he brought it as a mu'allaq (suspended report) in the form of uncertainty (tamrīḍ). In it, the narration is from Ibn ʿAbbās and Jābir together.

Al-Bukhārī narrated it in al-Tārīkh al-Kabīr, in the biography of "Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Riʾāb" (1/2/207–208), with three chains, in his precise and exacting manner, in brevity and in pointing to the chains and their defects:

The first of them: "Ḥaddathanī ʿAmr ibn Zurārah, he said: Zīyād narrated to us: Ibn Isḥāq said: a client of Zayd ibn Thābit narrated to me, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and ʿIkrimah, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās and Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh: that Abū Yāsir ibn Akhṭab passed by the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was reciting (Alif-Lām-Mīm. That is the Book)."

This is al-Bukhārī's pointing to the first of the three chains. "Ziyād" in this chain is al-Bakkāʾī. So this chain is sound up to Ibn Isḥāq. But there is weakness in it because one of its narrators is unknown: "a client of Zayd ibn Thābit." It is like the chain of the Sīrah: from Ibn ʿAbbās and Jābir together. Perhaps ʿAmr ibn Zurārah, the teacher of al-Bukhārī, narrated the Sīrah from al-Bakkāʾī, as Ibn Hishām narrated it from him.

The second: "Salamah said: Ibn Isḥāq narrated to me, he said: Muḥammad ibn Abī Muḥammad narrated to me, from ʿIkrimah or Saʿīd, from Ibn ʿAbbās: (Alif-Lām-Mīm. That is the Book) — at length."

This is al-Bukhārī's pointing to the second chain. He means that Salamah — who is Ibn al-Faḍl in Ṭabarī's chain here — narrated it from Ibn Isḥāq. He did not mention the wording of the ḥadīth, being content with this pointer to it.

And Ibn Isḥāq, in this chain, narrates it from "Muḥammad ibn Abī Muḥammad," who is the Anṣārī Madanī, client of Zayd ibn Thābit. al-Dhahabī, in al-Mīzān, claimed that he is "unknown" (lā yuʿraf)! But he is known. Al-Bukhārī biographed him in al-Kabīr (1/1/225) and did not mention any criticism of him, and Ibn Ḥibbān mentioned him in al-Thiqāt. That is sufficient for recognition and authentication. Perhaps he is the "client of Zayd ibn Thābit" who was left unnamed in the first chain. But this chain was confused for Ibn Isḥāq, or for Salamah ibn al-Faḍl: so the narration in it is from ʿIkrimah or Saʿīd — meaning Ibn Jubayr — with doubt. Then it is from Ibn ʿAbbās alone, without mention of "Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Riʾāb."

The third: "And from Ibn Isḥāq: Among what the Qurʾān was revealed about from the rabbis, as Ḥaddathanī al-Kalbī narrated to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Riʾāb: Abū Yāsir ibn Akhṭab passed by the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was reciting (Alif-Lām-Mīm), at length — in the calculation."

This third report, with the chain found here in Ṭabarī, follows the second report from Salamah ibn al-Faḍl; he joined it to it by his saying "wa ʿan Ibn Isḥāq" and it is not a new suspended chain.

By this act, al-Bukhārī pointed to the confusion in the report of Salamah ibn al-Faḍl between this and that. For this reason he went to criticize "Salamah" on account of this confusion, and he said after that: "ʿAlī [meaning his teacher ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī, the imam of criticism and authentication] said: We did not leave al-Rayy until we had been struck with the ḥadīth of Salamah."

And in Salamah's biography (2/2/85) he said: "Salamah ibn al-Faḍl Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Abraṣ al-Rāzī al-Anṣārī; he heard Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq; ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad al-Jaʿfī narrated from him. He has munkars (rejected reports). It is said he is a client of them. He died after ninety (one hundred). ʿAlī weakened him," meaning his teacher Ibn al-Madīnī. He means that Salamah died after the year 190. And he said in al-Tārīkh al-Ṣaghīr, p. 217: "Salamah ibn al-Faḍl Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Abraṣ al-Rāzī al-Anṣārī died after one hundred and ninety. ʿAlī [meaning Ibn al-Madīnī] said: We were struck with his ḥadīth before we left al-Rayy. And Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm weakened him." And he also said in his biography in al-Ḍuʿafāʾ (p. 16): "He heard Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq; ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn Abān and Muḥammad ibn Ḥumayd narrated from him. But he has munkars. And there is consideration (fīhi naẓar) regarding him."

I, however, go to the authentication (tawthīq) of Salamah ibn al-Faḍl: Ibn Maʿīn declared him trustworthy, as narrated by Ibn Abī Ḥātim in his book, and he has with him a good and comprehensive biography (2/1/168–169). He also narrated from Jarīr, who said: "There is no one from Baghdad to Khurasan more reliable in (narrating) Ibn Isḥāq than Salamah ibn al-Faḍl." And I have also preferred his authentication in Sharḥ al-Musnad (886).

In my view, this confusion is from Ibn Isḥāq, or perhaps he narrated it with these chains as he heard it. And all of them are weak and confused. The weakest of them is the report here, which al-Bukhārī pointed to: the narration of al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ.]]

Ibn Kathir deserves praise, for he placed the truth where it belongs when he said in his Tafsir (1:69–70): "As for the one who claims that these letters indicate the knowledge of the time-period, and that from them one can derive the times of events, the tribulations and the great battles, he has claimed what is not his, and has flown in a place where there is no pursuit! A weak hadith has been transmitted on this matter, and it is, in addition, more indicative of the invalidity of this approach than of its soundness." Then he quoted this hadith from this same place in al-Tabari. He then said: "The hadith revolves around Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi, who is among those whose solitary reports are not used as proof. Moreover, if this approach were correct, one would have to calculate the value of each of the fourteen letters mentioned, which would amount to a large total. And if one were to count them with repetition, the total would be even greater and more enormous!"

Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi is extremely weak; he was accused of lying. Indeed, Ibn Abi Hatim related in his al-Jarh (3/1/270–271), in his biography, from Abu 'Asim al-Nabil, who said: "Sufyan al-Thawri claimed to me, saying: al-Kalbi told us: whatever I narrate from me on the authority of Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, it is a lie, so do not narrate it." Abu Hatim said: "The people are unanimous in abandoning his hadith; it is not to be occupied with. He is one whose hadith has gone."

Al-Tabari himself has, earlier on (p. 66), greatly weakened him, when he pointed to a report from Ibn 'Abbas: "All of that was related from Ibn 'Abbas, and the narration from him is not from one whose transmission may be used as proof," and then he mentioned that the one who related it was "al-Kalbi from Abu Salih." He described the hadith (p. 72) that he narrated by this route as "a report with a problematic chain."

So it is strange of him, after this, to argue with these incoherent narrations and to accept this objectionable interpretation through the reckoning of the abjad numerals (hisab al-jummal), when he chooses in what follows (this page, line 8 and onward) that these letters contain all the meanings he has recounted, except for one statement other than this objectionable meaning. Rather, he explicitly states afterwards (p. 222, line 8) that among the meanings he has accepted is that they are "from the letters of the abjad reckoning"!

Al-Suyuti quoted this hadith in al-Durr al-Manthur (1:22, and 2:4–5), and in the first place he described it as weak. Likewise, al-Shawkani quoted it (1:20) and deemed it weak.

His saying at its end, "and they claim that these verses…", is part of the narration; it is a statement of Ibn Ishaq, relating from those he narrated from.

They said: This report has clearly affirmed the soundness of what we have said regarding this interpretation, and the falsehood of what our opponents have said in this matter.

The correct view in my opinion regarding the interpretation of the opening letters of the surahs, which are the letters of the alphabet, is this: that Allah, mighty is His praise, made them separate letters and did not join some of them to others, so as to make them like the rest of speech whose letters are joined. This is because He, mighty is His remembrance, intended by His word the indication, through each letter in it, of many meanings, not one single meaning, as al-Rabi' ibn Anas said, although al-Rabi' limited it to three meanings, excluding what goes beyond them.

The correct interpretation of this in my opinion is that each letter of it contains what al-Rabi' said, and what other exegetes besides him said about it, except what I have mentioned from the statement of the one I mentioned from the people of Arabic grammar, who directed the interpretation of this toward it being letters of spelling (huruf hija'), where mentioning what has been mentioned of them in the openings of the surahs suffices in place of mentioning the remaining twenty-eight letters of the alphabet, by interpreting: "these letters, that Book, in which there is no doubt" as a whole. That is a wrong and corrupt statement, because it departs from the sayings of all the Companions, the Successors, and those after them among the later generations of the exegetes and interpreters. [[al-Khalifun is the plural of khalif: a people succeeded a people, succeeding them (yakhlifuna khalfan), so they are khalifun: they came after them and followed in their footsteps. You say: "I am his successor (khalifuh) and I succeeded him": meaning I came after him.]] Sufficient as evidence of its error is the testimony of proof against it that it is wrong, together with the invalidation by the one who says it of his own statement which we have quoted from him, since he moved to explain the raising of "that Book", saying once that each of the two is raised by its companion, and another time that it is raised by the pronoun referring back to it in His saying "in which there is no doubt", and another time by His saying "a guidance for the God-fearing." That is his abandonment of his own statement that "alif-lam-mim" raises "that Book", and a departure from the view he claimed in interpreting "alif-lam-mim that Book," namely that the meaning is: "these letters are that Book."

If someone says to us: How is it permissible for one letter to comprise the indication of many different meanings?

It is said: Just as it is permissible for one word to contain many different meanings, as when they say for a group of people: ummah; for a period of time: ummah; for a devout man obedient to God: ummah; and for religion and creed: ummah. And as when they say for recompense and retribution: din; for authority and obedience: din; for humility: din; for reckoning: din; and in many similar examples which would make the book too long to enumerate, of speech with one word that contains many meanings. Likewise is the saying of God, mighty is His praise: "alif-lam-mim," "alif-lam-ra," "alif-lam-mim-sad," and what is similar to these of the letters of the alphabet which are the openings at the beginnings of the surahs. Each letter of them indicates various meanings, all of which include, from the names and attributes of God, mighty is He, what the exegetes have said, of the sayings we have mentioned from them. And they, together with that, are openings of surahs, as the one who said that has said.

That these are from the letters of God's names and attributes, mighty is His praise, does not prevent them from being openings of surahs. This is because God, mighty is His praise, has opened many surahs of the Qur'an with praise of Himself and laudation of Himself, and many of them with glorifying and magnifying them. So it is not impossible that He begins some of them with an oath by them.

As for those with which the beginnings are the letters of the alphabet, one of the meanings of their beginnings is that they are the openings of the surahs of the Qur'an with which they open. And they are among what He has sworn by, because one of their meanings is that they are from the letters of the names and attributes of God, exalted is His remembrance, as we have previously explained, and there is no doubt about the validity of the meaning of swearing by God and His names and attributes. And they are from the letters of the abjad reckoning. And for the surahs which open with them they are a sign and names. That comprises the meanings of all that we have described, which we have made clear, in its aspects. For if God, mighty is His praise, had intended by that, or by something of it, the indication of one single meaning from among what it may bear, to the exclusion of the other meanings besides it, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would have clarified that for them with a clarification that is not ambiguous. Since He, mighty is His praise, sent down His Book upon His Messenger (ﷺ) only to make clear to them what they differed about. And in the Messenger's (ﷺ) leaving the clarification of that — that the intended meaning of it from its aspects of interpretation is some and not others — is the clearest proof that all its aspects which it is capable of bearing are intended by it. For there was nothing impossible in reason about any of its aspects being part of its interpretation and meaning, just as it is not impossible for many meanings to be combined in one word with one utterance, in a single speech.

Whoever refuses what we have said about this should be asked for the difference between that and the rest of the words which come with one utterance while comprising many different meanings, such as ummah and din and what is similar to them of nouns and verbs. He will not say anything about one of those except that he is obliged to say the same about the other.

Likewise, everyone who interprets any of that in a manner other than the other aspects we have described should be asked for the proof of his claim, in the aspect which must be accepted. Then his claim is set against the view of his opponent in this matter, and he is asked for the difference between his view and theirs, from a principle, or from what a principle indicates. He will not say anything about either of them except that he is obliged to say the same about the other.

As for what some of the grammarians claimed: that this is like "bal" (rather) in the saying of the reciter of poetry:

"bal * mā hāja aḥzānan wa-shajwan qad shajā"

and that it has no meaning, and that it is only an addition to the speech whose meaning is discarding — then he erred in several respects. [[See what has passed: p. 210.]]

The first of them: he described God, exalted is His remembrance, as having addressed the Arabs with something that is not of their language, nor of the language of any human being. For the Arabs, although they used to open the beginnings of their poetic recitations with "bal," it is known of them that they did not begin any speech with "alif-lam-mim," "alif-lam-ra," or "alif-lam-mim-sad" in the sense of beginning it with "bal." Since that was not part of their beginnings — and God, mighty is His praise, addressed them only with what He addressed them with of the Qur'an, using what they know of their languages and what they use among themselves in their speech, in all of its verses — there is no doubt that the way of what we have described of the letters of the alphabet, with which the beginnings of the surahs were opened, for which they are openings, is the way of the rest of the Qur'an, in that He did not divert them from their languages, which they knew, and which they used in their speech among themselves. For if that were diverted from the way of their languages and their speech, it would be outside the meaning of clarity with which God, mighty is He, described the Qur'an, when He, exalted is His remembrance, said: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart, that you may be among the warners, in a clear Arabic tongue.﴾ And how could something be clear when no one among the worlds understands or comprehends it, according to the statement of the one who makes this claim, and which is not known in the speech of any created being, in his saying? And in God's report, mighty is His praise, about it being a clear Arabic, there is something which refutes this claim, and indicates that the Arabs had knowledge of it, and it was clear to them. This is one of the aspects of his error.

The second aspect of his error in this matter: his attributing to God, mighty is His praise, that He addressed His servants with what has no benefit for them and no meaning, from speech in which addressing with it and not addressing with it are equal. That is attributing to God, exalted is His remembrance, the futility which is denied of God in the saying of all the monotheists.

The third aspect of his error: that "bal" in the speech of the Arabs has an understood interpretation and meaning, and that they use it in their speech to retract a statement that has already been completed, as in their saying: "Your brother did not come to me, rather (bal) your father"; "I did not see 'Amr, rather (bal) 'Abd Allah," and what is similar to such speech, as the poet A'sha Bani Tha'laba said:

"Wa-la-ashrabanna thamānīyan wa-thamānīyan ... wa-thalāth ʿashrata wa-thnatayn wa-arba'ā"

And he continued in his poem until he reached his saying:

"bi-l-julsāni, wa-ṭayyibun ardānuhu ... bi-l-wunni yaḍribu lī yakurru al-iṣba'ā"

Then he said:

"bal ʿaddi hādhā, fī qarīḍin ghayrihi ... wa-dhkur fatan samḥa al-khalīqati arwaʿā"

It is as if he said: Leave this and take up the poetry of someone else. So "bal" comes in the speech of the Arabs in this manner of speech. As for opening their speech as a beginning with the meaning of prolongation and deletion [[See what has passed: p. 18, note 2; by prolongation he means addition]], without indicating any meaning, that is something we do not know anyone among the people of knowledge of the Arabic language and its speech to have claimed, except the one whose saying I have mentioned. So it could be a principle by which the letters of the alphabet, which are the openings of the surahs of the Qur'an with which they open, are compared — if it were comparable to it — but how, when they are far from being like it?

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Dhalika al-Kitab﴾ (That is the Book).

The commentators in general said: The interpretation of God, may He be exalted, His words ﴿Dhalika al-Kitab﴾ are: "This is the Book."

Mention of those who said this:

247- Harun ibn Idris al-Asamm al-Kufi related to me, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad al-Muharibi related to us, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid: "Dhalika al-Kitab" — he said: it is this Book.

248- Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah related to us, saying: Khalid al-Hadhdha' informed us, from 'Ikrimah, who said: "Dhalika al-Kitab": this is the Book.

249- Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri related to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His words "Dhalika al-Kitab", he said: this is the Book. [[The report 249: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr (with a dammed ẓāʾ) al-Fazari, Abu Muhammad, known as Ibn Abi Layla al-Kufi: very weak, accused of fabricating hadith. Al-Bukhari said in al-Kabir: "They abandoned him; he is a munkar al-hadith." Ibn Abi Hatim said in al-Jarh, citing Abu Zur'ah: "weak in hadith." Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin, no. 239: "He used to revile the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ and narrated fabricated reports from reliable narrators."]]

250- al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan related to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Dawud related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, regarding his words "Dhalika al-Kitab": this is the Book. He said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "Dhalika al-Kitab": this is the Book. [[All these reports 247–250 are mentioned by Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir 1:70, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:24, and al-Shawkani 1:21.]]

If someone says: How can "dhalika" mean "hadha" (this)? "Hadha" undoubtedly indicates something present and visible, whereas "dhalika" indicates something absent, neither present nor visible? It is said: This is permissible, because whatever has passed, through the nearness of its passing to the reporting of it [[In the printed edition: "wa-qurb taqaddihi" — he means: the mention of what has passed, whose passing is near to your report about it.]], then it—although it has become of the sense of the absent—is like the present to the addressee. This is like a man who relates a narration to a man, and the listener says: "Indeed that, by God, is as you said," and "this, by God, is as you said," and "it, by God, is as you mentioned," so he refers to it at one time with the sense of the absent, since it has already passed and gone, and at another time with the sense of the present, because his answer is near to the speech of the one reporting it, as if it had not yet ended. Likewise "dhalika" in His words ﴿Dhalika al-Kitab﴾, because He, dhikruhu jalla, when He placed before "dhalika al-Kitab" the "Alif-Lam-Mim," whose various meanings we have mentioned as we described, said to His Prophet ﷺ: O Muhammad, this which I have mentioned and made clear to you is the Book. Therefore it was appropriate to place "dhalika" in the place of "hadha," because it is pointed to as a report about what the words "Alif-Lam-Mim" contained of meanings, after the report about it by "Alif-Lam-Mim" had passed. So, because the report about it is near its passing, it became like the present pointed-to, and so it is reported by "dhalika" because it has passed, and the report about it becomes like the report about the absent. The commentators interpreted it [[tarjamahu: i.e., the commentators explained and clarified it by placing one particle in place of another. See above, 70 note 1/93: 4/ and other places.]] as meaning "hadha," because the report about it is near its passing, so it was like the witnessed thing pointed to by "hadha," like what we described of speech circulating among people in their discourse, and as He, dhikruhu jalla, said: ﴿And remember Isma'il and al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl, and each is of the choice ones. This is a reminder﴾ [Surah Sad: 48, 49]. This is what "dhalika" carries when it is intended to mean "hadha."

And His words, dhikruhu jalla, ﴿Dhalika al-Kitab﴾ may possibly mean the surahs revealed before Surat al-Baqarah at Makkah and Madinah, so it is as if He, may He be exalted, said to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: O Muhammad, know that what the surahs of the Book which I have sent down to you contain is the Book in which there is no doubt. Then the commentators interpreted it [[tarjamahu: see above.]] as meaning "dhalika" = "hadha al-Kitab," since those surahs revealed before Surat al-Baqarah are part of the whole of this our Book which God, the Mighty and Majestic, sent down upon our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

The first interpretation is more fitting to what the commentators said, because it is the more apparent of the meanings of their statement about "dhalika."

Some have directed the meaning of "dhalika" toward a parallel of the meaning of the verse of Khufaf ibn Nudbah al-Sulami:

*"If my horses have indeed had their core struck, then certainly I aimed straight at Malik with purpose and sure aim,*
*I say to him, while the spear bends his side: 'Look at Khufaf — indeed I am that one.'"* [[Al-Aghani 2:329/13:134–135/16:134, al-Khizana 2:470, and others; it appears in al-Tabari 1:314, 437. He speaks in the verse about the killing of his cousin Mu'awiyah ibn 'Amr, brother of al-Khansa'. Malik is Malik ibn Himar al-Shamkhi al-Fazari. "Horses" here means the raiding cavalry; Mu'awiyah and Khufaf had raided Banu Murrah and Fazarah. "Samim" means the pure, unmixed core of anything. He meant Mu'awiyah and his killing that day. It is said: "I did this matter 'amd 'ayn, and 'amdan 'ala 'ayn," if you undertake it face-to-face with earnestness and certainty. "Tayammama" means he aimed for and headed toward. "Atara al-matn" — the spear bends the side: he means the heat of the wound made him writhe from its pain, then he bowed to fall prostrate when the spear struck his vital point. I see that the pointing in this verse is toward something absent, as if he said: "I am that one you heard of and of his valor." This meaning takes the verse out of being evidence for what al-Tabari intended.]]

As if he meant: "Look at me — I am that one." He claimed that "dhalika al-Kitab" means "hadha," being similar to it. Khufaf made his name appear in the form of a report about an absent person, while he was reporting about himself. Likewise "dhalika" appears with the sense of a report about the absent, while its meaning is pointing to the present and witnessed.

The first statement is more fitting for the interpretation of "al-Kitab," for the reasons we mentioned.

Some have said: "Dhalika al-Kitab" means by it the Torah and the Gospel. When the interpretation of "dhalika" is directed to this way, there is no burden upon its interpreter in that, because "dhalika" would then be a report about an absent thing, in soundness.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿La rayba fihi﴾ (there is no doubt in it).

Its interpretation: "la rayba fihi" = "la shakka fihi" (no doubt in it), as:

251- Harun ibn Idris al-Asamm related to me, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman al-Muharibi related to us, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid: "la rayba fihi" — he said: no doubt in it.

252- Salam ibn Salim al-Khuza'i related to me, saying: Khalaf ibn Yasin al-Kufi related to us, from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Rawwad, from 'Ata': "la rayba fihi" — he said: no doubt in it. [[Report 252: Salam, Tabari's teacher: I have found no biography of him except in Tarikh Baghdad 9:198, which says: "Salam ibn Salim Abu Malik al-Khuza'i al-Darir: he narrated from Yazid ibn Harun, 'Umar ibn Sa'id al-Tanukhi, Musa ibn Ibrahim al-Marwazi, and al-Fadl ibn Jubayr al-Warraq. Al-Husayn ibn Isma'il al-Muhamili narrated from him." Nothing more. As for his teacher in this chain, "Khalaf ibn Yasin al-Kufi": I have found only an entry in al-Mizan 1:211 and Lisan al-Mizan 2:405 for a narrator named "Khalaf ibn Yasin ibn Mu'adh al-Zayyat," who was a contemptible liar, not to be occupied with. I do not know whether this is he or someone else.]]

253- Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi related to me, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri related to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr related to us, from al-Suddi, who said: "la rayba fihi" — no doubt in it.

254- Musa ibn Harun al-Hamdani related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas — and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the companions of the Prophet ﷺ: "la rayba fihi," no doubt in it.

255- Muhammad ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "la rayba fihi," he said: no doubt in it.

256- al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "la rayba fihi," meaning: no doubt in it.

257- al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq related to us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah: "la rayba fihi," meaning: no doubt in it.

258- It was related to me from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: his words "la rayba fihi," meaning: no doubt in it. [[All these reports 251–258 are cited by Ibn Kathir 1:71, and some in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:24, and al-Shawkani 1:22. Ibn Kathir said after citing them: "Ibn Abi Hatim said: I know of no disagreement on this."]]

"Rayb" is a verbal noun from the speaker's saying: "raabani al-shay yaribuni raybuan" (the thing troubled me). From this is the saying of Sa'idah ibn Ju'ayyah al-Hudhali:

*"They said: 'We left the tribe, they have surrounded it with him,' so there is no doubt that a slain man was there."* [[Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin 1:232, and Lisan (hasar).]]

It is narrated as "hasaru" and "hasiru," with the fatha more common and the kasra permissible. By his words "hasaru bihi" he means: they encircled him. By his words "la rayb" he means: no doubt in it. By his words "anna qad kana tharma lahim" he means a slain man; it is said: "qad luhima," when he was killed.

The ha' in "fihi" refers back to the Book, as if he said: there is no doubt about that Book, that it is from God, a guidance for the God-fearing.

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Hudan﴾ (guidance)

259- Ahmad ibn Hazim al-Ghifari related to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Bayan, from al-Sha'bi, "hudan": he said: guidance from misguidance. [[Report 259: Bayan, with a fatha on the b and a light ya: he is Ibn Bishr al-Ahmasi, a reliable narrator among the reliable, as Ahmad said. Sufyan, who narrates from him, is al-Thawri. This report was cited by al-Suyuti 1:24, attributing it to Waki' and al-Tabari.]]

260- Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat ibn Nasr related to us, from Isma'il al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet ﷺ: "hudan lil-muttaqin," he says: light for the God-fearing. [[Report 260: Ibn Kathir 1:71 cited it, al-Suyuti 1:24 and al-Shawkani 1:22 cited it together with the following report 263, treating them as one report and attributing it to Ibn Mas'ud only.]]

"Al-huda" in this place is a verbal noun from your saying: "hadaytu fulanan al-tariq" — when you guide him to it, direct him to it, and make it clear to him — "uhdihi hudan wa hidayatan."

If someone says to us: Is not the Book of God a light only for the God-fearing, and a right direction only for the believers? It is said: That is as our Lord, may He be exalted, described it. Had it been a light for others than the God-fearing, and a right direction for others than the believers, God, may He be exalted, would not have specified the God-fearing as those for whom it is guidance; rather, it would have encompassed all who are warned. But it is guidance for the God-fearing, a healing for what is in the breasts of the believers, a deafness in the ears of the deniers, a blindness to the eyes of the rejecters, and a conclusive proof of God against the disbelievers. So the believer in it is guided, and the disbeliever in it is refuted [[hajjahu yahujjuhu fahuwa mahjuj: he overcame him with proof, so he is defeated.]].

His words "hudan" may bear several meanings:

One of them: it is in the accusative, by way of being a circumstantial qualifier cut off from the Book, since it is indefinite and the Book is definite [[He means by "cut off": that it is detached from being a qualifier of the Book and becomes a circumstantial accusative (hal).]]. Then the interpretation would be: "Alif-Lam-Mim, that Book, [being] guiding for the God-fearing." "Dhalika" is nominative by "Alif-Lam-Mim," and "Alif-Lam-Mim" is complete by it, and "al-Kitab" is a qualifier of "dhalika."

It may also be accusative, cut off from the pronoun referring back to the Book in "fihi," so the meaning then would be: "Alif-Lam-Mim, that which there is no doubt in, [being] guiding."

It may also be accusative on these two readings, namely by way of being cut off both from the ha' in "fihi" and from "al-Kitab," on the basis that "Alif-Lam-Mim" is a complete utterance, as Ibn 'Abbas said its meaning is: "I am God, the All-Knowing." Then "dhalika al-Kitab" is a new, independent statement, and "al-Kitab" would be in the nominative by "dhalika," and "dhalika" by "al-Kitab," and "hudan" would be a cut-off [accusative] from "al-Kitab"; or "dhalika" would be nominative by the ha' referring back to it in "fihi," with "al-Kitab" as its qualifier, and "hudan" cut off from the ha' in "fihi." If "hudan" is placed in the nominative, then "dhalika al-Kitab" can only be a new independent statement, and "Alif-Lam-Mim" a complete utterance standing on its own, except in one respect: that "hudan" is then raised in the sense of praise, as God, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. These are the verses of the wise Book, a guidance and mercy for the good-doers﴾ [Surah Luqman: 1–3], in the reading of the one who reads "rahmatun" with the nominative, as praise of the verses.

The nominative in "hudan" in that case is permissible in three ways: one of them is what we mentioned, that it is a new expression of praise. The second: that it be made the predicate of "dhalika," with "al-Kitab" a qualifier of "dhalika." The third: that it be made to follow the position of "la rayba fihi," with "dhalika al-Kitab" raised by the pronoun referring back in "fihi." So it would be as He, dhikruhu, said: ﴿And this is a Book which We have sent down, blessed﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 92].

Some of the early grammarians among the Kufans claimed that "Alif-Lam-Mim" is the subject of "dhalika al-Kitab," meaning: these letters from the letters of the alphabet are that Book which I promised to reveal to you [[He means by the speaker of this view al-Farra' in his Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:10.]]. Then he refuted that from his own words, quickly undoing his refutation, and tore down what he had built, quickly tearing it down: he claimed that the nominative in "hudan" is of two kinds and the accusative of two kinds. One of the two nominatives: that "al-Kitab" is a qualifier of "dhalika," and "hudan" in the position of nominative as predicate of "dhalika."

As if you said: "That is guidance, there is no doubt in it" [[In the printed text and the manuscript: "dhalika la shakka fihi"; the correction is from al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:11.]]. He said: If you make "la rayba fihi" its predicate, you also raise "hudan" by making it follow the position of "la rayba fihi," as God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And this is a Book which We have sent down, blessed﴾, as if he said: "And this is a Book, guidance, of such and such a description." He said: As for one of the two accusatives, it is that you make "al-Kitab" the predicate of "dhalika" and put "hudan" in the accusative by way of cut-off, because "hudan" is indefinite, attached to a definite [word], and its predicate has been completed, so you put it in the accusative, for an indefinite cannot be a proof of a definite. And if you wish, you may put "hudan" in the accusative as cut off from the ha' in "fihi," as if you said: "there is no doubt in it, guiding."

Abu Ja'far said: He abandoned the principle he had established regarding "Alif-Lam-Mim," that it is raised by "dhalika al-Kitab," and cast it behind his back. And what was necessary for him, according to the principle he had established, was that he not permit the nominative in "hudan" under any condition except one aspect, and that is by way of a new statement, since it is praise. As for its being the predicate of "dhalika," or following the position of "la rayba fihi," then by his own view it would be an error. That is because when "Alif-Lam-Mim" governs "dhalika al-Kitab," there is no doubt that "hudan" then cannot be a predicate of "dhalika" in the sense of what raises it, nor follow the position of "la rayba fihi," because its position then is accusative, due to the completion of the predicate before it, and its separation from it by its difference from it.

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿lil-muttaqin﴾ (for the God-fearing)

261- Sufyan ibn Waki' related to us, saying: my father related to us, from Sufyan, from a man, from al-Hasan, his words "lil-muttaqin": he said: they guarded against what was forbidden to them, and performed what was obligated upon them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 2 (part 2 of 2):

262- Muhammad ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: "for those who are mindful (lil-muttaqin)", meaning: those who fear from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, His punishment for abandoning the guidance they know, and who hope for His mercy by affirming what He brought.

263- Musa ibn Harun related to me, he said: Amr ibn Hammad related to us, he said: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas; and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ: "a guidance for those who are mindful (hudan lil-muttaqin)", he said: They are the believers.

264- Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash related to us, he said: al-A'mash asked me about "al-muttaqin", he said: I answered him, and he said to me: "al-Kalbi was asked about it." So I asked him, and he said: "Those who avoid the major sins (kaba'ir al-ithm)." He said: So I returned to al-A'mash, and he said: "We think it is so." And he did not deny it.

265- al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim al-Tabari related to me, he said: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj related to us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah, he said: Umar Abu Hafs related to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah, from Qatadah: "a guidance for those who are mindful (hudan lil-muttaqin)", they are those whom He described and characterized, so He affirmed their attribute, saying: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen, establish the prayer, and spend from what We have provided them﴾.

266- Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Uthman ibn Sa'id related to us, he said: Bishr ibn Umarah related to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas: "for those who are mindful", he said: the believers who guard against associating others with Me (al-shirk bi), and who act in obedience to Me.[[The reports 261–266 were all cited by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir 1: 71–72, and some of them in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 24, and al-Shawkani 1: 22.]]

The most correct interpretation of the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿a guidance for those who are mindful﴾, is the interpretation of one who describes these people as those who fear Allah, Blessed and Exalted, in committing what He has forbidden them to commit, so they shun His acts of disobedience, and fear Him in what He has commanded them of His obligations, so they obey Him by fulfilling them. That is because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, described them with taqwa, and did not restrict their taqwa of Him to some of what they deserve of it rather than others.[[In the printed edition: "for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, only described them", where the word "only" (innama) adds nothing. Then the manuscript and printed edition read: "so He did not restrict their taqwa of Him to some of those among them rather than others", which is a garbled sentence; its correct form is what I have adopted, as the meaning becomes clear below.]] So no one among people may restrict the meaning of describing them with some aspect of the fear of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to the exclusion of another, except with a proof that must be accepted. For that, as an attribute of these people, if it were restricted to a particular aspect of the meanings of taqwa rather than its general sense, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, would not have left its clarification to His servants, either in His Book or through the tongue of His Messenger ﷺ, since there is no evidence in reason that describing them with the full generality of taqwa is impossible.

Thus it has become clear that the view of one who claims that the interpretation of this is merely: "those who guard against shirk and are free of hypocrisy (al-nifaq)" is corrupt. Because a person may be like that while being a wrongdoer (fasiq) who does not deserve to be among the mindful, unless, according to the one who holds this view, the meaning of hypocrisy is the committing of the abominations that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has forbidden, and neglecting His obligations that He has imposed. For a group of the people of knowledge have called whoever does such things a hypocrite. So he would be correct in the interpretation of Allah's words, Mighty and Majestic, "for the mindful", even if he differs in naming such a person by this name.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 3 (part 1 of 2):

The discussion of the Exalted's saying: ﴿Those who believe﴾
267- Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Razi narrated to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: "Those who believe" – he said: those who affirm as true.
268- Yahya ibn Uthman ibn Salih al-Sahmi narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas: "yu'minun" (they believe): yusaddiqun (they affirm as true) [[The report 267: its continuation will come with this same chain: 272. Ibn Kathir (1:73) cited the two separately. He cited 268 together with the first. al-Suyuti (1:25) cited all three together.]].
269- al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "yu'minun": yakhsharna (they fear).
270- Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la al-San'ani narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, who said: al-Zuhri said: faith is action [[The reports 269–270: Ibn Kathir cited them (1:73).]].
271- It was related to me from Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Ala' ibn al-Musayyab ibn Rafi', from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abd Allah, who said: Faith is affirmation [[The report 271: Abd Allah is Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn Kathir cited this report alone (1:73), then cited report 273 alone, detailing the chain of each. As for al-Suyuti (1:25), he combined the two wordings without explanation, and added to them the wording of report 277. This is an ill-considered treatment, first because the two chains differ, and second because 273 and 277 are not from Ibn Mas'ud alone, as you see.]].

The meaning of faith (iman) among the Arabs is affirmation (tasdiq). One who affirms something is called a believer in it with words, and one who affirms another's words by his deeds is called a believer too. Among this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And you would not believe us, even if we were truthful﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 17], meaning: you would not affirm us in what we say. The fear of God may enter into the meaning of faith, which is the affirmation of speech by action. Faith is a comprehensive term for acknowledging God, His books and His messengers, and affirming that acknowledgment by deed. Since this is so, the interpretation of the verse that is more appropriate, and more fitting to the description of the people, is that they are described as affirming the unseen in speech, belief and action, since the Exalted did not restrict them to one meaning of faith over another, but rather described them with it in general, without specifying any of its meanings, by which He would have excluded them from the description through report or reason.

* *

The discussion of the Exalted's saying: ﴿in the unseen﴾

272- Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Razi narrated to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: "in the unseen" – he said: by what has come of it, meaning: from God, the Exalted.
273- Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas – and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet ﷺ: "in the unseen": as for the unseen, it is what is hidden from the servants of the matters of Paradise and Hell, and what God, blessed and exalted, mentioned in the Qur'an. Their affirmation of that – meaning the believers among the Arabs – did not come from the origin of a book or knowledge they possessed.
274- Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Asim, from Zirr, who said: the unseen is the Qur'an [[Report 274: Sufyan is al-Thawri; Asim is Ibn Abi al-Najud, with the letter nun vowelled with a fatha, the reciter. Zirr, with a kasra on the zay and a shadda on the ra', is Ibn Hubaysh, with a damma on the ha'. He is a major and imam among the Successors. This report is in Ibn Kathir (1:73–74).]].
275- Bishr ibn Mu'adh al-Aqadi narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayn narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah, from Qatadah concerning His saying "Those who believe in the unseen", who said: They believe in Paradise and Hell, and resurrection after death, and the Day of Resurrection, and all of this is unseen [[Report 275: Ibn Kathir and al-Suyuti also mentioned it.]].
276- It was related to me from Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, "Those who believe in the unseen": they believe in God, His angels, His messengers, the Last Day, His Paradise, His Fire and His meeting, and they believe in life after death. All of this is unseen [[Report 276: Ibn Kathir (1:73) cited it thus: "Abu Ja'far al-Razi said, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-Aliyah..." And al-Suyuti (1:25) cited it thus: "Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-Aliyah..." I fear that the mention of "from Abu al-Aliyah" has dropped from the chain in the copies of al-Tabari, since it is established with these two who quote from him.]].

The root of the unseen (al-ghayb) is: everything that is absent from you of a thing. It derives from your saying: "So-and-so was absent (ghaba), absent (yaghibu) an absence (ghaybah)."

The scholars of interpretation have differed concerning the specific people whom God, exalted is His praise, meant by these two verses at the beginning of this surah, and concerning their attributes and the description by which He described them, of their belief in the unseen, and the other meanings the two verses contain of their qualities apart from it.

Some of them said: They are the believers of the Arabs specifically, to the exclusion of other believers from the People of the Book.

They cited as evidence for the soundness of their saying and the correctness of their interpretation the verse that follows these two verses, which is the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾. They said: The Arabs had no book before the Book which God, Mighty and Majestic, sent down to Muhammad ﷺ, by which they followed in affirming it, acknowledging it and acting upon it. The book was only for the People of the two Books, other than them. They said: When the Exalted related the account of those who believe in what was sent down to Muhammad and what was sent down before him – after His relating the account of the believers in the unseen – we know that each category is other than the other category, and that the believers in the unseen are a kind other than the kind who affirm the two books, one of which was sent down to Muhammad ﷺ, and the other to those before the Messenger of God [[In the manuscript: "والآخر منهما على من قبله رسول الله", and the apparent correct reading is "على من قبل رسول الله", as we have recorded it. As for the printed edition, it reads: "على من قبله من رسل الله تعالى ذكره".]].

They said: Since this is so, what we said is sound: that the interpretation of the Exalted's saying ﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾ is only those who believe in what is absent from them of Paradise and Hell, reward and punishment, and resurrection, and affirmation of God, His angels, His books and His messengers, and all that the Arabs did not follow in their jahiliyyah, of what God, exalted is His praise, obligated upon His servants to adhere to – to the exclusion of others.

Mention of those who said that:

277- Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas – and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet ﷺ: As for ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾, they are the believers from the Arabs, ﴿and establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them﴾. As for the unseen, it is what is hidden from the servants of the matters of Paradise and Hell, and what God mentioned in the Qur'an. Their affirmation of that did not come from the origin of a book or knowledge they possessed. ﴿And those who believe in the unseen and establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them﴾: these are the believers from the People of the Book [[Report 277: Its beginning was mentioned with this chain: 273.
