Ibn Kathir did not cite it in this lengthy wording. It has passed in the commentary on 271 that al-Suyuti combined the three wordings: 271, 273, 277, in one sequence!]].

Others said: Rather, these four verses were revealed concerning the believers from the People of the Book specifically, for their belief in the Qur'an, when God, exalted is His praise, informed them in it of the hidden matters that they used to conceal among themselves and disclose. Then when God, exalted is His praise, showed His Prophet ﷺ their secrets in His revelation, they knew that it was from God, Mighty and Majestic. So they believed in the Prophet ﷺ and affirmed the Qur'an and what it contains of information about the unseen matters of which they had no knowledge, because it was established for them – by the proof with which God, blessed and exalted, argued against them in His Book, from its information of what they used to hide of their inner thoughts – that all of that was from God.

Others said: Rather, the four verses from the beginning of this surah were sent down to Muhammad ﷺ describing all the believers who have that attribute, from the Arabs and non-Arabs, and the People of the two Books and others [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "وأهل الكتابين سواهم", and the correct reading is "وسواهم". For al-Tabari mentioned three sayings: the first, that it means the Arabs specifically; the second, that it means the People of the Book specifically; so the third is that it means both categories together and others than them among mankind.]]. This is the description of one category of people, and the one who believes in what God sent down to Muhammad ﷺ and what was sent down before him is the one who believes in the unseen.

They said: The Exalted described them with belief in what was sent down to Muhammad and what was sent down to those before him after finishing His description of them with belief in the unseen, because His description of them with what He described them with of belief in the unseen meant that they believe in Paradise, Hell, resurrection and the other matters which God, exalted is His praise, obligated them to believe in, of what they have not seen and what has not yet come but is to come, rather than informing about them that they believe in what Muhammad ﷺ and those before him of the messengers and the books brought.

They said: Since the meaning of the Exalted's saying ﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾ is not present in the saying ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾, the need of the servants to know their description by that was like their need to know them by the description they were described with of their belief in the unseen, so that they might know what God is pleased with of the actions of His servants and loves of their qualities, so that they would be, by it – if their Lord grants them success in it – [believers] [[This addition between brackets is necessary for the completeness of the meaning. It is in neither the printed edition nor the manuscript.]].

Mention of those who said that:

278- Muhammad ibn Amr ibn al-Abbas al-Bahili narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim al-Dahhak ibn Makhlad narrated to us, saying: Isa ibn Maymun al-Makki narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Abi Najih narrated to us, from Mujahid, who said: Four verses of Surah al-Baqarah are in description of the believers, two verses in description of the disbelievers, and thirteen concerning the hypocrites [[Report 278: Abu Asim is al-Nabil, the great memorizer. Isa ibn Maymun al-Makki is known as Ibn Dayah; Ibn Uyaynah said: "He was a reciter of the Qur'an; he recited upon Ibn Kathir." Abu Hatim and others deemed him trustworthy.]].

279- Sufyan ibn Wakee' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from a man, from Mujahid, with the like of it [[Report 279: This is a weak chain, due to the weakness of Sufyan ibn Wakee' and the anonymity of the man from whom Sufyan al-Thawri narrated. But the report is connected through the two chains before and after it.]].

280- al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Musa ibn Mas'ud narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it [[Report 280: Musa ibn Mas'ud is Abu Hudhayfah al-Nahdi, who is trustworthy; al-Bukhari narrated from him in his Sahih, and Ibn Sa'd and al-Ijli deemed him trustworthy. al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 4/1/295. Shibl is Ibn Abbad al-Makki the reciter, who is trustworthy; Ahmad, Ibn Ma'in and others deemed him so.

This report, with its three chains, is mentioned by Ibn Kathir (1:80) without detailing them, saying: "The apparent view is the saying of Mujahid – as narrated by al-Thawri from a man from Mujahid, and narrated by more than one from Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, that he said..."]].

281- It was related to me from Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: Four verses at the opening of this surah – meaning Surah al-Baqarah – are about those who believed, and two verses are about the leaders of the confederates.

The more correct of the two views in my opinion, and the more fitting to the interpretation of the Book, is the first view: that those whom God, remembered is He, described with belief in the unseen, and with what He described them with, exalted is His praise, in the first two verses, are other than those He described with belief in what was sent down to Muhammad and what was sent down to those before him of the messengers, for the reasons I mentioned earlier to the one who said that.

Among what also indicates the soundness of this view is that He, after describing the believers with the two attributes He described, and after classifying each category of them as He classified the disbelievers, divided them into two kinds [[His wording: "جنَّس... جنسين", with something between them separating them; the genus of a thing is making it into kinds, as one classifies it into categories.]] – one of which He made sealed upon its heart, sealed over, despairing of its return [[In the printed edition: "إيمانه", which is also correct in meaning. Al-iyab means returning to God in repentance and obedience. From it is His saying: ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength; indeed, he was one who turns back (awwab)﴾]] – and the other hypocritical, showing off the display of faith outwardly while concealing hypocrisy inwardly. Thus He made the disbelievers two kinds, just as He made the believers at the beginning of the surah two kinds. Then He made His servants know the description of each category of them and their attributes, and what He prepared for each group of them of reward or punishment, censured the blameworthy among them, and thanked the striving of the people of obedience among them.

* *

The discussion of the Exalted's saying: ﴿and establish﴾

Its establishment is its performance – with its limits, its obligations and what is required in it – in the manner it was prescribed. As one says: the people established their market (aqama suqahum), when they did not leave it idle of buying and selling in it, and as the poet said:

We established for the two Iraqs the market of striking, but they shrank back and turned away, all of them [[In the printed edition: "فحاسوا", and in the manuscript: "مجآمرا". Kham in war from its adversary, yakhimu khaiman: he became cowardly, recoiled and broke. I did not know the composer of the verse.]]

282- As al-Hasan... [report text]: Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, "and establish the prayer": he said: those who establish the prayer with its obligations.
283- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Bishr ibn Umarah, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, "and establish the prayer", he said: The establishment of the prayer is the completion of the bowing and prostration, the recitation, the humility, and turning toward it while in it [[Reports 282–283: in Ibn Kathir (1:77), al-Durr al-Manthur (1:27), and al-Shawkani (1:25).]].

* *

The discussion of the Exalted's saying: ﴿the prayer﴾

284- Yahya ibn Abi Talib narrated to me, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Juwaybir narrated to us, from al-Dahhak concerning His saying "Those who establish the prayer": meaning the obligatory prayer [[Report 284: Its chain is extremely weak. Yahya ibn Abi Talib Ja'far ibn al-Zabarqan: al-Dhahabi said: "a well-known traditionist... al-Daraqutni and others deemed him trustworthy... and al-Daraqutni is the most informed of people about him." He died in 275 AH at age 95. Yazid is Ibn Harun, one of the illustrious memorizers, among the teachers of Imams Ahmad, Ibn Ma'in, Ibn Rahawayh and Ibn al-Madini. Juwaybir (diminutive) is Ibn Sa'id al-Azdi al-Balkhi, extremely weak; Yahya al-Qattan weakened him, as al-Bukhari reported in al-Kabir 1/2/256 and al-Saghir 176; al-Nasa'i said in al-Du'afa' 8: "matruk al-hadith (abandoned in hadith)"; and in al-Tahdhib 2:124, Abu Qudamah al-Sarakhsi said: Yahya al-Qattan said: "They were lax in taking tafsir from people whom they did not deem trustworthy in hadith," then he mentioned al-Dahhak, Juwaybir and Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib, and said: "Their narrations are not tolerated, though their tafsir may be written from them."]].

As for al-salah (the prayer), in the speech of the Arabs it is supplication (al-du'a'), as al-A'sha said:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 3 (part 2 of 2):

A guard is over her, who never leaves her house for ever... and if she is slaughtered, he prays over her and utters a murmur.

[Note: the poet describes wine in its jar. Zamzama (to murmur) refers to a non-Arab (ʿilj, from the Persians) who, when eating while his mouth is closed, attempts to speak with a faint voice that is barely understood. Their doing that is zamzama. "Slaughtered" means that it is opened and its seal is removed. At that moment he prays, fearing that it may be spoiled, and so suffer loss.]

This means: he prayed for her. Similar is the verse of al-Aʿsha also:

And he faced her toward the wind in her jar, and prayed over her jar and performed the rasm.

[Note: the Diwan of al-Aʿsha, p. 29. His saying "faced her toward the wind" means he placed her opposite the direction of the wind at the time of opening her and removing her seal. It is also narrated as "fa-aqbalaha al-rih," which has the same meaning. Irtasama al-rajul: he magnified (God), supplicated, and sought refuge, fearing that he would find her spoiled and his trade would be ruined.]

I am of the view that the obligatory prayer (salah) was named "salah" because the one who prays exposes himself to the success of his request for reward from God through his action, along with what he asks of his Lord of his needs, in the manner of one who supplicates his Lord seeking the success of his needs and his petition.

* *

Concerning the interpretation of His saying, majestic is His praise: ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ (3)

The exegetes differed in its interpretation. Some of them said:

285- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, mawla of Zayd ibn Thabit, from ʿIkrimah, or from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning "and from what We have provided them, they spend": he said: they give the zakah, seeking reward by it.

286- Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, from Muʿawiyah, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning "and from what We have provided them, they spend": he said: the zakah of their wealth.

287- Yahya ibn Abi Talib narrated to me, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak, concerning "and from what We have provided them, they spend": he said: expenditures were acts of drawing near (to God) by which they sought nearness to God according to their means and effort, until the obligatory charities were revealed: seven verses in Surat Bara'a in which charities are mentioned, which are the affirmed, abrogating ones.

Others said:

288- Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas - and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet ﷺ, concerning "and from what We have provided them, they spend": it is the spending of a man on his family. And this was before the zakah was revealed.

The most preferable of the interpretations of the verse, and the most worthy of the description of this people, is that they were those who fulfilled all that was incumbent upon them regarding their wealth, paying (what was due), whether it was zakah or the maintenance of one whose maintenance is obligatory upon them, from family and dependents and others, whose maintenance is obligatory upon them by kinship, ownership, and other things. For Allah, majestic is His praise, generalized their description when He described them as spending from what He had provided them, and praised them for that quality. It is therefore known that, since He did not restrict their praise and description to a particular type of praiseworthy expenditure over another, neither by report nor otherwise, they are described as possessing all meanings of praiseworthy expenditure, from the good of what their Lord provided them from their wealth and possessions, and that is the lawful part of it, which is not mixed with anything unlawful.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may His majesty be exalted: ﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾

The description of those characterized by this attribute has already been explained, and which categories of people they are [[See pp. 237–241.]]. However, we will mention what has been transmitted on this matter from those from whom an interpretation has been related:

289 – Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding "And those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you": that is, they affirm you in what you have brought from God, exalted and mighty, and in what was brought by those messengers before you, making no distinction between them, and they do not deny what they were brought from their Lord [[The report 289 is mentioned by Ibn Kathir (1:79) together with what follows, 291. Al-Suyuti (1:27) and al-Shawkani (1:25) also mention it with an additional element on the two reports, attributed to Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim.]].

290 – Musa ibn Harun related to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas – and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ – regarding "And those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain": these are the believers among the People of the Book [[Report 290 is also mentioned by Ibn Kathir, but only by way of reference without giving its wording, and al-Shawkani follows him.

After this, the manuscript has the following text:

Heard by Ahmad, Muhammad and al-Hasan, the sons of 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad al-Farghani, all of it.

Heard by Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Tarsusi and al-Hasan, the sons of Muhammad ibn 'Abdan, and al-Hasan ibn Ibrahim al-Hannas, all of it. And praise be to God abundantly.]].

* *

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may His majesty be exalted: ﴿And in the Hereafter they are certain (4)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: As for "the Hereafter" (al-akhirah), it is an attribute of the abode, as He, may His majesty be exalted, said: ﴿And indeed the Abode of the Hereafter – that is the true life, if only they knew﴾ [Surah al-'Ankabut: 64]. It was described thus because it becomes "the last" (akhirah) in relation to the first that came before it, as you say to a man: "I bestowed favour upon you once after another, yet you gave thanks for neither the first nor the last," and it became "last" in relation to the first because the first preceded it. Likewise, the Abode of the Hereafter was called "the last" because the first abode preceded it, so the one following it became "the last." It is also permissible that it was called "the last" because it is delayed beyond creation, just as the world was called "dunya" (the near) because of its nearness to creation.

As for what God, may His majesty be exalted, described the believers as having – through what was sent down to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and what was sent down to those before him of the messengers – of certainty regarding the matter of the Hereafter, it is their certainty concerning what the polytheists were denying: the resurrection, the rising, the reward and punishment, the reckoning, the balance, and other things which God has prepared for His creatures on the Day of Resurrection. As follows:

291 – Muhammad ibn Humayd related this to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding "And in the Hereafter they are certain": that is, in the resurrection, the Last Day, Paradise and Hellfire, the reckoning and the balance; that is, not those who claim that they believed in what came before you while disbelieving in what came to you from your Lord [[Report 291 is the continuation of the preceding report 289, to which we have referred there.]].

This interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas has clearly stated that the surah from its beginning – although the verses at its start describe the believers – is an allusion from God, exalted and mighty, rebuking the disbelievers among the People of the Book, who claimed that they affirm what the messengers of God who came before Muhammad brought – peace be upon them and upon him – while they are in fact denying Muhammad ﷺ and rejecting the revelation he brought, and who, despite their denial, claim to be guided, and claim that none will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians. God, exalted be His praise, refuted this claim of theirs with His words: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. This is the Book, there is no doubt in it, a guidance for the God-fearing, who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend of what We have provided them, and who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain.﴾ He informed His servants that this Book is a guidance only for the people of faith in Muhammad ﷺ and in what he brought, who affirm what was sent down to him and to those messengers before him of clear proofs and guidance – exclusively – not for those who deny Muhammad ﷺ and what he brought while claiming to affirm those before Muhammad, peace be upon him, and what they brought of scriptures. Then God, exalted be His praise, confirmed the matter of the believers among the Arabs and among the People of the Book who affirm Muhammad ﷺ and what was sent down to him and to those messengers before him, with His words: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful﴾. Thus He informed that they alone are the people of guidance and success, to the exclusion of others, and that others are the people of error and loss.

The discussion of the words of Allah, may His praise be exalted: ﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord﴾

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning whom Allah, may His praise be exalted, meant by His words: "They are upon guidance from their Lord." Some of them said: By this He meant the people of the two attributes mentioned earlier, namely: the believers in the unseen from among the Arabs, and the believers in what was sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ) and to those before him of the messengers. He described all of them as being upon guidance from Him, and that they are the successful ones.

Mention of those among the people of interpretation who said this:

292. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas; and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), that "those who believe in the unseen" are the believers from among the Arabs, and "those who believe in what has been sent down to you" are the believers from among the People of the Book. Then He gathered the two groups and said: "They are upon guidance from their Lord, and they are the successful ones." [[Report 292 – quoted by Ibn Kathir 1:81, and al-Shawkani 1:26. Al-Suyuti 1:25 quoted it at length, combining it with the earlier reports 273, 277, 281 as a single chain, from Ibn Mas'ud alone, and attributed it to al-Tabari.]]

Others said: Rather, by this He meant the God-fearing (al-muttaqun) who believe in the unseen, and they are the ones who believe in what was sent down to Muhammad and what was sent down to those before him of the messengers.

Others said: Rather, by this He meant those who believe in what was sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ) and what was sent down to those before him, and they are the believers among the People of the Book who affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ) and what he brought, and who had previously been believers in all the prophets and books.

On this second interpretation, it is possible that "And those who believe in what has been sent down to you" (wa-alladhina yu'minuna bima unzila ilayka) is in a position of genitive (khafd) or in a position of nominative (raf').

As for its nominative position, it may come in two ways: first, by coordination (al-'atf) with the "alladhina" in "who believe in the unseen"; second, that it is the predicate of an inchoative (khabar mubtada'), or that "They are upon guidance from their Lord" is its governing element.

As for its genitive position, it is by coordination with "al-muttaqin" (the God-fearing). When it is coordinated with the first "alladhina", two meanings are possible: first, that it and the first "alladhina" are both descriptions of the God-fearing, according to the view of those who held that the four verses after "Alif-Lam-Mim" were revealed concerning one category of believers. The second meaning: that the second "alladhina" is coordinated in grammatical case with "al-muttaqin" in the genitive, and in meaning it is a category other than the first. This is according to the view of those who held that the believers concerning whom the first two verses were revealed after "Alif-Lam-Mim" are different from those concerning whom the last two verses that follow them were revealed.

It is also possible that the second "alladhina" is in the nominative in this case, in the sense of resumption (al-i'tinaf) [[In the printed edition: "al-isti'naf" in this place and the one following. They have the same meaning.]], since it begins anew after the completion of a verse and the end of a narrative. It may also be permitted to be nominative by intention of resumption, since it stands at the beginning of a verse, even if it is a description of the God-fearing.

Thus the nominative may be correct in four ways, and the genitive in two.

The most preferable interpretation to me of His words "They are upon guidance from their Lord" is what I have mentioned from the sayings of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, and that "ula'ika" (those) refers to both groups, namely the God-fearing and those who believe in what was sent down to you; and that "ula'ika" is nominative by the returning pronoun from their mention in His words "upon guidance from their Lord"; and that the second "alladhina" is coordinated with what came before in speech, as we have explained.

We have seen that this is the most preferable interpretation of the verse because Allah, may His praise be exalted, described both groups with their praiseworthy qualities and then praised them. He, mighty and majestic, would not single out one of the two groups for praise while they are equal in the qualities for which they deserve praise, just as it would not be consistent with His justice that they be equal in the deeds for which they deserve reward, and then He single out one of them for reward and deprive the other of the reward of its deed. Likewise is the way of praise for deeds, since praise is one of the kinds of reward.

As for the meaning of His words "They are upon guidance from their Lord," the meaning is: they are upon light from their Lord, and proof, and rectitude, and soundness, by Allah's granting them firmness and His success for them. As:

293. Ibn Humayd narrated to me, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, "They are upon guidance from their Lord": that is, upon light from their Lord, and rectitude in what has come to them [[Report 293 – mentioned by Ibn Kathir 1:81 with its continuation below: 294.]].

* *

The discussion of the words of Allah, may His praise be exalted: ﴿And they are the successful ones﴾

The interpretation of His words "And they are the successful ones" means: they are the ones who attain their goals and obtain what they sought with Allah, may He be remembered, by their deeds and their faith in Allah, His books and His messengers, namely winning the reward, eternal abiding in the gardens, and deliverance from the punishment Allah, blessed and exalted, has prepared for His enemies. As:

294. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: "And they are the successful ones": that is, those who attained what they sought, and were saved from the evil of that from which they fled.

As evidence that one of the meanings of falah (success) is attaining one's aim and obtaining one's need, is the saying of Labid ibn Rabi'ah:

"Understand, if you are not yet understanding... and he has indeed succeeded who had reason" [[His Diwan 2:12; the address in the verse is to his female companion.]]

meaning: he gained his need and obtained good. And from it is the saying of the rajiz:

"May I lose a mother who bore Riyah... she came with him splay-legged, bow-legged..."
[[The second verse in al-Lisan (fi-r-k-h). Al-farkahah: the distance between the two buttocks. Al-farkah and al-mufarkah derived from it signify censure, that he cannot bear the burden of what is laid on him in war or in a lasting noble deed.]]
"You suppose she has given birth to success!... I testify that it does not increase her falah"

meaning: good and nearness to her need. Falah is a verbal noun from your saying: aflaha fulanun yuflihu ifläha, falahan, and falaha. Falah also means: survival, and from it is Labid's saying:

"We alight in lands, all of which have been alighted in before us, and we hope for falah after 'Ad and Himyar"
[[His Diwan, poem no. 14, lamenting those of his people who perished.]]

he means survival. And also from it is the saying of 'Ubayd:

"Aflih (survive) as you wish, for it is attained by weakness, and the shrewd may be deceived"
[[His Diwan: 7; in the printed edition and the Diwan it reads "fa-qad yublagh", both being well-known transmissions.]]

meaning: live and remain as you wish. Likewise the saying of Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan:

"Every youth, Shu'ub will seize him, even if he is wealthy, and even if he meets falah"
[[From a poem not among the additional verses of his Diwan, except three verses, and this is not one of them. Sha'ub: a name for death, undeclined, because it splits people, i.e., shatters and scatters them.]]

meaning: success in his need and survival.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 6:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾

The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning who is meant by this verse, and concerning whom it was revealed. Ibn 'Abbas used to say, as follows:

295 - Muhammad ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, the mawla of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Indeed, those who disbelieve", i.e., in what was sent down to you from your Lord, "and if they say, 'We have believed in what has come to us before you'" [[Narration 295: Ibn Kathir mentions it (1:82) together with what follows at 299. al-Suyuti (1:29) cites it in a longer form, adding what comes at 307 and 311, and attributes it also to Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim; al-Shawkani (1:28) cites it without the last addition.]].

Ibn 'Abbas held that this verse was revealed concerning the Jews who lived in the outskirts of Madinah during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), rebuking them for their denial of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and their rejection of him, despite their knowledge of him and their recognition that he was the Messenger of Allah to them and to all mankind.

296 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, the mawla of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrimah or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: that the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah up to its hundredth verse was revealed concerning men whom he named by their individual names and lineages, from the rabbis of the Jews, and from the hypocrites of the Aws and the Khazraj. We disliked lengthening the book by mentioning their names [[Narration 296: Ibn Kathir mentions it (1:86) in similar wording, from the narration of Ibn Ishaq. al-Suyuti (1:29) transmits it in al-Tabari's wording, from him and from Ibn Ishaq. al-Shawkani transmits it briefly (1:29). It is clear that his saying "We disliked lengthening the book..." is from al-Tabari himself. See also what follows at 312.]].

A different interpretation has also been transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning this, namely:

297 - al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim related to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih related to us, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his saying: "Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was eager that all people should believe and follow him in guidance, so Allah, majestic is His praise, informed him that none will believe except those for whom happiness has preceded from Allah in the first Remembrance, and none will go astray except those for whom wretchedness has preceded from Allah in the first Remembrance [[Narration 297: It is in Ibn Kathir (1:82), al-Suyuti (1:28–29), and al-Shawkani (1:28), who attribute it also to Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi.]].

Others said, as follows:

298 - It was related to me by 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: Two verses concern the leaders of the Confederates: "Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe. Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and over their eyes is a covering, and for them is a great punishment," [[and he said: They are those whom Allah mentioned in this verse: "Have you not seen those who exchanged the favor of Allah for disbelief and caused their people to settle in the abode of destruction — Hell, which they will enter, and wretched is the settlement" (Ibrahim 28–29)]], he said: They are those who were killed on the Day of Badr [[Narration 298: This is as it stands in al-Tabari, from the saying of al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Ibn Kathir (1:82–83) mentions it in abridged form from the narration of al-Rabi' ibn Anas from Abu al-'Aliyah, without naming who transmitted it. al-Suyuti (1:29) and al-Shawkani (1:28) cite it in a longer form than here, including narration 309 with it, from the saying of Abu al-'Aliyah as well, and attribute it to Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim. It appears that al-Tabari's chain is abbreviated, or that his unnamed shaykh abbreviated it.]].

The most fitting of these interpretations for the verse is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas that Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad transmitted from 'Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from him, although each saying of those we have mentioned has its own line of reasoning.

As for the line of reasoning of those who interpreted it as al-Rabi' ibn Anas did, it is that when Allah, exalted is His remembrance, informed about a people among the disbelievers that they will not believe, and that warning would not benefit them, and then among the disbelievers there were some whom Allah benefited by the warning of the Prophet (ﷺ) to them, because they believed in Allah and in the Prophet (ﷺ) and in what came from Allah after the revelation of this surah [[The phrasing of his statement is: "As for... when Allah, exalted is His remembrance, informed about a people... it is not permissible..."]] — it was not permissible that the verse was revealed except concerning a specific group of the disbelievers. Since this is so, and the leaders of the Confederates were undoubtedly among those whom Allah, mighty and majestic is He, did not benefit by the warning of the Prophet (ﷺ) to them, until Allah, blessed and exalted is He, killed them at the hands of the believers on the Day of Badr, it is known that they are among those whom Allah, majestic is His praise, meant by this verse.

As for our reason for choosing the interpretation we have chosen, it is that the saying of Allah, majestic is His praise, "Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe," comes directly after His report, majestic is His praise, about the believers among the People of the Book, and after His description and praise of them for their belief in Him, His books and His messengers. The most fitting matter with the wisdom of Allah is that this report should be followed by a report about their disbelievers, their attributes, a condemnation of their means and conditions [[al-asbab, plural of sabab, meaning the paths and means]], and a display of their reproach and of disassociation from them. For their believers and their polytheists, although their conditions differ with the difference of their religions, the common lineage gathers them all: they are the Children of Israel.

Allah, majestic is His praise, used the opening of this surah as proof for His Prophet (ﷺ) against the polytheistic Jews, the rabbis of the Children of Israel, who, despite their knowledge of his prophethood, denied it, by showing His Prophet (ﷺ) what the rabbis among them used to keep secret and conceal, which the common mass of the Jews did not know but the rabbis among them knew [[ʿazm al-yahud: most of them, the majority]] — so that they would know that the One who informed him of the knowledge of that is the One who sent down the Book to Musa. For that was among matters which neither Muhammad (ﷺ), nor his people, nor his tribe knew or recognized before the revelation of the Furqan to Muhammad (ﷺ); so it would not have been possible for them to claim confusion regarding his matter, peace be upon him, that he is a prophet and that what he brought is from Allah [[In the printed edition: "from Allah"]]. And how could confusion be claimed regarding the truthfulness of an unlettered man who grew up among unlettered people, who could neither write, nor read, nor calculate, so that it could be said that he read the books and thus knew, or calculated [[by calculation here is meant the calculation of the courses of the stars and their zodiacal signs, by which the astrologer knows the reports of what is claimed as knowledge of the unseen]] and so became an astrologer? And he arose against learned rabbis, readers and scribes [[In the printed edition: "and he arose against the rabbis"; it seems to be connected to a previous sentence, but it is not correct; rather it begins a new statement]] who had studied the books and led the nations, informing them of the hidden faults, the preserved knowledge, the concealed reports, and the obscure matters of their own which were unknown even to those below them among their rabbis. The matter of one who is like this is not unclear, and his truthfulness is evident.

Among what indicates the correctness of what we have said — that those whom Allah, exalted is His remembrance, meant by His saying "Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe" are the rabbis of the Jews who were killed in disbelief and died upon it — is Allah's relating their story and reminding them of the covenants and pledges taken from them concerning the matter of Muhammad, peace be upon him, after His relating what He related about the hypocrites, and His interjecting between that what He interjected concerning Iblis and Adam — in His saying: "O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you" (al-Baqarah 40 and what follows) — and His argument to His Prophet against them, with what He argued against them in it after their denial of his prophethood. Since the report was first about the believers among the People of the Book, and last about their polytheists, it is more fitting that it be in the middle concerning them, since the speech follows one part of another, unless clear evidence comes to them that some of it has turned away from the meanings with which it began, so that the turning away from it becomes known at that point.

As for the meaning of disbelief (kufr) in His saying "Indeed, those who disbelieve," it is denial (juhud). That is because the rabbis of the Jews of Madinah denied the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), concealed him from the people, and hid his matter, while they knew him as they know their own sons.

The root of kufr among the Arabs is covering a thing, and for this reason they called the night "kafir", because of the covering of its darkness over what it envelops, as the poet said:

So they both remembered a precious, well-stacked clutch [of eggs], after the sun had cast its hand into the darkness [[The poem is attributed to Tha'labah ibn Su'ayr al-Mazini; Sharh al-Mufadaliyyat: 257. The pronoun in "fa-tadhakkara" refers to the ostrich hen and cock. Thiql: the protected, precious eggs of the ostrich; the Arabs call any precious, valued, protected thing thiql. Rathid: arranged and piled one upon another. Dhaka': the sun.]]

And Labid ibn Rabi'ah said:

On a night when the stars were covered by its clouds [[From his famous mu'allaqah, which appears in the commentary on a verse of Surat al-Ma'idah: 12 (6:98 Bulaq). It is also narrated as "its darkness". Its first half: "rising along the ridge of its back, continuous"; it refers to the wild cow that entered her hiding place at the root of a tree while sand was falling upon her back.]]

meaning: covered them. Likewise the rabbis among the Jews covered the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and concealed it from the people, despite their knowledge of his prophethood and their finding his description in their books. So Allah, majestic is His praise, said concerning them: "Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of the clear proofs and the guidance after We made it clear to the people in the Book — those are cursed by Allah and cursed by those who curse" (al-Baqarah 159). They are those concerning whom Allah, mighty and majestic, sent down: "Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe."

* *

The interpretation of His saying, majestic is His praise: "It is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe."

The meaning of "sawa'" (same/equal): balanced, taken from equality, as in your saying, "These two matters are equal to me" and "they are sawa' to me", i.e., they are equal to me. From this is the saying of Allah, majestic is His praise: "So throw back to them on equal terms" (al-Anfal 58), meaning: inform them and notify them of war, until your knowledge and their knowledge of what each party holds regarding the other become equal. Likewise His saying "sawa' 'alayhim" means: balanced for them, whichever of the two matters came from you toward them — warning or not warning — because they will not believe, and I have sealed upon their hearts and their hearing. From this is the saying of 'Ubayd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat:

The gray mare hastens me toward the son of Ja'far; the night and the day are sawa' for her [[His Diwan: 163; al-Kamil of al-Mubarrad 1:398–399. He praises 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Talib. Aghadda al-sayr and aghadda fihi: he hastened. The Diwan and al-Kamil have "taqaddat". Taqada bi-ba'iruhu: he hastened on the usual road. al-Shahba': her horse, named for its color, al-ashhab, which is when white hairs streak its black or bay coat until they nearly overcome the black or bay.]]

meaning: the night and the day are balanced for her in travel, because there is no slackening in it. From this is the saying of another:

And a night in whose darkness a man says: "Sound-eyed and blind-eyed are sawa'"

because the one with sound eyes sees in it only weak sight because of its darkness.

As for His saying "it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe," the speech appears with the form of a question, though it is a statement; because it occupies the place of "ayy" (which), as you say, "We do not care whether you stood or sat," while you are informing, not asking, because that clause occupies the place of "ayy". The meaning when you say that is: We do not care which of these two you did. Likewise in His saying "It is all the same for them whether you warned them or did not warn them," since the meaning of the speech is: It is equal for them which of these two you did toward them, it is fitting in its place with sawa': "Whether you did or did not do."

Some grammarians of Basra claimed that the interrogative particle came only with sawa', and it is not an interrogative, because when the questioner asks another, saying, "Is Zayd with you or 'Amr?", he seeks to establish which of them is with him; neither of them has more right to the question than the other. Since His saying "It is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them" has the meaning of equalization, that resembles the interrogative in equalization. We have already explained the correct view on this.

So the interpretation of the speech is then: Balanced, O Muhammad, regarding these who denied your prophethood, among the rabbis of Madinah, after knowing it, and who concealed the explanation of your matter to the people, that you are My messenger to My creation, though I took from them the covenant and pledge that they would not conceal that, that they would make it clear to the people, and inform them that they find your description in their books — whether you warn them or do not warn them, they will not believe, nor return to the truth, nor affirm you and what you have brought them. As:

299 - Muhammad ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, the mawla of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrimah or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "It is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe," meaning: they have disbelieved in what they possess of knowledge of the Remembrance, and denied the covenant taken from them concerning you; so they have disbelieved in what came to you, and in what they possess of what came to them through others than you. How then would they listen to a warning and admonition from you, when they have disbelieved in what they possess of your knowledge? [[Narration 299: Its takhrij was given with narration 295.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 7 (part 1 of 2):

On the interpretation of His words, may His praise be exalted: ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The origin of khatm (sealing) is ṭab' (stamping). The khātam (seal) is the ṭābi' (stamper). It is said of it: "I sealed the letter" (khatamtu al-kitāba), when you stamped it.

If someone says to us: "How can He seal upon hearts, when sealing is only a stamp upon vessels, containers and wrappings [[al-ghulaf is the plural of ghilāf: the casing that encloses what is placed inside it.]]?"

It is said in reply: The hearts of the servants are vessels for what is deposited in them of knowledge, and containers for what is placed in them of recognition of matters [[In the manuscript: "min al-ma'ārif bil-'ulūm" (of recognition of sciences).]]. So the meaning of sealing upon them and upon the hearing, by which sounds are perceived and through which one reaches knowledge of the realities of reports concerning the unseen, is analogous to the meaning of sealing upon all other vessels and containers.

If he says: "Is there for that a description you can give us so that we may understand it? Is it like the seal which is known to what appears to the eyes, or is it otherwise?"

It is said: The people of interpretation have differed regarding the description of that, and we will inform about its description after mentioning their sayings:

300- ʿĪsā ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā al-Ramlī narrated to me, saying: Yaḥyā ibn ʿĪsā narrated to us, from al-Aʿmash, who said: Mujāhid showed us with his hand and said: "They used to consider that the heart is like this — meaning the palm — so when the servant commits a sin, a part of it is closed up" — and he pointed with his little finger, "like this" — "and when he sins, it is closed up" — and he pointed with another finger — "and when he sins, it is closed up" — and he pointed with another finger, like this, until he closed all his fingers. He said: "Then it is stamped with a seal." Mujāhid said: "And they used to consider that this is the rayn [[The report 300: ʿĪsā ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Tamīmī al-Nahshalī: al-Nasā'ī said: "ṣāliḥ" (sound). He is among the teachers of al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mandah and others; he died in the year 251. Al-Bukhārī also narrated from him in al-Tārīkh al-Ṣaghīr (p. 224), in the biography of his paternal uncle Yaḥyā ibn ʿĪsā. Aḥmad and al-ʿIjlī declared him trustworthy, and al-Bukhārī gave his biography in al-Ṣaghīr. This report is to come with this chain in the commentary on the verse of Surat al-Muṭaffifīn: 14 (30:63 Bulaq). Ibn Kathīr mentioned it (1:82), and al-Suyūṭī (6:326).]].

301- Abū Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Wakīʿ narrated to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Mujāhid, who said: "The heart is like the palm; when he commits a sin, he closes a finger, until he closes all his fingers." And our companions used to say that it is the rān [[Report 301: This will also come (30:63 Bulaq). Ibn Kathīr alluded to it (1:83) without mentioning its wording, and likewise al-Suyūṭī (6:325).]].

302- al-Qāsim ibn al-Ḥasan narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn ibn Dāwūd narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj narrated to us, saying: Mujāhid said: "I was informed that the sins surround the heart from its sides until they meet upon it; their meeting upon it is the ṭab', and the ṭab' is the khatm." Ibn Jurayj said: "The khatm is the sealing upon the heart and the hearing" [[Report 302: This is from Ibn Jurayj's narration from Mujāhid, and it is apparently discontinuous, since Ibn Jurayj narrates from Mujāhid through an intermediary, as will come in the following report. Ibn Kathīr mentioned this report (1:83), but it is corrupted in it by a copyist's or printer's error.]].

303- al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: ʿAbdullāh ibn Kathīr narrated to me, that he heard Mujāhid say: "The rān is easier than the ṭab', and the ṭab' is easier than the locks (aqfāl), and the locks are the hardest of all that." [[Report 303: ʿAbdullāh ibn Kathīr: he is al-Dārī al-Makkī, one of the famous seven readers, and he is trustworthy. He recited the Qur'an to Mujāhid. Ibn Abī Ḥātim, in al-Jarḥ wa-l-Taʿdīl (2/2:144), confused him with "ʿAbdullāh ibn Kathīr ibn al-Muṭṭalib ibn Abī Wadāʿa al-Sahmī." It appears from the words of al-Ḥāfiẓ in al-Tahdhīb (5:368) that this error was from al-Bukhārī himself, so Ibn Abī Ḥātim perhaps followed him in his error without verification. This report was mentioned by Ibn Kathīr (1:83), and likewise al-Suyūṭī (6:326), who added its attribution to al-Bayhaqī.]].

Some of them said: The meaning of His saying "Allah has sealed upon their hearts" is a report from Allah, may His praise be exalted, about their arrogance and their turning away from listening to what they were called to of the truth, just as it is said: "Indeed so-and-so is deaf to this speech," when he refuses to hear it and lifts himself above understanding it out of arrogance.

Abu Ja'far said: The truth in this matter, in my view, is what is authentically related by a report like it from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, which is:

304- Muḥammad ibn Bashshār narrated it to us, saying: Ṣafwān ibn ʿĪsā narrated to us, saying: Ibn ʿAjlān narrated to us, from al-Qaʿqāʿ, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, when the believer commits a sin, a black spot appears on his heart. If he repents, gives it up and seeks forgiveness, his heart is polished; but if he increases (sin), it increases until it closes his heart, and that is the 'rān' of which Allah, may His praise be exalted, said: ﴿Nay! Rather, what they used to earn has covered over their hearts﴾ [Surat al-Muṭaffifīn: 14]." [[Report 304: It will come in al-Ṭabarī with this chain at 30:62 Bulaq, and he narrated it there with another chain before it and two other chains after it, all through Muḥammad ibn ʿAjlān from al-Qaʿqāʿ.
Muḥammad ibn Bashshār: the hafiz of Basra, known by the title "Bundār". The authors of the six books and other imams narrated from him. In the printed edition here it reads "Muḥammad ibn Yasār", which is an error. Ibn ʿAjlān: Muḥammad ibn ʿAjlān al-Madanī, one of the trustworthy scholars who acted upon their knowledge. al-Qaʿqāʿ ibn Ḥakīm al-Kinānī al-Madanī: a trustworthy Successor. Abū Ṣāliḥ: al-Sammān, named "Dhakwān", a trustworthy Successor; Aḥmad said: "Trustworthy, trustworthy, among the best of people and the most reliable of them."
The hadith was narrated by Aḥmad in al-Musnad (7939; 2:297 Ḥalabī) from Ṣafwān ibn ʿĪsā with this chain. al-Ḥākim (2:517) narrated it through Bakkār ibn Qutayba al-Qāḍī from Ṣafwān, and said: "This is a sound hadith according to the condition of Muslim, though they did not record it," and al-Dhahabī agreed. al-Tirmidhī (4:210) and Ibn Māja (2:291) narrated it through Muḥammad ibn ʿAjlān. al-Tirmidhī said: "This is a ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ hadith."
Ibn Kathīr mentioned it (1:84) from this narration of al-Ṭabarī, then said: this hadith through this route has been narrated by al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasā'ī from Qutayba from al-Layth ibn Saʿd, and by Ibn Māja from Hishām ibn ʿAmmār from Ḥātim ibn Ismāʿīl and al-Walīd ibn Muslim, all three from Muḥammad ibn ʿAjlān. al-Tirmidhī said "ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ"; then he mentioned it again (9:143) from the narrations of these and from Aḥmad's Musnad. al-Suyūṭī mentioned it (6:325) and added its attribution to ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Ḥibbān, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī in Shuʿab al-Īmān.
In the text of this hadith here, in the printed edition: "kāna nukta... ṣaqala qalbahu... ḥattā yughlif qalbahu." In the report of al-Ṭabarī that comes later, as in the manuscript, except his words "ḥattā tughliq qalbahu," which there read "ḥattā ta'lū qalbahu."]] 

So he ﷺ informed that when sins follow one another upon the hearts, they lock them; and when they lock them, the khatm from Allah, may He be exalted, and the ṭab' then come upon them, so there is no path for faith to them and no escape for disbelief from them; that is the ṭab'. The khatm which Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, mentioned in His saying "Allah has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing" is analogous to the ṭab' and the khatm upon what sight perceives of vessels and containers, which cannot be reached in what they contain except by breaking that seal off them and then untying them. Likewise faith does not reach the hearts of those whom Allah described as sealed upon, except after breaking His seal and untying His knot from them.

And it is said to the proponents of the second view, who claim that the meaning of His saying "Allah has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing" is a description of them as arrogant and turning away from what they were called to, acknowledging the truth out of arrogance: Tell us about the arrogance of those whom Allah, may His praise be exalted, described with this attribute, and their turning away from acknowledging what they were called to of faith and the other meanings attached to it: is it an act from them, or an act from Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, upon them?

If they claim it is an act from them — and that is their view — it is said to them: Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, has informed that He is the one who sealed upon their hearts and hearing. And how can it be permissible that the disbeliever's turning away from faith and his arrogance against acknowledging it — which is his act according to you — be a sealing from Allah upon his heart and hearing, and His sealing upon his heart and hearing be the act of Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, rather than the disbeliever?

If they claim that this is permissible to be so, because their arrogance and turning away were from the sealing of Allah upon their hearts and hearing, and since the sealing was the cause of that, it is permissible to name the causer by it — then they have abandoned their saying and affirmed that the sealing from Allah upon the hearts and hearing of the disbelievers is a meaning other than the disbelief of the disbeliever, other than his arrogance and his turning away from accepting and acknowledging faith. And that is entry into what they denied.

This verse is among the clearest proofs against the corrupt view of those who deny the imposition of what cannot be borne except with the help of Allah, because Allah, may His praise be exalted, informed that He sealed upon the hearts of a category of His disbelieving servants and their hearing; then He did not remove the obligation from them, nor did He lift from any of them His obligations, nor did He excuse any of them for anything that came from them of disobedience to Him because of what was done to them of sealing and stamping upon their hearts and hearing. Rather, He informed that for all of them there is a great punishment from Him for their abandonment of His obedience in what He commanded them and forbade them of His limits and obligations, along with His decree against them that they would not believe.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, may His praise be exalted: ﴿And upon their eyes is a covering﴾

Abu Ja'far said: His saying ﴿and upon their eyes is a covering﴾ is a new independent statement after the completion of the statement about what Allah, may His praise be exalted, sealed upon the organs of the disbelievers whose stories have passed. That is because "ghishāwa" (covering) is in the nominative case by His saying "and upon their eyes", which is evidence that it is a new independent statement, and that His saying "Allah has sealed upon their hearts" ends at His saying "and upon their hearing."

This is the correct reading according to us, for two reasons:

The first: the agreement of the authoritative readers and scholars in testifying to its correctness, and the isolation of one who opposes them in that, and his deviation from what they are unanimous in considering erroneous. And the unanimity of the authorities in declaring his reading erroneous is sufficient as evidence of its error.

The second: the khatm is not attributed to the eyes in anything of the Book of Allah, nor in any report from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, nor is it found in the language of any Arab. Allah, may He be blessed, said in another surah: ﴿And He sealed upon his hearing and his heart﴾, then He said: (and He placed upon his sight a covering) [Surat al-Jāthiya: 23], so He did not include the sight in the meaning of the khatm. That is what is known in the speech of the Arabs. Therefore it is not permissible for us, nor for anyone among the people, to read "ghishāwa" in the accusative, for the two reasons I have described, although there is a well-known grammatical justification for its accusative form in Arabic.

And in accordance with what we have said in this matter of statement and interpretation, the report was transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās:

305- Muḥammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan narrated to me, from his father, from his grandfather, from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Allah has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing," and the covering upon their eyes [[Report 305: This chain is among the most frequently recurring chains in al-Ṭabarī's tafsir, and it passed the first time at 118, when I had not yet been guided to explain it. It is a chain made consecutive through weak narrators from one family, if this expression is accurate! It is known among scholars as "the tafsir of al-ʿAwfī", because the Successor at its top who narrates it from Ibn ʿAbbās is "ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfī", as we will mention. al-Suyūṭī said in al-Itqān (2:224): "The route of al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated many from it. Al-ʿAwfī is weak, not a liar, and al-Tirmidhī sometimes graded him ḥasan." We will explain it here in detail, God willing:

Muḥammad ibn Saʿd, from whom al-Ṭabarī narrates: he is Muḥammad ibn Saʿd ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAṭiyya ibn Saʿd ibn Janāda al-ʿAwfī, from "Banū ʿAwf ibn Saʿd," a branch of "Banū ʿAmr ibn ʿIyādh ibn Yashkur ibn Bakr ibn Wā'il." He is lax in narration, as al-Khaṭīb said. al-Dāraquṭnī said: "There is no harm in him." He died at the end of Rabīʿ al-Ākhir in the year 276. Al-Khaṭīb gave his biography in Tārīkh Baghdād (5:322–323), and al-Ḥāfiẓ in Lisān al-Mīzān (5:174). He is not "Muḥammad ibn Saʿd ibn Manīʿ", the scribe of al-Wāqidī and author of the great Ṭabaqāt, who was one of the great trustworthy and careful hafiẓ, who died early, in Jumādā al-Ākhira in the year 230.
His father, "Saʿd ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-ʿAwfī": very weak. Imam Aḥmad was asked about him and said: "That one is a Jahmī," then he did not regard him as a place for narration, and said: "Even if he were not this, he would not be one who deserves to be written from, nor would he be a place for that." His biography is in al-Khaṭīb (9:126–127) and Lisān al-Mīzān (3:18–19).
From his paternal uncle: that is the uncle of Saʿd, "al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAṭiyya al-ʿAwfī." He held the judgeship of Baghdad. Ibn Maʿīn said: "He was weak in judgment, weak in hadith." Ibn Saʿd said in al-Ṭabaqāt: "He heard a great deal, and he was weak in hadith." Abū Ḥātim and al-Nasā'ī also weakened him. Ibn Ḥibbān said in al-Majrūḥīn: "Munkar al-ḥadīth... it is not permissible to argue with his report." He had a very long beard, and al-Khaṭīb related amusing anecdotes about it. He died in the year 201. Biographies: al-Ṭabaqāt (7/2:74), al-Jarḥ wa-l-Taʿdīl (1/2:48), Ibn Ḥibbān's al-Majrūḥīn no. 228 p. 167, Tārīkh Baghdād (8:29–32), and Lisān al-Mīzān (2:278).
From his father: he is "al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAṭiyya ibn Saʿd al-ʿAwfī", who is also weak. al-Bukhārī said in al-Kabīr: "not that," and Abū Ḥātim said: "weak in hadith." Ibn Ḥibbān said: "He narrates from his father; his son Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan narrated from him; munkar al-ḥadīth. I do not know whether the calamity in his narrations is from him, or from his father, or from both together, for his father is nothing in hadith, and most of his narration is from his father; from here his matter became confused, and leaving him became obligatory." Biographies: al-Tārīkh al-Kabīr (1/2:299), Ibn Abī Ḥātim (1/2:26), Ibn Ḥibbān's al-Majrūḥīn no. 210 p. 158, and al-Tahdhīb.
From his grandfather: he is "ʿAṭiyya ibn Saʿd ibn Janāda al-ʿAwfī", who is also weak, but he is disputed. Ibn Saʿd said: "He was trustworthy, God willing, and he has good hadiths; and among the people is one who does not argue with him." Aḥmad said: "He is weak in hadith. It reached me that ʿAṭiyya used to go to al-Kalbī and take the tafsir from him. Al-Thawrī and Hushaym used to weaken the hadith of ʿAṭiyya." [He] said: "ṣāliḥ." We have already favored his weakness in the explanation of the Musnad hadith 3010, and the explanation of the Tirmidhī hadith 551; al-Tirmidhī graded that hadith ḥasan because of corroborating routes, not because of ʿAṭiyya. al-Nasā'ī also weakened him in al-Ḍuʿafā' (24). Ibn Ḥibbān weakened him severely in al-Majrūḥīn, saying: "...it is not lawful to write his hadith except as a matter of wonder," folio 178. See also: Ibn Saʿd (6:212–213), al-Bukhārī's al-Kabīr (4/1:8–9), al-Ṣaghīr (126), Ibn Abī Ḥātim (3/1:382–383), and al-Tahdhīb.
The report was transmitted by Ibn Kathīr (1:85), and al-Suyūṭī in al-Durr al-Manthūr (1:29), adding its attribution to Ibn Abī Ḥātim. Al-Shawkānī did likewise (1:28).]]

If someone says: What is the aspect of the accusative in it?

It was said to him: [the verb] "tansubuha" may be read with an implied "ja'ala" (placed), as if he had said, "And He placed over their eyes a covering (ghishawah)," and then "ja'ala" was dropped because the earlier part of the sentence indicates it. (In the printed edition the reading is "in nasabaha...".) Its being in the accusative may also be understood as following the position of "al-sam'" (hearing), since that position is accusative, even though it is not good to repeat the governing verb before "ghishawah." Rather, it is because the sentences follow one another, as the Exalted said: ﴿There will go round about them youths of perpetual youth with cups and ewers﴾, then He said: ﴿and fruit such as they choose, and the flesh of fowl such as they desire, and houris with wide, lovely eyes﴾ [Surah al-Waqi'ah: 17–22]. So He put "al-lahm" (the flesh) and "al-hur" (the houris) in the genitive by coordinating them with "al-fakihah" (the fruit), the end of the speech being made to follow its beginning. It is well known that flesh is not carried round, nor the houris with wide eyes, but it is as the poet said, describing his horse:

*I fed her straw and cold water, until she spent the winter, her eyes streaming.*

[The speaker is unknown. al-Farra' cited it in *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* 1:14, saying, "Some of the Banu Asad recited it to me, describing his horse." In *al-Khizanah* 1:499 it says: "I saw in a sound margin of the Sahih that it belongs to Dhu al-Rummah, but I searched his divan and did not find it." It will come in the commentary on a verse of Surah al-Ma'idah: 109 (7:81 Bulaq). "Shatta" comes from *shatā bi-l-makan*: he stayed in the place during the winter, which is the season of barrenness. "Hammalah" means her tears flow, that is, she pours them out and sheds them from the severity of the cold.]

It is well known that water is drunk and not fed to an animal, but he made it accusative in the manner I described earlier, as another poet said:

*And I saw your husband in battle, girded with a sword and a spear.*

[The derivation of this line has already passed on p. 140.]

Ibn Jurayj used to say, at the point where the report about the sealing ends at the words "and upon their hearing," and the report resumes after it, the same as what we have said about it, and he would interpret it with the Book of God: ﴿If God willed, He would seal upon your heart﴾ [Surah al-Shura: 24].

306 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj narrated to us, saying: "The sealing is upon the heart and the hearing, and the covering is upon the sight." God, the Exalted, said: ﴿If God willed, He would seal upon your heart﴾, and He said: ﴿And God sealed upon their hearing and their hearts, and placed upon their sight a covering﴾ [Surah al-Jathiyah: 23].

[The report 306 was cited by Ibn Kathir in his *Tafsir* 1:85 and al-Shawkani 1:28.]

"Ghishawah" in the speech of the Arabs means a covering, and from it is the saying of al-Harith ibn Khalid ibn al-'As:

*I followed you when my eye was covered over; but when it cleared, I cut myself off, blaming it.*

[The poet is al-Harith ibn Khalid al-Makhzumi. The verse occurs in the commentary on a verse of Surah al-A'raf: 18 (8:103 Bulaq), and its version there is: "I accompanied you when my eye... I blame it" (*udhayyimuha*), as evidence for "al-dhaam" (blame), which is more eloquent in censure than mere blame. Then Abu Ja'far said: "Most narrators recite it *alumuha* (I blame it)." The story of the verse: when 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan assumed the caliphate and performed the pilgrimage to the House, al-Harith travelled with him after his return to Damascus; a coldness appeared in him toward al-Harith, and he remained at his door for a month without gaining access to him. So he departed from him and said the verse in question, followed by: "It is not my humility that has made you distance me, nor has my soul become needy of one who wrongs it." (See al-Aghani 3:317.) 'Abd al-Malik heard his poetry and sent for him and brought him back.]

From it one says: *tagharrahu al-hamm*, when worry covered him and mounted him. From it is also the saying of Nabigha of the Banu Dhubyan:

*Would that you had asked the Banu Dhubyan about my lineage, when the smoke covers the old, grey-headed, and the one who does not take part in the game of chance.*

[From his divan: 52. "Al-ashmat" is one whose head has turned grey from age; "al-barm" is one who does not enter with the people into the game of maysir (chance). Ibn Qutaybah said in *al-Ma'ani al-Kabir* 410, 1238: "He specified the ashmat because he has grown old and weak, so he comes to the places of the flesh."]

He means by it: it covers him and mixes with him.

God, the Exalted, only informed His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) about those among the rabbis of the Jews who disbelieved in him, that He had sealed upon their hearts and stamped them, so they do not understand any admonition that God, blessed and exalted, admonished them with, in what He gave them of knowledge of what they had of His Books, and in what He set limits in His Book which He revealed and sent down to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), "and upon their hearing," so they do not hear from Muhammad (ﷺ), the Prophet of God, any warning, reminder, or proof that he established against them by his prophethood, so that they might remember and beware the punishment of God, the Mighty and Majestic, for their denial of him, while they knew his truthfulness and the soundness of his command. And He informed him, along with that, that upon their sight is a covering, preventing them from seeing the path of guidance, so that they might know the ugliness of what they were upon of error and perdition.

In accordance with what we have said about this, the report was transmitted from a group of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil):

307 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿God has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and upon their sight is a covering﴾, that is, from guidance, that they would never attain it by other than what they denied you of the truth that came to you from your Lord, until they believe in it, even if they believe in all that came before you.

[Report 307 is mentioned by al-Suyuti 1:29, connected with what has passed (295, 299) and with what follows (311). He cited them as one continuous chain.]

308 – Musa ibn Harun al-Hamdani narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas – and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "God has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing," meaning: so they do not understand and do not hear. And He says: "and placed upon their sight a covering," meaning: upon their eyes, so they do not see.

[Report 308 was cited by Ibn Kathir 1:85. Al-Suyuti 1:29 and al-Shawkani 1:28 mention it only from Ibn Mas'ud.]

Others, however, interpreted that those of the disbelievers about whom God informed that He did this to them were the leaders of the factions who were killed on the day of Badr.

309 – Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: These two verses, up to ﴿and for them is a mighty punishment﴾, are about ﴿those who exchanged God's blessing for disbelief and caused their people to settle in the abode of ruin﴾ [Surah Ibrahim: 28]; they are those who were killed on the day of Badr. None of the leaders entered Islam except two men: Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and al-Hakam ibn Abi al-'As.

[Report 309 is the continuation of the earlier report 298, also cited by al-Suyuti 1:29 and al-Shawkani 1:28. We have pointed to it there.]

310 – And it was related to me from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from al-Hasan, who said: As for the leaders, there is none among them who answered, nor who was saved, nor who was guided.

We have already shown in what has passed which of these two interpretations is more correct, so we disliked repeating it.

* *

Concerning the explanation of the words of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And for them is a mighty punishment (7)﴾

Its interpretation, in my view, is as Ibn 'Abbas said and interpreted it:

311 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "And for them, because of what they are upon of opposition to you, is a mighty punishment." He said: This is about the rabbis of the Jews, for what they denied you of the truth that came to you from your Lord after their recognition of it.

[Report 311 is the continuation of the reports 295, 299, 307; al-Suyuti 1:29 cited them in one continuous chain, as we pointed out earlier. But he omitted from its end what follows "this is about the rabbis of the Jews." Perhaps he took it to be from al-Tabari's own words. The context makes clear that it is part of the report.]

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is His praise: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ (2:8)**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: As for His saying, "And among the people" (*wa-min al-nas*), the word "people" (*al-nas*) has two possible readings.

The first: it is a plural with no singular from its own form. Its singular is *insan* (a human being), and its feminine singular is *insana*.[[In the printed edition: "its singular is *insan* and its feminine singular is *insanah*."]]

The second: its origin is *unas*, and the *hamza* was dropped from it because of frequent use. Then the definite article *al-* was added, and the *lam* of the article was assimilated into the *nun*, as is said in ﴿But as for me, He is God, my Lord﴾ (18:38), as we have explained concerning the name "God" (*Allah*).[[See what has passed, pp. 125–126.]] Some have claimed that *al-nas* is a different form from *unas*, and that they heard the Arabs diminutive it as *nuways* (from *al-nas*), and that if the origin were *unas*, the diminutive would be *unays*, so it has been returned to its original form.

All the people of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wil*) agreed (*ajma'a*, consensus) that this verse was revealed concerning a group of the hypocrites (*ahl al-nifaq*), and that this description applies to them.

**Mention of those who said this among the people of interpretation, by name:**

312. Muhammad ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾: he meant the hypocrites from the Aws and the Khazraj and those who were upon their affair.

The names of these people were mentioned in this report of Ibn Abbas, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, but I have omitted naming them, disliking to lengthen the book by mentioning them.[[Report 312: a similar meaning has passed at 296, and we pointed to this there. The names of the hypocrites from the Aws and the Khazraj, whom al-Tabari disliked to lengthen the book by mentioning, were preserved for us by Ibn Hisham in his abridgement of the *Sirah* of Ibn Ishaq, in full detail: pp. 355–361 (Europe edition), 2: 166–174 (al-Halabi edition), 2: 26–29 (*al-Rawd al-Unuf*).]]

313. Al-Husayn ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾, up to ﴿So their trade did not profit them, nor were they guided﴾ (2:16), he said: this is about the hypocrites.[[Report 313: al-Hasan ibn Yahya, the teacher of al-Tabari; the manuscripts here have "al-Husayn," which is an error. A similar chain has passed in the correct form, no. 257.]]

314. Muhammad ibn Amr al-Bahili related to us, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa ibn Maymun related to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Abi Najih related to us, from Mujahid, who said: this verse, up to thirteen (verses), describes the hypocrites.

315. Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

316. Sufyan related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Sufyan, from a man, from Mujahid, the like of it.

317. Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from Isma'il al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾: they are the hypocrites.

318. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, from Ibn Abi Ja'far, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, concerning His saying: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day"﴾, up to ﴿God increased them in sickness, and theirs is a painful punishment﴾ (2:10), he said: these are the people of hypocrisy.

319. Al-Qasim related to us, saying: Al-Husayn ibn Dawud related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His saying: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾, he said: this is the hypocrite, whose speech contradicts his action, whose secret is other than his public, whose entering is other than his exiting, and whose presence is other than his absence.[[Reports 314–319: Ibn Kathir (1: 86) cited some of them, partly quoting and partly alluding. Al-Suyuti (1: 29) and al-Shawkani (1: 29) also cited some of them.]]

**The meaning of this:** When God, exalted is His praise, gathered for His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) his affair in the abode of his migration (*dar al-hijrah*), where his residence was settled, where God made His word manifest, and where Islam spread in the homes of its people; when the Muslims overcame, in it, those of the idolaters who were there, the worshippers of idols, and those of the People of the Book (*ahl al-kitab*) who were there were humbled, the rabbis (*ahbar*) of its Jews displayed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) their rancor, and showed him enmity and hatred, out of envy and insolence,[[In the manuscript: "the enmity and the *shinar*," which is an error. *Al-shana'an* and *al-shana'ah* mean hatred that is revealed by intense rage; *shani'a al-shay'* (he hated the thing) means he hated it intensely.]] except for a few of them whom God guided to Islam, so they embraced it. As His saying, exalted is His praise, states: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back from your faith into disbelief, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them﴾ (2:109). And a group, from among the clans (*arahit*) of the Ansar who had sheltered the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and supported him, secretly conspired with them against the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions, and plotted calamities against them.[[The *ghawa'il* are the plural of *ghA'ilah*: the misfortune that overwhelms and destroys. *Arahit* is the plural of *rahat*, a group of between three and ten people, with no women among them. He meant by them a small number from the branches of the Ansar.]] They had been stubborn (*'asaw*) in their polytheism and their ignorance,[[In the printed edition: "they had been stubborn (*'utuw*) in their ignorance," and both are correct. *'Asa al-shay'* means it became hard and firm, and grew rough through the passage of time; *'asa al-rajul* means he grew old. *Al-'asi* is the harsh one, and *al-'ati* is similar. *'Ata ya'tu* has the same meaning. See what has passed, p. 36, note.]] and their names have been given to us, but we disliked lengthening the book by mentioning their names and lineages. They supported them in this, in concealment and not openly, out of fear of being killed and of being seized by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions, and out of inclination toward the Jews because of their polytheism and their poor insight into Islam. So when they met the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the people of faith in him among his companions, they would say to them, out of fear for themselves: "We believe in God and in His Messenger and in the Resurrection," and they gave them with their tongues the word of truth, in order to ward off from themselves the judgment of God upon whoever holds to what they were persisting in of polytheism, had they displayed with their tongues what they believed of their polytheism. And when they met their brethren from among the Jews and the people of polytheism and the denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) and what he brought, and they were alone with them, they said: ﴿We are with you; we were only mocking﴾ (2:14).
