It is the same whether one says: there was no mockery, scheming, deception or derision from Allah toward those whom He informed that He mocks, derides and schemes against — or says: Allah did not cause the earth to swallow those whom He informed He caused to be swallowed among the nations, nor did He drown those whom He informed He drowned.

It is said to the one who says that: Allah, blessed is His praise, informed us that He schemed against a people who passed before us, whom we did not see; and He informed of others that He caused the earth to swallow them, and of others that He drowned them. We affirm Allah, mentioned, in what He informed us of that, and we do not distinguish between any of it. So what is your proof for your distinction between what you distinguished, by your claim: that He drowned and caused to be swallowed those whom He informed He drowned and caused to be swallowed, but did not scheme against those whom He informed He schemed against?

Then we reverse the argument upon him in that matter: he will not say anything about one of them except that the same will be imposed on the other.

If he resorts to saying: mockery is play and sport, and that is negated from Allah, exalted and mighty:

It is said to him: If the matter is as you describe the meaning of mockery, do you not say "Allah mocks them," and "Allah derided them," and "Allah schemed against them," while there is, according to you, no mockery or derision from Allah?

If he says "No," he denies the Qur'an and leaves the religion of Islam.

If he says "Yes," it is said to him: Then do we say, in the sense you spoke of: "Allah mocks them," and "Allah derided them" — "Allah plays with them" and "Allah sports with them" — while there is no play or sport from Allah?

If he says "Yes!", he describes Allah with what the Muslims have agreed to negate from Him, and agreed on the error of the one who describes Him with it, and attributes to Him what the proof of reason has established as the error of the one who attributes it to Him.

If he says: I do not say "Allah plays with them" or "Allah sports with them," but I say "Allah mocks them" and "Allah derides them":

It is said: Then you have distinguished between the meaning of play and sport, mockery and derision, scheming and deception. From the aspect by which it is permissible to say this, and not permissible to say that, their meanings have diverged. So it is known that each of them has a meaning other than the meaning of the other.

For discussion of this type there is a place other than this, and we disliked lengthening the book by exhausting it. In what we have mentioned there is sufficiency for one who is granted understanding of it.

* *

The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿And He extends them﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation differed concerning the interpretation of His saying: ﴿wa-yamuddu-hum (and He extends them)﴾. Some of them said:

364 — Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas — and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "yamuddu-hum" means: He gives them respite.

Others said:

365 — al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated to us, from Ibn al-Mubarak, from Ibn Jurayj, reciting from Mujahid: "yumaddu-hum," he said: He increases them [[Reports 364, 365: cited by Ibn Kathir 1: 31, al-Suyuti 1: 31, and al-Shawkani 1: 33.]].

Some of the grammarians of Basra interpreted it to mean: "yamuddu lahum," and he claimed that this is like the Arabs' saying: "The boy plays with the knucklebones (al-ka'ab)," meaning "plays with the knucklebones." He said: That is because they do say "qad maddat lahu wa-amddtu lahu" in other than this meaning, and this is the saying of Allah, mentioned: ﴿And We extended them﴾ [Surah al-Tur: 22], and this is from "maddana-hum" [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "and this is from amddna-hum"; the correct reading is likely what we adopted. He means that His saying (wa-yamuddu-hum fi tughyani-him) is from "maddat lahu," which is like "amadtu lahu," after dropping the preposition, as in the Arabs' saying "the boy plays the knucklebones," i.e., "plays with the knucklebones."]]. He said: It is said: "The sea has extended (madda) so it is extending (madd)," and "the wound has extended (amadda) so it is extending (mumidd)." It is related from Yunus al-Jarmi that he used to say: whatever is of evil is "maddadtu," and whatever is of good is "amddtu." Then he said: It is as I have explained to you: if you mean that you left him, it is "maddadtu lahu," and if you mean that you gave him, you say "amddtu."

As for some of the grammarians of Kufa, he used to say: every increase that arises in a thing from itself is "maddadtu" without an alif, as you say: "the river extended (madda), and another river extended it," when it joins with it and becomes part of it; and every increase brought into a thing from other than it is with an alif, like your saying: "the wound extended (amadda)," because the extension is from other than the wound; and "I extended (amaddtu) the army with reinforcements (madad)."

The most correct of these views concerning His saying: "wa-yamuddu-hum" is that it means "yazidu-hum" (He increases them), in the manner of giving them respite and leaving them in their insolence and rebelliousness, as our Lord described that He did to their counterparts in His saying: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sight as they did not believe in it the first time, and We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 110]; meaning: We leave them and abandon them in it, and We give them respite so that they increase in sin upon their sin.

There is no basis for the view of one who said that it means "yamuddu lahum" (He extends for them), because there is no disagreement among the Arabs and those knowledgeable of their language that they permit the saying of the speaker: "another river extended the river" (madda al-nahra nahrun akhar), in the sense that it joined with it and the water of the joined river became increased by the water of the one joining — without any interpretation from them. That is because its meaning is: another river extended the river. So likewise is it in Allah's saying: ﴿And He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾.

The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿fi tughyani-him (in their transgression)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: "al-Tughyan" is "al-Fu'lan," from your saying: "Fulan transgressed (taghā) yatghā tughyanan," when he exceeds his limit in the matter and rebels. From it is Allah's saying: ﴿Nay, indeed, man transgresses (layatgha) when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [Surah al-'Alaq: 6, 7], meaning he exceeds his limit. From it is the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

And he called upon Allah a call, but it was not the time for it [[lat hanna]], after his transgression (tughyani-hi), so he remained pointing [[mushiran]].

[[His Diwan: 34, with variation in the transmission. The pronoun in "wa-da'a Allah" refers to Pharaoh when the drowning overtook him. The pronoun in "tughyani-hi" refers to Pharaoh, or to the water when it rose and enveloped him. "Lat hanna" is a phrase used in their speech meaning: "this is not the time for that"; the "ta" in "lat" is an added particle attached to "la," originally "la hana," meaning "there is not here what you wanted," i.e., that time has passed. "Hanna" is with the initial h vowelled and the n doubled, like "hunna" with the h vowelled and n light. "Mushiran" means pointing with his hand in supplication to his Lord to save him from drowning.]]

Allah, mentioned, intended by His saying ﴿wa-yamuddu-hum fi tughyani-him﴾ that He gives them respite, and leaves them to go on in their error and disbelief, bewildered, wandering. As:

366 — I was told from al-Minjab, saying: Bishr narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿fi tughyani-him ya'mahun (in their transgression they wander blindly)﴾, he said: in their disbelief they wander.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bari) on surah 2, verse 15 (part 2 of 2):**

367. Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "*fi tughyanihim*" means in their disbelief.

368. Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' related to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿in their rebellion they wander blindly﴾: that is, they wander blindly in their misguidance.

369. I was told on the authority of Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "*fi tughyanihim*," in their misguidance.

370. Yunus related to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words "*fi tughyanihim*": "Their rebellion" is their disbelief and their misguidance.

[[The reports 366–370: cited by Ibn Kathir 1:95, al-Suyuti 1:31, and al-Shawkani 1:33.]]

* *

**The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words: ﴿they wander blindly﴾ (15)**

Abu Ja'far said: *al-'amah* (wandering blindly) itself means misguidance. It is said of it: *'amiha* (فلان يعمه) *ya'mahu 'amahanan wa 'umuhan*, when he goes astray. [[In Ibn Kathir 1:95 the text reads "*'amaha wa 'umuhan*"; the reading in al-Tabari is correct: "*'amaha wa 'umuhan wa 'umuhatan wa 'amahanan*."]] From this is the verse of Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj describing a desert wilderness where one goes astray:

*And a wide, shimmering plain of mirages, and a wilderness of wilderness, *
*which they traverse, entering another waste, *
*blind to guidance, among the ignorant wanderers.*

[[His Diwan: 166. *Makhfaq*: a wide, level land in which mirages shimmer, i.e., move. *Lahlah*: a wide land in which mirages move; its plural is *lahalah*. *Mahmah*: a desert wasteland with neither water nor a living soul. *Jaba al-mafazah* and *ijtabaha*: he crossed it by travel. His words "*fi mahmah*" mean: they cross it and enter another waste, going deep into the desert.]]

*Al-'umm'ah* (the wanderers) is the plural of *'amih*, those who go astray in it and become bewildered. So the meaning of His words ﴿in their rebellion they wander blindly﴾ is: in their misguidance and disbelief, which has overwhelmed them with its filth and whose abomination has covered them, they wander about bewildered and astray, finding no way out of it, because Allah has sealed their hearts and set a seal upon them, and has blinded their sight to guidance and covered it, so they see no right direction and find no path.

The interpretation of the exegetes agrees with what we have said regarding *al-'amah*.

371. Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "*ya'mahun*," they continue in their disbelief.

372. al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih related to us, from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas: "*ya'mahun*," he said: they persist.

373. I was told on the authority of al-Minjab, who said: Bishr related to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas regarding His words "*ya'mahun*," he said: they hesitate.

374. Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ibn Abbas said: "*ya'mahun*": those who are bewildered (*al-mutaladdid*). [[*Taladdada lil-rajul* (فهو متلدد): when a man remains in his place bewildered and confused, looking right and left.]]

375. Muhammad ibn Amr al-Bahili related to us, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa ibn Maymun related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Najih related to us, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah ﴿in their rebellion they wander blindly﴾, he said: they hesitate.

376. al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

377. Sufyan ibn Waki' related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Sufyan, from a man, from Mujahid, the like of it.

378. al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr related to us, from Ibn al-Mubarak, from Ibn Juraij, by recitation, from Mujahid, the like of it.

379. I was told on the authority of Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "*ya'mahun*," he said: they hesitate.

[[Reports 372–379: cited by al-Suyuti 1:31 and al-Shawkani 1:33, who also cite the report of Mujahid on the verse: "that is, they play and wander about in misguidance."]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 16:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is His praise: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says: How could these people have bought error in exchange for guidance, when they were hypocrites, and their hypocrisy was not preceded by faith, so that it could be said of them that they sold their guidance, which they had been upon, for their error, and substituted it for it? And you know that the understood meaning of purchase (shira') is the exchange of one thing by giving another thing in its place as a substitute for it, while the hypocrites whom God described with this attribute had never been upon guidance so that they could leave it and exchange it for disbelief and hypocrisy? It is said: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have differed concerning the meaning of that. We shall mention what they said about it, then clarify the correct interpretation in that, God willing:

380- Muhammad ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾, i.e., disbelief in exchange for faith.

381- Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas - and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the companions of the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾, he says: They took error and left guidance.

382- Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾, they preferred error over guidance.

383- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa ibn Maymun related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾, they believed and then disbelieved.

384- Al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it [[The reports 380-384: Ibn Kathir cited them in his tafsir 1: 95, 96, al-Suyuti 1: 31, 32, and al-Shawkani 1: 33, 34.]].

Abu Ja'far said: Those who interpreted it as "they took error and left guidance" directed the meaning of purchase toward taking the thing purchased in place of the price paid for it. They said: Likewise the hypocrite and the disbeliever have taken disbelief in place of faith, so this was their purchase of disbelief and error, which they took by leaving the guidance they had left, and the guidance they left was the price which they made as a substitute for the error they took.

As for those who interpreted the meaning of His saying "they bought" as "they preferred," when they found that God, exalted is His praise, had described the disbelievers in another place, attributing to them their preference of disbelief over guidance, saying: ﴿And as for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Surah Fussilat: 17], they turned His saying ﴿they bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ toward that. They said: The particle "ba'" (with) may be used in place of "'ala" (upon), and "'ala" in place of "ba'", as one says: "Marartu bi-fulan" and "Marartu 'ala fulan," with the same meaning, and as the saying of God, exalted is His praise: ﴿And among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 75], i.e., upon a qintar. So the interpretation of the verse according to their meaning is: Those are the ones who chose error over guidance. They seem to have directed the meaning of God's saying "ishtaraw" to the meaning of "ikhtaraw" (chose), because the Arabs say: "Ishtaraytu kadhā 'alā kadhā" and "istaraytuhu," meaning: I chose it over it.

From the use of "istira'" is the saying of A'sha Bani Tha'labah [[In the printed edition it is "al-ishtira'" with the shin, which is an error; the correct form is with the sin (s) unpointed.]]:

"Then I brought out the maiden, the al-mustara..." (the one chosen) from her curtain, and I spread the gambling...

[[Diwan: 35; Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara': 36; al-Lisan (s-r-a). In the printed edition it is "al-mushtara(t)" in both places, and the correct form is what we have recorded. Al-kā'ib: the one whose breasts have swelled, i.e., full-bosomed; she is a delicate, pampered, veiled girl. Khidr of the girl: her covering which is stretched for her so that she remains in it after puberty. Ashā'a al-māl among the people: distributed it among them. By al-qimār he means the game of maysir, and he refers to the winner's share of the maysir of the slaughtered camel's meat, which he distributes among the people out of generosity.]]

He means by al-mustara: the chosen one.

And Dhu al-Rummah said, regarding "ishtira'" in the sense of "ikhtiyar":

"He drives away the rejected ones from a choice herd, as if they were heaps beneath the rain-laden, pouring clouds..." [[Diwan: 62. The pronoun in his saying "yadhubbu" refers to the stallion camel. Yadhubbu: pushes away and drives off. Al-qasaya: plural of qasiyyah, which are the worst of the camels, weakened and left behind. Jamahir: plural of jumhur, a sandy mound raised above its surroundings, whose sand has piled up and clumped. Al-mudjinat: from their saying "a dajinah and mudjinah cloud," meaning the dense, heavy-raining one. Al-hawadib: those whose rain has lasted and whose drops have grown large. He likens the camels in the grandeur of their form and bulk to heaps of sand clumped together in the eye of one viewing from afar.]]

He means by al-shara: the chosen one.

And another said in a similar sense:

"Indeed the shara is the choicest of wealth, and the heart's treasure is the best of property" [[The second line is in Lisan (h-z-r). The "ruqah" of people are their best and most splendid in appearance. It is said: this thing is the treasure of my soul and heart, meaning the best of what I have, and that to which the heart is attached for its preciousness.]].

Abu Ja'far said: This, though it is a possible interpretation, I do not prefer it, because God, exalted is His praise, said: ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾, which indicates that the meaning of His saying "those are the ones who bought error in exchange for guidance" is the meaning of purchase that people commonly recognize: substituting one thing for another, and taking one exchange in place of another.

As for those who said that the people were believers and then disbelieved, there is no difficulty for them, if the matter were as they described the people. For if the matter were so, they would have abandoned faith and substituted disbelief for guidance in exchange. That is the understood meaning of buying and selling. But the indications from the opening of the verses through their attributes to the end indicate that these people had never been illuminated by the light of faith, nor entered the community of Islam. Do you not hear God, exalted is His praise, from the beginning of describing them until He reached their description, that He described them only as displaying falsehood with their tongues: by their claim of believing in our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and in what he brought, deceiving God, His Messenger, and the believers in their own estimation, and mocking the believers in their souls, while inwardly they were other than what they showed. God, majestic is His majesty [[In the printed edition: "for the saying of God..."]], says: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾, then He related their account until His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾. So where is the evidence that they were believers and then disbelieved?

If the speaker of this view thought that His saying "those who bought error in exchange for guidance" is the proof that these people had been upon faith and then moved from it to disbelief, and therefore they were told "they bought" — that interpretation is not accepted, since purchase according to its opponents may be taking one thing by leaving another, and it may mean choosing, and other meanings. When a word admits several aspects, no one may turn its meaning to some of those aspects rather than others except by a proof that must be accepted.

Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation of the verse that is more preferable to me is what we have related from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying: ﴿they bought error in exchange for guidance﴾: they took error and left guidance. That is because every disbeliever in God substitutes disbelief for faith, by acquiring the disbelief that has come from him in place of the faith that he was commanded to have. Do you not hear God, exalted is His praise, saying about one who acquires disbelief in Him in place of faith in Him and His Messenger: ﴿And whoever substitutes disbelief for faith has certainly strayed from the sound way﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 108]? That is the meaning of purchase, for every buyer of something substitutes for what is taken from him another substitute in its place. Likewise the hypocrite and the disbeliever substituted error and hypocrisy for guidance, so God misguided them, and stripped them of the light of guidance, and left them all in darknesses where they do not see.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of that is that the hypocrites, by their purchase of error in exchange for guidance, lost and did not profit, because the profitable merchant is one who exchanges from his owned merchandise a substitute that is more precious than his owned merchandise or better than the price with which he bought it. As for one who exchanges from his merchandise a substitute that is less than it and less than the price with which he bought it [[In the printed edition: "yabtaiuha"]], he is without doubt the loser in his commerce. Likewise the disbeliever and the hypocrite, for they chose bewilderment and blindness over right guidance and direction, and fear and terror over protection and security, and they substituted in the immediate: bewilderment for right direction, error for guidance, fear for protection, and terror for security, in addition to what has been prepared for them in the hereafter of painful punishment and severe torment. So they failed and lost. That is the manifest loss.

In accordance with what we have said, Qatadah used to say the same.

385- Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' related to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah: ﴿So their commerce did not profit, nor were they guided﴾: By God, you have seen them come out from guidance into error, from the community into division, from security into fear, and from the Sunnah into innovation [[Report 385: in Ibn Kathir 1: 96, al-Suyuti 1: 32, al-Shawkani 1: 34.]].

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says: What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾? Is commerce something that profits or suffers loss, so that one says it profited or was diminished [[One says: he was diminished (wudi'a) in his commerce, meaning he was defrauded and lost in it; similar to it is wakasa.]]?

It is said: The meaning of that is other than what you supposed. Rather, the meaning is: they did not profit in their commerce, neither in what they bought nor in what they sold. But God, exalted is His praise, addressed the Arabs in His Book, and in His address to them and His explanation to them, He followed the manner of address that some of them use with one another and their customary speech among themselves [[In the manuscript: "al-musta'lam", probably a slip of the pen.]]. Since the saying of a speaker to another was eloquent among them — "Your effort has failed, your night has slept, your sale has been lost," and similar speech whose meaning is not hidden from the hearer — He addressed them with what was in their idiom, saying: ﴿So their commerce did not profit﴾, since it was understood among them that profit is in commerce, just as sleep is in the night. He was satisfied with the understanding of those addressed as to the meaning, instead of saying: "They did not profit in their commerce," although that is its meaning, as the poet said:

"And the worst of deaths is a dead man in the midst of his people, like the destruction of the maiden, whose present one has left the living..." [[It is by al-Hutay'ah, from verses not in his diwan, but in Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara': 95, Sibawayh 1: 109, and Amali al-Sharif al-Murtada 1: 38, with some variation in the transmission; the Tabaqat version is the best of them. "Awaqada al-hayy" means it awakened the tribe: the one present of death, so the wailing women rose, lamenting and mourning. And the transmission of one who narrates "aslama al-hayy" means it delivered them to weeping.]]

He means by that: and the worst of deaths is the death of a dead man in the midst of his people; he was satisfied with the hearer understanding his intent, instead of stating what was left unstated. As Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj said:

"O Harith! You have relieved my worry for me, so my night slept, and my grief was revealed..." [[Diwan: 142, praising al-Harith ibn Sulaym, of the family of 'Amr ibn Sa'd ibn Zayd Manat.]]

He attributed sleep to the night, while its meaning is that it is the one who slept. As Jarir ibn al-Khatafa said:

"And a one-eyed man from Nabhan: his day is blind, and his night is seeing..." [[Diwan: 206; al-Naqa'id: 35; al-Mu'talif wa'l-Mukhtalif: 39, 161; Mu'jam al-Shu'ara' 253, from a poem satirizing the one-eyed al-Nabhani, who had satirized Jarir, and Jarir devoured him. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "That is, he is one-eyed by day regarding good things, seeing by night regarding evil deeds: he steals and commits adultery."]]

He attributed blindness and sight to the night and the day, while his meaning is to describe the Nabhani with that.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿and they were not guided﴾ [[16]]

By His saying, exalted is His praise, ﴿and they were not guided﴾, He means: they were not rightly guided in their preference of error over guidance, in their substitution of disbelief for faith, and in their purchase of hypocrisy with affirmation and acknowledgment.

**The interpretation of His words: ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire; and when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see﴾ (2:17)**

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us, "How is it said, ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾, when you know that the ha' and mim in His words 'their' (*hum*) is a pronoun for a group, of men or of men and women, and 'the one who' (*alladhi*) indicates a single male? How then can the report about one person be made a likeness for a group? Why was it not said, 'Their likeness is that of those who kindled a fire'? And if, in your view, it is permissible to liken a group to an individual, then would you permit someone who saw a group of men, whose forms and complete physiques pleased him, to say, 'It is as if these people, or the bodies of these people, are a palm tree'?"

It is said in reply: As for the case in which our Lord, exalted is His praise, likens a group of hypocrites to a single person whom He made an example of their deeds, this is permissible and fine. [["And in its parallels" means that in its parallels it is likewise permissible and fine. Similar to it is what comes a few lines later in His words "nor in its parallels," where the omission occurs in both instances.]] Just as He, exalted is His praise, said in a parallel to this: ﴿Their eyes roll like one who is overcome by death﴾ (33:19), meaning, like the rolling of the eye of one who is overcome by death. And as in His words: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul﴾ (31:28), meaning: only like the resurrection of a single soul.

As for likening the physiques of a group of men, in height and completeness of form, to a single palm tree, this is not permissible, nor is its parallel, because of the difference between them.

As for the likening of a group of hypocrites to a single kindler of fire, it is permissible because what is intended by the report about the likeness of the hypocrites is the report about the likeness of their being illuminated by what they displayed with their tongues of affirmation, while inwardly they harbored other than it, namely their wretched beliefs and their mixing of inner hypocrisy with the outward profession of faith. The state of being illuminated, although the individuals who experience it differ, is one meaning, not many different meanings. Therefore the likeness for it is like the likeness of one individual, among things differing in their individuals.

The interpretation of this is: The likeness of the illumination of the hypocrites by what they displayed of affirmation of Allah, of Muhammad ﷺ, and of what he brought, in words, while they disbelieved in it in their hearts, is like the likeness of the illumination of one who kindled a fire. Then the mention of the illumination was dropped and the likeness was attributed to them, as the poet Nabigha of Banu Ja'dah said:

*"How can you keep company with one whose friendship is like that of Abu Marhab?"* [[The verse is by al-Nabigha al-Ja'di (Lisan, rhb and khll). Khallah and khalalah mean an exclusive friendship in which there is no flaw. Abu Marhab is a kunya for the shadow; he means that it passes away as a shadow passes away, leaving no lasting affection.]]

He means: like the friendship of Abu Marhab, so he dropped "friendship," since what was displayed in the speech gave its hearers an indication of what was omitted. Likewise is the matter in His words: ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾. Since it was known to His hearers, from what was displayed in the speech, that the likeness was struck only for the illumination of the people by the profession of faith and not for the bodily persons themselves, it was good to omit mention of the illumination and to attribute the likeness to its people. What is intended by the likeness is what we have mentioned. Having described it, the saying ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ is permissible and fine, and the likeness of a group is expressed in words in the form of a single individual, since the meaning intended by "likeness" is a single one.

As for when the intention is to liken a group of the actual persons of the children of Adam, or of the persons possessing forms and bodies, to something, the correct speech is to liken a group to a group and an individual to an individual, because the person of each one of them is other than the persons of the others.

For this reason, in terms of meaning, the discourse differs regarding the likening of actions and of nouns. It is permissible to liken the actions of a group of people and others, when they have one meaning, to the action of a single individual, and then to omit the names of the actions and attribute the likeness and comparison to those who perform the action. One says: "Your actions are only like the action of a dog," then one omits and says, "Your actions are only like a dog's or like dogs'," and one means: only like the action of a dog, only like the actions of dogs. But it is not permissible to say, "They are only a palm tree," while intending to liken their bodies to palm trees in height and completeness.

As for His words ﴿kindled [istawqada] a fire﴾, it is in the sense of *awqada* (kindled). As the poet said:

*"And a caller called out: 'O you who answers the call to generosity!' But no one answered him at that moment."* [[The verse is by Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi (al-Asma'iyyat 14; Amali al-Qali 2:151). It is among the finest elegies.]]

He means: "but no one answered him." So the meaning of the speech is then: The likeness of the illumination of these hypocrites, in their displaying to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and to the believers with their tongues, by their saying, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," and "We affirm Muhammad and what he brought," while they harbor disbelief within, [[The syntax of his expression: "The likeness of the illumination of these . . . in what Allah does to them, the likeness of the illumination . . ."]] in what Allah does to them, is like the likeness of one who kindles a fire with its fire, until the fire illuminates what is around him, meaning: what is around the one who kindled it.

Some grammarians of Basra have claimed that *alladhi* in His words, "like the likeness of the one who kindled a fire," means *alladhina* (those who), as in His words, exalted is His praise: ﴿And the one who brought the truth and affirmed it, those are the God-fearing﴾ (39:33), and as the poet said:

*"Indeed, those whose blood was spilled at Falj, they are the people, all of the people, O Umm Khalid."* [[The verse is by al-Ashhab ibn Rumaylah (al-Khizanah 2:507–508; al-Bayan 4:55; Sibawayh 1:96; al-Mu'talif wa'l-mukhtalif of al-Amidi, 33). Al-Baghdadi reports that Abu Tammam recited the verse among verses by Huraith ibn Mihfad in his book Mukhtar ash'ar al-qaba'il, with the reading "wa-inna al-alla". There is no evidence in it. They say that the nun was dropped from *alladhina*, so it became *alladhi* due to the length of the speech and for lightness, and it means the plural, not the singular. Falj is a valley between Basra and the protected land of Dhariyyah, where this battle mentioned took place.]]

Abu Ja'far said: The first view is the correct one, for the reason we have described. The one who holds this view has overlooked the difference between *alladhi* in the two verses and in the line of verse. For *alladhi* in His words, "and the one who brought the truth," has indication that its meaning is plural, which is His words: ﴿those are the God-fearing﴾. Likewise *alladhi* in the verse, which is His words "their blood." But this indication is absent from His words, "like the likeness of the one who kindled a fire." That is the difference between *alladhi* in His words, "like the likeness of the one who kindled a fire," and the rest of the examples he cited to prove that the meaning of *alladhi* in His words, "like the likeness of the one who kindled a fire," is the plural. It is not permissible for anyone to transfer a word, which is the most common in the usage of the Arabs, to another meaning, except by a proof that must be accepted.

Then the people of interpretation differed about its interpretation. Several reports were transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas regarding it:

The first of them:

386 – Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from 'Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Allah struck a likeness for the hypocrites, saying: ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire; and when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see﴾, meaning: they see the truth and speak by it, until, when they came out with it from the darkness of disbelief, they extinguished it by their disbelief and their hypocrisy in it, so He left them in the darkness of disbelief, and they do not see guidance nor stand upright on truth.

The second:

387 – Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to us, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ to the end of the verse. This is a likeness Allah struck for the hypocrites, that they used to be mighty through Islam, so the Muslims married them, inherited from them, and shared the spoils with them. When they died, Allah stripped them of that might, as He stripped the owner of the fire of its light. ﴿And left them in darkness﴾, He says: in punishment.

The third:

388 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire; and when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see﴾. He claimed that some people entered Islam at the arrival of the Prophet ﷺ in Medina, then they became hypocrites. Their likeness was that of a man who was in darkness and kindled a fire, which illuminated for him what was around him of filth or harm, so he saw and recognized what to guard against. While he was in that state, his fire went out, and he went on, not knowing what to guard against of harm. Likewise the hypocrite: he was in the darkness of polytheism, then he embraced Islam, so he knew the lawful from the unlawful, and good from evil. While he was in that state, he disbelieved, so he came to know neither the lawful from the unlawful, nor good from evil. As for the light, it is faith in what Muhammad ﷺ brought, and the darkness was their hypocrisy.

And another:

389 – Muhammad ibn Sa'id narrated to me, saying: My father Sa'id ibn Muhammad narrated to me [[In the printed edition: "Muhammad ibn Sa'id" and "Sa'id ibn Muhammad." The latter is correct, from the manuscript and the biographical sources. See the detailed explanation of this chain: 305.]] saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, from his father, from his grandfather, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ up to "so they do not return," that He struck it as a likeness for the hypocrite. As for His words: ﴿Allah took away their light﴾, he said: As for the light, it is their faith, which they speak with. As for the darkness, it is their misguidance and disbelief, which they speak with. They were a people who had been upon guidance, then it was taken from them, and after that they transgressed.

Others said:

390 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to me, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire; and when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see﴾: The hypocrite utters "There is no god but Allah," and it illuminates for him in this world, so he marries Muslims by it, makes war with the Muslims by it, inherits from the Muslims by it, and protects his blood and his property by it. But when death comes, the hypocrite is stripped of it, because it had no root in his heart nor reality in his knowledge.

391 – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah: "Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire; and when it illuminated what was around him": it is "There is no god but Allah." It illuminated for them, so they ate and drank by it, were secure in this world, married women, and protected their blood by it. But when they died, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see.

392 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Tumaylah narrated to me, from 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman [[Abu Tumaylah, with a dotted-less tha' and a fathah on the mim: he is Yahya ibn Wadih al-Ansari al-Marwazi al-Hafiz, one of the teachers of Ahmad, Ishaq, and other imams. He is trustworthy; Ibn Ma'in, Ibn Sa'd, Abu Hatim and others declared him reliable. Abu Hatim erred in attributing to al-Bukhari that he mentioned him among the weak transmitters, which was not so, for al-Bukhari biographed him in al-Kabir 4/2/309 and mentioned no criticism of him, nor did he mention him in al-Du'afa' al-saghir. Al-Dhahabi said in al-Mizan 3:305, when mentioning Abu Hatim's statement: "I have not seen that, nor was it so, for al-Bukhari has used him as a proof." In the printed edition of al-Tabari here it reads "Abu Numaylah" with a nun, which is a printing error. As for "'Ubayd ibn Sulayman": he is al-Bahili al-Kufi, Abu al-Harith. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat, and Ibn Abi Hatim (2/2/408) mentioned that he asked his father about him, and he said: "There is no harm in him."]], from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, regarding His words: "like the likeness of one who kindled a fire; and when it illuminated what was around him," he said: As for the light, it is their faith which they speak with. As for the darknesses, it is their misguidance and disbelief.

Others said:

393 – Muhammad ibn 'Amr al-Bahili narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa ibn Maymun narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Najih narrated to us, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah: "Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire; and when it illuminated what was around him": As for the illumination of the fire, it is their turning toward the believers and guidance; and the going away of their light is their turning toward the disbelievers and misguidance.

394 – Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, from Shibl, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire; and when it illuminated what was around him": As for the illumination of the fire, it is their turning toward the believers and guidance; and the going away of their light is their turning toward the disbelievers and misguidance.

395 – Al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the same.

396 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: He struck the likeness of the people of hypocrisy, saying: "Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire." He said: The light of the fire and its brightness are only what kindled it. When it is extinguished, its light goes away. Likewise is the hypocrite: whenever he speaks a word of sincerity, it shines for him; but when he doubts, he falls into darkness.

397 – Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd narrated to me, regarding His words: "like the likeness of one who kindled a fire" to the end of the verse, he said: This is the description of the hypocrites. They had believed, until faith illuminated in their hearts, just as the fire illuminated for these who kindled it. Then they disbelieved, so Allah took away their light, removing it, just as He took away the light of this fire, and left them in darkness, unable to see. [[Reports 386–397: all these preceding narrations, and those that follow up to His words "so they do not return," numbered 398–404, were cited by Ibn Kathir (1:97–99), al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-manthur (1:32–33), and al-Shawkani in Fath al-Qadir (1:35).]]

The most correct interpretations of the verse are those given by Qatadah and al-Dahhak, and what ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. The reason is that Allah, exalted is His praise, only struck this parable for the hypocrites (al-munafiqun), whose description He gave and whose circumstances He related, from the time He began mentioning them with His words: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ — not for those who openly announce disbelief and openly associate partners with Allah [[In the printed edition: "i.e., not the open announcers", and in the manuscript: "the openly disbelieving", and the context of his expression: "Allah only struck this parable for the hypocrites... not for the open announcers of disbelief".]]. Had the parable been for someone who believed with sound faith and then openly announced disbelief with sound announcement — as the one who interprets Allah's words, exalted is His praise, ﴿The example of those who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around them, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, not seeing﴾ supposes — namely that the light of the fire is a parable for their faith which they had sincerely, and that the loss of their light is a parable for their apostasy and their open announcement of disbelief with sincerity — then there would have been no deception or mockery among those people in their own estimation, nor hypocrisy [[The context: "Had the parable been for those who believed with sound faith... there would not have been among the people..."]]. How could there be deception and hypocrisy from one who has shown you neither word nor deed except what made known to you the state he is in and the resolve of his own soul which he persists upon? Without doubt this is far from hypocrisy and free of deception. Since the people had only two states — the state of apparent faith and the state of manifest disbelief — the name of hypocrisy has fallen away from them, for in their state of sound faith they were believers, and in their state of sound disbelief they were disbelievers. There is no third state in which they were hypocrites.

In Allah's description of them with the attribute of hypocrisy is an indication that the statement is other than the claim of the one who asserted that these people were believers who then apostatized into disbelief and persisted in it — unless the proponent of that view meant that they moved from the faith they had been upon to the disbelief which is hypocrisy. That is a statement which, if it were said, its soundness could only be known through a widely transmitted report, or through some meanings that necessitate its soundness. As for the apparent text of the Book, there is no indication of its soundness, since it allows of interpretations more fitting than it.

Since the matter is as we have described, the most correct interpretation of the verse is this: the illumination of the hypocrites — by what they manifested with their tongues to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of acknowledgment of him, and their saying to him and to the believers, "We believe in Allah, His books, His messengers and the Last Day," so that they were judged by that in the immediate world with the ruling of Muslims — in the preservation of blood and property, security for their offspring from captivity, and in marriage and inheritance — is like the illumination of one who kindles a fire with fire, until, when he benefits from its light and sees what is around him, illuminated by its brightness from the darkness, the fire dies down and is extinguished, so its light departs and the one who was illuminated by it returns to darkness and bewilderment.

That is because the hypocrite continued to be illuminated by the light of the speech which he defended in his life against killing and captivity, while concealing within himself what would have made killing and the seizing of property obligatory for him had he manifested it with his tongue. His own soul imagined to him that he was a mocker and deceiver of Allah, His Messenger and the believers, until his soul tempted him — when he came before his Lord in the Hereafter — that he would be saved from Him by the same means by which he was saved in the world, namely lying and hypocrisy. Do you not hear Allah, exalted is His praise, saying, after describing them, and then informing of their state upon their coming before Him: ﴿On the Day when Allah raises them all up, and they swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think that they are upon something. Unquestionably, they are the liars﴾ [Surah al-Mujadilah: 18], the people supposing that their salvation from the punishment of Allah in the Hereafter would be like that by which they were saved from killing, captivity and the seizure of property in the world: by lying and falsehood; and that their deception would benefit them there as its benefit to them in the world; until they witnessed of the affair of Allah what they were certain of, that they had been, in their suppositions, in delusion and error, mocking themselves and deceiving themselves, when Allah extinguished their light on the Day of Resurrection. They asked the believers to wait so that they might borrow from their light, and it was said to them: "Go back behind you and seek a light," and they were struck with a wall with a gate, its inner side containing mercy and its outer side from before it containing punishment... ﴿Go back behind you and seek light; so a wall with a door was set between them; within it is mercy, and without it is punishment﴾ [Surah al-Hadid: 13–15]. That is the time when Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, not seeing, just as the fire of the one who kindled it went out after illuminating him, so he remained in his darkness, bewildered and wandering.

If someone says to us: you have mentioned that the meaning of Allah's words, exalted is His mention, "The example of those who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around them," is: it died down and was extinguished, and that this is not present in the Qur'an. What is your evidence that this is its meaning?

It is said: We have said that it is among the habits of the Arabs to be concise and brief, when what they have uttered contains sufficient indication of what they omitted and left out, as Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali said:

ʿAsaytu ilayha al-qalba, innī li-amrihā ... samīʿun, famā adrī arushdun ṭilābuhā!
[Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin 1: 71; it will come in the interpretation of Al ʿImran: 113. Al-Tabari's version of the line in both places does not yield a sound meaning; the version in his diwan: ʿaṣānī ilayhā al-qalbu innī li-amrihi... Another version: "daʿānī ilayhā..." and both are sound narrations. The full meaning of the line is in the one that follows it: faqultu li-qalbī: yā laka al-khayru! innamā ... yudallīka lil-mawti al-jadīdi ḥibābuhā. So he consults his heart, but he obeyed it.]

He means by it: "So I do not know whether its pursuit is right guidance or error," so the mention of "or error" was omitted, since what was uttered indicates it.

And as Dhu al-Rummah said describing the wild asses of Himyar:

Falammā labisna al-layla, aw ḥīna naṣṣabat ... lahu min khadhā ādhānihā wa-huwa jānaḥ
[Diwan: 108; it will come in the interpretation of Yunus: 77, and the Surah al-Naba: 10. It describes a herd of wild asses which stood watching the setting of the sun, until when it set they set off rapidly toward the watering place they were aiming for. His words "labisna al-layl" mean the wild asses, when the night covered them while they were watching for the sunset. "Naṣṣabat": raised and held up their ears. "Khadhdhat al-udhn" means the ear drooped from its base, leaning toward the cheeks, and this happens to wild asses in summer from the heat of the sun and thirst. "Naṣṣabat khadhā ādhānihā" means they prepared for a run to the water. "Janaḥ al-layl" means it approached, and from "janaḥa al-ṭā'ir" when it breaks its wings and then approaches like one who falls and seeks refuge in a place. It is a fine description of the approach of darkness from the side of the horizon. Al-Tabari intended that Dhu al-Rummah meant to say: "or when the night approached, they raised their ears toward it, while it was approaching." There is no necessity requiring the omission that he claimed in this line.]

He means: "or when the night approached," among many similar instances, which we disliked to lengthen the book by mentioning. Likewise His words, "The example of those who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around them," since in it and in what follows from His words, "Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, not seeing," there is an indication of what was left out, sufficient without mention, so the speech omitted it seeking brevity.

Likewise, the omission of what was omitted and the abridgment of what was abridged in the report about the parable of the hypocrites after it is like what was abridged in the report about the parable of the one who kindled the fire. For the meaning of the speech is: "Likewise the hypocrites, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, not seeing — after the illumination they were in during the world, by what they manifested with their tongues of acknowledgment of Islam while they concealed other than it — just as the light of this kindler's fire departed, by its extinguishing and dying down, so he remained in a darkness where he could not see."

And the "hā' and mīm" in His words "Allah took away their light" refer back to the "hā' and mīm" in His words "their parable" (mathaluhum).

**The Interpretation of God's Words: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return﴾ (2:18)**

Abu Ja'far said: Since the interpretation of God's words, may He be exalted, "God took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see" is what we have described, namely that it is a report from God, may He be exalted, about what He will do to the hypocrites in the Hereafter, when He tears away their veils, exposes the disgrace of their secrets, and removes the light of their illumination, leaving them in the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, wandering, unable to see in its pitch darkness, then it is clear that His words, may He be exalted, "Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return" belong to what is postponed but whose meaning is preposed. The meaning of the speech is: "Those who bought error in exchange for guidance, their trade did not profit them, and they were not guided. Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return. Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire, and when it lit up what was around him, God took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see," or "like a heavy rain from the sky."

Since that is the meaning of the speech, it is known that His words "deaf, dumb, blind" may be read in the nominative in two ways and in the accusative in two ways.

As for one of the two nominative readings: it is by way of a new sentence (isti'naf), because of the blame it contains. The Arabs do this in praise and blame, using both the accusative and the nominative, even when the subject is definite, as the poet said:

*"May my people never perish, those who are the poison of the enemies and the bane of the slaughtered camels,*
*Who alight at every battlefield, and who are pure at the knots of their waistwraps."*

[[The poem is by al-Khansa' bint Badr ibn Hifan, sister of Tarafa through their mother, whose mother was Warda. Her Diwan: 10. She is lamenting her husband Bishr ibn 'Amr ibn Marthad. It will come in the interpretation of a verse of Surat Ghafir: 3 (24:27 Bulaq). It is also in Sibawayh 1:104, 246, 249, and Khizanat al-Adab 2:301. Her words "May my people never perish" mean: may my people not be destroyed; she is invoking blessing on them. Its verb: ba'ida, ya'badu, ba'dan (of the pattern faraha) means to perish. Al-'Idah is the plural of 'adin, meaning enemy. Al-juzur is the plural of jazur, the camel that is slaughtered. "The bane of the camels" means the cause of their destruction, since they do not spare their wealth out of generosity. The "battlefield" (ma'tarak) is the place of combat where they clash and grind each other down. When the battlefield is crowded, the horsemen dismount and thrust at one another, drawing close until they embrace each other when the fighting grows fierce. Al-azr is the plural of izar, which is what covers the lower half, while the rida' covers the upper half. "The knots of the waistwraps" are where they are tied so they do not fall. By this she alludes to their chastity and purity, that they do not approach indecency and so loosen the knots of their waistwraps.]]

It is narrated as "al-nazilun" and "al-nazilin," and likewise "al-tayyibun" and "al-tayyibin," according to what I have described of praise.

The other nominative reading: it is by way of repeating "those" (ulaika), so the meaning then is: "Those who bought error in exchange for guidance, their trade did not profit them, and they were not guided. Those, deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return."

As for one of the two accusative readings: it is that it be a circumstantial accusative (qat') from what is in "guided" (muhtadin) referring to "those" [[Qat': that is, a circumstantial qualifier (hal). See what has passed: 230, note 4.]], because the reference to them within it is definite, while "deaf" is indefinite.

The other: that it be a circumstantial accusative from "those" (alladhina), because "those" is definite and "deaf" is indefinite [[Qat': that is, a circumstantial qualifier (hal). See what has passed: 230, note 4.]].

The accusative may also be permissible here by way of blame, so that is a third accusative reading.

As for the interpretation based on what we have narrated from Ibn 'Abbas through a chain other than the transmission of 'Ali ibn Abi Talha from him, the nominative is not permissible in it except in one way, which is the new sentence.

As for the accusative, it is permissible in two ways: one, blame; the other, a circumstantial qualifier from the "ha'" and "mim" in "their leaving" (tarakahum), or from their reference in "they do not see."

We have already explained the view that is more correct in the interpretation of this. The reading that is the reading is the nominative, not the accusative [[In the printed edition: "and the reading which is the reading of the nominative..." and that is a plain error.]], because no one disputes the written form of the codices (rusum masahif) of the Muslims, and if it is read in the accusative it becomes a reading that contradicts their written codices.

Abu Ja'far said: This is a report from God, may He be exalted, about the hypocrites: that by their purchasing error in exchange for guidance, they were not guided to guidance and truth. Rather, they are deaf to them, so they do not hear them, due to the dominance of God's abandonment over them; dumb from speaking them, so they do not utter them, and "dumb" (bukm) means the mute, the plural of abkam; blind from perceiving them so that they understand them, because God has sealed their hearts by their hypocrisy, so they are not guided.

Those who are the scholars of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said about this:

398. Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrima, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "deaf, dumb, blind," from good.

399. Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas: "deaf, dumb, blind," he says: they do not hear the guidance, nor see it, nor understand it.

400. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murra, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "dumb" are the mute.

401. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada, regarding his words "deaf, dumb, blind": deaf to the truth so they do not hear it, blind to the truth so they do not see it, dumb about the truth so they do not speak it [[These reports 398–401 are a continuation of what preceded in the interpretation of the beginning of the verse, numbered: 386, 387, 388, 390.]].

* *

**The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿So they will not return﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: His words "so they will not return" are a report from God, may He be exalted, about these hypocrites, whom God described by their purchasing error in exchange for guidance, their deafness to hearing good and truth, their dumbness from speaking them, and their blindness from seeing them [[Its context: "a report from God, may He be exalted... that they will not return."]], that they will not return to giving up their error, nor repent and turn back from their hypocrisy. Thus He despaired the believers of these people ever seeing right guidance, or saying the truth, or hearing one calling to guidance, or being reminded and repenting of their error, just as He despaired of the repentance of the leaders of the disbelievers among the People of the Book and the polytheists and their rabbis, whom He described as those upon whose hearts and hearing He has set a seal, and over whose sight is a veil.

Those who are the people of interpretation said the same as what we have said about the interpretation of this.

Mention of those who said that:

402. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada: "so they will not return," meaning: they will not repent nor be reminded.

403. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murra, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "so they will not return": they will not return to Islam.

It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas a statement whose meaning differs from the meaning of this report, namely what:

404. Ibn Humayd narrated it to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrima, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "so they will not return," meaning: they will not return to guidance nor to any good, so they will not attain salvation while they remain in what they are upon [[These reports 402–404 are a continuation of what preceded in the interpretation of the beginning of the verse, numbered: 401, 400, 398.]].

This interpretation contradicts the apparent wording of the recitation. That is because God, may He be exalted, reported about the people that they will not return, from their purchasing of error in exchange for guidance, to seeking guidance and seeing the truth, without Him restricting that condition of theirs to a particular time over another, or to one state over another [[In the printed edition: "to a time other than a time," which is an error.]]. But this report we have mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas indicates that this attribute of theirs is restricted to a time [[In the printed edition: "indicates that..."]], namely while they remained upon their situation, and that for them there is a way to turn back from it. That, in interpretation, is a false claim [[In the manuscript: "a claim of an observer," and its correct form is "a claim of falsehood" in apposition.]], with no evidence for it from the apparent meaning or from a report by which a proof is established so that it can be accepted.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 19 (part 1 of 4):

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is His remembrance: ﴿Or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Al-sayyib is al-fay'il from your saying, ṣāba al-maṭaru yaṣūbu ṣawban, when it descends and comes down, as the poet said:

"I am not of mankind, but an angel (malak) who descended from the air of the sky, descending (yaṣūbu)."

[[This verse is attributed to ʿAlqama ibn ʿAbada, but it is not his, nor is it in his Diwan. It will come in the interpretation of the verse in Surat al-Baqara, 30 (1:155 Bulaq), in a different narration. It is among the verses of Sibawayh (1:379) and Sharh Shawahid al-Shafiya (p. 287), and Lisan (ʾlk), and others, unattributed. It is said that it belongs to a man of ʿAbd al-Qays from the pre-Islamic period who praises al-Nuʿman. Al-Sirafi related that it belongs to Abu Wajza al-Saʿdi, praising ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr. In the manuscript it appears as "wa-lakin malakan". Before the verse is: "You are exalted above being ascribed to mankind in quality, and among mankind is one who ascribes you (such), and he is a liar."]]

And as ʿAlqama ibn ʿAbada said:

"As if they were struck by a cloud over them, whose thunderbolts for their birds are a crawling."

[[Diwan: the first verse: 34, and the second before it: 19; Sharh al-Mufaddaliyat: 784, 769. He praises with it al-Harith ibn Jabala ibn Abi Shamir al-Ghassani, who had taken captive his brother Shaʾs, so he traveled to him seeking his release. In this verse he mentions the day of ʿAyn Abagh, in which al-Harith al-Ghassani raided al-Mundhir ibn al-Mundhir ibn Ma' al-Sama', and they met at ʿAyn Abagh, and the army of al-Mundhir was defeated, and al-Mundhir was killed that day. His saying "as if they" refers to the army of al-Mundhir. Ṣāba al-maṭar: it descended and poured. He had described the defeated army in the verse before it, among the fallen who were struck down, and among the slain who had perished. So he likened them to birds whom heavy rain struck and thunderbolts seized, so they were frightened and could not rise to fly, so they crawl seeking deliverance. The pronoun in his saying "li-ṭayrihinna" refers to the thunderbolts, i.e., the birds of the thunderbolts, and he meant the birds that the thunderbolts frightened and the rain beat down.]]

"So do not equate between me and the ignorant one (mughammar), may you be watered by the water-skins of the clouds when they pour."

[[This verse is at the beginning of the poem. He addresses his beloved. In the printed edition it is "muʿammar," which is an error. Al-mughammar and al-ghamr: the one ignorant of affairs who has not tested them, as if ignorance had covered him and overwhelmed him. The second half is a supplication for her with fertility and bounty. Al-rawaya is the plural of rawiya: the animal that carries water-skins. Al-muzn: the white clouds, he likened them to the water-skins carrying water. The narration in his Diwan and al-Mufaddaliyat is "saqatka."]]

Meaning: when it descends. Originally it is "ṣayḥwib," but since the waw was preceded by a sukun yaʾ, both were turned into a shadda-ed yaʾ, as it is said: sayyid, from sāda yasūdu, and jayyid, from jāda yajūdu. Likewise the Arabs do with the waw when it is vowelled and preceded by a sukun yaʾ, turning both into a shadda-ed yaʾ.

And in accordance with what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-taʾwil) said.

Mention of those who said that:

405 - Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Ahmasi narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd narrated to us, saying: Harun ibn 'Antara narrated to us, from his father [[The chain 405: Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Samura al-Ahmasi, shaykh of al-Tabari: trustworthy, narrated from him al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Maja and others. He has an entry in al-Tahdhib. Ibn Abi Hatim included him (3/2/190). Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd: he is al-Tanafisi al-Ahdab, a well-known trustworthy narrator, narrated from him Ahmad, Ishaq, Ibn Ma'in and others. Harun ibn 'Antara ibn 'Abd al-Rahman: trustworthy, deemed trustworthy by Ahmad, Ibn Sa'd and others. al-Bukhari included him in al-Kabir (4/2/221) without mentioning any criticism, and Ibn Sa'd (6:243). His father: he is 'Antara ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, whose kunya is "Abu Wakic," and he is a Successor (tabi'i). Al-Bukhari said in al-Kabir (4/1/84): "He saw 'Ali; his son Harun narrated from him, and Abu Sinan." Ibn Sa'd included him in al-Tabaqat (6:163), and Ibn Abi Hatim (3/2/35), and mentioned that he narrated from 'Uthman, 'Ali, and Ibn 'Abbas, and that Abu Zur'a was asked about him and said: "Kufan, trustworthy."]], from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying "or like a rain-cloud from the sky," he said: the rain.

406 - 'Abbas ibn Muhammad narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: 'Ata' said to me: al-sayyib is the rain.

407 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: al-sayyib is the rain.

408 - Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murra from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): al-sayyib is the rain.

409 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle al-Husayn narrated to me, from his father, from his grandfather, from Ibn 'Abbas, the like of it.

410 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada: "or like a sayyib," he says: the rain.

411 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, the like of it.

412 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr al-Bahili and 'Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to me, both saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa ibn Maymun narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: al-sayyib is al-rabi' [[In the printed edition: "al-sayyib: the rain." Al-rabi': the rain at the beginning of spring.]].

413 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: al-sayyib is the rain.

414 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Ja'far, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: al-sayyib is the rain.

415 - It was related to me from al-Minjab, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umara narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: al-sayyib is the rain.

417 - Sawwar ibn 'Abd Allah al-'Anbari narrated to us, saying: Sufyan said: al-sayyib is that in which there is rain.

418 - 'Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj narrated to us, from 'Ata', regarding His saying "or like a rain-cloud from the sky," he said: the rain [[Reports 405–418: Ibn Kathir (1:99) and al-Durr al-Manthur (1:33) related them in abridged form.]].

Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation of that: the likeness of the hypocrites' seeking light by the light of their profession of Islam, while concealing disbelief, is like the likeness of one who kindles a fire by the light of its fire, according to what His description, exalted is His praise, has described; or like a dark rain whose downpour pours down from the sky [[al-wadq: the rain that comes out through gaps in the clouds, loosely falling.]], carried by a dark cloud on a dark night. And that is the darknesses which Allah, exalted is His praise, informed is in it.

If someone says to us: Tell us about these two likenesses: are they two likenesses for the hypocrites, or one of them? If they are two likenesses for the hypocrites, then how is it said "or like a sayyib," when "or" comes in speech to denote doubt, and it was not said "wa-kasayyib" with the waw which joins the second likeness to the first? Or if the likeness of the people is one of them, then what is the reason for mentioning the other with "or"? And you know that "or," when it occurs in speech, enters it only in the manner of doubt by the informant regarding what he informs of, like the saying of the speaker: "Your brother or your father met me," while only one of them met him, but he did not know which of the two met him, while knowing that one of them had met him. And it is impermissible for Allah, exalted is His praise, that doubt be attributed to Him regarding anything, or that knowledge of anything be absent from Him, regarding what He informed of or left aside informing of.

It is said to him: The matter in that is contrary to what you have gone to. And "or" — although in some speech it comes to mean doubt — it may come indicating the same as what the waw indicates, either by preceding speech before it, or by what comes after it, like the saying of Tawba ibn al-Humayyir:

"Layla has claimed that I am wicked, for myself is its piety, or upon it is its wickedness."

[[From a qasida of his. Amali al-Qali 1:88, 131; Amali al-Sharif al-Murtada 3:146; Amali al-Shajari 2:317; al-Adhdad of Ibn al-Anbari: 243; and others are many.]]

And it is known that this is from Tawba not in the manner of doubt regarding what he said, but because "or" in this place indicated the same as what the "waw" would indicate had it been in its place, so he placed it in its place. And likewise the saying of Jarir:

"He attained the caliphate, or it was for him by decree, just as Moses came to his Lord by decree."

[[His Diwan: 275; it will come in his interpretation of the verse of al-Baqara: 74 (1:287 Bulaq), and the verse of Ta-Ha: 40 (16:128 Bulaq); Amali al-Shajari 1:317. He says it about the Commander of the Faithful ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz. Its narration is "idh kanat," and in the printed edition: "jaʾa al-khilafa," which is a feeble narration.]]

And as the other said:

"Had weeping been able to return anything, I would have wept over Bujayr or ʿFaqaq,"

[[The two verses are by Mutammim ibn Nuwayra al-Yarbuʿi. Lisan (ʿfq), Amali al-Shajari 2:318, Amali al-Murtada 3:147, al-Adhdad of Ibn al-Anbari: 243. In the printed and manuscript editions it is "ʿala Jubayr," which is pure error, and in the printed: "ʿInaq," which is also an error. This poetry Mutammim ibn Nuwayra says in lamenting Bujayr ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Harith al-Yarbuʿi, who is Bujayr ibn Abi Mulayl, and his brother ʿFaqaq ibn Abi Mulayl. The first of them was killed on the day of Qushawa, killed by Luqaym ibn Aws (al-Naqa'id: 20), and ʿFaqaq was killed on the day of al-ʿAzala, killed by al-Du'a', and it was said killed by al-Furays ibn Muslima (al-Naqa'id: 583).]]

"Over the two men when they both passed away, for their affair, with sorrow and longing."

[[It is narrated as "with sorrow and burning" and "with grief and longing." His saying "they passed for their affair" means they perished and met what every living thing meets.]]

So by his saying "over the two men when they both passed away," it is shown that his weeping which he wanted to weep was not intended to be directed at one of them to the exclusion of the other, but he wanted to weep for both of them together. Likewise it is with the saying of Allah, exalted is His praise: "or like a rain-cloud from the sky." Since it is known that "or" in this indicates the same as what the "waw" would indicate had it been in its place, it is equal whether "or" or "waw" is uttered in it. And likewise the reason for omitting "the likeness" from His saying "or like a sayyib": since His saying "like the one who kindled a fire" indicates that its meaning is: like a sayyib, the "likeness" was omitted, and he sufficed — by the indication of what preceded in speech in His saying "like the one who kindled a fire" that its meaning is: or like a sayyib — from repeating mention of the likeness, seeking brevity and conciseness.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is His praise: ﴿Therein are darknesses, thunder and lightning. They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts, for fear of death. And Allah encompasses the disbelievers (19). The lightning nearly snatches away their sight; whenever it lights for them they walk in it, and when it darkens over them they stand still﴾

Abu Ja'far said: As for the darknesses, it is a plural whose singular is ẓulma.

As for the thunder (al-raʿd), the people of knowledge differed regarding it:

Some of them said: It is an angel who drives the clouds.

Mention of those who said that:

419 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from al-Hakam, from Mujahid, he said: The thunder is an angel who drives the clouds with its voice.

420 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi 'Adi narrated to us, from Shu'ba, from al-Hakam, from Mujahid, the like of it.

421 - Yahya ibn Talha al-Yarbu'i narrated to me, saying: Fudayl ibn 'Iyad narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, the like of it [[Chain 421: Yahya ibn Talha al-Yarbu'i: al-Tirmidhi and others narrated from him, and Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy. al-Nasa'i weakened him, saying in al-Du'afa' (32): "He is nothing."]].

422 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Salim informed us, from Abu Salih, he said: The thunder is an angel among the angels who glorifies.

[[Chain 422: Isma'il ibn Salim al-Asadi: trustworthy, narrated from him al-Thawri and Abu 'Awana. Ibn Sa'd (7/2/67) said: "He was trustworthy and firm." Abu Salih is al-Sammán.]].

423 - Nasr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Azdi narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Ya'la narrated to us, from Abu al-Khattab al-Basri, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, he said: The thunder is an angel entrusted with the clouds who drives them, as the camel-driver drives the camels, glorifying. Whenever one cloud departs from another cloud, he shouts at it, and when his anger intensifies, fire flies from his mouth, and that is the thunderbolts that you have seen [[Chain 423: Nasr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Bakkar al-Tajji, shaykh of al-Tabari: trustworthy, narrated from him al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Maja and others; he is in al-Tahdhib, and he said "it is said: al-Azdi," so he is thus attributed here; likewise al-Tabari narrated from him in the History (2:128) and attributed him to "al-Azdi." In the printed edition it appears as "al-Awdi" with a waw instead of a zayn, which is a misreading. Muhammad ibn Ya'la: he is al-Sulami al-Kufi, and his laqab is "Zunbur," and he is weak; al-Bukhari said "they speak about him." Abu al-Khattab al-Basri: I do not know who he is; but al-Dulabi mentioned in al-Kuna (1:167) "Abu al-Khattab 'Abd Allah," then said: "Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ammar narrated from al-Mu'afa ibn 'Imran from 'Abd Allah Abu al-Khattab from Shahr ibn Hawshab," and then he mentioned a hadith. He did not clarify more than that, and I have not found his biography.]].

424 - It was related to me from al-Minjab ibn al-Harith, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umara narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: The thunder is an angel among the angels whose name is "al-Ra'd," and it is his voice that you hear.

425 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Malik ibn Husayn narrated to us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: The thunder is an angel who drives the clouds with glorification and magnification [[Chain 425: 'Abd al-Malik ibn Husayn: he is Abu Malik al-Nakha'i al-Wasiti, known by his kunya and biographed under it in al-Tahdhib (12:219), and Ibn Abi Hatim biographed him under his name (2/2/347). He is weak, nothing.]].
