Ibn Juraj said: "your witnesses" to it when you have brought it—that it is its like, like the Qur'an [[Narrations 496–500 are partly in Ibn Kathir 1:108, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:35, and al-Shawkani 1:40; in the manuscript in some places "unās" appears instead of "nās," and both are the same.]].

That is Allah's address to whoever among the disbelievers doubts what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. His saying "fa-ud'ū," means: seek help and call for aid [[In the printed edition: "wa-ista'īnū," which are close in meaning; the first is better, and it is so in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:19.]], as the poet said:

When our horsemen and their men met, they called out: "O Ka'b!" and we claimed kinship with 'Amir [[The verse is by al-Ra'i al-Numayri, cited in Lisan al-'Arab (ʿazā). Ista'zā: to claim kinship, and to call in battle as one says "O so-and-so," or "O emigrants," or "O helpers"; the noun is al-'azā'/al-'azwa, the claim of one seeking aid.]]

By his saying "they called out: O Ka'b!" he means they sought help from Ka'b and called upon them for aid [[In the printed edition: "wa-ista'ānū," as in its counterpart mentioned before.]].

As for "al-shuhada'," it is the plural of shahid, as al-shurakā' is the plural of shārik and al-khuṭabā' the plural of khaṭīb. A shahid is named as one who bears witness to a thing for another by what establishes his claim. It may also be applied to one who is present at a thing, as one says: so-and-so is the companion (jalīs) of so-and-so, meaning his companion and drinking-partner (nadīm), meaning his fellow-drinker (munādim); and likewise one says: "his shahid," meaning his one who is present (mushāhid).

Since "al-shuhada'" can be the plural of "shahid," which is inflected for the two meanings I have described, the most preferable of its two senses for the interpretation of the verse is what Ibn 'Abbas said, namely that it means: seek help, in order that you produce a surah like it, from your helpers and witnesses who are present with you and assist you in your denial of Allah and His Messenger and back you in your disbelief and hypocrisy—if you are right in your rejection that what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought is fabrication and invention—so that you may test yourselves and others: can you produce a surah like it, and could Muhammad then produce all of it by his own invention?

As for what Mujahid and Ibn Juraj said in interpreting this, there is no basis for it. For the people in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were of three kinds: people of sound faith, people of sound disbelief, and hypocrites in between. The people of faith believed in Allah and His Messenger, so it would have been impossible for the disbelievers to claim that they had witnesses—for the truth of what they were producing, were they to produce an invented message, and then claim that it had a counterpart to the Qur'an—from among the believers [[His saying "from among the believers" is connected to his earlier statement "that they had witnesses..." meaning witnesses from among the believers. Then he separates, because his saying "for the truth of what they were producing..." is also connected to "witnesses."]]. As for the people of hypocrisy and disbelief, there is no doubt that if they were called to establish falsehood and to nullify truth, they would hasten to it along with their disbelief and misguidance [[In the printed edition: "la-sāra'ū ilayhi," and tatāra'a to something means to hasten toward it, said of rushing toward evil or what is not fitting. The reading "tatāra'ū" in the manuscript is sound in Arabic derivation, though the dictionaries do not record it; it is equivalent to tasarra' and tasāra'a.]]—so from which of the two groups would their witnesses come, were they to claim that they had produced a surah like the Qur'an [[In the printed edition: "fa-min ayy al-firaq...," and al-Tabari's speech is interrogative and disapproving. For it is impossible for believers to testify to this falsehood while the disbelievers and hypocrites hasten to bear witness to falsehood to nullify truth; so it was impossible that the meaning of "al-shuhada'" here be those who bear witness for them that what they brought is a counterpart to what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought from Allah the Exalted. It became necessary that the meaning of "al-shuhada'" be those who back them and assist them, as the following verse shows.]]?

Rather, it is as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if some of them were aids to others" (17:88). Thus in this verse He informed that the like of the Qur'an cannot be produced by jinn and humans, even if they back and assist one another in producing it. And He challenged them, in a sense of rebuke, in Surat al-Baqara, saying: "And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it, and call upon your witnesses other than Allah, if you are truthful." He means by that: if you are in doubt about the truthfulness of Muhammad in what he brought you from Me, that it is from Me, then produce a surah like it, and let some of you help one another in that, if you are truthful in your claim—so that you may know that when you are unable to do that, no one can produce it, neither Muhammad (ﷺ) nor any human, and that it becomes sound for you that it is My revelation and My inspiration to My servant.

The Interpretation of His words, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His remembrance be exalted, "But if you do not," He means: if you do not bring a surah like it, then you and your partners and helpers have banded together in that [[In the printed edition: "And you have banded together," but what is in the manuscript is better, and the explanation of this will come shortly.]], and so it becomes clear to you, through your testing and trial, that you are unable, and that all of My creation is unable, to do so, and you know that it is from Me, and then you persist in denying it.

And His words, "and you will never do it," mean: you will never bring a surah like it, ever.

501- As Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah: "But if you do not, and you will never do it," meaning: you are not able to do that, and you cannot bear it [[Report 501: Al-Suyuti mentions it at 1:35 in similar wording and attributes it to 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir. A printing error reads "Ibn Juraij" in it.]].

502- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "But if you do not, and you will never do it," then the truth has become clear to you [[Reports 501 and 502: in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:35, and al-Shawkani 1:40. The wording of al-Tabari in interpreting this verse and the one after it, and what he cites from the last report, indicates that he holds the answer of the condition to be omitted, because it is known and the context indicates it. The answer of the condition is "then the truth has become clear to you, and you have persisted in denying it and My messenger," then he continued in a new sentence: "So beware of burning in the Fire by your denial of My messenger, that he came to you with My revelation and My sending down, after it has become clear to you that it is My Book and from Me."]].

I have not found anyone who noticed this except al-Zamakhshari, for he said in his interpretation of this verse in his book "al-Kashshaf," the following text: "If you say: what is the meaning of making the condition for avoiding the Fire the absence of their bringing a surah like it? I say: when they do not bring it, and their inability to oppose it becomes clear, the truth of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) becomes sound to them. And when his truthfulness becomes sound to them, then they persist in obstinacy and do not submit or follow, they deserve punishment by the Fire. So it was said to them: if you realize your inability, then abandon obstinacy. So "fear the Fire" is placed in its position, because avoiding the Fire is attached to and accompanies abandoning obstinacy, in that it is one of its results. For whoever avoids the Fire abandons obstinacy. Its parallel is that a king says to his attendants: 'If you desire honor with me, then beware of my wrath.' He means: obey me and follow my command, and do what is the result of being wary of wrath. This is from the kind of metonymy (kinayah), which is a branch of the branches of eloquence. Its benefit is brevity, which is the adornment of the Qur'an, and the magnification of the matter of obstinacy, by putting avoidance of the Fire in its place and displaying it in its form, accompanied by magnifying the description of the Fire and making its matter appalling."

Thus al-Tabari's intention becomes clear by this, and that he wished to show that avoiding the Fire is not included in the condition, nor is it part of its answer, so as to exclude that the meaning of the speech is restricting their avoidance of the Fire to their inability to bring its like. The explanation that follows clearly indicates this meaning. This is from the subtle insight of al-Tabari, may God have mercy on him, and forgive al-Zamakhshari.

* *

The Interpretation of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿So fear the Fire, whose fuel is people and stones﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His remembrance be exalted, "fear the Fire," He says: beware of burning in the Fire by your denial of My messenger in what he brought you from Me, that it is from My revelation and My sending down, after you have clarified that it is My Book and from Me, and the proof has been established against you that it is My speech and My revelation, by your inability and the inability of all My creation to bring its like.

Then He, may His remembrance be exalted, described the Fire whose burning He warned them of, and informed them that people are its fuel, and that stones are its fuel, and He said: "whose fuel is people and stones." By His words "its fuel" He means its firewood. The Arabs make it a verbal noun, though it is a noun, when the waw is vocalized with a fatha, in the sense of firewood.

When the waw of "al-wuqud" is vocalized with a damma, it is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: the fire blazed (waqadat al-nar), so it is blazing (taqid) waqudan and qidatan and waqadanan and waqdan, meaning that it has flared up.

If someone asks: how were stones singled out and paired with people, so that they became the firewood of the Fire of Hell? It is said: they are stones of sulfur, and they are the most intense of stones in heat when they are heated, as has reached us.

503- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from Mis'ar, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Maysarah al-Zarrad, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words, "whose fuel is people and stones," he said: they are stones of sulfur, which God created on the day He created the heavens and the earth, in the lowest heaven, preparing them for the disbelievers.

504- Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, he said: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ibn 'Uyaynah informed us, from Mis'ar, from 'Abd al-Malik al-Zarrad, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words, "whose fuel is people and stones," he said: stones of sulfur, which God made as He willed [[Reports 503 and 504: Mis'ar, with a kasra on the mim, a sukun on the sin and a fatha on the 'ayn, is Ibn Kidam, with a kasra on the kaf and a light dal; he is a well-known trustworthy narrator, one of the leading figures. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Maysarah al-Hilali al-Kufi al-Zarrad, named after the trade of making armor: trustworthy, a prolific narrator, among the junior Successors. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit al-Jumahi al-Makki: a trustworthy Successor. 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi: one of the senior Successors who lived through the Jahiliyyah and Islam, who was Muslim during the lifetime of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) but did not see him.

Al-Tabari narrated this report through these two chains and through the chain that follows: 507. In the first and third, 'Abd al-Malik ibn Maysarah narrates it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit from 'Amr ibn Maymun, while in the second, 504, it is "'Abd al-Malik al-Zarrad from 'Amr ibn Maymun" directly, omitting "'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit." Had this chain stood alone, it would be taken as continuous, given the possibility of contemporaneity, for 'Abd al-Malik al-Zarrad narrates from Ibn 'Umar, who died in 74 AH, and 'Amr ibn Maymun died in 74 or 75 AH. But these two chains, 503 and 504, show that he narrated it only from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit from 'Amr ibn Maymun.

The report was also transmitted by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:261, through the route of Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd from Mis'ar from 'Abd al-Malik al-Zarrad from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit from 'Amr ibn Maymun from Ibn Mas'ud. This is a third route that supports the two routes which contain the addition of 'Abd al-Rahman in the chain. Al-Hakim said: "This is a sound hadith according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), though they did not record it." Al-Dhahabi agreed with him. Ibn Kathir mentioned it at 1:110-111 from the narration of al-Tabari, attributed it to Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, and quoted their authentication of it without objection. Al-Suyuti mentioned it at 1:36 and added its attribution to: 'Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, al-Firyabi, Hannad ibn al-Sari in the Kitab al-Zuhd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman.]].

505- Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, he said: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, he said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Fear the Fire whose fuel is people and stones." As for the stones, they are stones in the Fire of black sulfur, by which they are tormented along with the Fire [[Report 505: Ibn Kathir mentions it at 1:111 without attribution, and al-Suyuti at 1:36, attributing it to Ibn Jarir alone.]].

506- Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij regarding His words, "whose fuel is people and stones," he said: stones of black sulfur in the Fire. He said: 'Amr ibn Dinar said to me: stones harder than these and greater [[Report 506: in Ibn Kathir 1:111 without attribution.]].

507- Sufyan ibn Waki' narrated to us, he said: my father narrated to us, from Mis'ar, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Maysarah, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, he said: stones of sulfur which God created with Him however He willed and as He willed [[Report 507: its detailed transmission was given above with 503 and 504.]].

* *

The Interpretation of His words: ﴿It has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ (24)

We have already shown earlier in this book that "al-kafir" in the speech of the Arabs is one who covers something with a covering, and that God, may His praise be exalted, named the kafir a kafir only because he denies His blessings that are with him, and covers His favors bestowed upon him.

So the meaning of His words, then: "It has been prepared for the disbelievers," means: the Fire has been prepared for those who deny that God, their Lord, is the One who alone created them and those before them, who made the earth a bed for them and the sky a structure, and sent down water from the sky and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for them, while they associate with Him others in worship, taking rivals and gods [[His saying "the polytheists" is a description of what was said just before: "the deniers."]], and He is the One who alone brings them into being, and the One who alone possesses their sustenance and provisions [[In the manuscript: "things," which is an error.]].

508- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, mawla of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id, from Ibn 'Abbas: "It has been prepared for the disbelievers," meaning: for whoever is upon the like of what you are upon of disbelief [[Report 508: in Ibn Kathir 1:111, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:36, and al-Shawkani 1:41.]].

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan) on Surah 2, verse 25 (part 1 of 2)**

**On the interpretation (ta'wil, meaning the explanation of the text) of His words: ﴿And give good news to those who believe and do righteous deeds, that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: As for His words, Exalted is He, "And give good news," He means: inform them. Bishara (good news) is originally information about something that gladdens the one informed, when the one informing is the first to bring it, apart from any other informant.

This is a command from God, Exalted is He, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to convey His good news to His creatures who believed in him, in Muhammad (ﷺ), and in what he brought from his Lord, and who confirmed that belief of theirs and their acknowledgment through their righteous deeds. So He said to him: "O Muhammad, give good news to the one who confirms that you are My messenger, and that what you have brought of guidance and light is from Me, and who makes his confirmation true by performing the righteous deeds that I have enjoined and made obligatory upon him in My Book through your tongue, that for him are gardens beneath which rivers flow", specifically, and not for the one who denied you, rejected what you brought of guidance from Me, and opposed you,[[In the printed edition: "what I brought of guidance."]] and not for the one who showed his confirmation of you,[[In the manuscript: "not for one who showed..." without the waw, which is close in meaning.]] and acknowledged with his tongue that what you brought is from Me, but denied it in his belief and did not realise it in action. As for those, there is the Fire whose fuel is men and stones, prepared by Me. Al-jannat (the gardens) is the plural of jannah, and jannah is an orchard.

God, mighty is His remembrance, by mentioning the Garden only intends what is in the Garden of its trees, its fruits, and its plantings, and not its ground. For this reason He, mighty is His remembrance, said: "beneath which rivers flow."[[In the printed edition: "So for this He said..." The manuscript reading is better.]] This is because it is known that He, mighty is His praise, intends only to inform about the water of its rivers, that it flows beneath its trees, plantings and fruits, and not that it flows beneath its ground. For if the water were flowing beneath the earth, there would be no benefit in it for the springs above it, except by uncovering the barrier between them and it. Moreover, what the rivers of Paradise are described by is that they flow without trenches.

509. As Abu Kurayb related to us, who said: al-Ash'ari related to us, from Sufyan, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Abu 'Ubayda, from Masruq, who said: The palm trees of Paradise are arranged in tiers from their base to their branches, and their fruit is like large jars; whenever a fruit is picked, another grows in its place; and its water flows without a trench.[[The report 509: in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:38. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir 1:113: "It has come in a hadith that its rivers flow without a trench," without specifying. See what follows, no. 517.]]

510. Mujahid [ibn Musa][[The isnad 510: The addition in brackets is from the manuscript. He is Mujahid ibn Musa ibn Farrukh al-Khawarizmi, Abu 'Ali al-Khatli (with a dammah then a fathah), whom Ibn Ma'in, al-Nasa'i and others declared trustworthy. He is covered in al-Tahdhib; al-Bukhari included him in al-Kabir 4/1/413 and al-Saghir 245; al-Khatib in Tarikh Baghdad 13:265–266; and Ibn al-Athir in al-Lubab 1:345. This Mujahid died in Ramadan in the year 244. His teacher Yazid is Yazid ibn Harun.]] said: Yazid related to us, who said: Mis'ar ibn Kidam informed us, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Abu 'Ubayda, with something similar.

511. Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, who said: Ibn Mahdi related to us, who said: Sufyan related to us, who said: I heard 'Amr ibn Murrah narrate, from Abu 'Ubayda, — and he mentioned something like it — he said: I said to Abu 'Ubayda: From whom did you hear this? He became angry and said: Masruq.

Since the matter is as such, that its rivers flow without trenches, there is no doubt that what is intended by "the gardens" is the trees of the gardens, their plantings and their fruits, and not their ground, since its rivers flow above its ground and beneath its plantings and trees, as Masruq mentioned. And that is more fitting to the description of Paradise than that its rivers should flow beneath its ground.

God, mighty is His praise, encouraged His servants to belief through this verse, and urged them to worship Him by informing them of what He has prepared for those who obey Him and believe in Him with Him, just as in the preceding verse He warned them of what He has prepared, of His punishment, for those who disbelieve in Him, who set up gods and equals with Him, for associating another with Him and exposing themselves to His punishment by committing disobedience and abandoning obedience to Him.[[In the manuscript: "and the separation from His punishment," which has no meaning.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His words, mighty is His praise: ﴿Whenever they are provided with fruit therefrom as provision, they say: This is what we were provided with before, and they are given it in resemblance﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, He, exalted is His remembrance, "whenever they are provided with fruit therefrom", He means: from the Gardens. The pronoun refers to the Gardens, but what is meant is their trees. So it is as if He said: Whenever they are provided, from the trees of the orchards that God prepared for those who believed and did righteous deeds in His Gardens, with fruit from its fruits as provision, they say: This is what we were provided with before.

Then the people of interpretation differed concerning the interpretation of His words: "This is what we were provided with before."

Some of them said: The meaning of that is: This is what we were provided with before this, in the world.

Those who said that:

512. Musa ibn Harun related to me, who said: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to us, who said: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas; and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), they said: "This is what we were provided with before," he said: They were brought the fruit in Paradise, and when they looked at it [[In al-Durr al-Manthur: "fa-yanzuruna" ("and they look"), and in al-Shawkani: "fa-nazaru," and so it is in the manuscript.]] they said: This is what we were provided with before, in the world.

513. Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, who said: Yazid ibn Zurai' related to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada: "They say: This is what we were provided with before," that is, in the world.

514. Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, who said: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa ibn Maymun, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "They say: This is what we were provided with before," they say: How much it resembles it!

515. al-Qasim related to us, who said: al-Husayn related to us, who said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the like of it.

516. Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to me, who said: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said: "They say: This is what we were provided with before," in the world; and he said: "and they are given it in resemblance," they recognise it.[[The reports 512–516: in Ibn Kathir 1:113–114, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:38, and al-Shawkani 1:42.]]

Abu Ja'far said: Others said: Rather, the interpretation of that is: This is what we were provided with of the fruits of Paradise before this, because of the strong resemblance of some of it to other parts in colour and taste. And the reason of those who held this view is that the fruits of Paradise, whenever something is picked from them, another like it grows in its place.

517. As Ibn Bashshar related to us, who said: Ibn Mahdi related to us, who said: Sufyan related to us, who said: I heard 'Amr ibn Murrah narrate, from Abu 'Ubayda, who said: The palm trees of Paradise are arranged in tiers from their base to their branches, and their fruit is like large jars; whenever a fruit is picked from them, another grows in its place.[[See the previous reports 509–511. In the manuscript: "amthal al-qilal" ("like large jars"), as was mentioned just above.]]

They said: They were only confused with one another in the sight of the people of Paradise, because the one that grew back is similar to the one that was picked and eaten in all its meanings. They said: For this reason God, mighty is His praise, said: "and they are given it in resemblance," because the whole of it is confused in all its meanings.

Some of them said: Rather, they said: "This is what we were provided with before," because it resembles what came before it in colour, even if it differs from it in taste.

Those who said that:

518. al-Qasim ibn al-Husayn related to us, who said: al-Husayn ibn Dawud related to us, who said: A shaykh from al-Massisa related to us, from al-Awza'i, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, who said: One of them is brought a dish, and he eats from it; then another is brought to him, and he says: This is what was brought to us before. The king says: Eat, for the colour is one and the taste is different.[[Report 518: in Ibn Kathir 1:114, and al-Durr al-Manthur 1:38.]]

This interpretation is the view of those who interpreted the verse. However, the apparent recitation repels its soundness. What indicates its soundness and confirms it is the apparent meaning of the verse and the view of those who said that the meaning of that is: This is what we were provided with before, in the world. For God, mighty is His praise, said: "Whenever they are provided with fruit therefrom as provision," so He informed, mighty is His praise, that among the speech of the people of Paradise, whenever they are provided with the fruit of Paradise as provision, they say: This is what we were provided with before. He did not specify that this speech of theirs is about some of it and not others. Since He, mighty is His remembrance, has informed about them that this is their speech about everything they were provided with of its fruit, there is no doubt that this is their speech concerning the first provision they were given of its fruits, which they were brought after entering Paradise and settling in it, and for which no fruit had preceded it among them. Since there is no doubt that this is their speech concerning the beginning, as it is their speech concerning the middle and what follows it,[[In the printed edition: "in its middle."]] it is known that it is impossible for it to be their speech about the first provision they were given of the fruits of Paradise: "This is what we were provided with before this, of the fruits of Paradise!" How could they say of the first provision they were given of its fruits, when nothing else had preceded it among them: "This is what we were provided with before"? Unless a person of misguidance and error attributes to them the speech of falsehood from which God has purified them,[[In the printed edition, instead of "dhu ghayya" it reads "dhu ghurra," and in the manuscript "dhu 'atah." Al-'Atah means deficiency of intellect or madness. The best of these is what I have recorded from the book Hadi al-Arwah by Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya 1:268, where he quoted al-Tabari's text.]] or someone objects that it is their speech about the first provision they were given of its fruits, and thus rejects the soundness that God made sound by His words: "Whenever they are provided with fruit therefrom as provision," without any clear indication that it refers to one state rather than another.

From what we have explained, it has become clear that the meaning of the verse is: Whenever those who believed and did righteous deeds are provided, in Paradise, with fruit from the fruits of Paradise as provision, they say: This is what we were provided with before this, in the world.[[This detailed explanation that al-Tabari gave is from excellent reflection on the meanings of speech.]]

If someone asks us and says: How did the people say, "This is what we were provided with before," when what they were provided with before has been lost through their eating it? And how could the people of Paradise say a thing that has no reality?

It is said: The matter is not as you suppose. Rather, its meaning is: This is of the kind that we were provided with before this, of fruits and provision. Like a man who says to another: So-and-so has prepared for you such and such food, of various kinds of cooking, grilled meat and sweets. The one addressed says: This is my food in my house. By this he means that the kind of food his companion told him he had prepared for him is his food, not that the very items his companion informed him he had prepared for him are his food. Indeed, it is not permissible for a listener who hears him say this to imagine that he meant or intended that, because that contradicts the usual way speech is uttered. The speech of every speaker is directed toward what is familiar among people in its usage, and not toward its unfamiliar meanings. Likewise is the case with His words, "They say: This is what we were provided with before," since what they had been provided with before has passed away and been lost. It is known that they meant by it: This is of the kind that we were provided with before, and of its genus in attributes and colours[[In the printed edition: "in names and colours," which is an error.]] — as we have explained in what has preceded in this book.[[That is, the explanation of the statement previously given, "Speech is directed toward what is familiar among people in its usage, and not toward its unfamiliar meanings," which was mentioned on p. 388. Also, a clear error occurred in the printed edition: what we have quoted here was placed in the wrong location. It belongs at p. 394, from the beginning of his words "Some of the grammarians have claimed..." to his words "...by its departure from the view of all the people of knowledge, a proof of its error."]]

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿and they are given it in resemblance﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The pronoun in His words "and they are given it in resemblance" refers to the provision. So its interpretation is: They are given that which was provided to them from its fruits, in resemblance.

The people of interpretation have differed concerning the interpretation of "resemblance" (mutashabihan) in this context:

Some of them said: Its resemblance is that all of it is choice, with nothing inferior in it.

Those who said that:

519. Khallad ibn Aslam related to us, who said: al-Nadr ibn Shumayl informed us, who said: Abu 'Amir informed us, from al-Hasan, concerning His words, "resembling": He said: Choice, all of it, with nothing inferior in it.

520. Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, who said: Ibn 'Ulayya related to us, from Abu Raja': al-Hasan recited verses from al-Baqara, and came to this verse, "and they are given it in resemblance." He said: Do you not see how the fruits of this world, you consider some of them inferior? And that there is nothing inferior in that.

521. al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, who said: 'Abd al-Razzaq related to us, who said: Ma'mar informed us, who said: al-Hasan said: "and they are given it in resemblance," he said: Some of it resembles other parts, with nothing inferior in it.[[In the printed edition: "there is nothing inferior in it."]]

522. Bishr related to us, who said: Yazid related to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada: "and they are given it in resemblance," that is, choice, with nothing inferior in it; and the fruits of this world are sifted and some of them are rejected, whereas the fruits of Paradise are entirely choice, and nothing in it is rejected.

523. al-Qasim related to us, who said: al-Husayn related to us, who said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Some of the fruit of this world is rejected, and some of it is pure; but the fruit of Paradise is all pure, some of it resembling others in goodness, and nothing in it is rejected.[[Reports 519–523: some of them are in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:38, and some in al-Shawkani 1:42.]]

* *

Others said: Its resemblance is in colour, while it differs in taste.

Those who said that:

524. Musa related to me, who said: 'Amr related to us, who said: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas; and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "and they are given it in resemblance," in colour and appearance, but it does not resemble in taste.

525. Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, who said: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "and they are given it in resemblance," like the cucumber.

526. al-Muthanna related to us, who said: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, who said: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "and they are given it in resemblance," its colour is alike and its taste is different, like the cucumber among the cucumbers.

527. It was related to me from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: "and they are given it in resemblance," some of it resembles other parts and the taste differs.

528. al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, who said: 'Abd al-Razzaq related to us, who said: al-Thawri informed us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words, "resembling," he said: resembling in colour and differing in taste.

529. al-Qasim related to us, who said: al-Husayn related to us, who said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid: "and they are given it in resemblance," like the cucumber.[[Reports 524–529: some are in Ibn Kathir 1:114–115, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:38, and al-Shawkani 1:42.]]

* *

Others said: Its resemblance is in colour and taste.

Those who said that:

530. Ibn Waki' related to us, who said: My father related to us, from Sufyan, from a man, from Mujahid, his words, "resembling," he said: the colour and the taste.

531. al-Muthanna related to me, who said: Ishaq related to us, who said: 'Abd al-Razzaq related to us, from al-Thawri, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, and Yahya ibn Sa'id, "resembling": both said: in colour and taste.

* *

Others said: Its resemblance is that the fruit of Paradise and the fruit of this world resemble one another in colour, even if their tastes differ.

Those who said that:

532. al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, who said: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, who said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada: "and they are given it in resemblance," he said: It resembles the fruit of this world, except that the fruit of Paradise is more delicious.

533. al-Muthanna related to us, who said: Ishaq related to us, who said: Hafs ibn 'Umar said: al-Hakam ibn Aban related to us, from 'Ikrima, concerning His words, "and they are given it in resemblance," he said: It resembles the fruit of this world, except that the fruit of Paradise is more delicious.

* *

Others said: Nothing in Paradise resembles anything in this world, except in names.

Those who said that:

٥٣٤- Abu Kurayb narrated to me, saying: al-Ashja'i narrated to us. [Another chain:] Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us. Both of them said: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Zabyan, from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Kurayb said in his narration from al-Ashja'i: "Nothing in Paradise resembles anything in this world, except the names." Ibn Bashshar said in his narration from Mu'ammal: "There is nothing in this world from what is in Paradise except the names."

٥٣٥- 'Abbas ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Zabyan, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "There is nothing in this world from Paradise except the names."

٥٣٦- Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said, concerning His words ﴿and they will be given it in semblance﴾: "They recognize its names as they used to in this world: apples with apples and pomegranates with pomegranates. They say in Paradise, ﴿This is what we were provided with before﴾, meaning in this world, ﴿and they will be given it in semblance﴾, they recognize it, but it is not the same in taste."

[[The reports 530–536 are partly in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:38 and al-Shawkani 1:42.]]

Abu Ja'far said: The most preferred of these interpretations (ta'wil, meaning the explanation of the verse) is the interpretation of the one who said: "﴿And they will be given it in semblance﴾ in colour and appearance, while the taste differs." This means that the fruits of Paradise resemble the fruits of this world in appearance and colour, while differing in taste and flavour, for the reason we have already mentioned in the interpretation of His words ﴿Every time they are provided with a fruit from it as provision, they say, "This is what we were provided with before"﴾, and that its meaning is: every time they are provided from the Gardens with a fruit of its fruits as provision, they say, "This is what we were provided with before," meaning before, in this world. So God, exalted is His praise, informed about them that they said this. And because what they were brought in Paradise was semblant to it, meaning the resemblance of what they were brought in Paradise to what they had been provided in this world, in colour, appearance and look, even though they differed in taste and flavour, so they were distinct, and there was nothing in what is in Paradise of that kind that has a counterpart in this world.

We have already demonstrated the corruption of the view of those who claimed that the meaning of His words ﴿They say, "This is what we were provided with before"﴾ is merely the statement of the people of Paradise in comparing some of the fruit of Paradise with other fruit. [[See what has passed, p. 387 and what follows.]] That demonstration of the corruption of that view is the same demonstration of the corruption of the view of those who opposed our view in the interpretation of His words ﴿and they will be given it in semblance﴾, because God, exalted is His praise, only informed about the meaning for which the people said ﴿This is what we were provided with before﴾ by His words ﴿and they will be given it in semblance﴾.

One should ask whoever denies this and claims that it is impossible for anything in Paradise to be a counterpart to anything in this world in any respect: Is it permissible that the names of the fruits, foods and drinks of Paradise be counterparts to the names of those in this world?

If he denies that, he contradicts the explicit text of the Book of God, because God, exalted is His praise, only made His servants know in this world what is with Him in Paradise through the names by which those things in this world are called.

And if he says: "That is permissible, indeed it is so."

It is said: Then what prevents you from holding that the colours of what is in it are counterparts to the colours of what is in this world, meaning white, red, yellow and all kinds of colours, even though they differ and are superior by the excellence of beauty of appearance and look, so that what is in Paradise of that has brilliance, beauty and good appearance and look that differ from what is in this world, just as it was permissible in the names despite the difference of the named things in their bodies by excellence? Then the statement on that is reversed against him, so he will not say anything about one of them except that the same will be imposed on the other.

And Abu Musa al-Ash'ari used to say about that:

٥٣٧- Ibn Bashshar narrated to me, saying: Ibn Abi 'Adiyy, 'Abd al-Wahhab, and Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, from 'Awf, from Qasama, from al-Ash'ari, who said: "When God brought Adam out of Paradise, He provided him with fruit from the fruits of Paradise and taught him the making of everything. So your fruits here are from the fruits of Paradise, except that these change and those do not change."

[[Report 537: This chain is sound. Although it is mawquf (attributed to a Companion) in wording, it is marfu' (traced to the Prophet) in ruling, because it is information about the unseen that cannot be known by opinion or analogy. Al-Ash'ari is Abu Musa, and he was not one who related from earlier books. 'Awf is Ibn Abi Jamila al-A'rabi, a trustworthy and firm narrator, from whom the authors of the six books related. Qasama (with a fatha on the qaf and a light sin) is Ibn Zuhayr al-Mazini al-Tamimi al-Basri, a trustworthy early Successor, though some included him among the Companions, which is an error. His biography is in al-Isaba 5:276 and Ibn Sa'd 7/1/110, where he said: "He was trustworthy, God willing, and he died during al-Hajjaj's governorship of Iraq." Also Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/147, who related his authentication from Ibn Ma'in.
The hadith was mentioned by Ibn Kathir in al-Tarikh 1:80, from the narration of 'Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar from 'Awf with this chain. It was mentioned by Ibn al-Qayyim in Hadi al-Arwah 1:273 (p. 125 of the second edition, Mahmud Rabi' edition, 1357 AH) from the narration of 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from 'Uqba ibn Mukarram al-'Ammi the memorizer, from Rabi' ibn Ibrahim ibn 'Ulayya, from 'Awf with this chain, explicitly marfu': "He said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said." Likewise al-Haythami mentioned it in Majma' al-Zawa'id 8:197–198 "from Abu Musa, raising it," and said: "Al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani related it, and its narrators are trustworthy." Ibn al-Qayyim also mentioned it earlier in Hadi al-Arwah (pp. 30–31) from the narration of "Hawdhah ibn Khalifa from 'Awf" with this chain, mawquf in wording. The narration of Hawdhah ibn Khalifa was related by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:543, but its chain, in my view and belief, is corrupted, and the error is most likely from the copyists. What it contains is: "Hawdhah ibn Khalifa narrated to us, from 'Awf, from Qasama ibn Zuhayr, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Musa al-Ash'ari, who said: When God brought Adam out..." etc. Then al-Hakim said: "Its chain is sound but they did not include it," and al-Dhahabi agreed! As far as I know and believe, it is not possible that al-Hakim would authenticate this chain and al-Dhahabi would agree with him if it were in this form, because Abu Bakr ibn Abi Musa al-Ash'ari is a trustworthy Successor. If the chain were like this, the hadith would be mursal (missing a Companion) and not a proof, whether he raised it or said it on his own authority. The likely explanation is that the early copyists of al-Mustadrak erred in adding "Abu Bakr ibn," and the correct reading is "from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari," as is shown by Ibn al-Qayyim's citation of Hawdhah's narration and by the other narrations we have cited. And praise be to God for success.]]

[[This whole paragraph, from His saying "And some of the grammarians have claimed..." was in the printed edition at the place we pointed to above, p. 389.]] Some grammarians (ahl al-'arabiyya, the experts in Arabic grammar and language) claimed that the meaning of His words ﴿and they will be given it in semblance﴾ is that it is similar in excellence, that is, each one of them has an excellence in its kind like the excellence of the other in its kind.

Abu Ja'far said: This is not a view we consider it proper to occupy ourselves with demonstrating its corruption, because it departs from the view of all the scholars of ta'wil (the scholars of interpretation). It is enough that a view, by departing from the view of all the people of knowledge, is evidence of its error.

* *

On the interpretation of His words ﴿And for them therein are purified spouses﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The "ha'" and "mim" in "lahum" (for them) refer to those who believed and did righteous deeds, and the "ha'" and "alif" in "fiha" (therein) refer to the Gardens. The meaning of this is: "And give good news to those who believe and do righteous deeds that for them are Gardens in which are purified spouses."

Al-azwaj (spouses) is the plural of zawj, which is a man's wife. It is said: "So-and-so is the zawj of so-and-so and his wife."

As for His words "purified" (mutahharah), its interpretation is that they are purified from every harm, impurity and filth that occurs among the women of this world, such as menstruation, postpartum bleeding, excrement, urine, mucus, spittle, semen, and whatever is similar to that of harm, defilements, impurities and disliked things.

٥٣٨- As Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murra, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ: As for "purified spouses," they do not menstruate, do not emit wind, and do not spit out mucus.

٥٣٩- Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to us, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words "purified spouses." He says: purified from filth and harm.

٥٤٠- Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Yahya al-Qattan narrated to us [[In the manuscript: "Yahya al-'Attar," which is an error.]], from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And for them therein are purified spouses." He said: They do not urinate, do not defecate, and do not emit prostatic fluid.

٥٤١- Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly, except that he added: "nor do they emit semen, nor do they menstruate."

٥٤٢- Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the words of God, may His remembrance be exalted: "And for them therein are purified spouses." He said: purified from menstruation, excrement, urine, nasal mucus, spittle, semen and child-bearing.

٥٤٣- Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of that.

٥٤٤- Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: They do not urinate, do not defecate, do not menstruate, do not give birth, do not emit semen, and do not spit.

٥٤٥- Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similar to the report of Muhammad ibn 'Amr from Abu 'Asim.

٥٤٦- Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada: "And for them therein are purified spouses," yes, by God, from sin and harm.

٥٤٧- Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, concerning His words "And for them therein are purified spouses." He said: God purified them from every urine, excrement and filth, and from every sin.

٥٤٨- I was told from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to me, from his father, from Qatada, who said: purified from menstruation, pregnancy and harm.

٥٤٩- I was told from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to me, from his father, from Layth, from Mujahid, who said: purified from menstruation and pregnancy.

٥٥٠- Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd: "And for them therein are purified spouses." He said: The purified one is the one who does not menstruate. He said: The wives of this world are not purified; do you not see them bleed and abandon prayer and fasting? Ibn Zayd said: Thus was Eve created until she disobeyed, and when she disobeyed God said: "I created you purified, and I will make you bleed as you made this tree bleed." [[In the manuscript: "as dumayt" with a doubled mim, both are the same, and it means the blood of menstruation. This report was quoted by Ibn Kathir 1:115 from this place, and in it is "adhmayt" (you made bleed), as in the printed text here. Ibn Kathir said after quoting it: "This is strange."]]

٥٥١- I was told from 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', from al-Hasan concerning His words "And for them therein are purified spouses," he said: He says: purified from menstruation.

٥٥٢- 'Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn Yazid narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far al-Razi narrated to us, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from al-Hasan concerning His words "And for them therein are purified spouses," he said: from menstruation.

٥٥٣- 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj narrated to us, from 'Ata' concerning His words "And for them therein are purified spouses," he said: from child-bearing, menstruation, excrement and urine, and he mentioned things of this kind. [[Reports 538–553: some are in Ibn Kathir 1:115, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:39, and al-Shawkani 1:42. We disliked lengthening by detailing their sources one by one. Ibn Kathir 1:115–116 also quoted a marfu' hadith with this meaning, namely "purified from menstruation, excrement, nasal mucus and spittle," from the Tafsir of Ibn Mardawayh with its chain: through Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd al-Kindi, from 'Abd al-Razzaq ibn 'Umar al-Buza'i, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, from Shu'ba, from Qatada, from Abu Nadra, from Abu Sa'id, raised to the Prophet. He said: "This is a strange hadith." Then he quoted from al-Hakim that he related it in al-Mustadrak by this route and authenticated it on the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Then he said: "What he claimed about it is open to question, for this 'Abd al-Razzaq ibn 'Umar al-Buza'i was said by Abu Hatim ibn Hibban al-Busti to be one whose narrations may not be used as proof. I say: The more evident view is that this is the statement of Qatada, as was mentioned earlier." And it is as Ibn Kathir said. See Mizan al-I'tidal 2:126.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His words ﴿And they therein are abiding forever﴾

Abu Ja'far said: God, may His remembrance be exalted, means by this: "And those who believed and did righteous deeds, in the Gardens, are abiding forever." The "ha'" and "mim" in His words "wahum" (and they) refer to those who believed and did righteous deeds. The "ha'" and "alif" in "fiha" (therein) refer to the Gardens. Their abiding therein is the continuance of their remaining there, in the delight and enduring bliss that God gave them therein. [[In al-Durr al-Manthur 1:41 and al-Shawkani 1:42, it is that Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words "And they therein are abiding forever": "That is, abiding forever; He informs them that the reward for good and the punishment for evil remains upon its people forever, without cessation."
This report will come in the commentary on verse 82 of this surah (1:307 Bulaq edition). Al-Suyuti transferred it to this place, and al-Shawkani followed him.]]

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 2, Verse 26 (Part 1 of 2)**

On the explanation (*ta'wil*, interpretation) of His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example, [even] of a gnat or what is above it﴾

Abu Ja'far [al-Tabari] said: The people of *ta'wil* differed about the meaning for which Allah, exalted is His praise, sent down this verse, and about its interpretation.

Some of them said:

554. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ: When Allah struck these two parables for the hypocrites, meaning His saying ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ and His saying ﴿or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾, the three verses, the hypocrites said: "Allah is too exalted and too majestic to strike such parables." So Allah sent down: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example, [even] of a gnat...﴾ up to His saying ﴿Those are the losers.﴾

Others said:

555. Ahmad ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Qurad narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example, [even] of a gnat or what is above it.﴾ He said: This is a parable which Allah struck for this world: the gnat lives as long as it is hungry, but when it becomes fat, it dies. Likewise is the likeness of these people for whom Allah struck this parable in the Qur'an: when they are filled with the world to satiety, Allah seizes them at that time. He said: Then he recited: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened to them the gates of every [good] thing until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were [then] in despair﴾ [Al-An'am: 44]. [[Report 555: "Qurad" is with a *damma* on the *qaf* and a *fatha* on the *ra* (lightened); it is his epithet (laqab). His name is "Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghazwan," with a *fatha* on the *ghayn* (dotted) and a *sukun* on the *zay*, al-Khuza'i. He is trustworthy (thiqah). Ahmad said: "He was an intelligent man." Ibn Abi Hatim included him in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 2/2/274.]]

556. Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, with something similar, except that he said: When their terms expire and their periods are cut off, [they become] like the gnat, which lives as long as it is hungry and dies when it is sated. Likewise are those for whom Allah struck this parable: when they are filled with the world to satiety, Allah seizes them and destroys them. That is His saying: ﴿until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly, and they were [then] in despair﴾ [Al-An'am: 44]. [[In the printed edition it reads "khala ajalahum" (their terms passed), while in the manuscript it reads "khala" (passed). The correct form is what I have recorded. *Khala al-'umr yakhlu khuluwwan* means: the life passed and came to an end.]]

Others said:

557. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example, [even] of a gnat or what is above it﴾, meaning: Indeed, Allah is not ashamed of the truth, [so as] to mention any part of it, whether little or much. When Allah mentioned the fly and the spider in His Book, the people of error said: "What did Allah intend by mentioning this?" So Allah sent down: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example, [even] of a gnat or what is above it.﴾ [[In the manuscript: "shay'an qall minhu aw kathur," without the "ma"; in Ibn Kathir: "mimma qall aw kathur." All these are close in meaning.]]

558. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, who said: When Allah mentioned the spider and the fly, the polytheists said: "What is the matter with the spider and the fly that they are mentioned?" So Allah sent down: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example, [even] of a gnat or what is above it.﴾ [[The reports 554–558: most of them are in Ibn Kathir 1:117, and some are in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:41 and al-Shawkani 1:45.]]

Each speaker whose statement we have mentioned regarding this verse, and regarding the meaning for which it was revealed, has gone in a direction. However, the view closest to the correct and most in accord with the truth is what we have mentioned from the statements of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas.

That is because Allah, exalted is His remembrance, informed His servants that He is not ashamed to strike an example, [even] of a gnat or what is above it, following parables that had already been mentioned in this surah, which He struck for the hypocrites, rather than the parables He struck in other surahs. So it is more fitting and more appropriate that this statement, meaning His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example...﴾, be a response to the disapproval of the disbelievers and hypocrites of the parables struck for them in this surah, than that it be a response to their disapproval of the parables struck for them in other surahs.

If someone says: "The reason it must be a response to their disapproval of the parables struck in other surahs is that the parables Allah struck for them and for their gods in other surahs are parables whose meaning agrees with what He reported, that He is not ashamed to strike a parable, since some of them are a representation of their gods as a spider, and some are a comparison of them in weakness and humiliation to a fly. None of that is present in this surah, so it cannot be said that Allah is not ashamed to strike an example [in this surah]." [[In the printed edition: "an yadriba mathalan ma," which is not correct.]]

The matter is contrary to what he supposed. That is because the saying of Allah, exalted is His praise: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example, [even] of a gnat or what is above it﴾, is merely a report from Him, exalted is His remembrance, that He is not ashamed to strike, in matters of truth, parables both small and great, as a test and trial for His servants, so that by it He may distinguish the people of faith and affirmation of it from the people of error and disbelief in it: misguiding some people by it, and guiding others by it.

559. As Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His saying: "a parable, [even] of a gnat," meaning parables, small and great, by which the believers have faith, and they know that they are the truth from their Lord, and Allah guides them by them and misguides the defiantly disobedient by them. He means: the believers recognize it and so believe in it, and the defiantly disobedient recognize it and so disbelieve in it.

560. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, with the like of it.

561. Al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the like of it. [[Reports 559–561 are all one report; they are in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:42, al-Shawkani 1:45, and will come below as no. 566.]]

Abu Ja'far said: Not that He, exalted is His remembrance, intended to report about the gnat itself that He is not ashamed to strike a parable with it, but because the gnat, being among the weakest of creatures—

562. As al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, who said: The gnat is the weakest of what Allah created.

563. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, with something similar. [[Report 562 is in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:41.]]

— [[The words "khassaha..." are the answer to his earlier saying: "...because it was the weakest of creatures."]] Allah singled it out for mention for its smallness, and He informed [us] that He is not ashamed to strike the smallest and most insignificant of parables in truth, and [the greatest] which rises without limit in height, as a response from Him, exalted is His remembrance, to whoever among the hypocrites of His creation denied the parable He struck for them with the one who kindles a fire and the rainstorm from the sky, according to the description He gave of them.

If someone says to us: "Where is the denial of the hypocrites of the parables you described, to which this report is the answer, so that we may know that the matter is as you said?"

It is said: The evidence for that is clear in the saying of Allah, exalted is His remembrance: ﴿As for those who believed, they know that it is the truth from their Lord; but as for those who disbelieved, they say, "What did Allah intend by this as an example?"﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 26]. The people for whom the parables were struck in the two preceding verses, in which He struck the parable of what the hypocrites are upon, namely the one who kindled a fire and the rainstorm from the sky, as described before His saying "Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example," have denied the parable and said: "What did Allah intend by this as an example?" So He, exalted is His remembrance, made clear to them the error of their saying that, and condemned for them what they uttered, and informed them of their ruling regarding what they said, and that it is misguidance and wickedness, and that the correct and the guidance is what the believers said, not what they said. [[In the printed edition: "The evidence for that is clear, exalted is He, in His saying..."]]

As for the interpretation of His saying "Indeed, Allah is not ashamed" (*yastahyi*), some of those ascribed to knowledge of the Arabic language used to interpret the meaning of "Indeed, Allah is not ashamed" as: "Indeed, Allah does not fear to strike a parable," and he cited as evidence the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿and you fear the people, while Allah has more right that You fear Him﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 37], claiming that its meaning is: "You are ashamed of the people, and Allah has more right that you be ashamed before Him." He said: *al-istihya'* (shame) means *al-khashyah* (fear), and *al-khashyah* means *al-istihya'*. [[I do not know who the person ascribed to knowledge of Arabic who said this is. But I saw Abu Hayyan say in his tafsir 1:121 that this is the meaning al-Tabari preferred. It is clear that he erred in what he imagined, for al-Tabari's wording indicates that he did not verify the meaning, nor accept it, nor support it. Nevertheless, I think the figurative use of the word permits what this person said, though I dislike taking this verse in this sense.]]

As for the meaning of His saying "to strike an example" (*an yadriba mathalan*), it means to make clear and to describe, as He, exalted is His praise, said: ﴿He struck for you an example from yourselves﴾ [Al-Rum: 28], meaning: described for you. And as al-Kumayt said:

*"That is the striking of akhmas (fifths) for asdas (sixths), perhaps they will not be..."* [[This is a line the poet Kumayt took by stealth as a proverb. Its origin: an old man had camels and his sons were herding them far from their family for a long time. One day he said to them: "Pasture your camels in rabi' (a grazing pattern: withhold from water for three days and return on the fourth day)," so they pastured in the rabi' toward their family's path. They said: "If only we pastured them in *khams* (withhold four days and return on the fifth)!" So they added a day before reaching their family. They said: "If only we pastured them in *sids* (withhold five days and return on the sixth)!" The old man realized what they intended and said: "You are nothing but striking *akhmas* for *asdas*; your concern is not their pasture, but your family!" And he composed: "That is the striking of akhmas, I see it, for asdas, perhaps they will not be..." So their saying "striking akhmas for asdas" became a proverb for one who is evasive and shows one matter while intending another.]]

meaning: describing *akhmas*.

*Al-mathal* is *al-shabah* (resemblance). It is said: "This is the *mathal* of this and its *mithl*," just as it is said "its *shabah*" and "its *shibh*." From this is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

*"The promises of 'Urqub were for them a proverb, and their promises were nothing but falsehoods."* [[His Diwan: 8. In the manuscript it reads "wa ma mawa'iduha"; 'Urqub, as they claim, is 'Urqub ibn Nasr, a man of the Amalekites who settled in Medina before the Jews settled there after 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him. He would evade fulfilling promises by procrastination, as is well known in his story.]]

meaning *shabah* (likeness). So the meaning of His saying, then, is: "Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example" means: Indeed, Allah does not fear to describe a likeness for that which He is compared to. [[This is the remainder of the explanation of the word according to the view of those who said that *istihya'* means *khashyah*, not what al-Tabari adopted; al-Tabari's explanation is clear at the end of the interpretation of the verse.]]

As for "ma" which is with "mathal," it means "alladhi" (the one which), because the meaning of the sentence is: Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike, as a parable, the one which is a gnat in smallness and insignificance, or what is above it.

If someone says to us: "If the matter is as you said, what is the grammatical basis for the accusative (*nasb*) of *ba'udah* (gnat), when you know that the sense of the sentence, as you interpreted, is: 'Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable [of] that which is a gnat'; so *ba'udah* by your view should be in the nominative case? How then did it come to be in the accusative?"

It is said: The accusative came from two angles. The first: since *ma* was in the accusative position as the object of *yadrib* (strike), and the gnat was its complement (*silah*), it took the inflection of *ma* by being made like it, and so it was made to have its inflection, as Hassan ibn Thabit said:

*"And it suffices us as a virtue over others than us, the love of the Prophet Muhammad for us."* [[It is not in his Diwan. It appears in al-Tabari 4:99 unattributed, and in al-Khizanah 2:545–546 it is attributed to Ka'b ibn Malik; it is also attributed to Hassan ibn Thabit but is not found in his poetry. It is attributed to Bashir ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Ka'b ibn Malik, and also to 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah. al-Suyuti mentioned it in Sharh Shawahid al-Mughni: 116, 252, and recorded a line before it: "They helped their Prophet with the help of his Friend, so Allah, mighty is He, named us by His help." He said: It means that Allah, mighty and majestic, named them "the Helpers" (*al-Ansar*), because they helped the Prophet ﷺ and those who allied with him. The *ba'* in "bi-nasri waliyyihi" means "with."]]

So "ghayr" was given the inflection of "man" (*u'ribat bi-i'rab "man"*). The Arabs do this especially with "man" and "ma," giving their complements the same inflection as them, because they can be definite at times and indefinite at times.

As for the second angle: the meaning of the sentence is: Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable [of what lies] between a gnat and what is above it; then the mention of "bayna" (between) and "ila" (to) was omitted, since the accusative of *ba'udah* and the entry of the *fa'* (then) on the second *ma* indicate them. Just as the Arabs said: "We were rained upon from *ma* Zubalah to *fa*-al-Tha'labiyyah" and "he has twenty from *ma* a she-camel to *fa* a male camel," and "she is the most beautiful of people from *ma* her horn to *fa* her feet," meaning: from between her horn to her feet. They say likewise in every case where it is good in speech to use "*ma bayna kadha ila kadha*" (from between such and such to such and such), putting the first and second in the accusative, so that the accusative in both indicates what is omitted from the speech. [[In the manuscript: "li-yadulla al-nasb fi al-asma' 'ala al-mahdhuf," and both are the same in meaning.]] So likewise in His saying "*ma ba'udah fa-ma fawqaha*."

[[Most of this is from al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:21–22, where he mentioned both of the preceding angles; his statement is more detailed and clearer than al-Tabari's.]]

Some of the grammarians have claimed that the *ma* that comes with *mathal* is a *silah* (filler, redundant element) in the speech, in the sense of *tatawwul* (expansion/extension), and that the meaning of the sentence is: "Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike a gnat as a parable, or what is above it." Based on this interpretation, *ba'udah* must be in the accusative as the object of *yadrib*, and the second *ma* in *fa-ma fawqaha* must be coordinated with *ba'udah*, not with the first *ma*. [[The term *tatawwul* was explained long ago (see: 18, 224, and what follows, pp. 406, 154 of the Bulaq edition); it means addition to speech. The one he called "some of the grammarians" is al-Farra himself, who mentioned this as the first of three angles on the verse in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:21, saying: "The first of them: that you place the striking on the gnat and make *ma* a *silah*, as in His saying: 'in a little while they will surely become regretful' [Al-Mu'minun: 40], meaning: 'after a little.' The meaning, Allah knows best, is: Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike a gnat as a parable, or what is above it." What al-Tabari (of the Baghdadi school) calls *tatawwul*, al-Farra (of the Kufan school) calls *silah*, which is the addition to speech.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 26 (part 2 of 2):

As for the interpretation of His words "fa-ma fawqahā" (and whatever is above it): it means what is greater than it [[In the manuscript: "fa-huwa ma qad 'azuma minhā" ("so it is what is great of it"), which is an error without meaning.]] in my view, on account of what we mentioned earlier from the statements of Qatadah and Ibn Juraij: that the gnat is the weakest of God's creatures. Since it is the weakest of God's creatures, it is the extreme in littleness and weakness. And since that is so, there is no doubt that what is above the weakest of things can only be stronger than it. So the meaning, according to what the two of them said, must be "and whatever is above it in size and greatness," since the gnat is the extreme in weakness and littleness.

It has also been said regarding the interpretation of His words "fa-ma fawqahā" that it refers to smallness and littleness, as one says of a man whom a speaker mentions and describes with meanness and stinginess, and the listener says: "Yes, and above that," meaning above what was described in stinginess and meanness [[In the printed edition: "above what was described." This interpretation mentioned by al-Tabari was suggested and explained by al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 20-21, where he said: "If you were to put into a similar expression 'fa-ma fawqahā', meaning smaller than it, that would be permissible. But I do not prefer it," meaning that he does not prefer it in this place of the tafsir of the Book of God.]]. This is a view contrary to the interpretation of the people of knowledge whose understanding of the Qur'an's interpretation is accepted.

Thus it has become clear, by what we have described, that the meaning of the speech is: God is not ashamed to set forth a likeness for whatever He compares it to, which ranges from a gnat up to what is above the gnat.

As for the interpretation of the speech if "al-ba'ūdah" (the gnat) were in the nominative case, it is not permissible for "mā" except as we have said, that it be a noun, not a relative pronoun in the sense of elaboration [[We have explained the meaning of "ṣilah" (relative clause) and "tatawwul" (elaboration) earlier, p. 405.]].

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿Then as for those who believed, they know that it is the truth from their Lord; but as for those who disbelieved, they say, "What did God intend by this as an example?"﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words "as for those who believed," He means: as for those who affirmed God and His Messenger. And His words "they know that it is the truth from their Lord" mean: they recognize that the parable God has struck, for what He struck it for, is a parable.

564. As al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj told us, saying: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: "As for those who believed, they know that it is the truth from their Lord": that this parable is the truth from their Lord, and that it is the speech of God and from Him [[Report 564: it is from al-Rabi' ibn Anas from Abu al-'Aliyah, as has passed many times; and likewise it appears in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 43.]].

565. And as Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' told us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, regarding His words "As for those who believed, they know that it is the truth from their Lord": i.e., they know that it is the speech of the Most Merciful, and that it is the truth from God [[Report 565: in Ibn Kathir 1: 118.]].

"But as for those who disbelieved, they say, 'What did God intend by this as an example?'"

Abu Ja'far said: His words "as for those who disbelieved" mean those who denied the signs of God, rejected what they had recognized, and concealed what they knew to be true. That is the description of the hypocrites, and God, may He be exalted and glorified, meant by this verse them, and whoever was like them among their counterparts and associates from the polytheists, from the People of the Book and others, saying: "What did God intend by this as an example?", as we have already mentioned earlier from the report we transmitted from Mujahid, which is:

566. Muhammad related to us from Amr, saying: Abu 'Asim told us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "As for those who believed, they know that it is the truth from their Lord," to the end of the verse, he said: The believers affirm it, and they know it is the truth from their Lord, and God guides them by it, and He leads astray the defiantly disobedient by it. He says: the believers recognize it and so believe in it, and the defiantly disobedient recognize it and so disbelieve in it [[Report 566: already passed as no. 559.]].

The interpretation of His words "What did God intend by this as an example?" is: what did God intend by this parable as an example? The "dha" with "mā" has the meaning of "alladhī" (which), and its relative clause is "arāda" (intended), and "hadhā" (this) refers to the parable [[In the printed edition: "fa-dhā ma' mā fī ma'nā..."]].

* *

On the interpretation of His words, may His praise be exalted: ﴿By it He leads many astray, and by it He guides many﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may He be exalted and glorified, "He leads many astray by it," God leads many of His creatures astray by it. The pronoun in "bihi" (by it) refers to the parable. This is a statement from God, may His praise be exalted, that begins anew, and the meaning of the speech is: God leads astray by the parable that He sets forth many of the people of hypocrisy and disbelief:

567. As Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet ﷺ: "He leads many astray by it," meaning the hypocrites, "and guides many by it," meaning the believers [[Report 567: in Ibn Kathir 1: 119, al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 42, and al-Shawkani 1: 45, where it appears complete and connected, and its completion is the report that follows it: 568. But Ibn Kathir erred, joining this report with the following statement of al-Tabari, as if all of it were from the tafsir of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, and this is pure error. Al-Tabari's statement after "so they increase these in misguidance..." is a continuation of his statement before this: "that God leads astray by the parable that He sets forth many of the people of hypocrisy and disbelief."]].

So He increases these in misguidance upon their misguidance, because they denied what they had known as certain truth of the parable God struck for what He struck it for, and that it accords with what it was struck for. That is God's leading them astray by it. And "He guides by it," meaning by the parable, many of the people of faith and affirmation, so He increases them in guidance upon their guidance and in faith upon their faith, because of their affirmation of what they had known as certain truth, that it accords with what God struck as a parable, and their acknowledgment of it. That is God's guidance to them by it.

Some have claimed that this is a report about the hypocrites, as if they said: "What did God intend by a parable that not everyone recognizes, by which He leads this one astray and guides that one?" Then the speech was resumed, and the statement is from God, so God said: "And He leads astray by it none but the defiantly disobedient." And in what is in Surah al-Muddaththir, from God's words: "that those in whose hearts is disease and the disbelievers may say, 'What did God intend by this as an example?' Thus God leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills" — there is an indication that in Surah al-Baqarah it is likewise a beginning, meaning His words: "He leads many astray by it and guides many by it."

* *

On the interpretation of His words, may His praise be exalted: ﴿And He leads astray by it none but the defiantly disobedient (26)﴾

The interpretation of this is:

568. Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet ﷺ: "And He leads astray by it none but the defiantly disobedient": they are the hypocrites [[Report 568: the completion of the preceding report, whose place we have mentioned.]].

569. And Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid told us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah: "And He leads astray by it none but the defiantly disobedient": they defied, so God led them astray for their defiance [[Report 569: in Ibn Kathir 1: 119, and in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 42, and al-Shawkani 1: 45, where in place of "'ala fisqihim" ("for their defiance") it reads "bi-fisqihim" ("by their defiance").]].

570. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq told us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: "And He leads astray by it none but the defiantly disobedient": they are the people of hypocrisy [[Report 570: in Ibn Kathir 1: 119.]].

Abu Ja'far said: The root of "fisq" (defiant disobedience) in the speech of the Arabs is departure from something. It is said of it: "fasaqat al-ruṭabah" (the date came out) when it emerged from its skin. From this the mouse was named "fuwaysiqah" (little defiant one), because it comes out of its hole [[See al-Tabari 15: 170 (Bulaq edition). His words there: "It is related from the Arabs by hearsay: fasaqat al-ruṭabah min qishrihā, idhā kharajat. Wa fasaqat al-fa'rah idhā kharajat min juḥrihā," and the rest of what he said there.]]. Thus the hypocrite and the disbeliever are called "fāsiqān" (defiantly disobedient), because they depart from obedience to their Lord. Therefore He, may His remembrance be exalted, said in describing Iblis: ﴿Except Iblis; he was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord﴾ [Surah al-Kahf: 50], meaning he departed from His obedience and from following His command.

571.
