As Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah told us, saying: Ibn Ishaq told me, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from 'Ikrimah, mawla of Ibn 'Abbas, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿because they used to defy﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 59], i.e., because they strayed from My command [[Report 571: I have not found it in its place in the tafsir of the verse of al-Baqarah, nor in any verse in which this word is mentioned. None of those we rely upon has recorded it. In the manuscript: "min amrī" ("from My command").]]. So the meaning of His words "And He leads astray by it none but the defiantly disobedient" is: God leads astray, by the parable He sets forth for the people of error and hypocrisy, none but those who depart from His obedience and abandon following His command, from among those who disbelieve in Him from the People of the Book, and the people of error from among the hypocrites.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 27:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification﴾

Abu Ja'far said: This is a description by Allah, mighty and majestic is He, of the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqin), whom He informed that He does not lead astray by the parable He struck for the hypocrites other than them. So He said: ﴿And Allah does not lead astray by it except the defiantly disobedient﴾ — according to what He described earlier in the preceding verses — ﴿who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification.﴾

Then the people of knowledge (ahl al-ma'rifa) differed concerning the meaning of the covenant by whose breaking Allah described these defiantly disobedient people:

Some of them said: It is the charge (wasiyya) of Allah to His creatures, and His command to them with what He commanded them of obedience to Him, and His prohibition to them of what He forbade them of disobedience to Him, in His books and upon the tongue of His Messenger ﷺ. Their breaking of that is their abandoning of acting upon it.

Others said: These verses were revealed concerning the disbelievers among the People of the Book and the hypocrites among them, and it is them that Allah, mighty and majestic is He, meant by His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾, and by His saying: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day"﴾. So everything in these verses is a rebuke and reproach to them until the end of their accounts (qasas). They said: The covenant of Allah which they broke after its ratification is what Allah took from them in the Torah — of acting by what is in it, and following Muhammad ﷺ when he is sent, and affirming him and what he brought from their Lord. Their breaking of that is their denial of him after knowing his reality, their rejection of that, and their concealment of the knowledge of that from the people [[In the printed edition: "ʿan al-nas" (from the people), and "al-nas" is in the accusative as a second object of the verbal noun "kitmanihim". The verb "katama" takes one object or two objects; you say: "katamtu fulanan sirri" and "katamtu ʿan fulanin sirri", and both are the same.]], after they had given Allah a covenant from themselves that they would make it clear to the people and not conceal it. So Allah, mighty is His praise, informed that they cast it behind their backs and sold it for a small price.

Others said: Allah meant by this verse all of the people of polytheism, disbelief and hypocrisy. His covenant to all of them concerning His oneness is what He set down for them of proofs indicating His lordship. His covenant to them concerning His command and prohibition is what He presented as evidence for His messengers of miracles which no one among mankind other than them can bring the like of, bearing witness to them for their truthfulness. They said: Their breaking of that is their abandoning of acknowledgement of what has become clear to them as true by the proofs, and their denial of the messengers and the books, while knowing that what they brought is true.

Others said: The covenant that Allah, mighty is His mention, mentioned is the covenant He took from them when He brought them forth from the loins of Adam, which He described in His saying: ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify." — lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this," or say, "Only our fathers associated others with Allah before, and we were descendants after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 172-173]. Their breaking of that is their failure to fulfil it.

The most correct of the sayings in my view concerning the truth is the saying of the one who said: These verses were revealed concerning the disbelieving rabbis of the Jews who were among the environs of the emigration of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and what was near them of the remnants of the Children of Israel, and whoever was upon their polytheism from the hypocrites, whose accounts we have explained earlier in this book of ours.

We have shown that the saying of Allah, mighty is His praise: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them﴾, and His saying: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day"﴾, were revealed concerning them, and concerning whoever was upon the likeness of what they were upon of associating others with Allah. However, these verses in my view, although they were revealed concerning them, are meant to include every person who is upon the likeness of what they were upon of error; and what agrees with the description of the hypocrites in them is specifically meant for all the hypocrites; and what agrees with the description of the disbelieving rabbis of the Jews is meant for all who were their counterparts in their disbelief.

That is because Allah, mighty is His praise, sometimes addresses all of them with the attribute, due to His mention of all of them at the beginning of the verses that recounted their accounts, and sometimes specifies some of them with the attribute, due to His distinguishing at the beginning of the verses between their two groups, namely: the group of hypocrites from the worshippers of idols and the people of associating others with Allah, and the group of disbelieving rabbis of the Jews. So those who break the covenant of Allah are those who abandon what Allah covenanted with them of acknowledging Muhammad ﷺ and what he brought, and of making his prophethood clear to the people, concealing the clarification of that after their knowledge of it, and of what Allah had taken from them in that regard, as Allah, mighty is His mention, said: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture, "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it." But they cast it behind their backs﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 187]. Their casting it behind their backs is their breaking of the covenant that was prescribed to them in the Torah, which we have described, and their abandoning of acting upon it.

I have only said that He meant by these verses those whom I have said He meant, because the verses — from the beginning of the five and six verses of Surah al-Baqarah — were revealed concerning them, up to the completion of their accounts.

In the verse after the report about the creation of Adam and its explanation in His saying: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil My covenant, and I will fulfil your covenant﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 40]. His address to them, mighty is His mention, with fulfilment in that matter specifically, rather than the rest of mankind, indicates that His saying: ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification﴾ is intended for their disbelievers and hypocrites, and whoever was of their partisans from the polytheists, the worshippers of idols, in their error. However, the address — although it is to those of the two groups I have described — encompasses within its rulings, and within what Allah made obligatory for them of threat, blame and rebuke, every person who was upon their path and method from all of creation and the categories of nations addressed by the command and prohibition.

The meaning of the verse, then, is: And He does not lead astray by it except those who abandon the obedience of Allah, who depart from following His command and prohibition, who break the covenants of Allah which He covenanted with them, in the books that He sent down to His messengers and upon the tongues of His prophets, by following the command of His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ and what he brought, and by obeying Allah in what He made obligatory for them in the Torah of making His command clear to the people, and informing them that they find it written with them that he is a messenger from Allah whose obedience is obligatory, and not concealing that from them. Their breaking of that and their violating it is their opposition to Allah in His covenant to them — in what I described as the covenant He made with them — after they had given their Lord the covenant to fulfil that. As our Lord, mighty is His mention, described them with it in His saying: ﴿Then there succeeded them a successor who inherited the Book, taking the goods of this lowest world, and saying, "It will be forgiven us." And if goods like it came to them, they would take it. Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them, that they would not say about Allah except the truth?﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 169].

As for His saying: "after its ratification" (min ba'di mithaqihi), it means: after Allah's making it firm (tawaththuq) with it, by taking their pledges to fulfil it to Him, with what He covenanted to them in that. However, tawaththuq is a verbal noun from your saying: "tawaththaqtu min fulanin tawaththuqan," and al-mithaq is a noun derived from it. The pronoun in "mithaqihi" refers to the name of Allah.

It may also enter into the ruling of this verse everyone who has the description with which Allah described these defiantly disobedient people, of hypocrites and disbelievers, in breaking the covenant, severing the ties of kinship, and causing corruption on the earth.

No. 572: As Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada, concerning His saying: ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification﴾: "Beware of breaking this covenant, for Allah has disliked its breaking and threatened concerning it, and has put forward in the verses of the Qur'an proof, admonition and advice concerning it. We do not know that Allah, mighty is His mention, threatened for any sin what He threatened for breaking the covenant. Whoever gives the covenant and pledge of Allah from the fruit of his heart, let him fulfil it for Allah." [[Narration 572: in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:42, and al-Shawkani 1:45. "Min thamarat qalbihi" means from the purest of his heart, taken from the fruit of a tree, because it is its essence and the best part of it. In the hadith of the pledge: "he gave him the clasp of his hand and the fruit of his heart," meaning the purest of his covenant; it is the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As in the Musnad: 6501, 6503, 6793. One says: "Fulan favoured me with the fruit of his heart," meaning the purest of his affection.]]

No. 573: Al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Ishaq narrated to us, he said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning His saying: ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth — it is they who are the losers.﴾ He said: These are six traits of the hypocrites. When they have the upper hand (al-zahara), [[al-zahara (with three vowels): abundance; he meant by it the manifestness of the matter and dominance. Had the ha' been sukun, it would be correct, from their saying: "I prevailed over so-and-so": if I rose above him and overcame him.]] they manifest all six traits: when they speak they lie, when they promise they break, when they are entrusted they betray, they break the covenant of Allah after its ratification, sever what Allah commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth. And when they are the ones who are overcome, they manifest three traits: when they speak they lie, when they promise they break, and when they are entrusted they betray. [[No. 573: in Ibn Kathir 1:120-121 from Abu al-Aliyah, then he said: "Likewise al-Rabi' ibn Anas said also." Al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur and al-Shawkani mention a report they attribute to Ibn Jarir from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas who said: "The Harurites are those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification; he said: Beware of breaking this covenant." And he used to name them: "the defiantly disobedient." Al-Durr al-Manthur 1:42, and al-Shawkani 1:45. As for Ibn Kathir, he narrated it in his tafsir 1:119 quoting Ibn Abi Hatim, with its chain, and did not attribute it to al-Tabari. I fear it is a mistake by al-Suyuti and al-Shawkani.]]

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾

Abu Ja'far said: What Allah encouraged to be joined and condemned severing of in this verse is the kinship tie (al-rahm). He has clarified that in His Book, saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then would you, if you were to turn away, cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾ [Surah Muhammad: 22]. He meant by al-rahm the kin who are bound together with you by the womb of one mother. Severing it is wronging them by failing to render what Allah obligated of their rights, and what He made binding of showing them kindness. Joining it is rendering the obligatory due to them of the rights of Allah which He made binding for them, and showing them the compassion that is due.

The "an" (that) with "yusal" (be joined) is in the genitive position, meaning it is returned to the place of the pronoun in "bihi" (by it): so the meaning of the speech is: "and they sever what Allah commanded to be joined." The pronoun in "bihi" is a reference to the mention of "an yusal". Concerning this interpretation of His saying "and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined", that it is the kinship tie, Qatada used to say:

No. 574: Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada: "and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined" — by Allah, they severed what Allah commanded to be joined by severing the kinship tie and kinship. [[No. 574: in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:42, and al-Shawkani 1:46 abridged, and its text there: "and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined; he said: the kinship tie and kinship."]]

Others have interpreted it this way: that Allah condemned them for severing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers in him, and their kin. They cited as evidence the general apparent meaning of the verse, and that there is no indication that only some of what Allah commanded to be joined is meant by it, to the exclusion of others.

Abu Ja'far said: This is a view of interpreting the verse that is not far from the truth, but Allah, mighty is His praise, has mentioned the hypocrites in more than one verse of His Book, describing them with severing kinship ties. So this is a counterpart to that, though although it is so, it indicates Allah's condemnation of every severer who severed what Allah commanded to be joined, whether a kin tie or otherwise.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, mighty is His praise: ﴿and cause corruption on the earth﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Their causing corruption on the earth is what we described earlier of their disobedience to their Lord, their disbelief in Him, their denial of His Messenger, their rejection of his prophethood, and their denial of what he brought them from Allah, that it is the truth from Him.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, mighty is His praise: ﴿Those are the losers (27)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The "khasirun" (losers) is the plural of "khasir". The losers are those who diminish their own shares of it — by their disobedience to Allah — from His mercy, just as a man suffers loss in his trade by being reduced from his capital in his sale. Likewise the disbeliever and the hypocrite suffer loss through Allah's depriving them of His mercy, which He created for His servants on the Day of Resurrection, when they are most in need of His mercy. From it one says: "khasira al-rajulu yakhsaru khasran wa khusranan wa khasaran," as Jarir ibn Atiyyah said:

Indeed Sulayt are in loss; indeed they are
the sons of a people created as slaves (aqinnah).

[[His Diwan: 598; al-Naqa'id: 4; al-Lisan (qnn); its version is "abna'u qawmin" (sons of a people). Sulayt: a clan of Banu Yarbu', Jarir's people; the name Sulayt is Ka'b ibn al-Harith ibn Yarbu'. Ghassan ibn Dhuhayl al-Sulayti had satirised Banu al-Khatafi, so Jarir satirised him with this rajaz. "Aqinnah" is the plural of "qinn" (with a kasra on the qaf): the slave whose father and mother were both owned. The feminine is also "qinn" without a ha'.]]

He means by his saying "fi al-khasar" (in loss): that is, in what diminishes their shares of nobility and generosity. It has been said that the meaning of "Those are the losers" is: "Those are the ones who perish." It is also permissible that the speaker of that intended what we have said, of the perishing of the one whom Allah described with the description by which He described him in this verse, through Allah's depriving him of what He deprived him of His mercy, by his disobedience to Him and his disbelief in Him. So he took the interpretation of the speech according to its meaning, without explaining the interpretation of the very word itself, for the interpreters of the Qur'an often do so for many reasons that prompt them to it.

Some of them said concerning that:

No. 575: It was related to me by al-Minjab, he said: Bishr ibn Ammarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Everything that Allah ascribed to non-Muslims with a term like "khasir", He means by it disbelief; and what He ascribed to the people of Islam, He means by it sin.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 28 (part 1 of 2):

The discussion of the interpretation (ta'wil) of God's words: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life, then to Him you will be returned? (28) It is He who created for you all that is on the earth⟩﴾

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding its interpretation.

Some of them said:

576. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas; and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life." He said: You were not anything, then He created you; then He will cause you to die; then He will bring you to life on the Day of Resurrection.

577. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abdullah, regarding His words: ﴿You made us die twice and You gave us life twice⟩ [Surah Ghafir: 11]. He said: It is like that in al-Baqarah: "You were dead, then He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life."

578. Abu Husayn Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Abdullah ibn Yunus narrated to me, saying: Abthar narrated to us, saying: Husayn narrated to us, from Abu Malik, regarding His words: "You made us die twice and You gave us life twice." He said: You created us and we were not anything; then You made us die; then You gave us life.

579. Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Husayn, from Abu Malik, regarding His words: "You made us die twice and You gave us life twice." He said: They were dead, so God gave them life, then He caused them to die, then He gave them life.[[The report 579: "Husayn" with a dammed unpointed ha is Ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami. And "Abu Malik" is al-Ghifari al-Kufi, whose name is "Ghazwan". His biography has already been mentioned at 168.]]

580. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Dawud narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His words: "How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life." He said: You were not anything when He created you; then He will cause you to die the true death; then He will bring you to life. And His words: "You made us die twice and You gave us life twice" are similar to it.

581. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ata al-Khurasani narrated to me, from Ibn Abbas, who said: It is His words: "You made us die twice and You gave us life twice."

582. I was told by Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: Abu al-Aliyah narrated to me, regarding God's words: "How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead," he says: When you were not anything, then He gave you life when He created you; then He caused you to die; then He will give you life on the Day of Resurrection; then you were returned to Him after life.

583. I was told by al-Minjab, who said: Bishr ibn Ammarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: "You made us die twice and You gave us life twice." He said: You were dust before He created you; this is a death. Then He gave you life and created you; this is a giving of life. Then He will cause you to die, and you will return to the graves; this is another death. Then He will resurrect you on the Day of Resurrection; this is a giving of life. So they are two deaths and two lives. This is His words: "How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life, then to Him you will be returned."

Others said:

584. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-Suddi, from Abu Salih: "How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life, then to Him you will be returned." He said: He will give you life in the grave, then He will cause you to die.

Others said:

585. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead," the verse. He said: They were dead in the loins of their fathers,[[In the manuscript: "fi aslibah", and the correct reading is "salbah" (with kasra on the sad and fath on the lam), or "asleb" (with sukun on the sad and damma on the lam). All of them are plurals of salb (with damma then sukun): the bone of the back from the upper back down to the coccyx.]] then God gave them life and created them; then He caused them to die the death that is unavoidable; then He gave them life for resurrection on the Day of Resurrection. So they are two lives and two deaths.[[The reports 575–585: some of them are in Ibn Kathir 1:122 in summary, and some in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:42 and al-Shawkani 1:46. We have disliked lengthening by detailing them.]]

Some of them said:

586. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding God's words: "Our Lord, You made us die twice and You gave us life twice." He said: He created them from the back of Adam when He took the covenant from them, and he recited: ﴿And when your Lord brought forth from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants﴾, until: ﴿Or you should say, "It was only that our fathers associated others with God before, and we were descendants after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 172–173]. He said: So He gave them intellect and took the covenant from them. He said: And He extracted a rib from the ribs of Adam, the qusayra (the lowest rib), and created Hawwa' (Eve) from it. He mentioned it from the Prophet (ﷺ). He said: That is God's words: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from one soul and created from it its mate and spread from both of them many men﴾ [Surah al-Nisa': 1]. He said: And He spread from them after that in the wombs a great creation.[[In the printed edition: "wa bathth fihima ba'da dhalik", which is an error.]] And he recited: ﴿He creates you within the wombs of your mothers, a creation after a creation﴾ [Surah al-Zumar: 6]. He said: A creation after that. He said: When He took the covenant from them, He caused them to die; then He created them in the wombs; then He caused them to die; then He gave them life on the Day of Resurrection. That is God's words: ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, You made us die twice and You gave us life twice; so we acknowledge our sins."﴾ And he recited God's words: ﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾ [Surah al-Ahzab: 7]. He said: That day. He said: And he recited God's words: ﴿And remember the favor of God upon you and His covenant with which He bound you when you said, "We hear and we obey"﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 7].[[The report 586: in Ibn Kathir 1:122 and al-Shawkani 1:47, very briefly.]]

Abu Ja'far said: Each of these sayings that we have reported from those from whom we have related them has an aspect and a method of interpretation.

* * *

As for the aspect of the interpretation of the one who interpreted His words, "How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life," to mean "you were not anything," he went in the direction of the Arabic saying about a thing that has become effaced or a matter of obscure mention: "This is a dead thing" and "This is a dead matter," meaning by describing it with death: the obscurity of its mention and the effacement of its trace among people. Likewise it is said of its opposite: "This is a living matter" and "a living mention," meaning by describing it with that: that it is prominent and well known among people, as Abu Nukhayla al-Sa'di said:

*You revived my remembrance, though I was not obscure,*
*but some remembrance is more prominent than other.*[[Al-Aghani 18:140, and al-Mu'talif wa'l-Mukhtalif by al-Amidi: 193. Abu Nukhayla is his kunya, not his name, as Abu al-Faraj said; it is said his name is Ya'mur ibn Hazn ibn Za'idah, of the Banu Sa'd ibn Zayd Manat. He was mostly known for rajaz verse, and he has a small amount of qasida, and he was undutiful to his father, so his father disowned him. The line is from verses in which he praises Maslamah ibn Abd al-Malik.]]

He means by his words, "You revived my remembrance," that you raised it and made it famous among people until it became prominent, becoming living and mentioned, after it had been obscure and dead. Likewise is the interpretation of the one who said, regarding His words, "and you were dead," that you were not anything, meaning you were obscure, having no mention; that was your death. Then He gave you life, making you human beings who are alive, who are mentioned and known. Then He will cause you to die by seizing your spirits and returning you, as you were before He gave you life, with your mention effaced, your traces erased, and your affairs obscure. Then He will bring you to life by restoring your bodies to their forms and blowing the spirit into them, making you human as you were before the causing of death, recognizing one another at your resurrection and at your gathering.[[In the printed edition: "li-ta'arafu", which is close in meaning.]]

* * *

As for the aspect of the interpretation of the one who interpreted it as the death that is the departure of the spirit from the body, he must have meant by His words, "and you were dead," that it is an address to the people of the graves after their being given life in their graves. That is a distant meaning, because the rebuke there is only a rebuke for what they had previously done and neglected of their crimes, not a request for amends and a call to return.[[Al-isti'tab: asking to be pleased, i.e., that they should seek to be pardoned by Him and beg His forgiveness, turning back from their wrongdoing and seeking His pleasure. Ista'tabahu: he asked him to return to what pleases. Al-istirja'": asking to return; istarja'ahu: God returned him to obedience.]] His words, glorified be His mention, "How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead," are a rebuke of one who asks His servants to make amends and a reproach of one who calls His creation back from sins to obedience, and from error to repentance. There is no repentance in graves after death, and no turning back in them after departure.

* * *

As for the aspect of the interpretation of Qatadah's saying, that they were dead in the loins of their fathers: he meant by that that they were drops of semen with no spirits in them, so they were like the rest of the dead things that have no spirits. His giving them life, glorified be His mention, is His blowing spirits into them; and His causing them to die after that is His seizing their spirits. His giving them life after that is the blowing of spirits into their bodies on the day the Trumpet is blown and the creation is raised for the promised day.

* * *

As for Ibn Zayd, he has made clear what he intended by his interpretation, namely that the first death is at God's restoration of His servants in the loins of their fathers after He took them from the loins of Adam; that the second giving of life is the blowing of spirits into them in the wombs of their mothers; that the second death is the seizing of their spirits for return to the dust and their going into the barzakh (intermediate state) until the day of resurrection; and that the third giving of life is the blowing of spirits into them for the resurrection of the Hour and the spreading of the Last Day.

When the one who ponders this interpretation contemplates it, he will find it contrary to the apparent meaning of God's words, which the one who explained it claimed is the meaning of what we described. That is because God, glorified be His mention, informed in His Book about those of His creation whom He informed about: that they said, "Our Lord, You made us die twice and You gave us life twice." Ibn Zayd claimed in his explanation that God gave them life three times and caused them to die three times. The matter, according to us, even if what he described of God's extraction of His descendants from the loins of Adam and His taking of their covenant is as he described, is not part of the interpretation of these two verses, I mean His words, "How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead," the verse, and His words, "Our Lord, You made us die twice and You gave us life twice," are not about it. This is because no one has claimed that God caused to die those whom He created on that day other than the death by which they went into the barzakh until the day of resurrection; so it is not permissible to direct the interpretation of the verse toward what Ibn Zayd directed it to.

* * *

Some of them said: The first death is the separation of the man's semen from his body into the woman's womb, so it is dead from its separation from his body until the blowing of the spirit into it. Then God gives it life by blowing the spirit into it, making it a complete human after stages that pass over it. Then He causes it to die the second death by seizing the spirit from it, so it is dead in the barzakh until the day the Trumpet is blown, when He returns its spirit into its body, and it returns alive and complete for the resurrection. So that is two deaths and two lives.

These people were led to this saying because they said: The death of a living being is the separation of the spirit from it. They claimed that everything of the son of Adam is alive as long as it has not separated from his living body that has a spirit. So everything that has separated from his living body that has a spirit has been left by life and has become dead, like a limb of his limbs, such as a hand of his hands or a foot of his feet: if it is cut off and separated, while the one from whom it was cut is alive, the part that separated from his body is dead, with no spirit in it, by its separation from the rest of his body in which the spirit is. They said: Likewise his semen is alive by his life as long as it has not separated from his body that has a spirit. When it separates from him, becoming detached from him, it becomes dead, like the case of the hand, the foot, and the rest of his limbs, as we described. This is a saying and an aspect of interpretation, if it had a sayer among those of authority whose interpretations of the Qur'an are accepted.

* * *

The most preferable of the sayings we have mentioned for the interpretation of God's words, glorified be His mention, "How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life," the verse, is the saying we have mentioned from Ibn Mas'ud and from Ibn Abbas: that the meaning of His words, "and you were dead," is dead in mention, obscure in the loins of your fathers as drops of semen, not recognized and not mentioned. Then He gave you life by creating you as complete humans, until you were mentioned, recognized, and alive. Then He will cause you to die by seizing your spirits and returning you to crumbled remains, not recognized and not mentioned, in the barzakh until the day you are raised. Then He will give you life after that by blowing spirits into you for the resurrection of the Hour and the cry of the Day of Resurrection. Then to God you will be returned after that, as He said, "Then to Him you will be returned," because God, glorified be His praise, gives them life in their graves before their gathering, then He gathers them for the standing of reckoning, as He, glorified be His mention, said: ﴿On the day they will come forth from the graves quickly, as if they were rushing to a idol they were making for⟩ [Surah al-Ma'arij: 43]. And He said: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and at once they will rise from the graves to their Lord⟩ [Surah Ya-Sin: 51]. The reason for which we chose this interpretation is what we have already mentioned for those who hold it, and the corruption of what opposes it through what we have already clarified before.

This verse is a rebuke from God, glorified be His praise, to those who said, "We believe in God and the Last Day," whom God informed about: that despite their saying that with their mouths, they were not believers in Him, and that they only say that to deceive God and the believers. So God censured them with His words, "How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life," and rebuked them and argued against them, in denouncing what they denounced and rejecting with their sick hearts what they rejected. He said: How can you disbelieve in God, denying His power to give you life after your death, [for the resurrection of the Hour, and the recompense of the wrongdoer among you with wrongdoing and the good-doer with good; and you were once dead drops in the loins of your fathers, and He created you as complete creatures and made you living, then caused you to die after your creation. You know that the One who did that by His power, not failing to do so by the power by which He did that to you, is able to give you life after your death and to restore you after your annihilation, and to gather you to Him for your recompense for your deeds.][[What is between the brackets is omitted from the printed edition.]]

Then our Lord, glorified be His mention, enumerated to them and to their allies among the rabbis of the Jews, whose stories He combined with the stories of the hypocrites in many verses of this surah, which opened the report about them with His words, "Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe" [[The phrase "His favors" is the object of the phrase "Then our Lord enumerated," and what is between them is a parenthetical clause.]] — His favors that had passed from Him to them and to their fathers, whose occasions were great among them. Then He deprived many of them of many of them because of the sins they had committed, the crimes they had perpetrated, and their disobedience to Him by turning from obedience to disobedience, warning them thereby of the hastening of punishment for them, as He had hastened it for their predecessors and forebears before them, and frightening them with the arrival of His punishments in their courtyard, as He brought down upon their forebears, and informing them of what salvation they had in hastening to return to Him and hastening repentance, the deliverance for them on the Day of Resurrection from the punishment.[[In the printed edition: "yuhadhdhiruhum. . . wa-yukhawwifuhum. . . ahalla bi-awwalihim, wa-ya'rifuhum", and see what will come at p. 154 Bulaq. In the manuscript and printed edition: "min al-khalas. . ." without the waw, which does not make sense, so we added it. His words "hulul mathulatihi" are the plural of mathula (with fatha on the mim and damma on the tha): meaning punishment, torment, and retribution.]]

Then, after enumerating to them the blessings in which they dwell, He began by mentioning our father and their father, Adam, father of mankind (ﷺ may peace be upon him), and what preceded from his honor with Him, and His favors toward him, and what He brought upon him and upon his enemy Iblis of swift punishment for their disobedience, which was committed by them both, and their opposition to His command which He had enjoined upon them. And [He mentioned] His covering Adam with His mercy when he repented and turned back to Him; and what He brought upon Iblis of His curse in this world, and the eternal punishment He prepared for him in the Hereafter, when he was arrogant and refused to repent and turn back to Him. [He did this] as a warning to them about His judgment concerning those who turn back to Him in repentance, and His decree concerning those who are arrogant and refuse to turn back, as an excuse from God to them and a warning to them, "that they may ponder His signs and that those of understanding may take heed" [cf. Q. 38:29]. And [He addressed] especially the People of the Book, through what He mentioned of the stories of Adam and the rest of the stories He related with it and after it, which the People of the Book knew and the unlettered nation of idolatrous worshippers of idols were ignorant of, with argumentation against them, to the exclusion of other categories of nations who have no knowledge of that, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) [[The context of this phrase: "and especially the People of the Book... with argumentation against them... to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ)". Between these words and their referents is a continuous digression, as is al-Tabari's habit in his writing.]], so that they might know, by his informing them of that, that he is a messenger sent by God, and that what he brought them is from Him, since what he related to them of these stories was from the hidden knowledge they possessed, and the preserved contents of their books, and the concealed matters of their affairs, which none claimed knowledge of except themselves and those who had taken from them and read their books.

* *

It was known of Muhammad (ﷺ) that he had never been a scribe, nor a reader of their books, nor a companion or sitter with any of them, so they could not claim that he took that from their books or from some of them. Therefore, He, mighty is His remembrance, in enumerating to them the blessings in which they dwell, despite their disbelief in Him and their neglect of thanking Him for them with the obedience to Him that is due, said: ﴿He it is who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it; then He turned to the heaven and fashioned them as seven heavens; and He is Knower of all things﴾ [Q. 2:29]. He, mighty is His remembrance, informed them that He created for them whatever is on the earth, all of it, because the earth and all that is in it are benefits for the children of Adam. As for religion, it is evidence of the oneness of their Lord; and as for this world, it is sustenance and provision for them toward His obedience and the performance of His obligations.

Therefore He, mighty is His remembrance, said: "He it is who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it."

His saying "He" is a pronoun referring to the name of God, mighty is His remembrance, returning to His name in His saying "How do you disbelieve in God?" The meaning of His creating what He created, may His praise be exalted, is His originating its very substance and bringing it from the state of non-existence into existence. And "mā" here means "alladhī" (who/which).

The meaning of the speech, then, is: How do you disbelieve in God, when you were sperm-drops in the loins of your fathers, and He made you living humans, then He causes you to die, then He gives you life again after that and resurrects you on the Day of Gathering for reward and punishment; and He is the one who bestows favor upon you by what He created for you on the earth of your means of livelihood and your indications of the oneness of your Lord.

"Kayfa" here carries the sense of wonder and reproach, not interrogation, as if he said: Woe to you, how do you disbelieve in God? As He said: ﴿Then where are you going?﴾ [Q. 81:26]. And the clause "while you were dead and He gave you life" stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). In it is an implied "qad" [in the printed edition: "and in it is an implied qad", and the term 'damīr' here is not used in the sense the grammarians use it, but rather the hidden, concealed pronoun. See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:23–25], but it is omitted because the context indicates it. This is because when a verbal clause (fa'ala) occupies the position of a circumstantial clause, it is understood that it implicitly requires "qad", as He, mighty is His praise, said: ﴿or they come to you with their hearts constricted﴾ [Q. 4:90], meaning: their hearts having become constricted. And as you say to a man: "You have risen, your livestock has increased," meaning: your livestock has increased.

In a manner similar to what we have said regarding His saying "He it is who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it," Qatadah used to say:

587 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, regarding His saying "He it is who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it": "Yes, by God, He subjected to you whatever is on the earth [[The report: 587 – in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:42 and al-Shawkani 1:48, and in both there is an addition beyond what is in the originals of al-Tabari, which is: "...whatever is on the earth, all of it, as a dignity from God and a blessing for the son of Adam, as enjoyment and sustenance and benefit until a term."
Both of them also added another report which they said was transmitted by Ibn Jarir from Mujahid: "Regarding His saying: He it is who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it, he said: He subjected to you whatever is on the earth, all of it." The chain of this report is the one that comes at number 591, since it is its completion, as is made clear in what al-Suyuti and al-Shawkani transmitted. It is likely that the copies of al-Tabari in our hands have an omission that forced the copyists, given the length of the book; such a gap and such an addition have occurred earlier.]]

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then He rose over the heaven and made them seven heavens﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The scholars differed over the interpretation of His words, "Then He rose (istawa) toward the heaven."

Some of them said: The meaning of "istawa ila al-sama'" ("rose toward the heaven") is that He turned toward it, as you say: "So-and-so was facing (muqbilan) so-and-so, then he istawa over me, cursing me," and "istawa toward me, cursing me," meaning: he turned toward me, cursing me. They cited as evidence that istawa means turning toward the verse of the poet:

*I say, when they had cut through Sharwara with us,*
*Swift camels, and they turned (istawayna) from the resting place (al-dujuu')*

[The verse is by Tamim ibn Ubayy ibn Muqbil (Mu'jam maAsta'jam: 795, 857), and its reading is "thawani" instead of "sawamid." Sharwara is a mountain between Banu Asad and Banu 'Amir, on the road from Mecca to Kufa. Al-Dujuu', with a dotted dad, is also a place between the lands of Hudhayl and Banu Sulaym. "Sawamid" is the plural of "samid": the camels "samadat" in their journey, meaning they pressed on and travelled constantly without showing fatigue. "Sawamid" means camels that do not tire. The "nun" in "qata'n" refers to the camels.]

He claimed that the poet meant they went out from the resting place, and that this meant "turned toward" in his view. But this interpretation of the verse is wrong. The meaning of "istawayna min al-dujuu'" is: they set themselves straight upon the road, leaving the resting place, meaning they kept themselves steady upon it.

Others said: That was not from God, exalted is His remembrance, as a change of place, but it means His act, as you say: "The caliph was dealing with the people of Iraq, then he moved (tahawwala) to Syria," meaning: the moving of his action. [Some of them said: The words "Then He rose toward the heaven" mean: "istawat" (it rose/was straight)] [This sentence between the brackets is not in the manuscript, and it seems to have been inserted.] As the poet said:

*I say to him, when he was laid in his dust:*
*"Over which religion did Mus'ab kill the people?"*

[I have not found this verse. In the printed edition it reads "qabl al-ra's Mus'ab," which is certainly an error. In the manuscript it reads "fi tharatihi," which has no meaning; perhaps it is "fi turathihi." I am in doubt about all of that. However, the Mus'ab mentioned in the poetry is, in my estimation, Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr.]

Others said: "Then He rose toward the heaven" means He intended it ('amada laha). [In the printed edition: "'amada ilayha."] He said: Every person who abandons an action and turns to another is one who has set himself straight (mustawin) for what he intended, and turned toward it.

Others said: Istawa is ascending, and ascending is elevation. Among those who said this was al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

588. It was related to me from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: "Then He rose toward the heaven": he says, He ascended toward the heaven.

[The report 588 is in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:43; the following report, 589, is part of it.]

Then those who interpreted istawa as elevation and ascent differed about who rose toward the heaven. Some said: The one who rose toward the heaven and was high above it is its Creator and its Originator. Others said: Rather, the one high above it is the smoke, which God made the heaven for the earth. [In the printed edition: "al-'ali ilayha."]

Abu Ja'far said: In the language of the Arabs, istawa has several meanings. Among them: the end of a man's youth and strength; when he reaches that state it is said, "The man has istawa." Among them: the straightening of something that had been crooked among affairs and matters; it is said of this: "His affair istawa for So-and-so," meaning it became straight after being crooked. From this is the verse of al-Tirimmah ibn Hakim:

*The long time passed over the traces of Muhaddad, its eternity,*
*And it was effaced, and its country istawa with it.*

[From his Diwan: 110. Al-Lisan (s-w-y) says: "This verse is of mixed metre: its first hemistich is from al-Munsarih, and its second from al-Khafif." Al-Rasm: the remnants of the dwellings lying on the ground. Muhaddad is the name of a woman. Al-Abad: the long age, and the "ha'" in "abadahu" refers to the traces. 'Afa: it was worn away and its trace went. Al-Balad: the trace. He says: its traces were erased until it istawa with no trace.]

That is, it became straight with it. Among them: turning toward a thing, as it is said, "So-and-so istawa over So-and-so" with what he dislikes and what displeases him, after having been good to him. Among them: taking possession and seizing control [In the manuscript: "al-istila' wa al-ihtiwa'"], as in the saying: "So-and-so istawa over the kingdom," meaning he took control of it and possessed it. Among them: height and elevation, as in the saying of the speaker: "So-and-so istawa on his throne," meaning his being high above it.

The meaning most fitting to the words of God, exalted is His praise, "Then He rose toward the heaven and made them complete," is: He was high above them and ascended; He governed them by His power, and created them as seven heavens.

It is strange how someone who denies the meaning understood in the language of the Arabs, in the interpretation of God's words "Then He rose toward the heaven," which means height and elevation, does so in fear, in his own view, that he would be obliged, by his claim, if he interpreted it in its evident meaning in this way, to say that He rose and was high only after He had been beneath it. Then he interpreted it by the unknown from among its strange interpretations, yet he did not escape what he fled from! It is said to him: You claim that the interpretation of His words "istawa" is "turned toward"; was He then turned away from the heaven and then turned toward it? If he claims that this is not a turning of action but a turning of governance, it is said to him: Then say likewise: He was high above it with the height of kingship and authority, not the height of movement and cessation. Then he will not say anything in this matter without being obliged, in the end, to something similar. Had we not disliked prolonging the book with what is not of its kind, we would have informed you of the corruption of the saying of every speaker who spoke on this matter in a way that contradicts the saying of the people of truth. What we have made clear of it is enough, if God wills, for the person of understanding to be guided to what suffices him.

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: Tell us about God's istawa toward the heaven, was it before the creation of the heaven or after it?

It is said: After it, and before He made them seven heavens, as He, exalted is His praise, said: ﴿Then He rose toward the heaven while it was smoke, and said to it and to the earth: Come, willingly or unwillingly﴾ [Surah Fussilat: 11]. The istawa was after He created it as smoke, and before He made it seven heavens.

Some said: He only said "istawa toward the heaven," and there was no heaven yet, like a man saying to another, "Make this garment," while he only has yarn.

As for His words "fa-sawwahunna" (and made them complete), He means: He prepared them, created them, governed them, and straightened them. In the language of the Arabs, taswiyah (making complete) means straightening, setting right, and preparing, as one says: "So-and-so prepared this matter for So-and-so," meaning he straightened it, set it right, and made it ready for him. Likewise God's making His heavens complete means: His straightening them according to His will, His governing them according to His purpose, and His unfastening them after they had been sealed. [In the printed edition: "ba'da irtaqihinna," which is nothing; in the manuscript: "ba'da an tataqahunna," and it is apparent that it is a distortion of what we have established. Irtataqa the thing means: it was joined and knit until there was no crack in it. This is an interpretation of what is in Surah al-Anbiya', 30, from God's words: ﴿Did not those who disbelieved see that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, and We unfastened them?﴾ The fatq is the splitting.]

589. As: It was related to me from 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: "fa-sawwahunna sab'a samawat": he says, He made complete their creation, "and He is Knower of all things."

[Report 589 is in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:43, and it is part of the previous report, 588.]

He, exalted is His remembrance, said: "fa-sawwahunna," bringing their pronoun into the form of the pronoun of the collective. [The pronoun (al-mukannan) is what the grammarians have agreed to call the pronoun, because it is a substitute for what its mention is hidden. In the printed edition: "al-jam'" in place of "al-jami'" wherever it is mentioned in the following passages in this phrase.] He had said before: "Then He rose toward the heaven," so He brought it out as singular. He brought their pronoun out in the form of the pronoun of the plural, because "al-sama'" is a plural whose singular is "samawa," so the reckoning of its singular and its plural is like that of "baqarah" and "baqar," and "nakhlah" and "nakhl," and similar things. For this reason it is made feminine at one time, and it is said: "hadhihi sama'" (this is a heaven), and it is made masculine at another, and it is said: "al-sama' munfatir bihi" (the heaven is split by it) [Surah al-Muzzammil: 18], as is done with the plural that has no difference from its singular except the entry and exit of the "ha'" (ta marbutah): one says, "hadha baqar" and "hadhihi baqar," "hadha nakhl" and "hadhihi nakhl," and similar things.

Some of the Arabic grammarians claimed that the heaven is one, but it indicates the heavens, so He said "fa-sawwahunna," meaning by that the one mentioned and what it indicates of the rest of the heavens that were not mentioned with it. [The "Arabic grammarians" is al-Farra', though the wording is not his, in his book Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:25, but he went this way also in his book, pp. 126–131.] He said: It is only made masculine when it is made masculine while being feminine, so it is said: "al-sama' munfatir bihi," as the feminine is made masculine, and as the poet said:

*No cloud poured its rain,*
*And no earth grew its herbage.*

[The verse is from the poetry of 'Amir ibn Juwayn al-Ta'i, in Sibawayh 1:240, Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:127, al-Khizana 1:21–26, Sharh Shawahid al-Mughni: 319, al-Kamil 1:406, 2:68. Before it, describing an army: "And a girl among the daughters of kings, I jingled her anklet with the horses. Like a cloud of rain with its lightning, it throws the clouds and they throw for it. I promised her after the passing of the stars, a golden-haired girl who causes much rain..." Then "Fa-la mazna..."]

And as the poet of Banu Tha'laba, A'sha, said:

*If you see my hair has been changed,*
*Then the events have humiliated it.*

[This is A'sha of Banu Tha'laba, and A'sha of Banu Qays, and al-A'sha are all one person; his Diwan 1:120. In Sibawayh 1:239, Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:128, al-Khizana 4:578. The Diwan's version: "If you care for me, and I have a forelock, then the events have humbled it." The version of Sibawayh as in al-Tabari, except that he related "awda biha" (destroyed it). "Alwa bihi" means: went with it and destroyed it. "Awda bihi" means: destroyed it, too. As for "azra biha": that is, belittled it and brought humiliation upon it, from zirariyya, which is disparagement. All are good.]

Some said: The heaven, even if it is a heaven above a heaven and an earth above an earth, is in interpretation one, if you wish, and then that one becomes a plural, as one says: "thawb akhlaq wa asmal" (a worn garment and rags), and "burmah a'shar" (a pot in pieces) for the broken, and "burmah akhsar wa ajbar" (a pot in pieces). "Akhlaq" means that its sides are worn. [Akhlaq is the plural of khalq (with two vowels): worn out. Asmal is the plural of simal (with two vowels): thin, torn and worn. "Burmah ajbar," the opposite of their saying "burmah aksar," seems to be the plural of "burmah jabr" (with a fatha and sukun), even though they did not say it in the singular, just as they did not say "burmah kasr" in the singular. Its origin is from "jabr al-'azm," which is the setting of the bone after its breaking.]

If someone says to us: You have said that God, exalted is His praise, rose toward the heaven while it was smoke before He made it seven heavens, and then He made it seven after His istawa toward it; how then do you claim that it is a collective?

It is said: They were seven, not yet straightened, and so He, exalted is His remembrance, said: "fa-sawwahunna sab'an" (and made them seven, complete). As:

590. Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to me, who said: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: The first thing God, blessed and exalted, created was light and darkness; then He distinguished between them, making darkness a black, dark night, and making light a bright, seeing day. Then He raised the seven heavens from smoke (it is said, and God knows best, from the smoke of water), until they stood without being fastened together. He made dark the night of the lowest heaven and brought forth its forenoon, so night and day ran in it, and in it there was no sun, moon, or stars. Then He spread out the earth and set it firm with mountains, measured in it the sustenance, and scattered in it what He willed of creatures. He finished the earth and what He measured in it of its sustenance in four days. Then He rose toward the heaven while it was smoke, as He said, and fastened them together, and placed in the lowest heaven its sun, moon, and stars, and inspired in each heaven its command. He completed their creation in two days, and finished the creation of the heavens and the earth in six days. Then He rose on the seventh day above His heavens, then He said to the heavens and the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly, for what I intend for you," so they became calm about it, willingly or unwillingly. They said: "We came obedient."

[Report 590 is, in reality, an explanation of verses 9–12 of Surah Fussilat. Al-Tabari did not mention it at its place when interpreting them (24:60–65, Bulaq edition). Likewise Ibn Kathir, al-Suyuti, and al-Shawkani did not mention it at this place, nor at its place in the tafsir of Surah Fussilat. It is from the words of Ibn Ishaq, and there is no fault in them for turning away from quoting it. Al-Tabari later stated clearly that he mentioned it as corroboration, not as proof, since he found it clearer in explanation and better in exposition.]

Ibn Ishaq has informed us that God, exalted is His praise, rose toward the heaven after creating the earth and what is in it, and the heavens were seven from smoke, so He made them complete as He described. We cited Ibn Ishaq's saying as corroboration for what we said on this matter only because he is clearer in exposition concerning the creation of the heavens, that they were seven from smoke before our Lord's istawa toward them for their completion, than others, and better in explanation of what we intended to use as proof: that the meaning of the heaven of which God, exalted is His remembrance, said "Then He rose toward the heaven," is the meaning of the whole, as we have described. And that He, exalted is His praise, only said "fa-sawwahunna," since the heaven means the whole, as we have explained.

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: What is the description of God's completing the heavens, which He mentioned in His words "fa-sawwahunna," since they had been created seven before His completing them? And what is the reason for mentioning their creation after mentioning the creation of the earth? Is it because it was created before it, or for some other meaning? [In the printed edition: "am bi-ma'na," and this is better.]

It is said: We have mentioned that in the report we related from Ibn Ishaq, and we will confirm it with emphasis by adding to it reports from some earlier predecessors and their sayings. [In the printed edition: "wa nazid dhalika tawkidan."]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 29 (part 2 of 2):

591. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas; and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is He who created for you all that is on the earth. Then He rose to the heaven and made it seven heavens" [Qur'an 2:29]. He said: Indeed, Allah, blessed and exalted, His Throne was upon the water, and He had created nothing other than what He had created before the water. When He wanted to create the creation, He brought forth smoke from the water, and it rose above the water and towered over it, so He named it "sky" (sama'). Then He dried up the water and made it one earth, then He split it apart and made seven earths in two days, on Sunday and Monday. He created the earth upon a fish, and the fish is the nun that Allah mentioned in the Qur'an: "Nun. By the pen" [Qur'an 68:1]. The fish is in the water, the water is on the back of a rock (safah), the rock is on the back of an angel, the angel is on a stone, and the stone is in the wind, which is the stone that Luqman mentioned, neither in the heaven nor in the earth. Then the fish moved and convulsed, so the earth quaked, and He set the mountains upon it and it became still. The mountains then fell upon the earth, and that is His saying: "And He cast upon the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you" [Qur'an 16:15]. [In the originals: "and He made for it firm mountains lest it shake with you," which is an error that the pen of the copyists slipped into, in my judgment, and the verse is as I have cited it in Surah al-Nahl, and similarly in Surah Luqman: 10] [Surah al-Nahl: 15]. He created the mountains in it, and its sustenance for its inhabitants, its trees, and what befits it, in two days, on Tuesday and Wednesday, and that is when He says: "Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days and set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds. And He placed in it firm mountains above it and blessed it," meaning: He caused its trees to grow. "And He measured therein its sustenance," meaning: its sustenance for its people, "in four days, equal for those who ask" [Qur'an 41:9-10], meaning: say to whoever asks you: the matter is thus. [In the manuscript: "He says: whoever asked, so the matter is thus."] "Then He rose to the heaven when it was smoke" [Qur'an 41:11]. That smoke was from the breath of the water when it breathed, so He made it one heaven, then split it apart and made it seven heavens in two days, on Thursday and Friday. The day of Friday was so named because on it the creation of the heavens and the earth was gathered (jama'a). "And He revealed in each heaven its command" [Qur'an 41:12]. He said: He created in each heaven what He created of angels and of the creation within it, of seas, mountains of hail, and what is not known. Then He adorned the lowest heaven with the stars, making them an adornment and a protection, guarding against the devils. When He finished creating what He willed, He established Himself upon the Throne. That is when He says: "He created the heavens and the earth in six days" [Qur'an 7:54]. And He says: "They were a closed mass, and We unclosed them" [Qur'an 21:30]. [Report 591: cited in Ibn Kathir 1:123, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:42-43, and al-Shawkani 1:48. The discussion of this chain has passed, and my brother al-Sayyid Ahmad Shakir fully investigated it in its place (see report 168). Al-Tabari's statement has also passed when he addressed this chain in report no. 465, p. 353: "If that is sound, and I do not know it to be sound, since I am doubtful about its chain..." Al-Tabari, in his commentary, has transmitted reports whose chains he did not consider sound, knowing that the scholars of his time were engaged in examining chains and scrutinizing them, and accepted nothing except after close scrutiny of its chain. If you ask: why does al-Tabari cite a report like this, whose chain he doubts? The answer: he did not cite it to argue from what is in it, but to draw a lesson of one meaning, namely that Allah exalted raised the seven heavens from smoke, then spread out the earth and set it firm with mountains, then rose to the heaven when it was smoke, so He made them seven firmly fashioned, and revealed in each heaven its command. There is no harm in drawing a lesson from such a report, because the meaning he intended is the apparent and explicit meaning of the Qur'an. Even if the report itself was among what some Companions received from the Children of Israel, not from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). There is no proof except in what Allah revealed in His Book, or in what He revealed to His Prophet and which is confirmed to have come from him. Whatever is confirmed from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), we accept it and do not let anyone judge it, for his word is the guardian over the sayings of men.] [Surah al-Anbiya: 30].

592. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: "It is He who created for you all that is on the earth. Then He rose to the heaven." He said: He created the earth before the heaven. When He created the earth, smoke erupted from it, and that is when He says: "Then He rose to the heaven and made it seven heavens." He said: some of them above others, and seven earths, some of them beneath others [Report 592: cited in Ibn Kathir 1:124, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:42, and al-Shawkani 1:48].

593. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "and made them seven heavens," he said: some of them above others, between every two heavens a distance of five hundred years' journey.

594. Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying, where He mentioned the creation of the earth before the heaven, then mentioned the heaven before the earth, and that is because Allah created the earth with its sustenance without having spread it out before the heaven: "Then He rose to the heaven and made them seven heavens," then He spread out the earth after that, and that is His saying: "And the earth after that He spread out" [Qur'an 79:30].

595. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Abu Ma'shar narrated to me, from Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id, from Abd Allah ibn Salam that he said: Indeed Allah began the creation on Sunday. He created the earths on Sunday and Monday, created the sustenance and the firm mountains on Tuesday and Wednesday, and created the heavens on Thursday and Friday, and He finished in the last hour of Friday, creating Adam in it in haste. That is the hour in which the Hour will be established.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The meaning of the speech, then, is: He is the One who bestowed favor upon you, so He created for you all that is on the earth and subjected it to you, as a bounty from Him upon you, so that it would be a provision for you in your worldly life and an enjoyment until the arrival of your appointed terms, and a sign for you of the oneness of your Lord. Then He ascended to the seven heavens, while they were smoke, and He made them complete and firmly fashioned, and caused to run in some of them His sun, moon and stars, and determined in each of them what He determined of His creation [Reports 593-595: not found in any of those references].

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: "And He is, of all things, Knowing" (29)

By His saying "He" (huwa) is meant Himself, and by "of all things, Knowing" is meant that He who created you, and created for you all that is on the earth, and perfected the seven heavens with what is in them, making them firm from the smoke of water, and perfecting their making, nothing is hidden from Him, O hypocrites and unbelievers who disbelieve in Him from the People of the Book (in the manuscript: "and the People of the Book," as a conjunction), of what you reveal and what you conceal within yourselves, even if your hypocrites display with their tongues their saying: "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," while they are in denial of it inwardly. And your rabbis denied what My Messenger brought them of guidance and light, while they knew its truth. They rejected it and concealed what I had taken as a covenant from them, in clarifying to My creation the matter of Muhammad and his prophethood, while they knew it. Rather, I am aware of that and of your other affairs and the affairs of others. Indeed, I am Knowing of all things.

His saying "'alim" means "'alim" (knowing). It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he would say: it is the one whose knowledge is complete.

596. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated to me, from Ibn Abbas, who said: the knowing one whose knowledge is complete [Report 596: not found in our references].

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 1 of 6):

The discussion of His saying: ﴿And when your Lord said﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: Some of those ascribed to knowledge of the Arabic languages from among the people of Basra [[This is Abu 'Ubayda (see Tafsir Ibn Kathir 1:125), as has already passed in several places in al-Tabari's words. What supports this is that al-Baghdadi, in explaining the verse of ʿAbd Manaf ibn Rabiʿi (al-Khizana 3:171), transmitted from Ibn al-Sayyid: "Abu 'Ubayda said: idhā (إذا) is superfluous, therefore no answer is given to it." However, the two witnesses that follow concern the superfluity of "idhā," not of "idh" (إذ), and this is from the boldness and error of Abu 'Ubayda. Whoever the speaker is, he is bold and mistaken.]] claimed that the meaning of His saying, "And when your Lord said," is "and your Lord said," and that "idh" (إذ) is one of the superfluous particles, its meaning being omission. He argued for what he had described from him with the verse of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur:

﴿fa-idhā wa-dhālika lā mahāha li-dhikrihi ... wa-l-dahru yuʿqibu ṣāliḥan bi-fasād﴾

[[From the Mufaḍḍaliyyāt, poem no. 44. The verse is not in the recension of Ibn al-Anbari, the commentator on the Mufaḍḍaliyyāt. Regarding "lā mahāha": it is said, "laysa li-ʿaysinā mahhun" (with two fatḥas) and "mahāh," meaning there is no pleasantness or freshness in it. They have claimed that the waw in His saying "fa-idhā wa-dhālika..." is superfluous and intrusive, as if he said: "fa-idhā dhālika..." Al-Tabari said in his commentary on His saying, exalted is He: "until, when they come to it and its gates are opened, and its keepers say to them, 'Peace be upon you; you have done well, so enter it, to abide therein'" (vol. 24, p. 24): "The people of Arabic disagreed about the place of the answer to 'idhā' in His saying, '(until when they come to it).' Some of the grammarians of Basra said: it is said that His saying '(and its keepers said to them)' has the meaning of 'said to them,' as if it cancels the waw. Something has come in poetry that resembles the waw being superfluous, as the poet said: 'fa-idhā wa-dhālika yā kubayshatu lam yakun ... illā tawahhuma ḥālimin bi-khayāl,' so it seems he meant: 'fa-idhā dhālika lam yakun.'" Abu Sa'id al-Sukkari said in his explanation of the poems of the Hudhayl (2:100), in explanation of the verse of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali: "fa-idhā wa-dhālika laysa illā ḥīnahu ... wa-idhā maḍā shayʾun ka-an lam yuf'al," Abu Sa'id said: "The waw is superfluous. I said to Abu 'Amr: a man says, 'Our Lord and to You is the praise.' He said: a man says, 'I have taken this for such and such,' and he says, 'and it is for you.'"

Ibn al-Shajari said in his Amali (1:358): "It has been said that in the verse the waw is intrusive, but that is nothing, because the superfluity of the waw has not been established in any eloquent speech." What Ibn al-Shajari adopted is correct, and each of the witnesses they cited has an explanation that is not the place to detail. Sufficient as a refutation of what Abu 'Ubayda claimed about the superfluity of "idh" is al-Tabari's statement in this place, as will come: "It is not permissible to nullify a particle that was evidence for a meaning in the speech," and so on to the end of what he said. It is from sound understanding. His explanation of the verse afterwards shows that he does not hold the superfluity of the waw, in his saying in its explanation: "So then what we are in, and what has passed of our life."

Then he said: its meaning is: "that is, there is no pleasantness in its remembrance." And with the verse of ʿAbd Manaf ibn Rabiʿ al-Hudhali:

﴿ḥattā idhā aslaknūhum fī Qutāʾida ... shallan kamā taṭrudu al-jammālatu al-shurudā﴾

[[From the Diwan of the Hudhayl (2:42); it occurs in al-Tabari's commentary at 14:8, 18:13, 24:25 (Bulaq edition), al-Khizana 3:170–174, Amali Ibn al-Shajari 1:358, 2:289, and many others. "Aslaka al-rajul al-ṭarīq" means he took the road, and "aslakahu ghayruhu fīhi" means another made him take it, and "asaklahu al-ṭarīq" means he made him enter it or compelled him to it. Qutaʾida: a mountain between al-Munsarif and al-Ruḥaʾ, that is, on the road between Mecca and Medina. "Shalla al-sāʾiq al-ibil" means he drove the camels ahead of him with driving. "Marra fulān yashullu al-ʿaduww bi-l-sayf" means he drives them with the sword so that they flee before him. Al-jammāla are the owners of camels. "Sharada al-baʿīr" means the camel fled and went off into the land; the plural of shārid is shurud (with two fathas), like khādim and khadam. The plural of shurūd is shurud (with two ḍammas). ʿAbd Manaf mentions a people who raided their enemy, dislodging them from their dwellings and compelling them to "Qutaʾida," driving them with swords, spears and arrows, as camels that have bolted are driven. The answer to "idhā" is estimated as: "they drove them, a driving," a verb omitted and indicated by the verbal noun, as will come in al-Tabari's speech later.]]

He said: its meaning is "until they made them enter."

Abu Ja'far said: The matter in this is contrary to what he said. That is because "idh" is a particle that comes with the meaning of a condition and indicates an unknown time. It is not permissible to nullify a particle that was evidence for a meaning in the speech. Whether someone says it has the meaning of "superfluity," while it is evidence in the speech for a understood meaning, or someone else says, regarding the entire speech spoken, that it is evidence of what is intended, and it has the meaning of "superfluity" [[In the manuscript: "huwa bi-maʿnā al-tatawwul fī al-kalām." This is an error. "Al-tatawwul," in the terminology of al-Tabari and others, is addition in speech in the sense of nullification, as has passed above on p. 140 of Bulaq. Al-Tabari wanted to negate what some grammarians insisted upon regarding the claim of meaninglessness and superfluity in speech. He says: if a particle or word has an understood meaning in speech, and then you claim it is a nullified superfluity, it is permissible for someone else to claim that a complete sentence with an understood meaning, or a complete speech with an understood meaning, is likewise merely a nullified superfluity. Thereby every meaning of every speech would be nullified, since a claimant could nullify whatever he wishes by whatever boldness and assertion he desires. This supports our school which we have accepted in the earlier commentary.]].

And for what the one we described claimed, in the verse of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, that "idhā" means "superfluity," there is no understood way; rather, if it were removed from the speech, the meaning that al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur intended by his saying would be nullified:

﴿fa-idhā wa-dhālika lā mahāha li-dhikrihi﴾

That is because he meant by His saying: "so then what we are in, and what has passed of our life." He indicated by his saying "dhālika" what was described before of his life in which he was. "Lā mahāha li-dhikrihi" means there is no taste or excellence in it, because time has followed that righteousness with corruption. Likewise is the meaning of the saying of ʿAbd Manaf ibn Rabiʿ:

﴿ḥattā idhā aslaknūhum fī Qutāʾida ... shallan .................﴾

If "idhā" were dropped from it, the meaning of the speech would be nullified, because its meaning is: "until when they made them enter Qutaʾida, they drove, a driving." So his saying "asalkūhum shallan" indicates the omitted meaning, and it is dispensed with mentioning it by the indication of "idhā" upon it, so it was omitted, as what we have mentioned earlier in our book [[In the printed edition: "as what we have mentioned earlier in our book according to what the Arabs do..." In the manuscript: "as he said, we have mentioned earlier..." Both are errors; the first is a change by the editors, the second a misreading of "qāl" for "dalla," and the black dot is a blank in the original copied from, or the "mā" lost its alif and "m" was smudged, so someone took it for a separation mark. It should be noted that al-Tabari referred to what passed in this book at pp. 114 and 327, so consult it.]] — according to what the Arabs do in similar cases. And as al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

﴿fa-inna al-maniyyata man yakhshāhā ... fa-sawfa tuṣādifuhu aynamā﴾

[[From a well-made poem in the Mukhtarat of Ibn al-Shajari (1:16), al-Khizana (4:438), and Sharh Shawahid al-Mughni (p. 65); after it: "wa-in tatakhaṭṭāka asbābuhā ... fa-inna quṣāraka an tahrama"]]

He means: wherever he goes. And as the Arabs say: "I came to you from before and from after," meaning from before that and from after that. Thus is that in "idhā," as the speaker says: "If your brother honours you, then honour him, and if not, then do not honour him." He means: "If he does not honour you, then do not honour him."

And from that is the saying of another:

﴿fa-idhā wa-dhālika lā yaḍurruka ḍurruhu ... fī yawmin as'alu nā'ilan aw ankadu﴾

[[I do not know its speaker. In the printed edition: "fī yawm athil nā'ilan aw ankadā," which is an ancient error. In the printed edition: "as'al nā'ilan," which is closer to correct. "Al-ḍurr": bad condition, from poverty, hardship, affliction or grief. "Al-nā'il": what one obtains and reaches of kindness from a person. "Nakada" means: he asked him; he diminished the giving, or did not give him at all. The speaker says: "Give what you have given, kindly; there is no good in the one who is refused and the one who refuses."]]

is similar to the meaning we have mentioned in the verse of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur. Likewise is the meaning of God's saying, exalted is His praise: "And when your Lord said to the angels," for if "idh" were nullified and removed from the speech, the speech would depart from the meaning it has, and in it is "idh."

If someone says to us: What is the meaning of that? And what brings in "idh," since there is nothing before it in the speech to which it is joined? [[In the printed edition: "fa-in qāla qā'il," without "lanā."]]
