It is said to him: We have mentioned earlier [[See what has passed at p. 424 and following.]] that God, exalted is His praise, addressed those whom He addressed with His saying, "How do you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life," with these verses and those that follow, rebuking them, making their evil conduct and their station in misguidance ugly to them, along with the blessings He bestowed upon them and their forefathers; and reminding them, by enumerating His blessings upon them and their forefathers, of His might, that they should follow the way of those of their forefathers who perished in disobeying Him, so that He would make them follow their way in punishment; and informing them of what came from Him of His inclination toward the penitent among them, as a way of making them repent. So among what He enumerated of His blessings upon them was that He created for them all that is in the earth, and subjected to them what is in the heavens of its sun, moon and stars, and other benefits of it which He made for them and for all the children of Adam along with them. So in His saying, exalted is His mention, "How do you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life, then He causes you to die, then He gives you life, then to Him you will be returned," there is the meaning: remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, when I created you and you were nothing, and I created for you all that is in the earth, and I fashioned for you what is in the sky. Then He connected, by His saying, "And when your Lord said to the angels," upon the meaning implied by His saying, "How do you disbelieve in God," since it implied what I have described from His saying: remember My blessing when I did with you and I did, and remember My doing with your father Adam, when I said to the angels: I am placing on the earth a khalifa [[What Abu Ja'far said, may God cover him with His forgiveness, is among the finest reflection on the interpretation of the Book of God, and of good insight into Arabic and the secrets of its concision, its reliance on sufficing with few words that indicate much meaning, and its taking of particles as links for comprehensive meanings, not for returning one particle upon another that preceded it.]].

If someone says: Is there for that a parallel in the speech of the Arabs by which we know the soundness of what you said? It is said: Yes, more than can be counted. Among that is the saying of the poet:

﴿a-ajiddaka lan tarā bi-thuʿaylibāt ... wa-lā baydāna nājiyatan dhamūlā﴾

[[It is by al-Mirar ibn Saʿid al-Fiqʿasi; Maʿani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:171; Majalis Thaʿlab p. 159; Lisan (bayd), (ṭafl), (nashgh); and Muʿjam al-Buldan (thuʿaylibat). Thuʿaylibat and Baydan are two places. "Al-nājiya": the swift she-camel, from najāʾ, which is swiftness of travel. "Al-dhamūl": the she-camel that travels a swift, gentle pace; "dhamalat dhamīlan and dhamalānan."]]

﴿wa-lā mutadārikin wa-l-shamsu ṭiflun ... bi-baʿḍi nawāshighi al-wādi ḥumūlā﴾

[[It is narrated as "wa-lā mutalāfiyan" in the accusative. "Tadāraka al-qawm" (transitive) means he overtook them, or tried to catch up with them. "Talāfāhu" means he also overtook him. "The sun is a child": here it means at its rising, not at its setting, it took from the small child. "Nawāshigh al-wādī" is the plural of nāshigha: the watercourse into the valley. "Al-ḥumūl" are the howdahs in which women are carried by camels. The camels and what is upon them were called ḥumūl because they carry howdahs on them for the journey. He says: you will not overtake them, for they set out early on the journey.]]

He said: "wa-lā mutadārik," and no verb preceded it with a form to join it to, nor an inflected particle taking its case, so that "mutadārik" would be returned upon it in its case. But since before it there was a negated verb with "lan" indicating the intended meaning of the omitted element in the speech, he dispensed with mentioning what was omitted by the indication of what appeared of it, and treated the speech in meaning and case as if what was omitted from it were manifest. Because His saying:

﴿a-ajiddaka lan tarā bi-thuʿaylibāt﴾

means: "a-ajiddaka lasta bi-rāʾin," so he returned "mutadāriken" upon the place of "tarā," as if "lasta" and "bāʾ" were both present in the speech. Likewise His saying, "And when your Lord said," since before it had preceded God's reminder to those addressed of what had preceded before them and before their forefathers of His favours and blessings, and His saying "And when your Lord said to the angels," together with what follows of the blessings He enumerated to them and drew their attention to their occasions, returned "idh" upon the place of "wa-kuntum amwātan fa-aḥyākum." That is because the meaning of that is: remember these of My blessings, and this in which I said to the angels. Since the first was requiring "idh," He connected with "idh" upon its place in the first, as we described from the poet's saying in "wa-lā mutadārik."

\* \*

The discussion of His saying: ﴿lil-malāʾika﴾ (to the angels)

Abu Ja'far said: "al-malāʾika" is the plural of "malak," except that the singular without the hamza is more common and better known in the speech of the Arabs than with the hamza. That is because they say in the singular: "malak min al-malāʾika," dropping the hamza from it, and they vowel the lām which would have been quiescent if the noun were hamzated. They vowel it with fatḥa, because they transfer the vowel of the hamza that is in it, upon its dropping, to the quiescent letter before it. When they make the plural of the singular, they return the plural to the original and hamza it, and say "malāʾika."

The Arabs do much of that in their speech, leaving the hamza in a word that is hamzated, so their speech proceeds leaving its hamza in one state and hamzating it in another, as in their saying: "ra'aytu fulānan" (I saw so-and-so), then their speech went on hamzating "ra'aytu," then they said "nará, tará, yará," and their speech went on in "yafʿalu" and its counterparts leaving the hamza, until the hamza with them became anomalous, though the hamza in them is original. Likewise it is with "malak and malāʾika": their speech went on leaving the hamza from the singular, and hamzating it in the whole plural. Sometimes the singular comes hamzated, as the poet said:

﴿fa-lasta li-insiyyin wa-lākin li-malʾakin ... taḥaddara min jawwi al-samāʾi yaṣūbu﴾

[[The discussion of this verse has passed at p. 333; the manuscript's reading at this place is: "wa-lasta li-jinniyyin wa-lākin malʾakan"]]

It may also be said for the singular "mal'ak," so that is like their saying "jabadha" and "jadhaba," "sha'mal" and "shim'al," and what is similar to those inverted letters. However, what must be the case, when its singular is named "mal'ak," is that when it is pluralized it is pluralized on that pattern as "ma'ālik." I do not remember their plural in that form by transmission, but they do sometimes pluralize: "malāʾik" and "malāʾika," as "ashʿath" is pluralized "ashāʾith" and "ashāʾitha," and "misma'" "masāmiʿ" and "masāmiʿa." Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said in their plural in that manner:

﴿wa-fīhimā min ʿibādi llāhi qawmun ... malāʾika dhullilū wa-hum ṣiʿābu﴾

[[From his Diwan p. 19. "Dhullilū" from the humbling (dhull, with kasra on the dhāl) and "dhallalahu": he tamed him until he became humble, gentle and obedient.]]

The root of "malʾak" is the message, as 'Adi ibn Zayd al-'Ibadi said:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 2 of 6):

أَبْلِغِ النُّعْمَانَ عَنِّي مَلأَكًا ... إِنَّهُ قَدْ طَالَ حَبْسِي وَانْتِظَارِي [[al-Aghani 2:14, al-'Iqd al-Farid 5:261; in the printed edition it reads "wa-intizari" (and intizari), and it is one of the poems of 'Adi, which he wrote to al-Nu'man when he imprisoned him in a place where no one was allowed to enter. After it comes the well-known verse, which completes it: law bi-ghayri al-ma'i halqi shariqun ... kuntu ka-l-ghassani bi-l-ma'i i'tisari]]
It is also recited: مألَكًا (ma'alakan), according to the other dialect. Whoever says malakan (ملأكًا) takes it as maf'al, from la'aka ilayhi (لأك إليه), yal'aku, when he sends him a message, risalatun mal'akah [[In the printed and manuscript texts: "yal'uk", but this triliteral "la'aka yal'aku" I have not found stated in the lexicons; rather, what they state is the quadriliteral "alka-ni ila fulan: abligh-hu 'anni. Asluhu al'ikni, fa-hudhifat al-hamzah wa-ulqiyat harakatuha 'ala ma qablaha" (bring to him from me; its origin is al'ikni, the hamza was dropped and its vowel placed on the letter before it), but they state that it is metathesized (maqlub). If that is correct, then it is also valid that la'aka is a metathesis of the triliteral alaka, which they did state.]]; and whoever says ma'alakan (مألَكًا) takes it as maf'al from alaktu ilayhi ala'uku (ألكت إليه آلك), when I send to him a ma'alakah and ulukan [[Al-Tabari's speech suggests he meant the pattern "maf'al" with a fatha on the 'ayn, so it is ma'alak, with a fatha on the lam. The more famous and eloquent forms are al-ma'alak and al-ma'alakah (with fatha on the mim and damma on the lam in both).]], as Labid ibn Rabi'ah said [[In the printed edition: "Labid ibn Abi Rabi'ah", which is an error.]]:
A youth whose mother sent him
with a messenger, so we gave what he asked.
[[His Diwan, poem no. 37, verse 16; "wa-ghulamin" is in the genitive after the "rubba" particle. He sent the youth, his mother, seeking the kindness of Labid, so he gave her what she asked.]]
This is from alaktu, and from it the saying of Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan:
Alkini, O 'Uyayn, to him a saying;
I will convey it to you, away from me.
[[In the printed edition: "satahdihi al-ruwat ilayka" (the narrators will convey it to you), and we have kept the manuscript text. The Diwan: 85, and others. They vowel it "sa-ahdihi" with a damma on the hamza, from the gift (hadiyyah), i.e., I will give it to you, but I do not approve of it, and the poetry's meaning is corrupted by that. In my view it is with a fatha on the hamza, from "hadaytuhu al-tariq" when I made the road known to him and explained it to him. From it they derived their saying: hadani fulan al-shi'r and hadaytuhu: i.e., he satirized me and I satirized him. His saying "ilayka ilayka" means take it, as al-Qitami said: "When the stout one with thick muscles, we say: ilayka ilayka! its forearm became narrow for it."
His saying "'anni" means "from me," as in their saying "'anka ja'a hadha," meaning from you, or from your side. Likewise is His saying, exalted is He: "And He it is who accepts repentance from His servants" (42:25), meaning from His servants; and His saying, exalted is He: "Those from whom We accept the best of what they did" (46:16), meaning from whom We accept. The saying of Nabigha is not from their saying "ilayka 'anni," meaning withdraw and hold back. The poetry that follows indicates this, and the verse that follows this one contains the word in the accusative governed by "ilayka ilayka": qawafiya ka-l-sallami idha istamarrat ... fa-laysa yaruddu madhhabaha al-tazanni
i.e., take them, verses like stones, which are the stones.
His saying "'Uyayn" means 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari, who had helped Banu 'Abs against Banu Asad, allies of Banu Dhubyan, the kin of Nabigha.]] And 'Abd Banu al-Hasḥas said:
Alkini ilayha, by your life, O youth,
with a sign that did not come to us but bearing gifts.
[[The discussion of this verse preceded: 106 above.]]
He means by that: convey my message to her. The angels were named "malaikah" (angels) for the message, because they are the messengers of God between Him and His prophets, and between Him and whomever of His servants He sends to.
* *
Concerning the interpretation of His saying, majestic is His praise: ﴿Indi ja'ilun fi al-ard﴾ (I am placing on the earth)
The interpreters differed regarding His saying, "Inni ja'il," some saying: "Inni fa'il" (I am doing).
Those who said that:
597 - Al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Jarir ibn Hazim and Mubarak, from al-Hasan, and Abu Bakr - meaning al-Hudhali - from al-Hasan, and Qatadah, they said: God, mentioned be His remembrance, said to His angels: "Inni ja'ilun fi al-ardi khalifah" (I am placing on the earth a khalifah). He said to them: I am doing. [[Report 597: Ibn Kathir (1:127) transmitted it from al-Tabari. A gap occurred in its chain there, and the apparent cause is a printing error. al-Suyuti (1:44) mentioned it in abridged form. It will come again: 611, in full, with this same chain. Here it has two chains, indeed three: Hajjaj - that is Ibn al-Minhal - narrated it from Jarir ibn Hazim, and from Mubarak - that is Ibn Fudalah - then he narrated it from Abu Bakr al-Hudhali; all three from al-Hasan al-Basri. The first two chains are sound, and the third is weak, due to the weakness of Abu Bakr al-Hudhali, whom Ibn al-Madini weakened greatly, and Ibn Ma'in said: "He is nothing." al-Bukhari recorded him in al-Kabir (2/2/199) under the name "Salma Abu Bakr al-Hudhali al-Basri," and said: "He is not a hafiz according to them. 'Amr ibn 'Ali said: I deliberately turned away from Abu Bakr al-Hudhali." Ibn Abi Hatim likewise recorded him (2/1/313-314) and made clear his weakness. "Salma" is with a damma on the sin, a sukun on the lam, and imalah of the final alif.]]
Others said: "Inni khaliq" (I am creating).
Those who said that:
598 - I was told about al-Minjab ibn al-Harith, who said: Bishr ibn 'Imarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, who said: Everything in the Qur'an that is "ja'ala," it is "khalaqa" (created). [[Report 598: al-Suyuti (1:44) transmitted it from al-Tabari, but attributed it to the speech of al-Dahhak. Abu Rawq often narrates tafsir from al-Dahhak, so perhaps the mention of "al-Dahhak" fell out from some copyists in some copies of al-Tabari. Whatever the case, this chain is weak; its weakness was explained previously: 137. Its weakness is further increased here by the anonymity of the shaykh from whom al-Tabari narrated from al-Minjab, in his saying "I was told," with the anonymity of the one who told him.]]
Abu Ja'far said: The correct interpretation of His saying, "Inni ja'il fi al-ardi khalifah," is: "mustakhlif fi al-ard khalifatan" (one who appoints a successor on the earth), and "musayyir fiha khalafan" (one who makes in it a succession). [[In the manuscript: "khalqan" with a qaf.]] That is more like the interpretation of al-Hasan and Qatadah.
It was said: The earth mentioned by God in this verse is "Makkah."
Those who said that:
599 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from 'Ata', from Ibn Sabit: that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The earth was spread out from Makkah, and the angels used to circumambulate the House; so it is the first to be circumambulated, and it is the 'earth' of which God said: 'I am placing on the earth a khalifah.' When his people perished and he and the righteous were saved, he and those with him came to it and worshipped God there until they died. The grave of Nuh, Hud, Salih and Shu'ayb is between Zamzam, the Corner, and the Maqam." [[Report 599: Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (1:127) quoted its meaning from the tafsir of Ibn Abi Hatim: "My father narrated to us, Abu Salamah narrated to us, Hammad narrated to us, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit," and then mentioned it as marfu' (traced to the Prophet) in similar but abbreviated form. Ibn Kathir said: "This is mursal (its chain omits the companion), and in its chain there is weakness, and in it there is idraj (interpolation), namely that the meaning of 'the earth' is Makkah, and God knows best - for the apparent meaning of 'the earth' is more general than that." As for its being mursal: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit is a tabi'i, and he is trustworthy, but he did not meet the Prophet ﷺ, nor even the senior Companions such as 'Umar, Sa'd and Mu'adh and others. It is said that he is "'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Sabit." There is great disagreement about this, so the hafiz recorded him for his father in both places as "Sabit" or "'Abd Allah ibn Sabit" (al-Isabah 3:51-52, 4:73). al-Suyuti (1:46) transmitted it and attributed it to al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Asakir, at length like the narration of al-Tabari; and al-Shawkani (1:50) transmitted it in abridged form like the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim, and transmitted Ibn Kathir's explanation of it.
In the printed edition: "ata hu wa-man ma'ahu" (came he and those with him). In the manuscript: "fa-ya'buduu Allah biha" (so they worshipped God in it).]]
* *
Concerning the interpretation of His saying: ﴿khalifah﴾ (a successor)
The khalifah is the fa'ilah form from your saying: "khalafa fulan fulanan fi hadha al-amr" (so-and-so succeeded so-and-so in this affair), when he stood in his place in it after him. As God, mentioned be His praise, said: ﴿Then We made you successors in the earth after them, that We might see how you would act﴾ (Yunus 10:14). He means by that that He replaced you in the earth after them, making you successors after them. From this the supreme ruler is called khalifah, because he succeeds the one who was before him, standing in the affair in his place, becoming a successor from him. It is said of him: "khalafa al-khalifah, yakhlufu khilafah wa-khilifa" [[In the manuscript and printed text: "wa-khalifan," and what we have written is correct. In the hadith of 'Umar: "Had it not been for al-khilifa, I would have given permission" (with kasrah on the kha' and a shaddah on the lam with kasrah, followed by a ya', then an open fa'). They said: it and similar forms like al-ramy and al-dulayli are a verbal noun indicating the meaning of abundance. 'Umar means: the abundance of his striving in regulating the affairs of the caliphate and directing its reins.]].
Ibn Ishaq used to say:
600 - Ibn Humayd narrated it to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq: "Inni ja'ilun fi al-ardi khalifah," he says: an inhabitant and a populator who inhabits it and populates it, a successor, not from you. [[Report 600: In Ibn Kathir (1:127), and in the printed edition here, and in 615, "khalqan laysa minkum" (a creation not from you) with a qaf, which is an error; the correct reading is in Ibn Kathir (1:127). His saying "khalfan" means: a replacement for those who passed away, who were the inhabitants of the earth before our father Adam, peace be upon him, as will come in the complete report: 615. His saying "laysa minkum" is a new statement: i.e., not from you, O angels. As for the manuscript, it contains "laysa khalfan minkum," which is pure error.]]
What Ibn Ishaq said about the meaning of khalifah is not its interpretation - although God, mentioned be His praise, only informed His angels that He is placing on the earth a khalifah who inhabits it - but its meaning is what I described before.
If someone says: What was on the earth before the children of Adam, populating it, so that the children of Adam became a replacement from it and a succession in it?
It is said: The interpreters have differed concerning that.
601 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Imarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The first to inhabit the earth were the jinn, and they corrupted in it, shed blood in it, and some of them killed others. So God sent to them Iblis with a host of angels, and Iblis and those with him killed them until he drove them to the islands of the seas and the edges of the mountains. Then He created Adam and settled him in it, and that is why He said: "I am placing on the earth a khalifah." [[Report 601: In Ibn Kathir (1:127). al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (2:261) narrated a report resembling it in some meaning but differing in wording, saying: "'Abd Allah ibn Musa al-Saydalani informed us, Isma'il ibn Qutaybah narrated to us, Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah narrated to us, Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Bukayr ibn al-Akhnas, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas:..." and said: "This hadith is of sound chain, but they did not record it." al-Dhahabi agreed. As for al-Tabari's chain here, it is weak, as we explained earlier: 137.]]
Thus according to this view, "Inni ja'il fi al-ardi khalifah" refers to jinn, who succeed them there, inhabiting it and populating it.
602 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, concerning His saying: "Inni ja'il fi al-ardi khalifah," the verse, he said: God created the angels on Wednesday, created the jinn on Thursday, and created Adam on Friday. Some of the jinn disbelieved, so the angels would descend to them on the earth and fight them, so there was bloodshed, and corruption was on the earth. [[Report 602: al-Tabari narrated it in al-Tarikh (1:43) with this same chain. It will come again with this chain in a longer form: 612. Ibn Kathir (1:128) and al-Suyuti (1:45) transmitted the extended narration, but both made it a saying of Abu al-'Aliyah. So it is from the narration of al-Rabi' ibn Anas from Abu al-'Aliyah. al-Suyuti added that Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah also narrated it.]]
Others said concerning His saying: "Inni ja'il fi al-ardi khalifah," that is, a successor who succeeds one another, and they are the children of Adam, who succeed their father Adam, and each generation of them succeeds the generation that passed before it. This is a view transmitted from al-Hasan al-Basri.
A parallel to it is what:
603 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to me, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Ibn Sabit concerning His saying: "Inni ja'il fi al-ardi khalifah, qalu ataj'alu fiha man yufsidu fiha wa-yasfiku al-dima'" (They said: will You place therein one who corrupts therein and sheds blood?), he said: They meant by it the children of Adam ﷺ.
604 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: God, mentioned be His remembrance, said to the angels: "I intend to create in the earth a creation and to place therein a khalifah." And there was no creation of God at that time except the angels, and the earth had no creatures in it. [[Reports 603, 604: in Ibn Kathir (1:128).]]
This view allows for what was transmitted from al-Hasan, and it may be that Ibn Zayd meant that God informed the angels that He is placing on the earth a khalifah of His own, who will judge among His creation by His judgment, similar to what:
605 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas - and from Murrah, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some people of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ: that God, majestic is His praise, said to the angels: "Inni ja'il fi al-ardi khalifah." They said: Our Lord, and what will that khalifah be? He said: He will have offspring who will corrupt in the earth, envy one another, and some of them will kill others. [[Report 605: in Ibn Kathir (1:127).]] So the interpretation of the verse according to this narration that we mentioned from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas is: "Inni ja'il fi al-ardi khalifatan minni" (I am placing on the earth a khalifah from Me) who will succeed Me in judging among My creation. That khalifah is Adam and whoever stood in his place in obedience to God and judging with justice among His creation.
As for corruption and the shedding of blood without right, it is from other than His khalifah, and other than Adam and whoever stood in his place among God's servants - because the two of them reported that God, majestic is His praise, said to His angels when they asked Him: What is that khalifah? He said: He is a khalifah who will have offspring who will corrupt in the earth, envy one another, and some of them will kill others. So He attributed corruption and the shedding of blood without right to the offspring of His khalifah, not to him, and excluded from him His khalifah.
This interpretation, although it differs from what was transmitted from al-Hasan in the meaning of khalifah in one respect, agrees with it in another. As for its agreement with it: the redirecting of its interpreters of the attribution of corruption in the earth and the shedding of blood in it to other than the khalifah. As for its disagreement with it: their attribution of the succession to Adam in the sense of God's appointing him in it. And the attribution by al-Hasan of the succession to his offspring, in the sense of one succeeding another, and a generation of them standing in the place of a generation before them, and the attribution of corruption in the earth and the shedding of blood to the khalifah.
What led the interpreters of His saying, "Inni ja'il fi al-ardi khalifah," in the interpretation mentioned from al-Hasan, to what they said about it, is that they said that the angels only said to their Lord - when their Lord said to them, "Inni ja'il fi al-ardi khalifah" - "Ataj'alu fiha man yufsidu fiha wa-yasfiku al-dima'" (Will You place therein one who corrupts therein and sheds blood?), informing about the khalifah whom God, mentioned be His praise, said He would place in the earth, not about anyone else. For the discourse between the angels and their Lord was about him. They said: If that is so - and God had cleared Adam of corruption in the earth and the shedding of blood, and purified him from that - it is known that what was meant was other than him, from his offspring. Thus it is established that the khalifah who corrupts in the earth and sheds blood is other than Adam, and that they are his sons who did that, and that the meaning of the succession mentioned by God is only the succession of a generation of them to another, as we described.

Those who stated this view, and those who interpreted the verse in this way, overlooked the proper method of interpretation (ta'wil). When the Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I am going to place a successor (khalifah) on earth" (﴿إني جاعلٌ في الأرض خليفة﴾), they did not, in their reply to their Lord, attribute corruption and the shedding of blood to His successor on His earth. Rather, they said: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?" (﴿أتجعل فيها من يُفسد فيها﴾). It is not impossible that their Lord had informed them that His successor would have descendants from whom corruption and the shedding of blood would proceed, so they said: "O our Lord, will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?" (﴿أتجعل فيها من يُفسدُ فيها ويسفكُ الدماء﴾). This is what Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas said, as did others among the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) whom we have cited.

[In the original manuscript, after this point, there is the following statement:
"I have read its beginning under the guidance of the judge Abu al-Hasan al-Khasib ibn 'Abd Allah al-Khasibi, from Abu Muhammad al-Farghani, from Abu Ja'far al-Tabari. My brother 'Ali ibn Ahmad ibn 'Isa and Nasr ibn al-Hasan al-Tabari heard it with me. Abu al-Fath Ahmad ibn 'Umar al-Jahari heard it from the place of his hearing.
And Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn 'Isa al-Sa'di wrote this in Jumada al-Akhirah of the year 408 AH."]

* *

"Reminder" (tadhkirah): It has become clear to me, from what I have reviewed of al-Tabari's discourse, that al-Tabari's use of these reports which he narrates with their chains (asanid) is intended only to establish the meaning of a word or to explain the context of an expression. He has adduced here the reports he transmitted with their chains in order to indicate the meaning of "khalifah" and "khilafah," and how the early exegetes (mufassirun) differed over the meaning of "khalifah." His use of these reports is like the use of a poem by one who cites poetry to establish the meaning of a word in the Book of God. This is evident in the paragraph following report no. 605, where he mentions what was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, and what was narrated from al-Hasan, in explaining the meaning of "khalifah," and he deduces what the statement of each of them implies. Because of this manner of argument, he was not concerned about the weakness in the chain that he does not approve. The proof of this is that al-Tabari himself said regarding the chain of report no. 465 from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, mentioned earlier on page 353: "If this is correct, and I do not know it to be correct, since I am doubtful about its chain..." So, despite his doubt about this chain, he adduced the report only to indicate the meaning of the word alone, as Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas understood it, if it is authentically transmitted from them, or as the early narrators understood its meaning. This is a method that is not objectionable in argumentation. Similarly, he also cites reports and narrations whose weakness he does not doubt, or which are of the Isra'iliyyat (narrations from Jewish and Christian sources), and he did not cite them to be authoritative over the interpretation of the verses of the Noble Revelation. Rather, he cites lengthy accounts to explain the meaning of a word or the context of an event, even if the report itself is not something on which proof in religion or in the complete interpretation (tafsir) of the verses of God's Book can rest.

Thus, al-Tabari's argument with what the objectors reject was nothing but an attempt to deduce the meanings indicated by the words of this Noble Book, just as one deduces meanings by means of poetry. It is therefore an argument that is nearly linguistic. And since it is not objectionable to argue with poetry whose composer lied, even if its language is sound, it is not objectionable to cite narrations that the people of hadith do not approve of, and which do not constitute proof in religion, to indicate the meaning understood from the explicit wording of the Qur'an, and how the early generations understood it, whether they were Companions or those after them.

I hope this reminder will benefit the reader of al-Tabari's book when he encounters something of what the scholars of hadith have counted as gharib (unusual) and munkar (rejected). My brother, Sayyid Ahmad Shakir, did not fall short in explaining the rank of al-Tabari's narrators according to the scholars of biographical evaluation (al-rijal), and in this there is sufficiency for whoever wishes to know the knowledge of the earlier scholars as it truly was. All praise is due to God, first and last.]

* *

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is His praise, reporting about His angels: ﴿They said: Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: If someone says to us: How did the angels say to their Lord, when He informed them that He would place a successor on earth, "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?", when Adam had not yet been created, nor his descendants, so that they would know by direct observation what they would do? Did they know the unseen (al-ghayb) and so said that, or did they say what they said by conjecture? For that would be a testimony by conjecture and a statement about what they do not know, and that is not their attribute. Or what was the reason for their saying that to their Lord? It is said: The scholars of the people of interpretation have offered various opinions on this, and we will mention their opinions, then indicate the most sound of them in proof and the clearest of them in argument. It was reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning this:

606 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Ammarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Iblis was from a tribe of the angels called "al-Hinn" (the Hinn), who were created from the scorching fire (nar al-samum) among the angels. [In the printed edition, both occurrences read "al-Jinn" with a jim, which is an error, as shown by the context of this report, since it distinguishes between Iblis and the jinn mentioned in the Qur'an. Iblis was created from the scorching fire, and the others were created from a smokeless flame of fire (marij min nar). The jinn (with jim) were the first to inhabit the earth, and Iblis came to fight them with a host of angels. This is clear. Al-Jahiz said in al-Hayawan 7:177 that some people divide the jinn into two categories, saying: they are jinn and hinn (with ha), and they make the one with ha the weaker of the two. He also said in 1:291-292 that some people claim the hinn and the jinn are two different kinds, and they went to the saying of a Bedouin who came to the door of some ruler to enroll among the disabled, and he said concerning that:
"If you record the disabled, then I am disabled,
from an outward affliction and a hidden affliction.
I spend my nights flying among devils that hum,
their kind differing: jinn and hinn."
So he distinguished between these two kinds. See also al-Hayawan 6:193, and Lisan al-Arab (under j-n-n), and others.]

He said: His name was al-Harith. He said: He was one of the treasurers of Paradise. He said: All the angels were created from light other than this living kind. He said: The jinn mentioned in the Qur'an were created from a smokeless flame (marij) of fire, which is the tongue of fire that appears at its tip when it blazes. He said: Man was created from clay. The first to inhabit the earth were the jinn. They caused corruption therein, shed blood, and some of them killed others. He said: So God sent Iblis to them with a host of angels, who are this living kind called al-Hinn [in the printed edition both occurrences read "al-Jinn" with a jim, which is an error, as noted above] - and Iblis and those with him killed them until he drove them to the islands of the seas and the edges of the mountains. When Iblis did that, he became vain within himself and said: "I have done something no one has done!" He said: God perceived that from his heart, but the angels who were with him did not perceive it. God said to the angels who were with him: "Indeed I am placing a successor on earth." The angels replied to Him, saying: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, as the jinn caused corruption and shed blood, and we were only sent against them for that?" He said: "Indeed I know what you do not know," meaning: I have perceived from the heart of Iblis what you have not perceived, of his arrogance and his vanity. He said: Then He ordered the dust of Adam to be raised, and God created Adam from clay that sticks (tin lazib) - and the lazib is the sticky, hard one - from black mud (hama' masnun) that stinks. He said: It was black mud shaped only after it had been dust. He said: So He created him with His hand. He said: He remained forty nights as a body lying prostrate. Iblis would come to him and strike him with his foot, and it would ring out (yusalsil), that is, it would make a sound. He said: That is the saying of God: ﴿from clay like pottery﴾ [Surah al-Rahman: 14]. He means: like a thing blown into that is not solid (musmat). [Al-musmat is that which has no hollow; every thing with a hollow, when struck, produces a sound, whereas the musmat is silent and has no sound. The word is derived from silence (samt).] He said: Then Iblis would enter his mouth and exit from his anus, and enter from his anus and exit from his mouth, then say: "You are nothing! - because of the ringing - and not for anything were you created! If I am given power over you, I will destroy you, and if you are given power over me, I will disobey you." He said: When God breathed into him of His spirit, the breath reached first his head, and nothing of it flowed into his body without becoming flesh and blood. When the breath reached his navel, he looked at his body and was pleased by what he saw of its beauty, so he tried to rise but could not. This is the saying of God: ﴿And man was ever hasty﴾ [Surah al-Isra: 11]. He said: impatient, having no patience in ease or hardship. He said: When the breath was complete in his body, he sneezed and said: "Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds," by inspiration from God, Exalted, so God said to him: "May God have mercy on you, O Adam." He said: Then God said to the angels who were with Iblis specifically, not the angels in the heavens: "Prostrate to Adam." So they all prostrated except Iblis, who refused and was arrogant, because of what he had been speaking to himself of his arrogance and vanity. He said: "I will not prostrate to him, and I am better than him, older, and stronger in creation. You created me from fire and created him from clay," meaning: fire is stronger than clay. He said: When Iblis refused to prostrate, God made him despair (abalsahu), that is, made him despair of all good, and made him an accursed devil (shaytan rajim) as punishment for his disobedience. Then he taught Adam all the names, and these are the names by which people recognize one another: man, beast, earth, plain, sea, mountain, donkey, and similar things among the kinds and others. Then He presented these names to those angels - meaning the angels who were with Iblis, who were created from the scorching fire - and said to them: "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful, if you know that I am placing a successor on earth." [In the printed edition: "that you know that I place in the earth a successor," and the statement "I did not place" lacked the particle "lam" in the manuscript also. The correct reading is from al-Durr al-Manthur and al-Shawkani, whose takhrij comes below, and it will come in the correct form also in no. 671, p. 490, which is an abridgement of this report.] He said: When the angels knew God's censure of them for what they had said of the knowledge of the unseen, which none knows but Him, and which they had no knowledge of, they said: "Glory be to You" - exalting God above anyone knowing the unseen other than Him - "We repent to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us," disavowing knowledge of the unseen, except what You have taught us, as You taught Adam. He said: "O Adam, inform them of their names," meaning: inform them of their names. When he informed them of their names, He said: "Did I not tell you - O angels, specifically - that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and none knows it but Me, and I know what you reveal and what you were concealing?" meaning: I know the secret as I know the open, referring to what Iblis concealed in himself of arrogance and vanity.

[Report 606: Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur, dispersed, 1:44-45, 49, 50, and al-Shawkani 1:52 cited part of it dispersed. Al-Tabari narrated a portion of it with this chain in his History, 1:42-43.]

Abu Ja'far said: This report from Ibn 'Abbas indicates that the saying of God, exalted is His praise: "And when your Lord said to the angels, Indeed I am placing a successor on earth," is an address from God, exalted is His praise, to a specific group of the angels, not all of them, and that those to whom this was said among the angels were specifically the tribe of Iblis, who fought with him against the jinn of the earth before the creation of Adam. God specifically addressed them with this saying as a trial and test from Him, to make them know the limitation of their knowledge, and the superiority over them of many who are weaker in creation than they are among His creatures, and that His honor is not attained by strength of bodies and firmness of physiques, as Iblis, the enemy of God, supposed. And it makes clear that their saying to their Lord: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?" was a slip on their part and a conjecture about the unseen. God, exalted is His praise, informed them of the harm of what they had uttered, and made them stand on it until they repented and turned back to Him from what they had said and uttered, of guessing the unseen by conjectures, and they disavowed before Him that anyone other than Him knows the unseen, and He showed them what Iblis had concealed within himself of the arrogance that had been hidden from them.

[This commentary following Ibn 'Abbas's report is evidence for what we have maintained concerning al-Tabari's method of argumentation with reports and narrations (see pp. 453-454). He did not narrate it because he relied on its authenticity, but to show that God's saying, "And when your Lord said to the angels, Indeed I am placing a successor on earth," is an address containing the general term "the angels," which is intended as specific for some angels, as is well known in the Arabic language. And that the saying of these angels, "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein...", was not based on knowledge of the unseen that they knew, but was a conjecture they conjectured. What follows will clarify al-Tabari's method of argumentation, as I shall indicate in its place.]

It has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas a report contrary to this narration, which is:-

607. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and from Murra, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "When God had finished creating what He willed, He established Himself upon the Throne, and He appointed Iblis over the dominion of the lowest heaven. He was from a category of angels called the Jinn [[In the manuscript: "al-Hinn" with a ḥāʾ, but the following explanation shows it is with a jīm. See what we wrote earlier on p. 455, note 1.]], and they were named the Jinn only because they were the guardians of Paradise. Iblis, along with his dominion, was a guardian, and pride entered his heart, and he said: 'God has given me this only because of a distinction in me'" (thus said Musa ibn Harun, though another narrated it to me and said: "a distinction in me over the angels") [[The other narrator, whom al-Tabari left unnamed here, is identified in the History 1: 43, where he says: "Ahmad ibn Abi Khaythama narrated it to me, from Amr ibn Hammad."]]. "When that pride settled in his soul, God became aware of it, and God said to the angels: 'Indeed I am appointing a khalifa (successor/vicegerent) on the earth.' They said: 'Our Lord, what will that khalifa be?' He said: 'He will have offspring who will cause corruption on the earth, envy one another, and some of them will kill others.' They said: 'Our Lord, "will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You?" He said: "Indeed I know what you do not know."' This refers to the matter of Iblis. Then He sent Jibril to the earth to bring him some clay from it, but the earth said: 'I seek refuge in God from you, that you would diminish me or disfigure me.' So he returned and did not take any. He said: 'My Lord, it sought refuge in You, so You have granted it refuge.' Then God sent Mika'il, and it sought refuge from him, so he granted it refuge, and he returned and said what Jibril had said. Then He sent the Angel of Death, and it sought refuge from him. He said: 'And I seek refuge in God from returning without carrying out His command.' So he took from the surface of the earth, mixing it, and did not take from one place alone, and he took from red, white and black soil, and for this reason the children of Adam came out differing. Then he ascended with it, and moistened the dust until it became sticky clay (lāzib, which is that which sticks its parts to one another), and then he left it until it became foul and changed [[In the printed edition: "ḥīna anta" ("when it stank"); the correct reading is "ḥattā anta" ("until it stank"), as in al-Tabari's History and Ibn Kathir's Tafsir, as shown by its takhrīj (sourcing)."]]. This is when He says: ﴿from black mud, moulded﴾ (Surah al-Hijr: 28). He said: 'Stinking.' Then He said to the angels: ﴿Indeed I am creating a human from clay; so when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down in prostration to him﴾ (Surah Sad: 71-72). So God created him with His two hands, so that Iblis would not be arrogant toward him, so that He could say to him: 'Are you arrogant toward what I made with My two hands, and I was not arrogant toward it?' So He created him as a human. He was a body of clay for forty years, measured in days of Friday. The angels passed by him and were terrified of him when they saw him. The one most terrified of him was Iblis, so he would pass by him and strike him, and the body would make a sound like the sound of pottery, and it would ring, and this is when He says: ﴿from clay like pottery﴾ (Surah al-Rahman: 14), and he would say: 'For what reason were you created!' He entered through his mouth and came out through his posterior. He said to the angels: 'Do not be afraid of this, for your Lord is al-Samad (the Eternal, Self-Sufficient), and this is hollow [[al-Samad here means the one who has no hollow; al-muṣammad and al-muṣmat are the same. See what has preceded on p. 456, note 1.]]. If I were given power over him, I would destroy him.' When the appointed time came for which God, may His praise be exalted, willed to breathe the spirit into him, He said to the angels: 'When I have breathed into him of My spirit, then prostrate to him.' When He breathed the spirit into him and the spirit entered his head, he sneezed, and the angels said to him: 'Say: All praise is for God.' He said: 'All praise is for God,' and God said to him: 'May your Lord have mercy on you.' When the spirit entered his eyes, he looked at the fruits of Paradise. When it entered his belly, he desired food, and he leapt, before the spirit reached his legs, hastily toward the fruits of Paradise, and this is when He says: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ (Surah al-Anbiya: 37). So all the angels prostrated, every one of them, except Iblis, who refused to be among those prostrating, that is, he was arrogant, and he was among the disbelievers." God said to him: "What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you, regarding what I created with My two hands?" He said: "I am better than him; I would not prostrate to a human whom You created from clay." God said to him: "Get out of it, for it is not for you (yakūnu laka, meaning: it is not befitting for you) to be arrogant therein; so get out, for you are among the humbled." And ṣaghār (humiliation) is abasement. He said: "He taught Adam all the names, then presented the creatures to the angels, and said: 'Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful, that the children of Adam will cause corruption on the earth and shed blood.' They said to Him: 'Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.' God said: 'O Adam, inform them of their names.' When he informed them of their names, He said: 'Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?' He said, referring to their statement: 'Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?' that was what they revealed. 'And I know what you concealed': this refers to what Iblis secretly held in his soul of arrogance."

[[The report: al-Tabari narrated part of it in his History 10: 41-42, with this chain. Another part also in 1: 43, a third in 1: 45-46, a fourth in 1: 47, a fifth in 1: 47-48, and a sixth in 1: 50. Some of it is quoted from al-Suyuti 1: 45-47 and al-Shawkani 1: 50. The reasoning behind this chain has passed on p. 168, and al-Tabari's own view of it is on p. 452, where he considered it doubtful. Ibn Kathir quoted it in full at 1: 137-138, then said: "This chain going back to these Companions is well known in the tafsir of al-Suddi, and it contains many Isra'iliyyat (narrations from Jewish and Christian sources). Perhaps some of them are interpolated and are not the words of the Companions, or they took them from some earlier books, and God knows best. Al-Hakim narrates in his Mustadrak with this very same chain some matters, and says: 'It meets the condition of al-Bukhari!'"]]

Abu Ja'far said: This report, its beginning has a meaning contrary to the report narrated from Ibn Abbas through the narration of al-Dahhak, which we mentioned earlier, and its end agrees with its meaning. That is because it mentions at the beginning that the angels asked their Lord about that khalifa, when He said to them: "Indeed I am placing a khalifa on the earth." He replied that it would have offspring who would cause corruption on the earth, envy one another, and some of them would kill others. The angels then said: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?" So the statement of the angels was what they said to their Lord, after God had informed them that this would come from the offspring of the khalifa He would place on the earth. This is the meaning contrary to the beginning, which is the report of al-Dahhak that we mentioned.

As for its agreement with it in the end, it is their statement in the interpretation of His words: "Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful," that the children of Adam would cause corruption on the earth and shed blood, and that the angels said, when their Lord said that to them, disclaiming knowledge of the unseen: "Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise."

When a person of understanding reflects on this, he knows that its beginning corrupts its end, and its end invalidates the meaning of its beginning. For if God, may His praise be exalted, informed the angels that the offspring of the khalifa He would place on the earth would cause corruption therein and shed blood, then the angels' statement to their Lord, "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?", is unjustified as a rebuke for reporting about those whom God had informed them would cause corruption on the earth and shed blood, in the same way their Lord had informed them about them. Thus it could not be said to them, concerning what was hidden from them of knowledge: "If you are truthful in what you know from God's informing you that it will occur among the matters, then inform us of what God has hidden from your knowledge, just as you informed us of what God has made you aware of." Rather, that would be a misinterpretation and a claim against God that it is not right for Him to have such an attribute [[al-Tabari's criticism also shows what we have concluded about reasoning from reports, just as an arguer reasons from poetry. You see him demolish this report completely, and show the error in its context and the contradiction in its meaning. This is clear, God willing.]]. I fear that some of the transmitters of this report are the ones who erred regarding the one from whom they narrated it among the Companions, and that the interpretation from them was like this: "Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful in what you supposed you had grasped of knowledge from My informing you that the children of Adam would cause corruption on the earth and shed blood, to the extent that you permitted yourselves to say: 'Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?'" Then the rebuke would fall upon what they supposed they had grasped from God's saying to them: "Indeed there will be for him offspring who will cause corruption on the earth and shed blood," not upon their reporting what God had informed them would occur. That is because God, may His praise be exalted, although He had informed them about what would occur from some of the offspring of His khalifa on the earth, of the corruption and bloodshed that would come from them, He had kept hidden from them the information about what would come from many of them: their obedience to their Lord, their reform in His earth, the preservation of blood, His elevating their rank, and their honour before Him. He did not inform them of that. So the angels said: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?", supposing, according to the interpretation of these two reports I have mentioned and their apparent meaning, that all the offspring of the khalifa He would place on the earth would cause corruption therein and shed blood therein. So God said to them, when He taught Adam all the names: "Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful, that you know that all the children of Adam will cause corruption on the earth and shed blood, as you supposed in yourselves": a denial by Him, may His praise be exalted, of their saying that about all and generally, while it is a characteristic only of a specific part of the offspring of the khalifa. What we have mentioned here is our description of the interpretation of the report, not the view we choose in interpreting the verse [[This is also clear evidence that al-Tabari's use of reports and narrations does not mean he accepted them. Rather, he brought them to show the context of the verse's interpretation on one occasion, and to show the corruption of the reports themselves on another. Many who quoted al-Tabari have misunderstood his intention, and others who did not know his approach to this tafsir have criticised him unfairly.]].

Among what supports what we have mentioned, regarding the direction of the angels' report about the corruption and bloodshed of the khalifa's offspring in general, is:

608. Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, regarding His words: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?" He said: They mean the people [[Report 608: I have not found it.]].

Others said concerning that, based on:

609. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "And when your Lord said to the angels, 'Indeed I am placing a khalifa on the earth,'" that He consulted the angels about creating Adam. They said: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?" (the angels knew from God's knowledge that nothing is more hateful to God than bloodshed and corruption on the earth) "while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You." "He said: Indeed I know what you do not know." So there was in God's knowledge, may His praise be exalted, that there would come from that khalifa prophets, messengers, righteous people and the dwellers of Paradise. He said: It was mentioned to us that Ibn Abbas used to say: When God began creating Adam, the angels said: "Will God create a creation more honoured by Him than us, or more knowing than us?" So they were tested by the creation of Adam, for every creation is tested, just as the heavens and the earth were tested by obedience, and God said: ﴿Come willingly or unwillingly.' They said: 'We come willingly﴾ (Surah Fussilat: 11) [[Report 609: In Ibn Kathir 1: 129, and part of it scattered in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 45, 46, 50.]].

This report from Qatadah shows that Qatadah held that the angels said what they said, "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?", without a previously certain knowledge that this would occur, but out of opinion and supposition. And that God, may His praise be exalted, rejected this from their saying, and answered what they thought with His words: "Indeed I know what you do not know," that there would come from the offspring of that khalifa the prophets, the messengers, and those striving in the obedience of God.

A report from Qatadah contrary to this interpretation has also been transmitted, namely:

610. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?" He said: God had informed them that when there were creatures on the earth, they would cause corruption therein and shed blood, and that is His saying: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?" [[Report 610: I have not found it.]].

Similar to Qatadah's view, a group of the people of interpretation said so, including al-Hasan al-Basri:

611. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Jarir ibn Hazim and Mubarak, from al-Hasan (and Abu Bakr, from al-Hasan and Qatadah), and both said: God said to His angels: "Indeed I am placing a khalifa on the earth." He said to them: "Indeed I am doing so." They offered opinions, so He taught them a knowledge and kept hidden from them a knowledge that He knew and that they did not know. They then said, with the knowledge He had taught them: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?" (the angels had known from God's knowledge that there is no sin greater before God than bloodshed) "while we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You. He said: Indeed I know what you do not know." When He began creating Adam, the angels whispered among themselves, saying: "Let our Lord create whatever He wills to create. He will not create any creature except that we will be more knowing than it and more honoured by Him than it." When He created him and breathed into him of His spirit, He commanded them to prostrate to him, as they had said, and He favoured him over them. They knew they were not better than him, so they said: "If we are not better than him, then we are more knowing than him, because we were before him, and the nations were created before him." When they were pleased with their deeds, they were tested. So "He taught Adam all the names, then presented them to the angels, and said: 'Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful'" (that I will not create any creature except that you will be more knowing than it). "Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful." He said: The people then hastened to repentance (to which every believer hastens), and they said: "Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise." He said: "O Adam, inform them of their names." When he informed them of their names, He said: "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?" (regarding their saying: "Let our Lord create what He wills, for He will not create a creature more honoured by Him than us, or more knowing than us"). He said: He taught him the name of everything: these mountains, these mules, the camels, the jinn and the wild beasts. He began naming each thing by its name, and every nation was presented to him. Then He said: "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?" He said: As for what they revealed, it is their saying: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?" As for what they concealed, it is the saying of some of them to others: "We are better than him and more knowing" [[Report 611: part of it was previously given verbatim with this chain, and we explained the soundness of some of it and the weakness of some. al-Suyuti 1: 49 quoted part of it from this place in al-Tabari's tafsir. Ibn Kathir 1: 128 mentioned a section from the tafsir of Ibn Abi Hatim: from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah, from Sa'id ibn Sulayman, from Mubarak ibn Fudalah, from al-Hasan, i.e., al-Basri. This is a sound chain to al-Hasan al-Basri: al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sabbah is al-Za'farani, the trustworthy and reliable, a student of al-Shafi'i and a transmitter of his books in Iraq. Sa'id ibn Sulayman is Sa'dawayh al-Dabbi al-Wasiti, a trustworthy reliable narrator, one of al-Bukhari's teachers and a contemporary of Imam Ahmad. Mubarak ibn Fudalah is trustworthy, one of those closest to al-Hasan al-Basri, having sat with him for 13 or 14 years.]].

612. Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim also narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, regarding His words: "Indeed I am placing a khalifa on the earth," the verse, he said: God created the angels on Wednesday, created the jinn on Thursday, and created Adam on Friday. He said: Some of the jinn disbelieved, so the angels would descend to them on the earth and fight them, and there was bloodshed, and corruption on the earth. For this reason they said: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood?", the verse [[Report 612: its beginning was given under number 602, and we pointed to this there.]].

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 5 of 6):

613. [Muhammad ibn Jarir said:] I was told on the authority of Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far informed us, on the authority of his father, on the authority of al-Rabi', with the like of it: "Then He presented them to the angels and said: 'Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful.'" [He recited] up to His words: "Indeed, You are the Knowing, the Wise." He said: That was when they said: "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?" He said: When they realized that He was going to place a vicegerent on the earth, they said among themselves: "God will not create a creature except that we are more knowledgeable than it and more honourable." So God wished to inform them that He had preferred Adam over them. Adam was taught all the names, and He said to the angels: "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful," up to His words: "and I know what you reveal and what you conceal." What they had revealed was when they said: "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood," and what they had concealed among themselves was their saying: "God will not create a creature except that we are more knowledgeable than it and more honourable." Thus they knew that God had preferred Adam over them in knowledge and honour. [Editor's note: 613 is another version of the earlier report. I have not found it in the earlier sources.]

Ibn Zayd said:

614. It was narrated to me by Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la, who said: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said: When God created the Fire, the angels were struck with intense terror and said: "Our Lord, why did You create this Fire? For what purpose did You create it?" He said: "For those of My creation who disobey Me." He said: At that time God had no creation except the angels, and the earth had no creatures in it; Adam was created only after that. He recited God's words: "Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning?" [al-Insan 76:1]. He said: Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "O Messenger of God, I wish that period had lasted," [Editor's note: Umar's words, "I wish that period had lasted," mean: I wish man had remained something not worth mentioning, a clay that clings. He said it out of fear of his Lord's punishment on the Day of Resurrection. In al-Durr al-Manthur (6:297) it is reported: "Ibn al-Mubarak, Abu Ubayd in his Fada'il, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab that he heard a man recite: (Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning), and Umar said: 'I wish it had been completed.'" This is the meaning of Umar's words here.] Then he said: The angels said: "O Lord, will there come upon us a period when we disobey You in it?" — they did not see any creation other than themselves — He said: "No. I want to create on the earth a creature and make in it a vicegerent, and they will shed blood and cause corruption on the earth." So the angels said: "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?" And [they said]: "You have chosen us, so make us the ones in it. We exalt You with praise, sanctify You, and act in it by Your obedience." The angels were greatly troubled that God would place on the earth one who would disobey Him. He said: "Indeed, I know that which you do not know." "O Adam, inform them of their names." He said: [Adam] said: "So-and-so and so-and-so." He said: When they saw what God had given him of knowledge, they acknowledged Adam's superiority over them. But the wicked Iblis refused to acknowledge it and said: "I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay." He said: "Then descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein." [Editor's note: Part of its meaning will come with this chain (p. 176, Bulaq edition). As for this text, al-Suyuti mentioned part of it (1:45) and attributed it only to Ibn Jarir, and he did not mention Umar ibn al-Khattab's words in it. We have pointed out the occurrence of its meaning by another route in the footnote before this one. Umar's words here are presented in the manner of a hadith traced to the Prophet, since he said: "O Messenger of God, I wish that period had lasted." It would then be a mursal (disconnected) marfu' hadith, or rather munqati' (broken), because Ibn Zayd, who is Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, did not meet anyone except some of the Successors. Moreover, he is extremely weak, as was mentioned earlier at 185.]

Ibn Ishaq said:

615. It was narrated to us by Ibn Humayd, who said: Salamah ibn al-Fadl informed us, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: When God wished to create Adam by His power, to test him and to test others through him, given His knowledge of what was in His angels and all His creation — and the first trial the angels were subjected to contained for them what they loved and what they hated, for trial and purification regarding what was in them that they did not know, and God's knowledge encompassed it from them — He gathered the angels from the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, then said: "I am placing on the earth a vicegerent" — one who would dwell and build it, to inhabit it and cultivate it — a successor, not of you. [Editor's note: In the printed edition: "one who dwells and builds, a creature who will inhabit it and cultivate it, not of you." See what passed at no. 600 and its takhrij below.] Then He informed them of His knowledge about them, and said: They will cause corruption on the earth, shed blood, and act in disobedience. They all said: "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?" — We will not disobey, nor do anything You dislike? He said: "Indeed, I know that which you do not know." He said: I know about you and among you, and He did not reveal to them — the disobedience, corruption, shedding of blood, and doing what He dislikes from them, which will happen on the earth, which I mentioned concerning the children of Adam. God said to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿I had no knowledge of the Exalted Assembly when they disputed. It is only revealed to me that I am but a clear warner. When your Lord said to the angels: Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay. So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down to him in prostration﴾ [Sad 38:69–72]. Thus He mentioned to His Prophet ﷺ what was among the mention of Adam when He intended to create him, and the angels' disputing with Him concerning what He had told them about him. When God, may His remembrance be exalted, resolved to create Adam, He said to the angels: "I am creating a human being from dried clay, from black mud, molded, by My hands" — honouring him, magnifying his affair, and ennobling him. The angels preserved His covenant, understood His word, and all obeyed except the enemy of God, Iblis, who remained silent about what was in himself of envy, rebellion, arrogance, and disobedience. God created Adam from the surface of the earth, from clay that clings, from black mud, molded, by His hands, honouring him, magnifying his affair, and ennobling him above the rest of His creation. Ibn Ishaq said: It is said, and God knows best: God created Adam, then placed him, looking at him for forty years before breathing the spirit into him, until he became dry clay like pottery, untouched by fire. He said: It is said, and God knows best: When the spirit reached his head, he sneezed and said: "Praise be to God!" His Lord said to him: "May your Lord have mercy on you." The angels fell in prostration to him as soon as he was erect, preserving the covenant of God which He had made with them, and obeying His command which He had commanded them. The enemy of God, Iblis, stood up from among them and did not prostrate, out of arrogance, haughtiness, rebellion, and envy. He said to him: ﴿O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My hands?﴾ up to ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and whoever follows you among them, all together﴾ [Sad 38:75–85].

He said: When God finished with Iblis and rebuking him, and he refused except disobedience, He cast the curse upon him and expelled him from Paradise. Then He turned to Adam, after having taught him all the names, and said: "O Adam, inform them of their names." When he informed them of their names, He said: "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?" They said: "Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the Knowing, the Wise." That is, we only answered You about what You taught us, but what You did not teach us, You know best. So whatever name Adam gave to anything, that was its name by which it is known until the Day of Resurrection. [Editor's note: The first part of this report was given earlier under no. 600.]

Ibn Jurayj said:

616. It was narrated to us by al-Qasim, who said: al-Husayn informed us, who said: Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, who said: They only spoke of what He had informed them would exist from the creation of Adam, so they said: "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?" Some of them said: The angels only said what they said — "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood" — because God had permitted them to ask about that, after He had told them that this would happen from the children of Adam. So the angels asked Him, saying, in astonishment: "How will they disobey You, O Lord, when You are their Creator?" Their Lord answered them: "Indeed, I know what you do not know," meaning: that this will happen from them, even if you do not know it, and from some whom you see as obedient to Me. He thereby made them aware of the deficiency of their knowledge compared to His. [Editor's note: I have not found this report anywhere else.]

Some of the scholars of Arabic said: The angels' saying, "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein," was not a rejection of their Lord on their part; rather they asked Him so that they might know, and they informed about themselves that they glorify Him. He said: They said that because they disliked that God should be disobeyed, since the jinn had previously been commanded and had disobeyed.

Some of them said: That was from the angels in the manner of seeking guidance about what they did not know of that, as if they had said: "O Lord, inform us," a question of inquiry from them to God, not in the manner of a question of reproach.

Abu Ja'far said: The most preferable of these interpretations regarding the words of God, the Majestic, reporting His angels' saying to Him, "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You," is the interpretation of those who say that it was from them a request for information from their Lord, meaning: "Inform us, O our Lord, whether You are placing on the earth one with these characteristics, and leaving us from placing Your successors among us, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You" — not a denial from them of what their Lord had informed them He would do, even though they were greatly troubled when they were told that God would have a creature who disobeys Him.

As for the claim of one who asserts that God, the Majestic, had permitted them to ask about that and they asked in the manner of astonishment, it is a claim for which there is no indication in the apparent text of the revelation, nor any report from proof that closes the excuse. It is not permissible to interpret the Book of God with what has no indication in it from some of the aspects by which proof is established.

As for describing the angels, in their asking their Lord about it, as attributing corruption on the earth and the shedding of blood, there is nothing impossible in what was narrated from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud — the saying transmitted by al-Suddi, in agreement with them by Qatadah — in interpretation: that God, the Majestic, informed them that He is placing on the earth a vicegerent who will have offspring who will do such-and-such, so they said: "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein," in the manner of inquiry as I have described.

If someone says to us: What is the manner of their inquiry, given that the matter is as you have described, that they had already reported that this would happen?

It is said: The manner of their inquiry then would be about their state at the occurrence of that: would that be from them? And their asking their Lord to make them the vicegerents on the earth, so that they would not disobey Him. Also not corrupt is what al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas followed him in it, that the angels said that because of what they had of knowledge of the inhabitants of the earth before Adam, of the jinn. They said to their Lord: "Will You place therein, like them, creatures who will do the like of what they used to do?" — in the manner of seeking knowledge from them of their Lord, not in the manner of asserting that this would definitely happen as such. Thus it would be from them an informing about what they had not been made aware of from the knowledge of the unseen. Also not wrong is what Ibn Zayd said, that the angels' saying what they said was in astonishment that God should have a creature that disobeys its Creator.

We left aside the saying narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, which al-Rabi' ibn Anas agreed with, and what Ibn Zayd said in interpreting that, because we have no report of what they said from a route whose transmission closes the excuse and binds the hearer with proof. Information about what has passed and is past can only have its soundness known through a transmission that precludes collusion and fabrication, and in which falsehood, error, and forgetfulness are impossible. [Editor's note: In the manuscript and the printed edition: "it precludes from it... and it is impossible from it," which is not correct. In the manuscript the word "al-tashaghub" appears as an unclear word.] That is not found in this way in what al-Dahhak reported from Ibn Abbas and al-Rabi' agreed with, nor in what Ibn Zayd said.

So the most preferable interpretation of the verse, given that the matter is so, is the one that the apparent text of the revelation indicates and whose meaning can be sound.

If someone says: If the most preferable interpretation of the verse is what you mentioned, that God informed the angels that the descendants of His vicegerent on the earth would cause corruption and shed blood, and because of that the angels said: "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein," then where is the mention of God's informing them of that in His Book?

It is said to him: He relied on the indication of what has been made apparent from the speech about it, as the poet said:

"So do not bury me, for my burial is forbidden to you, / but rather let the she-wolf Umm Amir hide [in my remains]."

[Editor's note: The verse is by al-Shanfara al-Azdi in a story. See Sharh al-Hamasa 2:24–26, al-Aghani 21:89, and others. It is also narrated as: "Do not bury me, for my grave..." and "but rather give me good news." His words "khamiri" mean: hide yourself. It derives from al-khamrah (with kasra and sukun), meaning concealment. They mean by that the approach of the hyena, hidden and staying in its place until it mingles with the slain and takes from it. Umm Amir is the kunya of the hyena. The hunter says this to it when he wants to hunt it, deceiving it so that he can overpower it, saying: "Good news, Umm Amir, of lean sheep and withered locusts, and the broken bones of slain men," and the hyena inclines toward him and he hunts it.]

So he omitted his words "leave me for the one who is called at her hunting: hide yourself, Umm Amir," since in what appeared from his speech there was an indication of the meaning he intended. Likewise is that in His words: "They said: Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein," since in it there is an indication of what He left mentioned after His words "I am placing on the earth a vicegerent," of the information about what would happen from the corruption of His descendants on the earth; He relied on its indication and omitted it, leaving out its mention as we have mentioned from the poet's words. Such parallels in the Qur'an, in the poetry of the Arabs, and in their speech are more than can be counted. Because of what we have mentioned, we have chosen what we have chosen regarding the interpretation of His words: "They said: Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood."

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You﴾

Abu Ja'far said: As for His words, "while we exalt You with praise," it means: we magnify You by praising You and thanking You, as the Majestic said: ﴿So exalt your Lord with praise﴾ [al-Nasr 110:3], and as He said: ﴿And the angels exalt with praise of their Lord﴾ [al-Shura 42:5]. Every remembrance of God among the Arabs is tasbih (glorification) and prayer. A man among them says: "I have completed my subha (devotional recitation) of remembrance and prayer." It has been said that tasbih is the prayer of the angels.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 6 of 6):

617- Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ya'qub al-Qummi narrated to us, from Ja'far ibn Abi al-Mughira, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: The Prophet ﷺ was praying when a man from among the Muslims passed by a man from among the hypocrites, and said to him: "The Prophet ﷺ is praying and you are sitting!" He replied: "Go on to your work, if you have any work." He said: "I do not think that someone who will object to you will not pass by you." Then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab passed by him and said: "O so-and-so, the Prophet ﷺ is praying and you are sitting!" He said to him the same words, and he replied: "This is from my deeds." So he leapt upon him and beat him until he finished, then he entered the mosque and prayed with the Prophet ﷺ. When the Prophet ﷺ turned from his prayer, 'Umar stood up to him and said: "O Prophet of Allah, I passed a little while ago by so-and-so while you were praying, and I said to him: 'The Prophet ﷺ is praying and you are sitting!' He said: 'Go on to your work, if you have any work.'" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Why did you not strike his neck?" So 'Umar rose hastily.
