Abu Ja'far said: As for the interpretation of His saying, "Then Adam received" (fa-talaqqa Adam), it is said that he took and accepted [[In the printed edition: "took. And it was said: its origin is..." which is an error.]]. Its root is the tafa''ul form (tafa''ul, the reflexive pattern) from liqa' (meeting), as a man receives (yatalaqqa) another man, meeting him upon his arrival from his absence or journey. So it is as if that were the case in His saying "fa-talaqqa", as if he met it and received it with acceptance when it was revealed to him or he was informed of it. The meaning of that, then, is: God presented (laqqa) Adam with words of repentance, and Adam received them (talaqqaha) from his Lord and took them from Him, repentant, so God turned to him (taba Allah alayhi) by his accepting them and his acceptance of them from his Lord. As related:

777 - Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying, "Then Adam received from his Lord words," the verse. He said: He taught them the following verse: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [[Report 774: Ibn Kathir 1:147, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:59, al-Shawkani 1:58, and it will come under No. 792.]] [Surah al-A'raf: 23].

* *

Some readers recited: "fa-talaqqa Adamu min rabbihi kalimatun" (with the words as subject), making the words the ones who receive Adam. This, although it is permissible from the standpoint of Arabic grammar, since everything a man receives is received by him and whatever meets him has met him, so it is open to the speaker to direct the verb to whichever he wishes and to omit whichever he prefers, is in my view not permissible in recitation except with the nominative "Adam" as the one who receives the words, owing to the consensus of the authoritative reciters (al-qurra') and the exegetes of the earlier and later scholars, on directing the receiving to Adam rather than to the words. It is also not permissible to object to a reading upon which there is consensus, on the word of one who is subject to error and forgetfulness.

* *

The exegetes differed concerning the specific words that Adam received from his Lord. Some of them said:

Did You not create me with Your hand?" He said: "Yes." He said: "O Lord, did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?" He said: "Yes." He said: "O Lord, did You not settle me in Your Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "O Lord, did Your mercy not precede Your wrath?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do You see, if I repent and act righteously, will You return me to the Garden?" He said: "Yes."

He said: That is His saying, "Then Adam received from his Lord words."

So his Lord said to him: "Indeed I will return you to the Garden."

He said: "Yes." So Adam repented, and his Lord turned to him. [[Report 790: I have not found it elsewhere.]]

[[Report 791: Ibn Kathir 1:147, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:59.]]

[[Report 792: Ibn Kathir 1:147, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:59, and it passed as No. 774.]]

* *

These sayings that we have related from those from whom we have related them, although their wordings differ, their meanings agree that God, mighty is His praise, presented (laqqa) Adam with words, and Adam received them from his Lord, accepted them, acted upon them, and repented by his acceptance of them and his acting upon them to God from his sin, acknowledging his sin, disavowing his sin before his Lord, regretful over what had preceded from him of opposition to His command. So God turned to him by His accepting the words that he received from Him, and his regret over the past sin.

What the Book of God indicates is that the words which Adam received from his Lord are the words that God informed us he spoke, disavowing his sin by their utterance before his Lord and acknowledging his sin, and that is His saying: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers." What was said by those who opposed our view—among the sayings we have related—is not rejected outright, but it is a saying for which there is no evidence from a proof that must be accepted, so it is permissible for us to attribute it to Adam, and that it is among what he received from his Lord when he turned to Him in repentance from his sin. This report that God related about Adam—of the words He taught him, so that he said them repentant to Him from his sin—is an instruction from Him, exalted is His mention, to all those addressed in His Book regarding the manner of repenting to Him from sins [[In the manuscript: "the repentance from sins," without the preposition.]], and an admonition to those addressed by His saying: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 28], concerning the place of repentance from the disbelief in God in which they are, and that their deliverance from the error in which they remain is like the deliverance of their father Adam from his sin, together with reminding them of the blessings that preceded to them, with which He singled out their father Adam and others of their forefathers.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He turned to him﴾

Abu Ja'far said: His saying, "Then He turned to him," means: to Adam. The pronoun in "alayhi" (to him) refers to "Adam." And His saying, "Then He turned to him," means He granted him repentance from his sin. Repentance (tawbah) means returning to God, and turning back to His obedience from what He dislikes of disobedience.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He is the Ever-Returning, the Most Merciful (37). We said: Go down from it, all of you﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation of His saying, "Indeed, He is the Ever-Returning, the Most Merciful," is that God, mighty is His praise, is the Ever-Returning toward whoever of His sinning servants turns to Him from their sins, forgoing their punishment by their return to His obedience after their disobedience, by what preceded of their sin. We have mentioned that the meaning of repentance from the servant to his Lord is his return to His obedience and his turning back to what pleases Him, by abandoning what displeases Him of the matters in which he had persisted, which his Lord dislikes. Likewise, God's turning to His servant is that He grants him that, and turns back for him from His anger toward him to approval of him, and from punishment to pardon and forgiveness of him.

* *

As for His saying, "the Most Merciful," it means that He is the one who bestows favor upon him, together with repentance, through mercy. His mercy toward him is the pardoning of his slip and his overlooking the punishment of his offense.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We have mentioned the discussion of the interpretation of His saying, "We said: Go down from it, all of you," earlier [[See p. 534.]], so there is no need for us to repeat it, since its meaning in this place is its meaning in that place.

793 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim has related to me, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Salim informed us, from Abu Salih, regarding His saying, "Go down from it, all of you," he said: Adam, Eve, the serpent, and Iblis. [[Report 793: I have not found it with this isnad; see what passed, Nos. 754 and after.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 38:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He and remembered: ﴿Then if guidance comes to you from Me﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of His saying "fa-immā yaʾtiyannakum" is "fa-in yaʾtikum" (if there comes to you). The "mā" that accompanies "in" is for emphasis of the speech. Because it enters with "in," the heavy nun was added to "yaʾtiyannakum," as a distinction between the "mā" that comes to mean emphasis of the speech, which the grammarians call ṣila (a filler or redundant particle) and ḥashw, and the "mā" that means "alladhī" (who/which). By its entry into the verb, the "mā" that accompanies "in" in the sense of conditional is shown to be for emphasis, and not the "mā" meaning "alladhī."

Some grammarians of the Basrans [in the printed edition: "the Basran grammarians"] said: "immā" is "in" to which "mā" was added, and the verb after it takes the light or heavy nun, though it may also occur without a nun. The nun is good in it when "mā" enters, because "mā" is a negation, and so it is of what is not obligatory, and it is the particle that negates the obligatory, so the nun is good in it, like their saying: "bi-ʿaynin mā aranneka" (with an eye I see you), where when "mā" was added the nun became good in what is here.

A group of Arabic grammarians rejected the claim of the one who said this view: that the "mā" with "bi-ʿaynin mā aranneka" has the meaning of denial, and they supposed that this has the meaning of emphasis of the speech. [in the printed edition: "a group rejected the claim of its proponents..."]

Others said: rather it is superfluous in the speech, and its meaning is elision, and the meaning of the speech is "bi-ʿayn arāka" (with an eye I see you). It is not permissible, given the disagreement over it, to make it a basis upon which other things are measured.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He and remembered: ﴿guidance from Me. So whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾

Abu Ja'far said: "Al-hudā" in this place means clear explanation and right guidance, as:

794 – Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Adam al-ʿAsqalani narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabiʿ, from Abu al-ʿAliyah, regarding His saying "fa-immā yaʾtiyannakum minnī hudan": He said: "The guidance" is the prophets, the messengers, and the clear explanation. [Source note: Ibn Kathir 1:148, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:63, al-Shawkani 1:58.]

If what Abu al-ʿAliyah said in this is as he said, then the address in His saying "ihbiṭū" (descend) is to Adam and his wife, and if it is for Adam and his wife, then it must be that Adam and his wife and their offspring are meant by it. This would then be like His saying: ﴿He said to it and to the earth: "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said: "We come willingly"﴾ [Surah Fussilat: 11], meaning: we come with what is in us of creation, willingly. And like His saying in the reading of Ibn Masʿud: ﴿Our Lord, and make us submissive to You, and of our descendants a submissive nation to You, and show us our rites﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 128], where he used the plural before they were descendants, whereas in our reading it is "wa-arinā manāsikanā." And like when a speaker says to another: "As if you have married and a child has been born to you, and you have multiplied and become strong," and similar speech.

We said that this is necessary according to the interpretation we mentioned from Abu al-ʿAliyah, because Adam was the prophet during his lifetime after he was sent down to the earth, [in the printed edition: "he was the Prophet ﷺ"] and the messenger from God, may His praise be exalted, to his offspring. It is not permissible that what is meant by His saying "fa-immā yaʾtiyannakum minnī hudan" addressed to him and his wife, the Messenger ﷺ being meant, "fa-immā yaʾtiyannakum minnī anbiyāʾu wa-rusul" [in the printed edition: "...minnī hudan anbiyāʾ wa-rusul..."], except according to the interpretation I have described.

Abu al-ʿAliyah's statement on this, although it is an aspect of interpretation that the verse can bear, is closer to the truth in my view and more consistent with the apparent wording of the recitation: that its interpretation is: "If there comes to you, O assembly of those who were sent down to the earth from My heaven [in the printed edition: "O assembly of those I sent down"], namely Adam, his wife, and Iblis, as we have already mentioned in the interpretation of the preceding verse, a clear explanation of My command and My obedience, and guidance to My path and My religion, then whoever of you follows it, there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve, even if there had previously proceeded from them disobedience to Me and opposition to My command and My obedience." By this He informs them, may His praise be exalted, that He is the Accepter of repentance from whoever repents to Him of his sins, and the Merciful to whoever turns to Him, as He described Himself by His saying: "Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful."

This is because the apparent address in this is to those to whom He, may His praise be exalted, said: "Descend from it, all of you," and those addressed by it are those we named in the saying of the proof among the Companions and the Followers, whose narrations from them we have already presented. [in the printed edition: "the narration from them" without the particle] And that, although it is an address from God, may His remembrance be exalted, to those who were then sent down from the heaven to the earth, it is the sunnah of God in all of His creation, and a declaration from Him of those about whom He informed at the beginning of this surah with what He informed about them in His saying [in the printed edition: "and a declaration from Him of this to those who..."]: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 6], and in His saying: ﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 8], and that His ruling concerning them, if they repent to Him, turn back to Him, and follow what came to them of clear explanation from God upon the tongue of His messenger Muhammad ﷺ, is that they are with Him in the Hereafter among those on whom there is no fear and who do not grieve; and that if they perish upon their disbelief and misguidance before turning back and repenting, they will be among the people of the Fire, abiding in it forever.

And His saying "fa-man tabiʿa hudāy" means: whoever follows My clear explanation which I gave upon the tongues of My messengers, or with My messengers. [in the printed edition: "...My clear explanation which I make clear upon the tongues of My messengers."] As:

795 – Al-Muthanna narrated it to us, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabiʿ, from Abu al-ʿAliyah: "fa-man tabiʿa hudāy" — meaning: My explanation. [Source note: I have not found it elsewhere.]

* *

And His saying "fa-lā khawfun ʿalayhim" means: they will be safe from the terrors of the Resurrection and from God's punishment, not fearing His chastisement, because they obeyed God in the world and followed His command, His guidance, and His path; "wa-lā hum yaḥzanūn" means: they will not grieve that day over what they left behind after their death in the world. As:

796 – Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "There is no fear upon them" — he says: there is no fear upon you before you [Source note: I have not found it elsewhere.]

And nothing is greater in the breast of one who dies than what comes after death. So He gave them security from it, and consoled them about the world, saying: "nor will they grieve."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 39:

And His saying: ﴿But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs – they are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾.

Meaning: And those who denied My signs and rejected My messengers. The "signs of Allah" are His proofs and evidences of His oneness and lordship, and the marks and indications that the messengers brought to confirm that, and to confirm their truthfulness in what they reported of their Lord. We have already explained that the meaning of kufr (disbelief, the covering over of something) is [[See what has passed, p. 255.]].

"They are the companions of the Fire": that is, its people, those who are truly its people and no others, who will abide therein forever, without any term or end. As follows:

797 – ʿUqbah ibn Sinan al-Basri narrated to us, saying: Ghassan ibn Mudar narrated to us, saying: Saʿid ibn Yazid narrated to us – and Sawwar ibn ʿAbd Allah al-ʿAnbari narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Abu Maslamah Saʿid ibn Yazid narrated to us – and Yaʿqub ibn Ibrahim and Abu Bakr ibn ʿAwn narrated to me, both saying: Isma'il ibn ʿUlayyah narrated to us, from Saʿid ibn Yazid, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "As for the people of the Fire who are its people, they will not die therein nor live. But there will be people whom the Fire afflicts because of their sins or their misdeeds, and it causes them to die a death, until when they become charcoal, intercession is permitted [[Hadith 797: Al-Tabari narrates it here through three chains, all ending with Saʿid ibn Yazid. Ibn Kathir mentions it (1:158), but erred in saying he narrated it through two routes, when in fact there are three, as you see.

ʿUqbah ibn Sinan ibn ʿUqbah ibn Sinan al-Basri – the teacher of al-Tabari in the first chain: trustworthy; Abu Hatim heard from him and said: "Sadūq" (truthful). I have found no biography of him except in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 3/1/311. Ghassan ibn Mudar al-Azdi al-Basri: trustworthy, among the early teachers of Ahmad; Ahmad said: "a trustworthy, trustworthy shaykh." al-Bukhari included him in al-Kabir 4/1/107, and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/51. Abu Bakr ibn ʿAwn – the teacher of al-Tabari in the third chain: I could not determine who he is, and there is no trace of him in the chain, for al-Tabari narrated it from him and from Yaʿqub ibn Ibrahim al-Duraqi, both from Ibn ʿUlayyah. Saʿid ibn Yazid ibn Maslamah Abu Maslamah al-Azdi al-Basri: a trustworthy Successor, whose narrations are recorded by the group. al-Bukhari included him in 2/1/476, and Ibn Abi Hatim in 2/1/73. His kunya is "Abu Maslamah" with mim at its beginning. In Ibn Kathir's Tafsir it occurs as "Abu Salamah" without the mim, which is a typographical error.

This hadith is narrated by Muslim (1:67-68) and Ibn Majah (4309), both through Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal, from Saʿid ibn Yazid Abu Maslamah, but in both it is longer than here. No one among the authors of the six books other than these two narrated it, as its takhrij in Jami' al-Usul by Ibn al-Athir (8085) shows. Likewise Imam Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad (11093; 3:11 Halabi) from Ibn ʿUlayyah. Ahmad also narrated it (11769; 3:78-79), and Muslim (1:68), both through Shuʿbah, from Saʿid ibn Yazid.

In reality it is part of a long hadith, which Ahmad narrated in al-Musnad, both in full and abridged, through several routes from Abu Nadrah, including: 11029, 11168, 11218-11220 (3:5, 20, 25-26 Halabi).]].

**On the interpretation of His words, may He be remembered:** ﴿O Children of Israel﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His words, may His praise be exalted, "O Children of Israel," He means the descendants of Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, the Friend of the Merciful [[In the printed edition: "O descendants of Ya'qub..." with the addition of the vocative particle.]]. Ya'qub was called "Isra'il," meaning the servant of God and His chosen one among His creatures. "Il" is God, and "Isra" is the servant, just as it is said "Jibril" means the servant of God. And as the following report has it:

798. Ibn Humayd related to us: Jarir related to us, from al-A'mash, from Isma'il ibn Raja', from Umayr, the freedman of Ibn 'Abbas, from Ibn 'Abbas, that "Isra'il" is like your saying "Abd Allah" (the servant of God).

[[Report 798: It appears in Ibn Kathir 1:149 and al-Durr al-Manthur 1:63. This chain is sound. Isma'il ibn Raja' ibn Rabi'a is trustworthy; Muslim included him in his Sahih. Umayr, freedman of Ibn 'Abbas, is Umayr ibn 'Abd Allah al-Hilali, freedman of Umm al-Fadl, and he is sometimes attributed to the clientage of her husband al-'Abbas, as appears in another chain in the Musnad (77), and sometimes to the clientage of some of her children, as in this chain. He was a trustworthy Successor (tabi'i); Ibn Abi Hatim recorded his biography (3/1/380), and the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others narrated from him.]]

799. And Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, who said: "Il" means "God" in Hebrew.

[[Report 799: It appears in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:63. "al-Minhal" is Ibn 'Amr al-Asadi. "'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith" is al-Ansari al-Basri Abu al-Walid, a trustworthy Successor.]]

God, may His praise be exalted, addressed with His words "O Children of Israel" the rabbis of the Jews from among the Children of Israel who were living among the emigrants to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He attributed them, may His remembrance be exalted, to Ya'qub, just as He attributed the descendants of Adam to Adam, saying: ﴿O Children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of worship﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 31], and similar to that. He singled them out for address in this verse and in the verses that follow it, in which He reminds them of His blessings, although what was revealed concerning them and concerning others at the beginning of this surah has already been mentioned. The reason is that the proofs and signs He presented, which contain reports about their forebears and accounts of their earliest ancestors, and the stories of matters whose knowledge is specific to them, to the exclusion of all other nations, are not known to anyone else with the same certainty of their authenticity and reality, except for those who have acquired knowledge of them from them. He made them know that Muhammad's knowledge of these matters, despite the distance of his people and kin from knowing them and the scarcity of Muhammad (ﷺ) in studying the books that contain reports of those matters [[His words "wa-qillat muzawalat Muhammad (ﷺ) dirasat al-kutub" ("and the scarcity of Muhammad's practice of studying the books") correspond to what we say today in modern phrasing: "and the non-practice of Muhammad..." Al-Jahiz said in al-Bayan wa-al-Tabyin 1:285: "Awn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba ibn Mas'ud sought protection from Muhammad ibn Marwan at Nasibin, and he married a woman there. Muhammad said: 'How do you find Nasibin?' He said: 'Many scorpions, few relatives.' He meant by "few" what the speaker means in saying "so-and-so has little shame," and he did not mean that there is some shame, however little. They use "qalilan" in the place of "laysa" (not)." End of quote.

I say: From this is the saying of Durayd ibn al-Simma about his brother:
*Little complaining at calamities, guarding*
*from today the consequences of talk for tomorrow.*

And al-Tabari's explanation of His words in Surah al-Baqarah: 88, "fa-qalilan ma yu'minun" ("so little do they believe"), will come (1:324, Bulaq edition): "It is said 'fa-qalilan ma yu'minun' while they are all disbelievers, as the Arabs say: 'I have hardly ever seen the like of this.' They have related from them, from their hearing: 'I passed through lands where hardly anything grows except leeks and onions,' meaning that nothing grows except leeks and onions, and similar speech that describes a thing with scarcity while the meaning is the negation of the whole." End of quote.

In a hadith: "He used to hardly utter idle speech," meaning he never engaged in idle speech at all. Ibn al-Athir said: this word is used to negate the very essence of a thing (Lisan al-'Arab: q-l-l).

Were it not for a time in which the tongue has decayed, faith has diminished, and boldness has grown among the presumptuous in interpreting words and hunting for doubts, and were it not that a speaker would say and falsely attribute to al-Tabari that he said the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to study the books of the People of the Book, I would have been free of such lengthy discussion.]], that Muhammad (ﷺ) did not reach knowledge of that except through revelation from God and a descent of it to him from Him, because they are in a position concerning knowledge of its authenticity that no other nation holds. Therefore He, may His praise be exalted, singled them out with His words "O Children of Israel" for address, as:

800. Ibn Humayd related this to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from 'Ikrima, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words "O Children of Israel," that he said: O People of the Book, addressing the rabbis of the Jews.

**The Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted: "And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you"**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His praise be exalted, "believe" (āminū) means: affirm as true (ṣaddiqū), as we have already explained earlier. [[See what has passed: 234, 235.]] By "what I have sent down" He means what was sent down upon Muhammad ﷺ of the Qur'an. By His words "confirming what is with you" He means that the Qur'an confirms what the Jews of the Children of Israel have of the Torah. So He commanded them to affirm the Qur'an as true, and He informed them, may His praise be exalted, that in their affirming the Qur'an there is an affirmation by them of the Torah, because what is in the Qur'an of the command to acknowledge the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, to affirm him and to follow him, is like what is of that in the Torah and the Gospel. So in their affirming what was sent down upon Muhammad there is an affirmation by them of what they have of the Torah, and in their denying it there is a denial by them of what they have of the Torah.

His words "confirming" (muṣaddiqan) are a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun that is left out in "anzaltuhu" (I have sent it down), referring back to "mā" (what). The meaning of the sentence is: "Believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, O Jews." What is with them is the Torah and the Gospel. As related:

[8814] Muhammad ibn 'Amr al-Bahili narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa ibn Maymun narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of God: "And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you," he said: "I have only sent down the Qur'an confirming what is with you, the Torah and the Gospel." [[The report 8814 is in Ibn Kathir 1:150 in summarized form, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:264, and al-Shawkani 1:61.]]

[8815] And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

[8816] And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far informed us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyya: "And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you," he said: "O people of the Book, believe in what I have sent down upon Muhammad, confirming what is with you." He said: "Because they find Muhammad ﷺ written with them in the Torah and the Gospel." [[The report 8815 is in Ibn Kathir 1:150, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:64, and al-Shawkani 1:61.]]

* * *

**The Interpretation of His Words: "And do not be the first to disbelieve in it"**

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: How is it said, "And do not be the first to disbelieve in it," when the address in it is to a plural group, while "disbeliever" (kāfir) is singular? And if it is permissible, would one allow someone to say, "Do not be the first man to stand"?

It is said to him: The singular is only permissible for what is joined to the form "afʿal" (more... / first), when it is a predicate of a plural, if it is a noun derived from "faʿala / yafʿalu," because it conveys the meaning of the omitted word in the speech, which is "man" (whoever), and it stands in its place in conveying the sense of plurality and femininity that "man" would convey, while being in a singular form. Do you not see that you say: "Do not be the first of those who disbelieve in it"? "Man" here has the meaning of the plural, and it does not inflect like nouns for dual, plural and feminine. So when the derived noun from "faʿala / yafʿalu" is placed in its position, it operates, though singular, in the manner of "man" in conveying the sense of plurality and femininity that "man" would convey, as in your saying: "The army is routed" (al-jaysh munhazim) and "the troops are advancing" (al-jund muqbil), where you make the verb singular to match the singular form of "army" and "troops." [[In the printed edition: "the army runs away, and the troops advance," which is a clear error.]] It is not permissible to say: "The army is a man, and the troops are a boy," until you say: "The troops are boys and the army is men," because the singular of the countable nouns that are not derived from "faʿala / yafʿalu" does not convey the meaning of a group of them. Among this is the poet's verse:

*And when they have eaten, the basest eater among them [is the one];*
*And when they have hungered, the worst of the hungry [is the one].* [[Nawadir of Abu Zayd, p. 152, attributed to a pre-Islamic man. Also in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:33. It is three lines in Nawadir, and before it is: "And a wretched one, a snarling dog, insults me / so hear the wailing of dogs' rear ends." / "Is there anything other than your enemy against your neighbors / for your bellies, the dark night's dawn-calls?" "Ta'imu" means "they were sated," so then they are the basest of the sated. And in a hadith: "The food of one suffices two, and the food of two suffices four," meaning sufficiency. The one's sustenance is the two's food, and the two's fullness is the four's food.]]

So he used the singular once, in accordance with what I have described, by the intention of "man" and by placing the apparent derived noun from "faʿala / yafʿalu" in its position, and he used the plural another time, by the expression according to the number of the nouns referring to those spoken of. If he had used the singular where he used the plural, or the plural where he used the singular, it would have been correct and permissible. [[See the same as what al-Tabari said in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:32–33.]]

As for the interpretation of that, it means: "O assembly of the rabbis of the People of the Book, affirm as true what I have sent down upon My messenger Muhammad ﷺ of the Qur'an, which confirms your Book, and what you have of the Torah and the Gospel, in which it was entrusted to you that he is My messenger and My prophet, sent with the truth. And do not be the first of your community to deny it and to reject that it is from Me, while you have among you knowledge of it that others do not have." [[In the printed edition: "the first to deny it," but what we have set down is the correct version of al-Tabari's explanation.]]

And their disbelief in it is their rejection that it is from God. [[In the manuscript: "their disbelief in it and their rejection..." which is an error.]] The "hā'" in "bihi" (in it) refers back to "mā" (what) in His words: "And believe in what I have sent down." As related:

[8817] Al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj said regarding His words "And do not be the first disbeliever in it," that it refers to the Qur'an. [[The report 8817 is in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:64 and al-Shawkani 1:61.]]

Abu Ja'far said: And there is related from Abu al-'Aliyya concerning this:

[8818] Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyya: "And do not be the first to disbelieve in it," he said: "Do not be the first to disbelieve in Muhammad ﷺ." [[The report 8818 is in Ibn Kathir 1:150, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:64, and al-Shawkani 1:61.]]

Some of them said: "And do not be the first to disbelieve in it" means: in your Book. And they interpret that their denial of Muhammad ﷺ is a denial by them of their Book, because in their Book there is the command to follow Muhammad ﷺ.

These two opinions are far from what the recitation apparently indicates. That is because God, may His praise be exalted, commanded the addressees of this verse at its beginning to believe in what was sent down upon Muhammad ﷺ, when He said, may His remembrance be exalted: "And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you." It is understood that what God sent down in the time of Muhammad ﷺ is the Qur'an, not Muhammad, because Muhammad, upon him be the blessings of God, is a messenger who was sent, not a revelation that was sent down, and what is sent down is the Book. Then He forbade them to be the first to disbelieve in what He had commanded them to believe in at the beginning of the verse [[In the printed edition an addition appears between these two clauses, which is inserted, corrupts the speech, and is out of context. Its text: "...at the beginning of the verse from the People of the Book," which is the apparent and understood meaning. And there has not been mention of Muhammad...]], and there has not been in this verse any apparent mention of Muhammad ﷺ, so that the pronoun would refer back to him in His words "and do not be the first disbeliever in it." Although it is not impossible in speech to mention a pronoun for a name that has not had an apparent mention in the speech. [[Al-Tabari's explanation is sound and precise, although some of those who quoted his words thought that both opinions are correct, since they are mutually implicating: whoever disbelieves in the Qur'an has disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ, and whoever disbelieves in Muhammad ﷺ has disbelieved in the Qur'an (Ibn Kathir 1:150). Indeed, both opinions are correct in meaning in themselves, but al-Tabari determines the significance of the words and pronouns in the verse, identifies what the apparent recitation and revelation bear, and separates one meaning from another, even if both are correct in reason, correct in judgment, and correct in religion. People are often lax when meanings are close, and no one separates one meaning from another except one who is expert in Arabic, such as Abu Ja'far, may God be pleased with him.]]

Likewise there is no sense in the opinion of one who claims that the returning pronoun in "bihi" refers to "mā" in His words "what is with you." Because that, although it is a possibility of the apparent speech, is far from what the apparent recitation and revelation indicate, for the reason we described before, that the one commanded to believe in it at the beginning of the verse is the Qur'an. Thus it is necessary that the one forbidden to disbelieve in it at its end is the Qur'an. [[In the manuscript: "...that the command to believe in it at the beginning of the verse... that the prohibition of disbelief in it at its end..." while what is in the printed edition is better and clearer.]] As for whether the one commanded to believe in it is other than the one forbidden to disbelieve in it, in one speech and one verse, that is not the more famous and apparent use in speech. Moreover, its meaning in interpretation is distant. [[This also is of good insight regarding Arabic logic, although some think it is near to what is nearer.]]

[8819] Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrima, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it," and with you is knowledge of it that others do not have. [[The report 8819 is a continuation of the reports numbered 8805 and 8811 above, in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:63.]]

* * *

**The Interpretation of His Words, may His remembrance be exalted: "And do not exchange My signs for a small price"**

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding the interpretation of that. [[Ta'wil: the explanation or the ultimate meaning of a text; here, the exegetical interpretation of the Qur'an.]]

[8820] Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyya: "And do not exchange My signs for a small price," he said: "Do not take a wage for it." He said: "It is written with them in the earlier Book: O son of Adam, teach freely as you were taught freely." [[The report 8820 is a continuation of the report 8818 above and its references there. In Ibn Kathir 1:151. "Majjan" (freely) means giving a thing without favor or price. Abu al-'Abbas said: I heard Ibn al-A'rabi say: "Majjan" among the Arabs means falsehood, and they said: "water that is majjan" (ample water). Al-Azhari said: The Arabs say: "majjan" dates and "majjan" water, meaning abundant and sufficient. He said: A Bedouin asked me for dates, and I gave him a handful, and I apologized to him for the small amount, and he said: "By God, this is majjan," meaning abundant and sufficient. And their saying "He took it majjan" means without exchange, and it is a fa'al form because it is inflected (Lisan al-'Arab: m-j-n).]]

And others said:

[8821] Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And do not exchange My signs for a small price," he said: "Do not take a small greed and conceal the name of God, and that price is greed." [[The report 8821 is in Ibn Kathir 1:151. In the printed edition and in Ibn Kathir: "So that greed is the price," but what we have set down from the manuscript is better.]]

So the interpretation of the verse is therefore: "Do not sell what I have given you of knowledge of My Book and its signs for a vile price and a small worldly good." Their selling it, that is, their abandonment of making clear to the people what is in their Book concerning Muhammad ﷺ, and that it is written in it that he is the unlettered prophet whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, is for a small price, namely their contentment with leadership over their followers from among the people of their religion and creed, and their taking wages from those to whom they explained that, in exchange for what they explained to them of it.

We only said that the meaning of that is "do not sell," because the buyer of a small price in exchange for the signs of God is a seller of the signs for the price, so each of the price and the priced thing is sold to the other, and the other is a buyer for it. The meaning is, as Abu al-'Aliyya interpreted it: "Make clear to the people the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, and do not seek a wage from them for it." So then His prohibition of taking a wage for making it clear is the prohibition of buying a small price in exchange for His signs.

* * *

**The Interpretation of His Words, may His remembrance be exalted: "And fear Me"**

Abu Ja'far said: He says: "fear Me" — in your selling of My signs for a vile price, and your buying with them a small worldly good, and your disbelief in what I have sent down upon My messenger and your denial of the prophethood of My prophet — lest I bring upon you what I brought upon your predecessors who followed your path, of exemplary punishments and vengeances.

* * *

**The Interpretation of His Words: "And do not mix truth with falsehood"**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words "and do not mix" He means: do not confound. And "labs" (confusion, mixing) is mixing.

It is said from it: "labistu 'alayhi hadha al-amr, albisuhu labsan" (I confused this matter for him), when I mixed it up for him. As related:

[8822] I was told from al-Minjab, from Bishr ibn 'Amara, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "And We would have confused for them what they confuse" [Surat al-An'am: 9], he said: "We would have mixed up for them what they mix up." [[The report 8822 I have not found in any place, and al-Tabari did not mention it in its place in the tafsir of this verse in Surat al-An'am (7:98, Bulaq edition).]]

And from it is the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

*When they confused the truth with the feigned,*
*they were content and exchanged Zayd for me.* [[His Diwan: 65. "Ghina 'an al-shay'" and "istaghna": he cast it off and threw it from his sight and did not turn to it.]]

By His words "labasna" (they confused) he means: they mixed.

As for "al-libs" (clothing), it is said from it: "labistuhu albasuhu libsan wa malbasan" (I put it on, I wear it), and that is the garment one puts on and wears. [[In the printed edition: "and that is in the garment," with an addition.]] From "al-libs" is the saying of al-Akhtal:

*Indeed I have worn the ages of this time,*
*until gray hair covered my head and blazed.* [[His Diwan: 142, where it is "Indeed I have worn." "A'sur" is the plural of "'asr," meaning the age and time. Here it refers to the changing of days, sweet and bitter, so it is in the plural. "Labisa lahu a'surahu" means he lived through its ages and endured its good and evil. "Tajallala al-shayb ra'sahu" means gray hair covered his head.]]

And from "al-libs" is the saying of God, may His praise be exalted: "And We would have confused for them what they confuse." [Surat al-An'am: 9]

* * *

If someone says to us: How did they mix truth with falsehood while they were disbelievers? And what truth did they have with their disbelief in God?

It is said: Among them were hypocrites who outwardly showed affirmation of Muhammad ﷺ and inwardly concealed disbelief in him. Most of them said: "Muhammad is a prophet who was sent, but he was sent to others than us." So the hypocrite's confusion of truth with falsehood was his outward showing of the truth with his tongue, and his acknowledgment of Muhammad ﷺ and what he brought openly, and his mixing of that apparent truth with what he concealed inwardly. And the confusion of the one who acknowledged among them that he was sent to others, while denying that he was sent to them, was his acknowledgment that he was sent to others, which is the truth, and his denial that he was sent to them, which is falsehood, although God had sent him to all creation. This is their mixing of truth with falsehood and their confusing of it with that. As related:

[8823] Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Amara narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: "And do not mix truth with falsehood," he said: "Do not mix truthfulness with lying." [[The report 8823 is in Ibn Kathir 1:152, al-Durr al-Manthur 1:64, and al-Shawkani 1:62.]]

[8824] And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyya: "And do not mix truth with falsehood," he said: "Do not mix truth with falsehood, and render the counsel to God's servants regarding the matter of Muhammad ﷺ." [[The report 8824 is in Ibn Kathir 1:152.]]

٨٢٥ - Al-Qasim related to us, he said: al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hajjaj related to me, he said: Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid said regarding ﴿and do not confuse the truth with falsehood﴾: [it means] Judaism and Christianity mixed with Islam. [[The report: ٨٢٥ - I have not found it from Mujahid. A similar report from Qatadah is in Ibn Kathir, 1:152, and in al-Durr al-Manthur (al-Durr al-Manthur fi al-Tafsir bi al-Ma'thur), 1:64.]]

٨٢٦ - Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words, ﴿and do not confuse the truth with falsehood﴾: "The truth is the Torah which God sent down to Moses, and the falsehood is what they wrote with their own hands." [[The report: ٨٢٦ - In al-Durr al-Manthur, 1:64, and al-Shawkani, 1:62.]]

**The exegesis of the words of the Exalted: ﴿And conceal the truth while you know [it]﴾ (2:42)**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: Regarding His words, "and conceal the truth," there are two possible interpretations:

The first: Allah, great is His praise, forbade them from concealing the truth, just as He forbade them from mixing the truth with falsehood. The meaning would then be: "Do not mix the truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth." In this case, "and conceal" is in the jussive mood, governed by the same particle that governs "mix" (*talbisu*), as a conjunction to it.

The second: that the prohibition from Allah, great is His praise, is only against mixing the truth with falsehood, and His words "and conceal the truth" are a report from Him about their concealing of the truth which they know. In this case, "and conceal" is in the accusative, because it has shifted away from the meaning of His words "do not mix the truth with falsehood," since "do not mix" is a prohibition while "and conceal the truth" is a report conjoined to it. It is not permissible for the jussive particle that operated on "mix" to be repeated on it. This is what the grammarians call *ṣarf* (a shift in construction).[[This was mentioned by al-Farra' in his book *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* 1:33–34, then he said: "If you say: What is *ṣarf*? I say: It is that you bring a *wa* (and) conjoining a statement at its beginning whose repetition does not hold with what it is conjoined to. When that is the case, it is *ṣarf*, like the poet's saying:..." and he recited the verse and said: "Do you not see that it is not permissible to repeat 'do not' before 'come like it,' and therefore it was called *ṣarf*, since it is conjoined and it does not hold to repeat the preceding operator in it."]] A parallel to this in meaning and grammatical form is the saying of the poet:

*Do not forbid a trait while you commit its like;*
*It is a great shame upon you when you do it.*[[This is one of the verses transmitted in several poems. As the author of *al-Khizana* said (3:617), it is attributed by Sibawayh (1:424) to al-Akhtal, and it is in a poem of al-Mutawakkil al-Laythi. It is also attributed to Sabiq al-Barbari, and to al-Tirimmah, and to Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali. A poem cited by the author of *al-Khizana* (3:618) is not in his *Diwan*, which was published by Professor Muhammad Hasan Al Yasin in *Nafa'is al-Makhtutat*, printed by al-Ma'arif Press in Baghdad in 1373 AH (1954 CE). This *Diwan* is from a copy in the hand of Abu al-Fath Uthman ibn Jinni. The editor did not add it to the scattered poetry of Abu al-Aswad which he collected.]]

So "come" (*ta'ti*) is in the accusative according to the interpretation we mentioned for His words "and conceal" [[In the printed edition: "and conceal, the verse, because..." which is an error in reading what is in the manuscript, which is: "and conceal, except that it was not intended."]], because it is not intended to mean: "Do not forbid a trait nor come like it." Rather its meaning is: "Do not forbid a trait while you come like it." So the first is a prohibition and the second is a report, and the report is put in the accusative because it is conjoined to something of a different form.

As for the first of these two interpretations which we mentioned the verse can bear, it is in accordance with the view of Ibn 'Abbas, who said:

827 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umara narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words "and conceal the truth": he says, "Do not conceal the truth while you know."

828 – And Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from 'Ikrima or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "and conceal the truth," i.e., "and do not conceal the truth."[[The two reports 827 and 828: I have not found them in this wording elsewhere. The second is within the report of Ibn 'Abbas previously cited as No. 819, and in Ibn Kathir 1:152 and *al-Durr al-Manthur* 1:63.]]

As for the second of the two, it is in accordance with the view of Abu al-'Aliya and Mujahid.

829 – al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliya: "and conceal the truth while you know," he said: "They concealed the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ)."[[The report 829: I have not found it elsewhere.]]

830 – And Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa ibn Maymun, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

831 – And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

As for the interpretation of the truth which they concealed while knowing it, it is what:

832 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrima, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "and conceal the truth," he says: "Do not conceal what you have of knowledge of My messenger and what he brought, while you find it with you in what you know from the books which are in your hands."[[The report 832: in Ibn Kathir 1:152, *al-Durr al-Manthur* 1:63, and al-Shawkani 1:61.]]

833 – And Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umara narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: "and conceal the truth," he says: "Indeed you know that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, so He forbade them from that."[[The report 833: in *al-Durr al-Manthur* 1:64 and al-Shawkani 1:62, except his words "so He forbade them from that." In the printed edition: "...Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."]]

834 – And Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah: "and conceal the truth while you know," he said: "The People of the Book conceal Muhammad (ﷺ), while they find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel."[[The report 834: in Ibn Kathir 1:152, in summarized form.]]

835 – And al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

836 – And Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "and conceal the truth while you know," he said: "The truth is Muhammad (ﷺ)."[[The report 836: in Ibn Kathir 1:152, in summarized form; in *al-Durr al-Manthur* 1:64, and al-Shawkani 1:62.]]

837 – And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliya: "and conceal the truth while you know," he said: "They concealed the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), while they find him written with them."[[The report 837: I have not found it elsewhere.]]

838 – And al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: "You conceal Muhammad while you know, and you find him with you in the Torah and the Gospel."[[The report 838: I have not found it in this exact wording elsewhere. In the printed edition: "You conceal Muhammad..."]]

So the interpretation of the verse is therefore: "Do not confuse the people, O rabbis of the People of the Book, regarding the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and what he brought from his Lord, and do not claim that he has been sent only to some categories of nations rather than others, or be hypocritical about his matter, while you know that he has been sent to all of you and to all nations other than you. Thereby you would mix truth with falsehood, and conceal what you find in your Book of his description and attributes, and that he is My messenger to mankind entirely, while you know that he is My messenger, and that what he brought to you is from Me, and you recognize that among My covenant, which I took from you in your Book, is belief in him, in what he brought, and affirmation of him."

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah and bow with those who bow [in worship]﴾ (43).

Abu Ja'far said: It has been mentioned that the rabbis of the Jews and the hypocrites used to order the people to establish prayer and give zakah, but they did not do it themselves. So God commanded them to establish prayer along with the Muslims who affirm Muhammad and what he brought, and to give the zakah of their wealth along with them, and to submit to God and His Messenger as they submitted.

839 - As I was told by Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "And establish prayer and give zakah," he said: "Two obligatory duties; so fulfil them to God."[[The report 839: I did not find it in any place.]]

We have already explained the meaning of establishing prayer earlier in this book of ours, so we disliked repeating it.[[See what preceded, pp. 241-242.]]

As for giving zakah, it is the payment of the obligatory charity. The root of zakah is the growth, increase and multiplication of wealth. From this it is said: "the crop grew (zakā)" when what God brought forth from it increased; and "the expense grew (zakat)" when it increased. It is also said: "the odd number became even (zakā)" when the surplus added to it made it an even number, as the poet said:

They were an odd number or an even one, apart from four; they were not created, and the grandfathers of people are wrestling.[[Al-Lisan (khasa). In it: "Al-Farra': the Arabs say of an even number zakā, and of an odd number khasā... He said: the Dubayriyya recited to me..." and he recited the verse. Ta'talij: to wrestle and contend with one another.]]

And another said:

Neither odd in its count nor even, like the worst of the herbs, the tips of the sufa thorn.[[By a man of Banu Sa'd, then one of Banu al-Harith, regarding 'Amr ibn Ka'b ibn Sa'd. This verse is in a report about al-Aghlab al-Ajli (Tabaqat fuhul al-shu'ara': 572; Mu'jam al-shu'ara': 490; al-Aghani 18: 164). The version in the Tabaqat and al-Aghani is: "like the worst of the pasture (al-ra'y)." Al-ra'y (with a kasra and sukun) is the herbage itself, and also the pasture. Al-sufa: the thorn of the bahmi and the spike, and everything with thorns. He says: you among your people are like the sufa among the bahmi, its worst and most wicked part. The first verse is an addition not found in the cited sources.]]

Abu Ja'far said: al-sufa is the thorn of al-buhmi, and al-buhmi is what is round in the thorny sheaths.[[Al-buhmi: one of the noble herbs (that is, what is tender and moist and eaten uncooked), which grows as grain does, until its growth reaches the point of becoming like grain, rising about a span, its growth finer than that of wheat, its taste like barley; when it dries, a thorn comes out on it like the spike's thorn (this is al-sufa), and when it falls into the noses of camels they recoil from it, until people pull it from their mouths and noses. In the printed edition: "fi al-sula" with a shadda on the yā'; in the manuscript "fi al-sulā" with a ḍamma on the sīn and shadda on the lām. The correct reading is what I have given; al-sala'a is the plural of sala'a, which is the thorn of the palm, and by it he means the sufa of the buhmi, i.e., its thorn.]]

By His words "nor even" He means: He did not make them an even number from an odd one by its occurrence among them.[[His words "by its occurrence among them" mean by its presence among these people. Al-'adid (in the verse) comes from the saying "so-and-so is the 'adid of such-and-such a people," i.e., he is counted among them without being one of them. He means that if he joins a people he counts for nothing among them: if they are even, his joining does not make them odd, and if they are odd, it does not make them even; he is as nothing in the count. He is satirizing him and making him fall in estimation.]]

The reason zakah is called zakah, being wealth that leaves wealth, is that by giving it out from what it is taken from, God multiplies what remains of the owner's wealth. It is also possible that it was named zakah because it purifies what remains of a man's wealth and frees it from any injustice to the shares of the rightful claimants,[[Al-suhmān: plural of sahm, like al-sihām, meaning portion or share.]] as the Exalted said, reporting of His Prophet Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Have you killed an innocent soul?﴾ [Surah al-Kahf: 74], meaning: free of sins, pure. And as one says of a man: he is a just and upright (zakiyy) person, for that meaning.[[In the printed edition: "bi-dhalika al-ma'na," which is nothing.]] This interpretation is more pleasing to me, regarding the meaning of zakat al-mal, than the first, though the first is also acceptable as an interpretation.

As for giving it (ītā'uhā), it means handing it to its people.

As for the interpretation of rukū', it is submission to God through obedience. It is said: "so-and-so bowed (raka'a) to such-and-such," when he submitted to him. From this is the poet's saying:

She was sold for a miserable low price, and her father sought help through her from the poverty after he had bowed (raka'a).[[This verse is from verses by Isam ibn 'Ubayd al-Zamani (of Banu Zaman ibn Malik ibn Sa'b ibn 'Ali ibn Bakr ibn Wa'il), which Abu Tammam narrated in al-Wahshiyyat no. 130 (a manuscript in my possession), and al-Jahiz narrated in al-Hayawan 4: 281, where it says: "al-Ziyadi said," which is a distortion and corruption as you see. These verses are from a counter-poem between al-Zamani and Yahya ibn Abi Hafsa. Yahya had married the daughter of Talba ibn Qays ibn 'Asim al-Minqari, so Isam al-Zamani satirized him, saying: "I see the stone has changed and shivered, and sweet life has been replaced by bitterness." Yahya answered with verses including: "Is there anyone who will convey to Isam from me that I will overturn what I have made bitter." Thus al-Marzubani narrated in Mu'jam al-shu'ara': 270; Abu al-Faraj narrated in his al-Aghani 10: 75 that Yahya proposed to Muqatil ibn Talba al-Minqari for his daughter and two sisters, and he consented. Yahya sent to his sons Sulayman, Umar and Jamil, who came and married them to his three sons, and they went in to them and then carried them to Hajr (a place). The verses of Isam al-Zamani and the counter-verses Yahya answered him with are of fine poetry; read them in al-Wahshiyyat, al-Hayawan, and al-Shi'r wa al-shu'ara': 740. The version in al-Hayawan and al-Wahshiyyat is: "sold for a little price, and it was light for him to have her." Al-wakas: the lowering of the price in a sale. In the manuscript and printed edition it reads "bi-kasr la'im," which is a distortion with no meaning; I think the correct reading is what I have given by reasoning. Al-kasr: the most base of the little. His words "she was sold": the pronoun refers to the daughter of Muqatil ibn Talba al-Minqari whom Yahya or one of his sons married. He says: her father sold her for a base, lowly, mean price, and he married her seeking help by selling her from the hardship and want that befell him, so this base, miserly wealth married her to be helped by her dowry.]] He means: after he submitted from the severity of hardship and need.

Abu Ja'far said: This is a command from God, exalted is His praise, to those of the rabbis of the Children of Israel and their hypocrites whom He mentioned, to turn back in repentance to Him, to establish prayer and give zakah, to enter among the Muslims in Islam, and to submit to Him in obedience; and it is a prohibition from Him to them against concealing what they knew of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, after the proofs of Him had been made manifest to them, as we have described earlier in this book of ours, and after giving them warning and admonition, and after reminding them of His blessings upon them and upon their forefathers, as a kindness from Him toward them and a fuller establishment of the proof against them.[[In the printed edition: "wa-ibla'an ilayhim..." with the addition.]]

* *

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The Interpretation of His words, exalted is He: "Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves?"

Abu Ja'far said: The exegetes differed concerning the meaning of "righteousness" (al-birr) which those addressed in this verse used to enjoin upon the people while they forgot themselves, after all of them agreed that every obedience to God is called "birr." It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas:

840 – Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from 'Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding: "Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Book? Will you not then reason?" He said: i.e., you forbid the people from disbelief, by means of the prophethood you possess and the covenant (al-'ahdah) from the Torah,[[In the printed edition, and in the references: "wa-l-'ahd min al-Tawrah" (and the covenant from the Torah). Al-'ahd and al-'ahdah are the same.]] while you forsake yourselves, i.e., while you disbelieve in what it contains of My covenant with you concerning the confirmation of My messenger, and you break My compact, and you deny what you know of My Book.

841 – And Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umarah related to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people" – he says: Do you enjoin upon the people entry into the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), and other things you were commanded, such as establishing the prayer, while you forget yourselves.

* *

Others said:

842 – Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to me, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves?" He said: They used to enjoin the people to obey God and to be mindful of Him, while they themselves disobeyed Him.

843 – And al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves?" He said: The Children of Israel used to enjoin the people to obey God, to be mindful of Him, and to righteousness, and they would oppose it, so God reproached them.

844 – And al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: al-Hajjaj related to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: "Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people" – the People of the Book and the hypocrites used to enjoin the people to fasting and prayer, and they would neglect acting on what they enjoined upon the people, so God reproached them for that. Whoever enjoins good, let him be the most eager of people in it.

* *

Others said:

845 – Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: These Jews – when a man came to ask them about something in which there was no right, no bribe, and nothing, they would order him toward the truth. So God said to them: "Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Book? Will you not then reason?"[[The report: 845 – in Ibn Kathir 1:154, and in it: "When a man came, he asked them about a thing that was not in it..." And in the manuscript: "yas'aluhum laysa fihi".]]

846 – And 'Ali ibn al-Hasan related to me, saying: Muslim al-Jarmi related to us, saying: Mukhallad ibn al-Husayn related to us, from Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, from Abu Qilabah, regarding the saying of God: "Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, and you recite the Book?" He said: Abu al-Darda' said: A man does not understand fully until he dislikes people for the sake of God, then returns to himself and is more disgusted with himself.[[The report: 846 – quoted by Ibn Kathir 1:154 from this place. Al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1:64, attributing it also to 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa-l-Sifat, and al-Shawkani followed him, 1:65. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it, p. 210, through 'Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from Ayyub, similarly. As for "Muslim al-Jarmi": Ibn Kathir in this place has "Aslam," which is a Mut'i printing error. Both it and the copies of al-Tabari have "al-Harmi" with a ḥā'. We preferred in his biography earlier (p. 154) that it is with a jīm, and we mentioned his biographical sources there; we add here that Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned him in al-Jarh wa-l-Ta'dil 4/1/188, describing him as "from the raiders." His teacher Mukhallad ibn al-Husayn – with a fatḥah on the mīm and a silent unmarked kha' between the lām and the ya' – is a well-known trustworthy narrator; Ibn Sa'd said: "He was a trustworthy, excellent man," and Abu Dawud said: "He was the most intelligent person of his time." Abu Qilabah is 'Abd Allah ibn Zayd al-Jarmi, one of the great trustworthy Successors; I hold that his narration from Abu al-Darda' is mursal, for Abu al-Darda' died in 32 AH, while Abu Qilabah died late, in 104 AH, and it was said 107.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: All of what was said by those whose statements we mentioned regarding the interpretation of this verse is close in meaning; for although they differed on the description of the "righteousness" which those people used to enjoin upon others, whom God described with what He described them, they agree that they used to enjoin the people to what pleases God, in word or deed, while they opposed what they enjoined on others by their own actions.

So the interpretation that is indicated as correct by the apparent recitation is: "Do you enjoin the people to obey God, and leave yourselves disobeying Him? Will you not enjoin yourselves to what you enjoin the people – obedience to your Lord?" – rebuking them for it and making their conduct repugnant to them.[[In the printed edition: "wa-muqabbihan ilayhim."]]

* *

The meaning of "their forgetting themselves" in this place is analogous to the forgetting of which He, may His praise be great, said: "They forgot God, so He forgot them" [al-Tawbah: 67], meaning: they abandoned obedience to God, so God abandoned them from His reward.

* *

The Interpretation of His words: "while you recite the Book"

Abu Ja'far said: By His words "tatlūna" (you recite) He means: you study and read. As related:

847 – Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Bishr related to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: "while you recite the Book" – he says: you study the Book thereby. By "the Book" he means the Torah.[[The report: 847 – in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:64, its continuation is in the following report except for the words "and by the Book he means the Torah," which I fear may be from al-Tabari's own speech.]]

* *

The Interpretation of His words: "will you not then reason?"

Abu Ja'far said: By His words "Will you not then reason?"[[In the manuscript: "He means by that: will you not understand..."]] he means: will you not understand and comprehend the ugliness of what you do of disobedience to your Lord, which you enjoin the people to avoid and forbid them from committing while you yourselves commit it; and you know that what is incumbent upon you of God's right and obedience, and following Muhammad and believing in him and in what he brought, is like what is incumbent upon those whom you order to follow him. As:

848 – Muhammad ibn al-'Ala' related to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umarah related to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Will you not then reason?" – he says: Will you not understand? So He forbade them from this ugly conduct.[[The report: 848 – a continuation of the earlier report. In the printed edition: "fa-nahahum."]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This indicates the correctness of what we said regarding the matter of the rabbis of the Children of Israel ordering others to follow Muhammad (ﷺ), and that they used to say: "He is sent to others, not to us!" as we mentioned before.[[See what preceded, nos. 840–841.]]

* *

The Interpretation of His words: "And seek help in patience and prayer"

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His praise: "seek help in patience" he means: seek help in fulfilling My covenant which you pledged Me in your Book – of obedience to Me and following My command, and abandoning what you desire of leadership and love of the world, in favor of what you dislike of submitting to My command and following My messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) – by patience in it, and prayer.

* *

It has been said that the meaning of "patience" (al-sabr) in this place is fasting, and "fasting" is one of the meanings of "patience." Yet the interpretation of those who interpreted it so, in our view, is that God, dhikruhu, commanded them to be patient with what their souls dislike of obedience to God and abandoning His disobediences. The root of patience (al-sabr) is restraining the self from what it loves and holding it back from its desires; therefore the one who endures a calamity is called "sabir," for restraining his self from lamentation; and the month of Ramadan is called "the month of patience," because its fasters are patient against food and drink during the day, and its restraining of them from that is holding them back and withholding them from it, just as one "sabara" a man for killing – that is, one holds him back for killing until he kills him. Therefore it is said: "So-and-so killed so-and-so sabran," meaning he held him back for it until he killed him; the one killed is "masbur," and the killer is "sabir."

* *

As for prayer, we have mentioned its meaning earlier.[[See what preceded: 1:242–243.]]

* *

If someone says to us: We have understood the meaning of the command to seek help in patience for fulfilling the covenant and guarding obedience, so what is the meaning of the command to seek help in prayer for obedience to God, abandoning His disobediences, stripping oneself of leadership, and abandoning the world? It is said: In prayer there is recitation of the Book of God, whose verses call to renouncing the world and abandoning its bliss, which console souls about its adornment and delusion, and remind of the Hereafter and what God has prepared therein for its people. So in reflecting upon them there is help for the people of obedience to God in striving in it, as it is related from our Prophet (ﷺ) that when a matter distressed him, he turned to prayer.

849 – Isma'il ibn Musa al-Fazari related to me, saying: al-Husayn ibn Ratiq al-Hamadani related to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ikrimah ibn 'Ammar, from Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd ibn Abi Qudamah, from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn al-Yaman, from Hudhayfah who said: "When a matter distressed the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he turned to prayer."[[The report: 849 – "al-Husayn ibn Ratiq al-Hamadani": so it is in the printed edition. I have not found a narrator by this name or anything similar in the references available to me; in the manuscript it is "al-Husayn ibn Ziyad al-Hamadani" – and I found among narrators only two named "Husayn ibn Ziyad," neither of whom is described as Hamadani, and neither fits this isnad: one is "Husayn ibn Ziyad" without further description, whom al-Bukhari mentions in al-Kabir 1/2/387 no. 2881, saying he narrates from 'Ikrimah and Jarir ibn Hazim narrates from him; Jarir died in 175, so this is too early for Isma'il ibn Musa al-Fazari, who died in 245. The second is "Husayn ibn Ziyad Abu 'Ali al-Marwazi," whom al-Bukhari mentions right after, saying he died in 220, which is too late to have met Ibn Jurayj, who died in 150. 'Ikrimah ibn 'Ammar is al-'Ijli al-Yamami. In the manuscript it reads "'Ikrimah 'an 'Ammar," which is an error. The hadith will follow immediately with another sound isnad.]]

850 – And Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Jabbar related to me, saying: Khalaf ibn al-Walid al-Azdi related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Zakariyya related to us, from 'Ikrimah ibn 'Ammar, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Du'ali, who said: 'Abd al-'Aziz, brother of Hudhayfah, said, Hudhayfah said: "When a matter distressed the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he prayed."[[The report: 850 – it is the same as the previous one in meaning. "Khalaf ibn al-Walid": he is Abu al-Walid al-'Atki al-Jawhari; "al-'Atki" is a nisba to "al-'Atik," a clan of the Azd, and he was one of the trustworthy teachers of Ahmad. Yahya ibn Zakariyya is Ibn Abi Za'idah. Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Du'ali is "Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd Abu Qudamah," who appears in the previous isnad. In the originals here it reads "Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd ibn Abi Qudamah," which is an error; rather "Abu Qudamah" is the kunyah of "Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd." We have verified his biography in the explanation of another hadith in the Musnad, no. 6548, and we preferred that Ibn Abi Za'idah erred in his name, calling him "Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah." The hadith is narrated by Ahmad in the Musnad 5:388 (Halabi) from Isma'il ibn 'Umar and Khalaf ibn al-Walid, both from Yahya ibn Zakariyya. Abu Dawud narrated it, no. 1319, from Muhammad ibn 'Isa, from Yahya ibn Zakariyya, with this same isnad. Al-Bukhari alluded to it in al-Kabir 1/1/172, in the biography of "Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd Abu Qudamah al-Hanafi," saying: "al-Nadr narrated from 'Ikrimah, from Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd Abu Qudamah, who heard 'Abd al-'Aziz, brother of Hudhayfah, from Hudhayfah: the Prophet (ﷺ), when a matter distressed him, prayed. And Ibn Abi Za'idah said: from 'Ikrimah, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Du'ali." The "al-Nadr" to whom al-Bukhari alludes is al-Nadr ibn Muhammad al-Jarishi al-Yamami. "'Abd al-'Aziz ibn al-Yaman" is the brother of Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, as explicitly stated in the previous report, and as described in this report and in the reports of the Musnad and al-Bukhari's al-Kabir. But Abu Dawud's narration reads "'Abd al-'Aziz, son of Hudhayfah's brother," and so also in the narration of Ibn Mandah, which al-Hafiz alluded to in al-Isabah 5:159. In that place and in al-Tahdhib 6:364–365, al-Hafiz preferred that he is the son of Hudhayfah's brother, not his brother. But most narrators mention that he is his brother, as we noted, and none differed except Muhammad ibn 'Isa, the teacher of Abu Dawud, as far as I have seen. So I do not know what the basis of this preference is. Rather, what I see is preferring the narration of the majority, among them al-Nadr ibn Muhammad, who was prolific in narrating from 'Ikrimah ibn 'Ammar. Ibn Abi Hatim affirmed this in the biography of "'Abd al-'Aziz ibn al-Yaman" in al-Jarh wa-l-Ta'dil 2/2/399, mentioning no dispute or other view. The hadith is also mentioned by Ibn Kathir 1:157–158 from the narrations of the Musnad, Abu Dawud and al-Tabari, then he mentioned something similar at length, from the narration of Muhammad Nasr al-Marwazi in the Book of Prayer.]]

851 – Likewise it is related from him (ﷺ) that he saw Abu Hurayrah lying prone on his belly, and said to him: "Ishkanb dard?" He said: Yes. He said: Stand and pray, for in prayer there is healing.[[The report: 851 – thus al-Tabari mentions it without an isnad. Ahmad narrated it in the Musnad, no. 9054 (2:390 Halabi), from Aswad ibn 'Amir, from Dhawwad Abu al-Mundhir, from Layth, from Mujahid, from Abu Hurayrah. He narrated it again, no. 9229 (2:403 Halabi), from Musa ibn Dawud, from Dhawwad. Likewise Ibn Majah narrated it, no. 3458, with two isnads from Dhawwad. "Dhawwad" is with a dhal with a dot, a shaddah on the waw, and a final unpointed dal. The author of al-Khulasah vocalized it as "Dhu'ad" with a dotted dhamma and a following hamzah with a fatha, which is an error. Dhawwad is Ibn 'Ulbah al-Harithi, an elderly, righteous, truthful man, whom Ibn Ma'in weakened, saying: "He is nothing." Al-Bukhari mentioned him in al-Kabir 2/1/241 and in al-Saghir, p. 214, and said: "He contradicts in some of his narrations." In al-Saghir he narrated this hadith from Ibn al-Asbahani, from al-Muharibi, from Layth, from Mujahid: "Abu Hurayrah said to me: O Persian, shkm dard," then al-Bukhari said: "Ibn al-Asbahani said: Dhawwad raised it to the Prophet, and it has no basis; Abu Hurayrah was not Persian, rather Mujahid is Persian." This is a precise critique by Ibn al-Asbahani, and then by al-Bukhari, which concludes that the isnad of the hadith is weak as a marfu'. As to the wording in the text, "ishkanb dard": in the Bulaq edition there is written on it: "meaning: you complain of your belly, in Persian. Thus in the margin of the original." Likewise this wording is found in the Musnad, except that in its first occurrence "dard" is written "dhard" with a dot over the first dal, which is a misreading. This wording is found in al-Bukhari's narration in al-Tarikh al-Saghir, p. 214: "shkm dard." In Ibn Majah's narration: "ishkamt dard." Ustadh Fu'ad 'Abd al-Baqi wrote explaining it: "In Persian: ishkam, meaning belly; dard, meaning pain; the ta' is for address; the hamzah is a hamzat wasl. Thus Dr. Husayn al-Hamadani verified it. It means: do you complain of your belly? But in the supplement to Majma' Bihar al-Anwar, p. 7, there is (ashkanb dadam), and in a narration with a sukun on the ba'." I hold that the last transmission contains an error, for I earlier noted in old notes on the Musnad that its correct form is "ashkanb dardam." My strongest present suspicion is that I took that from the supplement to Majma' Bihar al-Anwar, which is not within reach as I write this.]]

Thus God, exalted is His praise, commanded those whose conduct He described, from among the rabbis of the Children of Israel, to make their recourse in fulfilling God's covenant which they pledged, to be seeking help through patience and prayer, just as He commanded His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) to do so. He said to him: "So be patient," O Muhammad, "at what they say, and glorify the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day, that you may be pleased" [Ta-Ha: 130]. So He commanded him, may His praise be great, in his calamities, to turn to patience and prayer. And:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 44 (part 2 of 2):

852- Muhammad ibn al-Ala and Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, both saying: Ibn Idris... [no]

Let me correct that and give the proper translation:

852- Muhammad ibn al-Ala' and Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, both saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us, saying: 'Uyaynah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from his father: that Ibn 'Abbas was informed of the death of his brother Quthum while he was on a journey, and he said, "Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un." Then he moved aside from the road, made his camel kneel, prayed two rak'ahs, prolonging his sitting in them, then rose and walked toward his mount, saying: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer, and indeed it is difficult except for the humble [khashi'in]﴾.

[[Report 852: its chain is sound (sahih). 'Uyaynah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman is trustworthy (thiqah). His father, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Jirshin al-Ghatafani, is a trustworthy Successor (tabi'i).
The report is mentioned by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:68, and he also attributes it to Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman.
Qutham ibn al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, brother of 'Abd Allah ibn al-'Abbas. His mother was Umm al-Fadl, and he resembled the Prophet (ﷺ). His hearing from the Prophet (ﷺ) is not authentic, for he was in the final period of the Prophet's life (ﷺ) at over eight years of age. He went out with Sa'id ibn 'Uthman during the time of Mu'awiyah to Samarqand, and was martyred there. Istirja': he said, "Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un."]]
* *
As for Abu al-'Aliyah, he used to say regarding it:
