853- Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, regarding ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾: he said, "He says: seek help through patience and prayer for the pleasure of God, and know that they are both obedience to God."
* *
And Ibn Jurayj said regarding it:
854- Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said regarding His words ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾: "They are two aids toward the mercy of God." [[Report 854: al-Husayn is Sunayd ibn Da'ud al-Massisi, and "Sunayd" is a laqab (epithet) for him, as has passed: 144.]]
855- And Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾, the verse: The polytheists said, "By God, O Muhammad, you are calling us to a great matter!" He said, "To prayer and belief in God, may His praise be exalted."

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed it is burdensome except for the humble (khashi'in)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His praise, ﴿and indeed it﴾, He means: and indeed the prayer. The "hā'" and "alif" in "wa-innahā" (and indeed it) refer back to "the prayer." Some have said that His words ﴿and indeed it﴾ mean: indeed the answering of Muhammad ﷺ (the call). But there has been no mention of this in the wording of "answering," so that "the hā' and alif" could be made to refer to it. And it is not permissible to abandon the apparent meaning understood from the speech in favor of a hidden meaning for which there is no evidence of its soundness. [[al-Zahir (the apparent meaning): what the Arabs understand from their speech. al-Batin (the hidden meaning): what is derived by inference from the apparent meaning according to the Arab method of expression. See what has passed, 1:72, note 2.]]

* *

By His words ﴿burdensome (kabirah)﴾ He means: heavy and difficult. As related:

856 - Yahya ibn Abi Talib narrated to me, saying: Ibn Yazid informed us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak, regarding His words ﴿and indeed it is burdensome except for the humble﴾, he said: It is indeed heavy. [[The report 856: In the printed edition it reads "Ibn Zayd informed us," and the correct reading is "Yazid" from the manuscript, meaning "Yazid ibn Harun." A similar chain has passed correctly at 284.

Among the narrators from Juwaybir is "Hammad ibn Zayd," but he cannot be intended in this chain, because Hammad ibn Zayd died in the year 179 AH. Yahya ibn Abi Talib cannot have narrated from him, since he was born in the year 182 AH, as stated in his biography in Tarikh Baghdad of al-Khatib 14:220-221.]]

* *

By His words ﴿except for the humble (al-khashi'in)﴾ He means: except for those who submit to His obedience, who fear His punishment, and who affirm His promise and His threat. As related:

856 - al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿except for the humble﴾, meaning those who affirm what Allah has revealed.

857 - And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam al-Asqalani narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah regarding His words ﴿except for the humble﴾, he said: meaning those who fear.

858 - And Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Jabir, from Mujahid: ﴿except for the humble﴾, he said: the true believers. [[Report 858: Muhammad ibn Amr is Muhammad ibn Amr ibn al-Abbas, Abu Bakr al-Bahili, one of al-Tabari's trustworthy teachers, from whom he narrated frequently; he died in the year 249 AH. He has a biography in Tarikh Baghdad 3:127. "Abu Asim" is al-Nabil, al-Dahhak ibn Makhlad. "Sufyan" is al-Thawri. "Jabir" is Ibn Yazid al-Ju'fi.

This chain occurs in this form in this place in the manuscript. The printed edition has "Muhammad ibn Ja'far" in place of "Muhammad ibn Amr," which is an undoubted error.

The difficulty here is that this chain, "Abu Asim, from Sufyan, from Jabir," is narrated by al-Tabari in most places "from Muhammad ibn Bashshar," from Abu Asim. As for his narration from "Muhammad ibn Amr," it is for the chain "Abu Asim, from Isa ibn Maymun, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid." The matter is close, and perhaps he narrated both.]]

859 - And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

860 - And Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: al-khushu' (humility) is fear and awe before Allah. And he recited the words of Allah: ﴿humbled (khashi'in) from the abasement﴾ [al-Shura: 45], and said: The fear that came upon them has humbled them, and they were humbled before it.

* *

The original meaning of "al-khushu'" is humility, lowliness and submissiveness, and from it is the saying of the poet: [[The verse is by Jarir.]]

When the news of al-Zubayr arrived, the walls of Medina humbled themselves, and the humbled mountains.

[[Diwan of Jarir: 345; al-Naqa'id: 969. It has been attributed to him in his Tafsir (1:289 / 7:157 Bulaq), Tabaqat Ibn Sa'd 3/1/79, Sibawayh 1:25, al-Adhdad of Ibn al-Anbari: 258, and al-Khizana 2:166. Sibawayh cited it as evidence that the feminine ending came with the verb because "sur" was attached to a feminine noun, "al-Madina," of which it is a part. Sibawayh said: "Sometimes in speech they say: 'Some of his fingers went,' and they made it feminine because he attached it to a feminine noun of which it is a part; had it not been of it, he would not have made it feminine, because if he said: 'the slave of your mother went,' it would not be good." (1:25)

Jarir's verse is used by al-Farazdaq to reproach and satirize him for treachery. When al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, may Allah be pleased with him, turned away on the Day of the Camel, a man from the Banu Mujashi', kinsmen of al-Farazdaq, met him, shot him and killed him treacherously. He described the mountains as "khushu'," meaning that at his death they bowed and lowered themselves from the awfulness of the calamity suffered by the disciple of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and from the foulness of the treachery of the Banu Mujashi'.]]

Meaning: and the mountains are humbled and lowly because of the greatness of the calamity of his loss.

* *

So the meaning of the verse: Seek help, O rabbis of the People of the Book, by restraining yourselves to obey Allah and withholding them from the disobedience of Allah, and by establishing the prayer which forbids indecency and wrongdoing and brings one near to the pleasure of Allah, whose establishment is great, except upon those who are humble before Allah, submissive to His obedience, and abased from fear of Him.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 46:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He, ﴿Those who think﴾

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: How does God, may His praise be majestic, report of those whom He has described as humbly submissive to Him in obedience, that they "think" (yazunnuna) that they will meet Him, when "thinking" (al-zann) is doubt, and one who doubts the meeting with God is, in your view, a disbeliever in God?

It is said to him: The Arabs sometimes call certainty "zann" (thinking/assumption), and they call doubt "zann" too, like their calling darkness "sadfa" and light "sadfa," and calling the one who seeks help "sarikh" and the one who gives help "sarikh," and similar words by which they name a thing and its opposite. What indicates that it is used for certainty is the verse of Durayd ibn al-Simma:

"I said to them: be certain (zunnu) of two thousand armored men, their chiefs in the Persian mail laced tight."

[Al-Asma'iyyat: 23; Sharh al-Hamasa 2: 156; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubayda: 40. It appears unattributed later at 25:83 and at 13:58 with another version: "fa-zannu bi-alfayi fāris mutalabbib." Before the verse, in al-Asma'i's transmission: "And I said to 'Ariḍ and the companions of 'Ariḍ... and the clan of Banu al-Sawda', and the people were witnesses openly, they were certain..." Abu Tammam's transmission: "nasahtu li-'āriḍ... 'fa-qultu lahum zunnu...". This poem was said in mourning for his brother 'Abd Allah ibn al-Simma, who is 'Ariḍ mentioned in his poetry. Al-mudajjaj: the horseman who has clad himself in his armour, i.e. entered into his weapons, as if covered by it. Al-sarāt is the plural of sarī: the best of the people among their horsemen. Al-fārisī al-musarrad: meaning the Persian coats of mail. 'Amr ibn Imru' al-Qays al-Khazraji said: "When we walk in the Persian mail as the camels walk, sturdy and..." Al-sard: inserting the rings of a mail-shirt into one another. Al-musarrad: the closely woven, interlocked links. He warns his brother and his people that they will meet an enemy of might who has completed his implements of war.]

He means by this: be certain of two thousand armored men coming to you. And the saying of 'Umayra ibn Tariq:

"Lest you raid my people, while I sit among you, and I make my thinking (zann) a hidden, cast-away matter."

[Naqa'id Jarir wa al-Farazdaq: 53, 785; al-Addad of Ibn al-Anbari: 12. He is 'Umayra ibn Tariq ibn Disiq al-Yarbu'i, who said it in a report concerning him with al-Hawfazan. The version in the Naqa'id reads: "and I sit among you..." and "and I make my knowledge a hidden, cast-away thing." Before the verse: "So do not command me, O son of Asma', with that which drags the young man with a taste (dhu al-tu'm) from speaking." Dhu al-tu'm: dhu al-hurm. Tajurr, from al-ijrar: this is to slit the tongue of the weaning camel-foal when they want to wean it, so that it does not suckle; he means it prevents him from speech. Ghaza al-amr and ightazāhu: he aimed at it; from it comes al-ghazw: going out to fight the enemy and plundering him. Al-marjam: the one whose true affair cannot be ascertained, because it is cast at without certainty, from al-rajm: casting.

Moreover, the verse, as transmitted in the Naqa'id, is not evidence that zann means certainty. The version of al-Tabari is the one suitable as evidence for this meaning.]

He means: "and I make my certainty a hidden, cast-away matter." The evidence from the poetry and speech of the Arabs that "zann" has the sense of certainty is more than can be counted, and what we have mentioned is sufficient for one whom God has granted understanding.

From it is the saying of God, may His praise be majestic: ﴿And the guilty will see the Fire and will think that they are about to fall into it﴾ [al-Kahf: 53]. Similar to what we have said regarding this is the interpretation of the exegetes.

861 - Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Adam related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliya, regarding His words: ﴿yazunnuna annahum mulaqu rabbihim﴾ he said: Indeed the zann here is certainty.

862 - And Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Jabir, from Mujahid, who said: Every zann in the Qur'an is certainty: "innī ẓanantu" and "wa-zannū."

863 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Abu Dawud al-Hafari related to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: Every zann in the Qur'an is knowledge. [Note on report 863: Ishaq is Ibn Rahawayh, the imam and hafiz. Abu Dawud al-Hafari, with the unpointed ḥāʾ and the opened fā', is 'Umar ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ubayd. In Ibn Kathir's tafsir (1:159) "Abu Dawud al-Jibri" occurs, which is a scribal error. Sufyan is al-Thawri.]

864 - Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿Those who think that they will meet their Lord﴾ — as for "yazunnun," they are certain.

865 - Al-Qasim related to me, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, who said: Ibn Jurayj said: ﴿Those who think that they will meet their Lord﴾ — they knew that they would meet their Lord; it is like His saying: ﴿Indeed I thought that I would meet my reckoning﴾ [al-Haqqa: 20], meaning: I knew.

866 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: ﴿Those who think that they will meet their Lord﴾ — he said: Because they had not witnessed it, so their thinking was certainty, not thinking in doubt. And he recited: ﴿Indeed I thought that I would meet my reckoning﴾.

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿that they will meet their Lord﴾

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: How is it said "that they are meeting their Lord," with the participle "mulaqun" being put in annexation to the Lord, may He be blessed and exalted, when you know its meaning is: "those who think that they will meet their Lord"? And since the meaning is so, the Arabic usage is to drop the annexation and keep the nun; the nun is dropped and the annexation made only in the nominal forms derived from verbs when they have the sense of the past tense (fa'ala), whereas when they have the sense of "yaf'alu" and "fa'il," the rule is to keep the nun and not annex.

It is said: There is no disagreement among all the people of knowledge of the Arabic language and its dialects on permitting the annexation of a noun formed from "fa'ala" and "yaf'alu," with the dropping of the nun, when it has the sense of "yaf'alu" and "fa'il" — I mean the sense of the future, and of the present action that has not yet been completed. So there is no point in the questioner's asking why it was said. The grammarians of Arabic have only differed over the cause for which the annexation is made and the nun dropped.

The grammarians of Basra said: The nun is dropped from "mulaqu rabbihim" and similar verbal forms which are in the form of nouns while carrying the sense of "yaf'alu" and of what has not yet been completed, because of their heaviness; and they are intended, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ [Al 'Imran: 185; al-Anbiya': 35; al-'Ankabut: 57], and as He said: ﴿Indeed We are sending the she-camel as a trial for them﴾ [al-Qamar: 27], while she has not yet been sent. And as the poet said:

"Are you sending a dinar for our need, or a slave of Rabb, a brother of 'Awn ibn Mikhraq?"

[Sibawayh 1:87; al-Khizana 3:476; al-'Ayni 3:563. The author of al-Khizana said: "This verse is among the verses of Sibawayh whose speaker is unknown. Ibn Khalaf said: it is said to be by Jabir ibn Ra'lan al-Sanbasi, and Sanbas is a clan of Tayy. Others besides the editor of Sibawayh attribute it to Jarir, to Ta'abbata Sharran, and say it is fabricated; God knows best." Dinar and 'Abd Rabb are two men. The evidence in it is the accusative of "'abd rabb" in the place of "dinar," because the meaning is: "Are you sending a dinar or a slave of Rabb?"]

So he annexed "ba'ith" to "dinar" though it has not yet been sent, and he put "'abd rabb" in the accusative as a coordination with the place of "dinar," because it is in an accusative position though it is in the genitive. And as the other said: [This is 'Amr ibn Imru' al-Qays, of the Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj; it is 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha, may God be pleased with him, an early pre-Islamic poet.]

"The guards of the honor of the clan, to whom there comes not from behind them any nutf..."

[Jamharat ash'ar al-'Arab 127; Sibawayh 1:95; al-Lisan (wakf); al-Khizana 2:188, 337, 483 / 3:400, 473. It is from a qasida he says to Malik ibn al-'Ajlan al-Najjari concerning a report that is mentioned. The 'awra: the place from which the enemy's approach is feared. The nutf: fault and suspicion; it is said: they are people of suspicion and nutf. This is the version of Sibawayh and al-Tabari; in other versions it reads "min wara'ina wakf," and al-wakf is fault and deficiency.]

with the accusative "al-'awra" and the genitive of it: the genitive is by annexation, and the accusative is by dropping the nun because of its heaviness, though it is intended. This is the view of the grammarians of Basra. [Sibawayh 1:95 said: "He did not drop the nun for annexation, nor so that the noun would take the place of the nun, but they dropped it as they dropped it in al-ladhayn and al-ladhin, when the speech was long, and the first noun's end was the second noun."]

* *

As for the grammarians of Kufa, they said: It is permissible in "mulaqu" to annex, and it has the sense of "yalqawna," and dropping the nun from it is because it is in the form of nouns, so it has in annexation to nouns the share of nouns. The same ruling applies to every noun which had a like counterpart. They said: when in any of these the nun is kept and the annexation is left out, it is done with it because it has the sense of "yaf'alu," which has not occurred and has not yet been required. They said: so the annexation is for the wording, and leaving out the annexation is for the meaning.

* *

The interpretation of the verse, then, is: seek help in fulfilling My covenant through patience in it and through prayer; and indeed prayer is heavy except upon the humble, those who fear My punishment, who submit to My command, who are certain of meeting Me and of returning to Me after their death.

God, may His praise be majestic, only informed that prayer is heavy except upon one with this description, because whoever is not certain of the return, nor believes in a resurrection, nor in reward or punishment, prayer for him is toil and error, since he does not hope by performing it to gain any benefit or to ward off any harm. It is right that for one with this description prayer be heavy, its performance burdensome upon him, and a grievous thing for him.

It is light upon the believers who affirm the meeting with God, who hope through it for His abundant reward, who fear through neglecting it His painful punishment: because of what they hope for by performing it in their return of attaining what God promised its people, and because of what they dread by neglecting it of what He threatened its neglecter. So God, may His praise be majestic, commanded the rabbis of the Children of Israel whom He addressed with these verses, that they be among those who establish it, hoping for its reward, when they are people of certainty that they will return to God, and that they will meet Him on the Day of Resurrection.

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿and that they will return to Him﴾ (46)

Abu Ja'far said: The "hā' and mīm" in His words "wa-annahum" refer to the humble ones, and the "hā'" in "ilayhi" refers to the Lord, exalted is His remembrance, in His words "mulaqū rabbihim." So the interpretation of the phrase is: and indeed it is heavy except upon the humble, those certain that they will return to their Lord.

* *

Then they differed on the interpretation of "return" in His words "wa-annahum ilayhi raji'un." Some of them said, by what:

867 - Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Adam related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliya regarding His words: ﴿and that they will return to Him﴾, he said: They are certain that they will return to Him on the Day of Resurrection.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is that they return to Him by their death.

* *

The more preferable of the two interpretations for the verse is the saying of Abu al-'Aliya, because God, may His remembrance be exalted, said in the verse before it: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life, then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Baqara: 28]. So He informed, may His praise be majestic, that their return to Him is after their resurrection and their revival from their death, and that is without doubt the Day of Resurrection. Likewise the interpretation of His words: ﴿and that they will return to Him﴾.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 47:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, "O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you"

Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation of this in this verse is similar to its interpretation in the previous one, in His saying: "Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you and fulfil My covenant." I have already mentioned it there [see 1: 555-559].

* *

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, "And that I preferred you over the worlds" (47)

Abu Ja'far said: This too is among what He, mighty is His praise, reminded them of from His blessings and favours upon them. By His saying, "And that I preferred you over the worlds," He means: that I preferred your forefathers. He attributed His favours upon their fathers and forebears to them as favours from Him upon them, since the merits of the fathers are merits for the sons, and the blessings bestowed upon the fathers are blessings upon the sons, because the sons come from the fathers. He, mighty is His remembrance, expressed His saying, "And that I preferred you over the worlds," in a general form, while He intends something specific, for the meaning is: "And that I preferred you over the world of those among whom you lived and in whose time you were" [[See 1: 143-146, then 151-152. It is said of anything that is in the middle of a thing and its main part: "He is between our backs and our backs" (bayna zahrayna wa-zahraynina), on the basis that he stays between the back of one behind him and the back of one in front of him, so he is shielded on both sides. Then it became widespread until it was used for dwelling among a people in general. It is also said: "He stays among them" (huwa bayna adhharihim muqim) with this meaning. It is also said: "I met him in the midst of the night" (bayna zahrani al-layl), meaning between nightfall and dawn; and on this basis, judge the usage of this word.]], like what has been related:

868 - Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la al-San'ani narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar; and al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning "And that I preferred you over the worlds," he said: He preferred them over the world of that time.

869 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah: "And that I preferred you over the worlds," he said: By what they were given of kingship, messengers and scriptures, over the world of those who were in that time, for every age has a world.

870 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Mujahid said concerning His saying, "And that I preferred you over the worlds," he said: Over those among whom they were.

871 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: Over those among whom they were.

872 - Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: I asked Ibn Zayd about the saying of God, "And that I preferred you over the worlds," and he said: The world of the people of that time. And he recited the saying of God: "And We chose them knowingly over the worlds" [al-Dukhan: 32], and said: This is for whoever obeyed Him and followed His command, though among them were apes, and they were the most hated of His creation to Him. And He said to this Ummah: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind" [Al 'Imran: 110], and he said: This is for whoever obeyed God, followed His command and avoided His prohibitions.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The evidence for the correctness of what we have said, that its interpretation is specific in the manner we described, is:

873 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us; and al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, all of them, from Bahz ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Verily you complete seventy nations" — Ya'qub said in his narration: "You are the last of them" — and al-Hasan said: "You are the best of them and the most honoured by God." [[The hadith 873: Bahz, with a fatha on the ba' and a silent ha': he is Ibn Hakim ibn Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah al-Qushayri. He is trustworthy (thiqah); Ibn Ma'in, Ibn al-Madini and others declared him trustworthy, and there is no proof for those who spoke against him. al-Bukhari included him in al-Kabir 1/2/143, and Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/430-431. Indeed al-Bukhari included a narration from him in the Sahih as a mu'allaq report, as al-Hafiz mentioned in al-Isabah 6: 112, in the biography of his grandfather. His father Hakim ibn Mu'awiyah is a trustworthy Successor (tabi'i); al-Bukhari included him in 2/1/12, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/207. His grandfather Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah is a Companion (sahabi) whose companionship is established; Ibn Sa'd said in al-Tabaqat 7/1/22: "He came to the Prophet (ﷺ), embraced Islam and kept his company, asked him about things, and related hadiths from him." al-Bukhari included him in 4/1/329 and said: "He heard the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Al-Tabari related this hadith here by two chains: through Ibn 'Ulayyah from Bahz, and through Ma'mar ibn Rashid from Bahz. It will come with these two chains separately (4: 30, Bulaq).

al-Tirmidhi related it (4: 82-83) through 'Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from Bahz, from his father, from his grandfather: "that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say, concerning the saying of God (You are the best nation brought forth for mankind), 'You complete seventy nations, you are the best of them and the most honoured by God.'" Then al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan hadith. More than one has related this hadith from Bahz ibn Hakim, similar to this, but they did not mention in it (You are the best nation brought forth for mankind)." Ibn Majah related it (4288) through Ibn 'Ulayyah, from Bahz. Imam Ahmad related it in al-Musnad (5: 3, Halabi) from Yazid ibn Harun, from Bahz. He related it (5: 5) from Yahya al-Qattan, from Bahz.

al-Darimi related it (2: 313) from al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, from Bahz. Ibn Majah also related it (4287) through Ibn Shawdhab, from Bahz.

Then Bahz did not transmit it alone from his father Hakim, for Sa'id ibn Iyas al-Jurayri also related it: Imam Ahmad related it (4: 447) from 'Affan, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from al-Jurayri, from Hakim ibn Mu'awiyah, from his father, in similar form. He also related it in a longer version (5: 3) from Hasan ibn Musa, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from al-Jurayri. Ibn Kathir mentioned the hadith (1: 160), attributing it to "the Masanid and the Sunan." Then he mentioned it again (2: 214), from "the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, the Sunan of Ibn Majah, and the Mustadrak of al-Hakim." Then he said after it: "It is a well-known hadith, and al-Tirmidhi declared it hasan."]]

* *

This report from the Prophet (ﷺ) has informed us that the Children of Israel were not preferred over the community of Muhammad (peace be upon him), and that the meaning of His saying, "And We preferred them over the worlds" [al-Jathiyah: 16], and His saying, "And that I preferred you over the worlds," is according to what we have explained of its interpretation.

We have already explained the interpretation of His saying, "the worlds" (al-'alamin), sufficiently in another place, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it [see above 1: 143-146].

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 48 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation of His words ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾ is: "And guard yourselves against a Day on which no soul will avail another soul in anything." It is also permissible that its interpretation be: "And guard yourselves against a Day which no soul will avail another soul in anything," as the rajaz poet said:

"She has been given her morning drink, and the morning drink of her, may peace be upon it, [is] with a liver that has been mixed with hump-fat,
In an hour when food is loved by her."

[Al-Kamil 1: 22, and Amali Ibn al-Shajari 1: 6, 186 and others. Sabbaha al-qawm (lit. "he gave the people their morning drink"): he gave them the sabuh, which is what is drunk in the morning of milk or wine. He prays for her good for the goodness of what he fed her after a hunger she endured.]

He means: "in which food is loved by her." The "ha'" (pronoun) referring back to "the Day" has been omitted, since the omission is a sufficiency, by what has appeared of His words ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul [will avail another]﴾, which indicates what has been omitted from it, so what has been omitted is dispensed with, since its meaning is known.

Some people of Arabic grammar claimed that it is not permissible that what is omitted in this position be anything except the "ha'". Others said: it is not permissible that what is omitted be anything except "fihi" (in it). We have already shown earlier the permissibility of omitting whatever the apparent text indicates. [See 1: 139–141, 179, and see Lisan al-Arab (j-z-y).]

* *

As for the meaning of His words ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾, it is a warning from Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, to His servants whom He addressed with this verse, lest His punishment befall them on the Day of Resurrection, which is the Day on which no soul will avail another soul in anything, and on which no father will avail his child, nor will a child avail his father in anything. [An embedding of a verse from Surah Luqman: 33.]

* *

As for the interpretation of His words "no soul will avail": it means "will not suffice," as:

874 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail": as for "tajzi", it is "tughni" (will suffice).

* *

The root of "al-jaza'" in the speech of the Arabs is: settlement and compensation. It is said: "jaziituhu qardahu wa daynahu ajziihi jaza'an" (I repaid him his loan and his debt), meaning: I settled his debt for him. From this it is said: "Jazaa Allahu fulanan 'anni khayran aw sharran" (May God reward so-and-so on my behalf with good or evil), meaning: may He recompense him on my behalf and settle on my behalf what I owed him for his deed that preceded toward me.

Some people of knowledge of the Arabic language have said: "It is said: 'ajzaytu 'anhu kadha'" when I help him with it, and "jazaytu 'anka fulanan" when I reward him.

Others among them said: rather, "jazaytu 'anka" means I settled on your behalf, and "ajzaytu" means I sufficed.

Others among them said: rather, both have one meaning. It is said: "jazat 'anka shah wa ajzat" (a sheep sufficed for you and did suffice), "jaza 'anka dirham wa ajza" (a dirham sufficed for you and did suffice), and "la tajzi 'anka shah wa la tujzi" (a sheep will not suffice for you), with one meaning; except that they mentioned that "jazat 'anka, wa la tujzi 'anka" is from the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and that "ajza'a wa tajzi'" is from the dialect of others. And they claimed that the Tamim tribe alone among the tribes of the Arabs says: "ajza'at 'anka shah, wa hiya tujzi'u 'anka" (a sheep sufficed for you, and it suffices for you).

Others claimed that "jazaa" without hamza means "qada" (settled), and "ajza'a" with hamza means "kafa'a" (compensated). [See what has come in this regarding in Lisan al-Arab (j-z-y), and what al-Tabari brought is more complete and clearer.] So the meaning of the statement then is: "And guard yourselves against a Day on which no soul will settle for another soul anything, nor will it suffice it in any sufficiency."

If someone says to us: What is the meaning of "no soul will settle for another soul, nor suffice it in any sufficiency"?

It is said: it is that one of us today may settle his child's or his father's or one bound by friendship and kinship's debt. As for the Hereafter, then in what the reports have brought us about it—a man would be pleased that a right be established for him against his child or his father [yurudd 'alayhi haqq: it became obligatory and binding; yurudd li kadha wa kadha: it became established. And it is said: li 'alayhi alf barid, meaning established]. That is because the settlement of rights on the Day of Resurrection is from the good deeds and the evil deeds, as:

875 - Abu Kurayb and Nasr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Azdi narrated to us, both saying: al-Muharibi narrated to us, from Abu Khalid al-Dalani Yazid ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Zayd ibn Abi Unaysa, from Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id al-Maqbari, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "May Allah have mercy on a servant who has an injustice against his brother concerning his honour"—Abu Kurayb said in his hadith: "or property or standing"—"so he seeks his pardon before it is taken from him, and there is no dinar or dirham [there]. If he has good deeds, they will take from his good deeds, and if he has no good deeds, they will load upon him from their evil deeds." [The hadith 875: this is a sound chain. Nasr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Azdi: mentioned previously at 423, and in the commentary there "al-Tajir" was written, which is a mistake; the correct is "al-Naji" with n. And "al-Azdi" with z; in the printed edition here it is "al-Awdi" with w, which is an error. Al-Muharibi: is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad, mentioned previously at 221. Abu Khalid al-Dalani, Yazid ibn 'Abd al-Rahman: they spoke about him, and the truth is that he is trustworthy; Abu Hatim and others declared him thiqa; al-Bukhari in al-Kabir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded him and mentioned no criticism of him. He is in al-Tahdhib under the kunyas, due to difference over his father's name, but al-Tirmidhi and al-Tabari preferred what we mentioned, as did al-Bukhari and Ibn Abi Hatim. "al-Dalani" in the printed edition here is "al-Dulabi," which is an error; we corrected it from the manuscript.

The hadith was transmitted by al-Tirmidhi 3: 292, from Hannad and Nasr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, both from al-Muharibi, with this chain, and he said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith. Malik ibn Anas narrated from Sa'id al-Maqbari, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ, something similar."

And his words within the hadith "Abu Kurayb said", in the printed edition "Abu Bakr", which is a clear error; its correctness is from the manuscript.]

876 - Abu 'Uthman al-Muqaddami narrated to us, saying: al-Furawi narrated to us, saying: Malik narrated to us, from al-Maqbari, from his father, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ, similarly. [The hadith 876: it is the previous hadith in meaning, but from the narration of Malik. It is the narration whose reference by al-Tirmidhi we quoted. Abu 'Uthman al-Muqaddami—with the mim dammed, qaf open and the dal muhmala doubled and fatha: he is Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr, attributed to "Muqaddam," one of his grandfathers. He is thiqa; Ibn Abi Hatim recorded him, 1/1/73, and said: "I heard from him in Mecca, and he is sadduq," and al-Sam'ani in al-Ansab and al-Khatib in Tarikh Baghdad recorded him; died 264. al-Furawi: with fa fatha and ra sukun, attributed to one of his grandfathers; in the printed edition it is with qaf instead of fa, which is a mistake. He is Ishaq ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Farwa, one of the narrators from Malik and one of al-Bukhari's teachers; he is thiqa, though some spoke of him without proof. We have favoured his tawthiq in the commentary of the Musnad: 7425. The hadith by way of Malik was transmitted by al-Bukhari 11: 343–344 (Fath al-Bari), from Isma'il—Ibn Abi Uways, son of Malik's sister and his relative—from Malik. Ahmad transmitted it in al-Musnad: 9613 (2: 435, Halabi), by way of Malik and Ibn Abi Dhi'b, both from al-Maqbari. Then he also transmitted it: 10580 (2: 506), by way of Ibn Abi Dhi'b. al-Bukhari also transmitted it 5: 73, by way of Ibn Abi Dhi'b. And its beginning in these narrations: "Whoever has an injustice..." and he mentioned something similar in meaning.]

877 - Khallad ibn Aslam narrated to us, saying: Abu Hammam al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id informed us, from Sa'id, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ, similarly. [The hadith 877: it is the previous hadith, similar in meaning, through another route. Abu Hammam al-Ahwazi: he is Muhammad ibn al-Zabriqan, a thiqa; al-Bukhari recorded him in al-Kabir 1/1/87 and said: "well-known in hadith"; Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/260; and the two Shaykhs in the Sahihayn included narrations from him. 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id: I lean toward it being 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id ibn Abi Hind, who is thiqa. It is unlikely that it is 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id al-Maqbari, since the context of the chain rules it out; had it been him it would have been "'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id 'an abihi." As it is "'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id 'an Sa'id," it is apparent that he is other than Ibn Sa'id al-Maqbari. The hadith is sahih in any case, by the previous chains.]

878 - Musa ibn Sahl al-Ramli narrated to us, saying: Nu'aym ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-'Aziz al-Darawardi narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Abi 'Amr, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Let none of you die while he owes a debt, for there is no dinar or dirham there; they will only divide there the good deeds and the evil deeds," and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gestured with his hand to the right and to the left. [The hadith 878: this is a sahih connected chain from Ibn 'Abbas. I did not find it in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, nor in the Six Books, nor in Majma' al-Zawa'id, nor did al-Tirmidhi point to it with his phrase "and in the chapter." So it is an added benefit, derived from the narration of Abu Ja'far, may Allah have mercy on him.]

879 - Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, saying: Salim ibn Qadim narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiya Hashim ibn 'Isa narrated to us, saying: al-Harith ibn Muslim informed me, from al-Zuhri, from Anas ibn Malik, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, similar to the hadith of Abu Hurayra. [The hadith 879: this is a chain with a difficulty I could not resolve. As for "Salm ibn Qadim": it is "Salm" with fa... (sin fatha and lam sukun). In the printed edition here it is "Salim" with an alif after the sin, which is an error. This Salm is a Baghdadi thiqa, who narrates from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, Baqiyya ibn al-Walid and others. Recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/268 and al-Khatib in Tarikh Baghdad 9: 145–146. He has a brief entry in Lisan al-Mizan 3: 65.

Abu Mu'awiya Hashim ibn 'Isa: he is Hashim ibn Abi Hurayra al-Himsi, known for being attributed to the kunya of his father, namely "Hashim ibn Abi Hurayra." Ibn Abi Hatim's entry 4/2/105, and he mentioned no criticism of him. He has an unrefined entry in Lisan al-Mizan 6: 184, in which the name of his narrator from him is mentioned as "Muslim ibn Qadim," which is a distortion.

As for the difficulty in the chain: it is in "al-Harith ibn Muslim," the narrator here from al-Zuhri. I do not know who he is, nor what his soundness is; perhaps there is a distortion I could not perceive. Furthermore, I did not find this hadith from the hadith of Anas at all, after long search and tracing. There is in al-Mustadrak of al-Hakim 4: 576 another hadith from Anas, by another route, containing some of this meaning; its chain is weak.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: That is the meaning of His words, may His praise be exalted: ﴿no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾, meaning: it will not settle for another anything that was obligatory upon it, because settlement there is from the good and evil deeds as we have described. And how can one settle for another what was obligatory upon him, one who would be pleased that a right be established for him against his child or his father, so that it is taken from him and he does not waive it for him? [In the printed edition: "fa-ya'khudhuhu minhu," and what is in the manuscript is more eloquent. Tajafa lahu 'an al-shay': he turned away from it and did not persist in demanding it, and overlooked it for him.]

Some grammarians of Basra claimed that the meaning of His words ﴿no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾ is: "it will not suffice from it that it be in its place."

This is a view whose falsehood the apparent Qur'an testifies to. [See what passed concerning the meaning of "zahir" 1, 72, note 2, and this part 2: 15.] That is because it is not understood in the speech of the Arabs that a speaker says: "ma aghnayta 'anni shay'an" (you did not avail me anything), meaning: you did not avail me by being in my place. Rather, when they wish to report that something does not suffice from something, they say: "la yajzi hadha min hadha" (this does not suffice from this), and they do not permit themselves to say: "la yajzi hadha min hadha shay'an" (this does not suffice from this anything).

Had the interpretation of His words ﴿no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾ been what the one whose words we have related said, it would have said: ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul﴾, as one says: "la tajzi nafs min nafs" (no soul suffices from a soul), and it would not have said "no soul will avail another soul in anything." In the soundness of the revelation with "no soul will avail another soul in anything" is clearest evidence for the soundness of what we have said and the falsehood of the view of the one whose words we mentioned. [This is from fine exposition of the meanings of the language, and it is a method of reasoning that al-Tabari preceded all who spoke on distinguishing the meanings of Arabic speech.]

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words ﴿and no intercession will be accepted from it﴾

Abu Ja'far said: "al-Shafa'a" (intercession) is a verbal noun from the saying of a man: "shafa'a li fulan ila fulan shafa'a" (so-and-so interceded for me with so-and-so), and it is his asking him to settle his need. The intercessor was only called "shafi' and shaft" because he made the one sought for intercession a pair (shaf'), so that the one with the need, before he sought intercession through him in his need, was single (fard), and his companion became for him in it an intercessor, and his request for it and in his need was an intercession. Therefore the shafi' in the house and in the land was called "shafi'" because the seller became a pair (shaf') through him. [Ibn Qutayba said in explaining "al-shufa'a": "A man in the Jahiliyya, when he wished to sell a house, a man would come to him and intercede with him regarding what he sold, so he would grant him the pre-emption and make him more entitled to the property than one further from its cause. So it was called shufa'a, and its claimant was called shafi'." And shufa'a in house and land: the judgment in favour of its owner (Lisan al-Arab: sh-f-'.)]

* *

So the interpretation of the verse then is: "And guard yourselves against a Day on which no soul will settle for another soul any right that was obligatory on it, to Allah, may His praise be exalted, nor to anyone else, and on which Allah will not accept the intercession of an intercessor, so that what was obligatory on it of right is left for it."

It was said: Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, addressed the people of this verse with what He addressed them with in it, because they were from the Jews of the Children of Israel, and they used to say: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved, and the children of His prophets, and our fathers will intercede for us with Him." So Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, informed them that no soul will avail another soul in anything on the Day of Resurrection, and no intercession of anyone will be accepted from it for it, until each one entitled to a right from it has his right fully given. As:

880 - Abbas ibn Abi Talib narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj ibn Nusayr narrated to us, from Shu'ba, from al-'Awwam ibn Maraijim—a man from Qays ibn Tha'laba—from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The hornless (animal) will indeed be avenged upon the horned on the Day of Resurrection, as Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything﴾ [al-Anbiya: 47], the verse..." [The hadith 880: Abbas ibn Abi Talib: he is Abbas ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zabriqan al-Baghdadi, a thiqa, mentioned in al-Tahdhib; recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/215 and al-Khatib in Tarikh Baghdad 12: 411–412. "al-'Awwam ibn Maraijim" with ra and jim: in the originals it is "Muzahim" with zay and ha, which is a distortion.

The hadith's chain is weak, because of Hajjaj ibn Nusayr al-Fasatiti. 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad transmitted it in al-Zawa'id 'ala al-Musnad: 520, from 'Abbas ibn Muhammad and Abu Yahya al-Bazzar, both from Hajjaj ibn Nusayr. We have discussed his weakness in detail there.

As for its meaning, it is sound and established, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, transmitted by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 7203. Muslim and al-Tirmidhi transmitted it, and al-Tirmidhi declared it sahih. "al-Jamma'": having no horn. "al-Qarna'": having a horn.]

So Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, despaired them of what they had raised hopes in themselves of, namely salvation from the punishment of Allah—despite their denial of the truth they had recognised and their opposition to Allah's command in following Muhammad ﷺ and what he brought them from Him—by the intercession of their fathers and others of all mankind. He informed them that nothing will benefit them with Him except repentance to Him from their disbelief and return from their error, and He made what He established among them of that a model for everyone who was on the like of their path, so that anyone of deviation would not hope for Allah's mercy. [In the printed edition: "fi rahmat Allah," which is not a good reading.]

And this verse, though its outward form is general in recitation, the meaning of it in interpretation is specific, because of the abundance of reports from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "My intercession is for the people of major sins from my community," and that he said: "Every prophet has been given a supplication, and I have hidden my supplication as an intercession for my community, and it will reach, God willing, those of them who do not associate anything with Allah." [The hadith "My intercession is for the people of major sins": Al-Tabari mentions it without a chain. It is a sahih hadith; al-Suyuti mentioned it in al-Jami' al-Saghir and attributed it to Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim, from Anas; and al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim from Jabir. See al-Munawi's large commentary, no. 4892 (vol. 4, p. 163).

And the hadith "There is no prophet..." etc.: likewise Al-Tabari brought it without a chain. Its meaning is established and sound, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, transmitted by al-Bukhari and Muslim. See al-Targhib wa al-Tarhib 4: 213.]

So it has become clear that God, may His praise be mentioned, may pardon His believing servants, through the intercession of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) on their behalf, for much of the punishment for their sins between them and Him [[In the printed edition: "إجرامهم بينه وبينهم" ("their crimes against Him and between them"), but what is in the manuscript is the correct and good reading.]], and that His saying: ﴿nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾ applies only to one who died in his disbelief, not repenting to God, Mighty and Majestic. This is not the place for an extended discussion of intercession, promise and threat; we will examine the arguments on that at length, and we will come to what suffices on it in its proper places, God willing.
* *
On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and no compensation will be taken from it﴾
Abu Ja'far said: "al-'adl" (with a fatha on the ayn) in the speech of the Arabs means the ransom (fidya), as:-
881 - Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, regarding ﴿and no compensation will be taken from it﴾: he said: it means ransom (fida').
882 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat ibn Nasr narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿and no compensation will be taken from it﴾: as for 'adl, it is "fa-ya'diluha" from the root 'adl; he says: even if it came with the earth filled with gold, with which it sought to ransom itself, it would not be accepted from it.
883 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿and no compensation will be taken from it﴾: he said: even if it came with everything, it would not be accepted from it.
884 - Al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Mujahid said: Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿and no compensation will be taken from it﴾: he said: "badal" (substitute), and the badal is the ransom.
885 - Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: regarding ﴿and no compensation will be taken from it﴾: he said: even if it had the earth filled with gold, no ransom would be accepted from it. He said: and even if it came with everything, it would not be accepted from it.
886 - Najih ibn Ibrahim also narrated to me, saying: 'Ali ibn Hakim narrated to us, saying: Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from his father, from 'Amr ibn Qays al-Mala'i, from a man of the Banu Umayyah, one of the people of Syria, whose praise was excellent, who said: It was said: "O Messenger of God, what is 'adl?" He said: "'Adl: the ransom" [[The hadith 886: Najih ibn Ibrahim: I did not find in all the references before me except an entry for "Najih ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Karmani" in Lisan al-Mizan 6:149, that he was a Kufan, trustworthy, who narrates from Abu Nu'aym, so he belongs to the generation of Tabari's teachers. It is most likely that he is the one. 'Ali ibn Hakim (with fatha on the ha') is al-Awdi al-Kufi, a trustworthy narrator and one of al-Bukhari's and Muslim's teachers. Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Humayd al-Ru'asi, and his father: both trustworthy. 'Amr ibn Qays al-Mala'i (with damma on the mim and light lam), al-Kufi: trustworthy, one of the successors of the successors. This hadith has been transmitted as marfu', from a man whose name is unspecified but whose praise is given, and the most likely view is that he was a Successor (tabi'i). So the isnad is mursal or munqati', and it is weak. I have not found it except in Tabari; Ibn Kathir (1:161) and al-Suyuti (1:68) transmitted it from him.]].
The ransom given for a thing, and its substitute, is called "'adl" because it equals it, even though it is of a different kind; it becomes its equivalent in terms of recompense, not in terms of resemblance in form and appearance, as He, may His praise be mentioned, said: ﴿And if she offers every compensation, it will not be taken from her﴾ [al-An'am: 70], meaning: and if she ransoms with every ransom, it will not be taken from her. [[The sentence on the interpretation of the verse is missing from the manuscript.]] From this one says: "This is its 'adl and its 'adil (equivalent)." As for "'adl" with a kasra on the ayn, it is like the load carried on the back; one says from this: "I have a slave who is the 'adl of your slave, and a sheep that is the 'adl of your sheep" (with a kasra on the ayn), when one slave equals another slave and one sheep equals another sheep. [[In the manuscript this sentence appears as: "يقال من ذلك: عندي غلام عدل غلاما وشاة عدل شاة", and it is limited to this amount, with its evident error.]] Likewise this applies to everything that is an equivalent of a thing of its own kind. When one wishes to say that he has its value from a different kind, the ayn is given a fatha, and one says: "I have the value of your sheep in dirhams" ("'adl shatika min al-darahim"). It is reported from some Arabs that they use a kasra on the ayn in "'adl" meaning ransom, for equalling what equals it in terms of recompense, because the meanings of 'adl and 'adl are close in their usage; as for the singular of "al-a'dal" (the loads), only "'adl" with a kasra on the ayn has been heard. [[This is also a good explanation, rarely found in a book of lexicography.]]
* *
On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾ (48)
The interpretation of His saying: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾ means that on that Day no helper will help them, just as no intercessor will intercede for them, and no compensation or ransom will be accepted from them. Favouritism is then abolished, bribes and intercessions are dissolved, and mutual aid and support between people is lifted [[In the printed edition: "وارتفع من القوم", which is an error. "وارتفع" here means "passed away and ended", a figurative use of "rising", which means "elevation".]], and judgement passes to the Just, the Mighty, for whom neither intercessors nor helpers are of any benefit; so He repays an evil deed with its like and a good deed with multiples of it. This is similar to His saying, may His praise be mentioned: ﴿And stop them, for they are to be questioned. What is the matter with you that you do not help one another? Rather, they are today submitting [themselves]﴾ [al-Saffat: 24-26]. Ibn 'Abbas used to say concerning the meaning of ﴿do not help one another﴾:-
887 - I was told on the authority of al-Minjab, who said: Bishr ibn 'Imarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?﴾ What is the matter with you that you do not defend yourselves against us? Far-fetched! That is not available to you today! [[The report 887: He did not mention it in the commentary on the verse of Surat al-Saffat; see (23:32, Bulaq edition).]]
* *
Some have said concerning the meaning of His saying: ﴿nor will they be helped﴾: "And they will have no helper from God on that Day who will defend them against God when He punishes them." It has also been said: "Nor will they be helped" by seeking support for them, intercession, or ransom.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The first view is more appropriate for the interpretation of the verse, for the reason we have described: God, may His praise be mentioned, only informed those addressed by this verse that the Day of Resurrection is a day on which there is no ransom for whoever among His creatures deserves His punishment, no intercession on it, and no helper for him. That is because these things existed for them in this world, so He informed them that on the Day of Resurrection these things are absent, and they have no way to them.

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 49 (part 1 of 2):

**On the interpretation of His words ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾**

As for the interpretation of His words ﴿And when We delivered you﴾, it is conjoined (*'atf*) to His words ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour﴾. It is as if He said: Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and remember Our bounty upon you, ﴿when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾, by Our delivering you from them. [[In the printed edition: "by Our delivering us from them for you"; they changed it so that it would fit what they were accustomed to in common speech.]]

* *

As for ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾, they are his people, his kin, and his followers.

The root of *āl* (family, people) is *ahl* (people). The *hā'* was changed to a *hamzah*, as they said *mā'* (water), [[In the printed edition: "as they said: māh", which is a clear error.]] and the *hā'* was changed to a *hamzah*. When they diminutive it, they say *muwayh*, so they return the *hā'* in the diminutive and bring it back to its original form. Likewise, when they diminutive *āl*, they say *uhayl*. It has also been transmitted from the Arabs, as a heard usage, the diminutive *uwayl*. [[See the entries (ahl) and (awl) in Lisan al-Arab.]] It may be said: "So-and-so is of the *āl* of women," meaning that he was created from them, and that expression is also used to mean that he desires them and is fond of them, as the poet said:

*Indeed you are of the āl of women, and they only incline to the near one; there is no union with the absent one.* [[I have not found this verse and I do not know its speaker. His saying "they incline to the near one" means to the one who is near and present; they attach their ties to him in affection, while the absent one's ties are cut. That is their nature, I seek God's forgiveness; rather it is the nature of the sons of our father Adam.]]

The best place for *āl* to be pronounced is with well-known proper names, such as their saying: *āl* the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), *āl* 'Ali, *āl* 'Abbas, *āl* 'Aqil. Its use with the unknown, with names of lands and the like, is not preferred. It is not considered good, according to the scholars of the Arabic language, to say: "I saw the *āl* of the man," or "the *āl* of the woman saw me," nor: "I saw the *āl* of Basra" or "the *āl* of Kufa." It has been reported from some Arabs, as a heard usage, that they say: "I saw the *āl* of Mecca and the *āl* of Medina." But that is not a widespread, commonly used form in their speech.

* *

As for ﴿Pharaoh﴾, it is said that it is a name by which the kings of the Amalekites in Egypt were called, just as the kings of Rome were called, some of them *Caesar* and some *Heraclius*, and as the kings of Persia were called *al-Akasira* (the Chosroes), whose singular is *Kisra*, and the kings of Yemen were called *al-Tababi'a* (the Tubba's), whose singular is *Tubba'*.

As for "Pharaoh of Moses," from whom God, exalted is He, informed that He delivered the Children of Israel, it is said that his name was *al-Walid ibn Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan*. Muhammad ibn Ishaq likewise mentioned that he had received this report about his name.

888 – Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to us this, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, that his name was al-Walid ibn Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan. [[See Tarikh al-Tabari 1:199.]]

* *

It is permissible to say ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾, while the address is to those who did not witness Pharaoh nor were among those delivered from him, because those addressed were the sons of those whom God delivered from Pharaoh and his people. So He attributed to them the favours bestowed upon their fathers, and likewise the ingratitude of their fathers, in the manner of attribution. This is like a speaker saying to another: "We did such-and-such to you, and we did such-and-such to you, and we killed you and took you captive," and the speaker either means by that his own people and clan, or the people of his city and homeland, whether or not the one addressed witnessed what was done to them. Just as al-Akhtal said, satirizing Jarir ibn 'Atiyah:

*And indeed al-Hudhayl attacked you and overtook you at Iraab, where he divides the spoils.* [[From his Diwan: 48, and Naqa'id Jarir wa al-Akhtal: 77–78. Al-Tabari said earlier (1:366): "Sama fulan li-fulan" means when he overlooked him and advanced toward him, rising above him. Al-Hudhayl is al-Hudhayl ibn Hubayrah al-Taghlibi, who raided the Banu Yarbu' at Iraab (a water of the Banu Riyah ibn Yarbu') and killed among them a devastating slaughter, and seized many camels and took many captives, among them al-Khatfa, the grandfather of Jarir, so al-Hudhayl was named "the one who mutilated the nose" and the Banu Tamim began frightening their children with his name. (See the account in al-Naqa'id 473, and Naqa'id Jarir wa al-Akhtal: 78.) *Nalakum* means: overtook you and inflicted upon you what he inflicted. *Al-Anfal* is the plural of *nafl* (with two vowels): it means spoils. In the printed edition: "taqsim", which is correct and acceptable.]]

*In a great host that calls the Aqarim; their horsemen were not unarmed nor incapable.* [[*Al-Fayliq*: a great battalion. His saying "calls" refers to al-Hudhayl. *Al-Aqarim* are Jusham, Malik, al-Harith, Tha'labah, Mu'awiyah and 'Amr, sons of Bakr ibn Habib ibn 'Amr ibn Ghanm ibn Taghlib, the kinsmen of al-Hudhayl. They were named *al-Aqarim* because their soothsayer looked at them when they were children, while they were under their covering, and she uncovered the covering, and when she saw them she said: "It is as if they looked at me with the eyes of snakes." *Al-Aqarim* is the plural of *aqram*, the most vicious of snakes and the most intent on pursuing and seeking people. *Al-'Uzl* is the plural of *a'zal*, one without a weapon. *Al-Akfal* is the plural of *kifl* (with a kasrah and a sukun), one who cannot stay on the back of his horse and does not ride well.]]

Jarir did not reach al-Hudhayl, nor did he witness him, nor did he reach Iraab or attend it. [[In the printed edition: "Jarir did not meet…"]] But when there was a day of the people of al-Akhtal against the people of Jarir, he attributed the address to him and to his people. Likewise, the address of God, mighty and majestic is He, to those addressed by His words ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾: because what was done by them to the people of those addressed by the verse, and to their fathers, He attributed that deed which was done to their fathers to those addressed by the verse and their people. [[See what preceded shortly, pp. 23–24.]]

* *

**On the interpretation of His words ﴿who subjected you to a terrible torment﴾**

In His words ﴿who subject you﴾ there are two interpretations. One is that it is a new, independent statement about Pharaoh's action toward the Children of Israel, so its meaning would be: Remember My favour upon you when I delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, and they had previously been subjecting you to a terrible torment. In that case the position of ﴿yusawmunakum﴾ is in the nominative case. [[In the printed edition: "when We delivered you…" according to the context of the verse, and this is better.]]

The second is that ﴿yusawmunakum﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), so its interpretation would be: And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who were subjecting you to a terrible torment.

* *

As for the interpretation of His words ﴿yusawmunakum﴾, it means: they make you encounter, cause you to taste, and entrust you with (suffering). It is said from this: "He made him undergo a harsh humiliation" (*sāmahu khuṭṭata ḍaym*), when he inflicted it upon him and made him taste it, as the poet said: *If he is made to suffer humiliation, his face turns dark…*. [[I have not found this verse. *Al-khasf* is injustice, degradation and humiliation, which are the worst of what befalls a human being, and the most ugly thing that one brother inflicts upon another. *Tarabbada wajhuh* means his face changed with anger and altered, as if its places had blackened. His saying "wajhuh" is a preposed subject, meaning his face turned dark.]]

* *

As for the interpretation of His words ﴿a terrible torment﴾, it means: the torment that distressed them. Some have said: the most severe torment. But if that were its meaning, it would be said *asw' al-'adhab* (the most terrible torment).

* *

If someone says to us: What was that torment with which they subjected them, which distressed them? [[His saying "which distressed them" does not appear in the manuscript; it fell out of it.]]

It is said: It is what God, exalted is He, described in His Book, when He said: ﴿They slaughter your sons and spare your women﴾. Muhammad ibn Ishaq also said regarding this:

889 – Ibn Humayd narrated this to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq informed us, saying: Pharaoh used to torment the Children of Israel, making them servants and slaves, and he classified them into his works: one group would build, [and one group would plough,] and one group would farm for him. They were engaged in his works, and whoever was not among them in a craft from his labour was liable to the poll-tax. So he subjected them, as God, mighty and majestic, said: a terrible torment. [[Report 889 is from a long account in Tarikh al-Tabari 1:199; the addition between the brackets is from its place there. It is said: "these are the *khawal* (servants) of so-and-so" when he takes them as slaves.]]

Al-Suddi said: He placed them in filthy works, and he killed their sons and spared their women.

890 – Musa ibn Harun narrated this to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi. [[Report 890 is from a long account in Tarikh al-Tabari 1:200; see what will come at no. 895.]]

* *

**On the interpretation of His words ﴿They slaughter your sons and spare your women﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: God, mighty is His praise, attributed what the people of Pharaoh did to the Children of Israel, namely their subjecting them to a terrible torment, their slaughter of their sons, and their sparing of their women, to them, not to Pharaoh. Though their doing those things was by the power of Pharaoh and on his command, it was because they carried these things out with their own hands. Thereby He made clear that every perpetrator who kills a soul or tortures a living being with his own hand, even if it is by the command of another, is the one who carries it out and deserves that the act be attributed to him, even if the one who commands is a dominant power over the one who carries out the command, whether the commander was a ruler, or a fierce thief (*khārib*), or an overbearing tyrant. [[*Al-khārib*: a thief of great corruption, from the saying "fulan sahib kharbah" (so-and-so is a man of corruption and suspicion), and from it *al-khārib* means one of the hardships of time. As for the lexicographers, they say: *al-khārib* is the thief of camels specifically, then it was transferred to other thieves by extension.]] Just as God, mighty is His praise, attributed the slaughter of the sons of the Children of Israel and the sparing of their women to the people of Pharaoh rather than to Pharaoh, though they did what they did by the power of Pharaoh and his command to them, along with his domination and subjugation of them. Likewise, every person who kills a soul unjustly on the command of another is, in our view, the one to be killed in retaliation, even if his killing of it was under compulsion from another to kill it. [[In the printed edition: "and if his killing of him," which is an alteration with no benefit.]]

* *

As for the interpretation of their slaughter of the sons of the Children of Israel and their sparing of their women, [[In the printed edition: "slaughter" in place of "their slaughter"; and the word "sons" dropped out of the manuscript.]] it was, as has been related to us from Ibn 'Abbas and others, as follows:

891 – Al-'Abbas ibn al-Walid al-Amuli and Tamim ibn al-Muntasir al-Wasiti narrated this to us, both saying: Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: al-Asbagh ibn Zayd informed us, saying: al-Qasim ibn Ayyub narrated to us, saying: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated to us, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Pharaoh and his companions discussed what God had promised Abraham, His friend, that He would place prophets and kings among his descendants. They conspired and agreed to send men with knives (*shifar*) [[*Al-shifar* is the plural of *shafrah*: a large, broad iron knife, used for cutting meat and other things.]] who would go about among the Children of Israel, and whenever they found a male newborn they would slaughter him. They did so. But when they saw that the elders of the Children of Israel were dying of their own terms, and that the young ones were being slaughtered, he said: You are about to annihilate the Children of Israel, and you will be left to do the labour and service which they used to do for you. So kill every male newborn one year, so that their numbers decrease; and leave them alone for one year. Then Moses' mother became pregnant with Aaron in the year when the young boys were not slaughtered, so she bore him openly and safely. Then, when the following year came, she became pregnant with Moses. [[Report 891: this is *mawquf* (a report ending with a Companion), and its chain to Ibn 'Abbas is sound. As for the soundness of the text, we cannot be certain of it; perhaps it is something the Companions used to relate about ancient history, transmitted from the People of the Book. 'Abbas ibn al-Walid ibn Mazid al-Amuli al-Bayruti: trustworthy, biographed in al-Tahdhib, and Ibn Abi Hatim biographed him at 3/1/214–215. Tamim ibn al-Muntasir ibn Tamim al-Wasiti: trustworthy, biographed in al-Tahdhib, and Ibn Abi Hatim at 1/1/444–445. Al-Asbagh ibn Zayd ibn 'Ali al-Juhani al-Wasiti al-Warraq: trustworthy, deemed so by Ibn Ma'in and others, biographed in al-Tahdhib, and al-Bukhari biographed him in al-Kabir 1/2/36, and Ibn Abi Hatim at 1/1/320–321. Al-Qasim ibn Abi Ayyub al-Asadi al-Wasiti: trustworthy, biographed in al-Tahdhib, and in al-Bukhari's al-Kabir 4/1/168–169, and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/107. In the printed edition here it reads "al-Qasim ibn Ayyub," which is an error. It occurs in full in Tarikh al-Tabari 1:202, with a slight difference in wording. In the manuscript at this point there are scribal errors which we have passed over without mentioning. In the printed edition and the manuscript: "so his mother bore him openly," and the correct reading from the history is as given.]]

892 – 'Abd al-Karim ibn al-Haytham also narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Bashshar al-Ramadi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us, saying: Abu Sa'id narrated to us, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The soothsayers said to Pharaoh: A child will be born this year who will take away your kingdom. He said: So Pharaoh appointed over every thousand women a hundred men, over every hundred ten, and over every ten a man, and he said: Look at every pregnant woman in the city; when she gives birth, look at the child. If it is male, slaughter it; if it is female, leave her alone. That is His words: ﴿They slaughter your sons and spare your women; and in that there is a great trial from your Lord﴾. [[Report 892: like the preceding one, it is *mawquf*, and its chain to Ibn 'Abbas is sound. Al-Tabari narrated it with this chain in the history as well, 1:225. 'Abd al-Karim ibn al-Haytham ibn Ziyad al-Qattan: trustworthy and reliable, died in 278 AH. Biographed by al-Khatib in Tarikh Baghdad 11:78–79, and Yaqut in Mu'jam al-Udaba' 4:154. Ibrahim ibn Bashshar al-Ramadi: trustworthy, who sometimes errs in one matter after another. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, in al-Kabir 1/1/277, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/89–90. Abu Sa'id, the narrator from 'Ikrimah, is 'Abd al-Karim ibn Malik al-Jazari. I have not found the report in its place in Tarikh al-Tabari.]]

893 – Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, regarding His words: ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who subjected you to a terrible torment﴾, he said: Pharaoh ruled them for four hundred years. Then the soothsayers said: A boy will be born this year in Egypt, and your destruction will be at his hands. So he sent into the people of Egypt midwives [[*Qawabil* is the plural of *qabilah*: a woman who receives the child at birth.]] and whenever a woman gave birth to a boy, he was brought to Pharaoh, who killed him, and he spared the girls.

894 – Al-Muthanna also narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, regarding His words: ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ to the end of the verse, he said: Pharaoh ruled them for four hundred years, and there came to him one who said: A boy will grow up in Egypt from the Children of Israel, who will overcome you, and your destruction will be at his hands. So he sent into Egypt women. He then mentioned something similar to the report of Adam.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 49 (part 2 of 2):

895 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat ibn Nasr narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: The matter of Pharaoh was that he saw in his dream that a fire came from Bayt al-Maqdis until it enveloped the houses of Egypt, burning the Copts and sparing the Children of Israel, and it ruined the houses of Egypt. So he summoned the sorcerers, the kahins (soothsayers), the 'a'if (augurs), the qa'if (physiognomists) and the hazah (astrologers), and asked them about his dream [[al-kahinun is the plural of kahin: one who claims knowledge of unseen events in the future. al-'a'ifah is the plural of 'a'if: one who practises 'iyafah, a form of divination that existed in the pre-Islamic period; it is reported that it consisted of interpreting the flight of birds and taking omens from their names and calls. In Lisan al-Arab (h-z-w): the 'a'if is one who knows matters and is consulted only if he is learned, tested and recognised. Perhaps what the lexicographers describe is only one type of 'iyafah. al-qafah is the plural of qa'if: one who follows and recognises traces, and recognises a man's resemblance to his brother and father; it is not sorcery, soothsaying or jibt. Perhaps the mention of it here is an addition by copyists, for what occurs in the narration of the History (al-Tarikh) is "al-qafah" and does not mention "al-'afah"; so perhaps what is in the History is a corruption of the correct "al-'afah". al-hazzah is the plural of hazin, and al-hazi is one who looks into the stars and their judgements by his conjecture and estimation, so he sometimes hits the mark; it is also al-hazza' (with the zay doubled).]] They said to him: 'There will emerge from this city from which the Children of Israel came - meaning Bayt al-Maqdis - a man who will be the cause of the destruction of Egypt.' So he ordered that no boy born to the Children of Israel be left alive but be slaughtered, and that no girl born to them be killed but be left. He said to the Copts: 'Look at your male slaves who work outside, and bring them in, and make the Children of Israel take on those filthy tasks.' So he placed the Children of Israel in the work of their boys, and they brought in their boys. This is the time when Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh was haughty in the land﴾ - meaning: he acted tyrannically in the land - ﴿and made its people into factions﴾ - meaning the Children of Israel, when he made them do the filthy tasks - ﴿oppressing a group among them, slaughtering their sons﴾ [al-Qasas: 4]. So no male child was born to the Children of Israel without being slaughtered, and the young would not grow up. Allah cast death upon the elders of the Children of Israel, and it spread quickly among them. The chiefs of the Copts entered upon Pharaoh and spoke to him, saying: 'These people have been struck by death, and it is likely that the work will fall upon our boys, if their sons are slaughtered; the young will not reach maturity and the old will perish!' [[In the printed edition: "nadhbah abna'ahum" (we slaughter their sons), and the correct reading is from the History.]] 'So if only you would leave some of their children alive!' So he ordered that they be slaughtered one year and left alive the next year. In the year they did not slaughter, Harun was born and was spared; and in the year they did slaughter, Musa was conceived.
[[Narration 895: it is in Tarikh al-Tabari 1:200, and its isnad there is the isnad that recurs in the tafsir, and its completion is: "... from al-Suddi in his report, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas - and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ..."]]

896 - Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: It was related to me that when the time of Musa drew near, the astrologers and soothsayers of Pharaoh came to him and said: 'You know that we find in our knowledge that a boy from the Children of Israel has approached the time of his birth, who will take your kingdom from you, overpower your authority, expel you from your land and change your religion.' When they said that to him, he ordered that every boy born to the Children of Israel be killed, and he ordered that the women be spared. He gathered the midwives from the women of [the people of] his kingdom and said to them: 'Let no boy of the Children of Israel fall into your hands without your killing him.' So they did this, and he would slaughter the boys who were above that age, and he would order the pregnant women to be tortured until they expelled what was in their wombs. [[Narration 896: in Tarikh al-Tabari 1:199; the words in parentheses are an addition, and the correction is from it.]]

897 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Abdullah ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: It has been related to me that he would order reeds to be split until they became like blades, then arrange some of them alongside others; then pregnant women from the Children of Israel would be brought and made to stand upon them, and their feet would be cut. So much so that a woman would give birth, and the child would fall from between her legs, and she would keep treading on it, protecting her leg from the edge of the reed, out of the extremity of her exhaustion. He went to excess in this and nearly exterminated them, until it was said to him: 'You have destroyed the people and cut off the offspring! And they are your servants and your workers!' So he ordered that the boys be killed one year and spared one year. Harun was born in the year the boys were spared, and Musa was born in the year they were killed. [[Narration 897: in Tarikh al-Tabari 1:199-200.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: What those whose sayings we have mentioned say is that the slaughter by the people of Pharaoh of the sons of the Children of Israel and their sparing of their women [[This is an incomplete sentence lacking the predicate of "kana" (was); it is so in the manuscripts, and I think its correct form is: "The slaughter by the people of Pharaoh of the sons of the Children of Israel and their sparing of their women was that Pharaoh ordered the killing of every boy born among the sons of the Children of Israel, and the sparing of their women," as in the two narrations 891 and 896, so a line appears to have been dropped by the copyist.]]. So the interpretation of His words, according to what those we have mentioned interpret, is: ﴿and they spare your women﴾ - they keep them alive and do not kill them.

It must follow, according to the interpretation of those who said what we have mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and al-Suddi regarding His words ﴿and they spare your women﴾, that their leaving the females from killing at their birth is permissible, and that the young girl in the state of her childhood and after her birth may be called "woman", and the small girls who are children are "women".
