It means: "And you were placing worship in other than its proper place, for worship is not befitting except to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; and you worshipped the calf, wronging yourselves and placing worship in other than its proper place." We have explained in another place earlier in our book that the root of every wrong is placing a thing in other than its proper place, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it here. [[See what passed: 1: 523-524.]]

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted be His mention: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that, that you might be grateful﴾ [2:52]

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of His saying: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾ is: We withheld hastening punishment upon you, "after that," that is, after your taking the calf as a god. As follows:

926 - al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim related this to me, saying: Adam al-Asqalani related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾, meaning after you had taken the calf.

* *

As for the interpretation of His saying: ﴿that you might be grateful﴾, it means: that you might give thanks. The meaning of "la'alla" in this place is the meaning of "kay" (so that). I have already explained earlier that one of the meanings of "la'alla" is "kay," which is sufficient so that it need not be repeated here. [[See what passed: 1: 364-365.]]

* *

So the meaning of the speech is: Then We pardoned you after your taking the calf as a god, so that you might give thanks to Me for My pardon of you, since pardon necessitates gratitude from people of understanding and intellect.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion, that perhaps you might be guided﴾ (5:53)

Abu Ja'far said: By His words ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion﴾ He means: remember also when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion. By "the Book" He means the Torah, and by "the Criterion" the distinction between truth and falsehood, as follows:

928 - Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliyah, regarding His words ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion﴾, he said: He distinguished by it between truth and falsehood.

929 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr al-Bahili narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of God: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion﴾, he said: "The Book" is the Criterion, a criterion between truth and falsehood. [[In the manuscript: "it is the Criterion between truth and falsehood," and what is in the printed edition is better.]]

930 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

931 - And al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion﴾, he said: "The Book" is the Criterion, which distinguishes between truth and falsehood.

932 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Criterion" is the comprehensive name of the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Criterion.

Ibn Zayd said on this matter:

933 - Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated this to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: I asked him, meaning Ibn Zayd, about the words of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion﴾, and he said: As for "the Criterion" which God, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned in ﴿the Day of the Criterion, the day the two hosts met﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], that is the Day of Badr, the day God distinguished between truth and falsehood, and the decree by which He distinguished between truth and falsehood. He said: Likewise God gave Moses the Criterion, God distinguished between them, and He saved him and delivered him; He distinguished between them through victory. Just as God made that between Muhammad ﷺ and the polytheists, so too He made it between Moses and Pharaoh. [[In the printed edition: "between Muhammad and the polytheists," and I have adopted what is in the manuscript.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most preferable of these two interpretations for the meaning of the verse [[In the printed edition: "So the most preferable of these two interpretations..."]] is what has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah and Mujahid: that the Criterion which God mentions He gave to Moses in this place is the Book by which He distinguished between truth and falsehood, and it is a description and attribute of the Torah. The meaning of the verse then is: And when We gave Moses the Torah, which We wrote for him on the tablets, and by which We distinguished between truth and falsehood.

Thus "the Book" is an attribute of the Torah, standing in its place, sufficing without mentioning the Torah, and then "the Criterion" is joined to it by conjunction, since it is one of its attributes.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "the Book" earlier in this our book, and that it means "the written." [[See what preceded, 1: 97–99.]]

* *

We said this interpretation is more preferable for the verse, though other interpretations are possible, because what precedes it is a mention of "the Book," and that the meaning of "the Criterion" is the distinction [[In the printed edition: "because what precedes it mentions the Book," without "min".]] — and we have shown this earlier in this our book [[See what preceded, 1: 98–99.]] — so attaching it, since this is the case, to the attribute of what immediately precedes it is more preferable than attaching it to the attribute of what comes after it.

As for the interpretation of His words ﴿that perhaps you might be guided﴾, it is like the interpretation of His words ﴿that perhaps you might be thankful﴾, and its meaning is: that you may be guided. [[See what preceded, 2: 69.]]

It is as if He said: Remember also when We gave Moses the Torah, which distinguishes between truth and falsehood, that you may be guided by it, and follow the truth that is in it, for I made it a guidance for whoever is guided by it and follows what is in it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 54:

On the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is His mention: ﴿And when Musa said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf, so turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is better for you in the sight of your Creator." Then He accepted your repentance; indeed He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ (54)

The meaning of this is: Remember also when Musa said to his people from the Children of Israel: "O my people, you have wronged yourselves." Their wronging themselves was their doing to themselves what they had no right to do, which made them deserving of punishment from God, exalted is He. Likewise, everyone who commits an act for which he deserves punishment from God is a wrongdoer to himself, since he has made punishment from God due upon himself. The act they committed, by which they wronged themselves, is what God reported about them: their apostasy by taking the calf as a lord after Musa had parted from them.

Then Musa commanded them to return from their sin, and to turn back to God from their apostasy, by repenting to Him and submitting to His obedience in what He had commanded them. He informed them that the repentance from the sin they had committed was their killing themselves.

* *

We have already shown earlier that the meaning of "repentance" (tawbah) is returning from what God dislikes to what He is pleased with of obedience to Him. [[See what has passed: 1: 547.]]

* *

So the people responded to what Musa had commanded them of repentance from the sins they had committed, turning to their Lord as he had ordered them, as follows:

934 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah ibn al-Hajjaj narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu Abd al-Rahman, that he said concerning this verse, ﴿kill yourselves﴾: "They went to the daggers, and some of them began stabbing others."

935 – Abbas ibn Muhammad narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj ibn Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah informed me that he heard Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid say: "Some of them rose up against others with daggers, killing one another; no man showed compassion to a man, near or far, [[hanna alayhi: he showed kindness to him. In Ibn Kathir 1: 169 it reads "la yahnu", which has the same meaning.]] until Musa waved his garment, [[alwa bi-thawbihi: he gestured with it, signaling. Musa was commanding them to stop what they were doing.]] and they dropped what was in their hands. Then seventy thousand dead were uncovered." And God revealed to Musa: "Enough for Me, I am satisfied!" That is when he waved his garment. [[In the printed edition: "qad iktafayt, fa-dhalika hina alwa..." and in the manuscript "bi-dhalika"; I have chosen what Ibn Kathir 1: 169 transmits.]]

936 – Abd al-Karim ibn al-Haytham narrated to me, saying: Ibrahim ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Sufyan ibn Uyaynah narrated to us, saying: Abu Sa'id said, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Musa said to his people: ﴿Turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is better for you in the sight of your Creator. Then He accepted your repentance; indeed He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ He said: Musa commanded his people, by the command of his Lord, exalted is He, that they kill themselves. He said: Those who had been devoted to the calf sat down, drawing their legs up, [[In the manuscript: "fa-ikhtaba alladhi 'akafu..." In Ibn Kathir: "fa-akhbara", which is an outright error. Ihtiba' with one's garment means to draw the legs to the belly and bind them with a garment that gathers them with the back, tying it around them; it may also be done with the arms instead of the garment. See al-Baghawi 1: 169, which supports the reading I preferred for this word.]] while those who had not been devoted to the calf stood up, took the daggers in their hands, and a fierce darkness came upon them, and they began killing one another. The darkness then cleared from them, and seventy thousand had been uncovered as dead. [[ajla 'an kadha: it was uncovered from it, i.e., revealed.]] Every one of them who was killed had repentance, and every one of them who remained had repentance.

937 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: When Musa returned to his people he said: ﴿O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?﴾ up to His words: ﴿Thus did the Samiri cast [it].﴾ [Ta-Ha: 86–87]. Then Musa threw down the Tablets and seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward himself. ﴿[Harun] said, "O son of my mother, do not seize my beard or my head. I feared that you would say, 'You have caused a division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word.'"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 94]. So Harun left him and turned to the Samiri, and [Musa] ﴿said, "What is your business, O Samiri?" ... then we will surely burn it and scatter it into the sea, a scattering.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 95–97]. Then he seized it, slaughtered it, then burned it with a file, [[harraqa al-hadid bi-l-mibrad harqan: he filed the iron. Harraqahu (with shaddah on the ra') means he rubbed it down and scraped parts of it against one another. Similarly this came from Ibn Ishaq in Tarikh al-Tabari 1: 220, where he said: "I heard some of the people of knowledge say: its burning was only sahlah." Sahl means grinding and scraping with a file.]] then he scattered it into the sea, so that no flowing sea that day remained without some of it falling into it. Then Musa said to them: "Drink from it." They drank, and whoever had loved it had gold come out on his lips. That is the meaning of His words: ﴿And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts because of their disbelief.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 93]. When the Children of Israel were overcome with regret (saqata fi aydihim) when Musa came and they saw that they had gone astray, they said: "If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers." God refused to accept the repentance of the Children of Israel except in the condition they had disliked, that He fight them when they worshipped the calf, [[In the printed edition: "an yuqatilahum", and I have kept what is in the manuscript and Tarikh al-Tabari.]] so Musa said to them: ﴿O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf, so turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves.﴾ He said: They lined up in two rows, then struck one another with swords. Those who had worshipped it and those who had not worshipped it fought with swords, and whoever was killed from either group was a martyr, until the killing grew heavy and they nearly perished, until seventy thousand were killed among them. Then Musa and Harun prayed: "Our Lord, the Children of Israel are destroyed! Our Lord, leave a remnant, leave a remnant!" [[al-baqiyah: sparing them, as the two called upon their Lord to leave a remnant, so He would not uproot them by killing themselves.]] So He commanded them to lay down their weapons, and He accepted their repentance. Whoever was killed was a martyr, and whoever remained had his sins expiated. That is His saying: ﴿So He accepted your repentance; indeed He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ [[The report: 937 – in Tarikh al-Tabari 1: 219.]]

938 – Muhammad ibn Amr al-Bahili narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning God's words: ﴿because of your taking the calf﴾, he said: Musa had commanded his people, by the command of his Lord, that they kill one another with daggers, so a man would kill his father and kill his son, and God accepted their repentance.

939 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "because of your taking the calf," he said: The command of Musa to his people, by the command of his Lord, was that they kill one another, but a man was not to kill his father or his brother. So that reached seventy thousand in an hour of a day. [[The report: 939 – this entire report has fallen out of the printed edition.]]

940 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah, concerning God's words: ﴿And when Musa said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves..."﴾ up to the verse. He said: They became two rows, and they began killing one another, until the dead reached what God willed. Then it was said to them: "The one who kills and the one who is killed have both been accepted in repentance."

941 – al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: al-Layth narrated to me, saying: Uqayl narrated to me, from Ibn Shihab, who said: When the Children of Israel were commanded to kill themselves, they went out with Musa among them, and they struck at one another with swords and stabbed one another with daggers, while Musa was raising his hands. When he tired, some of them came to him and said: "O Prophet of God, pray to God for us." They took hold of his upper arms, supporting his hands. [[In the printed edition: "yashuddunah", and the correct reading is from the manuscript and Ibn Kathir. He means: they supported his hands while Musa was raising his hands in supplication to God.]] The matter continued this way until, when God accepted their repentance, He restrained the hands of some of them from others, and they dropped their weapons. Musa and the Children of Israel grieved over the killing that had taken place among them, so God, exalted is His praise, revealed to Musa: "What grieves you? As for those among you who were killed, they are alive with Me and provided for; and as for those who remained, their repentance has been accepted!" So Musa gave the Children of Israel this good news. [[In the printed edition and Ibn Kathir: "fa-sarra bi-dhalika Musa wa-bani Isra'il".]]

942 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri and Qatadah, concerning God's words: ﴿So kill yourselves,﴾ he said: They stood in two rows, killing one another, until they were told: "Stop." Qatadah said: It was martyrdom for the one killed and repentance for the living.

943 – al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Dawud narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ata' said to me: I heard Ubayd ibn Umayr say: They rose up against one another, killing one another, and a man would not spare his brother, his father, his son, or anyone, until the repentance was revealed. [[In the printed edition: "ma yatawaqqa al-rajul", and in the manuscript: "ma yatarana". Tarabba'a fulanan means to be wary of him and he is wary of you; the root appears in "urba' bika 'an kadha", meaning I raise you above it and do not want it for you. It is also said: "ma 'abba'a bihi wa-la rabba'a", meaning I did not care about it and was not concerned. So his words "ma yatarabba'" mean the man would not care whether he killed his brother.]]

Ibn Jurayj said, and Ibn Abbas said: Their dead reached seventy thousand. Then God, exalted is He, lifted the killing from them and accepted their repentance. Ibn Jurayj said: They lined up in two rows and fought among themselves, and God made the killing of those among them who were killed a martyrdom, and it was repentance for those who remained. The killing of one another happened because God knew that some of them had known that the calf was false, but what prevented them from denouncing those who worshipped it was only fear of fighting. Therefore He commanded that they kill one another.

944 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: When Musa returned to his people, he burned the calf and scattered it into the sea, [[At the start of this report in the History 1: 220, the burning of the calf is its sahl, as has passed on p. 70, footnote 1.]] and he went out to his Lord with those whom he had chosen from his people, and the thunderbolt seized them, then they were raised up. Musa asked his Lord to accept the repentance of the Children of Israel from worshipping the calf, and He said: "No, unless they kill themselves." He said: It reached me that they said to Musa: "We will be patient with the command of God!" So Musa ordered those who had not worshipped the calf to kill those who had worshipped it. They sat in the courtyards, and the people drew their swords against them and began killing them. Musa wept, and women and children came to him crying, seeking pardon for them. [[bahasha ilayhi: he approached him and hurried toward him, and prepared himself to weep.]] So He accepted their repentance and pardoned them, and Musa ordered that the swords be lifted from them. [[The report 944: in Tarikh al-Tabari 1: 221, and Ibn Kathir 1: 170; in the History alone: "that the sword be lifted from them."

Now, in the manuscript we have adopted, there is a lacuna from his words in this report: "asked his Lord to accept the repentance of the Children of Israel from worshipping" until his words: "The discourse on the interpretation of His words: 'Then We raised you after your death.'" This is the beginning of the second volume of this copy, and the endowment document written on the back of this volume indicates that this copy is divided into twenty-two parts.]]

945 – Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: When Musa returned to his people, there were seventy men who had withdrawn with Harun and had not worshipped the calf. Musa said to them: "Go to the appointment of your Lord." They said: "O Musa, is there no repentance for us?" He said: "Yes! ﴿Kill yourselves. That is better for you in the sight of your Creator. Then He accepted your repentance...﴾" the verse. So they drew out swords, sickles, daggers, and knives. [[ikhtarata al-sayf: he drew it. Al-jirzah (with a kasrah on the jim and a fathah on the zay) is the plural of jirz (with a dammah and a sukun), an iron club, a weapon used for fighting.]] He said: He sent a fog over them, and they began feeling one another with their hands, and they killed one another. He said: A man would meet his father and his brother and kill him without knowing it, and they would call out to one another in it: "May God have mercy on a servant who restrained himself until he attains God's pleasure." [[In the printed edition: "sabara hatta yablugha" without "nafsahu". The addition is from Ibn Kathir 1: 170.]] He recited the words of God, exalted is His praise: ﴿And We gave them of the signs that which contained a clear trial.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 33]. He said: Their dead were martyrs, and their living had repentance accepted, and he recited: ﴿So He accepted your repentance; indeed He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ [[The report 945: in Ibn Kathir 1: 170.]]

* *

So what we have mentioned, from those from whom we have related the reports we have transmitted, was the repentance of the people from the sin they committed among themselves and with their Lord, by worshipping the calf, together with their regret over what had passed from them of that.

* *

As for the meaning of His words, ﴿so turn in repentance to your Creator﴾, He means by it: return to the obedience of your Creator, and to what pleases Him concerning you, as follows:

946 – al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me with it, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah: ﴿so turn in repentance to your Creator﴾, that is, to your Creator.

* *

The word bari' comes from "bara'a Allah al-khalq yabra'uhu fa-huwa bari'," meaning God created creation, so He is the Creator. And "al-bariyyah" means creation. It is of the pattern "fa'iliyyah" in the sense of "maf'ulah," except that it is not hamzated, just as "malik" is not hamzated although it derives from "la'aka," but it has gone that way without the hamzah. [[See what passed: 1: 444–447.]] The poet of Banu Dhubyan, Nabighah, said:

Except Sulayman, when the King said to him: "Stand over the creation and restrain it from error."

[[His Diwan: 29, from his poem in which he mentions al-Nu'man and apologizes to him; and before the verse:

"And I see no one among the people who resembles him, nor do I exempt any of the peoples, nor any one of them."

hadadtu fulanan 'an al-sharr: I restrained him and held him back from evil. Al-fanad: error in opinion and speech.]]

It has been said that "al-bariyyah" was not hamzated only because it is "fa'iliyyah" from "al-bara," and "al-bara" means dust. So its interpretation, according to those who interpret it thus, is that it was created from dust.

* *

Some of them said: "al-bariyyah" is taken from your saying, "baraytu al-'ud" (I shaped the stick). Therefore it was not hamzated.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Omitting the hamzah from "bari'kum" is permissible, and substituting it is also permissible. Since that is permissible in "bari'kum," it is not objectionable that "al-bariyyah" from "bara Allah al-khalq" be without a hamzah.

* *

As for His words, ﴿That is better for you in the sight of your Creator﴾, He means by it: your repentance through killing yourselves and obeying your Lord is better for you in the sight of your Creator, because by it you will be saved from God's punishment in the Hereafter for your sin, and by it you deserve reward from Him.

* *

As for His words, ﴿So He accepted your repentance﴾, meaning: for what you did of what He commanded you, namely killing one another. This is from what is omitted, the part that is dispensed with by what is manifest of it in place of what is left out. The meaning of the speech is: "So turn in repentance to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is better for you in the sight of your Creator, so you repented, and so He accepted your repentance." The mention of "you repented" is omitted, since in His words ﴿He accepted your repentance﴾ there is clear indication that the speech requires "you repented."

* *

By His words ﴿So He accepted your repentance﴾ He means: your Lord returned to what you loved: pardon for your sins and for the enormity of what you committed, and forgiveness for your offense, ﴿indeed He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾; He means: the One who returns to whoever turns back to Him in obedience, to what He loves of pardon for him. By "the Merciful," He means: the One who returns to him with His mercy that saves from His punishment.

**Commentary on the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not believe you until we see God openly"﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The interpretation of this is: "Remember also when you said: 'O Moses, we will not believe you or acknowledge what you have brought us, until we see God openly' (*jahratan*), face to face (*'iyanan*), with the screen between us and Him removed and the covering between us and Him lifted, so that we look at Him with our eyes, just as a well is made clear (*tajhar al-rakiyyah*). That is when its water has been covered by mud, and what has covered it is cleared away until the water appears and becomes pure." It is said of this: [[This is the exact wording of al-Akhfash (*Lisan*, entry *jahara*). In the printed edition it reads "fanafa" (he removed) instead of "fanqa" (he cleared), which is acceptable, but I have kept what is in the *Lisan*.]] "I made the well open (*jahartu al-rakiyyah ajharuha jahran wa jahratan*)." [[His phrase "*wa jahratan*" is a verbal noun I have not found in the *Lisan* or elsewhere.]] Hence it is said: "So-and-so has openly (*jahara*) declared this matter (*jahara fulan bihadha al-amr mujaharatan wa jihaaran*)," [[In the printed edition: "*jahara fulan bihadha al-amr mujaharatan wa jihaaran*." It is not right to say it this way, because *mujaharah* can never be the verbal noun of *jahara*, although *jihar* may be its verbal noun, as in the *Lisan*: "*jahara bikalamihi yajharu jahran wa jihaaran*." For this reason I preferred to replace "*jahara*" with "*jahara*"... (sic) with "*jaahara*", so that the sense stands correctly.]] meaning when he makes it visible to the eye and proclaims it, as al-Farazdaq ibn Ghalib said:

*"Of those who keep a thousand of them*
*kneeling in fear of him, openly..."*

[[From his *Diwan*, p. 443, and *al-Naqa'id*, p. 255, in satire of Jarir. Before the verse is:

*"He howled, and roused a lion, a tawny one,*
*woe to the son of al-Muraghah! What did he rouse?"*

His phrase "*awa*" refers to Jarir. His phrase "*min al-la'i*" originally is "*min al-la'in*." *Al-la'un* is the plural of *alladhi* from a different form, meaning *alladhina* ("those who"). It has dialect forms: *al-la'un* in the nominative, *al-la'in* in the genitive and accusative; *al-la'u* with *-n* dropped, and *al-la'i* with the *ya'* kept in every case. It applies to men and women alike, and from it is the saying of 'Abbad ibn Tahfah, who was Abu al-Rabis, an Umayyad poet:

*"Of the company who are those who, when the base-born
fear to knock, they rattle the door-ring."*

Abu al-Rabis permitted combining "*al-la'i*" and "*alladhina*" because the two words differ, or by dropping one of them. The saying of al-Farazdaq, "*min al-la'i*," means "of those who." Then he broke off and omitted something, because the speech indicates what he intended, as if he had said: "He is one of those you know, O Jarir." Then he resumed and said: "*yazillu al-alfa minhu...*" The pronoun in "*minhu*" refers to his phrase "*aghlaba dayghaman*," that is, the lion, and he means himself. "*Al-alf*" means a thousand men. His phrase "*munikhan*" means that the thousand have made their mounts kneel from fear of him, and he has cut the road on them.

Moreover, the version in *al-Naqa'id* and the *Diwan* has "*nahaaran*" (by day) in place of "*jihaaran*" (openly). Its meaning is explained in *al-Naqa'id*: "He said *nahaaran*, and did not say *layla* (by night), because the lion's courage and strength are greatest by night. So he says: 'This lion keeps a thousand of them kneeling by day; how much more so by night!'" The version of al-Tabari, "*jihaaran*," is close in meaning to the version that has "*nahaaran*." They say: "I met him openly, by day," because the day reveals everything, makes it known, and makes it visible. That is, they made their mounts kneel while they saw him with their own eyes, and that was in daylight.]]

*Hadith with chain (isnad) no. 947:* As al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said regarding ﴿until we see God openly﴾: "Openly (*'alaniyah*)."

*Hadith no. 948:* And it was narrated to me from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding ﴿until we see God openly﴾: he means "face to face (*'iyanan*)."

*Hadith no. 949:* And Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said regarding ﴿until we see God openly﴾: "Until He looks down upon us."

*Hadith no. 950:* Bishr ibn Mu'adh told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatadah regarding ﴿until we see God openly﴾: that is, "face to face."

Thus, by mentioning it, the Exalted reminded them of the disagreement of their forefathers and the poor conduct of their predecessors toward their prophets, despite the many signs of God, the Mighty and Majestic, and the lessons they had witnessed, of which even a few would cool the hearts (*tuthlij*, [[*Thalaja nafsuhu bil-shay'* (with a kasra on the *lam*) *tathlaju wa tathlaju* (with a fatha or damma on the *lam*) *thulujan*: he found satisfaction and calm and was settled and at rest with it, and trusted in it.]]) and with which souls would be reassured in belief. This was alongside the successive proofs against them and the abundance of God's favours upon them. [[The commentary on a similar word was given earlier, p. 58; in the manuscript it read "*shuyu' alaihi ladaihim*" (the spreading of His blessings among them). And "*subugh al-ni'mah*" means its completeness, perfection and breadth. I still prefer "*shuyu'*" here because of his words "*ladayhim*." But if he says "*subugh al-ni'am 'alayhim*," as will come at the end of this paragraph, then it is undoubtedly "*subugh*."]] Yet at the same time, at one point they asked their prophet to make for them a god other than God; at another they worshipped the calf instead of God; at another they said, "We will not believe you until we see God openly"; and at yet another, when called to fight, they said to him, "Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting here." At another point it was said to them: "Say *hittah* (a word of repentance) and enter the gate prostrating; We shall forgive you your sins," but they said *hintah fi sh'irah* ("wheat in barley," a mockery) and entered the gate on their backsides. [[Refer to the above: "*hinta fi shi'irah*."]] Besides these and other deeds with which they harmed their prophet, peace be upon him, which are too many to count.

So our Lord, blessed and exalted is His remembrance, informed those whom He addressed with these verses, the Jews of the Children of Israel who were living among the emigrants of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that they would be no different, in denying Muhammad (ﷺ), rejecting his prophethood, refusing to acknowledge him and what he brought, despite knowing him and recognising the truth of his matter, from their forefathers and predecessors, whose stories were detailed to them regarding their apostasy from their religion time after time, and their assaults upon their prophet Moses, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, time after time, despite God's great trial among them, the Mighty and Majestic, and the abundance of His favours upon them. [[See the previous commentary, p. 77, note 2.]]

\* \*

**Commentary on the words of the Exalted: ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on﴾**

The exegetes differed about the nature of the thunderbolt (*sa'iqah*) that seized them. Some of them said:

*Hadith no. 951:* Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated this to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding the words ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾: "They died."

*Hadith no. 952:* And it was narrated to me from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾: "They heard a sound and were struck senseless (*sa'iqu*), meaning, they died."

\* \*

And others said:

*Hadith no. 953:* Musa ibn Harun al-Hamdani narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi regarding ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾: "The thunderbolt is fire."

\* \*

And others said:

*Hadith no. 954:* Ibn Humayd narrated this to us, saying: Salamah told us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: "The earthquake (*rajfah*) seized them, and it is the thunderbolt, and they all died."

\* \*

The root meaning of *sa'iqah* (thunderbolt) is any terrifying matter that a person sees or witnesses or that befalls him, until through its awfulness and great significance it results in destruction and ruin, and in loss of reason and dullness of understanding, [[His phrase "*ghumur fahm*" I have not found in the lexicographical books. It seems to be a verbal noun of *ghamara 'alayhi* (passive): he was overcome, i.e., he fainted. In a hadith, that when the Prophet (ﷺ) first fell ill, in the house of Maymunah, his illness grew severe until he was *ghumira 'alayhi*, that is, he fainted, as if it covered his reason and concealed it, from their saying: "I *ghamartu* the thing" when I covered it; and "*ghushiya 'alayhi*" and "*ughmiya 'alayhi*" also carry the meaning of concealment (*Lisan*, *al-Fa'iq*).]] or loss of some bodily faculty, whether it is a sound, or fire, or an earthquake, or a trembling. And among what shows that a person may be struck senseless while still alive, not dead, is the saying of God, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And Moses fell down in a swoon﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], meaning he fainted. And from it is the saying of Jarir ibn 'Atiyyah:

*"Was al-Farazdaq anything but a monkey*
*whom the thunderbolts struck, so that he turned round?"*

[[From his *Diwan*, p. 281, and *al-Naqa'id*, p. 251, and after it, in satire of al-Farazdaq, and it is among its most severe:

*"Whenever I alighted at the abode of a people,*
*I departed with disgrace and left them shame."*

How severe is what he said! In *al-Naqa'id*, explaining the verse, it says: "His language, that is Jarir's, is *al-sawaqi'*. *Fastadara*: that is, he turned into a human after he had been a monkey." It seems he missed the meaning, for he meant that he was transformed into a monkey in the form he had before becoming a human. So his phrase "*istadara*" means he returned to the point from which he began. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) at the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Time has turned round (*istadara*) as it was on the day God created the heavens and the earth," that is, it returned as it began. So he is saying: al-Farazdaq was in origin a monkey, then he changed into a human; when the thunderbolts of my poetry struck him, he returned as he was originally, a plain monkey.]]

It is therefore known that Moses was not dead when he fell down senseless, because God, the Mighty and Majestic, reported about him that when he came to himself he said: ﴿I have repented to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. Nor did Jarir liken al-Farazdaq, while he was alive, to a monkey that was dead. But the meaning is what we have described.

\* \*

And by His words ﴿while you were looking on﴾, He means: while you were looking at the thunderbolt that struck you. He says: the thunderbolt seized you in plain sight (*'iyanan jahratan*) while you were looking at it.

Commentary on the words of God Most High: ﴿Then We raised you up after your death, that you might give thanks﴾

He means by His words ﴿Then We raised you up﴾: then We brought you back to life.

* *

The original meaning of "al-ba'th" (raising) is stirring a thing up from its place. From this it is said: "So-and-so raised (ba'atha) his riding-camel," when he stirred her up from her resting place to set out, as the poet says:

"So I stir her up, and she is well-fed for a year, like the peak of al-Ra'n, a swift and hardy she-camel."

[The verse is not located in any source. The word "hiya" is pronounced with a doubled yaa, which is the dialect of Hamdan, who double the waw in "huwa" as in the saying of one speaker: "Indeed my tongue is a sweet thing by which one is healed, and he, upon whom God has poured it, is bitter"; and they double the yaa in "hiya" as in the saying: "The soul is not commanded to be harsh, which I obey, and it, if commanded with gentleness, obeys."

The pronoun in "abtha'uha" refers to his she-camel. "Sani' hawl" means that she has grazed for a year, a full year, until she became fat and strong. It is said: "He fed his horse (sana'a) a fattening (sana'a), so it is a well-kept horse (sani'), and the feminine is without the taa'." When one tends to it well, feeds and fodders it, and fattens it, and everything you have cared for until it is excellent is "sani'." "Al-Ra'n" is the great projecting ridge of a mountain that you see standing forward. He likened her in her majesty and strength to a mountain peak. "Dhi'labah" is a swift she-camel that persists in travel. "Waqah" is hard and enduring, the male and the female alike.]

"Al-Ra'n" is the extremity of a mountain's ridge; "al-dhi'labah" is the light, swift one; "al-waqah" is the one with a hard hoof or sole. From this it is said: "I raised (ba'atha) so-and-so for my need," when I made him rise from the place where he was in order to set off on it. From this too the Day of Resurrection is called "the Day of Ba'th" (Raising), because it is the day when people are stirred up from their graves to the place of reckoning.

* *

He means by His words ﴿after your death﴾: after your death by the thunderbolt that destroyed you.

* *

As for His words ﴿that you might give thanks﴾, He says: We did that for you so that you would give thanks to Me for the blessing I bestowed upon you, by reviving you, sparing you from Me, so that you would return in repentance from your great sin, after I had inflicted punishment upon you by the thunderbolt that I sent down on you, which caused you to die because of the great wrong you had committed between yourselves and your Lord.

This statement accords with the interpretation of those who explained His words ﴿Then We raised you up﴾ as "then We revived you."

* *

Others said: the meaning of His words ﴿Then We raised you up﴾ is: We raised you up as prophets.

9559 - Musa ibn Harun related this to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat related to us from al-Suddi.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The sense of the statement according to what al-Suddi interpreted is: The thunderbolt seized you, then We revived you after your death while you were looking on at Our reviving you after your death, then We raised you up as prophets, that you might give thanks.

Al-Suddi claimed that this is a case of the earlier being meant as the later, and the later as the earlier.

9560 - Musa related this to us, saying: Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat related to us from al-Suddi.

This interpretation is one whose apparent wording contradicts it, along with the consensus of the interpreters on its being wrong. The necessary consequence of al-Suddi's interpretation that we have related from him is that the meaning of His words ﴿that you might give thanks﴾ is: that you might give thanks to Me for making you prophets.

* *

The reason for their saying to Musa is what God, Mighty and Majestic, reported of them, that they said to him: ﴿We will never believe you until we see God openly﴾. As for what was said:

9557 - Muhammad ibn Humayd related this to me, saying: Salama ibn al-Fadl told us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: When Musa returned to his people, and saw what they were engaged in of worshipping the calf, and said to his brother and to the Samiri what he said, and burned the calf and scattered it into the sea [in the manuscript: "into the sea"], Musa chose from them seventy men, the best of the best, and said: Set out to God, Mighty and Majestic, repent to Him of what you have done, and ask Him to accept repentance for those you have left behind among your people. Fast and purify yourselves and wash your garments. He went out with them to Mount Sinai at the appointed time which his Lord had set for him, and he would not come to it except by His permission and knowledge. Then the seventy said to him, as has been related to me, when they had done what he commanded them and went out to meet their Lord: O Musa, ask your Lord on our behalf that we may hear the speech of our Lord. He said: I will do so. When Musa drew near the mountain, a column of cloud descended upon it until it covered the whole mountain, and Musa drew near and entered it, and said to the people: Come near. Whenever his Lord spoke to him, a bright light would settle on his forehead, such that no human could look at it, so a veil was drawn between them. The people drew near, and when they entered the cloud they fell down in prostration, and they heard Him speaking to Musa, commanding and forbidding: Do, and do not. When He had finished His command to him, the cloud cleared away from Musa, and he came toward them. They said to Musa: ﴿We will never believe you until we see God openly﴾, and the thunderbolt, which is the trembling, seized them, [and their souls departed] and they all died. [What is between the brackets is an addition from the History of al-Tabari, where it reads: "their souls departed"; the correct reading is what is given here. It is said: "his soul was snatched away" (in the passive), he died suddenly, meaning abruptly; and in a hadith that a man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: My mother's soul was snatched away, and she died without making a bequest; shall I give charity on her behalf? He said: Yes.] Musa stood imploring his Lord, calling on Him, desiring Him, and saying: My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me too! They have acted foolishly; will You destroy those behind me among the Children of Israel for what the foolish among us have done? [In the History: "They acted foolishly, so there will perish those behind me... this is destruction for them", with "i.e." omitted.] That is: this is destruction for them. I chose from them seventy men, the best of the best, and I return to them with not one man of them with me! What, then, will they believe me about or trust me with after this? ﴿Indeed we have turned back to You﴾. Musa continued to implore his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and to ask of Him, [the words "and to ask Him" are not in the printed edition], until their souls were returned to them. He then asked Him to accept the repentance of the Children of Israel for worshipping the calf, and He said: No, unless they kill themselves. [Report 9557 is in the History of al-Tabari 1: 220-221.]

9558 - Musa ibn Harun related this to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat ibn Nasr related to us, from al-Suddi: When the Children of Israel repented of worshipping the calf, and God accepted their repentance by having some of them kill others as He had commanded them, God, Exalted, commanded Musa to come to Him with some men of the Children of Israel, to apologise to Him for the worship of the calf, and He set them an appointment. Musa chose from his people seventy men, handpicked by him, and went with them so that they might make their apology. When they arrived at that place, they said: ﴿We will never believe you until we see God openly﴾, for you have spoken with Him, so show Him to us. The thunderbolt seized them and they died. Musa stood weeping and calling on God, saying: My Lord, what shall I say to the Children of Israel when I come to them, having destroyed their best? My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me too! Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us have done? God revealed to Musa: These seventy are among those who took the calf; that is the time of which Musa says: ﴿It is only Your trial; You lead astray by it whom You will and guide whom You will﴾ [to His words] ﴿Indeed we have turned back to You﴾ [Al-A'raf: 155-156]. [He says: We have repented to You.] [The addition between the brackets is from the History of al-Tabari; the first of them is an addition that is indispensable.] That is His words: ﴿And when you said, O Musa, we will never believe you until we see God openly, the thunderbolt seized you﴾. Then God, Mighty is His praise, revived them; they rose and lived, one by one, each looking at the others to see how they were brought back to life. They said: O Musa, you call upon God and He grants whatever you ask; so call on Him to make us prophets! He called on God, Exalted, and He made them prophets. That is His words: ﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾, but He placed one letter before and another after. [The History: 1: 221. The words "placed one letter before and another after" refer to what he mentioned in interpreting the verse according to al-Suddi's view (p. 85): "The thunderbolt seized you, then We revived you..."]

9559 - Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la related this to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: When Musa returned from his Lord with the tablets, on which the Torah had been written, he found them worshipping the calf, so he commanded them to kill themselves, and they did so, and God accepted their repentance. [In the printed edition: "He said: Indeed these tablets..."] He said: Indeed these tablets contain the Book of God, in which is His command that He commanded you, and His prohibition that He forbade you. They said: Who will take it on your word alone? No, by God, we will not, until we see God openly, until God looks down upon us [in the printed edition: "looks upon us"] and says: This is My Book, take it. Why does He not speak to us as He spoke to you, O Musa, [in the printed edition: "as He speaks to you"; the correct form will come in no. 1115], and say: This is My Book, take it? He recited God's words: ﴿We will never believe you until we see God openly﴾. He said: Then a wrath from God came, and a thunderbolt came upon them after their repentance, and it struck them, so they all died. He said: Then God revived them after their death, and he recited God's words: ﴿Then We raised you up after your death, that you might give thanks﴾. Musa said to them: Take the Book of God. They said: No. He said: What has happened to you? They said: We died and were revived. He said: Take the Book of God. They said: No. Then God sent angels who uprooted the mountain over them. [Report 9559; it will also come as no. 1115, where the full account is given: "nataqu al-jabal" means they uprooted it from its base and raised it over them.]

9560 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning God's words: ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on. Then We raised you up after your death﴾: He said: The thunderbolt seized them, then God raised them up to complete the rest of their lifespans.

9561 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq told us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, concerning God's words: ﴿So the thunderbolt seized them﴾: He said: They were the seventy whom Musa chose, who set out with him. He said: They heard a sound, and said: ﴿We will never believe you until we see God openly﴾. He said: They heard a voice and were struck dead, meaning they died. That is God's words: ﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾. They were raised after their death, because that death was a punishment for them, so they were raised to complete the rest of their lifespans.

* *

This is what has been transmitted concerning the cause for which they said to Musa: ﴿We will never believe you until we see God openly﴾. We have no report of established soundness for any of what was said by those whose statements on the cause of their saying that to Musa we have mentioned, such that it would constitute proof and be accepted as settled. [In the printed edition: "so he is granted to them", which is an error and faulty wording; what is meant is acceptance of the sound report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). This statement of al-Tabari shows that he cited these reports only to clarify some meanings, even though they do not establish proof in tafsir, as we said in the notice we wrote in the first volume, pp. 453-454. See the rest of al-Tabari's discussion in this section, for it is a highly eloquent statement, useful for understanding al-Tabari's method in his tafsir.] It is possible that some of it is what they said. Since there is no report establishing it as proof, the correct thing to say about it is: God, Mighty and Majestic, has told us that the people of Musa said to him: ﴿O Musa, we will never believe you until we see God openly﴾, just as He reported that they said it. God, Mighty and Majestic, reported this of them only to those addressed by these verses, as a rebuke for their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ), and his proof has been established against those to whom it was presented; those who receive it have no need to know the particular cause that prompted them to say it. Those whose statements we have related above did speak, and it is possible that some of them are true, as one of them said.

**Discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾**

﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾ is conjoined to His saying: ﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾. So the meaning of the verse is: "Then We raised you up after your death, and We shaded you with the clouds," and He enumerated the rest of the blessings He bestowed upon them, "so that you may give thanks."

* *

*Al-ghamam* is the plural of *ghamamah*, just as *al-sahab* is the plural of *sahabah*. *Al-ghamam* is that which covers the sky and clothes it with cloud and dust and other things that conceal it from the eyes of onlookers. The Arabs call anything that is covered *maghmum* (covered).

* *

It has been said that the clouds with which God shaded the Children of Israel were not clouds (*sahab*).

962 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾, he said: "It is not the sahab."

963 – And al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Abu Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾, he said: "It is not the sahab. It is the cloud in which God will come on the Day of Resurrection, and it was not [given] except to them."
[Editor's note: In the manuscript, this report stops at the words "he said: It is not the sahab," and then adds after it: "And with its chain from Mujahid, he said: It is not the sahab; it is the cloud in which..." to the end of the report.]

964 – And Muhammad ibn Amr al-Bahili narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God, may His praise be exalted: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾, he said: "It is in the position of the sahab."

965 – And al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Abbas said: "And We shaded you with the clouds," he said: "It is a cloud more cool and pleasant than this, and it is the one in which God, Mighty and Majestic, will come on the Day of Resurrection, in His saying: ﴿in canopies of clouds﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:210]; and it is the one in which the angels came on the day of Badr." Ibn Abbas said: "And it was with them in the wilderness (al-tih)."
[Editor's note: In the manuscript: "fihi fi qawlihi" without "yawm al-qiyamah" (the Day of Resurrection).]
[Editor's note: The pronoun in his saying "wa-kana" ("and it was") refers to the cloud.]

* *

Since the meaning of *al-ghamam* is as we have described, that which covers the sky with something that conceals its face from the one looking at it, then the one with which God, Mighty and Majestic, shaded the Children of Israel, and which He described as being a cloud, is no more entitled to being called a sahab than to being anything else that covers the face of the sky.
[Editor's note: In the printed edition: "fa-ghatta wajhaha" ("so it covered its face"), and that is better.]

* *

It has been said: it is what is white of the clouds.

* *

**Discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And We sent down upon you al-manna﴾**

The people of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wil*) differed concerning the description of *al-manna*. Some of them said:

966 – Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me this, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And We sent down upon you al-manna﴾, he said: "Al-manna is a gum (sumghah)."

967 – al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

968 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And We sent down upon you al-manna and al-salwa﴾, he said: "al-Manna used to descend upon them like snow."

* *

Others said: "It is a drink."

Mention of who said that:

969 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: "Al-manna is a drink that used to descend upon them like honey, and they would mix it with water and then drink it."

* *

Others said: "Al-manna is honey."

Mention of who said that:

970 – Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "Al-manna: it is honey that used to descend for them from the sky."

971 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from Jabir, from Amir, who said: "Your honey here is one part of seventy parts of al-manna."

* *

Others said: "Al-manna is thin bread (khubz al-raqaq)."
[Editor's note: In the printed edition: "khubz al-raqaq." Raqaq is an adjective, like tawil and tiwal; it is flat, thin bread.]

Mention of who said that:

972 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Abd al-Karim narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Samad narrated to me, saying: "I heard Wahb – and he was asked: 'What is al-manna?' – he said: 'Thin bread, like corn (al-dhurah), and like the purest flour (al-naqiy).'"
[Editor's note: This is part of a report that will come later under no. 995. In the manuscript it reads "min al-dhurah," and in Ibn Kathir it is as in the printed edition, and it will come likewise under no. 995.]

* *

Others said: "Al-manna is ginger (al-zanjabil)."
[Editor's note: In the printed edition it is "al-tarankhubin," and likewise in al-Baghawi: "al-tarankhubin." In Taj al-Arus: "al-tarankhubin," with a damma, is the manna mentioned in the Qur'an. It will come after no. 977; here it is "al-zanjabil" as in Ibn Kathir and the manuscript. See Lisan al-Arab, under (m-n-n).]

Mention of who said that:

973 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Al-manna used to fall upon the ginger tree (shajar al-zanjabil)."
[Editor's note: In the printed edition: "shajar al-tarankhubin."]

* *

Others said: "Al-manna is that which falls upon the tree that people eat."

Mention of who said that:

974 – al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Abbas said: "Al-manna used to descend upon their trees, and they would go out to it in the morning and eat from it whatever they wished."
[Editor's note: This report is in the manuscript after no. 976.]

975 – And Musa narrated to me, saying: al-Hammani narrated to us, saying: Shurayk narrated to us, from Mujalid, from Amir, regarding His saying: ﴿And We sent down upon you al-manna﴾, he said: "Al-manna is that which falls upon the tree."

976 – It was narrated to me from al-Minjab ibn al-Harith, who said: Bishr ibn Imarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿al-manna﴾, he said: "Al-manna is that which falls from the sky upon the tree, and the people eat it."

977 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Shurayk narrated to us, from Mujalid, from Amir, who said: "Al-manna is this which falls upon the tree."

* *

It has been said: al-manna is al-tarankhubin.

* *

Some of them said: "Al-manna is that which falls upon the thyme (al-thimam) and the 'ushar plant, and it is sweet like honey." It is this that al-A'sha – Maymun ibn Qays – meant by his saying:

*If they had been fed the manna and the salwa in their place,*
*the people would not have seen any food among them that was bountiful.*

[Editor's note: From his Diwan, p. 87, from a long qasidah in which he mentions Dhu al-Taj Hawdhah ibn Ali al-Hanafi, lord of al-Yamamah. The Banu Tamim had attacked a property and a caravan that was being driven to Kisra, so al-Muka'bir the Persian, Kisra's governor over Bahrain, struck them and brought them into al-Mushaqqar, a fortress in Bahrain, by a deception he played on them; he killed their men and spared the boys. On that day Hawdhah ibn Ali spoke to al-Muka'bir about a hundred of the Banu Tamim captives, and he granted them to him on the day of Fitr (or Fasah), so he freed them. Then al-A'sha said, mentioning what had happened before at the hand of Hawdhah among the Banu Tamim:

*Ask Tamim about the days of their bargain, when all their captives came to him in submission.*
*In the midst of al-Mushaqqar, in a dark, long-necked [fortress], they could not find any way to escape there.*
*If they had been fed the manna...* [the rest of the line is missing in the source]

So he described the Banu Tamim as ungrateful for his favour. (Tarikh al-Tabari 2:132–134.) *Al-ta'm* is what is eaten of food. *Najaa al-ta'am fi al-insan* means here: its eating was complete and its nourishing effect became apparent, and he digested it well and it agreed with him.]

And the reports concerning the Messenger of God (ﷺ) became widely attested that he (ﷺ) said:

978 – "The truffle is of al-manna, and its water is a cure for the eye."
[Editor's note: al-Tabari narrated this without a chain. He was right that the reports for it are widely attested. It was narrated by Ahmad, the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), and al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd. It was also narrated by Ahmad, the two Shaykhs, and Ibn Majah, from the hadith of Abu Sa'id and Jabir. It was narrated by Abu Nu'aym in al-Tibb (Medicine), from the hadith of Ibn Abbas and Aisha. See for example al-Musnad: 1625, 1626; al-Jami' al-Saghir: 6463; Zad al-Ma'ad of Ibn al-Qayyim 3:383; and Tafsir Ibn Kathir 1:174–176, where he quotes many of its chains.]

Others said: "Al-manna is a sweet drink that they used to cook and then drink."

* *

As for Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, he made it honey in his poetry, when he described their situation in the wilderness and what they were provided with there. He said:

*So God saw that they were in a place of loss, neither one with cultivated fields nor one that was settled.*
[Editor's note: From his Diwan, pp. 34–35, in the originals and the Diwan: "wa-la mathmuran" ("nor fertile" in the sense of ruined). Mudi'a: a place of loss, ruin and destruction. It is said: "He is in a house of loss" (with the mim fathah and the dad kasrah), as if he were lost in it. It is a mafil form, and the taa' has been dropped from it, as they say: al-manzil and al-manzilah. Mazra': a mimi verbal noun from "zara'a," meaning not one with crops. Ma'mur: one inhabited, whose ruin has gone. "Wa-la ma'muran" is in the accusative, as a conjunction to the place of "bi-dhi mazra'," which is accusative. I chose this word because it is the one that accords with the context of the poem, and because the error between "ma'mur" and "mathmur" is easy, as you will see in the explanation of the third line.]

*Then He made to descend upon them early in the morning clouds, and He milked their rain upon them like the milk of hairy she-camels, like those that are kept for milking*
[Editor's note: In the originals: "fa-ansaha" / "fa-'afaha" / "fa-sanaha." There is no sense in any of these. I am inclined to read it from the manuscript as "fa-nasaha," originally "fa-nasa'aha" with a hamza, as they said: "bara'a Allah al-khalq wa-baraahum" with the hamza dropped. Nasa'a al-dabbah / al-ibil yansa'uha nas'an: he drove it and urged it on. He means: he drove the clouds over them. Ghadiyat: plural of ghadiyah, the cloud that forms in the morning. Maraa al-naqah maryan: he rubbed her udder so that she would let down her milk. Al-muzn: plural of muznah, the cloud that has water. Khalaya: plural of khaliyyah, the she-camel left for milking because of her generosity and abundant milk. Al-khawar: reddish camels with a tinge of grey, thin-skinned, long-furred, having hair that penetrates the wool; it is longer than the rest of the wool, and when they are like this they are abundant and very milky. He likened the cloud with abundant water to these two kinds of she-camels abundant in milk, whose rain is milked upon them, and then in the next line he specified the kinds of things sent down upon them from the sky.]

*Honey dripping, and sweet water, and milk, pleasing and abundant.*
[Editor's note: Nataf, from natafa yantufu: to drip. It is explained later: i.e., it drips from the sky. Al-furat: the sweetest of waters. He described the milk as having "bahjah," which is beauty and freshness, because its cream had not been taken, so it did not thin out and lose the sheen of the cream; so he used "bahjah" figuratively for this. As for his saying "mathmuran," the printed edition has "mamrura," and in the manuscript it was originally "mathmuran," then the scribe's pen played with the tha' and the mim, and he himself wrote in the margin "mazmuran," then explained at the edge of the page: "al-mazmur: the pure part of the milk." That is something with no existence in the lexicons. I have seen that he wrote "mathmuran" in the first line, and I preferred its correct form to be "ma'muran," and I preferred in this line that it be confused for him when he wrote "mathmuran," and then he returned and made it "mazmuran." I did not find "mathmuran" in the lexicons, but it is said: al-thamir and al-thumayrah: milk whose cream has appeared and become granular. Ibn Shumayl said: when it is churned, the likes of the spots of a lizard's skin are seen upon it, then it gathers and becomes cream, and as long as they are small it is thamir. They say: "Your milk is of good thamar (yield), and your churning has yielded (athmara makhadhuka)." So it is as if he said "mathmuran," meaning "thamiran," because fa'il here has the sense of maf'ul.]

*Al-mathmur: the pure part of the milk.* [In the printed edition it was "al-mamrur," and I noted in the footnote that in the margin of the manuscript it is "al-mazmur."]

So he made the manna that used to descend upon them honey dripping (*nataf*), and *al-nataf* is that which drips.
[Editor's note: The phrase "So he made the manna..." up to the end of the sentence is not in the manuscript.]

* *

**Discussion on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿and al-salwa﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: "Al-salwa" is the name of a bird resembling the quail (al-sumana). Its singular and its plural are of one form, just as the plural and singular of al-sumana are the same in form. It has also been said that the singular of salwa is salwah.

Mention of who said that:

979 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to me, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some people among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Al-salwa is a bird resembling the quail."
[Editor's note: The report: In the manuscript it is limited to part of this chain, to his saying "from al-Suddi," and omits the rest, which is the chain that recurs throughout his tafsir. So it seems every chain that stopped at al-Suddi is this chain, and he used a part of it instead of all of it, as has passed just before and will come after.]

980 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: "It was a bird larger than the quail."

981 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, who said: "Al-salwa: a bird which the south wind used to gather for them."

982 – Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "Al-salwa: a bird."

983 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Al-salwa: a bird."

984 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Abd al-Karim narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Samad narrated to me, saying: "I heard Wahb – and he was asked: 'What is al-salwa?' – he said: 'A fat bird like the pigeon.'"
[Editor's note: Part of a report that will come later under no. 995.]

985 – Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "Al-salwa: a bird."

986 – al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: "Al-salwa was a bird that used to come to them like the quail."

987 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hammani narrated to us, saying: Shurayk narrated to us, from Mujalid, from Amir, who said: "Al-salwa is the sumana."

988 – It was narrated to me from al-Minjab, who said: Bishr narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Al-salwa is the sumana."

989 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad informed us, saying: Shurayk narrated to us, from Mujalid, from Amir, who said: "Al-salwa is the sumana."

990 – Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu Amir narrated to us, saying: Qurrah narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, who said: "The sumana is al-salwa."

* *

If someone says: "What was the reason for God, Mighty and Majestic, shading them with the clouds and sending down the manna and the salwa upon these people?"

It is said: The people of knowledge differed concerning that. We will mention what has reached us of it:

991 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat ibn Nasr narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "When God accepted the repentance of the people of Musa, and revived the seventy whom Musa had chosen after he had caused them to die, God commanded them to set out toward Jericho (Ariha), which is the land of Bayt al-Maqdis. So they set out until, when they were near it, Musa sent twelve chieftains (naqib). What happened with them, with the Jabbarin (tyrants), and with the people of Musa, is what God has related in His Book."
[Editor's note: This is an abridgement. Its detailed account is in the history books in its place, as will come in its place with mention of its sources.]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 57 (part 2 of 2):

The people of Moses said to Moses: ﴿Go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting right here.﴾ Moses became angry and invoked [a curse] upon them, saying: ﴿My Lord, I control none but myself and my brother, so part us from the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ That was a hasty act by Moses, which he hurried into. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, it is forbidden to them for forty years; they will wander in the land.﴾ When the wandering (al-tih) was imposed upon them, Moses regretted [his words], and his people who had been with him and who used to obey him came to him and said: "What have you done to us, O Moses?" When he regretted, Allah revealed to him: "Do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people," meaning: do not grieve over the people whom you named as defiantly disobedient. So he did not grieve. They said: "O Moses, how can we have water here? Where is the food?" So Allah sent down to them the manna, which used to fall upon the tree of tarangabin [in the manuscript alone: "al-zanjabil"; see above: 92] and the quail, which is a bird resembling the quail (al-samani). A man would come and look at the bird: if it was fat he would slaughter it, and otherwise he would release it; and when it grew fat, it would come to him. They said: "This is the food; where is the drink?" So Moses was commanded, and he struck the rock with his staff, and twelve springs gushed forth from it, and each tribe drank from its own spring. They said: "This is food and drink; where is the shade?" So the clouds were made to shade them. They said: "This is shade; where is the clothing?" So their garments would grow with them as children's clothes grow, and no garment of theirs would tear. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds and sent down upon you the manna and the quail﴾, and His saying: ﴿And when Moses asked water for his people, We said: Strike the rock with your staff, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew its drinking place.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 60] [[The report: 991 – in Tarikh al-Tabari 1: 221–222.]]

992 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: When Allah the Mighty and Majestic accepted the repentance of the Children of Israel, and commanded Moses to lift from them the sword [of punishment] for worshipping the calf, Moses was commanded to lead them toward the Holy Land, [[In the manuscript: "an yasbiqa bihim" (that he should precede them), and the copyist intended to correct it in the margin, writing "-" but did not complete it.]] and [Allah] said: "Indeed I have decreed it for you as a home, a dwelling and a residence, so go forth to it and fight whoever among the enemy is in it, for I will give you victory over them." So Moses set out with them toward the Holy Land by the command of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, until, when they alighted at the wilderness of wandering (al-tih) between Egypt and Syria, a land in which there was neither shade-giving tree nor shelter [[al-khamar (with two fatha vowels): anything that covers you, whether a tree, a building, or other.]], Moses called upon his Lord when the heat afflicted them, so He shaded them with clouds; and he prayed for their provision, so Allah sent down to them the manna and the quail.

993 – al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, he said: Ishaq narrated to us, he said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas –

994 – And it was narrated to me from Ammar ibn al-Hasan: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' [[This second chain is missing from the manuscript.]], regarding His saying: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾, he said: The clouds shaded them in the wandering. They wandered within five or six farsakhs; whenever they rose in the morning and traveled onward, by evening they would find themselves at the very place from which they had set out. They remained so until forty years had passed. [[In the manuscript: "hatta qamarat arba'īna sanatan" (a corrupted reading).]] He said: During that time the manna and the quail continued to descend upon them, and their garments did not wear out. They had with them a stone from the stones of Mount Sinai which they carried with them; whenever they alighted, Moses struck it with his staff, and twelve springs gushed forth from it.

995 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Ishaq narrated to us, he said: Isma'il ibn Abd al-Karim narrated to us, he said: Abd al-Samad narrated to me, he said: I heard Wahb say: When Allah forbade the Children of Israel to enter the Holy Land for forty years, during which they would wander in the land, they complained to Moses and said: "What shall we eat?" He said: "Indeed Allah will bring you what you will eat." They said: "From where for us? Unless He rains bread upon us!" He said: "Indeed Allah the Mighty and Majestic will send down upon you bread that has been baked." So the manna would descend upon them. Wahb was asked: What is the manna? He said: Thin flat bread like millet, or like pure flour. [[This sentence has been cited previously in report no. 972.]] They said: "What shall we eat with it? Is there any need for us to have meat?" He said: "Indeed Allah will bring it to you." They said: "From where for us? Unless the wind brings it to us!" He said: "Indeed the wind will bring it to you." So the wind would bring them the quail. Wahb was asked: What is the quail? He said: A fat bird like the pigeon, [[This sentence has been cited previously in report no. 984.]] which would come to them, and they would take from it from Sabbath to Sabbath. [[In the printed edition: "from the Sabbath to the Sabbath."]] They said: "What shall we wear?" He said: "No garment of any of you will wear out for forty years." They said: "What shall we put on our feet?" He said: "The thong of any of your sandals will not break for forty years." [[al-shise: one of the thongs of a sandal which passes between the two toes.]] They said: "If children are born among us, what shall we clothe them with?" [[In the printed edition: "fa-inna fina awladan."]] He said: "The garment of the child will grow with him." They said: "From where shall we have water?" He said: "Allah will bring it to you." They said: "From where? Unless it gushes for us from the rock!" So Allah the Blessed and Exalted commanded Moses to strike the rock with his staff. They said: "How shall we see? Darkness covers us!" [[In the printed edition: "fa-bim nubsir."]] So He set up for them a pillar of light in the middle of their camp, which illuminated their entire camp. They said: "With what shall we be shaded? The sun is very harsh upon us!" He said: "Allah will shade you with clouds." [[Report: 995. Ishaq is Ibn Rahawayh, the great imam. Isma'il ibn Abd al-Karim ibn Ma'qil ibn Munabbih al-San'ani: trustworthy, biography in al-Tahdhib, al-Bukhari's biography 1/1/367, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/187. Here he narrates from his paternal uncle Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil ibn Munabbih, who is also trustworthy, biography in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/50. Abd al-Samad narrates from his uncle Wahb ibn Munabbih, this report.]]

996 – Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, Ibn Zayd said, then he mentioned something similar to the report of Musa ibn Harun, from Amr ibn Hammad, from Asbat, from al-Suddi.

997 – al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated to me, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, he said: Ibn Jurayj said: Abdullah ibn Abbas said: There were created for them in the wandering garments that do not wear out nor become soiled. [[Daran al-thawb yadran daranan fa-huwa daran wa-adran: it became stained with dirt.]] He said, and Ibn Jurayj said: If a man took from the manna and quail more than the food of one day, it would spoil, except that on Friday they would take the food for Saturday, and it would not turn bad by the morning.

* *

Regarding the interpretation of His saying, ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾:

This is among the matters left unstated because its outward meaning indicates what has been omitted. The meaning of the verse is: "And We shaded you with the clouds and sent down upon you the manna and the quail, and We said to you: Eat of the good things with which We have provided you." The words "and We said to you" have been omitted, because of what the outward sense of the address indicates. By His saying, ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾, He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: Eat of the delicious things of Our provision which We have provided you. It has also been said that by His saying, ﴿of the good things with which We have provided you﴾, He means: of its lawful portion which We have permitted to you and made your provision.

The first of the two opinions is more correct as an interpretation, because it describes the pleasant life in which the people were, which He gave them; describing it as "good" (ṭayyib), which carries the sense of pleasure, is more fitting than describing it as merely lawful and permitted.

The "mā" in "razaqnākum" (with which We have provided you) means "alladhī" (which). As if it were said: Eat of the good things of the provision which We have provided you.

* *

Regarding the interpretation of His saying, ﴿And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves﴾ (57):

This too is among the matters left unstated because its outward meaning indicates what has been omitted. The meaning of the speech is: "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you." But they opposed what We commanded them, disobeyed their Lord and His messenger sent to them, and "they did not wrong Us." So what appears is sufficient regarding what has been omitted.

His saying, ﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾, means: they did not wrong Us by their deed and their disobedience, but they were wronging themselves.

By His saying, ﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾, He means: they did not place their deed and their disobedience toward Us in a position of harm to Us or diminishment for Us; rather, they placed it from themselves in a position of harm to themselves and diminishment for them. As:

999 – Narrated to us by al-Minjab, he said: Bishr narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves﴾: he said: "They were harming themselves."

* *

We have already shown earlier that the root of "zulm" (wronging) is placing a thing in other than its proper place, and that has been sufficient, so there is no need to repeat it.

* *

Likewise, our Lord, may His remembrance be exalted, is not harmed by the disobedience of any disobedient one, nor does the wrong of any wrongdoer diminish His treasuries; nor does the obedience of any obedient one benefit Him, nor does the justice of any just one increase His dominion. Rather, the wrongdoer wrongs only his own self, the disobedient one diminishes only his own share, and it is only his own self that the obedient one benefits, and his own share that the just one attains.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 58 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town"﴾
