The "town" (al-qaryah) which Allah, may His praise be exalted, commanded them to enter, that they might eat from it abundantly wherever they wished, is, as has been reported to us, Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

Mention of the narrations to this effect:

999 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿Enter this town﴾, he said: Bayt al-Maqdis.

1000 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Hammad narrated to me, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town"﴾ As for "the town," it is the town of Bayt al-Maqdis.

1001 - I was told on the authority of ʿAmmar ibn al-Hasan, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ: ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town"﴾, meaning Bayt al-Maqdis.

1002 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: I asked him, meaning Ibn Zayd, about His words: ﴿Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish﴾. He said: It is Jericho, which is near Bayt al-Maqdis.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿and eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance﴾

He means by this: eat from this town wherever you wish, a pleasant and ample sustenance without reckoning. We have already explained the meaning of "raghad" (abundance) earlier in our book, and mentioned the opinions of the people of interpretation regarding it. [[See what has passed, 1: 515–516.]]

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿and enter the gate prostrating﴾

As for the "gate" (bab) which they were commanded to enter, it has been said that it is the Gate of Repentance (Bab Hittah) of Bayt al-Maqdis.

Mention of those who said this:

1003 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr al-Bahili narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾, he said: The Gate of Hittah, from the Gate of Iliya', of Bayt al-Maqdis.

1004 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

1005 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿And enter the gate prostrating﴾, as for "the gate," it is a gate of the gates of Bayt al-Maqdis.

1006 - Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿And enter the gate prostrating﴾, that it is one of the gates of Bayt al-Maqdis, and it is called the Gate of Hittah. As for His words: ﴿prostrating﴾, Ibn ʿAbbas used to interpret it to mean bowing (rukʿan).

1007 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to me, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-Aʿmash, from al-Minhal ibn ʿAmr, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾, he said: Bowing, through a small gate.

1008 - Al-Hasan ibn al-Zabarqan al-Nakhaʿi narrated to us, saying: Abu Usamah narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-Aʿmash, from al-Minhal, from Saʿid, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿Enter the gate prostrating﴾, he said: They were commanded to enter bowing.

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The original meaning of "sujud" (prostration) is bending down toward one to whom one prostrates, out of reverence for him. Thus every one who bends down to something out of reverence for it is "sajid" (prostrating). From this is the saying of the poet: [[He is Zayd al-Khayl ibn Muhalhil al-Ta'i, the famous horseman.]]

With a host in whose sides the piebald horses go astray; you see the hills prostrating themselves before the hooves.

[[It will come later in this part, 1: 289 (Bulaq edition); also al-Kamil 1: 258, al-Maʿani al-Kabir 890, al-Adddad by Ibn al-Anbari 256, Hamasah of Ibn al-Shajari 19, Majmuʿat al-Maʿani 192, and others. The "bi" in his saying "bi-jamʿ" is linked to a preceding verse, which is: "Banu ʿAmir, do you recognize, when Abu Mikhnaf rises in the morning, the one who has tied the knot of the rear-riders?"

"Al-bulq" is the plural of "ablaq" and "balqaʾ": a horse whose white markings rise to the thighs. "Al-hujarat" is the plural of "hujrah" (with fatha then sukun): a direction/side. "Al-akam" (with damma then sukun, originally two dammas) is the plural of "ikam," the plural of "akamah": a mound higher than what surrounds it, below a mountain, rough with stones. Ibn Qutaybah said in al-Maʿani al-Kabir: "He says: when the piebald horses go astray in it despite their fame and are not recognized, then others are all the more likely to go astray. He describes the multitude of the army, and means that the hills have humbled themselves from the impact of the hooves." In the printed edition here it is "fihi," and the correct reading is what I have established; the pronoun in "minhu" refers to the army or the gathering.]] By his saying "sujjadan" he means humble and submissive.

From this is the saying of Aʿsha of Banu Qays ibn Thaʿlabah:

He alternates between the prayers to the King, at times prostrating, at times crying out.

[[His Diwan: 41; it will come at 18: 28 (Bulaq), with another verse at 14: 82 (Bulaq). "Rawaha, yurawihu murawahah": to do two acts in one act, to work at one thing and at another. Labid said describing a horse: "He turned, intending the folds of Falj, alternating between preservation and abandonment."

As for his saying "min salawat" (from the prayers), "min" here is explanatory of the kind, like His words: "They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and they will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade." The "bayna" which "yurawih" requires has been omitted, because what follows indicates it, namely his saying "at times... and at times." "Al-juʾar" is raising the voice in supplication with humility, entreaty and distress. One cries out (jaʾara) to his Lord, yajʾaru, juʾaran.]]

That is Ibn ʿAbbas's interpretation of His words: ﴿prostrating﴾ as bowing, because the one who bows is bent, although the one who prostrates is more deeply bent than he.

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿and say, "Hittah"﴾

As for the interpretation of His words: ﴿Hittah﴾, it is a form (fi'lah) from the saying of the speaker: "God removed your sins from you, so He removes them, a removal (hittah)," like the rudda, al-hiddah and al-middah from ḥaddadtu and maddadtu.

* *

The people of interpretation differed regarding its meaning. Some of them said in accordance with what we have said regarding it.

Mention of those who said this: [[In the printed edition: "that from them," with the addition.]]

1009 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us: ﴿And say, "Hittah"﴾, he said: Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: That is, "Lower (uhutt) our sins from us."

1010 - Yunus narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: (And say, "Hittah"), by it Allah removes from you your sin and your error. [[In the printed edition: "and your errors."]]

1011 - Al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said, Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿Say "Hittah"﴾, he said: He removes your errors from you.

1012 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-Aʿmash, from al-Minhal ibn ʿAmr, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿Hittah﴾, forgiveness.

1013 - I was told on the authority of ʿAmmar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ regarding His words: ﴿Hittah﴾, he said: He removes your errors from you.

1014 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj informed me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: ʿAta' said to me regarding His words: ﴿And say, "Hittah"﴾, he said: We have heard that He removes their errors from them.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: say "There is no god but Allah," as if they directed its interpretation: say that which removes your errors from you, and it is the statement "There is no god but Allah."

Mention of those who said this:

1015 - Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim and Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam al-Misri narrated to me, both saying: Hafs ibn ʿUmar informed us, saying: Al-Hakam ibn Aban narrated to us, from ʿIkrimah: ﴿And say, "Hittah"﴾, he said: Say, "There is no god but Allah."

* *

Others said, in agreement with the meaning of ʿIkrimah's saying, except that they made the statement they were commanded to say to be seeking forgiveness.

Mention of those who said this:

1016 - Al-Hasan ibn al-Zabarqan al-Nakhaʿi narrated to us, saying: Abu Usamah narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-Aʿmash, from al-Minhal, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿And say, "Hittah"﴾, he said: They were commanded to seek forgiveness.

* *

Others said, similar to the saying of ʿIkrimah, except that they said: the statement they were commanded to say is: "This matter is true, as it was said to you."

Mention of those who said this:

1017 - I was told on the authority of al-Minjab, who said: Bishr narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: ﴿And say, "Hittah"﴾, he said: Say, "This matter is true, as it was said to you."

* *

The grammarians of Arabic differed regarding the reason for which "hittah" was put in the nominative case.

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: "Hittah" is raised in the sense of "say, let there be from you a removal (hittah) of our sins," as you say to a man: "your hearing" (samʿuka).

Others among them said: It is a word which God commanded them to say in the nominative, and He obligated them to say it thus.

Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: "Hittah" is raised by a pronoun referring to "hadhihi" (this), as if he said: "And say: 'This' is a removal." [[Al-damir: the implied pronoun, or ellipsis (al-idmar), as passed in 1: 427 note 1. We have also seen in a statement which al-Sharif al-Murtada cited in his Amali 1: 334 from Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari, who said: "kad, is not implied, and it must be pronounced; if its pronoun were permissible, it would be permissible to say: qama ʿAbd Allah, meaning kada ʿAbd Allah yaqum..." and here it is undoubtedly in the sense of ellipsis. It will also come in the following paragraph, in the sense of the implied.]]

Others among them said: It is raised by a pronoun whose meaning is the predicate, as if he said: "Say what is a removal," so that "hittah" is then the predicate of "ma".

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: What is closest to the truth in this in my view, and most resembling the apparent sense of the Book, is that "hittah" is raised by the intention of an omitted predicate which the apparent recitation indicates, namely: "our entering the gate prostrating is a removal." Its repetition in this wording is sufficient, since the apparent sense of the revelation indicates it, namely His words: ﴿And enter the gate prostrating﴾, just as His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And when a community among them said, "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?" They said, "As an excuse to your Lord"﴾ [al-A'raf: 164], [[Our reading: "maʿdhiratan" with the accusative in our copies. Al-Tabari mentioned in the commentary on this verse, 9: 63 (Bulaq), that the nominative is the reading of the general readers of the Hijaz, Kufa and Basra, and that some of the readers of Kufa read "maʿdhiratan" with the accusative.]] meaning: our admonition to them is an excuse to your Lord. Likewise, in my view, the interpretation of His words: ﴿and say, "Hittah"﴾ means: "And when We said, 'Enter this town, and enter the gate prostrating, and say: our entering that prostrating is a removal of our sins.'" This view is on the pattern of the interpretation of al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd, which we mentioned just above.

[[Here begins the first part in the old division from which the copyist of our manuscript transcribed. Its beginning: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate, Lord, make it easy, by Your mercy."]] Abu Jaʿfar said: As for the interpretation of the saying of ʿIkrimah, it is necessary that the reading in "hittah" be accusative, because if the people were commanded to say "There is no god but Allah," or to say "We seek forgiveness from Allah," then it has been said to them: "Say this statement," so "say" then falls upon "hittah," since "hittah," according to the saying of ʿIkrimah, is the statement "There is no god but Allah." And if it is the statement "There is no god but Allah," then "saying" falls upon it, just as if a man commanded another man to say good and said to him: "Say good" in the accusative, and it would not be correct for him to say "Say good [in the nominative]" except with severe strain.

In the consensus of the readers upon the nominative of "hittah" [[In the printed edition: "al-qurrāʾ," as is the practice throughout what has passed] there is clear evidence against the interpretation which ʿIkrimah gave of His words: ﴿and say, "Hittah"﴾. Likewise, on the interpretation we have related from al-Hasan and Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿and say, "Hittah"﴾, [[See no. 1010 above.]] it is necessary that the reading of "hittah" be accusative, because the custom of the Arabs, when they place verbal nouns (masadir) in the position of verbs and omit the verbs, is to put the verbal nouns in the accusative, as the poet said: [[He is al-Farazdaq]]

They were destroyed by the hands of a band and their swords, striking upon the brains of heads, a Syrian blow.

[[His Diwan: 890, in an ode praising Yazid ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and mentioning his defeat of Yazid ibn al-Muhallab in the year 102 (see his account in Tarikh al-Tabari 8: 151–160). The version in his Diwan: "They knelt by the hands of obedience, and their swords": his saying "anakhu" means they were humbled and submitted, or were struck down and died, as if they were camels that knelt and settled. His saying "aydi taʿah" means people of obedience.]]

And like the saying of one who says to a man: "Sam'an wa ta'atan," meaning: "I hear, hearing, and obey, obedience," and as His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Allah forbid [ma'adha Allah]﴾ [Yusuf: 23], meaning: "We seek refuge in Allah."

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿We will forgive you [naghfir lakum]﴾

He means by His words: ﴿We will forgive you﴾: We shall cover your sins with mercy and conceal them upon you, so that We do not expose you by punishment for them.

* *

The root of "al-ghafr" is covering and concealment. Every one who conceals something is its "ghafir" (concealer). From this it is said of the iron helmet worn as protection for the head that it is a "maghfar," because it covers the head and shields it. Similarly "ghimd al-sayf" (the scabbard of the sword), which is what sheathes it and hides it. [[In the printed edition: "and from it ghimd al-sayf," which makes the statement disordered and interpolated, so I prefer that it be "and from it" and "similarly," because he explained "naghfir" with his saying "natatammad" (we envelop). In the printed edition: "what sheathes it and conceals it," and I have kept what is in the manuscript.]] And for this reason the nap of cloth is called "ghafrah," because it covers the cloth and comes between the viewer and seeing it. From this is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

So I do not reproach my cousin if he is ignorant, and I forgive him his ignorance if he is most ignorant.

[[His Diwan, ode 31. This version appears in Sharh Shawahid al-Mughni: 137; in other books it is "if he is unjust," which is better. His saying "ajhal" means "jahil," as they say "awjal" for "wajil," "amil" for "ma'il," "awhad" for "wahid," and others. The first half of the line is correctly "alla aʿtib" as in al-Mufaḍḍaliyyat 590 and elsewhere, or "wa-qad aʿtib" as in al-Qurtayn 2: 69. It is also narrated as "wa la ashtim ibn al-ʿamm." He says: I reach his satisfaction when he is wronged or ignorant, so I leave for him what he does not like for what he likes.]]

He means by his saying: "And I forgive him his ignorance": I cover his ignorance upon him by my forbearance toward him.

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿your errors [khataya-kum]﴾

"Al-khataya" is the plural of "khatiyah" without hamzah, as "al-mataya" is the plural of "matiyah," and "al-hashaya" the plural of "hashiyah." The plural "khataya" was used without hamzah because omitting the hamzah in "khati'ah" is more common than with hamzah, so it was pluralized as "khataya," on the basis that its singular is unhamzated. Had "al-khataya" been pluralized from "khati'ah" with hamzah, it would have been said "khata'i," like "qabilah" and "qaba'il," and "sahifah" and "sahai'if." "Khati'ah" may also be pluralized with the ta', and then it is hamzated and said "khati'at." "Al-khati'ah" is of the form fa'ilah, from "khati'a al-rajulu yakhta' khit'" (the man erred), and that is when he deviates from the path of truth. From this is the saying of the poet: [[He is Umayyah ibn al-Askar (Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shuʿara: 159–160)]]

And if two emigrants surround him, by the life of God, they have erred and failed.

[[Amali al-Qali 3: 109; Kitab al-Muʿammarin: 68; al-Khizanah 2: 405. Its first half is narrated as "atahu muhajiran takannafahu." As for its second half, its narrations differ: "bi-tark kabirah khati'a..." and "li-yatruk shaykhahu khati'an..." and "fa-farraqa shaykhahu..." Umayyah had grown old, lived a long life in the Jahiliyyah, and Islam found him elderly. Then came the time of ʿUmar, when his son Kilab went out to fight, leaving him a dying man, today or tomorrow. He said some verses, of which this line is one. When ʿUmar heard them, he wrote to Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas: "Send Kilab ibn Umayyah ibn al-Askar back home," and he was sent back. He has a good story with ʿUmar in this incident (in al-Qali 1: 109).]]

He means: they erred from the truth and sinned.

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And We will increase the good-doers [wa-sanazidu al-muhsinin]﴾ (58)

Its interpretation is what has been related to us from Ibn ʿAbbas, namely:

1018 - Al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated it to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said, Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿And We will increase the good-doers﴾: whoever among you is a good-doer, his goodness will be increased, and whoever is in error, We will forgive him his sin.

The interpretation of the verse: "And when We said: Enter this town and eat from it [wherever and whatever] you wish, freely, in abundance; and enter the gate prostrating, and say: 'Forgiveness,' We will forgive you your sins and increase [the reward of] the good-doers." Its meaning: enter this town, which is permitted to you, every good thing in it being made lawful for you, provided to you abundantly without reckoning; and enter the gate prostrating, and say: "Our prostration to God is a remission from our Lord for our sins, by which He will wipe away our transgressions; We will cover over the sins of the sinner among you, concealing them for him, and remove his burdens from him; and We will increase the good-doer among you, beyond his previous good deeds with Him, in goodness."

Then God, may His praise be exalted, informed of their great ignorance, their evil obedience to their Lord, their disobedience to their prophets, and their mockery of His messengers, despite the great blessings of God, the Mighty and Majestic, upon them and the wondrous signs and lessons He showed them, rebuking by this their sons who were addressed by these verses, and informing them [that]{{Context of the sentence: "...innahum in ta'addu" and "in" here is negating, in the sense of "ma," like the one in His saying: "Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near," and His saying: "I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you."}} if they transgress in denying Muhammad (ﷺ) and rejecting his prophethood, despite the great favour of God in sending him to them and the wondrous proofs He manifested at his hands among them, [they would be] like their predecessors whose description He gave and whose stories He related to us in these verses, saying, may His praise be exalted: "But those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them, so We sent upon those who did wrong a plague from the sky..." (the verse).

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿So those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them﴾

The interpretation of His words ﴿fabaddala﴾ (so substituted) means: changed. By His words ﴿alladhina zalamu﴾ (those who did wrong) He means those who did what was not theirs to do. By His words ﴿qawlan ghayra alladhi qila lahum﴾ (a word other than that which had been said to them) He means: they substituted a word other than the one they were commanded to say, and instead said something contrary to it. That is the substitution and alteration that came from them. Their substitution of the word they were commanded to say, with another word, [Note: "qawlan" is the object of "tabdiluhum" (their substitution). As for the predicate of "kana" (was), it is His words: "ma haddathana bihi al-Hasan..."] was:

1019 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Hammam ibn Munabbih, that he heard Abu Hurayra say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Allah said to the Children of Israel: "Enter the gate prostrating and say: Hitta (forgive), and We will forgive you your sins." But they substituted, and entered the gate dragging themselves on their buttocks, and said: "A grain in barley." [Hadith 1019: Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad (8213), from ʿAbd al-Razzaq, with this chain, but with the wording "a grain in a hair." Likewise al-Bukhari narrated it (6:312, 8:228-229, Fath al-Bari) from the route of ʿAbd al-Razzaq. Al-Hafiz (8:229) mentioned that the wording "shaʿra" (hair) is the narration of most of al-Bukhari's transmitters, and that the narration of al-Kushmihani is "shaʿira" (barley). Ibn Kathir (1:180) also mentioned it and attributed it to Muslim and al-Tirmidhi, from the narration of ʿAbd al-Razzaq.]

[Hadith 1020, 1021: This is the previous hadith, but al-Tabari narrated it here by two chains. One is sound and continuous, and the other is weak, containing an unidentified narrator between Ibn Ishaq and Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad.

Salih ibn Kaysan al-Madani: a trustworthy Successor (tabiʿi). Salih, mawla of al-Tawama, is Ibn Nabhan, and he too is trustworthy, except that he changed in his later years; whoever narrated from him in earlier times, his hadith is sound. * *

Commentary on the interpretation of His words: ﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky﴾

By His words ﴿fa-anzalna ʿala alladhina zalamu﴾ (so We sent down upon those who did wrong) He means: upon those who did what was not theirs to do, from their substitution of the word that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had commanded them to say, with another word, and their disobedience to Him in what He commanded them, and their committing what He had forbidden them to commit. ﴿Rijzan min al-sama bima kanu yafsuqun﴾ (a punishment from the sky because they were defiant).

* *

"Rijz" in the language of the Arabs means punishment, and it is different from "Rujz" (with a u vowel). [Al-Rijz (with a kasra) is what came in His words in Surat al-Muddaththir: "wal-rujza fahjur". Al-Tabari explained the difference between them at 29:92 (Bulaq), saying: "al-rujz with a damma on the ra... the idols."] That is because "rijz" is a pustule, [A pustule: small boils, like those that occur with plague and smallpox.] and from it is the report narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning plague, that he said: "It is a rijz with which some of the nations before you were punished."

1036 - Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Yunus informed me, from Ibn Shihab, who said: ʿAmir ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas informed me, from Usama ibn Zayd, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "This affliction, or sickness, is a rijz with which some nations before you were punished." [Hadith 1036: Its chain is sound. Ibn Kathir mentioned it (1:182) and said: "This hadith is originally recorded in the two Sahihs, from the hadith of al-Zuhri, and from the hadith of Malik from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir and Salim Abi al-Nadr, from ʿAmir ibn Saʿd, in similar wording." Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad through the route of al-Zuhri (5:207-208). He also narrated it (5:209) through the route of Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Ibrahim ibn Saʿd, from Usama ibn Zayd, in fuller form.]

1037 - Abu Shayba ibn Abi Bakr ibn Abi Shayba narrated to me, saying: ʿUmar ibn Hafs narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from al-Shaybani, from Riyah ibn ʿUbayda, from ʿAmir ibn Saʿd, who said: I witnessed Usama ibn Zayd with Saʿd ibn Malik saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Plague is a rijz sent down upon those before you, or upon the Children of Israel." [Hadith 1037: This is another sound chain for the previous hadith. Abu Shayba ibn Abi Bakr ibn Abi Shayba is Ibrahim ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Muhammad, a trustworthy narrator from whom al-Nasa'i, Abu Zur'a and Abu Hatim also narrated; he is biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim. ʿUmar ibn Hafs ibn Ghiyath is trustworthy, and al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from him in the Sahihs. His father Hafs ibn Ghiyath is trustworthy, reliable and well known; the compilers all narrated from him. Al-Shaybani is Abu Ishaq Sulayman ibn Abi Sulayman, trustworthy and a proof. Riyah ibn ʿUbayda: the "ra" is vocalized with a kasra and the yaa' with a light sukun, and in the printed edition it appears as "Rabah" with a baa', which is an error. "ʿUbayda" has a fatha on the ʿayn and a kasra on the baa'. This Riyah is from Basra and is trustworthy; Ibn Ma'in and Abu Zur'a declared him trustworthy. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib (3:299-300), al-Kabir of al-Bukhari, and Ibn Abi Hatim. He is distinct from "Riyah ibn ʿUbayda al-Sulami al-Kufi," whom al-Mizzi and al-Dhahabi distinguished in al-Tahdhib and al-Mushtabih. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar rejected that distinction from al-Mizzi, but followed al-Dhahabi in Tabsir al-Muntabih without comment, and that is the correct view, God willing.]

* *

Those who held the same view as we have stated in the interpretation of this said so, the people of interpretation.

Those who said so:

1038 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatada regarding His words ﴿rijzan﴾, he said: punishment.

1039 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam al-ʿAsqalani narrated to us, saying: Abu Jaʿfar narrated to us, from al-Rabiʿ, from Abu al-ʿAliya regarding His words ﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky﴾, he said: the rijz is anger.

1040 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: When it was said to the Children of Israel: "Enter the gate prostrating and say Hitta," and those among them who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent upon them the plague, and it left none of them. He recited: ﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky because they were defiant﴾. He said: The children remained, and in them were the virtue and worship attributed to the Children of Israel, and goodness, while all the fathers perished; the plague destroyed them.

1041 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: al-rijz is punishment. Everything in the Qur'an that is "rijz" means punishment.

1042 - It was narrated to me from al-Minjab, saying: Bishr narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words ﴿rijzan﴾, he said: Everything in the Book of Allah that is "rijz" means punishment.

* *

We have already shown that the interpretation of "rijz" is punishment. The punishments of Allah, may His praise be exalted, are of different kinds. Allah, may His praise be exalted, has informed us that He sent down upon those whose affair we have described a rijz from the sky. It is possible that it was plague, and it is possible that it was something else. There is no indication in the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, nor in an established report from the Messenger, as to which kind it was.

The correct statement on this is to say as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: So We sent down upon them a punishment from the sky for their defiance.

However, what the statement of Ibn Zayd affirms is more likely to be sound, due to the report I mentioned from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) describing plague as a rijz, and that a people before us were punished by it. Yet I do not say with certainty that it was so, because the report from the Messenger of Allah does not specify which nation was punished by it. It is possible that those punished by it were not the ones Allah described in His words: ﴿So those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them﴾.

* *

Commentary on the interpretation of His words: ﴿because they were defiant﴾

We have already shown, earlier in this book, that the meaning of "fisq" (defiance) is going out from something. [See what has passed, 1:409-410, where he mentioned the verse in a report from Ibn ʿAbbas containing: "i.e., they strayed from His command" (p. 410).]

So the interpretation of His words ﴿bima kanu yafsuqun﴾ (because they were defiant) is: because they used to abandon obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, going out from it into disobedience to Him and opposition to His command.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 60:

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people, We said: Strike the rock with your staff, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew its drinking place﴾

The meaning of His words ﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people﴾ is: and when Moses asked Us to give his people water to drink. The one who was asked is omitted, and the thing requested, which is water, is also omitted, since the apparent speech indicates the meaning of what has been left out. [[His words "and the thing requested (al-ma'na alladhi sa'ala Musa)", meaning "and the thing", which is water.]]

Likewise, His words ﴿We said: Strike the rock with your staff, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾ are a case where what is left unsaid is dispensed with by the evidence of what is apparent. The meaning of the speech is: We said, "Strike the rock with your staff," so he struck it, and it gushed forth. The report of Moses striking the rock is omitted, since what was mentioned indicates what is meant.

Likewise, His words ﴿Every people knew its drinking place﴾ mean: every people among them knew its drinking place. The word "among them" is omitted because the speech points to it.

* *

We have already shown earlier that "anas" (people) is a plural with no singular from its own form, [[In the printed edition: "that al-nas is a plural with no singular from its own form". That was mentioned before, but here he meant "anas", which is mentioned in the verse, and it is likewise a plural with no singular from its own form, although some have said it is the plural of insi (human).]] and that if "al-insan" (the human) were pluralized from its own form, it would be said "anasiyy" and "anasiyya". [[See what preceded, 1: 268.]]

* *

The people of Moses are the Children of Israel, whose accounts Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has related in these verses. Moses asked his Lord for water for them at the time they wandered in the wilderness (al-tih), as follows:

1043 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh told us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' told us, from Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people﴾, the verse. He said: This occurred when they were in the desert and complained to their prophet of thirst. They were commanded to strike a rock of Tur, that is, from Mount Sinai, with his staff. They carried it with them, and when they stopped, Moses struck it with his staff, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs, each tribe having a known spring whose water flowed for them.

1044 - Tamim ibn al-Muntasir told me, saying: Yazid ibn Harun told us, saying: Asbagh ibn Zayd told us, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Ayyub, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: That was in the wilderness. The clouds shaded them, manna and quails were sent down upon them, and they were given garments that would neither wear out nor become soiled. A square rock was placed among them, and Moses was commanded to strike the rock with his staff, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs, three springs from each side, one for each tribe. They never journeyed a stage without finding that rock with them, in the place where it had been with them at the first halting place. [[al-Minqalah: a stage of a journey; the plural is manaqil.]]

1045 - 'Abd al-Karim told me, saying: Ibrahim ibn Bashshar told us, saying: Sufyan told us, from Abu Sa'id, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: That was in the wilderness. Moses struck the rock for them, and there became in it twelve springs of water, one for each tribe of them, from which they drank.

1046 - And Muhammad ibn 'Amr told me, saying: Abu 'Asim told us, saying: 'Isa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿So We said: Strike the rock with your staff, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾, one spring for each tribe of them. All of that occurred during their wandering, when they wandered.

1047 - Al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid regarding His words ﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people﴾, he said: They feared thirst during their wandering when they wandered, so the rock burst forth for them twelve springs, which Moses struck. Ibn Juraij said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "The tribes (al-asbat)" are the sons of Ya'qub; they were twelve men, each of whom fathered a tribe, a community of people. [[In the printed edition: "wa-lad sibtan wa-ummatan min al-nas", but the correct reading omits the conjunction, since his words "ummatan min al-nas" are an explanation of "sibtan".]]

1048 - Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la told me, saying: Ibn Wahb told us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: Moses asked water for them in the wilderness, and they were watered from a rock like a sheep's head. He said: They would put it on the sides of the juwaliq when they journeyed, [[al-Jawaliq: a large bag woven from wool or hair, in which food is carried; in our lands we call it "al-shawal," a corruption of "al-jawaliq".]] and Moses would tap it with the staff when they stopped, and twelve springs would gush from it, one for each tribe of them, and the Children of Israel would drink from it. When it was time to depart, the springs would stop, and it would be lifted and placed on the side of the juwaliq. [["Qila bihi" is passive of "qala bihi". "Qala bil-shay'" means he lifted or carried it. The Arabs use "qawl" to denote all kinds of actions and apply it to things other than speech and the tongue. They say: "qala bi-rijlihi," when he begins to advance and walk, or when he gestures with it to kick. They say: "qala bil-ma' 'ala yadihi," meaning he turned it over and poured it. And similar things. Something similar has passed above, p. 54 note 3, p. 64 note 4.] When they stopped, he would set it down and tap it with the staff, and a spring would gush forth from every side like the sea.

1049 - Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told me, from al-Suddi, who said: That was in the wilderness.

* *

As for His words ﴿Every people knew its drinking place﴾, Allah informed of them concerning this, because their manner of drinking, in respect of what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, brought forth for them from the rock whose description He gave in this verse, differed from the drinking of all other people in the waters that Allah brings forth from the mountains and lands, which no one owns except Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Allah had made for each of the twelve tribes a spring from the rock whose description is given in this verse, from which that tribe alone drank, and no tribe entered into the drinking of another tribe. Moreover, each of those twelve springs had a place in the rock known to the tribe that drank from it. Therefore He, glorified be His praise, singled them out in the report about them: that every people among them knew its drinking place, to the exclusion of others among mankind, since others, in the water that no one possesses, were partners in its sources and channels, whereas each of these tribes had exclusive drinking from one source of the rock, apart from the rest of its sources, belonging to them alone and not to the other tribes. Therefore they were singled out in the report about them: that every people among them knew its drinking place.

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Eat and drink of the provision of Allah﴾

This too is a case where what is apparent is sufficient to dispense with what is left unsaid. The meaning of the speech is: ﴿We said: Strike the rock with your staff﴾, so he struck it and there gushed forth from it twelve springs, every people knew its drinking place, and it was said to them: Eat and drink of the provision of Allah. Allah, glorified be His praise, informed that He commanded them to eat what He provided them in the wilderness, the manna and quails, and to drink the water He caused to gush forth for them from the rock that is passed from hand to hand, [[al-Hajar al-mutawa'ir: the rock that is exchanged, passed from one hand to another. From "ta'awarū al-shay'": when they exchange a thing. A thing is not passed about among people unless it is movable; what is fixed is not passed about or exchanged.] which has no firm place in the earth and no way to it except for its owners, [[In the printed edition: "la sabil ilayhi li-malikiyhi", which is meaningless. The correct reading is what we have given, with the addition of "illa", and what preceded in the interpretation of the earlier part of the verse confirms this.] which pours forth springs of water and surges with fountains of sweet, sweet water, by the power of the Lord of Majesty and Bounty.

Then He, glorified be His remembrance, bade them forth, [[taqaddama ilayhi bi-kadha: when he commanded him.] along with permitting them what He permitted and bestowing upon them the blessing of pleasant life, with the prohibition against striving in the earth to cause corruption and acting wickedly in it with arrogance, and He said to them: ﴿And do not commit abuse in the earth, causing corruption﴾.

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And do not commit abuse in the earth, causing corruption (60)﴾

By His words ﴿do not commit abuse﴾ He means: do not transgress, and do not strive in the earth causing corruption. As follows:

1050 - Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Adam told us, saying: Abu Ja'far told us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah: ﴿and do not commit abuse in the earth, causing corruption﴾, he says: do not strive in the earth to cause corruption.

1051 - Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb told us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿and do not commit abuse in the earth, causing corruption﴾: do not commit abuse means do not transgress.

1052 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh told us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatadah: ﴿and do not commit abuse in the earth, causing corruption﴾, that is, do not travel in the earth as corrupters.

1053 - It was reported to me from al-Minjab, who said: Bishr told us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿and do not commit abuse in the earth, causing corruption﴾, do not strive in the earth.

The root of "al-'atha" is intense corruption, indeed the most intense corruption. [[al-'atha: a verbal noun of "'atha yu'thi", like "radiya yardha", and it is the dialect of the Hijaz. I have found this verbal noun only in Taj al-'Arus, and I do not know whether the 'ayn is vocalized with fatha or kasra, but I lean toward fatha being more likely.] It is said from it: "'athiya fulan fi al-ard" when he exceeded in corruption to its extreme, "ya'tha 'atha", with the verb in the short form; and for the plural: "hum ya'thun". There are two other dialects for it: one is "'atha ya'thu 'utuwwan". Whoever recites it in this dialect should vowel the thā' of "ya'thu" with a damma, and I know of no reciter whose recitation is followed who recited with it. [["Recitation is a tradition, and one does not recite with what the reciters did not recite." Lisan al-'Arab (ʿthy).] Whoever speaks in this dialect reporting about himself says: "'athawtu a'thu," and whoever speaks in the first dialect says: "'athiytu a'tha."

The other of the two is: "'aththa ya'īthu 'aytha, 'uyūthan, and 'aythanan," all with one meaning. From "al-'ayth" is the verse of Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj:

"And he who acts unlawfully (mustahill) has spread corruption among us: a tax collector or a merchant who..." [[His Diwan, p. 30. Mustahill: one who has made their property lawful and seized it. The musaddiq is the agent who collects the zakat of people's wealth, and is the agent of the poor in collection, and he may dispose for them according to what his judgment leads him to, so he may act unjustly if he is not among the pious. Qa'atha al-shay' yaq'athuhu: he uprooted and exhausted it. And "qa'athahu fa-nqa'atha": when he uprooted it from its root and it was pulled up. The lexicons do not mention "qa'ith fa-huwa muqa'ith," but since he intended that the merchant comes with his oppression and injustice and raising of prices, uprooting people's wealth, while people defend their wealth against him, he derived from the form of mufa'alah that occurs between two: "qa'ith fa-huwa muqa'ith," meaning he tries to uproot the wealth of the people, and the people defend their wealth against him.]]

By His words "'atha fina" he means: he corrupted among us.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 61 (part 1 of 3):

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions."﴾

I have already shown earlier (in the previous part of this volume, 2:11) the meaning of "patience" (ṣabr), that it is restraining the self and holding it back from something. Given that this is so, the meaning of the verse is: Remember when you said, O assembly of the Children of Israel: "We cannot bear to restrain ourselves to one kind of food." That "one kind of food" was what God, the Exalted and Praised, informed that He fed them during their wandering (tīh), and it is the quail (salwā) according to some of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wīl), while according to Wahb ibn Munabbih it was pure bread with meat. So ask your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows, of the herbs and cucumbers, and what God named along with that. It is reported that they asked Moses for it.

* *

The reason for their asking Moses this, as has reached us, is what:

1054 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿And when you said, O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food﴾. He said: The people were in the wilderness, the clouds had been cast over them, and the manna and quail had been sent down upon them, but they grew weary of that and mentioned a life they had had in Egypt, so they asked Moses. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Go down to a city, for you will have what you asked.﴾

1055 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾. He said: They grew weary of their food and mentioned the life they had lived before that. They said: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows, its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic﴾, to the end of the verse.

1056 - al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding His words: ﴿And when you said, O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food﴾. He said: Their food was the quail and their drink was the manna. They asked for what was mentioned, and it was said to them: ﴿Go down to a city, for you will have what you asked.﴾

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Qatadah said: When they arrived in Syria they lost the foods they used to eat, so they said: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions﴾. The clouds had been cast over them and the manna and quail sent down upon them, but they grew weary of that and mentioned a life they had lived in Egypt.

1057 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, saying: I heard Ibn Abi Najih regarding His, the Mighty and Majestic, words: ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾: the manna and quail, and they exchanged it for herbs and what was mentioned with them.

1058 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same as that, exactly.

1059 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same as that.

1060 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: They were given in the wilderness what they were given, but they grew weary of it and said: ﴿O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions﴾.

1061 - Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd informed us, saying: The food of the Children of Israel in the wilderness was one kind, and their drink was one kind. Their drink was honey that descended to them from the sky, called manna, and their food was a bird called quail. They ate the birds and drank the honey, and they did not know bread or anything else. So they said: "O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs," and he recited until he reached: ﴿Go down to a city, for you will have what you asked.﴾

* *

As for His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿from what the earth grows﴾ — He did not mention what they asked Him to bring forth from the earth, so that it would say: "They said: call upon your Lord to bring forth for us such and such from what the earth grows, its herbs and cucumbers," — because "min" (from/some of) comes to mean partitive (tab'īḍ) of what follows it, so it is sufficient with it from mentioning the partitive, since it is known by its inclusion in the meaning of what the speech is about. Like the saying of a speaker: "Today he has morning food (ṭa'ām) from so-and-so," meaning some of it.

Some of them have said: "min" here means redundancy (ilghā') and omission (isqāṭ). As if the meaning of the speech, in his view, is: bring forth for us what the earth grows of its herbs. He cited in support of that the saying of the Arabs: "I did not see from anyone," meaning "I did not see anyone," and the words of God: ﴿and He will expiate from you some of your misdeeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 271], and their saying: "There was from talk, so leave me alone until I go," meaning: there was talk.

Some grammarians among the Arabic-language scholars have denied that "min" means redundancy in any part of speech, and claimed that its entry into every place it enters indicates that the speaker means part of what it enters, not all of it, and that it does not enter a place except for a comprehensible meaning.

So the interpretation of the speech, then, according to what we have described regarding the matter of "min" [in the printed edition: "according to what we have described regarding the matter of 'min' we mentioned," where "we mentioned" is undoubtedly superfluous, as is clear from the context of his preceding and following speech]: ask your Lord for us to bring forth for us some of what the earth grows of its herbs and cucumbers.

* *

"Al-baql" (herbs), "al-qithā'" (cucumbers), "al-'adas" (lentils) and "al-basal" (onions) are what people among themselves know of the plants of the earth and its grains.

* *

As for "al-fūm," the people of interpretation differ concerning it. Some of them said: it is wheat and bread.

Mention of those who said that:

1062 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad and Mu'ammal narrated to us, both saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from 'Ata': "al-fūm": bread.

1063 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata' and Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿and its fūm﴾: they both said its bread.

1064 - Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Abi Za'idah and Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to us, both saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa ibn Maymun, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿and its fūm﴾, he said: bread.

1065 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah and al-Hasan: al-fūm is the grain that people make bread from.

1066 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah and al-Hasan, the same.

1067 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Husayn informed us, from Abu Malik regarding His words: ﴿and its fūm﴾, he said: wheat.

1068 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat ibn Nasr narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿and its fūm﴾: wheat.

1069 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn 'Awn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Yunus, from al-Hasan and Husayn, from Abu Malik regarding His words: ﴿and its fūm﴾: wheat.

1070 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far al-Razi narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: al-fūm is the grain that people make bread from.

1071 - al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said to me regarding His words: ﴿and its fūm﴾: its bread, and Mujahid said it.

1072 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said to me: al-fūm is bread.

1073 - Yahya ibn 'Uthman al-Sahmi narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿and its fūm﴾, he says: wheat and bread.

1074 - It was related to me from al-Minjab, who said: Bishr narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: ﴿and its fūm﴾, he said: it is precisely al-Burr, wheat.

1075 - 'Ali ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Muslim al-Jarmi narrated to us, saying: 'Isa ibn Yunus narrated to us, from Rushdin ibn Kurayb, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the words of God, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and its fūm﴾, he said: al-fūm is wheat in the language of the Banu Hashim. [Hadith 1075 — Muslim al-Jarmi: it was previously established in 154, 649, 846 that it is "al-Jarmi" with a jim, and it is printed here with a jim as we preferred. Rushdin — with a kasra on the ra', sukun on the shin with dots, and a kasra on the dal — ibn Kurayb: weak; the discussion of his weakness has been given in the commentary on the Musnad: 2571. His father, Kurayb ibn Abi Muslim: a trustworthy Successor (tabi'i).]

1076 - 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Mansur narrated to us, from Nafi' ibn Abi Nu'aym, that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas was asked about the words of God: ﴿and its fūm﴾, and he said: wheat. Have you not heard the saying of Uhayhah ibn al-Julah, when he said:
"I used to think myself the richest of people, a single person, who came to Medina without the farming of fūm."
[Hadith 1076 — 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd al-Hakam al-Misri: trustworthy, one of the people of hadith, knowledgeable in history; he composed the History of Egypt and others, as in al-Tahdhib; he died in the year 257. He is the author of the book (Futuh Misr) published in Europe. His shaykh 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Mansur: I have not found any mention of him in the references before me, except in Futuh Misr, p. 40, lines 7–8, where Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam says there: "'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Mansur al-Yahsubi narrated to us, from 'Asim ibn Hakim..." His shaykh Nafi': he is Nafi' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Nu'aym al-Madani, one of the well-known seven readers; he did not meet Ibn 'Abbas, but narrated from the Successors, and he has an entry in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir of al-Bukhari 4/2/8, Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/456–457, and Tarikh Isbahan of Abu Nu'aym 2:326–327.
The verse is in Lisan al-'Arab (fawm), attributed to Abu Mahjan al-Thaqafi, recited by al-Akhfash, and its version is:
"I used to think myself like the richest single one... who alighted in Medina..."
In al-Rawd al-Anf 2:45 it is attributed to Uhayhah or to Abu Mahjan, and it narrates "sakan al-Madina" (dwelt in Medina).]

* *

Others said: it is garlic.

Mention of those who said that:

1077 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to me, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, who said: it is this garlic.

1078 - al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: al-fūm is garlic (thūm).

* *

And it is in some readings "wathūmihā" (with thā').

* *

It has been mentioned that the naming of wheat and bread together as "fūm" is from the ancient language. It was related by hearing from the people of that language: "fawmū lanā" (bake for us), meaning: knead bread for us.

* *

It is mentioned that this is the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "wathūmihā" with the thā'. [See the Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:41.] If that is correct, then it is among the interchanged letters, like their saying: "They fell into 'aathur sharr" and "'afur sharr," and their saying: "to the athafi (stones of hearth), athathi," and "to the maghafir (sweet gum), maghathir," and what is similar to that, where the thā' is turned into fā' and the fā' into thā', because the articulation point of fā' is close to that of thā'. "Al-maghafir" is something resembling a sweet substance, likened to honey, descending from the sky sweet, falling upon trees and the like.

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿He said: Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾

The meaning of His words: ﴿He said: Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾ is: Moses said to them: Do you take what is lower in worth, value and rank of life, in exchange for what is better than it in worth, value and rank? That was their exchange.

* *

The root of "istibdal" (exchange) is leaving something for another in place of what was left.

* *

The meaning of His words: ﴿adná﴾ (lower) is baser, more lowly, and smaller in rank and worth. Its origin is from their saying: "This is a man who is dunī (base) to the utmost baseness," and "innahu layudanni fi al-umur" without hamza, when he pursues its base aspects. It has been mentioned with hamza from some Arabs in this regard, by hearing from them. They say: "Ma kunta dā'nan, wa-laqad danu'ta [this is all from al-Farra's words in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:42; the printed text had "ma kunta duniyyan," and the correct reading is what I have recorded from al-Farra's book], and one of our companions recited to me from another that he heard some of Banu Kilab recite the verse of al-A'sha [the one who heard this is al-Farra; see his Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:42; al-Tabari always ignores him]:
"Bāsilat al-waq'i sarābīluhā, bīḍun ilā dā'inihā al-ẓāhir [its meaning: its coats of mail are sturdy in impact, white toward the base of it that appears]."
with hamza on dā'in, and that he heard them say: "innahu la-dā'in khabīth" with hamza. [In al-Farra's Ma'ani there is an addition between brackets from some copies: [if he was dissolute].] If that is correct from them, then hamza in it is one dialect and omitting it is another.

* *

There is no doubt that whoever exchanged the manna and quail for herbs, cucumbers, lentils, onions and garlic has exchanged the lowly of life for the noble from it.

* *

Some of them have interpreted His words: ﴿what is lower﴾ as meaning: what is nearer (aqrab), and the basis of His words "adná" as the comparative form (af'al) of "dunuww", which means nearness.

* *

A number of people of interpretation have said in their interpretation of His words: ﴿what is lower﴾ something similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

1079 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, who said: ﴿Would you exchange what is lower for what is better?﴾ He says: Would you exchange what is evil for what is better than it?

1080 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿what is lower﴾, he said: worse.

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted and Mentioned, words: ﴿Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you asked﴾

Its interpretation is: So Moses called upon God, and We responded to him, and We said to them: "Go down to a city." It is one of the omitted elements, the apparent meaning of which suffices to indicate what was omitted and left out of it.

* *

We have already shown earlier that the meaning of "descent" (hubūṭ) to a place is only to go down to it and settle in it. [See what preceded in 1:534.]

* *

So the interpretation of the verse, then: Remember when you said: "O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows, its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions." Moses said to them: "Would you exchange what is baser and worse of life for what is better than it?" So Moses called upon his Lord for them to give them what they asked Him, and God responded to his supplication, and He gave them what they sought, and God said to them: ﴿Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you asked.﴾

* *

Then the readers (qurra') differed in their recitation of His words ﴿miṣran﴾ [in the printed edition: "al-Farra'," and we returned it to what the text of al-Tabari followed earlier, in all the places where they followed substituting it from "qurra'" to "qurra'"]. The majority of readers recited "miṣran" with tanwin (nunation) on "al-miṣr" and treated it as declinable. Some of them recited it without tanwin and with the alif removed. As for those who put tanwin on it and declined it, they meant by it a city (miṣr) of the cities, not a specific city. So its interpretation, according to their reading, is: "Go down to a city of the cities, because you are in the desert, and what you sought does not exist in the wastelands and deserts, but only in villages and cities; so indeed for you, when you descend to it, is what you asked of the living." It is also possible that some of those who read it with declension and tanwin meant by the speech: "Go down to a city," the town known by this name, which is "Egypt" from which they had departed. However, he declined it and put tanwin on it, following the orthography of the Mushaf, because in the Mushaf there is a fixed alif in "miṣr," so the way of his reading with declension and tanwin is like the way of one who read: "qawārīra qawārīra min fiḍḍa" [al-Insan: 15–16] with tanwin, following the orthography of the Mushaf. As for the one who did not put tanwin on "miṣr," he undoubtedly meant "Egypt" known by this name specifically, to the exclusion of all other lands. [See what al-Farra' said in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:42–43.]

* *

The people of interpretation differed concerning this, paralleling the difference of the readers in its recitation.

1081 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah: ﴿Go down to a city﴾, that is, a city of the cities, "for indeed you will have what you asked."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 61 (part 2 of 3):

1082 - Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿Go down to a city﴾, [meaning] one of the cities, "for you will have what you asked for." When they came out of the wilderness (al-tih), He lifted the manna and the quails from them, and they ate the herbs.

1083 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Adam related to me, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: ﴿Go down to a city﴾, he said: It means a city from among the cities.

1084 - Al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: ﴿Go down to a city﴾, he said: a city from among the cities. They claimed that they did not return to Egypt.

1085 - Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: ﴿Go down to a city﴾, he said: a city from among the cities. And "Misr" is not declined in speech. It was said to him: "Which Misr?" He said: The holy land that Allah prescribed for them. And he recited the words of Allah, may His praise be exalted: ﴿Enter the holy land which Allah has prescribed for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21].

* *

Others said: It is Egypt, where Pharaoh was.

Mention of those who said that:

1086 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Adam related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, concerning His words: ﴿Go down to Egypt﴾, he said: It means the Egypt of Pharaoh.

1087 - It was related to us from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, from Ibn Abi Ja'far, from his father, from al-Rabi', the like of it.

* *

The argument of those who said that Allah, may His praise be exalted, meant by His words ﴿Go down to a city﴾ a city from among the cities, not the Egypt of Pharaoh specifically, is that Allah made the land of al-Sham (Syria) a dwelling for the Children of Israel after He brought them out of Egypt. He afflicted them with the wandering only because of their refusal, under Moses, to fight the tyrants, when he said to them: ﴿O my people, enter the holy land which Allah has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, lest you return as losers. They said: O Moses, indeed therein is a people of tyrants, and we will never enter it until they leave it. If they leave it, then we will enter. Two men of those who feared, upon whom Allah had bestowed favor, said: Enter upon them through the gate, and when you enter it, you will surely be victorious. And upon Allah rely, if you are believers. They said: O Moses, we will never enter it as long as they are within it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting here﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21-24]. So Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, forbade those who said this, as has been related to us, from entering it, until they died in the wilderness. He afflicted them with wandering in the land for forty years. Then He sent down their descendants to al-Sham, and settled them in the holy land, and the destruction of the tyrants was accomplished at their hands, with Joshua ibn Nun, after the death of Moses ibn 'Imran. We see that Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, has informed us that He prescribed for them the holy land, and He did not inform us that He returned them to Egypt after bringing them out of it. Therefore it is not permissible for us to read "Go down to Egypt" and interpret it as meaning that He returned them there.

They said: If someone argues with the words of Allah, may His praise be exalted: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs, and treasures and a noble station. Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 57-59], it is said to them: [[In the printed edition: "qila lahum" (it was said to them), which is an error. The pronoun in "lahu" refers back to "fa-in ihtajja muhtajj" (if someone argues).]] Indeed Allah, may His praise be exalted, only gave them that as an inheritance, by granting them possession of it, and He did not return them to it, and He made their dwellings in al-Sham.

* *

As for those who said that Allah meant by His words, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿Go down to Egypt﴾, Egypt, their argument is the verse in which He said: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs, and treasures and a noble station. Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 57-59], and His words: ﴿How much they left behind of gardens and springs, and crops and a noble station, and luxury they had been enjoying. Thus, and We caused other people to inherit them﴾ [al-Dukhan: 25-28]. They said: Allah, may His praise be exalted, informed that He had caused them to inherit that and made it theirs, so they would not inherit it and then not benefit from it. They said: They would not benefit from it except by some of them going to it; otherwise there is no way to benefit from it if they do not go there, or some of them do not go there. They said: [[The words "wa-ukhra" mean "and another [argument]". See Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 43.]] And another [argument] is that it is in the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "Go down to Misr" without the alif. They said: In that is the clear indication that it is Misr itself.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: What we hold concerning this is that there is no indication in the Book of Allah for the correctness of either of these two interpretations, nor is there any report from the Messenger (ﷺ) that would remove the excuse. The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differ in its interpretation. So the most preferable of the sayings in this regard to us, as correct, is to say: [[In the printed edition: "'indana wa-al-sawab", which is a copyist's error.]] that Moses asked his Lord to give his people what they had asked for of the plants of the earth, as Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, explained in His Book, while they were wandering in the land. So Allah answered Moses' supplication and commanded him to go down with those who were with him of his people to a settled place on the earth which would produce for them what he had asked for them, since what they asked for is only grown in towns and cities. And He had given them that when they reached it. It is possible that this settled place is "Misr," and it is possible that it is "al-Sham."

As for the recitation, it is with the alif and tanwin: ﴿Go down to a city (misran)﴾, and this is the recitation which, in my view, cannot be other than this, because of the agreement of the written copies of the Muslims' codices (mashahif), and the consensus of the reciters (qurra') upon it. No one has read it without the tanwin and with the alif dropped, except those whose objection to the proof (al-hujjah) is not permissible, [[al-hujjah here means: those by whom proof is established.]] regarding what has come in recitation widely transmitted between them.

* *

The discussion of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words ﴿were stamped﴾, He means: were decreed (furidat), and placed upon them, humiliation, and they were made to bear it. From the saying of the speaker: "The imam imposed (darraba) the jizyah on the people of the dhimmah," and "The man imposed (darraba) the kharaj on his slave," meaning he placed it upon him and obliged him to it. And from their saying: "The commander imposed (darraba) the mobilization (al-ba'th) on the army," meaning: he obliged them to it. [[al-Ba'th: the sending of troops to raid.]]

* *

As for "al-dhillah" (humiliation), it is a form of "al-fi'lah" from the saying of the speaker: "So-and-so was humbled (dhalla yadhillu dhullan wa-dhillah)," like "al-saghrah" from "saghura al-amr" (the matter was small), and "al-qi'dah" from "qa'ada" (sat). [[I have not found in the books available to me any text stating "saghirah" or "qi'dah" as verbal nouns of the form fi'lah, like "nishdah" for "nashada al-dabbah" (he sought the animal); it does not indicate a state, though it agrees with it in pattern.]]

And "al-dhillah" is the lowliness (al-sagharr) which Allah, may His praise be exalted, commanded His believing servants not to grant safe-conduct to remain in what they are upon of disbelief in Him and His Messenger, unless they pay the jizyah to them. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day, and do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and do not adopt the religion of truth from those who were given the Scripture, until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29]. As:

1088 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Hasan and Qatadah, concerning His words: ﴿And humiliation was stamped upon them﴾, they both said: They give the jizyah willingly, while they are humbled.

* *

As for "al-maskanah" (poverty), it is a verbal noun of "al-miskin" (the needy). It is said: "There is none among them more wretched (askan) than so-and-so," and "He was not destitute (maskinan)," and "He has truly become destitute (tamaskana maskanah)." Some of the Arabs say: "tamaskana tamaskunan." And "al-maskanah" in this place is the poverty of need and want, and it is their humility and lowliness, as:

1089 - Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim related this to me, saying: Adam related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, concerning His words: ﴿And poverty﴾, he said: destitution.

1090 - Musa related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, concerning His words: ﴿And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them﴾, he said: poverty.

1091 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words: ﴿And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them﴾, he said: These are the Jews, the Children of Israel. I said to him: Are they the Copts of Egypt? He said: What have the Copts of Egypt to do with this? No, by Allah, they are not them. Rather, they are the Jews, the Jews of the Children of Israel.

* *

Allah, may His praise be exalted, informed them that He would replace their might with humiliation, their blessing with misery, and their pleasure with Him with wrath, as a recompense from Him to them for their disbelief in His signs, their killing of His prophets and messengers, their transgression and wrongdoing without right, their disobedience to Him, and their opposition to Him.

* *

The discussion of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And they returned with wrath from Allah﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words ﴿and they returned with wrath from Allah﴾, He means: they turned back and went back. And "ba'u" is not said except joined to either good or evil. It is said of it: "Fulan ba'a bi-dhanbihi yabu'u bihi bawan wa-bawa'an" (so-and-so bore his sin). And from it is the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿Indeed, I wish that you would bear my sin and your sin﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 29], meaning: you would turn back, bearing them and returning with them, while they have become upon you, not me.

* *

So the meaning of the statement is: And they returned turning back, bearing the wrath of Allah, and wrath from Allah had come upon them, and indignation from Him was due upon them, as:

1092 - I was told by 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning His words: ﴿And they returned with wrath from Allah﴾, so wrath from Allah befell them.

1093 - Yahya ibn Abi Talib related to us, saying: Yazid informed us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak, concerning His words: ﴿And they returned with wrath from Allah﴾, he said: They deserved the wrath of Allah.

* *

We have previously mentioned the meaning of Allah's wrath toward His servant in what has passed in this book of ours, so it suffices from repeating it in this place. [[See what has passed: 1: 188-189.]]

* *

The discussion of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may He be exalted, "that" (dhalika), He means: the stamping of humiliation and poverty upon them, and the sending down of His wrath upon them. Thus He indicated by His words "that" — and it refers to what we have described — that the saying of the speaker "that" includes many meanings when pointed to with it.

* *

By His words ﴿because they used to disbelieve﴾, He means: because of their disbelieving. He says: We did to them — the sending down of humiliation, poverty and wrath upon them — because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right, as the poet of the Banu Tha'labah, A'sha, said:

"A queenly woman dwelt, in al-Hijaz,
among a people who were enemies, and a distant land,
because of her settling in the spring pasture of the sandgrouse
and the meadow of the tanadib, until she became a traveler."

[[His Diwan: 67. "Maliki-yyah" is attributed to "al-malik" (the king), meaning of the plants of kings. "al-'adah" is the plural of "'aad," meaning the enemy. "al-shatir": the far, the strange; he intended that she was in an unknown land. He mentioned the land in this verse. He means that she settled the homes of a people between whom and us enmity was established, in a far-off exile, so that I can no longer reach her.

"Bi-ma" here means "because of" her settling, and the people "tarabba'" and "irtabaʿa" the place: they stayed there in the season of spring. "Rawd al-qata" (the meadow of the sandgrouse) is among the most famous meadows of the Arabs in the land of al-Hijaz. "Rawd al-tanadib" is also in al-Hijaz near Sarif. His saying "hatta tasira" (until she becomes a traveler) comes from the saying "sara al-rajul yasiru fa-huwa sa'ir," meaning: when he arrives at the water; the people who arrive at the water are called "al-sa'irah." And "al-sayr" (with a kasra on the sad) is the water which people arrive at. He says: she became a stranger among other than her people, as the pursuit of spring and fertility and the places of water in the lands drove her to that.]]

He means by that: this woman dwelt in this place, among a people who were enemies and a land far from its people — because of the closeness she had to him and his people and his land — [[This sentence in the manuscripts and the printed edition was: "wa-ardan ba'idatan min ahlihi bi-makan qurbiha kana minhu wa-min qawmihi wa-min tarabbiha..." and it is a sentence without meaning. I have made "bi-makan" into "li-makan," "wa-badalan" into "baladihi," so that it has a meaning the soul can rest in. The part between the two lines is an interjection and an explanation of his saying: "ardan ba'idatan min ahlihi" (a land far from its people).]] because of her settling in the spring pasture of the sandgrouse and the meadow of the tanadib.

So likewise His words: ﴿And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them, and they returned with wrath from Allah. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾ — He says: That was from Us because of their disbelief in Our signs, and as a recompense to them for their killing of Our prophets.

* *

We have explained previously in this book of ours that the meaning of "kufr" (disbelief) is the covering and concealing of a thing, [[See what has passed: 1: 255.]] and that "the signs of Allah" (ayat Allah) are His proofs, His markers, and His evidences of His oneness and the truthfulness of His messengers. [[See what has passed: 1: 552.]]

So the meaning of the statement is: We did that to them because they used to deny the proofs of Allah for His oneness and the confirmation of His messengers, and reject their validity, and call them lies.

* *

By His words ﴿and kill the prophets without right﴾, He means: and kill the messengers of Allah whom He sent, to convey what He sent them with from Him, to those to whom they were sent.

* *

[The word] "nabiyyin" is the plural, and its singular is "nabiy," unhamzated. Its origin is with hamzah, because it derives from "anba'a 'an Allah, fa-huwa yunbi'u 'anhu inba'an" (he informed about Allah, so he informs about Him). The name derived from it is "munbi'" (informer), but it was changed to the pattern "fa'il" from "maf'il," as "sami'" was changed to "fa'il" from "musmi'" and "basir" from "mubsir," and similar things. [[In the printed edition: "maf'il" in place of "musmi'." He does not mean by his saying "sami'" the attribute of Allah, may He be exalted, but what came in the poetry of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib: "Min Rayhanah al-da'i al-sami'? (Is it from Rayhanah, the caller, the one who listens?) — yu'arriquni wa-ashabi hujU' (it keeps me awake, and my companions are sleeping)" meaning: al-da'i al-musmi' (the caller who makes [others] hear). See what has passed: 1: 283.]] And the hamzah was replaced by a "ya'" in "al-nabi'," so it became "nabiy." Furthermore, "al-nabiy" is also pluralized as "anbiya'," and they pluralized it this way because they connected "al-nabi'" with the attributes that come on the pattern "fa'il" of the roots of "ya'" and "waw," by replacing the hamzah with a "ya'". That is because when they pluralize the attributes that are on the pattern "fa'il" of the roots of "ya'" and "waw," they pluralize them as "af'ila'" such as their saying: "waliy" (ally) and "awliya'" (allies); "wasiy" (executor) and "awsiya'" (executors); and "da'iy" (claimant) and "ad'iya'" (claimants). But if they pluralized it on its original form, and the singular "nabi'" with hamzah, they would pluralize it as "fu'ala'," so it would be said: "al-nubaʾ," on the pattern of "al-nubaha'," because that is the plural of attributes on the pattern "fa'il" that are not of the roots of "ya'" and "waw," like their pluralization of "al-sharik" as "shuraka'," "al-'alim" as "'ulama'," "al-hakim" as "hukama'," and what is similar to that. It has been transmitted by hearing from the Arabs that the plural of "al-nabiy" is "al-nubaʾ," and that is from the dialect of those who hamzate "al-nabi'," and then pluralize it as "al-nubaʾ," as I have explained. Among that is the saying of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas in praise of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"O seal of the prophets, indeed you are sent
with goodness; every guidance of the path has guided you."

[[From verses of his in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham 4: 103 and elsewhere. The implied subject in his saying "hadaka" is Allah, glorified and exalted, indicated by what is in his saying "innaka mursal bi-l-khayr" (indeed you are sent with goodness), for it is Allah who sent him. It is vocalized in most books as "kullu" with a damma, and "huda" and "hadaka" with a damma on the ha'.]]
