"O seal of the prophets" — [he read it as] with the hamza, as in the singular of them being "nabi'" with a hamza. Some have said: [[It seems he means al-Kisa'i (al-Bahr al-Muhit 1: 220). I found in Mu'jam al-Buldan 8: 249: "Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said in al-Zahir, regarding the verse of al-Qatami: '...inna al-nabi fi hadha al-bayt huwa al-tariq' (that al-nabi in this verse means the road)." But Abu Ja'far does not mean him, for Abu Bakr was born in the year 271 and died in 328. This view was refuted by Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaj, as transmitted by Yaqut, who said: "How can that be among the names of the road, when he says, 'lamma waradna nabiyyan' (when we came upon a nabi), and before coming upon it they were on the road? It would then mean 'lamma waradna tariqan' (when we came upon a road), and this has no meaning, unless he meant a particular road in a specific place, which returns to it being the name of a specific place. It was said: it is a particular sand dune, and it was said: it is the name of a mountain." See the verification of this in Mu'jam al-Buldan, Mu'jam ma Ista'jam, and others.]] "Nabi" and "nubuwwah" are without a hamza, because they are derived from "al-nabwah", which is like "al-najwah", meaning an elevated place. He used to say that the origin of "nabi" is the road, and he cited the verse of al-Qatami:

*Lamma waradna nabiyyan wa-staatabba biha*
*musahnfirun ka-khutut al-saihi munsahil*

[[Diwan: 4, from his famous well-known qasida. The pronoun in "waradna" refers to the camels mentioned before. Its narration is "wa-staatabba bina". Nabi is a high sand dune in the dwellings of Banu Taghlib, which al-Qatami mentioned in much of his poetry. Istatabba al-amr wa-l-tariq: it became settled, straight, clear, continuous and extended. Musahnfir is an adjective of the road: wide, extended, going on. Al-saih: a type of striped cloak or mantle, worn or used as a covering and spread out. He likened the traces of travel on it to the stripes of the cloak. Sahalat al-rih al-ard fa-nsahalat: the wind scraped away what was on the ground. The road was described this way because it had become settled through travel and had become clear and evident.]]

He says: the road was only called "nabi" because it is apparent and clear, from "al-nubuwwah". He says: I have not heard anyone pronounce "al-nabi" with a hamza. He said: We have mentioned what is in this matter, and explained what is sufficient, God willing.

* *

By His saying ﴿and they kill the prophets without right﴾, He means that they used to kill the messengers of God without God's permission to kill them, denying their message and rejecting their prophethood.

* *

On the interpretation of His exalted words ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾

His saying ﴿That﴾ refers back to the first "that". The meaning of the statement is: humiliation and poverty were struck upon them, and they returned bearing anger from God, because of their disbelief in the signs of God and their killing of the prophets without right, on account of their disobedience to their Lord and their transgression of His limits. Then He, may His praise be exalted, said ﴿That is because they disobeyed﴾, meaning: that is due to their disobedience and disbelief, being transgressors.

* *

"Al-i'tida'" is going beyond the limit that God has set for His servants to something else. Every one who goes beyond the limit of a thing to something else has transgressed to what he has gone beyond to. The meaning of the statement: I did to them what I did of that, because they disobeyed My command and exceeded My limits by doing what I had forbidden them from.

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: As for "those who believed" (alladhina amanu), they are those who affirmed the Messenger of God in what he brought them of truth from God, and their faith in that is their affirmation of it, as we have explained earlier in this book of ours. [[See what preceded, 1: 234-235.]]

* *

As for "those who were Jews" (alladhina hadu), they are the Jews. The meaning of "hadu" is "they repented." It is said of it: "hada al-qawm yahudu hawdan wa hadatan." [[His saying "hadah" is a verbal noun I have not found in the lexicon books.]] It has also been said: the Jews were named "Yahud" only because of their saying: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾. [Surah al-A'raf: 156.]

1094 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: The Jews were named only because they said: "Indeed, we have turned back to You."

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted and mighty is He: ﴿And the Christians﴾

Abu Ja'far said: "al-Nasara" (the Christians) is a plural, its singular being "nasran," just as the singular of "al-sakara" (the intoxicated) is "sakran," and the singular of "al-nashawa" (the drunken) is "nashwan." Likewise, the plural of every adjective whose singular is on the pattern "fa'lan" is formed as "fa'ala." However, the widespread usage of the Arabs for the singular of "al-Nasara" is "nasrani" (Christian). It has been transmitted from them, by hearing, "nasran" with the "ya'" dropped, and from it is the poet's saying:

*Seen when the evening comes, turning away from the wrong, and at dawn, while it is a Christian facing the sun*. [[I do not know who said it. Al-Adhdad of Ibn al-Anbari: 155; he narrated it as: "tarahu wa yudha wa huwa..." and Abu Hayyan transmitted it in al-Bahr al-Muhit 1: 238 from al-Tabari, and in both it is "idha dar al-'ashi". Al-Qurtubi erred (his Tafsir 1: 369) when he said: "Sibawayh recited" and mentioned the verse, but Sibawayh did not recite it. He narrated its first half: "(Seen when the evening turns, turning away)". The verse describes the chameleon. "Muhannafan" means he has turned away, or has become a hanif (one who inclines to monotheism). He means that it faces the qibla. His saying "ladayhi" means "beside him," i.e., beside the evening, and he means before the evening is complete, or beside the forenoon. And he has mentioned it in a previous verse. His saying "shamis" means facing the sun, before the east. He says it faces the sun as a Christian does. It is like the saying of Dhu al-Rummah also describing the chameleon: "When the shade turns in the evening, you see it a hanif, and at the time of forenoon it turns to the sun."]]

And it was heard from them, in the feminine: "nasranah" (a female Christian). The poet said: [[It is Abu al-Akhzar al-Hammani.]]

*So both of them fell, and her head bowed down, as a Christian woman prostrates, not inclining.* [[Sibawayh 2: 29, 104; and Lisan al-Arab (h-n-f). It describes two she-camels who lowered their heads from exhaustion, so he compares the camel's head in its drooping with the head of a Christian woman when she lowers it in her prayer. "Asjada al-rajul": he lowered and bent his head. Humayd ibn Thawr said, describing she-camels: "When they were twisted on a wrist, and a hand dyed with henna and its bracelets, the excess of their reins prostrated them in the prostration of the Christians to their monks."]]

It is said: "asjada" means "he leaned." [[Al-Tabari's explanation of the meaning of "asjada" is not good.]] It has also been heard in their plural "ansar," with the meaning of "al-Nasara." The poet said:

*When I saw Nabat as ansar, I raised my waistcloth above my knees, I was for them a neighbor among the Christians.* [[I do not know the speaker of the rajaz. The verses are in Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 44, and Amali Ibn al-Shajari 1: 79, 371. He recited it as evidence for the omission of the conjunctive waw: meaning "wa-kuntu lahum min al-nasara jaran," then he recited it in another place as evidence for the omission of the conjunctive fa': meaning "fa-kuntu lahum..."]]

These verses that I have mentioned indicate that they were named "Nasara" because some of them supported others, and assisted one another among themselves. It has also been said that they were named "Nasara" because they settled in a land called "Nasirah."

1095 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: "al-Nasara" were named Nasara only because they settled in a land called "Nasirah."

* *

Others say: it is because of His saying: ﴿Who are my helpers toward God?﴾ [Surah al-Saff: 14].

* *

It has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas, through a route not accepted, that he used to say: The Christians were named Nasara because the village of Jesus son of Mary was called "Nasirah," and his companions were called "al-Nasiriyyun," and Jesus was called "al-Nasiri."

1096 - I have been told this from Hisham ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

1097 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: They were named Nasara because they were in a village called Nasirah, which Jesus son of Mary used to inhabit. It is a name they named themselves with, and they were not commanded with it.

1098 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿Those who say: "Indeed, we are Christians"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 82], he said: They named themselves after a village called "Nasirah," where Jesus son of Mary used to live.

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the Sabians﴾

Abu Ja'far said: "al-Sabi'un" (the Sabians) is the plural of "sabi'," which means one who newly adopts a religion other than his own, like an apostate from the people of Islam from his religion. Every person who leaves the religion he was upon for another is called by the Arabs "sabi'." It is said of it: "sabi'a fulan yasba' sab'an" (so-and-so turned). It is also said: "sabi'at al-nujum" (the stars rose) when they appeared; and "sabi'a 'alayna fulan mawdi'a kadha wa kadha" means he appeared (talaʿa).

* *

The people of interpretation differed concerning who among the people of religions is bound by this name. Some said: it applies to everyone who left one religion for a non-religion. They said: those whom God meant by this name are a people who have no religion.

Mention of those who said that:

1099 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us.

1100 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya also narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, both from Sufyan, from Layth, from Mujahid, who said: The Sabians are neither Jews nor Christians, and they have no religion.

1101 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-Hajjaj ibn Artah, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Mujahid, the like of it.

1102 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from 'Anbasah, from al-Hajjaj, from Mujahid, who said: The Sabians are between the Magians and the Jews; their slaughtered animals are not eaten, and their women are not married.

1103 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from 'Anbasah, from Hajjaj, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, the like of that.

1104 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih: "al-Sabi'in" are between the Jews and the Magians, and have no religion.

1105 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

1106 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid said: "al-Sabi'in" are between the Magians and the Jews, they have no religion. Ibn Jurayj said: I said to 'Ata': "al-Sabi'in," they claim it is a tribe from the direction of al-Sawad [[Meaning the Sawad of Iraq.]], who are neither Magians, nor Jews, nor Christians. He said: We have heard that, and the polytheists said to the Prophet: "He has become a Sabian."

1107 - Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la also narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His saying: "and the Sabians," he said: The Sabians are [people of] a religion among the religions, who were in the island of Mosul. [[In the printed edition: "al-Sabi'un din min al-adyan," and the addition between the brackets is necessary.]] They say: "There is no god but God," and they have no deed, no book, and no prophet, except the statement: "There is no god but God." He said: They did not believe in the Messenger of God, and for that reason the polytheists used to say to the Prophet ﷺ and his companions: "These are the Sabians," likening them to them.

* *

Others said: They are a people who worship the angels and pray toward the qibla.

Mention of those who said that:

1108 - Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from his father, from al-Hasan, who said: Ziyad [[Ziyad is Ziyad ibn Abihi, the governor of Iraq in the time of Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] told me that the Sabians pray toward the qibla and perform the five prayers. He said: He wanted to remove the jizya (poll tax) from them. He said: Then it was made known afterward that they worship the angels.

1109 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh also narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿and the Sabians﴾, he said: The Sabians are a people who worship the angels, pray toward the qibla, and recite the Zabur (Psalms).

1110 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: The Sabians are a sect of the People of the Book who recite the Zabur. Abu Ja'far al-Razi said: It has also reached me that the Sabians are a people who worship the angels, recite the Zabur, and pray toward the qibla.

* *

Others said: Rather, they are a group of the People of the Book.

Mention of those who said that:

1111 - Sufyan ibn Wakee' narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Sufyan, who said: al-Suddi was asked about the Sabians, and he said: They are a group of the People of the Book.

* *

The interpretation of His words, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, and does righteous deeds, for them is their reward with their Lord﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying: ﴿Whoever believes in God and the Last Day﴾, He means: whoever affirms and acknowledges resurrection after death on the Day of Resurrection, and does righteous deeds, obeying God. ﴿For them is their reward with their Lord﴾ means: for them is the reward of their righteous deeds with their Lord.

* *

If someone says to us: Where is the completion of His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians﴾?

It is said: Its completion is the phrase: ﴿Whoever believes in God and the Last Day﴾. Because its meaning is: whoever among them believes in God and the Last Day, the word "minhum" (among them) has been omitted, because the context indicates it, being sufficient with what is mentioned for what is left out.

If he says: What is the meaning of this statement?

It is said: Its meaning is: Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians—whoever believes in God and the Last Day, for them is their reward with their Lord.

If he says: How does the believer believe?

It is said: The meaning of "believer" here is not the meaning you supposed, of transferring from one religion to another, like the transfer of the Jew and the Christian to faith. Although it has been said that those meant by that are those of the People of the Book who were upon their faith in Jesus and what he brought, until they reached Muhammad ﷺ and believed in him and affirmed him; so it was said to those who had been believers in Jesus and what he brought, when they reached Muhammad ﷺ: "Believe in Muhammad and in what he brought." But the meaning of the believer's faith in this place is his steadfastness in his faith and his leaving its alteration. As for the faith of the Jews, Christians, and Sabians, it is affirmation of Muhammad ﷺ and what he brought. So whoever among them believes in Muhammad, and in what he brought, and in the Last Day, and does righteous deeds, not altering or changing, until he dies upon that, for him is the reward of his deed and his recompense with his Lord, as His majesty, exalted is His praise, described.

If someone says: How did He say: "for them is their reward with their Lord," when the word "man" (whoever) is singular in form, and the verb with it is singular?

It is said: "Man," although the verb following it is singular, its meaning includes the singular, dual, and plural, and masculine and feminine, because in all these states it is in one form and one appearance that does not change. So the Arabs make the verb singular with it, although its meaning is plural, for its wording; and they make the verb plural with it at another time, for its meaning, as His majesty, exalted is His praise, said: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you; but can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not understand? And among them are those who look at you; but can you guide the blind, even though they do not see?﴾ [Yunus: 42-43]. So He made the verb plural with "man" once, for its meaning, and made it singular with it another time, because it is in the wording of the singular, as the poet said:

*Greet Salma for both of you, if you pass by, and say to her: "Turn back to those who stayed behind."* [[In the Diwan of Imru' al-Qays, attributed to him, from an ode of twenty-three verses, and in it: "It is said it is for a man from Kindah," and its beginning: "Abodes in which the gazelles and the wild cattle..." The Adhdad of Ibn al-Anbari: 288 says: al-Farra' recited it, and its narration is its first half: "Greet Salma with a glance when you stood." What is in al-Tabari's narration, "'ankuma," is superfluous in the speech; the Arabs say "sir 'anka" and "anfidh 'anka," meaning "pass on," and "jiz," there is no meaning for "'anka" here. In a hadith of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: that he circumambulated the House with Ya'la ibn Umayyah, and when he reached the western corner facing the Black Stone, he said to him: "Will you not touch it?" He said: "Pass on, for the Prophet ﷺ did not touch it." The hadith explains it: i.e., leave it and pass it by. And His saying "'arradtuma" is from their saying: "'arada al-rajul" when he came to the 'Arud (with a fatha on the 'ayn), which is Mecca and Medina and what is around them.]] He said: "takhallafu" (they stayed behind), and made "man" in the position of "alladhina" (those who). And al-Farazdaq said:

*Come, for if you pledge to me that you will not betray me, we will be like the two who keep company, O wolf.* [[His Diwan: 870; Sibawayh 1: 404; al-Kamil 1: 216; Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara': 310; al-Adhdad: 288; Amali Ibn al-Shajari 2: 311. In the narration of his Diwan: "ta'al fa-in wathaqtani" ("come, if you trust me"). It is a verse from his excellent ode which he said when a wolf came upon him and he entertained it as a guest.]]

So he made "yastahibani" (they two keep company) dual, for the meaning of "man." Likewise His saying: ﴿Whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, for them is their reward with their Lord﴾: He made "amana" and "'amila salihan" singular for the wording of "man," and made their mention plural in His saying: ﴿for them is their reward﴾, for its meaning, because it has the meaning of the plural.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ (62).

He, may His remembrance be exalted, means by it: no fear upon them regarding what they face of the terrors of the Resurrection, and they will not grieve over what they left behind of the world and its life, when they witness what God has prepared for them of reward and everlasting bliss with Him.

* *

Mention of those who said that by His saying: ﴿Whoever believes in God﴾ is meant the believers among the People of the Book who reached the Messenger of God ﷺ:

1112 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat ibn Nasr narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews﴾, the verse, he said: This verse was revealed concerning the companions of Salman al-Farisi. Salman was from Jundaysabur, and he was of its nobles, and the son of the king was a close friend of his, a brother bonded to him; neither of them would decide a matter without the other, and they used to ride out together to hunt. While they were hunting, a tent of a 'abaʾ (a cloak) appeared to them from afar. [[Ruffi'a lahu al-shay' (passive): he saw it from a distance. In the printed edition: "bayt min khibaʾ" (a tent of felt), and the khibaʾ is a tent of camel-hair or wool. That is a statement without meaning. In al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 73, the report is narrated in full: "min 'abaʾah." The correct reading is what I have set down. The 'abaʾ is a kind of cloak with large black stripes, and here it is singular, its plural being a'biyah. "'Abaʾ" is also the plural of "'abaʾah."]] They came to it, and there in it was a man in front of him a codex, reading in it while weeping. They asked him: What is this? He said: The one who wants to know this does not stand in your position. If you both wish to know what is in it, then come down until I inform you. So they came down to him, and he said to them: This is a book that came from God, in which He commanded obedience to Him and forbade disobedience to Him; in it: you shall not commit adultery, nor steal, nor take the wealth of people by falsehood. He recounted to them what was in it, which is the Gospel that God revealed to Jesus. It entered their hearts, and they followed him and became Muslims. He said to them: Indeed, the slaughter of your people is forbidden to you.

They remained with him in that state, learning from him, until there was a festival of the king, and he made food, [[In al-Durr al-Manthur: "fajama'a ta'aman" (he gathered food), and I think the correct reading is "fasana'a ta'aman" (he prepared food); this is confirmed by his later saying: "he invited him to his feast." One says: "sana'a lahum ta'aman" (he prepared food for them), and "kuntu fi sana'i fulan" (I was at the feast of so-and-so), meaning his banquet and invitation.]] then he gathered the people and the nobles, and sent to the king's son, inviting him to his feast to eat with the people. The youth refused and said: I am busy with you, so eat, you and your companions. When the messengers insisted upon him, he informed them that he would not eat of their food. The king sent to his son and summoned him, and said: What has commanded you this? He said: We do not eat from your slaughtered animals; you are unbelievers, your slaughter is not lawful. The king said to him: Who commanded you with this? He informed him that the monk had commanded him with that. So he summoned the monk and said: What is my son saying? He said: Your son has spoken truly. He said to him: Were it not that blood is great among us, I would kill you, but leave our land. He gave him a term. Salman said: So we stood weeping over him, and he said to the two of them: If you both are truthful, then indeed we are in a church in Mosul with sixty men, worshipping God therein; come to us there.

The monk departed, and Salman and the king's son remained. Salman kept saying to the king's son: Let us go! And the king's son would say: Yes. The king's son began selling his goods, wanting the provisions. When it was slow for Salman, Salman went out until he reached them, and he settled with his companion, who was the lord of the church.

The people of that church were among the best of the monks. [In al-Durr al-Manthur: "So the people of that church were of the highest rank among the monks."] Salman would strive in worship with them and exhaust himself. The shaykh said to him: "You are a young lad who imposes upon himself worship beyond what he can bear, and I fear you will slacken and grow weak. So be gentle with yourself and ease up on it." Salman said to him: "Tell me, is what you order me to do better, or what I am doing?" He said: "Rather, what you are doing." Salman said: "Then leave me alone."

Then the master of the church summoned him and said: "Do you know that this church is mine, and that I have the greatest right to it? Had I wished to expel these people from it, I would have done so! But I am a man who is weak for the worship of these people, and I want to transfer from this church to another church whose worship is lighter than theirs. If you wish to stay here, then stay; and if you wish to go with me, then go." Salman said to him: "Which of the two churches is better in its people?" He said: "This one." Salman said: "Then I will remain in this one." So Salman stayed there, and the master of the church entrusted Salman to the scholar of the church, and Salman worshipped with them.

Then the learned shaykh wished to go to Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and said to Salman: "If you wish to go with me, then go; and if you wish to remain, then remain." Salman said to him: "Which is better, that I go with you or that I remain?" He said: "No, rather go with me." So he went with him. They passed by a paralytic lying on the side of the road, and when he saw them he called out: "O master of the monks, have mercy on me, may God have mercy on you!" But he neither spoke to him nor looked at him. They continued until they reached Bayt al-Maqdis, and the shaykh said to Salman: "Go out and seek knowledge, for the scholars of the earth come to this mosque." Salman went out and listened to them. Then he returned one day sad, and the shaykh said to him: "What is wrong with you, O Salman?" He said: "I see that all the good has been taken by those who came before us, the prophets and their followers!" The shaykh said to him: "O Salman, do not grieve, for there remains a prophet, and no prophet is better in his followers than him, and this is his time in which he will emerge. I do not think I will reach him, but as for you, you are a youth and perhaps you will reach him. He will emerge in the land of the Arabs; so if you reach him, believe in him and follow him." Salman said to him: "Then tell me something of his signs." He said: "Yes, he has the seal of prophethood marked on his back, and he eats gifts but does not eat charity."

Then they returned until they reached the place of the paralytic, who called out to them: "O master of the monks, have mercy on me, may God have mercy on you!" The shaykh turned his donkey toward him, took him by the hand and lifted him, then struck him against the ground and supplicated for him, saying: "Stand up by God's permission!" He stood up healthy, running briskly. [Ishtadda: ran and hastened.] Salman began to marvel as he watched him run. The monk proceeded and disappeared from Salman's sight, and Salman did not know [where he went].

Then Salman was alarmed and sought the monk. He met two men of the Arabs from Kalb, and asked them: "Did you see the monk?" One of them made his mount kneel and said: "Yes, this is the shepherd of the herd!" [Al-sirmah: a herd of camels and sheep.] They seized him and took him off to Medina.

Salman said: "I was struck with a grief the like of which I had never experienced. He was bought by a woman from Juhayna, and he would tend the sheep for her, he and a boy of hers, taking turns with the flock, one day this one and one day that one. Salman would gather dirhams, awaiting the emergence of Muhammad (ﷺ). Then one day, while he was tending, his companion who relieved him came to him and said: 'Did you know that a man has arrived today in Medina claiming to be a prophet?' [Ash'arta: I knew.] Salman said to him: 'Remain with the sheep until I come to you.'"

Salman descended to Medina, looked at the Prophet (ﷺ) and circled around him. When the Prophet (ﷺ) saw him, he understood what he wanted, so he let his garment slip so that the seal showed. When Salman saw it, he came to him and spoke with him. Then he went and bought with a dinar, with part of it a sheep and with part of it bread, and brought it to him. He said: "What is this?" Salman said: "This is charity." He said: "I have no need of it; take it away, and let the Muslims eat it." Then he went and bought with another dinar bread and meat, and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with it. He said: "What is this?" He said: "This is a gift." He said: "Sit and eat." So he sat and they both ate from it together. While he was conversing with him, he mentioned his companions and told him about their condition. He said: "They used to fast, pray, believe in you, and bear witness that you would be sent as a prophet." When Salman finished praising them, the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said to him: "O Salman, they are among the people of the Fire." This weighed heavily upon Salman, for Salman had said to him: "Had they encountered you, they would have affirmed you and followed you." Then God revealed this verse: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians—whoever believes in God and the Last Day﴾.

[Hadith: 1112. This is a broken (munqati') report concerning the conversion of "Salman al-Farisi." Al-Hafiz said in al-Isabah 3:113: "His story has been related through many routes; the most authentic of them is what Ahmad transmitted from his own narration. Al-Hakim transmitted it through another route from him as well. Al-Hakim also transmitted it from the hadith of Buraydah. Al-Bukhari recorded a portion of it. In the course of his account of his conversion there is a difference that is hard to reconcile." His reference to the narration of Ahmad is in al-Musnad 5:441–444 (Halabi), and it is with the same chain in Ibn Sa'd 4:53–57. See also al-Mustadrak of al-Hakim 3:599–604, Tarikh Isbahan of Abu Nu'aym 1:48–57, and al-Hilyah of Abu Nu'aym 1:190–195.]

The faith of the Jews was: whoever adhered to the Torah and the sunnah of Moses, until 'Isa (Jesus) came. When 'Isa came, whoever adhered to the Torah and followed the sunnah of Moses, without abandoning it and without following 'Isa, was lost. The faith of the Christians was: whoever among them adhered to the Gospel and the laws of 'Isa was a believer, accepted by Him, until Muhammad (ﷺ) came; whoever of them did not follow Muhammad (ﷺ) and abandon what he had been upon of the sunnah of 'Isa and the Gospel was lost.

* *

1113 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews﴾ – the verse. He said: Salman al-Farisi asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about those Christians and what he had seen of their deeds. He said: "They did not die upon Islam." Salman said: "The earth grew dark for me, and I recalled their diligence, so this verse was revealed: 'Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews.'" [The verse did not appear in the printed edition; it appears in the text of al-Durr al-Manthur.] Then he called Salman and said: "This verse was revealed concerning your companions." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies upon the religion of 'Isa and dies upon Islam before hearing of me, he is upon good; and whoever hears of me today and does not believe in me has perished."

[Hadith: 1113 – This is also a broken report.]

* *

And Ibn 'Abbas said:

1114 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians﴾ up to His words ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾. Then God revealed after this: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him, and he will be among the losers in the Hereafter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85].

This report indicates that Ibn 'Abbas held that Allah, exalted is His praise, had promised whoever among the Jews, Christians and Sabians did righteous deeds a reward in the Hereafter, the Garden, for his deeds; then that was abrogated by His words: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him.﴾

* *

The interpretation of the verse, then, according to what we have mentioned from Mujahid and al-Suddi, is: Indeed, those who believed from this nation, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians – whoever among the Jews, Christians and Sabians believed in God and the Last Day – for them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.

* *

What we have stated as the first interpretation is more consistent with the apparent sense of the revelation, because Allah, exalted is His praise, did not single out some of His creatures among them over others for reward on righteous deeds combined with faith; and the statement ﴿whoever believes in God and the Last Day﴾ is a report applying to all that was mentioned at the beginning of the verse.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 63:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when We took your covenant﴾

Abu Ja'far said: "al-Mithaq" (the covenant) is the form "mif'al" from "al-wathiqah" (the binding bond), whether it is by an oath, or by a pledge, or by some other binding document. [See what has preceded, 1:414, in His saying: "after its covenant" (Surah al-Baqarah: 27).]

By His saying: ﴿And when We took your covenant﴾, He means the covenant which He, may His praise be glorified, informed that He had taken from them in His saying: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship none but Allah, and be good to parents"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83-85] and the verses that were mentioned along with it. The reason the covenant was taken from them, as reported by Ibn Zayd, was:

1115 - Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: When Musa returned from his Lord with the tablets, he said to his people, the Children of Israel: "Indeed, these tablets contain the Book of Allah, in which is His command that He has commanded you and His prohibition that He has forbidden you." [In the printed edition: "and His command that He commanded you," and the correction is from its narration in no. 959.] They said: "And who will take it on your word? No, by Allah, not until we see Allah openly, until Allah comes to us and says: 'This is My Book, so take it!' Why does He not speak to us as He spoke to you, O Musa, and say: 'This is My Book, so take it'?" He said: Then a wrath came from Allah, and a thunderbolt came upon them and struck them, and they all died. He said: Then Allah revived them after their death, and Musa said to them: "Take the Book of Allah." They said: "No." He said: "What has befallen you?" They said: "We died, then we were revived!" [In no. 959: "They said: we were struck that we died..."] He said: "Take the Book of Allah." They said: "No." So He sent His angels, and they uprooted the mountain over them, and it was said to them: "Do you recognize this?" They said: "Yes, this is the Tur." He said: "Take the Book, or else we will cast it upon you." He said: So they took it with the covenant, and he recited the saying of Allah: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship none but Allah, and be good to parents"﴾ until reaching: ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83-85]. He said: "Had they taken it the first time, they would have taken it without a covenant." [The report no. 1115: most of it has passed in no. 959.]

* *

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We raised over you the Tur﴾

Abu Ja'far said: As for "al-Tur", it is the mountain in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of al-Ajjaj:

"He drew near his two wings from the Tur, then swooped, / Like the falcon when the falcon folds..."

[His Diwan: 17. It is from a good qasidah in which he mentions the virtues of Umar ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Ma'mar al-Taymi, who held great governorships, conquered many conquests, and fought the Kharijites. The pronoun in his saying "danā" refers to a later noun, which is "al-bazi" (the falcon) mentioned in the next verse. Before it, he mentions Umar ibn Ubayd Allah and his battalions around him: "Around Ibn Ghara'... a steed, if he is pursued he escapes, and if he seeks vengeance he prevails / When the noble ones rush to the goal, he rushes..." He means: "He rushed, swooping like the falcon's swoop from the Tur, drawing near his two wings... then passed", with things placed before and after. It is among the fine examples of inversion. His saying "danā" means he folded his wings, drew them close and narrowed the space between them in readiness for the swoop from the mountain's peak. "Marr" means he hastened very swiftly. His saying "taqaḍḍā" originally was "taqaḍḍaḍa", and the last ḍād was changed to yā', as they found three ḍāds burdensome, as they did in "ẓannan" and "tazannā" by transformation. "Taqaḍḍaḍa al-ṭā'ir" means the bird fell in its flight, intending to alight. "Al-bāzī" is a kind of falcon, strong. "Kasara al-ṭā'ir janāḥayhi" means he gathered some of them, that is, a little, while intending to fall.]

It is also said that it is the name of a particular mountain, and it is mentioned that it is the mountain on which Allah spoke with Musa. It is also said that it is of the mountains whatever grows vegetation, as opposed to what does not. [I have not found this saying in the lexicon books under its root.]

* *

Mention of those who said: it is the mountain whatever it was:

1116 - Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: Musa commanded his people to enter the gate prostrating and to say "Hittah," and the gate was lowered for them so they would prostrate, but they did not prostrate, and they entered on their backsides, and said "Hintah." Then the mountain was uprooted over them — he means: the base of the mountain was pulled out of the earth and raised above them like a canopy = and "al-Tur," in Syriac, is the mountain = as a warning, or a fear, Abu Asim doubted, so they entered prostrating in fear, and their eyes were on the mountain. It is the mountain upon which his Lord manifested Himself. [The report no. 1116: its beginning has passed in no. 1027.]

1117 - And Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Huthayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: The mountain was raised above them like a cloud, and it was said to them: "You will either believe, or it will fall upon you." So they believed. And "al-Jabal" in Syriac is "al-Tur."

1118 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised over you the Tur﴾, he said: al-Tur is the mountain; they were at its base, so it was raised over them above their heads, and it was said: "You will surely take My command, or I will drop it on you."

1119 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah: ﴿And We raised over you the Tur﴾, he said: al-Tur is the mountain. Allah uprooted it and raised it over them, and He said: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾, so they acknowledged that.

1120 - And Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah: ﴿And We raised over you the Tur﴾, he said: The mountain was raised over them, frightening them with it.

1121 - Ibn Wakic narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from al-Nadr, from Ikrimah, who said: al-Tur is the mountain.

1122 - And Musa narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: When Allah said to them: "Enter the gate prostrating and say 'Hittah'," they refused to prostrate, so Allah commanded the mountain to fall upon them. They looked at it, and it had overshadowed them, so they fell prostrating on one side, and looked with the other side, and Allah had mercy on them and lifted it from them. That is His saying: ﴿And when We shook the mountain over them as though it were a canopy﴾ [al-A'raf: 171], and His saying: ﴿And We raised over you the Tur﴾.

1123 - Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: The mountain in Syriac is "al-Tur."

* *

And others said: "al-Tur" is the name of the mountain upon which Allah spoke with Musa.

Mention of those who said that:

1124 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ibn Abbas said: al-Tur is the mountain upon which the Torah was sent down to Musa, and the Children of Israel were beneath it. Ibn Juraij said: Ata' said to me: The mountain was raised over the Children of Israel, and it was said: "You will either believe in it, or it will fall upon you." That is His saying: ﴿as though it were a canopy﴾.

* *

And others said: "al-Tur" is, among the mountains, only that which produces vegetation.

Mention of those who said that:

1125 - It was reported from al-Minjab, who said: Bishr ibn Umarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿al-Tur﴾: al-Tur is among the mountains what produces vegetation; what does not produce vegetation is not a tur.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, may He be remembered: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The scholars of Arabic grammar differed regarding the interpretation of this. Some grammarians of Basra said: it is of what is dispensed with by the evidence of the apparent statement, from what its mention was left out. That is because the meaning of the speech is: "And We raised the Tur over you, and We said to you: Take what We have given you with strength, or else We will hurl it upon you."

And some grammarians of Kufa said: The taking of the covenant is a saying, so there is no need to supply a saying within the speech, making it two speeches; however, every speech that differs from the saying — which has the meaning of saying — must be accompanied by "an" (that), as Allah, may His praise be glorified, said: ﴿Indeed, We sent Nuh to his people, that warn your people﴾ [Nuh: 1]. He said: It is permissible to omit "an".

The correct view regarding this, in our opinion, is that every speech uttered which conveys the meaning intended is sufficient without anything else.

By His saying: ﴿Take what We have given you﴾, He means what We commanded you in the Torah.

And the root of "al-iitā'" (giving) is "al-i'ṭā'" (bestowing). [See what has preceded, 1:574.]

* *

By His saying: ﴿with strength﴾, He means with diligence in fulfilling what He commanded you and obligated upon you, as:

1126 - It was reported from Ibrahim ibn Bashshar, who said: Ibn Uyaynah narrated to us, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾. He said: Act by what is in it.

1127 - And Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Huthayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

1128 - And Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾, he said: with obedience.

1129 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾. He said: "al-Quwwah" is diligence, "or else I will hurl it upon you." He said: So they acknowledged that they would take what they were given with strength.

1130 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿with strength﴾, meaning: with diligence and effort.

1131 - And Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said — and I asked him about Allah's saying: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ — he said: Take the Book that Musa brought, affirming and establishing it.

* *

So the interpretation of the verse is: Take what We have obligated upon you in Our Book of obligations, accept it, and act upon it with your own diligence in fulfilling it, without negligence or slackness. That is the meaning of their taking it with strength, with diligence.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, may He be remembered: ﴿And remember what is in it, that you may become righteous (63)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He means: Remember what is in what We have given you of Our Book of promise and severe warning, and of encouragement and deterrence; recite it, take lessons from it, and reflect upon it when you do so, so that you may be righteous and fear My punishment, [See what has passed regarding the explanation of "la'alla" meaning "kay" (so that), 1:364-365, and this part 2:68.] by your persistence in your error, so that you may desist and turn to My obedience, and cease from what you are upon of disobedience to Me. As:

1132 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to us, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿that you may become righteous﴾, he said: that you may desist from what you are upon.

* *

And what Allah gave them is the Torah. As:

1133 - Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah: ﴿And remember what is in it﴾, he says: Remember what is in the Torah.

1134 - And as narrated to me from Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His saying: ﴿And remember what is in it﴾, he says: They were commanded with what is in the Torah.

1135 - And Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: I asked Ibn Zayd about Allah's saying: ﴿And remember what is in it﴾, and he said: Act upon what is in it, with obedience to Allah and sincerity. [In the printed edition: "bi-ṭā'at Allāh wa-ṣidq" is an error.] He said: And he said: Remember what is in it, do not forget it or neglect it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 64 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Then you turned away after that﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, exalted is His praise, ﴿Then you turned away﴾, He means: then you turned aside. It is in fact "tafa'altum" from the expression "tawallani fulan dubURAHU" (so-and-so turned his back to me), when he turned his back on him and put him behind his back. This is then used for every one who abandons an obedience he has been commanded to observe and turns his face away. It is said: "So-and-so has turned away from the obedience of so-and-so, and turned away from his companionship." And from this is the saying of God, exalted is His praise: ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty, they were stingy with it and turned away, while they were averse﴾ [al-Tawbah: 76]. He means by this: they contradicted what they had promised God, from their saying: (If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely be among the righteous) [al-Tawbah: 75], and they cast that behind their backs.

* *

It is a habit of the Arabs to borrow a word and place it in the position of its counterpart, as Abu Kharash al-Hudhali said:

It is not like the old state of the abode, O Umm Malik...
But the chains have encircled the necks.

[Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin 2: 150; Sirat Ibn Hisham 4: 116; al-Aghani 21: 41; al-Kamil 1: 267. These are fine verses in lament for a friend. Zuhayr ibn al-Ajwa al-Hudhali, of the Banu Amr ibn al-Harith, who was a cousin of Abu Kharash and his friend, went out seeking spoils on the day of Hunayn, was captured and bound along with people whom the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had taken. Jamil ibn Mu'ammar al-Jumahi saw him, and there had been enmity between them in the pre-Islamic period. He said to him: "Are you the one who walks before us with provocations?" and struck off his neck. Abu Kharash then lamented him, and said to Jamil ibn Mu'ammar: "Indeed, if you had confronted him when you met him... and fought him, or you were among those who fight..., Jamil would have been the worst of the people in ignominy, but the back-binding is a preoccupation for a man." It is not like the old state... In the printed edition "fa-laysa li-ahd al-dar" is an error. By "the abode" he means Mecca and what surrounds it and borders it. He says: the matter is not as you knew it and as we knew it; Islam came and demolished all of that.]

And the youth became like an elder who speaks not, except the truth, and rests.

[He means: the youth departed from the habits of his youth and its wildness, and became like the elder in his deliberation and steadiness, for religion has stunned the strong-willed youths and calmed them from fear of the punishment of their Lord for killing without fighting or battle. So the blamers rested, because they no longer found anything to blame their husbands for, such as exposing themselves to destruction.]

By His saying, "the chains have encircled the necks," he means that Islam has become, in its prohibition to us of what we used to do in the pre-Islamic period, of what God has forbidden us in Islam, like the chains encircling our necks, which prevent the one who has a shackle on his hand from reaching for what he tries to take.

Parallels to this in the speech of the Arabs are more than can be counted. Likewise His saying: (Then you turned away after that), He means by it: you abandoned acting upon what We took as your covenant and pledges to act upon with earnestness and diligence, after you gave your Lord covenants to act upon it and to carry out what He commanded you in your Book, so you cast it behind your backs.

By His saying, exalted is His mention, "that," He refers to everything before it in the preceding verse, namely His saying: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you﴾.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is His mention: ﴿Had it not been for the bounty of God upon you and His mercy﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, exalted is His mention, ﴿Had it not been for the bounty of God upon you﴾, had it not been that God showed favour to you by repentance, after your breaking the covenant which you pledged when He raised the mountain above you, that you would strive in His obedience, in performing His obligations, in carrying out what He commanded you, and in refraining from what He forbade you in the Book which He gave you, and He bestowed upon you Islam and His mercy with which He had mercy on you, and He overlooked your sin which you committed, by your returning to the obedience of your Lord, you would have been among the losers.

Although this is an address to those among the People of the Book who were living among the emigrants of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the days of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), it is in fact a report about their forefathers. The report is presented in the form of a report about them, in the manner we have explained earlier, that a tribe of the Arabs addresses another tribe at a time of boasting or otherwise, with what the forefathers of the one addressed did to the forefathers of the one addressing, and it attributes the deeds of its forefathers to itself, saying: "We did this to you, and we did that to you." We have mentioned some evidence for this from their poetry earlier. [See what has passed in this part 2: 38-39.]

* *

Some have claimed that the address in these verses was given in the form of attributing the act to those addressed by it, while the act belonged to others, because those addressed were allies of those among the early Children of Israel who did that, so God made them part of them because of their alliance with them.

* *

Others said: It was said in this way because its hearers were aware, and although the address went out as an address to the living among the Children of Israel and the People of the Book, the meaning in that is only a report about what God related of the tidings of their forefathers. So the knowledge of the hearers of that made it unnecessary to mention their forefathers by name. A poet similarly says:

When we trace our lineage, she did not bear me as a base woman,
And you did not find any way to make it appear otherwise.

[It will come in this part 1: 333 (Bulaq), and in 3: 49 (Bulaq), and in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an: 61, 178. Before the verse he speaks to his wife: "She shot at me from the bow of the enemy and kept away... Abidah; may God increase what is between us in distance."]

He said, "when we trace," and "when" requires a future verb, then he said, "she did not bear me as a base woman," reporting a past verb, because the birth has already passed and occurred. He did this, according to the one who cites it, because the hearer has understood its meaning. So what we have mentioned, of God's address to the People of the Book who were living among the emigrants of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the days of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), attributing the deeds of their forefathers to them, is a parallel to this.

The first view that we stated is the prevalent one in the speech and address of the Arabs.

* *

Abu al-'Aliyah used to say, regarding His saying: ﴿Had it not been for the bounty of God upon you and His mercy﴾, as was related to us, something similar to what we have said.

1136 - Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Nadr narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah: ﴿Had it not been for the bounty of God upon you and His mercy﴾, he said: "The bounty of God" is Islam, "and His mercy" is the Qur'an.

1137 - And it was narrated to me by Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us [from his father], from al-Rabi', the like of it. [What is between the brackets is an addition that is indispensable; see the end of the chain from Ammar ibn al-Hasan, number 1134.]

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿you would have been among the losers﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Had it not been for the bounty of God upon you and His mercy to you, by His rescuing you through repenting towards you from your sin and your offence, you would have been those who diminish their own shares forever, destroyed by what you committed of breaking your covenant and opposing His command and obedience.

We have previously explained the meaning of "loss" with evidence earlier, sufficient so as not to repeat it in this place. [See what has passed, 1: 417.]

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, ﴿And you certainly knew﴾, he means: you certainly recognized. [The evidence for this will come from the exegesis of Ibn Abbas, number 1138.] Like your saying: "I have known your brother," and "I did not know him," meaning: I recognized him, and I did not recognize him, as He, exalted is His praise, said: ﴿And others besides them whom you do not know; God knows them﴾ [al-Anfal: 60], meaning: you do not recognize them, God recognizes them.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath﴾, that is, those who exceeded My limit, and committed what I forbade them in the day of Sabbath, and disobeyed My command.

I have shown earlier that "transgression" originally means exceeding the limit in everything, sufficiently so as not to repeat it here. [See what has passed in this part 2: 142.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This verse and the verses following it, which recount what He, exalted is His praise, enumerated against the Children of Israel, those who were among the houses of the Ansar in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), those whose early forefathers' breaking of God's covenant and pledge He mentioned at the beginning of this surah, and what they used to conclude of contracts, and the warning to those addressed by them that there befall them, through their persistence in their disbelief and their remaining upon denial of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and their abandonment of following him and believing in what came to them from their Lord, the like of what befell their forefathers of transformation, quaking and thunderbolt, and what they had no power to bear of the wrath and anger of God. As follows:

1138 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn Ammarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath﴾, he says: "And you certainly recognized." This is a warning to them against disobedience. He says: beware lest there befall you what befell the people of the Sabbath, when they disobeyed Me, they transgressed - he says: they became bold - in the Sabbath. He said: God did not send a prophet except that He commanded him with the Friday prayer, and informed him of its excellence and greatness in the heavens and with the angels, and that the Hour will be established on it. Whoever followed the prophets in the past, as the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) followed Muhammad, honoured the Friday, heard and obeyed, recognized its excellence and persisted in it, as God, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ). [In the printed edition: "by what God, exalted is He, commanded him and His Prophet (ﷺ)," which is an incorrect sentence; I have corrected it as you see.] And whoever did not do so was in the position of those whom God mentioned in His Book when He said: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them: Be apes, despised.﴾ This is because the Jews said to Moses, when he commanded them with the Friday and informed them of its excellence: "O Moses, how do you command us with the Friday and prefer it over all the days, while the Sabbath is the best of all days, because God created the heavens and the earth and the sustenance in six days, and every thing submitted to Him in obedience on the Sabbath day [sabt: rested; their saying "sabata lahu" means: he humbled himself to Him and ceased from every work except His worship, glory be to Him; see what follows, p. 174], and it was the last of the six?" He said: And likewise the Christians said to Jesus son of Mary, when he commanded them with the Friday: they said to him: "How do you command us with the Friday, when the first of the days is the best of them and its lord, and the first is better, and God is One, and the One who is first is better?" So God revealed to Jesus: "Leave them and Sunday, but let them do in it such and such," of what He commanded them. They did not do it, so God, exalted is He, related their story in the Book for their disobedience. He said: And likewise God said to Moses, when the Jews said what they said about the matter of the Sabbath: "Leave them and the Sabbath; let them not hunt fish in it or anything else, nor do any work, as they have said." He said: When the Sabbath came, the fish appeared upon the water; this is His saying: ﴿when their fish come to them on their Sabbath day, openly on the surface﴾ [al-A'raf: 163], that is, visible upon the water; this was because of their disobedience to Moses. And when it was not the Sabbath day, they became game like the rest of the days; this is His saying: ﴿and on the day they do not keep Sabbath, they do not come to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]. So the fish did that as long as God willed. When they saw them thus, they coveted taking them and feared punishment; some of them took some of them, and they were not withheld from him, and the punishment which Moses had warned them of from God did not befall him. When they saw that the punishment did not befall them, they returned, and some of them informed others that they had taken the fish and nothing had befallen them, so they multiplied in that, and thought that what Moses had said to them was false. This is the saying of God, exalted is His praise: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them: Be apes, despised﴾ — that is, to those who hunted the fish — so God transformed them into apes for their disobedience. He says: they did not live on the earth beyond three days. [He said: No transformed creature ever lived more than three days.] [This addition is from Ibn Kathir's tafsir 1: 193 and al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 75, and it is indispensable. In the printed edition after it, "and he did not eat, nor drink, nor reproduce," is an error.] And God created apes and swine and the rest of creation in the six days which God mentioned in His Book. So He transformed these people into the form of apes, and thus He does to whom He wills, as He wills, and changes him as He wills.

1139. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, who said: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from Ikrimah, the client of Ibn Abbas, who said: Ibn Abbas said: "Allah only enjoined upon the Children of Israel the day that He enjoined upon you for your festival, which is Friday. But they differed and turned to Saturday, and exalted it, and abandoned what they had been commanded. When they refused anything but adherence to Saturday, Allah tested them in it, and forbade them what He had permitted them on other days. They lived in a town between Aylah and al-Tur called Madyan. Allah forbade them, on Saturday, the fish: hunting them and eating them. Whenever it was Saturday, the fish would come towards them in schools to the shore of their sea, and when Saturday passed, they would leave, and they would not be seen, neither small fish nor large. Then, when it was Saturday again, they would come to them in schools, and when Saturday passed, they would leave. They continued in this way, until a long time passed over them and they craved the fish, [[al-qaram: intense desire for meat; qarima yaqrimu (with fatha on the ra') qaraman (with two fathas).]] and a man among them deliberately took a fish secretly on Saturday, pierced it with a thread, then released it into the water, and drove a stake into the shore for it and tied it, then left it. When the next day came, he came and took it, meaning: I did not take it on Saturday; then he went off with it and ate it. When the following Saturday came, he did the same, and the people smelled the scent of the fish, and the people of the town said: 'By Allah, we have smelled the scent of fish!' Then they discovered the deed of that man. [['athara 'ala al-amr: he became aware of it, and it had been hidden. In the printed edition: "according to what he did", and I have confirmed the text of Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir 1: 194.]] He said: So they did as he did, and they ate in secret for a long time, and Allah did not hasten punishment upon them, until they hunted them openly and sold them in the markets. A group among them, from the people of the remnant, [[In the printed edition: "from the people of taqiyya", which is a clear error. Ahl al-baqiyya are the people of discernment and understanding, who preserve themselves by obedience to Allah, and by their adherence to the approved religion. One who is a baqiyya has merit and goodness in what he is praised for. This will follow later correctly. Allah the Exalted said: "Why were there not among the generations before you those of remnant (baqiyya) who forbade corruption on the earth?" (Surah Hud: 116).]] said: "Woe to you! Fear Allah!" and they forbade them from what they were doing. Another group said, who did not eat the fish and did not forbid the people from what they did: "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah will destroy or punish with a severe punishment?" They said: "As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him." [Al-A'raf: 164] (i.e., we disapprove of their deeds) "and perhaps they will fear Him." Ibn Abbas said: While they were in that state, the remnant woke up in their assemblies and mosques, and they lost the people and did not see them. Some of them said to others: "Indeed, something has happened to the people! Go and see what it is!" So they went to look in their houses, and found them locked from the inside, for they had entered at night and locked them upon themselves, as people lock themselves in. In the morning they were monkeys in them, and they would recognize a man by his eye, and he was a monkey; a woman by her eye, and she was a monkey; a child by his eye, and he was a monkey. He said: Ibn Abbas says: Had Allah not mentioned that He saved those who forbade evil, we would have said He destroyed all of them. They said: It is the town of which Allah said to Muhammad (ﷺ): "And ask them about the town which was by the sea" [Al-A'raf: 163], to the end of the verse.

1140. Bishr narrated to us, who said: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, who said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them: Be apes, despised and cast out" (Al-Baqarah: 65). He said: The fish were made lawful to them, and were forbidden to them on the day of Saturday, as a trial from Allah, so that He might know who among them would obey Him and who would disobey Him. The people became three categories: one category refrained and forbade disobedience; another category refrained from violating Allah's sanctity; and a third category violated the sanctity of Allah and persisted in disobedience. When they refused anything but transgressing against what they had been forbidden, Allah said to them: "Be apes, despised and cast out," and they became apes with tails, howling, after they had been men and women.

1141. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, who said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, who said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His words: "And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath," he said: They were forbidden to hunt the fish on Saturday, and the fish would come to them on Saturday, and they were tested by that. They transgressed and hunted them, so Allah made them apes, despised and cast out.

1142. Musa narrated to me, who said: Amr narrated to us, who said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them: Be apes, despised and cast out." He said: They were the people of Aylah, which was the town that was by the sea. The fish, whenever it was Saturday, (and Allah had forbidden the Jews to do any work on Saturday), every fish in the sea would come out until they stretched their snouts out of the water. But when it was Sunday, the sea's bottom became dry and none of them was seen until Saturday came again. This is His words: "And ask them about the town which was by the sea, when they transgressed in the Sabbath, when their fish came to them on their Sabbath day openly, and on the day they did not keep the Sabbath, they did not come to them" [Al-A'raf: 163]. Some of them craved fish, so a man would dig a pit and make for it a channel to the sea. When Saturday came, he would open the channel, and the waves would bring the fish, striking them until they threw them into the pit. The fish would want to get out, but could not, because of the scarcity of water in the channel, so it would stay there [therein]. [[The addition is from Tafsir Ibn Kathir 1: 195.]] When Sunday came, he would come and take it. The man would roast the fish, and his neighbor would smell its scent, so he would ask him and he would inform him, and he would do what his neighbor had done. When the matter spread among them and they ate the fish, their scholars said to them: "Woe to you! You only hunt fish on Saturday, and it is not lawful for you!" They said: "We only hunted it on Sunday, when we took it." The jurists said: "No, but you hunted it on the day you opened the water for it, and it entered." They said: "No!" and they were arrogant and refused to desist. Some of those who admonished them said to others: "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah will destroy or punish with a severe punishment?" [Al-A'raf: 164], meaning: Why do you admonish them when you have already admonished them and they did not obey you? Some of them said: "As an excuse to your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him" [Al-A'raf: 164]. When they refused, the Muslims said: "By Allah, we will not live with you in one town." So they divided the town with a wall. The Muslims opened a door, and those who transgressed on Saturday opened a door. The Muslims would go out from their door, and the disbelievers from their door. One day the Muslims went out, and the disbelievers did not open their door. When they were slow to come out, the Muslims scaled the wall over them, and behold, they were apes leaping upon one another. They opened to them and they went off into the earth. That is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "So when they persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them: Be apes, despised and cast out" [Al-A'raf: 166]. That is when He said: "Those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed upon the tongue of Dawud and Isa, son of Maryam" [Al-Ma'idah: 78]. They were the apes.

1143. Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, who said: Abu Asim narrated to us, who said: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His words: "Those who transgressed among you in the Sabbath, so We said to them: Be apes, despised and cast out." He said: They were not transformed; rather it is a parable which Allah struck for them, like the parable of the donkey that carries books [[Surah al-Jumu'ah: 5.]].

1144. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, who said: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, who said: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath, so We said to them: Be apes, despised and cast out." He said: Their hearts were transformed, and they were not transformed into apes; rather it is a parable which Allah struck for them, like the donkey that carries books.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This view which Mujahid stated is a view contrary to the apparent meaning of what Allah's Book indicates. That is because Allah informed in His Book that He made from among them apes and swine, and worshippers of the taghut [[Surah al-Ma'idah: 60.]]; and as He informed about them that they said to their prophet: "Show us Allah openly" [An-Nisa: 153]; and that Allah, the Exalted, struck them dead when they asked their Lord that; and that they worshipped the calf, so their repentance was made the killing of themselves; and that they were commanded to enter the Holy Land, but they said to their prophet: "Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we will remain sitting here" [Al-Ma'idah: 24], so He tested them with wandering. So whoever says: "He did not transform them into apes," while He has informed that He made from them apes and swine, and whoever says: "Nothing of what Allah informed about the Children of Israel occurred among them" — from opposition to their prophets, and the punishments and penalties which Allah sent upon them. Whoever denies some of that and affirms another part, is asked for proof of his claim, and is confronted, regarding what he denied, with what he affirmed; then he is asked to distinguish between them, by a widely transmitted report or a sound narration.

This, together with the opposition of Mujahid's view to the view of all the authorities whose transmission is not permitted to be wrong or false, on what they have transmitted unanimously. And the unanimity of the authorities in refuting it is sufficient proof of the corruption of his view.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 65:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿So We said to them, "Be apes, despised."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words ﴿So We said to them﴾ He means: So We said to those who transgressed concerning the Sabbath, that is, on the day of the Sabbath.

* *

The root of "as-sabt" (the Sabbath) is stillness and calm, in ease and tranquility. For this reason the sleeper is called "masbut" (one in a state of sleep-stillness), because of his stillness, the stillness of his body, and his rest. As His mighty and majestic praise says: ﴿And We made your sleep a rest﴾ [al-Naba': 9], meaning a rest for your bodies. It is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: "Sabata fulan yasbutu sabtan" (so-and-so rested/ceased).

It has been said that it was named "sabt" because Allah, may His praise be exalted, finished the creation of all His creatures on Friday, which is the day before it.

* *

As for His words ﴿Be apes﴾, the meaning is: become such.

* *

And "al-khasi'" (despised) means one who is distanced and driven away, like a dog that is driven off. From this one says: "Khasa'tuhu akhsa'uhu khas'an wa khusu'an, wa huwa yakhsa'u khusu'an." He said: It is also said: "Khasa'tuhu fa-khasa'a wa-nkhasa'a." From it is the saying of the rajiz (the rajaz poet):

Like a dog: if you say to it "Khas'!" it withdraws [[Lisan al-'Arab: (khasa'a); its narration is: "in qila lahu" (if it is said to it).]]

meaning: if you drive it away, it is driven off, humiliated and abased.

So likewise the meaning of His words ﴿Be apes, despised﴾ is: distanced from good, humiliated, abased [[Ṣāghir, its plural ṣaghara (with vowels). This is what they stated, and I did not find "ṣaghrā'" on the pattern of jahlā', which is a plural of some adjectives on the pattern of "fā'il", such as shā'ir and shu'arā', and 'ālim and 'ulamā'. They liken "fā'il" to "fa'īl", as in karīm and kuramā', so they pluralize it like its plural.]] as follows:

1145 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿Be apes, despised﴾, he said: "Abased."

1146 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from a man, from Mujahid, the like of it.

1147 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

1148 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah: ﴿Despised﴾, he said: "Abased."

1149 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His words ﴿Be apes, despised﴾, meaning: humiliated and abased.

1150 - And it was related to me from al-Minjab, who said: Bishr ibn 'Imarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: "khasi'an" (despised), meaning: humiliated.

Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So We made it﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The exegetes differed concerning the interpretation of the "hā' and alif" in His words ﴿So We made it﴾, and to what they refer. Two opinions are narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning it. The first of them is what:

1151 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umarah narrated to us, saying: Abu Rawq narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿So We made it﴾, meaning: We made that punishment, which is the transformation, a deterrent ("nakal").

On this statement of Ibn 'Abbas, the "hā' and alif" in ﴿So We made it﴾ refer to "the transformation" (al-maskhah), which is a form (fi'lah) of the verb: God transformed them with a transformation (maskhah). [[It seems he means it is a verbal noun, like their saying "Allah had mercy on him with mercy (rahmah)", and he did not intend a single instance; what he says two lines later will confirm this.]]

So the meaning of the statement on this interpretation is: We said to them, "Be apes, despised," and they became transformed apes; ﴿So We made it﴾, meaning We made Our punishment and Our transformation of them, ﴿a deterrent for what lay before it and what came after it, and an admonition to the God-fearing﴾.

* *

The other of Ibn 'Abbas's two statements is what:

1151 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿So We made it﴾, meaning: the fish.

On this view, the "hā' and alif" refer to the fish, though no mention of them has preceded; but since the context gives an indication of them, their mention is left implicit. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed in the Sabbath﴾.

* *

Others said: "We made the town whose people transgressed on the Sabbath." Thus the "hā'" and "alif" in the view of these people refer to the town of the people who were transformed.

* *

Others said: The meaning is: We made the apes who were transformed a deterrent "for what lay before it and what came after it," so the "hā' and alif" refer to the apes.

* *

Others said: ﴿So We made it﴾ means: We made the community that transgressed on the Sabbath a deterrent.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿a deterrent (nakal)﴾

"Nakal" is a verbal noun from the saying, "Fulan punished (nakkala) Fulan with a punishment (tankil) and a deterrent (nakal)." The original meaning of "nakal" is punishment, as 'Adi ibn Zayd al-'Ibad said:

"He does not anger the King with what the servant can bear,
nor in his punishment is there anything to be disapproved."

[[I have not found this verse in any of the sources that mention the poem of 'Adi ibn Zayd which he wrote to al-Nu'man from his prison. I have recorded the verse as it stands in the defective manuscripts of Tafsir al-Tabari that have survived, but my own view is that the verse should be: "He does not overwhelm the King with what the servant can bear, nor in his punishment is there anything to be disapproved." The copyist misread "yakuzzu" as "yaskhatu," and put "al-Dalil" in place of "al-Malik." "Kazzahu al-amr" means: it burdened him and was hard on him. He says to al-Nu'man: You are a King who is capable, so let not what your servants bear of pardon toward those who have done wrong and transgressed overburden you; if you punish, there is nothing in your punishment to be disapproved, for you are the lord obeyed, whose command is effective over your subjects, small and great.]]

* *

In agreement with what we have said on this matter, the report from Ibn 'Abbas has been narrated:

1152 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umarah narrated to us, saying: Abu Rawq narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿a deterrent﴾, he says: a punishment.

1153 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to me, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to me, from his father, from al-Rabi' concerning His words: ﴿So We made it a deterrent﴾, meaning: a punishment.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿for what lay before it and what came after it﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The exegetes differed concerning the interpretation of this. Some of them said:

1154 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿for what lay before it﴾, he says: so that those after them would beware of My punishment. ﴿And what came after it﴾, he says: those who had remained with them.
