1155 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': ﴿for what lay before it and what came after it﴾, for what had passed for them of sins, [[khalā: passed, departed, and ended.]] ﴿and what came after it﴾, meaning: a lesson for whoever remained of the people.

* *

Others said:

1156 - Ibn Humayd narrated to me, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from 'Ikrimah, mawla of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what lay before it and what came after it﴾, meaning: from the towns.

* *

Others said:

1157 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, with it, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said, God said: ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what lay before it﴾, from the sins of the people, ﴿and what came after it﴾, meaning: for the fish they had caught.

1158 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah concerning His words: ﴿for what lay before it﴾, from its sins, ﴿and what came after it﴾, from the fish.

1159 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to me, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿for what lay before it﴾, what had passed of their wrongdoings until they were destroyed by it.

1160 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿a deterrent for what lay before it and what came after it﴾, he says: "what lay before it" is what had passed of their wrongdoings, ﴿and what came after it﴾ is their wrongdoings by which they were destroyed.

1161 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same, except that he said: ﴿and what came after it﴾, their error by which they were destroyed.

* *

Others said:

1162 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what lay before it and what came after it﴾, he said: As for "what lay before it," it is what had passed of their deeds; ﴿and what came after it﴾ is what came after them of the nations, that they might disobey and God would do to them the like of that.

* *

Others said:

1163 - Ibn Sa'd narrated to me, with it, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, his statement: ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what lay before it and what came after it﴾, meaning the fish; He made it a deterrent "for what lay before it and what came after it," from the sins they committed before the fish and what they committed after the fish. This is His words: ﴿what lay before it and what came after it﴾.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these interpretations for the interpretation of the verse is what al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. This is because of what we have described: that the "hā' and alif" in His words ﴿So We made it a deterrent﴾ refer more appropriately to the punishment and the transformation which those people underwent than to anything else. This is because Allah, majestic is His praise, warns His creatures only of His might and wrath, and with this He frightens them. In His clarification, He, dear is His mention, by His words ﴿a deterrent﴾, that He meant by it the punishment which He brought down upon the people, and He is known to have meant by His words ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what lay before it and what came after it﴾: So We made Our punishment which We brought upon them a deterrent for what lay before it and what came after it, rather than any other meaning. Since the "hā' and alif" referring to the transformation and the punishment is more appropriate than referring to anything else, likewise the referent of the "hā' and alif" in His words ﴿for what lay before it and what came after it﴾ should be the "hā' and alif" in His words ﴿So We made it﴾, rather than anything else [bracketed text is an addition necessary for the sense of the sentence].

So the meaning of the statement, since the matter is as we have described: We said to them, "Be apes, despised," and We made Our punishment of them a deterrent for what lay before it of their former sins, by Our transforming them and Our punishing them, and for what came after it of the like of their sins: that anyone who practices them would be transformed as they were transformed, and that there would befall him the like of what befell them, as a warning from God, dear is His mention, to His servants, that they should not commit of His disobedience the like of what the transformed committed, and so be punished with their punishment.

As for the one who said that the interpretation of ﴿So We made it﴾ refers to the fish, meaning a punishment for what lay before the fish of the sins of the people and what came after it of their sins, this is further removed from the derivation. This is because the fish were not previously mentioned so as to say ﴿So We made it﴾. If someone supposes that this is permissible, even though the fish were not previously mentioned, because the Arabs may refer to a noun without it having been mentioned, then even if that is so, it is not permissible to abandon what is understood from the apparent meaning of the Book, which is clear in the address and revelation, for an inner meaning for which there is no indication from the apparent revelation, nor any report transmitted from the Messenger ﷺ, nor any consensus widely attested in it.

As for the interpretation of one who interprets it as "for what lay before it of the towns and what came after it," this is to be considered alongside the interpretation of one who interprets it as "for what lay before the fish and what came after it."

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿and an admonition﴾

"Admonition (mawidhah)" is a verbal noun from the saying, "I admonished the man, I admonish him, admonition (wa'z) and admonition (mawidhah)," when one reminds him.

* *

So the interpretation of the verse: ﴿So We made it a deterrent for what lay before it and what came after it, and a reminder to the God-fearing﴾, that they might take admonition from it, take heed, and be reminded by it, as:

1164 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿and an admonition﴾, he says: and a reminder and a lesson to the God-fearing.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿to the God-fearing (5:66)﴾

As for "the God-fearing (al-muttaqun)," they are those who guard themselves, by performing His obligations and avoiding His disobedience, as:

1165 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn 'Umarah narrated to us, saying: Abu Rawq narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿and an admonition to the God-fearing﴾, he says: to the believers who guard against polytheism and act in obedience to Me.

* *

So God, dear is His mention, made what He brought down upon those who transgressed on the Sabbath of His punishment an admonition specifically to the God-fearing, and a lesson to the believers, and not to those who disbelieve in Him, until the Day of Resurrection, as:

1166 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from 'Ikrimah, mawla of Ibn 'Abbas, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿and an admonition to the God-fearing﴾, until the Day of Resurrection.

1167 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿and an admonition to the God-fearing﴾, meaning: after them.

1168 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, the same.

1169 - Musa narrated to us, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: as for "an admonition to the God-fearing," they are the community of Muhammad ﷺ.

1170 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': ﴿and an admonition to the God-fearing﴾, he said: so it was an admonition specifically to the God-fearing.

1171 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His words: ﴿and an admonition to the God-fearing﴾, meaning: to those after them.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 67:**

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow." They said, "Do you take us in ridicule?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: This verse is one in which Allah rebukes those being addressed from the Children of Israel for their forefathers' breaking of the covenant that Allah had taken from them to obey His prophets. So He said to them: "Remember also your breaking of My covenant. ﴿When Moses said to his people﴾," and his people were the Children of Israel, when they disputed concerning the murdered man who had been killed among them: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow. They said, "Do you take us in ridicule?"﴾

"Al-Huzu' (the ridicule)" means play and mockery, as the rajaz poet said: [[He is Sakhir ibn Umayr al-Tamimi. It is also said that the poem belongs to al-Asma'i himself.]]

*Indeed, Umm Tulaysa has mocked me,*
*she said, "I see him destitute, with nothing at all."* [[Al-Asma'iyyat: 58; Amali al-Qali 2: 284. For what has been said about it, see the commentary on Simt al-Lali by al-Rajkuti: 930. Their narration in full is: "Akht Al Tulaysa has mocked me..." and so on. It is also narrated as "destitute (mumlaqan) with nothing at all" and "mublatan"; all of them have the same meaning: poor, with nothing at all.]]

By his words "has mocked" he means: has scorned and played.

It is not fitting that a prophet of Allah—regarding what he reports from Allah, whether a command or a prohibition—should be subject to ridicule or play. So they assumed of Moses that in his command to them—by the command of Allah, exalted is His remembrance, to slaughter a cow when they disputed before him concerning the murdered man—he was mocking and playing. It was not for them to assume that of the prophet of Allah, when he was informing them that Allah is the One who commanded them to slaughter the cow.

* *

The "fa'" (then) has been omitted from His words ﴿They said, "Do you take us in ridicule?"﴾, and it is the response (to the statement before it), because what precedes it in speech makes it unnecessary, and silence after His words ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾ is good. Therefore, it is permissible to drop the "fa'" from His words ﴿Do you take us in ridicule?﴾, just as it is permissible and good to drop it from His exalted words ﴿He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?" They said, "Indeed, we have been sent..."﴾ [Al-Hijr: 57–58; Adh-Dhariyat: 31–32]. It was not said "fa-qalu" (so they said). It would also have been good and permissible to say "fa-qalu." But if it were a single word, the "fa'" would not have been dropped from it. That is because when you say "qumtu fa-fa'altu kadha wa kadha" (I stood up, so I did such and such), you would not say "qumtu fa'altu kadha wa kadha" (I stood up, I did such and such), because it is a conjunction, not an interrogative that one stops at. [[In the printed edition it reads "qumtu wa-fa'altu" and in another printed edition "wa lam taqul: qumtu..." with an added "wa", which is corrupt. See Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 44.]]

So Moses informed them—when they said to him what they said—that one who reports from Allah, mighty is His praise, with mockery and derision, is among the ignorant. [[The meaning in context: Moses informed them that one who reports from Allah with mockery and derision is among the ignorant.]] He cleared himself of what they had assumed of him from that, and said: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾, meaning from among the foolish who attribute to Allah lies and falsehood.

* *

The cause of Moses' statement to them, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾, was what follows:

**1172.** Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from 'Ubayda, who said: Among the Children of Israel there was a man who was sterile—or barren—he said: His guardian killed him, then carried him and threw him into a tribe other than his own. He said: Strife broke out among them over it until they took up weapons. He said: The people of understanding said, "Will you fight each other while the Messenger of Allah is among you?" He said: So they came to the prophet of Allah, and he said, "Slaughter a cow!" They said, "Do you take us in ridicule?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant." [They then said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow..." up to His words, ﴿So they slaughtered it, and they almost did not do it﴾.] He said: Then he struck (the body) and informed them of its killer. He said: The cow was not obtained except for its weight in gold. He said: Had they taken any cow at all, it would have sufficed for them. And so no killer inherited after that. [[Narration 1172: "Ubayda," with a fatha on the 'ayn and a ya' below after the bi'; it is 'Ubayda al-Salmani. Ibn Kathir narrated this report 1: 197–198, from the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim, through Hisham ibn Hassan, "from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from 'Ubayda al-Salmani." Then he referred to this narration of al-Tabari.

Another report has already passed: 245, from the narration of Ayyub and Ibn 'Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from "'Ubayda." There we judged that the correct reading is "'Ubayda." This isnad here supports what we judged.]]

**1173.** And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to me, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliya, concerning Allah's words, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾. He said: There was a man from the Children of Israel who was wealthy but had no child, and he had a relative who was his heir. So he killed him in order to inherit from him, then threw him at a crossroads. [[Majma' al-tariq: the place where people meet and gather, or where roads meet.]] He came to Moses and said to him: "My relative has been killed, and a great matter has come upon me, and I find no one who will make clear to me who killed him except you, O prophet of Allah." He said: So Moses called out among the people: "I adjure Allah, whoever has knowledge of this, to make it clear to us." But they had no knowledge of it. The killer approached Moses and said: "You are the prophet of Allah; ask your Lord for us to make it clear." So he asked his Lord, and Allah revealed to him: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow.﴾ They were astonished and said: ﴿Do you take us in ridicule?﴾ He said: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant.﴾ They said: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is.﴾ He said: ﴿Indeed, He says it is a cow, neither old nor virgin, but between that﴾ — meaning: neither aged — ﴿nor virgin﴾ — meaning: nor young — ﴿between that﴾ — meaning: middle, between the virgin and the aged. ﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is.﴾ He said: ﴿Indeed, He says it is a cow, bright yellow in color﴾ — meaning: its color is pure — ﴿pleasing to the observers﴾ — meaning: it delights the observers. ﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is, for cattle have become confused to us, and we, if Allah wills, will be guided.﴾ He said: ﴿Indeed, He says it is a cow not trained to labor﴾ — meaning: its work has not made it tame — ﴿to plow the earth﴾ — meaning: it is not tame so as to plow the earth — ﴿nor to water the field﴾ — He says: nor to work the field — ﴿sound, with no blemish upon it﴾, meaning sound of defects — ﴿no mark upon it﴾ — He says: no whiteness upon it. (They said: "Now you have brought the truth," and they slaughtered it, though they almost did not do it.) He said: Had the people, when they were commanded to slaughter a cow, taken any cow from among the cattle and slaughtered it, it would have been sufficient for them. But they made things hard upon themselves, so Allah made it hard upon them. And had the people not made an exception, saying, ﴿And indeed, we, if Allah wills, will be guided,﴾ they would never have been guided to it. It has reached us that they did not find the cow described to them except with an old woman who had orphans and who was their guardian. When she knew that nothing else would benefit them, she raised the price upon them. So they came to Moses and informed him that they had found this description only with so-and-so, and that she had asked them for many times its price. Moses said to them: "Allah had indeed made it easy for you, but you made it hard upon yourselves. So give her what satisfies her and her judgment." They did so, bought it, and slaughtered it. Moses commanded them to take a bone from it and strike the slain man with it. They did so, and his soul returned to him, and he named his killer for them. Then he returned dead as he had been. They took his killer—who was the one who had come to Moses and complained to him—and Allah killed him for the evil of his deed.

**1174.** Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow."﴾ He said: There was a man from the Children of Israel who had much wealth, and he had a daughter, and he had a nephew who was in need. The nephew proposed marriage to his daughter, but he refused to marry her to him. The young man became angry and said, "By Allah, I will surely kill my uncle, take his wealth, marry his daughter, and eat his blood money!" Then the young man came to him, and merchants had arrived among the tribe of the Children of Israel. He said, "O uncle, come with me and take some of the goods of these people, perhaps I may profit from them. [[In the printed edition: "uṣība fīhā," which is an error; the correct reading is from Tafsir Ibn Kathir 1: 200. Asaba al-insan min al-mal wa ghayrihi means: he took and seized some of the wealth or other things. He means: that I may gain profit from it.]] For if they see you with me, they will give to me." So the uncle went out with the young man at night. When he reached that tribe, the young man killed the old man, then returned to his family.

When morning came, he came as if seeking his uncle, as if he did not know where he was, and did not find him. He set off toward him, and there he found that tribe gathered over him. He seized them and said, "You have killed my uncle, so pay me his blood money." He began to weep, throwing dust on his head and calling out, "O my uncle!" He brought them up before Moses, and Moses judged against them for the blood money. They said to him, "O Messenger of Allah, call upon your Lord for us, so that He may make clear to him who his companion is, and the perpetrator of the crime be seized. [[In the printed edition: "Ud'u lana hatta yatabayyana." Ibn Kathir's text in his tafsir 1: 200: "Ud'u lana rabbaka hatta yubayyina lana man sahibuhu, fa-yu'khadhu sahib al-qadiyya."]] By Allah, his blood money is a light matter for us, but we are ashamed to be disgraced by it." That is when Allah, mighty is His praise, says: ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed over it—and Allah is one who brings forth what you were concealing.﴾ So Moses said to them: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow.﴾ They said: "Do you ask us about the slain man and his killer, and you say, 'Slaughter a cow!'? Are you mocking us?" Moses said: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant.﴾ He said: Ibn 'Abbas said: Had they taken any cow at random and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed for them. But they became strict and pressed Moses with difficult questions, so Allah made it hard upon them. [[A'annahu and ta'annatahu: he asked him about something intending to confuse him and cause hardship.]] They said: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is.﴾ He said: ﴿Indeed, He says it is a cow, neither old nor virgin, but between that﴾ — the fari (old) is the aged one that does not bear, and the bikr (virgin) is the one that has borne only one calf, and the 'awan (middle) is the middle one, which has borne and whose offspring has borne — ﴿so do what you are commanded.﴾ They said: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is.﴾ He said: ﴿Indeed, He says it is a cow, bright yellow in color, pleasing to the observers.﴾ He said: pleasing to the observers. ﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is, for cattle have become confused to us, and we, if Allah wills, will be guided.﴾ He said: ﴿Indeed, He says it is a cow not trained to labor, to plow the earth, nor to water the field, sound, with no blemish upon it.﴾ — with no whiteness, no blackness, and no redness. ﴿They said: Now you have brought the truth.﴾ So they searched for it, but they could not find it.

There was a man from the Children of Israel who was among the most dutiful of people to his father. A man passed by him carrying pearls to sell. His father was sleeping, with the key under his head. The man said to him, "Will you buy these pearls from me for seventy thousand?" The young man said to him, "Wait until my father wakes up, and I will take them for eighty thousand." The other said, "Wake your father, and it is yours for sixty thousand." The merchant kept reducing the price for him until it reached thirty thousand, while the other insisted on waiting until his father woke up, until it reached one hundred thousand. When the merchant pressed him too much, he said, "No, by Allah, I will not buy it from you for anything at all," and he refused to wake his father. So Allah compensated him for that pearl by giving him that cow. The Children of Israel passed by him looking for the cow, and they saw the cow with him. They asked him to sell it to them, a cow for a cow, but he refused. They offered him two, but he refused. They increased until they reached ten, but he refused. They said, "By Allah, we will not leave you until we take it from you." So they took him to Moses and said, "O prophet of Allah, we found the cow with this man, and he refused to give it to us, though we have offered him a price." Moses said to him, "Give them your cow." He said, "O Messenger of Allah, I have more right to my property." He said, "You are right." And he said to the people, "Satisfy your companion." They gave him its weight in gold, but he refused, so they doubled for him what they had given, until they gave him its weight ten times over. Then he sold it to them and took its price. He said, "Slaughter it." They slaughtered it, and he said, "Strike him with part of it." They struck him with the piece between his shoulders, and he lived. They asked him, "Who killed you?" He said to them, "My nephew. He said, 'I will kill him, take his wealth, and marry his daughter.'" So they seized the youth and killed him.

**1175.** Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada—

**1176.** And Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, from Ibn Zayd, from Mujahid—

**1177.** And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn Yazid narrated to me, from Mujahid—

**1178.** And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Karim narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil narrated to me, that he heard Wahb mention—

**1179.** And al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid; and Hajjaj, from Abu Ma'shar, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and Muhammad ibn Qays—

**1180.** And Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father informed me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas—

All of them mentioned that the cause for which Moses said to them, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾, was similar to the cause mentioned by 'Ubayda, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Suddi, except that some of them mentioned that the one who killed the slain man whose case was brought before Moses was the brother of the deceased, and some mentioned that he was his nephew, and some said that they were a group of heirs who were impatient for his death. But they all agree that Moses only commanded them to slaughter the cow because of the slain man, when they brought the dispute before him, by Allah's command to him to do so. [[It is more correct to read "'an amri Allahi iyyahu bi-dhalik" (from Allah's command to him concerning that).]] So they said to him: "And what is the slaughtering of a cow to do? Make clear to us our dispute which we brought before you concerning the killing of the one who was killed, and you claim that one of us is the killer! Are you mocking us?" As follows:

**1181.** Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: A slain man from the Children of Israel was killed and thrown into the territory of one of the tribes. The people of the slain man came to that tribe and said, "You, by Allah, have killed our companion!" They said, "No, by Allah." So they came to Moses and said, "This is our slain man among them, and by Allah, they killed him!" They said, "No, by Allah, O prophet of Allah, he was thrown upon us!" Moses said to them: "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow." They said: "Are you mocking us?" And he recited the words of Allah, mighty is His praise: ﴿Do you take us in ridicule?﴾ They said: "We come to you to mention our slain man and what we are in, and you mock us?" Moses said: (I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant.)

**1182.** Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid; and Hajjaj, from Abu Ma'shar, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, and Muhammad ibn Qays: When the guardians of the slain man and those they accused of killing their companion came to Moses and related their story to him, Allah revealed to him that they should slaughter a cow. So Moses said to them, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow.﴾ ﴿They said: Do you take us in ridicule?﴾ ﴿He said: I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant.﴾ They said: "What are the cow and the slain man?" He said: "I say to you, 'Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow,' and you say, 'Do you take us in ridicule?'"

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 68:**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is."  He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow neither old nor virgin"﴾

[[The entire verse is missing from the manuscripts, so I have placed it in its proper position.]]

Abu Ja'far said: Those to whom it was said, ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾, after they had known and it had been established among them that what Moses had commanded them concerning this was from the command of Allah to slaughter a cow, said, in earnest and truth, [[His words "in earnest and truth" are the predicate of his words "that what Moses had commanded them…"]] ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is.﴾ So they asked Moses to ask his Lord on their behalf for what Allah had already spared them by His saying to them, "Slaughter a cow." For He, exalted is His praise, had only commanded them to slaughter a cow from among cattle, meaning any cow they wished to slaughter, without restricting it for them to one type rather than another or one kind rather than another. Yet, out of the coarseness of their characters, the harshness of their natures, their poor understanding, and their taking upon themselves what Allah had lifted from them as a burden, they said this, seeking to provoke the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as follows:

1183 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: When Moses said to them, ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾, they said to him, seeking to provoke him: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is.﴾

When they, out of ignorance, took upon themselves what they took upon themselves by searching into the description of the cow they had been commanded to slaughter, which had already been spared them, seeking to provoke their prophet Moses, may God's blessings be upon him, after they had already shown him ill opinion regarding what he told them from Allah, exalted is His praise, by their saying: ﴿Do you make us a mockery?﴾ [[The sequence of the phrase is: "When they took upon themselves out of ignorance what they took upon themselves… He punished them…", and there is a separation between them.]] — He, mighty and exalted, punished them by restricting the slaughter of what He had commanded them to slaughter of cattle to one type rather than another. [[In the printed edition it reads "by specifying the slaughter of what He had commanded them…", but I believe al-Tabari's wording is what I have recorded here. He had said earlier (189): "without restricting it for them to one type rather than another," and he will say later (197): "so they restricted it to one type rather than the other types."]] So He, exalted is His praise, said to them, when they asked Him, saying, "What is it? What are its description and attributes? Make it clear to us so that we may know it!" [[Al-hilyah (with a kasra and then a sukun) means description and form: he described the man's appearance and condition (ḥallā al-rajul yuḥallīhi taḥliyah). Taḥallaytu al-rajul means I came to know his description.]] — He said: ﴿Indeed, it is a cow neither old nor virgin﴾.

* *

The meaning of His words, exalted is His praise, ﴿neither old﴾ is: neither a decrepit aged cow. It is said of it: "The cow became fāriḍ (faradat al-baqaratu tafriḍu furūḍan)," meaning that it became aged. From this is the poet's saying:

"O Lord of a rival who bears a grudge against me, an old enemy, who has cycles like the cycles of a menstruating woman." [[Majalis Tha'lab: 364; al-Ma'ani al-Kabir: 850, 1143; al-Hayawan 6: 66–67; al-Addad: 22; Kitab al-Qartayn 1: 44, 77; al-Lisan (f-r-d); and others. The correct version of the verse is: "O Lord, a master who is envious, hostile toward me, with an old and buried grudge."

al-Dabb means anger and rancor that one conceals in the heart. Qurū' and aqrā' are plurals of qar' (with a damma and sukun), which means a time of menstruation. Ibn Qutaybah said: "That is, he has times when his enmity is stirred." Al-Jahiz said: "It is as though he went to the idea that his rancor subsides and then flares up again, then subsides and flares up again."]]

By his words "fāriḍ" he means "ancient": describing an ancient grudge. From this is another's saying:

"For her are glass-like eyelids and a fāriḍ uvula, wide and drooping, like a waterskin that the one who churns has tilted." [[The first line is in al-Lisan (z-j-j), and the second in al-Mukhassas 1: 162. In the original it read: "lahu zujāj wa lahāh fāriḍ … hadlā'u ka'l-waṭb nahāh al-mākhiḍ," which is a corruption. Zujāj is the plural of zajj, the iron piece fitted to the bottom of a spear, with which it is stuck into the ground, and he borrowed it here for the eyelids. Al-lahāh is the red flesh in the palate, hanging over the root of the tongue and overlooking the throat. The fāriḍ in this verse means wide, great and large: one says "laḥyah fāriḍ" (a huge beard), "shiqshiqah fāriḍ" (a huge camel's palate), and "dalw fāriḍ" (a large bucket). Abu Muhammad al-Fuqa'si, describing a wide bucket (al-gharb), said: "And the gharb is a fāriḍ large bucket of cattle hide."

Hadlā' and ahdal: this is one who walks with a sideways gait, with his shoulders and neck bent forward over his chest and bowed. Al-waṭb is a container for milk, made of hide. Nahāh means turned and inclined. Al-mākhiḍ comes from makhaḍa al-laban, when milk is put into the churn to extract its butter. Perhaps he is satirizing his wife, mentioning the ugliness of her teeth, the width of her uvula out of her excessive greed, and describing her gait as leaning to one side with her body heaped up piece upon piece, as if she were a waterskin being tilted to the right and left by the one churning it.]]

And with the like of what we have said about the interpretation of "fāriḍ," the interpreters said:

Those who said that:

1184 – Ali ibn Sa'id al-Kindi related to me, saying: 'Abd al-Salam ibn Harb related to us, from Khusayf, from Mujahid: ﴿neither old﴾, he said: not large. [[Report 1184: Ali ibn Sa'id ibn Masruq al-Kindi, the teacher of al-Tabari: a Kufan, reliable, whose biography is in al-Tahdhib and in Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/189–190; he died in 249 AH. 'Abd al-Salam ibn Harb al-Mala'i al-Kufi, the hafiz: reliable and authoritative; the authors of the six books related from him. Ibn Abi Hatim gives his biography at 3/1/47.]]

1185 – Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn 'Atiyyah related to us, saying: Shurayk related to us, from Khusayf, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, or from Ikrimah (Shurayk was uncertain): ﴿neither old﴾, he said: large.

1185 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father informed me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿neither old﴾: al-fāriḍ is the decrepit one.

1186 – It was related to me from al-Minjab, saying: Bishr related to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿neither old﴾, he says: not large and decrepit.

1187 – Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿neither old﴾: the decrepit one.

1188 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "al-fāriḍ" is the large one.

1189 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri related to us, saying: Shurayk related to us, from Khusayf, from Mujahid, his words: ﴿neither old﴾, he said: the large one.

1190 – Al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Adam related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah: ﴿neither old﴾, meaning: not decrepit.

1191 – It was related to me from 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the like of it.

1192 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "al-fāriḍ" is the decrepit one.

1193 – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar said, Qatadah said: "al-fāriḍ" is the decrepit one. He says: not decrepit and not virgin, but ʿawān between these two.

1194 – Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "al-fāriḍ" is the decrepit one that does not give birth.

1195 – Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "al-fāriḍ" is the large one.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿nor virgin﴾

Abu Ja'far said: "al-bikr" is used of female animals and of human beings, as long as the male has not mounted her. It is pronounced with a kasra on the bā' (bikr), and no form of fa'ala or yaf'alu is heard from it. As for "al-bakr" with a fatha on the bā', it means a young camel.

* *

Allah, mighty and exalted, by His words ﴿nor virgin﴾ meant one that is young and has not given birth, as follows:

1196 – Ali ibn Sa'id al-Kindi related to me, saying: 'Abd al-Salam ibn Harb related to us, from Khusayf, from Mujahid: ﴿nor virgin﴾: young.

1197 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "al-bikr," the young one.

1198 – Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: al-Hasan ibn 'Atiyyah related to us, saying: Shurayk related to us, from Khusayf, from Sa'id, from Ibn Abbas, or Ikrimah (he was uncertain): ﴿nor virgin﴾, he said: the young one.

1199 – Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿nor virgin﴾: the young one.

1200 – Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Abu Sufyan related to me, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah: ﴿nor virgin﴾ and not young.

1201 – It was related to me from al-Minjab, saying: Bishr related to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿nor virgin﴾, and not a weak young one.

1202 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Adam related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah: ﴿nor virgin﴾, meaning: nor young.

1203 – It was related to me from 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the like of it.

1204 – Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, concerning "al-bikr": she has given birth only to one offspring.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿ʿawān﴾

Abu Ja'far said: "ʿawān" is the middle-aged one who has given birth, one litter after another, and it is not an adjective for the virgin. It is said of it: "qad 'awwanat" when it has become so.

The meaning of the speech is that He says: "Indeed, it is a cow neither fāriḍ nor bikr, but ʿawān between those." It is not permissible for "ʿawān" to be other than the subject (mubtada'), because His words ﴿between that﴾ refer back to the fāriḍ and the bikr, so it cannot precede them. From this is al-Akhtal's saying:

"In Mecca there are no grey-haired women who gather in crowds, nor in Yathrib any ʿawān or virgins." [[His Diwan: 119. This differs from what al-Tabari related; before it is: "I swear by the Lord of the dancing (birds) and what stands in Mecca of veils and curtains / and by the offering, when its forelegs are reddened, on the day of sacrifice, the Tashriq, and the slaughtering / and what is in Zamzam of shaved-headed grey-haired men, and in Yathrib of ʿawān and virgins."

He means: they shaved their heads, having exited the state of ihram and completed their pilgrimage. Shamt is the plural of ashmat, the one whose black hair is mixed with the white of grey. If the version of al-Tabari, "shamt muhaffalah," is correct, it may derive from al-hafil and al-ihtifal, which is striving and diligence; one says: a man with hafil, dhū ḥafl and ḥafla: he has striving, diligence and exaggeration in what he undertakes of matters. So it seems he means: those who strive in worship and pilgrimage.]]

Its plural is ʿawn, and one says: "imra'ah ʿawān min niswah ʿawn" (a woman who is ʿawān among women who are ʿawn). From this is the saying of Tamim ibn Muqbil:

"And a gathering like statues, with dark-eyed women whose tears are…, they have not known the hardship of life, neither as virgins nor as ʿawn." [[Jamharat Ash'ar al-'Arab: 162, from the fine poetry of Tamim ibn Ubayy ibn Muqbil. In Arabic usage, al-ma'tam is a group of women, or men, in good or in evil. They say the common people err and think that al-ma'tam means lamentation and wailing. Al-dumā is the plural of dumyah: a picture or statue, whose craft is perfected and whose beauty is exaggerated; the Arabs often compare women to statues. Al-ḥūr is the plural of ḥawrā'; al-ḥawar is when the whiteness of the white of the eye is intense and the blackness of its black is intense, its pupil is round, its lids are thin, and what is around it is white. His words "lam tabʾas" mean that hardship of life did not befall her, or that she did not complain of the hardship of life; one says: bi'isa yabʾas bu'sa, so he is bā'is and ba'īs, he became poor and hardship was severe upon him. In the printed edition, and in al-Lisan (a-t-m), it reads "lam tayʾas" with a yā', which is an error.]]

And one says: "baqarah ʿawān, and baqar ʿawn." He said: The Arabs sometimes say "baqar ʿuwun" like "rusul," wanting by that to distinguish the plural of ʿawān from cattle from the plural of ʿānah from wild asses. It is said: "hādhihi ḥarb ʿawān," when it is a war that has been fought in it time after time, likened to the woman who gave birth litter after litter. Likewise it is said: "ḥājah ʿawān," when it has been fulfilled time after time.

1205 – Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, that Ibn Zayd recited to him:

"Sitting at the doors, seekers of need, of needs that are ʿawān, or a need that is virgin." [[Diwan al-Farazdaq: 227; Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara': 256; Tarikh al-Tabari: 138; and others. It will come at 7/188 (Bulaq). The verse is about Ziyad, and before it: "Ziyad called me for a gift, and I was not one to approach him with what a man of noble lineage drives of abundance / and with Ziyad, if he wished to give them their gift, there are many men whom he sees as poor."

It is related as "qu'udan," and Ibn Sallam's version is "ṭālib ḥājah," and the "or a need that is virgin" is in the accusative, in conjunction with the place of "ḥājah ʿawān," whose place is accusative by his saying: "ṭalāb."]]

Abu Ja'far said: The verse is by al-Farazdaq.

And in a similar way to what we have said about this, the interpreters interpreted it.

Those who said that:

1206 – Ali ibn Sa'id al-Kindi related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Salam ibn Harb related to us, from Khusayf, from Mujahid: ﴿ʿawān between that﴾: middle, who has given birth to one or two litters. [[Report 1206: "Ali ibn Sa'id al-Kindi": we have given his biography at 1184. In the manuscripts here it reads "Sa'd" instead of "Sa'id," which is an error.]]

1207 – Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿ʿawān﴾, he said: "al-ʿawān": the spinster, the middle-aged.

1208 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "al-ʿawān," the middle-aged.

1209 – Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn 'Atiyyah related to us, saying: Shurayk related to us, from Khusayf, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, or Ikrimah (Shurayk was uncertain): ﴿ʿawān﴾, he said: between that.

1210 – It was related to me from al-Minjab, saying: Bishr related to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿ʿawān﴾, he said: between the young and the old, and she is at her strongest and most beautiful among cattle and beasts.

1211 – Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿ʿawān﴾, he said: the middle-aged.

1212 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Adam related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah: ﴿ʿawān﴾, middle-aged (naṣaf).

1213 – It was related to me from 'Ammar, from Ibn Abi Ja'far, from his father, from al-Rabi', the like of it.

1214 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ related to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah: "al-ʿawān," middle-aged, between that.

1214 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri related to us, saying: Shurayk related to us, from Khusayf, from Mujahid: ﴿ʿawān﴾, the one who produces something, on condition that she has given birth once or twice.

1215 – Musa related to us, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "al-ʿawān," the middle-aged who is between that, who has given birth and whose offspring has also given birth.

1216 – Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "al-ʿawān," between that, not a virgin and not an old one.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿between that﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words ﴿between that﴾ he means between the virgin and the decrepit one, as follows:

1217 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Adam related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah: ﴿between that﴾, that is, between the virgin and the decrepit.

* *

If someone says: You know that "bayna" can only be used with two things or more, so how is it said "bayna dhālika" when "dhālika" is singular in form?

It is said: It is valid even though it is singular, because "dhālika" has the meaning of two, and the Arabs combine in "dhālika" and "dhāka" two things and two meanings of actions, as the speaker says: "I think your brother is standing, and ʿAmr was your father," [[al-Farra's wording here is clearer: he said: "There must be two things for 'kāna,' and there must be two things for 'aẓunn,'" and then it is permissible to say: "qad kāna dhāka, wa aẓunna dhālika." Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 45.]] then he says: "qad kāna dhāka, wa aẓunna dhālika." So with "dhālika" and "dhāka" he combines the subject and the predicate, which "aẓunna" and "kāna" must have. [[In the printed edition it reads: "which 'al-ẓann' and 'kāna' must have," which is confused speech.]]

* *

So the meaning of the speech is: He said: "Indeed, it is a cow that is neither an aged decrepit one, nor a young one who has not given birth, but a middle-aged cow who has given birth, one litter after another, between old age and youth." So "dhālika" combines the meaning of old age and youth, as we have described. Had the words in place of "fāriḍ" and "bikr" been the names of two individuals, it would not have been combined with "bayna." That is because "dhālika" does not refer to the names of two individuals, and it is not permissible for one who says "I was between Zayd and ʿAmr" to say "I was between that." It is only with the names of actions, not with the names of persons. [[See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 45.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾ (68)

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, mighty and exalted, says to them: Do what I command you, and you will attain your needs and requests with Me; and slaughter the cow that I have commanded you to slaughter, so that you may reach—by ending your obedience to Me in slaughtering it—the knowledge of the killer of your slain.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 69:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: Call upon your Lord for us that He show us what its color is. He said: Indeed He says, "It is a yellow cow."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of that is: the people of Moses said to Moses: "Call upon your Lord for us that He show us what its color is?" That is, what color is the cow you commanded us to slaughter? This was also another act of obstinacy on their part after the first, and an overburdening with a request they had been spared in the second and last question. For they had not been restricted in the second instance, when after their question about the age of the cow they had been commanded to slaughter, they refused except to overburden themselves with what they had been spared, asking about its description. So they were restricted to one type rather than the other types, as a punishment from God for them, for the question they put to their Prophet ﷺ, out of obstinacy toward him. Then He did not restrict them to one color rather than another, so they refused except to overburden themselves with what they had been free of overburdening, and they said, out of obstinacy toward their Prophet ﷺ, as Ibn Abbas reported: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us that He show us what its color is.﴾ So it was said to them as a punishment: ﴿Indeed He says, "It is a yellow cow, bright in color, pleasing to the beholders."﴾ So they were restricted to one color rather than another. The meaning is: the cow I commanded you to slaughter is yellow, bright in its color.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of His saying ﴿what its color is?﴾ is: what thing is its color? Therefore the word "color" is in the nominative, because it is the subject of the interrogative "ma". The reason "ma" is not put in the accusative by "show us" is that the original form of "ayy" and "ma" is a collective of separate interrogatives. The speaker says: "Show us whether this cow is black or yellow?" Since "show us" cannot govern an interrogative in its separated form, it cannot govern "ayy", which is a collection of that separated form. [The printed edition had here "like the saying of the speaker", which is an error. And the sentence in the printed edition read: "Since it is not like his saying: show us, it is raised as an interrogative, separate, it cannot be raised as ayy..." which is a passage marred by textual corruption; see the Ma'ani al-Farra' 1:46-48, which gives a clear and sufficient explanation.] The same applies to all its analogues, the governing is one in "ma" and "ayy".

The people of interpretation differed concerning the meaning of His saying ﴿yellow﴾. Some of them said: the meaning of that is black, intensely black.

Those who said that among them:

1218 - Abu Mas'ud Isma'il ibn Mas'ud al-Jahdari related to me, saying: Nuh ibn Qays related to us, from Muhammad ibn Sayf, from al-Hasan: ﴿yellow, bright in color﴾, he said: black, intensely black.

1219 - Abu Za'ida Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Abi Za'ida and al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim related to me, both saying: Muslim ibn Ibrahim related to us, saying: Nuh ibn Qays related to us, from Muhammad ibn Sayf, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, the like of it.

* *

Others said: the meaning of that is: yellow of horn and hoof.

Those who said that:

1220 - Hisham ibn Yunus al-Nahshali related to me, saying: Hafs ibn Ghiyath related to us, from Ash'ath, from al-Hasan concerning His saying: ﴿yellow, bright in color﴾, he said: yellow of horn and hoof.

1221 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Hushaym related to me, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from Kathir ibn Ziyad, from al-Hasan concerning His saying: ﴿yellow, bright in color﴾, he said: it was wild.

1222 - Ya'qub related to me, saying: Marwan ibn Mu'awiya related to us, from Ibrahim, from Abu Hafs, from Mughra' - or from a man -, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿a yellow cow, bright in color﴾, he said: yellow of horn and hoof.

1223 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: it is yellow.

1224 - Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: al-Dahhak ibn Makhlad related to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Indeed it is a yellow cow, bright in color﴾, he said: if they had taken any yellow cow, it would have sufficed them.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: I think that whoever said, concerning His saying ﴿yellow﴾, that it means black, went by the saying used in describing black camels: "These are yellow camels, and this is a yellow she-camel," meaning black. That is said of camels because their blackness inclines toward yellowness, and from it is the saying of the poet: [This is al-A'sha al-Kabir.]

"Those are my horses from him, and those are my mounts... their young are yellow like raisins."

[From his qasida praising Abu al-Ash'ath Qays ibn Ma'd Yakrib al-Kindi. The original read "from him" incorrectly... the meaning of the poem is that Qays... and I do not think al-Tabari errs in transmitting this verse. Al-rikab are camels ridden upon, having no singular of their own form; their singular is rahila. Al-zabib is withered grapes, the blackest of which is the finest, though it is not pure black. He says: all that I possess of horses and of camels that have borne me the best of what camels bear is from the generosity of Abu al-Ash'ath.] He means by his saying "yellow" black, and that is so when it is applied to camels; it is not something by which a cow is described. Moreover, the Arabs do not describe blackness as "intense" (faqu'), but when they describe blackness they describe it by its intensity, with words such as "jet-black", "pitch-black", "deep black", and they say: "he is black, jet-black, pitch-black, and deep-black" - and they do not say: "he is fāqi' black". They say: "he is fāqi' yellow." So his describing it as fāqi' is clear evidence against the interpretation of the one who interpreted His saying ﴿indeed it is a yellow cow, fāqi'﴾ as meaning intensely black.

* *

On His saying: ﴿bright in color﴾

Abu Ja'far said: It means pure in its color. The "fuqu'" (brightness) in yellow is like the "nusu'" (purity) in white, which is its intensity and clarity, as:

1225 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, saying: Qatada said: ﴿bright in color﴾, it is the clear in its color.

1226 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Adam related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliya: ﴿bright in color﴾, i.e., clear in its color.

1227 - I was told by Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the like of it.

1228 - Musa related to us, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿bright﴾, he said: pure in its color.

1229 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿bright in color﴾, intensely yellow, nearly white from its yellowness. Abu Ja'far said: I think it is white! [Abu Ja'far seems to object to the saying "nearly white from its yellowness", saying in effect: if that were correct, then "bright in color" would mean white, and yellowness intensifies while becoming pale when it lightens. This is what I believe his meaning to be.]

1230 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His saying ﴿bright in color﴾: it is intensely yellow.

* *

From this it is said: "faqu'a lawnuhu, yafqa'u and yafqu'u, fuqu'an, fahuwa fa'iq", as the poet said:

"I charged upon him with the bay horse until I left him humbled, dragging in the dust, and his color is bright (fa'iq)." [I do not know who said it. The "ward" is his horse.]

* *

On His saying: ﴿pleasing to the beholders﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying ﴿pleasing to the beholders﴾ is meant that this cow amazes the one who looks at it, in the goodness of its form, its appearance and its shape, as:

1231 - Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada: ﴿pleasing to the beholders﴾, i.e., amazing the beholders.

1232 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Abd al-Karim related to us, saying: Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil related to me that he heard Wahb: ﴿pleasing to the beholders﴾; when you look at it, it seems to you as if the rays of the sun emerge from its skin.

1233 - Musa related to us, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿pleasing to the beholders﴾, he said: amazing the beholders.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 70 (part 1 of 2):

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is. Indeed the cows are alike to us, and we, if God wills, will surely be guided."﴾ (2:70)**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His words "They said" he means the people of Moses, those who were commanded to slaughter the cow, speaking to Moses. The mention of Moses is omitted, and the pronoun referring back to him is also omitted, relying on what the apparent sense of the speech indicates. The meaning of the speech is: they said to him, "Call upon your Lord," and "to him" is not mentioned for the reason we have described.

As for His words, "Make clear to us what it is," this is a report from God about the people, concerning their third act of ignorance. Had they, when commanded to slaughter a cow, slaughtered whichever cow was easiest to obtain, of those that fall under the name "cow," it would have sufficed for them, and nothing else would have been required of them, since they had not been obligated to a particular attribute over another. But when they asked for its description, asking what attribute it had, He made clear to them that it was of a certain age, distinct from the ages of the rest of the cattle. It was said to them: "It is a *'awan* (a middle-aged cow), between the *fariḍ* (old cow past breeding) and the *bikr* (young cow) and the *ḍari'* (the weak, emaciated one)." [The *ḍari'* is the weak, wasted, thin one.] So, once its age had been made clear to them, had they slaughtered the least of cows of the age that had been made clear to them, it would have sufficed for them, since they had not been obligated to anything other than the age that had been specified for them, nor had they been restricted to one color over another. But when they refused except that it be known to them by its descriptions, defined by its limits that distinguish it from all the other beasts of the earth, they made things hard for themselves, and God made things hard for them in return, because of their excessive questioning of their Prophet and their disputing with him. For this reason our Prophet ﷺ said to his community:

1234 — "Leave me alone as long as I leave you alone, for those before you were destroyed by their excessive questioning and their disputing with their prophets. So when I command you to do something, do it, and when I forbid you from something, avoid it as much as you are able."

[Note on the hadith: 1234 — He narrated it here without an isnad. It is from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. An error occurred at its end, which reversed its meaning. The correct wording, with the correct meaning, is: "So when I forbid you from something, avoid it, and when I command you to do something, do of it as much as you are able." This is the wording of al-Bukhari. The Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) elaborated on its explanation in Fath al-Bari 13: 219–226. Ahmad also narrated it, 7361, with approximately its meaning, and we pointed to many of its chains in the Musnad and elsewhere. Muslim also narrated it, 2: 221, with similar wording, through several chains. Ibn Hibban also narrated it in his Sahih through several chains: 17, 18, 19, 20 (in our edition). In Ibn Hibban's narration 17: "Ibn 'Ajlan said: I narrated it to Aban ibn Salih, and he said to me: How excellent is this statement, His saying: 'so do of it as much as you are able.'" It is the ninth hadith of the Forty Hadith of al-Nawawi, and Ibn Rajab explained it at length in Jami' al-'Ulum wa'l-Hikam. The error that occurred here is probably from the copyists, for I do not think al-Tabari would have been unaware of the incoherence in this wording.]

Abu Ja'far said: But when the people increased the harm and obstinacy toward their Prophet Moses ﷺ, God increased them in punishment and hardship, as:

1235 — Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthām ibn 'Ali narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Minhal ibn 'Amr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Had they taken the least cow, they would have been satisfied with it, but they made things hard, so God made things hard for them."

1236 — Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir narrated to us, saying: I heard Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from 'Ubaydah, who said: "Had they taken the least cow, it would have sufficed for them."

[Note on the report: 1236 — Al-Tabari's shaykh here is named "'Amr ibn 'Abd al-A'la"! I have not found any narrator by this name. It is rather "Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la al-San'ani," one of the shaykhs of Muslim, Abu Dawud and others, as this same isnad appeared correctly earlier: 1172. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la was a trustworthy Basran who died in 245 AH, biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir of al-Bukhari 1/1/174, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/16.]

1237 — al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ayyub—

1238 — And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from Hisham ibn Hassan, all together, from Ibn Sirin, from 'Ubaydah al-Salmani, who said: "They asked and made things hard, so God made things hard for them."

1239 — al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn 'Uyaynah informed us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from 'Ikrimah, who said: "Had the Children of Israel taken any cow, it would have sufficed for them. Had it not been for their saying: 'And we, if God wills, will surely be guided,' they would not have found it."

1240 — Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the words of God: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed God commands you to slaughter a cow"﴾: "Had they taken any cow, it would have sufficed for them." ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is." He said, "Indeed He says it is a cow neither old nor young"﴾: he said: "Had they taken a cow of this description, it would have sufficed for them." ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is." He said, "Indeed He says it is a yellow cow, bright in its color, pleasing to the beholders"﴾: he said: "Had they taken a yellow cow, it would have sufficed for them." ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is." * He said, "Indeed He says it is a cow not trained to plow the earth nor to water the tilth"﴾ — the verse.

1241 — al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly, and he added in it: "But they made things hard, so He made things hard for them."

1242 — al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid said: "Had they taken any cow at all, it would have sufficed for them." Ibn Jurayj said: 'Ata' said to me: "Had they taken the least cow, it would have been enough for them." Ibn Jurayj said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "They were only commanded to take the least cow, but when they made things hard for themselves, God made things hard for them; by God, had they not made an exception, I would never have made clear to them the final end."

[Note on the report: 1242 — At its end is a marfu' hadith, which Ibn Jurayj mentioned. It is mursal (its chain omits a Companion) and cannot be used as proof. Also coming: 1244, from Qatadah, mursal. Ibn Kathir mentioned its meaning in his Tafsir 1: 203, from the tafsirs of Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh, with their chains, from the narration of al-Hasan, from Abu Rafi', from Abu Hurayrah, marfu', with similar wording. Ibn Kathir said: "This is a strange hadith from this route. The best that can be said of it is that it is a statement of Abu Hurayrah, as a similar one was mentioned earlier from al-Suddi."]

1243 — al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: "Had the people, when they were commanded to slaughter a cow, picked any cow at random and slaughtered it, it would have been the right one. But they made things hard for themselves, so God made things hard for them. Had it not been that the people made an exception, saying, 'And we, if God wills, will surely be guided,' they would never have been guided to it, ever."

1244 — Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of God ﷺ used to say: 'The people were only commanded with the least cow, but when they made things hard for themselves, it was made hard for them. By Him in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, had they not made an exception, I would never have made clear to them the final end.'"

1245 — Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Had they picked any cow and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed for them. But they made things hard and were obstinate toward Moses, so God made things hard for them."

1246 — Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "Had the people looked at the least cow—meaning the Children of Israel—it would have sufficed for them, but they made things hard, so it was made hard for them, and they bought it for its hide filled with dinars."

[Note on the report: 1246 — This chain is broken (munqati') between Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash and Ibn 'Abbas, as is evident, since Abu Bakr narrates from the Successors (tabi'un), and his birth was long after the death of Ibn 'Abbas. This report was mentioned by al-Suyuti 1: 77, and attributed to Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim "through several routes."]

1247 — Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "Had they taken a cow as God commanded them, that would have sufficed for them. But the trial lies in these questions. They said: 'Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is,' so He made things hard for them, and He said: 'Indeed He says it is a cow neither old nor young, but between that,' and they said: 'Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is.' He said: 'Indeed He says it is a yellow cow, bright in its color, pleasing to the beholders.' He said: And He made things harder for them than the first time, and recited until He reached: ﴿sound, with no spot in it﴾. They refused again and said: ﴿Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is. Indeed the cows are alike to us, and we, if God wills, will surely be guided.﴾ So He made things hard for them, and He said: 'Indeed He says it is a cow not trained to plow the earth nor to water the tilth, sound, with no spot in it.' He said: So they were compelled to a cow whose description no one knew except it, and it was yellow, with no black or white in it."

[Note on the report: 1247 — Its completion will come at no. 1273.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: These statements we have mentioned from those whom we have mentioned—from the Companions, the Successors, and those who followed them after them—that had the Children of Israel taken the least cow and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed for them, but they made things hard, so God made things hard for them, are among the clearest proofs that the people held that God's ruling, in what He commanded and forbade in His Book and upon the tongue of His Messenger ﷺ, is according to the apparent generality, not the hidden specificity [see our discussion of "the apparent and the hidden" in the Tafsir: 2: 15 and the references], unless some part of what the apparent wording of the revelation generalizes is specified by a Book from God or by the Messenger of God; and that if the revelation or the Messenger specifies some part of what the apparent wording of the revelation generalizes with a ruling contrary to what the apparent sense indicates, then what is specified is excluded from the ruling of the verse that generalized that category, and the rest of the ruling of the verse remains general. This is as we have explained in our book "al-Risalah" in the section "Subtle Speech on Explaining the Foundations of Rulings," in our statements on generality and specificity; their agreement with us on this, their doctrine is our doctrine, and their rejection of the view of those who hold that rulings are specific, and their testimony to the corruption of the view of him who said: the ruling of a verse that comes in general form remains general unless some part of what the verse generalizes is specified. If some part is specified, then the ruling of the verse is specific.

This is because all those whose statements we have just mentioned—those who blamed the Children of Israel for asking their Prophet ﷺ about the description of the cow they were commanded to slaughter, its age and its adornment—saw that they were in error in asking Moses ﷺ that question. They saw that had they picked the least cow of the cattle when they were commanded to slaughter it, by His words, "Indeed God commands you to slaughter a cow," and slaughtered it, they would have fulfilled what was obligatory upon them from God's command in that matter, and obeyed the truth, since the people had not restricted themselves to one kind of cow over another, or one age over another.

They also saw that, when they asked Moses about its age and he informed them of it, restricting them to one age over another and one kind over another, singling out from all kinds of cows one kind, they were in their second question, after what had been specified for them of the kinds of cows, in the same error as they were in their first question.

Likewise they saw that in the third question they were in the same situation as in the first and second. And that what was required of them in the first case was to act by the apparent sense of the command, slaughtering whatever beast they wished of those that fell under the name "cow." Likewise they saw that what was required of them in the second case was to act by the apparent sense of the command, slaughtering whatever beast they wished of those that fell under the name "cow," a middle-aged one, neither old nor young. They did not see that their ruling—when some cows were specified for them over others in the second case—had moved away from the requirement they had in the first case, namely acting by the apparent sense of the command, to specificity. In their unanimous agreement on what we have transmitted from them concerning this, together with the report we have transmitted from the Messenger of God ﷺ agreeing with their statement, there is clear evidence for the soundness of our view regarding generality and specificity, and that God's rulings in the verses of His Book, in what He commands and forbids, are general, unless something is specified that must be submitted to. And that if something from it is specified, what is specified from it is excluded from the ruling of the general verse, and the rest of the ruling of the verse remains on its general apparent sense. This also confirms the truth of what we have said on this, and it is a just witness against the corruption of the view of whoever opposed our view on it.

Some who were great in ignorance and intense in confusion claimed that the people asked Moses what they asked after God's command to them to slaughter a cow from among the cattle, because they thought they had been commanded to slaughter a particular cow singled out for that, just as the staff of Moses was singled out in its meaning, so they asked him to make it clear to them so they would recognize it.

Had this ignorant man reflected on his statement, what he found difficult to say would have been easy for him. For he considered it a grave matter that the people asked their Prophet what they asked, as a form of excessive strictness in their religion; then he attributed to them a matter even greater than what he rejected that they had done. He claimed that they believed it was permissible for God to impose an obligation upon them, and to require them to worship in a certain way, and then not make clear to them what He had obligated them to and required them to worship, until they asked for that to be made clear to them! Thus he attributed to God, exalted is His remembrance, what is not permissible to attribute to Him, and ascribed to the people an ignorance that is not ascribed even to madmen. He claimed that they were asking their Lord to impose obligations on them. So we seek refuge in God from confusion, and we ask Him for success and guidance.

* *

As for His words, "Indeed the cows are alike to us," "al-baqar" is the plural of "baqarah" (cow).

Some have read: ﴿Indeed the *al-bāqir* are alike to us﴾, and this, although it is permissible in speech since it occurs in the language and poetry of the Arabs, as Maymun ibn Qays said [meaning al-A'sha al-Kabir]:

*And what is his fault if the cattle (bāqir) refuse the water,*
*Yet they refuse the water only so that he may strike?*

[Diwan: 90; al-Hayawan 1: 19 (see also 1: 301, 6: 174); al-Lisan (th-w-r) and others. From a qasida he says to the Banu Qays ibn Sa'd, and about the estrangement that existed between him and them after friendship and affection. Before the verse: "I, and what you charged me with—and your Lord—/ so that he who has become more disobedient and more hostile may know."

"Like the bull, while the jinn strikes his back, / and what is his fault if they refuse the drink?"

Al-Jahiz said: "When they brought the cattle to water and they did not drink, either because the water was muddy or because they were not thirsty, they struck the bull so that he would plunge in, because the cattle follow him as the she-camels follow the stallion, and as the wild asses follow the male ass. They used to believe that the jinn were what turned the bulls away from the water, so the cattle would hold back from drinking until they perished... It is as if he said: if he is always struck because they refused the water, then it is as if they only refused the water so that he would be struck."]

And as Umayyah said [meaning Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt]:

*And they drive the cattle (bāqr) of the plain to the mountain, / emaciated, lest they perish.*

[Diwan: 35; al-Hayawan 4: 467; al-Azminah wa'l-Amkinah 2: 124, and others. In the printed original: "bāqir al-tawd lil-sahl," but the Diwan and al-Hayawan have "bāqiran yaṭrud al-sahl," and the correct reading is what I have set down from al-Azminah. al-Jahiz said in mentioning the fires of the Arabs: "Another fire: the fire by which they sought rain in the first Jahiliyyah. When years of drought followed them in succession, and calamity settled on them, and dearth grew severe, and they needed rain, they gathered together and gathered what cattle they could, then tied in their tails and between their hocks bundles of brushwood, then they climbed with them onto a rugged mountain and lit fires in them, and they cried out in supplication and humility, and they believed that this was among the causes of watering." Ibn al-Kalbi said: "They would kindle fires as an omen for lightning." "Al-mahazil" is the plural of "mahzul" (emaciated), like "hazil," whose plural is "hazla," meaning one who has become extremely weak and whose fat has gone. "Tabur": to perish.]

— So it is not permissible to read it that way, because it contradicts the reading that came with the proof, transmitted by those who, in what they transmitted, are unanimously agreed, cannot be subject to error, forgetfulness, or lying.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 70 (part 2 of 2):

As for the interpretation of ﴿tashabaha ʿalayna﴾ (﴿it has become confused to us﴾), it means: it has been made ambiguous (iltabasa) for us. The readers (qurra') differ in its recitation. Some of them used to recite it as "tashabaha ʿalayna" with the shin lightened and the ha' in the accusative, in the pattern of "tafaʿala," and they made the verb masculine, even though "al-baqar" (the cattle) is a collective noun. This is because it is a habit of the Arabs to make masculine every verb whose singular form takes a ha' (ta' marbuta) and whose plural form drops the ha', and to make it feminine as well (wa-ta'nithuhu), just as Allah the Exalted said of its counterpart in the masculine: ﴿as if they were trunks of hollowed-out palm trees﴾ [al-Qamar 54:20], where He used "munqaʿir" (uprooted), which describes palm trees, in the masculine because the word "al-nakhl" (palm trees) is masculine in form. And He said in another place: ﴿as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:7], where He made "khawiyah" (hollow) feminine, though it describes "al-nakhl," in agreement with the meaning of "al-nakhl." Although it has the form of a masculine singular, as we described earlier, it is the plural of "nakhlah" (a single palm tree).

* *

Others used to recite it as ﴿inna al-baqara tashshabahu ʿalayna﴾ (﴿indeed the cattle have become confused to us﴾) with the shin doubled and the ha' in the nominative, so that the verb is feminine, agreeing with the feminine sense of "al-baqar." They add to the beginning of "tashabaha" a taʾ indicating its feminine form, then the second taʾ is assimilated into the shin of "tashabaha" because their articulation points are close, so it becomes a doubled shin, and the ha' is raised because the verb is in the imperfect (al-istiqbal) and free of the jussive and subjunctive particles.

* *

Others used to recite it as ﴿inna al-baqara yashshabahu ʿalayna﴾, so that "yashabihu" takes the form of a report about a masculine subject, for the reason we mentioned in the reading of the one who recited "tashabaha" with the lightened shin and the ha' in the accusative. Except that he raised it with the yaʾ which he prefixes to the beginning of "tashabaha," which denotes the imperfect, and he assimilated the taʾ into the shin, as the reader did in "tashabaha" with the taʾ and the doubling.

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The correct recitation in this matter, in our view, is ﴿inna al-baqara tashabaha ʿalayna﴾, with the shin of "tashabaha" lightened and its ha' in the accusative, in the sense of "tafaʿala," because the authoritative consensus of the readers agrees on its correctness and on rejecting what differs from it. The proof is not to be contradicted by the statement of someone who is liable to error, forgetfulness and mistake in what is transmitted.

* *

As for His saying ﴿wa-inna in shaʾa Allahu la-muhtadun﴾ (﴿and indeed, if Allah wills, we will be guided﴾), they meant: and indeed, if Allah wills, He will make clear to us what has become confused and ambiguous to us about the matter of the cow that we were commanded to slaughter. The meaning of their "being guided" (ihtidaʾ) in this context is the meaning of "being made clear" (tabayyun), i.e., that which was incumbent upon them to slaughter as distinct from the other kinds of cattle. [That is, this is from their saying: "hadahu," meaning he made it clear to him; and from it the saying of Allah the Exalted: "As for Thamud, We guided them," meaning We made clear to them the path of guidance.]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 71 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: Indeed, He says it is a cow neither broken to plow the earth nor to water the tilth﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of this is: Moses said, "Indeed Allah says that the cow which I commanded you to slaughter is a cow neither broken [to labour]."

By His saying ﴿neither broken﴾ He means: not made docile by work. So the meaning of the verse is: it is a cow that has not been made docile by plowing the earth with its hooves, nor by drawing water on it to irrigate the crops. [[sanaytu al-naqa yasnu; wa sana al-rajul yasnu sanwan wa sanaya: if he irrigated the land. Al-saniya is the water-carrying animal, that is, the camel or other animal by which crops are watered, and its plural is al-sawani.]] Just as one says of a beast that has been made docile by riding or work: "a docile beast, clearly docile," with the dhal vowelled with a kasra.
