Among faith in Him is the affirmation that there is no god but God. Likewise, among His covenant which He made with them is that whoever comes to God on the Day of Resurrection with a proof that will be his salvation from the Fire, He will save him from it. All of that, though the wording of those who say it differs, is in agreement in meaning, according to what we have said concerning it. And God, the Exalted, knows best.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 81:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾

Abu Ja'far said: His words, ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾, are a refutation by God of the Jewish speakers who said: ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾, and an announcement from Him to them that He punishes whoever associates others with Him and disbelieves in Him and His messengers, and whose sins encompass him; so he is eternal in the Fire, for Paradise is not inhabited except by the people of faith in Him and His Messenger, the people of obedience to Him, and those who keep His limits. As follows:

1420 - Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad narrated to me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr or 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him﴾. That is: whoever does the like of your deeds and disbelieves in the like of what you disbelieved in, until his disbelief encompasses whatever good he has; those are the companions of the Fire, therein they will abide eternally.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for ﴿Yes (bala)﴾, it is an affirmation in every statement that begins with a denial, just as "naam" (yes) is an affirmation in a question that contains no denial. Its origin is "bal" (rather), which is a retraction from pure denial, as in your saying: "'Amr did not stand; rather, Zayd [did]." The letter "ya'" was added to it so that pausing on it would be proper, since "bal" is not suitable for pausing, being a conjunction and a retraction from denial. And so that "bala" – I mean – would be a retraction from denial only, and an affirmation of the act that follows the denial; the "ya'" in it indicates the meaning of affirmation and granting. [[Al-in'am: confirmation. It is said: an'ama, meaning he answered with his saying "na'am" (yes), and it is confirmation.]] And the word "bal" indicates retraction from denial. [[See Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 52-53, where al-Tabari counted the final letter of "bala" as a "ya'", while al-Farra' counted it as an "alif".]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for the "evil deed" (sayyi'ah) that God mentions in this place, it is associating partners with God. As follows:

1421 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Sufyan, saying: 'Asim narrated to me, from Abu Wa'il: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾, he said: Associating partners with God.

1422 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾, [meaning] polytheism.

1423 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

1424 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, his words: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾, he said: As for the evil deed, it is polytheism.

1425 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, the like of it.

1426 - Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾, as for the evil deed, it is the sins for which the Fire has been promised.

1427 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to 'Ata': ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾. He said: Polytheism. Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid said: ﴿evil deed﴾ [means] polytheism.

1428 - I was told from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', his words: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾, meaning: polytheism.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We have only said that the "evil deed" – whose earner, God, may He be exalted, mentioned, and whose sin encompasses him, is among the people of the Fire who abide therein eternally – in this place, God meant by it only some evil deeds and not others, although its apparent meaning in the recitation is general, because God has decreed for its people eternity in the Fire. Eternity in the Fire belongs to the people of disbelief in God and not to the people of faith in Him, due to the abundance of reports from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that the people of faith will not abide therein, and that eternity in the Fire belongs to the people of disbelief in God and not to the people of faith. For God, may He be exalted, has joined, in His words: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him, those are the companions of the Fire, therein they will abide eternally﴾ – to His words – ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds, those are the companions of Paradise, therein they will abide eternally﴾. So it was thereby known that those who have eternity in the Fire from among the people of evil deeds are other than those who have eternity in Paradise from among the people of faith.

* *

If someone supposes that those who have eternity in Paradise from among those who believe are those who did righteous deeds, not those who did evil deeds, then in God's announcement that He expiates our evil deeds through our avoidance of the major sins of what we are forbidden, and our entering the noble entrance, there is what indicates the soundness of what we have said regarding the interpretation of His words: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾, that it refers to a particular category of evil deeds and not to all of them.

* *

If someone says to us: God, may He be exalted, has only guaranteed us the expiation of our evil deeds through avoiding the major sins of what we are forbidden, so what is the evidence that major sins are not included in His words: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾?

It is said: Since it is established that minor sins are not included in it, and that what is meant by the verse is particular and not general, it is established and confirmed that judgment and ruling by it is not permissible for anyone against anyone, except against one whom God has informed of it by proof from a decisive report that excuses the one who has received it. It is established and confirmed that God, may He be exalted and remembered, meant by it the people of polytheism and disbelief in Him, by the testimony of the whole community. It is therefore necessary to judge that the people of polytheism and disbelief are among those whom God meant by the verse. As for the people of major sins, the decisive reports that excuse one who has received them have been widely attested to us as indicating that they are not meant by it. Whoever denies this – among those who contest the proof of the abundant reports and the widespread accounts – it is necessary for him to abandon firmly testifying against the people of major sins that they abide eternally in the Fire, on the basis of this verse and its counterparts, which came in general terms regarding them in the threat. For the interpretation of the Qur'an is not attained except through the clarification of the one to whom God has entrusted the clarifying of the Qur'an, and the verse may come general in the category of its apparent meaning, while being particular in that category in its inner meaning. [[See the explanation of "the apparent and the inner" above: 2: 15 and references.]]

The defenders of the report are asked – that the people of major sins are among the people of exception – the same question we ask those who deny the stoning of the married adulterer and the removal of the obligation of prayer from a menstruating woman during menstruation. For the question against them is the same as the question against these, equally. [[This is a response to the Mu'tazilah, in their obligation that the people of faith abide eternally in the Fire. Stoning of the married adulterer and the removal of the obligation of prayer from a menstruating woman during menstruation are among what came in reports, and no Qur'anic text was revealed concerning them.]]

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may He be exalted and praised: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, he means: it gathered upon him, so that he died upon it, before repenting and turning back from it.

* *

The original meaning of "encompassing a thing" is surrounding it, like the "wall" by which a house is surrounded, so that it encircles it. From this is God's, may He be exalted and praised, saying: ﴿A Fire whose enclosure surrounds them﴾ [al-Kahf: 29].

* *

The interpretation of the verse therefore is: whoever associates partners with God and commits many sins, dying upon them before repenting and turning back, those are the companions of the Fire, therein they will abide eternally forever. The commentators have said in accordance with what we have said regarding its interpretation.

Those who said so:

1429 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, he said: He died in his sin.

1430 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Jarir ibn Nuh narrated to us, saying: al-A'mash narrated to us, from Abu Razin, from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, he said: He died upon it.

[[The report 1430 – al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym al-Thawri al-Kufi: one of the senior and best of the Successors, trustworthy, about whom one does not ask the like. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir of al-Bukhari 2/1/246, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/459. His father "Khuthaym," with a dammed initial kha' and a diminutive form, as vocalized by Ibn Duraid in al-Ishtiqaq: 112-113, and by al-Hafiz in al-Taqrib; in the printed edition it appears as "Khaythim" with the ya' before the tha', and that is how the author of al-Khulasah vocalized it. It is a plain error.]]

1431 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq informed me, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad narrated to me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr or 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, he said: His disbelief encompasses whatever good he has.

1432 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to me, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, he said: That for which God has made the Fire obligatory.

1433 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, he said: As for the sin, it is the obligating major sin.

1434 - al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us [saying: Ma'mar informed us], from Qatadah: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, he said: The sin: the major sins.

1435 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Waki' and Yahya ibn Adam narrated to us, from Salam ibn Miskin, who said: A man asked al-Hasan about His words: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾. He said: We do not know what the sin is, my son. Recite the Qur'an; every verse in which God has promised the Fire, that is the sin.

1436 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid regarding His words: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him﴾, he said: Every sin that encompasses is that for which God has promised the Fire.

1437 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Razin: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, he said: He died in his sin.

1438 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: al-A'mash narrated to us, saying: Mas'ud Abu Razin narrated to us, from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym regarding His words: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, he said: It is the one who dies upon his sin before repenting.

1439 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Waki' said: I heard al-A'mash say regarding His words: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾: he died in his sins.

1440 - I was told from 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, the obligating major sin.

1441 - Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, so he died without repenting.

1442 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hassan narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to 'Ata': ﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾. He said: Polytheism, then he recited: ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾ [al-Naml: 90]. [[See what passed in his discussion of "khati'ah" in this volume 2: 110.]]

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide eternally (81)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may He be exalted and praised: "Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide eternally", he means: those who earned evil deeds and whose sins encompassed them are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide eternally.

* *

By His words, may He be exalted and praised: ﴿companions of the Fire﴾, he means: the people of the Fire. He made them its companions because of their preference, in their worldly life, for what brings them to it and to its blaze, over the deeds that bring them to Paradise. So He, may His remembrance be exalted, made them its companions, because of their preferring its causes over the causes of Paradise, just as the companion of a man is one who keeps company with him, preferring his company over the company of others, until he is known by it.

* *

﴿Therein they are﴾, meaning: they are in the Fire, abiding eternally. By His words ﴿abiding eternally﴾ he means: remaining. As follows:

1443 - Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to me, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad narrated to me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr or 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿Therein they are abiding eternally﴾, that is, abiding forever.

1444 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿Therein they are abiding eternally﴾, they will not come out of it forever.

**The interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds—they are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally﴾ (2:82)**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words ﴿those who believe﴾ He means: those who affirmed the truth of what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. By His words ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ He means: they obeyed Allah, upheld His limits, performed His obligations, and avoided His prohibitions. By His words ﴿Those﴾ He means: those who are like this, ﴿are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally﴾, meaning: its people, who are its people, will remain therein ﴿eternally﴾, dwelling forever.

* *

This verse and the one before it are a report from Allah to His servants concerning the permanence of the Fire and the permanence of its people within it, [and the permanence of Paradise and the permanence of its people within it].¹ and the lasting of what has been prepared in each of them for its people. It is a refutation by Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, of those among the Jews of the Children of Israel who said: "The Fire will not touch us except for a few counted days," and that they would afterward go on to Paradise. So He informed them of the eternal abiding of their disbelievers in the Fire and the eternal abiding of their believers in Paradise, as follows:

1445 – Ibn Humayd related to me, he said: Salamah related to us, he said: Ibn Ishaq related to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad related to me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr or 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds—they are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally﴾: that is, whoever believed in what you disbelieved in, and acted upon what you abandoned of his religion, for them is Paradise, abiding therein eternally. He informs them that the reward for good and evil remains upon its people forever, with no cessation of it ever.

1446 – Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions—﴿they are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally﴾.

¹ The words between the brackets are an addition that is necessary for the flow of the discourse.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 83 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship none but Allah"﴾

Abu Ja'far said: We have already shown, earlier in this book of ours, that "al-mithaq" (the covenant) is of the pattern "mif'al," derived from "making a solemn pledge" (tawthuq bi'l-yamin) and similar matters that confirm a statement. [See what preceded, 1:414, and this part, 2:156.] So the meaning of the statement is: "And remember also, O assembly of the Children of Israel, when We took your covenant: you shall worship none but Allah," as follows:

1447 - Ibn Humayd narrated to me, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad narrated to me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr or Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ — that is, your covenant — ﴿"Worship none but Allah"﴾.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The readers differ in the reading of His saying ﴿tabudun﴾ [ta'budun, "you worship"]. Some read it with the "ta" (second person), and some read it with the "ya" (third person), and the meaning in that is one. The reading with "ya" and "ta," and saying ﴿la ta'budun﴾ and ﴿la ya'budun﴾ [they worship], while they are absent (ghayb, plural of ghā'ib, "absent," like khadim and khadam), is permissible because the taking of the covenant means causing someone to swear an oath. Just as you say, "I made your brother swear that he would stand up," and you report about him what you report about an absent person because he is absent from you; and you say, "I made him swear that you would stand up," and you report about him what you report about the addressee, because you had addressed him with that — so that is correct and permissible.

Likewise His saying: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship none but Allah"﴾ and ﴿ya'budun﴾ [they worship]. Whoever reads it with "ta" — the meaning is address, since the address had indeed been made with that. And whoever reads it with "ya" — it is because they were not being addressed with that at the time of the report about them.

* *

As for the case of ﴿la ta'budun﴾ being in the nominative, it is by the "ta" in "ta'budun," and it is not in the accusative governed by "an" (that), which could enter upon ﴿la ta'budun illa Allah﴾. For when its entering upon a verb is valid, but it is omitted and does not enter, the proper construction in it is the nominative, as His, may His praise be exalted, said: ﴿Say: "Is it other than Allah that you order me to worship, O ignorant ones?"﴾ [al-Zumar: 64], where "a'budu" is in the nominative since "an" did not enter it — with the alif indicating the sense of the future; and as the poet said:

Are you my blamer, that I should attend the battle,
and that I should witness pleasures? Will you make me immortal?

[The poet is Tarafah ibn al-'Abd. Diwan: 317 (Ash'ar al-Sitta al-Jahiliyyin), from his precious mu'allaqah; it will come at 21:22 / 30:130 (Bulaq), and Sibawayh 1:452.]

So "uhdur" is in the nominative, though "an" could enter it — since it was omitted, with the alif that comes to mean the future.

The omission of "an" from His saying ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship..."﴾ is valid because of what appeared in the statement indicating it, so he dispensed, by the indication of the apparent, from it. [See the Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:53–54.]

* *

Some grammarians of Basra said: the meaning of His saying ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship none but Allah"﴾ is a quotation (hikayah), as if you said: "We made them swear: 'By Allah, you shall not worship,'" that is, "We said to them: 'By Allah, you shall not worship'" — and they said: "By Allah, they shall not worship." What he said of that is close in meaning to the view we have stated on it.

In the manner of what we have said regarding His saying ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship none but Allah"﴾, the people of interpretation have interpreted it.

Those who said that:

1448 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah: He took their covenants that they should be sincere to Him, and that they should not worship other than Him.

1449 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far informed us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His saying: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship none but Allah"﴾, he said: We took their covenant that they should be sincere to Allah and not worship other than Him.

1450 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship none but Allah"﴾, he said: The covenant which was taken from them in al-Ma'idah. [His saying, exalted be He, in Surat al-Ma'idah: 12: "Allah had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve leaders" to the end of the verse.]

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And to parents, good treatment﴾

Abu Ja'far said: His, may His praise be exalted, saying ﴿And to parents, good treatment﴾ is a conjunction upon the position of the omitted "an" in ﴿la ta'budun illa Allah﴾. So the meaning of the statement was: "And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel, that you should worship none but Allah, and [that you should show] good treatment to parents." So ﴿la ta'budun﴾ is in the nominative because "an" was omitted; then "bil-walidayni" is conjoined upon its position, as the poet said: [ 'Uqaybah ibn Hubayrah al-Asadi, from the pre-Islamic and Islamic periods.]

Mu'awiyah, we are but human, so be lenient,
for we are not mountains nor iron.

[Sibawayh 1:34, 375, 448; al-Khizanah 1:343; Simt al-La'ali: 149, which contains good verification. This verse is one in which Sibawayh erred. 'Uqaybah had come as a delegation to Mu'awiyah and handed him a paper containing these verses:
Mu'awiyah, we are but human, so be lenient,
for we are not mountains nor iron.
So consider it a nation that has perished in ruin,
whose ruler is Yazid and Abu Yazid.
You have eaten our land and stripped it bare,
so is there any standing crop or harvest?
Leave the treacherous ones of the caliphate and set things straight,
and the appointing of the base and the slaves.
Give us equal treatment, lest your armies be met
by armies following armies.
Mu'awiyah summoned him and said: "How bold you are against me!" He said: "I advised you when they deceived you, and I was truthful to you when they lied to you." Mu'awiyah said: "I do not think you are anything but truthful."]

So "al-hadid" is put in the accusative by conjunction upon the position of "al-jibal," for had it not been for the preposition "ba'" in it, it would have been in the accusative; so "al-hadid" was conjoined upon the meaning of "al-jibal," not its wording. Likewise what I described of His saying ﴿And to parents, good treatment﴾.

* *

As for "al-ihsan" (good treatment), it is in the accusative by a hidden verb whose sense is conveyed by His saying ﴿and to parents﴾, since its meaning is understood. So the meaning of the statement, were the omitted element made explicit, would be: "And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel, that you should worship none but Allah, and that you should do good to parents with good treatment." He dispensed with His saying ﴿and to parents﴾ from saying "and that you should do good to parents with good treatment," since that its meaning is understood by what appeared in the statement.

* *

Some of the people of Arabic grammar claimed regarding this that its meaning is: "and to parents, so do good, good treatment," making the "ba'" in "al-walidayn" a complement of the verb "ihsan," placed before it.

* *

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: "that you should worship none but Allah, and do good to parents with good treatment." They claimed that the "ba'" in "al-walidayn" is a complement of the omitted element, namely "ahsanu" (do good), and so they made it two statements. But the statement is only turned toward what they claimed when there is no coherent way for the statement to be consistent as one statement. As for when the statement has an understood way of being consistent as one statement, there is no reason to turn it into two statements. Furthermore: if the matter were as they said, it would be said "wa ila al-walidayni ihsanan" (and to parents, good treatment), for one says "Fulan did good to his parents" (ahsana ila walidayhi), and one does not say "ahsana bi-walidayhi" except in a forced usage of speech.

But the matter is as we have said, namely: "And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel with such-and-such, and [with] to parents, good treatment" — as we explained before. So "wa-l-ihsan" (and the good treatment) is then an infinitive from the sense of the statement, not from its wording, as we explained earlier regarding its parallels. [See what preceded, 1:138.]

* *

If a sayer says: "And what is that 'good treatment' which was taken from them, and the covenant regarding parents?" It is said: the like of what Allah has made obligatory upon our community for them, of doing kindness to them, speaking gently, lowering the wing of humility out of mercy toward them, showing tenderness toward them, compassion for them, supplicating for good for them, and similar acts which Allah has urged His servants to do toward them.

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And to the near of kin, the orphans, and the needy﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying ﴿and to the near of kin﴾, and by "the near of kin," he means that they should join their relatives, their kin.

* *

"Al-qurba" (kinship) is a verbal noun on the pattern "fu'la," from your saying, "The kinship of so-and-so's relative has become near to me in kinship (qarabah), nearness (qurba) and closeness (qurban)," with one meaning.

* *

As for "al-yatama," they are the plural of "yatim" (orphan), like "asir" and "asara" (captive, captives). Both males and females among them are included in "al-yatama."

* *

The meaning of that is: "And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: that you shall worship none but Allah alone, apart from any rivals besides Him; and to parents, good treatment; and to the near of kin: that you join their kinship and recognize their right; and to orphans: that you show them compassion and tenderness; and to the needy: that you give them their rights which Allah has obligated upon your wealth."

* *

"Al-miskin" (the needy) is the one who is humbled and abased by poverty and need, and it is on the pattern "mif'il" from "miskanah" (humble state). "Miskanah" is the abasement of need and poverty. [See what preceded in this part, 2:137.]

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And speak to people good words﴾

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says: "How is it said ﴿And speak to people good words﴾, bringing the statement as a command when nothing preceded it as a command, rather the statement from the beginning of the verse proceeds in the manner of a report?" It is said: the statement, although it proceeded at the beginning of the verse in the manner of a report, is something in whose place the address by command and prohibition is fitting. For if, in place of "la ta'budun illa Allah" [you worship none but Allah], it had been "la ta'budu illa Allah" [worship none but Allah] — in the form of a prohibition from Allah to them against worshipping other than Him — it would have been fitting and correct. It has been mentioned that this is so in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b. And it was fitting and permissible — if it were recited thus — because the taking of the covenant is a saying.

So the meaning of the statement, were it recited thus, would be: "And when We said to the Children of Israel: 'Worship none but Allah,'" as He, may His praise be exalted, said in another place: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mountain above you: "Take what We have given you with strength"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]. Since it was fitting to place the command and prohibition in the position of ﴿la ta'budun illa Allah﴾, it was conjoined by His saying ﴿And speak to people good words﴾ upon the position of ﴿la ta'budun﴾, even though each of them differs in meaning from what is in the other, due to what we described regarding the permissibility of placing address by command and prohibition in the position of "la ta'budun." So it is as if it were said: "And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: 'Worship none but Allah, and speak to people good words.'" This is like what we previously explained: that the Arabs sometimes begin a statement in the form of a report about the absent in the place of narration of what was reported, then return to the report in the form of address; and sometimes begin in the form of address, then return to report in the form of reporting about the absent, because of the two meanings in the narration, as the poet said: [This is Kuthayyir 'Azzah.]

Treat us ill or treat us well — no blamer
is ours, nor one who is despised if she turns away.

That is, "taqallat" (she turned away).

* *

As for "al-husn" (good), the readers differed in its reading. The majority of the readers of Kufa, except 'Asim, read ﴿wa-qulu li'l-nasi hasanan﴾ with a fatha on the ha and the sin. The majority of the readers of Madinah read ﴿husnan﴾ with a damma on the ha and sukun on the sin. And it has been related from some readers that he used to read "wa-qulu li'l-nasi 'husna'" on the pattern "fu'la."

* *

The people of Arabic grammar differed regarding the distinction between the meaning of "husnan" and "hasanan." Some Basran grammarians said: it is on one of two aspects: either "al-hasan" is meant as "al-husn," and both are dialects, as it is said "al-bukhl" and "al-bakhl" (stinginess); or "al-husn" is made to be "al-hasan" in the sense of comparison. This is because "al-husn" is a verbal noun, while "al-hasan" is the good thing. In that case it would be like your saying: "You are nothing but eating and drinking," and as the poet said: [It is said to be 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib al-Zubaydi. (al-Khizanah 4:56). It is not in his qasidah of this meter in al-Asma'iyyat: 43, but it occurs in Nawadir Abi Zayd: 149–150 as belonging to 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib. So it seems to be his, and it seems to have dropped from al-Asma'i's transmission, though it is in others'.]

And horses have advanced toward horses,
their greeting among them is a painful blow.

[Nawadir Abi Zayd: 150; Sibawayh 1:365, 429; al-Khizanah 4:53; and others.]

So he made "greeting" (tahiyyah) a blow.

Another said: rather, "al-husn" is the general name comprising all meanings of goodness, and "al-hasan" is a part of the meanings of "al-husn." He said: for this reason, when He, may His praise be exalted, enjoined regarding parents, He said: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man regarding his parents, goodness (husnan)﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 8], meaning that He enjoined him regarding both of them with all the meanings of goodness; and He commanded regarding the rest of people with some of what He commanded regarding his parents, saying: ﴿And speak to people good words (hasanan)﴾, meaning by that some of the meanings of goodness.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: What this speaker said regarding the meaning of "al-hasan" with damma on the ha and sukun on the sin is not far from the truth, and that it is a name for its kind which is named by it. As for "al-hasan," it is an attribute applied to what is described by it, and that occurs with a particular thing. Since this is so, the correct reading in His saying ﴿wa-qulu li'l-nasi hasanan﴾ — because the people were commanded, in this covenant, when it was said to them "and speak to people" — is to use the good (hasan) of speech, rather than the other meanings of goodness which occur without speech. That is an attribute of a particular meaning of goodness, namely speech. Therefore I chose its reading with a fatha on the ha and the sin over its reading with a damma on the ha and sukun on the sin.

* *

As for the one who read it "wa-qulu li'l-nasi husna," he, by his reading thus, opposed the reading of the people of Islam. It is sufficient as evidence of the error of reading it thus that it departs from the reading of the people of Islam, even if there were no other evidence of its error. How much more so when it is also outside what is known of Arabic speech! For the Arabs hardly ever speak "fu'la" and "af'al" except with the definite article or with a genitive construction. It is not said "jaa'ani ahsan" (a better one came to me) until they say "al-ahsan" (the best). Nor is it said "ajmal" until they say "al-ajmal." For "af'al" and "fu'la" are hardly found as attributes except for a known, recognized referent, as you say: "Rather, your brother is the best (al-ahsan)," and "rather, your sister is the most beautiful (al-husna)." And it is not permissible to say: "a woman, husna" (most beautiful), or "a man, ahsan" (best).

* *

As for the interpretation of the good saying which Allah commanded those whose affair He described from the Children of Israel in this verse to say to people: it is what:

1451 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Bishr ibn 'Umarah, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And speak to people good words﴾: He commanded them also after this creation: that they say to people good words: that they command whoever has not said "la ilaha illa Allah" and has turned away from it, to say it until they say it as they said it, for that is a means of nearness to Allah, may His praise be exalted. And al-Hasan also said: gentle speech is from good manners, the beautiful character and noble disposition, and it is something Allah approves and loves.

1452 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah: ﴿And speak to people good words﴾, he said: say to people what is customary and kind.

1453 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj: ﴿And speak to people good words﴾, he said: truthfulness regarding the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ).

1454 - And it was reported to me from Yazid ibn Harun, who said: I heard Sufyan al-Thawri say regarding His saying ﴿And speak to people good words﴾: command them with what is right and forbid them from what is wrong. [The report 1454: I fear that something may have fallen from its chain of narration.]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 83 (part 2 of 2):

1455 - Harun ibn Idris al-Asamm narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad al-Muharibi narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I asked 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah about the words of Allah, may His praise be exalted: ﴿And speak to people good [words]﴾. He said: Whoever you meet from among the people, say to him good speech. He said: I also asked Abu Ja'far, and he said the same. [[The report: 1455 - Harun ibn Idris al-Asamm, a shaykh of al-Tabari: I have not found a biography for him, nor have I found him anywhere except in al-Tabari's narration from him in the History as well, 1: 253, and 2: 126. He narrated from him, from al-Muharibi. 'Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman: he is al-'Arzami, one of the trustworthy and memorizing imams. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, and in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/366-368.]]

1456 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Malik informed us, from Abu Ja'far and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, regarding His words: ﴿And speak to people good [words]﴾. He said: To people, all of them.

1457 - Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Malik informed us, from 'Ata', the like of it.

* *

The discussion of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And establish prayer﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words ﴿And establish prayer﴾, He means: perform it with its obligatory rights upon you in it, as:

1458 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Bishr ibn 'Ammara, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: ﴿And establish prayer﴾: this, and "the establishment of prayer" is the completion of bowing, prostration, recitation, humility, and devotion to it within it. [[See what has passed: 1: 241, 573.]]

* *

The discussion of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And give zakat﴾

Abu Ja'far said: We have already explained earlier the meaning of "zakat" and what its origin is. [[See what has passed: 1: 573-574.]]

* *

As for the zakat which Allah commanded the Children of Israel, whose matter is mentioned in this verse, it is what:

1459 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us with it, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Bishr ibn 'Ammara, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And give zakat﴾, he said: The giving of zakat is what Allah had made obligatory upon them regarding their wealth of zakat, and it was a sunnah that they had, other than the sunnah of Muhammad (ﷺ). The zakat of their wealth was an offering, a fire would descend upon it and consume it, and that was its acceptance. Whoever the fire did not do that to was not accepted, and what was offered was from an income that was not lawful: from injustice or deception, or taking by other than what Allah had commanded him and made clear to him.

1460 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And give zakat﴾, meaning by "zakat": obedience to Allah and sincerity.

* *

The discussion of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then you turned away, except for a few of you, and you were [habitually] refusing (83)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: This is a report from Allah, may His praise be exalted, about the Jews of the Children of Israel, that they broke His covenant and violated His pact, after Allah had taken their pledge to fulfill it to Him, by not worshipping other than Him, by being good to parents, by joining ties of kinship, by showing kindness to orphans, by giving the rights of the needy to them, by commanding the servants of Allah with what Allah had commanded them and urging them to obey Him, by establishing prayer with its limits and obligations, and by giving the zakat of their wealth. They opposed His command in all of that and turned away, refusing, except for those whom Allah protected from among them, who fulfilled to Allah His covenant and pact, as:

1461 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Bishr ibn 'Ammara, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, made obligatory upon them - meaning: upon those whose matter Allah described in His Book from the Children of Israel - this which He mentioned He had taken their covenant with, they turned away from it out of distaste and aversion to it, and sought what was light for them, except a few of them, and they are those whom Allah excepted when He said: ﴿Then you turned away﴾, meaning: you turned away from My obedience, ﴿except for a few of you﴾, he said: the few whom I have chosen for My obedience. My punishment will descend upon whoever turned away and refused it, meaning: abandoned it, considering it light. [[See the meaning of "tawalla" in what has passed in this part: 2: 162.]]

1462 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad narrated to me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, or from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿Then you turned away, except for a few of you, and you were [habitually] refusing﴾, i.e., you abandoned all of that.

* *

Some of them said: By His words ﴿and you were [habitually] refusing﴾, Allah, may His praise be exalted, meant the Jews who were in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and by the rest of the verse He meant their forefathers. It is as if he went to the meaning that the speech is: ﴿Then you turned away, except for a few of you﴾: then your predecessors turned away, except for a few of them, but He made it an address to the remnants of their descendants, as we have mentioned earlier. Then He said: "and you, O remnants of them, are also refusing from the covenant that was taken upon you by that, and abandoning it as your predecessors abandoned it."

* *

Others said: Rather, His words ﴿Then you turned away, except for a few of you, and you were [habitually] refusing﴾ are an address to those among the Jews of the Children of Israel who were present in the vicinity of the emigration of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a censure of them for breaking the covenant that was taken from them in the Torah, changing the command of Allah, and committing His disobedience.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 84:

The explanation of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And when We took your covenant: Do not shed your blood, and do not expel yourselves from your homes﴾

Abu Ja'far said: His words, ﴿And when We took your covenant: Do not shed your blood﴾, are in meaning and grammatical construction similar to His words: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: Do not worship except Allah﴾.

* *

As for "safk al-dam" (shedding blood), it means pouring it out and spilling it.

* *

If someone says: What is the meaning of His words, ﴿Do not shed your blood, and do not expel yourselves from your homes﴾? Did the people kill themselves and expel themselves from their homes, so that they were forbidden from that? It is said: The matter is not as you suppose; rather, they were forbidden from killing one another. So when a man among them killed another man, it was as if he killed himself, since their religion was one [and the two were], in status, like one man. As the Prophet ﷺ said: [[The words in parentheses are necessary, otherwise the sentence is corrupt.]]

1463 - "The believers in their mutual mercy, their compassion and their kindness towards one another are like one body: when one part of it complains, the rest of the body responds to it with wakefulness and fever."

[[Hadith 1463: al-Tabari narrated it in this form without a chain. Apparently he also related it by meaning. Its wording in Sahih Muslim 2:284, from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, is: "The likeness of the believers in their mutual affection, mercy and kindness is like the body: if one organ complains, the rest of the body responds to it with wakefulness and fever." It is likewise narrated in Musnad Ahmad (4:270, Halabi). Al-Bukhari narrated it with a similar meaning, 10:367 (Fath edition).]]

* *

It is also possible that the meaning of His words, ﴿Do not shed your blood﴾, is: a man among you should not kill another man among you, so that he is subjected to retaliation (qisas), and thereby he becomes one who kills himself, because he is the one who caused for himself that which made him deserve killing. Thus the killing by the victim's guardian in retaliation is attributed to him. It is like saying to a man who commits an act for which he deserves punishment and is punished: "You have brought this upon yourself."

* *

Those who interpret the verse have said things similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

1464 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And when We took your covenant: Do not shed your blood﴾, that is: none of you should kill another, ﴿and do not expel yourselves from your homes﴾, and your self, O son of Adam, is the people of your religion.

1465 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah regarding His words: ﴿And when We took your covenant: Do not shed your blood﴾, he says: none of you should kill another, ﴿and do not expel yourselves from your homes﴾, he says: none of you should expel another from the homes.

1466 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿Do not shed your blood﴾, he says: none of you should kill another without right, ﴿and do not expel yourselves from your homes﴾, so O son of Adam, you would be shedding the blood of the people of your religion and your call.

* *

The explanation of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then you affirmed﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, ﴿Then you affirmed﴾, He means: with the covenant that We took from you, that you would not shed your blood and would not expel yourselves from your homes, as:

1467 - al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah: ﴿Then you affirmed﴾, he says: you affirmed this covenant.

1468 - And I was told on the authority of Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the same.

* *

The explanation of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And you are witnesses﴾ (84)

Abu Ja'far said: The interpreters differed concerning whom the words ﴿And you are witnesses﴾ address. Some of them said: That is an address from Allah, the Exalted, to the Jews who were among the residents of Medina during the days of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ's migration to it, rebuking them for neglecting the rulings of what was in their hands of the Torah, whose judgments they used to acknowledge. So Allah, the Exalted, said to them: ﴿Then you affirmed﴾, meaning by that the affirmation of your forefathers and predecessors, ﴿and you are witnesses﴾ to their affirmation of the taking of the covenant upon them, that they would not shed their blood and would not expel themselves from their homes, and you attest that this is true from My covenant upon them. Among those from whom this view is related is Ibn Abbas.

1469 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad narrated to me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, or Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: ﴿And when We took your covenant: Do not shed your blood and do not expel yourselves from your homes. Then you affirmed and you are witnesses﴾, that this is true from My covenant upon you.

* *

Others said: Rather, that is a report from Allah, may His praise be exalted, about their forefathers, but He, may His remembrance be exalted, presented the report about them in the form of direct address, in the manner we described in the other verses that are similar to it, whose interpretation we have explained earlier. [[See what has passed: 2:298, note 2, and the references.]]

* *

They interpreted His words ﴿And you are witnesses﴾ to mean: and you are witnesses.

Mention of those who said that:

1470 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Adam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah, regarding His words: ﴿And you are witnesses﴾, he says: and you are witnesses.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the sayings in interpreting this, in my view, is that His words ﴿And you are witnesses﴾ are a report about their predecessors, and include among them those addressed who lived to see the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, just as His words ﴿And when We took your covenant﴾ are a report about their predecessors, even though it is an address to those who lived to see the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. [[In the printed edition: "bi-anna kana khitaban..." which does not make sense.]] Because Allah, the Exalted, took the covenant of those among the Children of Israel who were in the time of the Messenger of Allah Musa ﷺ, as He has clarified to us in His Book, and obligated all who came after them of their descendants to the rulings of the Torah, like the obligation imposed on those who were in the time of Musa among them. Then He rebuked those He addressed with these verses for breaking and for their predecessors' breaking that covenant, and for denying what they had pledged upon themselves of the covenants of fidelity, [[The sentence's order: "wa-takdhibuhum ma wakkadu min al-'uhud 'ala anfusihim bil-wafa' lahu", with transposition.]] by His words: ﴿Then you affirmed and you are witnesses﴾. Since it goes out in the form of address to those among them who were in the time of our Prophet ﷺ, it refers to every one of them who was bound by the covenant in the time of Musa and after him, and every one of them who testified to the confirmation of what is in the Torah. For Allah, may His praise be exalted, did not restrict by His words ﴿Then you affirmed and you are witnesses﴾, and similar verses, some of them over others. The verse is capable of meaning all of them. Since that is so, [[The printed edition reads "fa-in kana dhalika kadhalik" which is also incorrect.]] no one may claim that some of them specifically were meant over others. The same ruling applies to the following verse, namely His words: ﴿Then you, these are they who kill yourselves﴾, and so on, because it has been mentioned to us that their predecessors used to do of that what their latter ones did, those who lived in the era of our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

The interpretation of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Then you are those who kill yourselves and expel a group of your own people from their homes, supporting [their enemies] against them in sin and aggression﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The phrase ﴿Then you are these﴾ admits of two interpretations. The first is that it means: "Then you, O these people," and the "O" (ya) is omitted because the context indicates it, as in His words ﴿Joseph, turn away from this﴾ [Yusuf 29], whose meaning is "O Joseph, turn away from this." The meaning of the statement would then be: "Then you, O assembly of the Jews of the Children of Israel, after your acknowledgment of the covenant that I took from you, that you would not shed your own blood nor expel yourselves from your homes, and after your testimony against yourselves [that this is a binding right of Mine over you, obligatory for you to fulfil to Me], you kill yourselves and expel a group of you from their homes, supporting one another in expelling them, in sin and aggression." [In the printed edition: "then you acknowledged and after your testimony..." The waw has no place here.] [In the printed edition: "supporting one another against it in expelling you..." which is an error.]

* *

"Ta'awun" (cooperation) is "tazahur" (backing). The word "tazahur" was used for cooperation because each party strengthens the back of the other. It is a form of "tafa'ul" from "zahr" (back), meaning that they lean their backs against one another's backs for support. [In the printed edition: "And tazahur was said of cooperation..." which is nothing.]

* *

The second interpretation: its meaning is "Then you are a people who kill yourselves." It then refers back to the address "you" (antum). The words "these" (ha'ula') intervene between them and the predicate, as the Arabs say: "Anā dhā aqūmu" (I am this one standing) and "Anā hādhā ajlisu" (I am this one sitting). [In the printed edition: "If it were said: 'Anā hādhā ajlisu'..." The correct reading is what I have recorded.] When one says "Anā hādhā ajlisu," it is sound and permissible; likewise: "Anta dhāka taqūmu" (You are that one standing).

Some of the Basran grammarians claimed that His words "these" in ﴿Then you are these﴾ serve as an alert and emphasis for "you" (antum). They maintained that although "antum" is a pronoun for the collective addressees, "these" and "ulā'" may be used to emphasise it because it is a pronoun for the addressees, just as Khafaf ibn Nadbah said:

"I say to him while the spear bends his side: 'Know, Khafaf, that I am that one.'" [This was previously cited, vol. 1, p. 227.]

meaning: "I am this one." And as His words, may His praise be exalted, say: ﴿Until when you were in the ship and they sailed with them...﴾ [Yunus 22].

* *

The commentators then differed about who is meant by this verse, similar to their difference about who is meant by His words ﴿while you witness﴾. Here is the mention of the disputes on this:

1471 – Muhammad ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad related to me, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: ﴿Then you are these, killing yourselves and expelling a group of you from their homes, supporting [their enemies] against them in sin and aggression﴾, referring to the people of polytheism [in the Tafsir of Ibn Kathir, vol. 1, p. 223, and al-Durr al-Manthur, vol. 1, p. 86, read: "i.e., the people of polytheism." The correct reading is that in al-Tabari. His words "to the people of polytheism" mean: you expel a group of you to the people of polytheism], until you shed their blood along with them and expel them from their homes along with them. [In the printed edition: "then he said, Anbahum" and it is better to omit it.] He said: God informed them [of this] about their deed. [What is between the brackets is an addition that cannot be dispensed with. As for Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir, vol. 1, p. 223, he wrote: "God informed them of this about their deed," which is a distortion.] He had forbidden them in the Torah to shed their blood, and had made it obligatory upon them to ransom their captives. They were two groups: one group from Banu Qaynuqa', allies of the Khazraj, and al-Nadir and Qurayza, allies of the Aws. Whenever war broke out between the Aws and the Khazraj, Banu Qaynuqa' went out with the Khazraj, and al-Nadir and Qurayza went out with the Aws. Each of the two factions backed its allies against their brethren, until they shed one another's blood, while they held the Torah in their hands, knowing from it what was obligatory for them and what was lawful for them. The Aws and the Khazraj were people of polytheism who worshipped idols, [in the printed edition: "the people of polytheism," the correct reading is in Ibn Hisham's Sirah, vol. 2, p. 188, and Ibn Kathir, vol. 1, p. 224] who knew neither Paradise nor Hell, nor resurrection nor the Last Day, nor a scripture, nor the forbidden nor the lawful. When the war laid down its burdens, they ransomed their captives, in confirmation of what was in the Torah and in adherence to it, some of them from others. Banu Qaynuqa' would ransom whoever of their captives was in the hands of the Aws, and al-Nadir and Qurayza would ransom whoever of them was in the hands of the Khazraj. And they would waive the blood they had spilled, [tall damahu wa-atallahu: he rendered it void and nullified it,] and the slain whom they had killed among themselves, [in the printed edition: "and they killed those they killed," the correct reading from Ibn Hisham, vol. 2, p. 189,] as backing for the people of polytheism against them. God, may His remembrance be exalted, said when He informed them of that [in the printed edition: "informed them of that," the correct reading is what I have recorded from Ibn Hisham's Sirah, vol. 2, p. 189, and you will see this in the commentary on the verse itself later]: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ That is: you ransom it according to the ruling of the Torah, yet you kill it. And in the ruling of the Torah it is that one should not be killed, nor expelled from one's home, nor should anyone who associates others with God and worships idols besides Him back [their enemies] against him [in the printed edition: "from that," which is pure error] — seeking the goods of this worldly life.

It is in that [deed of theirs] with the Aws and the Khazraj — so I have been informed — that this account was revealed. [This last sentence is from Ibn Ishaq's words, not from Ibn Abbas's.]

1472 – Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad related to me, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿And when We took your covenant: that you shall not shed your blood nor expel yourselves from your homes; then you acknowledged it while you bore witness﴾. He said: God took from the Children of Israel in the Torah that none of them should kill another, and whatever slave or female slave of the Children of Israel you found, you should buy them with the price of their value and free them. [In the printed edition: "with what he offered of his hand, then free him," which is a grave corruption. One says: "The slave-girl was valued at a hundred dinars" (qāmat al-amatu mi'ata dinar), meaning her value reached a hundred dinars. And one says: "How much was your slave-girl valued at?" meaning, how much did she reach? And I found it in al-Baghawi's Tafsir, in the correct form: "with what was the price of its value," vol. 1, p. 224, in the margin of Ibn Kathir's Tafsir.] So Qurayza were allies of the Aws, and al-Nadir allies of the Khazraj, and they would fight in the war of Sumayr. [The war of Sumayr: it was in the pre-Islamic period between the Aws and the Khazraj. Sumayr was a man from Banu Amr ibn Awf. See the account of this war in al-Aghani, vol. 3, p. 18, 26.] Qurayza fought together with their allies, al-Nadir and their allies, and al-Nadir fought Qurayza and their allies, and they defeated them, ruined their houses, and expelled them from them. When a man of either of the two factions was taken captive, they gathered for him until they ransomed him. The Arabs reproached them for this and said: "How do you fight them and ransom them?" They said: "We were commanded to ransom them, and fighting them was forbidden to us." They said: "Then why do you fight them?" They said: "We are ashamed that our allies be humiliated." So when God, may He be mighty and majestic, reproached them, He said: ﴿Then you are these, killing yourselves and expelling a group of you from their homes, supporting [their enemies] against them in sin and aggression﴾.

1473 – Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: Qurayza and al-Nadir were two brothers, and they were in this position [al-mathaba: meaning the city of the Messenger of God, ﷺ; al-mathaba is the dwelling, because its people go about their affairs and then return to it, come back to it. God, may He be exalted, said: "And when We made the House a place of return (mathaba) for the people and a sanctuary"], and the Book was in their hands. The Aws and the Khazraj were two brothers, then they split, and Qurayza and al-Nadir split, so al-Nadir were with the Khazraj and Qurayza were with the Aws, and they fought. Some of them would kill others. So God, may His praise be exalted, said: ﴿Then you are these, killing yourselves and expelling a group of you from their homes﴾, the verse.

* *

Others said something different:

1474 – It was related to me by al-Muthanna, saying: Adam related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: Among the Children of Israel, when they found a people weak, they expelled them from their homes. The covenant had been taken from them that they should not shed their blood, nor expel themselves from their homes.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for "al-'udwan" (aggression), it is the verbal noun of "al-ta'addi" (transgression). It is said of it: "Fulan 'adā fī kadhā 'udwan wa-'udwānan, wa-i'tadā ya'tadī i'tidā'an" (So-and-so transgressed in such-and-such, a transgression), and that is when one exceeds one's limit in wrongdoing and oppression.

* *

The readers differed in the reading of ﴿tazāharūn﴾. [In the printed edition: "the readers differed," and I have returned it to al-Tabari's method.] Some of them read it "tazāharūn" on the pattern of "tafā'alūn," removing the extra letter, which is the final tā'. Others read it ﴿taẓẓāharūn﴾ with a shadda, in the sense of "tatazāharūn," but they assimilated the second tā' into the ẓā' because their articulation points are close, making them one doubled ẓā'. These two readings, although their wordings differ, agree in meaning. Whichever of them the reader recites is correct, because both are well-known dialects and widely transmitted readings in the cities of Islam with one meaning. Neither of them carries a meaning that merits preferring it over the other, except that someone who chooses the doubled "taẓẓāharūn" does so seeking completeness of the word.

* *

The interpretation of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while their expulsion is forbidden to you. Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His praise be exalted, ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾, He means the Jews. He reproaches them with this and makes them recognise the ugliness of the deeds they used to commit. He said to them: "Then you — after your acknowledgment of the covenant that I took from you, that you would not shed your blood nor expel yourselves from your homes — kill yourselves," meaning: some of you kill others, "and you — along with your killing of those of you whom you kill, when you find a captive from among you in the hands of others, your enemies — ransom him, while another of you expels some of you from their homes. Your killing of them and your expelling them from their homes is forbidden to you, and leaving them as captives in the hands of your enemy [is forbidden to you]," [the addition between the brackets is indispensable for the sentence to be sound]. "How do you permit yourselves to kill them, and do not permit yourselves to leave off ransoming them from their enemy? Or how do you not permit yourselves to leave off ransoming them, while you permit yourselves to kill them?" [In the printed edition: "and they are all alike" and the correct reading is what I have recorded.] "Both are equal in the ruling binding upon you concerning them, because what I have forbidden you — killing them and expelling them from their dwellings — is like what I have forbidden you — leaving them as captives in the hands of their enemy. Do you believe in part of the Book — in which I imposed My obligations upon you, and clarified My limits for you, and took from you a covenant to act upon what is in it — so that you affirm it, and ransom your captives from the hands of your enemy; and disbelieve in part of it, so that you deny it, and kill those whose killing I forbade you from among the people of your religion and your people, and expel them from their homes? Do you not know that your disbelief in part of it is a breaking by you of My covenant and My pact?" As follows:

1475 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: ﴿Then you are these, killing yourselves and expelling a group of you from their homes, supporting [their enemies] against them in sin and aggression. And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while their expulsion is forbidden to you. Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ [Do you believe in part of the Book, ransoming, and disbelieve in part, killing and expelling?]. [In the printed edition: "...and disbelieve in part, ransoming. By God, ransoming them is faith, and expelling them is disbelief." It is a disordered statement, so I added what is between the brackets as a reasoned supplement until the sentence is sound.] By God, ransoming them is faith, and expelling them is disbelief. So they would expel them from their homes, and when they saw them captive in the hands of their enemy, they would ransom them.

1476 – Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq related to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad related to me, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, or from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾ — you knew that this was obligatory upon you in your religion — ﴿while their expulsion is forbidden to you﴾ in your Book. ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ Do you ransom them, believing in that, and expel them, disbelieving in it?

1477 – Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾, meaning: If you find him in the hand of another, you ransom him, while you kill him with your own hand?

1478 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far said: Qatadah used to say concerning His words: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾: their expulsion was disbelief, and their ransoming was faith.

1479 – al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Adam related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah concerning His words: ﴿Then you are these, killing yourselves﴾, the verse. He said: Among the Children of Israel, when they found a people weak, they expelled them from their homes. The covenant had been taken from them that they should not shed their blood nor expel themselves from their homes, and the covenant had been taken from them: if some of them were captured, they should ransom them. So they expelled them from their homes, then ransomed them. Thus they believed in part of the Book and disbelieved in part: they believed in the ransom, so they ransomed, and they disbelieved in the expulsion from the homes, so they expelled.

1480 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Adam related to us, saying: Abu Ja'far related to us, saying: al-Rabi' ibn Anas related to us, saying: Abu al-'Aliyah informed me: that 'Abd Allah ibn Salam passed by the Exilarch (Ra's al-Jalut) in Kufa, while he was ransoming women whom the Arabs had not had intercourse with, and not ransoming those with whom the Arabs had had intercourse. 'Abd Allah ibn Salam said to him: "Indeed it is written in your book: 'Ransom them all.'"

1481 – al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij: ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part?﴾ He said: Their disbelief was killing and expulsion, and their faith was ransoming. Ibn Juraij said: He means: when they were with you, you killed them and expelled them from their homes, but when they were captured, you ransomed them? And it has reached me that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said concerning the story of the Children of Israel: "The Children of Israel have passed away, and you are the ones meant by this account."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The readers differed in the reading of His words: ﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾.

Some of them read: ﴿asra tafdūhum﴾ [ʼasrā tafdūhum]; some: ﴿ʼasārā tufādūhum﴾; some: ﴿ʼasārā tafdūhum﴾; and some: ﴿asra tufādūhum﴾.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for whoever reads ﴿And if they come to you as captives [asra]﴾, he intends the plural of "asīr" (captive), since it is on the pattern "fa'īl," like the plurals of names of people with afflictions whose singular comes on the measure "fa'īl." For the state of captivity is similar in meaning — in the harm and hardship that befall the captive — to some meanings of afflictions, and he attached the plural of what is attached to it to the plural of what we have described, so it is said: "asīr" and "asrā," just as one says: "marīḍ" and "marḍā" (sick), "kasīr" and "kasrā" (broken), "jarīḥ" and "jarḥā" (wounded).

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for those who read ﴿ʼasārā﴾, they gave it the form of the plural of "fa'lān," since the plural of "fa'lān" whose feminine is "fa'lā" may share the plural of "fa'īl," as they said: "sakārā and sakrā" (drunk), "kasālā and kaslā" (lazy). So they likened "asīr" — and pluralised it sometimes as "asārā" and other times as "asrā" — to that.

* *

Some of them claimed that the meaning of "al-asrā" differs from the meaning of "al-asārā," and claimed that the meaning of "al-asrā" is the surrender of a people without their being taken captive by one who takes them captive, and that the meaning of "al-asārā" is the state of a people who are captured in the hands of their captors through their capture and their being seized by force and conquest.

Abu Ja'far said: That is a view that has no intelligible basis in the language of any Arab. Rather, it is as I have described: the plural of "asīr" is sometimes on the pattern "fa'lā," for the reason I have explained, and sometimes on the pattern "fu'ālā," for what I have mentioned: their likening its plural to the plural of "sakrān" (drunk) and "kaslān" (lazy) and what is similar to that.

* *

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 85 (part 2 of 2):

The most correct reading in this matter is the reading of the one who recited ﴿And if they come to you as captives﴾, because the pattern *fa'ālā* as the plural of *fa'īl* is not widespread in the speech of the Arabs. Since this pattern is not widespread in their speech, while the plural of descriptive adjectives that denote afflictions and infirmities, whose singular is measured as *fa'īl* and whose plural is *fa'lā* (as we described earlier), is widespread and common among them, and since *al-asīr* (the captive) is one of these, it is necessary that it be assimilated to its counterparts and forms, so that its plural follows their plural rather than that of those that differ from them.
* *
As for the one who recited ﴿you ransom them﴾ (*tufādūhum*, with the reciprocal form), he intended: you ransom them from their captivity, and they ransom you, those whom they captured, with them, your captives from them.
* *
As for the one who recited it as ﴿you ransom them﴾ (*tafdūhum*, without the reciprocal form), he intended: you, O assembly of Jews, if those whom you expelled from their homes come to you as captives, you ransom them and rescue them.
This reading is more pleasing to me than the first, I mean ﴿captives you ransom﴾ [[In the printed edition: "أسرى تفدوهم" (asra tafdūhum), which is not the correct form, according to the reading that Abu Ja'far chose.]] because what is incumbent upon the Jews in their religion is the ransoming of their captives in every case, whether those who captured their captives ransomed them from them or did not ransom them.
* *
As for His saying: ﴿And it is forbidden for you to expel them﴾, in His saying ﴿And it﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: that it refers back to the expulsion mentioned earlier, as if He said: "And you expel a group of you from their homes, and their expulsion is forbidden for you." Then "the expulsion" that comes after "it is forbidden for you" is repeated as a repetition of "it," because a statement intervened between "the expulsion" and "it."
The second interpretation: that it is a *'imād* (a pronoun of separation). This is what the Basran grammarians called *ḍamīr al-faṣl* (the pronoun of separation); it is also called *di'āma* (support) and *ṣifa* (attribute). By his saying "the verb" here, he meant the derived noun that governs what follows it in the manner of a verb. His intent will become clear in the expressions that follow. Because the *wāw* that is with *huwa* requires a noun to follow it rather than a verb, when the verb was placed before the noun that the *wāw* requires to follow it, *huwa* was placed after the *wāw*, since it is a noun, as you say: "I came to you while he, your father, is standing," meaning: "while your father is standing," since the *wāw* requires a noun. So *huwa* was used as a support, since the verb preceded the noun, so that the sentence would be sound. [[Al-Farra' has fully covered all of this in *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* 1: 50-52.]] As the poet said:
So convey to Abu Yahya, when you meet him, [that] upon the she-camels, in whose armpits is dried sweat,
That the Salami who is in Dariyya, the commander of the protected pasture, has sold my right to the Banu 'Abs
For a garment, a dinar, a sheep, and a dirham. So is there, here, a head that is raised?" [[The second half of the last line will come at 11: 34 and 17: 73. I did not find this poetry except in *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* of al-Farra' 1: 52, and I did not know its composer. The *'īs* are white camels mixed with a slight reddish tint, and they are among the noblest camels. "Yabs" means dry. The sweat has dried in their armpits from the length of the journey. The Salami: he means a man who was, as I believe, a collector and agent for zakat, and commander of the protected pasture of Dariyya. I do not know his lineage, whether it is a tribe or a town. The protected pasture of Dariyya is in Najd, on the road from Basra to Mecca, and it is closer to Mecca; it is a good land mentioned in their poetry. In the verse there is *iqwā'* (a defect in the poetic rhyme).]]
[[The second half will come shortly: 374. His saying "for a garment" is connected to his earlier saying "sold." He says: he took these bribes that he enumerated from the Banu 'Abs, and handed over my right to them. As for his saying "So is there, here, a head that is raised?", he says it to Abu Yahya whom he mentioned, meaning: "Is there any helper who will help us and take our right, so that we may raise our heads after the injustice that has befallen us?" This is a phrase they say in such situations. Al-Ra'i said (*Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara'*: 442):
If I raise their heads with them, I lift them up, and if they meet the like of it in the future, they will corrupt.
A Bedouin said: "A youth like the light of the sun, not stingy with good, nor does he reproach the stingy;
Nor a speaker of foul speech that harms his companion, nor one who raises his head with a foul-speaking retort."
This expression also occurs in the chapter "The virtue of one who has knowledge and teaches" in the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) (al-Bukhari 1: 23): "That is the likeness of one who has understanding in the religion of God and benefits from what God sent me with, so he knows and teaches; and the likeness of one who does not raise his head with that and does not accept the guidance of God with which I was sent."]]
Thus *hal* (is there) was followed by *huwa* because it requires the noun of support.
[[In the printed edition: "فأوليت هل لطلبها" (fa-uliyat hal li-talabiha), and the addition of "huwa" is indispensable.]]
* *
The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Then what is the recompense of those among you who do that except disgrace in the life of this world﴾
Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted: ﴿Then what is the recompense of those among you who do that﴾: there is no recompense for whoever among you kills a person, and thereby disbelieves by killing him, by breaking the covenant of God which He imposed upon him in the Torah, and expels a group of you from your homes, aiding their enemies against them from among the people of polytheism, wrongfully and transgressively, and in opposition to what God commanded him in His Book which He sent down to Moses, except disgrace. "Recompense" here means reward: the compensation for what one did of that, and the wage for it. [[See what has passed at 2: 27-28 of this part.]] ﴿except disgrace in the life of this world﴾. "Disgrace" (*khizy*) means humiliation and abasement; it is said from it: "the man was disgraced, he is disgraced, disgrace (*khizyan*)." ﴿in the life of this world﴾ means: in the immediate world before the Hereafter.
* *
Then the scholars differed concerning the disgrace with which God disgraced them because of their past disobedience to Him. Some of them said: That is the ruling of God which He sent down to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): that the killer is taken for the one he killed, and retaliation is exacted for him as *qisas* (retribution in kind), and the oppressed is avenged against the oppressor.
* *
Others said: Rather, that is the imposition of the *jizya* (poll tax) upon them as long as they remain upon their religion, as a humiliation and abasement for them.
* *
Others said: Rather, that is the disgrace for which they were repaid in this world: the expulsion by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of the Banu al-Nadir from their homes at the first gathering (*li-awwal al-hashr*), and the killing of the fighting men of the Banu Qurayza and the taking captive of their children, and that was a disgrace in this world, while for them in the Hereafter there is a great punishment.
* *
The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment﴾
Abu Ja'far said: By His saying: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment﴾: on the Day when the Hour is established, those among you who do that will be returned, after the disgrace that befalls them in this world as a recompense for disobedience to God, to the most severe punishment that God has prepared for His enemies.
* *
Some have said: the meaning of that is: "And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to a punishment more severe than the punishment of this world." [[In the printed edition: "إلى أشد العذاب من عذاب الدنيا" (ila ashadd al-'adhab min 'adhab al-dunya), and the correct form is to delete "al-'adhab".]]
But there is no meaning to the saying of one who says that. [[In the printed edition: "ولا معنىلقول ذلك بأن" (wa-la ma'na li-qawl dhalika bi-anna), and the correct form is to add "dhalika".]] Rather, God, may His praise be exalted, only informed that they will be returned to the most severe meanings of punishment, and for that reason the definite article ("al-" in *al-'adhab*) was added, because He meant by it the whole category of punishment, not a specific type of it.
* *
The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾ (85)
Abu Ja'far said: The reciters differed concerning the recitation of this.
