1703 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada: ﴿So they learn from them what they use to separate between a man and his wife﴾. Their separation is that each one of them is made to be held back from the other (yu'khadha 'an sahibihi), and each of them is made to hate the other.

* *

As for those who refused to say that the two angels taught people the separation between a man and his wife, they directed the interpretation of His words ﴿So they learn from them﴾ to mean "so they learn in place of what the two taught them of that by which they separate between a man and his wife," like the speaker's saying: "Would that we had such-and-such from such-and-such," meaning "in place of such-and-such," as the poet said:

"You gathered from the good things a leather water-skin, a bowl, and a tie
for the udders of the notched she-camels, the full-grown ones."
[[I do not know who said these two lines, and I have found them only in al-Amali of al-Sharif al-Murtada, 1: 421. It seems he transmitted them from al-Tabari, because they came in the interpretation of this verse with this meaning. "Al-wat": a leather water-skin for milk specifically. "Al-'ilba": a piece of skin taken from the side of a camel, shaped round, then filled with soft sand, then its edges are closed with twigs until it dries and hardens, then its top is cut off, and it stands upright from its dryness, resembling a round bowl, as if it were carved out. The herdsman hangs it and drinks from it, and has gentleness and lightness with it, because it does not break if the camel shakes it or it falls to the ground. "Al-sirr": tying the udders of milking she-camels when they are sent out to graze, and they call that binding "sirar." "Al-akhlaf" is the plural of "khalf" (with a kasra and sukun), which is the udder of a she-camel or camel when it has completed its eighth year and entered its ninth, and its tooth is "buzil," meaning it has split from flesh; this is its utmost age and the completion of its strength. In the printed edition here it is "al-muddhimma," in al-Amali of al-Sharif: "al-muzammama," and in another copy of it: "al-muzahhama." One of the commentators on the Amali said: "al-muzammama is the one on which the bridle is hung." I chose that it be "al-muzannama," as it is more fitting to this poetry. It is said: a she-camel "muzannama," which is one that bears the mark of tazneem, which is cutting the tip of its ear and leaving a raised piece of flesh. This is done only to noble camels. This is a satire: it says to him, "You are only a lowly herdsman, who herds the noble camels of the masters, and you gather of the good things that your masters enjoy nothing but a water-skin, a bowl, and a tie for their camels which you herd for them."]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 102 (part 7 of 8):

And of all the qualities of the noble: tale-bearing ... and striving against the adjoining neighbour with slander (al-najl) [[al-jar (the neighbour): the one whose house is near yours. He is described as "the adjoining" (al-mujawir) to show how close he is, and he is the immediate neighbour (al-jar al-junub), who has the greatest sanctity because he has settled in your vicinity and under your protection, and because he relies on the security of your pledge. Al-najl: tearing apart his honour through backbiting, defamation and reviling in his absence. In a hadith: "Whoever slanders people, they will slander him," meaning, whoever reviles people and cuts their honour with abuse, as one cuts with a mangal (sickle); they will repay him in kind.]]

He means by his saying "you have gathered from the good things": in place of the good things of this world, these base qualities and vile deeds. From this is the saying of another:

"Your qualities have become too hard to be softened in their protrusions, and you have inherited disobedience (uquq) from the noble forebears." [[I have not identified its speaker. Saladat: became hard and stiff. As-safah: a hard, smooth, massive stone that grows nothing. Al-hiyud is the plural of hayd: a protrusion in a mountain, a horn or other things. This is a simile: he says to him, "You are coarse and harsh; nothing can improve you, and there is no good in you, like a smooth stone with protrusions, nothing can improve it and it brings no good." As-salaf (forebears) of a man: those who preceded him among his fathers and kinsmen who are above him in age and merit. He says: you inherited disobedience from your parents in place of the glorious qualities of the noble forebears, so you disobey them, just as they disobeyed their own fathers. You are thus a successor who curses an ancestor who was base and disobedient, cursing his forefathers. You are therefore deeply rooted in disobedience, which is the worst of human qualities.]]

That is: you have inherited disobedience from your parents in place of the noble forebears.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: "And they could not harm anyone thereby except with the permission of God"

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His praise be exalted, "And they could not harm anyone thereby except with the permission of God," He means: the learners from the two angels, Harut and Marut, could not, by what they learned from them of the means by which they separate a man from his wife, harm anyone among mankind, except one for whom God had decreed that this would harm him. As for the one whom God protects from harm, and guards from the evil of sorcery, spells and incantations, it does not harm him, nor does its injury reach him.

* *

The word "permission" (idhn) in the speech of the Arabs has several meanings. Among them: command, not in the sense of obligation. It is not permissible that His words "And they could not harm anyone thereby except with the permission of God" should bear this meaning, because God, may His praise be exalted, has forbidden separating a man from his spouse without sorcery, by the tongue of the community. How then could it be by way of sorcery? [[As if he means: He forbade the separation through the tongue of the community: that they speak it and command its doing.]]

Among them: leaving free, the one given permission and the one left free to him.

Among them: knowledge of a thing. It is said from this: "I have been informed (adhintu) of this matter" when you know of it, "ādhana bihi idhnan" (he informed him of it). From this is the saying of al-Hutay'a:

"Ah, Hind, if you renew union, / and if not, then inform me of the severance." [[I did not find this line in the published Diwan of al-Hutay'a. His words "fa-adhini-ni" indicate that the verb is transitive: "adhanahu bi-l-shay' yadhanuhu idhnan" meaning he informed him of it, like "ādhanahu bihi." This is not mentioned in any lexicon, and the line is evidence for it; al-Tabari's explanation after it also points to his meaning.]]

That is: inform me. From this is His saying, exalted is He: "Then be warned of war from God" [Surah al-Baqarah: 279]. This is the meaning of the verse: it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "And they could not harm anyone thereby, by what they learned from the two angels, except by the knowledge of God," meaning: by what has preceded in God's knowledge that it will harm him. As related:

1704: Al-Muthanna b. Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Suwayd b. Nasr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Sufyan, concerning His words, "And they could not harm anyone thereby except with the permission of God," he said: "By the decree of God."

* *

On the interpretation of His words: "And they learn what harms them and does not benefit them"

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, "and they learn" He means the people who learn from the two angels what was sent down to them of the means by which they separate a man from his wife. They learn from them the sorcery that harms them in their religion and does not benefit them in their return. As for the immediate worldly life, they have indeed earned by it and gained livelihood through it.

* *

On the interpretation of His words: "And they knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter"

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His praise be exalted: [[In the printed edition: "By this, may His praise be exalted." "And they learn, that is, the people who learn..." This is not a correct statement; it seems to be an alteration by some copyist.]] "And they knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter," He means the group who, when a messenger from God came to them confirming what was with them, cast the Book of God behind their backs as if they did not know, and followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon. So He, may His praise be exalted, said: The ones who discarded it, from the Jews of the Children of Israel, certainly know My Book, which they cast behind their backs in ignorance, the ones who abandon acting upon what it contains of following you, O Muhammad, and following what you have come with, after My sending down to you My Book confirming what they have, and after your being sent to them to acknowledge what they have and what is in their hands; those who prefer over it the following of the sorcery which the devils recited in the time of Solomon, and which was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut: for whoever bought sorcery in exchange for My Book, which I sent down to My messenger, and preferred it over that, there is no share for him in the Hereafter. As related:

1705: Bishr b. Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid b. Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His words, "And they knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter": He says: the People of the Book knew this from God's covenant to them: that the sorcerer has no share with God on the Day of Resurrection.

1706: Musa narrated to us, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, concerning His words, "And they knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter," meaning the Jews. He says: the Jews knew that whoever learned it or chose it has no share in the Hereafter.

1707: And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words, "And they knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter": for whoever bought what separates a man from his wife.

1708: Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words, "And they knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter": He said: The Jews knew that in God's Book, in the Torah, whoever buys sorcery and abandons the religion of God, has no share in the Hereafter. So the Fire is his abode and his refuge.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for His words, "whoever bought it" (liman ishtarahu), "man" is in the nominative position, and "And they knew" is not what governs it, because His words "And they knew," [[In the printed edition: "because the words 'they knew' mean an oath." I have preferred to keep "And they knew," because the whole sentence means an oath.]] carry the meaning of an oath; therefore it is in the nominative position. The meaning of the speech is: "By God, whoever bought sorcery, has no share in the Hereafter." Because His words "they knew" carry the meaning of an oath, it is emphasised with the "lam of oath," so it is said, "liman ishtarahu," as one says: "I swear that whoever stood is better than whoever sat," and as one says: "You have known, by Amr, that he is better than your father."

As for "man," it is a conditional particle. The word "ishtarahu" was used, not "yashtaruhu," because the "lam of oath" enters upon "man." It is the custom of the Arabs, when they place the lam of oath before a conditional particle, not to use the verb after it except in the past form ("fa'ala") rather than the present ("yaf'alu"), except rarely, out of aversion to putting in the conditional a jussive element, as God, may His praise be exalted, says: "If they are expelled, they will not go forth with them" [Surah al-Hashr: 12]. It is permissible also to pronounce the verb after it in the present form in the jussive. [[All of this is in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:65–69, with some alteration of the wording.]]

As the poet said:

"Even if your houses have become too narrow for you, / let my Lord know that my house is spacious." [[Al-Farra' narrates it in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:66 without attribution. But the author of al-Khizanah 4:220 attributes it to Kumayt b. Ma'ruf. I have not found it attributed to him in any other book, and I fear that the author of al-Khizanah may have erred. Moreover, this line and what precedes it are all in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:65–66.]]

* *

The interpreters have differed concerning the interpretation of His words: "whoever has no share in the Hereafter." Some of them said: "khalaq" (share) in this place means portion.

Those who said this:

1709: Al-Muthanna b. Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "whoever has no share in the Hereafter," he says: "from a portion."

1710: Musa b. Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "whoever has no share in the Hereafter": "from a portion."

1711: Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to me, saying: Waki' narrated to us; Sufyan said: We heard concerning "And whoever has no share in the Hereafter" that he has no portion in the Hereafter.

* *

Others said: "khalaq" here means proof.

Those who said this:

1712: Al-Hasan b. Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah: "And whoever has no share in the Hereafter," he said: He has no proof in the Hereafter.

Others said: khalaq means religion.

Those who said this:

1713: Al-Hasan b. Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, saying: al-Hasan said: "whoever has no share in the Hereafter," he said: He has no religion.

* *

Others said: "khalaq" here means stability (qiwam).

Those who said this:

1714: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said, Ibn 'Abbas said: "whoever has no share in the Hereafter," he said: stability.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these sayings is the saying of the one who said: the meaning of "khalaq" in this place is portion, because that is its meaning in the speech of the Arabs.

From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ):

1715: "Surely God will support this religion with people who have no share (khalaq) [in it]." [[The hadith: 1715 – Al-Tabari transmitted this hadith without an isnad. Ahmad has narrated it in al-Musnad 5:45 (Halabi), from the hadith of Abu Bakrah, with the wording: "Surely God will support this religion with people who have no share." Al-Haythami mentioned it in Majma' al-Zawa'id 5:302, then said: "Ahmad and al-Tabarani narrated it, and its men are trustworthy." He also mentioned it after that from the hadith of Anas and said: "al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated it, and one of al-Bazzar's chains has trustworthy men." (Thus in the original.) Al-Suyuti mentioned it in al-Jami' al-Saghir: 1838, attributing it to al-Nasa'i and Ibn Hibban from the hadith of Anas, and to Ahmad and al-Tabarani from the hadith of Abu Bakrah. His commentator al-Manawi related that al-Hafiz al-'Iraqi said: "Its chain is good." The hadith of Anas was also narrated by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah 6:262, and he narrated before it 3:13 from the mursal hadith of al-Hasan. Then he pointed to the hadith of Anas.]]

That is: they have no portion and no share in Islam and the religion. From this is the saying of Umayyah b. Abi al-Salt:

"They call for woe therein; they have no share (khalaq) / except garments of pitch and shackles." [[His Diwan: 47, a single line. His words "therein," I think, mean the Fire. Qitr: molten copper.]]

By this he means: they have no portion and no share, except the garments and the shackles.

* *

Likewise His words, "whoever has no share in the Hereafter": he has no portion of the Garden in the abode of the Hereafter, because he had no faith, no religion, and no righteous deed by which he would be rewarded in the Garden and recompensed, so that he would have a portion and share of the Garden. God, may His praise be exalted, said, "whoever has no share in the Hereafter," describing him as having no share in the Hereafter; and He means by it: he has no portion of reward, recompense or Garden, apart from his portion of the Fire, since His censure of their deeds, for which He denied them a share in the Hereafter, indicated His intended meaning of the statement: that they have no share in the good things there, but as for the evils, they do have a share there.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: "And how wretched is that for which they sold their souls, if only they had known"

Abu Ja'far said: We have already shown earlier that the meaning of "shara" (sold) is "sold." [[See what has gone before in this part, 2:340–342.]] The meaning of the speech then is: "And how wretched is that for which he sold his soul, from learning sorcery, if he had known the evil of its consequence," as:

1716: Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And how wretched is what they sold their souls for," he says: how wretched is what they sold their souls for.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: How does He, may His praise be exalted, say "And how wretched is what they sold their souls for, if only they had known"? Yet He said before: "And they knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter." How can they be knowers that whoever learns sorcery has no share, while they are ignorant that they have sold their souls for sorcery in a wretched bargain?

It is said: the meaning of that is other than what you imagine, that they are described as ignorant of what they are described as knowing. Rather, that is of the postponed which means the advanced. The meaning of the speech is: "They could not harm anyone thereby except with the permission of God, and they learn what harms them and does not benefit them, and how wretched is what they sold their souls for, if only they had known. And they knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter." So His words, "How wretched is what they sold their souls for, if only they had known," are a censure from God, may His remembrance be exalted, of the act of those who learned from the two angels the separation between a man and his wife, and a report from Him, may His praise be exalted, about them that they sold their souls for a wretched thing, by their contentment with sorcery in place of their religion through which their souls would be saved from destruction, out of ignorance of the evil consequence of their deed and the loss of the bargain they made. For one who does not know God, nor knows His lawful and unlawful, His command and His prohibition, may learn that from the two.

Then He returned to the group whom God told us had cast His Book behind their backs as if they did not know, and followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon and what was sent down to the two angels. He reported about them that they knew that whoever bought sorcery has no share in the Hereafter. He described them as committing acts of disobedience to God while knowing them, and disbelieving in God and His messengers, and preferring to follow the devils and to act by what they introduced of sorcery over acting by His Book, His revelation and His sending down, out of obstinacy, rebellion against His messengers and transgression of His limits, with knowledge on their part of the punishment and torment that is due to whoever does that from God. That is the interpretation of His words.

* *

Some of those who claim something have asserted that His words "And they knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter" mean the devils, and that His words "if only they had known" mean the people. But this is a view opposed to all the interpreters, for they are unanimous that His words "And they knew that whoever bought it" refer to the Jews and not to the devils. Furthermore, it contradicts what the Qur'an indicates, because the verses before His words "And they knew that whoever bought it" and after His words "if only they had known" came from God to censure the Jews and rebuke them for their misguidance, and to blame them for casting aside God's revelation and the verses of His Book behind their backs, while knowing the error of their deed. So His words "And they knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter" are one of those reports about them.

* *

Some have said: those whom God, may His praise be exalted, described with His words "And how wretched is what they sold their souls for, if only they had known," and whom He denied knowledge, are the ones He described with His words "And they knew that whoever bought it would have no share in the Hereafter." He denied them knowledge with His words "if only they had known," after describing them as having known with His words "And they knew," because they did not act upon what they knew. The one who knows is the one who acts on his knowledge; but when his deeds contradict his knowledge, he is among the ignorant. It is also said of one who does an act contrary to what he should do, even though he knows it, "If you had known, you would have desisted," as Ka'b b. Zuhayr al-Muzani said, describing a wolf and a crow which followed them to eat their food and provisions:

"When they both came to me I said: If only you two knew it! / Do you not both know that I am one who has run out of provisions?" [[His Diwan: 51, and Amali al-Sharif al-Murtada 1:424. It seems he was quoting al-Tabari's explanation of this verse, with alteration. "Muramal" means one whose provisions are spent; "armala al-rajul" means the man became "mumlal" as if he stuck to the sand when he was shaken.]]

So he reported that he said to them both, "If only you knew it," denying them knowledge, then questioned them, saying: "Do you not both know?" They answered: So likewise is His saying "And they knew that whoever bought it" and "if only they had known."

* *

This is an interpretation which, though it has some justification and a certain basis, goes against the apparent meaning understood from the very wording itself, I mean His words: ﴿And they certainly knew﴾ and His words: ﴿If only they knew﴾, and it is merely an extraction. And the interpretation of the Qur'an according to the apparent, understood meaning of the address is preferable to a hidden, inner meaning drawn from it, unless there comes an indication—from a source that must be accepted—giving a meaning contrary to its apparent evidence as commonly understood among the people of the tongue in whose language the Qur'an was revealed. [[He says: "The interpretation of the Qur'an according to the apparent, understood meaning of the address... is preferable." He elaborated and went on at length.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 103:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah, the reward from Allah would have been better, if they had known.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah﴾, meaning: if those who learn from the two angels that by which they separate a man from his wife, "had believed," that is, affirmed Allah and His Messenger and what had come to them from their Lord, and "feared" their Lord, that is, feared Him and so feared His punishment, obeying Him by performing His obligations and avoiding His disobedience, then Allah's recompense to them and His reward for them for their faith in Him and their fear of Him would have been better for them than sorcery and what they had acquired by it, "if they had known" that Allah's reward for them for that is better for them than sorcery and what they had acquired by it. By His saying ﴿if they had known﴾ He negated knowledge from them: that they should know the extent of Allah's reward and the measure of His recompense for obeying Him.

* *

And "al-mathubah" (reward) in the speech of the Arabs is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: "athabtuka ithabatan wa thawaban wa mathubatan." Its root derives from "thaba ilayka al-shay'," meaning: it returned. Then it is said: "athabtuhu ilayka," meaning: I returned it to you and gave it back. So the meaning of "a man's recompense of another man for a gift or other thing" is: his returning to him something of it in exchange and giving it back to him as a substitute. Then every one who compensates another for his deed, his gift, or a favour that the other had extended to him, is called "muthib" (one who rewards) to him. From this is Allah's "thawab" (reward) to His servants for their deeds, meaning His giving them compensation and recompense for it, so that there returns to them, in place of their deed which they performed for Him, a return.

* *

Some grammarians of Basra claimed that His saying ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah, the reward from Allah would have been better﴾ is one whose answer has been omitted, the meaning being understood from the context. Its meaning is: "And if they had believed and feared Allah, they would have been rewarded," but He dispensed with the words "they would have been rewarded," since the report about the reward indicates it.

* *

But some grammarians of Basra denied this, holding that the answer to His saying ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah﴾ is ﴿the reward﴾ (mathubah), and that "law" (if) is answered with "mathubah," even though it is followed by a past-tense verb, because its meaning is close to that of "la'in" (if indeed), in that both are conditionals, and both are answers to faith. So the answer of each of them has been placed after the other: "law" is answered with the answer of "la'in," and "la'in" with the answer of "law," for this reason, even though their answers differ. The rule for "law" is that it is answered by the past tense of the verb, and the rule for "la'in" is that it is answered by the future tense of the verb, because of the closeness of their meanings that we have described. So the interpretation of His saying ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah﴾ is: "And if indeed they had believed and feared Allah, the reward from Allah would have been better."

* *

Those who held the view we have stated about the interpretation of "al-mathubah" were the people of interpretation.

Mention of those who said that:

1717 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying ﴿the reward from Allah﴾: he says, a reward from Allah.

1718 - Yunus told me, saying: 'Amr told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi, concerning ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah, the reward from Allah would have been better﴾: as for "al-mathubah," it is the reward (al-thawab).

1719 - Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ishaq told us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning ﴿And if they had believed and feared Allah, the reward from Allah would have been better﴾: he says, a reward from Allah.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 104 (part 1 of 2):

The explanation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Ra'ina"﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The exegetes differed concerning the interpretation of His words: ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina."﴾ Some of them said: its interpretation is: "Do not say, 'Opposition'."

Mention of those who said this:

1720 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Mu'ammal related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata', regarding His words: ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina,"﴾ he said: Do not say, "Opposition."

1721 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina,"﴾ "Do not say, 'Opposition'."

1722 - And al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

1723 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from a man, from Mujahid, the like of it.

1724 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* *

Others said: its interpretation is: "Arina sam'aka" (make us hear you / give us your attention), meaning: listen to us and we will listen to you.

Mention of those who said this:

1725 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq related to me, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from 'Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿Ra'ina,﴾ meaning: "Arina sam'aka" (give us your attention).

1726 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the words of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Ra'ina,"﴾ "Do not say: listen to us and we will listen to you."

1727 - And it was related to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say, concerning His words: ﴿Ra'ina,﴾ he said: A man among the polytheists used to say: "Ari'ni sam'aka" (give me your attention).

* *

Then the exegetes differed concerning the reason for which God forbade the believers to say "Ra'ina." Some of them said: It was a word the Jews used with the intent of mockery and abuse, so God, exalted is His remembrance, forbade the believers to say it to the Prophet ﷺ.

Mention of those who said this:

1728 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Ra'ina,"﴾ a saying the Jews used in mockery, so God rebuked the believers from saying the like of what they said.

1729 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri related to us, from Fudayl ibn Marzuq, from 'Ata'iyyah: ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina,"﴾ he said: Some people among the Jews used to say, "Arina sam'aka!" until some people among the Muslims said it too. So God disliked for them what the Jews said, and He said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Ra'ina,"﴾ as the Jews and Christians said it.

1730 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina" and say, "Unzurna,"﴾ he said: They used to say: "Ra'ina sam'aka!" and the Jews would come and say the like of it mockingly, so God said: ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina," and say, "Unzurna."﴾

1731 - And it was related to me from al-Minjab, who said: Bishr ibn 'Imarah related to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina,"﴾ he said: They used to say to the Prophet ﷺ: "Ra'ina sam'aka!" And "Ra'ina" is like your saying "'Aținā" (give us).

1732 - And Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Ra'ina," and say, "Unzurna,"﴾ he said: "Ra'ina" is the saying the people said. They said: ﴿We hear and disobey, and hear without being heard, and "Ra'ina" with their tongues, and as a slander upon the religion﴾ [Surah al-Nisa: 46]. He said: "He said: this is the 'Ra'in'" - and "ra'in" means the mistaken - he said: So He said to the believers: Do not say "mistaken," as the people said, but say: "Unzurna" and listen. He said: They used to look at the Prophet ﷺ and speak to him, and he would listen to them, and they would ask him and he would answer them. [[The statement "al-Ra'in: al-Khata'" I have not found in any other source so far. What is in the books of tafsir and lexicography is different, and perhaps it was "al-Khata'" (error). They have also said: "Ra'ina: al-hujr min al-qawl" (abusive speech). And they said it is derived from ra'unah, which is foolishness, ignorance and slackness.]]

* *

Others said: Rather, it was a word the Ansar used to say in the Jahiliyyah, so God forbade them in Islam from saying it to His Prophet ﷺ.

Mention of those who said this:

1733 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Hushaym related to me, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, from 'Ata', regarding His words: ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina,"﴾ he said: It was a dialect among the Ansar in the Jahiliyyah, so this verse was revealed: ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina," but say, "Unzurna,"﴾ to the end of the verse.

1734 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, from 'Abd al-Malik, from 'Ata', he said: ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina,"﴾ he said: It was a dialect of the Ansar.

1735 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from 'Abd al-Malik, from 'Ata', the like of it.

1736 - And al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, from Ibn Abi Ja'far, from his father, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, regarding His words: ﴿Do not say, "Ra'ina,"﴾ he said: The polytheists of the Arabs, when some of them spoke with others, one of them would say to his companion: "Ari'ni sam'aka!" So they were forbidden from that.

1737 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: "Ra'ina" is the saying of the mocker. So He forbade them to mock the words of Muhammad ﷺ.

* *

Some said: Rather, it was the speech of a particular Jew, called Rifa'ah ibn Zayd. He would address the Prophet ﷺ with it in a manner of abuse toward him, and the Muslims had taken it from him, so God forbade the believers from saying it to the Prophet ﷺ.

Mention of those who said this:

1738 - Musa related to me, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Ra'ina" and say, "Unzurna,"﴾ there was a man of the Jews - from a Jewish tribe called Banu Qaynuqa' - who was called Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Sa'ib - Abu Ja'far said: This is an error; it is in fact Ibn al-Tabut, not Ibn al-Sa'ib - who used to come to the Prophet ﷺ, and when he met him and spoke to him, he would say: "Arina sam'aka," and "isma' ghayr musma'" [[In the printed edition: "fa-qala", the fa' has no place here.]]. So the Muslims thought that the Prophets were honored with this, so some of them would say: "isma' ghayr musma'," like your saying "isma' ghayr sagir" (listen without being humbled). This is the verse in al-Nisa: ﴿Among those who are Jews, they distort words from their places and say: "We hear and disobey, and hear without being heard, and Ra'ina," twisting with their tongues and slandering the religion﴾ [Surah al-Nisa: 46]. He says: He only intends by His words "slander upon the religion." Then He addressed the believers, saying: "Do not say, 'Ra'ina.'" [[Taqaddama ilayhi: amarahu (he commanded him).]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view concerning the prohibition by God, mighty is His praise, of the believers saying to His Prophet "Ra'ina," is that it is said: it is a word which God disliked for them to say to His Prophet ﷺ, similar to what is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said:

1739 - "Do not say to grapes 'karm,' but say: 'al-habalah'." [[Hadith 1739: al-Tabari mentioned it as a suspended narration without a chain. It was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (7509) from Abu Hurayrah, raised: "And do not call grapes 'karm'." It was narrated by the Two Shaykhs and others, as we explained there. He had also narrated it before in brief allusion: 7256.

Muslim (2:197) narrated from 'Alqamah ibn Wa'il, from his father, raised: "Do not say 'al-karm,' but say: 'al-habalah,' meaning grapes."]]

1740 - And "Do not say: 'my slave' ('abdi), but say: 'my young man' (fata-y)." [[Hadith 1740: This too is suspended, and it is part of a long hadith. It was narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, from Abu Hurayrah, raised: "... and let none of you say 'my slave' ('abdi), 'my female slave' (amati); let him say 'my young man' (fata-y), 'my young woman' (fatati), 'my boy' (ghulami)." See al-Bukhari 5:128-131 (Fath), and Muslim 2:197.]]

And the like of that, of the two words which are used with one meaning in the speech of the Arabs, so the disapproval or prohibition comes with the use of one of them, and the choice of the other over it in address.

* *

If someone says to us: We have understood the meaning of the Prophet's ﷺ prohibition regarding "grapes" that it be called "karm," and regarding "slave" that he be called "slave"; so what is the meaning in His words "Ra'ina" then, for which God, mighty is His praise, forbade the believers to say it, until He commanded them to prefer His words "Unzurna"?

It is said: What is in it of that is like what is in the saying of one who says "karm" for grapes and "slave" for the owned. For the saying "my slave" applies to all the servants of God, so it was disliked for the Prophet ﷺ that some of God's servants be attributed - in the sense of servitude - to other than God; and he was commanded that this be attributed to another, in a sense other than that in which it is attributed to God, mighty and majestic, so it is said "my young man." Likewise the reason for his prohibition regarding "grapes" that it be called "karm" is fear of the supposition that it is described with generosity (karam), even though it is vocalized with a sukun, for the Arabs sometimes soften some vowels when they follow one pattern. So he disliked that grapes be described by that. Likewise God, mighty and majestic, forbade the believers to say "Ra'ina," because the saying "Ra'ina" might carry the meaning "ihfazna wa-nahfazaka" (guard us and we will guard you), and "urqubna wa-narqubka" (watch over us and we will watch over you), from the Arabs' saying to one another "ra'aka Allah" (may God watch over you and keep you) - meaning "hafizaka Allah wa-kala'aka" (may God guard you and protect you) - and it might carry the meaning: "Arina sam'aka" (give us your attention), from their saying "ara'tu sam'i i'ra'an - aw ra'aytuhu sam'i ri'a'an aw mura'atan" (I gave my hearing to him), meaning: I emptied it for hearing his speech. As al-A'sha Maymun ibn Qays said:

He gives heed to the words of the chiefs of men when they / display to him resolve, or whatever he invents.

[[His Diwan: 86; it will come in this part, 2:540. Some verses of this poem were previously cited in 1:106, 2:94; it is about Hawdhah ibn 'Ali, as was previously mentioned. Before it he says: "O Hawdh, best of those who walk upon the earth / a sea of bounties for the seekers and the travelers..." Ibtada'a: invented whatever he willed.]]

By his words "yar'a" he means: he inclines his hearing to him, emptying it for that.

God, exalted is His praise, had commanded the believers to honor and revere His Prophet ﷺ, until He, exalted is His remembrance, forbade them in what He forbade them from raising their voices above his voice, and from speaking loudly to him as some of them speak loudly to one another, and warned them that their deeds would be nullified because of that. [[Read the saying of God, exalted, at the beginning of "Surat al-Hujurat".]]

So He addressed them with rebuke, forbidding them to say to him any words that contain rudeness, and commanded them to choose for their address the best of words and the most refined of meanings. Among that was their saying "Ra'ina," because of what it contains of the possibility of the meaning: "Arina nara'ak" (watch us, we will watch you), since the form of mufa'alah (reciprocity) occurs only between two parties, as one says: "'Atina, haddithna, jalisna" (give us, speak to us, sit with us), meaning: do for us and we will do for you; and the meaning: "Arina sam'aka" (give us your attention), until we understand you and you understand us. So God, exalted is His remembrance, forbade the companions of Muhammad to say it in that way, and to single out their request for waiting and delay, so that they may understand him with honor and reverence from them toward him; and that they should not ask him what they asked of that in a manner of rudeness and contempt from them toward him, nor with harshness and coarseness, imitating the Jews in their address to the Prophet of God ﷺ by their saying to him: ﴿"Isma' ghayr musma'" and "Ra'ina."﴾

What supports the correctness of what we have said on this is His words: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, desire that any good should be sent down upon you from your Lord﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 105]. [[This is the verse that follows the verse being explained.]] This indicates that what He rebuked them for is what pleases the Jews and the polytheists.

* *

As for the interpretation related from Mujahid concerning His words "Ra'ina," that it means "opposition," it is something that is not sensible in the speech of the Arabs. For "ra'aytu" in the speech of the Arabs is only in one of two ways: one of them in the sense of "fa'altu" from "al-ri'yah" (guardianship) and "al-kala'ah" (protection). The other in the sense of emptying the hearing, meaning "ari'tuhu sam'i." As for "ra'aytu" in the sense of "kharaftu" (I opposed), there is no understandable meaning for it in the speech of the Arabs. Unless he read it with tanwin, then directed it toward the meaning of ra'unah (foolishness), ignorance and error, in the manner which 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said about it; then it would have a understandable meaning, although it contradicts the readings of the reciters.

* *

As for the other view related from 'Ata'iyyah and those from whom it is related: that His words "Ra'ina" were a word of the Jews with the meaning of abuse and derision, which the believers used by taking it from them; this is impermissible regarding the description of the believers: that they take from the speech of the polytheists words whose meaning they do not know, and then use them among themselves and in addressing their Prophet ﷺ. But it is possible that this is what was related from Qatadah, that it was a correct word understood in the speech of the Arabs, which coincided with a word from the speech of the Jews in a non-Arabic tongue, which for the Jews is abuse, and for the Arabs means: "Arina sam'aka" and empty it to understand me. So God, mighty and majestic, knew the intention of the Jews in their saying that to the Prophet ﷺ, and that its meaning from them differs from its meaning in the speech of the Arabs; so God, mighty and majestic, forbade the believers from saying it to the Prophet ﷺ, lest one whose meaning in it is other than the meaning of the believers in it should dare to address the Messenger of God ﷺ with it. This is an interpretation for which no report has come in a way that establishes proof. Since this is so, what is more appropriate for the interpretation of the verse is what we have described, since that is the apparent meaning understood from the verse, rather than anything else.

* *

It has been related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he used to read it: ﴿Do not say "ra'inan"﴾ with tanwin, meaning: "Do not say a saying 'ra'inan'," from "al-ra'unah," which is foolishness and ignorance. But this is a reading contrary to the readings of the Muslim reciters, and it is impermissible for anyone to recite with it, due to its irregularity and its departure from the readings of the earlier and later generations, and its contradiction of what the proof from the Muslims has brought.

Whoever gives "ra'ina" tanwin, gives it tanwin because of His words "Do not say," since then it is governed by it. Whoever does not give it tanwin, leaves off its tanwin because it is a quoted command. For the people were as if they used to say to the Prophet ﷺ: "Ra'ina," meaning a request: either that he give them his hearing, or that he watch over them and observe them, as I have explained earlier. So it was said to them: Do not say in your request to him "Ra'ina." Then the indication of the meaning of command in "ra'ina" then is the dropping of the ya' that would be in "yur'ihi," and what indicates it - I mean the dropped "ya'" - is the kasrah of the "'ayn" in "ra'ina."

* *

It is mentioned that the reading of Ibn Mas'ud is: ﴿Do not say "ra'unaa"﴾, meaning a quoted command suitable for a group, to be watchful of them. If that reading from him is sound, it is possible that the people were forbidden from using it among themselves in addressing one another, whether their address was to the Prophet ﷺ or to someone else. But we do not know this to be sound by the route through which reports are authenticated.

* *

The explanation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And say, "Unzurna"﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is He: ﴿And say, "Unzurna,"﴾ He means: say, O believers, to your Prophet ﷺ: "Unzurna" and "irqubna" - so that we may understand and clarify what you say to us, and teach us - as:

1741 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿And say, "Unzurna,"﴾ "Fahimna, bayyin lana ya Muhammad" (Make us understand, explain to us, O Muhammad).

1742 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿And say, "Unzurna,"﴾ "Fahimna, bayyin lana ya Muhammad."

1743 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* *

It is said from it: "nazartu al-rajul anzuruhu nazratan," meaning: I waited for him and watched over him, and from it is the saying of al-Hutay'ah:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 104 (part 2 of 2):

Among its uses is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿On the Day when the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women will say to those who believed, "Wait for us (unzurūnā) that we may borrow from your light"﴾ [Surah al-Hadid: 13]. He means by it: "Wait for us" (intaẓirūnā).

[[His Diwan: 53; and Lisan al-Arab, entries (nẓr), (ḥwz), (nss), (ʿshy). From a qasida in which he satirizes al-Zibriqan ibn Badr and praises Bughayd ibn ʿAmir ibn Shammas. Al-aʿshāʾ is the plural of ʿishan (with a kasra and then a sukun), meaning what camels graze on in the evening. Al-ṣādira refers to camels that come back from the water. Al-khams refers to the watering intervals of camels: they remain in pasture for three days after the day of watering and come back to the water on the fourth day. Al-ḥawz means gentle driving; ḥāza al-ibil means he drove the camels slowly and gently. Al-tanassās and al-nass is the verbal noun from your saying "nassa al-ibil baynahā," meaning he drove them hard to reach the water. It is also transmitted as "ītāʾ ṣādira." Al-ītāʾ is the verbal noun of "ātā al-shayʾ," meaning he delayed it. He says to al-Zibriqan, when he (the poet) had stopped at his house and then moved on to the house of Bughayd (see the account of their dispute in Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shuʿara: 96–98): "I waited for the best of you the way thirsty camels wait for their evening pasture." This is because camels, when they return from water, graze for a long time, and there is much water in their bellies, so they need much herbage. He describes how long he waited, when he had no patience for a long wait. Al-Zibriqan complained about this poem to ʿUmar, and about his saying in it: "Leave generosity, do not travel to seek its aim; sit, for you are the one who eats and clothes [others]."]]

* *

It has been recited as "anẓirnā" and "unẓirūnā" with a cut hamza (ʾalif) in both places. [[I added the words of Allah the Exalted, "unẓirūnā," because of the difference between the two letters.]] Whoever recites it that way intends "akhkhirnā" (delay us), as Allah, may His praise be exalted, said: ﴿He said, "My Lord, give me respite (fa-anẓirnī) until the day they are raised"﴾ [Surah Sad: 79], meaning "akhkhirnī" (delay me). But there is no justification for reciting it that way in this place. The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were only commanded to draw near to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), to listen to him, to address him gently, and to lower their wings to him, not to delay away from him, nor to ask him to delay them. So the correct reading, given that this is so [[In the printed edition: "in kāna dhālika..." is nothing.]], is the reading of the one who connects the hamza in His saying ﴿unẓurnā﴾, and does not cut it, meaning "intaẓirnā" (wait for us).

* *

It has been said that the meaning of ﴿anẓirnā﴾ with a cut hamza is "amhilnā" (give us time). It is related from some Arabs by hearing: "Anẓirnī ukallimuka" (give me time, and I will speak with you). The one who heard this from some of them reported that he asked them for clarification of its meaning, and they informed him that they meant "amhilnī" (give me time). If this is correctly transmitted from them, then "fa-anẓirnā" and "anẓirnā," with a cut hamza or a connected hamza, are close in meaning. However, even if this is so, the recitation that I do not permit anything other than is the recitation of the one who recites: ﴿wa-qūlū unẓurnā﴾ with a connected hamza, meaning "intaẓirnā" (wait for us), because the authorities have agreed on its correctness and their rejection of the other readings.

* *

Concerning the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And listen. For the disbelievers is a painful punishment﴾ [2:104]

Abu Jaʿfar said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, ﴿wa-smaʿū (and listen)﴾, He means: listen to what is said to you and recited to you from the Book of your Lord, and retain it, understand it, as:

1744 – Musa narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿wa-smaʿū﴾: "Listen to what is said to you."

* *

So the meaning of the verse is: O you who believe, do not say to your Prophet: "Ra'ina" (attend to us), give us your hearing and empty it for us, that we may make you understand and you may understand from us what we say. Rather, say: "Wait for us and watch for us, until we understand from you what you teach us and make clear to us. And listen to him in what he says to you, retain it, memorize it, and understand it." Then Allah, may His praise be exalted, informed them that for those among them and among others who deny His signs, oppose His command and prohibition, and reject His Messenger, there is a painful torment in the Hereafter. So He said: "And for the disbelievers in Me and My Messenger, a painful punishment." By His saying "al-alim" (painful) He means "al-mujiʿ" (agonizing). We have already mentioned the evidence for this earlier, and the reports concerning it. [[See what has passed: 1:283; then this part: 2:140, 377.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 105:

The exposition of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, and the polytheists, do not wish that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words ﴿ma yawadd﴾ (do not wish), He means: do not love. That is, many of the People of the Book do not love. It is said from this: "Fulan wadda kadhā yawadduhu waddan, wuddan, and mawaddatan" (Fulan loved such-and-such).

* *

As for "al-mushrikin" (the polytheists), it is in the genitive case by conjunction with "ahl al-kitab" (the People of the Book). The meaning of the statement is: those who disbelieve among the People of the Book do not love, nor do the polytheists, that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord.

* *

As for ﴿an﴾ in His words ﴿an yunazzal﴾ (that there be sent down), it is in the accusative governed by His words ﴿yawadd﴾. We have already explained the reason for the entry of "min" in His words ﴿min khayr﴾ (any good), and similar statements that begin with a negation in the past, so that this suffices and there is no need to repeat it in this place. [See what has passed in this volume, 2:126, 127. He should have mentioned it in the exegesis of verse 102, or referred to it, as he refers to it here.]

* *

So the meaning of the statement is: the disbelievers among the People of the Book and the polytheists who worship God with idols do not love that there be sent down to you any of the good that was with God, so that He sends it down to you. The polytheists and the disbelieving People of the Book wished that God would not send down to them the Criterion (al-Furqan) and what He revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ) of His judgments and signs. The Jews and their followers among the polytheists loved only this out of envy and spite toward the believers.

In this verse there is clear evidence that God, blessed and exalted, forbade the believers to incline toward their enemies among the People of the Book and the polytheists, to listen to their words, or to accept anything they bring them under the guise of counsel, because He informed them of what the People of the Book and the polytheists conceal of rancor and envy, even if they display with their tongues the opposite of what they conceal.

* *

The exposition of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And God singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and God is the Possessor of great bounty﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His praise, ﴿And God singles out for His mercy whom He wills﴾, He means: God singles out whom He wills with His prophethood and His messengership, so He sends him to whomever He wills of His creation, and bestows faith as a favor upon whom He loves, guiding him to it. And "His singling them out" (ikhtisasuhu) with it means distinguishing them with it apart from others of His creation. God made His sending of messengers to those to whom He sent them among His creation, and His guidance of whom He guided among His servants, a mercy from Him to them, so that by it they reach His pleasure and His love, and their success with it in Paradise, and their deserving His praise by it. All of that is a mercy from God to them.

* *

As for His words, ﴿And God is the Possessor of great bounty﴾, it is a report from God, exalted is His praise, that every good that His servants attain in their religion and their worldly life is from Him at the outset and as a favor from Him to them, without their deserving it from Him.

* *

In His words, ﴿And God singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and God is the Possessor of great bounty﴾, there is an allusion by God, mentioned and exalted, to the People of the Book: that the guidance which He gave to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and to the believers in him is a favor from Him, and that His blessings are not attained by wishful desires, but are gifts from Him which He singles out with whom He wills of His creation.

On the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He: "Whatever sign We abrogate..."

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His praise, "Whatever sign We abrogate [ma nansakh min ayah]," He means: whatever We transfer from the ruling of a sign to another, changing it and substituting it. [[In the printed edition: "ma nasakh min ayah ila ghayrihi fa-nabdhu", and the addition is from Tafsir Ibn Kathir 1: 273.]] This is when the permitted becomes forbidden, the forbidden becomes permitted, and the allowed becomes prohibited, and the prohibited becomes allowed. This happens only in commands and prohibitions, in restriction and release, in forbidding and permitting. As for reports (akhbar), there is no abrogating (nasikh) or abrogated (mansukh) element in them.
* *
The root of "naskh" (abrogation) is from "nasakh al-kitab" (copying a book), which is transferring it from one copy to another different from it. Likewise, the meaning of abrogating a ruling to something else is only transforming it and transferring its wording from it to something else. [[In the printed edition: "ʿanhu ila ghayrihi"; in Ibn Kathir: "wa naql ʿibarah ila ghayriha". The correct reading is what I have adopted.]] When this is the meaning of abrogating a sign, then it is the same, when its ruling is abrogated and its obligation is changed and replaced, and the obligation of the servants is transferred from what was binding upon them, whether its script (khatt) remains recorded, or its trace is erased, so it is effaced and forgotten. [[In the printed edition: "awfara hazzaha fa-turika, aw muhiya athāruhā fa-ʿufiyya aw nusiya", a sentence that has been corrupted and garbled. Al-Tabari's meaning is that abrogation, which is the change of a ruling, may occur while the script remains as it is, with a different ruling expressed in other wording — or the script is lifted and people forget what they had memorized at the time of revelation. "ʿAfiya" comes from their saying: ʿafa al-athar yaʿfu, meaning it was obliterated and went away; and ʿaffāhu yuʿaffīhi (with doubled letter) means he wiped it out and removed it.
Furthermore, the following sentence, "for in both of its states it is abrogated," and the report of al-Hasan that follows, indicate the correctness of what I have recorded in reading al-Tabari's text.]] For in that case it is abrogated in both its states, and the new ruling that replaces the first ruling, and to which the obligation of the servants is transferred, is the abrogating element (nasikh). It is said of it: "Allah abrogated such-and-such a sign, abrogating it (yansakhuhu) with abrogation (naskhan), and the 'nuskhah' is the noun." In accordance with what we have said, al-Hasan al-Basri used to say:
1745 - Sawwar ibn ʿAbd Allah al-ʿAnbari narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn al-Harith narrated to us, saying: ʿAwf narrated to us, from al-Hasan, that he said concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause you to forget, We bring one better than it or the like of it" [Q 2:106], he said: "Your Prophet (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an, then he forgot it, and it was nothing, [[In the printed edition: "qāla uqriʾa qurʾānan", a part of which is missing; it will appear correctly in the report numbered 1754, and I have added this addition from there.]] and among the Qur'an is what has been abrogated while you still recite it."
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation differed concerning the interpretation of His words, "Whatever We abrogate," and some of them said:
1746 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Whatever sign We abrogate": as for its abrogation, it is its taking away.
* *
And others said:
1747 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate," he says: "whatever We substitute from a sign."
* *
And others said:
1748 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from the companions of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, that they said: "Whatever sign We abrogate," we keep its script [and substitute its ruling].
1749 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Whatever sign We abrogate," we keep its script and substitute its ruling. I related it from the companions of Ibn Masʿud.
1750 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Bakr ibn Shawdhab narrated to me, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from the companions of Ibn Masʿud: "Whatever sign We abrogate," we keep its script [and substitute its ruling]. [[Report 1750: the words between brackets are from Ibn Kathir 1: 273–274.]]
* *
On the Interpretation of His Words: "Or cause you to forget [aw nunsiha]"
Abu Ja'far said: The readers differed concerning His words. The people of Medina and Kufa read it: "aw nunsiha" (or We cause it to be forgotten). The reading of those who read it thus has two interpretive possibilities.
The first: that its interpretation is: "Whatever sign We abrogate, O Muhammad, changing its ruling, or cause you to forget." It is mentioned that in the codex of ʿAbd Allah it reads: "ma nunsika min ayah aw nansakhha najiʾ bi-mithlihā" (Whatever We cause you to forget of a sign, or abrogate it, We bring one like it), and this is the interpretation of "forgetting" (al-nisyan). And this interpretation was held by a group of the people of interpretation.
Those who said this:
1751 - Bishr ibn Muʿadh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause you to forget, We bring one better than it or the like of it": he used to abrogate a sign by the sign after it, and the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) would recite a sign or more than that, then it would be forgotten and lifted.
1752 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause you to forget," he said: Allah, exalted is His remembrance, would cause His Prophet (ﷺ) to forget what He willed and abrogate what He willed.
1753 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr used to say: "nunsiha" means: We lift it from among you.
1754 - Sawwar ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn al-Harith narrated to us, saying: ʿAwf narrated to us, from al-Hasan, that he said concerning His words: "or cause you to forget," he said: Your Prophet (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an, then forgot it. [[Report 1754: see the preceding report 1745 and the commentary on it.]]
* *
Likewise Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas used to interpret the verse, except that he read it: "aw tansaha" in the sense of addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as if he meant: "or you cause it to be forgotten, O Muhammad." Reports on this:
1755 - Yaʿqub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Yaʿla ibn ʿAta' informed us, from al-Qasim [ibn Rabiʿah], who said: I heard Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas say: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause you to forget." I said to him: "Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab reads it: 'aw tunsaha'," [[In the printed edition: "aw nunsiha". The correct reading is what I have recorded, and in Ibn Kathir 1: 275 it reads "aw nansāha"; but Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr al-Muhit 1: 334 states that the reading of Sa'id is "aw tansaha" without hamza, with the ta vowelled with damma; and Ibn Khalawayh in Shawadh al-Qira'at: 9 states: "aw tunsaha" similarly, without naming its subject. I have recorded this because it matches the script of al-Tabari's text. See the following reports 1756, 1757, and al-Hakim's al-Mustadrak 2: 242.]] He said: Saʿd said: "The Qur'an was not revealed to al-Musayyab or to the family of al-Musayyab!" God said: "We shall make you recite, so you will not forget" [Q 87:6], "and remember your Lord when you forget" [Q 18:24]. [[Report 1755: the words between brackets are from Ibn Kathir 1: 275. al-Qasim ibn Rabiʿah is al-Qasim ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Rabiʿah ibn Qanif al-Thaqafi, and is sometimes ascribed to his grandfather. He is the grandson of the nephew of Layla bint Qanif, the Companion. He narrated from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas concerning His words "Whatever sign We abrogate," and from him narrated Yaʿla ibn ʿAta' al-ʿAmiri. Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the reliable (thiqat). Ibn Hajar said: I read in the hand of al-Dhahabi: "No one narrated from him except Yaʿla." (Tahdhib al-Tahdhib 8: 320). See nos. 1756 and 1757.]]
1756 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Hushaym informed us, saying: Yaʿla ibn ʿAta' narrated to us, saying: al-Qasim ibn Rabiʿah ibn Qanif al-Thaqafi narrated to us, saying: I heard Ibn Abi Waqqas mention something similar. [[Report 1756: in the printed edition: "ibn Qanif", which is "Qanif" with qaf, then nun, then fa. So stated in al-Isabah in the biography of "Layla bint Qanif".]]
1757 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and Adam al-ʿAsqalani narrated to us, both together, from Shuʿbah, from Yaʿla ibn ʿAta', who said: I heard al-Qasim ibn Rabiʿah al-Thaqafi say: I said to Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas: "I heard Ibn al-Musayyab read: 'Whatever sign We abrogate or cause you to forget'," and Saʿd said: "Allah did not reveal the Qur'an to al-Musayyab or to his son! Rather it is: 'Whatever sign We abrogate or cause you to forget,' O Muhammad." Then he recited: "We shall make you recite, so you will not forget" and "and remember your Lord when you forget." [[Report 1757: see the two preceding reports. al-Hakim said in al-Mustadrak 2: 242: "This is a sound hadith according to the condition of the two Shaykhs, though they did not record it."]]
1758 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten [aw nunsiha]," he says: "nunsiha" means: We lift it. And Allah, blessed and exalted, had sent down matters of the Qur'an and then lifted them.
* *
The other meaning of the two is that it is in the sense of "leaving" (al-tark), from the words of Allah, exalted is His praise: "They forgot Allah, so He forgot them" [Q 9:67], meaning: they left Allah, so He left them. The interpretation of the verse then, according to this interpretation, is: "Whatever sign We abrogate, changing its ruling and substituting its obligation, We bring one better than what We abrogated or its like." A group of the people of interpretation followed this interpretation.
Those who said this:
1759 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiyah narrated to me, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: "or cause it to be left [aw nansaha]," he says: "or We leave it, not substituting it." [[Report 1759: in Ibn Kathir: "aw nansāhā". The correct reading is what is in al-Tabari, with the nun vowelled with fatha.]]
1760 - Musa narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, his words: "or cause it to be forgotten": "we leave it, not abrogating it."
1761 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten," he said: the abrogating and the abrogated.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd used to say about this:
1762 - Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words: "nunsiha," "we erase it" (namhāhā).
* *
Others read it: "aw nansaʾha" with a fatha on the nun and a hamza after the sin, in the sense of "We postpone it," from your saying: "nasaʾtu hadha al-amr ansaʾuhu nasʾan wa-nasaʾan," when you postponed it. It is from their saying: "I sold it on credit (bi-nasaʾ), meaning with deferment." From this is the verse of Tarafah ibn al-ʿAbd:

*La-ʿamruka inna al-mawta ma ansaʾa al-fata... la-ka-l-tawali al-murkhā wa-thiniyāhu bi-l-yadi*
"By your life, death does not postpone the youth, but it is like the long rope let loose, and its end held in the hand." [[His Diwan: 318 (from the poems of the six pre-Islamic poets), from his famous mu'allaqah. Their version is "ma akhta'a al-fata" (what misses the youth). Al-tawal: a rope lengthened for the animal so it can graze while tied to it. Thiniyah: the end. That is, it does not escape the ropes of death, even if its term is deferred. How true what he said! But we forget!]]
He means by "ansaʾa": postponed.
Among those who read it thus were a group of Companions and Successors, and a group of the readers of Kufa and Basra read it so, and a multitude of the people of interpretation interpreted it so.
Those who said this:
1763 - Abu Kurayb and Yaʿqub ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, both saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Malik informed us, from ʿAta' concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate or postpone [aw nansaʾha]," he said: we postpone it.
1764 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, saying: I heard Ibn Abi Najih say concerning the words of Allah: "or postpone it [aw nansaʾha]," he said: "nurjiʾuha" (we defer it).
1765 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "aw nansaʾha," we defer it and postpone it.
1766 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Fudayl narrated to us, from ʿAtiyyah: "aw nansaʾha," he said: we postpone it, so we do not abrogate it.
1767 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir informed me, from ʿUbayd al-Azdi, from ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr: "aw nansaʾha," its deferment and postponement.
Thus al-Qasim narrated to us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir, "from ʿUbayd al-Azdi," but it is actually "from ʿAli al-Azdi." [[Reports 1767 and 1768: al-Tabari clarified in the first chain that his teacher al-Qasim said in the chain "ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir, from ʿUbayd al-Azdi," and showed that the correct version is "from ʿAli al-Azdi." He then cited the second chain in its correct form. This is as he said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir al-Dari al-Makki, the reader, one of the seven readers; he is reliable, biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/144. ʿAli al-Azdi is ʿAli ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Azdi al-Bariqi, a reliable Successor, biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/193. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr (both diminutives): he is al-Laythi al-Jundaʿi al-Makki, a reliable senior Successor; some even counted him among the Companions, and people praised him highly in the assembly of Ibn ʿUmar. In the Musnad: 5359. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Isabah 5: 79, Ibn Sa'd 5: 341–342, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/409.]]
1768 - Ahmad ibn Yusuf narrated to me, saying: al-Qasim ibn Sallam narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir, from ʿAli al-Azdi, from ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr that he read it: "nansaʾha."
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation of those who read it thus is: "Whatever sign We substitute from a sign We sent down to you, O Muhammad, so We nullify its ruling and keep its script, or We postpone it and let it stand, so We do not change it or nullify its ruling; We bring one better than it or its like."
* *
Some of them read it: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten [aw tunsaha]." The interpretation of this reading is similar to the interpretation of the reading of one who read "aw nunsiha," except that the meaning of "aw tunsaha" is: you, O Muhammad.
* *
Some read: "Ma nunsakh min ayah" with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the sin, meaning: "What We cause you, O Muhammad, to abrogate of a sign," from "ansakhtuka fa-ana ansakhuka" (I made you abrogate, so I abrogate you). In our view this is an error in recitation, because it departs from what the readers transmitted with widespread authority. Likewise the reading of one who read "tunsaha" or "tansaha" is anomalous (shadh) and departs from the reading which the readers of the community transmitted as authoritative.
The most correct reading concerning His words, "aw nunsiha," is the reading of one who reads "aw nunsiha," meaning: "we leave it." Because Allah, exalted is His praise, informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that whenever He substitutes a ruling or changes it, or does not substitute or change it, He brings something better than it or its like. The one most fitting to the verse, since that is its meaning, is that when He has mentioned the report of what He does when He changes and substitutes a ruling of a sign, it should be followed by the report of what He does when He does not substitute or change it. So the report that must follow His words, "Whatever sign We abrogate," is: "or We leave its abrogation," since this is the customary usage in the speech of people. Moreover, when it is read thus in the meaning I have described, it includes the meaning of "nisyan" (causing to forget), which means leaving, and the meaning of "nasa'" (postponement), which means deferment, since everything left is deferred in the state of being left.
* *
Some people denied the reading of one who reads "aw nansaha" when it means forgetting, and said: It is not permissible that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forgot any part of the Qur'an that was not abrogated, unless he forgot some of it and then remembered it. They said: Furthermore, if he forgot some of it, it would not be permissible for all those among his Companions who recited and memorized it to forget it together. They said: And in the words of Allah, exalted is His praise: "And if We willed, We would surely take away what We have revealed to you" [Q 17:86], there is an indication that Allah, exalted is His remembrance, did not cause His Prophet to forget anything of the knowledge He had given him.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: This is a view whose length and corruption is witnessed by the widespread reports from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions to the effect of what we have said.
1769 - Bishr ibn Muʿadh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah who said: Anas ibn Malik narrated to us: that those seventy Ansar who were killed at Bi'r Ma'unah, we recited with them and among them a writing: "Inform our people on our behalf that we have met our Lord, and He is pleased with us and has made us pleased." Then that was lifted. [[Report 1769: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ (with damma on the zayn) al-ʿAyshi: reliable, a memorizer, an authority; Shuʿbah, al-Thawri and other great scholars narrated from him. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/335, Ibn Sa'd 7/2/44, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/263–265. Saʿid is Ibn Abi ʿArubah. This hadith is an abridgement of a hadith from Anas, concerning the story of the reciters who were killed at Bi'r Ma'unah. The imams narrated it from Anas through various channels.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 106–107 (part 2 of 3):

Among these reports: al-Bukhari narrated it (7: 297, Fath al-Bari), from Abd al-A'la ibn Hammad, from Yazid ibn Zurai', with this same chain. At its end: "Anas said: We recited a Qur'an concerning them, then that was abrogated: Convey on our behalf to our people that we have met our Lord, and He is pleased with us and has made us pleased."
Muslim narrated it (1: 187-188) through the transmission of Malik, from Ishaq ibn Abd Allah ibn Abi Talhah, from Anas. For a detailed account of this, see Ibn Kathir's History (4: 71-74).]]
1770 - What we have mentioned from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, that they used to recite: "If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth, he would seek a third; and nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust; and Allah turns in mercy to whoever repents." Then it was abrogated. [[The hadith 1770: al-Tabari mentions it in passing. It is part of a long hadith narrated by Muslim (1: 286) from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. Al-Suyuti mentioned it in al-Durr al-Manthur (1: 105), attributing it also to Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il.
Al-Suyuti also expounded on this topic at length in al-Itqan (2: 29-32, Al-Matba'a al-Musawiyya edition, Cairo, 1287 AH), and quoted many reports concerning it.]]
And similar to that are reports which would take too long to enumerate in this book.
It is not impossible, according to the nature of a sound mind, nor by the proof of any report, that Allah should cause His Prophet ﷺ to forget some of what He had sent down to him. Since that is not impossible on either of these two aspects, it is not permissible for anyone to say that it is impossible.
As for His saying: ﴿And if We willed, We could surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾, He, may His praise be glorified, did not state that He would not take away any of it; rather He stated that if He willed, He could take away all of it. He did not take it away, praise be to Allah, but only took away what they had no need of, since what is abrogated is something the servants have no need of. Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, said: ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget, except what Allah wills﴾ [Al-A'la: 6-7], informing that He causes His Prophet to forget what He wills of it. So what was taken away is that which Allah excepted.
As for us, we have chosen the interpretation we have chosen seeking the coherence of the speech in an ordered meaning, not denying that Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, had caused His Prophet to forget some of what He had abrogated of His revelation and His sending down. [[In the printed edition: "had given his Prophet some of what We abrogate", and the correct reading is what I have established.]]
* *
The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾
Abu Ja'far said: The interpreters differed concerning the interpretation of His saying: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾. Some of them said:
1771 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾, he says: better for you in benefit, and more gentle for you.
* *
And others said:
1772 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾, he says: a verse in which there is lightening, in which there is mercy, [[In Ibn Kathir's Tafsir (1: 275): "in which there is concession" in place of "in which there is mercy".]] in which there is a command, in which there is a prohibition.
* *
Others said: We bring a better one than that which We abrogated, or one better than that which We left and did not abrogate.
Those who said that:
1773 - Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿We bring a better one than it﴾, he says: We bring one better than that which We abrogated, or its like, or the like of that which We left.
* *
The "ha' and alif" in His saying ﴿minha (than it)﴾ refer to this statement, to the verse in His saying ﴿whatever verse We abrogate﴾. And the "ha' and alif" in His saying ﴿aw mithliha (or its like)﴾ refer to the "ha' and alif" in His saying ﴿aw nunsiha (or cause it to be forgotten)﴾.
* *
Others said:
1774 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: Ubayd ibn Umayr used to say: ﴿nunsiha﴾: We lift it from among you; We bring one like it or better than it. [[The report 1774: part of it has passed as no. 1753.]]
1775 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': ﴿aw nunsiha (or cause it to be forgotten)﴾, we lift it, We bring one better than it or its like. [[The report 1775: part of it has passed as no. 1758.]]
1776 - And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Bakr ibn Sharwadh narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from the companions of Ibn Mas'ud, the like of it.
* *
