The correct statement concerning the meaning of this, in our view, is: whatever ruling of a verse We change and alter, or leave its alteration and let it remain in its state, We bring a better one than it for you, from the ruling of the verse which We abrogated and changed its ruling, either in the immediate for its lightness upon you, because it imposed an obligation that was upon you, so He removed its burden from you, as with what was upon the believers of the obligation of qiyam al-layl (night prayer), then that was abrogated and lifted from them, so that was better for them in their immediate life, by the removal of its weight and the lifting of its burden from them; or in the hereafter for the greatness of its reward, on account of the hardship of bearing it and the heaviness of its burden upon the bodies. Like what was upon them of fasting a number of days in the year, which was abrogated and in its place was made obligatory upon them the fasting of a whole month each year, so the obligation of fasting a whole month each year was heavier upon the bodies than fasting a number of days. Yet although that is so, the reward for it is more abundant and the recompense for it is greater, because of the excess of its hardship upon those charged with it compared with fasting a number of days. So although it is harder upon the bodies, it is better than the first in the hereafter, for the excess of its reward and the greatness of its recompense, which was not the like of fasting the numbered days. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿We bring a better one than it﴾, because it is either better than it in the immediate, for its lightness upon the one charged with it, or in the hereafter for the greatness of its reward and the abundance of its recompense.
Or it may be its like in the hardship upon the body and the equality of the recompense and reward upon it, like the abrogation by Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, of the obligation of prayer facing the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis to its obligation facing the direction of the Sacred Mosque.
So turning toward Bayt al-Maqdis, though it differs from turning toward the Mosque, the burden of turning—toward whichever one is turned—is one. For the burden upon one turning toward Bayt al-Maqdis in turning toward it is like the burden upon one whose body turns toward the Ka'bah; they are equal. That is the meaning of "its like" which He, may His praise be glorified, mentioned: ﴿or its like﴾.
* *
Allah, may His praise be glorified, only meant by His saying: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾: whatever ruling of a verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten. But since the addressees of the verse understood its meaning, the mention of "the verse" sufficed in place of mention of "its ruling". This is like the other examples we have mentioned earlier in this book of ours, such as His saying: ﴿and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 93], meaning the love of the calf, and the like.
[[See what has passed in this part 2: 357-360.]]
* *
The interpretation of the verse, then: whatever ruling of a verse We change and alter, or leave without altering, We bring a ruling better for you—O believers—than it, or its like in lightness, heaviness, reward and recompense.
* *
If someone says: We know that the calf is not drunk into the hearts, and that no one who hears His saying: ﴿and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ is confused that its meaning is: "and they were made to drink love of the calf into their hearts." So what indicates that His saying: ﴿whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring a better one than it﴾ is a parallel to that?
It is said: What indicates that it is so is His saying: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾. It is not permissible that some of the Qur'an be better than other parts of it, because all of it is the speech of Allah, and it is not permissible concerning the attributes of Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, to say that some of them are more excellent than others, or that some are better than others. [[Whoever wishes to see how Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, would perceive the meaning of every letter, seeking the truth and the correct, eager for the indication of every word, let him read similar statements of his earlier and later.]]
* *
The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾ (106)
Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His praise be glorified: ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent﴾, He means: Do you not know, O Muhammad, that I am capable of compensating you for what I have abrogated of My rulings and changed of My obligations which I had imposed upon you, with what I will of that which is better for you and for My believing servants with you, and more beneficial for you and for them, either immediately in this world or in the hereafter later—or by replacing for you and for them its like in benefit to them, immediately in this world and later in the hereafter, and similar in lightness upon you and upon them? So know, O Muhammad, that I am capable of that and of all things.
* *
The meaning of His saying ﴿qadir (competent)﴾ in this place is: powerful. It is said from it: "qad qadirtu 'ala kadha wa kadha" when one is powerful over such-and-such: "aqdiru 'alayhi, qudratan wa qidranan wa maqdiratan". The Banu Murra of Ghatafan say "qadirtu 'alayhi" with a kasra on the dal.
As for "taqdir" from the speaker's saying "qaddartu al-shay'", it is said from it: "qaddartuhu uqaddiruhu qadran wa qadaran".
* *
The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that you have, besides Allah, no protector or helper?﴾ (107)
Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: Did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ not know that Allah is over all things competent, and that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, until he was told that? It is said: Indeed! Some of them used to say: That is merely from Allah, may His praise be glorified, a report that Muhammad had known that, but the speech has been brought out in the form of affirmation, as the Arabs do in addressing one another, when one says to his companion: "Did I not honour you? Did I not favour you?" meaning an informing that he had honoured him and favoured him; he intends: Did I not honour you? Did I not favour you? meaning: you have known that.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: This has no basis in our view. That is because His saying, may His praise be glorified: ﴿Do you not know﴾ means only: Have you not known? It is a negative particle to which an interrogative particle is attached, and interrogative particles enter speech either to seek confirmation or to express negation. As for their use to express affirmation, that is not known in the speech of the Arabs, especially when they are attached to negative particles. But in my view, even though it apparently is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, it is in fact meant for his companions whom Allah, may His praise be glorified, mentioned: ﴿Do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna" and listen﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 104]. What indicates that this is so is His saying, may His praise be glorified: ﴿And you have, besides Allah, no protector or helper﴾, for He returned in address at the end of the verse to all of them, though He began its beginning with address to the Prophet ﷺ by saying: ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. For the intended ones are those whose affair you have described, from among his companions. This is widespread and eloquent in the speech of the Arabs: that a speaker brings his speech in the form of address to some people while intending others, and in the form of address to one while intending others, or to a group while the one addressed is one of them, and in the form of address to a group while the intended one is one of them. Among that is the saying of Allah, may His praise be glorified: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise. And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord; indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 1-2]. He returned to address the group, though He had begun the speech with address to the Prophet ﷺ. A similar example is the saying of al-Kumayt ibn Zayd in praise of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

*To the bright lamp, Ahmad, nothing diverts me,*
*neither desire nor fear, from him to another, though the eyes of people be raised to me and they wait.*
It was said: "You have exceeded!" No, rather I aimed justly, even if those who blame me reproached or defamed me.
My devotion to your praise is a tongue that, even if it were to much clamour and uproar over you,
you are the pure, unadulterated, refined in lineage, if your people's lineage raises them.

He brought out his speech in the form of address to the Prophet ﷺ, while intending by it the people of his house, and concealed their description and praise by mentioning the Prophet ﷺ, and referred to the Umayyads with "the ones who blame". For it is known that no one is described as reproaching the praiser of the Prophet ﷺ and his exalter, nor as increasing clamour and uproar in lengthy speech about his excellence.

[[Whoever wishes to know the difference between two intellects of the people of acumen and perception, let him look at the difference between Abu Ja'far's statement in its graceful handling and al-Jahiz's statement in his self-assertion by his cleverness, where he says in his book al-Hayawan (5: 169-171).

Among the faulty praise, of which I have never seen anything more wondrous, is the saying of al-Kumayt ibn Zayd, praising the Prophet ﷺ: If his praise were for the Banu Umayya, it would be permissible for some of the Banu Hashim to fault them for it; or if it were for some of the Banu Hashim, it would be permissible for some of the Banu Umayya to object to it; or if it praised Abu Bilal the Kharijite, it would be permissible for the common people to fault it; or if it praised Amr ibn Ubayd, it would be permissible for the opponent to fault it; or if it praised al-Muhallab, it would be permissible for the companions of al-Ahnaf to fault it. But as for the praise of the Prophet ﷺ, who would be displeased by it? Then he recited the earlier verses and said: "Had he said nothing about him, peace be upon him, except like his saying: 'Blessed is a grave in which you lie, and blessed are you therein, and Yathrib has its people with it by that...' 'They have buried generosity, prudence and bounty, the evening the poured earth covered you...' Had he not praised him, peace be upon him, except with these poems which are not suitable among the Arabs generally, he would not be praised; how then with what we have related before this?"

Al-Jahiz's pen is sometimes seized like an itch, not calmed from its outbursts until it is satisfied by some speech, some self-assertion, and excess of intellect! Yet the critics follow al-Jahiz, trusting his excellence and intellect, and often they abandon what is more fitting, being seduced by what he says.]]

And as Jamil ibn Ma'mar said:

*Surely my neighbours, this evening, have departed,*
*calls of desire and wide lands have summoned them.*
[[I have not found the verse in what has been printed of Jamil's poetry, nor in what I have collected of it. "al-manadih": wide, distant lands, as if plural of mandihah, its yâ' dropped. Tamim ibn Ubayy ibn Muqbil said: "When I incline my mount to its resting place, I mount, and I am not too weak for the wide lands." It may be well said that it is a plural with no singular from its own form, like mahasin mashabih; its singular is nadh, and its plural andah: that which is wide of land.]]

He said: "Surely my neighbours this evening" — beginning the report about a group of his neighbours, then said "has departed", because his intention, in what he began of his speech, was to report about one of them rather than the group. And as Jamil also said in his other ode:

*O my two friends, in what you have lived, have you seen*
*a slain man who wept for love of his killer before me?*
[[Al-Amali 2: 74, al-Aghani 1: 117, 7: 140; this is an ode from the fine poetry of Jamil.]]

He means the female killer, for he describes a woman, and he named the man to refer to her, meaning her. So likewise His saying: ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾ and ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ — though the apparent speech is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, it is intended for his companions. This is clear by the indication of His saying: (And you have, besides Allah, no protector or helper. Or do you desire to ask your Messenger as Moses was asked before?) — the three verses after it — that it is so. [[See what will come shortly after: 499-500.]]

* *
As for His saying: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, and He did not say "the dominion of the heavens" — He meant by it "mulk" (dominion) of sovereignty and kingdom, not "milk" (ownership). When the Arabs wish to inform about "kingdom" which is sovereign rule, they say: "Allah has given the creation dominion (mulk)." And when they wish to inform about "milk" (ownership) they say: "So-and-so owns (malaka) this thing, so he possesses it (yamlikuhu) as ownership (milkan), possession (malakah) and holding (malkan)."

The interpretation of the verse, then, is: Do you not know, O Muhammad, that to Me belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and their sovereignty, apart from any other? I judge in them and in what is in them as I will, I command in them and in what is in them as I will, I forbid what I will, and I abrogate (naskh), substitute, and alter, from My rulings by which I judge My servants, whatever I will, whenever I will, and I confirm of them whatever I will?

* *

Although this statement is, from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, an address to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) in the form of a report about His greatness, it is also from Him, may His praise be exalted, a refutation of the Jews who denied the abrogation of the rulings of the Torah, rejected the prophethood of Jesus, and denied Muhammad (ﷺ), because they came with what they came with from Allah by altering what Allah had changed in the rulings of the Torah. So Allah informed them that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and their sovereignty, since all creatures are the people of His kingdom and obedience, upon them is hearing and obeying Him and submitting to His command and prohibition, and that to Him belongs the commanding of them as He wills, the forbidding of them as He wills, the abrogating of what He wills, the confirming of what He wills, and the causing to be forgotten of what He wills of His rulings, His commands and His prohibitions. Then He said to His Prophet (ﷺ) and to the believers with him: Submit to My command and hasten to obey Me in what I abrogate and in what I leave unabrogated, of My rulings, My limits and My obligations. Let not the opposition of an opponent to you in My command, My prohibition, My abrogating and My abrogated rulings alarm you, for no one manages your affairs besides Me, and no helper for you except Me, and I am the sole one who holds your guardianship, the defender of you, and the one who alone grants you victory, by My might, My authority and My power, against whoever opposes you and is hostile to you, and sets up the war of enmity between him and you, until I raise up your proof and make it against them for you.

* *

The word *al-wali* (الولي) means *fa'il* (فعيل) from the saying of the speaker: "I took charge of the affair of so-and-so" (وَلِيت أمر فلان), when I became its overseer, so "I am its *wali*, and he is its *wali*," meaning its guardian and its manager. From this it is said: "So-and-so is the *wali al-'ahd* of the Muslims" (ولي عهد المسلمين), meaning the one who carries out what he has been entrusted with regarding the affairs of the Muslims.

* *

As for *al-nasir* (النصير), it is *fa'il* (فعيل) from your saying: "I supported you, I support you, so I am your supporter and your *nasir*," and it means the one who strengthens and empowers.

* *

As for the meaning of His words ﴿apart from Allah﴾ (من دون الله), it means other than Allah and beyond Allah, and from it is the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

"O soul, what do you have apart from Allah of any protector,
and what remains after the vicissitudes of time?"

[His Diwan: 43. Similar to it is the verse of Ibn Ahmar: "We are only a people of grazing livestock, and for them there is no tilled land nor cultivated fields," meaning: we have no property other than livestock, so we have no crops and no horses.]

He means: what protects you from adversities other than Allah and beyond Allah?

* *

The meaning of the statement, then, is: You, O believers, have no one besides Allah who manages your affairs, nor any helper who will support and strengthen you and aid you against your enemies.

On the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He: "Whatever sign We abrogate..."

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His praise, "Whatever sign We abrogate [ma nansakh min ayah]," He means: whatever We transfer from the ruling of a sign to another, changing it and substituting it. [[In the printed edition: "ma nasakh min ayah ila ghayrihi fa-nabdhu", and the addition is from Tafsir Ibn Kathir 1: 273.]] This is when the permitted becomes forbidden, the forbidden becomes permitted, and the allowed becomes prohibited, and the prohibited becomes allowed. This happens only in commands and prohibitions, in restriction and release, in forbidding and permitting. As for reports (akhbar), there is no abrogating (nasikh) or abrogated (mansukh) element in them.
* *
The root of "naskh" (abrogation) is from "nasakh al-kitab" (copying a book), which is transferring it from one copy to another different from it. Likewise, the meaning of abrogating a ruling to something else is only transforming it and transferring its wording from it to something else. [[In the printed edition: "ʿanhu ila ghayrihi"; in Ibn Kathir: "wa naql ʿibarah ila ghayriha". The correct reading is what I have adopted.]] When this is the meaning of abrogating a sign, then it is the same, when its ruling is abrogated and its obligation is changed and replaced, and the obligation of the servants is transferred from what was binding upon them, whether its script (khatt) remains recorded, or its trace is erased, so it is effaced and forgotten. [[In the printed edition: "awfara hazzaha fa-turika, aw muhiya athāruhā fa-ʿufiyya aw nusiya", a sentence that has been corrupted and garbled. Al-Tabari's meaning is that abrogation, which is the change of a ruling, may occur while the script remains as it is, with a different ruling expressed in other wording — or the script is lifted and people forget what they had memorized at the time of revelation. "ʿAfiya" comes from their saying: ʿafa al-athar yaʿfu, meaning it was obliterated and went away; and ʿaffāhu yuʿaffīhi (with doubled letter) means he wiped it out and removed it.
Furthermore, the following sentence, "for in both of its states it is abrogated," and the report of al-Hasan that follows, indicate the correctness of what I have recorded in reading al-Tabari's text.]] For in that case it is abrogated in both its states, and the new ruling that replaces the first ruling, and to which the obligation of the servants is transferred, is the abrogating element (nasikh). It is said of it: "Allah abrogated such-and-such a sign, abrogating it (yansakhuhu) with abrogation (naskhan), and the 'nuskhah' is the noun." In accordance with what we have said, al-Hasan al-Basri used to say:
1745 - Sawwar ibn ʿAbd Allah al-ʿAnbari narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn al-Harith narrated to us, saying: ʿAwf narrated to us, from al-Hasan, that he said concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause you to forget, We bring one better than it or the like of it" [Q 2:106], he said: "Your Prophet (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an, then he forgot it, and it was nothing, [[In the printed edition: "qāla uqriʾa qurʾānan", a part of which is missing; it will appear correctly in the report numbered 1754, and I have added this addition from there.]] and among the Qur'an is what has been abrogated while you still recite it."
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation differed concerning the interpretation of His words, "Whatever We abrogate," and some of them said:
1746 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Whatever sign We abrogate": as for its abrogation, it is its taking away.
* *
And others said:
1747 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate," he says: "whatever We substitute from a sign."
* *
And others said:
1748 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from the companions of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, that they said: "Whatever sign We abrogate," we keep its script [and substitute its ruling].
1749 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Whatever sign We abrogate," we keep its script and substitute its ruling. I related it from the companions of Ibn Masʿud.
1750 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Bakr ibn Shawdhab narrated to me, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from the companions of Ibn Masʿud: "Whatever sign We abrogate," we keep its script [and substitute its ruling]. [[Report 1750: the words between brackets are from Ibn Kathir 1: 273–274.]]
* *
On the Interpretation of His Words: "Or cause you to forget [aw nunsiha]"
Abu Ja'far said: The readers differed concerning His words. The people of Medina and Kufa read it: "aw nunsiha" (or We cause it to be forgotten). The reading of those who read it thus has two interpretive possibilities.
The first: that its interpretation is: "Whatever sign We abrogate, O Muhammad, changing its ruling, or cause you to forget." It is mentioned that in the codex of ʿAbd Allah it reads: "ma nunsika min ayah aw nansakhha najiʾ bi-mithlihā" (Whatever We cause you to forget of a sign, or abrogate it, We bring one like it), and this is the interpretation of "forgetting" (al-nisyan). And this interpretation was held by a group of the people of interpretation.
Those who said this:
1751 - Bishr ibn Muʿadh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause you to forget, We bring one better than it or the like of it": he used to abrogate a sign by the sign after it, and the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) would recite a sign or more than that, then it would be forgotten and lifted.
1752 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause you to forget," he said: Allah, exalted is His remembrance, would cause His Prophet (ﷺ) to forget what He willed and abrogate what He willed.
1753 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr used to say: "nunsiha" means: We lift it from among you.
1754 - Sawwar ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn al-Harith narrated to us, saying: ʿAwf narrated to us, from al-Hasan, that he said concerning His words: "or cause you to forget," he said: Your Prophet (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an, then forgot it. [[Report 1754: see the preceding report 1745 and the commentary on it.]]
* *
Likewise Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas used to interpret the verse, except that he read it: "aw tansaha" in the sense of addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as if he meant: "or you cause it to be forgotten, O Muhammad." Reports on this:
1755 - Yaʿqub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Yaʿla ibn ʿAta' informed us, from al-Qasim [ibn Rabiʿah], who said: I heard Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas say: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause you to forget." I said to him: "Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab reads it: 'aw tunsaha'," [[In the printed edition: "aw nunsiha". The correct reading is what I have recorded, and in Ibn Kathir 1: 275 it reads "aw nansāha"; but Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr al-Muhit 1: 334 states that the reading of Sa'id is "aw tansaha" without hamza, with the ta vowelled with damma; and Ibn Khalawayh in Shawadh al-Qira'at: 9 states: "aw tunsaha" similarly, without naming its subject. I have recorded this because it matches the script of al-Tabari's text. See the following reports 1756, 1757, and al-Hakim's al-Mustadrak 2: 242.]] He said: Saʿd said: "The Qur'an was not revealed to al-Musayyab or to the family of al-Musayyab!" God said: "We shall make you recite, so you will not forget" [Q 87:6], "and remember your Lord when you forget" [Q 18:24]. [[Report 1755: the words between brackets are from Ibn Kathir 1: 275. al-Qasim ibn Rabiʿah is al-Qasim ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Rabiʿah ibn Qanif al-Thaqafi, and is sometimes ascribed to his grandfather. He is the grandson of the nephew of Layla bint Qanif, the Companion. He narrated from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas concerning His words "Whatever sign We abrogate," and from him narrated Yaʿla ibn ʿAta' al-ʿAmiri. Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the reliable (thiqat). Ibn Hajar said: I read in the hand of al-Dhahabi: "No one narrated from him except Yaʿla." (Tahdhib al-Tahdhib 8: 320). See nos. 1756 and 1757.]]
1756 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Hushaym informed us, saying: Yaʿla ibn ʿAta' narrated to us, saying: al-Qasim ibn Rabiʿah ibn Qanif al-Thaqafi narrated to us, saying: I heard Ibn Abi Waqqas mention something similar. [[Report 1756: in the printed edition: "ibn Qanif", which is "Qanif" with qaf, then nun, then fa. So stated in al-Isabah in the biography of "Layla bint Qanif".]]
1757 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and Adam al-ʿAsqalani narrated to us, both together, from Shuʿbah, from Yaʿla ibn ʿAta', who said: I heard al-Qasim ibn Rabiʿah al-Thaqafi say: I said to Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas: "I heard Ibn al-Musayyab read: 'Whatever sign We abrogate or cause you to forget'," and Saʿd said: "Allah did not reveal the Qur'an to al-Musayyab or to his son! Rather it is: 'Whatever sign We abrogate or cause you to forget,' O Muhammad." Then he recited: "We shall make you recite, so you will not forget" and "and remember your Lord when you forget." [[Report 1757: see the two preceding reports. al-Hakim said in al-Mustadrak 2: 242: "This is a sound hadith according to the condition of the two Shaykhs, though they did not record it."]]
1758 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten [aw nunsiha]," he says: "nunsiha" means: We lift it. And Allah, blessed and exalted, had sent down matters of the Qur'an and then lifted them.
* *
The other meaning of the two is that it is in the sense of "leaving" (al-tark), from the words of Allah, exalted is His praise: "They forgot Allah, so He forgot them" [Q 9:67], meaning: they left Allah, so He left them. The interpretation of the verse then, according to this interpretation, is: "Whatever sign We abrogate, changing its ruling and substituting its obligation, We bring one better than what We abrogated or its like." A group of the people of interpretation followed this interpretation.
Those who said this:
1759 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiyah narrated to me, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: "or cause it to be left [aw nansaha]," he says: "or We leave it, not substituting it." [[Report 1759: in Ibn Kathir: "aw nansāhā". The correct reading is what is in al-Tabari, with the nun vowelled with fatha.]]
1760 - Musa narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, his words: "or cause it to be forgotten": "we leave it, not abrogating it."
1761 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten," he said: the abrogating and the abrogated.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd used to say about this:
1762 - Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words: "nunsiha," "we erase it" (namhāhā).
* *
Others read it: "aw nansaʾha" with a fatha on the nun and a hamza after the sin, in the sense of "We postpone it," from your saying: "nasaʾtu hadha al-amr ansaʾuhu nasʾan wa-nasaʾan," when you postponed it. It is from their saying: "I sold it on credit (bi-nasaʾ), meaning with deferment." From this is the verse of Tarafah ibn al-ʿAbd:

*La-ʿamruka inna al-mawta ma ansaʾa al-fata... la-ka-l-tawali al-murkhā wa-thiniyāhu bi-l-yadi*
"By your life, death does not postpone the youth, but it is like the long rope let loose, and its end held in the hand." [[His Diwan: 318 (from the poems of the six pre-Islamic poets), from his famous mu'allaqah. Their version is "ma akhta'a al-fata" (what misses the youth). Al-tawal: a rope lengthened for the animal so it can graze while tied to it. Thiniyah: the end. That is, it does not escape the ropes of death, even if its term is deferred. How true what he said! But we forget!]]
He means by "ansaʾa": postponed.
Among those who read it thus were a group of Companions and Successors, and a group of the readers of Kufa and Basra read it so, and a multitude of the people of interpretation interpreted it so.
Those who said this:
1763 - Abu Kurayb and Yaʿqub ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, both saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Malik informed us, from ʿAta' concerning His words: "Whatever sign We abrogate or postpone [aw nansaʾha]," he said: we postpone it.
1764 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, saying: I heard Ibn Abi Najih say concerning the words of Allah: "or postpone it [aw nansaʾha]," he said: "nurjiʾuha" (we defer it).
1765 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "aw nansaʾha," we defer it and postpone it.
1766 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Fudayl narrated to us, from ʿAtiyyah: "aw nansaʾha," he said: we postpone it, so we do not abrogate it.
1767 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir informed me, from ʿUbayd al-Azdi, from ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr: "aw nansaʾha," its deferment and postponement.
Thus al-Qasim narrated to us, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir, "from ʿUbayd al-Azdi," but it is actually "from ʿAli al-Azdi." [[Reports 1767 and 1768: al-Tabari clarified in the first chain that his teacher al-Qasim said in the chain "ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir, from ʿUbayd al-Azdi," and showed that the correct version is "from ʿAli al-Azdi." He then cited the second chain in its correct form. This is as he said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir al-Dari al-Makki, the reader, one of the seven readers; he is reliable, biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/144. ʿAli al-Azdi is ʿAli ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Azdi al-Bariqi, a reliable Successor, biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/193. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr (both diminutives): he is al-Laythi al-Jundaʿi al-Makki, a reliable senior Successor; some even counted him among the Companions, and people praised him highly in the assembly of Ibn ʿUmar. In the Musnad: 5359. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Isabah 5: 79, Ibn Sa'd 5: 341–342, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/409.]]
1768 - Ahmad ibn Yusuf narrated to me, saying: al-Qasim ibn Sallam narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir, from ʿAli al-Azdi, from ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr that he read it: "nansaʾha."
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation of those who read it thus is: "Whatever sign We substitute from a sign We sent down to you, O Muhammad, so We nullify its ruling and keep its script, or We postpone it and let it stand, so We do not change it or nullify its ruling; We bring one better than it or its like."
* *
Some of them read it: "Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten [aw tunsaha]." The interpretation of this reading is similar to the interpretation of the reading of one who read "aw nunsiha," except that the meaning of "aw tunsaha" is: you, O Muhammad.
* *
Some read: "Ma nunsakh min ayah" with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the sin, meaning: "What We cause you, O Muhammad, to abrogate of a sign," from "ansakhtuka fa-ana ansakhuka" (I made you abrogate, so I abrogate you). In our view this is an error in recitation, because it departs from what the readers transmitted with widespread authority. Likewise the reading of one who read "tunsaha" or "tansaha" is anomalous (shadh) and departs from the reading which the readers of the community transmitted as authoritative.
The most correct reading concerning His words, "aw nunsiha," is the reading of one who reads "aw nunsiha," meaning: "we leave it." Because Allah, exalted is His praise, informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that whenever He substitutes a ruling or changes it, or does not substitute or change it, He brings something better than it or its like. The one most fitting to the verse, since that is its meaning, is that when He has mentioned the report of what He does when He changes and substitutes a ruling of a sign, it should be followed by the report of what He does when He does not substitute or change it. So the report that must follow His words, "Whatever sign We abrogate," is: "or We leave its abrogation," since this is the customary usage in the speech of people. Moreover, when it is read thus in the meaning I have described, it includes the meaning of "nisyan" (causing to forget), which means leaving, and the meaning of "nasa'" (postponement), which means deferment, since everything left is deferred in the state of being left.
* *
Some people denied the reading of one who reads "aw nansaha" when it means forgetting, and said: It is not permissible that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forgot any part of the Qur'an that was not abrogated, unless he forgot some of it and then remembered it. They said: Furthermore, if he forgot some of it, it would not be permissible for all those among his Companions who recited and memorized it to forget it together. They said: And in the words of Allah, exalted is His praise: "And if We willed, We would surely take away what We have revealed to you" [Q 17:86], there is an indication that Allah, exalted is His remembrance, did not cause His Prophet to forget anything of the knowledge He had given him.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: This is a view whose length and corruption is witnessed by the widespread reports from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions to the effect of what we have said.
1769 - Bishr ibn Muʿadh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah who said: Anas ibn Malik narrated to us: that those seventy Ansar who were killed at Bi'r Ma'unah, we recited with them and among them a writing: "Inform our people on our behalf that we have met our Lord, and He is pleased with us and has made us pleased." Then that was lifted. [[Report 1769: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ (with damma on the zayn) al-ʿAyshi: reliable, a memorizer, an authority; Shuʿbah, al-Thawri and other great scholars narrated from him. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/335, Ibn Sa'd 7/2/44, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/263–265. Saʿid is Ibn Abi ʿArubah. This hadith is an abridgement of a hadith from Anas, concerning the story of the reciters who were killed at Bi'r Ma'unah. The imams narrated it from Anas through various channels.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 106–107 (part 2 of 3):

Among these reports: al-Bukhari narrated it (7: 297, Fath al-Bari), from Abd al-A'la ibn Hammad, from Yazid ibn Zurai', with this same chain. At its end: "Anas said: We recited a Qur'an concerning them, then that was abrogated: Convey on our behalf to our people that we have met our Lord, and He is pleased with us and has made us pleased."
Muslim narrated it (1: 187-188) through the transmission of Malik, from Ishaq ibn Abd Allah ibn Abi Talhah, from Anas. For a detailed account of this, see Ibn Kathir's History (4: 71-74).]]
1770 - What we have mentioned from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, that they used to recite: "If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth, he would seek a third; and nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust; and Allah turns in mercy to whoever repents." Then it was abrogated. [[The hadith 1770: al-Tabari mentions it in passing. It is part of a long hadith narrated by Muslim (1: 286) from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. Al-Suyuti mentioned it in al-Durr al-Manthur (1: 105), attributing it also to Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il.
Al-Suyuti also expounded on this topic at length in al-Itqan (2: 29-32, Al-Matba'a al-Musawiyya edition, Cairo, 1287 AH), and quoted many reports concerning it.]]
And similar to that are reports which would take too long to enumerate in this book.
It is not impossible, according to the nature of a sound mind, nor by the proof of any report, that Allah should cause His Prophet ﷺ to forget some of what He had sent down to him. Since that is not impossible on either of these two aspects, it is not permissible for anyone to say that it is impossible.
As for His saying: ﴿And if We willed, We could surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾, He, may His praise be glorified, did not state that He would not take away any of it; rather He stated that if He willed, He could take away all of it. He did not take it away, praise be to Allah, but only took away what they had no need of, since what is abrogated is something the servants have no need of. Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, said: ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget, except what Allah wills﴾ [Al-A'la: 6-7], informing that He causes His Prophet to forget what He wills of it. So what was taken away is that which Allah excepted.
As for us, we have chosen the interpretation we have chosen seeking the coherence of the speech in an ordered meaning, not denying that Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, had caused His Prophet to forget some of what He had abrogated of His revelation and His sending down. [[In the printed edition: "had given his Prophet some of what We abrogate", and the correct reading is what I have established.]]
* *
The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾
Abu Ja'far said: The interpreters differed concerning the interpretation of His saying: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾. Some of them said:
1771 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾, he says: better for you in benefit, and more gentle for you.
* *
And others said:
1772 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾, he says: a verse in which there is lightening, in which there is mercy, [[In Ibn Kathir's Tafsir (1: 275): "in which there is concession" in place of "in which there is mercy".]] in which there is a command, in which there is a prohibition.
* *
Others said: We bring a better one than that which We abrogated, or one better than that which We left and did not abrogate.
Those who said that:
1773 - Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿We bring a better one than it﴾, he says: We bring one better than that which We abrogated, or its like, or the like of that which We left.
* *
The "ha' and alif" in His saying ﴿minha (than it)﴾ refer to this statement, to the verse in His saying ﴿whatever verse We abrogate﴾. And the "ha' and alif" in His saying ﴿aw mithliha (or its like)﴾ refer to the "ha' and alif" in His saying ﴿aw nunsiha (or cause it to be forgotten)﴾.
* *
Others said:
1774 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: Ubayd ibn Umayr used to say: ﴿nunsiha﴾: We lift it from among you; We bring one like it or better than it. [[The report 1774: part of it has passed as no. 1753.]]
1775 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': ﴿aw nunsiha (or cause it to be forgotten)﴾, we lift it, We bring one better than it or its like. [[The report 1775: part of it has passed as no. 1758.]]
1776 - And al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Bakr ibn Sharwadh narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from the companions of Ibn Mas'ud, the like of it.
* *
The correct statement concerning the meaning of this, in our view, is: whatever ruling of a verse We change and alter, or leave its alteration and let it remain in its state, We bring a better one than it for you, from the ruling of the verse which We abrogated and changed its ruling, either in the immediate for its lightness upon you, because it imposed an obligation that was upon you, so He removed its burden from you, as with what was upon the believers of the obligation of qiyam al-layl (night prayer), then that was abrogated and lifted from them, so that was better for them in their immediate life, by the removal of its weight and the lifting of its burden from them; or in the hereafter for the greatness of its reward, on account of the hardship of bearing it and the heaviness of its burden upon the bodies. Like what was upon them of fasting a number of days in the year, which was abrogated and in its place was made obligatory upon them the fasting of a whole month each year, so the obligation of fasting a whole month each year was heavier upon the bodies than fasting a number of days. Yet although that is so, the reward for it is more abundant and the recompense for it is greater, because of the excess of its hardship upon those charged with it compared with fasting a number of days. So although it is harder upon the bodies, it is better than the first in the hereafter, for the excess of its reward and the greatness of its recompense, which was not the like of fasting the numbered days. That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿We bring a better one than it﴾, because it is either better than it in the immediate, for its lightness upon the one charged with it, or in the hereafter for the greatness of its reward and the abundance of its recompense.
Or it may be its like in the hardship upon the body and the equality of the recompense and reward upon it, like the abrogation by Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, of the obligation of prayer facing the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis to its obligation facing the direction of the Sacred Mosque.
So turning toward Bayt al-Maqdis, though it differs from turning toward the Mosque, the burden of turning—toward whichever one is turned—is one. For the burden upon one turning toward Bayt al-Maqdis in turning toward it is like the burden upon one whose body turns toward the Ka'bah; they are equal. That is the meaning of "its like" which He, may His praise be glorified, mentioned: ﴿or its like﴾.
* *
Allah, may His praise be glorified, only meant by His saying: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾: whatever ruling of a verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten. But since the addressees of the verse understood its meaning, the mention of "the verse" sufficed in place of mention of "its ruling". This is like the other examples we have mentioned earlier in this book of ours, such as His saying: ﴿and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 93], meaning the love of the calf, and the like.
[[See what has passed in this part 2: 357-360.]]
* *
The interpretation of the verse, then: whatever ruling of a verse We change and alter, or leave without altering, We bring a ruling better for you—O believers—than it, or its like in lightness, heaviness, reward and recompense.
* *
If someone says: We know that the calf is not drunk into the hearts, and that no one who hears His saying: ﴿and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ is confused that its meaning is: "and they were made to drink love of the calf into their hearts." So what indicates that His saying: ﴿whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring a better one than it﴾ is a parallel to that?
It is said: What indicates that it is so is His saying: ﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾. It is not permissible that some of the Qur'an be better than other parts of it, because all of it is the speech of Allah, and it is not permissible concerning the attributes of Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, to say that some of them are more excellent than others, or that some are better than others. [[Whoever wishes to see how Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, would perceive the meaning of every letter, seeking the truth and the correct, eager for the indication of every word, let him read similar statements of his earlier and later.]]
* *
The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾ (106)
Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His praise be glorified: ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent﴾, He means: Do you not know, O Muhammad, that I am capable of compensating you for what I have abrogated of My rulings and changed of My obligations which I had imposed upon you, with what I will of that which is better for you and for My believing servants with you, and more beneficial for you and for them, either immediately in this world or in the hereafter later—or by replacing for you and for them its like in benefit to them, immediately in this world and later in the hereafter, and similar in lightness upon you and upon them? So know, O Muhammad, that I am capable of that and of all things.
* *
The meaning of His saying ﴿qadir (competent)﴾ in this place is: powerful. It is said from it: "qad qadirtu 'ala kadha wa kadha" when one is powerful over such-and-such: "aqdiru 'alayhi, qudratan wa qidranan wa maqdiratan". The Banu Murra of Ghatafan say "qadirtu 'alayhi" with a kasra on the dal.
As for "taqdir" from the speaker's saying "qaddartu al-shay'", it is said from it: "qaddartuhu uqaddiruhu qadran wa qadaran".
* *
The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that you have, besides Allah, no protector or helper?﴾ (107)
Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: Did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ not know that Allah is over all things competent, and that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, until he was told that? It is said: Indeed! Some of them used to say: That is merely from Allah, may His praise be glorified, a report that Muhammad had known that, but the speech has been brought out in the form of affirmation, as the Arabs do in addressing one another, when one says to his companion: "Did I not honour you? Did I not favour you?" meaning an informing that he had honoured him and favoured him; he intends: Did I not honour you? Did I not favour you? meaning: you have known that.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: This has no basis in our view. That is because His saying, may His praise be glorified: ﴿Do you not know﴾ means only: Have you not known? It is a negative particle to which an interrogative particle is attached, and interrogative particles enter speech either to seek confirmation or to express negation. As for their use to express affirmation, that is not known in the speech of the Arabs, especially when they are attached to negative particles. But in my view, even though it apparently is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, it is in fact meant for his companions whom Allah, may His praise be glorified, mentioned: ﴿Do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna" and listen﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 104]. What indicates that this is so is His saying, may His praise be glorified: ﴿And you have, besides Allah, no protector or helper﴾, for He returned in address at the end of the verse to all of them, though He began its beginning with address to the Prophet ﷺ by saying: ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. For the intended ones are those whose affair you have described, from among his companions. This is widespread and eloquent in the speech of the Arabs: that a speaker brings his speech in the form of address to some people while intending others, and in the form of address to one while intending others, or to a group while the one addressed is one of them, and in the form of address to a group while the intended one is one of them. Among that is the saying of Allah, may His praise be glorified: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites; indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise. And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord; indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 1-2]. He returned to address the group, though He had begun the speech with address to the Prophet ﷺ. A similar example is the saying of al-Kumayt ibn Zayd in praise of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

*To the bright lamp, Ahmad, nothing diverts me,*
*neither desire nor fear, from him to another, though the eyes of people be raised to me and they wait.*
It was said: "You have exceeded!" No, rather I aimed justly, even if those who blame me reproached or defamed me.
My devotion to your praise is a tongue that, even if it were to much clamour and uproar over you,
you are the pure, unadulterated, refined in lineage, if your people's lineage raises them.

He brought out his speech in the form of address to the Prophet ﷺ, while intending by it the people of his house, and concealed their description and praise by mentioning the Prophet ﷺ, and referred to the Umayyads with "the ones who blame". For it is known that no one is described as reproaching the praiser of the Prophet ﷺ and his exalter, nor as increasing clamour and uproar in lengthy speech about his excellence.

[[Whoever wishes to know the difference between two intellects of the people of acumen and perception, let him look at the difference between Abu Ja'far's statement in its graceful handling and al-Jahiz's statement in his self-assertion by his cleverness, where he says in his book al-Hayawan (5: 169-171).

Among the faulty praise, of which I have never seen anything more wondrous, is the saying of al-Kumayt ibn Zayd, praising the Prophet ﷺ: If his praise were for the Banu Umayya, it would be permissible for some of the Banu Hashim to fault them for it; or if it were for some of the Banu Hashim, it would be permissible for some of the Banu Umayya to object to it; or if it praised Abu Bilal the Kharijite, it would be permissible for the common people to fault it; or if it praised Amr ibn Ubayd, it would be permissible for the opponent to fault it; or if it praised al-Muhallab, it would be permissible for the companions of al-Ahnaf to fault it. But as for the praise of the Prophet ﷺ, who would be displeased by it? Then he recited the earlier verses and said: "Had he said nothing about him, peace be upon him, except like his saying: 'Blessed is a grave in which you lie, and blessed are you therein, and Yathrib has its people with it by that...' 'They have buried generosity, prudence and bounty, the evening the poured earth covered you...' Had he not praised him, peace be upon him, except with these poems which are not suitable among the Arabs generally, he would not be praised; how then with what we have related before this?"

Al-Jahiz's pen is sometimes seized like an itch, not calmed from its outbursts until it is satisfied by some speech, some self-assertion, and excess of intellect! Yet the critics follow al-Jahiz, trusting his excellence and intellect, and often they abandon what is more fitting, being seduced by what he says.]]

And as Jamil ibn Ma'mar said:

*Surely my neighbours, this evening, have departed,*
*calls of desire and wide lands have summoned them.*
[[I have not found the verse in what has been printed of Jamil's poetry, nor in what I have collected of it. "al-manadih": wide, distant lands, as if plural of mandihah, its yâ' dropped. Tamim ibn Ubayy ibn Muqbil said: "When I incline my mount to its resting place, I mount, and I am not too weak for the wide lands." It may be well said that it is a plural with no singular from its own form, like mahasin mashabih; its singular is nadh, and its plural andah: that which is wide of land.]]

He said: "Surely my neighbours this evening" — beginning the report about a group of his neighbours, then said "has departed", because his intention, in what he began of his speech, was to report about one of them rather than the group. And as Jamil also said in his other ode:

*O my two friends, in what you have lived, have you seen*
*a slain man who wept for love of his killer before me?*
[[Al-Amali 2: 74, al-Aghani 1: 117, 7: 140; this is an ode from the fine poetry of Jamil.]]

He means the female killer, for he describes a woman, and he named the man to refer to her, meaning her. So likewise His saying: ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾ and ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ — though the apparent speech is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, it is intended for his companions. This is clear by the indication of His saying: (And you have, besides Allah, no protector or helper. Or do you desire to ask your Messenger as Moses was asked before?) — the three verses after it — that it is so. [[See what will come shortly after: 499-500.]]

* *
As for His saying: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, and He did not say "the dominion of the heavens" — He meant by it "mulk" (dominion) of sovereignty and kingdom, not "milk" (ownership). When the Arabs wish to inform about "kingdom" which is sovereign rule, they say: "Allah has given the creation dominion (mulk)." And when they wish to inform about "milk" (ownership) they say: "So-and-so owns (malaka) this thing, so he possesses it (yamlikuhu) as ownership (milkan), possession (malakah) and holding (malkan)."

The interpretation of the verse, then, is: Do you not know, O Muhammad, that to Me belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and their sovereignty, apart from any other? I judge in them and in what is in them as I will, I command in them and in what is in them as I will, I forbid what I will, and I abrogate (naskh), substitute, and alter, from My rulings by which I judge My servants, whatever I will, whenever I will, and I confirm of them whatever I will?

* *

Although this statement is, from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, an address to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) in the form of a report about His greatness, it is also from Him, may His praise be exalted, a refutation of the Jews who denied the abrogation of the rulings of the Torah, rejected the prophethood of Jesus, and denied Muhammad (ﷺ), because they came with what they came with from Allah by altering what Allah had changed in the rulings of the Torah. So Allah informed them that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and their sovereignty, since all creatures are the people of His kingdom and obedience, upon them is hearing and obeying Him and submitting to His command and prohibition, and that to Him belongs the commanding of them as He wills, the forbidding of them as He wills, the abrogating of what He wills, the confirming of what He wills, and the causing to be forgotten of what He wills of His rulings, His commands and His prohibitions. Then He said to His Prophet (ﷺ) and to the believers with him: Submit to My command and hasten to obey Me in what I abrogate and in what I leave unabrogated, of My rulings, My limits and My obligations. Let not the opposition of an opponent to you in My command, My prohibition, My abrogating and My abrogated rulings alarm you, for no one manages your affairs besides Me, and no helper for you except Me, and I am the sole one who holds your guardianship, the defender of you, and the one who alone grants you victory, by My might, My authority and My power, against whoever opposes you and is hostile to you, and sets up the war of enmity between him and you, until I raise up your proof and make it against them for you.

* *

The word *al-wali* (الولي) means *fa'il* (فعيل) from the saying of the speaker: "I took charge of the affair of so-and-so" (وَلِيت أمر فلان), when I became its overseer, so "I am its *wali*, and he is its *wali*," meaning its guardian and its manager. From this it is said: "So-and-so is the *wali al-'ahd* of the Muslims" (ولي عهد المسلمين), meaning the one who carries out what he has been entrusted with regarding the affairs of the Muslims.

* *

As for *al-nasir* (النصير), it is *fa'il* (فعيل) from your saying: "I supported you, I support you, so I am your supporter and your *nasir*," and it means the one who strengthens and empowers.

* *

As for the meaning of His words ﴿apart from Allah﴾ (من دون الله), it means other than Allah and beyond Allah, and from it is the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

"O soul, what do you have apart from Allah of any protector,
and what remains after the vicissitudes of time?"

[His Diwan: 43. Similar to it is the verse of Ibn Ahmar: "We are only a people of grazing livestock, and for them there is no tilled land nor cultivated fields," meaning: we have no property other than livestock, so we have no crops and no horses.]

He means: what protects you from adversities other than Allah and beyond Allah?

* *

The meaning of the statement, then, is: You, O believers, have no one besides Allah who manages your affairs, nor any helper who will support and strengthen you and aid you against your enemies.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 108 (part 1 of 2):

The explanation of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the cause for which this verse was revealed. Some of them said:

1777 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to me. And Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us. [[In the printed edition: "qal haddathana Ishaq" (he said: Ishaq narrated to us), and the correct reading is what has been established here.]] Both said: Ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, the client (mawla) of Zayd ibn Thabit, narrated to me, saying: Sa'id ibn Jubayr, or Ikrimah, narrated to me, from Ibn 'Abbas: Rafi' ibn Huraymilah and Wahb ibn Zayd said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Bring us a Book from heaven that we may read it, and cause rivers to gush forth for us, and we will follow you and believe you!" So Allah revealed concerning that their words: [[In the printed edition: "min qawlihim" (their words), and the correct reading is what has been established from the Sirah of Ibn Hisham.]] ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾, the verse. [[The report 1777 is in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 2:197.]]
* *
Others said:
1778 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah concerning His words: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾ Moses used to ask, and it was said to him: ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾.
1889 [sic] - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi concerning: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾ that they asked that Allah show Himself to them openly. The Arabs asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to bring them Allah so that they might see Him openly.
* *
Others said:
1780 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning the words of Allah: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾ that Allah show them openly. The Quraysh asked Muhammad ﷺ that Allah make Safa gold for them. He said: "Yes! And it will be for you like the table (ma'idah) of the Children of Israel, if you disbelieve!" But they refused and turned back.
1781 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, who said: The Quraysh asked Muhammad to make Safa gold for them. He said: "Yes! And it will be for you like the table of the Children of Israel, if you disbelieve!" But they refused and turned back. So Allah revealed: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾ that Allah show them openly.
1782 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.
* *
Others said:
1783 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, if only our expiations were like the expiations of the Children of Israel!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allahumma, we do not desire it! What Allah has given you is better than what He gave the Children of Israel. When one of the Children of Israel committed a sin, he would find it written on his door along with its expiation. If he expiated it, it was a disgrace for him in this world, and if he did not expiate it, it was a disgrace for him in the Hereafter. But Allah has given you better than what He gave the Children of Israel." He said: ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness of Allah, will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa: 110]. He said, and said: "The five prayers, and Friday to Friday, are expiations for what is between them."
And he said: "Whoever intends a good deed and does not do it, a good deed is recorded for him; if he does it, ten times its like is recorded for him, and none perishes before Allah except one who is destined to perish."
Then Allah revealed: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾ [[The report 1783 is a mursal (broken) hadith, from the mursal reports of Abu al-'Aliyah. Ibn Kathir (1:279) transmitted it from al-Tabari, and al-Suyuti (1:107) transmitted it and attributed it to al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim. Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi is a trustworthy (thiqah) senior Successor, as we mentioned at 184, and we add here that he is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/1/298, al-Saghir: 109, Ibn Sa'd 7/1/81-85, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/510, and al-Isabah 2:221. But reliance on his narrations, like that of other Successors and those after them, is in a connected chain (isnad muttasil); as for the mursal and the munqati', there is no proof in them.]]
* *
The scholars of Arabic differed concerning the meaning of ﴿am﴾ in His words: ﴿am turidun﴾ (or do you wish). Some of the Basran grammarians said: it has the meaning of interrogation (istifham). The sense of the speech: "Do you wish to question your Messenger?"
* *
Others among them said: it has the meaning of a new, disconnected interrogation within speech, as if you incline with it to the beginning, like the Arabs' saying: "Verily it is camels, O people, or sheep?" and "Such and such happened, or did my soul deceive me?" He said: The words ﴿am turidun﴾ are not expressing doubt, but are said to make their conduct appear ugly. He cited for his statement the verse of al-Akhtal:
"Your eye deceived you, or did you see in Wasit, / At the dimness of night, from al-Rabab, an apparition?" [[Diwan: 41; Naqa'id Jarir wa-al-Akhtal: 70. Wasit: a village west of the Euphrates opposite al-Raqqah, among the districts of al-Jazirah, and among the dwellings of Banu Taghlib; it is not the Wasit built by al-Hajjaj between Basra and Kufa. Al-Ghalas: the darkness of the end of the night when it mixes with the first glimmers of dawn, a blackness mixed with whiteness and redness.]]
* *
Some of the Kufan grammarians said: If you wish, you may make His words ﴿am turidun﴾ an interrogation upon a speech that has preceded it, as He, great is His praise, said: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds. Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 1-3]. Here "am" came without an interrogation before it, and that was, in his view, evidence that it is an interrogation initiated upon a speech that preceded it. The speaker of this opinion said: "am" in meaning comes as a response to an interrogation in two ways: one of them is that it distinguishes the meaning of "ayy" [[In the printed edition: "ta'rifu ma'na ayy" (you know the meaning of ayy), and in Lisan al-'Arab (amm 14:300): "an tufariq ma'na am" (that it separates the meaning of am); both are plainly erroneous. The correct text is in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:71. That is because your saying: "Is Zayd with you or 'Amr?" means: which of them is with you. It is clear that "am" separates the interrogation, and "ayy" gathers the dispersed interrogation. Al-Tabari has already said in an earlier part of this volume 2:198: "The original of 'ayy' and 'ma' is gathering the dispersed interrogation."]], and the other is that it is used interrogatively in a sequential manner, while the one who intends it intends a beginning, except that it is a beginning connected to speech. [[In the printed edition: "wa-takunu 'ala jihat al-naskh, wa-li-alladhi yunawa bihi al-ibtida'" (and it is in the manner of sequence, and for the one who intends a beginning), and the correct text is from al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an.]] If you began a speech with nothing preceding it and then asked a question, it could only be with the "alif" or with "hal". [[This is the exact text of al-Farra in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:71.]]
He said: If you wish, you may say that in His words ﴿am turidun﴾ there is an interrogation before it, and it is a response to it, which is in His words: ﴿Do you not know that Allah has power over all things?﴾ [[This is also part of al-Farra's text in Ma'ani al-Qur'an.]]
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The correct view concerning this, in my opinion, according to what the reports we have mentioned from the people of interpretation indicate, is that it is an initiating interrogation, meaning: "Do you wish, O people, to question your Messenger?" It was permissible for the people to interrogate with "am," even though one of the conditions of "am" is that it be a sequential interrogation following what precedes it of speech, because it is an initiating interrogation when a preceding speech comes before it. No interrogation with it without preceding speech has been heard from the Arabs. Its parallel is His, great is His praise, saying: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds. Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 1-3]. "Am" may also have the meaning of "bal" (rather) when preceded by an interrogation in which "ayy" does not fit, as they say: "Do you have a right over us, or are you a man known for injustice?" [[This too was mentioned by al-Farra, and he said after it: "They mean: rather, you are a man known for injustice."]] And a poet said:
"By Allah, I do not know: has Salma appeared to me in a ghoul's form, / or is it sleep, or is every beloved to me?" [[I have not identified its speaker. It will come in his tafsir 20:6 (Bulaq) correctly, and in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:72, Lisan (amm), and al-Sahibi: 98. In the printed edition here: "taqawwalat... am al-qawl," which is a pure error. His words "taghawwalat" mean she took on the form of a woman whom he perceives and sees, from the ghoul's transformation: that is, the ghoul takes many forms and appears in various shapes. He means she is far away, with no doubt about her distance, yet he imagines he sees her standing before him. al-Akhtal said: "And she appeared to you in the valleys after / you had crossed the lava-field and the joining..." and "The ghoul appeared to frighten us, a jinn-woman, / and the young women show you terrors." Then he says: "or is it sleep," meaning: or is it a dream. Rather, both are beloved to me, meaning whichever it was, she is beloved to me.]]
That is: rather, every beloved to me.
Some of them used to say, rejecting the view of one who claims that "am" in His words ﴿am turidun﴾ is a new interrogation disconnected from speech, inclined toward what precedes it: the first is a statement, the second an interrogation, and interrogation does not occur within a statement nor a statement within an interrogation; rather, doubt overtook him—by his claim—after the statement had passed, so he questioned.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: When the meaning of "am" is what we have described, the sense of the speech is: "Do you wish, O people, to question your Messenger about things similar to what the people of Moses asked before you, so that you disbelieve—if it is withheld from you—in your questioning what it is not permissible in Allah's wisdom to give you, or that you perish if it is among what is permissible in His wisdom to give you, and He gives it to you, then you disbelieve after that, as those nations who came before you perished, who asked their prophets for what it was not theirs to ask of them; so when it was given to them, they disbelieved, and were hastened with punishments for their disbelief after Allah had given them what they asked." [[In the printed edition: "aw atahlikun" (or do you perish), which is an error.]]
* *
The explanation of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾
Abu Ja'far said: By His words, great is His praise, ﴿whoever exchanges﴾ He means: whoever substitutes (yastabdil) "disbelief" [[See what has preceded in this volume 2:130.]], and by "disbelief" He means denial of Allah and His signs, [[See what has preceded in this volume 1:255, 382, 552 and what follows.]] ﴿for faith﴾, meaning: affirmation of Allah and His signs and acknowledgment of Him. [[See what has preceded 1:234-235, 271, 560 and what follows.]]
It has been said: by "disbelief" in this place is meant hardship, and by "faith" ease. But I do not know hardship as a meaning of "disbelief," nor ease as a meaning of "faith," unless the one who says this intends by his interpretation of "disbelief" in the sense of hardship in this place, and by his interpretation of "faith" in the sense of ease: what Allah has prepared for the disbelievers in the Hereafter of hardships, and what Allah has prepared for the people of faith in it of bliss; so that would be a valid view, though far from the apparent sense of the address.
Mention of those who said this:
1784 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Abu al-'Aliyah: ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾, he says: he exchanges hardship for ease.
1785 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Abi Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, the like of it.
* *
In His words: ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith has strayed from the sound way﴾ there is clear evidence for what we have said [[See what has preceded shortly: 462-466, 484-488, and see what follows shortly: 498, 499]] that these verses from His words ﴿O you who believe, do not say "Ra'ina"﴾ are an address from Allah, the Exalted, to the believers among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and a rebuke from Him to them for a matter that had occurred from them, which pleased the Jews and which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked for them, so Allah disliked it for them, and rebuked them for it, and informed them that the Jews are people of deceit toward them, envy and oppression, that they wish them harm and plot their ruin, and He forbade them to take them as advisers, and informed them that whoever of them apostatized from his religion and exchanged his faith for disbelief has missed the right path.

* *
The explanation of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So he has strayed from the sound way (108)﴾
Abu Ja'far said: As for His words ﴿has strayed﴾, He means: went astray and deviated. The root of "dalal 'an al-shay'" (straying from a thing) is going away from it and swerving; then it is used of a thing that is lost and of a thing that is not regarded, as they say of a lowly man who has no mention and no distinction: "ḍull ibn ḍull" and "qull ibn qull," and as al-Akhtal said of a thing that is lost:
"You were the chaff on a turbid, foaming sea / which the torrent cast forth, so it perished in perishing." [[Diwan: 50; Naqa'id Jarir wa-al-Akhtal: 83; it will come in Tafsir al-Tabari 3:219 / 21:61 (Bulaq). "You were," meaning Jarir, and it is the answer to "idha" (when); before the verse: "And when Wa'il's branches rose toward glory / and the valley gathered against you and flowed." "Wa'il's branches" means Bakr and Taghlib, the kin of al-Akhtal. "Al-qadhi" is what lies on the water of straw, leaves and sticks. In the printed edition here: "akbar" for "akdar," which is a misreading; it is correctly written in the other two places in the tafsir. "Akdar" means a surging sea, clouded after clarity. "Muzbid" means a raging, roiling sea that casts up foam. "Al-ati" is the flood that comes from a distant place. His words "qadhafa al-ati bihi" describe the chaff: he says, you were then like chaff cast by the flood into a foaming sea whose waves never settle, so you perished in perishing. The diwan's version: "in lujjin akdar."]]
That is: he perished and was lost.
* *
What Allah, the Exalted, meant by His words ﴿has strayed from the sound way﴾ is that he has gone away from the sound way and deviated from it.
* *
As for the explanation of His words ﴿the sound way﴾, by "al-sawa'" He means the middle and the method.
The root of "sawa'" is the middle. It is reported from 'Isa ibn 'Umar the grammarian that he said: "I kept writing until my middle ran out" (inqata'a sawa'i), meaning my middle. Hassan ibn Thabit said:
"Woe to the Ansar of the Prophet and his kin / after his burial in the midst of the tomb." [[Diwan: 98; it will come in Tafsir al-Tabari 10:20 (Bulaq). The reading here is "naslihi" (his offspring), and I suspect it is an error of a copyist or a misreading. The diwan's version and what comes in al-Tabari and elsewhere is "wa-rahtihi" (and his kin). It is from Hassan's elegy for the Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be ransom for him, ﷺ. By "wa-rahtihi" he means the Muhajirun, may Allah be pleased with them. "Al-maghib" is the verbal noun of "ghayyabahu fi al-ard," he buried him in the earth. "Al-mulhad" with a dammah on the mim and a fathah on the ha with a silent lam between them is the lahd, the grave.]]
By "sawa'" he means the middle. The Arabs say: "He is in the sawa' of the path," meaning in the level of the path; and "sawa' al-ard" is its level, in their usage.
As for "al-sabil," it is the trodden path, changed from "masbul" to "sabil." [[I have not found a verb "masbul" for his word; it seems he wished to return it to its root, since "fa'il" must have a triliteral verb "sabal," even if they did not use it, and it is turned from "maf'ul." So al-Tabari said "masbul." This is made easier by their saying "al-sabilah," which is "fa'ilah" from a triliteral verb, but they did not use it; its meaning is "the people who travel the road." And they said "sabil sabilah," meaning travelled, so this too is "fa'ilah" in the sense of "maf'ulah." Thus by "al-masbul" in both places he means the travelled.]]
* *
So the meaning of the speech, then, is: whoever substitutes disbelief for faith in Allah and His Messenger, so that he apostatizes from his religion, has deviated from the way of the path, its clear, trodden middle. [[I have not found a verb "masbul" for his word; it seems he wished to return it to its root, since "fa'il" must have a triliteral verb "sabal," even if they did not use it, and it is turned from "maf'ul." So al-Tabari said "masbul." This is made easier by their saying "al-sabilah," which is "fa'ilah" from a triliteral verb, but they did not use it; its meaning is "the people who travel the road." And they said "sabil sabilah," meaning travelled, so this too is "fa'ilah" in the sense of "maf'ulah." Thus by "al-masbul" in both places he means the travelled.]]

This statement, on its face, reports the going astray from the path of the one who exchanges faith for disbelief, and what is meant by it is the report that he has abandoned the religion of God which He has approved for His servants, and made for them a way to travel toward His good pleasure and a road to ride toward His love and the attainment of His gardens. So He, exalted is His praise, made the path—whose traveler, if he rides its clear course and keeps to its middle, is saved, attains his need, and reaches his goal—an example of His religion to which He called His servants: their attainment, by adhering to it and following it, of their aims in the Hereafter, [[In the printed edition: "لإدراكهم بلزومه واتباعه إدراكهم طلباتهم. . " The word "إدراكهم" is an addition by a copyist.]] is like one who reaches the clear road by keeping to it, the aim of his salvation from it and arrival at the place he intended and sought. And He made the likeness of one who swerves from His religion and turns aside from following what He called him to of His worship—[[In the printed edition: "والحائد عن اتباع ما دعاه. . ", and I think the correct reading is what I have recorded.]] in his missing what he hoped to attain by his deeds in the Hereafter and to gain by it in his return, [[In the printed edition: "في حياته ما رجا أن يدركه. . ", which is without doubt a corruption; I have recorded what my reasoning led me to in reading it, since they say "he missed the path" and "he missed what he sought," and similar expressions.]] and his going away from the reward of his deeds that he hoped for, and his distance from his Lord—like the one who swerves from the course of the road and the intended way, who, the more he goes astray in the direction he has taken, [[Al-wughul is the verbal noun of "waghala yaghulu wughulan," meaning to go away and go far in one's course.]] only grows farther from the place of his need, and further from the place he intended and desired.

And this way about which God informed, that whoever exchanges disbelief for faith has strayed from its straightness, is the straight path, which He commanded us to ask Him to guide us to, saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 109:
