1844- Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Hisham ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: My father related to me, from Qatadah, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Your brother al-Najashi has died, so pray over him." They said: "Shall we pray over a man who is not a Muslim?" He said: Then this was revealed: ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Scripture are those who believe in Allah and what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them, humbly submissive to Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 199]. Qatadah said: They said: "Indeed he did not pray toward the qiblah," so Allah, majestic and exalted, revealed: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west; wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾. [[The hadith: 1844 - it is a weak hadith, because it is mursal. Al-Suyuti quoted it 1: 109, attributing it to Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir. Ibn Kathir quoted it 1: 291, from this place, then said: "This is strange." I say: its context indicates its weakness and its odd nature.]]
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this matter is that Allah, mighty is His remembrance, specified the report about the easts and the wests in this verse as belonging to Him in possession, although nothing exists that does not belong to Him in possession, informing His believing servants that He possesses them and the creation that lies between them, and that obedience to Him is incumbent upon all of them, since they belong to Him, in what He commanded and forbade them, in what He obligated upon them of duties, and in turning toward the direction to which they were turned; since it is a rule of owned things that they obey their owner. So the report about the easts and the wests was given, and what is meant is the creation between them, in the manner I have explained, of being satisfied with a report about the cause of a thing in place of mentioning the thing and reporting about it, just as it was said: ﴿And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾, and what is similar to that. [[See what has passed in this part 2: 357-360, 483.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 115 (part 2 of 2):

The meaning of the verse, then, is: To Allah belongs the dominion of the creation between the east and the west; He worships them as He wills and judges among them as He wishes, obliging them to obey Him. So turn your faces, O believers, toward My face, for wherever you turn your faces, there is My face.
* *
As for the question of whether this verse is abrogating (nasikh), abrogated (mansukh), or neither, the correct position is to say that it came in a general (ʿumum) form while the intended meaning is specific (khass). That is because His saying ﴿So wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ is open to several readings: wherever you turn, during your travels, in your voluntary prayers, and while you are fighting your enemy, in your voluntary and obligatory prayers, there is the Face of Allah, as Ibn ʿUmar and al-Nakhaʿi said, and as those whom we mentioned earlier from them said.
= It also allows: wherever you turn, from the land of Allah in which you dwell, there is the qibla of Allah toward which you turn your faces, because the Kaaba is possible for you to face from there. As he said:
1845 – Abu Kurayb said: Waki reported to us, from Abu Sinan, from al-Dahhak and al-Nadr ibn ʿArabi, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾. He said: "The qibla of Allah. Wherever you are, east or west, face it."
1846 – al-Qasim told us: al-Husayn told us: Hajjaj told us, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibrahim informed me, from Ibn Abi Bakr, from Mujahid, who said: "Wherever you are, you have a qibla that you face." He said: "It is the Kaaba."
= It also allows: wherever you turn your faces in your supplication, there is My face; I respond to your supplication, as:
1847 – al-Qasim told us: al-Husayn told us: Hajjaj told me, Ibn Jurayj said, Mujahid said: When the verse ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Surah Ghafir: 60] was revealed, they asked, "To where?" And then ﴿So wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ was revealed.
* *
Since the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿So wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ admit of the aspects we have mentioned, it is not permissible for anyone to claim that it is abrogating or abrogated unless he has a proof that must be accepted.
For abrogation exists only where there is something abrogated, and no proof has been established that must be accepted showing that His words ﴿So wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ mean: wherever you turn your faces in your prayers, there is your qibla. Nor is there proof that it was revealed after the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, as a command from Allah to them to turn toward the Kaaba, so that one could say it abrogated the prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis. For among the people of knowledge, among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the leading Successors (tabiʿun), there are those who deny that it was revealed with that meaning, and no report from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is established that it was revealed concerning it, and disagreement about it existed, as I have described.
= Nor, since it is not abrogating in the sense we have described, has a proof been established that it is abrogated, since it admits of what we have described: that it came in general terms, and its meaning is either: in one circumstance rather than another [[In the printed edition: "or its meaning is in one circumstance rather than another", which is corrupt. His intent is that the verse came in general form and admits of one of two meanings: either in one circumstance rather than another, if the intended sense is turning in prayer, or in every circumstance, if the intended sense is supplication, and other meanings we have mentioned.]], if by it is meant facing in prayer, and in every circumstance if by it is meant supplication, and other meanings we have mentioned.
We have shown in our book "The Book of Clarification on the Foundations of Rulings" (Kitab al-Bayan ʿan Usul al-Ahkam) that there is no abrogation in the verses of the Qur'an or the reports of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ except what negates an established ruling and obligates the servants to its duty, admitting of no other meaning in its outward or inward sense. [[In the printed edition: "in its outward sense"; see what preceded regarding "the outward and inward" (al-zahir wa al-batin) 2:15 and its references.]] As for what admits of other meanings, such as being an exception, or specific and general, or unspecified (mujmal) or explained (mufassar), it is far from abrogation and abrogated, which suffices so as not to repeat it in this place. And there is no abrogated except what negates a ruling that had been established and obligatory.
Neither of these two meanings has been shown to be correct for His words ﴿So wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾ by a proof that must be accepted, so that it could be said of it that it is abrogating or abrogated.
* *
As for His words ﴿fa-aynama﴾, its meaning is: wherever (ḥaythuma).
* *
As for His words ﴿tawallu﴾, the more appropriate interpretation is that it means: you face toward it and towards it, as one says, "I turned my face (wallaytu wajhi) and I turned it toward him," meaning: I faced him and confronted him. We say this is the more appropriate interpretation of the verse because the proof (hujja) is in agreement that this is its interpretation, and the one who interprets it as "you turn away from it so that you turn your backs to it" is an outlier. What you turn toward is the Face of Allah, meaning the qibla of Allah.
* *
As for His words ﴿thamma﴾, it means: there (hunalika).
* *
Scholars differed regarding the interpretation of His words ﴿thamma wajhu Allah﴾ [[In the printed edition: "thamma, and some of them said", which is corrupt; the correct reading is to keep "wajh Allah".]]. Some said: its interpretation is: there is the qibla of Allah, meaning by that His face toward which He directed them.
Those who said this:
1848 – Abu Kurayb told us: Waki told us, from al-Nadr ibn ʿArabi, from Mujahid: ﴿thamma wajhu Allah﴾, he said: "The qibla of Allah."
1849 – al-Qasim told us: al-Husayn told us: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibrahim informed me, from Mujahid, who said: "Wherever you are, you have a qibla that you face."
* *
Others said: the meaning of the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, ﴿thamma wajhu Allah﴾ is: there is Allah, blessed and exalted.
* *
Others said: the meaning of His words ﴿thamma wajhu Allah﴾ is: there, by turning toward Him, you attain the good pleasure of Allah, to whom belongs the noble Face.
* *
Others said: by "the Face" is meant the one who has the face; those who held this view said: "the Face of Allah" is an attribute of Him.
* *
If someone asks: how does this verse relate to the one before it?
It is said: it is connected to it. The meaning is: And who is more unjust than the Christians who prevented the servants of Allah from His mosques, that His name be mentioned in them, and strove for their ruin? To Allah belong the east and the west; wherever you turn your faces, remember Him, for His Face is there. His bounty, His earth, and His lands encompass you, and He knows what you do. The destruction by one who destroyed the mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis, and the prevention by those who prevented the remembrance of Allah in it, shall not stop you from remembering Allah wherever you are in the land of Allah, seeking by it His Face.
* *
The interpretation of His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing (115)﴾
Abu Jaʿfar said: By His words, may His praise be exalted, ﴿All-Encompassing (wasiʿ)﴾, He means that He encompasses all His creatures with sufficiency, bounty, generosity, and management.
As for His words ﴿All-Knowing (ʿalim)﴾, He means that He knows their deeds; nothing of them is hidden from Him or escapes His knowledge, but He knows all of them.
* *
The interpretation of His words, exalted is He, ﴿And they say, "Allah has taken a son." Glory be to Him. Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are obedient to Him (116)﴾
Abu Jaʿfar said: By His words, may His praise be exalted, ﴿And they say, "Allah has taken a son"﴾, He means those who prevented the mosques of Allah from His name being mentioned in them, and ﴿And they say﴾ is coordinated with His words ﴿and strove for their ruin﴾.
* *
The interpretation of the verse: Who is more unjust than one who prevented the mosques of Allah from His name being mentioned in them and strove for their ruin, and said, "Allah has taken a son"? They are the Christians who claimed that ʿIsa is the son of Allah. So Allah, may His praise be exalted, refuted what they said and disassociated Him from what they ascribed to Him by their lies and fabrications: ﴿Glory be to Him (subhanahu)﴾, meaning by it: exalted and far removed from having a son, and high above that. We have already explained the meaning of the saying "Subhan Allah" in what preceded, sufficiently to avoid repeating it here. [[See what preceded: 1:474, 495.]]
* *
Then He, may His praise be exalted, informed that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, by dominion and creation. The meaning is: how could the Messiah be a son of Allah, when he is in one of these places, either in the heavens or on the earth, and to Allah belongs the dominion of whatever is in them? And if the Messiah were a son as you claim, he would not be like the rest of what is in the heavens and the earth, of His creation and servants, in the manifestation of the signs of workmanship in him.

The Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted: ﴿Everything is devoutly obedient to Him﴾ (2:116)

Abu Ja'far said: The people of ta'wil (interpretation) differed regarding the meaning of this. Some of them said: its meaning is: obedient.

Those who said this:

1850. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿Everything is devoutly obedient to Him﴾, meaning: obedient.

1851. Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Everything is devoutly obedient to Him﴾. He said: obedient. He said: the obedience of the disbeliever is in the prostration of his shadow.

1852. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly, except that he added: "by the prostration of his shadow while he is unwilling."

1853. Musa narrated to us, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿Everything is devoutly obedient to Him﴾, he said: everything is obedient to Him on the Day of Resurrection.

1854. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to me, from one he mentioned, from Ikrimah: ﴿Everything is devoutly obedient to Him﴾, he said: the obedience.

1855. It was related to me from al-Minjab ibn al-Harith, saying: Bishr ibn Ammarah narrated to us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿devoutly obedient﴾, meaning: obedient.

* *

Others said: the meaning of that is: everything acknowledges its servitude to Him.

Those who said this:

1856. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Waqid narrated to us, from Yazid al-Nahwi, from Ikrimah: ﴿Everything is devoutly obedient to Him﴾, everything acknowledges its servitude to Him.

* *

And others said, with what:

1857. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, with it, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding his words: ﴿Everything is devoutly obedient to Him﴾, he said: everything stands before Him on the Day of Resurrection.

* *

The word "qunut" (devout obedience) in the speech of the Arabs has several meanings: one of them is obedience; another is standing; and a third is refraining from speech and holding one's tongue from it.

* *

The most preferable of the meanings of "qunut" in His words: ﴿Everything is devoutly obedient to Him﴾ is obedience and affirmation to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, of servitude, by the testimony of their bodies, with what is in them of the traces of craftsmanship, and the indication of the oneness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that Allah, He whose remembrance is exalted, is the Originator of them and their Creator. This is because Allah, whose praise is exalted, refuted those who claimed that Allah has a son, by His words: ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, in ownership and creation. Then He informed about all that is in the heavens and the earth that they affirm, by their indication, their Lord and Creator, and that Allah, He whose remembrance is exalted, is their Originator and Maker. And if some of them deny that, then their tongues submit to Him in obedience, by their testimony to Him through the traces of craftsmanship in them, and that the Messiah is one of them. How then could He have a son, when this is his description?

* *

Some who fell short in understanding the speech and its proper direction claimed that His words: ﴿Everything is devoutly obedient to Him﴾ are specific to the people of obedience and not general. It is not permissible to claim a specific meaning for a verse whose apparent meaning is general, except by a proof that must be accepted, as we have explained in our book: "Kitab al-Bayan 'an Usul al-Ahkam" (The Book of Clarification on the Foundations of Rulings).

* *

This is information from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that the Messiah, whom the Christians claimed to be the son of Allah, along with the heavens and the earth and what is in them, refutes them, either by tongue or by indication. This is because Allah, whose praise is exalted, informed about all of them, of their obedience to Him and their affirmation of His servitude, following His words: ﴿And they said: Allah has taken a son﴾. This indicates the soundness of what we have said.

The Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted: "The Originator of the heavens and the earth"

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His praise be exalted, "the Originator of the heavens and the earth" (Badi' al-samawati wa'l-ard), He means: its originator (mubdi'uha).

* *

It is actually "mubdi'" (the active form), turned into "fa'il" (the intensive form), just as "al-mu'lim" (the painful) was turned into "alim", and "al-musmi'" (the one who makes hear) into "sami'" (the All-Hearing). [[See what has passed: 1:251, and this volume 2:140, 377, 506.]] The meaning of "mubdi'" is: the one who brings into existence and creates something new, which no one before him has created or originated. For this reason, one who introduces innovation in religion is called "mubtadi'" (innovator), because he introduces into it what no one before him had introduced. Likewise, every person who originates an action or a statement that no one before him had done or said is called "mubtadi'" by the Arabs. Among this is the verse of A'sha Banu Thaʿlaba [[In the printed edition: "al-A'sha ibn Tha'laba", which is a plain error.]], in praise of Hawdha ibn Ali al-Hanafi:

*He takes counsel from the words of the chiefs of men when ... they reveal to him resolve, or whatever he wills he originates (ibtada'a)*

That is: he creates whatever he wills. And from this is the verse of Ru'ba ibn al-Ajjaj:

*O you who travels the far distant path (al-qidhdhaf al-atya'a), if you are truly the most devout and most obedient to God,*
*then it is not the way of truth that you should innovate (an tabad'a).* [[Its text in his Diwan: 87, and in Lisan (b-d-ʿ), from a long rajaz in which he boasts of his clan, Banu Tamim. The Diwan's reading is "al-qidhdhaf al-atbaʿa", which has no intelligible meaning; al-Tabari's reading has a basis in Arabic. "Al-ghashi" from their saying: ghashiya al-shay': he aimed at it, engaged it, or it descended upon him. Al-qidhdhaf: rapid travel and going far in it, or as if he meant the far distant region, though I have not found it in the books of Arabic. Al-atya': I have not found it in anything; perhaps he took it from their saying: tatayya'a al-qawm fi'l-ard: when they spread apart in it blindly and with hardship. He says: O you who goes in distant paths far from the customary way — meaning: whoever innovates matters for which people have no precedent, and follows in his innovation strange paths.]]

That is: to bring into existence in religion what was not there.

* *

So the meaning of the statement is: Glory be to God! How could He have a son when He is the owner of whatever is in the heavens and the earth, all of which testify to Him by their indication of His oneness, and acknowledge His lordship, while He is their Creator, their Originator, who brought them into being without a root or a model upon which He patterned them?

* *

This is a declaration from God, the Exalted, to His servants that among what bears witness to this is the Messiah, whom they attributed to God, may His praise be exalted, as a son. And it is an informing from Him to them that the One who originated the heavens and the earth without any origin and without any model, is the One who originated the Messiah without a father, by His power. [[Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir (1:294) quoted al-Tabari's words and then said: "This, from Ibn Jarir, may God have mercy on him, is a good statement and a correct expression," approving what was light in meaning; but what was heavy for him earlier (see p. 522 note 1) was the subject of his objection, although it is higher, better, more precise, subtler, more correct in expression, and deeper in profundity. This is one of the wonders regarding what Ibn Jarir suffered from people's lack of knowledge of the soundness of his understanding and the subtlety of his perception.]] Similar to what we have said on this, a group of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said.

Mention of those who said that:

1858. Al-Muthanna told us, saying: Ishaq told us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "the Originator of the heavens and the earth" — he says: He originated their creation, and no one shared with Him in their creation.

1859. Musa told me, saying: Amr told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "the Originator of the heavens and the earth" — he says: He originated them and created them, and nothing was created before them that could be taken as a model. [[The report 1859: in the printed edition it read: "and nothing had created its like, so it would be imitated," which is corrupt speech. The correct text is in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:110.]]

* *

The Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted: "And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is."

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His praise be exalted, "And when He decrees a matter" (wa-idha qada amran), He means: when He firmly establishes a matter and makes it binding. [[Hatama al-amr: he decreed it with binding decree.]]

* *

The root of every "decree of a matter" is establishing it firmly and completing it. [[In the printed edition: "qada' al-ihkam", and the correct reading is what I have set.]] From this, the judge between people is called "al-qadi" (the judge), because he separates the judgment between adversaries, and cuts off the ruling between them and completes it. [[In the printed edition: "farāghihi", and the addition of "minhu" is necessary.]] From this it is said of the dead: "qad qada" (he has decided/passed away), meaning he has finished with the world and departed from it. From this it is said: "ma yanqadi ʿajabi min fulan" (my wonder at so-and-so does not end), meaning does not cease. From this it is said: "taqadda al-nahar" (the day has passed), when it has run out. And from this is the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: "And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him" [Surah al-Isra: 23], meaning: He has settled the ruling on it among His servants by His command to them of that. Likewise His words: "And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book" [Surah al-Isra: 4], meaning: We informed them of that and told them of it, and so We completed (fa-faraghna) it for them. And from this is the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

*And upon them two coats of mail, woven, which Dawud decreed, or which Tubba' (a king) had made with skill.* [[His Diwan: 19; al-Mufaddaliyyat: 881; Ta'wil Mushkil al-Qur'an: 342; it will come in al-Tabari's Tafsir 11:65 and 22:47 (Bulaq). It is from his ode, which surpassed all poetry, in which he mourns his sons who died of plague. The pronoun in "upon them" refers to two champions whom he described earlier in the poem, each of whom had prepared his weapons... "Masrudatan" means two coats of mail, from al-sard, which is stringing or weaving, their rings woven tightly. Dawud: he is the Prophet of God, peace be upon him. Tubba': a name for every king of Himyar (see what passed 2:237). Ibn al-Anbari said: "He heard that iron was made pliable for Dawud, peace be upon him, and he heard of the Tubbaʿi coats of mail, so he thought that Tubba' made them. But Tubba' was too great to make anything with his own hand; they were made in his time and in his reign." Al-sani': one skilled in his work; and the feminine is sanna'. It is also narrated as: "wa-ʿalayhima maziyatan," meaning two coats of mail. The mazyah: a coat of mail of pure iron, soft and smooth.]] It is also narrated:

*And the two champions exchanged two coats of mail, which he decreed* [[" Ta'awara" means, as they say: they exchanged with spears, two coats of mail, from their saying: we exchanged so-and-so with blows, when you struck him and then your companion did. My view is that this is a rejected narration, not fitting the poetry, for he says after it: "And each of them had in his hand a spear with a point, like a minaret, bald..." and "each of them wrapped in a sharp, bright sword which cuts when it strikes the blow," and "then they snatched each other's souls with thrusts like the windows of the camels which are not raised." He describes, then informs that they struck each other with deadly blows, and there is no sense in putting the spearing first and then returning to describing the weapon, except with distance and strain.]]

By His words "qada-huma", he means: "ahkamahuma" (he firmly established them). From this is the saying of another in praise of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him: [[He is Juz' ibn Dirar, brother of al-Shammakh ibn Dirar. Its attribution has been disputed; it is attributed to al-Shammakh and to others, until they attributed it to the jinn (see Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara: 111; Hamasa Abi Tammam 3:65; Ibn Sa'd 3:241; al-Aghani 9:159; Nahj al-Balagha 3:147; al-Bayan wa'l-Tabyin 3:364; Ta'wil Mushkil al-Qur'an: 343; and many others). The correct thing is that he says: "in the elegy of Umar ibn al-Khattab."]]

*You decided matters, then after them you left calamities in their husks, not yet split open.* [[" Al-bawa'iq" is the plural of baa'iqa: the distressing disaster that opened a breach which cannot be closed. "Al-akmam" is the plural of kumm (with damma and kasra of the kaf), the sheath of the fruit before it splits open. His words "lam tufattaq": its original form was tatafattaq, one of the two taa's being omitted. Tafattaqa al-kumm 'an zahratihi: it split open and burst. May God have mercy on Umar, the imam who gathered the affairs of people during his life, until when he passed away their affairs scattered.]]

It is also narrated: "bawa'ij." [[Bawa'ij is the plural of bai'ija: the calamity that bursts open with a distressing bursting, which covers people, and whose evils follow one after another, from their saying: "baja al-barq wa-inbaja wa-tabawwaja": when lightning flashed, uncovered, and the cloud covered, and its light spread.]]

* *

As for His words, "Then He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is" (fa-innama yaqulu lahu kun fa-yakun), He means by this: when He firmly establishes a matter and makes it binding, He only says to that matter, "Be," and that matter becomes as God commanded it to be and willed it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: What is the meaning of His words, "And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is"? And in what state does He say "Be" to the matter He decrees: in the state of its non-existence, a state in which His command is impermissible, since it is impossible to command except one who is commanded, and if there is no one commanded, the command is impossible; just as a command without a commander is impossible, so too is a command from a commander except to one who is commanded? [[In the printed edition: "kama mahal al-amr" without the waw; the waw must be retained. By "al-ma'mur" he means the existing one who is commanded.]] Or does He say it to it in the state of its existence? — and that is a state in which His command to come into being is impermissible, because it is an existing thing, and it is not said to the existing "be existent" except without the meaning of commanding its very coming into being?

It is said: The interpreters have disputed the meaning of this, and we will report what they said, and the reasons each group gave for its statement on this: [[I wish to alert the reader of this tafsir to give attention to the context of the sayings of those who spoke, and how he himself separates the meanings from one another, how he reaches the proof with reason and subtle perception, and sound clarity about the meanings of the speech and the interpretation of the verses of the Book of our Lord, glory be to Him. Then let him consider the sayings of the commentators, and how they avoided going deep into what he went deep into, trusting in God's help for him, and then following the most guided paths in seeking the goals.]]

* *

Some of them said: That is a report from God, may His praise be exalted, about His binding command, in the manner of a decree upon the one upon whom He decrees from His creatures who exist, that when He commands him with a command, His decree is carried out in it and His command proceeds in it. Like His command to some of the Children of Israel that they be apes, cast out, while they existed at the time of His command to them, and His binding decree upon them with what He decreed for them; and like what the earth swallowed up with its dwelling, and what is similar to that of His command and decree concerning one who existed among His creation at the time of His binding command upon him.

Those who held this view took His words, "And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is," to be specific rather than general.

* *

Others said: Rather, the verse, though its apparent meaning is general, its interpretation is specific, because a command is not permissible except to one who is commanded, as I described earlier. They said: Since that is so, the interpretation of the verse is: "And when He decrees a matter of giving life to the dead, or causing the living to die, and the like, He only says to the living, 'Be dead,' or to the dead, 'Be alive,' and what is similar to that of the command."

* *

Others said: Rather, that is from God, Mighty and Majestic, a report about everything He brings into being and makes to exist: that when He decrees it, creates it, and brings it into being, it comes to be and is found — and there is no speech there, according to the proponents of this view, except the existence of the created thing and the coming into being of the decreed thing. They said: The saying of God, Mighty and Majestic, "And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is," is like the saying of one who says: "So-and-so spoke with his head" or "spoke with his hand," when he moves his head or gestures with his hand without saying anything; and like the saying of Abu al-Najm:

*And the girths said to the belly: "Be lean, be lean," and it became like a stallion camel, enraged.* [[I have not found the full rajaz; the two verses are in Lisan (h-n-q). It describes a she-camel whom travel has worn out. "Al-ansa'" is the plural of nas' (with kasra then sukun), a strip of leather braided broad with which saddles are tied. "Lahiqa al-batn" means it grew lean: that is, the saddle-girths said to the camel's belly: be lean. He means by this what travel had worn her down with. "Qadaman": that is, since long ago, as Bashama ibn al-Ghadir said: "Do not wrong us, and do not forget our kinship... turn toward us, for the kinship has long bent toward us." Abu al-Najm means: that her emaciation has lasted long, for the girths said that a long time ago. "Ada": became and returned. "Al-fanīq": the stallion camel set aside for stud, not ridden and not humiliated because of their honor for it, so it is huge and very robust. "Al-muhnaq": lean, with little flesh. "Al-ihnaq": the belly cleaving to the spine.]]

But there is no speech there; he meant only that the back had joined the belly. And as 'Amr ibn Hamma al-Dawsi said: [[He is also called Ka'b ibn Hamma, and he is one of the long-lived; they claimed he lived four hundred years less ten. He was one of the judges of the Arabs, and it is said he is the "Dhu al-Hilm" for whom the staff was struck, from which a proverb came.]]

*So he became like the eagle whose chicks have flown; when he wants to fly, it is said to him: "Settle down!"* [[Kitab al-Mu'ammarin: 22; Hamasa al-Buhturi: 205; Mu'jam al-Shu'ara: 209; these are verses.]]

There is no speech there either; its meaning is: when he wanted to fly, he came down. And as another said:

*The basin filled up, and it said: "Enough, enough, gently, for I have filled my belly!"* [[Amali Ibn al-Shajari 1:313, 2:140; Lisan (q-t-t). In the printed edition: "sila", and the correct reading is in Lisan and Amali Ibn al-Shajari; the well-known reading is "mahlan ruwaydan". "Qatani": enough for me and sufficient; the grammarians have much discussion on "qatani". His words "sala": it seems to be from their saying: insalla al-sayl (the flood ran out), which is the first beginning when it flows, before it intensifies. As if he says: gently, slowly.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the sayings regarding His words, "And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is," is that it should be said: it is general concerning everything God has decreed and created, because the apparent meaning of this is general, and it is not permissible to turn the apparent meaning toward an inner interpretation without proof, as we have shown in our book "Kitab al-Bayan 'an Usul al-Ahkam." Since that is so, the command of God, Mighty and Majestic, to a thing, when He wills to bring it into being as existent by His words, "Be," in the state of His willing it to be brought into being, the existence of what He wills to bring into being and create does not precede His willing it, nor His command to become and exist, and does not lag behind it. [[In the printed edition: "wujudahu alladhi arada ijadahu" with an addition of the pronoun in "wujud" which has no place.]] It is therefore impermissible that a thing be commanded to exist and willed in this way unless it already exists, nor that it exist unless it is commanded to exist and willed in this way. [[He says: the existence of a thing does not precede God's will and command, nor does it lag behind them.]] The parallel to His words, "And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is," is His words: "And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command. Then when He calls you with a call from the earth, behold, you will come forth" [Surah al-Rum: 25], meaning that the emergence of people from their graves does not precede God's call, nor lag behind it.

* *

And we question him who claims that His words, "And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is," is specific in interpretation, arguing that a command to what does not exist is impermissible: [[He means: "We question the one who claimed..." regarding the call of the people of the graves.]] regarding the call of the people of the graves before they come out of their graves, or after? Or is it concerning a specific part of creation? He will say nothing on this without being bound to the same on the other point.

And we question those who claimed that the meaning of His words, may His praise be exalted, "then He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is," is like the saying of one who says: "So-and-so spoke with his head or his hand," when he moves it and gestures, and like the saying of the poet: [[He is al-Muthaqqib al-Abdi.]]

*She says, when I spread out her saddle-girth for her: "Is this her religion forever, and my religion?"* [[Al-Mufaddaliyyat: 586; al-Kamil 1:193; Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara: 231; it will come in his tafsir 4:112 (Bulaq), from a fine ode in which before this he says about his she-camel: "When I rise to saddle her in the night, she groans with the groan of a sorrowful man." Daraʾa al-wadin for the she-camel: spreading it on the ground, then making her kneel upon it to tie her saddle on. Al-wadin: a broad leather girth of woven hide with which a camel's saddle is tied. Al-din: habit and custom.]]

...and the like of that: they have not hit the mark of the language, nor of the Book of Allah, nor have they followed what the proofs point to as sound. So it is said to those who say this: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, informed about Himself that when He decrees a matter, He says to it, "Be," and it is. Do you deny that He says this? If they deny it, they have denied the Qur'an and departed from the religion (millah).

If they say, "Rather, we affirm it, but we claim that it is like the saying of a speaker, 'The wall spoke, so it leaned,' where there is no speech, and it is only a report about the wall's leaning":

It is said to them: Do you permit the one who reports about the wall's leaning to say, "The wall's speech, when it wanted to lean, was to say this, and so it leaned"?

If they permit that, they have departed from the recognized speech of the Arabs and opposed their logic and what is known in their language.

If they say, "That is not permitted,"

it is said to them: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, informed them about Himself that His saying to a thing, when He wills it, is to say to it "Be," and it is. Thus He informed His servants of the saying by which the thing comes into being, and its description and its emphasis. Yet this, according to you, is not permitted in describing that which has no speech and no clarity, as in the saying of the speaker, "The wall spoke, so it leaned." So how did they not know the difference between the meaning of Allah's words, ﴿And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾, and the saying of the speaker, "The wall spoke, so it leaned"? The explanation of the corruption of this statement has a place other than this, where we will address it sufficiently, if Allah wills.

* *

Since the matter in His words, majestic is His praise, ﴿And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾, is as we have described, that the state of His command to a thing to exist is the state of the existence of the one commanded to exist, it becomes clear that the more appropriate reading of His words ﴿fa-yakūnu (and it is)﴾ is the nominative (raf') by coordination (ʿaṭf) on His words ﴿yaqūlu (He says)﴾, because "saying" (al-qawl) and "being" (al-kawn) have one state. This is like the saying of a speaker, "So-and-so repented and was guided," and "So-and-so was guided and repented," because he is not a penitent except while he is guided, and not guided except while he is penitent. Likewise, it is not possible for Allah to command a thing to exist except while it exists, nor for it to exist except while He is commanding it to exist.

For this reason, whoever permitted the accusative (naṣb) of ﴿fa-yakūna﴾ read, ﴿Our saying to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Naḥl: 40], according to the meaning we have described, meaning: that We say, and it becomes.

As for the one who read it in the nominative, [and this is the reading of our codex (muṣḥaf) today], he saw that the statement was complete at His words ﴿when We intend it, that We say to it, "Be"﴾, since it is known that when Allah decrees His judgment upon a thing, the one upon whom it is decreed exists. Then he began with His words, "fa-yakūnu (and it is)," as He, majestic is His praise, said: ﴿So that We may make clear to you, and settle in the wombs what We will﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 5], and as Ibn Aḥmar said:

He treats a barren mare that has defeated him,
so that he may impregnate her and she bears him a foal.

[Al-Maʿānī al-Kabīr: 846, 1134; Sībawayh 1: 341, from verses describing a friend he had, saying: "He is still for us a close friend like the belly's ache, a heavy or sharp pain; and he claims that he has come upon us with his evil, and so he leaves us in ruin. This friend is like the belly's ache: one does not know from where it will come or how it will reach him. He treats evil that he cannot control, as though he seeks offspring from a barren woman. He made that an example. The ḥiwār is the calf of a cow. The sharrah is the sharpness of evil, and the tabār is destruction."]. He means: so that he, behold, bears her as a foal.

* *

The meaning of the verse, then, is: They said, "Allah has taken a son." Exalted is He above having a son! Rather, He is the Owner of the heavens and the earth and what is in them; all of it attests to His servitude by its indication of His oneness. How could He have a son, when He is the One who originated the heavens and the earth without any precedent, just as He originated Jesus without a father, by His power and authority, by which nothing He wills is beyond Him? Rather, He only says to it, when He decrees it and wills its existence, "Be," and it is existent as He willed and intended. Thus was His origination and creation of Jesus, when He willed to create him without a father.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 118:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And those who do not know say: "Why does Allah not speak to us, or a sign not come to us?"﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The exegetes differed concerning whom Allah meant by His saying: ﴿And those who do not know say: "Why does Allah not speak to us?"﴾. Some of them said: He meant by this the Christians.

Mention of those who said this:

1860 – Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And those who do not know say: "Why does Allah not speak to us, or a sign not come to us?"﴾, he said: The Christians say it.

1861 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it – and he added to it regarding ﴿And those who do not know﴾: the Christians.

* *

Others said: Rather, Allah meant by this the Jews who were in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Mention of those who said this:

1862 – Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr related to us. And Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us; both of them said: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad related to me, saying: Sa'id ibn Jubayr or 'Ikrimah related to me, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Rafi' ibn Huraymilah said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "If you are a messenger from Allah as you claim, then say to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, that He should speak to us so that we hear His speech!" So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed concerning that His saying: ﴿And those who do not know say: "Why does Allah not speak to us, or a sign not come to us?"﴾, the whole verse. [[The report: 1862 – Sirat Ibn Hisham 2: 198.]]

* *

Others said: Rather, He meant by this the polytheists of the Arabs.

Mention of those who said this:

1863 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: ﴿And those who do not know say: "Why does Allah not speak to us, or a sign not come to us?"﴾ – they are the unbelievers of the Arabs.

1864 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': ﴿And those who do not know say: "Why does Allah not speak to us?"﴾, he said: They are the unbelievers of the Arabs.

1865 – Musa related to me, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿And those who do not know say: "Why does Allah not speak to us?"﴾ – as for "those who do not know," they are the Arabs.

* *

The most correct and sound of these statements is the statement of the one who says: Allah, exalted is He, meant by His saying ﴿And those who do not know say﴾ the Christians, to the exclusion of others. This is because it comes within the context of Allah's report about them, and about their slander against Him and their claim that He has a son. So He, mighty is His praise, reporting about them in what He reported of their misguidance, says that along with their fabrication of falsehood against Allah by His saying ﴿Allah has taken a son﴾, they wished for vain things from Allah, and said, out of ignorance of Allah and of their own standing with Him, while they themselves were polytheists: ﴿Why does Allah not speak to us?﴾, as He speaks to His messenger and His prophets, "or a sign come to us as it came to them?" It is not fitting for Allah to speak except to His friends, nor to bring a miraculous sign upon the claim of a claimant except to one who is truthful in his claim and who calls to Allah and His unity. As for one who is lying in his claim and who calls to the fabrication against Him and to the ascription of sons and daughters to Him, it is not permissible that Allah, mighty is His praise, speak to him, or give him a miraculous sign that would confirm his lie and his fabrication against Him.

As for the one who asserts that by His saying ﴿And those who do not know﴾ Allah meant the Arabs [[In the printed edition: "And the one who asserts..." – the correct reading is what is established here, as the editor of the printed edition corrected it.]], he is saying a statement for which there is no report of its soundness and no proof of its truth in the apparent meaning of the Book. When a statement comes to that, its error is evident, because he has claimed what has no proof of its soundness, and claiming the like of that is not difficult for anyone.

* *

As for the meaning of His saying ﴿Why does Allah not speak to us?﴾, it means: "Why does Allah not speak to us!" as al-Ashhab ibn Rumaylah said: [[It is not by al-Ashhab but by Jarir; Ibn al-Shajari followed him in his Amali 2: 210, as if he had transmitted it from him as is his habit.]]

*You consider the slaughter of she-camels the best of your glory, O sons of Dhawtara, were it not for the armored brave man* [[Diwan of Jarir: 338; al-Naqa'id: 833; cited later in the Tafsir 7: 119 (Bulaq) without attribution; Majaz al-Quran: 52; Amali Ibn al-Shajari 1: 279, 334 / 2: 210; al-Khizanah 1: 461. The Diwan and al-Naqa'id have "your best striving" instead. The verse is from a long qasidah in refutation of Jarir and al-Farazdaq. "Aqr al-nayb": 'aqr of a she-camel or horse means striking its legs and cutting them; when they wished to slaughter a camel they would hamstring it, then slaughter it, and they did this so that it would not run off at the slaughter. The Arabs used to vie in generosity through al-mu'aqarah, which is that one man hamstrings a she-camel, and the other hamstrings one too, competing in generosity and bounty, and insisting in this until one of them overcomes his companion. Al-nayb is the plural of nab: the aged she-camel, so named for the length of her tooth. Jarir refers by this to what al-Farazdaq boasted of regarding the mu'aqarah of his father Ghalib ibn Sa'sa'ah with Suhaym ibn Wathil al-Riyahi at a place called "Sawwar"; Suhaym hamstrung five, then changed his mind, while Ghalib hamstrung a hundred or two hundred. This is one of the matters of the Jahiliyyah. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Do not eat from the mu'aqarah of the Bedouins, for I do not feel safe that it is among what was dedicated to other than Allah." 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O people, it is not lawful for you, for it was dedicated to other than Allah." (See the account of the mu'aqarah in al-Naqa'id: 625–626.)

As for his saying "Sons of Dhawtara," it means: "O sons of the fools." This is what has been said, though I fear it is not so, for "Dhawtara" is a nickname for a man of the Banu Mujashi' ibn Darim, whom they did not name. Jarir said to al-Farazdaq: "Ibn Shari'ah, and al-Qarin, and Dhawtara... the worst of horsemen on the night of calamity." This is evidence that it refers to a specific person, which I hope to verify in another place. He intended to disparage him by his ancestors in general. *Al-Kamy* is the brave man who does not fear, who does not turn away from his opponent, whether or not he had weapons.

As for his saying "ta'uddun" – meaning "you reckon and make" – the verb "a'adda" was transitive to two objects, by the implication of the meaning of "ja'ala and hasiba," as Dhu al-Rummah said: "A noble, white, bright, lordly one... those who seek him reckon him as dependents."]]

meaning: "Why then do you not reckon the armored brave man!" As:

1866 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿Why does Allah not speak to us?﴾, he said: "Why then does Allah not speak to us!"

Abu Ja'far said: As for "the sign" (al-ayah), it has been established earlier that the meaning of "ayah" is the sign (al-'alamah). [[See what preceded: 1: 106.]] Allah only reported about them that they said: "Why does a sign not come to us in accordance with what we desire and ask, as came to the prophets and messengers?" So He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Thus said those who were before them, similar to their saying.﴾

* *

The interpretation of His exalted saying: ﴿Thus said those who were before them, similar to their saying. Their hearts are alike.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The exegetes differed concerning whom Allah meant by His saying: ﴿Thus said those who were before them, similar to their saying.﴾ Some of them said concerning that what follows:

1867 – Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Thus said those who were before them, similar to their saying﴾ – they are the Jews.

1868 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Those who were before them﴾ – the Jews.

* *

Others said: They are the Jews and the Christians, because "those who do not know" are the Arabs. [[In the printed edition: "They are the Jews," the correct reading is what is established here, as the editor of the printed edition inferred; the evidence is that it will be reported after from Qatadah, and it has passed in No. 1763 with this chain from Qatadah that "those who do not know" are the unbelievers of the Arabs, and the following report is a continuation of this earlier report.]]

Mention of those who said this:

1869 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' related to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah: ﴿Those who were before them﴾, meaning the Jews and the Christians and others.

1870 – Musa related to me, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, who said: They said – meaning the Arabs – as the Jews and Christians before them had said.

1871 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': ﴿Thus said those who were before them, similar to their saying﴾, meaning the Jews and the Christians.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We have shown that those whom Allah, mentioned is His, meant by His saying ﴿And those who do not know say: "Why does Allah not speak to us?"﴾ are the Christians, and that those who said the like of their saying are the Jews [[In the printed edition: "and those who said" – the pronoun in "and those who said" refers back to the Christians. See its evidence earlier, shortly before: 550.]] who asked Musa ﷺ to show them their Lord openly, and to let them hear the speech of their Lord, as we have explained earlier in this our book – [[See what preceded in the explanation of the verse: 55, and the report: 959.]] and they asked for signs which they had no right to ask, presuming upon their Lord. Likewise the Christians wished upon their Lord, presuming upon Him that He let them hear His speech and show them the signs they desired. Allah, mighty is His praise, reported about them that they said in this matter the like of what the Jews said, and wished upon their Lord like their wishes, and that their saying which they said in this respect resembles the saying of the Jews because of the similarity of their hearts in misguidance and disbelief in Allah. Although their schools differ in their lying against Allah and their fabrication against Him, their hearts are alike in disbelief in their Lord and fabrication against Him, and in their presumption over Allah's prophets and messengers, peace be upon them. Mujahid said in accordance with what we have said regarding this.

1872 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Their hearts are alike﴾ – the hearts of the Christians and the Jews.

* *

Another said: [[In the printed edition: "And others said," the correct reading is what is established here, for he reported Mujahid's statement alone.]] The meaning of that is: the hearts of the unbelievers of the Arabs, the Jews, the Christians and others are alike.

Mention of those who said this:

1873 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: ﴿Their hearts are alike﴾, meaning the Arabs, the Jews, the Christians and others.

1874 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': ﴿Their hearts are alike﴾, meaning the Arabs, the Jews, the Christians and others.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: It is not permissible in His saying ﴿tashabahat﴾ to read it with the doubled letter (tathqil), because the "ta'" at its beginning is an added letter introduced into the form "tafa'ala"; if it were doubled, it would become two ta's, and it is not permissible to introduce two added ta's as a sign of a single meaning. It is only permissible in the future tense, because the meaning of their insertion differs: one of them enters as a sign of the future, and the other is the one of "tafa'ala," then one of them is assimilated into the other and doubled, so it is said: "Tashabbaha qulubuna ba'da al-yawm" (our hearts will resemble one another after today). [[See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Quran 1: 75; Tabari's expression here corrects the error there.]]

* *

The meaning of the verse: The Christians said, ignorant of Allah and of His greatness: "Why does our Lord, Allah, not speak to us, as He spoke to His prophets and messengers, or why does a sign from Allah not come to us by which we know the truth of what we are upon, according to what we ask and desire?" Allah, mighty is His praise, said: Just as these ignorant Christians said and wished upon their Lord, so did those before them, the Jews, who asked their Lord to show them Allah Himself openly, and to give them a sign, and presumed over Him and His messengers, and wished vain wishes. Thus the hearts of the Jews and the Christians were alike in their rebellion against Allah, their little knowledge of His greatness, and their audacity toward His prophets and messengers, just as their statements that they said were alike.

* *

The interpretation of His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain (118).﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, mighty is His praise, ﴿Indeed We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain﴾, He means: We have made clear the indications because of which Allah became angry with the Jews, and made of them apes and swine, and prepared for them a humiliating punishment in their return; and the ones because of which Allah disgraced the Christians in this world, and prepared for them disgrace and a painful punishment in the Hereafter; and the ones because of which He made the dwellers of the gardens, those who submitted their faces to Allah while being good-doers, in this surah and others. So He made known the causes because of which each group deserved from Allah what was done to them, and Allah specified for this the people who are certain, because they are the people of firmness in matters and those who seek knowledge of the realities of things with certainty and soundness. Allah, mighty is His praise, reported that He made clear to the one who has this attribute what He made clear, so that his doubt would vanish and he would know the reality of the matter, since it is a report from Allah, mighty is His praise, and the report of Allah is one whose hearer is not excused for doubting it. Other reports may carry what is possible in them of accidental causes of forgetfulness, error, and lying, but that is negated from the report of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

* *

The interpretation of His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed We have sent you with the truth, as a bringer of good news and a warner﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of His saying, mighty is His praise, ﴿Indeed We have sent you with the truth, as a bringer of good news and a warner﴾ is: Indeed We have sent you, O Muhammad, with Islam, which I do not accept from anyone other than it of the religions, and it is the truth; as a bringer of good news to whoever follows you, obeys you, and accepts from you what you call to of the truth – with victory in this world, success with reward in the Hereafter, and enduring bliss therein; and as a warner to whoever disobeys you, opposes you, and rejects what you call to of the truth – with disgrace in this world, humiliation therein, and a humiliating punishment in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 119:

The explanation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ (119)

Abu Ja'far said: The majority of reciters read: ﴿Wa la tus'alu 'an ashab al-jahim﴾, with a dammah on the "ta" of "tus'alu" and a raf' (nominative) on the "lam" of it, as a statement of fact, meaning: O Muhammad, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner. You have conveyed what you were sent with, and you are only responsible for conveying and warning. You are not held accountable for those who disbelieved in what you brought of the truth and who were among the people of the Blazing Fire.

Some of the people of Medina read it: ﴿Wa la tas'al﴾ with a jazm (apocopate), as a prohibition, with a fatha on the "ta" of "tas'al" and a jazm on its "lam". According to the reading of these people, the meaning is: We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner so that you may convey what you were sent with, not so that you would be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire; so do not ask about their condition. Those who read this reading interpreted it with what follows:

1875- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Musa ibn Ubaydah, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I wish I knew what my parents did." So it was revealed: ﴿And do not ask about the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾

1876- Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from Musa ibn Ubaydah, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I wish I knew what my parents did. I wish I knew what my parents did. I wish I knew what my parents did," three times. Then it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and you will not be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ He did not mention them until Allah took him. [[The two hadiths 1875 and 1876 are both mursal, for Muhammad ibn Ka'b ibn Sulaym al-Qurazi is a Successor (tabi'i), and a mursal report does not establish proof. Furthermore, both chains are weak due to the weakness of their narrator Musa ibn Ubaydah ibn Nashit al-Rabadhi, who is very weak, biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir of al-Bukhari 4/1/291, al-Saghir 172-173, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/151. Al-Bukhari said: "Munkar al-hadith, as stated by Ahmad ibn Hanbal. 'Ali ibn al-Madini said, on the authority of al-Qattan: 'We used to avoid him in those days.'" Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Jawzajani who said: "I heard Ahmad ibn Hanbal say: 'Narration from Musa ibn Ubaydah is not permissible in my view.' We said: 'O Abu 'Abd Allah, is it not permissible?' He said: 'In my view.' I said: 'But Sufyan and Shu'bah have narrated from him?' He said: 'If it were clear to Shu'bah what is clear to others, he would not have narrated from him.'" Ibn Ma'in said: "His hadith is not used as proof." Abu Hatim said: "Munkar al-hadith." His father is "Ubaydah," in diminutive form; in the printed edition both chains read "'Abdah," which is an error.]]

1877- Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Dawud ibn Abi 'Asim informed me that the Prophet (ﷺ) said one day: "I wish I knew where my parents are." Then it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and you will not be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ [[This report is also mursal and does not establish proof. Dawud ibn Abi 'Asim ibn 'Urwah ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi is a trustworthy Successor, and he also narrates from some Successors. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/1/210, and al-Jarh 1/2/421. In the printed edition it reads "Dawud 'an Abi 'Asim," which is a distortion; we corrected it from Ibn Kathir 1:297.

Ibn Kathir (1:296) quoted al-Qurtubi as saying: "We have mentioned in al-Tadhkirah that Allah revived his parents until they believed in him, and we answered his saying: 'Indeed my father and your father are in the Fire.'" Then Ibn Kathir commented: "The hadith narrated about the lifetime of his parents, peace be upon him, is not in any of the six books nor elsewhere, and its chain is weak."

I see that elaborating at length on such matters is unprofitable, and we were not commanded to burden ourselves with speculation about it.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct reading in my view is the reading of the one who reads with raf', as a statement of fact. Because Allah, mighty is His praise, recounted the stories of peoples from among the Jews and Christians, and mentioned their misguidance, their disbelief in Allah, and their audacity toward His prophets. Then He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Indeed, We have sent you﴾ O Muhammad ﴿with the truth as a bringer of good tidings﴾ to those who believed in you and followed you, from among those whose accounts I have related to you and whose accounts I have not related to you, ﴿and a warner﴾ to those who disbelieved in you and opposed you. So convey My message. There is no responsibility upon you for the deeds of those who disbelieve in you after you have conveyed My message to them, nor are you accountable for what they did afterward. There has been no mention, in the context of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) asking his Lord about the companions of the Blazing Fire, that would make the words "and you will not be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire" have a direction to which they could be directed. Rather, the speech is directed toward the meaning indicated by its apparent sense, unless a clear indication establishes proof that its intended meaning differs from what its apparent sense shows; then that would be submitted to the established proof. There is no report establishing proof that the Prophet (ﷺ) was forbidden from asking about the companions of the Blazing Fire in this verse, nor any indication that this is so in the apparent meaning of the revelation. The obligation is that the interpretation of that statement be in accordance with what has been mentioned before this verse, and concerning those mentioned after it from among the Jews, Christians, and others of the disbelievers, not a prohibition against asking about them. [[A strong, irrefutable argument, and insight into the context and sequence of the meanings of the Qur'an. But many people overlook the places of truth in a specific passage, because the matter becomes confused for them due to its resemblance to another place in a different passage, as you will see in the following note no. 40.]]

* *

If someone supposes that the report narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b is sound, then the impossibility of doubt on the part of the Messenger (peace be upon him) regarding whether the people of polytheism are among the people of the Fire, and that his parents were among them, refutes the soundness of what Muhammad ibn Ka'b said, if the report from him is sound. Moreover, Allah began the statement after His words ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ with "wa" (and) — with His words ﴿and you will not be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ — and He did not connect it to what precedes with "fa" (so), which would make it: "Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, so do not ask about the companions of the Blazing Fire" — [[In the printed edition it read: "with 'wa' says: fa la tus'al 'an ashab al-jahim... bashiran wa nadhiran wa la tus'al 'an ashab al-jahim," which is an error, as the printed edition's editor corrected in his note.]] which most clearly indicates that the statement with "wa la tus'al" is a report, and that it is more appropriate than a prohibition, and the raf' is more appropriate than the jazm. It has been mentioned that in the reading of Ubayy it is: ﴿Wa ma tus'al﴾, and in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿Wa lan tus'al﴾, and both of these readings attest to the raf' and its being a statement, not a prohibition. [[Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (1:297): "Ibn Jarir rejected this statement transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b and others, because doubt on the part of the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning the matter of his parents is impossible, and he chose the first reading. What he followed here is open to scrutiny, because it is possible that this was during his seeking forgiveness for his parents, before he knew their state; then when he knew that, he disowned them and reported that they were among the people of the Fire, as this is established in the Sahih. There are many similar instances and parallels to this, and what Ibn Jarir mentioned does not necessarily follow, and Allah knows best."]]

Ibn Kathir, may Allah forgive him, forgot what al-Tabari repeated and began with: the mention of the sequence of consecutive verses. And the context, as he himself said, concerns the Jews and Christians and their accounts, the similarity of their hearts in disbelief in Allah, their scant knowledge of the greatness of their Lord, their audacity toward the messengers and prophets of Allah, and all of this necessitates the torment of the Blazing Fire. So what brought the disbelieving Arabs into this context? Indeed, they do enter into the meaning of being among the companions of the Blazing Fire, as does every polytheist among the Arabs and others. We have already explained earlier (p. 521, note 1) that these preceding verses and those following them show most clearly that their whole story concerns the Jews and Christians, and the polytheists of the Arabs have no part in it. Even if these polytheists enter into the meaning of being among the companions of the Blazing Fire, the context of the verses requires that it be about the Jews and Christians; thus restricting one part of a verse to having been revealed about some polytheists of the Jahiliyyah is an arbitrary judgment without report or proof. (See also p. 565.)

Ibn Kathir overlooked al-Tabari's meaning. Al-Tabari intended to show two things: that the report from Muhammad ibn Ka'b is not sound, and that even if it were sound from one route, the revelation of the verse was not for this that was narrated from him. The explanation: the report is not sound, because it came in the form of doubt from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding the state of one of the people of the Jahiliyyah: whether he is in a garden or in the Fire! And this is something the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is far above. There is a great difference between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) seeking forgiveness for his parents who were from the people of the Jahiliyyah and upon such a state of polytheism, and his doubting their condition and saying: "I wish I knew what my parents did." Ibn Kathir's words would be correct only if there were a link between this doubt and the seeking of forgiveness, such that one necessarily implies the other or is caused by it. Moreover, the report is rejected because the context of the verses clearly indicates that they were revealed concerning the Jews and Christians, so it is impossible to restrict one part of these consecutive verses to a report that is not sound, for a weakening reason. I do not know why Ibn Kathir inserted seeking forgiveness and disavowal into this place, despite the clarity of al-Tabari's argument in the preceding paragraph from the standpoint of context, and in this paragraph from the standpoint of grammar.

Indeed, some of the problems over which people's disputes revolve may cause the likes of Ibn Kathir to overlook the places of precision, correctness, and careful verification, while they interpret the Book of Allah, which does not contradict itself and in which falsehood cannot approach from before it or behind it. O Allah, we ask You for protection from error, and we seek Your guidance in clarifying the meanings of Your Book.

* *

Some grammarians of Basra directed His words ﴿and you will not be asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ toward the circumstantial sense (hal), as if he saw that its meaning was: "We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, not being asked about the companions of the Blazing Fire." This applies when the "ta" is read with a dammah and it is read as a statement; and he would permit on that basis the reading "wa la tas'al" with a fatha on the "ta" and a dammah on the "lam" as a statement, meaning: "We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, not asking about the companions of the Blazing Fire." We have already explained what we hold to be correct in this matter.

These two opinions that I have mentioned from the Basran grammarian are refuted by what has been transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy in the readings, [[In the printed edition: "yarfa'uhuma ma ruwiya..." and the correct form is what I have adopted.]] because bringing into them what they brought, namely "ma" and "lan," indicates that the speech is cut off from its beginning and that "wa la tas'al" is a new beginning. And when it is a beginning, it cannot be a circumstantial clause.

* *

As for ﴿ashab al-jahim﴾, "al-jahim" is the Fire itself when its fuel has been kindled, and from it is the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

When Jahannam is kindled and then it whirls... and the Jahim turns away from its quddamisah [[His Diwan: 53; the narration there is "thumma faara" (then it boiled), and that appears to be the correct form, and I fear the line may be distorted. I did not know the meaning of "qawabisuha" there; I think it may be "qadamisuha," the plural of qadmus, which means large, hard stones, like His saying, exalted is He: "its fuel is men and stones." "A'rada al-shay'" means it spread and widened, and His saying "'an" means because of the casting of these stones into it. This is the closest meaning I have reached, and the following line supports it, where the answer to "idha" appears: "it is stirred with hard, solid, strong sandal wood... as though the palm-like ones (al-dahiyat) had white tips for it." He apparently means by al-dahiyat: the palm trees. The poetry of Umayyah is in any case obscure.]]

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan) on Surah 2, Verse 120**

The interpretation of His word, exalted is He: ﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion (millah). Say, "Indeed, the guidance of God is the [true] guidance."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His word, exalted is His praise: ﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion﴾, He means: O Muhammad, the Jews and the Christians will never be pleased with you, ever. So leave off seeking what would please them and agree with them, and turn instead to seeking the pleasure of God by calling them to the truth with which God has sent you. For what you call them to is indeed the way to unite with you in harmony and in the upright religion. There is no way for you to please them by following their religion, because Judaism is opposed to Christianity, and Christianity is opposed to Judaism. Christianity and Judaism cannot be combined in one person at one time. The Jews and the Christians will not agree to be pleased with you unless you become a Jew-Christian, and that will never happen from you, because you are one person, and two opposing religions cannot be combined in you at one time. If there is no way for them to be combined in you at one time, then there is no way for you to please both groups. If there is no way for you to do that, then hold fast to the guidance of God, by which He has provided a way to bring creation together in harmony.

* *

As for "millah," it means religion (din), and its plural is milal.

* *

Then He, exalted is His praise, said to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Say, O Muhammad, to these Christians and Jews who said: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾, ﴿Indeed, the guidance of God is the [true] guidance﴾, meaning: indeed, the clarification of God is the convincing clarification and the decisive judgment between us. So come to the Book of God and His explanation, in which He has made clear to His servants what they differed about, which is the Torah that you both acknowledge to be from God. In it, the truth of us will become clear to you from the falsehood, and which of us are the people of Paradise and which of us are the people of the Fire, and which of us is upon what is correct and which upon what is wrong.

God commanded His Prophet ﷺ to call them to the guidance and clarification of God only because in it is the refutation of the Jews and Christians in what they said, that none would enter Paradise except those who were Jews or Christians, and the clarification of the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, and that the one who denies him is among the people of the Fire, not the one who affirms him.

* *

The interpretation of His word, exalted is He: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have from God no protector or helper.﴾ (120)

Abu Ja'far said: By His word, exalted is His praise, ﴿And if you were to follow﴾, O Muhammad, the desires of these Jews and Christians, in what would please them with regard to you, becoming a Jew or a Christian and turning, in that, to pleasing them, agreeing with their wishes, after the knowledge that has come to you of their misguidance and their disbelief in their Lord, and after what I have related to you of their news in this surah, ﴿you would have from God no protector﴾, meaning: you would have, O Muhammad, no protector who would manage your affairs and no guardian who would look after them, ﴿nor helper﴾, who would help you against God, averting from you what descends upon you of His punishment and preventing you from it, should your Lord bring it upon you. The meanings of "protector" (wali) and "helper" (nasir) have already been explained earlier.

It has been said that God, may His remembrance be exalted, revealed this verse to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ because the Jews and Christians invited him to their religions, and each faction among them said: the guidance is what we are upon and not what others among the rest of the religions are upon. So God admonished him not to do that, and taught him the decisive proof that distinguishes between them regarding what each group claimed.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 121:

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The exegetes differed concerning those whom God, mighty and majestic is He, meant by His words: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾. Some of them said: They are the believers in the Messenger of God ﷺ, and in what he brought, from among his Companions.

Mention of those who said this:

1878 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾: These are the Companions of the Prophet of God ﷺ; they believed in the Book of God and affirmed it.

* *

Others said: Rather, God meant by this the scholars of the Children of Israel, who believed in God and affirmed His messengers, and so they acknowledged the judgment of the Torah, and acted upon what God had commanded in it of following Muhammad ﷺ, believing in him, and affirming what he brought from God.

Mention of those who said this:

1879 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it with its due recitation; those believe in it, and whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers﴾, he said: Whoever among the Jews disbelieved in the Prophet ﷺ, those are the losers.

* *

This view is more correct than the view stated by Qatadah, because the verses before it have passed with reports about the People of the Two Books, and the alteration by those among them who altered the Book of God, their interpreting it other than its true meaning, and their attributing falsehoods to God. No mention of the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ occurred in the verse before it, so that His words ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ would be directed to a report about them; nor is there any mention of them in the verse that follows it, so that it would be directed to being a fresh report about the stories of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ after the ending of the stories of others; nor has any report come that this is a report about them which must be accepted. [[May God have mercy on Abu Ja'far; he does not omit sound argumentation at every verse. But some exegetes go beyond the bounds and are lax; would that they had followed his method in precision, preservation and inference.]]

Given that this is so, the more appropriate meaning of the verse is that it is directed as a report about those whom God, mighty and majestic is He, related [their stories] in the verse before it and the verse after it, [[What is between the brackets is an addition that is necessary.]] and they are the People of the Two Books: the Torah and the Gospel. Given that this is so, the interpretation of the verse is: Those to whom We have given the Book, which you know, O Muhammad, that is the Torah, read it and followed what is in it, so they affirmed you and believed in you, and in what you brought from Me; those recite it with its due recitation.

* *

The definite article and the noun "al-Kitab" were introduced because it is definite, and the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions knew which book was meant by it.

* *

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿they recite it with its due recitation﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The exegetes differed concerning the interpretation of His, the Mighty and Majestic's, words: ﴿they recite it with its due recitation﴾. Some of them said: The meaning of that is: they follow it with its due following.

Mention of those who said this:

1880 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ibn Abi 'Adi and 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me; and 'Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi 'Adi narrated to us, all of them, from Dawud, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿they recite it with its due recitation﴾: they follow it with its due following.

1881 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from Ikrimah, the like of it.

1880 (repeated numbering) - 'Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Dawud ibn Abi Hind narrated to us, from Ikrimah, the like of it.

1883 - al-Hasan ibn 'Amr al-'Anqazi narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from Asbat, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His, the Mighty and Majestic's, words: ﴿they recite it with its due recitation﴾, he said: They make lawful its lawful and make unlawful its unlawful, and they do not distort it. [[Report 1883: in the printed edition: "al-Hasan ibn 'Amr al-'Abqari"; see the note on report no. 1625. Likewise, "al-Hasan" occurred in report 1655, which is an error; we correct it.]]
