1886 - It was narrated to me on the authority of 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: By Him in whose hand is my soul, the due recitation of it is that its lawful be made lawful and its unlawful be made unlawful, and that one recite it as God sent it down, and not distort the words from their places, nor interpret anything from it other than its true interpretation.

1887 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah and Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir, from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: ﴿they recite it with its due recitation﴾, that one makes lawful its lawful and unlawful its unlawful, and does not distort it from its places.

1888 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: [Abu Ahmad] al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: 'Abbad ibn al-'Awwam narrated to us, from one he mentioned, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿they recite it with its due recitation﴾: they follow it with its due following.

1891 - 'Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to me, saying: Sufyan narrated to us; and Nasr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Azdi narrated to me, saying: Yahya ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, from Sufyan — they all said: from Mansur, from Abu Razin, the like of it.

1893 - Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Malik informed us, from Qays ibn Sa'd: ﴿they recite it with its due recitation﴾, he said: they follow it with its due following. [[Report 1899: Abu Qutaybah is Salm ibn Qutaybah al-Shu'ayri, a trustworthy and reliable transmitter from whom al-Bukhari and the authors of the Sunan related. al-Hasan ibn Abi Ja'far al-Jufri: good in narration, though criticized; we preferred to grade his reports as good in detail in the commentary on the Musnad. "Ayyub" is al-Sakhtiyani; the printed edition has "Abu Ayyub", which is an error corrected from the biographical works. Abu al-Khalil is Salih ibn Abi Maryam al-Dab'i, a trustworthy transmitter.]]

[[Report 1901: Mubarak is Ibn Fudalah, one of the closest people to al-Hasan al-Basri, as we said at no. 611.]]

1902 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿they recite it with its due recitation﴾, he said: they make lawful its lawful and unlawful its unlawful, and act upon what is in it. It was mentioned to us that Ibn Mas'ud used to say: the due recitation of it is that one makes lawful its lawful, makes unlawful its unlawful, and recites it as God, mighty and majestic, sent it down, and does not distort it from its places.

1903 - 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Abu Dawud narrated to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn 'Utayyah narrated to us, I heard Qatadah say: ﴿they recite it with its due recitation﴾, he said: they follow it with its due following. He said: its following: they make lawful its lawful and unlawful its unlawful, and recite it as it was sent down.

1904 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn 'Awn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym informed us, from Dawud, from Ikrimah regarding His words: ﴿they recite it with its due recitation﴾, he said: they follow it with its due following. Have you not heard the words of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿and the moon when it follows it﴾ [Surah al-Shams: 2], he said: when it follows it.

* *

Others said: ﴿they recite it with its due recitation﴾ means they recite it with its due recitation. [[See what has passed in this part 2: 411.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view concerning the interpretation of this is that it means: they follow it with its due following, from the saying of the speaker: "I continued to recite its trace" (ma zilt atlu athrahu), meaning he followed its trace. [[See what has passed in this part 2: 411.]] This is because the authoritative consensus of the exegetes is that this is its interpretation.

Given that this is its interpretation, the meaning of the speech is: Those to whom We have given the Book, O Muhammad, from the People of the Torah, who believed in you and in the truth which I have brought them through you, follow My Book which I sent down upon My Messenger Musa, may God's blessings be upon him, so they believe in it and acknowledge what is in it of your description and attributes, and that you are My Messenger; obedience to Me is incumbent upon them in believing in you and affirming what I have brought them from Me; they act upon what I have made lawful for them, and avoid what I have made unlawful for them in it; and they do not distort it from its places, nor alter it, nor change it, as I sent it down to them, by any interpretation or otherwise.

* *

As for His words: ﴿with its due recitation﴾, it is an intensification in describing their following of the Book and their adherence to acting upon it, as one says: "Indeed so-and-so is a scholar of the true sort," and as one says: "Indeed so-and-so is every bit an excellent man." [[See Sibawayh 1: 223-224.]]

* *

The grammarians differed concerning the annexation of "haqq" (true/due) to a definite noun. Some grammarians of Kufa said: its annexation to a definite noun is not permissible, because it has the sense of "ayy" (which), and the sense of your saying "afdal rajul Fulan" (the best man is so-and-so), and "afʿal" is not annexed to a single definite noun, because it is partitive, and a partitive single thing cannot be definite. So they rejected saying "marartu bi-l-rajuli haqqa al-rajul" (I passed by the man, the due man), and "marartu bi-l-rajuli jidda al-rajul," just as they rejected "marartu bi-l-rajuli ayya al-rajul" (I passed by the man, which man), while they permitted it with "kull al-rajul," "ayn al-rajul," and "nafs al-rajul." [[In the printed edition: "ghayr al-rajul".]] They said: We only permitted that because these words were originally intensifiers, and when they became nouns, they retained their status as definite nouns according to their origins.

They claimed that His words ﴿they recite it with its due recitation﴾ permit the annexation to "recitation," which is itself annexed to a definite noun, because the Arabs count the pronoun "hu" (it) — when it refers to an indefinite — as indefinite, so they say: "marartu bi-rajulin wahidin ummuhu (I passed by a single man whose mother...), and nasij wahdihi (unique, by himself), and sayyid qawmihi (the lord of his people)." They said: likewise His words ﴿haqqa tilawatihi﴾: the annexation of "haqq" to "tilawah" is permitted, and "tilawah" is annexed to the pronoun "hu," because the Arabs count the "hu" in such analogous cases as an indefinite. They said: If it were "haqq al-tilawah," it would be permissible to say "marartu bi-l-rajuli haqqa al-rajul."

On this view, the meaning of the speech is: Those to whom We have given the Book recite it with a recitation that is due.

* *

Some grammarians of Basra said: The annexation of "haqq" to indefinites with indefinites, and to definites with definites, is permissible; and this is analogous to the saying of the speaker: "marartu bi-l-rajuli ghulam al-rajul" (I passed by the man, the servant of the man), and "bi-rajulin ghulam rajulin."

So the interpretation of the verse according to these is: Those to whom We have given the Book recite it with the recitation of it that is due. [[The correct wording should be: "haqq tilawat al-Kitab" (the due recitation of the Book); perhaps the copyist erred.]]

* *

The first view is more correct in our opinion, because the meaning of His words ﴿haqqa tilawatihi﴾ is "the recitation" in the sense of praising the recitation they recite and extolling it. "Ayy" is not permissible to be annexed to a single definite noun according to all of them; and likewise "haqq" is not permissible to be annexed to a single definite noun.

The annexation in ﴿haqqa tilawatihi﴾ to what contains the "hu" is due to the reason I described, whose explanation was given earlier.

* *

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Those believe in it﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words ﴿Those﴾, mighty and majestic is He means: these are the ones of whom He reported that they recite what He gave them of the Book with its due recitation. As for His words ﴿believe﴾, it means: they affirm it. The "hu" in His words "bihi" (in it) refers back to the "hu" in "tilawatihi," and both are a mention of the Book which God said: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾.

God, mighty and majestic is He, reported that the believer in the Torah is the one who follows what is in it of its lawful and unlawful, and acts upon what is in it of God's obligations which He imposed in it upon its people; and that its people, who are truly its people, are those who have this description, not those who distort it, alter its interpretation, change its ways, and abandon what God imposed upon them in it.

* *

God, mighty and majestic is He, described those who were described with what He described them, among the followers of the Torah, and praised them for what He praised them, because in following it lies following Muhammad, the Prophet of God ﷺ, and affirming him, since the Torah commands its people to do that, and informs them of God, mentioned be He, concerning his prophethood, and the obligation of obeying him upon all of God's creation of the children of Adam; and that in denying Muhammad is denying it. So God, mighty and majestic is He, reported that the followers of the Torah are the believers in Muhammad ﷺ, and they are those who act upon what is in it, as:

1905 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: ﴿those believe in it﴾: He said: whoever among the Children of Israel believed in the Messenger of God ﷺ and in the Torah. And whoever disbelieves in Muhammad ﷺ is the one who disbelieves in it, the loser, as God, mighty and majestic is He, said: ﴿and whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers﴾. [[See what has passed concerning the meaning of "al-khasir" (the loser) at 1: 417, then this part 2: 166.]]

* *

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers (121)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿and whoever disbelieves in it﴾ is meant: whoever disbelieves in the Book which He reported that they recite — from among those to whom He gave it, of the believers — with its due recitation. By His words, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿disbelieves﴾ is meant: denies what is in it of God's obligations and the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and his truthfulness, and distorts it, altering its interpretation. Those are the ones who lost their knowledge and their deeds, cheated themselves of their portion of God's mercy, and exchanged for it God's wrath and anger. Ibn Zayd said regarding His words, with what follows:

1906 - Yunus narrated to me this, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers﴾: he said: whoever among the Jews disbelieved in the Prophet ﷺ, ﴿those are the losers﴾.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 122:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you and that I preferred you over the worlds﴾ (2:122).

Abu Ja'far said: This verse is an admonition from God, dhikruhu, to the Jews who were living among the emigrants of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and a reminder from Him to them of what had passed of His favours toward them through their forefathers, seeking to win them over to His religion and to the confirmation of His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ. So He said: "O Children of Israel, remember My favours toward you, My benefactions among you, and My rescuing you from the hands of your enemy Pharaoh and his people, and My sending down upon you the manna and the quails during your wandering, and My establishing you in the land after you had been humiliated and subdued, and My choosing messengers from among you, and My preferring you over a world among whom you lived, at a time when you were obedient to Me," [[If the phrase "and I admonish you to follow My Messenger..." has not dropped out here, then the phrase "to follow My Messenger" is connected to his saying at the beginning of the address: "Remember My favours upon you..."]] "by following My Messenger sent to you, by confirming him and confirming what has come to you from Me, and by abandoning persistence in error and deviation."

We have previously mentioned, in what has gone before, the blessings which God bestowed upon the Children of Israel, the meanings of the favours of His which He reminded them of, and the world over which they were preferred, with narrations and evidences. We disliked lengthening the book by repeating it, since the meaning in that matter here and there is one.

[[See what has preceded in this volume, 2: 23-26.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 123:

The explanation of the words of His, ﴿And guard against a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will any compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped﴾ (2:123).

Abu Ja'far said: This verse is a warning from God, may His praise be exalted, to those whose admonition He had already given through what He admonished them with in the preceding verse. God says to them: "Guard against" (wa-ttaqu), O assembly of the Children of Israel, who alter My Book and My revelation (tanzil), who distort its interpretation (ta'wil) from its proper meaning, who deny My Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ): the punishment of a Day on which no soul will settle anything for another soul, nor will it suffice for it in any way. Guard against perishing in your present state of disbelief in Me and denial of My Messenger, so that you die upon it. For that is a Day on which no ransom will be accepted from a soul for what it owes, no one who has a right against it will intercede for what is due from it, and it will not be helped by any helper from God when He takes vengeance upon it for its disobedience to Him. [[In the printed edition: "wa-la hum yunsaruhum" ("and they will not be helped them"), which is an error; the correct reading is what has been established here.]]

* *

The explanation of all the meanings of this verse has already passed in its counterpart earlier, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it in this place. [[See what has preceded in this part, vol. 2: pp. 26–36.]]

* *

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

**The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan) on Surah 2, Verse 124 (Part 1 of 3)**

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His words, exalted is His praise, ﴿And when He tried﴾, is meant: and when He tested.

It is said of this verb: "I tried so-and-so (ibtalaytu fulanan), I try him, a trial (ibtila')." From it is the words of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿And test the orphans﴾ [Surah al-Nisa': 6], meaning: test them. [[See what has preceded in volume 2: 48, 49.]]

God's testing of Abraham, remembered be He, was a testing by obligations He imposed upon him and commands He ordered him with. These are the "words" (kalimat) which He revealed to him and charged him to act upon, as a trial and test from Him for him.

Then the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the nature of the "words" with which God tried His prophet and intimate friend Abraham, may the blessings of God be upon him.

Some of them said: They are the laws of Islam, and they are thirty "portions" (sahm). [[The sahm, originally, is one of the arrows by which lots are cast in the game of maysir, which are the qidah (lots). Then what the winner of the game obtains was called a sahm, and then it became widespread until every share was called a sahm. His statement here indicates that they used it for every part of a thing that can be divided and is a single whole. So his saying "sahm" here means a characteristic and a branch. Its evidence will come in the reports that follow.]]

Mention of those who said this:

1907. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: "And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words," he said: Ibn 'Abbas said: No one was tested with this religion and established it except Abraham. God tested him with words, and he completed them. He said: So God wrote for him acquittal, and He said: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled﴾ [Surah al-Najm: 37]. He said: Ten of them are in "al-Ahzab," ten of them are in "Bara'ah," and ten of them are in "al-Mu'minun" and "Sa'ala sa'il." And he said: Indeed this Islam is thirty portions. [[Its explanation will come in the following report.]]

1908. Ishaq ibn Shahin narrated to us, saying: Khalid al-Tahhan narrated to us, from Dawud, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: No one was tested with this religion and then carried it out entirely except Abraham. He was tested with Islam and completed it, so God wrote for him acquittal, and He said: "And Abraham who fulfilled." Then he mentioned ten in "Bara'ah" [112], He said: ﴿The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers﴾ up to the end of the verse, [[In the printed edition: "al-Ayat" (the verses), and the correct reading is what I have set down.]] and ten in "al-Ahzab" [35]: ﴿Indeed the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾, and ten in "Surat al-Mu'minun" [1-9] up to His words: ﴿And those who are attentive to their prayers﴾, and ten in "Sa'ala sa'il" [22-34]: ﴿And those who are attentive to their prayers﴾.

1909. 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Shabawayh narrated to us, saying: 'Ali ibn al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Kharijah ibn Mus'ab narrated to us, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Islam is thirty portions, and no one was tested with this religion and established it except Abraham. God said: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled﴾, so God wrote for him acquittal from the Fire. [[Report 1909: 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Shabawayh is 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Thabit ibn Mas'ud ibn Yazid, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, known as Ibn Shabawayh, and he is among the imams of hadith, as al-Khatib said. He is biographed in Tarikh Baghdad 9: 371, and he has a brief biography in Ibn Abi Hatim. In the printed edition here it occurs as "'Ubayd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Shabarmah," which is a distortion and an error. We have corrected it from the Tarikh and from what will come in the Tafsir.
'Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Shaqiq ibn Dinar: trustworthy (thiqah), one of the shaykhs of Ahmad, al-Bukhari, and others. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, and in Sharh al-Musnad: 7437.
This report will come with this isnad in the Tafsir: 27: 43 (Bulaq edition). Likewise Abu Ja'far narrated it with this isnad in the Tarikh 1: 144.
Ibn Kathir mentioned it, 1: 302, and attributed it also to Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim. al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1: 111-112, and added its attribution to Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir. And this isnad is sound (sahih).]]

Others said: They are ten characteristics from the sunan of Islam.

Mention of those who said this:

1910. al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words," he said: God tried him with purification: five in the head and five in the body. In the head: trimming the moustache, rinsing the mouth (madmadah), sniffing water into the nose (istinshaq), the siwak, and parting the hair. In the body: paring the nails, shaving the pubic area, circumcision, plucking the armpit hair, and washing away the traces of excrement and urine with water. [[The report: 1910: This isnad is also sound.
It is in the Tafsir of 'Abd al-Razzaq (manuscript of Dar al-Kutub, photographed), with this isnad.
Likewise Abu Ja'far narrated it in the Tarikh 1: 144, from the Tafsir of 'Abd al-Razzaq, with this isnad.
Likewise al-Hakim narrated it, 2: 266, by way of Ibn Tawus from his father, with the same. He said: "This is a hadith sound according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), though they did not record it," and al-Dhahabi agreed with him.
Ibn Kathir mentioned it, 1: 301. Likewise al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1: 111, and attributed it further to 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan.]]

1911. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Ibn 'Abbas, the like of it, but he did not mention the trace of urine.

Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Sulayman narrated to us, saying: Abu Hilal narrated to us, saying: Qatadah narrated to us regarding His words: "And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words," he said: He tried him with circumcision, shaving the pubic area, washing the front and back passages, the siwak, trimming the moustache, paring the nails, and plucking the armpit hair. Abu Hilal said: And I have forgotten one characteristic.

It was reported to me from 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Matar, from Abu al-Khald, who said: Abraham was tried with ten things, which are in the human being, a sunnah: sniffing water into the nose, trimming the moustache, the siwak, plucking the armpit hair, paring the nails, washing the knuckles (al-baraghim), circumcision, shaving the pubic area, and washing the back passage and the private part. [[The report: 1913: Matar is Ibn Tahman al-Warraq. Abu al-Jild, with the letter jim vowelled and the lam sukun, was explained previously: 434. In the printed edition it is "Abu al-Khald" with the letter kha' instead of jim, which is a distortion that recurs there frequently.
al-Baraghim is the plural of barjamah (with the ba' damma, the ra' sukun, and the jim damma): it is the protrusions of the bones at the joints of the fingers.]]

Mention of those who said this:

1930. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Salm ibn Qutaybah narrated to us, from Yunus ibn Abi Ishaq, from al-Sha'bi: "And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words," he said: among them is circumcision.

Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn Abi Ishaq narrated to us, who said: I heard al-Sha'bi, and Abu Ishaq asked him about the words of God: "And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words," and he said: among them is circumcision, O Abu Ishaq.

Mention of those who said this:

1933. Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us, from Abu Raja', who said: I said to al-Hasan: "And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words, and he completed them." 1934. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, who said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: al-Hasan used to say: Yes, by God, He tried him with a matter and he was patient with it: He tried him with the star, the sun, and the moon, and he did well in that, and he recognised that his Lord is enduring and does not cease. Then He tried him with the migration, and he left his lands and his people until he reached al-Sham, migrating to God. Then He tried him with the fire before the migration, and he was patient with that. Then God tried him with the slaughter of his son and with circumcision, and he was patient with that.

1935. al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from one who heard al-Hasan say regarding His words: "And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words," he said: God tried him with the slaughter of his son, and with the fire, and with the star, the sun, and the moon.

1936. Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Salm ibn Qutaybah narrated to us, saying: Abu Hilal narrated to us, from al-Hasan: "And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words," he said: He tried him with the star, and with the sun and the moon, and found him patient.

Others said, with what:

1937. Musa ibn Harun narrated it to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: The words with which Abraham was tried by his Lord: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us. Indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing. Our Lord, and make us Muslims to You, and from our descendants a Muslim nation to You, and show us our rites, and turn to us. Indeed You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful. Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 127-129].

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this matter, in our opinion, is to say: Allah, mighty and majestic, informed His servants that He tested His intimate friend Ibrahim with words that He revealed to him, and commanded him to act upon them, so he fulfilled them, just as Allah, may His praise be exalted, informed of him that he did. [In the printed edition: "wa-atammahunna" with a waw, and what I have established is the better reading.] It is permissible that those words are all of what was mentioned by those whose statements we have cited in interpreting "the words," and it is permissible that they are some of it. For Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was tested, as has reached us, with all of that, and acted upon it, and carried out in it the obedience of Allah and the duty incumbent upon him in it. Since that is the case, it is not permissible for anyone to say that Allah meant by the words with which Ibrahim was tested a specific part of that to the exclusion of the rest, nor that He meant all of it, except with a proof that must be accepted: either a report from the Messenger ﷺ or a consensus of the authorities. No report from the Messenger concerning any of that has been authenticated, neither by a single transmitter nor by a group of transmitters whose transmission must be accepted. However, two reports have been related from the Prophet ﷺ with a meaning similar to this, and if either of them, or both, were established, the view based on them in interpreting this would be correct. The first of them is:

1938- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Rashdin ibn Sa'd narrated to us, saying: Zabban ibn Fa'id narrated to me, from Sahl ibn Mu'adh ibn Anas, from his father, who said: The Prophet ﷺ used to say: Shall I not inform you why Allah named Ibrahim His intimate friend: "who fulfilled" (al-ladhi waffa)? [Surah al-Najm: 37] Because he used to say every morning and every evening: "So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning" [Surah al-Rum: 17] until he finished the verse. [Editor's note: The hadith's chain is severely weak and has no standing. al-Tabari himself weakened it, as well as the following hadith. Ibn Kathir (1:304) said after pointing to this: "It is as he said, for it is not permissible to narrate them except with a clarification of their weakness, and their weakness is due to several reasons, for each of the two chains includes more than one weak narrator, in addition to what is in the text that indicates its weakness."
Rashdin ibn Sa'd: very weak; we have discussed him at length in the commentary on the Musnad (no. 5748). "Rashdin" is with a kasra on the ra, sukun on the shin, kasra on the dal, and a nun after the ya; the printed edition and Ibn Kathir have "Rashid," which is an error.
Zabban ibn Fa'id al-Misri al-Himrawi: also weak. Ahmad said: "His hadiths are munkar (rejected)," and Ibn Ma'in weakened him. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/1/405, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/616. Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin (p. 210, manuscript photocopy in my possession): "Extremely munkar al-hadith; he uniquely narrates from Sahl ibn Mu'adh a copy that looks fabricated." "Zabban" is with a zay and a doubled ba. The printed edition has "Rayyan" with a ra and a ya, which is an error.
Sahl ibn Mu'adh ibn Anas al-Juhani: also weak; Ibn Ma'in weakened him. Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin (p. 232): "Zabban ibn Fa'id narrated from him; extremely munkar al-hadith. I do not know whether the confusion in his hadith is from him or from Zabban ibn Fa'id. If it is from either of them, then the reports narrated by that one are discarded."
This hadith, despite its severe weakness, was narrated by Ahmad in the Musnad (15688; vol. 3, p. 439, Halabi edition). Indeed, he narrated this copy, which Ibn Hibban almost decided was fabricated.]] The other of the two is:

1939- Abu Kurayb narrated to us with it, saying: al-Hasan ibn 'Atiyya narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, from al-Qasim, from Abu Umama, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "And Ibrahim who fulfilled" [and the one who fulfilled]. He said: Do you know what "fulfilled" means? They said: Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: It is for his work of the day: four rak'ahs during the day. [Editor's note: al-Tabari weakened this too, and Ibn Kathir agreed, as we said regarding the previous one. al-Hasan ibn 'Atiyya ibn Najih al-Kufi: trustworthy; al-Bukhari narrated from him in al-Kabir 2/1/299, mentioning no criticism of him, and Abu Hatim and Abu Zur'a narrated from him; Abu Hatim said: "Saduq (truthful)." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/27. He is not "al-Hasan ibn 'Atiyya ibn Sa'd al-'Awfi," whose biography appeared earlier at 305.
Isra'il: this is Ibn Yunus ibn Ishaq al-Sabi'i, and he is trustworthy; he appeared at 1291.
Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr al-Hanafi or al-Bahili, al-Dimashqi then al-Basri: very weak. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, in al-Bukhari's al-Kabir 1/2/191, in his al-Du'afa p. 7, where he said: "Matruk al-hadith (abandoned in hadith); they abandoned him," and in Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/479. Ibn Hibban said in al-Majruhin (p. 142): "He narrated from al-Qasim, mawla of Mu'awiya, and others, things that look fabricated." Abu Hatim said: "Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr narrated from al-Qasim, from Abu Umama, a fabricated copy, more than a hundred hadiths."
As for al-Qasim: he is Ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Shami, his kunya is Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, and he has been disputed; the preponderant view is that he is trustworthy, and that what is criticized in him comes from the weak transmitters who narrated from him. We have explained this in the commentary on the Musnad (no. 598) and in our notes on al-Mundhiri's Tahdhib al-Sunan (no. 2376).
The hadith was mentioned by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (6:129), and he also attributed it to Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and others, and said: "With a weak chain."]]
* *
Abu Ja'far said: Had the report of Sahl ibn Mu'adh from his father been sound in its chain, it would have been clear that the words with which Ibrahim was tested and by which he stood were his saying every morning and evening: "So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon" — or if the report of Abu Umama had been transmitted by reliable narrators, it would have been known that the words revealed to Ibrahim, with which he was tested in acting upon them, were that he pray four rak'ahs every day. However, these are two reports whose chains are open to scrutiny.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on the meaning of the "words" with which Allah informed that Ibrahim was tested is what we have shown above.
Had someone said regarding this that what Mujahid, Abu Salih and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said is more correct than what others said, it would have been a valid position. For His saying: "Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people" and His saying: "And We charged Ibrahim and Isma'il: purify My House for those who circumambulate" and all the verses similar to these serve as an explanation of the words by which Allah mentioned that Ibrahim was tested. [Ibn Kathir quoted this passage in his tafsir (1:304) from the beginning of "Had someone said," and then commented: "I say: what he first said, that the words include everything mentioned, is stronger than this which he permitted from the statement of Mujahid and whoever said the like. For the context gives something other than what they said, and Allah knows best." Ibn Kathir has offered nothing, for al-Tabari's statement is clear, and it indicates that the correct view is the first, and that this second one, had it been said, would be a valid position. This is a wording of weakening, not of strengthening.]
* *
On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: "He completed them"
Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "fa-atammahunna," Allah, mighty is His praise, means: Ibrahim completed the words. "His completing them" means his fulfilling them by standing for Allah in what He obligated upon him concerning them, and this is the fulfillment about which Allah, mighty is His praise, said: "And Ibrahim who fulfilled" [Surah al-Najm: 37], meaning he fulfilled what he was charged with, "the words," meaning what He commanded him of His obligations and the trials in them, [In the printed edition: "meaning: he fulfilled what was charged to him by the Book, so He commanded him of His obligations and trials in them," which is a disordered phrase that does not hold together, and it seems the correct reading is what I have established.] as:

1940- Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas: "fa-atammahunna," meaning: he discharged them.

1941- Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada: "fa-atammahunna," meaning: he acted upon them and completed them.

1942- It was narrated to me from 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "fa-atammahunna," meaning: he acted upon them and completed them.
* *
On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: "He said: Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people"
Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people," Allah, mighty is His praise, said: O Ibrahim, I will make you an imam for the people, one who is followed and emulated, as:

1943- It was narrated to me from 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people": to be followed and emulated.
* *
It is said from this: "I led the people in prayer, so I lead them, leading and imamate," when one is their imam.
* *
Allah, mighty is His praise, by His saying to Ibrahim, "Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people," meant: I will make you one who leads, after you, those of the people of faith in Me and My messengers, you going before them, [In the printed edition: "fa-taqaddamahum anta" [then you go before them], which is nothing.] and they follow your guidance and take as their example your practice, which you carry out by My command to you and My revelation to you.
* *
On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: "He said: And from my offspring"
Abu Ja'far said: By this, Allah, mighty is His praise, means: Ibrahim said, when Allah had raised his station and honored him, informing him of what He would do with him, by making him an imam in goodness for those of his time, and for those of his descendants who came after him and for all other people, who would be guided by his guidance and emulate his deeds and character: "O Lord, and from my offspring, appoint leaders whom they may follow, as You made me an imam who is followed and emulated." This is a request from Ibrahim to his Lord, which he asked of Him, as:

1944- It was narrated to me from 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: Ibrahim said: "And from my offspring," meaning: appoint from my offspring those who are followed and emulated.
* *
Some people have claimed that Ibrahim's saying, "And from my offspring," was a request from him to his Lord that his progeny be upon his covenant and religion, as He said: "And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols" [Surah Ibrahim: 35], and Allah, mighty is His praise, informed that among his descendants is the wrongdoer who opposes his religion, by His saying: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers."
* *
The apparent meaning of the revelation indicates other than what the proponent of this view said. For Ibrahim's saying, peace be upon him, "And from my offspring," follows Allah's saying, mighty is His praise: "Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people." It is known that what Ibrahim asked for his descendants, if it were other than what his Lord informed him He had given him, would have been made clear. [His saying "it would have been made clear" means that what Ibrahim asked his Lord would have come explicitly in the verse.] But since the request was of what had already been mentioned, He sufficed with the mention that had already passed, by repeating and restating it, and so said: "And from my offspring," meaning: and from my offspring, make the like of what You made me, of imamate over the people.
* *
On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: "He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers (124)"
Abu Ja'far said: This is an announcement from Allah, mighty is His praise, that the wrongdoer cannot be an imam whom the people of goodness follow. It is from Allah, mighty is His praise, a reply to what might be supposed from Ibrahim's request that He make among his descendants imams like himself. So He informed that He would do that, except that whoever among them was of the wrongdoers, He would not make him so, nor place him in the station of His friends with Him, by honoring him with imamate. For imamate belongs only to His friends and the people of His obedience, not to His enemies and the disbelievers in Him. [In the printed edition: "lama tawahhama," which is an error; the correct is what I have established, in the passive voice.]
* *
The exegetes differed concerning the "covenant" which Allah, mighty is His praise, forbade the wrongdoers to attain.
Some of them said: That "covenant" is prophethood.
Those who said that:

1945- Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers," meaning: My covenant, my prophethood.
So the meaning of the one who holds this view regarding the verse is: prophethood does not reach the people of wrongdoing and polytheism.
* *
Others said: The meaning of "covenant" is the covenant of imamate.
So the interpretation of the verse according to their view is: I will not make any of your descendants who are wrongdoers an imam for My servants to be followed.
Those who said that:

1946- Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers," he said: a wrongdoer cannot be an imam.

1947- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: Allah said: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers," he said: a wrongdoer cannot be an imam.

1948- al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from 'Ikrima, with the like of this.

1949- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid concerning His saying: "He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers," he said: a wrongdoer cannot be an imam to be followed.

1950- Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, the like of this.

1951- Musharraf ibn Aban al-Hattab narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Khusayf, from Mujahid concerning His saying: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers," he said: I will not make a wrongdoer an imam to be followed. [Report 1951: Musharraf ibn Aban Abu Thabit al-Hattab, al-Tabari's shaykh: al-Khatib biographed him in Tarikh Baghdad 13:224, and mentioned that he narrated from Ibn 'Uyayna and others. He died in Baghdad in 243 AH. I found no other biography or mention of him beyond that. "Musharraf" is on the pattern of "Muhammad," as al-Dhahabi stated in al-Mushtabih p. 484, and Ibn Hajar's al-Tabsir (manuscript photocopy).
The printed edition has "Masruq," which is a clear error; it appeared earlier at 1383 as "Bishr ibn Aban al-Hattab," which is also an error. It will later come with the correct "Musharraf" at 2382.
As for "al-Hattab," this is how it stands here with the unpointed ha, while in Tarikh Baghdad it is "al-Khattab" with the dotted kha. I was unable to determine between them.]
1952- Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd al-Muharibi narrated to us, saying: Muslim ibn Khalid al-Zanji narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning His saying: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers," he said: I will not make a wrongdoer an imam to be followed.

1953- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers": he said: a wrongdoer cannot be an imam.
Ibn Jurayj said: As for 'Ata', he said: "Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people. He said: And from my offspring," so he refused to make a wrongdoer among his descendants an imam. I said to 'Ata': What is His covenant? He said: His command.
* *
Others said: The meaning of that is: there is no covenant for a wrongdoer that you should obey him in his wrongdoing.
Those who said that:

1954- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, his statement: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers," meaning: there is no covenant for a wrongdoer over you in his wrongdoing, that you obey him in it.

1955- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us, from Isra'il, from Muslim al-A'war, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas: "He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers," he said: The wrongdoers have no covenant, and if you make a covenant with him, break it.

1956- al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Sufyan, from Harun ibn 'Antara, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A wrongdoer has no covenant.
* *
Others said: The meaning of "covenant" in this place is: safety/security (aman).
So the sense of the statement according to their meaning is: Allah said: My covenants of security do not reach My enemies and the people of wrongdoing among My servants; that is, I will not grant them security from My punishment in the Hereafter.
Those who said that:

1957- Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada: "He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers," that is with Allah on the Day of Resurrection; the wrongdoers do not attain His covenant. As for in this world, they have attained the covenant of Allah, and they shared inheritance with the Muslims through it, fought alongside them, and married through it. [In the printed edition: "wa-'adawhum" (and they were enemies to them), but the correct reading from al-Durr al-Manthur 1:118 is "wa-ghazawhum," and his saying "ghazawhum" means they were with them in the raids and shared the spoils.] When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah restricts His covenant and honor to His friends.

1958- al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada concerning His saying: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers," he said: The wrongdoers do not attain the covenant of Allah in the Hereafter; but in this world the wrongdoer has attained it, and has eaten by it and lived.

1959- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Isra'il, from Mansur, from Ibrahim: "He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers," he said: The wrongdoers do not attain the covenant of Allah in the Hereafter. As for in this world, the wrongdoer has attained it, felt secure by it, eaten, seen, and lived.
* *
Others said: Rather, the "covenant" mentioned by Allah in this place is: the religion of Allah.
Those who said that:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 124 (part 3 of 3):

1960- Ammar narrated to me, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: God said to Ibrahim: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers." He said: "The covenant of God which He made with His servants is His religion. He means: His religion does not reach the wrongdoers. Do you not see that He said: ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And of their descendants are those who do good and those who clearly wrong themselves﴾ [Surah al-Saffat: 113]? He means: not all your descendants, O Ibrahim, are upon the truth."

1961- Yahya ibn Ja'far narrated to me, saying: Yazid informed us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak, regarding His words: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers." He said: "My covenant does not reach an enemy of Mine who disobeys Me, and I do not bestow it except upon a friend of Mine who obeys Me." [Note on the report: 1961 - Yahya ibn Ja'far is Yahya ibn Abi Talib; see report no. 284.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Although the apparent meaning of this statement is the apparent meaning of a report, it is [in fact] a notification that the covenant of God, which is prophethood and leadership for the people of goodness, in the sense of being emulated in this world, and the covenant by fulfilling which one is saved in the Hereafter, from one who fulfilled it to God in this world, will not be attained by whoever among his descendants is a wrongdoer, a transgressor, an oppressor who deviates intentionally from the path of truth. [Context of this parenthetical clause: "...the covenant of God does not reach from the descendants of Ibrahim... whoever among them is a wrongdoer..."; and the context of this clause which the long preceding clause interrupts: "Although its apparent meaning is the apparent meaning of a report... then it is an announcement from God..." – and this is the practice of Abu Ja'far, may God be pleased with him.] It is therefore an announcement from God, may His remembrance be exalted, to Ibrahim, that among his offspring will be those who associate partners with Him, who deviate intentionally from the right path, and who wrong themselves and His servants, as in the report:

1962- Ishaq ibn Ibrahim ibn Habib ibn al-Shahid narrated to me, saying: Attab ibn Bashir narrated to us, from Khusayf, from Mujahid regarding His words: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers," he said: "Indeed there will be wrongdoers among your descendants." [Note on the report: 1962 - In the printed edition it reads "Attab ibn Bashr," which is an error. He is Attab ibn Bashir al-Jazari, Abu al-Hasan, also called Abu Sahl al-Harrani (Tahdhib al-Tahdhib); and al-Tarikh al-Kabir of al-Bukhari 4/1/56.]

* *

As for the accusative case of "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers), it is because the covenant is what does not reach the wrongdoers.

It is mentioned that in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers" (al-zalimun), meaning: the wrongdoers are those who do not attain the covenant of God.

* *

The nominative and accusative cases are both permissible in "al-zalimin" and likewise in "al-'ahd" (the covenant), because whatever a person attains, the person has attained it, as one says: "The good of so-and-so reached me, and I attained its good," so the verb is directed once to the good and once to the self.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "al-zulm" (wrongdoing) earlier, so we dislike repeating it. [See what preceded: 1: 523-524.]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 125 (part 1 of 3):

The Explanation of His Words, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people﴾

Abu Ja'far said: As for His words, "And when We made the House a place of return," it is conjoined with "and when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words" by the particle "when" (idh). And His words, "and when Abraham was tried," are conjoined to His words, "O Children of Israel, remember My favour," so that "remember" governs "when Abraham was tried by his Lord" and "when We made the House a place of return."

* *

And "the House" which God made a place of return for the people is the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram).

* *

As for "mathabah" (place of return), the grammarians of Arabic differ regarding its meaning and the reason for which it takes the feminine form.

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: the "ha'" (ta' marbuta) was added to "mathabah" because many people return to it, just as it is said "sayyarah" (one who travels much) and "nassabah" (one who genealogizes much).

And some of the grammarians of Kufa said: rather, "mathab" and "mathabah" have the same meaning, like "maqam" and "maqamah" [[In the printed edition: "nazirahu," and the more likely reading is what I have adopted.]]. "Maqam" is masculine in their view because it is intended as the place where one stands, and "maqamah" is feminine because it is intended as the spot. These [Kufans] denied that "mathabah" is like "sayyarah" and "nassabah," and said: the "ha'" was only added to "sayyarah" and "nassabah" by analogy with "da'iyah."

* *

"Mathabah" is a "mafʿalah" form from "thaba al-qawm ila al-mawdi'," meaning when people returned to it; so they return to it, mathaban, mathabah and thawaban. [[These sources are not mentioned in the lexicographical works. The masdars "mathab" and "mathabah" are regular mimi masdars, so their omission from the lexicons is not strange. As for his words "wa-thawaban," if this is correctly attributed to al-Tabari, it is also permissible in Arabic; but the lexicographers stated that the verbal noun of "thaba" is "thawaban, thawban, thu'udan," so I fear it may be a corruption of one of these. As for "al-thawab" in the known Arabic books, it is the noun from "athabahu yuthibuhu ithabatan, wa-huwa al-thawab," meaning recompense for a deed.]]

So the meaning of His words, "And when We made the House a place of return for the people," is: and when We made the House a place of return and refuge for the people, who come to it every year and return to it, and they are never satiated with it. And from "mathab" is the saying of Waraqah ibn Nawfal describing the Sanctuary:

A place of return for the scattered tribes, all of them... the swift she-camels come to it at a trot, lean and worn. [[From long verses by Waraqah ibn Nawfal in al-Bidayah wa'l-Nihayah of Ibn Kathir 2: 297; the verse is in Tafsir Abi Hayyan 1: 380 in this transmission, and before the verse in mention of our father Abraham, peace be upon him: "So he followed the religion of the one who founded the foundations, and he had a preponderant favour upon the people. And he founded a firm structure in Mecca, shining in it are lamps against the darkness. A place of return for the scattered tribes..." with "mathaban" in the accusative; however al-Shafi'i narrated this verse in al-Umm 2: 120 attributed to Waraqah ibn Nawfal, and its second half: "The swift she-camels come to it at a trot, the swift ones (dhawamil)..." Likewise it appears in al-Qurtubi 2: 100; Abu Hayyan counted it a variant in the verse, and with this transmission the author of Lisan al-Arab mentioned it in (thawb) attributed to Abu Talib, and in (dhamal) unattributed. It is apparent that al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, erred in narrating the verse. And the author of Lisan erred in its attribution; it was confused for him with the poetry of Abu Talib in his famous ode.
"Afna' al-qaba'il": their mixed and scattered groups from here and there. "Khabbat al-dabbah yakhubbu khababan": a swift kind of running. "Al-ya'malat" is the plural of "ya'malah," the she-camel that is swift and made for travel, her name derived from "'amal," and "'amal" means hastening and haste. "Al-tala'i'" is the plural of "tali'." "Naqah tali' asfar": one whose journey has exhausted her and whose leanness has worn her down, so she is lean and emaciated. It means the camels whose owners wore them out in their haste to the pilgrimage to the House. As for "al-dhawamil" in the other transmission, it is the plural of "dhaміlah." "Naqah dhumul and dhamilah": one that walks a gentle, swift pace.]]

And from it is said: "thaba ilayhi 'aqluh" (his reason returned to him), when it came back to him after being absent from him.

* *

And the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said this:

1963. Muhammad ibn 'Amr told me, saying: Abu 'Asim told us [and] 'Isa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding God's words, "And when We made the House a place of return for the people," he said: they never become satiated with it.

1964. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

1965. Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah told us, saying: Shibl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And when We made the House a place of return for the people," he said: they return to it, never becoming satiated with it.

1966. Musa told me, saying: 'Amr told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "And when We made the House a place of return for the people," he said: As for "mathabah," it is that to which they return every year; a person who has come to it once does not leave it from returning to it.

1967. Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, saying: my father told me, saying: my paternal uncle told me, saying: my father told me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas his words: "And when We made the House a place of return for the people," he said: they never become satiated with it; they come to it, then return to their families, then come back to it.

1968. 'Abd al-Karim ibn Abi 'Umayr told me, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim told me, saying: Abu 'Amr said: 'Abdah ibn Abi Lubabah told me regarding His words: "And when We made the House a place of return for the people," he said: no one who departs from it departs thinking he has become satiated with it.

1969. Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim told me, saying: Hushaym told us, saying: 'Abd al-Malik informed us, from 'Ata' regarding His words: "And when We made the House a place of return for the people," he said: they return to it from every place, and are never satiated with it.

1970. Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Jarir told us, from 'Abd al-Malik, from 'Ata', the like of it.

1971. Muhammad ibn 'Umarah al-Asadi told me, saying: Sahl ibn 'Amir told us, saying: Malik ibn Mighwal told us, from 'Atiyyah regarding His words: "And when We made the House a place of return for the people," he said: they are never satiated with it. [[The report: 1971. Al-Tabari's teacher "Muhammad ibn 'Umarah al-Asadi," as passed in 645, 1511, and as we mentioned, he is often narrated from in the History. In the printed edition: "Muhammad ibn 'Ammar."
Sahl ibn 'Amir: he is al-Bajali, and he is very weak. Al-Bukhari included him in al-Saghir, p. 234, and said: "munkar al-hadith, his hadith is not written." Ibn Abi Hatim included him 2/1/202 and narrated from his father, who said: "He is weak in hadith; he narrated falsehoods! I met him in Kufa, and he used to fabricate hadith." He is also in Lisan al-Mizan 3: 119-120. The name of his father in al-Tarikh al-Saghir is "'Ammar," which is a scribal or printing error.]]

1972. Muhammad ibn Bashshar told us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman told us, saying: Sufyan told us, from Abu al-Hudhayl who said: I heard Sa'id ibn Jubayr say: "And when We made the House a place of return for the people," he said: they make pilgrimage and return.

1973. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from Abu al-Hudhayl, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His words: "a place of return for the people," he said: they make pilgrimage, then make pilgrimage again, and are never satiated with it. [[The two reports 1972-1973: Abu al-Hudhayl is Ghalib ibn al-Hudhayl al-Awdi, who narrates from Anas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others; he is trustworthy, and Ibn Ma'in deemed him trustworthy. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir of al-Bukhari 4/1/99, and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/47. He will be named by his name in the report after these two.]]

1974. Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ibn Bukayr told us, saying: Mis'ar told us, from Ghalib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "a place of return for the people," he said: they return to it. [[The report: 1974. Ghalib is Abu al-Hudhayl in the two reports before it. Mis'ar, with a kasra on the mim, sukun on the sin and fatha on the 'ayn: he is Ibn Kidam (kasra on the kaf, lightened dal), and he is one of the great authorities, the trustworthy.]]

1975. Bishr ibn Mu'adh told us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatadah regarding His words: "And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary," he said: a gathering place.

1976. Al-Muthanna told me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih told me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas: "a place of return for the people," he said: they return to it.

1977. It was related to me from 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "a place of return for the people," he said: they return to it.

1978. Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "And when We made the House a place of return for the people," he said: they return to it from all lands and come to it.

* *

The Explanation of His Words: ﴿and a sanctuary﴾

Abu Ja'far said: "al-Amn" (security) is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: "amina yamanu amnan."

* *

God only named it "amnan" (a sanctuary of security) because in the pre-Islamic period it was a refuge for whoever sought refuge in it, and a man among them who met the killer of his father or his brother would not harm him or confront him until he left it. It was as God, may His praise be majestic, said: ﴿Have they not seen that We have made a sacred sanctuary secure, while people are snatched away from around them?﴾ [Surah al-'Ankabut: 67]

1979. Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "and a sanctuary," he said: whoever enters it is secure; a man would meet the killer of his father or his brother and would not confront him.

1980. Musa told me, saying: 'Amr told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: As for "amnan," whoever enters it is secure.

1981. Muhammad ibn 'Amr told me, saying: Abu 'Asim told us, saying: 'Isa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding God's words: "and a sanctuary," he said: its sanctity; no one who enters it is to fear.

1982. It was related to me from 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His words: "and a sanctuary," meaning: a security from the enemy, that weapons may not be carried in it; and in the pre-Islamic period people were snatched from around it while they themselves were secure and not taken captive.

1983. It was related to me from al-Minjab, saying: Bishr informed us, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "and a sanctuary," he said: a sanctuary for the people.

1984. Al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid regarding His words: "and a sanctuary," he said: its sanctity; no one who enters it is to fear.

* *

The Explanation of His Words: ﴿And take, from the standing-place of Abraham, a place of prayer﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The readers differed regarding the recitation of this:

Some of them recited: "wa-attakhidhu min maqami Ibrahima musalla" with a kasra on the "kha'," in the form of a command to take it as a place of prayer. This is the reading of the majority of the two garrison cities of Kufa and Basra, and the reading of the majority of the readers of Mecca and some readers of Medina. [[In the printed edition: "qura'" in these places; I have returned it to what al-Tabari followed in the earlier parts.]] Those who recited it thus adopted the report which:

1985. Abu Kurayb and Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim told us, both saying: Hushaym told us, saying: Humayd informed us, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: I said: O Messenger of God, if only you would take the standing-place as a place of prayer! So God revealed: "And take, from the standing-place of Abraham, a place of prayer."

1986. Muhammad ibn Bashshar told us, saying: Ibn Abi 'Adi told us -and Ya'qub told me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah told us- both from Humayd, from Anas, from 'Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, the like of it.

1987. 'Amr ibn 'Ali told us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' told us, saying: Humayd told us, from Anas who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: I said: O Messenger of God, and he mentioned the like of it. [[The reports 1985-1987 are one report with four sound chains. It is an abridgement of a longer report narrated by Ahmad in the Musnad: 157, 160, 250, from Hushaym, from Ibn Abi 'Adi, and from Yahya — all three from Humayd, from Anas. Al-Bukhari also narrated it from Musaddad, from Yahya. Ibn Kathir mentioned it 1: 309-310 from the narrations of al-Bukhari and Ahmad, then mentioned that al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah also narrated it, and al-Tirmidhi said: "hasan sahih."]]

* *

They said: God, may His remembrance be exalted, only revealed this verse as a command from Him to His Prophet ﷺ to take the standing-place of Abraham as a place of prayer. It is not permissible to recite it, being a command, in the form of a statement.

* *

Some grammarians of Basra have claimed that His words, "and take, from the standing-place of Abraham, a place of prayer," are conjoined to His words, "O Children of Israel, remember My favour" and "and take, from the standing-place of Abraham, a place of prayer." So the command of this verse, and the taking of the place of prayer from the standing-place of Abraham, according to this speaker, was for the Jews of the Children of Israel who were in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, ..... as related to us [from] al-Rabi' ibn Anas [[In the printed edition: "as al-Rabi' ibn Anas related to us," which is an error, so I added "from" in parentheses, for a long time lies between Abu Ja'far al-Tabari and al-Rabi' ibn Anas. See the following note.]] with what:

1988. It was related to me from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, who said: Among the words with which Abraham was tried is His saying: "and take, from the standing-place of Abraham, a place of prayer." He commanded them to take the standing-place of Abraham as a place of prayer, so they pray behind the standing-place. [[The report: 1988 is part of the earlier report no. 1922, which is "from Ibn Abi Ja'far, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas," and I added what is between the parentheses so the speech is coherent. It will also come later as no. 2001, but I placed these dots at the earlier place because I fear there is a lacuna in the text. For he began by saying: the command of this verse, according to this Basran's opinion, was for the Jews of the Children of Israel in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Then he followed it by saying: "so he commanded them to take the standing-place of Abraham as a place of prayer, so they pray behind the standing-place." I do not know that the Jews who were in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ used to pray in the Sacred House behind the standing-place, so I placed these dots, as I judge that something has dropped from al-Tabari's words at this point which would make this speech coherent. I have not found in the books that transmit from the tafsir of al-Tabari anything that guides to the correct wording here.
What I surmise is that a passage has dropped out here: that the address of this verse was directed to Abraham and his descendants from the line of Ishmael, so the pronoun in his words "he commanded them to take the standing-place of Abraham as a place of prayer, so they pray behind the standing-place" refers to the descendants of Abraham from the line of Ishmael, namely the Arabs of the followers of the religion of Ishmael, and their remnants from the people of the pre-Islamic period, whom the Messenger of God ﷺ came to establish upon the hanifiyyah, the religion of Abraham, which is Islam.]]

* *

So the interpretation of the speaker of this view: "And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them, He said: I am making you an imam for the people," and He said: "take, from the standing-place of Abraham, a place of prayer."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The report we mentioned earlier from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, indicates the opposite of what these said, and that it is a command from God, may His remembrance be exalted, to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and to the believers in him, and to all mukallaf creation.

* *

Some readers of Medina and Syria recited: ﴿wa-ittakhadhu﴾ with a fatha on the "kha'," in the form of a statement.

* *

Then they differed concerning what it is conjoined to with His words "wa-ittakhadhu," since it is recited thus as a statement,

Some grammarians of Basra said: its interpretation, if it is recited thus: "And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary, [and when] they took, from the standing-place of Abraham, a place of prayer." [[The addition between the parentheses is necessary, otherwise there would be no difference between this view and the one that follows. The Basran in this interpretation means that the conjunction is to the sentence "when We made," so that "when" is implied in His words "and they took."]]

And some grammarians of Kufa said: rather, it is conjoined to His word "We made," so the meaning of the speech is: "And when We made the House a place of return for the people, and they took it as a place of prayer." [[See the Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 77, which is his interpretation.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct statement and reading regarding this, in our view, is "wa-ittakhadhu" with a kasra on the "kha'," as the interpretation of the command to take the standing-place of Abraham as a place of prayer, on account of the established report from the Messenger of God ﷺ that we mentioned just before, and that:

1989. 'Amr ibn 'Ali told us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id told us, saying: Ja'far ibn Muhammad told us, saying: my father told me, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that the Messenger of God ﷺ recited: "wa-ittakhadhu min maqami Ibrahima musalla." [[The report: 1989. 'Amr ibn 'Ali is al-Fallas, one of the great trustworthy memorizers, from whom the authors of the six books and others narrated. His teacher Yahya ibn Sa'id is al-Qattan the Imam.
The report is part of the long report of Jabir concerning the Hajj, as we will mention in 2003, God willing.]]

* *

Then the people of interpretation differed regarding the explanation of His words, "and take, from the standing-place of Abraham, a place of prayer," and regarding "the standing-place of Abraham." Some of them said: "the standing-place of Abraham" is the whole of the Hajj.

Those who said this:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 125 (part 2 of 3):

1990 – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn Jurayj informed us, from ʿAta', from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: "the station of Ibrahim," he said: "All of the Hajj is the station of Ibrahim."

1991 – Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ishaq told us, saying: Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding: "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer," he said: "All of the Hajj."

1992 – Abu Kurayb told us, saying: Waki' told us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAta', who said: "All of the Hajj is 'the station of Ibrahim'."

* *

Others said: "The station of Ibrahim" refers to ʿArafah, al-Muzdalifah and the jamarat (the pillars stoned during Hajj).

Mention of those who said this:

1993 – Muhammad ibn ʿAmr told me, saying: Abu ʿAsim told us, saying: ʿIsa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah: regarding "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer," he said: "Because I have made him an imam, so his station is ʿArafah, al-Muzdalifah and the jamarat."

1994 – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His words: "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer," he said: "Its station is Jam' (Muzdalifah), ʿArafah and Mina – I do not know it except that he mentioned Makkah."

1995 – ʿAmr ibn ʿAli told us, saying: Abu ʿAsim told us, saying: ʿIsa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from ʿAta', from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His words: "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer," he said: "Its station is ʿArafah."

1996 – ʿAmr ibn ʿAli told us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ told us, saying: Dawud told us, from al-Sha'bi, who said: "The verse was revealed to him while he was standing at ʿArafah, [regarding] the station of Ibrahim: 'Today I have perfected for you your religion' [Surah al-Ma'idah: 3], the verse."

1997 – ʿAmr told us, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal told us, saying: Dawud told us, from al-Sha'bi, the like of it.

* *

Others said: "The station of Ibrahim" is the Haram.

Mention of those who said this:

1998 – It was narrated to me from Hammad ibn Zayd, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His words: "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer," he said: "The entire Haram is 'the station of Ibrahim'."

* *

Others said: "The station of Ibrahim" is the stone on which Ibrahim stood when his building rose high and he became too weak to lift the stones.

Mention of those who said this:

1999 – Sinan al-Qazzaz told us, saying: ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Majid al-Hanafi told us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Nafi' told us, saying: I heard Kathir ibn Kathir narrate, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Ibrahim began building it, and Isma'il would hand him the stones, and they were both saying: 'Our Lord, accept from us; indeed You are the Hearing, the Knowing.' When the building rose high and the old man became weak at lifting the stones, he stood upon a stone, and it is the 'station of Ibrahim'." [[The hadith 1999 is a part of the hadith that follows at 2056, which we will takhrij there, God willing. The teacher of al-Tabari here, "Ibn Sinan al-Qazzaz," is "Muhammad ibn Sinan," whose biography passed at 157. In the printed edition it is "Sinan" without "ibn," which is an error.]]

* *

Others said: Rather, "the station of Ibrahim" is his station which is in the Masjid al-Haram.

Mention of those who said this:

2000 – Bishr ibn Muʿadh told us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ told us, saying: Saʿid told us, from Qatadah: "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer." They were only commanded to pray beside it, and they were not commanded to wipe it. This nation has gone to lengths that the nations before it did not go to. And some of those who saw its trace were told about its footprint and fingers, and these nations kept wiping it until it wore away and was effaced. [[In the printed edition: "mimma takallafathu" – the correct reading is from Tafsir Ibn Kathir 1:311. In the printed edition: "asabiʿahu fiha" – the correct reading is from Ibn Kathir. Khalaqa, akhlaqa and ikhlawlaqa mean: to wear out.]]

2001 – It was narrated to me from ʿAmmar, saying: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar told us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer," they pray behind the station. [[The report 2001 is the earlier report 1988; see the commentary on it.]]

2002 – Musa told me [[In the printed edition it was "Yunus told me," which is a plain error; rather it is his chain which recurs in the tafsir – to al-Suddi, and the nearest of it is number 1980.]], saying: ʿAmr told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer," meaning the prayer beside his station during Hajj.

The "maqam" is the stone which the wife of Isma'il placed under the foot of Ibrahim when she washed his head. Ibrahim placed his foot on it while riding; she washed one side, then lifted it from beneath him, and his foot had sunk into the stone. She placed it under the other side and washed it, and his foot sank into it too. So God made it one of His signs, and He said: "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer."

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The most correct of these sayings in our view is what those said who held that "the station of Ibrahim" is the well-known station bearing this name, which is in the Masjid al-Haram, due to what we narrated just before from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab [[See what preceded, numbers 1985–1987]], and due to what:

2003 – Yusuf ibn Sulayman told us, saying: Hatim ibn Isma'il told us, saying: Ja'far ibn Muhammad told us, from his father, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) touched the corner, ran (ramal) three times, and walked four times, then advanced to the station of Ibrahim and recited: "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer." He placed the station between himself and the House, and prayed two rak'ahs. [[Hadith 2003: Yusuf ibn Sulayman, teacher of al-Tabari, is Abu ʿUmar al-Bahili al-Basri, trustworthy, biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/223–224. In the printed edition "Sulayman" is written instead of "Sulayman"; this is an error.
Hatim ibn Isma'il al-Madani: trustworthy, reliable, narrates much; the group (al-jama'ah) narrated from him. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir of al-Bukhari 2/1/72, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/258–259, and Ibn Sa'd 5:314.
Ja'far ibn Muhammad: this is Ja'far al-Sadiq, son of Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn al-Husayn ibn ʿAli ibn Abi Talib. He is trustworthy, truthful, reliable, one of the leaders of the People of the House in jurisprudence, knowledge and virtue. Only the Rafidi Shia lie about him. As for the narrations of the trustworthy from him, they are sound.
This hadith is a part of the long hadith of Jabir concerning the description of the Farewell Pilgrimage. A part of it has passed at 1989, through the narration of Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan from Ja'far al-Sadiq.
A part of it will come with this chain at 2365.
The full hadith was narrated by Imam Ahmad in al-Musnad, 14492 (vol. 3, pp. 320–321, Halabi edition), from Yahya al-Qattan, from Ja'far.
Muslim also narrated it in his Sahih 1:346–347, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh – both from Hatim ibn Isma'il, from Ja'far al-Sadiq, with it.]]

* *

These two reports indicate that God, mentioned be He, by "the station of Ibrahim" which He commanded us to take as a place of prayer meant that which we have described.

Even if there were no report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) confirming the correctness of what we have chosen in interpreting this, the obligation regarding it would still be what we have said. That is because speech is to be understood according to its apparent, well-known meaning, not its hidden, unknown inner meaning [[See the explanation of "the apparent and the hidden" in what passed, 2:15, and seek it in the indexes]], until something comes that indicates otherwise, which must be accepted. There is no doubt that what is known among people as "the station of Ibrahim" is the prayer place which God, mentioned be He, spoke of: "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer."

* *

[Abu Jaʿfar said: As for His words, "place of prayer" (muṣallā)] – the people of interpretation differ on its meaning. [[The addition between brackets is necessary.]] Some of them said: it is "the place of supplication (mudda')."

Mention of those who said this:

2004 – Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ishaq told us, saying: Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And take the station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer," he said: "The place of prayer of Ibrahim is a place of supplication (mudda')."

* *

Others said: The meaning is: take a place of prayer where you pray.

Mention of those who said this:

2005 – Bishr ibn Muʿadh told me, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ told us, saying: Saʿid told us, from Qatadah, who said: They were commanded to pray beside it.

2006 – Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi, who said: It is the prayer beside it.

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: It seems that those who said the interpretation of "al-muṣallā" here is "al-mudda'" took "al-muṣallā" to be a "mufaʿʿal" form derived from the saying of one who says "ṣallaytu" in the sense of "I supplicated (da'awtu)." [[See what preceded, 1:242–243.]]

The ones who held this view are those who said: the station of Ibrahim is the entire Hajj.

* *

So its meaning in the interpretation of this verse is: take ʿArafah, al-Muzdalifah, al-Mash'ar and the jamarat, and all the places of Hajj where Ibrahim stood, as places of supplication, calling upon Me there, and following Ibrahim, My intimate friend, peace be upon him, in them; for I have made him, for those after him – from among My friends and the people of My obedience – an imam whom they follow along with his traces, so follow him.

* *

As for the interpretation of those who held the other view, it is: O people, take from the station of Ibrahim a place of prayer where you pray, as an act of worship from you and as an honouring from Me of Ibrahim.

* *

This view is the more correct, due to the report we mentioned from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

* *

On the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He: "And We charged Ibrahim and Isma'il, [saying]: Purify My House"

Abu Jaʿfar said: By His words, "And We charged," He, mentioned be He, means: "and We commanded," as:

2007 – Al-Qasim told us, saying: Al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I asked ʿAta': "What is His 'ahd (charge)?" He said: "His command."

2008 – Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed me, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "And We charged Ibrahim," he said: "We commanded him."

* *

So the meaning of the verse is: "And We commanded Ibrahim and Isma'il to purify My House for those who circumambulate." The "purification" which God commanded them regarding the House is its purification from idols, from the worship of idols in it, and from shirk with God.

* *

If someone says: What is the meaning of His words, "And We charged Ibrahim and Isma'il that they purify My House for those who circumambulate"? And was there, in Ibrahim's time – before his building the House – a house in the Haram which would be purified from shirk and the worship of idols, such that they could be commanded to purify it?

It is said: There are two interpretations for this, and a group of the people of interpretation held each of the two views.
