The teacher of al-Tabari in the first chain, "Hannad," is Ibn al-Sari ibn Mus'ab al-Darimi al-Tamimi, and he is reliable. One of the teachers of al-Bukhari and Muslim and others. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/248, al-Saghir p. 245, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/119-120.
In the printed edition it reads "'Abbad," which is a distortion; its correction comes from al-Tabari's Tarikh 1:128-129, where he narrated this report with this first chain, "Hannad ibn al-Sari narrated to us." Ibn Kathir also quoted it at 1:224 from al-Tabari.

2059- Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Simak, who said: I heard Khalid ibn 'Ar'arah narrating from 'Ali, with something similar.

2060- Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Dawud narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah, Hammad ibn Salamah, and Abu al-Ahwas all narrated to us, from Simak, from Khalid ibn 'Ar'arah, from 'Ali, with something similar.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for the one who says, "Ibrahim and Isma'il raised the foundations," or who says, "Ibrahim raised them while Isma'il was handing him the stones," then the correct view in his statement is that the implied speaker of the words is Ibrahim and Isma'il. The sentence then becomes: "And when Ibrahim and Isma'il were raising the foundations of the House, they were saying, 'Our Lord, accept from us.'" It was possible, on this interpretation, that the implied speaker of the words be Isma'il alone, without Ibrahim, or Ibrahim alone, without Isma'il, were it not for what the majority of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) hold, namely that the implied speaker of the words is Ibrahim and Isma'il together.
As for the interpretation transmitted from Ali, that Ibrahim alone raised the foundations without Isma'il, then the implied speaker of the words can only be Isma'il alone.
* *
The correct view in our opinion on this matter is that the implied speaker of the words is Ibrahim and Isma'il, and that Ibrahim and Isma'il together raised the foundations of the House. This is because, if Ibrahim and Isma'il themselves built it and raised it, then it is as we have said. And if Ibrahim alone undertook its building while Isma'il was handing him (the stones), then both of them still raised it, since its raising was by both of them: from one of them the building, and from the other the carrying of the stones to it and the assistance in placing the stones in their places. The Arabs do not refrain from attributing the building to the one by whose cause and assistance the building took place.
We have said what we have said on this matter because all the people of interpretation agree that Isma'il is meant by the report that God related about him and his father, that they were saying it: "Our Lord, accept from us, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing." It is known that Isma'il would not have said this unless he was either a mature man or a youth who understood the distinction between harm and benefit, and to whom God's obligations and rulings applied. Since, during his father's building, he was what God commanded him to build and raise the foundations of the House of God, so it is known that he did not abstain from helping his father, either in the building or in the carrying of the stones. Whichever of these he did, he entered into the meaning of one who raised the foundations of the House, and it is established that the implied speech is a report about him and his father Ibrahim, peace be upon them both.
* *
So the meaning of the statement: "And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House, and Isma'il (with him), they were saying: Our Lord, accept from us our deed, our obedience to You, and our worship of You, in our compliance with Your command which You have commanded us, in the building of Your House which You have commanded us to build. Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."
* *
In God's report, exalted is His remembrance, that they raised the foundations of the House while saying, "Our Lord, accept from us; indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," is clear evidence that their building was not a dwelling in which they would live, nor a residence in which they would stay. Rather, it is evidence that they built it and raised its foundations for everyone who wished to worship God, seeking nearness to God through that. For this reason they said, "Our Lord, accept from us." Had they built it as a dwelling for themselves, there would be no understandable sense in their saying, "Accept from us," for in that case they would have been asking that there be accepted from them what contains no nearness to Him. And their station is not one in which they ask God to accept what contains no nearness to Him. [[He means: they hold a rank and station in knowledge and prophethood, so they do not ask God to accept a deed that is not one of the acts of nearness to God.]]
* *
On the interpretation of His statement: ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing (127)﴾
Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation of His statement, "Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," means: Indeed You are the All-Hearing of our supplication and our request to You to accept what we ask You to accept from us, of obedience to You in the building of Your House which You have commanded us to build, the All-Knowing of what is in the inner depths of our souls of submission to You in obedience, and of turning toward what brings You good pleasure and love, and of what we reveal and conceal of our deeds. [[His statement "and what we reveal..." is conjoined to his statement "the All-Knowing of what is in the inner depths of our souls."]] As related:

2061 - Al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Abu Kathir informed me, saying: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated to us, from Ibn Abbas: "Accept from us, indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," he said: Accept from us, indeed You are the All-Hearing of the supplication.
* *
On the interpretation of God's statement, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, and make us submissive to You, and from our descendants a Muslim nation submissive to You﴾
Abu Ja'far said: This too is a report from God, exalted is His remembrance, about Ibrahim and Isma'il: that they were raising the foundations of the House while saying, "Our Lord, and make us submitting (muslimayn) to You," meaning by that: make us surrendered to Your command, humbled to Your obedience, not associating with You in obedience anyone other than You, nor in worship anyone besides You.
* *
We have already shown earlier that the meaning of "Islam" (al-Islam) is submission to God through obedience. [[See what has passed: 2:510, 511.]]
* *
As for His statement, "and from our descendants a Muslim nation submissive to You," they singled out some of their descendants with this, because God, exalted is His remembrance, had already informed Ibrahim, His friend (khalil), peace be upon him, before this request of his, that among his descendants there would be those whose covenant would not be attained because of their wrongdoing and immorality. So they singled out some of their descendants for the supplication.
* *
It has been said that they meant by this the Arabs.
Mention of who said that:
2062 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "and from our descendants a Muslim nation submissive to You," meaning the Arabs.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: This is a view whose apparent meaning of the Book contradicts. For its apparent meaning indicates that they asked God to make from their descendants people of His obedience and guardianship, and those who respond to His command. Among the sons of Ibrahim there were Arabs and non-Arabs, and those who respond to God's command and submit to Him in obedience were from both groups. So there is no basis for the view of one who says that Ibrahim, by this supplication, meant a particular group of his descendants specifically, to the exclusion of others, except for an arbitrary judgment that no one is unable to make.
* *
As for "the nation" (al-umma) in this place, by it is meant a community of people, [[See what has passed: 1:221, line 14.]] from the words of God: ﴿And among the people of Musa is a nation who guide by the truth and by it act justly﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 159]. [[Ibn Kathir's commentary 1:332 contains the following text:
Ibn Jarir said: The correct view is that it encompasses the Arabs and others, because among the descendants of Ibrahim are the Children of Israel, and God, exalted is He, has said: "And among the people of Musa is a nation who guide by the truth and by it act justly."
As you see, this is not in the original text of al-Tabari. I do not know whether it is an paraphrase by Ibn Kathir, or whether there is a lacuna in the manuscripts of al-Tabari at this place; both are possible, and I do not assert anything with certainty.
Furthermore, Ibn Kathir intended to refute what al-Tabari held, claiming that al-Suddi's specification that they are the Arabs does not exclude others. He then said: "The context is only about the Arabs, and for this reason He said after it: 'Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who recites to them Your verses and teaches them the Book and wisdom and purifies them' (the verse), and the intended meaning of that is Muhammad ﷺ, who was sent among them."
This objection of Ibn Kathir does not stand, and his argument from context here does not hold. The supplication is the supplication of Ibrahim and Isma'il together, and each of them has descendants whom the supplication includes. And the context here is the context of consecutive verses, not of a single verse. In the verses that follow this verse there is mention of the creed of Ibrahim and its explanation: "When his Lord said to him, 'Submit,' he said, 'I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds.' And Ibrahim enjoined it upon his sons, and Ya'qub (did likewise): 'O my sons, indeed God has chosen for you the religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims. Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub, when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we are Muslims."'"
These are consecutive verses, so specification in them is not permissible, together with the clarity of the indication that the descendants of Ibrahim other than Isma'il, namely the descendants of Ishaq, were upon the creed of Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq, and were Muslims to Him. This is also evidence for what I held in the introduction to the first part, that al-Tabari abridged his commentary here, for had he wished he would have elaborated and argued with what you argued with. It is also evidence that reading al-Tabari requires following verse after verse, and that reading him in fragments leads to error in understanding his intent and argument. And it is evidence that al-Tabari was very attentive to the context and connection of verses, though he may have omitted to mention this connection in detail with his argument, because he had already exhausted that in earlier places, so he abridged the other places, trusting his reader to follow what he intended. Another evidence that this commentary is still of unrecognized standing, despite its high station among our predecessors, may God forgive us and them.]]

**Commentary on the Words of God Most High: ﴿And show us our rites﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: The reciters differed over the reading of this. [[In the printed edition: "al-qurra'" and "qurra'", and I have restored them to the form Tabari uses in his wording. Al-qara'a is the plural of qari' (reciter), like hafiz and huffaz, as has been noted many times before.]] Some read *"wa-arina manasikana"* in the sense of seeing with the eye, that is, make them manifest to our eyes so that we see them. This is the reading of the common people of the Hijaz and Kufa.

Some of those who interpret it in this sense would vowel the *ra'* of *"arina"* with a sukun, except that they would give it a faint kasra sound.

* *

Those who held this view and read it this way differed over the meaning of *"manasikana"*.

Some said: they are the rites of the Hajj and its landmarks.

Those who said this include:

2063. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿And show us our rites﴾: God showed them their rites: the circumambulation of the House, the running between al-Safa and al-Marwa, the departure from Arafat, the departure from Jam', and the stoning of the pillars, until God completed the religion, or His religion.

2064. al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿And show us our rites﴾. He said: Show us our rites and our pilgrimage.

2065. Musa narrated to us, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: When Ibrahim and Isma'il finished building the House, God commanded him to proclaim, so He said: ﴿And proclaim to the people the pilgrimage﴾ [Surah al-Hajj 22:27]. So he proclaimed between the two mountains of Makkah [[The two mountains of Makkah are the two mountains surrounding it: Abu Qubais and al-Ahmar, which overlooks Qu'aiqi'an. Al-akhshab is any rough, coarse mountain. In a hadith: "Makkah will not cease to exist until its two akhshab cease to exist."]]: "O people! God commands you to make pilgrimage to His House." He said: It sank into the heart of every believer, and everyone who heard him, whether mountain, tree, or animal, answered: "Here I am, here I am." And they answered him with the talbiyah: "Here I am, O God, here I am," and whoever came to him came. Then God commanded him to go out to Arafat and described it to him [[The addition in parentheses, I think, is more correct.]]. So he went out. When he reached the tree near the 'Aqaba, Satan confronted him, and he pelted him with seven pebbles, glorifying God with each pebble, and Satan flew and landed at the second pillar, and he pelted him and glorified God. Then Satan flew and landed at the third pillar, and he pelted him and glorified God. When Satan saw that he could not withstand him, and Ibrahim did not know where to go, he set off until he came to Dhu al-Majaz. When Satan looked at him and did not recognize him, he passed by, and for this reason it was named Dhu al-Majaz. Then he set off until he arrived at Arafat, and when he looked at it he recognized the description. He said: "I have recognized it!" So it was named 'Arafat. Ibrahim stood at Arafat until evening, and then he drew near to Jam' [[Izdalafa ila al-shay' means to come close to it and approach it. Jam' (with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the mim) is Muzdalifah.]], and it was named al-Muzdalifah, and he stood at Jam'. Then he came back until he reached Satan at the place where he had first met him, and he pelted him with seven pebbles, seven times. Then he remained at Mina until he finished the Hajj and its rites. This is His words: ﴿And show us our rites﴾. [[Part of this report will come later under number 3792 in this volume.]]

* *

Others said, among those who read it this way: *"al-manasik"* means the sacrificial slaughterings. So the meaning of this verse, according to those who say this, is: "Show us how to sacrifice our offerings to You, O our Lord, so that we may slaughter them for You." [[Nasaka yansuku nusukan (with a damma on the sin) means to slaughter. An-nasika is the sacrificial animal.]]

Those who said this include:

2066. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata': ﴿And show us our rites﴾. He said: our slaughterings.

2067. al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata', who said: our places of slaughter.

2067 (repeated). Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

2067 (repeated). al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

2067 (repeated). al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: 'Ata' said: I heard 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr say: ﴿And show us our rites﴾, he said: show us our places of slaughter.

* *

Others said: ﴿And show us our rites﴾ is read with a sukun on the *ra'*. [[In the printed edition: "Others said", and from the context I deduced that it should be "others read", so I have written what I deduced. He will say later: "This is a reading that was transmitted..."]] They claimed that the meaning of this is: "Teach us and guide us to them", not that it means "show them to us with our eyes." They claimed that this is like the verse of Hutaith ibn Ya'fur, brother of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur: [[They are two brothers from Banu Nahshal ibn Darim, both of the pre-Islamic period. Their mother was Rahm bint al-'Abbab.]]

*Ruini jawadan mata hazlan la'allani ... ara ma tarin aw bakhilan mukhalladan*

[[The poem appears in al-Shi'r wa-al-shu'ara' (pp. 201–202, 211), which contains research on an ancient dispute about its attribution; in Majaz al-Qur'an (p. 55); and in al-Khizana (1:195–196), which both cite many sources. The line is attributed to Hatim al-Ta'i and to Ma'n ibn Aws. In Lisan al-'Arab (under *anna* and *'alal*) it is cited from Ibn Barri, who said: "Hutaith ibn Ya'fur, and it is said to be by Durayd." It will come in Tabari's Tafsir attributed to Durayd ibn al-Simma (7:213, Bulaq edition), with a difference in the first half: *Dharini atuffu fi al-bilad la'annani*.

I have not found this version in the books available to me, and I fear that Tabari, or the one who recited the line to him, has erred. The words of Hutaith before or after it are: *Dharini akun lil-mal ribban, wa la yakun / li al-mal ribban, tahmadi ghibbahu ghadan*; *Dharini fa-la a'ya bima halla sahati / aswadu fa-akfi, aw uti'u al-musawwadan*. He addresses his mother Rahm bint al-'Abbab in these verses, for she used to blame him for his generosity and squandering of wealth. *Al-hazl* (with fatha and sukun) and *al-hazl* (with damma and sukun) and *al-hizal* mean the opposite of fatness, together with weakness and slackness. His words "la'anni" with a fatha on the hamza mean "la'alli" [perhaps]. It comes from their saying "an" in the sense of "'al" and "la'an" in the sense of "la'al". I believe the hamza is altered from the 'ayn and the nun is altered from the lam. Both are dialects of the Arabs, and they combined in this word.]]

By his words "*arini*" he means: guide me to it and make its place known to me, not seeing with the eye.

This is a reading that was transmitted from some of the early authorities. [[It would have been better for this sentence to come after his words: "Others read: 'wa-arna manasikana' with a sukun on the ra'." But this is how it appears in the manuscripts.]]

Those who said this include:

2068. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: 'Ata' said: *"Arina manasikana"*: bring them out for us, teach them to us.

2069. al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn Jurayj informed us, who said: Ibn al-Musayyib said: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: When Ibrahim finished building the House, he said: "I have done it, O Lord, so show us our rites" — make them manifest to us, teach them to us — so God sent Gabriel, and he performed the Hajj with him.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning is one, for whoever vowels the *ra'* makes the sign of the jussive the dropping of the *ya'* in the phrase of the speaker: *"yurinihi"* → *"arnhu"* [[Thus it appears in the printed edition as "urinhu", but I think the correct form of this word is "yurinihi", the imperfect in the nominative, so that it agrees with his words: "and I keep the ra' with a kasra as it was before the jussive."]], and he keeps the *ra'* with a kasra as it was before the jussive. Whoever gives the *ra'* of *"arna"* a sukun imagines that the inflection of the word falls on the *ra'*, so he gives it a sukun in the jussive, as they did in *"lam yakun"* and *"lam yak"*. [[The apparent sense of Tabari's words here indicates that his words "lam yak" have a sukun on the kaf, on the assumption that the inflection of this word falls on the kaf, so he gave it a sukun when the jussive particle entered. I have not found this view in any book available to me, and I fear that there is a lacuna in Tabari's text at this point that I have not identified.]]

Whether it is seeing with the eye or seeing with the heart, it makes no difference. There is no sense in the distinction made by those who distinguish between seeing with the eye and seeing with the heart in this matter.

* *

As for *"al-manasik"*, it is the plural of *"mansak"*, which is the place where one worships God and draws near to Him by what pleases Him of righteous deeds: either by slaughtering an animal for Him, or by prayer, circumambulation, running, or other righteous deeds. For this reason the sites of the Hajj are called "its rites," because they are signs and landmarks that people habitually frequent and return to.

* *

The original meaning of *"al-mansak"* in the speech of the Arabs is the familiar place that a man frequents and is accustomed to. One says: "For so-and-so there is a *mansak*," when he has a place that he frequents for good or evil. For this reason the rites were called *"manasik"*, because they are frequented, and people return to them for the Hajj and the 'Umra and the deeds by which one draws near to God.

* *

It has been said that the meaning of *"al-nusk"* is the worship of God, and that *"al-nasik"* is so named only because of his worship of his Lord.

So those who hold this view interpret His words: ﴿And show us our rites﴾ as: "Teach us Your worship: how should we worship You, and where should we worship You, and what pleases You of us so that we may do it?"

Although this view is a possible meaning the speech can bear, the dominant sense of *"al-manasik"* is what we have described before, namely that they are "the rites of the Hajj," whose meaning we have explained.

* *

This speech proceeded from Ibrahim and Isma'il as a request they made to their Lord on their own behalf. In fact it was a request they made to their Lord on behalf of themselves and their Muslim descendants. When they joined their Muslim descendants to themselves, they became like those who speak on their own behalf in this matter. We say that this is so because of the supplication they made earlier on behalf of their Muslim descendants at the beginning of the verse, and its continuation later in another verse. As for what is at the beginning of the verse, it is their words: ﴿Our Lord, and make us submissive to You, and from our descendants a Muslim nation submissive to You﴾. Then they included themselves and the Muslim nation from their descendants in their request to their Lord that He show them their rites, saying: ﴿And show us our rites﴾. As for what comes in the verse that follows: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from among them﴾, they made the request specifically for their descendants.

It has been mentioned that in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: *"wa-arhum manasikahum"* [and show them their rites], meaning: "Show our Muslim descendants their rites."

* *

**On the Words of God Most High: ﴿And accept our repentance; indeed You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ (2:128)**

Abu Ja'far said: As for *"al-tawba"* (repentance), its root is returning from what is disliked to what is loved. So the repentance of the servant to his Lord is his returning from what God dislikes in him, by regret for it, abandonment of it, and resolve not to return to it. The repentance of the Lord toward His servant is His returning to him by pardoning his sin, forgiving his offense, and granting him forgiveness and grace from Himself. [[See the meaning of "al-tawba" above in 1:547 and 2:72–73.]]

* *

If someone asks us: Did they have sins that required them to ask their Lord for repentance?

It is said: No one among God's creatures is free of deeds, between himself and his Lord, from which he must turn back in repentance. It is possible that what they asked was for what had occurred before them, and they singled out for it the situation they were in: the raising of the foundations of the House. For that was the most fitting place in which God would answer their supplication, and so that they might make what they did there a sunna to be followed after them, and so that people might take that place after them as a site for seeking exoneration from sins before God. It is also possible that by their words: "and accept our repentance" they meant: "accept the repentance of the wrongdoers among our children and descendants, whose affairs You have made known to us, from their wrongdoing and their association [of others with You], until they turn back in obedience to You." Then the apparent sense of the speech would be a supplication on their own behalf while the one meant would be their descendants, just as one says: "So-and-so honoured me through my son and my family, and so-and-so was kind to me," when he is kind to his son.

* *

As for His words: ﴿Indeed You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾, He means: You are the One who returns to Your servants with bounty, and who grants them pardon and forgiveness out of grace; the Merciful toward them, who rescues by Your mercy whom You will from their destruction, and delivers by Your compassion from Your wrath whom You wish to save among them.

The exegesis of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses﴾

Abu Ja'far said: This is the supplication of Ibrahim and Isma'il for our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) specifically, and it is the supplication to which our Prophet (ﷺ) referred when he said: "I am the answer to the supplication of my father Ibrahim, and the glad tidings of Isa":

2070 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Thawr ibn Yazid, from Khalid ibn Ma'dan al-Kala'i: that a group of the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O Messenger of God, tell us about yourself." He said: "Yes, I am the answer to the supplication of my father Ibrahim, and the glad tidings of Isa (ﷺ)."

[Editor's note: Thawr ibn Yazid al-Kala'i al-Himsi is a trustworthy narrator, among the most reliable transmitters. He is listed in al-Tahdhib, in al-Bukhari's al-Kabir 1/2/180-181, and in Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/468-469.

Khalid ibn Ma'dan al-Kala'i al-Himsi is a trustworthy, firm Successor (tabi'i), listed in al-Tahdhib, in al-Bukhari's al-Kabir 2/1/161-162, in Ibn Sa'd 7/2/162, and in Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/351.

This chain is mursal (broken), because Khalid ibn Ma'dan did not mention hearing from any of the Companions. It appears likewise in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham (p. 106-107, Europe edition; 1:175, Halabi edition), in a lengthy narrative. Al-Tabari also narrated it in his History 2:130 with this same chain, likewise lengthy and mursal.

However, it is established as connected (muwassal) through Ibn Ishaq as well: al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak 2:600, by way of Yunus ibn Bukayr, from Ibn Ishaq who said, "Thawr ibn Yazid narrated to me, from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that they said: 'O Messenger of God, tell us about yourself?'" He then mentioned the hadith in abridged form, similar to what is here. Al-Hakim then said: "Khalid ibn Ma'dan is among the best of the Successors; he accompanied Mu'adh ibn Jabal and those after him among the Companions. So whenever he narrates a hadith traced back to the Companions, its chain is sound, even if they did not record it." Al-Dhahabi agreed with his authentication.]

2071 - Imran ibn Bakkar al-Kala'i narrated to me, saying: Abu al-Yaman narrated to us, saying: Abu Kurayb narrated to us, from Abu Maryam, from Sa'id ibn Suwayd, from al-Irbad ibn Sariyah al-Sulami, who said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'Indeed I am, with God, in the Mother of the Book, the Seal of the Prophets, while Adam was still lying in his clay. I shall inform you of the interpretation of this: I am the answer to the supplication of my father Ibrahim, the glad tidings of Isa to his people, and the vision of my mother.'"

[Editor's note: Imran ibn Bakkar al-Kala'i is trustworthy, one of the teachers of al-Nasa'i, and he was declared trustworthy by him and others. He is listed in al-Tahdhib and in Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/294, which mentions that he heard from him. Al-Tabari's narration from him has already passed at 149, where we did not translate him. al-Tahdhib records that he died "in the year one hundred and seventy-one," which is an error of a copyist or printer, since it is inconceivable that al-Nasa'i and al-Tabari and this generation heard from him. The correct date is 271.

Abu al-Yaman is al-Hakam ibn Nafi' al-Himsi, a trustworthy teacher of Ahmad ibn Hanbal and al-Bukhari. He is listed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 1/2/342, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/129, which says: "He is noble, trustworthy, and truthful."

As for his saying "Abu Kurayb narrated to us" here, this is certainly an error by the copyists, for Abu Kurayb Muhammad ibn al-‘Ala' (whose biography has already passed, at 1291) died after Abu al-Yaman. This is one point. The other is that Abu al-Yaman narrated this hadith from Ibn Abi Maryam, as will come. Either it is a copyist's error, or the correct wording is "Abu Kurayb and he (Abu al-Yaman) both said: narrated to us," in which case Imran ibn Bakkar narrated it from two teachers.

Ibn Abi Maryam is "Abu Bakr ibn ‘Abd Allah ibn Abi Maryam al-Ghassani al-Shami," who is weak due to poor memory and confusion, as we explained in the commentary on the Musnad: 1464, 6165. Here in the printed edition it says "from Abu Maryam" without "ibn," which is a clear error. Moreover, the weakness of Ibn Abi Maryam due to his memory is compensated in this hadith, since others narrated it. But he erred in it by omitting the Successor from its chain.

Sa'id ibn Suwayd al-Kalbi al-Shami is a trustworthy Successor who heard from some Companions and met them. Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy (p. 475) among the followers of the Successors. Al-Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) included him in al-Ta'jil: 152, noting this hadith, and transmitted that al-Bukhari said: "His hadith is not authentic." I do not know where al-Bukhari said this, for he did not mention him in al-Saghir, nor in al-Du'afa'. He is listed in al-Kabir 2/1/436 without any criticism mentioned, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/29 likewise mentions no criticism. The two narrators differed concerning him in this chain and the two chains after it: was it "from al-Irbad," or is there another Successor between them? Ibn Abi Maryam erred in omitting the Successor between Sa'id and al-Irbad, as will come, God willing.]

2072 - Yunus ibn ‘Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah informed me; and ‘Ubayd ibn Adam ibn Abi Iyas al-Asqalani narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: al-Layth ibn Sa'd narrated to us, from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, both of them together, from Sa'id ibn Suwayd, from ‘Abd Allah ibn Hilal al-Sulami, from al-Irbad ibn Sariyah al-Sulami, from the Prophet (ﷺ), with something similar.

[Editor's note: This is another chain for the preceding hadith, indeed two chains: al-Tabari narrated it from Yunus ibn ‘Abd al-A'la, from Ibn Wahb, and then from ‘Ubayd ibn Adam al-Asqalani, from his father, from al-Layth ibn Sa'd, and Ibn Wahb and al-Layth both narrated it from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih.

The first is clear. ‘Ubayd ibn Adam ibn Abi Iyas al-Asqalani, in the second, is trustworthy; Abu Zur'ah, Abu Hatim, al-Nasa'i and others also narrated from him. He is listed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/402. His father Adam ibn Abi Iyas has had his biography pass at 187. Al-Layth ibn Sa'd and Mu'awiyah ibn Salih also passed at 187.]

2073 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Suwayd, from ‘Abd al-A'la ibn Hilal al-Sulami, from al-Irbad ibn Sariyah, that he said: "I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say," and he mentioned something similar.

[Editor's note: This is another chain for the preceding hadith. Abu Salih is ‘Abd Allah ibn Salih, the scribe of al-Layth ibn Sa'd; his biography has passed at 186. Regarding the name of ‘Abd al-A'la ibn Hilal al-Sulami: the name differed on Mu'awiyah ibn Salih in the preceding chain and this one: there "‘Abd Allah ibn Hilal," and here "‘Abd al-A'la ibn Hilal." I incline to "‘Abd al-A'la" for reasons that will come, God willing.

This Successor was not given a biography by al-Hafiz in al-Ta'jil under either of the two names, although he is among the narrators of Musnad Ahmad. His predecessor al-Hafiz al-Husayni did list him in al-Ikmal, p. 64, saying: "‘Abd Allah ibn Hilal al-Sulami, also called ‘Abd al-A'la, a Syrian. He narrated from al-Irbad ibn Sariyah and Abu Umamah al-Bahili. From him Suwayd ibn Sa'id al-Kalbi narrated. Unknown!" But the man was never unknown at all. He is listed in Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/25 under "‘Abd al-A'la," and Ibn Hibban also mentioned him among the trustworthy, p. 267, and mentioned this hadith from al-Irbad ibn Sariyah. Al-Bukhari also mentioned him in al-Kabir, in the biography of Sa'id ibn Suwayd, under the name "‘Abd al-A'la ibn Hilal," and Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Hibban did likewise.

Moreover, the narrators from al-Layth ibn Sa'd also differed on it. In the narrations of Ahmad and Ibn Sa'd, via al-Layth, it is "‘Abd al-A'la ibn Hilal," as we will mention.

Indeed, ‘Abd al-A'la has mention in another hadith in the Musnad (5:261, Halabi) in the Musnad of Abu Umamah al-Bahili, where Imam Ahmad narrated with his chain to Khalid ibn Ma'dan who said: "We attended a feast of ‘Abd al-A'la ibn Hilal, and when we finished the food, Abu Umamah stood up and said..." etc.

Whatever the case, these chains are sound, despite this difference. Such things are frequent and have no effect on the soundness of the hadith.

As for the hadith through Abu Bakr ibn Abi Maryam (2071): Ahmad also narrated it in the Musnad: 17230 (vol. 4 p. 127, Halabi), from Abu al-Yaman al-Hakam ibn Nafi', from Abu Bakr, from Sa'id ibn Suwayd, from al-Irbad, similarly. Its ending in his version is: "and the vision of my mother, in which she saw that a light came out of her that illuminated the palaces of Syria; and thus do the mothers of the prophets see, peace and blessings of God upon them."

Al-Hakim narrated something similar, with some abridgment, in al-Mustadrak 2:600, by way of Abu al-Yaman, from Ibn Abi Maryam, and he and al-Dhahabi authenticated it.

Ahmad also narrated it: 17217 (vol. 4 p. 127, Halabi), from ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi, from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, from Sa'id ibn Suwayd, from "‘Abd Allah ibn Hilal al-Sulami," from al-Irbad ibn Sariyah, similarly. So ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi named the Successor "‘Abd Allah," as Ibn Wahb and Adam ibn Abi Iyas did here in their narration from al-Layth.

Ahmad also narrated it: 17218, and Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat 1/1/95-96, both from Abu al-‘Ala' al-Hasan ibn Sawwar al-Khurasani, from al-Layth ibn Sa'd, from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, from Sa'id ibn Suwayd, from "‘Abd al-A'la ibn Hilal al-Sulami," from al-Irbad.

Al-Haythami mentioned this hadith in Majma' al-Zawa'id 8:223, with wordings from al-Irbad. Then he said: "Ahmad narrated it with several chains, and al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani with something similar... One of Ahmad's chains has narrators who are the narrators of the Sahih, other than Sa'id ibn Suwayd, and Ibn Hibban has declared him trustworthy."

It is also in al-Suyuti 1:139, who attributed it, besides what we have mentioned, to Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il.

Furthermore, the hadith has another witness suitable for citation, despite weakness in its chain: Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated in his Musnad: 1140, from al-Faraj ibn Fudalah, from Luqman ibn 'Amir, from Abu Umamah al-Bahili, from the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar to this hadith.

Likewise Imam Ahmad narrated it in the Musnad (5:262, Halabi), from Abu al-Nadr Hashim ibn al-Qasim, from al-Faraj ibn Fudalah, with this chain. Al-Faraj ibn Fudalah is weak, as we said at 1688.

Al-Suyuti mentioned it at 1:139, attributing it also to al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi.]

* *

Those who said this among the people of interpretation include a group.

Those who said so:

2074 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves," so God did that, and sent among them a messenger from themselves, whom they recognize by his face and lineage, who brings them out of darkness into light, and guides them to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy.

2075 - Musa narrated to us, saying: ‘Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves," it is Muhammad (ﷺ).

2076 - It was narrated to me from ‘Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves," it is Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said to him: "That has been answered, and he is at the end of time."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His remembrance be exalted, "who will recite to them Your verses," He means: who will read to them Your Book which You reveal to him.

* *

The exegesis of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and teach them the Book and the Wisdom﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By "the Book" He means the Qur'an.

I have already explained previously why the Qur'an is called "a Book," and what its interpretation is. This is the view of a group of the people of interpretation.

Those who said so:

2077 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "and teach them the Book," the Qur'an.

* *

Then the people of interpretation differed on the meaning of "the Wisdom" mentioned by God in this place.

Some of them said: it is the Sunnah.

Those who said so:

2078 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "and the Wisdom," that is, the Sunnah.

* *

Others said: "the Wisdom" is knowledge of the religion and understanding of it.

Those who said so:

2079 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: I said to Malik: "What is the Wisdom?" He said: knowledge of the religion, understanding of the religion, and following it.

2080 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words "and the Wisdom," he said: "the Wisdom" is the religion which they know only through him (ﷺ), who teaches them it. He said: "and the Wisdom" is intellect within the religion, and he recited: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 269], and He said to Isa: ﴿and He will teach him the Book and the Wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 48]. He said, and Ibn Zayd recited: ﴿And recite to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our verses, but he detached himself from them﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 175]. He said: he did not benefit from the verses, since wisdom was not with them. He said: "and the Wisdom" is something God places in the heart, by which it is illuminated.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view in our opinion regarding "the Wisdom" is that it is knowledge of God's rulings, which cannot be grasped except through the explanation of the Messenger (ﷺ), and knowledge of them, and what those rulings indicate of their counterparts. It is, in my view, derived from "al-hukm" meaning the distinction between truth and falsehood, like "al-jilsah" and "al-qi'dah" from "al-julus" and "al-qu'ud." It is said of it: "Indeed so-and-so is wise (hakim) to the utmost degree," meaning: he is most accurate in speech and action.

Since this is so, the interpretation of the verse is: Our Lord, send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses, and teach them Your Book which You send down to them, and the decisive judgment of Your rulings which You teach him.

* *

The exegesis of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and purify them﴾

Abu Ja'far said: We have already shown previously that the meaning of "tazkiyah" is purification, and that the meaning of "zakah" is growth and increase.

So the meaning of His words "and purify them" in this place: purify them from associating partners with God and worshipping idols, and cause them to grow and multiply through obedience to God, as:

2081 - al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: ‘Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from ‘Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn ‘Abbas: "who will recite to them Your verses and purify them," he said: by purification is meant obedience to God and sincerity.

2082 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj said regarding His words "and purify them": he said, He purifies them from polytheism and frees them from it.

* *

The exegesis of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed You, You are the Mighty, the Wise (129)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: Indeed You, O Lord, are "the Mighty," the Strong whom nothing He wills can overpower; so do for us and for our offspring what we have asked and requested of You. And "the Wise," whose planning admits no flaw or error; so give us what benefits us and benefits our offspring, and which will not diminish You or diminish Your treasuries.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 130:

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And who would turn away from the creed of Abraham﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His, the Exalted's, words "And who would turn away from the creed of Abraham," God, may His remembrance be exalted, means: and which of the people would renounce the creed of Abraham and abandon it, out of aversion to it, in favour of something else? [[The explanation of "millah" (creed, religious community) will come after several pages, p. 104.]]

* *

God, may His remembrance be exalted, meant by this the Jews and the Christians, because of their choosing what they chose of Judaism and Christianity over Islam. For "the creed of Abraham" is the upright monotheism (al-hanifiyyah) that submits to God, as He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was an upright man, a Muslim﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 67]. So He, may His remembrance be exalted, said to them: And who would turn away from the creed of Abraham, the upright submitting creed, except one who has foolishly wronged himself, as:

2083 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "And who would turn away from the creed of Abraham except one who has foolishly wronged himself": The Jews and the Christians turned away from his creed, and they adopted Judaism and Christianity as an innovation not from God, and they abandoned the creed of Abraham, meaning Islam, as upright monotheists. Likewise God sent His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) with the creed of Abraham.

2084 - I was told by Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His words: "And who would turn away from the creed of Abraham except one who has foolishly wronged himself," he said: The Jews and the Christians turned away from the creed of Abraham, and they invented Judaism and Christianity, which are not from God, and they abandoned the creed of Abraham: Islam.

* *

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿except one who has foolishly wronged himself﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His, the Exalted's, words "except one who has foolishly wronged himself," He means: except one whose self has been made foolish. We have already explained earlier that the meaning of "safah" (foolishness) is ignorance. [[See what has passed, 1: 293-295.]]

So the meaning of the statement is: None turns away from the upright creed of Abraham except a foolish ignorant person, unaware of the place of his own good in what benefits it and what harms it in its final return, as:

2085 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "except one who has foolishly wronged himself," he said: except one who has missed his share.

* *

The word "nafs" (self) has been put in the accusative to express the sense of a specifier (tamyiz). This is because "safah" originally belongs to the self; when it was transferred to "man," "nafs" was put in the accusative, in the sense of specification. [[Tafsir and mufassar: meaning tamyiz, which is also called "tabyin" (clarification).]] As one says: "He is the most spacious of you in home," so "home" enters the statement to indicate that the spaciousness is in it, not in the man. Likewise "nafs" is introduced because foolishness belongs to the self, not to "man." That is why it is not permitted to say: "Your brother has been foolish." It is permitted that it be specified by "nafs," though it is attached to a definite noun, because it is in the sense of an indefinite. [[See the explanation of this in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 79, and Lisan al-'Arab (safah).]]

* *

Some grammarians of Basra said: His statement "safah nafsahu" follows the pattern of "safiha" when the verb is intransitive; it has been made transitive to "nafsahu" and "ra'yahu" and similar things which in meaning resemble "safiha" when it is not transitive. As for "ghabina" and "khasira," they may be transitive to something else; one says: "He cheated fifty (people)" and "he lost fifty."

* *

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And We had certainly chosen him in this world﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His, the Exalted's, words "And We had certainly chosen him in this world," He means: We had certainly chosen Abraham. The "hu" (him) in His words "chosen him" refers to the mention of Abraham.

* *

"Al-istifa'" (choosing) is the "ifti'al" form from "safwah" (pure best), and likewise "istafayna" is "iftaʻalna" from it; its "ta'" has been changed to "ta'" (ṭā') because its point of articulation is close to that of the "sad."

By His words "We chose him" is meant: We selected him and elected him for friendship (al-khullah), [[Al-khullah (with a dammah and a shaddah): friendship and love. Al-khalil: the close, beloved friend. Here it is a station of the stations of God's love for some of His servants whom He has chosen and loved.]] and We made him in this world an imam for those after him.

* *

This is information from God, may His remembrance be exalted, that whoever opposes Abraham in what he established for those after him, opposes God; and it is a declaration by Him to His creation that whoever opposes what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought, opposes Abraham. For God, may His remembrance be exalted, informed that He chose him for friendship, made him an imam for the people, and informed that his religion was the upright submitting creed. In this is the clearest explanation from God, may His remembrance be exalted, that whoever opposes him is an enemy of God, because of his opposition to the imam whom God appointed for His servants.

* *

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And indeed he, in the Hereafter, is among the righteous (130)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His, the Exalted's, words "And indeed he, in the Hereafter, is among the righteous," He means: And indeed Abraham, in the abode of the Hereafter, is among the righteous.

* *

"Al-salih" (the righteous) among the children of Adam is the one who discharges the rights of God upon him.

Thus He, may His remembrance be exalted, informed about Abraham, His friend, that in this world he is chosen (safi), and in the Hereafter he is a close friend (wali), and that he arrives at the stations of His friends who fulfil His covenant.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ (2:131)

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, "When his Lord said to him, 'Submit,'" He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: when his Lord said to him, "Devote worship sincerely to Me, and humble yourself to Me in obedience." We have already explained the meaning of "islam" (submission) in the usage of the Arabs in earlier passages, so there is no need to repeat it. [[See what has preceded at 2:510-511, and this part at 3:74.]]

* *

As for the meaning of His words, "He said, 'I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds,'" He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: Abraham replied to his Lord, "I have humbled myself in obedience and devoted worship sincerely to the Master of all creatures and their Governor, to the exclusion of any other."

* *

If someone says: You know that "idh" (when) denotes a time, so what is the time it denotes, and what is it that it relates to (its complement)? [[In the printed edition: "wa-ma alladhi silatuhu" (and what is its complement). The correct reading is what has been established here.]]

It is said: It relates to His words, "And We certainly chose him in this world." The sense of the statement is: "And We certainly chose him in this world, when his Lord said to him, 'Submit.' He said, 'I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds.'" The meaning of the statement is: "And We certainly chose him in this world when We said to him, 'Submit.' He said, 'I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds.'" The name "Allah" appears in His words, "When his Lord said to him, 'Submit,'" in the manner of reporting about an absent party, although His mention had occurred earlier in the manner of speaking about Himself, as Khufaf ibn Nadbah said:

"I say to him, while the spear bends his side: 'Look at Khufaf, for indeed I am that one.'" [[The citation of this verse was given earlier at 1:227 and 2:304.]]

* *

If someone among us asks: Did God call Abraham to Islam?

It is said to him: Yes, He did call him to it.

If he says: At what time did He call him to it?

It is said: When he said, "O my people, I am free of what you associate. Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth, as a monotheist, and I am not of those who associate others with God" (Qur'an 6:78-79). That is the time when his Lord said to him, "Submit," after He had tested him with the stars, the moon, and the sun. [[He recited the verses of Surah al-An'am: 6:74-78.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 132:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and [so did] Jacob﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His, may He be exalted, words "and enjoined it," He means: enjoined this word. By "the word" He means His words "I have submitted myself to the Lord of the worlds" [[In the printed edition: "a'ni bil-kalima" ("I mean by the word"), which is a plain error.]], and it is "Islam" (submission), which he (ﷺ) was commanded to follow, namely sincerely devoting worship and monotheism to God, and the submission of the heart and limbs to Him. [[See the explanation of "Islam" above: 2:510, 511, and this part 3:74, 92.]]

* *

By His words "Abraham enjoined it upon his sons," He means: he charged them with it and commanded them to it.

* *

As for His words "and Jacob," the meaning is: Jacob also enjoined that upon his sons, as:

2086 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words "and Abraham enjoined it upon his sons, and [so did] Jacob," he says: Jacob enjoined it upon his sons after Abraham.

2087 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: "And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons," he charged them with Islam, and Jacob enjoined the like of that.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Some have said: His words "And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons" are a complete statement, and His words "and Jacob" begin a new clause. The meaning is: "And Abraham enjoined upon his sons" that they say: "We have submitted to the Lord of the worlds." "And Jacob enjoined upon his sons": "O my sons, indeed God has chosen for you the religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims."

But there is no sense in what this one says, because what Jacob enjoined upon his sons is similar to what Abraham enjoined upon his sons: urging obedience to God, submission to Him, and Islam.

* *

If someone says: If the matter is as you have described, that its meaning is: "Abraham enjoined it upon his sons and Jacob, [saying]: 'O my sons,'" then why is "that" (an) omitted from the speech?

It is said: Because enjoining is a kind of speech, so it is treated according to its meaning. For if it had come in the form of the verb "say," "an" would not have been appropriate with it; rather it would have been said: "And Abraham said to his sons and Jacob: 'O my sons.'" Since enjoining is speech, it was treated according to its meaning rather than its wording, [[In the printed edition: "ʿala maʿnāhā dūna qawlihā" ("according to its meaning rather than its saying"), which is an error; the correct reading is what is adopted here.]] so "an," which would suit it, was omitted, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿God enjoins you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females﴾ [Surah an-Nisa: 11], and as the poet said:

"Indeed I will reveal to you, of what I reveal, / I have two longings: one longing in Najd, / and another longing for me in the lands of Sind." [[Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:80, 180, and Lisan al-Arab (shajan). "Shajan" means the inclination and need of the soul; it is a metaphor from "shajan," which is grief and worry. They use it to refer to a beloved woman who occupies the heart with worry and sorrow, through separation, coquetry, or aloofness. Muslim ibn al-Walid al-Ansari says: "And a flock of sorrows, folded over the chest, / whoever meets it is stupefied."

He means women. He also said: "Has he prolonged my life, or extended my term, / or is there not among the departing ones one longing for me?"

That is, a woman I love, or a desire whose separation and absence grieve me.]]

So "an" was omitted, since the declaring by tongue is, in meaning, speech, so it was treated according to its meaning rather than its wording. [[See the detailed treatment of this in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:80-81.]]

* *

Some of the grammarians of Arabic said: "An" was omitted from His words "and Abraham enjoined it upon his sons and Jacob" due to sufficiency of the vocative, meaning the vocative formula "O my sons." He claimed that the reason for this is that it is the habit of the Arabs to dispense with "an" using interrogative particles, as in their saying: "I called out: 'Did you stand?' — I called out: 'Where is Zayd?'" He said: Sometimes they include it with the particles, so they say: "I called out: 'an, did you stand?'"

* *

Some of the readers recited: "wa-awṣā bihā Ibrāhīm" (with the alif, "and he enjoined"), meaning: he charged.

As for one who recited "wa-waṣṣā" with the doubled letter, he means by it that he charged them with a charge after a charge, and enjoined an injunction after an injunction.

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿O my sons, indeed God has chosen for you the religion﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His, may He be exalted, words "indeed God has chosen for you the religion," He means: God has chosen for you this religion, about which He charged you, and selected it for you. [[See the meaning of "ișṭifā'" (choosing) earlier: 91.]]

* *

The definite article "al-" was attached to "religion" because those addressed, their descendants and sons, had come to know it through their fathers' enjoining it upon them and their charge concerning it. Then they said to them, after having made them aware of it: "Indeed God has chosen for you this religion about which He has charged you, so fear God lest you die except while you are upon it."

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: Is death and life in the hands of the children of Adam, so that one of them is forbidden to die except in one state rather than another?

It is said to him: The meaning of that is other than the way you supposed. Rather, the meaning of "so do not die except while you are Muslims" is: do not depart from this religion, which is Islam, during your lifetimes. This is because no one knows when his death will come upon him, so they said to them: "So do not die except while you are Muslims," because you do not know when your deaths will come upon you, by night or by day. So do not depart from Islam, lest your deaths come upon you while you are on other than the religion your Lord has chosen for you, and you die while your Lord is angry with you, and you perish.

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His remembrance be exalted, "Or were you witnesses," He means: were you? But He used the interrogative "am" (or) because it introduces a new question following a preceding speech, as in His words: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, from the Lord of the worlds. Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [Surah as-Sajda: 1-3]. The Arabs do the same with every question that they begin after a preceding speech, asking with "am." [[Al-Tabari treated the topic of "am" earlier, at 2: 492-494. See also Majaz al-Qur'an by Abu 'Ubayda: 56.]]

* *

"Ash-shuhada'" is the plural of "shahid" (witness), as "ash-shurakaa'" is the plural of "shareek" (partner) and "al-khusama'" is the plural of "khasim" (adversary). [[The interpretation of "ash-shuhada'" was discussed earlier, at 1: 376-378.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of the speech is: Were you, O company of Jews and Christians, who deny Muhammad ﷺ and reject his prophethood, present at the time of Ya'qub's (Jacob's) presence and witnessing, when death approached him? That is, you were not present for that. So do not fabricate falsehoods about My prophets and messengers, and do not attribute to them Judaism and Christianity. I sent My intimate friend Ibrahim (Abraham), and his son Ishaq (Isaac) and Isma'il (Ishmael) and their descendants, with the pure monotheistic faith (al-hanifiyya al-muslima), and with it they enjoined their sons, and with it they bequeathed to their descendants after them. So if you had been present with them and had heard from them, you would have known that they were upon other than the religions and creeds that you attribute to them after them. [[In the printed edition: "ʿalā ghayr mā tanḥalūhum," and the correct reading is what is established here.]]

* *

These verses were revealed as a refutation from God, exalted is He, of the Jews and Christians in their claim regarding Ibrahim and his son Ya'qub, that they were upon their religion. So He said to them in this verse: "Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?" so that you would know what he said to his sons and what his sons said to him. Then He informed them of what he said to them and what they said to him. The people of ta'wil (interpretation of meaning) have said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said so:

2088- Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His words: "Or were you witnesses," meaning the People of the Book.

* *

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿When he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God; and to Him we are submitting."﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His remembrance be exalted, "When he said to his sons," He means: when Ya'qub said to his sons.

* *

This "idh" (when) is repeated as an apposition (badal) of the first "idh," meaning: Were you witnesses of Ya'qub when Ya'qub said to his sons at the time of his approaching death?

* *

By His words, "What will you worship after me?" he means: what thing will you worship after me? That is, after my death? They said: "We will worship your God." They meant: Your sons said to him: We will worship the object of worship that you worship, and the object of worship of your fathers, Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq, "one God," that is: we will purify worship for Him and declare His lordship alone, so we will not associate anything with Him, and we will not take a lord besides Him.

* *

By His words, "and to Him we are submitting," he means: and to Him we are humbly submissive in servitude and obedience.

His words, "and to Him we are submitting," may be understood as a circumstantial clause (haal), as if they said: We worship your God, submitting to Him by our obedience and our worship of Him. It may also be an independent new statement, meaning: we will worship your God after you, and to Him we are submitting now and in every state.

* *

The better of these two possibilities in its interpretation is that it be a circumstantial clause, and that it mean: We worship your God and the God of your fathers Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq, submitting to His worship.

* *

It is said that the mention of Isma'il was placed before Ishaq because Isma'il was older than Ishaq.

Those who said so:

2089- Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq," he said: It is said that he began with Isma'il because he was the eldest.

* *

Some of the earlier readers recited "wa-ilaha abika Ibrahima" (the God of your father Ibrahim), thinking that Isma'il, since he was the paternal uncle of Ya'qub, could not be included among those named by way of substitution for the fathers and counted among them. This reading by its reciter reflects little knowledge on his part of the courses of Arabic speech. The Arabs do not refuse to make paternal uncles equivalent to fathers, and maternal uncles equivalent to mothers. [[See Majaz al-Qur'an by Abu 'Ubayda: 57, where he says: "The Arabs treat the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle as a father."]] Therefore Isma'il entered among those named by way of substitution for the fathers. "Ibrahim," "Isma'il" and "Ishaq" are a substitution (tarjama, i.e., badal, apposition) for "the fathers" in the genitive position, but they are put in the accusative because they are not declined (they are diptotes). [[Tarjama (substitution) and what derives from it means "badal" (apposition), as was said earlier at 2: 340, 420, and in this volume at 3: 52. His words "but they are put in the accusative because they are not declined" mean that these are proper names that are not inflected, as is clear; but this is an elegant expression.]]

* *

The correct reading in our view is "wa-ilaha abaika" (the God of your fathers), because the readers agree on approving it, and the readings of those who differed from it are irregular.

* *

The accusative of His words, "ilahan" (one God), is a circumstantial accusative (haal) referring to "ilahaka" (your God).

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 134:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿That was a community that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn. And you will not be questioned about what they used to do.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, means by His words "That was a community that has passed away": Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and their offspring.

He says to the Jews and the Christians: O assembly of Jews and Christians, leave off claiming Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the Muslims among their descendants for what they were not, and do not attribute to them the disbelief of Judaism and Christianity, so that you attach it to them. For they are a community (by "community" in this place is meant the group and the generation of people) [see what has preceded regarding the meaning of "ummah" (community) 1:221, and this part 3:74] that has passed away: it has gone its way.

* *

The saying "it has passed away" (qad khalat) is said of one who has died and departed, because he has become empty of (takhallī) the world and alone, free of the companionship he had with his people and associates in his life in this world. [In the printed edition: "bima kana min al-uns" (with what had been of intimacy), and the correct reading is what is established here: i.e., his being emptied of what had been of intimacy with his people.]

Its origin is from the expression "the man has become empty (khalā al-rajul)," when he is in a place where he has no companion, and is alone away from people. So this was used for one who dies, in that sense.

* *

Then He, may His remembrance be exalted, said to the Jews and Christians: indeed, for those whom you have attributed to yourselves, your error and your disbelief in which you are [in the printed edition: "bi-dalālikum wa-kufrikum" with an added bā', while the context of al-Tabari requires dropping this bā'] — from among My prophets and My messengers — is what they earned [in the printed edition: "kasabat", which is an error; the correct reading is what is established here].

The "hā'" and "alif" in His words "lahā" refer, if you wish, to "tilka" (that), and if you wish, to "al-ummah" (the community).

* *

By His words "lahā mā kasabat," He means: what it did of good. And for you, O assembly of Jews and Christians, is the like of that which you did. You will not be held to account, you who claim as yours the creeds you have attributed to them, for what Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and their offspring used to do, so that you would be asked about it, for they earned good and evil, because for every soul is what it earned and against it is what it has acquired. So abandon your claiming them and claiming their creeds, for mere claims will not avail you with God; what will avail you with Him is only the righteous deeds you previously did, if you did them and sent them forward.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 2, verse 135**

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they say: "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided."﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, "And they say: 'Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided,'" exalted is His remembrance, the Jews said to Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions among the believers: "Be Jews and you will be guided." And the Christians said to them: "Be Christians and you will be guided."

* *

By their words "you will be guided" they mean: you will reach the path of truth. [[See the meanings of "guidance" (al-huda) above, 1:166-170, 230, 249, 549-551; 2:393.]] As related:

2090. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, and Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Ishaq, who said: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, the client of Zayd ibn Thabit, told me, saying: Sa'id ibn Jubayr, or Ikrimah, told me, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Suriya al-A'war said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "There is no guidance except what we are upon! Follow us, O Muhammad, and you will be guided!" And the Christians said the same. So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning them: ﴿And they say: "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided." Say: "Rather, the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the polytheists."﴾ [[The report: 2090. Sirat Ibn Hisham 2:198.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Allah argued on behalf of His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with the most eloquent, concise and complete argument, and taught it to Muhammad His Prophet ﷺ, so He said: "O Muhammad, say, to those among the Jews and Christians who speak to you and to your Companions: '"Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided"': Rather, let us follow the religion of Abraham, upon whose testimony to its being the religion of Allah, which He approved and chose and commanded, all of us agree, for his religion was the upright Islamic monotheism (al-ḥanīfiyyah al-muslimah), and let us leave the other creeds about which we differ, some of us denying them and some of us affirming them. For that, in its disagreement, gives us no way to unite upon it, whereas we do have a way to unite upon the religion of Abraham."

* *

Concerning the grammatical parsing of His words "Rather, the religion of Abraham," there are three possibilities. The first: that the meaning of His words "And they say: 'Be Jews or Christians'" be taken to mean: "And they say: Follow Judaism and Christianity." For when they said "Be Jews or Christians," they were calling them to Judaism and Christianity; then this meaning is followed by a conjunction with "religion." So the meaning of the speech becomes: "Say, O Muhammad, we will not follow Judaism and Christianity, nor take them as a creed; rather, we will follow the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf." Then the second "follow" is omitted, and "religion" is conjoined in the case of "Judaism" and "Christianity."

The second: that it be governed by a hidden verb with the sense of "follow."

The third: that what is intended is: "Rather, let us be the companions of the religion of Abraham, or the people of the religion of Abraham." Then "the people" and "the companions" are omitted, and "religion" is put in their place, since it conveys the meaning of the speech. [[See Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:82. In this last view he means that the accusative is governed by "let us be," which is from the sense of His words "Be Jews...," and then "let us be" was omitted.]] As the poet said: [[He is Dhu al-Kharq al-Tuhawi. On the dispute about his name, and who else bore it, see al-Mu'talif wa al-Mukhtalif: 119, and al-Khizanah 1:20-21.]]

*"I thought the bleating of my she-camel was a she-goat!*
*And it was not, woe to you, a she-goat."*

Meaning: the voice of a she-goat. In this case, "the religion" is in the accusative by conjunction in grammatical case with "the Jews and the Christians."

* *

It is also permissible that it be in the accusative by way of exhortation (al-ighra'), meaning: follow the religion of Abraham. [[See Majaz al-Qur'an by Abu 'Ubaydah: 57, where he says: "Upon you is the religion of Abraham."]]

Some reciters read it in the nominative. Its interpretation according to the reading of one who reads it in the nominative is: "Rather, guidance is the religion of Abraham."

* *

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Rather, the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf, and he was not of the polytheists."﴾ (135)**

Abu Ja'far said: "Religion" (al-millah) means the creed (al-din).

* *

As for "ḥanīf," it means upright in every matter. It has been said that the man whose one foot turns toward the other is called "aḥnaf" because of his looking toward soundness, just as the desert waste is called "mafāzah" in the sense of success in escaping it and safety, and as the snake-bitten one is called "salīm" (the safe one), optimistically hoping for his safety from destruction, and similar things.

* *

The meaning of the speech, then, is: "Say, O Muhammad: Rather, we follow the religion of Abraham, upright."

In this case "ḥanīf" is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "Abraham."

* *

As for the people of interpretation, they differed about its interpretation. Some of them said: "The ḥanīf is the pilgrim (al-ḥājj)." It has also been said: the religion of Abraham was named the ḥanīfiyyah because he was the first leader whom the servants of his time, and those who came after him until the Day of Resurrection, were bound to follow in the rites of the Hajj and to take as their model in it. They said: So whoever performs the Hajj to the House and performs the rites of Abraham according to his creed is a ḥanīf, a Muslim upon the religion of Abraham.

Mention of those who said this:

2091. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from Kathir Abu Sahl, who said: I asked al-Hasan about "ḥanīfiyyah," and he said: "The Hajj to the House."

2092. Muhammad ibn 'Ubadah al-Asadi told me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Fudayl informed us, from 'Ata'ah, concerning His words "ḥanīfan," who said: "The ḥanīf is the pilgrim." [[The report: Muhammad ibn 'Ubadah al-Asadi, the teacher of al-Tabari: this shaykh has appeared several times in the printed edition in various forms. Among them: 645 and 1511, under the name "Muhammad ibn 'Umarah al-Asadi," and we noted in the second of these that we found no biography or mention of him except in al-Tabari's narrations from him repeatedly in the History. We did not find him in the indexes of the History except so. Among them: 1971, under the name "Muhammad ibn 'Ammar," and we corrected it there according to what we had seen before, "Muhammad ibn 'Umarah." But here, as you see, he comes as "Muhammad ibn 'Ubadah." My current preference is that this is the correct form. If so, the copies of al-Tabari in the Tafsir and the History are distorted in every place he is mentioned in another way.

This shaykh is "Muhammad ibn 'Ubadah ibn al-Bakhtari al-Asadi al-Wasiti": a trustworthy, truthful thinker, who was a specialist in grammar and literature. He is among the teachers of al-Bukhari, Abu Hatim, Abu Dawud and others. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib and in Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/17. al-Bukhari narrated two hadiths from him in the Sahih (8:26 and 9:93 of the Sultaniyyah edition; 10:429 and 13:214 of al-Fath; 9:53 and 10:246 of al-Qastallani, the first Bulaq edition). The margin of the Sultaniyyah edition states that "'Ubadah" in both places is with a fatha on the 'ayn. The two commentators also vocalized it so. al-Hafiz (13:214) said: "With a fatha on the unpointed letter and a light ba', and the name of his grandfather is al-Bakhtari, with a ba' vowelled, sukun on the dotted letter, and a fatha on the taa' from above; a trustworthy Wasiti, kunyah Abu Ja'far. He has nothing in al-Bukhari except this hadith and another that preceded in the Book of Manners," meaning the one that passed in al-Fath (8:26).

Similarly, the vocalization of his father's name is given in al-Dhahabi's al-Mushtabih: 333, and by al-Hafiz in Tahrir al-Mushtabih (manuscript).

I preferred here that he is "Muhammad ibn 'Ubadah" because "Muhammad ibn 'Umarah al-Asadi" is missing from the books of biographies and transmission, as far as my knowledge reaches, and because many of his narrations in the History and the Tafsir are from "'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa," as in the Tafsir: 1511, and the History 1:57, 2:266, 3:76, 78. Indeed, it is possible that there is another teacher, whose knowledge has not reached us, named "Muhammad ibn 'Umarah," who agrees with this one in his teachers and in those who narrate from him. But I consider what I have mentioned to be the more probable.

"'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa" is al-'Absi, the memorizer (al-hafiz), trustworthy. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib and in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/334-335, and in Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 1:322-323. His name occurs in the printed edition here as "'Abd Allah," which is an evident distortion.

Fudayl is Ibn Marzuq al-Raqashi, and he is trustworthy. We preferred his authentication in Sharh al-Musnad: 1251, because whoever spoke against him spoke because of hadiths he narrates from 'Ata'ah al-'Awfi, who is narrated from here, and 'Ata'ah is weak, as has passed in 305.]]

2093. al-Husayn ibn 'Ali al-Sada'i told me, saying: My father narrated to us, from Fudayl, from 'Ata'ah, the like of it. [[The report: al-Husayn ibn 'Ali al-Sada'i, with the sad vowelled and the dal lightened, the Akfani: trustworthy, upright, among the righteous; al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others narrated from him. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/56, and Tarikh Baghdad 8:67-68.

His father, "'Ali ibn Yazid ibn Sulaym al-Sada'i," is also trustworthy, though some spoke against him. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/209.]]

2094. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam ibn Salm narrated to us, [[In the printed edition it is "Hakkam ibn Salim," which is an error. It has passed many times in the chain of al-Tabari.]] from 'Anbasah, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Mujahid, who said: "The ḥanīf is the pilgrim."

2095. al-Hasan ibn Yahya told me, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn al-Taymi informed us, from Kathir ibn Ziyad, who said: I asked al-Hasan about "ḥanīfiyyah," and he said: "It is the Hajj to this House."

Ibn al-Taymi said: Juwaybir informed me, from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, the like of it. [[The report: Ibn al-Taymi: I have not found a text that identifies who he is. The attribution "al-Taymi" is broad. I am inclined to think it is Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman ibn Tarkhan al-Taymi, for he belongs to this generation and 'Abd al-Razzaq narrates from him. Perhaps 'Abd al-Razzaq mentioned him with this attribution so that he would not be confused with Ma'mar, who is Ibn Rashid, since 'Abd al-Razzaq narrates much from Ma'mar. He feared a transcriptional confusion if he said "Mu'tamir" here, so he went out of it by saying "Ibn al-Taymi."]]

2096. Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-Suddi, from Mujahid: "ḥunafā'" (ḥanīfs), he said: "pilgrims." [[See what will come in report 2098, for this is from the explanation of the verse of Surah al-Hajj mentioned there.]]

2097. al-Muthanna told me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih told me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words "ḥanīfan," he said: "Pilgrim."

2098. It was narrated to me from Waki', from Fudayl ibn Ghazwan, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Qasim, who said: The people of Mudar used to make the Hajj to the House in the pre-Islamic period, and were called "ḥunafā'." So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿Ḥunafā' for Allah, not associating anything with Him.﴾ [Surah al-Hajj: 31]

* *

Others said: "The ḥanīf" is the follower, as we described before, from the words of those who said that its meaning is uprightness.

Mention of those who said this:

2099. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "ḥunafā'," he said: "Followers."

* *

Others said: The religion of Abraham was named the ḥanīfiyyah because he was the first to establish circumcision for the servants, and those after him followed him in it. They said: So whoever is circumcised in the manner of Abraham's circumcision is upon what Abraham was upon of Islam, and he is a ḥanīf upon the religion of Abraham. [[See Majaz al-Qur'an by Abu 'Ubaydah: 58.]]
