Others said: "Rather, the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf": rather, the religion of Abraham, sincere. So "the ḥanīf," in their view, is one who makes his religion sincerely for Allah alone.

Mention of those who said this:

2100. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And follow the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf," he says: "sincere."

* *

Others said: Rather, "ḥanīfiyyah" is Islam. Whoever takes Abraham as his model in his creed and stays upright upon it, is a "ḥanīf."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: "Ḥanf," in my view, is uprightness upon the religion of Abraham, and following him in his creed. [[In the printed edition: "The ḥanīf in my view is uprightness," which is an inconsistent statement; its correct form is what I have established.]] This is because if ḥanīfiyyah were the Hajj to the House, it would necessarily follow that those who made the Hajj to it in the pre-Islamic period, who were polytheists, were ḥanīfs. But Allah has denied that this was genuine ḥanīfism by His words: ﴿But he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ [Surah Ali 'Imran: 67]

The same applies to circumcision. For if ḥanīfiyyah were circumcision, the Jews would necessarily be ḥanīfs. But Allah excluded them from that by His words: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim.﴾ [Surah Ali 'Imran: 67]

It is therefore established that ḥanīfiyyah is not circumcision alone, nor the Hajj to the House alone, but is what we described: uprightness upon the religion of Abraham, following him in it, and taking him as a model in it.

* *

If someone says: Were not those who came before Abraham, from the prophets and their followers, upright in what they were commanded of obedience to Allah, with the uprightness of Abraham and his followers?

It is said: Yes.

If he says: Then how is ḥanīfiyyah attributed to Abraham and his followers upon his creed specifically, to the exclusion of the other prophets before him and their followers?

It is said: Every one of the prophets before Abraham was a ḥanīf, following the obedience of Allah. But Allah, mighty and majestic, did not make any of them a leader for those after him among His servants until the Hour, as He did with Abraham, when He made him a leader in what He clarified of the rites of the Hajj and circumcision, and other laws of Islam, as worship for him forever until the Hour. He made what was established of that a distinguishing sign between the believers and disbelievers among His servants, and between the obedient among them and the disobedient. Thus the one among the people who is upright is called "ḥanīf" by following his creed and his steadfastness upon his guidance and path, and whoever deviates from his creed is called by all the names of the creeds, so it is said: "Jew, Christian, Magian," and other kinds of creeds.

* *

As for His words, "and he was not of the polytheists," He says: he was not one who worshipped idols and images, nor was he a Jew or a Christian, but he was a ḥanīf, a Muslim.

**Commentary on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He:** ﴿Say: "We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and in what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting."﴾ [2:136]

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, exalted is His remembrance, means by this: "Say," O believers, to these Jews and Christians who have said to you, "Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided": "We believe" (amanna), that is, "We affirm as true" (saddaqna) "in God."

We have already shown earlier that the meaning of "faith" (iman) is affirmation as true (tasdiq), so there is no need to repeat it. [See what has passed: 1:235-236, then 2:143, 348, and other places besides these.]

* *

"And in what has been sent down to us": he also says, "We affirm as true the Book that God sent down to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ)." He attributed the address of the revelation to them, since they were his followers, commanded and forbidden by it. So it, although it was sent down to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), carries the meaning of being sent down to them, because of the meanings for them in it that I have described.

* *

By His words, "and in what was sent down to Abraham," He means: "We also affirm as true and believe in what was sent down to Abraham, and Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes," who are the prophets among the descendants of Jacob.

* *

As for His words, "and in what was given to Moses and Jesus," He means: "We also believe in the Torah that God gave to Moses, and in the Gospel that God gave to Jesus, and in the books that He gave to all the prophets, and we acknowledge and affirm that all of that is truth, guidance and light from God, and that all of those whom God mentioned among His prophets were upon truth and guidance, confirming one another, on one path in calling to the Oneness of God (tawhid) and acting in obedience to Him." "We make no distinction between any of them": He says, "We do not believe in some of the prophets and disbelieve in others, nor disown some and befriend others, as the Jews disowned Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, while acknowledging others of the prophets, and as the Christians disowned Muhammad (ﷺ) while acknowledging others of the prophets. Rather, we bear witness for all of them that they were the messengers and prophets of God, sent with truth and guidance."

* *

As for His words, "and to Him we are submitting," He, exalted is His remembrance, means: "We are humbly obedient to Him, yielding to Him in servitude."

* *

It is related that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said this to the Jews, but they disbelieved in Jesus and in those who believed in him, as follows:

2101. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, the client (mawla) of Zayd ibn Thabit, narrated to me, saying: Sa'id ibn Jubayr, or Ikrimah, narrated to me, from Ibn Abbas, who said: A group of Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), among them Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab, [In the Sirah of Ibn Hisham 2:216, "among them: Abu Yasir."] Rafi' ibn Abi Rafi', Azar, Khalid, Zayd, Azar ibn Abi Azar, and Ash'a. They asked him about which of the messengers he believed in, and he said: "I believe in God, and in what was sent down to us, and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and what was given to Moses and Jesus, and what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting." When he mentioned Jesus, they denied his prophethood and said: "We do not believe in Jesus, nor in whoever believes in him." Then God revealed concerning them: ﴿Say: "O People of the Book, do you find fault with us only because we believe in God and in what has been sent down to us and what was sent down before, and because most of you are defiantly disobedient?"﴾ [5:59] [Report 2101: it will come in the commentary on Surat al-Ma'idah: 59 (6:188-189, Bulaq edition), with its chain through Hannad ibn al-Sarri from Yunus ibn Bukayr. It is in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham 2:216 with slight variation in some of its wording. See also the following report.]

2102. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad narrated to me, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas. He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came, and he mentioned something similar, except that he said "Nafi' ibn Abi Nafi'" in place of "Rafi' ibn Abi Rafi'." [Report 2102: thus it occurs in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham 2:216. See also the Sirah of Ibn Hisham 1:161-162, "Rafi' ibn Abi Rafi'" and "Nafi' ibn Abi Nafi'." Confusion in the names of the Jews of that era is common in the books of biography.]

* *

Qatadah said: This verse was revealed as a command from God, exalted is His remembrance, to the believers to affirm as true all His messengers.

2103. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "Say: We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us and what was sent down to Abraham," through His words, "and to Him we are submitting." God commanded the believers to believe in and affirm as true all His prophets and messengers, and not to make a distinction between any of them.

* *

As for the "Tribes" (al-Asbat) that he mentioned, they are twelve men from the descendants of Jacob ibn Isaac ibn Abraham. Each man among them had offspring who became a nation of people, so they were called "Tribes." As follows:

2104. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: The Tribes are Joseph and his brothers, the sons of Jacob. He had twelve sons, and each of them had offspring who became a nation of people, so they were called "Tribes."

2105. Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: As for the Tribes, they are the sons of Jacob: Joseph, Benjamin, Reuben, Judah, Simeon, Levi, Dan, and Qahath. [Report 2105: in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:140. I have not found "Qahath" among the sons of Jacob; in al-Durr al-Manthur it is "Tahan." Both appear to be distortions of "Naphtali," the son of Dan's mother, Bilhah, the maidservant of Rachel, as will come in the following report, 2107, and as is in the Book of Genesis that is in our hands. Al-Tabari here restricted himself to eight of the Tribes. Al-Suyuti, in al-Durr al-Manthur, in his narration from al-Tabari, added a ninth, "Wakunu" (with the letter nun), and there is no such name among the sons of Jacob, unless it is a misreading of "Zebulun," as it is in the books of that people. See the note on the following report, 2107.]

2106. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: "The Tribes" are Joseph and his brothers, the sons of Jacob, twelve men, and each man among them had offspring who became a nation of people, so they were called "the Tribes."

2107. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, saying: [Report 2107: I have not verified these names, despite the variation in them, but I will mention the points of difference in their spelling in the Book of the Children of Israel that is in our hands, in the notes that follow.] Jacob ibn Isaac, who is Israel, married his maternal cousin Leah, daughter of Laban ibn Bathuel ibn Ilyas, [Leah daughter of Laban son of Bethuel, and Rachel daughter of Laban...] and she bore him Reuben ibn Jacob, who was his eldest son; Simeon ibn Jacob; Levi ibn Jacob; Judah ibn Jacob; Zebulun ibn Jacob; [Zebulun ibn Jacob] Issachar ibn Jacob; and Dinah, daughter of Jacob. Then Leah daughter of Laban died. Jacob then married her sister Rachel daughter of Laban ibn Bathuel ibn Ilyas, and she bore him Joseph ibn Jacob and Benjamin, which in Arabic means "lion." He also had four sons by two of his concubines, one named Zilpah and the other named Bilhah: Dan ibn Jacob, Naphtali ibn Jacob, Gad ibn Jacob, and Asher ibn Jacob. [Asher ibn Jacob; see all of these in the Book of Genesis, chapters 29, 30, and 35.] So the sons of Jacob were twelve men, and God multiplied from them twelve tribes, whose number no one can count and whose lineages no one knows except God. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations.﴾ [Surat al-A'raf: 160]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 137:

The explanation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And if they believe in the like of what you have believed, then they are guided﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, "And if they believe in the like of what you have believed": if the Jews and the Christians believe in God, and in what has been sent down to you, and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and what was given to the prophets from their Lord, and acknowledge that, just as you, O believers, have believed and acknowledged, then they have been granted success and have been rightly guided, and have held to the path of truth and been guided. They would then be of you and you of them, by their entry into your religion (millah) through their acknowledgment of that.

By this verse, may His remembrance be exalted, He indicated that He does not accept any deed from anyone except with faith in these meanings which He enumerated before it, as:

2108 - Al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih related to us, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: "And if they believe in the like of what you have believed, then they are guided," and similar to this, he said: God, glorified be He, informed that faith is the firmest handhold, and that He does not accept any deed except with it, and that Paradise is forbidden only to whoever abandons it.

* *

A reading has been reported from Ibn Abbas regarding this, which the codices of the Muslims contradict, and the reciters of the Qur'an have agreed to abandon it. It is that:

2109 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far related to us, saying: Shu'bah related to us, from Abu Hamzah, who said: Ibn Abbas said: "Do not say: 'And if they believe in the like of what you have believed, then they are guided' — for there is no like of God — but say: 'And if they believe in that which you have believed, then they are guided'" — or he said: "And if they believe in what you have believed."

* *

So Ibn Abbas, in this report, if it is authentically from him, directs the interpretation of the reading of one who recited: "And if they believe in the like of what you have believed," as meaning: if they believe in a like of God, and in a like of what was sent down to Abraham and Ishmael. And that, if it is turned toward this sense, is associating partners with the Mighty God without doubt, for God, may His remembrance be exalted, has no like, so that we would believe in Him or disbelieve in Him.

* *

But the interpretation of that is other than the meaning toward which he directed its interpretation. Its meaning is what we have described, namely: if they affirm a like of your affirmation in what you have affirmed, from all that we have enumerated to you of the books of God and His prophets, then they are guided. The comparison occurs only between the two affirmations and the two acknowledgments, which are the faith of these people and the faith of those. Like the saying of a speaker: "Amr passed by your brother the way I passed by him," meaning: Amr passed by your brother like my passing by him. The comparison entered only as a comparison between the two passings, not between Amr and the speaker. Likewise His saying: "And if they believe in the like of what you have believed," the comparison occurs only between the two faiths, not between the object of belief.

* *

The explanation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿But if they turn away, then they are only in opposition﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, "And if they turn away", meaning: if those who said to Muhammad ﷺ and his companions, "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided," turn away and refuse [[See the meaning of "tawalla" previously: 2: 162, 163 / then 298, 299.]] — and do not believe in the like of your faith, O believers, in God and in what the prophets brought and what the messengers were sent with, and they distinguish between the messengers of God and between God and His messengers, believing in some and disbelieving in others — then know, O believers, that they are only in disobedience, separation, and hostility toward God, His messenger, and you, as:

2110 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah: "But they are only in opposition," that is, in separation. [[The report 2110: "from Sa'id" has fallen out of the printed edition in its chain, and it is a recurring chain in the tafsir, affirmed previously at 2104.]]

2111 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "Then they are only in opposition", meaning separation.

2112 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "And if they turn away, then they are only in opposition," he said: opposition (shiqaq) is separation and hostility. When one opposes, he has fought, and when one fights, he has opposed, and both are one in the speech of the Arabs. And he recited: ﴿And whoever opposes the Messenger﴾ [Surah an-Nisa': 115].

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The root of "shiqaq," in our view, and God knows best, is derived from the saying of the speaker: "This matter was difficult for him (shagga 'alayhi hadha al-amr)," when it distressed and harmed him. Then it was said: "So-and-so opposed so-and-so (shaqqa fulan fulanan)," meaning: each of them inflicted upon the other what distressed and harmed him, and his offense weighed heavily upon him. From it is the saying of God, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿And if you fear a breach (shiqaq) between them﴾ [Surah an-Nisa': 35], meaning: separation between them.

* *

The explanation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿So God will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ (137)

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, "So God will suffice you against them," meaning: God will suffice you, O Muhammad, against those who said to you and your companions, "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided," from among the Jews and Christians, if they turn away from believing like the faith of your companions in God, in what was sent down to you, in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac and the other prophets, and separate between God and His messengers — whether by the sword's killing, or by expulsion from your neighborhood, or other punishments. For God is "the All-Hearing" of what they say to you with their tongues and what they display to you with their mouths, of ignorance, of calling to disbelief, and of misguided creeds; "the All-Knowing" of what they conceal for you and your believing companions in their souls of envy and hatred.

God did that to them quickly and fulfilled His promise, and He sufficed His Prophet ﷺ by giving him power over them, until He killed some of them, expelled some, and humiliated some and disgraced them with the jizyah and abasement.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan) on Surah 2, verses 138–139**

**On the interpretation of His words, ﴿Sibghat Allah. And who is better than Allah in sibghah (dye/colouring)? And we are worshippers of Him﴾ (2:138)**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By *al-sibghah* (the dye/baptism), He, may His mention be exalted, means the *sibghah* of Islam. This is because when the Christians wished to make their children Christians, they would immerse them in water which they claimed was a sanctification for them, similar to the ritual bath of impurity (*ghusl al-janabah*) for the people of Islam, and they claimed it was their *sibghah* in Christianity. [See Ma'ani al-Qur'an (al-Farra'), 1:82–83.]

Then Allah, may His mention be exalted, said, when they said to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his believing companions, "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided": Say to them, O Muhammad, "O Jews and Christians, rather, follow the religion of Ibrahim, the *sibghah* of Allah, which is the best of colourings, for it is the *hanifiyyah* (pure monotheism) that submits (to Allah). And leave off associating partners with Allah and going astray from the path of His guidance."

* *

The word *al-sibghah* is in the accusative (*nasb*) for the one who reads it in the accusative, as a substitution (*radd*) for *al-millah* (the religion). Likewise, whoever reads *al-sibghah* in the nominative (*raf'*) reads *al-millah* in the nominative, as its substitution.

It is also permissible to read it in the nominative in another way, namely as a new predicate (*ibtida'*), meaning: "It is the *sibghah* of Allah."

It is also permissible to read it in the accusative in a way other than substitution for *al-millah*, rather as (an object of a verb implied in) His words, "Say: We believe in Allah," up to His words, "and we are submitting to Him," meaning: "We have believed with this belief," so that the belief itself is then the *sibghah* of Allah. [See Ma'ani al-Qur'an, 1:82–83.]

* *

Scholars of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wil*) in general agree with what we have said about the interpretation of *al-sibghah*.

Those who said this:

2113. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words, "Sibghat Allah. And who is better than Allah in sibghah": The Jews dye their children as Jews, and the Christians dye their children as Christians, and the *sibghah* of Allah is Islam. There is no *sibghah* better than Islam, nor purer, and it is the religion of Allah with which He sent Nuh and the prophets after him.

2114. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: 'Ata' (said regarding) "Sibghat Allah": The Jews dyed their children (in Judaism), contrary to the *fitrah* (innate nature).

* *

Scholars of interpretation differed regarding the interpretation of His words, "*Sibghat Allah*." Some of them said: It is the religion of Allah.

Those who said this:

2115. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah: "Sibghat Allah," he said: the religion of Allah.

2116. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding His words, "Sibghat Allah," he said: the religion of Allah. "And who is better than Allah in sibghah" – who is better than Allah in religion.

2117. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the like of it.

2118. Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from a man, from Mujahid, the like of it.

2119. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mujahid, the like of it.

2120. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

2121. Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Fudayl ibn Marzuq narrated to us, from 'Atiyyah regarding His words, "Sibghat Allah," he said: the religion of Allah.

2122. Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Sibghat Allah. And who is better than Allah in sibghah," he says: the religion of Allah, and who is better than Allah in religion.

2123. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Sibghat Allah," he said: the religion of Allah.

2124. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding the words of Allah, "Sibghat Allah," he said: the religion of Allah.

2125. Ibn al-Barqi narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Abi Salamah narrated to us, saying: I asked Ibn Zayd about the words of Allah, "Sibghat Allah," and he mentioned the like of it.

* *

Others said: "*Sibghat Allah*" is the *fitrah* of Allah. [See Majaz al-Qur'an (Abu 'Ubaydah), p. 59.]

Those who said this:

2126. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding the words of Allah, "Sibghat Allah," he said: the *fitrah* of Allah upon which He created people.

2127. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Harb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Lahi'ah narrated to us, from Ja'far ibn Rabi'ah, from Mujahid: "And who is better than Allah in sibghah," he said: the *sibghah* is the *fitrah*.

2128. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, who said: "*Sibghat Allah*" is Islam, the *fitrah* of Allah upon which He created people. Ibn Juraij said: 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir said to me: "*Sibghat Allah*," he said: the religion of Allah, and who is better than Allah in religion. He said: It is the *fitrah* of Allah.

* *

As for whoever held this view and directed *al-sibghah* to mean the *fitrah*, its meaning is: "Rather, we follow the *fitrah* of Allah and His religion upon which He created His creation, and that is the upright religion," from the words of Allah, may His mention be exalted: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 14], meaning: the Creator of the heavens and the earth. [See Majaz al-Qur'an, p. 59.]

* *

**On the interpretation of His words, ﴿And we are worshippers of Him﴾ (2:138)**

Abu Ja'far said: His words, may His mention be exalted, "And we are worshippers of Him," are a command from Allah, may His mention be exalted, to His Prophet ﷺ to say to the Jews and Christians, who said to him and to those who followed him among his companions, "Be Jews or Christians." So He said to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Say, "Rather, we follow the religion of Ibrahim, a *hanif* (upright in monotheism), the *sibghah* of Allah, and we are worshippers of Him." That is, the religion of those who humble themselves before Allah and submit to Him, in our following the religion of Ibrahim, and our submission to Him in that, without arrogance in following His command and in acknowledging His messengers, as the Jews and Christians were arrogant and disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ out of arrogance, transgression, and envy.

* *

**On the interpretation of His words, ﴿Say: Do you argue with us about Allah, when He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds, and we are sincere to Him﴾ (2:139)**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His mention be exalted, "Say: Do you argue with us about Allah," He means: Say, O Muhammad, to the assembly of the Jews and Christians, who said to you and your companions, "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided," and claimed that their religion is better than your religion, and their book better than your book, because it came before your book, and they claimed that for this reason they are closer to Allah than you: "Do you argue with us about Allah, when He is our Lord and your Lord? In His hand is all good, to Him belongs reward and punishment, and recompense for deeds, the good and bad among them. Yet you claim that you are closer to Allah than we are, because your prophet came before our prophet and your book before our book, while your Lord and our Lord is One, and that for each group of us is what it has done and earned of good and evil deeds, and it will be recompensed for them, rewarded or punished [for them]" [in the printed edition: "and it will be recompensed, rewarded or punished." The correct reading seems to require deleting the "and" and adding "for them." The phrase "for lineage over deeds" is coordinated with "and the recompense for deeds"]. Not on account of lineage or the precedence of religion and book.

* *

By His words, "Say: Do you argue with us," He means: Say, do you dispute with us and debate us? As:

2129. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Say: Do you argue with us about Allah?" Say: Do you dispute with us?

2130. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "Say: Do you argue with us?" Do you dispute with us?

2131. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Do you argue with us?" Do you debate us?

* *

As for His words, "And we are sincere to Him," it means: And we are sincere to Allah in worship and obedience, associating nothing with Him, and worshipping no one other than Him, as the people of idols worshipped idols alongside Him, and the people of the calf worshipped the calf alongside Him.

* *

This is a reproach from Allah, may His mention be exalted, to the Jews, and an argument for the people of faith, through His words, may His mention be exalted, to the believers among the companions of Muhammad ﷺ: Say, O believers, to the Jews and Christians who said to you, "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided": "Do you argue with us about Allah?" By His words "about Allah," He means: about the religion of Allah, which He commanded us to adopt, and our Lord and your Lord is One, just and not unjust, and He only recompenses His servants for what they have earned. And you claim that you are closer to Allah than we are, because of the antiquity of your religion, your book, and your prophet, while we are sincere to Him in worship, having associated nothing with Him. Yet you have associated partners in your worship of Him: some of you worshipped the calf, and some of you worshipped the Messiah. So how can you be better than us and closer to Allah than we are? [In the printed edition: "how can you be better than us," and the correct reading is what is recorded here. "Anna" is an interrogative meaning "how."]

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan) on Surah 2, verses 138–139**

**On the interpretation of His words, ﴿Sibghat Allah. And who is better than Allah in sibghah (dye/colouring)? And we are worshippers of Him﴾ (2:138)**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By *al-sibghah* (the dye/baptism), He, may His mention be exalted, means the *sibghah* of Islam. This is because when the Christians wished to make their children Christians, they would immerse them in water which they claimed was a sanctification for them, similar to the ritual bath of impurity (*ghusl al-janabah*) for the people of Islam, and they claimed it was their *sibghah* in Christianity. [See Ma'ani al-Qur'an (al-Farra'), 1:82–83.]

Then Allah, may His mention be exalted, said, when they said to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his believing companions, "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided": Say to them, O Muhammad, "O Jews and Christians, rather, follow the religion of Ibrahim, the *sibghah* of Allah, which is the best of colourings, for it is the *hanifiyyah* (pure monotheism) that submits (to Allah). And leave off associating partners with Allah and going astray from the path of His guidance."

* *

The word *al-sibghah* is in the accusative (*nasb*) for the one who reads it in the accusative, as a substitution (*radd*) for *al-millah* (the religion). Likewise, whoever reads *al-sibghah* in the nominative (*raf'*) reads *al-millah* in the nominative, as its substitution.

It is also permissible to read it in the nominative in another way, namely as a new predicate (*ibtida'*), meaning: "It is the *sibghah* of Allah."

It is also permissible to read it in the accusative in a way other than substitution for *al-millah*, rather as (an object of a verb implied in) His words, "Say: We believe in Allah," up to His words, "and we are submitting to Him," meaning: "We have believed with this belief," so that the belief itself is then the *sibghah* of Allah. [See Ma'ani al-Qur'an, 1:82–83.]

* *

Scholars of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wil*) in general agree with what we have said about the interpretation of *al-sibghah*.

Those who said this:

2113. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words, "Sibghat Allah. And who is better than Allah in sibghah": The Jews dye their children as Jews, and the Christians dye their children as Christians, and the *sibghah* of Allah is Islam. There is no *sibghah* better than Islam, nor purer, and it is the religion of Allah with which He sent Nuh and the prophets after him.

2114. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: 'Ata' (said regarding) "Sibghat Allah": The Jews dyed their children (in Judaism), contrary to the *fitrah* (innate nature).

* *

Scholars of interpretation differed regarding the interpretation of His words, "*Sibghat Allah*." Some of them said: It is the religion of Allah.

Those who said this:

2115. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah: "Sibghat Allah," he said: the religion of Allah.

2116. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah regarding His words, "Sibghat Allah," he said: the religion of Allah. "And who is better than Allah in sibghah" – who is better than Allah in religion.

2117. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the like of it.

2118. Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from a man, from Mujahid, the like of it.

2119. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mujahid, the like of it.

2120. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

2121. Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Fudayl ibn Marzuq narrated to us, from 'Atiyyah regarding His words, "Sibghat Allah," he said: the religion of Allah.

2122. Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Sibghat Allah. And who is better than Allah in sibghah," he says: the religion of Allah, and who is better than Allah in religion.

2123. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Sibghat Allah," he said: the religion of Allah.

2124. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding the words of Allah, "Sibghat Allah," he said: the religion of Allah.

2125. Ibn al-Barqi narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Abi Salamah narrated to us, saying: I asked Ibn Zayd about the words of Allah, "Sibghat Allah," and he mentioned the like of it.

* *

Others said: "*Sibghat Allah*" is the *fitrah* of Allah. [See Majaz al-Qur'an (Abu 'Ubaydah), p. 59.]

Those who said this:

2126. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding the words of Allah, "Sibghat Allah," he said: the *fitrah* of Allah upon which He created people.

2127. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Harb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Lahi'ah narrated to us, from Ja'far ibn Rabi'ah, from Mujahid: "And who is better than Allah in sibghah," he said: the *sibghah* is the *fitrah*.

2128. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, who said: "*Sibghat Allah*" is Islam, the *fitrah* of Allah upon which He created people. Ibn Juraij said: 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir said to me: "*Sibghat Allah*," he said: the religion of Allah, and who is better than Allah in religion. He said: It is the *fitrah* of Allah.

* *

As for whoever held this view and directed *al-sibghah* to mean the *fitrah*, its meaning is: "Rather, we follow the *fitrah* of Allah and His religion upon which He created His creation, and that is the upright religion," from the words of Allah, may His mention be exalted: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 14], meaning: the Creator of the heavens and the earth. [See Majaz al-Qur'an, p. 59.]

* *

**On the interpretation of His words, ﴿And we are worshippers of Him﴾ (2:138)**

Abu Ja'far said: His words, may His mention be exalted, "And we are worshippers of Him," are a command from Allah, may His mention be exalted, to His Prophet ﷺ to say to the Jews and Christians, who said to him and to those who followed him among his companions, "Be Jews or Christians." So He said to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Say, "Rather, we follow the religion of Ibrahim, a *hanif* (upright in monotheism), the *sibghah* of Allah, and we are worshippers of Him." That is, the religion of those who humble themselves before Allah and submit to Him, in our following the religion of Ibrahim, and our submission to Him in that, without arrogance in following His command and in acknowledging His messengers, as the Jews and Christians were arrogant and disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ out of arrogance, transgression, and envy.

* *

**On the interpretation of His words, ﴿Say: Do you argue with us about Allah, when He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds, and we are sincere to Him﴾ (2:139)**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His mention be exalted, "Say: Do you argue with us about Allah," He means: Say, O Muhammad, to the assembly of the Jews and Christians, who said to you and your companions, "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided," and claimed that their religion is better than your religion, and their book better than your book, because it came before your book, and they claimed that for this reason they are closer to Allah than you: "Do you argue with us about Allah, when He is our Lord and your Lord? In His hand is all good, to Him belongs reward and punishment, and recompense for deeds, the good and bad among them. Yet you claim that you are closer to Allah than we are, because your prophet came before our prophet and your book before our book, while your Lord and our Lord is One, and that for each group of us is what it has done and earned of good and evil deeds, and it will be recompensed for them, rewarded or punished [for them]" [in the printed edition: "and it will be recompensed, rewarded or punished." The correct reading seems to require deleting the "and" and adding "for them." The phrase "for lineage over deeds" is coordinated with "and the recompense for deeds"]. Not on account of lineage or the precedence of religion and book.

* *

By His words, "Say: Do you argue with us," He means: Say, do you dispute with us and debate us? As:

2129. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Say: Do you argue with us about Allah?" Say: Do you dispute with us?

2130. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "Say: Do you argue with us?" Do you dispute with us?

2131. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Do you argue with us?" Do you debate us?

* *

As for His words, "And we are sincere to Him," it means: And we are sincere to Allah in worship and obedience, associating nothing with Him, and worshipping no one other than Him, as the people of idols worshipped idols alongside Him, and the people of the calf worshipped the calf alongside Him.

* *

This is a reproach from Allah, may His mention be exalted, to the Jews, and an argument for the people of faith, through His words, may His mention be exalted, to the believers among the companions of Muhammad ﷺ: Say, O believers, to the Jews and Christians who said to you, "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided": "Do you argue with us about Allah?" By His words "about Allah," He means: about the religion of Allah, which He commanded us to adopt, and our Lord and your Lord is One, just and not unjust, and He only recompenses His servants for what they have earned. And you claim that you are closer to Allah than we are, because of the antiquity of your religion, your book, and your prophet, while we are sincere to Him in worship, having associated nothing with Him. Yet you have associated partners in your worship of Him: some of you worshipped the calf, and some of you worshipped the Messiah. So how can you be better than us and closer to Allah than we are? [In the printed edition: "how can you be better than us," and the correct reading is what is recorded here. "Anna" is an interrogative meaning "how."]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 140:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians? Say: Are you more knowing, or is God?﴾

Abu Ja'far said: There are two readings of this. The first is "Am taqulun" with a "ta" (you say). Whoever reads it thus, its interpretation is: Say, O Muhammad, to those among the Jews and Christians who say to you, "Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided": "Do you dispute with us about God, or do you say that Abraham...?" Thus this is coordinated with His saying: "Do you argue with us about God?"

The other reading is "am yaqulun" with a "ya" (they say). Whoever reads it thus directs His saying "am yaqulun" to being a new interrogative sentence, like His saying: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [Surah al-Sajdah: 3], and as one says: "Is it camels or sheep?" [[See what has passed concerning the report on "am" in 2:492-494, and this part 3:97.]] He made it a new interrogative because a new statement has come, as one says: "Are you standing, or is your brother standing?" so that his saying "or is your brother standing" becomes a new statement for a sentence that is not part of the first, and a fresh interrogative. Had it been a coordination with the first interrogative, it would have been a statement about the first, and one would say: "Are you standing or sitting?"

Some scholars of Arabic have claimed that, when read thus with "ya", if what follows "am" is a complete sentence, it is a coordination with the first interrogative, because the meaning of the speech is: It was said, "Which of these two matters is occurring: this or that?"

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct reading in our view is "am taqulun" with "ta" rather than "ya", as a coordination with His saying "Say: Do you argue with us?", in the sense: Which of these two matters do you do? Do you dispute with us about the religion of God, claiming that you are more worthy than us and more rightly guided in the way, while our affair and yours is as we have described, as we have already explained [[In the printed edition: "aydan" (also), and the correct is what is recorded.]] — or do you claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and whomever God named, were Jews or Christians according to your creed, so that their falsehood and your lies become clear to the people [[I fear the correct reading is "fayattadih lil-nas" (becomes clear to the people), but what is in the original is not objectionable.]], because Judaism and Christianity came into being after those prophets whom God named? It is not permissible to read it with "ya", because it is anomalous against the reading of the reciters.

* *

This verse is also an argument from God, exalted is He, to His Prophet ﷺ against the Jews and Christians whose stories God has mentioned. God says to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Say, O Muhammad, to these Jews and Christians: Do you dispute with us about God, and claim that your religion is superior to ours, that you are upon guidance while we are upon error, by a proof from God, exalted is He, so that you call us to your religion? Then bring your proof for that, and we will follow you in it. Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians according to your religion? Then bring — for your claim — whatever you have claimed of that as proof, and we will believe you, for God has made them imams to be followed.

Then He, exalted is He, said to His Prophet ﷺ: Say to them, O Muhammad, if they claim that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians: Are you more knowing about them and about what they were upon of religions, or is God?

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God?﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He means: If the Jews and Christians — who said to you and your companions, "Be Jews or Christians" — claim, O Muhammad, that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians, then who is more unjust than them? He says: And which person is more unjust than them? For they concealed a testimony they had from God, that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Muslims. They concealed that and attributed to them Judaism and Christianity.

* *

The people of interpretation differed concerning the meaning of this.

2132: Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, he said: Abu 'Asim related to us, he said: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His saying: "And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God," he said: In the saying of the Jews about Abraham, Ishmael and those mentioned with them, that they were Jews or Christians. God says: Do not conceal from Me a testimony if it is with you concerning them. And He knows that they are liars.

2133: Al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, he said: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God," in the saying of the Jews about Abraham, Ishmael and those mentioned with them: that they were Jews or Christians. God said to them: Do not conceal from Me the testimony concerning them, if it is with you concerning them. And God knew that they were liars.

2134: Al-Qasim related to us, he said: Al-Husayn related to us, he said: Ishaq related to me, from Abu al-Ashhab, from al-Hasan that he recited this verse: "Am taqulun inna Ibrahima wa Isma'il" up to His saying "Say: Are you more knowing or is God? And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God?" Al-Hasan said: By God, the people had from God a testimony that His prophets were innocent of Judaism and Christianity, just as the people have from God a testimony that your wealth and your blood are sacred among you. Then with what did they make them lawful?

2135: It was reported from 'Ammar, he said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' concerning His saying: "And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God": the People of the Book concealed Islam while they knew that it is the religion of God, and they found it written with them in the Torah and the Gospel that they were neither Jews nor Christians, and that Judaism and Christianity came after these by a period of time.

* *

God, exalted is His mention, meant by that that the Jews and Christians, if they claim that Abraham and whoever was named with him in this verse were Jews or Christians, will be made clear to the polytheists who are their helpers, their lie and their false claim against the prophets of God, because Judaism and Christianity came into being after them. And if they negate Judaism and Christianity from them, it will be said to them: Come to the religion they were upon, for we and you all agree that they were upon the truth, and we differ regarding what opposes the religion they were upon.

* *

Others said: Rather, God, exalted is His mention, meant by His saying "And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God" the Jews in their concealing the matter of Muhammad ﷺ and his prophethood, while they know it and find it in their books.

Those who said that:

2136: Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, he said: Yazid related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians?" Those are the People of the Book who concealed Islam while they knew it is the religion of God, and adopted Judaism and Christianity, and concealed Muhammad ﷺ while they knew he is the Messenger of God ﷺ, finding him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel.

2137: Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, he said: 'Abd al-Razzaq related to us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah concerning His saying: "And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God": he said: The testimony is the Prophet ﷺ, written with them, and he is the one they concealed.

2138: Al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Ishaq related to us, he said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to me, from his father, from al-Rabi', similar to the report of Bishr ibn Mu'adh from Yazid. [[Report 2138: In the printed edition, "al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to me" appears, dropping "Ishaq related to us" from the chain; it is a recurring chain in the tafsir, the nearest of which is number 117.]]

2139: Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said concerning His saying: "And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God," he said: They are the Jews, who are asked about the Prophet ﷺ and his description in the Book of God that is with them, and they conceal the description.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We chose the view we have stated in interpreting this because His saying, exalted is His mention, "And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God," comes right after the story of the prophets God named, and before their story. What is closest to that is more fittingly part of their stories rather than other than that.

* *

If someone says: What testimony do the Jews and Christians have from God concerning the matter of Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes? It is said: The testimony they have from God concerning their affair is what God sent down to them in the Torah and the Gospel, and their command in it to follow their way and adhere to their creed, and that they were upright Muslims (hunafa' muslimin). This is the testimony they have from God that they concealed, when the Prophet of God ﷺ invited them to Islam, and they said to him: ﴿None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 111], and they said to him and his companions: "Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided." So God sent down these verses concerning them, in refutation of their lying, their concealing of the truth, and their fabrication against the prophets of God of falsehood and lies.

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾ (140)

Abu Ja'far said: God, exalted is His mention, means by that: Say — to these Jews and Christians who dispute with you, O Muhammad — "And God is not unaware of what you do," of your concealing the truth which He obligated you in His Book to make clear to the people concerning the matter of Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes in the matter of Islam, and that they were Muslims, and that the upright Islamic monotheism (al-hanifiyyah al-muslimah) is the religion of God which all creation is obligated to follow, not Judaism, Christianity, or other sects. Nor is He heedless of His punishment for your doing that, but rather He keeps account of you, until He requites you with the recompense you deserve in the hasty life of this world and the delayed Hereafter. He requited them quickly in this world, by killing some of them and expelling them from their homeland and dwellings, and He will requite them in the Hereafter with a humiliating punishment.

**The exegesis of His words, may He be exalted:** ﴿That is a community (ummah) that has passed away. It shall have what it earned, and you shall have what you earn, and you will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾ (2:141)

Abu Ja'far said: By His words "That is a community," God, may He be remembered, means Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the *Asbat* (the tribes, the descendants of Jacob's sons).

As related to us:

2140. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, regarding His words, may He be exalted, "That is a community that has passed away," meaning: Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the *Asbat*.

2141. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the same.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We have already explained earlier that *al-ummah* means the group [[See what preceded at 1:221, then this volume 3:74, 100. Then see "khala" and "kasaba" in this volume 3:101 and the references there.]].

* *

The meaning of the verse, then, is: Say, O Muhammad, to those who dispute with you concerning God among the Jews and the Christians, if they conceal what they possess of testimony regarding the matter of Abraham and those we have named along with him, and that they were Muslims, and they claim that they were Jews or Christians, while they are lying: Indeed Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the *Asbat* are a community that has passed away, that is, has gone its way [[See what preceded at 1:221, then this volume 3:74, 100. Then see "khala" and "kasaba" in this volume 3:101 and the references there.]], and has come to its Lord, and has passed on with its deeds and its hopes. For it is what it earned of good during the days of its life, and upon it is what it acquired of evil. Nothing benefits it except its righteous deeds, and nothing harms it except its evil ones. So know this, O Jews and Christians, for indeed you, if these—[[In the printed edition: "they are those with whom...", and the correct reading is "and they are those..."]] and they are those in whom you take pride, and you claim that through them you hope for deliverance from the punishment of your Lord, despite your misdeeds and your great sins—will not benefit from anything before God except what they have sent forward of righteous deeds, and will not be harmed except by their evil ones, then you are even more deserving that nothing will benefit you before God except what you have sent forward of righteous deeds [[The context of this phrase: "If these... nothing benefits them before God except what they sent forward... then you are even more deserving that nothing benefits you except righteous deeds..."]], and nothing will harm you except your evil deeds. So beware for your own souls, and hasten, before their departure, to repentance and turning back to God from the disbelief, misguidance, and slander against God and His prophets and messengers in which you are engaged. Abandon reliance on the virtues of your fathers and grandfathers, for to you is only what you have earned, and upon you is only what you have acquired, and you will not be asked about what Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and the *Asbat* used to do of deeds, because every soul that comes before God on the Day of Resurrection will be asked only about what it earned and sent forward, not about what others sent forward.

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His saying, the Exalted, "The foolish will say," He means: "The ignorant will say," "among the people," and they are the Jews and the hypocrites (ahl al-nifaq).

Allah the Mighty and Majestic named them "foolish" (sufaha') because they made the truth foolish (safiha al-haqq).[[Safah al-haqq: he was ignorant of it. For the meaning of "safah" see what has passed at 1: 293-294, and then this part 3: 90.]] The rabbis of the Jews grew arrogant, their ignorant ones and their dull-witted ones (ahl al-ghaba') refused to follow Muhammad (ﷺ), since he was from the Arabs and not from the Children of Israel, and the hypocrites were perplexed and became dull.

* *

Those who interpreted the Qur'an (ahl al-ta'wil) said what we have said about "the foolish": that they are the Jews and the people of hypocrisy.

The mention of those who said they are the Jews:

2142. Narrated to me Muhammad ibn 'Amr, who said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: "The foolish among the people will say: What turned them from their qibla?" He said: The Jews say it, when he (ﷺ) abandoned Bayt al-Maqdis.

2143. Narrated to me al-Muthanna, who said: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, who said: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

2144. I was told, from Ahmad ibn Yunus, from Zuhayr, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara': "The foolish among the people will say," he said: The Jews.[[The report 2144: This chain is not sound (laysa bi-dhak), for al-Tabari narrated it from an unnamed person, from Ahmad ibn Yunus, who is Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yunus al-Tamimi. He is trustworthy (thiqa), and the compilers all narrated from him, and he is sometimes attributed to his grandfather. He was born in 133 or 134 and died in 227. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 1/2/6, al-Saghir p. 239, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/57, and Ibn Sa'd 6: 283. Zuhayr is Ibn Mu'awiya Abu Khaythama al-Kufi, trustworthy, firm and well known. Abu Ishaq is al-Sab'i, 'Amr ibn 'Abd Allah, the great and well-known Successor (tabi'i). al-Bara' is Ibn 'Azib, a Companion (sahabi).]]

2145. Narrated to us Abu Kurayb, who said: Waki' narrated to us, from Isra'il, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara': "The foolish among the people will say," he said: The Jews.

2146. Narrated to me al-Muthanna, who said: al-Hammani narrated to us, who said: Shurayk narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', concerning His saying: "The foolish among the people will say," he said: The People of the Book.

2147. Narrated to me al-Muthanna, who said: Abu Salih narrated to us, who said: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Jews.

* *

Others said: "The foolish" are the hypocrites.

The mention of those who said that:

2148. Narrated to us Musa, who said: 'Amr narrated to us, who said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: "The foolish among the people will say" was revealed concerning the hypocrites.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿What turned them from their qibla which they had been facing?﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, the Mighty and Majestic, "What turned them" (ma wallahum): What thing turned them from their qibla? It is from the speech of one who says: "So-and-so turned his back to me (wallani fulan dubura-hu)," when he turned his face away from him and turned his back to him. So likewise His saying "What turned them?" means: What thing turned their faces?[[See what has passed concerning the meaning of "wall" at 2: 162, and this part 3: 115.]]

* *

As for His saying "from their qibla," the qibla of everything is what faces its face. It is a form (fi'la) like "the sitting and the sitting posture (al-jilsa wa al-qi'da)",[[See what he said about that in "al-Hikma" in this part 3: 87.]] from the speech of one who says: "I faced (qabalt) so-and-so," when I came to face him, facing him. So he is my qibla and I am his qibla, when each of the two faces the other with his face.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: So the meaning of the speech, then, since that is its meaning [[In the printed edition: "since its meaning is," with "dhalika" dropped, and the speech is not complete except with it.]]: "The foolish among the people will say to you, O believers in Allah and His Messenger, when you turn your faces from the qibla of the Jews which was your qibla before My command to you to turn your faces from it toward the Sacred Mosque: What thing turned the faces of these people, and turned them from the place they used to face with their faces in their prayer?"

So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, informed His Prophet (ﷺ) of what the Jews and the hypocrites would say when his qibla and the qibla of his Companions was changed from Syria to the Sacred Mosque, and taught him what response he should give them. He said to him: "If they say that to you, O Muhammad, then say to them: ﴿To Allah belong the East and the West; He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾."

* *

The reason for that was that the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for a period whose length we will mention later, if Allah the Exalted wills. Then Allah the Exalted wished to turn the qibla of His Prophet (ﷺ) to the Sacred Mosque. So He informed him of what the Jews would say when he turned his face and the faces of his Companions toward it, and what response he should give them.

* *

The mention of the period in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, what was the reason for his praying toward it, and what prompted the Jews and the hypocrites to say what they said when Allah changed the qibla of the believers from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'ba?

The people of knowledge differed about the period in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis after the Hijra. Some of them said, with what follows:

2149. Narrated to us Abu Kurayb, who said: Narrated to us Yunus ibn Bukayr, and narrated to us Ibn Humayd, who said: Salama narrated to us. They both said together: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad narrated to me, who said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr informed me, or 'Ikrima (Muhammad's doubt), from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When the qibla was turned from Syria to the Ka'ba, and it was turned in Rajab, seventeen months after the arrival of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Medina, Rifa'a ibn Qays came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Qardam ibn 'Amr, and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and Nafi' ibn Abi Nafi' (thus said Ibn Humayd; Abu Kurayb said: and Rafi' ibn Abi Rafi'),[[See what has passed in this part 3: 111, note 1.]] and al-Hajjaj ibn 'Amr, ally of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and al-Rabi' ibn al-Rabi' ibn [Abi] al-Haqiq, and Kinana ibn Abi al-Haqiq,[[The addition between the brackets is from the Sira of Ibn Hisham. In it: "and Kinana ibn al-Rabi' ibn Abi al-Haqiq."]] and they said: "O Muhammad, what turned you from your qibla which you were facing, while you claim that you are upon the religion and creed of Abraham? Return to your qibla which you were facing, and we will follow you and believe you!" They only wanted to tempt him away from his religion. So Allah revealed concerning them: ﴿The foolish among the people will say, What turned them from their qibla which they had been facing?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾.[[The report 2149: The text is that of Ibn Hisham's Sira 2: 198-199.]]

2150. Narrated to us Abu Kurayb, who said: Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, who said: al-Bara' said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for seventeen months, and he used to long to be turned toward the Ka'ba. He said: While we were praying one day, a passer-by passed us and said: "Do you not know that the Prophet (ﷺ) has been turned toward the Ka'ba?" He said: We had already prayed two rak'as toward here, and two rak'as toward here. Abu Kurayb said: It was said to him: "Did Abu Ishaq narrate it?" So he was silent.[[The hadith 2150: Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash is trustworthy and well known, except that they criticized him for some errors, because when he grew old his memory deteriorated and he changed. Here he narrates the hadith as a disconnected report (munqati'an) from al-Bara', because he did not meet him. One of his hearers asked him, as Abu Kurayb related at the end of the hadith: "Did Abu Ishaq narrate it?" The questioner wanted to make sure of it: Did he hear it from Abu Ishaq al-Sab'i from al-Bara'? But he was silent and did not answer him. If this alone existed, the hadith would be weak. But it is established through the narration of Abu Ishaq al-Sab'i from al-Bara' in the three chains that follow, the first of which is through Ibn 'Ayyash himself, and through the other sources of the hadith, as will come.]]

2151. Narrated to us Ibn Wakic, who said: Yahya ibn Adam narrated to us, from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', who said: After the arrival of the Prophet (ﷺ) at Medina, we prayed seventeen months toward Bayt al-Maqdis.[[The hadith 2151: This chain is weak, because of the weakness of Sufyan ibn Wakic, the teacher of al-Tabari. But it is strengthened by the reports that follow and others.
Ibn Majah narrated it: 1010, from 'Alqama ibn 'Amr al-Darimi, from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', at length. In it he mentioned that their prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis was "eighteen months." 'Alqama ibn 'Amr al-Darimi is trustworthy. al-Busayri said in his Zawa'id of Ibn Majah: "The hadith of al-Bara' is sound, and its narrators are trustworthy."]]

2152. Narrated to us Muhammad ibn Bashshar, who said: Yahya narrated to us, from Sufyan, who said: Abu Ishaq narrated to us, from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: I prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ) toward Bayt al-Maqdis sixteen months or seventeen months (Sufyan's doubt), then we were turned to the Ka'ba.[[The hadith 2152: This chain is very sound. Yahya is Ibn Sa'id al-Qattan. Sufyan is al-Thawri. The hadith is abridged. Thus al-Bukhari narrated it, 8: 132 (Fath al-Bari), and Muslim 1: 148, both through Yahya, from Sufyan, in abridged form.]]

2153. Narrated to me al-Muthanna, who said: al-Nufayli narrated to us, who said: Zuhayr narrated to us, who said: Abu Ishaq narrated to us, from al-Bara', that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he first arrived at Medina, stayed with his grandfathers, or his maternal uncles, from the Ansar, and that he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis sixteen months, and he liked that his qibla should be toward the House. He prayed the 'Asr prayer with some people. A man from among those who prayed with him went out and passed by the people of the mosque while they were bowing, and said: "I bear witness that I prayed with the Messenger of Allah toward Mecca." So they turned as they were, toward the House. He liked to be turned toward the House. The Jews had been pleased that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and the People of the Book; but when he turned his face toward the House, they denounced that.[[The hadith 2153: This is a detailed report. The chain is very sound. Imam Ahmad narrated it in the Musnad 4: 283 (Halabi), from Hasan ibn Musa, from Zuhayr, who is Ibn Mu'awiya, through this chain, similarly, and at greater length. Ibn Sa'd narrated it in al-Tabaqat 1/2/5, from al-Hasan ibn Musa, through this chain. Likewise al-Bukhari narrated it, 1: 89-90, from 'Amr ibn Khalid, from Zuhayr, through it. He also narrated it, 8: 130, from Abu Nu'aym, from Zuhayr, somewhat abridged.
Al-Bukhari also narrated it, 1: 421-422, and 13: 202, and Muslim 1: 148, by several ways, from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.
Its remainder will come through this chain: 2222.]]

2154. Narrated to me 'Imran ibn Musa, who said: 'Abd al-Warith narrated to us, who said: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Ibn al-Musayyab, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis after he arrived at Medina sixteen months, then he was turned toward the Ka'ba two months before Badr.[[The hadith 2154: 'Imran ibn Musa ibn Hayyan al-Qazzaz al-Laythi, the teacher of al-Tabari: trustworthy. Biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/305-306.
'Abd al-Warith is Ibn Sa'id ibn Dhakwan, one of the leading scholars. Yahya ibn Sa'id is al-Ansari al-Bukhari, trustworthy and a proof, one of the teachers of al-Zuhri, Malik, al-Thawri and others.
Ibn al-Musayyab is Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, the great Successor. In the printed edition it reads "al-Musayyab" without "ibn," which is a clear error by the copyists.
This hadith is mursal (disconnected at the Companion level), as is clear, and Malik narrated it likewise in the Muwatta', p. 196, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, as a mursal. Al-Shafi'i also narrated it from Malik in al-Risala, in our edition, no. 366. Ibn Sa'd also narrated it in al-Tabaqat 1/2/4, from Yazid ibn Harun, from Yahya ibn Sa'id.
It has been connected by al-'Utaradi, from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Sunan al-Kubra 2: 3, through Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Jabbar al-'Utaradi: "Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl narrated to us, Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: I heard Sa'd say..." and he mentioned the hadith. Then al-Bayhaqi said: "Thus al-'Utaradi narrated it from Ibn Fudayl. But Malik, al-Thawri and Hammad ibn Zayd narrated it from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Ibn al-Musayyab, as a mursal, without mention of Sa'd."
This is a good chain, suitable as a good supporting narration for the mursal report. Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Jabbar al-'Utaradi was already mentioned at 66, where Abu Hatim said of him: "not strong." But one who considers his biography in al-Tahdhib 1: 51-52, and Tarikh Baghdad 4: 262-265, will see that his reliability is more likely, and that the criticism of him was not based on clear proof. Therefore al-Khatib said: "Abu Kurayb was among the great teachers, truthful and righteous. Abu 'Ubayda al-Sari ibn Yahya was also a noble teacher, trustworthy, of the generation of al-'Utaradi. Each of the two has testified for him concerning hearing, and the other concerning his uprightness. That indicates the goodness of his condition and the permissibility of narrating from him, since no statement affirmed for anyone other than them requires dropping his hadith or rejecting his report." This suffices for accepting his addition in this hadith, by connecting it through the narration of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.]]

* *

Others said with what follows:

2155. Narrated to us 'Amr ibn 'Ali, who said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, who said: 'Uthman ibn Sa'd the scribe narrated to us, who said: Anas ibn Malik narrated to us, who said: The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis nine or ten months. While he was standing praying the Zuhr prayer at Medina, and had prayed two rak'as toward Bayt al-Maqdis, he turned his face toward the Ka'ba. So the foolish said: ﴿What turned them from their qibla which they had been facing?﴾[[The hadith 2155: 'Amr ibn 'Ali is al-Fallas, whose biography has passed at 1989.
Abu 'Asim is al-Nabil, whose name is "al-Dahhak ibn Makhlad." He was a trustworthy, firm jurist, one of the teachers of Ahmad, Ishaq, Ibn al-Madini and other imams. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/2/337, al-Saghir p. 231, Ibn Sa'd 7/2/49, Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/463, and al-Jam' bayn rijal al-Sahihayn pp. 228-229. He was truly noble, in quality and in epithet. al-Bukhari said in al-Kabir: "I heard Abu 'Asim say: I have not backbitten anyone since I knew that backbiting harms its people." He was born in 122 and died in 212, at the age of 90 years and 4 months. His mother bore him when she was 12 years old. May Allah have mercy on both of them.
'Uthman ibn Sa'd al-Tamimi al-Katib al-Mu'allim: trustworthy. Abu Nu'aym and al-Hakim and others declared him trustworthy, and some spoke of him without proof. Some reported from al-Nasa'i that he said: "not trustworthy," but al-Hafiz reported that he saw in the handwriting of Ibn 'Abd al-Hadi: "The correct statement of al-Nasa'i is that he is not strong." This is the correct statement from al-Nasa'i, and it is what is in his book al-Du'afa', p. 22. Ibn Abi Hatim biographed him 3/1/153 and said: "He heard from Anas ibn Malik." His hearing from Anas is established for us in another hadith in the Musnad: 13201.
So this chain, according to us, is sound. The hadith was mentioned by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 143, attributing it to al-Bazzar and Ibn Jarir. al-Haythami mentioned it in Majma' al-Zawa'id 2: 13 and said: "al-Bazzar narrated it, and in it is 'Uthman ibn Sa'd, whom Yahya al-Qattan and Ibn Ma'in and Abu Zur'a declared weak, and Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz declared trustworthy, and Abu Hatim said: a shaykh." al-Haythami also said: "The hadith of Anas is in the Sahih, except that it placed this in the Fajr prayer, while here it is the Zuhr." He points by that to the fact that its origin is in the Sahih, which is the hadith in Sahih Muslim 1: 148, from the narration of Hammad ibn Salama, from Thabit, from Anas, similar to it, and in it: "A man from the Banu Salama passed by, while they were bowing in the Fajr prayer, and called out: 'Indeed the qibla has been changed!' So they turned as they were toward the qibla." Ibn Sa'd also narrated it in 1/2/4, through Hammad ibn Salama. It is clear that this is a different story from the one al-Tabari narrated here. For what is here is that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself turned his face toward the Ka'ba. This is the first change of the qibla. As for the report of Muslim, it concerns other people, in the mosque of Quba', who were informed while they were praying that the qibla had been changed, so they turned toward it, as is established in the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar. It is in the Musnad: 4642, 4794, 5934, 5827.]]

* *

Others said with what follows:

2156. Narrated to us Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, who said: Abu Dawud narrated to us, who said: al-Mas'udi narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Murra, from Ibn Abi Layla, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Medina and prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis thirteen months.[[The hadith 2156: Abu Dawud is al-Tayalisi, the great hafiz imam, whose name is "Sulayman ibn Dawud ibn al-Jarud." Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/2/11, Ibn Sa'd 7/2/51, Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/111-113. He died in 203 at the age of 92 years, which he did not complete, as Ibn Sa'd said.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 142 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Mas'udi: He is ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUtba ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, and he is trustworthy (thiqa), though his memory deteriorated toward the end of his life. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib (Tahdhib al-Tahdhib), and in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/250-252. We have discussed him in our commentary on the Musnad several times, the last being in hadith no. 7105.

Ibn Abi Layla: He is ʿAbd al-Rahman, the well-known Successor (tabiʿi). However, he did not hear from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, as Ali ibn al-Madini, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Khuzayma affirmed with certainty, since he was born in the year of Muʿadh's death, or before it, or shortly after it.
Therefore this chain is discontinuous (munqati).

The hadith with this chain, in abridged form, was narrated by Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi in his Musnad (no. 566), with the wording: "The Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina and prayed seventeen months facing towards Bayt al-Maqdis. Then this verse was revealed to him: 'We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven' [2:144], to the end of the verse," he said, "so God turned him toward the Kaʿba."

It is part of a long hadith narrated by Abu Dawud al-Sijistani in his Sunan (no. 507), through two chains: from Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, the shaykh of al-Tabari here, from Abu Dawud (that is, al-Tayalisi), and then he narrated it from Nasr ibn al-Muhajir, from Yazid ibn Harun, both from al-Mas'udi. But Abu Dawud made clear that the narration of Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna is abridged, like the narration in the Musnad of al-Tayalisi, but that he mentioned their prayer facing Bayt al-Maqdis was "thirteen months," like the narration of al-Tabari here from Ibn al-Muthanna. I lean toward the view that Ibn al-Muthanna's narration is from al-Tayalisi, and I prefer it over the narration in al-Tayalisi's Musnad, since that work was not compiled by him but by one of the transmitters from him.

Furthermore, the hadith of Muʿadh, in full, was narrated by Ahmad in the Musnad (5: 246-247), from Abu al-Nadr Hashim ibn al-Qasim, from Yazid ibn Harun, both from al-Mas'udi, with this chain. But in it the wording is "seventeen months," like the narration of the Musnad of al-Tayalisi.

The Hafiz [Ibn Hajar] in Fath al-Bari (1: 89-90) pointed to many narrations on this matter, and attempted to reconcile them or to give preference to one. In my view, such a matter cannot be precisely determined unless it was recorded at the time, or people directed their resolve to preserving it.

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said (1: 345-346): "The point is that the turning toward Bayt al-Maqdis came after his ﷺ arrival in Medina. The matter continued thus for some months, and he ﷺ would often supplicate and beseech that he be turned toward the Kaʿba, which is the qibla of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). So he was answered, and he was commanded to turn toward the Ancient House." See also Ibn Kathir's History (3: 252-254).

* *

Hadith 2157: Ahmad ibn al-Miqdam al-ʿIjli narrated to us, saying: al-Muʿtamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard my father say: Qatada narrated to us, from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab: that the Ansar prayed the first qibla three years before the Prophet ﷺ came, and that the Prophet ﷺ prayed the first qibla sixteen months after his arrival in Medina, or as he said. Both hadiths are narrated by Qatada from Saʿid.

* *

Mention of the reason for which the Messenger of God ﷺ used to pray facing Bayt al-Maqdis before the obligation was imposed upon him to face the direction of the Kaʿba.

* *

The scholars differed regarding this.

Some of them said: That was by the choice of the Prophet ﷺ.

Mention of those who said so:

Hadith 2158: Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih Abu Tamila narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Waqid narrated to us, from ʿIkrima — and from Yazid al-Nahwi, from ʿIkrima — and al-Hasan al-Basri, both said: The first thing abrogated in the Qur'an was the qibla. That is because the Prophet ﷺ used to face the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, which was the qibla of the Jews, and the Prophet ﷺ faced it for seventeen months, so that they would believe in him and follow him, and to call the Arab Ummiyyun (gentiles) to it. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "To Allah belong the East and the West; wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing" [Surat al-Baqara: 115].

Hadith 2159: Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ, concerning His saying: "The foolish among the people will say: What has turned them from their qibla which they used to face?" — meaning Bayt al-Maqdis. Al-Rabiʿ said: Abu al-ʿAliya said: The Prophet of God ﷺ was given the choice to turn his face wherever he wished, and he chose Bayt al-Maqdis in order to win over the People of the Book, so his qibla was sixteen months, and during that time he was turning his face in the sky. Then God turned him toward the Sacred House.

* *

Others said: Rather, that act — by the Prophet ﷺ and his companions — was by the obligation imposed on them by Allah, Mighty is His mention.

Mention of those who said so:

Hadith 2160: Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiya ibn Salih narrated to us, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: When the Messenger of God ﷺ migrated to Medina, and most of its inhabitants were Jews, God commanded him to face Bayt al-Maqdis.
