The Jews rejoiced. So the Messenger of God ﷺ faced it for some months, and the Messenger of God ﷺ loved the qibla of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), and he would supplicate while looking at the sky. Then God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven" [2:144], to the end of the verse. The Jews were then suspicious of this and said: "What has turned them from their qibla which they used to face?" So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "Say: To Allah belong the East and the West." [Note: the report 2160 has passed as no. 1833 and will come as no. 2236; the additions between the parentheses are from both places.]

Hadith 2161: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: The Messenger of God ﷺ first prayed facing the Kaʿba, then he was turned toward Bayt al-Maqdis. The Ansar prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis three years before his coming, and he prayed after his coming sixteen months, then God, Mighty is His praise, turned him to the Kaʿba.

* *

Mention of the reason for which those who said "What has turned them from their qibla which they used to face?" said it.

* *

The commentators differed regarding this. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that there are two opinions on it. One of them:

Hadith 2162: Ibn Humayd narrated it to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad narrated to me, from ʿIkrima, or from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Some Jews said that to the Prophet ﷺ, saying to him: "Return to your qibla which you were on, and we will follow you and believe you!" They intended to tempt him away from his religion. [Note: this is part of the earlier report no. 2149.]

The other opinion is what I have mentioned from the hadith of ʿAli ibn Abi Talha from him, which passed before. [Meaning the report no. 2160.]

* *

Hadith 2163: Bishr ibn Muʿadh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, from Saʿid, from Qatada, concerning His saying: "The foolish among the people will say: What has turned them from their qibla which they used to face?" He said: The Ansar prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for two years before the Prophet ﷺ came to Medina, and the Prophet of God ﷺ prayed after his arrival in Medina as an emigrant, toward Bayt al-Maqdis, for sixteen months, then God turned him after that toward the Ka'ba, the Sacred House. Some of the people said concerning that: "What has turned them from their qibla which they used to face?" The man has longed for his birthplace! So God, Mighty and Majestic, said: "Say: To Allah belong the East and the West; He guides whom He wills to a straight path."

* *

It was said: The speakers of this statement were the hypocrites, and they only said it mocking Islam.

Mention of those who said so:

Hadith 2164: Musa narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: When the Prophet ﷺ was turned toward the Sacred Mosque, people differed about it and became divided. The hypocrites said: What is the matter with them, that they were on one qibla for a time, then abandoned it and turned to another? So God revealed concerning the hypocrites: "The foolish among the people will say," the whole verse.

* *

Interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Say: To Allah belong the East and the West; He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ (142)

Abu Jaʿfar [al-Tabari] said: By this, Almighty God means: Say, O Muhammad, to those who said to you and your companions: What has turned you from your qibla, Bayt al-Maqdis, which you were facing, to facing the direction of the Sacred Mosque? — To Allah belongs the dominion of the East and the West; meaning by this: the sovereignty over what lies between the two regions of the rising of the sun and the two regions of its setting, and what is between them of the world; He guides whom He wills of His creation, [i.e.] He makes him steadfast and grants him success to the upright path, which is the "straight path" — and by this He means: toward the qibla of Ibrahim, whom He made an imam for the people — and He forsakes whom He wills of them, leading him astray from the way of truth.

* *

By His, the Exalted's, saying "He guides whom He wills to a straight path," God means: Say, O Muhammad: Indeed God guided us by turning toward the Sacred Mosque, the qibla of Ibrahim, and He led you astray — O Jews, hypocrites, and the community of polytheism against God — and forsook you from what He guided us to in that.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (*Jami al-Bayan* (comprehensive exposition) of Qur'anic *tafsir* (exegesis)) on surah 2, verse 143 (part 1 of 4)**

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Thus We have made you a community of the middle way﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His praise be exalted, "And thus We have made you a community of the middle way," He means: just as We guided you, O believers, to Muhammad (ﷺ) and to what came to you from Allah, We singled you out for success in following the *qibla* (direction of prayer) of Abraham and his religion, and We favoured you thereby over all others among the peoples of the religions. Thus We singled you out and favoured you over others among the people of faiths, by making you a community of the middle way.

* * *

It has been explained that *al-umma* (the community) is a generation of people, or a category of them, and other than that. [See what preceded, 1: 221, and then this part, 3: 74, 100, 128.]

* * *

As for *al-wasat* (the middle), in the speech of the Arabs it means the best, the choicest. It is said of it: "So-and-so is *wasat al-hasab* (of middling/central lineage) among his people," meaning of central lineage, when they intend by that the elevation of his lineage. And "he is *wasat* among his people, and *wasit*" [the evidence for their saying *wasit* from their poetry is the verse of Jabir ibn Tha'laba al-Ta'i:

*Whoever becomes poor among his people, praises wealth,*
*Even if he is among them, *wasit* al-amm, of the middling/less noble mother's kin.*]

Just as it is said: "a sheep dry of milk" (*yabisat al-laban* and *yabasat al-laban*), and as His praise has said: ﴿So strike for them a dry path in the sea﴾ [Surah Ta-Ha: 77]. Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma said, using *wasat*:

*They are a middle (*wasat*) whose judgment the people are pleased with,*
*When one of the nights of calamity descends upon the great.*

[This appears to be from his Mu'allaqa; his *Diwan* 2: 27. But the first half of the verse in the *Diwan* reads: "For a tribe of lawful (descent), their affairs protect the people." I did not find this version among the published versions of his *Diwan*. However, al-Jahiz recited the verse in this version, unattributed, in *al-Bayan* 3: 225. It is attributed to Zuhayr in *Asas al-Balagha*, under *wasat*. The version of the *Diwan* and al-Jahiz has "when one of the nights came upon," and they are the same.]

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: I hold that *al-wasat* in this context is the *wasat* that means the part that lies between two extremes, like "the middle of the house" (*wasat al-dar*), with the *sin* vowelled with a short vowel and with a doubled consonant, not permitted to be pronounced with the *sin* lightened.

I hold that Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, described them as "middle" only because of their moderation in religion: they are neither people of excess in it, like the excess of the Christians, who went to extremes in asceticism and said what they said about Jesus, nor people of deficiency in it, like the deficiency of the Jews, who altered the Book of Allah, killed their prophets, lied against their Lord and disbelieved in Him. Rather, they are people of moderation and balance in it. Allah described them thus, since the most beloved of matters to Allah is the most moderate of them.

* * *

As for the interpretation (*ta'wil*), it has come that *al-wasat* means the just. That is the meaning of "the best," because the best among people are their just ones.

**Mention of those who said that *al-wasat* means the just**

2165. Salm ibn Junada and Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, both saying: Hafs ibn Ghiyath narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words, "And thus We have made you a community of the middle way," he said: "Just."

[Hadith 2165: Salm ibn Junada, a teacher of al-Tabari, whose biography appeared at 48. Al-Tabari narrated from him often, and he is Abu al-Sa'ib. In the printed edition here it says "Salim," which is an error repeated in it. There is no need to point this out again.
Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim: he is al-Dawraqi, the hadith memorizer, passed at 237.
This chain and the two chains after it are for one hadith, abridged from a hadith that will come at 2179.
Ahmad also narrated it abridged in *al-Musnad*: 11084, from Abu Mu'awiya, from al-A'mash, with it. He also narrated something similar: 11291, from Waki', from al-A'mash (*al-Musnad* 3: 9, 32, Halabi edition). Ibn Kathir quoted it, 1: 348, from *al-Musnad*. al-Haythami mentioned it in *Majma' al-Zawa'id* 6: 316 and said: "Ahmad narrated it, and its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih."
The author of *al-Zawa'id* erred in including it there, because it is an abridgment of the lengthy hadith that comes, and al-Bukhari and others narrated it, so it is not among the additions.
These abridged versions in al-Tabari were pointed to by the hafiz (memorizer) Ibn Hajar in *Fath al-Bari* 8: 131, while explaining the lengthy version.
All the versions we have seen have "*'adlan*" (just, singular) instead of "*'udulan*" (just, plural). Perhaps what is here is an error of the copyists, because the better form is the singular, used as a descriptive by the verbal noun, which is the same for the masculine, feminine, dual and plural. In *Lisan al-'Arab*: "If you see it in the plural, dual or feminine, then it is because it has been treated as a descriptive that is not a verbal noun." What Ibn Hajar transmitted in *Fath al-Bari*, and al-Suyuti in *al-Durr al-Manthur* 1: 144, has *'adlan* as well. Indeed, the words of Abu Ja'far himself, before this hadith, indicate that, since he said: "Mention of those who said: *al-wasat* is the just."]

2166. Mujahid ibn Musa and Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, both saying: Ja'far ibn 'Awn narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of it.

2167. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "And thus We have made you a community of the middle way," he said, "just."

2168. 'Ali ibn 'Isa narrated to me, saying: Sa'id ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His words, "We have made you a community of the middle way," he said: "Just."

[Hadith 2168: 'Ali ibn 'Isa ibn Yazid al-Baghdadi al-Karajiki: trustworthy, among the teachers of al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Khuzayma, biographized in *al-Tahdhib*, Baghdad 12: 12-13. Al-Khatib said: "I know nothing of his condition but good." He died in the year 247.
Sa'id ibn Sulayman: he is Abu 'Uthman al-Wasiti al-Bazzaz, whose nickname is "Sa'dawayh," whose trustworthiness was mentioned previously in the commentary at 611. Biographized in *al-Tahdhib*, *al-Kabir* 2/1/440, Ibn Sa'd 7/2/81, Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/26, and *Tarikh Baghdad* 9: 84-87. He died in the year 225, aged 100.
Hafs ibn Ghiyath: passed at 1037. But his narration here from Abu Salih Dhakwan al-Samman is certainly disconnected (*munqati'*), since Abu Salih died in the year 101, and Hafs was born in the year 117. He narrates from al-A'mash and his generation, from Abu Salih, as in the chain that passed at 2165.
Probably the phrase "from al-A'mash" fell out of al-Tabari's copy at this point between them, so that the chain is consistent and sound. I could not be certain of this, because I did not find this hadith of Abu Hurayra in another book with a chain. Al-Suyuti mentioned it only in *al-Durr al-Manthur* 1: 144, attributing it to al-Tabari alone.
The omission of "al-A'mash" from this chain is perhaps supported by the fact that Ibn Hajar, when he pointed in *Fath al-Bari* 8: 131 to al-Tabari's abridged versions of the hadith of Abu Sa'id mentioned earlier, mentioned from them that al-Tabari narrated it "through the route of Waki' from al-A'mash, with the wording: 'and the middle is the just,' abridged, traced to the Prophet. And through the route of Abu Mu'awiya from al-A'mash, the like of it." So these are two chains for the hadith of Abu Sa'id, which Ibn Hajar, who is what he is in precision and scrupulousness, transmitted from this place in al-Tabari, and which are not in the copy between our hands. So it is not unlikely that in this chain too there is a deficiency: the words "from al-A'mash" between Hafs ibn Ghiyath and Abu Salih.]

2169. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Ash'ath, from Ja'far, from Sa'id: "And thus We have made you a community of the middle way," he said, "just."

* * *

2170. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "And thus We have made you a community of the middle way," he said, "just."

2171. Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

2172. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, his words: "a community of the middle way," he said, "just."

2173. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding His words: "a community of the middle way," he said, "just."

2174. Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His words: "a community of the middle way," he said, "just."

2175. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "And thus We have made you a community of the middle way," he says: He made you a community of the just.

2176. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Rishd ibn Sa'd, saying: Ibn An'am al-Ma'afiri informed us, from Hibban ibn Abi Jabala, attributing it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "And thus We have made you a community of the middle way," he said: "The *wasat* is the just."

[Hadith 2176: It is a fragment of a lengthy hadith, which will come at 2195. "Rishdin ibn Sa'd" appears in the printed edition here as "Rashid ibn Sa'd." That is an error, as we will show there, if Allah wills.]

2177. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata', Mujahid and 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir, regarding "a community of the middle way," they said: "just." Mujahid said: "*'adlan*" (justly).

[In the printed edition: "Mujahid said: just," and it seems the correct reading is what is established here, otherwise it would be superfluous speech with no meaning.]

2178. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding "And thus We have made you a community of the middle way," he said: "They are a middle between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the nations."

* * *

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people, and that the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: "*al-shuhada'*" (witnesses) is the plural of "*shahid*" (witness). [See the explanation of "*al-shuhada'*" in what preceded, 1: 376-378, and this part, 3: 97.]

So the meaning is: And thus We have made you a community of the middle way, just, [*li-takunu*] witnesses for My prophets and My messengers over their nations by conveying, [The words in brackets are an addition that is indispensable, by the indication of the verse, and by the indication of what will come of His words: "and that My messenger may be."] that they have conveyed what they were commanded to convey of My messages to their nations, and that My messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) may be a witness over you, by your faith in him and in what came to you from Me, as follows:

2179. Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to me, saying: Hafs narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Noah, peace be upon him, will be called on the Day of Resurrection and it will be said to him: "Did you convey what you were sent with?" He will say: "Yes." It will be said to his people: "Did he convey to you?" They will say: "No warner came to us!" It will be said to him: "Who knows that?" He will say: "Muhammad and his community." That is His words: "And thus We have made you a community of the middle way, that you may be witnesses over the people, and that the Messenger may be a witness over you."

[Hadith 2179: It and the two chains after it are for one hadith, part of which passed with these chains at 2165-2167, except that there are additional teachers of al-Tabari in the first two chains here.
The hadith was narrated by Imam Ahmad in *al-Musnad*, in similar form: 11130, from Waki' from al-A'mash, and 11579, from Abu Mu'awiya from al-A'mash (3: 32, 58, Halabi edition).
Al-Bukhari narrated it, 6: 264, through 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad; 8: 130-131, through Jarir and Abu Usama; and 13: 266, through Abu Usama and Ja'far ibn 'Awn, all from al-A'mash, with this chain, in similar form.
Ibn Kathir quoted it in *al-Tafsir* 1: 347-348, from the two narrations of Imam Ahmad, and said: "It was narrated by al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, through many routes, from al-A'mash."
Al-Suyuti attributed it at 1: 144 to these and to others.]

2180. Mujahid ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Ja'far ibn 'Awn narrated to us, saying: al-A'mash narrated to us, from Abu Salih, from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), similar to it, except that he added in it: "They will be called and they will testify that he conveyed."

2181. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Sa'id: "And thus We have made you a community of the middle way, that you may be witnesses over the people" [meaning: that the messengers have conveyed], "and that the Messenger may be a witness over you." [meaning:] by what you have done, or performed.

2182. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Fudayl narrated to us, from Abu Malik al-Ash'ja'i, from al-Mughira ibn 'Utayba ibn al-Nahhas: that a *mukatab* (a slave in a contract of manumission) of theirs narrated to them, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, I and my community are upon a hill on the Day of Resurrection, overlooking the creation. No nation will be but that it wishes it were from it, O this community. [In the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik: "So we were left behind, O you three" - he means their being left behind from the expedition of Tabuk, and the delay of their repentance. This expression is used for specification, and is specific to the one who speaks about himself and the one addressed. You say: "As for me, I will do such and such, O man," meaning himself. So the meaning of Ka'b's words "O you three" is: those specified as left behind. (*Lisan al-'Arab*, root: *aya*).] And no prophet whose people denied him, but we will be his witnesses on the Day of Resurrection, that he conveyed the messages of his Lord and advised them." He said: "and that the Messenger may be a witness over you."

[Hadith 2182: This chain is weak, because of the anonymity of the Successor (*tabi'i*) who narrated it from Jabir, and the name of the narrator from the Successor requires investigation to verify.
Ibn Fudayl: he is Muhammad ibn Fudayl ibn Ghazwan, passed at 1840. Abu Malik al-Ash'ja'i: he is Sa'd ibn Tariq ibn Ashyam, a trustworthy Successor. Biographized in *al-Tahdhib*, *al-Kabir* 2/2/59, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/86-87.
al-Mughira ibn 'Utayba ibn al-Nahhas: in al-Tabari here "'Uyayna" is recorded, instead of "'Utayba." He is not biographized in *al-Tahdhib* or its appendices. Ibn Abi Hatim biographized him at 4/1/227 thus: "Mughira ibn 'Utayba ibn Nahhas al-'Ijli. He was a judge for the people of Kufa. He narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Musa ibn Talha, and from Mukatab, from Jabir," etc. Al-Bukhari biographized him in *al-Kabir* 4/1/322-323 thus: "Mughira ibn 'Uyayna ibn 'Abis. Ibn al-Mubarak said: Ibn al-Nahhas, from . . . and from Mukatib ibn Jabir . . ."
The scholar 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yahya al-Yamani, corrector of the two books, decided in favour of what Ibn Abi Hatim's book has, because it agrees with what is established in *al-Thiqat* of Ibn Hibban and *al-Ikmal* of Ibn Makula. That is correct. Al-Mughira has many narrations in al-Tabari's *History*, and his father's name is established correctly in many of them, and his name and lineage are mentioned in full there at 4: 81: "al-Mughira ibn 'Utayba ibn al-Nahhas al-'Ijli."
As for the words here, "that a *mukatab* of theirs narrated to them from Jabir," it is understood from them that the anonymous Successor who narrated from Jabir is a client of the family of al-Mughira, the narrator from him, and that he is a *mukatab* of theirs. But what is in the books of al-Bukhari and Ibn Abi Hatim, as you see, is: "and from Mukatib, from Jabir." The scholar 'Abd al-Rahman said in his commentary on Ibn Abi Hatim: "I think it is Sa'id ibn Ziyad al-Mukatib," but before that, in his commentary on *al-Tarikh al-Kabir*, he mentioned that only as a possibility, and almost rejected it, by saying that "Sa'id ibn Ziyad al-Mukatib, client of Ziyad al-Mukatib, client of the Banu Zuhra" was biographized by al-Bukhari, that is in 2/1/433, "but he did not mention his narration from Jabir or any other of the Companions." That is what he said, and likewise he was biographized in *al-Tahdhib* and elsewhere. Therefore I greatly doubt that he is the one meant by the words of al-Bukhari and Ibn Abi Hatim among the teachers of al-Mughira, "from Mukatib, from Jabir." Rather, I almost prefer what is here in al-Tabari: that it is from "*mukatab*" [with the alif], and that it was mentioned in some narrations this way; perhaps some early copyists, when they copied it, omitted the alif.
I did not find this hadith in another book with a chain, so as to be able to go beyond this limit in the investigation. But al-Suyuti mentioned it at 1: 114 - without a chain of course - and attributed it only to Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh.
Ibn Kathir mentioned it at 1: 348, quoting from Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Abi Hatim, through 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad, from Abu Malik al-Ash'ja'i, with this chain. In it is "from Mughira ibn 'Utayba ibn Niyas"! That is an obvious error.]

2183. 'Isam ibn Rawwad ibn al-Jarrah al-'Asqalani narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to us, saying: al-Awza'i narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi al-Fadl, from Abu Hurayra, who said: I went out with the Prophet (ﷺ) to a funeral. When he had prayed over the deceased, the people said: "What an excellent man!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is obligatory!" Then I went out with him to another funeral. When they had prayed over the deceased, the people said: "What a wretched man!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is obligatory." Ubayy ibn Ka'b stood up to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what do you mean by 'it is obligatory'?" He said: "The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'that you may be witnesses over the people.'"

[Hadith 2183: 'Isam ibn Rawwad ibn al-Jarrah al-'Asqalani: trustworthy. Ibn Abi Hatim biographized him at 3/2/26, and said: "My father narrated from him, and I wrote from him," then said: "My father was asked about him, and he said: truthful." In *Lisan al-Mizan*: "Abu Ahmad al-Hakim softened his assessment of him. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in *al-Thiqat*."]

His father, "Rawad ibn al-Jarrah": his biography has already passed (no. 126). We add here that he is also mentioned in *Mizan al-I'tidal* (the Balance of Moderation, a critical dictionary of narrators). The overall assessment of him supports his weakness. Al-Tabari also narrates from him, later on (22:72-73), a fabricated hadith with no basis. He also narrated something indicating that this shaykh had that hadith inserted into his narrations. If that is so, it reveals serious carelessness, which means nothing from his narrations can be accepted. As for this hadith here, he did not narrate it alone, as will come in the following chain.

In the printed edition, the name appears here as "Issam ibn Warrad," with the waw placed before the ra, which is a clear error.

Abdullah ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Madini: Ibn Abi Hatim recorded his biography (2/2/137), and narrated from his father, who said: "Only Yahya ibn Abi Kathir narrated from him, and we do not know him." Al-Dhahabi said in *al-Mizan* about this: "Unknown." Al-Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) said in *Lisan al-Mizan*: "Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy (*al-thiqat*)." In our view, this is sufficient to justify relying on his hadith, since he is a tabi'i (a second-generation Muslim who met Companions) whose person is known, and Ibn Hibban judged him trustworthy. In our view, the tabi'un are accepted unless a acceptable form of criticism is established against one of them.

In the printed edition, the name appears here as "Abdullah ibn al-Fadl," with the word "Abi" omitted, which is an error. It is correctly given in the following chain.

2184: Ali ibn Sahl al-Ramli narrated to me, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, saying: Abu Amr narrated to me, from Yahya, who said: Abdullah ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Madini narrated to me, saying: Abu Hurayra narrated to me, saying: A funeral bier was brought to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the people said: "What a good man!" Then he mentioned something similar to the hadith of Issam from his father.

[[Hadith 2184: This is another chain for the previous hadith. Ali ibn Suhayl al-Ramli has passed (no. 1384). Al-Walid ibn Muslim al-Dimashqi, the scholar of al-Sham (Greater Syria): trustworthy, precise, sound in knowledge and in hadith, one of the teachers of Ahmad, Ishaq and others; he died in 195 AH. He is mentioned in *al-Tahdhib*, *al-Kabir* (4/2/152-153), Ibn Sa'd (7/2/173), and Ibn Abi Hatim (4/2/16-17). He narrated from Marwan ibn Muhammad, who said: "al-Walid ibn Muslim was knowledgeable in the hadith of al-Awza'i."

His teacher in this chain, "Abu Amr," is al-Awza'i.

The hadith, through this route, is sahih (sound). Al-Suyuti mentions it (1:145) and attributes it to al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim.

Its origin is established from the hadith of Abu Hurayra. Ahmad narrated it in *al-Musnad* (7543). Abu Dawud, al-Nasai and Ibn Majah also narrated it, as we have shown here. However, the question of Ubayy ibn Ka'b is not mentioned in it, nor is the citing of the verse. In *Majma' al-Zawa'id* (3:4) there is another, lengthier version of it, in which the questioner is Umar. It is said that "al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat, and its narrators are the narrators of the sahih."]]

2185: Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Zayd ibn al-Habbab narrated to us, saying: Ikrima ibn Ammar narrated to me, saying: Iyas ibn Salama ibn al-Akwa' narrated to me, from his father, who said: We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) when a funeral bier passed by him, and it was praised with a good praise. He said: "It is due (*wajabat*)!" Then another bier passed by him, and it was praised less than that. He said: "It is due!" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is due?" He said: "The angels are the witnesses of Allah in the heavens, and you are the witnesses of Allah on earth. Whatever you testify about someone, it is due for him." Then he recited: ﴿And say: Act, for Allah will see your deeds, and His Messenger, and the believers﴾ [Surah al-Tawba: 105].

[[Hadith 2185: This is a sound chain, according to the condition of Muslim.

Zayd ibn al-Habbab (with a dammed ha and a lightened ba) al-Ukli: trustworthy, one of the teachers of Ahmad, Ibn al-Madini and other imams. He is mentioned in *al-Tahdhib*, *al-Kabir* of al-Bukhari (2/1/358), Ibn Sa'd (6:281), and Ibn Abi Hatim (1/2/561-562).

Ikrima ibn Ammar al-Ijli: trustworthy; Shu'ba and al-Thawri and Waki' and others narrated from him. He is mentioned in *al-Tahdhib*, *al-Kabir* of al-Bukhari (4/1/50), Ibn Sa'd (5:404), and Ibn Abi Hatim (3/2/10-11).

Iyas ibn Salama ibn al-Akwa': a trustworthy tabi'i who narrated many hadiths; the authors of the six books (al-Kutub al-Sitta) narrated from him. He heard from his father, the Companion, and al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated hadiths from him on the authority of his father. He is mentioned in *al-Tahdhib*, *al-Kabir* of al-Bukhari (1/1/439), Ibn Sa'd (5:184), and Ibn Abi Hatim (1/1/279-280). Also *Rijal Sahihayn* (the narrators of the two sahih books), p. 47.

The hadith is mentioned by al-Suyuti (1:145), abridged at its end. He attributes it to Ibn Abi Shayba, Hannad, Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani. al-Haythami, in *Majma' al-Zawa'id* (3:4-5), quoted it from two chains of al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, in each of which there is a weak narrator. Thus the hadith is established as sound through this sound chain according to Ibn Jarir. In the printed edition: "فما شهدتم عليه وجبت" ("whatever you testified about him, it was due"), but the correct reading is what is recorded here.]]

* *

2186: Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾: "that you may be witnesses for Muhammad (peace be upon him) over the nations: the Jews, the Christians and the Magians."

2187: al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

2188: Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, who said: On the Day of Resurrection the Prophet (ﷺ) will come "nadiyahu" (alone/with his assembly?), with no one with him, and the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) will testify that he delivered the message to them.

[[Narration 2188: In the printed edition it reads "Abu Asim" (with "Asim" alone). The correct reading is what is recorded here. This is a chain that recurs in the commentary; the nearest instance is 2186. As for his words "nadiyahu" (his assembly), this is how it appears in the printed edition, in other printed editions, in the manuscripts, and in *al-Durr al-Manthur* (1:146) it reads "bi-idhnihi" (with his permission), but the latter has no meaning. As for "nadiyahu," it seems he meant his station on the Day of Resurrection. *Al-nadi* means the gathering of a people and the members of a council. However, I incline to think that the wording is distorted from a word meaning "alone, or by himself," since the context requires that. As for his words "the Prophet (ﷺ) comes nadiyahu," I incline to think that "(ﷺ)" is an addition of a copyist, and the context requires that it read: "The Prophet comes on the Day of Resurrection nadiyahu, with no one with him."]]

2189: al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from his father, that he heard Ubayd ibn Umayr the like of it.

2190: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Abi Najih narrated to me, from his father, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) will come on the Day of Resurrection, and he mentioned the like of it, but did not mention Ubayd ibn Umayr, the like of it.

2191: Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾, i.e., that their messengers had conveyed the message to their peoples from their Lord, "and the Messenger will be a witness over you," that he had conveyed the messages of his Lord to his community.

2192: al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Zayd ibn Aslam: that the people of Noah will say on the Day of Resurrection: "Noah did not convey to us!" So Noah (peace be upon him) will be called and asked: "Did you convey to them?" He will say: "Yes." It will be said: "Who are your witnesses?" He will say: "Ahmad (ﷺ) and his community." So you will be called and asked, and you will say: "Yes, he conveyed to them." Then the people of Noah will say: "How do you testify against us when you did not live in our time?" They will say: "The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) came and informed us that he had conveyed to you, and it was revealed to him that he had conveyed to you, so we believed him." He said: Then Noah (peace be upon him) will be confirmed, and they will be called liars. He said: [Allah said]: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind, and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾.

2193: al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾: that this community would be witnesses over mankind that the messengers had conveyed to them, and the Messenger would be a witness over this community that he had conveyed what he was sent with.

2194: al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Zayd ibn Aslam: that the nations will say on the Day of Resurrection: "By Allah, this community has almost become all prophets, because of what they see that Allah has given them!"

2195: al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Rishdin ibn Sa'd, who said: Ibn An'am al-Mu'afiri informed me, from Hayyan ibn Abi Jabala, attributing it (*yusniduhu*) to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "When Allah gathers His servants on the Day of Resurrection, the first to be called will be Israfil. His Lord will say to him: 'What did you do with my covenant? Did you convey my covenant?' He will say: 'Yes, my Lord, Jibril (peace be upon both of them) has conveyed it to me.' Jibril will be called and it will be said to him: 'Did Israfil convey my covenant to you?' [[In the printed edition: "Did you convey to Israfil," which is an error; the correct reading is what is recorded here.]] He will say: 'Yes, my Lord, he conveyed it to me.' Israfil will be released, and Jibril will be asked: 'Did you convey my covenant?' He will say: 'Yes, I conveyed it to the messengers.' Then the messengers will be called and it will be said to them: 'Did Jibril convey my covenant to you?' They will say: 'Yes, our Lord.' Jibril will be released. Then the messengers will be asked: 'What did you do with my covenant?' They will say: 'We conveyed it to our nations.' Then the nations will be called and it will be said: 'Did the messengers convey my covenant to you?' Some of them will deny and some will confirm. The messengers will say: 'We have witnesses against them who testify that we conveyed, along with your testimony.' He will say: 'Who will testify for you?' They will say: 'The community of Muhammad.' The community of Muhammad (ﷺ) will be called, and He will say: 'Do you testify that these messengers of mine conveyed my covenant to those to whom they were sent?' They will say: 'Yes, our Lord, we testify that they conveyed.' Those nations will say: 'How can someone who did not live with us testify against us?' The Lord, blessed and exalted, will say to them: 'How can you testify against those you did not live with?' They will say: 'Our Lord, You sent to us a messenger and You sent down to us Your covenant and Your Book, and You related to us that they had conveyed, so we testify according to what You committed to us.' The Lord will say: 'They have spoken the truth.' That is His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a community of the middle way﴾ — and *al-wasat* means the just — ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind, and the Messenger may be a witness over you.﴾" Ibn An'am said: "It has reached me that on that day the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) will testify, except those who harbour *hinna* (a grudge) against their brother."

[[Hadith 2195: This is a weak hadith, on two grounds: first, it is mursal (its narrator, a tabi'i, did not attribute it to a Companion); second, Rishdin ibn Sa'd is weak, as will be explained.

A piece of it has passed with this same chain (2176), and we referred its takhrij (tracing of sources) to this place.

Rishdin ibn Sa'd: very weak; his case was explained at 1938. In the printed edition, here and at 2176, he appears as "Rashid," as was the case at 1938. This is an error.

Ibn An'am al-Mu'afiri: he is Abd al-Rahman ibn Ziyad ibn An'am (with a fatha on the hamza, a sukun on the nun and a damma on the ain), al-Mu'afiri al-Ifriqi, the judge. He is trustworthy. Many scholars spoke against him without valid proof. He heard from distinguished tabi'un, and was bold in speaking the truth. Ahmad ibn Salih used to say: "He is trustworthy," and he would object to whoever criticised him. Abu Bakr al-Maliki said in *Riyad al-Nufus*: "He was one of the leading hadith scholars, known for asceticism and piety, firm in his religion, and accomplished in various sciences." Ibn Hibban went to an extreme in his criticism of him, saying in *al-Majruhin* (pp. 283-284): "He used to narrate fabricated reports from trustworthy narrators, and he would bring from the reliable narrators what was not part of their hadiths, and he used to make tadlis (concealment of sources) from Muhammad ibn Sa'id ibn Abi Qays al-Mathlub." He then narrated a hadith through him to support what he said. That hadith is fabricated, but Ibn An'am is innocent of its responsibility, for the blame lies with one of the liars, Yusuf ibn Ziyad al-Basri. al-Daraqutni responded to Ibn Hibban's claim, as is recorded in the margin of a manuscript of *al-Majruhin*.

The easterners (mashariqa) erred in identifying Ibn An'am, and so came what was said in criticising him. Indeed they also erred about the date of his death, dating it to 156 AH, whereas the westerners (maghariba) knew him better and dated it to 161 AH.

He has full biographies in: *al-Tahdhib* (6:173-176), *al-Saghir* of al-Bukhari (p. 180), Ibn Abi Hatim (2/2/334-335), *al-Majruhin* of Ibn Hibban (283-284), *al-Mizan* of al-Dhahabi (2:104-105), *Tabaqat Ulama' Ifriqiya* of Abu al-Arab (27-32), *Riyad al-Nufus* of Abu Bakr al-Maliki (1:96-103), and *Tarikh Baghdad* (10:214-218).

Hayyan (with a kasra on the ha and a shadda on the ba) ibn Abi Jabala al-Misri: a trustworthy tabi'i. He was one of the ten whom Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz sent to teach the people of Ifriqiya the matters of their religion. He is mentioned in *al-Tahdhib*, *al-Kabir* of al-Bukhari (2/1/83), and Ibn Abi Hatim (1/2/269).

This hadith is mursal, since its narrator attributes it from a tabi'i that he "attributes it (yusnidu) to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," without mentioning who related it to him.

As for his wording "yusnidu" (attributing it), in the printed edition here and at 2176 it is written "bi-sanadihi" with a ba, which is a misreading. The hadith is mentioned by al-Suyuti (1:145), who attributes it only to al-Tabari and to Ibn al-Mubarak in *al-Zuhd*.

In the printed edition it read "hiqd 'ala akhihi" (a grudge against his brother). In *al-Durr al-Manthur* (1:146) it reads "ihna," and what I have recorded is from al-Qurtubi and some manuscripts. *Al-hinna* means grudge, from "wahana, yahinu, hinna" (with the kasra on the ha and fatha on the nun), like "wa'ada, ya'idu, 'idda." al-Azhari said: "It is not from the speech of the Arabs; rather, it is *ihna*, meaning a grudge." al-Asma'i denied "hinna," and Abu Nasr reported from him that he said: "We used to think al-Tirimmah was something until he said: 'I dislike that my people should criticise me for my coming to the lowest ones, possessors of *hinnat*'" [the verse, the poet's line, as cited in Diwan al-Tirimmah, p. 134], because it is *ihna* and *ihan*, and one does not say *hinnat*. al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Fa'iq* (under *ahann*): "As for what is reported from al-Asma'i... it is a belittling of him! 'Wahana' is a hasty judgment on the hamza being original or on dropping the waw in usage."]]

2196: al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Zuhayr narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak regarding His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾: he means by this those who held firm to guidance; they are the ones who will be witnesses over mankind on the Day of Resurrection, because of their denial of the messengers of Allah and their disbelief in the signs of Allah.

2197: It was narrated to me by Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾: he says: that you may be witnesses over the nations who passed before you, concerning what their messengers brought them and how they denied them. They will say on the Day of Resurrection and marvel: "A nation was not in our time, so they believed in what their messengers brought, while we denied what they brought!" So they will marvel exceedingly. His saying: ﴿and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾: means through their belief in him and in what was sent down to him.

2198: Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾, meaning: they testified about the generations according to what Allah, mighty and majestic, named for them.

2199: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: I asked Ata': "What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾?" He said: "The community of Muhammad: they will testify against those who abandoned the truth when faith and guidance came to them, from among those who were before us." He said: "Abd Allah ibn Kathir said it." He said: Ata' said: "Witnesses against those among mankind who abandoned the truth, all of them, which was brought to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) in their Book; ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾, that they believed in the truth when it came to them and confirmed it."

2200: Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over mankind, and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is a witness over his community, and they are witnesses over the nations. They are one of the four categories of witnesses whom Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned: ﴿And the Day when the witnesses stand﴾ [Surah Ghafir: 51]. The four are: the angels who count our deeds, for us and against us; he recited His saying: ﴿And every soul will come with it a driver and a witness﴾ [Surah Qaf: 21], and said: 'This is the Day of Resurrection.' He said: 'And the prophets are witnesses over their nations.' He said: 'And the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) are witnesses over the nations.' He said: '[And the *atwar*] are the bodies and the skins.'"

[[Narration 2200: al-Suyuti mentioned it in *al-Durr al-Manthur* (5:352) under the tafsir of [Surah Ghafir, verse 51], though not in this wording, and attributed it to Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim in their tafsirs. Its text is:

"From Zayd ibn Aslam: The witnesses are four: the angels who count our deeds over us; he recited: 'And every soul will come with it a driver and a witness.' And the prophets are witnesses over their nations; he recited: 'How then, when We bring from every nation a witness.' And the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) are witnesses over the nations; he recited: 'that you may be witnesses over mankind.' And the bodies and the skins; he recited: 'And they will say to their skins: Why did you testify against us? They will say: Allah has made us speak, who makes everything speak.'"]]

The first paragraph, which opens with the editor's remark on a passage marked in brackets, reads:

As for what came in the text of al-Tabari, which I have placed between brackets, it is an undoubted error, and I fear that its correct form is "al-atraf wa-l-ajsad wa-l-julud" (the limbs, the bodies and the skins). By "al-atraf" he means the *jawarih* (the bodily members), namely the hands and feet, as in His words, exalted is He, in [Surat Ya-Sin: 65]: (Today We seal their mouths, and their hands speak to Us, and their feet bear witness to what they used to earn).

* *

The discussion of the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you used to face except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His praise be great, "And We did not make the qibla which you used to face," He means: We did not make the turning away of you, O Muhammad, from the qibla which you used to face, so that We turned you away from it, except that We might know who follows you from who does not follow you, of those who turn back on their heels.

* *

The qibla which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) faced, which God meant by His words, "And We did not make the qibla which you used to face," is the qibla which you used to face before He turned you toward the Ka'ba, as:

2201 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And We did not make the qibla which you used to face," meaning: Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

2202 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to 'Ata': "And We did not make the qibla which you used to face." He said: The qibla was Bayt al-Maqdis.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: He omitted mention of "the turning away from it," being satisfied with what the indication of the preceding speech shows of its meaning, like all the other examples of this kind that we have mentioned in the past. [[See what has passed: 1:139-141, 179, and many others; seek it in the indexes.]]

We only say that this is its meaning because God's trial of the Companions of His Messenger concerning the qibla occurred, as the reports agree, at the change from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'ba, to the point that, it is mentioned, men who had embraced Islam and followed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) apostatized, and many of the hypocrites, on account of that, revealed their hypocrisy and said: "What is the matter with Muhammad, changing us once to this place and once to that place!" The Muslims said, concerning their brethren who had passed away while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis: "Our deeds and theirs have been nullified and lost!" The polytheists said: "Muhammad has become bewildered in his religion!" So that was a trial for the people and a purification for the believers.

Therefore His words, may His praise be great, "And We did not make the qibla which you used to face except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels" mean: And We did not make your turning away from the qibla which you used to face, and your being turned to another, except [as a test], as He, may His praise be great, said: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾ [Surat al-Isra': 60], meaning: And We did not make your report of the vision which We showed you [a trial]. That is because, had he not told the people what he had been shown, no one would have been tested by it. Likewise, the first qibla, which was toward Bayt al-Maqdis, had it not been turned away from toward the Ka'ba, no one would have been tested or tried by it.

* *

Mention of the reports which were transmitted with the meaning of what we have said:

2203 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada, who said: The qibla was a trial and a purification. The Ansar prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for two years before the arrival of the Prophet of God (ﷺ), and the Prophet of God (ﷺ), after his arrival in Medina as an emigrant, prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for seventeen months. Then God turned him toward the Ka'ba, the Sacred House. Concerning that, some of the people said: "What has turned them from their qibla which they used to face?" The man has longed for his birthplace! God, mighty and majestic, said: "Say: to God belong the East and the West; He guides whom He wills to a straight path." Some people said, when the qibla was turned toward the Sacred House: "What about our deeds which we performed toward our first qibla?" So God, mighty and majestic, revealed: "And God would not let your faith go to waste." God tests His servants with whatever He wills of His command, command after command, that He may know who obeys Him from who disobeys Him, and all of it is accepted, since in it there is faith in God, sincerity toward Him, and submission to His decree. [[The report: 2203 - in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:143, and part of it has passed as no. 2163. In the printed edition it read: "and all of it is accepted, and if there is in it faith in God..." a clumsy expression, so I made "idha" into "idh" and added "dhalika" so that the expression would be sound. As for al-Durr al-Manthur, its wording is even weaker, and its text is: "and all of that is accepted, in degrees of faith in God, sincerity, and submission to God's decree."]]

2204 - Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray facing Bayt al-Maqdis, and then the Ka'ba abrogated it. When he was turned toward the Sacred Mosque, the people differed concerning it and became groups. The hypocrites said: "What is wrong with them, that they were on one qibla for a time and then abandoned it and turned to another?" The Muslims said: "Would that we knew about our brethren who died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis! Has God accepted from us and from them, or not?" The Jews said: "Muhammad has longed for the land of his father and his birthplace; and had he remained on our qibla, we would have hoped that he is the one we are waiting for!" The polytheists of Mecca said: "Muhammad's religion has become bewildered, so he has turned his qibla toward you, and he knows that you were better guided than he; he is about to enter your religion!" So God, may His praise be great, revealed concerning the hypocrites: "The foolish among the people will say: What has turned them from their qibla which they used to face?" down to His words: "And it is indeed a great thing, except for those whom God has guided," and He revealed the verses after them concerning the others. [[The report: 2204 - part of it has passed as no. 2164, and it is in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:142-143.]]

2205 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to 'Ata': "Except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels"? 'Ata' said: He tests them, that He may know who submits to His command. Ibn Jurayj said: It has reached me that some people who had embraced Islam turned back and said: "Once here and once there!"

* *

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: Did God not know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels, except after the follower had followed and the one who turned back had turned back on his heels, so that He said: "We did not do what We did, of changing the qibla, except that We might know the one who follows the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from the one who turns back on his heels"?

It is said: God, may His praise be great, is the One who knows all things before they exist. His words: "And We did not make the qibla which you used to face except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels" do not inform that He did not know that except after its existence. [[In the printed edition: "it informs that He did not know that. . ." and the correct form is what I have set down, with the addition between brackets.]]

If he says: Then what is the meaning of that?

It is said to him: As for its meaning according to us, it is: "And We did not make the qibla which you used to face except that My Messenger, My party and My friends might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels." He, may His praise be great, said: "except that We might know," and its meaning is: that My Messenger and My friends might know. Since the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his friends are of his party, and it is among the habits of the Arabs to attribute what the followers of a chief do, and what is done to them, to the chief, as in their saying: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab conquered the land of Iraq and collected its tribute," whereas it was his companions who did that, on account of a cause that came from him in that. And like what has been reported in a similar case from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: God, may His praise be great, says: "I was ill and My servant did not visit Me; I asked him for a loan and he did not lend to Me; he insulted Me, and it was not fitting for him to insult Me."

2206 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Khalid narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far, from al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: God said: "I asked My servant for a loan and he did not lend to Me; he insulted Me, and it was not fitting for him to insult Me! He says: O my time! And I am Time, I am Time."

2207 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from his father, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), with something similar. [[The two reports: 2206 and 2207 are one hadith with two sound chains.
Khalid: in the first of them, he is Khalid ibn Makhlad al-Qitwani, with fath on the qaf and the ta'. He is trustworthy, one of al-Bukhari's teachers, from whom he and Muslim both narrated in the two Sahihs. He has been criticized for his excessive Shi'ism, but he is truthful in narration. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir of al-Bukhari 2/1/160, Ibn Sa'd 6:283, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/354. His teacher Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn Abi Kathir al-Ansari al-Zurqi is a well-known trustworthy narrator, from whom the authors of the six books narrated.
The hadith was also narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 1:418, through the route of Yazid ibn Harun, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, with the second chain, similar to it. He said: "This is a sound hadith according to the condition of Muslim, though they did not record it." al-Dhahabi agreed with him.
The prohibition of insulting time, in the Qudsi hadith, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, is established through several routes, in the two Sahihs and others. See al-Musnad: 7244, 7509; al-Bukhari 8:441, 10:465, 13:389; and Sahih Muslim 2:196-197.]]

* *

Thus He, may His mention be exalted, attributed the lending and the visiting to Himself, though it was done by another, since it was on account of His cause.

It has been related from the Arabs by hearsay: "I am hungry though not in my belly, and I am naked though not on my back," meaning: the hunger of his family and dependents and the nakedness of their backs.

Likewise His words: "except that We might know," meaning: that My friends and party might know.

Those who interpret the Qur'an (ahl al-ta'wil) said something similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

2208 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas: "And We did not make the qibla which you used to face except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels," Ibn 'Abbas said: That We might distinguish the people of certainty from the people of polytheism and doubt.

* *

Some of them said: It was said that way because the Arabs put "al-'ilm" (knowledge) in place of "al-ru'ya" (seeing), and "al-ru'ya" in place of "al-'ilm," as He, mighty is His mention, said: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [Surat al-Fil: 1], and he claimed that the meaning of "alam tara" is: did you not know? And he claimed that the meaning of His words "except that We might know" is: except that We might see who follows the Messenger. And he claimed that the saying of the speaker: "I saw, I knew, I witnessed" are letters that alternate, so that some of them are placed in the place of others, as Jarir ibn 'Atiyya said:

As if you had not witnessed Luqayt and Hajib
and 'Amr ibn 'Amr when he called on the tribe of Darim [[His Diwan: 563, and al-Naqa'id: 409, from his rhyming ode, in refutation of al-Farazdaq's ode. In it he enumerates the days of his people. The address in his words "as if you" is to al-Farazdaq, and he mentions "the day of Jabala," which is among the greatest of their days; it was forty years before Islam, the year the Prophet (ﷺ) was born, and it was between 'Amir and 'Abs against Dhubyan and Tamim. Luqayt ibn Zurara was killed that day, Hajib ibn Zurara was captured, and 'Amr ibn 'Amr ibn 'Adas was captured; they were of the Banu 'Abd Allah ibn Darim, and they were paternal uncles of al-Farazdaq, who was of the Banu Mujashi' ibn Darim.
The reading in the Diwan and al-Naqa'id is "idha da'aw" (when they called), and both are sound in meaning.]]
meaning: as if you had not known Luqayt, because between the destruction of Luqayt and Hajib and the time of Jarir there is a distance in time that is not hidden. For those he mentioned perished in the Jahiliyya, and Jarir was after a period had passed since the coming of Islam.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This interpretation is far-fetched, because "seeing," even if it is used in the place of "knowing," because it is impossible for someone to see a thing without its seeing necessarily constituting knowledge that he has seen it, when his nature is sound. So it is permissible, from the aspect I have established as seeing, that his establishing it be attributed to it as knowledge, and it is sound that by mentioning "seeing" one indicates the meaning of "knowing" for that reason. But that is not, although it is permissible in seeing for the reason we have described, permissible in knowing, so that by mentioning the report about "knowing" one indicates "seeing." That is because a person may know many things that he has not seen and does not see, and it is impossible for him to see something without knowing it, as we have already set out the explanation [of it]. [[An addition required by its context.] Moreover, it is not found in any of the Arabs' speech that one says "I knew such-and-such" meaning "I saw it." Rather, it is permissible to direct the meanings of what is in the Book of God, which He sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ), of speech, toward what is found similarly in the speech of the Arabs, and not toward what is not found in their speech. So "ra'aytu" in the sense of "'alimtu" (I saw, meaning I knew) is found in their speech, while "'alimtu" in the sense of "ra'aytu" (I knew, meaning I saw) is not found in their speech. Thus it is permissible to direct "except that We might know" toward the meaning "except that We might see."

* *

Others said: It was said: "except that We might know," because the hypocrites, the Jews, and the disbelievers in God denied that God, may His mention be exalted, knows a thing before its existence. They said, when it was said to them that some people among the people of the qibla would turn back on their heels when the qibla of Muhammad (ﷺ) was turned to the Ka'ba: "That will not happen!" Or they said: "That is false!" When God did that, turned the qibla, and those who disbelieved on account of that disbelieved, God, may His praise be great, said: "I did not do it except that We might know what your knowledge does not know [i.e. what is known to none of you], O polytheists who deny My knowledge of what is to exist of things before its existence": that I am knowing of what will exist of what has not yet been. [[In the printed edition: "except that We might know what is with you..." and this makes the sentence unsound and not understandable. I saw that the context before it shows that it is as I have set down, for the believers knew that some people would apostatize if the qibla was turned, and the Jews and hypocrites denied that this would happen. So the context required that the interpretation combine this knowledge from those and that denial from those. Then al-Tabari came with a wording that corrects what I have gone to in his words: "except to make clear to you that We know." So the meaning of the verse according to the speaker of this view is: We did not make the qibla which you used to face, and except for the knowledge that We know who follows the Messenger. . .]]

So the meaning of the speakers of this view in the interpretation of His words "except that We might know" is: except that We might make clear to you that We know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels. And this, although it is a view that has a way out, is far from what is understood.

* *

Others said: It was said: "except that We might know," and He is knowing of it before its existence and in every state, on the basis of kindness toward His servants and winning them over to His obedience [[In the printed edition: "on the basis of kindness (tarfiq)" and this is an error]], as He, may His praise be great, said: ﴿Say: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? Say: God. And indeed we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾ [Surat Saba': 24]. He knows that he is upon guidance and that they are upon clear error, but He was gentle with them in the address, and did not say: "We are upon guidance and you are upon error." Likewise His words "except that We might know" mean, according to them: except that you might know, since you were ignorant of it before it existed. So He attributed the knowledge to Himself, out of gentleness toward their address.

* *

We have already made clear the statement which is more fitting in that to the truth.

* *

As for His words: "who follows the Messenger," He means: the one who follows Muhammad (ﷺ) in what God commands him, so he turns toward the direction toward which Muhammad (ﷺ) turns.

* *

As for His words: "from who turns back on his heels," He means: the one who turns back from his religion, so that he becomes a hypocrite, or disbelieves, or opposes Muhammad (ﷺ) in that, among those who outwardly show following, as:

2209 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words: "And We did not make the qibla which you used to face except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels," he said: It is the one who, when doubt enters him, turns back from God and becomes a disbeliever on his heels.

* *

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 143 (part 4 of 4)**

The original root of "al-murtadd ʿalā ʿaqibayh" (the one who turns back on his heels) is "al-munqalib ʿalā ʿaqibayh": one who returns backwards, retracing the path he had already traversed and turning away from it. This phrase is used of anyone who turns back from something he was engaged in, whether a religion or a good deed. Among its uses is the words of Allah: ﴿So they both retraced their steps, following their own tracks﴾ [Surah al-Kahf: 64], meaning they returned along the path they had taken. The apostate is called "murtadd" because he turns back from his religion and the creed he had been upon.

It is said "rajaʿa ʿalā ʿaqibayh" (he returned upon his heels) because he returns backwards upon his heels, to the direction in which he had begun his journey before turning back from it. This is therefore made a parable for everyone who abandons one thing and takes up another, when he turns away from what he had been in, toward that which he had abandoned and then taken up again. It is said: "Fulan turned back on his heels (irtadda) and reversed upon his heels (inqalaba ʿalā ʿaqibayh)."

* * *

**On the interpretation of Allah's words: ﴿And indeed it was a great matter, except for those whom Allah guided﴾**

Abu Jaʿfar (al-Tabari) said: The exegetes differed concerning what Allah, may He be exalted, described as having been "a great matter, except for those whom Allah guided."

Some said: By "al-kabira" (the great matter) He, may His praise be exalted, meant the turning away from Bayt al-Maqdis toward the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram) and the change of direction. The feminine form "kabira" was used because "al-tawliya" (the turning) is feminine.

Those who said this include:

2210. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Allah's words "And indeed it was a great matter, except for those whom Allah guided" mean: its change (taḥwīl).

2211. Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa ibn Maymun narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning the words of Allah, mighty and majestic: "And indeed it was a great matter, except for those whom Allah guided," he said: [it refers to] what they were commanded regarding the shift to the Kaʿba from Bayt al-Maqdis.

2212. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

2213. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatada concerning His words: "Indeed it was a great matter, except for those whom Allah guided," he said: It was a great matter when the qibla was changed to the Sacred Mosque, so it was a great matter except for those whom Allah guided.

* * *

Others said: Rather, "al-kabira" is the qibla itself, the very direction which the Prophet (ﷺ) used to face from Bayt al-Maqdis before the change.

Those who said this include:

2214. I was told by ʿAmmar ibn al-Hasan, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ, from Abu al-ʿAliya: "And indeed it was a great matter" — that is, the qibla of Bayt al-Maqdis — "except for those whom Allah guided." [In the printed edition: "from his father from Abu al-ʿAliya," with "from al-Rabiʿ" omitted; this is a circular chain in al-Tabari, the nearest to it being no. 1886.]

Others said: Rather, "al-kabira" is the prayer which they used to perform toward the first qibla.

Those who said this include:

2215. Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "And indeed it was a great matter, except for those whom Allah guided," he said: [It means] your prayer, until Allah, mighty and majestic, guides you to the qibla. [The report 2215 will come complete as 2217, where it reads "guides you to the qibla"; both are correct.]

2216. Yunus related it to me again, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "And indeed it was a great matter," he said: Your prayer here — meaning toward Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen months — and your turning away from here.

* * *

Some grammarians of Basra said: "Al-kabira" is feminine because the qibla is feminine, and it is this that He, may His praise be exalted, meant by His words: "And indeed it was a great matter."

Some grammarians of Kufa said: Rather, "al-kabira" is feminine because of the feminine "al-tawliya" and "al-taḥwīla" (the turning and the change).

So the meaning of the speech according to those who hold this view is: "We did not make your change from the qibla which you were upon, nor our turning you away from it, except that We might know who follows the Messenger from among those who turn back on his heels. And indeed our change of you from it and our turning you away was a great matter, except for those whom Allah guided."

* * *

This interpretation is, in my view, the most correct of the interpretations, because the people found it great that the Prophet (ﷺ) turned his face from the first qibla to the other, not the qibla itself, nor the prayer, since the first qibla and the prayer were not burdensome to them. Unless one takes the feminine "kabira" as referring to "al-qibla" and says that "al-qibla" was mentioned in place of "al-tawliya wa-l-taḥwila" (the turning and the change), because the context indicates that meaning, as we have described for you in similar cases. [See what has preceded in the indexes of the earlier volumes.] Then that would be a sound reading and an understandable interpretation.

* * *

The meaning of "kabira" is "great" [See the explanation of "kabira" above, 2:15.] as follows:

2217. Yunus narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "And indeed it was a great matter, except for those whom Allah guided," he said: [It was] a great matter in the breasts of people, by which Satan enters the son of Adam. He said: "What is wrong with them? They prayed toward here for sixteen months, then they turned away!" So that became great in the breasts of those who neither know nor understand, and of the hypocrites, and they said: "What kind of religion is this?" As for those who believed, Allah, mighty and majestic, made it firm in their hearts. He recited the words of Allah: "And indeed it was a great matter, except for those whom Allah guided," he said: Your prayer, until He guides you to the qibla. [Report 2217: see what preceded as 2215 and the commentary on it.]

* * *

Abu Jaʿfar said: As for His words "except for those whom Allah guided," He means:

"And indeed the turning of you away from the qibla which you were upon is a great matter, except for those whom Allah, mighty and majestic, has granted success, guiding them to believe you, to believe in you and in that, to follow you in it, and in what Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, has revealed to you," as:

2218. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiya ibn Salih related to me, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "And indeed it was a great matter, except for those whom Allah guided," he says: except for the humble ones (al-khashiʿin), meaning those who affirm what Allah, blessed and exalted, has revealed. [Report 2218: I fear this report is the same as the earlier report no. 856.]

* * *

On the interpretation of Allah's words: ﴿And Allah would never make your faith (īmānakum) go to waste﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: It has been said that by "faith" (al-īmān) in this place is meant the prayer.

* * *

The reports transmitted to this effect, and the statement of those who said it:

2219. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Wakiʿ and ʿUbayd Allah narrated to us — and Sufyan ibn Wakiʿ narrated to us, saying: ʿUbayd Allah ibn Musa narrated to us — all of them, from Israʾil, from Simak, from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was turned toward the Kaʿba, they said: "What about those of our brothers who died before that, while they were praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis?" So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste." [Report 2219 is with two chains together: the first is sound, being the narration of Abu Kurayb from Wakiʿ and ʿUbayd Allah ibn Musa; the second is weak, being the narration of Sufyan ibn Wakiʿ from ʿUbayd Allah ibn Musa. ʿUbayd Allah ibn Musa al-ʿAbsi was mentioned at 2092. The hadith was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 3249, from Wakiʿ, from Israʾil, with this chain, similar. He also narrated it in full and in abridged form from several routes from Israʾil: 2691, 2776, 2966. We gave its takhrij there at 2691.]

2220. Ismaʿil ibn Musa related to me, saying: Sharik informed us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Baraʾ concerning the words of Allah, mighty and majestic: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste," he said: Your prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis.

2221. Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Baraʾ, similarly. [Reports 2220–2221 are one hadith with two chains. Al-Suyuti mentioned it at 1:146 and also attributed it to Saʿid ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Abi Hatim.]

2222. Al-Muthanna also related to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Nufayl al-Harrani narrated to us, saying: Zuhayr narrated to us, saying: Abu Ishaq narrated to us, from al-Baraʾ, who said: Men died upon the qibla before it was turned to the House, and some were killed, and we did not know what to say about them. So Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, revealed: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste." [Report 2222: ʿAbd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Nufayl is ʿAbd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Nufayl, Abu Jaʿfar al-Nufayli al-Harrani, the trustworthy, reliable, and memorizing transmitter, biographied in al-Tahdhib, and in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/159. Zuhayr is Ibn Muʿawiya al-Jaʿfi Abu Khaythama, mentioned at 2144. Abu Ishaq is al-Subaʿi al-Hamdani. The hadith is the remainder of the earlier hadith with this chain: 2153, whose takhrij we explained there.]

2223. Bishr ibn Muʿadh al-ʿAqadi narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatada, who said: Some people said, when the qibla was turned toward the Sacred House: "What about our deeds which we used to perform in our (former) qibla?" So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste."

2224. Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Hammad related to me, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was turned toward the Sacred Mosque, the Muslims said: "Would that we knew about our brothers who died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis! Has Allah accepted from us and from them or not?" So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning them: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste." He said: Your prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis — meaning: "This is one obedience and that is another obedience." [In the printed edition: "when he was turned (tawajjaha)..."; see what preceded at 2204 and the commentary on it. Report 2224: it passed as 2164, then 2204, and here it has an addition.]

2225. I was told by ʿAmmar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ, who said: Some people said, when the qibla was turned to the Sacred House: "What about our deeds which we used to perform in our first qibla?" So Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, revealed: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste," the verse.

2226. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Dawud ibn Abi ʿAsim informed me, saying: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was turned toward the Kaʿba, the Muslims said: "Our companions who used to pray toward Bayt al-Maqdis have perished!" So it was revealed: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste."

2227. Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to us, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste," he says: Your prayer which you prayed before the qibla was (changed). The believers had been apprehensive for those among them who had prayed, that their prayers would not be accepted.

2228. Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste," your prayer.

2229. Muhammad ibn Ismaʿil al-Fazari narrated to us, saying: al-Muʾammal informed us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Saʿid narrated to us, from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab concerning this verse: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste," he said: Your prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis.

* * *

Abu Jaʿfar said: We have already shown in what preceded that "al-īmān" (faith) means "tasdiq" (affirmation/belief), and that affirmation may be by speech alone, by action alone, or by both together. [See what preceded at 1:234–235 and elsewhere; seek it in the index of language terms.]

So the meaning of His words "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste," according to what the reports have been unanimous upon, that it is the prayer, is: "Allah would never make the affirmation of His Messenger, peace be upon him, go to waste through your prayer which you performed toward Bayt al-Maqdis in obedience to his command, because that was from you an affirmation of My messenger, and following My command, and obedience from you to Me."

* * *

He (Allah) said: "And the waste of it" — may His praise be exalted — if He had wasted it, would be: abandoning the rewarding of His companions and those who worked upon it, so that it would perish in vain and become null, like the "waste of a man's wealth," and that means destroying it in a matter from which he receives no recompense, either in this world or the next.

* * *

Allah, may His praise be exalted, thus informed that He would not nullify the work of a worker who performed a deed for Him, which was an obedience to Him, so that He would not reward him for it, even if that obligation were abrogated after the worker had performed it, in accordance with what He had enjoined upon him of his work.

* * *

If someone says: How did Allah, may His praise be exalted, say: "And Allah would never make your faith go to waste," attributing the faith to the living addressees, when the people addressed had been apprehensive about their brothers who had died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and this verse was revealed concerning their situation?

It is said: Although the people were apprehensive about that, they were also apprehensive that the reward of their prayers which they had prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis before the change to the Kaʿba would be cancelled, and they thought their deed had become null and gone to waste. So Allah, may His praise be exalted, revealed this verse at that time, directing the address to the living, and the dead among them were included. For it is the custom of the Arabs, when in a report both the addressed and the absent are gathered, that they give precedence to the addressed, and the absent is included in the address. So they say to a man whom they address, while speaking about him and about another absent person who is not present: "We did such-and-such to you two, and we made such-and-such for you two," in the manner of their address to both of them while both are present. And they do not consider it permissible to say: "We did this to both of them," while they are addressing one of them, thereby returning the addressee to the category of the absent. [Al-ghayb (with two vowels) is the plural of ghaʾib (absent), like khadim and khadam.]

* * *

On the interpretation of Allah's words: ﴿Indeed Allah is, toward mankind, Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾ (143)

Abu Jaʿfar said: By His words, may His praise be exalted: "Indeed Allah is, toward mankind, Most Kind, Most Merciful," He means: that Allah is possessed of compassion toward all His servants.

* * *
