"Al-raʾfa" (compassion/tenderness) is the highest meaning of mercy, and it is general to all creation in this world, and to some of them in the next.

* * *

As for "al-Rahim" (the Merciful), He is the one who has mercy upon the believers in this world and the next, as we have explained earlier. [See what preceded at 1:126–134.]

* * *

He, may His praise be exalted, intended by this that Allah, mighty and majestic, is more merciful to His servants than to let go to waste an obedience they performed for Him without rewarding them for it, and more tender toward them than to hold them accountable for abandoning what He had not obligated upon them — that is: "Do not grieve over your dead who died while praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis." Indeed, I (shall reward) them for their obedience to Me through their prayers which they prayed in that manner, for I am more merciful toward them than to waste a deed they performed for Me. And do not grieve over them, for I shall not hold them accountable for abandoning the prayer toward the Kaʿba, since I had not obligated that upon them, and I am more tender toward My creatures than to punish them for abandoning what I had not commanded them to do.

* * *

As for "al-Raʾuf" (the Compassionate), it has several readings. One is "raʾuf" in the pattern of "faʿul," as al-Walid ibn ʿUqba said:

"And the worst of the seekers — and do not be him — is the slayer of his paternal uncle, the Compassionate, the Merciful."

[In the printed edition it read "al-Raʾuf al-Rahima" with a final alif; the correct reading is in al-Qurtubi 2:145 and Abu Hayyan 1:427, which both contain another error: the first has "yuqatil" and the second "yuqabil." It seems this verse is from a poem by al-Walid ibn ʿUqba, who wrote to Muʿawiya urging Muʿawiya to fight ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both. It is found in Ansab al-Ashraf: 140, Tarikh al-Tabari 5:236–237, Hamasat al-Buhturi: 30, al-Lisan (h-l-m), and elsewhere, but this verse is not in them. It may have come before the verse which says: "Woe to you! Hurl it upon them, for the best of those who seek vengeance is the one who is violent." His words "do not be him" are a supplication for him and a disapproval that he be like this seeker who rebels, demanding the blood of his uncle, while being compassionate and merciful toward his enemy and the slayer of his uncle, and he is the worst of avengers.]

It is the reading of the majority of the readers of Kufa. Another is "raʾuf" in the pattern of "faʿul" (raʾūf), which is the reading of the majority of the readers of Medina. And "raʾif," which is the dialect of Ghatafan, in the pattern of "faʿil," like "hadhir." And "ra'f" in the pattern of "faʿl," with the ʿayn vowelless, which is the dialect of Banu Asad.

The recitation is according to one of the first two forms.

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven; so We will surely turn you to a qibla (direction of prayer) that you will be pleased with. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: "We have certainly seen, O Muhammad, Our turning of your face toward the heaven."

* *

By "al-taqallub" (the turning) is meant the changing and the redirecting.

By His words "in the heaven" is meant toward the heaven and its direction.

* *

It was said to him (ﷺ), according to what has reached us, because before the change of his qibla from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) to the Ka'bah, he used to raise his gaze to the heaven, awaiting from Allah, may His praise be exalted, His command to change toward the Ka'bah, as related:

2230. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words, "We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven": He (ﷺ) used to turn his face toward the heaven, wishing that Allah, mighty and majestic, would turn it toward the Ka'bah, until Allah turned it toward it.

2231. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His words, "We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven": The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray toward Bayt al-Maqdis, while he was longing for and desiring the qibla toward the Sacred House, so Allah, may His praise be exalted, turned him toward the qibla that he longed for and desired.

2232. Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ishaq narrated to me, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to me, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning His words, "We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven," he says: your looking toward the heaven. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to turn his face during the prayer while he was praying toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and he was longing for the qibla of the Sacred House, so Allah turned him to a qibla that he longed for.

2233. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: The people used to pray facing Bayt al-Maqdis. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah, eighteen months after his migration, whenever he prayed he would raise his head to the heaven, looking for what he would be commanded. He used to pray facing Bayt al-Maqdis, and then the Ka'bah abrogated it (nasakha-ha). So the Prophet (ﷺ) loved to pray facing the Ka'bah, and Allah, may His praise be exalted, revealed: "We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven," to the end of the verse.

* *

Then they differed concerning the reason for which he (ﷺ) longed for the qibla of the Ka'bah.

Some of them said: He disliked the qibla of Bayt al-Maqdis because the Jews said: "He follows our qibla and opposes us in our religion!"

Those who said this:

2234. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, who said: The Jews said: "Muhammad opposes us, and follows our qibla!" So he would supplicate to Allah, may His praise be exalted, and would seek to have the qibla made obligatory for him [[In the printed edition: "yasta'rid lil-qiblah" (seeks to display for the qibla); I have confirmed what is in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:147. The word "yastafrid" means he asks that its obligation be imposed upon him and upon the believers. This is not attested in the lexicographical books, but it is correct Arabic. As for "yasta'rid lil-qiblah," it is nothing.]]. Then it was revealed: "We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven; so We will surely turn you to a qibla that you will be pleased with. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque," and the saying of the Jews, "He opposes us and follows our qibla!" ceased. [This was] in the midday prayer [[The construction of his wording: "fa-nazalat... fi salat al-zuhr" (then it was revealed... in the midday prayer).]]. So he made the men take the place of the women, and the women take the place of the men.

2235. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: I heard him (i.e., Ibn Zayd) say: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, said to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "Wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "These are the people of the Jews, who face a house from the houses of Allah, namely Bayt al-Maqdis; if only we had faced it!" So the Prophet (ﷺ) faced it for sixteen months. Then it reached him that the Jews were saying: "By Allah, Muhammad and his companions did not know where their qibla was until we guided them!" [[In the printed edition: "ma daraa Muhammad (ﷺ)," which the Jews did not say, so I have corrected it. Likewise it came in no. 1838.]] So the Prophet (ﷺ) disliked that, and he raised his face to the heaven, and Allah, may His praise be exalted, said: "We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven; so We will surely turn you to a qibla that you will be pleased with. So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque," to the end of the verse. [[The report: 2235. Passed previously as no. 1838.]]

* *

Others said: Rather, he longed for that because it was the qibla of his father Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

Those who said this:

2236. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to us, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) migrated to Madinah, and most of its people were Jews, Allah, mighty and majestic, commanded him to face Bayt al-Maqdis. The Jews rejoiced, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) faced it for sixteen months. But the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved the qibla of Ibrahim, so he would supplicate and look toward the heaven. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: "We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven," to the end of the verse. [[The report: 2236. Passed previously as nos. 1833 and 2160.]]

* *

As for His words, "so We will surely turn you to a qibla that you will be pleased with," it means: We will surely turn you away from Bayt al-Maqdis to a qibla "that you will be pleased with": that you will desire and love. [[See the meanings of "wallā" in what has passed, 2:162, 535, and in this part, 3:131.]]

* *

As for His words, "So turn your face," it means: turn your face and redirect it.

* *

And His words, "toward the Sacred Mosque," mean: by "shatr" (toward), the direction, the intent, and the facing, as the Hudhali poet said: [[He is Qays ibn al-'Izarah al-Hudhali. "Al-'Izarah" is his mother, and his name is Qays ibn Khuwaylid ibn Kahil.]]

*Indeed the difficult-birthing she-camel, with a disease mingling with her... her direction is a gaze of two eyes, exhausted.* [[His diwan in Ash'ar al-Hudhaliyyin by al-Sukkari: 261 (Europe); Risalat al-Shafi'i: 35, 487; Sirah of Ibn Hisham 2:200; al-Kamil 1:12, 2:3; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubaydah: 60; Lisan al-'Arab (shatr, hasar), and others. The version in al-Shafi'i's Risalah reads "inna al-'asib" with a ba' at its end, and the version in his diwan and Ibn Hisham reads "inna al-nu'us." Al-'Asir: the one who makes her tail difficult when pregnant, from her ferocity. Al-Nu'us: the one who closes her eyes at milking. Al-'Asib: the palm frond when its leaves are stripped off. I believe he did not describe the she-camel by any of these three words, but rather it is the name of his she-camel. All of them could be names for a she-camel. Ibn Hisham said: "Al-nu'us: his she-camel, and she had a disease, so he looked at her with a gaze of exhaustion (hasir), from his saying, 'and he is exhausted.'" It is also narrated: "dā' yukhāmiruhā fa-nahwahā..." His diwan's version is "makhzur." "Mahsur" is the hasir, the one who has grown weary and tired. "Makhzur" comes from the saying "kharaza basaruhu" (his sight squinted): when he drew his eyelids together and looked with the corner of his eye. He is describing his she-camel and mentioning his sorrow and love for her; he is concerned about her because of the disease that has mingled with her, and he prolongs his gaze at her until his eyes become exhausted and weary.]]

By His words "shatrahā" is meant: toward her. And as Ibn Ahmar said:

*They run with us toward Jam', while she is tying her tail, as the tying has nearly reached the saddle-strap (haqab) from her speeding.* [[Sirah of Ibn Hisham 2:199; al-Rawd al-Unuf 2:38; al-Khizanah 3:38; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubaydah: 60. In the printed edition: "min infadiha," which is an error. Before it he said: "I began asking him about the state of his companions, so he said: 'Hayyi, for the caravan has grown weary'" ... "Hayyi": hurry. "Nasab": struggled hard in the journey. His saying "Jam'" is Muzdalifah, referring to the Hajj. His saying "'aqidah": that she had bent her tail between her thighs. His saying "kārab": meaning nearly, came close, and drew near. "Awfadat al-naqatu iyfādan": the she-camel hastened. "Al-haqab": the girth with which the saddle is tied on the belly of the camel, on the side near its belly, so that the saddle-hitting does not harm it. He says: They hastened quickly toward Muzdalifah, so she began bending her tail, sealing her vulva with it, until the knot of her tail nearly reached the girth. The she-camel closes her vulva with her tail in her haste. Al-Mukhbil al-Sa'di says: "And when I raised the whip, it frightened her beneath the ribs of a terrified, noble one. And she closes her two haunches with one of the tufted ones, which were barren, and fresh vegetation grew from the barrenness." And al-Muthaqqib al-'Abdi, describing his hastening she-camel, says: "She closes with the lasting one of the drawn-out tail-hair, a thick-haired one, the vulva of a slender, oily she-camel."]]

* *

The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) also said something similar to what we have said on this matter.

Those who said this:

2237. Sufyan ibn Wakf' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from Abu al-'Aliyah: "Shatr al-Masjid al-Haram" means: its direction.

2238. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Shatr al-Masjid al-Haram," its direction.

2239. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words: "So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque," its direction.

2240. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

2241. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah: "So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque," that is, facing the Sacred Mosque.

2242. Al-Husayn ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque," he said: toward the Sacred Mosque.

2243. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque," that is, facing it.

2244. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Juraij said: 'Amr ibn Dinar informed me, from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Shatrahu," toward it.

2245. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hamani narrated to us, saying: Shurayk narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara': "Fa-wallu wujuhakum shatrahu" (So turn your faces toward it). He said: its side.

2246. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "Shatrahu," its side, its flank. He said: and its flanks are "shutur."

[[The report: 2246: it and what precedes it of reports interpret "shatrahu" as: its side, or: toward it. Compare what al-Shafi'i said in al-Risalah, in our edition: 105–111, 1378–1381, which supports this.]]

* *

Then they differed concerning the place toward which Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to turn his face within the Sacred Mosque.

Some of them said: It is the qibla to which the Prophet (ﷺ) was turned, and which Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, meant by His words, "So We will surely turn you to a qibla that you will be pleased with": opposite the spout (mizab) of the Ka'bah.

Those who said this:

2247. 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ziyad narrated to me, saying: 'Uthman narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah informed us, from Ya'la ibn 'Ata', from Yahya ibn Qamtah, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr: "So We will surely turn you to a qibla that you will be pleased with": opposite the spout of the Ka'bah. [[The report: 2247. 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ziyad, the shaykh of al-Tabari: he is attributed to his grandfather. He is "'Abd Allah ibn al-Hakam ibn Abi Ziyad al-Qatawani," and the name of "Abu Ziyad" is "Sulayman." This 'Abd Allah is trustworthy (thiqah); Abu Zur'ah, Abu Hatim, Ibn Khuzaymah and others narrated from him. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib. And Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/38. As for his shaykh "'Uthman," I do not know who he is. The strong likelihood is that it is a distortion, and the correct form is "'Affan."

Yahya ibn Qamtah: a trustworthy Successor (tabi'i). Al-Bukhari biographed him in al-Kabir 4/2/229, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/181, and mentioned that he was a Hijazi, and neither of them mentioned any criticism of him. Al-Bukhari mentioned that he narrates "from Ibn 'Umar." Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned that he narrates "from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr." Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat, p. 371, and said: "He narrates from Ibn 'Umar and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr." Ya'la ibn 'Ata' narrated from him.

His father's name is "Qamtah," with a qaf, then a mim, then an unmarked ta'. I have not found anything that confirms the vocalization of these letters. But it is recorded thus in al-Tabari, in the tafsir of 'Abd al-Razzaq, and in the references for biography. In Ibn Kathir and al-Mustadrak it appears as "Qatah" without the mim. This is an error, because it contradicts what we mentioned from the references.

The hadith was also narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:269, through Muslim ibn Ibrahim, from Shu'bah, with this chain, in a longer version similar to the narration after this one. Al-Hakim said: "This is a hadith with a sound chain, though they (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not include it." Al-Dhahabi agreed with him.]]

2248. And al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Ya'la ibn 'Ata', from Yahya ibn Qamtah, who said: I saw 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr sitting in the Sacred Mosque opposite the spout, and he recited this verse: "So We will surely turn you to a qibla that you will be pleased with." He said: This is the qibla; this is the qibla.

2249. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, with his chain from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, similar, except that he said: He faced the spout and said: This is the qibla that Allah said to His Prophet: "So We will surely turn you to a qibla that you will be pleased with." [[The two reports: 2248, 2249: these are two other chains for the hadith before them. The first of them is from the narration of 'Abd al-Razzaq, from Hushaym, from Ya'la ibn 'Ata'.

Hushaym (diminutive): he is Ibn Bashir, with a fatha on the ba' (mu-wahhadah) and a kasra on the shin. He is Abu Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Khazim, a hafiz, trustworthy and firm. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/242, Ibn Sa'd 7/2/61, 70, Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/115–116, and Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 1:229–230.

The hadith is in the tafsir of 'Abd al-Razzaq, p. 13, with this chain. And it does not have the word "hiya" (it is) added here after "this is the qibla." I fear that its addition is neither good nor established.

Ibn Kathir 1:352 mentions that Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it "from al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah, from Hushaym, from Ya'la ibn 'Ata'." The name "Hushaym" in it appears distorted, and it is corrected from this place.

The hadith is also in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:147, and he attributed it additionally to Ibn Abi Shaybah, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad ibn Mani' in his Musnad, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir. It is in Majma' al-Zawa'id 6:316, and he said: "al-Tabarani narrated it through two routes, and the narrators of one of them are trustworthy."]]

* *

Others said: Rather, that whole House is a qibla, and the qibla of the House is the door.

Those who said this:

2250. Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: The whole House is a qibla, and this is the qibla of the House, meaning the one in which is the door. [[The report: 2250. al-Suyuti narrated it, 1:147, from al-Tabari alone, with the wording: "The whole House is a qibla, and the qibla of the House is the door."]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct position on this matter, in my view, is what Allah, may His praise be exalted, said: "So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque." So the one who turns his face toward the Sacred Mosque is the one who hits the qibla. Rather, what is required of the one whose intention is directed toward it in his heart is that he is facing it, just as the one who follows an imam is only required to follow him, even if his body is not directly opposite the imam's body, and even if he is at the end of the row while the imam is at the other end, to his right or to his left, provided that the one behind him is following him and praying toward the direction in which the imam prays. Likewise the rule of the qibla: even if not every worshipper and one who faces it is directly opposite it with his body, he is nonetheless facing it. If one is to its right or its left, opposite it, then he is facing it, however far or near he is from it, to its right or its left, provided that he is not turning his back to it, nor deviating from it with his body and face, as related:

2251. Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Isra'il informed us, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Umayrah ibn Ziyad al-Kindi, from 'Ali: "So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque," he said: its direction, its side. [[The report: 2251. Abu Ishaq: he is al-Sabi'i al-Hamdani.

'Umayrah (with a fatha on the 'ayn) ibn Ziyad al-Kindi: a trustworthy Successor. Ibn Sa'd biographed him in al-Tabaqat 6:141, and said: "He narrated from 'Abd Allah." He meant by that 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud. Al-Bukhari biographed him in al-Kabir 4/1/69, and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/24. Neither of them mentioned any criticism of him, nor a narration from anyone other than Ibn Mas'ud. They both mentioned that the one who narrates from him is Abu Ishaq.

The hadith was narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:269, through Muhammad ibn Kathir, from Sufyan (that is, al-Thawri), from Abu Ishaq, with this chain. Al-Hakim said: "This is a hadith with a sound chain, though they did not include it." Al-Dhahabi agreed with him. Likewise al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Sunan al-Kubra, vol. 2, p. 3, from al-Hakim.

al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1:147, and additionally attributed it to 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Dinawari in al-Mujalasah.

Ibn Kathir mentioned it, 1:268, quoting from al-Hakim.]]

Tabari's wording in all of them is: "He said: 'Its side is before it'" (shatruhu qablahu), as we have established. In the printed edition here, however, it reads: "He said: 'Its side is among us, a qiblah'!!" This is a ridiculous error, from a copyist or a typesetter.

In the chain of narration in Ibn Kathir, "Muhammad ibn Ishaq" appears instead of "Abu Ishaq." This is an error, contradicting what is established here and what is established in all other sources.

In Ibn Kathir, al-Mustadrak and its abridgment by al-Dhahabi (both printed and manuscript), "Umayr ibn Ziyad" appears. This too is an error. It is correctly given in al-Bayhaqi's narration from al-Hakim.]]
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The qiblah of the House is its door, as in:
2252 - Yaqub ibn Ibrahim and al-Fadl ibn al-Sabbah told me, both saying: Hushaym told us, saying: Abd al-Malik informed us, from Ata, who said: Usama ibn Zayd said: "I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ when he came out of the House, he turned his face toward the door and said: 'This is the qiblah, this is the qiblah.'" [[Hadith 2252 - al-Fadl ibn al-Sabbah al-Baghdadi: trustworthy (thiqah); Ibn Ma'in declared him trustworthy. Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi said: "He was one of the best of God's servants." Biographed in al-Tahdhib, and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/63.
Abd al-Malik: he is Ibn Abi Sulayman al-Arzami, passed at 1455.
Ata: he is Ibn Abi Rabah, the great Tabi'i, the proof, the authority of knowledge, mufti and muhaddith of the people of Makkah. Biographed in al-Tahdhib; Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/330-331; Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 1:92-93; Tarikh al-Islam 4:278-280; Ibn Sa'd 2/2/133-134 and 5:344-346.
Usama ibn Zayd ibn Harithah: he is the beloved of the Messenger of God ﷺ and the son of his beloved.
Abu Hatim, as related from him by his son in al-Marasil (p. 57), claimed that Ata did not hear from Usama. However, the following narration contains Ata's explicit statement of hearing from him. Moreover, contemporaneity is sufficient to establish continuity, as is the preponderant view among the scholars of hadith.
Ata was born in 27 AH and died in 114 AH. Al-Dhahabi even mentioned that he died at 90 years of age. Usama ibn Zayd died in 54 AH; Mus'ab al-Zubayri dated his death at the end of Mu'awiyah's caliphate, in 58 or 59 AH.
This hadith was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (5:209), from Hushaym, with this chain and wording. Then he narrated it after it, with the same chain, in a fuller form, similar in meaning.]]
2253 - Ibn Humayd and Sufyan ibn Waki' told us, both saying: Jarir told us, from Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman, from Ata, who said: "Usama ibn Zayd told me, saying: The Prophet ﷺ came out of the House and prayed two rak'ahs facing the Ka'bah with his face, and said: 'This is the qiblah,' twice." [[Hadith 2253 - Ibn Humayd: he is Muhammad ibn Humayd ibn Hayyan al-Razi, the hafiz. Tabari's narration from him has been cited many times before, and we authenticated him at 2028. We add here that Ibn Ma'in and others declared him trustworthy, and some disputed certain hadiths from him; Ibn Ma'in answered that "these hadiths he narrates are not from him, but from the shaykhs from whom he narrates them." al-Khalili said: "He was a hafiz and scholar of this discipline; Ahmad and Yahya approved of him." Abd Allah ibn Ahmad presented to his father what he had written from him, and he said: "As for his narrations from Ibn al-Mubarak and Jarir, they are sound; as for his narrations from the people of al-Ray, he is more knowledgeable." Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 1/1/69-70, Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/232-233, al-Khatib 2:259-264, Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 2:67-69.
Jarir: he is Ibn Abd al-Hamid ibn Qurt al-Razi, a trustworthy proof. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir of al-Bukhari 1/2/214, Ibn Sa'd 7/2/110, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/505-507, al-Khatib 7:253-261, Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 1:250.
This is a sound chain, in which Ata explicitly states hearing from Usama ibn Zayd, as was noted in the previous chain.
This hadith was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (5:210), within a story, from Yahya, meaning al-Qattan, from Abd al-Malik: "Ata narrated to us, from Usama ibn Zayd."]]
2254 - Abu Kurayb told us, saying: Abd al-Rahim ibn Sulayman told us, from Abd al-Malik, from Ata, from Usama ibn Zayd, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, something similar. [[Hadith 2254 - Abd al-Rahim ibn Sulayman: he is al-Marwazi al-Ashall, whose biography has passed at 2030. This hadith is a repetition of the previous one, but in this chain Ata's hearing from Usama is not explicitly stated.]]
2255 - Sa'id ibn Yahya al-Umawi told us, saying: My father told us, saying: Ibn Jurayj told us, saying: I said to Ata: "Did you hear Ibn Abbas say: 'You were only commanded to circumambulate, and you were not commanded to enter it'?" He said: "He did not forbid entering it, but I heard him say: 'Usama ibn Zayd told me that the Messenger of God ﷺ, when he entered the House, supplicated in all its corners, and did not pray until he came out. When he came out, he prayed two rak'ahs facing the qiblah and said: "This is the qiblah."'" [[Hadith 2255 - Sa'id ibn Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Umawi: trustworthy and firm; indeed Ali ibn al-Madini said: "A group of sons are more firm in our view than their fathers... and this Sa'id ibn Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Umawi is firmer than his father." He is among the shaykhs of al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Zur'ah and Abu Hatim. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/1/477, Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/74, al-Khatib 9:90-91. His father, Yahya ibn Sa'id ibn Aban ibn Sa'id ibn al-As: a trustworthy hafiz. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/277, Ibn Sa'd 6:277-278 and 7/2/80-81, Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/151-152, al-Khatib 14:132-135, Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 1:298.
This hadith was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (5:208), from Abd al-Razzaq and Rawh, both from Ibn Jurayj, with this chain, similar in meaning.
He had narrated it earlier (p. 201) from Abd al-Razzaq alone, in abridged form, omitting the story.
Nothing in this hadith negates that Ata heard the hadith from Usama ibn Zayd, because here he is only answering the questioner about the statement of Ibn Abbas and negating that Ibn Abbas forbade entering the House. Therefore he mentions Ibn Abbas's narration from Usama for this purpose. This does not preclude that the hadith was known to Ata directly from Usama.
This hadith is also narrated by Muslim (1:376-377), through Muhammad ibn Bakr, from Ibn Jurayj, with this chain, similar to this story, slightly longer.
Al-Bukhari narrated it (1:420-421, Fath al-Bari), through Abd al-Razzaq, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ata, from Ibn Abbas, in abridged form. He did not mention the story, nor that it was from Usama; he made it a hadith of Ibn Abbas. The hafiz mentioned that al-Isma'ili and Abu Nu'aym narrated it in their collections, through Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, from Abd al-Razzaq, with this chain, making it "a narration of Ibn Abbas from Usama ibn Zayd." The hafiz said: "And this is the more probable."
The disagreement over whether the Messenger of God ﷺ prayed inside the Ka'bah or not is mentioned in the major collections. The preponderant view is that he prayed in it, since an affirmation takes precedence over a negation. See Nasb al-Raya 2:319-322.]]
* *
Abu Ja'far said: Thus he ﷺ informed that the House is the qiblah, and that the qiblah of the House is its door.
* *
On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾
Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means by this: Wherever you are on the earth, O believers, turn your faces in your prayer toward the Sacred Mosque and toward its direction.
The "ha'" in "shatrah" refers to the Sacred Mosque.
By this verse, He, may His praise be exalted, made obligatory upon the believers the fard (obligation) of facing the Sacred Mosque in their prayer wherever they are in God's earth, may He be blessed and exalted.
The "fa'" was introduced in His words "fa-wallu," as a response to the conditional. This is because His words "wherever you are" are a condition, and its meaning is: wherever you may be, turn your faces toward it.
* *
On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾
He, may His praise be exalted, by His words "And indeed those who were given the Scripture" means the rabbis of the Jews and the scholars of the Christians.
* *
It has also been said: He meant by this only the Jews.
Those who said this:
2256 - Musa ibn Harun told us, saying: Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "And indeed those who were given the Scripture" was revealed concerning the Jews.
* *
His words "they know that it is the truth from their Lord" mean: these rabbis and scholars of the People of the Book know that facing the mosque is the truth which God, exalted is He, prescribed for Abraham, his descendants, and all His servants after him.
* *
His words "from their Lord" mean that it is the obligation imposed upon the servants of God, may He be remembered, and it is the truth from their Lord, which He prescribed for them.
* *
On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And God is not unaware of what they do﴾ (144)
Abu Ja'far said: He, may He be blessed and exalted, means by this: And God is not unaware of what you do, O believers, in your obedience to His command and your submission to His obedience in what He has obligated upon you of His duties, and your faith in Him in your prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis, and then your prayer after that toward the direction of the Sacred Mosque; nor is He heedless of it. [[See the explanation of "heedless" in what has passed, 2:243-244, 315, and this part 3:127.]] Rather, He, may His praise be exalted, counts it for you, stores it up for you with Him, until He recompenses you for it with the best recompense and rewards you with the best reward.
* *
On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if you were to bring those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah, nor are you a follower of their qiblah, nor are some of them followers of the qiblah of others﴾
Abu Ja'far said: He, may His name be blessed, means by this: And if you were to bring, O Muhammad, to the Jews and the Christians every proof and argument, which is the "sign," [[See its explanation in what has passed, 1:106 / 2:553.]] showing that the truth is what you brought them, namely the obligation of turning from the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis in prayer to the qiblah of the Sacred Mosque, they would not have believed it, nor would they have followed your qiblah, to which I turned you, which is facing the Sacred Mosque, even with the establishment of the proof against them in this regard.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: "La'in" (if indeed) was followed by the past tense of the verb, though its ruling is that it takes a future response, likening it to "law" (if), so it takes the response that "law" takes, because of the closeness of their meanings.
The explanation of a similar case has passed earlier. [[See what has passed, 2:458, and see Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:84.]] "Law" takes the response of oaths. The Arabs do this only in conditionals specifically, because the conditional resembles the oath: each of them is not complete in its beginning except by its end, is not complete alone, and is not valid except with what confirms it after it. So when it begins with an oath and it is introduced upon the conditional, the first "lam" takes the place of an oath, and the second takes the place of its response, as it is said: "La-'umrka la-taqumanna" (By your life, you will surely stand), when the "lam" of "la-'umrka" became frequent until it became like a letter of its letters, so it takes the response that oaths take, since the "lam" in oaths substitutes for the oath itself, unlike the other letters, which are more appropriate for the oath. It indicates the oath and functions as the responses do, and the other responses of oaths do not indicate the oath for us. [[The phrase "ajwibat al-ayman lana 'ala al-aymān" is an obscure expression; I have not found a reading for it that I can accept, and I have no doubt that it is corrupted or deficient.] So the "lam" that is in the response of oaths was likened to the oath, for what we have described, and so it takes their responses.
* *
Thus the meaning of the speech, given that the matter is as we have described, is: "Even if you brought those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah."
* *
As for His words "nor are you a follower of their qiblah," He says: nor do you have any way, O Muhammad, to follow their qiblah. This is because the Jews pray facing Bayt al-Maqdis, and the Christians face the east; how could you have a way to follow their qiblah, with their directions differing? He says: So hold to your qiblah, to which you were commanded to turn, and leave aside what the Jews and Christians say and what they call you to of their qiblah and facing it.
* *
As for His words "nor are some of them followers of the qiblah of others," He means by it: the Jews do not follow the qiblah of the Christians, nor do the Christians follow the qiblah of the Jews, but each faces its own, as:
2257 - Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "Nor are some of them followers of the qiblah of others." He says: The Jews are not followers of the qiblah of the Christians, nor the Christians followers of the qiblah of the Jews. He said: This verse was revealed because when the Prophet ﷺ was turned toward the Ka'bah, the Jews said: "Muhammad has longed for the land of his father and birth! If he had remained on our qiblah, we would have hoped that he is the one we are awaiting!" So God, exalted is He, revealed concerning them: "And indeed those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord," up to His words "They conceal the truth while they know." [[The report: 2257 - see what has passed, no. 2204.]]
2258 - Yunus told us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words "nor are some of them followers of the qiblah of others": like that.
* *
God, exalted is He, means by this: the Jews and the Christians do not unite upon one qiblah, while each faction maintains its own religion. So He, may His praise be exalted, said to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: O Muhammad, do not make yourself hope for the pleasure of these Jews and Christians, for this is a matter with no way to it. Since their religions differ, you have no way to please each faction among them. For if you follow the qiblah of the Jews, you will anger the Christians, and if you follow the qiblah of the Christians, you will anger the Jews. So leave what has no way to it, and call them to what has a way to it: unity upon your upright Islamic religion, and your qiblah, the qiblah of Abraham and the prophets after him.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 145:

The explanation of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, indeed you would then be among the wrongdoers﴾ (2:145).

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "And if you were to follow their desires," [He means]: If you, O Muhammad, were to seek the approval of these Jews and Christians, who said to you and your companions, "Be Jews or Christians and you will be guided," and you were to follow their qibla, that is, you were to turn back to their qibla.

By His saying, "after the knowledge that has come to you," [He means]: after the knowledge has reached you, through My informing you that they persist in falsehood, out of enmity toward the truth and with their own awareness that the qibla toward which I have turned you is the qibla that I prescribed for your forefather Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and for all his descendants among the messengers after him, namely turning toward it. "Indeed, you would then be among the wrongdoers" means: indeed, if you did that, you would be among the servants who wrong themselves, who oppose My command and abandon My obedience, and you would be counted among them. [[Context: "from among the wrongdoing servants... and he is among them."]]

Tafsir of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognise it as they recognise their own sons﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words "Those to whom We gave the Book recognise it", He, may His praise be lofty, means the rabbis of the Jews and the scholars of the Christians. He says: these rabbis from among the Jews and these scholars from among the Christians recognise that the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram) is their qibla, and the qibla of Abraham and the qibla of the prophets before you, "as they recognise their own sons". As follows:

2259 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, concerning His words "Those to whom We gave the Book recognise it as they recognise their own sons", he said: they recognise that the Sacred House is the qibla.

2260 - Al-Muthanna narrated to us: Ishaq narrated to us: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "Those to whom We gave the Book recognise it as they recognise their own sons", he means: the qibla.

2261 - It was related to me from Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' concerning His words: "Those to whom We gave the Book recognise it as they recognise their own sons", they knew that the qibla of the Sacred House is their qibla, which they were commanded to face, just as they knew their sons.

2262 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me: my father narrated to me: my paternal uncle narrated to me: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: "Those to whom We gave the Book recognise it as they recognise their own sons", he means by that: the Ka'bah, the Sacred House.

2263 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Those to whom We gave the Book recognise it as they recognise their own sons", they recognise the Ka'bah from the qibla of the prophets, as they recognise their sons. [[In the printed edition: "they recognise the Ka'bah from the qibla of the prophets".]]

2264 - Yunus narrated to me: Ibn Wahb informed us: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words: "Those to whom We gave the Book recognise it as they recognise their own sons", he said: the Jews recognise that it is the qibla, Makkah.

2265 - Al-Qasim narrated to us: al-Husayn narrated to us: Hajjaj narrated to me: Ibn Jurayj said, concerning His words: "Those to whom We gave the Book recognise it as they recognise their own sons", he said: the qibla and the House.

* *

Tafsir of the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed a party of them conceal the truth while they know﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be lofty, says: And indeed a group of those who were given the Book — and they are the Jews and the Christians. Mujahid used to say: they are the People of the Book.

2266 - Muhammad ibn Amr — meaning al-Bahili — narrated to me: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, with that.

2267 - Al-Qasim narrated to us: al-Husayn narrated to us: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, the like of it.

2268 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, the like of it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for His words "they conceal the truth" — and that truth is the qibla to which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, directed His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). He says: "So turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque" — the qibla which the prophets before Muhammad (ﷺ) used to face. The Jews and the Christians concealed it, so some of them faced east and some faced towards Bayt al-Maqdis, and they abandoned what Allah had commanded them. Along with that, they concealed the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), while they find it written with them in the Torah and the Gospel. So Allah, Blessed and Exalted, informed Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community of their treachery against Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and their treachery against His servants, and their concealment of that. He informed that they do what they do of that with knowledge on their part that the truth is other than it, and that the obligation upon them from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is its opposite. So He said: "they conceal the truth while they know", that it is not permissible for them to conceal it, so that they deliberately disobey Allah, Blessed and Exalted, as follows:

[[From the words "as Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us" up to where we mention in p. 207, note 2, is found in sixteen pages remaining from the lost section of the old manuscript.]]

2269 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "And indeed a party of them conceal the truth while they know", they concealed Muhammad (ﷺ).

2270 - Al-Muthanna narrated to us: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "they conceal the truth while they know", he said: they conceal Muhammad (ﷺ) while they find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel.

2271 - Al-Muthanna narrated to us: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj narrated to us: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "And indeed a party of them conceal the truth while they know", he means the qibla.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters (147).﴾

Abu Ja'far said: His remembrance is exalted, says: [In the printed edition: "Allah, His praise is exalted, says," but I have adhered to the text of the manuscript.] Know, O Muhammad, that the truth is what your Lord has informed you of and brought to you from Him, not what the Jews and Christians say to you.

This is a report from Allah, His remembrance is exalted, to His Prophet, peace be upon him, concerning the fact that the qiblah toward which he turned is the true qiblah, the one upon which Abraham, the Friend of the Merciful (Khalil al-Rahman), and those prophets of Allah, mighty and majestic, after him were upon. [In the printed edition: "And this is from Allah, His remembrance is exalted, a report," but I have adhered to the manuscript.]

His remembrance, exalted, says to him: So act upon the truth that has come to you from your Lord, O Muhammad, and do not be among the doubters.

* *

By His words "so do not be among the doubters," He means: do not be among those who doubt that the qiblah to which I have turned you is the qiblah of Abraham, my friend, peace be upon him, and the qiblah of the prophets other than him, as:

2272 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to me, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: Allah, His remembrance is exalted, said to His Prophet, peace be upon him: "The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters," meaning: do not be in doubt, for it is your qiblah and the qiblah of the prophets before you. [In the printed edition: "Do not be in doubt that it is," with the fa' of "fa-innaha" omitted.]

2273 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "So do not be among the doubters," he said: among the doubters. He said: Do not doubt in that.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The word "al-mumtari" is of the form "mufta'il," derived from "al-mirya," and "al-mirya" means doubt. Among its uses is the verse of al-A'sha:

It runs upon the shins of those who dispute, galloping, when the mirage swells... [Source: his Diwan p. 20, and Lisan al-Arab (r-j-h-n), from a qasidah of which a line appeared earlier at 1:345-346, describing swift, daring horses of Qays ibn Ma'dikarib al-Kindi, which raided a people; while the people were disputing, they suddenly...:
"Its daring warriors outpace the glass, in dust like smoke..."
"It runs upon the shins..." 
The verb "darra al-faras yadurru durayran wa dirrah" means: it ran a very intense run, nothing turned it back. "Al-asw uq" is the plural of "saq" (shin), also pluralized as "suq" and "siqan." He says: while they were disputing, the horses overtook them and struck them down, trampled them with heavy trampling, and passed over their shins at a run. "Arjahanna al-sarab" means it rose, widened, and quivered, which happens at the time of sunrise.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: Was the Prophet ﷺ in doubt that the truth is from his Lord, or that the qiblah to which Allah turned him is true from Allah, His remembrance is exalted, such that he was forbidden from doubting it, so it was said to him: "So do not be among the doubters"?

It is said in reply: That is from the speech that the Arabs use in the form of a command or prohibition addressed to the one spoken to, while the intended meaning is someone else, as His words, mighty and majestic, say: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [Surah al-Ahzab: 1], then He said: (And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord. Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted) [Surah al-Ahzab: 2]. The speech thus takes the form of a command and prohibition to the Prophet ﷺ, while the intended addressees are his believing companions. We have already explained the like of this earlier, enough to dispense with repeating it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 148:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And every one has a direction toward which he turns﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His remembrance, "wa-likull" (and for every...), He means: and for every community of a religion (ahl milla). The phrase "ahl al-milla" (the people of the religion) has been omitted, the context being sufficient to indicate it, as in:

2274 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of God, mighty and majestic, "wa-likulli wijhah," he said: "For every possessor of a religion."

2275 - al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "wa-likull wijhatun huwa muwalliha," so for the Jew there is a direction toward which he turns, and for the Christians a direction toward which they turn, and God, mighty and majestic, has guided you, O community, to the qibla which is the qibla (of truth).

2276 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to 'Ata', "wa-likull wijhah huwa muwalliha": he said, "For every people of a religion, the Jews and the Christians." Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid said, "For every possessor of a religion."

2277 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words, "wa-likull wijhatun huwa muwalliha": "For the Jews there is a qibla, and for the Christians a qibla, and for you a qibla," meaning the Muslims.

2278 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words, "wa-likullin wijhatun huwa muwalliha," he meant by it the people of the religions: he says, "For every one there is a qibla that they are content with, and the face of God, blessed and exalted is His name, is wherever the believers turn. That is because God, mighty is His remembrance, said: ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God; indeed God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 115]."

2279 - Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding "wa-likullin wijhatun huwa muwalliha": he says, "For every people there is a qibla which they have turned toward."

* *

So the interpretation of the people of this view regarding this verse: For every people of a religion there is a qibla which he faces and toward which he turns his face.

* *

Others said otherwise:

2280 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related this to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq related to us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding "wa-likull wijhatun huwa muwalliha": it is their prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis and their prayer toward the Ka'bah.

* *

The interpretation of the speaker of this statement: For every direction toward which your Lord turned you, O Muhammad, there is a qibla, which God, mighty and majestic, turns His servants toward.

* *

As for "al-wijhah," it is a verbal noun like "al-qi'dah" and "al-mishyah," from "al-tawajjuh" (facing toward). Its meaning is "muttawajjih" (one who faces), toward which one turns his face in prayer, as in:

2281 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "wijhah": a qibla.

2282 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

2283 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "wa-likull wijhah," he said: "a face."

2284 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "wijhah": a qibla.

2285 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, saying: I said to Mansur: "wa-likull wijhatun huwa muwalliha," he said: "We recite it, and for each one We have made a qibla which they are content with."

* *

As for His words, "huwa muwalliha," it means: he turns his face toward it and faces it, as in:

2286 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "huwa muwalliha," he said: "he faces it."

2287 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

* *

The meaning of "al-tawliyah" here is facing toward, as one says to another, "turn toward me," meaning: come toward me. "Al-infiraf" (turning away) as commonly used is turning away from something; then one says "infaraf ila al-shay'" (he turned toward the thing), meaning: he came toward it, turning away from something else. Likewise one says "wallaytu 'anhu" (I turned away from him) when you turn your back on him, then one says "wallaytu ilayhi" (I turned toward him), meaning I came toward him, turning away from another.

* *

The verb, namely "al-tawliyah," in His words "huwa muwalliha" refers to "kull" (every). The "huwa" that accompanies "muwalliha" refers to "al-kull," and it is in the singular because of the wording "kull."

* *

The meaning of the statement, then, is: For every people of a religion there is a direction, all of them turning their faces toward it.

* *

It has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas and others that they recited it as "huwa mawlaha," meaning that it is directed toward it. In that case "al-kull" has an unnamed subject. Had its subject been named, the statement would be: "wa-likull dhi milla wijhatun, Allahu muwalliyhi iyyaha," meaning: God directs him toward it.

* *

It has been mentioned that some of them recited it as "wa-likulli wijhatin" without tanwin and with idafa. That is a grave error, and the recitation with it is not permissible, because, if recited thus, the statement would be incomplete and meaningless, and it is not permissible that it be from God, may His praise be exalted.

* *

The correct recitation in our view is: "wa-likullin wijhatun huwa muwalliha," meaning: for every one there is a direction and a qibla, toward which that whole is turning its face. This is due to the consensus of the authoritative reciters on this recitation and their affirmation of it, and the deviation of those who differed to other readings. What is transmitted by widespread report is authoritative, while what is held by one who is liable to error and mistake is not permissible to set against the authoritative transmission.

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿So race to good deeds﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, "fa-istabiqu," He, exalted is His remembrance, means: hasten and hurry, from "al-istibaq," which is hurrying and hastening, as in:

2288 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His words, "fa-istabiqu al-khayrat": he says, "so hasten to the good things."

* *

By His words, "fa-istabiqu al-khayrat," He means: I have made the truth clear to you, O believers, and guided you to the qibla from which the Jews and the Christians and all the other people of religions besides you have strayed. So hasten with righteous deeds, in thanks to your Lord, and provide for your afterlife in your worldly life. Indeed I have made the paths of salvation clear to you, so there is no excuse for you in neglect. Preserve your qibla and do not lose it as the nations before you lost theirs, lest you go astray as they went astray; like what:

2289 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "fa-istabiqu al-khayrat," he says: "Do not let yourselves be overcome regarding your qibla."

2290 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words, "fa-istabiqu al-khayrat," he said: "the righteous deeds."

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Wherever you may be, God will bring you all together; indeed God is Able over all things﴾ (148)

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of His words, "wherever you may be, God will bring you all together," is: in whatever place or spot you perish, God will bring you all together on the Day of Resurrection, indeed God is Able over all things, as in:

2291 - I was told by 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "wherever you may be, God will bring you all together," he says: "Wherever you may be, God will bring you all together on the Day of Resurrection."

2291m - Musa related to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "wherever you may be, God will bring you all together," meaning: on the Day of Resurrection.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: By this verse God, mighty and majestic, urged the believers to obey Him and to provide for the afterlife in this world. So He, may His praise be exalted, said to them: Hasten, O believers, to act in obedience to your Lord, and to hold fast to what He has guided you to of the qibla of Abraham His friend and the laws of his religion. For God, mighty is His remembrance, will bring you together, along with those who opposed your qibla, your religion and your law, all of you on the Day of Resurrection, from wherever you are in the regions of the earth, until He repays the good-doer among you for his goodness, and the evildoer for his evil, or He will graciously pardon.

* *

As for His words, "indeed God is Able over all things," He, mighty is His remembrance, means: indeed God, over gathering you after your deaths from your graves to Him, from wherever you are, and whether your graves are in one place or another, and over whatever else He wills, is Able. So hasten to bring forth your souls with righteous deeds before your deaths, for the Day of your resurrection and gathering.

The Interpretation of His, the Exalted's, Words: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed, it is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ (2:149)

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, "And from wherever you set out," He, may His praise be exalted, means: from whatever place you go out to, toward whatever place you head. "So turn your face," O Muhammad, means: turn your face. We have already shown that "al-tawliyah" (turning) in this context toward the Sacred Mosque means only directing the face toward it. We have also explained the meaning of "shatr" (toward, direction) earlier. [[See what has preceded regarding "al-tawliyah" in this volume, 3:194, note 3, and what has preceded in the interpretation of "shatr" in this volume, 3:175.]]

* *

As for His words, "And indeed, it is the truth from your Lord," He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: indeed, facing toward it is the truth, about which there is no doubt, from your Lord. So preserve it, and obey Allah in your turning toward it.

* *

As for His words, "And Allah is not unaware of what you do," He says: Indeed, Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, is not heedless of your deeds, nor unaware of them, but He records them for you, until He recompenses you for them on the Day of Resurrection. [[See the meaning of "ghafil" (unaware) in what has preceded in this volume, 3:174, note 1, and the references there.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 150 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His saying, exalted be His mention: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, exalted be His mention, "And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque," He means: from whatever place and spot you depart, O Muhammad, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque, facing it and in its direction.

And by His saying, "And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it," He means: wherever you are, O believers, from the lands of God, turn your faces in your prayer toward it, facing it, directed to it and aiming at it. [[In the manuscript: "fa-wallu fi salatikum" ("turn in your prayer"), omitting "wujuhakum" ("your faces").]]
* *
The interpretation of His saying: ﴿So that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who do wrong. So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: A group of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said: By "the people" in His saying, "So that people will have no argument against you," God means the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab).

Mention of those who said that:

2292. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying, "So that people will have no argument against you," meaning by it the People of the Book. They said, when the Prophet of God ﷺ was turned toward the Ka'bah, the Sacred House: "The man has longed for his father's house and the religion of his people!"

2293. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His saying, "So that people will have no argument against you," meaning by it the People of the Book, who said, when the Prophet of God ﷺ was turned toward the Ka'bah: "The man has longed for his father's house and the religion of his people!"
* *
If someone says: What argument did the People of the Book have concerning the prayer of the Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions toward Jerusalem, against the Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions?

It is said: We have already mentioned what was related about that earlier. It is said: They used to say: "Muhammad and his companions did not know where their qibla was until we guided them! And [they say]: Muhammad opposes us in our religion and follows our qibla!" [[See what preceded in this part, nos. 2234, 2235.]] This is the argument with which they argued against the Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions, by way of their contention with them, and their deception thereby of the ignorant and the dullards among the polytheists. [[In the printed edition: "and the people of obstinacy among the polytheists," the correct reading being from the manuscript.]]

We have already explained earlier that the meaning of the people's disputing with him, which God, exalted be His mention, mentioned in His Book, is only contention and debate. God, may His majesty be exalted, cut off that argument of theirs and put an end to it, by changing the qibla of His Prophet ﷺ and the believers in him from the qibla of the Jews to the qibla of His friend Abraham, peace be upon him. That is the meaning of God's saying, exalted be His praise: "So that people will have no argument against you," meaning by "the people" those who used to argue against them with what I have described.
* *
As for His saying: "except those of them who do wrong," they are the polytheists of the Arabs from Quraysh, according to what the people of interpretation have explained.

Mention of those who said that:

2294. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "except those of them who do wrong": the people of Muhammad ﷺ.

2295. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: They are the polytheists of the people of Makkah.

2296. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "except those of them who do wrong," meaning the polytheists of Quraysh.

2297. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah and Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: "except those of them who do wrong," he said: They are the polytheists of the Arabs.

2298. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "except those of them who do wrong," and "those who do wrong": the polytheists of Quraysh.

2299. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: 'Ata' said: They are the polytheists of Quraysh. Ibn Jurayj said: 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir informed me that he heard Mujahid say the same as the saying of 'Ata'.
* *
If someone says: What argument did the polytheists of Quraysh have against the Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions, in their turning in prayer toward the Ka'bah? And is it permissible that the polytheists should have an argument against the believers, regarding what God commanded them or forbade them? [[In the printed edition: "...has an argument against the believers regarding what God, exalted be His mention, commanded them with, or forbade them," where "argument" is moved forward and praise of God added.]]

It is said: The meaning of that is contrary to what you suppose and what you have gone to. Rather, "argument" in this place means contention and debate. [[See what preceded in the tafsir of "Do you argue with us?" in this part, 3: 121.]] The meaning of the speech is: so that no one among the people will have against you contention and a claim of falsehood other than the polytheists of Quraysh, for they have against you a false claim and contention without right, [[In the printed edition: "false claim" in both places, which is acceptable; one says "da'wa batil" and "batila".]] by their saying to you: "Muhammad has returned to our qibla, and he will return to our religion." That claim of theirs and their false wishes are the "argument" which Quraysh had against the Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions. For this reason God, exalted be His mention, excepted "those who do wrong" from Quraysh out of the rest of the people, since He denied that any of them had an argument against them regarding the qibla to which He directed them.

And the people of interpretation have said the same as what we have said about that.

Mention of those who said that:

2300. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God, exalted be His mention: "So that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who do wrong": the people of Muhammad ﷺ. Mujahid said: "Their argument is their saying: You have turned back to our qibla!"

2301. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same, except that he said: their saying: "You have returned to our qibla!"

2302. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar narrated to us, from Qatadah and Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: "So that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who do wrong," both said: They are the polytheists of the Arabs. They said when the qibla was turned toward the Ka'bah: "He has returned to your qibla, so he will soon return to your religion!" God, mighty and majestic, said: "So do not fear them, but fear Me."

2303. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "except those of them who do wrong," and "those who do wrong": the polytheists of Quraysh. He says: They will argue against you with that; their argument against the Prophet of God ﷺ, at his turning toward the Sacred House, was that they said: "He will return to our religion as he returned to our qibla!" So God, exalted be His mention, sent down concerning all of that. [[Report 2303 is in Ibn Kathir 1: 358 and al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 148. What is in the manuscript and the printed edition is identical: "So God sent down concerning all of that." In al-Durr al-Manthur: "So God sent down concerning that: 'O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer; surely God is with the patient.'" What is in al-Tabari barely makes sense, and what is in al-Durr does not make sense; the likely correct wording is: "So God sent down concerning that, all of that, up to His saying: 'O you who believe...'."]]

2304. Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the same.

2305. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, concerning what is mentioned, from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas; and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some people among the companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said: When the Prophet of God ﷺ was turned toward the Ka'bah, after his prayer toward Jerusalem, the polytheists of Makkah said: "Muhammad's religion has become confused! He has turned his qibla toward you, and he knows that you were better guided than he in the way, and he will soon enter your religion!" So God, may His praise be exalted, sent down concerning them: "So that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who do wrong. So do not fear them, but fear Me." [[Report 2305: see the earlier report 2204.]]

2306. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I asked 'Ata' about His saying: "So that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who do wrong." He said: Quraysh said, when he returned to the Ka'bah and was commanded toward it: "He did not need us! He has faced our qibla!" So that is their argument, and they are "those who do wrong." Ibn Jurayj said: 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir informed me that he heard Mujahid say the same as the saying of 'Ata'; Mujahid said: Their argument is their saying: "You have returned to our qibla!"
* *
So the interpretation of those whose interpretation we have mentioned has made clear His saying, "except those of them who do wrong," regarding the correctness of what we have said about its interpretation, and that it is an exception in the sense of the well-known exception, in which what follows the particle of exception is affirmed of those, while what precedes it is negated. [[In the printed edition: "the one that is affirmed of them for what follows the exception particle is what was negated of what precedes them," which is a grammatically confused reading; the correct reading is that of the manuscript.]] As when one says: "No one among the people traveled except your brother," affirming for the brother the travel which is negated of every person. Likewise His saying: "So that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who do wrong," negates that anyone have contention, dispute, or false claim against the Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions because of their turning in prayer toward the Ka'bah, except those of them who wronged themselves from Quraysh, for they have against them contention and a false claim, by saying: "You only turned toward us and toward our qibla, because we were better guided than you, and because you, by turning toward Jerusalem, were in error and falsehood."

Since that is the meaning of the verse by the consensus of the authorities among the people of interpretation, it is clear that the view of one who claims that the meaning of His saying "except those of them who do wrong" is "nor those of them who do wrong," and that "illa" means "wa" (and), is mistaken. [[The one who made this claim is Abu 'Ubaydah in Majaz al-Qur'an: 60-61; see also al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 89-90.]] For if that were its meaning, the first negation regarding all people, that they should have an argument against the Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions in their turning toward the Ka'bah with their faces, would be explaining the intended meaning, and there would be no point in mentioning afterward "except those of them who do wrong," except confusion, which is exalted above being attributed to Him or described by it. [[Al-Tabari's refutation of Abu 'Ubaydah is more sound and more upright than his refutation of al-Farra'.]]

Along with this, the meaning of the speech, if "illa" is taken to mean "wa" and the sense of conjunction, is outside the usage of the Arabs. That is because "illa" is not found in any of their speech with the meaning of "wa," except with a preceding exception that has already come before it. As when one says: "The people traveled except 'Amr, except your brother," meaning: except 'Amr and your brother; then "illa" in that case conveys what "wa" conveys, because the second "illa" is attached to the first "illa." [[In the manuscript: "to the first," which seems incorrect.]] It may also combine "illa" and "wa" in it, saying: "The people traveled except 'Amr and except your brother," and then one of them is dropped, and the other stands in its place, so one says: "The people traveled except 'Amr and your brother, or except 'Amr except your brother," as we described before.

Since that is the case, it is not permissible for any claimant among the people to assert that "illa" in this place means "wa" in the sense of conjunction.
* *
It is also evident that the view of one who claims that the meaning is: "except those of them who do wrong; for they have no argument, so do not fear them," is corrupt. This is like the speaker's saying: "All people praise you except the wrongdoer who transgresses against you," for his enmity is not counted, nor is his withholding of praise, because of the enmity. Likewise the wrongdoer has no argument, and he has been called a wrongdoer... [[The context: "And the corruption of the view of one who claims... is evident, by the consensus of all the people of interpretation on the error of what he claimed as interpretation in that."]] by the consensus of all the people of interpretation in declaring erroneous what he claimed as interpretation in that. And the consensus of their agreement on its error suffices as a witness to the error of his statement.
* *
And the falsehood of the view of one who claimed that "those who do wrong" here are some Arabs who were Jews and Christians, who used to argue against the Prophet ﷺ, while the rest of the Arabs had no argument, and the argument of the one who argues was broken, is evident. For you say to one whose argument you wish to break: "You do have an argument against me, but it is broken; you argue without argument; your argument is weak." And it directed the meaning of "except those of them who do wrong" toward the meaning: except those of them who wronged, from the People of the Book, for they have against you a feeble argument or a weak argument.
* *
And the weakness of the view of one who said that "illa" in this place means "but" (lakin).

And the weakness of the view of one who claimed that it is a new beginning, meaning: "except those of them who do wrong, so do not fear them." [[His saying "and the weakness of the view..." is conjoined with his earlier saying: "and the falsehood of the view of one who claimed..."]]

For the interpretation of the people of interpretation came in this matter to the effect that this is a statement from God, mighty and majestic, about those of them who wronged: that they argue against the Prophet ﷺ and his companions with what we have mentioned. He did not intend in that to inform about the description of their argument as weak or strong, although it was weak because it was false; rather He intended to affirm for those who wronged what He had negated for those before the particle of exception regarding the description.

2307. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, who said: al-Rabi' said: A Jew disputed with Abu al-'Aliyah, and said: Moses, peace be upon him, used to pray toward the rock of Jerusalem. Abu al-'Aliyah said: He used to pray by the rock toward the Sacred House. He said: So between me and you is the Mosque of Salih, for he hewed it out of the mountain. Abu al-'Aliyah said: I have prayed in it, and its qibla is toward the Sacred House. Al-Rabi' said: Abu al-'Aliyah informed me that he passed by the mosque of Dhu al-Qarnayn, and its qibla was toward the Ka'bah.
* *
As for His saying: "So do not fear them, but fear Me," it means: do not fear these whose affair I have described to you as wrongdoers in their argument and contention, and what they say, that Muhammad ﷺ has returned to our qibla and will return to our religion; or that they might have power over you in harm to your religion or in turning you away from what God, exalted be His mention, has guided you to of the truth. But fear Me, fear My punishment, in your opposing My command if you oppose it.

That is an admonition from God, mighty and majestic, to His believing servants, urging them to adhere to their qibla and pray toward it, and forbidding them to turn toward anything else. He, mighty and majestic, says: Fear Me, O believers, in abandoning My obedience in what I have commanded you, the prayer toward the Sacred Mosque.

It has been related from al-Suddi concerning that:

2308. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "So do not fear them, but fear Me," he says: Do not fear that I will return you to their religion [[Up to here is what we found of the papers mentioned on p. 189 note 1, and at its end is the following text...]]

The second volume is complete, by the help of God Most High, and blessings and peace be upon His Prophet Muhammad, his family, and his companions. Following it in the third volume, God willing, is: The Discussion on the Interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, Most High: ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you and that you may be guided﴾, God willing, and it is the remainder of the twenty-sixth part??

* *

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His saying, Most High: ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you and that you may be guided (150)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾, and from wherever you set out from the lands and the earth, and to whatever place you travel, ﴿turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [[In the printed edition: "إلى أي بقعة" without the waw; the correct reading is what is given here.]], and wherever you are, O Muhammad, and the believers, turn your faces in your prayers toward it, and take it as your qiblah, so that people will have no argument against you, except the polytheists of Quraysh. And that I may complete by this, from My guidance to you to the qiblah of My intimate friend Abraham, peace be upon him, whom I made an imam for the people, My favor; so I perfect for you My bounty upon you, and complete through it the laws of your upright, submitting religion, which I enjoined upon Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and the rest of the prophets besides them. That is the favor which He, may His praise be exalted, declared that He would complete upon His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers in him among his companions.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿and that you may be guided﴾, it means: and so that you may be guided to the right direction of the qiblah. [[See what has passed regarding the meaning of "la'alla" as "kay" (so that): 1: 364 / then 2: 69, 72, 161.]] And "la'allakum" is conjoined to His saying, ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾, and ﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you﴾ is conjoined to His saying, ﴿so that there will not be﴾.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 151:
