Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The correct view on this matter, in our opinion, is to say: God, may His remembrance be exalted, has made the circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwa one of the symbols of God, just as He made the circumambulation of the House one of its symbols.

As for His saying: ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around between them﴾, it is possible that it was said to both groups, of whom some feared circumambulating between them because of the two idols that al-Sha'bi mentioned, and some because of their aversion to circumambulating between them in the Jahiliyya, as is narrated from 'A'isha.

Whichever of the two matters it was, there is no indication in the saying of God, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around between them﴾, the verse, that He meant by it the removal of blame from those who circumambulate between them, because the circumambulation between them was impermissible by God's prohibition, and then the circumambulation between them was made a concession. This is because all agree that God, may His remembrance be exalted, did not prohibit it at any time and then granted concession in it by His saying: ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around between them﴾.

* * *

The disagreement among the people of knowledge on this matter is on several views. Some of them held that one who leaves the circumambulation between them has left out one of the rites of his pilgrimage, and that nothing suffices in place of it except its exact making up, just as one who leaves the circumambulation that is the circumambulation of return (tawaf al-ifada) is not compensated except by making it up exactly. They said: These are two circumambulations: God commanded one of them at the House, and the other between al-Safa and al-Marwa.

* * *

Some of them held that one who leaves the circumambulation between them may compensate for leaving it with a ransom (fidya), and they held that the ruling on circumambulating between them is the ruling on throwing some of the pebbles (al-jamarat), standing at al-Mash'ar, the farewell circumambulation (tawaf al-sadr), and similar things, for which the one who leaves them may compensate with a ransom, and he is not obliged to return to make up for it exactly.

* * *

Others held that circumambulating between them is voluntary: if its doer does it he is a good-doer, and if one leaves it, he is not obliged to anything by leaving it. [[In the printed edition: "he is not obliged to anything by leaving it, and God knows best," and this is undoubtedly an addition by a copyist.]]

* * *

Mention of those who said: The running (sa'y) between al-Safa and al-Marwa is obligatory, and it is not compensated by a ransom, and whoever leaves it must return. [[In the printed edition: "then he must return," and the better reading is what I have set down, which is more like the expression of al-Tabari and his contemporary jurists. It will come similarly many times later in his expression, and perhaps this is a change by a copyist or editor.]]

2353. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, from his father, from 'A'isha, who said: "By my life, the one who did not run between al-Safa and al-Marwa has not made the pilgrimage, because God said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of God.﴾"

2353 bis. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Malik ibn Anas said: "Whoever forgets the running between al-Safa and al-Marwa until he gets far from Mecca, let him return and run. And if he has had intercourse with women, he must perform 'umra and offer a sacrificial animal (hady)." [[See Malik's wording in al-Muwatta': 374-375.]]

* * *

al-Shafi'i used to say: Whoever leaves the running between al-Safa and al-Marwa until he returns to his own land, he must return to Mecca and circumambulate between them, and nothing else suffices for him. [[See al-Shafi'i's wording in al-Umm 2:178.]]

2354. al-Rabi' narrated this from him.

* * *

Mention of those who said: A sacrifice (dam) suffices for it, and there is no return to make it up.

al-Thawri said with that:

2355. 'Ali ibn Sahl narrated to me from Zayd ibn Abi al-Zarqa', from him; and Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said: If the one who leaves the circumambulation between them returns to make it up, that is good; and if he does not return, then he must offer a sacrifice (dam).

* * *

Mention of those who said: The circumambulation between them is voluntary, and nothing is incumbent on the one who leaves it, and of those who read: ﴿so there is no blame upon him that he not circumambulate between them﴾.

2356. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj narrated to us, saying: 'Ata' said: "If a pilgrim had departed (from 'Arafat) after throwing the pebble at Jamrat al-'Aqaba, and circumambulated the House but did not run, and then had intercourse with his wife, there is nothing upon him, neither pilgrimage nor 'umra, because of God's saying in the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud: ﴿So whoever makes pilgrimage to the House or performs 'umra, there is no blame upon him that he not circumambulate between them.﴾" Then I went back to him after that and said: "He has indeed abandoned the sunna of the Prophet ﷺ." He said: "Do you not hear Him say: ﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾?" But he refused to impose anything upon him.

2357. Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Malik informed us, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, that he used to read: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of God﴾, the verse, ﴿there is no blame upon him that he not circumambulate between them﴾.

2358. 'Ali ibn Sahl narrated to me, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Asim, who said: "I heard Anas say: The circumambulation between them is voluntary."

2359. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, saying: 'Asim al-Ahwal informed us, who said: Anas ibn Malik said: "They are voluntary."

2360. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, something similar.

2361. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of God. So whoever makes pilgrimage to the House or performs 'umra, there is no blame upon him that he go around between them﴾. He said: "He did not make it a sin for the one who did not circumambulate between them."

2362. al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, from 'Isa ibn Qays, from 'Ata', from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "They are voluntary." [[Report 2362: I have not been able to be certain about 'Isa ibn Qays, the narrator from 'Ata'. In Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/284 there are two biographies: "'Isa ibn Qays", who narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and from whom al-Layth narrated; and "'Isa ibn Qays al-Sulami", from whom Hushaym narrated. Nothing else is mentioned about either of them. However, the first is unknown. So it is possible that the narrator here is one of them. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah died in the year 114, so the narrator from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab (who died in 73) is very likely to narrate from 'Ata'. Al-Layth and Hushaym are close in generation: al-Layth died in 175 and Hushaym in 183. As for "Ahmad", the narrator here from "'Isa ibn Qays", I have not been able to identify him.

Then it became clear to me that "Hajjaj" in this chain is "Hajjaj ibn al-Sha'ir", that is, Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Hajjaj al-Thaqafi al-Baghdadi, known as Ibn al-Sha'ir because his father Yusuf was a poet who was a companion of Abu Nuwas. This Hajjaj is trustworthy (thiqa), one of the teachers of Muslim, Abu Dawud and others. Ibn Abi Hatim said: "He was one of the memorizers, of those who are good at narrating hadith and memorizing it." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/168, Tarikh Baghdad 8:240-241, and Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 2:117-118.

And his teacher "Ahmad" is Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Yunus, who is trustworthy, precise, a memorizer, one of the teachers of al-Bukhari and Muslim, whom Imam Ahmad named "Shaykh al-Islam". Reference to him has already passed: 2144.

If the chain is as we have concluded, then "'Isa ibn Qays" is a distortion, and the correct form is "'Umar ibn Qays", who is the Meccan known as "Sandal", with a fatha on the sin and dal (unpointed) and a silent nun between them. He is very weak, a denounced narrator (munkar al-hadith), as al-Bukhari said. Ibn 'Adi said: "He is weak by unanimous agreement; no one has doubted it, and Malik denounced him as a liar." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib. See also al-Saghir of al-Bukhari, p. 190; al-Du'afa' of his, p. 25; al-Nasa'i, p. 24; Ibn Sa'd 5:358; and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/129-130.

I incline to think this chain is as such, but I cannot be certain of that, nor change the name "'Isa ibn Qays", until I establish it by another proof.]]

2364. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from 'Asim, who said: "I said to Anas ibn Malik: Is the running between al-Safa and al-Marwa voluntary?" He said: "It is voluntary."

* * *

The correct view on this matter, in our opinion, is that the circumambulation between them is an obligatory duty (fard wajib), and that whoever leaves it must return to make it up, whether he forgot or did it deliberately, because nothing other than that suffices for him, due to the abundance of reports from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he performed the pilgrimage with the people, and among the rites of their pilgrimage that he taught them was the circumambulation between them.

* * *

Mention of the narration from him to that effect:

2365. Yusuf ibn Salman narrated to me, saying: Hatim ibn Isma'il narrated to us, saying: Ja'far ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from his father, from Jabir, who said: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ approached al-Safa in his pilgrimage, he said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of God﴾. Begin with what God began with in mentioning it." So he began with al-Safa and climbed upon it. [[Hadith 2365: It is a portion of the long hadith of Jabir about the description of the Farewell Pilgrimage (hajjat al-wada'). A part of it has passed with this chain: 2003. And another from the narration of Yahya al-Qattan, from Ja'far al-Sadiq: 1989.]]

2366. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Mahmud ibn Maymun Abu al-Hasan narrated to us, from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, from Ibn 'Ata', from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: that the Prophet ﷺ said: ﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the symbols of God﴾, and he came to al-Safa and began with it, and stood upon it, then he came to al-Marwa and stood upon it, and he circumambulated and ran. [[Hadith 2366: Mahmud ibn Maymun Abu al-Hasan: I do not know who he is, nor what his situation is. I have not found a biography of him or any mention of him.

Ibn 'Ata', from his father: this is Ya'qub ibn 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, who is trustworthy; we explained this in al-Musnad: 1809. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/298, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/211.

I have not found this hadith in any of the sources, although Ibn 'Abbas has other hadiths concerning al-Safa and al-Marwa and the running between them. Among them is the hadith that has passed: 2342, and a hadith in al-Mustadrak 2:270-271, which al-Hakim and al-Dhahabi declared sound.]]

* * *

Since it is established, by the unanimous agreement of the whole Community, that the circumambulation between them is by the teaching of the Messenger of God ﷺ to his community in their rites, and his practice in his pilgrimage and 'umra, and his ﷺ explanation to his community of the general principles of what God established in His Book, made obligatory in His revelation, and commanded, which could not be known except through his explanation, binding the community to act upon it, as we have explained in our book "The Book of Clarification on the Foundations of Rulings" (Kitab al-Bayan 'an Usul al-Ahkam), when the Community disagreed about its obligation, while the circumambulation between them was disputed as to whether it is obligatory or not obligatory, it became clear that its obligation falls upon the one who performs the pilgrimage or 'umra, for the reason we have described.

[[In the printed edition it read: "as we have explained", which is an error that disrupts the sentence. And his saying: "and his explanation..." up to his saying: "when the Community disagreed about its obligation" is a parenthetical clause linked to what precedes it, and its context and the context of its meaning are: "and his explanation to his community of the general principles of what God established in His Book - which cannot be known except through his explanation - binding the community to act upon it... when the Community disagreed about its obligation." And this clause is part of his saying, and from its context: "Since it is established by the unanimous agreement of the Community... it became clear that its obligation falls upon the one who performs the pilgrimage or 'umra."]]

Likewise, the obligation to return to make up the circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwa, since there is disagreement about what is required of the one who leaves it, along with the unanimous agreement of all of them that this is something the Messenger of God ﷺ did and taught his community in their pilgrimage and 'umra, when he taught them the rites of their pilgrimage, just as he circumambulated the House and taught his community in their pilgrimage and 'umra, when he taught them the rites of their pilgrimage and 'umra, and when all agreed that the circumambulation of the House cannot be compensated by any ransom or substitute, and that its leaver can only be required to return to make it up, the circumambulation between al-Safa and al-Marwa is its counterpart: no ransom or compensation suffices for it, and its leaver can only return to make it up, since both are circumambulations: one of the House and the other between al-Safa and al-Marwa.

Whoever distinguishes between their rulings is turned back on the argument, and then he is asked for the proof of the distinction between them.

If he argues with the reading of the one who read: ﴿so there is no blame upon him that he not circumambulate between them﴾,

it is said: That is contrary to what is in the codices of the Muslims, and it is not permissible for anyone to add to their codices what is not in them. It makes no difference whether a reader recited it like that or a reader recited: ﴿Then let them complete their untidiness, and let them fulfill their vows, and let them circumambulate the ancient House﴾ [Surat al-Hajj: 29], "so there is no blame upon them that they not circumambulate it." [[In the printed edition: "so there is no blame upon him", which is a clear error. He means that the reader makes the saying "so there is no blame upon them that they not circumambulate between them" part of the preceding verse of Surat al-Hajj, thereby adding to the Qur'an what is not in it.]] If one of the two additions that are not in the codex is permissible, the other is its counterpart; otherwise, whoever permits one of them while forbidding the other is arbitrary, and arbitrariness is something no one is unable to do. [[In the printed edition: "If there came one of the two additions," which is a corruption; the correct reading is what I have set down.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 158 (part 4 of 4):

It has been narrated that this reading (qira'ah) was denied, and that the revelation was not in this form, from ʿĀʾishah.

2367. Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Mālik ibn Anas informed me, from Hishām ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, who said: I said to ʿĀʾishah, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), and I was then young: "Have you considered the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: 'Indeed, aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever makes ḥajj to the House or performs ʿumrah, there is no blame upon him for going around them'? For we see no fault upon anyone in not going around them!" ʿĀʾishah said: "Nay! If it were as you say, it would be: 'There is no blame upon him for not going around them.' Rather, this verse was revealed concerning the Anṣār, who used to pronounce the talbiyah for Manāt, and Manāt was at Quddayd. They used to be reluctant to go around between aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah. When Islam came, they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about that, and Allah revealed: 'Indeed, aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever makes ḥajj to the House or performs ʿumrah, there is no blame upon him for going around them.'"

* *

Abū Jaʿfar said: The reading of the one who read "fa-lā junāḥa ʿalayhi an lā yaṭṭawwafa bihimā" may admit that the "lā" with "an" is a superfluous particle (ṣilah) in the speech [Note: "ṣilah" means an added, non-functional particle; see what has preceded at 1:190, 405 and the glossary of terms, and see also the Maʿānī al-Qurʾān of al-Farrāʾ 1:95, where he mentions this interpretation], since a negation preceded it in the preceding speech, namely His words: ﴿so there is no blame upon him﴾. It is then like the saying of Allah, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿He said: "What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?"﴾ [Sūrat al-Aʿrāf: 12], meaning: what prevented you from prostrating. And as the poet said: [Note: this is Jarīr.]

"The Messenger of Allah did not approve of their act, nor did the two good ones, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar."

[Note: its takhrij was previously cited at 1:191–192.]

And if the written form of the Muṣḥaf were like that, there would be no argument for the one who argues, given that the speech admits of what we have described, because we have explained that this is something the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught his community in their rites, as we mentioned, and because analogy confirms its soundness. So how much more so, when it contradicts the written forms of the Muslims' copies of the Qur'an, and is something which, if a reciter recited it today, he would deserve punishment for adding to the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, what is not part of it?

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever volunteers good, then indeed Allah is Appreciative and Knowing﴾ (158).

Abū Jaʿfar said: The reciters differed regarding the reading of this. The majority of the reciters of Madina and Basra recited it: "wa-man tatawwaʿa khayran," in the past tense with a "tā'" and a fatḥah on the "ʿayn." The majority of the reciters of Kufa recited it: "wa-man yaṭṭawwaʿ khayran," with a "yā'," a sukūn on the "ʿayn," and a shaddah on the "ṭā'," meaning: "and whoever volunteers (yatatawwaʿ)." It is reported that it is in the reading of ʿAbdullāh: "wa-man yatatawwaʿ," and the reciters of Kufa read it as we have described, following the reading of ʿAbdullāh mentioned, except ʿĀṣim, who agreed with the Madinans. They doubled the "ṭā'" seeking the assimilation of the "tā'" into the "ṭā'." Both readings are well known and sound, and their meanings agree without differing, because the past tense of the verb with conditional particles carries the meaning of the future. So whichever of the two readings a reciter uses, he is correct.

* *

[Note: I added what is between the parentheses, relying on his later statement: "We only said that the correct meaning of his words..." and it is apparent that it was dropped by a copyist.] [Our view on this is that] the meaning is: whoever volunteers ḥajj and ʿumrah after fulfilling his obligatory ḥajj, then indeed Allah is Appreciative of his volunteering with what he volunteers from that, seeking His face, and He will reward him for it, and He is Knowing of what he intended and willed by his volunteering with what he volunteered.

We only said that the correct meaning of His words "whoever volunteers good" is what we have described, rather than the view of one who claimed it refers to: whoever volunteers the sa'y and the circumambulation between aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah, because the one who performs sa'y between them is not volunteering the sa'y between them except in a voluntary ḥajj or a voluntary ʿumrah, as we described before. Since that is so, it is known that by volunteering in that he meant volunteering with what this act is part of, namely ḥajj or ʿumrah.

* *

As for those who claimed that circumambulating between them is a voluntary act and not obligatory, the correct interpretation of it according to their view is: whoever volunteers the circumambulation between them, then indeed Allah is Appreciative [of his volunteering that] — because according to them, for the pilgrim and the one performing ʿumrah, the circumambulation between them is optional: if he wills he performs it, and if he wills he leaves it. So the meaning of the speech according to their interpretation is: whoever volunteers the circumambulation between aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah, then indeed Allah is Appreciative of his volunteering that, Knowing of what the one circumambulating between them intended and intended in the same way, as:

2368. Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid: "And whoever volunteers good, then indeed Allah is Appreciative, Knowing," he said: whoever volunteers good, it is good for him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) volunteered, and it became one of the sunan.

* *

Others said: the meaning of that is: whoever volunteers good and performs ʿumrah.

Those who said this:

2369. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: "And whoever volunteers good, then indeed Allah is Appreciative, Knowing," whoever volunteers good and performs ʿumrah, then indeed Allah is Appreciative, Knowing. He said: The ḥajj is obligatory, and the ʿumrah is voluntary; ʿumrah is not obligatory upon anyone among the people.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 159 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down of clear proofs and guidance after We had made it clear to the people in the Scripture﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, [[In the printed edition: "He says: 'Indeed those who conceal...'", which is a scribal error; the correct reading is what I have recorded.]] "Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down of clear proofs," he means the scholars of the Jews and their rabbis, and the scholars of the Christians, because they concealed from the people the matter of Muhammad ﷺ and abandoned following him, while they found him written down with them in the Torah and the Gospel.
* *
And the "clear proofs" which Allah sent down are: [[In the printed edition: "min al-bayyinat" (of the clear proofs), as if it were connected to the preceding speech, and this does not stand; the correct reading appears to be what I have recorded.]] what made clear the matter of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, his sending, and his description, in the two Scriptures in which Allah, exalted is His remembrance, informed that their people find his description.
* *
By "the guidance," He, exalted is His remembrance, means what He made clear to them of his matter in the books which He sent down to their prophets. So He, exalted is His remembrance, said: Indeed, those who conceal from the people what We sent down in their books of clarification concerning the matter of Muhammad ﷺ and his prophethood, and the soundness of the religion with which We sent him and its truth, so they do not inform them of it, nor do they make known my clarifying of that to the people and my making it clear to them, [[In the printed edition it reads "wa-la ya'lamuna min tabyini dhalika lil-nas wa-idahi lahum", a phrase that does not stand and the context of the verse requires what I have recorded: making "ya'lamuna" into "ya'linunahu", adding "ba'd", and making "idahi" into "idahihi".]] in the Scripture which I sent down to their prophets. "Those — Allah curses them, and those who curse curse them, except those who repent" — the verse. As:
2370 - Abu Kurayb told us, and Yunus ibn Bukayr told us, and Ibn Humayd told us, Salamah told us, [they said] all together: Muhammad ibn Ishaq told us, who said: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, told me, who said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr, or Ikrimah, told me, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Mu'adh ibn Jabal, brother of Banu Salamah, and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, brother of Banu Abd al-Ashhal, and Kharijah ibn Zayd, brother of Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj, asked a group of rabbis of the Jews — Abu Kurayb said: about what is in the Torah, and Ibn Humayd said: about some of what is in the Torah — so they concealed it from them and refused to inform them about it. So Allah, exalted is His remembrance, sent down concerning them: "Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down of the clear proofs and the guidance after We had made it clear to the people in the Scripture — those, Allah curses them, and those who curse curse them." [[Narration no. 2370: in Ibn Hisham's Sirah 2:200, as in the version of Ibn Humayd.]]
2371 - Muhammad ibn Amr told me, who said: Abu Asim told us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of Allah: "Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down of the clear proofs and the guidance," he said: they are the People of the Book.
2372 - Al-Muthanna told me, who said: Abu Hudhayfah told us, who said: Shibl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.
2373 - Al-Muthanna told me, who said: Ishaq told us, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His saying: "Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down of the clear proofs and the guidance," he said: They concealed Muhammad ﷺ while they found him written down with them, so they concealed him out of envy and insolence.
2374 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh told us, who said: Yazid told us, who said: Sa'id told us, from Qatadah: "Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down of the clear proofs and the guidance after We had made it clear to the people in the Scripture," those are the People of the Book; they concealed Islam, which is the religion of Allah, and they concealed Muhammad ﷺ, while they found him written down with them in the Torah and the Gospel.
2374 bis - Musa told me, who said: Amr told us, who said: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down of the clear proofs and the guidance after We had made it clear to the people in the Scripture," they claimed that a man from the Jews had a friend from the Ansar called Tha'labah ibn Ghanamah. [[In Ibn Hisham's Sirah and elsewhere it is written with a ghayn (gh) unvocalized, but Ibn Hajar vocalized it in al-Isabah and said: "with a fatha on the unmarked letter and the nun," and did not mention any doubt or disagreement in its pointing with the ghayn.]] He said to him: Do you find Muhammad with you? He said: No! = He said: Muhammad: "the clear proofs." [[The statement "He said: Muhammad, the clear proofs" is from the tafsir of al-Suddi, not from the dialogue between Tha'labah ibn Ghanamah and the Jew. It means that the clear proofs they conceal are Muhammad ﷺ, that is, his description and attributes in their Scripture.]]
* *
The interpretation of His saying: ﴿after We had made it clear to the people in the Scripture﴾
[Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, exalted is His remembrance, "after We had made it clear to the people,"] [[The bracketed addition is necessary, and I have inferred it from the method of Abu Ja'far throughout his tafsir. This is undoubtedly a omission by the copyist.]] some of the people, because knowledge of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, his description, and his sending was found only among the People of the Book and not among others; and it is them that He, exalted is His remembrance, meant by His saying "to the people in the Scripture," and by that He means: the Torah and the Gospel.
* *
And although this verse was revealed concerning a particular group of people, it is intended to apply to every person who conceals knowledge which Allah has obligated him to make clear to the people.
This is similar to the report transmitted from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said:
2375 - "Whoever is asked about a knowledge which he possesses and conceals it, will be bridled on the Day of Resurrection with a bridle of fire." [[The hadith: 2375 - This is a sahih hadith. al-Tabari mentioned it here without an isnad. It was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 7561, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. We have traced it in our commentary on the Musnad, and in the Sahih of Ibn Hibban with our verification, no.: 95.]]
* *
And Abu Hurayrah used to say:
2376 - Nasr ibn Ali al-Jahdami told us this, who said: Hatim ibn Wardan told us, who said: Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani told us, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: Were it not for a verse of the Book of Allah I would not have narrated to you! And he recited: "Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down of the clear proofs and the guidance after We had made it clear to the people in the Scripture — those, Allah curses them, and those who curse curse them." [[The hadith: 2376 - Nasr ibn Ali ibn Nasr ibn Ali al-Jahdami: trustworthy, one of the teachers of the authors of the six books. Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/106, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/471. Hatim ibn Wardan al-Sa'di: trustworthy, narrated by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/1/72, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/260. Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani: passed at 2039. But his narration here from Abu Hurayrah is disconnected (munqati'), for he was born in the year 66 and Abu Hurayrah died in 59 or around it. The meaning of the hadith is sound and established from Abu Hurayrah through other connected narrations, as we will mention in the hadith after it.]]
2377 - Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam told me, who said: Abu Zur'ah Wahb Allah ibn Rashid told us, from Yunus, who said: Ibn Shihab said, Ibn al-Musayyib said: Abu Hurayrah said: Were it not for two verses which Allah sent down in His Book I would not have narrated anything: "Indeed, those who conceal what We sent down of the clear proofs," to the end of the verse, and the other verse: "And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture, that you shall make it clear to the people" to the end of the verse [Surah Al 'Imran: 187]. [[The hadith: 2377 - Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam: the Egyptian imam and hafiz, jurist of his age. Ibn Khuzaymah said: "I have not seen among the jurists of Islam one more knowledgeable of the sayings of the Companions and Successors than him." Biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/300-301, and Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 2:115-116. Abu Zur'ah Wahb Allah ibn Rashid al-Misri, muadhdhin of al-Fustat: trustworthy; Abu Hatim said: "his standing is truthfulness." Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/27 included him, and said: "Abd al-Rahman, Muhammad, and Sa'd, the sons of Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam, narrated from him." He is also biographed in Lisan al-Mizan 6:235, where it is cited from Ibn Yunus that he died in Rabi' al-Awwal in the year 211, "and the judges used to accept him." Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam narrated from him in Futuh Misr many times, among them on p. 182 lines 3-4: "Wahb Allah ibn Rashid told us, Yunus ibn Yazid informed us, from Ibn Shihab..." This chain is established in Tarikh Wulat Misr of al-Kindi, p. 33, from Ali ibn Qudayd, from Abd al-Rahman: "Abu Zur'ah Wahb Allah ibn Rashid told us." Al-Duwlabi mentioned it in al-Kuna wa-al-Asma' 1:182, and narrated: "Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam and al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman al-Jizi told us, both said: Abu Zur'ah Wahb Allah ibn Rashid told us, etc." The narration of al-Rabi' al-Jizi from him is also established in Kitab al-Wulat, p. 313. This name "Wahb Allah" is among rare names; I have not seen it, as far as I have seen, except for this shaykh, and the authors of the homonym works did not mention it, nor did al-Zabidi in his commentary on the Qamus, despite his wide knowledge. The matter was confused for the copyists or printers of al-Tabari, so in the printed edition it stands thus: "Thana Abu Zur'ah wa-Abd Allah ibn Rashid," and they altered "Wahb Allah" to "wa-Abd Allah," making them two narrators! Yunus: he is Ibn Yazid al-Aylî, and he is trustworthy, known for narrating from al-Zuhri and constant companionship with him. Ahmad ibn Salih said: "We do not put anyone before Yunus in regard to al-Zuhri," and he said: "When al-Zuhri came to Ayla he would stay with Yunus, and when he traveled to Medina Yunus would accompany him." Biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/406, Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/247-249, and Ibn Sa'd 7/2/206. This hadith is part of a longer hadith narrated by Muslim 2:261-262, through Ibn Wahb, from Yunus, from Ibn Shihab — he mentioned a hadith from A'ishah — then: "Ibn Shihab said: Ibn al-Musayyib said: Abu Hurayrah said..." It was also narrated by Abd al-Razzaq in his tafsir, pp. 14-15, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from al-A'raj, from Abu Hurayrah, similar and longer. Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad: 7691, from Abd al-Razzaq. Al-Bukhari narrated it in 5:21 (Fath), similar, from the narration of Ibrahim ibn Sa'd, from al-Zuhri, from al-A'raj. Al-Bukhari also narrated it in 1:190-191 (Fath) from the narration of Malik, from al-Zuhri, from al-A'raj; likewise Ibn Sa'd 2/2/118 and Ahmad in al-Musnad: 7274 — both through Malik. Al-Hakim narrated in al-Mustadrak 2:271, a similar abridged version, through Abu Usamah, from Talhah ibn Amr, from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Abu Hurayrah, and said: "This hadith is sahih in its isnad, though they did not record it." Al-Dhahabi agreed.]]
* *
The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Those — Allah curses them, and those who curse curse them﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, exalted is His remembrance, "Those, Allah curses them," he means: these who conceal what Allah sent down concerning the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, his description, and the matter of his religion, that it is the truth — after Allah had made it clear to them in their books — Allah curses them for their concealment of that and their abandoning of making it clear to the people.
* *
"Al-la'nah" is on the pattern "fa'lah", from "la'anahu Allah," meaning He removed him, distanced him, and banished him. The root of "al-la'n" is expulsion, [[See what has preceded at 2:328.]] as the poet al-Shammakh ibn Dirar said, describing water that he came to:
I startled with it the sandgrouse and I drove away from it
the station of the wolf, like the outcast one [al-la'in]...
[[Previously cited and explained at 2:328. In the note there an error; the correct reference is "Majaz al-Qur'an: 46".]]
That is: the station of the wolf, the expelled one. "Al-la'in" is an attribute of "the wolf," and he meant: the station of the expelled wolf, and the outcast like the man. [[In the printed edition: "al-tarid wa-al-la'in," and the correct reading omits the waw.]]
* *
So the meaning of the verse is then: those — Allah distances them from Himself and from His mercy, and those who curse ask their Lord to curse them, because the cursing of the children of Adam and all of Allah's creation when they curse is only that they say: "O Allah, curse him," since the meaning of "la'n" is what we have described: removal and distancing.
And we only said that the cursing of those who curse is what we have described — their asking their Lord to curse them, and their saying: "Allah has cursed him" or "upon him is the curse of Allah" — because:
2378 - Muhammad ibn Khalid ibn Khidash and Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim told me, both said: Isma'il ibn Ulayyah told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His saying: "Those, Allah curses them, and those who curse curse them," the beasts. He said: When the year becomes barren, [[The land and the year became barren: it lacked rain; a barren year is one lacking rain. "Sanah" means drought. In the printed edition it read "asanat", and the correct reading is what I have recorded. In al-Durr al-Manthur 1:162: "when the year became severe".]] the beasts say: "This is because of the disobedient children of Adam; Allah curses the disobedient children of Adam!"
* *
Then the people of interpretation differed about who Allah, exalted is His remembrance, meant by "those who curse." Some of them said: He meant by that the creatures of the earth and its insects.
Those who said that:
2379 - Muhammad ibn Humayd told us, who said: Jarir told us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, who said: The creatures of the earth curse them, and whatever Allah wills of the beetles and scorpions say: "We are withheld rain because of their sins."
2380 - Ibn Bashshar told us, who said: Abd al-Rahman told us, who said: Sufyan told us, from Mansur, from Mujahid: "Those, Allah curses them, and those who curse curse them," he said: the creatures of the earth, the scorpions and beetles, saying: "We have been withheld rain because of the errors of the children of Adam."
2381 - Ibn Humayd told us, who said: Hakkam told us, from Amr, from Mansur, from Mujahid: "and those who curse curse them," he said: the vermin and creatures of the earth curse them, saying: "The rain has been withheld from us because of the errors of the children of Adam."
2382 - Mushrif ibn Aban al-Haththab al-Baghdadi told us, who said: Waki' told us, from Sufyan, from Khusayf, from Ikrimah regarding His saying: "Those, Allah curses them, and those who curse curse them," he said: everything curses them, even the beetles and scorpions, saying: "We have been withheld rain because of the sins of the children of Adam." [[The report: 2382 - Mushrif ibn Aban al-Haththab al-Baghdadi: here it is established correctly, as appeared at 1951. It was previously given garbled as "Bishr ibn Aban": 1383.]]
2383 - Muhammad ibn Amr told me, who said: Abu Asim told us, who said: Isa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "and those who curse curse them," he said: the cursers are the beasts.
2383 bis - Al-Muthanna told me, who said: Abu Hudhayfah told us, who said: Shibl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His saying: "and those who curse curse them," the beasts, which curse the disobedient children of Adam when Allah withholds rain from them because of the sins of the children of Adam, so the beasts come out and curse them.
2384 - Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la told me, who said: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Muslim ibn Khalid informed me, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His saying: "Those, Allah curses them, and those who curse curse them," the beasts: camels, cows, and sheep, which curse the disobedient children of Adam when the land becomes barren.
* *
If someone says to us: What is the basis of those who interpreted His saying "and those who curse curse them" as meaning that the cursers are beetles, scorpions, and similar vermin of the earth, when you know that when they gather what is of the kind of beasts and other than the children of Adam, [[The pronoun in "that they, when gathered" refers to the Arabs, even though no mention of them preceded in the speech.]] they gather it without the "ya' and nun" and without the "waw and nun," but rather with the "ta'," and what contradicts what we have mentioned, so you say: "al-la'anat" and similar?

It is said: The matter, even if it is so, is that it is among the customs of the Arabs, when they describe something of the beasts or others — of which the rule of its plural is "ta'" and not the form of the plural of the males of the children of Adam — with what is an attribute of humans, that they make its plural the plural of their males, as He, exalted is His remembrance, said: ﴿And they said to their skins: Why did you testify against us?﴾ [Surah Fussilat: 21], so He brought their address in the pattern of the address of the children of Adam, since they spoke to them and they spoke to them. And as He said: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 18], and as He said: ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars — I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 4].
* *
And others said: Allah, exalted is His remembrance, meant by His saying "and those who curse curse them" the angels and the believers.
Those who said that:
2385 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh told us, who said: Yazid ibn Zurayi' told us, who said: Sa'id told us, from Qatadah: "and those who curse curse them," he said: it says: the cursers are the angels of Allah and the believers. [[In the printed edition: "Yazid ibn Zurayi' from Qatadah," with "qala haddathana Sa'id" dropped; the correct reading is what I have recorded, and it is a chain that recurs throughout the tafsir, the nearest being no. 2374.]]
2386 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, who said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, who said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His saying: "and those who curse curse them," the angels.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 159 (part 2 of 2):

2387- Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: "Al-lā'inūn" (the ones who curse) refers to the angels of Allah and the believers.

* *

Others said: By "al-lā'inīn" (the ones who curse) is meant everything other than the children of Adam and the jinn.

Mention of those who said this:

2388- Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding "and those who curse cursed them": he said, al-Bara' ibn Azib said: When the disbeliever is placed in his grave, a beast comes to him whose eyes are like two copper cauldrons, with an iron club with it. It strikes him a blow between his shoulders, and he cries out. Every creature that hears his voice curses him, and nothing is left that does not hear his voice except the two weighty creatures, the jinn and mankind.

2389- Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Zuhayr narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying: "Those, upon them is the curse of Allah and the curse of the ones who curse": he said, when the disbeliever is placed in his grave, he is struck with a hammer [[al-mitraq and al-mitraqah: the blacksmith's tool with which iron is struck.]] and lets out a cry, which every thing hears except the two weighty creatures, the jinn and mankind; and no thing hears his cry without cursing him.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these sayings in our view is the saying of the one who said: "Al-lā'inūn" are the angels and the believers. This is because Allah, mentioned be He, has described the disbelievers as being subject to a curse that comes from Allah, the angels and all people, when He, mentioned be He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of mankind, all together﴾ [[This is verse no. 161, which comes shortly after.]]. Thus, the curse which Allah, mentioned be He, informed us would befall the other group, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of clear proofs and guidance after We have made it clear to people [[In the printed edition: "after We made it clear to people", which is a copyist's error.]], is the curse of Allah and the curse of those whose curse, He informed us, befalls those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers [[In the printed edition: "it is the curse of Allah whose curse, He informed us, befalls. . . ", and the correct reading is what has been established.]], and they are "al-lā'inūn", because both groups are people of disbelief.

* *

As for the saying of those who claimed that "al-lā'inīn" are the beetles, scorpions and the like of crawling creatures and insects of the earth [[Every creature walking on the face of the earth is called dabbah and dabib.]], this is a claim whose reality cannot be grasped except through a report from Allah that this is their action, by which proof is established, and there is no report of this from the Prophet of Allah ﷺ, so it could be said that it is so.

Since this is the case, the correct statement regarding what they have said is to say: the evidence from the apparent meaning of the Book of Allah contradicts the view of the people of interpretation [[What is between the brackets is an addition, which I fear may have dropped out from a copyist.]], and that is what we have described. For if it were permissible that the beasts and all of Allah's creation curse those who conceal what Allah has sent down in His Book concerning the description, praise and prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, after they have knowledge of it, and all the wrongdoers are cursed along with them, then it is not permissible to definitively assert that Allah meant by "al-lā'inūn" the beasts, insects and crawling creatures of the earth, except by a report that is a decisive proof. There is no such report, and the apparent meaning of the Book of Allah which we mentioned indicates the opposite [[In the printed edition: "and the Book of Allah which we mentioned", which is not a sound phrasing. The correct reading is what has been established. And what he mentioned just before: "the evidence from the apparent meaning of the Book of Allah. . . ".]].

This, and the refutation of these speakers for what they said, clarifies for you the method of al-Tabari and his exegesis, and reveals to you his way of rejecting the reports he narrated from the Successors, in every matter that requires a decisive report from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to explain what they mentioned. Al-Tabari may mention such reports and then not mention his argument for rejecting them, because he disliked repeating the same statement and redundancy in what he made a foundation of the exegesis, as he explained in his "Risalat al-Tafsir", and then in his own tafsir afterwards, and in the rejection of similar matters in various places in it. As for when there is in any of that a decisive report from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he does not omit mentioning it. So when he does not mention, in such matters, a report from the Messenger of Allah, know that he leaves to the reader of his book the knowledge of the way by which this view is refuted.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 160:

On the interpretation of His saying, ﴿Except for those who repent, make amends, and make [the truth] clear; those, I will turn to them in forgiveness, for I am the Ever-Turning, the Most Merciful﴾ (2:160).

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: Allah and those who curse, curse those who conceal from people what they know of the matter of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), his description and attributes, in the Book that Allah sent down and made clear to people, except for those among them who turn back from their concealment of that and return in repentance by believing in Muhammad (ﷺ), acknowledging him and his prophethood, affirming what he brought from Allah, and making clear what Allah sent down in His books, which were sent to His prophets, concerning the command to follow him; and who amend their own state by drawing near to Allah through righteous deeds that please Him; and who make clear what they knew of the revelation of Allah that He sent down to His prophets and entrusted to them in His books, so that they do not conceal it, and they make it manifest and do not hide it. "Those" means: these people who did what I have described of them, are those whom I will turn to, so I will make them among the people who return to my obedience and turn back to my pleasure.

Then He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: "And I am the Ever-Turning, the Most Merciful," meaning: I am the One who returns to Myself the hearts of My servants that have turned away from Me, and who turns them back after their retreat from My obedience to seeking My love, and who is Merciful to those who come back to Me after their turning toward Me; I cover them with My pardon, and I overlook the great sins they committed between Me and them, by the bounty of My mercy towards them.

* *

If someone says: How is one turned to in forgiveness when he has repented? And what is the meaning of His saying: "Except those who repent, those I will turn to in forgiveness"? Is there a penitent who is not one to whom forgiveness is turned, or one to whom forgiveness is turned who is not a penitent?

It is said: That is such that neither of the two occurs without the other with it; so whether it is said, "except those to whom forgiveness is turned, and they repent," or said, "except those who repent, for I turn to them in forgiveness," it is the same. We have already explained the reason for such a construction when it came in a similar form earlier in this book, so we disliked repeating it in this place. [[See what preceded, 2:549.]]

* *

The people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said on this.

Those who said that:

2390 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying, "Except those who repent, make amends, and make [it] clear," he said: They amended what was between them and Allah, and made clear what had come to them from Allah, so they did not conceal it nor deny it: "those, I will turn to them in forgiveness, and I am the Ever-Turning, the Most Merciful."

2391 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His saying, "Except those who repent, make amends, and make [it] clear," he said: They made clear what is in the Book of Allah for the believers, and what they were asked about concerning the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ). And all of this concerns the Jews.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Some have claimed that the meaning of His saying, "and make [it] clear," is only: and make repentance clear through sincerity of deed. But the apparent sense of the Book and the Revelation contradicts this, because these people were rebuked before this verse for concealing what Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, sent down and made clear in His Book concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his religion. Then He, may His remembrance be exalted, made an exception for those among them who make clear the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his religion, so they repent of what they had been upon of denial and concealment; He removed them from the number of those whom Allah curses and the cursers curse. And the rebuke was not for their failure to make repentance clear through sincerity of deed.

Those whom Allah excepted from those who conceal what Allah sent down of clear proofs and guidance after He made it clear to people in the Book, were Abdullah ibn Salam and his kinsfolk (dhawuh) from the People of the Book, who embraced Islam, its embrace was good, and who followed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 161:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers – upon them is the curse of Allah and of the angels and of mankind, all together.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His remembrance, "Indeed, those who disbelieve" – meaning: indeed, those who denied the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and called him a liar, from among the Jews and Christians and the rest of the people of the religions, and the polytheists who worship idols – "and die while they are disbelievers" – meaning: and die upon their denial and their rejection of Muhammad (ﷺ) – "upon them is the curse of Allah and the angels" – meaning: those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers, upon them is the curse of Allah; He says: may Allah remove them far away and banish them from His mercy – "and the angels" – meaning: and the angels curse them, "and mankind, all together." The cursing of the angels and of mankind toward them is their saying: "upon them is the curse of Allah."

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "al-la'nah" (curse) earlier, with sufficient explanation so that it need not be repeated. [[See what has passed in this part 3: 254, and the note: 1, and its references.]]

* *

If someone says: How can the curse of "mankind, all together" from the various categories of nations be upon the one who dies disbelieving in Muhammad (ﷺ) [the curse of all people], when most of them do not believe in him and affirm him? It is said: The meaning of that is contrary to what you have supposed. The people of interpretation have differed regarding the interpretation of this. Some of them said: By His words, "and mankind, all together," Allah means only the people of faith in Him and His Messenger, to the exclusion of the rest of mankind.

Mention of those who said that:

2392 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words: "and mankind, all together" – he said: by "mankind, all together" are meant the believers.

2393 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "and mankind, all together" – by "mankind, all together" are meant the believers.

* *

Others said: Rather, that refers to the Day of Resurrection, when the disbeliever is made to stand before the witnesses, and all people curse him.

Mention of those who said that:

2394 – It was related to me from Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah: that the disbeliever will be made to stand on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah curses him, then the angels curse him, then all of mankind curses him.

* *

Others said: Rather, that refers to the saying of any speaker, whoever he may be: "May Allah curse the wrongdoer," and this reaches every disbeliever, because he is among the wrongdoers.

Mention of those who said that:

2395 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi regarding His words: "upon them is the curse of Allah and the angels and mankind, all together" – for no two believers or two disbelievers curse each other, one of them saying: "May Allah curse the wrongdoer," without that curse being due upon the disbeliever, because he is a wrongdoer; so every one of creation curses him.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these opinions in our view is the statement of the one who said: Allah means by that all people, in the sense that they curse them by saying: "May Allah curse the wrongdoer – or the wrongdoers."

For every person among the children of Adam does not refrain from saying this, whoever he may be and whatever community he belongs to, and thereby every disbeliever, whoever he may be, enters into this curse. This is the same meaning as what Abu al-'Aliyah said, because Allah, exalted is His remembrance, informed about those who will be witnesses on the Day of Resurrection, that they will curse them, saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah? Those will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, "These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers."﴾ [Hud: 18]

As for what Qatadah said, that by it He meant some of the people, it is an opinion whose apparent wording of the revelation contradicts it, and there is no proof for its validity from report or reasoning. If he thought that those meant were the believers, because the disbelievers do not curse themselves or their allies, then Allah, exalted is His remembrance, has informed that they will curse them in the Hereafter. And it is known of them that they curse the wrongdoers, and every disbeliever is included among the wrongdoers, by his wronging of himself, his rejection of his Lord's blessing, and his opposition to His command.

The Interpretation of His, the Exalted's, Words: ﴿Abiding therein, the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved﴾ (162)

* *

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says to us: What is it that put "abiding therein" in the accusative?

It is said: It is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the "hā' and mīm" in "upon them" ('alayhim). The meaning of His words, "Those — upon them is the curse of Allah," is: Those — Allah curses them, and the angels and all of mankind curse them, abiding therein. For this reason, some read it as: "Those — upon them is the curse of Allah, and the angels and mankind, all of them," [[In the printed edition: "wal-nās ajmī'n," which is an error; the correct reading is what has been recorded, with "al-malā'ikah wal-nās ajma'ūn" in the nominative, and this is the reading of al-Ḥasan. See Ma'ānī al-Qur'ān by al-Farrā' 1: 96–97, and the treatment of this verse in the other books of tafsir.]] directing it toward the meaning I have described. Although this is permissible in Arabic, reciting with it is not permissible, because it contradicts the codices of the Muslims and what the Muslims have transmitted widely as recitation. It is therefore not permissible to object with an anomalous (shādh) statement against what has been established by widespread transmission.

* *

As for the "hā' and alif" in His words "fīhā" (therein), they refer back to "the curse," and the intended meaning of the speech is what the disbeliever arrives at through the curse from Allah, from His angels, and from mankind. And what he arrives at through it is the Fire of Hell. The speech was applied to "the curse," while the intended meaning is what the disbeliever arrives at, as we have already explained with similar examples earlier, as:

2396 — I was told by ʿAmmār, who said: Ibn Abī Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabīʿ, from Abu al-ʿĀliyah: "Abiding therein," he says: abiding in Hell, in the curse.

* *

As for His words, "the punishment will not be lightened for them," it is a report from Allah, dhikruhu, about the perpetuity of the punishment forever, without any limit or lightening, as He, dhikruhu, said: ﴿And those who disbelieve, for them is the Fire of Hell; it will not be decreed upon them so that they die, nor will its punishment be lightened for them﴾ [Sūrat Fāṭir: 36], and as He said: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins﴾ [Sūrat al-Nisā': 56].

* *

As for His words, "nor will they be reprieved," it means: nor will they be given respite to offer an excuse, as:

2397 — I was told by ʿAmmār, who said: Ibn Abī Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabīʿ, from Abu al-ʿĀliyah: "Nor will they be reprieved," he says: they will not be given respite so that they may make excuses, like His words: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak, nor will they be permitted, so that they may make excuses﴾ [Sūrat al-Mursalāt: 35–36].

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 163:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿And your God is one God; there is no god but Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: We have already explained earlier the meaning of "al-uluhiyyah" (divinity, i.e., being the object of worship), and that it is the worship of creation. [See what has preceded, 1:122–126.]

So the meaning of His words, "And your God is one God; there is no god but Him, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful," is: The One who deserves your obedience, O people, and merits your worship, is one object of worship and one Lord. So do not worship other than Him, and do not associate with Him anything else. For whoever you associate with Him in your worship of Him is a creature among the creatures of your God, like you, whereas your God is one God, with no like or equal.

* *

Scholars differed about the meaning of His, may He be exalted and remembered, oneness (wahdaniyyah).

Some of them said: The meaning of God's oneness is the negation of likenesses and equals from Him, as one says, "So-and-so is the one of the people (wahid al-nas)" and "he is the one of his people," meaning by that that he has no equal among people, and no likeness or peer among his people. Likewise the meaning of the saying "God is one" is: God has no like and no equal.

They claimed that what guided them to the soundness of this interpretation is that the saying of the speaker "one" (wahid) conveys four meanings. The first: that it is "one" of a kind, like "the one human" among mankind. The second: that it is undivided, like an atom that cannot be divided. [In the printed edition: "ghayr mutasarrif" (not disposing), which is a misreading; the correct reading is what has been recorded.] The third: that it means similarity and agreement, as the speaker says, "These two things are one," meaning by that that they are alike, until, because of their resemblance in qualities, they become like a single thing. The fourth: that it is intended to negate a counterpart and a likeness from Him.

They said: Since the three meanings of "one" are negated of Him, the fourth meaning that we described is the correct one.

* *

Others said: The meaning of His, may He be exalted and remembered, oneness is the meaning of His being singled out from things, and things being singled out from Him. They said: He is singular alone because He is not included in anything, nor is anything included in Him. They said: There is no soundness to the saying of the speaker "one" applied to all things except in this sense. The proponents of this view rejected the four meanings that the others stated.

* *

As for His words, "there is no god but Him," this is a report from Him, may He be exalted and remembered, that there is no Lord of the worlds other than Him, and that no one deserves worship from the servants apart from Him; that everything other than Him is His creation; that it is obligatory upon all of them to obey Him and submit to His command, and to abandon the worship of whatever else is taken as a rival or deity, and to forsake idols and images. For all of that is His creation, and it is obligatory upon all of them to acknowledge Him alone in oneness and divinity, and divinity is fitting only for Him, since whatever blessing they have in this world is from Him, not from what they worship of idols and what they associate with Him of partners (ashrak); [ashrak is the plural of shareek, as one says sharif and ashraf, and nasir and ansar; it is also pluralized as shuraka'.] and whatever blessing they will attain in the Hereafter is from Him; and that what they have associated with Him of partners neither harms nor benefits, in the immediate or the later, in this world or the Hereafter.

This is a warning from God, may He be exalted and remembered, to the people of associating others with Him about their error, and a call from Him to them to return from their disbelief and turn back from their polytheism.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 164 (part 1 of 2):

Then, may His remembrance be exalted, He made them aware, through the verse that follows, of the place where people of intellect could reason to the truth of what He had alerted them to regarding His oneness and His clear, decisive proofs, thereby removing their excuse. So He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: O polytheists, if you are ignorant of, or doubt, the truth of what I have informed you, namely that your God is one God, rather than what you claim to be divine among rivals and idols, then reflect upon My proofs and consider them. Among My proofs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, the ships that run upon the sea with what benefits people, what I send down from the sky as water by which I give life to the earth after its death, what I have dispersed in it of every creature, and the clouds that I have subjected between the sky and the earth. If what you worship of idols, gods, rivals, and all that you associate with Him, when all of it is gathered together and acts in concert, or when some of it acts alone without the rest, is able to create the like of anything from My creation that I have named to you, then for you, by your worship of what you worship besides Me, there would then be an excuse. Otherwise, there is no excuse for you in taking a god other than Me, and no god for you or for what you worship other than Me. So let people of intellect reflect upon the brevity with which God argues against all the people of disbelief in Him and the deniers of His oneness, in this verse and the one after it, with the most concise speech, the most eloquent proof, and the most subtle meaning, by which they may be brought to knowledge of the excellence of God's wisdom and His clarification.
* *
The discussion of the matter for which God sent down to His Prophet ﷺ His words: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day﴾
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The exegetes differed concerning the occasion for which God, may His remembrance be exalted, sent down this verse upon His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

Some of them said: He sent it down to him as an argument in his favor against the polytheists who worshipped idols. That is because when God, may His remembrance be exalted, sent down to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: "And your God is one God; there is no god except Him, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," and he recited that to his companions, and the idolaters among the worshippers of idols heard of it, the polytheists said: "What is the proof and evidence that this is so? We deny that, and we claim that we have many gods?" Then God sent down at that point: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth," as an argument for His Prophet ﷺ against those who said what we have mentioned of them.

Mention of those who said that:

2398- Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Ata', who said: It was sent down to the Prophet ﷺ in Medina: "And your God is one God; there is no god except Him, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." The disbelievers of Quraysh in Mecca said: "How can one God suffice for the people?" So God, may His remembrance be exalted, sent down: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day," up to His words: "are signs for a people who reason." By this you know that He is one God, the God of everything, and the Creator of everything.

* *
Others said: Rather, this verse was sent down upon the Prophet ﷺ because the people of polytheism asked the Messenger of God ﷺ [for a sign], [[The addition between the brackets is needed for the sentence to be complete, and what follows later in the reports confirms it.]] so God sent down this verse, informing them in it that in the creation of the heavens and the earth and all else that is mentioned along with it, there is a clear sign of God's oneness, and that He has no partner in His dominion, for whoever understands and reflects upon that with sound comprehension.

Mention of those who said that:

2399- Sufyan ibn Waki' related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Sufyan, from his father, from Abu al-Duha, who said: When "And your God is one God; there is no god except Him, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" was sent down, the polytheists said: "If this is so, then let him bring us a sign!" So God, may His remembrance be exalted, sent down: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day," the verse.

2400- Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, who said: Sa'id ibn Masruq related to me, from Abu al-Duha, who said: When "And your God is one God; there is no god except Him, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" was sent down, the polytheists said: "If this is so, then let him bring us a sign," so God, may His remembrance be exalted, sent down: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day," the verse.

2401- Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq ibn al-Hajjaj related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, who said: Sa'id ibn Masruq related to me, from Abu al-Duha, who said: When this verse was sent down, the polytheists began to marvel and say: "You say your God is one God, so let him bring us a sign if you are among the truthful!" So God sent down: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day," the verse.

2402- Al-Qasim related to us, saying: Al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, that the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Show us a sign!" So this verse was sent down: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth."

2403- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Ya'qub al-Qummi related to us, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, who said: Quraysh asked the Jews, saying: "Tell us about the signs that Moses brought to you!" So they related to them the staff and his white hand "for the beholders." They asked the Christians about the signs that Jesus brought them, and they informed them that he used to heal the blind and the leper and raise the dead by God's permission. Then Quraysh said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Ask God to turn the Safa into gold for us, so that we may increase in certainty and strengthen ourselves thereby against our enemy." The Prophet ﷺ asked his Lord, and it was revealed to him: "I shall give them what they want, and I will turn Safa into gold for them, but if they disbelieve, I will punish them with a punishment I have not inflicted on anyone among the worlds."

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Leave me with my people, and I will call them day by day." Then God sent down to him: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth," the verse: Indeed, in that is a sign for them, if they only want me to turn Safa into gold for them. The creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day is greater than that I should turn Safa into gold for them so that they might increase in certainty.

2404- Musa related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day," the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Change Safa into gold for us, if you are truthful that it is from Him!" So God said: "Indeed, in these signs are signs for a people who reason." And He said: "A people before you asked for signs, and then they became disbelievers in them."

* *
Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this matter is that God, may His remembrance be exalted, directed His servants, by this verse, to the evidence of His oneness and His singular divinity, apart from everything else. It is permissible that it was sent down concerning what Ata' said, and it is permissible that it was sent down concerning what Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu al-Duha said. We have no report establishing the soundness of either group's view that would settle the matter, so it is permissible for someone to rule in favor of one of the two groups' view over the other. Whichever of the two views is correct, the meaning of the verse is what I have said.

* *
On the interpretation of His words: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾
Abu Ja'far said: By His words "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth," may His remembrance be exalted means: indeed, in the bringing into being and originating of the heavens and the earth.

* *
The meaning of "khalq" (creation) when God creates things is His originating and bringing them into existence after they did not exist.
We have already explained earlier the reason why "the earth" is said in the singular and not pluralized as "the heavens" are, so there is no need to repeat it. [[See what preceded, 1: 431-437.]]

* *
If someone asks us: Does the heavens and the earth have a creation that is other than them, so that it is said: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth"?
It is said: People have differed on this. Some said: They have a creation which is other than them. They argued for this with this verse, and with the one in Surah al-Kahf: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves﴾ [Surah al-Kahf: 51], and they said: God created nothing except that God wills it. They said: So things came about by God's will, and the will is a creation of them.

* *
Others said: The creation of a thing is an attribute of it, neither it itself nor other than it. They said: If it were other than it, it would be necessary that its like be described. They said: If it were permissible for its creation to be other than it, and for it to be described, it would be necessary that it have an attribute which is its creation. If that were necessary, there would be no end to it. They said: So it was known by that that it is an attribute of the thing. They said: So the creation of the heavens and the earth is an attribute of them, as we have described. They also argued, with the claim that a thing has a creation which is not itself, from the Book of God in a manner similar to what the former argued.

* *
Others said: The creation of the heavens and the earth, and the creation of every created thing, is that very thing itself and not other than it.
So the meaning of His words "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth" is: indeed, in the heavens and the earth. [[Abu Ja'far did not follow in this place the preference for a view that he customarily adopts. This indicates what we have gone to, that he sometimes abbreviated his speech, fearing prolixity. This holds if there is no lacuna or abridgement by a copyist or scribe in the manuscripts.]]

* *
On the interpretation of His words: ﴿and the alternation of the night and the day﴾
Abu Ja'far said: By His words "and the alternation of the night and the day," may His remembrance be exalted means: and the succession of night and day over you, O people.

* *
"Ikhtilaf" in this place is the reflexive form (iftial) from "khulouf," each of the two succeeding the other, [["Khulouf" is the verbal noun of "khalafa"; I have not found it in the lexicographers' books, but it is an Arabic formation sound in its analogy.] as God, may His remembrance be exalted, said: ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day succeeding one another, for whoever wishes to remember or wishes gratitude﴾ [Surah al-Furqan: 62].
Meaning: each of them replaces the other; when the night departs, the day comes after it, and when the day departs, the night comes behind it. From this is said: "So-and-so replaced so-and-so with his family in evil," and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

With them are the eyes and the gazelles walking in succession, and their fawns rising from every resting place. [[From his famous Mu'allaqa (ancient ode). The pronoun in "bi-ha" refers to "the abodes of Umm Awfa," his beloved. "Al-'Ayn" is the plural of 'ayna': wild cattle, large and beautiful-eyed. "Al-Aram" is the plural of ram: white gazelles that dwell in sand. "Khilfa": when one group comes, another departs to replace it in its place. He describes their coming and going in the open expanse of this sandy tract. "Al-Atla'" is the plural of tala': the young of cattle and gazelles. He describes the young of the cattle and gazelles in this sandy tract, having risen from their resting places. He describes the difference of movement in this deserted abode that Umm Awfa left, where he had stood after twenty years, as he mentioned.]]

* *
As for "al-layl" (the night): it is the plural of "layla" (a night), like "al-tamr" which is the plural of "tamra" (a date). It may also be pluralized as "layali," and they add in its plural what was not in its singular; their addition of the "ya" in that is like their addition of it in "rubā'iyya," "thamaniya," and "karāhiyya."

* *
As for "al-nahar" (the day): the Arabs hardly pluralize it, because it is like light. It has been heard in its plural as "al-nuhur," the poet said:

Had it not been for the two thrids we would have perished from hunger, a thrid of night and a thrid with al-nuhur. [[Tahdhib al-Alfaz: 422, al-Mukhassas 9: 51, Lisan (n-h-r), al-Azmina wa al-Amkina 1: 77, 155 and elsewhere. The narration in Lisan and al-Mukhassas is "lamatna bi-l-damr." "Al-Dumr" (with the mim vowelled or sukun) like "al-'usr" and "al-'usr": emaciation and the belly clinging to the spine from hunger or other things. "Al-thurayd": bread broken up and moistened with the water of the cooking pot and dipped in it until it softens.]]
If it were said in the plural of its paucity "anhira," it would be analogical.

* *
On the interpretation of His words: ﴿and the ship that runs in the sea with what benefits people﴾
Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, means: indeed, in the ships that run in the sea.

* *
"Al-fulk" is the ships; its singular and plural have the same form, and it is masculine and feminine, as God, may His remembrance be exalted, said in the masculine in another verse: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Surah Ya-Sin: 41], so He made it masculine.

* *
In this verse He said "and the ship that runs in the sea," and it is "majrat" (made to run), since when it is made to run it is "the running one," so there is added to it the attribute that belongs to it. [[See what preceded 1: 196.]]

* *
As for His words "with what benefits people," their meaning is: it benefits people at sea.

* *
On the interpretation of His words: ﴿and what God sends down from the sky of water, and gives life thereby to the earth after its death﴾
Abu Ja'far said: By His words "and what God sends down from the sky of water," may His remembrance be exalted means: and in what God sends down from the sky of water, which is the rain that God sends down from the sky.
His words "and gives life thereby to the earth after its death": its giving life is its cultivation and the bringing forth of its vegetation. The "ha'" in "bihi" refers to "the water," and the "ha' and alif" in His words "after its death" refer to the earth.
"The death of the earth" is its ruin, the effacement of its cultivation, and the cessation of its vegetation, which is for the servants a sustenance and for the creatures provision.

* *
On the interpretation of His words: ﴿and He dispersed in it every kind of creature﴾
Abu Ja'far said: By His words "and He dispersed in it every kind of creature," may His remembrance be exalted means: and indeed, in what He dispersed in the earth of creatures.

* *
The meaning of His words "and He dispersed in it," and He spread it, from the saying of one who says: "The prince dispersed his expeditions," meaning: he dispersed them.
The "ha' and alif" in His words "in it" refer to "the earth."

* *
"Al-dabba" (the creature) is the active form, from the saying of one who says: "The creature crawled, crawls a crawling, so it is a creature." "Al-dabba" is a name for every living being that is not a bird with its wings, because of its crawling on the earth.

* *
On the interpretation of His words: ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾
