Abu Ja'far said: By His words "and the turning of the winds," may His remembrance be exalted means: and in His turning of the winds. He omitted mention of the agent and attributed the verb to the object, as you say: "The coming of your brother pleases me," meaning: your coming to your brother.

* *
"The turning" of God of them is that He sends them sometimes as fertilizing winds, sometimes makes them barren, and sends them as a punishment that destroys everything by its Lord's command, as:

2405- Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah concerning His words: "and the turning of the winds and the clouds subjected": he said: Capable is our Lord, by God, of that, if He wills; He made them a mercy, fertilizing for the clouds and a herald before His mercy, and if He wills, He makes them a punishing barren wind that fertilizes nothing; it is only a punishment upon whomever it is sent. [[The addition between the brackets is from the text of al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 164, from the text of Qatadah's tafsir which al-Tabari cited.]]

* *
Some scholars of Arabic grammar claimed that the meaning of His words "and the turning of the winds" is that they come sometimes from the south, north, east and west. Then he said: That is their turning. [[This is the view of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 97.] This description with which he described the winds is a description of their turning (tasarruf), not of their turning (tasrif), because "tasrif" is God's turning of them, and "tasarruf" is the variation of their blowing.
It is also permissible that the meaning of His words "and the turning of the winds" is God's, may His remembrance be exalted, turning of the blowing of the wind by the variation of its directions.

* *
On the interpretation of His words: ﴿and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth, are signs for a people who reason﴾
Abu Ja'far said: By His words "and the clouds subjected," may His remembrance be exalted means: and in the clouds. "Sahab" is the plural of "sahaba" (a cloud). This is shown by His words: ﴿and He raises the heavy clouds﴾ [Surah al-Ra'd: 12], where He made "al-musakhkhar" singular and masculine, as they say: "This is a date, and these are many dates" in its plural, and "this is a palm, and these are palms."
"Sahab" is said to be so called, God willing, because it drags parts of itself along and draws them, from the saying of one who says: "So-and-so passed dragging his skirt," meaning "drawing it."

* *
As for the meaning of His words "are signs," they are indications and evidences that the Creator of all that and its originator is one God. [[See the meaning of "ayah" in what preceded 1: 106, and the indexes of language. Al-Tabari left his explanation of "al-musakhkhar," and it seems there is abridgement in the originals by a copyist or scribe, if not by al-Tabari himself, as I pointed out earlier.]]

* *

"لقوم يعقلون" (for a people who reason), meaning: for whoever comprehends the places of the proofs and understands from God His indications of His oneness. Thus God, may His remembrance be exalted, informs His servants that the signs and proofs have been placed as a consideration only for those possessed of intellects and discernment, to the exclusion of other creatures, since they are the ones addressed by the command and prohibition, charged with obedience and worship, for whom is the reward and upon whom is the punishment.

* *

If someone says: How did He argue against the people of disbelief with His saying: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day..." (Qur'an 2:164), concerning the oneness of God? You know that some categories of the disbelievers deny that the heavens and the earth and the rest of what is mentioned in this verse are created.

It is said: The denial of whoever denies that does not prevent that all that God, may His remembrance be exalted, mentioned in this verse be a proof of its Creator and Fashioner, and that He has a Governor who resembles nothing, and a Originator who has no equal. And although this is so, God argued with it only against a people who acknowledged that God is their Creator, but who associated with His worship the worship of idols and images. [See what has preceded at 1:371, and the refutation of those who thought the Arabs did not acknowledge the oneness.] So He, may His remembrance be exalted, argued against them, saying—when they denied His saying: "And your God is one God," and claimed that He has partners among the gods: [Indeed your God is the One who created the heavens and caused the sun and the moon to run for your benefit, bringing your provisions, continuing in their courses. And that is the meaning of the alternation of the night and the day in the sun and the moon] [[A great deal has fallen out of this sentence, so it has become confused and disordered, and its correct form is probably what follows: [Indeed your God is the One who created for you the heavens and the earth, creating the earth and ordaining for you in it your provisions and sustenance, and creating the heavens and causing the sun and the moon to run in their courses—and that is the meaning of: (and the alternation of the night and the day)—and creating the winds that drive the ships which carry you, making them run in the sea, that you may seek of His bounty.]]] And that is the meaning of His saying: "And the ships that run in the sea with what benefits people." And He sent down to you water from the sky, and by it made your fertile land fruitful after its barrenness, and made it lush after its desolation, and raised you up by it after your despair [[Amra' al-ard: made the land fertile after drought. Al-dathur: the effacement, meaning its ruin and the erasure of the traces of its cultivation of vegetation and other things. In the printed edition it read "fayn'a-kum," and the correct reading is what is established here. Na'asha Allah yan'ashuhu: raised him up and restored him with His mercy.]], and that is the meaning of His saying: "And what God sends down from the sky of water, and gives life thereby to the earth after its death." And He subjected the livestock for you, in which you have food and sustenance, and in which is beauty and mounts, and in which are furnishings and clothing, and that is the meaning of His saying: "And He spread therein every moving creature." And He sent the winds for you as fertilizers for the trees of your fruits, your sustenance and your provisions, and drove for you the clouds whose rain is your life and the life of your cattle and livestock, and that is the meaning of His saying: "And the directing of the winds and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth."

He informed them that their God is God, who bestowed these blessings upon them and singled Himself out for them. Then He said: Is there any of your partners who does any of these things, so that you associate him in your worship of Me and make him a rival and equal to Me? If none of your partners does any of these things, then in what I have enumerated to you of My blessings and singled out for you with My favors are indications for you, if you are people who reason about the places of truth and falsehood, and of injustice and fairness. For how is it that you have goodness done to you by One who is alone, apart from Me, while you make for Me rivals in your worship of Me? This is the meaning of the verse.

* *

Those who were reminded by this verse and against whom it was argued are the people whose description I have given, not the deniers of the Creator and the materialists. And although in the smallest of what God counted in this verse there are conclusive proofs that suffice for all mankind, we have left explaining it, out of dislike of lengthening the book by mentioning it.

**Commentary on the words of God Almighty: "And among the people are those who take, besides God, rivals (andad) whom they love as they love God; but those who believe are stronger in love for God" (2:165)**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means that among the people are those who take, besides God, rivals to Him =

We have already explained earlier that *al-nidd* (the rival) means an equal, with the evidence that supports this, so we dislike repeating it. [[See what has preceded, 1: 368-370.]]

* *

= And that those who took these "rivals" besides God love their rivals as the believers love God. Then He informed them that the believers are stronger in love for God than those who take these rivals for their rivals.

* *

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the "rivals" which the people had taken. What were they?

* *

Some of them said: They are their gods which they worshipped besides God.

Those who said this:

2406. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada, concerning His words: "And among the people are those who take, besides God, rivals whom they love as they love God, but those who believe are stronger in love for God," that they are the unbelievers' love for their idols.

2407. Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words, may His remembrance be exalted: "They love them as they love God," out of boastfulness and imitation of the Truth through the rivals, "but those who believe are stronger in love for God," than the unbelievers' love for their idols.

2408. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

2409. It was reported to me from 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' concerning His words: "And among the people are those who take, besides God, rivals whom they love as they love God." He said: They are the gods that are worshipped besides God; he means: they love their idols as they love God, "but those who believe are stronger in love for God," that is, than the unbelievers' love for their idols.

2410. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words: "And among the people are those who take, besides God, rivals whom they love as they love God." He said: These are the polytheists. Their rivals are their gods whom they worshipped along with God; they love them as the believers love God. "But those who believe are stronger in love for God" than their love for their gods.

* *

Others said: Rather, the "rivals" in this place are only their leaders whom they obeyed in disobedience to God, may His remembrance be exalted.

Those who said this:

2411. Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And among the people are those who take, besides God, rivals whom they love as they love God." He said: The rivals are men whom they obey as they obey God; when they command them, they obey them and disobey God. [[The report 2411: in the printed edition, "Musa said: Asbat narrated to us" is given with "'Amr said" omitted; this is a chain that recurs in the tafsir, confirmed by no. 2404. Then see p. 288, line 11, where its interpretation and explanation of al-Suddi's statement will come.]]

* *

If someone says: How is it said "as the love of God"? Does God love rivals? And did those who took rivals love God, so that it is said "they love them as they love God"?

It is said: The meaning of that is other than what you have supposed. This is only like the saying of the speaker: [[In the printed edition: "and this is like," and I have preferred the wording more fitting to the context and meaning.]] "I sold my slave as the sale of your slave," meaning: I sold him as your slave was sold, and as your selling of your slave; and "I took my right from him as the taking of your right," meaning: as your taking of your right; so the pronoun of the addressee is dropped from the second, being sufficed by its pronoun in "slave" and "right." As the poet said:

*So I shall not greet, as long as I live,*
*Zayd with the greeting of the Amir.* [[I do not know who said it. It will come in this part, 3: 311. It is one of four verses in al-Bayan wa'l-Tabyin 4: 51, Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 100, and Amali al-Sharif 1: 215. After the verse:*
*An Amir who eats fine bread secretly,*
*and feeds his guest barley bread!*

*Do you remember when your qaba' was a sheepskin,*
*and your sandals were of camel hide?*

*Glory be to Him who gave you dominion*
*and taught you to sit upon the throne!!*]]

He means: as one greets the Amir.

* *

So the meaning of the speech is then: "And among the people are those who take, O believers, besides God, rivals whom they love as you love God." [[In the printed edition: "as the love of God." This is not an explanation in line with his speech and exposition, but the text of the verse itself, and the correct reading is what has been given.]]

* *

The interpretation of His words: **"And if only those who did wrong could see, when they see the punishment, that all power belongs to God and that God is severe in punishment" (2:165).**

Abu Ja'far said: The readers differed in reading this. The majority of the people of Medina and Syria read: *"Wa law tara alladhina zalamu"* with the *ta'* (you), *"idh yarawna al-'adhab"* with the *ya'* (they), *"anna al-quwwata lillahi jami'an wa anna Allaha shadid al-'adhab"* with the opening of both *anna*s, meaning: "And if you, O Muhammad, could see those who disbelieved and wronged themselves, when they see and witness the punishment of God, that all power belongs to God and that God is severe in punishment."

Then, in the accusative case of the two *anna*s in this reading, there are two possibilities. One is that they are opened with an omitted element of the speech which is required by it, so the interpretation of the speech will then be: "And if you, O Muhammad, could see those who did wrong when they see the punishment of God, they would acknowledge, — and *tara* means 'see' — that all power belongs to God, and that God is severe in punishment." The answer will then be, when *anna* is opened in this way, left out, having been sufficed by the speech's indication of it, and the meaning is as I have described. This is one of the two possibilities for opening *anna*, according to the reading of the one who reads *"wa law tara"* with the *ta'*.

The other possibility of opening is that its meaning is: "And if you, O Muhammad, could see those who did wrong when they see the punishment of God, because all power belongs to God and God is severe in punishment, you would know the extent of God's punishment." Then the *lam* is omitted, and it is opened with that meaning, the speech indicating it.

* *

Others among the early readers read: *"Wa law tara alladhina zalamu idh yarawna al-'adhab inna al-quwwata lillahi jami'an wa inna Allaha shadid al-'adhab"* [with *inna*, in the indicative]. Meaning: "And if you, O Muhammad, could see those who did wrong when they witness the punishment of God, you would know the state into which they shall come." Then He, may His remembrance be exalted, informed of a new statement about His power and authority, after the completion of the first statement, and said: *"inna al-quwwata lillahi jami'an"* — in this world and the next, apart from whatever else is rivals and gods — *"wa inna Allaha shadid al-'adhab"* for those who associate others with Him, claim partners with Him, and make rivals for Him.

* *

This reading may bear another possibility in the reading of the one who breaks *inna* in *"tara"* with the *ta'*. It means: "And if you, O Muhammad, could see those who did wrong when they see the punishment, saying: Indeed all power belongs to God and indeed God is severe in punishment." Then the "saying" is omitted and what is said is retained.

* *

Others read: *"Wa law yara alladhina zalamu"* with the *ya'*, *"idh yarawna al-'adhab anna al-quwwata lillahi jami'an wa anna Allaha shadid al-'adhab"* with the opening of the *alif* in both *anna*s, meaning: "And if those who did wrong could see God's punishment which He prepared for them in Hell, they would know when they see it and witness it that all power belongs to God and that God is severe in punishment, when they see the punishment." Then the first *anna* is in the accusative case because it is connected to the omitted answer of *law*, and the answer is left out, and the second is conjoined to the first. This is the reading of the majority of the Kufan, Basran and Meccan readers.

* *

Some grammarians of Basra claimed that the interpretation of the reading of the one who reads *"wa law yara alladhina zalamu idh yarawna al-'adhab anna al-quwwata lillahi jami'an wa anna Allaha shadid al-'adhab"* with the *ya'* in *yara* and the opening of the two *alif*s in *anna* and *anna*, is: "And if they knew," [[He means that *yara* means *ya'lam* (knows). Abu 'Ubayda said this in Majaz al-Qur'an: 62.]] because they had not known the extent of the punishment they witness. The Prophet (ﷺ) knew, so when He says "And if you could see," He is addressing the Prophet (ﷺ).

If *inna* were broken as a beginning, when He says "And if they could see," it is permissible, because *law yara* means *law ya'lam* (if they knew).

*Law* may also be used in a sense that needs nothing with it. You say to a man: "By God, if he knew, if you knew" [[In the printed edition: "law ya'lam" in both places; the correct form is to make one with *ya'* and the other with *ta'*.]] as the poet said: [[He is 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras.]]

*If your desire is the coquetry of flirtation, then 'law' was*
*in the bygone days and the years gone by!* [[From his Diwan: 37, from a fine ode in which he reproaches his wife, who had resolved to part from him; before it: "That is my wife, who desires my departure of old; is it for separation that she wishes, or for coquetry?" *Zayal* means separation. His words "your *tabb*" mean your desire, your will, your aim. He says to her: If it is coquetry that you desire and aim at, that time has passed, the days when we were young in the bygone ages and our past nights! When you were fair as a white gazelle, and when I came to you intoxicated, trailing my skirts behind me!]]

This has no answer except in meaning. And another poet said: [[He is also 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras, from the aforementioned ode.]]

*And take a portion of what we live on, and do not let*
*the vain trifles carry you away into the terrors!* [[From his Diwan: 37; it will come in the tafsir 7: 117, and in both places it is corrupted. Here it was: "and take a portion of what you live on." He said this to her after mentioning that she claimed he had grown old and his wealth had dwindled, and his brothers and helpers had withheld from him. Then he commanded her to reject the speech of the blamers, and advised her to live with him on what he lives on. *Al-tarahat* is the plural of *tarhah*, which means vain matters. *Al-ahwal* is the plural of *hawl*, which means a frightening matter. Then he mentioned to her the matter of her people if she left him to them and what she would meet of terrors, saying: Among them is one who withholds, and among them is one who is destitute, and a miser against you among misers.]]

So he omitted: "then live" [[In the printed edition: "then: live," and the correct form is what has been given, and it will come in the correct form in the seventh part.]].

He said: Some of them read *"wa law tara"* and opened *anna* after *tara*. But that is not sound, [[His words "not sound" mean a weak opinion, not a strong one.]] because the Prophet (ﷺ) knows, but He intended that people should know that, as He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: "Or do they say, 'He has forged it'" [Surah al-Sajda: 3], to inform people of their ignorance, and as He said: "Do you not know that to God belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth" [Surah al-Baqara: 107]. [[See what has preceded 2: 484-488.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Some people denied that *anna* could be governed by His words "law yara" (if he saw). They said: The people who did wrong already know, when they see the punishment, that all power belongs to God; so there is no sense in him who interprets it as: "If the wrongdoers saw that power belongs to God." They said: What governs *anna* is only the answer to *law*, which has the meaning of "knowing," because the first "knowing" precedes it. [[By the first "knowing," he means "law yara," meaning "law ya'lam," and the other is the omitted answer: "they would know."]]

* *

Some grammarians of Kufa said: Whoever puts *anna* in the accusative in "that all power belongs to God and that God is severe in punishment," from those who read *"law yara"* with the *ya'*, has put it in the accusative only by making "seeing" govern it, and made "seeing" fall upon it. As for whoever put it in the accusative of those who read *"law tara"* with the *ta'*, he put it in the accusative by way of interpretation: "Because all power belongs to God, and because God is severe in punishment." He said: Whoever broke them, of those who read with the *ta'*, breaks them as a statement.

* *

Others among them said: The opening of *anna* in the reading of the one who reads *"wa law yara alladhina zalamu"* with the *ya'*, by making *yara* govern, and the answer of the speech is then left out, as the answer of: "And if a Qur'an were such that the mountains were moved by it, or the earth were split by it" [Surah al-Ra'd: 31] was left out, because the meaning of Paradise and Hell is repeated and well known. [[See Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 97, where it reads "the meanings of Paradise...", and the correct form is what is in al-Tabari and one copy of Ma'ani al-Qur'an.]] They said: Breaking *inna* is permissible in the reading of the one who reads with the *ya'*, and the "seeing" falls upon *idh* in meaning. They permitted putting *anna* in the accusative in the reading of the one who reads it with the *ta'*, for the sake of an intention of another verb, and that the interpretation of the speech be: "And if you, O Muhammad, could see those who did wrong when they see the punishment [they see] that all power belongs to God and that God is severe in punishment." They claimed that breaking *inna* is the better form when read *"wa law tara"* with the *ta'*, as a resumption, because His words "law tara" have fallen upon "those who did wrong." [[This is the saying of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 97-98, with some alteration in wording. His word "fell" (waqa'a), and "falling" (al-wuquʻ), means that the verb is transitive to it. See the glossary of terms.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct reading in this matter, in our view, is: *"Wa law tara alladhina zalamu"* — with the *ta'* in *tara* — *"idh yarawna al-'adhab anna al-quwwata lillahi jami'an wa anna Allaha shadid al-'adhab,"* meaning: "You would see that all power belongs to God and that God is severe in punishment." So His words "you would see," in the second place, are omitted, being sufficed by the indication of His words "and if you could see those who did wrong," from mentioning it, even though it is the answer to *law*. [[In the printed edition: "and though it is the answer," and the correct form is what has been given.]]

The speech, though its exit is in the form of address to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), is meant for others, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was without doubt knowing that all power belongs to God and that God is severe in punishment. This is like His words: "Do you not know that to God belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth" [Surah al-Baqara: 107], which we have explained in its place. [[See what has preceded 2: 484-488.]]

We chose this over the reading with the *ya'* only because when the people see the punishment, they have certain knowledge that all power belongs to God and that God is severe in punishment; so there is no sense in saying: "If they saw that all power belongs to God" at that time. For one says "if you had seen" only to one who has not seen; as for one who has seen it, there is no sense in saying to him "if you had seen."

* *

The meaning of His words "when they see the punishment" is: when they witness the punishment, as:

2412. It was reported to me from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning His words: "And if only those who did wrong could see, when they see the punishment, that all power belongs to God, and that God is severe in punishment," he said: If they witnessed the punishment.

* *

What God, may His remembrance be exalted, meant by His words "And if you could see those who did wrong," and if you, O Muhammad, could see those who wronged themselves, who took besides Me rivals whom they love as you love Me, when they witness My punishment on the Day of Resurrection which I have prepared for them, you would know that all power belongs wholly to Me, apart from the rivals and gods, and that the rivals and gods avail them nothing there, and do not ward off from them a punishment I have sent down upon them; and you would be certain that My punishment is severe for whoever disbelieves in Me and claims with Me another god besides Me.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 166:

The interpretation (ta'wil, the explanation of the meaning) of His saying, ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment," He, may He be exalted, means: when those who were followed disown those who followed them. [[In the printed edition: "from those who followed" again, but the correct reading is "those who followed them" as I have established it; otherwise it would be mere repetition without meaning.]]

* *

Then the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed about those whom God, may He be exalted, meant by His saying, "When those who were followed disown those who followed." Some of them said:

2413. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying, "When those who were followed": they are the tyrants, the leaders and the chiefs in polytheism; "those who followed": they are the weak followers; "and they see the punishment."

2414. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "When those who were followed disown those who followed," he said: The leaders disowned their followers on the Day of Resurrection.

2415. Al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Juraij (narrated): I said to Ata': "When those who were followed disown those who followed," he said: Their chiefs, their leaders and their masters disowned those who followed them.

* *

Others said:

2416. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "When those who were followed disown those who followed": as for "those who were followed," they are the devils, who disowned humankind.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view in this matter, in my opinion, is that God, may He be exalted, informed that those who were followed in polytheism against God disown their followers when they witness the punishment of God. He did not single out some of them over others, but included all of them. Therefore, every leader in disbelief in God and error is included in this: he disowns his followers who used to follow him in error in the world, when they witness the punishment of God in the Hereafter.

* *

As for what the verse indicates regarding who is meant by His saying, "When those who were followed disown those who followed," it indicates only that the rivals (andad) whom he who was described by His saying, "And among people is he who takes rivals besides God," are those who disown their followers.

Since the verse indicates this, the interpretation given by al-Suddi of His saying, "And among people is he who takes rivals besides God" [[See report no. 2411.]], is sound: that "rivals" in this place means only the men whom they obeyed in what they commanded them, and disobeyed God in obeying them, just as believers obey God and disobey others. The interpretation of the one who said, "When those who were followed disown those who followed, they are the devils who disowned their allies among humankind," is therefore invalid. [[His saying "and was invalid" is conjoined to his saying "was sound."]] For this verse is in the context of reporting about those who take rivals.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And their means of connection are cut off from them﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this God, may He be exalted, means: God is severe in punishment, when those who were followed disown, and when their means (asbab) are cut off from them.

* *

Then the people of interpretation differed about the meaning of "al-asbab" (the means). Some of them said:

2417. Yahya ibn Talhah al-Yarbu'i narrated to me, saying: Fudayl ibn Iyad narrated to us; and Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Ubayd al-Mukattib, from Mujahid: "And their means are cut off from them," he said: the connection that existed between them in the world. [[Report 2417: Fudayl ibn Iyad ibn Mas'ud al-Tamimi, the ascetic from Khurasan: trustworthy (thiqah). Ibn Sa'd said: "He was trustworthy, firm, virtuous, a worshipper, pious, and a great narrator of hadith." He died at the beginning of Muharram in the year 187 in Mecca. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/1/123, al-Saghir 209, Ibn Sa'd 5:366, and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/73.

Abu Ja'far narrates this report by two isnads: through the two routes of Fudayl ibn Iyad, then through the two routes of Jarir, who is Ibn Abd al-Hamid al-Dabbi, both from Ubayd al-Mukattib. Then he will narrate it again immediately after, by two other isnads: 2418 and 2419, from the narration of Sufyan, who is al-Thawri, from Ubayd al-Mukattib.

"Ubayd al-Mukattib," with a damma on the mim, sukun on the kaf and a kasra on the taʼ, from "al-iktab," meaning teaching writing: he is Ubayd ibn Mihran al-Kufi, and he is trustworthy; Muslim included him in his Sahih. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Sa'd 6:237, and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/2.]]

2418. Ishaq ibn Ibrahim ibn Habib ibn al-Shahid narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ubayd al-Mukattib, from Mujahid: "And their means were cut off from them," he said: their connection in the world. [[Report 2418: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim ibn Habib ibn al-Shahid, a teacher of al-Tabari: trustworthy and reliable. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/211, and Tarikh Baghdad 6:370.]]

2419. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us; and Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, both saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ubayd al-Mukattib, from Mujahid, with the like of it.

2420. Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And their means were cut off from them," he said: the affection.

2421. Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, with the like of it.

2422. Al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, who said: a connection that existed between them by affection in the world.

2423. Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa, who said: Qays ibn Sa'd informed me, from Ata', from Ibn Abbas, concerning the saying of God, may He be exalted: "And their means were cut off from them," he said: the affection.

2424. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "And their means were cut off from them": the means of remorse on the Day of Resurrection, and the means of connection that existed between them in the world, by which they used to connect and love one another. These turned into enmity for them on the Day of Resurrection. Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disbelieve in others, and some of you will curse others, and some of you will disown others. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿The intimate friends on that day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [Surah al-Zukhruf: 67], so every friendship became enmity for its people, except the friendship of the righteous.

2425. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Mu'ammar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: "And their means were cut off from them," he said: it is the connection that existed between them in the world.

2426. It was narrated to me from Ammar ibn al-Hasan, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "And their means were cut off from them," he says: the means are remorse.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of "al-asbab" is the ranks (manazil) they had among the people of the world.

Mention of those who said that:

2427. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: "And their means were cut off from them," he says: their ranks were cut off from them.

2428. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas: "And their means were cut off from them," he said: the means are the ranks.

* *

Others said: "The means" are the kinship ties.

Mention of those who said that:

2429. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Juraij said, and Ibn Abbas said: "And their means were cut off from them," he said: the kinship ties.

* *

Others said: "The means" are the deeds they used to do in the world.

Mention of those who said that:

2430. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: as for "And their means were cut off from them," it is the deeds.

2431. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His saying: "And their means were cut off from them," he said: the means of their deeds. The people of piety were given the means of their deeds as a firm bond, so they grasp them and are saved; but the others were given the means of their wicked deeds, so they are cut off from them and go off into the Fire.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: [[From the beginning of this paragraph, it is Abu Ja'far's own speech, and I fear something may have fallen out before it. This opening, in any case, departs from the method his book followed before and after.]] "Al-asbab" are the things by which one attaches himself. He said: "al-sabab" is a rope. "Al-asbab" is the plural of "sabab," which is everything by which a man reaches his objective and need. A rope is called "sabab" because one reaches the need, which cannot be reached except by clinging to it, through clinging to it. A road is called "sabab," because by traveling it one reaches what cannot be attained except by crossing it. In-law relation is called "sabab," because it is a cause (sabab) of prohibition. A means of approach is called "sabab," because one reaches the need through it; and likewise everything by which the attainment of an objective occurs is a "sabab" for attaining it.

Since this is so, the correct view regarding the interpretation of His saying, "And their means were cut off from them," is to say: God, may He be exalted, informed that those who wronged themselves, from among the people of disbelief who died while disbelievers, disown, at their witnessing the punishment of God, the followed one from the follower, and their means are cut off from them.

God, may He be exalted, has informed in His Book that some of them curse others, and He reported about the Satan that he says to his allies: ﴿I cannot help you, nor can you help me. I have disbelieved in your associating me with God before﴾ [Surah Ibrahim: 22]. He, may He be exalted, informed that the intimate friends on that day will be enemies to one another except the righteous, and that the disbelievers on that day will not help one another; so He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned. What is wrong with you that you do not help one another?﴾ [Surah al-Saffat: 24-25]. And that a man among them will not benefit from his kinsman nor from his close relative, even if his kinsman was a friend of God. So He, may He be exalted, said concerning that: ﴿The plea of forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him; but when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to God, he disowned him﴾ [Surah al-Tawbah: 114]. And He, may He be exalted, informed that their deeds will become regrets upon them.

All these meanings are means (asbab) by which a person in the world reaches his aims. God cut off their benefits in the Hereafter from the disbelievers in Him, because these were contrary to His obedience and His good pleasure, so they are cut off with their people. Neither their friendships with one another benefited them when they came to their Lord, [[In the printed edition: "yanfa'uhum" (benefits them), but the correct reading is what I have established, since the verbs before and after it are all in the past tense. "Khilal" is the verbal noun of "khalla" (with a shadda on the lam) "yakhallu" "mukhalla" and "khilal," meaning friendship and affection. Imru' al-Qays says: "I turned love away from them out of fear of destruction... so I am not one who abandons friendship, nor one who is tired of it."]]

nor did their worship of their rivals, nor their obedience to their devils; nor did their kinship ties defend them and help them against the vengeance of God upon them; nor did their deeds avail them, but they became regrets upon them. So all the means of the disbelievers are cut off.

Therefore there is no meaning more eloquent, in the interpretation of His saying, "And their means were cut off from them," than the description of God [that] and that is what we have explained of the cutting off of all their means, not some of them, [[The addition between the brackets is necessary so that the beginning and end of the sentence are consistent, in the following clause. By his saying "the description of God" he means what God, glorified, described of the severing of the means of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, like what he enumerated just above in the previous paragraph.]] according to what we have said in this matter. And whoever claims that what is meant by that is a particular subset of the means, will be asked to provide proof for his claim from a principle that is not disputed, and will be countered with the statement of his opponent on it. He will not say anything in this matter without being bound in the end to something similar.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 167:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿And those who followed said, "If only we had a return [to the world], then we would disassociate ourselves from them as they have disassociated themselves from us."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His, may He be remembered, words, "And those who followed said," he means: the followers of men, those who had taken them as rivals to God, obeying them in disobedience to God and disobeying their Lord in obeying them, when they see God's punishment in the Hereafter, said: "If only we had a return."

* *

By "return" (karrah) he means the coming back to the world, from the saying of the speaker, "I charged against the people, charging (akurru) a charge (karran)," and "karrah" is a single occurrence, which is when one attacks them, returning upon them after having turned away from them, as al-Akhtal said:

"And indeed the mares turned back upon Fazarah with a turn, like the return of the sprinkled [arrow-lot?] ... and they circled there in a circle."

[Note: the Diwan has ... and the Fazarah ibn Dhubyan ibn Bughayd. al-Munih: an arrow with no share in the game of maysir (qidh al-maysir), the arrows of maysir being seven with shares and four without shares with the seven, but they are re-cast with them in every throw...]

And as for what is related:

2432 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah: "And those who followed said, 'If only we had a return, then we would disassociate ourselves from them as they have disassociated themselves from us'," i.e., for us there is a return to the world.

2433 - al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "And those who followed said, 'If only we had a return'," he said: The followers said: "If only we had a return to the world, so that we would disassociate ourselves from them as they disassociated themselves from us."

* *

His words, "then we would disassociate ourselves" (fa-natabarra'a), are in the accusative because it is an answer to the wish with "fa'" (the fa of response). For the people wished for a return to the world in order to disassociate themselves from those who used to obey them in disobedience to God, just as their leaders who were in the world, who were followed in it in disbelief in God, disassociated themselves from them, when they witnessed the magnitude of the punishment of God that had descended upon them, and they said: "Would that we were returned, and we would not deny the signs of our Lord, and we would be among the believers" [Qur'an 6:27].

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿Thus God will show them their deeds as regrets for them﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of His words, "Thus God will show them their deeds," says: just as He showed them the punishment that He mentioned in His words, "and they will see the punishment," which they used to deny in the world, so likewise He will show them their wicked deeds for which they deserved punishment from God, "as regrets for them," meaning: remorse.

* *

"Hasarat" is the plural of "hasrah." Likewise every noun whose singular is on the pattern "fa'lah" with an open first letter and a sukun second letter, its plural on the pattern "fa'alat," like "shahwah" and "tamrah," becomes "shahawat" and "tamarat," with the second letter vocalised. But if it is an adjective, you leave its second letter sukun, like "dakhmah," whose plural is "dakhmat," and "'ablah," whose plural is "'ablat." Sometimes the second letter is made sukun in nouns, as the poet said: [The speaker is unknown.]

"Perhaps the vicissitudes of time, or its turns, will make us prevail over its calamities, and the soul will rest from its sighs."

So he made the second letter of "zafarat" sukun, and it is a noun. It is said: "hasrah" is the most intense remorse.

* *

If someone says to us: How can they see their deeds as regrets for them, when a person only regrets abandoning good and missing it? And you know that the disbelievers had no deeds for which they would regret not increasing them, so that God would show them a little of it! Rather, all their deeds were acts of disobedience to God, and there is no regret for them in that; the regret is only for what they did not do of obedience to God?

It is said: The people of interpretation differ in interpreting that, so we will mention what they said, then we will inform of what is more apt as its interpretation, God willing.

Some of them said: The meaning of that: Thus God will show them their deeds, which He imposed upon them in the world, but they wasted them and did not act by them, until others were made worthy by their obedience to their Lord of what God had prepared for them, had they acted by them in their lives, of dwellings and blessings. Thus the reward that God had prepared for them with Him, had they obeyed Him in the world, which they witnessed upon entering the Fire or before that, became a grief and remorse and regret for them.

Those who said that:

2434 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Thus God will show them their deeds as regrets for them." He asserted that Paradise is raised up for them, and they look at it and at their houses in it, had they obeyed God, and it is said to them: "These are your dwellings had you obeyed God," then they are divided among the believers, who inherit them. That is when they regret.

2435 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, saying: Abu al-Za'ra' narrated to us, from Abdullah, in a story he mentioned, and he said: There is not a soul but that it looks at a house in Paradise and a house in the Fire, and that is the Day of Regret. He said: The people of the Fire see the people of Paradise, and it is said to them: "If only you had acted!" and regret seizes them. He said: The people of Paradise see the house that is in the Fire, and it is said: "Had God not bestowed His favour upon you!"

[Editorial note on the chain: Sufyan is al-Thawri. Salamah ibn Kuhayl al-Hadrami, previously authenticated. Al-Thawri said he was "a pillar of the pillars"; Ahmad said he was "precise in hadith"; Abu Zur'ah said he was "Kufan, trustworthy, reliable, intelligent." Abu al-Za'ra' is Abdullah ibn Hani' Abu al-Za'ra' al-Kabir, maternal uncle of Salamah ibn Kuhayl, a trustworthy senior Successor. This narration is a fragment of a long report, as al-Tabari says "in a story he mentioned"; another fragment appears at Tabari 15:97 (Bulaq). It is a mawquf report from Ibn Mas'ud, but since it concerns the end of time, trials, the end of the world, resurrection and intercession, which cannot be known by opinion, it is effectively marfu' in ruling. al-Hakim related it in full in al-Mustadrak 4:496-498 through al-Husayn ibn Hafs al-Isfahani, from Sufyan, with this chain, and said it was sahih by the standard of the two Shaykhs, and al-Dhahabi agreed. al-Haythami cited it in Majma' al-Zawa'id 10:328-330 and said it was mawquf and contradicts the sahih hadith and the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "I am the first intercessor." Al-Tayalisi related another fragment from it via Yahya ibn Salamah ibn Kuhayl from his father, but Yahya is very weak; al-Bukhari said "munkar al-hadith." The weakness of that chain does not harm, since this report has a sound chain through Sufyan al-Thawri from Salamah ibn Kuhayl.]

* *

If someone says: How can deeds that they did not do be attributed to them under this interpretation?

It is said: Just as a deed is presented to a man and it is said to him, before he does it: "This is your deed," meaning: this is what it is incumbent upon you to do, just as it is said to a man whose lunch is brought before he eats it: "This is your lunch today," meaning: this is what you will eat today. Likewise His words, "Thus God will show them their deeds as regrets for them," mean: thus God will show them the deeds that it was obligatory for them to perform in the world, as regrets for them.

* *

Others said: Thus God will show them their evil deeds as regrets for them: why did they do them? Why did they not act by other than them, which would please God, may He be remembered?

Those who said that:

2436 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "Thus God will show them their deeds as regrets for them": their wicked deeds became a regret for them on the Day of Resurrection.

2437 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words, "their deeds as regrets for them": Were not their wicked deeds, by which God caused them to enter the Fire, [made] regrets for them? He said: And He made the deeds of the people of Paradise theirs, and recited God's words: "For what you sent forth in the days that have passed" [Qur'an 69:24].

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more apt of the two interpretations of the verse is the interpretation of those who said: The meaning of His words, "Thus God will show them their deeds as regrets for them," is: thus God shows the disbelievers their wicked deeds as regrets for them: why did they act by them? And why did they not act by other than them? So they will regret what they neglected of their evil deeds, when they see their recompense from God and His punishment, because God informed that He would show them their deeds as remorse for them.

So what is more apt for the interpretation of the verse is what the apparent meaning indicates, not what an inner meaning might bear that has no indication that it is what is meant. As for what al-Suddi said about it, though it is a view the verse may bear, it is a far-fetched tendency, and there is no report stating that it is as he mentioned that would constitute a proof to be accepted, nor any indication in the apparent meaning of the verse that it is what is intended. Since the matter is thus, the apparent sense of the revelation is not to be diverted to an inner interpretation.

* *

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿And they will not come out of the Fire﴾ (167)

Abu Ja'far said: He, may He be remembered, means by that: and these whom I have described as disbelievers, even if they regret after witnessing what they witnessed of God's punishment, their remorse over what preceded from their wicked deeds becomes intense, and they wish for a return to the world to repent therein and to disassociate themselves from their misleaders and masters whom they used to obey in disobedience to God therein, are not going to come out of the Fire which God has made them enter by their disbelief in Him in the world, and their regret there does not save them from God's punishment at that time; rather, they are therein abiding forever.

* *

In this verse is the indication of God's refuting those who claim that the punishment of God upon the people of the Fire from among the disbelievers is terminated, and that it has an end, and that after that it perishes. For God, may He be remembered, informed about these whom He described in this verse, then concluded the report about them that they are not coming out of the Fire, without any exception from Him of a time over another. So that is without limit or end.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿O mankind, eat of what is in the earth, lawful and good, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾ (2:168)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: "O mankind, eat of what I have made lawful for you of the foods, through the tongue of My Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), and which I have made good for you, of what you forbid yourselves of the baheerah, the sawaa'ib, the waseelah and what is similar to that, which I have not forbidden to you, [as opposed to] what I have forbidden to you of the foods and victuals, which I have rendered impure: carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than God has been invoked." And leave the footsteps of Satan, which destroys you and causes you to perish, brings you to the places of ruin, and forbids you your property, so do not follow them and do not act upon them. Indeed, he (meaning by "he" that Satan, and the pronoun in "indeed, he" refers back to Satan) is to you, O mankind, a "clear enemy," meaning: he has made his enmity clear to you, by his refusal to prostrate to your father, his deception of him until he expelled him from the Garden, his causing him to slip into sin, and his eating from the tree.

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: So do not take him as an adviser, O mankind, despite his having made his enmity clear to you. Leave what he commands you to do, and hold fast to My obedience in what I have commanded you and forbidden you, of what I have made lawful for you and forbidden you, rather than what you have forbidden yourselves and made lawful, out of obedience of you to Satan and following his command.

* *

The meaning of His words "ḥalālan" is "ṭiqan" (free, unrestricted). [[Al-ṭalq (with kasra and sukun): the lawful. It is said: "it is ṭalq for you," meaning lawful. And in a hadith: "Horses are ṭalq," meaning that wagering on them is lawful.]] It is a verbal noun from the speaker's saying: "this thing has become lawful (ḥalla) for you," meaning it has become unrestricted for you, "so it is lawful for you (yaḥillu lak) as ḥalāl and ḥill." And among the speech of the Arabs: "it is ḥill for you," meaning ṭalq. [[In the printed edition: "from the speech of the Arabs...", with the waw affirmed; omitting it is also good.]]

* *

As for His words "ṭayyiban," it means pure, not impure and not forbidden.

* *

As for "al-khuṭuwāt" (the footsteps), it is the plural of "khuṭwa," and "khuṭwa" is the distance between the two feet of a walker. "Khaṭwa" with a fatha on the kha' is the single instance of the action, from the speaker's saying: "I took one step." "Khuṭwa" may be pluralized as "khuṭan," and "khaṭwa" as "khaṭawāt" and "khiṭā'."

* *

The meaning of the prohibition against following his footsteps is the prohibition against his path and his influence in what he calls to, which is contrary to the obedience of God, may His remembrance be exalted.

* *

The interpreters differed over the meaning of "khuṭuwāt." Some of them said: "The footsteps of Satan" are his deeds.

Those who said this:

2438 – Al-Muthanna b. Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah b. Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya b. Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali b. Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words "the footsteps of Satan," he said: his deeds.

* *

Others said: "The footsteps of Satan" are his sins.

Those who said this:

2439 – Muhammad b. 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His words "the footsteps of Satan," he said: his sin.

2440 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, he said: his sins.

2441 – Al-Hasan b. Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada regarding His words "and do not follow the footsteps of Satan," he said: his sins.

2442 – Yahya b. Abi Talib narrated to me, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak regarding His words "the footsteps of Satan," he said: the sins of Satan, which he commands.

* *

Others said: "The footsteps of Satan" are his obedience (to Satan).

Those who said this:

2443 – Musa b. Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi regarding "and do not follow the footsteps of Satan," he said: his obedience.

* *

Others said: "The footsteps of Satan" are vows made in disobedience.

Those who said this:

2444 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Sulayman, from Abu Mijlaz regarding His words "and do not follow the footsteps of Satan," he said: they are vows in acts of disobedience.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The sayings we have mentioned from those whom we have cited regarding the interpretation of His words "the footsteps of Satan" are close in meaning to one another, because each speaker among them, in what he said, pointed to the prohibition of following Satan in his traces and his actions. However, the true interpretation of the word is what I have explained: that it is the distance "between his two feet," and then it is used for all his traces and paths, as I have made clear.

**The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He only orders you to evil and immorality, and to say about Allah what you do not know﴾ (2:169)**

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "Indeed, He orders you," exalted is His remembrance, He means the Shaytan (Satan), "to evil and immorality, and to say about Allah what you do not know."

* *

"Al-su'" (evil) means sin, like "al-durr" (harm), from the speaker's saying, "This matter displeased you (sa'aka) with displeasure (su'an)," and it is what displeases the one who does it.

* *

As for "al-fahsha'" (immorality), it is a verbal noun like "al-sarra'" and "al-darra'" [[Perhaps the correct reading is, "fa-hiya ism masdar" (it is a noun of the verbal noun).]], and it is everything whose mention is considered shameful and whose hearing is ugly.

It has been said that the "su'" which Allah mentioned is the disobedience of Allah. If that is so, then Allah named it "su'" because it displeases its doer through its evil consequence for him with Allah. It has also been said that "al-fahsha'" is adultery. If that is so, then it is called [thus] [[What is between the brackets is an addition by which the sentence is made sound.]] because its hearing is ugly and it is detestable to mention the one who does it.

Mention of those who said that:

2445 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Indeed, He orders you to evil and immorality": as for "evil," it is disobedience, and as for "immorality," it is adultery.

* *

As for His saying, "and to say about Allah what you do not know," it refers to what they used to forbid of the *baha'ir* (she-camels whose ears were slit and released), the *sawa'ib* (animals released freely), the *wasa'il* (animals that gave twins), and the *hawami* (stallions set free after siring), while claiming that Allah had forbidden that. So Exalted is His remembrance said to them: ﴿Allah did not institute any bahira, sa'iba, wasila, or ham, but those who disbelieve invent lies against Allah, and most of them do not reason﴾ (5:103). Thus, in this verse, Exalted is His remembrance informed them [[In the printed edition it is "wa-akhbarahum" with a waw, and the correct and better reading is what I have established.]] that their saying, "Allah has forbidden this!" is from the lies to which the Shaytan orders them, and that He has in fact made it lawful for them and good, and did not forbid its eating to them. Rather, they say about Allah what they do not know the reality of, out of obedience to the Shaytan, following his footsteps, and imitating the traces of their misguided forefathers and their ignorant fathers, who were ignorant of Allah and of what He sent down to His Messenger, and astray from the truth and its path, and out of their excess, as Allah sent down in His Book to His Messenger (ﷺ). So Exalted is His remembrance said: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "No, we will follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾ (2:170).

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 170:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?﴾ (2:170)

Abu Ja'far said: In this verse there are two possible interpretations.

The first: the "ha" and "mim" in His saying "when it is said to them" refer back to "man" (some people) in His saying "And among the people are those who take, other than Allah, equals," so the meaning of the speech is: "And among the people are those who take, other than Allah, equals; and when it is said to them, 'Follow what Allah has sent down,' they say, 'Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon.'"

The second: the "ha" and "mim" in His saying "when it is said to them" refer to "the people" mentioned in His saying "O people, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good," so that this is a shift from direct address to a report about an absent party, as in His, may He be remembered, saying: ﴿until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them by a good wind﴾ (Surah Yunus: 22).

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more likely to be correct in my view, and more fitting to the interpretation of the verse [[In the printed edition: "and more likely in my view and more fitting to the verse," which is a broken sentence; I have restored it to al-Tabari's wording in his interpretation of most of the preceding verses.]], is that the "ha" and "mim" in His saying "to them" refer to "the people," and that this is a return from direct address to a report about an absent party, because it comes right after His saying "O people, eat of what is on the earth." It is therefore more fitting that it be a report about them than a report about those of whom He reported that among them are "those who take, other than Allah, equals," given what lies between them in verses and the cutting off of their account by a separate, new story; and that it was revealed concerning a group of Jews who said this [[In the printed edition: "and it was revealed concerning a group of Jews," which is a plainly erroneous reading that disrupts the sense. The correct text is as given here. Abu Ja'far means that the more correct view is that the verse was revealed concerning the pagan Arabs of the Jahiliyyah who forbade for themselves what they forbade, as mentioned in the interpretation of the two preceding verses (168, 169). He considers it unlikely that the verse refers to those mentioned in verse 165, just as he considers unlikely the view of those who said it was revealed concerning the Jews, in the report he will narrate after. Thus his words "and that it was revealed" are coordinated with his word "a report" in "more fitting that it be a report about them than a report about those...".]] when they were invited to Islam, as:

2446: Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited the Jews of the People of the Book to Islam and encouraged them towards it, and warned them of the punishment and vengeance of Allah. Rafi' ibn Kharijah and Malik ibn Awf said to him: "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon, for they were more knowledgeable and better than us!" So Allah revealed concerning their saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?﴾ [[In the printed edition: "Allah revealed concerning their saying that," which is a plain error; I have restored it to its text in Ibn Hisham's Sirah, as its source will be cited.]] [[Report no. 2446: in Ibn Hisham's Sirah 2: 200-201, with slight variation in wording.]]

2447: Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, narrated to me, saying: Sa'id ibn Jubayr, or Ikrimah, narrated to me, from Ibn Abbas, the like of it, except that he said: Abu Rafi' ibn Kharijah and Malik ibn Awf said to him. [[Report no. 2447: see report 2446.]]

* *

As for His saying "Follow what Allah has sent down," its meaning is: act upon what Allah has sent down in His Book to His Messenger; so make lawful what He has made lawful, make unlawful what He has made unlawful, and take it as a leader you follow and a guide whose rulings you obey.

* *

As for His saying "what we found (alfayna) our fathers upon," it means "we found (wajadna)," as the poet said: [[He is Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali.]]

*Then I found him, not one who seeks to make amends, nor one who remembers Allah except a little.*

[[His Diwan: 49 (Nafa'is al-Makhtutat); Sibawayh 1: 85; al-Aghani 11: 107; Amali Ibn al-Shajari 1: 283; al-Sadaqah wa al-Sadiq: 151; al-Khizanah 4: 554; Sharh Shawahid al-Mughni: 316; al-Lisan ('-t-b). These are from verses he composed about a woman he used to sit with in Basra, who was a attractive, bold woman. One day she said to him: "O Abu al-Aswad, would you like to marry me? I am a woman skilled with her hands, good at managing affairs, content with what is available." He said: "Yes." So she gathered her family and he married her. Then he found her to be other than she had claimed: she hastened to spend his wealth, reached out to betray him, and spread his secrets. So he went to those who had attended his wedding and asked them to gather at his place, and they did. He said to them: ...]]

Here the verses are given as in the source, followed by Ibn al-Shajari's remark on the grammar of the line, which I render as it stands.

"What makes the one who composed this line good is the omission of the tanwin for the meeting of two unvocalised letters, and the accusative for the name of Allah, the Exalted; and preferring this over omitting the tanwin for the annexation and the genitive for the name of Allah, because if he had annexed it, it would be defined by its annexation to a definite noun, and then the conjoined would not agree with the conjoined-to in indefiniteness. So he omitted the tanwin for the meeting of two unvocalised letters, and made the active participle operative."

"Isti'tab" (to be made to make amends) means: he turned back from wrongdoing and sought contentment; thus *mustatib* is one who makes amends.

He means: I found him. And as for:

2448: Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "They say, 'Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon,'" that is, what we found our fathers upon.

2449: Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' the like of it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: So the meaning of the verse: when it is said to these disbelievers, "Eat of what Allah has made lawful for you, and leave the steps and paths of Satan, and act upon what Allah has sent down to His Prophet (ﷺ) in His Book," they turn arrogantly away from submitting to the truth and say, "Rather, we will follow our fathers and follow what we found them upon, of making lawful what they used to make lawful and making unlawful what they used to make unlawful."

* *

Allah, may He be remembered, said: "Even though their fathers" — meaning: the fathers of these disbelievers who passed away in their disbelief in the Mighty God — "understood nothing" of the religion of Allah and its obligations, His command and His prohibition, so that they might be followed in the path they took and be taken as examples in their deeds, "and were not guided" to right guidance, so that others might be guided by them and those seeking religion, desiring truth and correctness, might follow them?

He, may He be remembered, says to these disbelievers: How then, O people, do you follow what you found your fathers upon, leaving what your Lord commands you, when your fathers understood nothing of the command of Allah, nor were they correct in truth, nor did they attain right guidance? A follower only follows one who has knowledge of the thing and acts upon it himself; as for the ignorant, no one follows him in what he is ignorant of except one who has no intellect or discernment.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 171 (part 1 of 2):**

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is as the likeness of one who calls out to that which hears nothing but calling and crying﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the meaning of this.

Some of them said: The meaning is: the likeness of the disbeliever, in his scant understanding of what is recited to him from God's Book, and his poor acceptance of what he is called to of the Oneness of God and what he is admonished with, is the likeness of a beast that hears a sound when it is called to, and does not comprehend what is said to it.

Mention of those who said this:

2450. Hannad ibn al-Sari narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Simak, from Ikrimah, concerning His words: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve is as the likeness of one who calls out to that which hears nothing but calling and crying." He said: It is the likeness of a camel or a donkey: you call to it, and it hears the sound but does not understand what you say.

2451. Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Zurai' narrated to me, saying: Yusuf ibn Khalid al-Samti narrated to us, saying: Nafi' ibn Malik narrated to us, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words: "as the likeness of one who calls out to that which does not hear." He said: It is like the likeness of a sheep and the like. [[The report: 2451. This is a report with a broken (munharim) isnad. As for "Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Zurai'", the teacher of al-Tabari, I have not found his biography. Al-Tabari narrates from "Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Bazi'", and I cannot be certain it is him; the letter of his grandfather's name differs.
As for "Yusuf ibn Khalid al-Samti": he is extremely weak. Ibn Ma'in said of him: "A liar, a zindiq; his hadith is not to be written." One should not occupy oneself with the likes of him. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/388, Ibn Sa'd 7/2/47, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/221-222. "Al-Samti": with a fatha on the sin and a sukun on the mim, a nisba to samt (bearing and appearance). Ibn Sa'd said: "It was said of him al-Samti because of his beard and his appearance and bearing"!!
Nafi' ibn Malik: he is al-Asbahi, Abu Suhayl, the paternal uncle of the Imam Malik ibn Anas, and he is a reliable Successor (tabi'i). He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/86, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/453.]]

2452. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, his words: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve is as the likeness of one who calls out to that which hears nothing but calling and crying": like the camel, the donkey and the sheep. If you say to one of them, "Eat!", it does not know what you say, except that it hears your voice. Likewise the disbeliever: if you command him to good, or forbid him from evil, or admonish him, he does not understand what you say, except that he hears your voice.

2453. al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ibn Abbas said: The likeness is of an animal that is called out to, so it hears but does not understand what is said to it. Likewise the disbeliever: he hears the sound but does not understand.

2454. Sufyan ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Khusayf, from Mujahid: "As the likeness of one who calls out to that which does not hear." He said: The likeness of the disbeliever is the likeness of the beast that hears the sound and does not understand.

2455. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "As the likeness of one who calls out": it is a parable God struck for the disbeliever, who hears what is said to him and does not understand, like the beast that hears the calling and does not understand.

2456. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve is as the likeness of one who calls out to that which hears nothing but calling and crying." He says: The likeness of the disbeliever is like the camel and the sheep: it hears the sound and does not understand, nor know what is meant by it.

2457. al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "as the likeness of one who calls out to that which hears nothing but calling and crying." He said: It is a parable God struck for the disbeliever. He says: The likeness of this disbeliever is the likeness of this beast that hears the sound and does not know what is said to it. Likewise the disbeliever does not benefit from what is said to him.

2458. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: It is a parable of the disbeliever, who hears the sound and does not understand what is said to him.

2459. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Juraij said: I asked Ata', then I said to him: It is said: the beast does not understand, except that it hears the call of the caller when he calls out to it; so they likewise do not understand while they hear. He said: Just so. He said: And Mujahid said: "The one who calls out" is the shepherd, "to that which does not hear" of the animals.

2460. Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "As the likeness of one who calls out" the shepherd "to that which does not hear" of the animals.

2461. Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "As the likeness of one who calls out to that which hears nothing but calling and crying": it does not understand what is said to it, except that when it is called it comes, or when it is summoned it goes. As for "the one who calls out", it is the shepherd of the sheep, just as the shepherd calls out to that which does not hear what is said to it, except when it is called or summoned. Likewise Muhammad (ﷺ) calls out to one who hears nothing but the babbling of speech. God says: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 18].

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of those who held this view, in their interpretation as they interpreted it, as I have related from them, is: And the likeness of the admonition of those who disbelieve and of their admonisher is as the likeness of the shepherd calling to his sheep and calling out to them. So "the likeness" has been attributed to "those who disbelieve", and the mention of "the admonition and the admonisher" has been dropped, because the context indicates it, as one says: "When you meet so-and-so, honour him with the honour of a ruler," meaning: as you honour a ruler; and as the poet said:

"I shall not greet, as long as I live, Zayd with the greeting of the Amir" [[The citation of this line was already given in this volume: 281, note 1. This view in the interpretation of the verse was mentioned by al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:100.]]

meaning: as one greets the Amir.

It may also be that the meaning, on this interpretation which these men adopted, is: And the likeness of those who disbelieve, in their scant understanding of God and His Messenger, is as the likeness of the beast being called, which understands from the command and prohibition nothing but the sound. For if it were said to it, "Graze! Go to the water!", it would not know what is said to it, except the sound it hears from the speaker. Likewise the disbeliever: his likeness, in his scant understanding of what he is commanded and forbidden, through his poor reflection upon it and his little consideration and thought about it, is the likeness of this one being called in what it is commanded and forbidden. So the meaning refers to the one being called, while the speech is directed at the caller, as the poet of the Banu Dhubyan, al-Nabigha, said:

"I have feared, until my fear does not exceed
the fear of a wild goat on the peak of al-Mutarah, a sheltered one." [[His Diwan: 90; it will come in the tafsir 30:146 (Bulaq); Majaz al-Qur'an: 65; Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:99; Mushkil al-Qur'an: 151; al-Insaf: 164; Amali Ibn al-Shajari 1:52, 324; Amali al-Sharif 1:202, 216; Mu'jam ma Musta'jam: 1238. It is from a qasidah of which a line was cited in this volume: 213. "Dhi al-Mutarah" (with the mim vowelled with a fatha) is the name of a mountain. "Aqil" means: he has taken refuge at the top of the mountain, sought shelter in it, and held back. "Al-Wa'l": the mountain goat, which shelters itself with its horns from the hunter. Al-Bakri mentioned that he saw, in Ibn al-A'rabi's report, that he means by "Dhi al-Mutarah" (with the mim vowelled with a damma) his she-camel, and that it is the "mutarah" of the heart from vigour and exuberance. And by that he means what is on her of the saddle and equipment. He says: It is as if I am on the saddle of this she-camel, and on one who is sheltered from fear and terror.]]

The meaning: until the fear of the wild goat does not exceed my fear. And as another (al-Nabigha al-Ja'di) said:

"Your saying was an obligation, just as
adultery was an obligation for stoning." [[Will come in the tafsir 2:198, 327 (Bulaq); Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:99, 131; Mushkil al-Qur'an: 153; al-Insaf: 165; Amali al-Sharif 1:216; al-Sahibi: 172; Simt al-La'ali: 368; al-Lisan (zana). Al-Tabari said in 2:327: "He means: as stoning was the obligatory punishment for the offence of adultery."]]

The meaning: just as stoning was the obligation of adultery, he made adultery the obligation of stoning, because the meaning of the speech is clear to its hearer. And as another said:

"Indeed a lamp is noble in its glory,
by which the eye is delighted when it is seen (tajharuh)" [[Will come in the tafsir (2; 198 Bulaq); Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:99, 131; Amali al-Sharif 1:216; al-Lisan (hala). It is said: "There is no one in the tribe whom my eye loves to behold (tajharuh)", meaning my eye takes him and I am pleased by him. And in the hadith describing the Messenger of God (ﷺ), Ali says: "He was neither short nor tall, and he was nearer to tall. Whoever saw him was struck by his beauty (jahharahu)", meaning he was great in the eye.]]

The meaning: it is delighted (yuhla) by the eye, so he made it that the eye is delighted by it. [[What has passed is more than the statement of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:99.]] And the parallels to this in the speech of the Arabs are more than can be counted, of what the Arabs direct from the report of what they speak of to what accompanies it, because the meaning of that is evident to its hearer. So you say: "Present the basin to the she-camel," whereas it is the she-camel that is presented to the basin, and similar things of their speech. [[This is from the text of Abu Ubaydah's words in Majaz al-Qur'an: 63-64.]]

Others said: The meaning of that is: And the likeness of those who disbelieve, in their calling upon their gods and idols that neither hear nor understand, is as the likeness of one who calls out to that which hears nothing but calling and crying; and that is the echo, whose sound is heard, and the caller does not understand anything from it.

So the interpretation of the speech according to the view of those who said this is: And the likeness of those who disbelieve and their gods, in their calling upon them while they neither understand nor comprehend, is as the likeness of the one calling out to that which does not hear the caller except calling and crying; that is, from which the caller hears nothing but his own call.

Mention of those who said this:

2462.
