Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His words: "And the likeness of those who disbelieve is as the likeness of one who calls out to that which hears nothing but calling and crying": He said: It is the man who shouts in the hollows of the mountains, and a voice answers him there, returning his call, which is called "al-sada" (echo). So the likeness of these people's gods to them is as the likeness of one who is answered with this sound, which does not benefit him; it hears only calling and crying. He said: The Arabs call that "al-sada".

Note: This verse may be understood, on this interpretation, in another way besides that. It would mean: And the likeness of those who disbelieve in their calling upon their gods that do not understand their calling is as the likeness of one who calls to his sheep from a place from which his sheep do not hear his voice, so he gains nothing from his calling except that he is in toil from calling and crying. Likewise the disbeliever in his calling upon his gods is only in toil from calling upon them and crying out to them, and nothing benefits him.

Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation most preferable to me for the verse is the first interpretation, which Ibn Abbas and those who agreed with him stated. It is that the meaning of the verse is: And the likeness of the admonition of the disbeliever and his admonisher is as the likeness of the one calling to his sheep and his calling out to them: he hears his call but does not understand his speech, as we have already explained.

As for the permissibility of omitting "admonition" by relying on the likeness of it, we have already explained it in His words: ﴿Their likeness is as the likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 17], and in other parallels of it among the verses, with sufficient explanation so as not to repeat it. [[See what has passed: 1:318-328, and seek that in the index of Arabic grammar from the earlier parts.]]

We have chosen this interpretation because this verse was revealed concerning the Jews, and it is them whom God, dhikruh exalted, meant by it. The Jews were not people of idols they worshipped, nor people of statues they venerated, hoping for their benefit or the repelling of their harm. So there is no basis, given that this is the case, for the interpretation of one who interpreted it to mean: the likeness of those who disbelieve in their calling out to the gods and their calling upon them.

If a speaker says: What is your proof that the intended people of this verse are the Jews?

It is said: Our proof for that is what precedes it of verses and what follows it, for they are the ones meant by it. So what lies between them is more fitting and more proper to be a report about them than a report about others, until clear proofs come showing that the report turns away from them to others. Besides this, there are the reports we have mentioned from those from whom it has been said that they were revealed concerning them, and the report we narrated from Ibn Abbas that the verse preceding this verse was revealed concerning them. [[This is a problematic point in the words of Abu Ja'far, may God be pleased with him, which required him to clarify it thoroughly. For the beginning of his expression indicates that all the verses before this verse were revealed concerning the Jews, and that is not so. Then after a little he returns to say: "This, with the report we narrated from Ibn Abbas that the verse before this verse was revealed concerning them" — meaning the Jews. Had the matter been as is understood from the beginning of his expression, there would be no meaning to his explicit statement afterwards that the verse "before this verse" was revealed concerning them, in what is narrated from Ibn Abbas.
The apparent meaning is that Abu Ja'far intended to say: the preceding verses were revealed concerning the Jews — except the final verses from the start of His words "Indeed those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers" to His words "And your God is One God" (163-170). Those were revealed concerning the Arab disbelievers, and Ibn Abbas mentioned that the last verse (170) was revealed concerning the Jews as well. Then the verses after them are without doubt about the Jews and the People of the Book, so for that reason he understood the meaning of this verse to be meant for the Jews. It is as though he made the verses (163-169) a parenthetical insertion in the narration of a single story, the story of the Jews.
If that is not the case, I do not know how his speech coheres. For from the time he began explaining these verses from 163-169, he mentioned none but the polytheists, and he made clear that what is meant by His words, "O mankind, eat of what is in the earth, lawful and good" — are those who forbade for themselves the bahira, the sa'iba and the wasila (p. 300). Then he returned in the interpretation of His words, "and that you say about God what you do not know," and said: it is what they used to forbid of the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the hami (p. 303). And the Jews, just as they were not people of idols they worshipped, or of statues they venerated, as Abu Ja'far said, so also they did not forbid a bahira, nor a sa'iba, nor a wasila, as he mentioned in the explanation of the preceding verses. So this is a contradiction on his part, may God have mercy on him, unless his speech is understood as an exception for the verses he explained as intended for the Arab polytheists who forbade for themselves what they forbade of the bahira, the sa'iba and the wasila.
The correct view in my opinion is that this verse follows the preceding verses, and that its story is similar to the story before it in mentioning the polytheists to whom God said: "O mankind, eat of what is in the earth, lawful and good." And that the return to the story of the People of the Book is from the beginning of His words, "Indeed those who conceal what God has sent down of the Book" and the verses that follow it. See what will come (317), for he returned there and made the verse specific to the polytheists of the age of ignorance by his mention of what they forbade for themselves of foods, and that is a severe contradiction.]] And according to what we have said, that this verse is intended for the Jews, Ata' used to say:

2463. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ata' said to me concerning this verse: They are the Jews, about whom God revealed: ﴿Indeed those who conceal what God has sent down of the Book, and take for it a small price﴾ to His words: ﴿How patient they are over the Fire!﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 174-175].

As for His words, "yan'iq" (calls out), it means: he cries out to the sheep. "Al-Na'iq" and "al-Nu'aq" (the calling). From it is the saying of al-Akhtal:

"So call out to your sheep, O Jarir, for indeed
your own soul has made you hope for error in the wilderness." [[His Diwan: 50; Naqa'id Jarir wa al-Akhtal: 81; Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara': 429; Majaz al-Qur'an: 64; al-Lisan (n'q). Some of its lines have passed in 2:38-39, 492, 496, and this volume 3:294. He had mentioned before the wars of his clan, the Banu Taghlib, then said to Jarir: You are only a shepherd of sheep, so cry out to your sheep, and leave the wars and their mention. You have no knowledge of them, nor do your forefathers. Whatever your soul tells you of that is error and falsehood.]]

I.e.: cry out to it.

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind; so they do not understand﴾ (171)

Abu Ja'far said: By His words "deaf, dumb, blind" (ṣumm bukm ʿumy), He, may His remembrance be exalted, means these disbelievers whose likeness is like that of one who shouts to what hears nothing but calling and crying out. "Deaf" (ṣumm) to the truth, so they do not hear it. "Dumb" (bukm) means mute (khurs) concerning the utterance of the truth and what is right, and concerning acknowledging what God commanded them to acknowledge, and clarifying to people what God, may His remembrance be exalted, commanded them to make clear about the matter of Muhammad ﷺ; so they do not speak it, nor say it, nor make it clear to people. "Blind" (ʿumy) to guidance and the path of truth, so they do not see it. [[See the explanation of "ṣumm," "bukm," "ʿumy" earlier, 1:328-331. Abu Ja'far here understood the meaning of the verse as referring to the Jews and the People of the Book. And see the earlier note, p. 314, no. 1.]] As follows:

2464 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah concerning His words "deaf, dumb, blind": he said: deaf to the truth, so they do not hear it, nor benefit from it, nor understand it; blind to the truth and guidance, so they do not see it; dumb concerning the truth, so they do not speak it.

2465 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "deaf, dumb, blind," he said: concerning the truth.

2466 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "deaf, dumb, blind," he said: they do not hear guidance, nor see it, nor understand it.

* *

As for the nominative case (raf') in His words "deaf, dumb, blind" (ṣumm bukm ʿumy), it comes from the beginning of a new sentence (ibtida' wa-istinaf), as shown by His words "so they do not understand" (fa-hum la yaʿqilun), just as one says in speech: "He is deaf who does not hear, and he is dumb who does not speak." [[See its i'rab in the other verse earlier, 1:329-330.]]

**The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words:** ﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you, and give thanks to God, if it is Him you worship﴾ (172)

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, "O you who believe," He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: O you who have affirmed God and His Messenger, acknowledged servitude to God, and submitted to Him in obedience, as related:

2467. Al-Muthanna told me, who said: Ishaq told us, who said: Abu Zuhayr told us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding His words, "O you who believe," that he said: "They affirmed."

* *

"Eat of the good things We have provided for you" means: eat of the lawful provision that We have made lawful for you, which became good for you by My making it lawful for you, rather than what you yourselves had forbidden, which I had not forbidden you, of foods and drinks.

"And give thanks to God" means: praise God as is due to Him from you, for the blessings with which He has provided you and made them good for you.

"If it is Him you worship" means: if you are submissive to His command, listening and obeying. So eat what He has permitted you to eat, made lawful, and made good for you, and abandon the steps of Satan in forbidding it.

We have already mentioned some of what they used to forbid themselves in their jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam) of foods, which He urged them to eat and forbade them from believing it to be unlawful, since their forbidding it in the jahiliyyah was obedience on their part to Satan and following the people of disbelief in God among their fathers and forefathers. Then He, may His remembrance be exalted, clarified to them what He had forbidden them and detailed it for them, explaining it.

[[In the printed edition: "wa fassala lahum" (and He detailed for them), and the correct reading is what I have established. What he says here is another proof that Abu Ja'far was confused about the story of these verses, for he went back and made some of the preceding verses concern the polytheists of the Arabs in their jahiliyyah, as you see; and this is also clear in his explanation of the following verse. See p. 314, note 1.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 173 (part 1 of 2):

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Indeed, He has forbidden you only the carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked.﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: Do not forbid to yourselves what I have not forbidden you, O believers in Allah and His Messenger, of the baha'ir (she-camels slit-eared and released), the sawa'ib (animals released freely), and the like. Rather, eat of them, for I have not forbidden you anything except carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which is invoked upon for other than Me.
* *
The meaning of His words, "Indeed He has forbidden you carrion," is: He has forbidden you only carrion.
"Innama" is a single particle, and for this reason "al-maytata" (carrion) and "al-dam" (blood) are in the accusative. In the case of "al-maytata," if "innama" is taken as a single particle, only the accusative is permissible. But if "innama" were two words, separated from "inna," then "al-maytatu" would be in the nominative, and what follows it likewise. The meaning of the sentence would then be: Indeed, what Allah has forbidden you of foods is carrion, blood, and the flesh of swine, and nothing else. [[See the detailed discussion of this in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an, 1:102-103.]]
It has been related from some reciters that they recited it in this way, according to this interpretation. I do not permit myself to recite it so, although it has a comprehensible basis in interpretation and in Arabic grammar, because the consensus of the authoritative reciters is against it. It is not permissible for anyone to object to them regarding what they have transmitted unanimously.
* *
If "ḥurrima" were read with a dammah on the ḥa' (ḥurrima, passive), then "al-maytatu" would have two possible nominative readings. The first: the subject is unnamed (passive), and "innama" is one particle.
The second: "inna" and "ma" have the value of two particles, "ḥurrima" is the relative clause of "ma," and "al-maytatu" is the predicate of "alladhi," nominative as the predicate. Although this too has a basis, I do not permit myself to recite by it, for the reason I have mentioned.
* *
As for "al-maytata," the readers differ in its recitation. Some of them read it with a light pronunciation (al-maytata with the yā' lightened), while its meaning involves the emphatic form (mayyita), but they lighten it just as those who say of "huwa hayyin layyin" (he is easy and gentle) say "al-hayn al-layn," as the poet said:
"He who has died and found rest is not a dead man; / the dead is the dead of the living."
[[From al-Asma'iyyat: 5; Mu'jam al-Shu'ara': 252; Tahdhib al-Alfaz: 448; al-Lisan (m-w-t); Hamasat Ibn al-Shajari: 51; al-Khizana 4:187; Sharh Shawahid al-Mughni: 138. It is from good, truthful verses; after it he says: "The dead is only he who lives humiliated, his condition dejected, with little hope. / So some people suck at trickles of water, and some have their throats in the water." Al-thimad is the little water that remains in pits. How true is what this noble free man said.]] He combined the two dialects in a single line, with a single meaning.
Others read it with the emphatic form and treated it as its original root, saying: it is originally "mayyit," the pattern "fayʿil," from death. But when the unvowelled yā' and the vowelled wāw came together, and the yā' with its sukun preceded, the wāw was changed to yā' and doubled, so they became a doubled yā', as they did in "sayyid" and "jayyid." They said: whoever lightens it has only sought lightness. Recitation with it in its original form is preferable.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The correct view of this matter, in my judgment, is that lightening and emphasis in the yā' of "al-maytah" are two well-known dialects both in recitation and in the speech of the Arabs, so whichever of them a reciter uses is correct, because there is no difference in their meaning.
* *
As for His words, "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked," He means by it: that which is slaughtered for the gods and idols, over which a name other than His is pronounced, or which is intended for other than Him, such as idols.
It is said "that over which is invoked" (ahalla bihi) because, when they wanted to slaughter what they offered to their gods, they would pronounce the names of the gods to whom they offered it and raise their voices with it. This became their custom, until anyone who slaughtered, whether he pronounced the name or not, and whether he raised his voice or not, was called "muhill." Their raising of voices with it is the "ihlal" which Allah, the Exalted, mentioned when He said, "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked." From this is said of one who utters the talbiyah in pilgrimage or umrah, "muhill," for his raising his voice with the talbiyah. And from it is "istihlal" of a child when it cries out at its fall from its mother's womb, and "istihlal" of rain, which is the sound of its falling on the earth, as 'Amr ibn Qami'ah said:
"The valleys were wronged by the ihlal of a [thirsty] rain-cloud, / so the clear water was pure for it after the clearing."
[[The attribution of this line was previously discussed in 1:523-524, and the correct attribution is to al-Hadirah al-Dhubyani.]]
The people of interpretation differed concerning this. Some of them said: By His words "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked," He means: what is slaughtered for other than Allah.
Those who said this:
2468- Bishr ibn Mu'adh told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatadah: "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked," he said: what is slaughtered for other than Allah.
2469- al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah concerning His words: "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked," he said: what is slaughtered for other than Allah, of what has not had the name of Allah pronounced over it.
2470- al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah told us, saying: Shibl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked," what is slaughtered for other than Allah.
2471- al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn 'Abbas said concerning His words: "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked," he said: what has been invoked for the tawaghit (false deities).
2472- Sufyan ibn Waki' told us, saying: Abu Khalid al-Ahmar told us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked," he said: what has been invoked for the tawaghit.
2473- al-Muthanna told me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, saying: Mu'awiyah told me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas: "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked," meaning: what has been invoked for all the tawaghit. That is: what is slaughtered for other than Allah by the people of disbelief, other than the Jews and Christians.
2474- Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Jarir told us, from 'Ata' concerning the saying of Allah: "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked," he said: it is what is slaughtered for other than Allah.
* *
Others said: The meaning of that is: what has been mentioned over it other than the name of Allah.
Those who said this:
2475- al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ishaq told us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi' concerning His words: "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked," he says: what has had mentioned over it other than the name of Allah.
2476- Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said—and I asked him about the saying of Allah: "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked"—he said: what is slaughtered for their gods, the idols (ansab) they worship, or over which they mention their names. He said: they say, "in the name of so-and-so," as you say, "in the name of Allah." He said: that is His words, "and that over which other than Allah has been invoked."
2477- Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Haywah told us, from 'Uqbah ibn Muslim al-Tujibi and Qays ibn Rafi' al-Ashja'i, that they both said: What is slaughtered for the festival of the churches is permitted to us, and what is offered to them of bread or meat, for it is only the food of the People of the Book. Haywah said: I said, "Have you seen the saying of Allah: 'and that over which other than Allah has been invoked'?" He said: That refers only to the Magians, the people of idols, and the polytheists.
* *
The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, then there is no sin upon him.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, "whoever is compelled," may His remembrance be exalted, He means: whoever is afflicted by the necessity of hunger, to what He has forbidden you of carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked—and he is in the state we have described—then there is no sin upon him in eating it, if he eats it.
* *
As for His words, "fa-man udturra" (whoever is compelled), it is an "iftaʿala" form from "ḍarūrah" (necessity).
* *
"Ghayra bāghin" (neither desiring) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "man," as if it were said: whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, and eats it, it is lawful for him.
* *
It has been said that the meaning of His words, "whoever is compelled," is: whoever is forced to eat it and eats it, there is no sin upon him.
Those who said this:
2478- Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi told us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri told us, saying: Isra'il told us, from Salim al-Aftas, from Mujahid concerning His words: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing": he said: a man whom the enemy seizes and invites to disobey Allah.
* *
As for His words, "neither desiring nor transgressing," the people of interpretation differ concerning its explanation.
Some of them said: By His words, "neither desiring," He means: one who does not rise against the rulers with his sword, rebelling against them without oppression, nor transgressing against them by war and aggression, thereby corrupting the path against them.
Those who said this:
2479- Abu Kurayb told us, saying: Ibn Idris told us, saying: I heard Layth, from Mujahid: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing": he said: not one who cuts the road, nor one who separates from the community, nor one who goes out in disobedience to Allah; for him there is a dispensation.
2480- al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah told us, saying: Shibl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing," he says: not one cutting the road, nor one separating from the rulers, nor one going out in disobedience to Allah; for him there is a dispensation. But whoever goes out desiring or transgressing in disobedience to Allah, there is no dispensation for him even if he is compelled to it.
2481- Hannad ibn al-Sari told us, saying: Sharik told us, from Salim, from Sa'id: "neither desiring nor transgressing": he said: he is one who cuts the road; there is no dispensation for him when he is hungry to eat carrion, nor when he is thirsty to drink wine.
2482- al-Muthanna told me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr told us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Sharik, from Salim—meaning al-Aftas—from Sa'id concerning His words: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing": he said: the desiring transgressor is the one who cuts the road; for him there is no dispensation and no honour.
2483- al-Muthanna told me, saying: al-Hammani told us, saying: Sharik told us, from Salim, from Sa'id concerning His words: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing": he said: if he goes out on one of the ways of Allah and is compelled to drink wine, he may drink; and if he is compelled to carrion, he may eat. But if he goes out cutting the road, there is no dispensation for him.
2484- al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hafs ibn Ghiyath told me, from al-Hajjaj, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah, from Mujahid, who said: "neither desiring" against the rulers, "nor transgressing" he said: one who cuts the road.
2485- Hannad told us, saying: Ibn Abi Za'idah told us, from Warqa', from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing": he said: not one who cuts the road, nor one who separates from the rulers, nor one who goes out in disobedience to Allah; for him there is a dispensation.
2486- Hannad told us, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah told us, from Hajjaj, from al-Hakam, from Mujahid: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing": he said: not desiring against the rulers, nor transgressing against the wayfarer.
* *
Others said concerning His words, "neither desiring nor transgressing": not desiring the forbidden in his eating, nor exceeding what has been permitted to him of it.
Those who said this:
2487- Bishr ibn Mu'adh told us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' told us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah concerning His words: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing": he said: not desiring in his eating, nor transgressing: by passing from the lawful to the unlawful while he has an alternative.
2488- al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Hasan concerning His words: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing": he said: not desiring in it, nor exceeding in eating it, while he is free of it.
2489- al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ishaq told us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq told us, from Ma'mar, from one who heard al-Hasan say that.
2490- al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Abu Tumaylah told us, from Abu Hamzah, from Jabir, from Mujahid and 'Ikrimah concerning His words: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing": "neither desiring" seeking it, "nor transgressing": exceeding what sustains himself.
2491- I was told by 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing," he says: without seeking the forbidden and exceeding it. Do you not see that He says: "But whoever seeks beyond that, those are the transgressors" [Surah al-Mu'minun: 7; Surah al-Ma'arij: 31].
2492- Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing": he said: that he eats that out of desire and transgression from the lawful to the unlawful, leaving the lawful which he has, and transgressing by eating this forbidden. This is the transgression. He denies that the two are different, and says: this and that are one!
* *
Others said the interpretation of that is: whoever is compelled, not desiring in his eating a pleasure, nor transgressing beyond what he must have.
Those who said this:
2493- Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing." As for "desiring," he seeks his appetite through it; and as for the "transgressor," he exceeds in his eating, eating until he is satisfied; rather, he eats of it only the amount that sustains himself until it reaches his need.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The most probable of these sayings for the interpretation of the verse is the saying of the one who said: whoever is compelled, not desiring by his eating what is forbidden to eat, nor transgressing in his eating, and he has, instead of eating it, sufficiency and independence through what Allah has made lawful to him.
This is because Allah, the Exalted, has not permitted anyone to kill himself under any circumstances. Since that is so, there is no doubt that the one who rebels against the Imam and the one who cuts the road, though they have done what Allah forbade them—namely this one's rising against the one he rebelled against, and this one's striving to corrupt the earth—do not, by their doing what they did of what Allah forbade them, make lawful for them what they did, [namely] the killing of themselves [by hunger]. [Their return to what Allah forbade them after their deed, though they had been made lawful for them before that act, and even if we do not regard their return to what Allah forbade them as a prohibition, does not permit for them what was forbidden to them before that.] Since that is so, it is obligatory upon the brigands and the rebels against the just Imams to return to the obedience of Allah, to return to what Allah obliged them to return to, and to repent from the disobedience of Allah—not to kill themselves by hunger, thereby adding to their sin another sin, and to their opposition to Allah's command another opposition. [[This paragraph is a refutation of the first view, the view that the "rebel" is one who rises against the rulers and the "transgressor" is the highwayman, and that they are excepted from the ruling of the verse permitting the compelled to eat what Allah has forbidden. But the wording in the original is corrupt and nearly devoid of meaning, and I did not presume to leave it as it stands. In the original it reads thus: [Rather, that is from their deed, even if it does not lead them to what Allah has forbidden them, so what was forbidden to them before that is not permitted to them.]
This is a sentence that does not stand. I have made an effort and judge that a whole line has probably fallen from the copyist between his words "killing themselves" and "before that from their deed," leaving "before" alone, so a later copyist, not grasping what he wrote, changed "qabl" to "bal," thinking this made the meaning sound in some way. Thus the speech became disordered as you see, to no clear meaning. What further corrupted and disordered it was the misreading of "wa-in lam nara raddahuma" as what was written: "wa-in lam yu'adhhuma," which produced a sentence heavily garbled.
Al-Tabari, in this paragraph, adduces two proofs to refute the view that the rebel is one who rises against the Imam and that the transgressor is the highwayman.
The first proof: that the rebel and the transgressor, although each has committed a forbidden act, the commission of this forbidden act does not make killing themselves lawful for them, since it was forbidden to them before they committed what they committed of Allah's prohibitions upon them.

The second argument: Allah has permitted every person compelled by necessity (mudtarr) to eat what is otherwise forbidden to him. Therefore, the exception of the one who transgresses (al-baghi) and the one who oversteps (al-adi) from the permission granted by Allah to the one compelled by necessity does not count, in his view, as a prohibition; rather, it is a return to what had been forbidden to them both before the transgression or the aggression. Nevertheless, this return to what had been forbidden to them, although what had been permitted to them and to every compelled person before the transgression and aggression has become forbidden to them, does not allow them to kill themselves, which was forbidden to them before the transgression and aggression.

Thus, it is obligatory upon them both to repent, not to kill themselves through hunger, so that they would increase in sin upon their sin, and in opposition upon their opposition through transgression and aggression, which Allah has commanded against.

As for the one who directed the interpretation of this to mean that he is not a transgressor in his eating by desire, so that he eats that out of desire and not to remove a necessity whose danger is death, from what Allah had already forbidden to him, then it is in meaning what we have said in its interpretation, although its wording differs.

As for the interpretation of His saying "nor transgressing" (wa la 'adin): it means not eating from it to satiety, but only what sustains him. This is part of the meanings of transgression in his eating. Allah has not restricted the meanings of transgression in his eating to a particular meaning, so it cannot be said that He meant only some of its meanings.

Since this is the case, the correct statement is what we have said: that it is transgression in all its forbidden meanings.

* *

As for the interpretation of His saying "then there is no sin upon him": it means that whoever eats that in the manner we have described, there is no blame upon him for his eating in that manner, nor any sin.

* *

The interpretation of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (173)

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful," the meaning is: If you obey Allah in your Islam, avoiding eating what He has forbidden you, and abandon following Satan in what you used to forbid in your ignorance, obeying Satan and following his footsteps, in what I did not forbid you, He will forgive what has passed from you in your disbelief and before your Islam of error, sin, and disobedience, overlooking it and abandoning punishment for it, and He is Merciful to you if you obey Him.

* *

The interpretation of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book and purchase with it a small price﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, "Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book," He means the rabbis of the Jews who concealed from people the matter of Muhammad ﷺ and his prophethood, while they found it written in their Torah, for bribes they were given for that, as:

2494: Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book," the whole verse: they are the People of the Book, who concealed what Allah had revealed to them and made clear to them of the truth and guidance, concerning the sending of Muhammad ﷺ and his command.

2495: al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His saying: (Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book and purchase with it a small price): He said: They are the People of the Book, who concealed what Allah had revealed to them of the truth, Islam, and the matter of Muhammad ﷺ.

2496: Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book": these are the Jews, who concealed the name of Muhammad ﷺ.

2497: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Ikrimah regarding His saying: "Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book," and the one in Al 'Imran: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 77], both were revealed concerning the Jews.

* *

As for the interpretation of His saying: "and purchase with it a small price," it means: they barter with it. The "ha'" in "bihi" (with it) refers to "concealment." So the meaning is: they bartered, through their concealment of what they concealed from people regarding the matter of Muhammad ﷺ and the matter of his prophethood, for a small price. That is because what they were given in exchange for distorting the Book of Allah and interpreting it other than its proper meaning, and for concealing the truth in that, was a small amount of worldly goods, as:

2498: Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "and purchase with it a small price," he said: They concealed the name of Muhammad ﷺ, and took for it a small greed, so that is the small price.

* *

I have already explained earlier the manner of their "purchasing," in a way that suffices without repeating it here.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 174:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿Those are they who eat into their bellies nothing but the Fire, and Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and for them is a painful punishment﴾ [2:174]

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, "Those" — he means those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), for a base bribe they are given, and so they distort the verses of Allah for that purpose and alter their meanings. "They eat into their bellies" — by their eating what they consumed of bribes for that and of the ja'alah (a stipulated fee, from ja'l, a reward promised to someone for doing or saying something), and the wage they took for it. "Nothing but the Fire" — meaning: nothing but that which brings them down into the Fire and makes them burn in it, as He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly, they only consume into their bellies a Fire, and they will [soon] burn in a Blaze﴾ [4:10]. The meaning is: they eat into their bellies nothing but what leads them into the Fire by their eating. So the mention of "the Fire" was sufficient, and the listeners' understanding of the meaning of the statement made unnecessary the mention of "what leads them to or causes them to enter." A group of the people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

2499 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding "Those eat into their bellies nothing but the Fire": he says, what they took as wages for it.

* *

If someone says: Does eating occur other than in the belly, so that it is said "they eat into their bellies"?

It is said: The Arabs do say: "I was hungry in other than my belly, and I was satiated in other than my belly," so it is said "in their bellies" for that reason, as one says "this man himself did it." We have explained this in other places earlier.

As for His saying "and Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection," he says: He will not speak to them with what they love and desire; but with what displeases and distresses them, He will indeed speak to them. For He, may His remembrance be exalted, has informed that He will say to them, when they say: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers.﴾ He said: ﴿Remain in it in humiliation, and do not speak to Me﴾ — the two verses [23:107–108].

* *

As for His saying "nor will He purify them," he means: He will not cleanse them from the defilement of their sins and their disbelief. "And for them is a painful punishment" — meaning: painful, causing agony.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 175:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error at the price of guidance and punishment at the price of forgiveness﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, exalted is His remembrance, "Those are the ones who have bought error at the price of guidance," He means: those who took error and abandoned guidance, and took what brings upon them the punishment of God on the Day of Resurrection, and abandoned what brings upon them His forgiveness and His good pleasure. He thus dispensed with mentioning the cause that necessitates "punishment" and "forgiveness," because His listeners understand its meaning and what is intended by it. We have already explained parallels to this in what has passed. [[See the indexes of the earlier linguistic discussions.]] Likewise we have explained the sense of "they bought error at the price of guidance" through the differing views of those who differ, and the evidence supporting what we have chosen among the sayings, earlier on, so we disliked repeating it. [[See what has passed, 1: 311-315.]]

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how patient they are over the Fire!﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation differed regarding the interpretation of this. Some of them said the meaning of this is: how bold they are in acting in a way that brings them near to the Fire.

Those who said this:

2500 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, he said: Yazid related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "So how patient they are over the Fire," he says: how bold they are in the deed that brings them near to the Fire.

2501 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His saying: "So how patient they are over the Fire," he says: how bold they are against it.

2502 - al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Amr ibn Awn related to us, he said: Hushaym related to us, from Bishr, from al-Hasan regarding His saying: "So how patient they are over the Fire," he said: By God, they have no patience over it, but how bold they are toward the Fire.

2503 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq related to us, he said: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri related to us, he said: Mis'ar related to us; and al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Abu Bukayr related to us, he said: Mis'ar related to us, from Hammad, from Mujahid, or Sa'id ibn Jubayr, or one of his companions: "So how patient they are over the Fire," meaning: how bold they are.

2504 - It was related to me from Ammar ibn al-Hasan, he said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His saying: "So how patient they are over the Fire," he says: how bold and how patient they are over the Fire.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: how much do they act in the manner of the people of the Fire.

* *

Those who said this:

2505 - Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, he said: Abu Asim related to us, he said: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His saying: "So how patient they are over the Fire," he said: how much they act in falsehood.

2506 - al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, he said: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* *

They differed regarding the interpretation of "ma" in His saying: "So how patient they are over the Fire." Some of them said: it has the sense of an interrogative, as if he said: What is it that made them patient? What thing made them patient? [[This is the view of Abu Ubaydah in Majaz al-Qur'an: 64.]]

Those who said this:

2507 - Musa ibn Harun related to me, he said: Amr related to us, he said: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "So how patient they are over the Fire," this is in the form of a question. He says: What is it that made them patient over the Fire?

2508 - Abbas ibn Muhammad related to me, he said: Hajjaj al-A'war related to us, he said: Ibn Jurayj informed us, he said: Ata said to me: "So how patient they are over the Fire," he said: What makes them patient over the Fire, when they abandoned the truth and followed falsehood?

2509 - Abu Kurayb related to us, he said: Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash was asked about: "So how patient they are over the Fire," he said: This is an interrogative. Had it been from patience, it would have said "fa-ma asbaru-hum" in the nominative. He said: One says to a man, "Ma asbarak," meaning: what has done this to you?

2510 - Yunus related to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: "So how patient they are over the Fire," he said: This is an interrogative. He says: What is this that made them patient over the Fire, so that it emboldened them to act in this way?

* *

Others said: It is an expression of wonder. That is: how intense is their boldness toward the Fire, in their doing the deeds of the people of the Fire!

Those who said this:

2511 - Sufyan ibn Waki' related to us, he said: My father related to us, from Ibn Uyaynah, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "So how patient they are over the Fire," he said: how much they act in the deeds of the people of the Fire!

This is also the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah, which we have mentioned earlier. [[See what has passed, nos. 2501, 2502.]]

* *

Whoever said it is an expression of wonder directs the interpretation of the speech to: "Those are the ones who have bought error at the price of guidance and punishment at the price of forgiveness," so how intense is their boldness, by their doing what they did of that, toward that which necessitates the Fire! Just as His remembrance, exalted is He, said: ﴿Killed is man, how disbelieving he is!﴾ [Surah Abasa: 17], expressing wonder at his disbelief in the One who created him and proportioned his creation.

* *

As for those who directed its interpretation to the interrogative, its meaning is: these are the ones who bought error at the price of guidance and punishment at the price of forgiveness, so what has made them patient over the Fire, though no one has patience over the Fire, until they exchanged it for God's forgiveness, taking it in its place as a substitute?

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most preferable of these sayings for the interpretation of the verse is the saying of the one who said: how bold they are toward the Fire, meaning: how bold they are toward the punishment of the Fire, and how much they act in the manner of its people. This is because it is heard from the Arabs: "Ma asbara fulanan 'ala Allah," meaning: how bold is so-and-so toward God! [[See the report of this in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 103.]] God only expresses wonder at His creation by disclosing the report about the people who conceal what God, blessed and exalted, has sent down concerning the matter of Muhammad ﷺ and his prophethood, and who sell the concealment of that for a small price of illicit gain and bribes they were given, in a manner of wonder at their rushing into that, [[qadima, taqaddama, aqdama, istaqdama are all with one meaning, when one is bold and rushes forward.]] while knowing that this necessitates for them the wrath of God and His painful punishment.

The meaning of that is only: how bold they are toward the punishment of the Fire! But mention of "the Fire" is sufficient from mention of "its punishment," just as one says: "How similar your generosity is to Hatim," meaning: how similar your generosity is to the generosity of Hatim, and "how similar your bravery is to 'Antarah." [[See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 103, also.]]

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿That is because Allah sent down the Book with truth; and indeed those who differ concerning the Book are in extreme dissension﴾ (2:176).

Abu Ja'far said: As for His words, "That is because Allah sent down the Book with truth," there is a difference of opinion regarding what "that" (dhalika) refers to.

* *

Some of them said: What "that" refers to is their action which they are doing, from their boldness toward the fire of Hell, in their opposition to the command of Allah, their concealing from people what Allah sent down in His Book and commanded them to make clear to them concerning the matter of Muhammad ﷺ and the matter of his religion. [This is] because Allah, blessed and exalted, "sent down the Book with truth," and His sending down the Book with truth is His report about them in His words to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is all the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe. Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and over their eyes is a veil, and for them is a great punishment﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 6-7]. So they—along with what Allah has reported about them, that they will not believe—will do nothing but exchange guidance for misguidance and forgiveness for punishment.

And others said: Its meaning is that "that" is known to them, namely that Allah sent down the Book with truth, because We have informed them in the Book that this [punishment] is theirs, and the Book is true.

It is as if the one who holds this view understood the verse to mean: "That [punishment]" which Allah, mentioned be He, spoke of—"how patient they are in the fire" is known to be theirs. For Allah has informed in several places of His revelation that the Fire is for the disbelievers, and His revelation is true; thus the report about "that" is, in their view, implied.

* *

And others said: The meaning of "that" is that Allah described the people of the Fire, saying, "How patient they are for the Fire," then He said: this punishment is because of their disbelief. "This" (hadha), in their view here, is what "that" (dhalika) may replace, [[See what has preceded, 1:225-227, on the explanation of "that" and "this".]] as if He said: We did that because Allah sent down the Book with truth, so they disbelieved in it. He said: Then "that," if this is its meaning, is in the accusative case, and it is in the nominative case with the preposition "bi" (because of).

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most preferable of the opinions regarding the interpretation of the verse, in my view, is that Allah, mentioned be He, pointed with His words "that" to everything contained in His words, "Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book," up to His words "That is because Allah sent down the Book with truth," from His report about the actions of the rabbis of the Jews, and His mention of what He, mentioned be He, has prepared for them of punishment for that. So He said: This which these rabbis of the Jews have done—by their concealing from people what they concealed of the matter of Muhammad ﷺ and his prophethood, while knowing it, seeking from them a base worldly gain—and by their opposition to My command and obedience [and this is because of My leaving them without purification, without purifying them, and without speaking to them, and My preparing for them a painful punishment]—is because I sent down My Book with truth, so they disbelieved in it and differed concerning it.

In that case, "that" has two grammatical possibilities: nominative and accusative. The nominative is with "bi" (the particle), and the accusative is in the sense: I did that because I sent down My Book with truth, so they disbelieved in it and differed concerning it. The mention of "so they disbelieved in it and differed" is omitted, being sufficiently indicated by what has been mentioned in the discourse.

* *

As for His words, "And indeed those who differ concerning the Book are in extreme dissension," by this He means the Jews and the Christians. They differed concerning the Book of Allah: the Jews disbelieved in what Allah related in it of the stories of Jesus son of Mary and his mother. The Christians believed in some of that and disbelieved in some of it, and all of them disbelieved in what Allah sent down in it concerning the command to believe in Muhammad ﷺ. So He said to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Indeed, these people who differed concerning what I sent down to you, O Muhammad, are in dispute and separation from the truth, far from right guidance and correctness, as Allah, mentioned be He, said: ﴿And if they believe in the like of what you have believed, then they have been guided; but if they turn away, then they are only in dissension﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 137]. As:

2512 - Musa related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "And indeed those who differ concerning the Book are in extreme dissension," he said: They are the Jews and the Christians. He said: They are in far-reaching enmity. And I have already explained the meaning of "shiqaq" (dissension) previously. [[See what has preceded in this volume, 3:115-116.]]

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 177 (part 1 of 3):**

**On the interpretation (ta'wil, meaning the explanation of the text) of His words, ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but righteousness is in one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets﴾:**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The people of ta'wil differed regarding the interpretation of this verse. Some of them said: The meaning is that righteousness is not prayer alone, but righteousness is the good qualities that I will explain to you.

2513: Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words, ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west﴾, meaning: prayer. He said: It is not righteousness that you pray and do not act. This was from the time he moved from Mecca to Medina, when the obligatory duties were revealed and the limits were set. So Allah commanded the obligatory duties and acting upon them.

2514: Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west﴾, but righteousness is what has been firmly established in the hearts of obedience to Allah.

2515: al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

2516: al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: This verse was revealed in Medina: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west﴾, meaning: prayer. He said: It is not righteousness that you pray and do not act otherwise than that. Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid also said: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west﴾, meaning: prostration. But righteousness is what has been firmly established in the heart of obedience to Allah.

2517: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Tumayla narrated to us, [[In the printed edition: "Abu Numayla" with an N, and the correct reading is what is established here. See narration no. 2490 and the commentary on it.]] from 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman, from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, that he said regarding it: He said: It is not righteousness that you pray and do not act otherwise than that. This was when he moved from Mecca to Medina, so Allah revealed the obligatory duties and set the limits in Medina, and commanded that the obligatory duties be taken up.

* *

Others said: Allah meant by that the Jews and the Christians. That is because the Jews prayed facing toward the west, and the Christians prayed facing toward the east, so Allah revealed this verse concerning them, informing them in it that righteousness is other than the action they perform, but it is what we have explained in this verse.

Mention of those who said that:

2518: al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, who said: The Jews used to pray facing toward the west, and the Christians used to pray facing toward the east, so this was revealed: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west﴾.

2519: Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada regarding His words, ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west, but righteousness is in one who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾. It was mentioned to us that a man asked the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) about righteousness, so Allah revealed this verse. And it was mentioned to us that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) called the man and recited it to him. The man, before the obligatory duties, if he testified that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger, and then died upon that, it was hoped for him and he was expected to receive good. So Allah revealed: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west﴾. The Jews had turned toward the west and the Christians toward the east: ﴿but righteousness is in one who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾, and the verse.

2520: al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: The Jews used to pray before the west, and the Christians before the east, so this was revealed: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west﴾.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more preferable of these two views for the interpretation of the verse is the view stated by Qatada and al-Rabi' ibn Anas: that by His words, ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west﴾, He meant the Jews and the Christians. This is because the verses before it had passed with their rebuke and blame, and the report about them and about the painful punishment prepared for them. And this is in the context of what came before it, since the matter is so: "It is not righteousness", O Jews and Christians, that some of you turn your faces toward the east and some of you toward the west. "But righteousness is in one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, and the Book", and the verse.

* *

If a speaker says: How is it said, "But righteousness is in one who believes in Allah", when you know that "righteousness" (al-birr) is a verb and "man" (the one who) is a noun, so how can the verb be the person?

It is said: The meaning of that is other than what you imagined. Rather, its meaning is: "But the righteous one is the one who believes in Allah and the Last Day." So "man" was placed in the position of the verb, being sufficient by its indication and the indication of its relative clause, which is a description of it, from the omitted verb, as the Arabs do. They place nouns in the places of their verbs for which they are well known, so they say: "Generosity is Hatim, and bravery is 'Antara", and "Generosity is only Hatim, and bravery is only 'Antara," meaning: The generosity is the generosity of Hatim. You suffice with mentioning "Hatim," since he was known for generosity, from repeating the mention of "generosity" after what you had mentioned, so you place it in the position of "his generosity," because the speech indicates what you omitted, dispensing with what you mentioned about what you did not mention. As it was said: ﴿And ask the town in which we were﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 82], and the meaning is: the people of the town. And as the poet said, he being Dhu al-Khiraq al-Tuhawi:

*You thought the bellowing of my she-camel was a she-camel of the mountain goat! And it was not so, woe to you, by the mountain goat!*

He means: the bellowing of a she-camel of the mountain goat, or the sound of [a mountain goat]. [[The addition in brackets is necessary.]] As one says: "You thought my shouting was your brother's", meaning by it: you thought my shouting was the shouting of your brother.

* *

It may also be that the meaning of the speech is: "But the one who is righteous is the one who believes in Allah", so "righteous" (al-birr) would be a verbal noun placed in the position of the name. [[This is the view of Abu 'Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an, p. 65, and al-Farra' mentioned it in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:104.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His words, ﴿and gave wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the wayfarer, those who ask, and for the freeing of slaves﴾:

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, ﴿and gave wealth in spite of love for it﴾, He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: He gave his wealth at the time of his love for it, and his stinginess with it, and his miserliness over it. [[See the meaning of "giving" (itaʾ) in what has passed: 1:574; 2:160, 317.]] As:

2521: Abu Kurayb and Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to us, both saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: I heard Layth, from Zubayd, from Murra ibn Sharahil al-Bakili, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: ﴿and gave wealth in spite of love for it﴾, that is: he gives it while he is healthy and miserly, hoping for life and fearing poverty. [[The report: 2521: Ibn Idris is 'Abd Allah ibn Idris ibn Yazid al-Awdi, who has passed (in 438 and 2030). Layth is Ibn Abi Sulaym, who has passed in the explanation of 1497. Zubayd (with a single bā', diminutive) is Ibn al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Karim al-Yami, and he is trustworthy and firm. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/1/411, Ibn Sa'd 6:216, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/623. Murra ibn Sharahil is al-Hamdani al-Kufi, one of the senior Successors, as his authentication has passed (168). He is biographed in al-Tahdhib 10:88-89, al-Kabir 4/2/5, Ibn Sa'd 6:79, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/366. "Al-Bakili", with a fatha on the bā' and a kasra on the kāf, is his nisba to Bakil, a clan of Hamdan. See al-Ishtiqaq of Ibn Durayd, pp. 250, 256, 312, and Jamharat al-Ansab of Ibn Hazm pp. 372-373. Murra is also attributed to Bakil in the book of Ibn Abi Hatim, and this is correct. In al-Tahdhib, "al-Saksaki" appears in its place; this is an undoubted error, since "al-Saksak" is the son of Ashras ibn Kinda. There is a great difference between Hamdan and Kinda; they meet only after several ancestors, in "Zayd ibn Kahlan ibn Saba'". See Jamharat al-Ansab, p. 405 and what precedes it.]]

2522: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, and al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, both of them together, from Sufyan, from Zubayd al-Yami, from Murra, from 'Abd Allah: ﴿and gave wealth in spite of love for it﴾, he said: while you are healthy, hoping for life and fearing poverty. [[The report: 2522: 'Abd al-Rahman is Ibn Mahdi the imam. Sufyan is al-Thawri. Al-Tabari narrates it through the chain of Ibn Mahdi, and through the chain of 'Abd al-Razzaq, both from Sufyan. The report is in the Tafsir of 'Abd al-Razzaq, p. 15, and in it: "while you are healthy and miserly", with the addition of "miserly".]]

2523: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Zubayd al-Yami, from 'Abd Allah, that he said regarding this verse: ﴿and gave wealth in spite of love for it﴾, he said: while you are greedy and miserly, hoping for wealth and fearing poverty.

2524: Ahmad ibn Ni'ma al-Misri narrated to us, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: al-Layth narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn A'yan narrated to us, from Shu'ba ibn al-Hajjaj, from Zubayd al-Yami, from Murra al-Hamdani, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said regarding the word of Allah: ﴿and gave wealth in spite of love for it to relatives﴾, he said: greedy and miserly, hoping for wealth and fearing poverty. [[The report: 2524: Al-Tabari's shaykh, Ahmad ibn Ni'ma al-Misri: I did not find a biography of him. Abu Salih is 'Abd Allah ibn Salih, the scribe of al-Layth. Al-Layth is Ibn Sa'd, the imam of the people of Egypt. Ibrahim ibn A'yan al-Shaybani al-Basri, who settled in Egypt, is weak. al-Bukhari said: "There is something to be considered in his isnad." Abu Hatim said: "This is a Basran shaykh, weak in narration, munkar al-hadith (his narrations are rejected), who came to Egypt." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, and a trustworthy different "Ibrahim ibn A'yan" was distinguished from him. Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/87 has three biographies, and al-Bukhari 1/1/272 has one biography. These three chains (2521-2523) are for a report whose wording stops at Ibn Mas'ud (mawquf, attributed to a Companion). In reality it is marfu' in ruling (traced to the Prophet), since this kind of thing is not known through opinion. Its meaning will also come as mawquf on him: 2529, 2531. Al-Hakim also narrated it, 2:272, through the narration of Mansur, from Zubayd, from Murra, from Ibn Mas'ud, as mawquf, and he said: "This is a sahih hadith according to the condition of the two shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), but they did not record it." Al-Dhahabi agreed with him. Al-Suyuti 1:170-171 attributed it to Ibn al-Mubarak, Waki', and others. Then he mentioned that al-Hakim also narrated it from Ibn Mas'ud as marfu'. Likewise Ibn Kathir 1:388 reported that al-Hakim narrated it as marfu'. I did not find it marfu' in al-Mustadrak. Then Ibn Kathir mentioned the mawquf narration and claimed that it was more sahih. This meaning is also established in a sahih marfu' hadith from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), when he was asked: Which charity is greatest in reward? He said: "That you give charity while you are healthy and miserly, fearing poverty and hoping for long life, and you do not delay until, when it reaches the throat, you say: to so-and-so such-and-such, and it was already for so-and-so." Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad: 7159, 7401. Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and Abu Dawud also narrated it, as we explained there.]]

2525: Abu Kurayb and Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, both saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Salim informed us, from al-Sha'bi, I heard him being asked: Does a man have a right in his wealth beyond zakat? He said: Yes! And he recited this verse: ﴿and gave wealth in spite of love for it to relatives, orphans, the needy, the wayfarer, those who ask, and for the freeing of slaves, and established prayer and gave zakat﴾.

2526: Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Suwayd ibn 'Amr al-Kalbi narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salama narrated to us, saying: Abu Hamza informed us, saying: I said to al-Sha'bi: If a man pays zakat on his wealth, is his wealth made pure for him? So he recited this verse: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east and the west﴾ up to ﴿and gave wealth in spite of love for it﴾ to its end. Then he said: Fatima bint Qays narrated to me that she said: O Messenger of Allah, I have seventy mithqals of gold. He said: Put it toward your relatives. [[The hadith: 2526: Suwayd ibn 'Amr al-Kalbi is trustworthy, one of the shaykhs of Ahmad. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/2/149, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/239. Abu Hamza is Maymun al-A'war al-Qassab, and he is very weak. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/1/343, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/235-236. I did not find this hadith with this wording in any other place. A similar meaning has been narrated with a weaker isnad. al-Daraqutni narrated in his Sunan, p. 205, through the chain of Abu Bakr al-Hudhali, from Shu'ayb ibn al-Habhab, from al-Sha'bi, from Fatima bint Qays, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a collar containing seventy mithqals of gold, and I said: O Messenger of Allah, take from it the obligatory amount, so he took from it one mithqal and three quarters of a mithqal." Al-Daraqutni said: "Abu Bakr al-Hudhali is abandoned (matruk), and no one narrated it except him." The weakness of this al-Hudhali has already been explained at 597.]]

2527: Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Adam narrated to us, from Sharik, who said: Abu Hamza narrated to us, as far as I know, from 'Amir, from Fatima bint Qays, that she heard him say: Indeed there is a right in wealth beyond zakat. [[The hadith: 2527: Sharik is Ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Sharik al-Nakha'i, the judge, and he is trustworthy. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/2/238, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/365-367. His saying: "from Fatima bint Qays: that she heard" means the Prophet (ﷺ), as is clear from the context of the report and from the other narrations. The hadith will also come: 2530, and its takhrij (sourcing) will be there, God willing.]]

2528: Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, from Abu Hayyan, who said: Mizham ibn Zafar narrated to me, saying: I was sitting with 'Ata', when a Bedouin came to him and said: I have camels, so is there a right for me in them beyond the charity? He said: Yes! He said: What? He said: Lending the bucket, the stallion's mating, and milking. [[In the printed edition: "'ariyyat al-dhalul" (the lending of the tame one), which is an error. In the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "We used to count al-ma'un (small necessities) in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): lending the bucket and the pot." In the hadith of Abu Hurayra, that he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "What is the right of camels? He said: Give the noble one, lend the abundant one, let the back be [milked], let the stallion mate, and give drink of milk." In the hadith of 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, a man said: O Messenger of Allah, what is the right of camels? — and he mentioned it similarly, adding: "and lending its bucket." (Sunan Abi Dawud 2:167, 168, chapter on the rights of wealth.) "Tarraqa al-fahl" means he mated the she-camel, mounting her and striking her; "itraq al-fahl" is lending him for mating. "Al-halab" (with two fatha vowels) is the milk that is milked, named by its verbal noun from: halaba al-naqa, yahlibuha, halaban and halaban (milked the she-camel).]]

2529: Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, mentioning from Murra al-Hamdani regarding ﴿and gave wealth in spite of love for it﴾, he said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: You give it while you are healthy and miserly, prolonging hope and fearing poverty. He also mentioned from al-Suddi that this is an obligatory matter in wealth, a right upon the owner of wealth to do, beyond what is due upon him of zakat.

2530: al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: Asad narrated to us, saying: Suwayd ibn 'Abd Allah narrated to us, from Abu Hamza, from 'Amir, from Fatima bint Qays, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "In wealth there is a right beyond zakat," and he recited this verse: "It is not righteousness" to the end of the verse. [[The hadith: 2530: Asad is Ibn Musa, who is called "Asad al-Sunna" (the lion of the Sunna). He has passed at 23. Suwayd ibn 'Abd Allah is thus established in the printed edition. In my view this is an error; the correct reading is "Sharik ibn 'Abd Allah", who appeared in the previous chain: 2527. The hadith is well known as being narrated by Sharik. Furthermore, among the narrators whose biographies we have seen, there is none named "Suwayd ibn 'Abd Allah" except a man of some standing, but not with this chain; he is known only from another munkar report, and he is biographed in Lisan al-Mizan. This hadith is a repetition of hadith 2527, slightly longer. Al-Darimi also narrated it, 1:385, from Muhammad ibn al-Tufayl. Al-Tirmidhi 2:22 narrated it through al-Aswad ibn 'Amir, and al-Darimi through Muhammad ibn al-Tufayl. Ibn Majah: 1789, through Yahya ibn Adam. Al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra 4:84, through Shadhan, all from Sharik, with this chain, in full and abridged form. Al-Tirmidhi said: "This hadith does not have a strong isnad. Abu Maymun al-A'war is weak." Al-Bayhaqi said: "This hadith is known through Abu Hamza Maymun al-A'war, the Kufan, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal and Yahya ibn Ma'in criticized him, along with those after them among the hadith memorizers."]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 177 (part 2 of 3):

Ibn Kathir (1: 389-390) reports that it was also transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim, from Yahya ibn Abd al-Hamid. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it from the hadith of Adam ibn Abi Iyas and Yahya ibn Abd al-Hamid, both from Shurayk. He then mentioned that it was also recorded by Ibn Majah and al-Tirmidhi.

The wording of the hadith in Ibn Majah is garbled and has the opposite meaning. It reads: "There is no right in wealth other than zakat"!

This is an old error found in some copies of Ibn Majah. Some scholars tried to support the authenticity of this wording in Ibn Majah, as in Ibn Hajar's al-Talkhis al-Habir (p. 177) and al-Munawi's Sharh al-Jami al-Saghir (no. 7641).

However, the earlier narration of al-Tabari (no. 2527), which comes through Yahya ibn Adam, from which Ibn Majah also transmitted, shows that the correct wording is the one found in all the other transmissions.

This is supported by the fact that Ibn Kathir attributed the hadith to both al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah together, without distinguishing between their versions. Al-Nabulisi did the same in Dhakha'ir al-Mawarith (no. 11699), attributing it to both as a single hadith.

It is further supported by the fact that al-Bayhaqi, after narrating it, said: "What our companions transmit in the commentaries is: 'There is no right in wealth other than zakat.' I do not know of any chain for it. What I narrated with this meaning is what I mentioned earlier." Had it been in Ibn Majah with this wording, he would not have said that, God willing.

**2531.** Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from Zubayd al-Yami, from Murrah ibn Sharahil, from Abd Allah, regarding His words: ﴿and gave away wealth though loving it﴾. He said: It means a man gives while he is healthy and miserly with it, hoping to live long and fearing poverty.

* *

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The interpretation of the verse is: he gave away wealth, while he loves it, is eager to accumulate it and is stingy with it, to his kin, thus joining their ties of kinship.

I have said that by His words ﴿the near of kin﴾ He meant the kin of the one who pays the wealth though loving it, on the basis of the report transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning his command to Fatimah bint Qays=

**2532.** And his (ﷺ) saying, when he was asked: "Which charity is best?" He said: "The utmost effort of the one of little means, given to a relative who is hostile." [[The hadith: 2532. Its meaning is established from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. Ahmad recorded it in al-Musnad (no. 8687; 2: 358, Halabi): "From Abu Hurayrah, that he said: 'O Messenger of God, which charity is best?' He said: 'The utmost effort of the one of little means, and begin with those you support.'"

Al-Mundhiri mentioned it in al-Targhib wa al-Tarhib (2: 28) and said: "Abu Dawud, Ibn Khuzaymah in his Sahih, and al-Hakim recorded it, and al-Hakim said: 'Sahih according to the conditions of Muslim.'"

Al-Hakim also narrated in al-Mustadrak (1: 406), from Umm Kulthum bint Uqbah, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'The best charity is that given to a relative who is hostile.'" Al-Hakim said: "This is a sahih hadith according to the conditions of Muslim, though they did not record it," and al-Dhahabi agreed with him.

Al-Haythami mentioned it in Majma al-Zawa'id (3: 116) and said: "al-Tabarani recorded it in al-Kabir, and its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih." He mentioned before it other hadiths similar to it.

"Al-kashih" means the one who harbors hatred. Ibn al-Athir said: "The enemy who conceals his enmity and folds his side (kashh) over it, that is, his inner self." The kashih is one who harbors enmity for you, as if he folds it within his side. The kashh is the space between the ribs and the lower ribs, or one who turns away from you with his face and presents you with his side.]]

* *

As for "the orphans" and "the needy," we have already explained their meanings earlier. [[See what has preceded regarding the meaning of "miskin" (2: 137, 293), and the meaning of "dhi al-qurba" and "al-yatama" (2: 292).]]

* *

As for "ibn al-sabil" (the wayfarer), it refers to the one who passes by a man. Then the scholars differed about his description. Some of them said: he is the guest among that group.

Those who said this:

**2533.** Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding "and the wayfarer," he said: "He is the guest." He said: "It has been mentioned to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) used to say: 'Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him say what is good or remain silent.' He also used to say: 'The right of hospitality is three nights, and whatever he offers beyond that is charity.'" [[The hadith: 2533. It is a mursal hadith. Qatadah, who is a Tabi'i (a Follower of the Companions), says: "It has been mentioned to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) used to say..." and then mentions it.

The "Sa'id" who narrates from Qatadah is Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah. The "Yazid" who narrates from him is Yazid ibn Zurai'.

The meaning of the hadith is established within a hadith recorded by Muslim (2: 45), from Abu Shurayh al-Adawi al-Khuza'i: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honour his guest with his gift." They said: "What is his gift, O Messenger of God?" He said: "His day and night. Hospitality is three days, and whatever is beyond that is charity for him. Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him say what is good or keep silent." Ahmad also recorded it, as did all the authors of the six canonical books, as in al-Fath al-Kabir (3: 231).]]

* *

Others said: He is the traveller who passes by you.

Those who said this:

**2534.** Sufyan ibn Wakf narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Jabir, from Abu Ja'far, regarding "ibn al-sabil": "The one who crosses from one land to another."

**2535.** Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid and Qatadah, regarding His words "ibn al-sabil": "The one who passes by you while travelling."

**2536.** Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from one he mentioned, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid and Qatadah, the same.

* *

The traveller was called "ibn al-sabil" because he keeps to the road, and the road is "al-sabil." He is called its "son" because of his constant presence on it during his journey, just as the water-bird is called "son of the water" because of its constant presence in it, and the man whom the ages have worn down is called "son of the days, nights and times." Dhu al-Rummah's verse is an example:

I came upon it by stumbling through the wilderness, while the Pleiades, as if on the crown of the head, were a "son of water" hovering aloft.

[[Diwan: 401. It is connected to a verse before it: "A stagnant water, long unvisited by people, / as if the locusts' spittle is in it, the water of the ghada tree." The ājin is the changed water. Al-dabā are young locusts. Al-ghaḍā is a tree. It is as if the locusts grazed it and spat their grazing into it, so it is yellowish-black. Al-i'tisaf is plunging forward and travelling without guidance. Al-muhalliq is high and lofty. Ibn al-Ma' is the bird of the cranes, known as the kurki, and the Iraqi goose, which is white-breasted, red-beaked and yellow-eyed. Al-Aqayshir says, describing a drinking gathering: "As if they, and the hands of the drinkers, are carrying / when they shine in the hands of the cranes, / daughters of water, seen white, their wings / red-beaked, yellow-eyed." Al-Thurayya are many stars gathered together, named in the singular. He placed them "on a summit," in the middle of the night, seen white and bright.]]

* *

As for His words "and the beggars," He means by them those who ask for food and seek it, as:

**2537.** Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, from Husayn, from Ikrimah, regarding His words "and the beggars," he said: "The one who asks you."

* *

As for His words "and in the freeing of slaves," He means by it: the freeing of necks from bondage, namely the mukatabun, who strive to free their necks from bondage by paying their contractual sums which they agreed upon with their masters. [[ "Al-ubudah" and "al-ubudiyyah" are the same, and it has no verb form according to Abu Ubayd. Al-Lihyani said its verb is "abada," on the pattern of "karama."]]

* *

**Concerning the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: "and who establish prayer, and give zakat, and those who fulfil their covenant when they make one"**
