Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His remembrance, "and establish prayer," He means: maintaining the act of it within its limits. By "and give zakat," He means: giving it in the manner He prescribed for them.

* *

If someone says: Is there any right that must be paid obligatorily from wealth other than zakat?

It is said: The interpreters have differed on this:

Some of them said: There are obligatory rights other than zakat. They based their view on this verse and said: When God, blessed and exalted, said, "and gave away wealth, though loving it, to the near of kin," and those He named with them, and then said afterwards, "and established prayer and gave zakat," we know that the wealth which He described the believers as giving to the near of kin and those named with them is other than the zakat which He mentioned they give. For if it were one and the same wealth, its repetition would have no understood meaning. They said: Since it is impossible for God, exalted is His remembrance, to say a word with no meaning, we know that the ruling on the first wealth is other than zakat, and that the zakat mentioned afterwards is other than it. They said: Moreover, the interpretation of the interpreters has made clear the correctness of what we have said on this.

Others said: Rather, the first wealth is zakat itself, but God described at the beginning of the verse the giving of the believers to those they give to. Through His description of their conduct, He made known to His servants the places in which they must place their zakat. Then He indicated, by His words afterwards, "and gave zakat," that the wealth which the people gave is the obligatory zakat, since the people entitled to its shares are those whom He informed, at the beginning of the verse, the people gave their wealth to.

* *

As for His words "and those who fulfil their covenant when they make one," He means, exalted is His remembrance: those who do not break the covenant of God after making it, but fulfil it and complete it according to what they agreed to with those with whom they made it. As:

**2538.** I was told by Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, regarding His words "and those who fulfil their covenant when they make one," he said: "Whoever gives the covenant of God and then breaks it, God will take revenge on him. And whoever gives the protection of the Prophet (ﷺ) and then betrays it, the Prophet (ﷺ) will be his adversary on the Day of Resurrection."

* *

I have already explained "the covenant" earlier, in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary. [[See what has preceded: 1: 410-415, 557. Then this part 3: 20.]]

* *

**Concerning the interpretation of His words: "and the patient in misfortune and in adversity"**

Abu Ja'far said: We have already explained the interpretation of "patience" earlier. [[See what has preceded: 2: 10-11, 124. Then this part 3: 214.]]

The meaning of the statement is: those who restrain themselves, in misfortune, adversity and the time of hardship, from what God dislikes for them, holding themselves back to obey His command. Then the interpreters differed about the meaning of "misfortune and adversity," saying:

**2539.** Al-Husayn ibn Amr ibn Muhammad al-Anqazi [[In the printed edition it reads "al-Abqari," and the correct form is what I have written. He was biographically noted earlier, no. 1625.]] narrated it to me, saying: My father narrated to me, and Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us. Both of them said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "As for al-ba'sa', it is poverty, and as for al-darra', it is sickness."

**2540.** Ibn Wakf narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hamani narrated to us. Both of them said: Shurayk narrated to us, from al-Suddi, from Murrah, from Abd Allah, regarding His words "and the patient in misfortune and adversity," he said: "The misfortune is hunger, and the adversity is illness."

**2541.** Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Shurayk narrated to us, from al-Suddi, from Murrah, from Abd Allah, who said: "The misfortune is need, and the adversity is illness."

**2542.** Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: "We used to narrate that the misfortune is distress and poverty, and the adversity is sickness." The Prophet Ayyub (ﷺ) said: ﴿Indeed, harm has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful﴾ [Surah al-Anbiya: 83].

**2543.** I was told by Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His words "and the patient in misfortune and adversity," he said: "Misfortune is destitution and poverty, and adversity is in the self, from pain or sickness that afflicts one's body."

**2544.** Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words "misfortune and adversity," he said: "Misfortune is distress, and adversity is affliction in the body."

**2545.** Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Ubayd narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, who said: "Misfortune and adversity" is sickness. [[The report: 2545. I fear that some part of this report has been dropped. It is the explanation of "misfortune," and it mentions "adversity" before the words "sickness." The correct text will come in the report that follows.]]

**2546.** Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding "and the patient in misfortune and adversity," he said: "Misfortune is distress and poverty, and adversity is sickness and pain."

**2547.** Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Ubayd ibn al-Tufayl narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim say regarding this verse, "and the patient in misfortune and adversity": "As for misfortune, it is poverty, and adversity is sickness." [[The report: 2547. Ubayd ibn al-Tufayl, his kunya is "Abu Sayyidan," with a kasra on the unpointed sin, a sukun on the lower-pointed ya', then an unpointed dal, as will come with his name and kunya in 2555. He is al-Ghatafani. Waki' and Abu Nu'aym al-Fadl ibn Dukayn also narrate from him. Abu Hatim said: "Saleh, there is no harm in him." He is biographically noted in al-Taqrib, al-Khulasa and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/409.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for the people of Arabic grammar, they differed about this. Some of them said: "al-ba'sa'" and "al-darra'" are nouns (masdar) that came on the pattern "fu'ala'," for which there is no "af'al," because it is a noun. Just as "af'al" has come in nouns for which there is no "fa'la'," such as "Ahmad." They have used "af'al" as an adjective, but no "fa'la'" has come for it. They said: "You are more fearful than that (awjal)," and they did not say "wajla'."

Others said: It is the name of the act. "Al-ba'sa'" is destitution, and "al-darra'" is harm. It is a noun which may be used, if you wish, for a feminine or for a masculine, as Zuhayr said:

So she will produce for you the boys of ill omen, all of them like the red-skinned one of 'Ad, then she will suckle and wean them.

[[Diwan: 20, from his unique mu'allaqa. These are verses from his description of war, which begins before this verse: "War is only what you know and have tasted, / and it is not a tale that is hidden or unspoken. / When you rouse it, you rouse it blameworthy / and it grows fierce, when you ignite it, and it flares. / It grinds you as the millstone grinds with its grindstones, / and it conceives as the she-camel conceives, then bears and then weans." He means that war conceives as the she-camel conceives, bearing twins in one womb. His words "red-skinned of 'Ad" mean "red-skinned of Thamud," but he erred and did not mind which one he said. The red-skinned of Thamud is Qidar, who hamstrung the she-camel of God, so their Lord destroyed them for what they did. He says that war suckles its ill-omened offspring and keeps them until they are weaned, after they have reached the age of striving for themselves in evil.]]

He means: "so she will produce for you boys of ill omen."

Others said: If that were a noun that could be applied to masculine and feminine, then "af'al" could be used in indefinite form. But it is a noun that stands in place of the masdar. The proof of this is His words: ﴿If you seek their help, you will find them not better﴾ (ghayra abad), without inflection. The phrase "fulan ghayr abad" is said, meaning "there is no good in him." It is also said, "ma 'inda fulan abad," meaning "there is no benefit in him." A man said to his son: "If you go out to the market and profit for us, or return with no abad," meaning with no benefit. He said: It was a noun for the masdar, because when it is mentioned it is understood that the masdar is meant.

Another said: If that were a masdar that came in the feminine, it would not come in the masculine, and if it came in the masculine, it would not come in the feminine. For whoever is named "af'al" is not inflected into "fu'la'," and whoever is named "fu'la'" is not inflected into "af'al," because every noun keeps its form and is not inflected into another. But these are two dialects. When it is used in the masculine, it follows the pattern of "ash'am," and when it is used as "al-ba'sa' wal-darra'," [[Meaning: when it is used in the feminine, it carries the sense of "the state of misfortune" and "the state of adversity."]] it means: "the state of misfortune" and "the state of adversity." Even though "al-darra'" was not formed as "al-adarr," nor "al-ash'am" as "al-sha'mā'," because the feminine of it is not intended as masculine, nor the masculine as feminine, just as they say "a beautiful woman" (hasna'), and do not say "a more beautiful man" (ahsan). And they say "a beardless man" (amrad), and do not say "a beardless woman" (marda'). So when it is said "the distressing trait" (al-khisla al-darra') and "the ill-omened matter" (al-amr al-ash'am), it indicates the masdar, and it does not need to be a noun, though it suffices instead of the masdar.

This is the view that contradicts the interpretation of those scholars we mentioned regarding "al-ba'sa' wa'l-darra'" (the adversity and the affliction), although it is sound according to the grammar of Arabic. The reason is that the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) took "al-ba'sa'" to mean destitution (al-bu's) and "al-darra'" to mean harm to the body (al-darr fi'l-jasad). Their interpretation is based on their having construed "al-ba'sa' wa'l-darra'" as nouns denoting actions (asma' al-af'al), rather than as descriptive nouns and their qualifiers (sifat al-asma' wa-nu'utuha). Therefore the more appropriate reading of "al-ba'sa' wa'l-darra'", according to the view of the people of interpretation, is that they are nouns denoting actions, so that "al-ba'sa'" is a noun for destitution and "al-darra'" is a noun for harm.
* *
As for "al-sabirin" (the patient ones), it is in the accusative case (nasb), and it is an attribute of "man" (those who) used for the purpose of praise. [[He means "man" in His saying, exalted is He: "But righteousness is (the righteousness of) one who believes..."]] This is because it is the custom of the Arabs, when the description of a single person is lengthened, to interpose praise or blame, sometimes in the accusative and sometimes in the nominative, [[See what has passed, 1:329.]] as the poet said: [[I do not know who said it.]]

*To the king, the lord, and the son of the noble warrior,*
*and the lion of the battalion in the crowd,*
*and the man of judgment when affairs are overcast*
*with the clanging and the bridles.*

[[Al-Farra' Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:105; al-Insaf: 195; Amali al-Sharif 1:205; Khizanat al-Adab 1:216. Al-qarm: the chief, the exalted one, the foremost in knowledge and experience of affairs. Al-mazdahim: the fray of battle where the brave men crowd together. He praises him for his boldness in battle. "Ghumma al-amr yaghummu" (passive form): it became obscure and dark, and the person was in confusion, unable to find the right course. Al-salil: the sound of iron. By "dhat al-salil" he means a battalion of infantry whose helmets, coats of mail and weapons clang. "Dhat al-lujum": a battalion of cavalry. He mentions his steadfastness and the composure of his mind and judgment when intellects waver amid the clashing of swords and the charging of horses in the battle of death. So his saying "bi-dhat al-salil" is connected to his saying "tughumm al-umur".]]

So "lion of the battalion" and "the man of judgment" are in the accusative, by way of praise, while the noun before them is in the genitive because it is an attribute of one person. Another poet said similarly: [[I do not know the speaker of either of them.]]

*Would that those among whom the stars were gathered had been piled up*
*over every lean and fat among them,*
*rains of the people in every barren year and hardship,*
*lions of the thicket protecting every lair.*

[[Al-Farra' Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:106; Amali al-Sharif 1:206. His saying "tawada'at" is, in my view, a "tafa'ala" form from their saying: the builder "waddha'a al-hajar tawdi'an" (stacked the stone, placing one on another). From it also comes "al-tawaddu'" (sewing the robe after laying the cotton). Also from it: "wada'at al-na'ama baydaha" (the ostrich laid her eggs) when she piled them and placed some of them upon others, and it is "bayd mawdi'" (eggs piled one upon another). He says: would that the sky had gathered over all of them, so they would be among its stars. His saying "ghath minhum wa-samin" is praise, meaning: there is no lean one among them, for even their lean ones deserve to be among the men of distinction. "Rains of the people" (ghuyuth al-wara): in every barren year and hardship. In the version of al-Farra' and al-Sharif it reads "wa-lazbatin." "Al-azma," "al-azba," and "al-lazba" have the same meaning: the severity of the year and drought. Their version also reads "ghuyuth al-hayya." "Al-hayya" is fertility, and rain is called "hayya" because it is the cause of fertility. "Al-thara": the place where lions take shelter.]]

* *

Some have claimed that His saying [[This view is mentioned by al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:108, and he rejected it.]] "and the patient ones in adversity" is in the accusative, coordinated (ataf) upon "al-sa'ilin" (the beggars).

As if the meaning of the sentence, in his view, was: "and gave wealth out of love for it to the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, the wayfarer, the beggars, and the patient ones in adversity and affliction." The apparent meaning of the Book of God indicates the error of this view, because "the patient ones in adversity and affliction" are those afflicted with disability in their bodies and those straitened in their wealth. The description of the people as giving wealth—to those whose description is this—has already passed in His saying "and the needy, the wayfarer, and the beggars." And the people of destitution and poverty are the people of "al-ba'sa' wa'l-darra'," because whoever is not among the people of affliction (darra') and of hardship (ba'sa') is not one who is entitled to receive charity. He is entitled to receive it only when he combines with his affliction a hardship. When he combines hardship with it, he is among the people of indigence (maskana) who have entered into the category of "the needy" mentioned earlier before His saying "and the patient ones in adversity." If this is so, and then "the patient ones in adversity" were put in the accusative by His saying "and gave wealth out of love for it," the sentence would be a repetition without any meaningful benefit. As if it were said: "and gave wealth out of love for it to the near of kin, the orphans, and the needy." God is exalted above addressing His servants in such a way. Rather, the meaning is: "But righteousness is (the righteousness of) one who believes in God and the Last Day, and the angels, and the Book, and the prophets... and the ones who fulfil their covenant when they make one, and the patient ones in adversity and affliction." "And the ones who fulfil" is in the nominative because it is an attribute of "man" (man), and "man" is in the nominative, so it is inflected according to its case. "And the patient ones" is in the accusative—although it is an attribute of it—by way of the praise we described earlier.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿and in the time of violence﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His remembrance, "and in the time of violence," He means: and the patient ones in the time of violence, which is the time of the severity of fighting in war, as:

2548 - Al-Husayn ibn 'Amr ibn Muhammad al-'Anqazi told me, saying: My father told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi, from Murra, from 'Abdullah, regarding God's saying "and in the time of violence," he said: "in the time of fighting." [[The report: 2548 - in the printed edition: "al-'Abqari," which has occurred many times before in error, and we have corrected it. See his biography at no. 1625.]]

2549 - Musa told me, saying: 'Amr told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi, from Murra, from 'Abdullah, the like of it.

2550 - Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa told us, saying: Shibl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "and in the time of violence" — the fighting.

2551 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh told us, saying: Yazid told us, from Sa'id, from Qatada regarding His saying "and in the time of violence," i.e., at the places of fighting.

2552 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq told us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada: "and in the time of violence," the fighting.

2553 - I was told from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "and in the time of violence," at the encounter with the enemy.

2554 - Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Nu'aym told us, saying: 'Ubayda told us, from al-Dahhak: "and in the time of violence," the fighting.

2555 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq told us, saying: Abu Ahmad told us, saying: 'Ubayd ibn al-Tufayl Abu Sayyidan told us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim say regarding His saying "and in the time of violence," he said: the fighting. [[The reports 2554-2555: Abu Nu'aym in the first of them is al-Fadl ibn Dukayn. Abu Ahmad in the second is al-Zubayri, Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr. The remainder of the chain has passed at 2547.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones who are truthful, and those are the God-fearing﴾ (177)

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His remembrance, "Those are the ones who are truthful," He means: those who believe in God and the Last Day, and whose description is the description He gave them in this verse. He says: whoever does these things, they are the ones who were truthful toward God in their faith, and who made their words true by their deeds—not he who turns his face toward the east and the west while opposing God in His command, breaking His covenant and His pact, concealing from the people the clarification that God commanded him to make, and denying His messengers.

* *

As for His words, "and those are the God-fearing," He means: those who feared the punishment of God, so they avoided disobeying Him, were wary of His threat, and did not transgress His limits, and they feared Him, so they performed His obligations.

* *

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas used to say in the same sense as what we have said regarding "Those are the ones who are truthful":

2556 - I was told from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "Those are the ones who are truthful," he said: they spoke words of faith, and its reality is action; they were truthful toward God. He said: al-Hasan used to say: this is a word of faith, and its reality is action; if there is no action with the speech, then there is nothing.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 178 (part 1 of 3):**

On the interpretation of God's words: ﴿O you who believe, retaliation (qisas) is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His words "retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain," God, may He be remembered, means: it is made obligatory upon you.

* *

If someone says: Is retaliation obligatory upon the guardian (wali) of the slain person, against the killer of his relative?

It is said: No. Rather, it is permitted for him to do so, as well as to pardon, or to accept blood money (diyah).

If someone says: How then did He say "retaliation is prescribed for you"?

It is said: The meaning of that is contrary to what you have supposed. Its meaning is: O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain, the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female. That is, when a free person kills a free person, the blood of the killer is equivalent to the blood of the slain, and retaliation is taken from him and not from anyone else among the people. So do not exceed in killing to someone other than the one who killed, for it is forbidden for you to kill other than the killer in return for your slain.

The obligation that God imposed upon us in retaliation is what I have described: abstaining from exceeding in retaliation, by killing the killer for his victim and not someone else. It does not mean that retaliation became an obligation upon us in the way the obligation of prayer and fasting is, such that we have no right to abandon it. Had it been an obligation that we could not lawfully abandon, His words "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any way" would have no intelligible meaning, for there is no pardon after retaliation, so it could not be said "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any way."

* *

It has been said that the meaning of retaliation (qisas) in this verse is the offsetting of the blood-money of some of the slain against the blood-money of others. The reason, according to them, is that the verse was revealed concerning two factions who waged war during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and some of them killed others. The Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to reconcile them by cancelling the blood-money of the women of one faction against the blood-money of the women of the other, and the blood-money of their men against the blood-money of their men, and the blood-money of their slaves against the blood-money of their slaves, as retaliation. That, according to them, is the meaning of "retaliation" in this verse.

* *

If someone says: God, may He be remembered, said: "retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female." So are we only permitted to take retaliation for a free person from a free person, and for a female only from a female?

It is said: Rather, we are permitted to take retaliation for a free person from a slave, and for a female from a male, by the word of God, may He be remembered: ﴿And whoever is killed unjustly, We have given his heir authority﴾ [Surah al-Isra: 33]. And by the widely transmitted report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said:

2557: The Muslims' blood is equal. [[Hadith 2557: al-Tabari narrated it here without a chain of narration. Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad (6797), from the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who is Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As: "The Muslims' blood is equal, and the least of them may extend protection on their behalf, and they are one hand against whoever is other than them." Ibn Majah narrated something similar (2685). Ahmad narrated it with different wordings, both longer and shorter (6692, 6970, 7012).]]

* *

If someone says: If that is so, what is the way to interpret this verse?

It is said: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed on this. Some of them said: This verse was revealed concerning a people who, whenever a man among them killed a slave of another people, would not accept, for their slain, the blood of his killer because he was a slave, until they killed his master in return. And if a woman from another group killed a man among them, they would not accept, for the blood of their companion, the female killer, until they killed a man from the woman's clan and kin. So God revealed this verse, informing them that the retaliation prescribed for them was that a man should be killed for a man, the killer and no one else, and a female for a female, the killer and no other man, and a slave for a slave, the killer and no other free person. He forbade them to exceed in retaliation from the killer to someone else.

The narrators of this view:

2558: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu al-Walid narrated to us, and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj narrated to us, the two of them saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from al-Sha'bi, concerning His words "the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female." He said: It was revealed concerning two tribes of the Arabs who fought a blind (ʿummiyyah) war. They said: We will kill for our slave so-and-so the son of so-and-so, and for such-and-such a woman we will kill so-and-so the son of so-and-so. So God revealed: "the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female." [[ʿUmmiyyah (with the ʿayn vowelled either with a damma or kasra, and the mim and yaʾ doubled): error, arrogance, obstinacy in falsehood, strife, and misguidance. In a hadith: "Whoever fights under a blind banner, becoming angry for a group, or supporting a group, or calling to a group, and is killed, is killed the death of jahiliyyah." Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: it is a blind matter of partisanship, whose direction is not clear.]]

2559: Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female." He said: The people of jahiliyyah had transgression in them and obedience to Satan. A tribe, if it had strength and protection, and a slave of another people was killed among them, would say: We will not kill for him except a free man! Out of arrogance, because of their superiority over others in themselves. And if a woman of theirs was killed by a woman of another people, they would say: We will not kill for her except a man! So God revealed this verse, informing them that a slave is for a slave and a female is for a female, and He forbade them from transgression. Then God, may He be remembered, revealed later in Surah al-Ma'idah: ﴿And We prescribed for them therein: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth, and wounds in retaliation﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 45].

2560: al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words "Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain." He said: Those before us had no blood-money; there was only killing, or pardon by the family. So this verse was revealed concerning a people who were more numerous than others. When a slave was killed from among their large clan, they would say: We will not kill for him except a free man. And if a woman among them was killed, they would say: We will not kill for her except a man. So God revealed: "the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female."

2561: Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: al-Mu'tamir narrated to us, saying: I heard Dawud, from Amir, concerning this verse: "Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female." He said: That applies only to a blind war, when a slave from one side and a slave from the other are harmed, they are equal; and likewise for two women, and likewise for two free persons. This is its meaning, God willing. [[The explanation of "ʿummiyyah" was already given on p. 359, note 1.]]

2562: al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: Included in God's words "the free for the free" is a man for a woman and a woman for a man. And Ata' said: There is no difference between them.

* *

Others said: Rather, this verse was revealed concerning two groups who had fought between them during the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and from each of the two groups a number of men and women were killed. So the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to reconcile them, by making the blood-money of the women from each group retaliation for the blood-money of the women of the other group, and the blood-money of the men for the men, and the blood-money of the slaves for the slaves. That is the meaning of His words "retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain."

The narrators of this view:

2563: Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, concerning His words: "Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female." He said: Two peoples of the Arabs fought, one of them Muslim and the other a covenanted people (mu'ahad), over some matter that arises among the Arabs. The Prophet (ﷺ) reconciled them, and they had killed free persons, slaves and women, on condition that the free man pay the blood-money of a free man, the slave the blood-money of a slave, and the female the blood-money of a female. So he offset some of them against others.

2564: al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Sufyan, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, who said: There was fighting between two clans of the Ansar. One of them had superiority over the other, and they sought excellence. The Prophet (ﷺ) came to reconcile them, and this verse was revealed: "The free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female." So the Prophet (ﷺ) made the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female.

2566: al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Shu'bah, from Abu Bishr, who said: I heard al-Sha'bi say concerning this verse: "Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain." He said: It was revealed concerning a blind war. Shu'bah said: It seems to be about a reconciliation. He said: They reconciled upon this.

2567: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, who said: I heard al-Sha'bi say concerning this verse: "Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female." He said: It was revealed concerning a blind war. [[The explanation of "ʿummiyyah" was already given on p. 359, note 1.]] He said: It was during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ).

* *

Others said: Rather, this is a command from God, may He be remembered, to offset the blood-money of a free person and the blood-money of a slave, and the blood-money of a male and the blood-money of a female, in intentional killing, if retaliation is taken from the killer for the slain, and the difference in excess between the blood-money of the slain and that of the one retaliated against is settled.

The narrators of this view:

2568: I was told, from Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning His words: "O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female." He said: We were told on the authority of Ali ibn Abi Talib that he used to say: Any free man who kills a slave, he is liable to qawad (retaliation) for him. If the slave's masters wish to kill the free man, they may kill him, and offset the value of the slave against the blood-money of the free man, and pay to the free man's heirs the remainder of his blood-money. And if a slave kills a free man, he is liable to qawad for him. If the free man's heirs wish, they may kill the slave and offset the value of the slave, and take the remainder of the free man's blood-money. If they wish, they may take the full blood-money and spare the slave. And any free man who kills a woman, he is liable to qawad for her. If the woman's heirs wish, they may kill him and pay half the blood-money to the heirs of the free man. And if a woman kills a free man, she is liable to qawad for him. If the heirs of the free man wish, they may kill her and take half the blood-money. If they wish, they may take the full blood-money and spare her. And if they wish, they may pardon.

2569: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, that Ali said concerning a man who killed his wife: If they wish, they may kill him and pay half the blood-money.

2570: Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Yahya narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Awf, from al-Hasan, who said: A man is not killed for a woman until they are given half the blood-money.

2571: Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mughirah, from Simak, from al-Sha'bi, who said: Concerning a man who intentionally killed his wife, they brought him to Ali, and he said: If you wish, kill him, and return the excess of the man's blood-money over the woman's blood-money.

* *

Others said: Rather, this verse was revealed in a situation in which the people did not kill a man for a woman, but they killed a man for a man and a woman for a woman. Then God made the ruling equal for all of them by His words: "And We prescribed for them therein: a life for a life" [Surah al-Ma'idah: 45], and made all of them liable to retaliation for one another.

The narrators of this view:

2572: al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words "and the female for the female." He said: That was because they did not kill a man for a woman, but they killed a man for a man and a woman for a woman. Then God revealed: "a life for a life." So He made the free persons equal in retaliation among themselves, in intentional killing, men and women alike, in killing and in injury short of killing. And He made the slaves equal among themselves in intentional killing, in killing and in injury short of killing, men and women alike.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: [[His words "since it is disputed" complete his reply to the question on p. 358, line 11: "It is said: The people of interpretation differed on this..."]] Since the disagreement I have described exists concerning the matter in which this verse was revealed, it is obligatory for us to apply it according to the ruling it indicates, by a decisive report that leaves no excuse. The reports from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) are widely corroborated, by general transmission, that the life of a free man is liable to qawad (retaliation) in exchange for the life of a free woman. Since that is so, and since the community differs about offsetting the difference between the blood-money of a man and that of a woman, as I have shown from the words of Ali and others, the invalidity of the view that retaliation applies in that case becomes clear. The offsetting of the difference between the two blood-monies is contrary to the consensus of all the people of Islam: it is forbidden for a man to destroy a limb of his body in exchange for compensation he receives for its destruction, so let alone the whole body; and it is forbidden for anyone else to destroy any part of it, of the same kind as what is forbidden in that, in exchange for a payment he receives for it. [[The construction of the sentence: "it was clear the invalidity of the one who said retaliation applies... by the consensus of all the people of Islam that it is forbidden for a man..."]] Therefore it is obligatory that the life of a free man be liable to retaliation in exchange for the life of a free woman.

Since that is so, it becomes evident that God, may He be remembered, did not intend by His words "the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female" that a slave should not be retaliated against for a free man, nor that a female should not be killed for a male, nor a male for a female. Since that is so, it is clear that the verse refers to one of the two other meanings: either our statement, that retaliation must not exceed to someone other than the killer and the offender, so that a male is taken for a female and a free man for a slave; or the other view, namely that the verse was revealed concerning particular people, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to reconcile by offsetting the blood-money of their slain one against another, as al-Suddi and those whose statements we have mentioned said.

The entire community agrees, without any disagreement, that offsetting rights against one another is not obligatory, and they agree that God did not issue a judgment on this and then abrogate it (naskh). Since that is so, and since God, may He be remembered, said "retaliation is prescribed for you," which indicates that it is an obligation, it is known that the view of the one who held this position is contrary to that. For what is an obligation upon the holders of rights to perform leaves them no choice in it; yet all agree that the holders of rights have the choice in offsetting their rights against one another. Since the invalidity of this view we have mentioned has become clear, the correct view on this matter is what we have stated.

* *

If someone says: Since you have said that the meaning of His words "retaliation is prescribed for you" is "retaliation is made obligatory for you," and since the word "kutiba" (was prescribed/written) has no meaning in the speech of people except "to write it out," to draw it as a line and a text, what is your proof that the meaning of His words "kutiba" is "made obligatory"?

It is said: This usage exists in the language of the Arabs, and it is widespread in their poetry. Among it is the saying of the poet: [[He is ʿUmar ibn Abi Rabiʿah, or Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr al-Asadi.]]

Killing and fighting have been prescribed for us,
and for chaste women, the trailing of skirts.
[[Diwan of ʿUmar, p. 421; al-Bayan wa al-Tabyin 2:236; al-Kamil 2:154; Tarikh al-Tabari 7:158; Ansab al-Ashraf 5:264; al-Aghani 9:229. This poem has a story behind it. When Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr went out against al-Mukhtar ibn Abi Ubayd al-Thaqafi, the self-proclaimed prophet, defeated and killed him, among those he seized was his wife ʿAmrah bint al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir. When he asked her about him, she said: May God have mercy on him, if he was one of the righteous servants of God. So Mus'ab wrote to his brother Abd Allah that she claimed he was a prophet! He ordered her killed. The man assigned to kill her killed her in a horrible manner, and people disapproved of it. Among those who composed verses about it was ʿUmar: "Among the greatest wonders to me is the killing of a fair, free, long-necked woman, who was slain thus without fault. May God's reward be great for her as a slain one!" ... "Killing has been prescribed..."]]

And the saying of Nabighah of Banu Ja'dah:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 178 (part 2 of 3):

Ya bint ammi, kitab Allah akhrajani ... 'ankum, fa-hal amna'anna Allah ma fa'ala! [[Lisan (k-t-b) and Asas al-Balagha (k-t-b), and Maqayis 5: 159. Some versions read "Ya ibnata ammi" (O daughter of my paternal uncle), and in the Asas it reads "akhharani" (has delayed me). I suspect "akhharani" is a scribal error.]]

Such usage is more frequent in their poetry and speech than can be counted. However, although that word may mean "was obligated" (furiḍa), in my view it is derived from "al-kitab," which means writing and inscription. God, may His remembrance be exalted, has written down everything He has obligated upon His servants and everything they will do in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). God, may His remembrance be exalted, said in the Qur'an: ﴿Nay, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a Preserved Tablet﴾ [Surah al-Buruj: 21-22], and He said: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an, in a Book well-guarded﴾ [Surah al-Waqi'a: 77-78]. Thus it has been made clear that everything He has imposed upon us is written in the Preserved Tablet.

So the meaning of His saying, since that is the case, "Retaliation (al-qisas) has been prescribed for you," is: retaliation for the slain has been written for you in the Preserved Tablet as an obligation, that you should not kill anyone for the slain other than his killer.

* *

As for "al-qisas" (retaliation), it comes from the saying of the speaker: "I retaliated against so-and-so for my right against him, which was from his right over me, qisasan and muqassa." So killing the killer in return for the one he killed is "qisas," because it is an act done to him similar to what he did to the one he killed, although one of the two acts is transgression and the other is right. Although they differ in this respect, they agree that each has done to his companion the like of what the other did to him. The first act of the victim's guardian, when he kills the killer of his guardee, is called qisas, since by the killing he deserved the killing of the one who killed him, so it is as if his slain guardee were the one who had himself killed his killer, and so he exacted retribution from him.

* *

As for "al-qatla" (the slain), it is the plural of "qatil," just as "al-sar'a" is the plural of "sari'," and "al-jarha" is the plural of "jarih." The pattern "fa'il" is pluralized as "fa'la" only when it is an attribute of a thing described by it, in the sense of a disability or harm from which its possessor cannot escape from his place or his fall, [[See what has preceded in the commentary on "asra" (captives), 2: 311.]] such as "al-qatla" in their battles, "al-sar'a" in their places, "al-jarha," and what is similar to that.

* *

So the interpretation of the statement is: Retaliation for the slain has been prescribed for you, O believers, that a free man be killed for a free man, a slave for a slave, and a female for a female. Then the mention of "that he be retaliated against" was omitted, being sufficiently indicated by His saying: "Retaliation has been prescribed for you."

* *

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then let there be prompt pursuit of the blood money and payment to him with good conduct﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have differed concerning the interpretation of this.

Some of them said: its interpretation is: whoever is left (unkilled) by way of relief from the killing, unjustly, from the obligation which was due to his brother upon him from retaliation, which is the thing God referred to as "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part," then there is prompt pursuit by the pardoner of the killer for what is due to him from him in blood money, and payment by the one pardoned of that to him with good conduct.

Mention of those who said this:

2573. Abu Kurayb and Ahmad ibn Hammad al-Dulabi narrated to us, both saying: Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna narrated to us, from 'Amr, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part": the pardon is that he accepts the blood money in a deliberate killing. "Prompt pursuit with kindness": that this one demands it reasonably, and that this one pays it with good conduct.

2574. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salama narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Dinar narrated to us, from Jabir ibn Zayd, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said concerning His saying: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then prompt pursuit with kindness and payment to him with good conduct": he said: it is the deliberate killing, where the family of the victim is content with the blood money. "Prompt pursuit with kindness": the claimant is commanded to do so, "and payment to him with good conduct" from the one demanded.

2575. Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Shaqiq narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, and al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated to us, both saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The one who accepts the blood money, that is pardon from him and prompt pursuit with kindness, and the one pardoned by his brother pays to him with good conduct. [[The report 2575: Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Shaqiq, a teacher of al-Tabari; narrations from him have also passed: 1591. And it will come again: 2594. In the printed edition here "Sufyan" appears instead of "Shaqiq." This is an error and a distortion. There is no narrator named "Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Sufyan," nor by the name of his father.]]

2576. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, His saying: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then prompt pursuit with kindness and payment to him with good conduct," and it is the blood money: that the claimant pursues well, and payment to him with good conduct: that the one demanded pays well.

2577. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then prompt pursuit with kindness and payment to him with good conduct," and the one who pardons is the one who pardons the blood and takes the blood money.

2578. Sufyan narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part": he said, the blood money.

2579. Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Yazid, from Ibrahim, from al-Hasan: "and payment to him with good conduct": he said, it is incumbent on this claimant to demand reasonably, and incumbent on this one demanded to pay with good conduct.

2580. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then prompt pursuit with kindness," and the pardoner is the one who pardons the blood and takes the blood money.

2581. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu al-Walid narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from al-Sha'bi concerning His saying: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then prompt pursuit with kindness and payment to him with good conduct": he said, it is the deliberate killing, where the family is content with the blood money.

2582. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Dawud, from al-Sha'bi, the like of it.

2583. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada concerning His saying: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then prompt pursuit with kindness and payment to him with good conduct," he says: he was killed deliberately, then pardoned, and the blood money was accepted from him. He says: "then prompt pursuit with kindness," so the pursuer is commanded to pursue reasonably, and the payer is commanded to pay with good conduct. The deliberate killing is qawad (retaliation) to him, qisas, with no 'aql in it, [[Al-'aql: the blood money. It was called 'aql because among the Arabs in the Jahiliyya the blood money was camels, since camels were their wealth. So the killer would drive the blood money to the courtyard of the heirs of the slain, tie it there (ya'qiluha), and hand it over to his guardians.]] unless they are content with the blood money. If they are content with the blood money, then it is a hundred *khilfa*. [[Al-khilfa (with the kha' vowelled with fatha and the lam with kasra): the pregnant she-camel. It has no plural from its own root; rather it is called "makhad," just as one says "woman" and "women."]] If they say: "We will not be content except with such-and-such," then that is theirs.

2584. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada concerning His saying: "then prompt pursuit with kindness and payment to him with good conduct": he said, the claimant pursues it reasonably, and the one demanded pays with good conduct.

2585. It was narrated to me on the authority of 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning His saying: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then prompt pursuit with kindness and payment to him with good conduct": he says, whoever kills deliberately and is pardoned, and the blood money is taken from him. He says: "then prompt pursuit with kindness": the owner of the blood money he takes is commanded to pursue it reasonably, and the payer is commanded to pay with good conduct.

2586. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: I said to 'Ata': His saying: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then prompt pursuit with kindness and payment to him with good conduct." He said: that is when he takes the blood money, and it is pardon.

2587. Al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazza informed me, from Mujahid, who said: If he accepts the blood money, then he has pardoned the retaliation, and that is His saying: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then prompt pursuit with kindness and payment to him with good conduct." Ibn Juraij said: al-A'raj informed me, from Mujahid, the like of that, and he added to it: if he accepts the blood money, then it is incumbent on him to pursue reasonably, and on the one pardoned to pay with good conduct.

2588. Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Aqil narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan said: Accepting the blood money is a good pardon.

2589. Yunus narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "and payment to him with good conduct": he said, you, O pardoned one.

2590. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, His saying: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then prompt pursuit with kindness and payment to him with good conduct," and it is the blood money: that the claimant pursue well, and payment to him with good conduct: that the one demanded pay well.

* *

Others said regarding His saying, "whoever is pardoned," that it means: whoever is left with a surplus, and some remainder is left for him. They said: the meaning of His saying, "in any part from his brother," is: from his brother's blood money, something, or from the compensation for his wound, [[Al-arsh: the blood money for injuries and wounds, such as a head wound and the like.]] so the one who is owed that remainder from the killer or the wounder pursues it reasonably, and the killer or wounder pays him what remains due to him of that with good conduct.

This is the view of one who claims that the verse was revealed, meaning His saying, "O you who believe, retaliation has been prescribed for you concerning the slain," concerning those who fought one another in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, so the Messenger of God ﷺ was commanded to reconcile between them, so that the blood money of some would be set off against the blood money of others, and some of them would return to others the surplus that remained for them over the others. I think that the proponents of this view directed the interpretation of "pardon" in this place to the meaning of "abundance," from the saying of God, exalted is His remembrance: ﴿until they had multiplied﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 95]. So the meaning of the statement for them is: whoever has an abundance over his brother the killer.

Mention of those who said that:

2591. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part," he says: some remainder is left for him from his brother's blood money, or from the compensation for his wound, so let him pursue it reasonably, and let the other pay him with good conduct.

* *

The obligation according to the interpretation of the statement we have transmitted from 'Ali and al-Hasan, concerning His saying, "retaliation has been prescribed for you," that it means: the setting-off of the blood money of a male soul against the blood money of a female soul, and of a slave against a free man, and the mutual adjustment by the surplus between the blood moneys of their two souls, is that the meaning of His saying, "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part," is: whoever is relieved of what is owed to his brother from him, from the retaliation of the blood money of one of them against the blood money of the other's soul, through consent to the blood money of the slain soul, then there is prompt pursuit by the guardian reasonably, and payment by the killer to him of that with good conduct.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the statements in my view regarding His saying, "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part," is: whoever is forgiven, from the obligation which was due to his brother from him of the retaliation, in any part of the obligation, in exchange for a blood money he takes from him, then there is prompt pursuit reasonably by the pardoner of the blood, who is content with the blood money for his guardian's blood, and payment to him, from the killer, of that with good conduct. This is because of the reasons we have already set forth earlier: that the meaning of God's saying, exalted is His remembrance, "retaliation has been prescribed for you," is only retaliation for the killing souls, or the wounding or head-wounding souls, deliberately. Likewise "pardon" also concerns that.

As for the meaning of His saying, "then prompt pursuit reasonably," it means: then pursuit of what God has made due to him as a right from the killer of his guardian, without demanding from him more than what is not his due, in the ages of the prescribed camels or otherwise [[Al-fara'id: plural of fariḍa, which is a camel taken in zakat; it was called fariḍa because it is an obligation incumbent upon the owner of the property. Then the usage broadened so that a camel in other than zakat was called fariḍa.]], or imposing upon him what God has not made obligatory upon him, as follows:

2592. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to me, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, who said: It has reached us from the Prophet of God ﷺ that he said: "Whoever adds or demands an extra camel" — meaning in the camels of blood money and their prescribed ages — then it is of the practice of the Jahiliyya. [[The hadith 2592: this is a mursal hadith, since it is transmitted by Qatada, who is a Successor (tabi'i). I did not find it elsewhere, nor did al-Suyuti mention it.]]

* *

As for the goodness of the other in payment, it is the payment of what he became liable for by his killing to the guardian of the slain, according to what God obligated and required upon him, without diminishing for him any right due to him from him on account of that, or compelling him to demand and pursuit.

* *

If someone says to us: how is it said, "then prompt pursuit reasonably and payment to him with good conduct," and not "then pursuit reasonably and payment to him with good conduct" in the accusative, as He said: ﴿So when you meet those who disbelieved, then striking of necks﴾ [Surah Muhammad: 4]? It is said: Had the revelation come in the accusative, and it were "fa-ittiba'an bil-ma'ruf wa-ada'an ilayhi bi-ihsan," it would have been permissible and sound in Arabic, in the manner of a command, as one says: "striking, striking," and "when you meet so-and-so, then honoring and magnifying." However, it came in the nominative, and that is more eloquent in the speech of the Arabs than its accusative. Likewise, it is so in everything that is its like, of what is an obligation of general application, for the one who has done it and for the one who has not done it if he does it, not a recommendation or encouragement. Its nominative case has the meaning: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, the ruling concerning it is: prompt pursuit reasonably and payment to him with good conduct," or "the judgment and decision concerning it is: prompt pursuit reasonably."

Some of the grammarians (ahl al-'arabiyya) have said: its nominative is on the meaning: "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then upon him is prompt pursuit reasonably." This is a valid position, but the first we have stated is the proper construction of the speech. Likewise, every similar case in the Qur'an, its nominative is in the manner we have stated. Such as His saying: ﴿And whoever kills it among you intentionally, then the penalty is the like of what he killed of the livestock﴾ [Surah al-Ma'ida: 95], and His saying: ﴿Then either keep in reasonable manner or release with good conduct﴾ [Surah al-Baqara: 229]. As for His saying, ﴿then striking of necks﴾, the correct reading is the accusative, which is the proper construction, because it is an exhortation from God, may His remembrance be exalted, to His servants to kill at the meeting with the enemy, as one says, "When you meet the enemy, then magnify God and declare His unity," as an urging to magnification, not as an obligation or binding requirement. [[See the Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 109-110.]]

* *

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, exalted is His remembrance, "that," He means this [[See "dhalika" in the sense of "hadha" 1: 235-237, and then this part 3: 335.]] which I have ruled and prescribed for you, namely my permitting you, O nation, to pardon retaliation against the killer of your slain, in exchange for a blood money which you take, thereby owning it as you own all your other property, which I had forbidden to those before you from the earlier nations, ﴿an alleviation from your Lord﴾, meaning: an alleviation from me for you, from what I had burdened others with, by forbidding that to them, ﴿and a mercy﴾ from me to you. As follows:

2593. Abu Kurayb and Ahmad ibn Hammad al-Dulabi narrated to us, both saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: In the Children of Israel there was retaliation, and there was no blood money among them. So God said in this verse: "Retaliation has been prescribed for you concerning the slain: the free for the free," to His saying, "whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part": the pardon is that he accepts the blood money in a deliberate killing. ﴿That is an alleviation from your Lord﴾: he says, He has lightened for you what was upon those before you, namely that this one pursue it reasonably, and that this one pay with good conduct. [[The hadith 2593: Ahmad ibn Hammad ibn Sa'id ibn Muslim al-Ansari al-Razi al-Dulabi: he is the father of "Abu Bishr Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Dulabi," the author of the book al-Kuna wa al-Asma'. We have elevated his lineage, quoting from Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 2: 291 in the biography of his son the hafiz. Ahmad ibn Hammad is trustworthy; Ibn Abi Hatim recorded his biography (1/1/49) and mentioned no criticism of him, and noted that his father Abu Hatim heard from him.

Sufyan: this is Ibn 'Uyayna.

The hadith was transmitted by 'Abd al-Razzaq in his tafsir, p. 16, in similar form, with two isnads: from Ma'mar, from Abu Najih, from Mujahid; and from Ibn 'Uyayna, like the isnad here to Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas.

It was also transmitted by al-Bukhari 12: 183 (Fath), from Qutayba ibn Sa'id, from Sufyan, with this same isnad.

Al-Suyuti mentioned it 1: 173, and added its attribution to Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, and others.]]

Ibn Kathir mentioned it (1:394) through the narration of Sa'id ibn Mansur, from Sufyan. Then he said: "Others besides him have narrated it from 'Amr, and Ibn Hibban included it in his Sahih from 'Amr ibn Dinar." He (may Allah have mercy on him) overlooked that al-Bukhari also narrated it in his Sahih. He attributed it to the Sahih of Ibn Hibban and did not mention al-Bukhari.

2594. Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Shaqiq narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, saying: 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Those before you used to kill the killer in retaliation for the slain, and blood money was not accepted from them. So Allah revealed: "O you who have believed, retribution is prescribed for you in the matter of the slain: the free for the free..." to the end of the verse. "That is an alleviation from your Lord" means: He lightened it for you. For those before you, blood money was not accepted. So accepting blood money from one who takes it is a pardon.

2595. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Dinar informed us, from Jabir ibn Zayd, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding "That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy" — concerning what was upon the Children of Israel, meaning: the prohibition of blood money for them.

2596. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Upon the Children of Israel was retribution for killing, with no blood money among them for a life or for a wound. This is the saying of Allah: "And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life, and the eye for the eye..." the whole verse [Surah al-Ma'idah: 45]. Allah lightened it for the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), so blood money was accepted from them for a life and for injury. This is His saying, the Exalted: "That is an alleviation from your Lord" among you.

2597. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His saying: "That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy." It is only a mercy by which Allah showed compassion to this Ummah. He fed them blood money and made it lawful for them, and it was not lawful for anyone before them. The People of the Torah had only retribution or pardon, with no compensation between them. The People of the Gospel had only pardon, which they were commanded to observe. Allah made for this Ummah retaliation, pardon, and blood money, if they wished, and made it lawful for them, which was not granted to any nation before them.

2598. It was narrated from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' with the same wording, except that he said: "there was nothing between them."

2599. al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His saying: "Retribution is prescribed for you in the matter of the slain," who said: There was no blood money for those before us. It was only killing or pardon to the family of the slain. This verse was revealed concerning a people who were more numerous than others.

2600. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: 'Amr ibn Dinar informed me, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Indeed the Children of Israel had retribution prescribed for them, and this Ummah was lightened. 'Amr ibn Dinar recited: "That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy."

* *

As for the view of the one who said that retribution (qisas) in this verse means the mutual settling of blood money among the slain, as stated by al-Suddi, then its interpretation should be: This which I have done for you, O believers — the settlement of blood money for your slain by blood money for one another, and the abandonment of requiring retaliation from the rest of you for the one he killed, and taking his blood money — is an alleviation from Me for you, lifting the burden of what was upon you by My ruling that you must choose either retaliation or blood money, and a mercy from Me to you.

* *

Concerning the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment﴾ [2:178]

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His saying, the Exalted, "whoever transgresses after that," He means: whoever exceeds what Allah has allowed him after taking the blood money, by transgression and wrongdoing, to the killing of his victim's killer and the shedding of his blood, which has not been allowed for him. For that act and his transgression into what He has forbidden him, there is a painful punishment.

I have already explained the meaning of "transgression" earlier, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary. [See above, 2:307.] The people of interpretation have said things similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

2601. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Whoever transgresses after that," by killing, "will have a painful punishment."

2602. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Whoever transgresses," after taking the blood money, "will have a painful punishment."

2603. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray'a narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah regarding His saying: "Whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment," meaning: whoever transgresses after taking the blood money by killing, will have a painful punishment. He said: It was mentioned to us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "I will not pardon a man who kills after taking the blood money."

[Editorial note on hadith 2603: This was also narrated by Qatadah the Successor as a marfu' report, so it is mursal. al-Suyuti also mentioned it (1:173) from Qatadah and attributed it only to al-Tabari and Ibn al-Mundhir. 'Abd al-Razzaq also narrated the marfu' wording in his Tafsir, p. 16, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, likewise mursal. Then al-Suyuti mentioned the marfu' wording and attributed it to Samuwayh in his Fawa'id, from Samurah. He was greatly deficient in this, as he was also deficient in al-Jami' al-Saghir (9701), where he mentioned it and attributed it only to al-Tayalisi, from Jabir, meaning Jabir ibn 'Abdullah. The hadith of al-Tayalisi from Jabir is in his Musnad (1763), from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Mutar al-Warraq, from a man, from Jabir, which he narrated as marfu'. Ahmad also narrated it in his Musnad (14968), from 'Affan, from Hammad ibn Salamah: "Mutar informed us, from a man I think was al-Hasan, from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah." Likewise Abu Dawud narrated it in his Sunan (4507), from Musa ibn Isma'il, from Hammad ibn Salamah, with the same chain. So al-Suyuti's deficiency is that he attributed it only to al-Tayalisi, though it is in one of the Six Books and in the Musnad of Ahmad. In any case, the hadith of Jabir is weak, because its chain includes an unnamed man, or a man about whom Mutar al-Warraq was uncertain. The hadith of al-Hasan from Samurah was also mentioned by Ibn Kathir (1:395), who said: "Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah said, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, from Samurah...," and narrated it as marfu'. This chain could be sound if we knew its chain to Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah and who narrated it through him, but I have not found that after lengthy search. If we found it, it would connect this mursal report which al-Tabari narrated through Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah from Qatadah.]

2604. al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His saying: "Whoever transgresses after that," who said: It is killing after taking the blood money. He means: whoever kills after taking the blood money, upon him is killing, and no blood money is accepted from him. [Editorial note: al-Tabari narrated this report through 'Abd al-Razzaq. It is in his Tafsir, p. 16, with this same chain.]

2605. It was narrated from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His saying: "Whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment," meaning: whoever transgresses after taking the blood money, will have a painful punishment.

2606. Sufyan ibn WakI' narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to me, from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, from al-Hasan, who said: When a man killed a victim in the Jahiliyyah, he fled to his people. His people came and reconciled on his behalf with blood money. He said: The fugitive would come out, having been granted safety for himself. He said: He would then be killed, and the blood money would be thrown to them. That is the "transgression."

2607. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Aqil narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Hasan on this verse: "Whoever is pardoned something from his brother's blood," who said: The killer, when he was sought and could not be caught, the blood money was taken from his family, then he was granted safety, and was caught and killed. al-Hasan said: This is not a permitted transgression (lit. "what is eaten" is not 'udwan).

2608. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Muslim narrated to us, saying: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Harun ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I said to 'Ikrimah: Who kills after taking the blood money? He said: Then he is to be killed! Have you not heard Allah say: "Whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment"?

2609. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Whoever transgresses after that," after he takes the blood money, then kills, "there is no painful punishment" [as stated].

2610. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Whoever transgresses after that," he says: whoever transgresses after taking the blood money, will have a painful punishment.

2611. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: "Whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment," who said: He took the 'aql (blood money), then killed the killer of his slain after taking the 'aql, so he will have a painful punishment.

* *

They differed concerning the meaning of "painful punishment" which Allah prescribed for one who transgresses after taking the blood money from the killer of his relative.

Some of them said: That "punishment" is killing: he is killed for the one he killed after taking the blood money from him, and his pardon of retaliation from him is by the blood of his relative.

Those who said this:

2612. Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim al-Dawraqi narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak regarding His saying: "Whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment," who said: He is killed, and that is the painful punishment, meaning: the punishment that hurts.

2613. Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to me, saying: Abu Ishaq narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said this.

2614. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Harun ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from 'Ikrimah: "Whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment," who said: Killing.

* *

Some others said: That "punishment" is a penalty which the ruler imposes on him, according to what the ruler sees fit as punishment.

Those who said this:

2615. al-Qasim ibn al-Hasan narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, who said: Ibn Jurayj said: Isma'il ibn Umayyah informed me, from al-Layth (except that he did not attribute it, and said: "a trustworthy man"), that the Prophet (ﷺ) made it obligatory, by oath or otherwise, that he not pardon a man who pardoned the blood and took the blood money, then transgressed and killed. Ibn Jurayj said: 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz informed me, saying: In a letter of 'Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: The "transgression" which Allah mentioned is that a man takes the 'aql or exacts retaliation, or the ruler decides concerning the wounds, then some of them transgress after fully receiving their right. Whoever does that has transgressed, and the ruling on it rests with the ruler, according to what he sees as the punishment. He said: Even if he pardoned him, none of those seeking the right would have the right to [pardon] [The words in parentheses are so in the original; the correct reading, in my judgment, is "to kill him." I did not find this report, nor the letter of 'Umar which he mentioned.] because this is among the matters about which Allah revealed His saying: "If you dispute over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger" [Surah al-Nisa': 59].

[Editorial note on hadith 2615: These are actually two reports, narrated by Ibn Jurayj, and I did not find them elsewhere. I cannot accept that their wording comes from the words of prophethood, nor does it bear the light of prophethood. It resembles the wording of jurists more! The first is narrated by Ibn Jurayj, from Isma'il ibn Umayyah, from a man named "al-Layth," though he did not name him. I do not know who this "al-Layth" is. As for Isma'il ibn Umayyah, he is trustworthy and narrates from the Successors. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir (1/1/34), Ibn Abi Hatim (1/1/159), Nasab Quraysh (182), and Jamharat al-Ansab of Ibn Hazm (74). The second is narrated by Ibn Jurayj from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, from "a letter of 'Umar from the Prophet (ﷺ)." The apparent meaning is a letter of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, though it is possible it is a letter of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. 'Abd al-'Aziz, son of the Commander of the Believers 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, is trustworthy; Ibn Ma'in and others declared him trustworthy. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim (2/2/389).]

2616. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad narrated to us, from Yunus, from al-Hasan: concerning a man who was killed and blood money was taken from him, then his relative killed the killer for him. al-Hasan said: The blood money he took is to be taken from him, and he is not to be killed for it.

[Editorial note on report 2616: Bishr ibn Mu'adh, the teacher of al-Tabari, has passed in 352. We add here that he is a well-known trustworthy narrator, biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim (1/1/368). It is mentioned that his father wrote from him, and when he was asked about him, he said: "truthful in narration, sincere." He narrates from early teachers, such as Hammad ibn Zayd, who died in 179, and 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad, his teacher here, who died that same year. 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad al-'Abdi al-Basri: one of the great trustworthy scholars. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Saghir of al-Bukhari (202), where it is said he died in 179; Ibn Abi Hatim (3/1/20-21); and Ibn Sa'd (7/2/44). Yunus: he is Ibn 'Ubayd ibn Dinar al-'Abdi, and he is trustworthy, among the most reliable and firmest of al-Hasan's companions. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir (4/2/402), al-Saghir (160), Ibn Sa'd (7/2/23-24), and Ibn Abi Hatim (4/2/242).]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two interpretations of His saying, "Whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment," is the view of those who said: whoever transgresses after taking the blood money and kills the killer of his relative, will have a painful punishment in the immediate life of this world, which is killing. This is because Allah, the Exalted, gave every guardian of a slain person who was killed unjustly authority over the killer of his relative. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have given his heir authority, but let him not exceed limits in killing﴾ [17:33]. Since this is so, and since all the scholars agreed that whoever kills the killer of his relative after pardoning him and taking the blood money for his slain, is a wrongdoer in his killing, it is clear that he who kills unjustly in this way does not have authority over the heirs of the victim in retaliation, pardon, or taking blood money, whichever they choose. [There is ambiguity in this phrasing, and I fear something may have dropped out of the sentence, but the general meaning is clear.] When this is so, it is known that this is his punishment, because whoever has his legal penalty carried out upon him in this world, that is his punishment for his sin, and he will not be pursued for it in the Hereafter, as the report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has established. [Like what al-Bukhari narrated from the hadith of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "I pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a group, and he said: I pledge you that you will not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor kill your children, nor bring slander that you invent between your hands and feet, nor disobey me in what is right. Whoever among you fulfills it, his reward is with Allah, and whoever is afflicted with any of that and is punished for it in this world, it is an expiation for him and a purification, and whoever Allah conceals, it is up to Allah: if He wills He punishes him, and if He wills He forgives him" (al-Bukhari, Book of Hudud, 8:162).]

As for what Ibn Jurayj said: that the ruling on one who kills the killer of his relative after pardoning him and taking the blood money of his slain relative is to be decided by the Imam rather than the heirs of the slain, this is an opinion contrary to what the apparent meaning of the Book of Allah indicates, and on which the scholars of the Ummah agreed. That is because Allah gave the guardian of every person slain unjustly authority over the killer, and not others, without specifying one slain person over another. So it is the same whether that was the slain of the guardian of the one who killed, or someone else. Whoever makes an exception in this must be asked for proof from a source or parallel, and the argument must be reversed against him; then he will never say anything about any of this without being bound to its equivalent in the other case.
