When the heir is numerous and the wealth is small, he bequeaths a third of all his wealth, and the one to whom the bequest is made, or the ruler, makes reconciliation between them. I asked: Is that during his life or after his death? He said: We have not heard anyone say it except after his death, and he is admonished at that time.

2701- al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn 'Uyaynah informed us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father regarding His words: "Whoever fears injustice or sin from a testator and makes reconciliation between them," he said: It is the man who bequeaths to the child of his daughter.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: Whoever fears, from a testator for his parents and relatives, injustice toward some of them over others, and makes reconciliation between the parents and relatives, then there is no sin upon him.

Mention of those who said this:

2702- Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Whoever fears injustice or sin from a testator and makes reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him." As for "injustice" (janafan): it is error in his bequest; and as for "sin" (ithman): it is deliberately intending injustice in his bequest. Not carrying it out is greater in reward for him, but he should make reconciliation between them according to what he sees as right, decreasing for some and increasing for others. He said: This verse was revealed concerning the parents and the nearest relatives.

2703- Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "Whoever fears injustice or sin from a testator and makes reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him," he said: "Janaf" is that he be unjust to some of them over others in the bequest, and "ithm" is that he commits sin regarding his parents, some over others. "Makes reconciliation between them": the one to whom the bequest is entrusted makes reconciliation between the parents and the nearest relatives – the son and the sons are "the nearest relatives" – then there is no sin upon him. This is the executor to whom it was entrusted and who was given authority over it. If he sees that one of them is unjust to this one over that one, and makes reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him. The testator was unable to bequeath as Allah, exalted is He, commanded, and the executor was unable to make reconciliation. So Allah, exalted is His remembrance, took that from them and established the obligatory shares.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the opinions regarding the interpretation of the verse is that its interpretation is: "Whoever fears injustice or sin from a testator" – that is, he inclines away from right by mistake, or deliberately intends sin in his bequest, by bequeathing to his parents and relatives who do not inherit from him more than what is permissible for him to bequeath to them from his wealth, and beyond what Allah has permitted to him, exceeding a third or the whole third, when the wealth is little and the heirs are many – then there is no harm upon the one who attends him in making reconciliation between those to whom the bequest is made and the heirs of the deceased, and between the deceased himself, by commanding the deceased in this matter with what is right, informing him of what Allah has permitted him and allowed him in bequeathing from his wealth, and forbidding him from exceeding in his bequest the good that Allah, exalted is His remembrance, mentioned in His Book: "Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is a bequest to parents and relatives in accordance with what is right" (2:180). That is the "reconciliation" that Allah, exalted is His remembrance, mentioned: "and makes reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him." Likewise, for one who has abundant wealth and few heirs, who wishes to limit his bequest to his parents and relatives below a third, the one who attends him makes reconciliation between him, his heirs, and his parents and relatives to whom he wishes to bequeath, by commanding the sick person to increase his bequest to them, bringing it up to the third that Allah has permitted. That too is part of reconciling them in accordance with what is right.

We chose this opinion because Allah, exalted is His remembrance, said: "Whoever fears injustice or sin from a testator," meaning: whoever fears that a testator will incline unjustly or commit sin. The fear of injustice and sin from the testator is only before the occurrence of injustice and sin. As for after it has occurred from him, there is no sense in fearing that he will be unjust or sinful; rather, that is the state of one who has already been unjust or sinful. If that were its meaning, it would have said: "Whoever ascertains from a testator injustice or sin" – or "is certain of it" or "knows it" – and would not have said: "Whoever fears from him injustice."

* *

If what we have said is unclear to some people, and they say: What is the meaning of reconciliation then, since reconciliation only occurs between those who differ over something?

It is said: Although that is among the meanings of reconciliation, reconciliation also includes making peace between the two parties regarding that which is feared will cause disagreement between them, so that disagreement is secured against. For "reconciliation" is only the act by which the well-being of relations is restored, whether that act occurs before the disagreement or after it.

If someone says: How is it said "and makes reconciliation between them," when no mention has preceded of the heirs or of the parties who disagree, or whose disagreement is feared? It is said: Indeed, mention has preceded of those to whom Allah, exalted is His remembrance, commanded the bequest, namely the parents of the testator and his relatives, and those commanded to make bequests in His words: "Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is a bequest to parents and relatives in accordance with what is right." Then He, exalted is His remembrance, said: "Whoever fears from a testator" – toward those to whom I commanded him to bequeath – "injustice or sin, and makes reconciliation between them" – and between those to whom I commanded him to bequeath – "there is no sin upon him." The reconciliation between him and them is reconciliation between them and the heirs of the testator.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The phrase "Whoever fears from a testator" has been recited with a light "ṣād" and a sukun on the "wāw," and also with a vowelled "wāw" and a doubled "ṣād."

As for the one who recited it with a light "ṣād" and a sukun on the "wāw," he recited it in the dialect of one who says: "Awṣaytu Fulānan bi-kadha" (I bequeathed to so-and-so such-and-such).

As for the one who vowelled the "wāw" and doubled the "ṣād," he recited it in the dialect of one who says: "Waṣṣaytu Fulānan bi-kadha" (I bequeathed to so-and-so such-and-such). These are two well-known dialects of the Arabs: "waṣṣaytuka" and "awṣaytuka." [[See the explanation of (wṣy) in what preceded in this part, 3: 93-96.]]

As for "janaf" (jaʾnaf), it means injustice and deviation from the truth in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of the poet: [[He is 'Amir al-Khasafi, of the Banu Khasafah ibn Qays 'Aylan.]]

They are the kinsmen, even if they are unjust toward us,
and we are from meeting them visitors who turn away.

[[Majaz al-Quran by Abu 'Ubaydah: 66, 67; Mushkil al-Quran: 219; al-Lisan (jnf, wly). Al-mawla: the paternal cousin; he used the singular in place of the plural, meaning "al-mawali." Abu 'Ubaydah said it is like His words: "Then He brings you out as a child" (22:5). Zawr is the plural of azwar, meaning one who turns away from a thing. He says: They are our cousins, and we dislike meeting them and fighting them, because of their right of kinship.]]

It is said of it: "Janafa al-rajulu 'ala sahibihi yajnafu" (the man was unjust toward his companion and inclined against him) – when he leaned against him and oppressed him – "janafan."

* *

So the meaning of the speech is: "Whoever fears from a testator injustice" in regard to the object of the bequest, and inclination away from correctness in it, and deviation from moderation, "or sin" by deliberately intending that with knowledge of the error of what he does, "and makes reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him."

* *

The people of interpretation said in agreement with what we have said regarding the meaning of "janaf" and "ithm."

Mention of those who said that:

2704- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: "Whoever fears from a testator injustice," meaning by "janaf": error.

2705- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Jabir ibn Nuh narrated to us, from 'Abd al-Malik, from 'Ata': "Whoever fears from a testator injustice," he said: inclination.

2706- Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Malik informed us, from 'Ata', the same.

2707- 'Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn al-Harith and Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, both saying: 'Abd al-Malik narrated to us, from 'Ata', the same.

2708- Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak, who said: "Janaf" is error, and "ithm" is deliberate.

2709- Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: [Abu Ahmad] al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from 'Ata', the same.

2710- Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Whoever fears from a testator injustice or sin." As for "janafan": error in his bequest; and as for "ithman": deliberately intending injustice in his bequest. [[The report: 2710 – passed as number 2702 in full.]]

2711- Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His words: "Whoever fears from a testator injustice or sin," he said: error or deliberate. [[The report: 2711 – in the printed edition: "Whoever fears from a testator janafan" he said: "janafan ithman," which is an unsettled and corrupt expression. I did not think it right to leave it in its corruption, so I have transmitted Mujahid's statement which Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah and 'Abd ibn Humayd related, as reported by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 175.]]

2712- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi': "Whoever fears from a testator injustice or sin," he said: "Janaf" is error, and "ithm" is deliberate.

2713- 'Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn Yazid, the owner of the pearls, narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, the same.

2714- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Qabisah narrated to us, from Sufyan, from his father, from Ibrahim: "Whoever fears from a testator injustice or sin," he said: "Janaf": error, and "ithm": deliberate.

2715- Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Fudayl ibn Marzuq narrated to us, from 'Atiyyah: "Whoever fears from a testator injustice," he said: error, "or sin" deliberately.

2716- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, from Ibn 'Uyaynah, from Ibn Tawus, from his father: "Whoever fears from a testator injustice," he said: inclination.

2717- Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "janafan," [meaning] unfairness (hayf), and "ithm," [meaning] his inclination toward some over others. All of it returns to one meaning, just as "Pardoning, Forgiving" and "Forgiving, Merciful" are.

2718- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "Janaf" is error, and "ithm" is deliberate.

2719- I was told from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: al-Fadl ibn Khalid narrated to us, saying: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, who said: "Janaf" is error, and "ithm" is deliberate. [[The report: 2719 – al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj al-Khayyat al-Baghdadi: a shaykh whose narration is not relied upon. Ibn Ma'in said of him: "a liar, a drunkard, a cunning man." He is biographed in Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/62-63, Tarikh Isbahan 1: 266-267, Tarikh Baghdad 8: 84-86, and Lisan al-Mizan 2: 307. Al-Tabari narrates from him often in the tafsir with an unknown chain, saying: "I was told from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj." Perhaps this is because of the weakness of his narration, so the chain does not reach him. In some instances in the history he named the one who narrated to him from him; see the History 1: 30, 42.]]

The printed edition gives his name correctly, as in 2898. It often appears in error as "al-Hasan ibn al-Faraj," as it does in this place and in 2750. Something similar happened earlier at 691, where I said there: "I did not know who he is." It should be corrected in that place and wherever it occurs in the tafsir.

al-Fadl ibn Khalid: his biography has already passed at 691.]]

* *

As for His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, the meaning is: Allah is Forgiving to the testator [[In the printed edition: "Forgiving, Merciful to the testator..." This is not correct, and the context of his wording supports the correction we have made.]] for what he had let his soul entertain of deviation (janaf) and sin, if he abandoned sinning and deviating in his bequest. So He overlooks for him what he had let his soul entertain of injustice, since he did not carry it out, and so He refrains from holding him accountable for it [[In the printed edition: "fa-yaf'al an yu'akhidhahu bihi" (then he does that, to hold him accountable for it), and the likely correct reading is what we have recorded.]]. "Merciful" to the one who reconciles between the testator and whoever wished to wrong someone else through him, or to sin on his behalf.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 183:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you, as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may become God-conscious﴾ (2:183)

Abu Ja'far said: By His, the Exalted's, words "O you who believe," He means: O you who believe in God and His Messenger, who affirm both and acknowledge them. [See the explanation of "faith" (al-iman) above, 1:234-235, and the references in the index of terms.]

By His words "fasting has been prescribed for you," He means: fasting has been made obligatory for you. [See the explanation of "prescribed" (kutiba) above in this part, 3:357, 364, 365.]

"Fasting" (al-siyam) is a verbal noun, from the saying of the speaker: "I fasted from such-and-such," meaning: I refrained from it. One says: "I fast from it, fasting (sawman) and fasting (siyaman)." The meaning of "siyam" is refraining from what God has commanded to refrain from. From this it is said: "the horses fasted" (samat al-khayl), when they refrained from running; and from it is the verse of the poet Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan:

Horses fasting, and horses not fasting,
beneath the dust-cloud, and others chewing their bits.

[Diwan: 106 (additions), and Lisan (ʿ-l-k) (ṣ-w-m). But it is from his ode whose opening is: "Su'ad has departed, and her cord has been severed."]

It has been explained that "the horse fasted" means it held back from moving. The phrase in the lexicography is: "the horse fasted" when it stood in its stall without eating, or stood still without taking any food. Abu ʿUbayda said: every one who refrains from food, speech, or movement is a fasting one. Al-ʿajaj: the dust that rises. The meaning is that they do not stand still in battle. ʿalaka the horse its bit: chewed it and moved it in its mouth.

From the same is the saying of God, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ (19:26), meaning: a silence from speech.

* *

As for His words "as it was prescribed for those before you," the meaning is: prescribed for you the like of what was prescribed for those before you.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Then the people of interpretation differed concerning those whom God meant by His words "as it was prescribed for those before you," and concerning the aspect in which the comparison between the prescription of our fasting and the fasting of those before us occurs.

Some of them said: Those about whom God informed us regarding the fasting He prescribed for us, that it is like what was incumbent upon them, are the Christians. They said: the aspect of comparison by which He likened one to the other is their agreement in the time and the duration, which is binding upon us today.

Those who said this:

2720. I was told, from Yahya ibn Ziyad, from Muhammad ibn Aban [al-Qurashi], from Abu Umayya al-Tanafisi, from al-Sha'bi, that he said: "If I fasted the whole year, I would break the fast on the day about which there is doubt, whether it is of Sha'ban or of Ramadan. That is because the Christians were obligated to fast the month of Ramadan as it was prescribed for us, but they shifted it to the season. For they would sometimes fast it in the summer and count thirty days. Then there came after them a generation which took the safe course for themselves, so they fasted ten days before the thirty and a day after them. Then the later ones continued to follow the practice of the generation before them until it reached fifty." That is His words: "Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you."

* *

Others said: Rather, the comparison is only because their fasting was from the night prayer ('isha') to the night prayer, and that was God's prescription for the believers at the first time fasting was made obligatory upon them. Those who held this view agreed with the first view that those God meant by "as it was prescribed for those before you" are the Christians.

Those who said this:

2721. Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you." As for those before us, they are the Christians: Ramadan was prescribed for them, and it was prescribed for them that they not eat, drink, or have intercourse with women after sleep during the month of Ramadan. The fasting of Ramadan became hard upon the Christians, and it kept shifting for them in winter and summer. When they saw that, they gathered and made a fast in the transition between winter and summer, and said: "We will add twenty days by which we atone for what we did!" So they made their fasting fifty days. The Muslims continued to do as the Christians did, until there occurred the matter of Abu Qays ibn Sirma and ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, what occurred [the report of Abu Sirma and ʿUmar will come in the traditions nos. 2935-2952], and God then made lawful for them eating, drinking, and intercourse until the break of dawn.

2722. Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ishaq told us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you," he said: fasting was prescribed for them from the 'atama to the 'atama.

* *

Others said: Those God meant by His words "as it was prescribed for those before you" are the People of the Book.

Those who said this:

2723. Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa told us, saying: Shibl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you," the People of the Book.

* *

Others said: Rather, that was prescribed for all people.

Those who said this:

2724. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding His words: "Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you," he said: the month of Ramadan was prescribed for the people as it was prescribed for those before them. He said: God had prescribed for people, before Ramadan was sent down, the fasting of three days of every month.

2725. Bishr told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatada, regarding His words: "O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you," Ramadan: God prescribed it for those who were before them.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these views is the view of the one who said: the meaning of the verse is:

O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you from among the People of the Book, "for a number of days" (ayyaman ma'dudat), and these are the whole month of Ramadan. Because whoever came after Abraham ﷺ was commanded to follow Abraham, since God, may He be exalted, had made him an imam for the people, and God, Mighty and Majestic, has informed us that His religion was the upright monotheistic submission (al-hanifiyya al-muslima), so He commanded our Prophet ﷺ with the like of what He commanded those prophets before him.

As for the comparison, it occurs only in the time: that those before us were prescribed the month of Ramadan just as it was prescribed for us, identically.

* *

As for the interpretation of His words "so that you may become God-conscious" (la'allakum tattaqun), it means: so that you may refrain from eating food, drinking drink, and intercourse with women during it. [See the explanation of "la'alla" meaning "so that" (li-kay) above, 1:364-365, then 2:69, 161, and seek it in the index also.] It says: I prescribed for you the fast and the abstaining from what you would break by failing to abstain from it, so that you may guard against what would break your fast during the time of your fasting.

* *

Among those who said the like of what we have said regarding this were a group of the people of interpretation:

Those who said this:

2726. Musa told me, saying: ʿAmr told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: As for His words "so that you may become God-conscious," he says: that you may guard against food, drink, and women, just as the Christians before you guarded against them.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 2, Verse 184 (Part 1 of 4)**

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Days numbered﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, exalted is His mention, means: "O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you, [for] a number of days."

"Days" (ayyaman) is in the accusative by an implied verb, as if it were said: "Fasting has been prescribed for you, as it was prescribed for those before you, that you fast for numbered days," as one says: "The striking pleased me, Zayd (as in: the striking of Zayd)."

* *

His words, "as it was prescribed for those before you," [refer to] the fasting, as if it were said: "There has been prescribed for you that which is like what was prescribed for those before you: that you fast for numbered days."

* *

Then the exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning what God, majestic and exalted, meant by His words, "numbered days."

Some of them said: "The numbered days" are the fasting of three days of every month. They said: That was the fasting prescribed for the people before the month of Ramadan was prescribed for them.

Those who said this:

2727 – Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Ata', who said: "The fasting of three days of every month was incumbent upon them, and he did not call the month 'numbered days.'" He said: "This was the fasting of the people before, then God, majestic and exalted, prescribed for the people the month of Ramadan."

2728 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words: "O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may be God-fearing." He said: "It was three days of every month. Then that was abrogated (nusikha, naskh: the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation) by what was revealed of the fasting of Ramadan. So this was the first fast, [which was] from the 'atamah (the night prayer time)."

2729 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah narrated to us, from Amr ibn Murrah, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Medina and fasted the day of 'Ashura' and three days of every month. Then God, majestic and exalted, revealed the prescription of the month of Ramadan, and God revealed: "O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you," until [He reached]: "And for those who are able to bear it, there is a ransom: the feeding of a poor man."

[[Hadith note: 2729 – Yunus ibn Bukayr: his biography has already passed, at no. 1605. In the printed edition here it reads "Bishr ibn Bukayr," which is a clear error. This hadith will come with this chain – longer than here – correctly, at no. 2733.

Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah: he is al-Mas'udi, and he is trustworthy (thiqah). They spoke about him, that he changed at the end of his life, a year or two before his death. He died in 160 AH. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib. [See also] Ibn Sa'd 6:254, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/250–252.

This hadith is a fragment of a long hadith on the states of prayer and the states of fasting. A small fragment of it, concerning the prayer toward Jerusalem, has passed: 2156, through the route of Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, from al-Mas'udi.

Ahmad related it in full in al-Musnad 5:246–247 (Halabi edition), from Abu al-Nadr, Yazid ibn Harun – both from al-Mas'udi. Likewise Abu Dawud al-Sijistani related it: 507, through the route of Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi and Yazid ibn Harun.

Al-Hakim related in al-Mustadrak 2:274 its portion concerning the states of fasting, through the route of Abu al-Nadr, from al-Mas'udi. He said: "This is a hadith whose chain is sound, though the two [Shaykhs, al-Bukhari and Muslim] did not record it." Al-Dhahabi agreed with him.

Ibn Kathir quoted it in full, 1:402–404, from the narration of al-Musnad, with its chain. Al-Suyuti also mentioned it in full, 1:175–176, and added its attribution to Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan.]]

2730 – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, who said: "God, He – His mention is exalted – had prescribed for the people, before Ramadan was revealed, the fasting of three days of every month."

* *

Others said: Rather, the three days which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to fast before the prescription of Ramadan were voluntary fasting. God, majestic and exalted, meant by His words, "Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you: numbered days," the days of the month of Ramadan, not the days which he used to fast before the obligation of the fast of the month of Ramadan.

Those who said this:

2731 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from Amr ibn Murrah, who said: Our companions (ashabuna) narrated to us: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when he came to them, commanded them to fast three days of every month as a voluntary act, not an obligation. He said: Then the fast of Ramadan was revealed. Abu Musa said: His words, "Amr ibn Murrah said: Our companions narrated to us," he means Ibn Abi Layla; it is as if Ibn Abi Layla were the one saying, "Our companions narrated to us."

[[Hadith note: 2731 – This is a fragment of the previous long hadith, which we indicated at 2729, but here it is narrated through another route: the route of Shu'bah from Amr ibn Murrah. Here Amr ibn Murrah says, "Our companions narrated to us: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ)," etc. If this were taken at face value, it would be a mursal (a report lacking a companion in its chain). Therefore Abu Musa – that is, Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, the teacher of al-Tabari – explained it as meaning that the one who said this was Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla. Then al-Muthanna followed it with a narration after it: 2732, from Abu Dawud – that is al-Tayalisi – from Shu'bah, who said: "I heard Amr ibn Murrah say: I heard Ibn Abi Layla." This is the chain we indicated a moment ago, in which al-Tabari related another fragment of the hadith, at 2156.

It appears that Ibn al-Muthanna heard the hadith from Muhammad ibn Ja'far twice or more: once in this form here, and some of it in the clear and explicit form, mentioning Ibn Abi Layla.

Abu Dawud al-Sijistani related the entire hadith in his Sunan: 506, by two chains, one of which is this chain of al-Tabari, namely from Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna. Abu Dawud said: "Amr ibn Marzuq narrated to us, Shu'bah informed us, from Amr ibn Murrah, who said: I heard Ibn Abi Layla – (and) – and Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from Amr ibn Murrah: I heard Ibn Abi Layla say: The prayer was transferred through three states; and our companions narrated to us that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said…"

So he repeated in the second chain – in the route of Shu'bah – the statement of Amr ibn Murrah: "I heard Ibn Abi Layla." Perhaps he intended by this repetition, in which the name of Ibn Abi Layla is explicitly stated, to remove the suspicion that someone might think that the narration in which Muhammad ibn Ja'far did not name "Ibn Abi Layla" is being corrected by this explicit one.

Or this is supported by al-Tabari's statement following the hadith: "Abu Musa said: His words, 'Amr ibn Murrah said: Our companions narrated to us,' he means Ibn Abi Layla; it is as if Ibn Abi Layla were the one saying, 'Our companions narrated to us.'" Abu Musa is Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna himself, the teacher of al-Tabari and Abu Dawud. So when he narrated the ambiguous narration – which is in al-Tabari here – he explained it with the other, clarifying narration, and stated explicitly that the one saying "Our companions narrated to us" was Ibn Abi Layla, not Amr ibn Murrah, out of caution against the impression that the chain would be mursal if the speaker were Amr ibn Murrah.

Al-Tabari has commented on this, with the chain through Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, in which there is the explicit statement that Amr ibn Murrah heard this from Ibn Abi Layla: 2732.

Ibn Abi Layla's statement, "Our companions narrated to us," he means by it the Companions (al-sahabah), such as Mu'adh and others. Ibn Abi Layla was one of the senior Successors (al-tabi'un). This is supported by the narration of al-Bukhari 4:164 (Fath al-Bari), a fragment of this same long hadith, a suspended narration (mu'allaq) in the form of a firm assertion. He said: "Ibn Numayr said: al-A'mash narrated to us, Amr ibn Murrah narrated to us, Ibn Abi Layla narrated to us: our companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) narrated to us." Al-Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) said: "Abu Nu'aym connected it in al-Mustakhraj, and al-Bayhaqi through his route… This hadith was recorded by Abu Dawud, through the route of Shu'bah and al-Mas'udi, from al-A'mash, in full, in the adhan, the qiblah, and the fasting. The chain of it differed greatly. The route of Ibn Numayr is the most preponderant of them."]]

2732 – Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Dawud narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, saying: I heard Amr ibn Murrah say: I heard Ibn Abi Layla… and he mentioned something similar.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We have mentioned the statement of the one who said that by His words, "Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you," He meant the month of Ramadan.

* *

The most correct interpretation in my view is the statement of the one who said: God, His praise is exalted, meant by His words, ﴿Numbered days﴾, the days of the month of Ramadan. This is because no report has come establishing a proof that a fast was prescribed for the people of Islam other than the fast of the month of Ramadan, and then abrogated by the fast of the month of Ramadan. And God, may He be exalted, has made clear within the context of the verse [[In the printed edition: "And that God, may He be exalted…" – an error. It is not coordinated with His words "that a fast…"; rather it is coordinated with His words, "because there has not come a report…"]] that the fasting which He, His praise is exalted, made obligatory upon us is the fast of the month of Ramadan and no other times, by distinguishing it from the days of which He informed that He had prescribed their fasting upon us with His words: "The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down." Whoever claims that a fast had become binding upon the Muslims, other than the fast of the month of Ramadan, whose obligation they agree upon, and then that was abrogated, should be asked for proof of that from a report that establishes a proof, since that cannot be known except by a report that cuts off excuses.

Since the matter in this is as we have described, the interpretation of the verse is: "O you believers, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that you may be God-fearing: numbered days, which are the month of Ramadan." It is also permissible that its meaning be: "Fasting has been prescribed for you" – the month of Ramadan has been prescribed for you.

* *

As for "numbered" (ma'dudat): they are those whose periods and hours of time are counted. By His words, "numbered," [He means] countable (muhsayat).

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then [the fast is] a number of other days. And for those who are able to bear it, there is a ransom: the feeding of a poor man﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may He be praised and exalted, "So whoever among you is ill," [[This part of the verse was not in the printed edition; I have included it according to its method in the commentary.]] whoever among you is ill, from among those obligated to fast, or who is healthy and not ill but is on a journey: "then [the fast is] a number of other days," that is: then upon him is the fasting of the number of days which he broke fast in his illness or on his journey, "from other days," meaning: from other days than the days of his illness or his journey.

* *

The nominative in His words, "then [the fast is] a number of other days," is like the nominative in His words, "then [there should be] following with kindness." The explanation of that has passed there with what suffices without repeating it. [[See what has preceded in this volume, 3:373.]]

* *

As for His words, "And for those who are able to bear it, there is a ransom: the feeding of a poor man," the reading of all the Muslims is: "And for those who are able to bear it," and upon that are the written copies of their codices (masahif). It is the reading that no one among the people of Islam is permitted to oppose, because all of them transmitted its correctness generation after generation.

Ibn Abbas used to read it, according to what is reported from him: "And for those who are made to bear it" (yuttawwaqunahu, from the root meaning to be burdened or put to a strain). [[See the rejection of this reading in what will come: 438.]]

* *

Then the readers (qurra') of "And for those who are able to bear it" differed about its meaning.

Some of them said: That was at the beginning when fasting was prescribed. Whoever among the residents was able to bear it fasted if he wished, and if he wished he broke his fast and paid the ransom, feeding a poor man for each day he broke his fast, until that was abrogated.

Those who said this:

2733 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah narrated to us, from Amr ibn Murrah, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Medina and fasted the day of 'Ashura' and three days of every month. Then God, majestic and exalted, prescribed the month of Ramadan, and God, His mention is exalted, revealed: 'O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you,' until [He reached] 'And for those who are able to bear it, there is a ransom: the feeding of a poor man.' So whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished broke his fast and fed a poor man. Then God, majestic and exalted, made the fasting obligatory upon the healthy resident, and the feeding was confirmed for the elderly one who is not able to fast. So God, majestic and exalted, revealed: 'So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it, and whoever is ill or on a journey,' to the end of the verse."

[[Hadith note: 2733 – This is a fragment of the hadith we took out at 2729, longer than the previous narration.]]

2734 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from Amr ibn Murrah, who said: "Our companions narrated to us that the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when he came to them, commanded them to fast three days of every month as a voluntary act, not an obligation." He said: "Then the fast of Ramadan was revealed." He said: "They were a people who had not accustomed themselves to fasting. He said: The fasting was hard upon them. He said: So whoever did not fast fed a poor man. Then this verse was revealed: 'So whoever of you witnesses [the month], let him fast it, and whoever is ill or on a journey [let him fast] a number of other days,' and so the concession was for the ill and the traveler, and we were commanded to fast." Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna said: His words, "Amr said: Our companions narrated to us," he means Ibn Abi Layla. It is as if Ibn Abi Layla were the one saying, "Our companions narrated to us."

2735 – Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Dawud narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, saying: I heard Amr ibn Murrah say: I heard Ibn Abi Layla… and he mentioned something similar.

[[Hadiths 2734 and 2735: These are also fragments of the hadith we indicated at 2731 and 2732. Al-Tabari, at the beginning of the first of them, here explicitly named "Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna," whom he had referred to there by his kunya, "Abu Musa."]]

2736 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, from Alqamah, concerning His words: "And for those who are able to bear it, there is a ransom: the feeding of a poor man." He said: "Whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished broke his fast and fed a poor man half a sa' (a measure). Then [the verse] abrogated it: 'The month of Ramadan,' to His words, 'So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it.'"

2737 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mughirah, from Ibrahim, similarly – and he added in it, he said: "Then this verse abrogated it, and the first verse became [applicable] to the old man who is not able to fast, who gives in charity for each day to a poor man half a sa'."

2738 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih Abu Tumaylah narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, from Yazid al-Nahwi, from Ikrimah and al-Hasan al-Basri concerning His words: "And for those who are able to bear it, there is a ransom: the feeding of a poor man." He said: "Whoever among them wished to fast, fasted; and whoever among them wished to ransom himself with the feeding of a poor man, ransomed himself, and his fast was complete for him. Then He said: 'So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it.' Then He made an exception to that, saying: 'And whoever is ill or on a journey, [let him fast] a number of other days.'"

2739 – Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: I asked al-A'mash about His words: "And for those who are able to bear it, there is a ransom: the feeding of a poor man," and he related to us from Ibrahim, from Alqamah. He said: "It was abrogated by: 'So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it.'"

[[Report note: 2739 – Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i: Muhammad ibn Yazid ibn Muhammad ibn Kathir ibn Rifa'ah al-Ijli, judge of Baghdad. He narrated from Abd Allah ibn Idris and Hafs ibn Ghiyath; Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and others narrated from him. Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy (al-thiqat) and said: "He errs and contradicts." Ibn Abi Hatim said: "I asked my father about him and he said: He is weak; they speak about him; and he has a book on the readings (qira'at). He died in 248 AH."]]

2740 – Umar ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, saying: Abd Allah narrated to us, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, who said: "This verse abrogated – meaning: 'And for those who are able to bear it, there is a ransom: the feeding of a poor man' – the one after it: 'So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it, and whoever is ill or on a journey, [let him fast] a number of other days.'"

[[Hadith note: 2740 – Umar ibn al-Muthanna: thus it is in the printed edition, and I incline to think its correct form is "Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna," the teacher of al-Tabari from whom he narrates much. I found no one called "Umar ibn al-Muthanna" except one man, mentioned in al-Tahdhib and Lisan al-Mizan as being among the Successors. I did not dare to correct it here, because it is possible that he is one of al-Tabari's teachers whose biographies we have not found.

Abd al-Wahhab: he is Ibn Abd al-Majid al-Thaqafi; his biography has passed at 2029.

Abd Allah: he is Ibn Umar ibn Hafs ibn Asim ibn Umar ibn al-Khattab, known by the epithet "al-Umari." He is trustworthy, biographed in al-Tahdhib, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/109–110.

It is possible that there is an error in the printed edition, and its correct form is "Ubayd Allah" with the diminutive. He is the brother of Abd Allah, older than him and more reliable according to the imams of criticism and endorsement (al-jarh wa-al-ta'dil). He is one of the seven jurists (fuqaha' al-sab'ah), biographed in al-Tahdhib, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/326–327. He and his brother share many teachers, among them "Nafi', client of Ibn Umar."]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 184 (part 2 of 4):

I suspected this possibility because the hadith is narrated through "Ubayd Allah," as I will mention, God willing:
Al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Sunan al-Kubra 4:200, through the route of Abd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi, "from Ubayd Allah ibn Umar, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar."
Al-Bukhari narrated it in abridged form, 4:164 and 8:136, through the route of Abd al-A'la, who is Ibn Abd al-A'la, from Ubayd Allah, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar.
Al-Bayhaqi also narrated it through one of al-Bukhari's two routes.
The hadith is sound in every case. Al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1:178, and added its attribution to Waki', Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah in his Musannaf, and Ibn al-Mundhir.]]

2741. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: I heard al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from Alqamah, regarding His words: "And for those who are able to fast [it is] a ransom: feeding a needy person" [2:184]. He said: "It was abrogated by: 'So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it' [2:185]."

2742. Al-Walid ibn Shuja' Abu Hammam narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn Mushir narrated to us, from Asim, from al-Sha'bi, who said: This verse was revealed: "And for those who are able to fast [it is] a ransom: feeding a needy person." A man would break his fast and give charity of food to a needy person for each day. Then this verse was revealed: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it, and whoever is ill or on a journey [then a number of other days]" [2:185]. Thus the concession was granted only to the sick and the traveler.

2743. Hannad ibn al-Sari narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn Mushir narrated to us, from Asim, from al-Sha'bi, who said: This verse was revealed for people in general: "And for those who are able to fast [it is] a ransom: feeding a needy person," and a man would break his fast and give his food in charity to a needy person. Then this verse was revealed: "And whoever is ill or on a journey [then a number of other days]." He said: Thus the concession was granted only to the sick and the traveler.

2744. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Layla, who said: I entered upon Ata' while he was eating in the month of Ramadan. He said: "I am an elderly old man. When fasting was revealed, whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished broke his fast and fed a needy person, until this verse was revealed: 'So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it, and whoever is ill or on a journey [then a number of other days]' [2:185]. Thereafter fasting became obligatory on everyone, except the sick, the traveler, or an elderly person like me, who pays a ransom."

2745. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: al-Layth narrated to me, saying: Yunus informed me, from Ibn Shihab, who said: God said: "O you who believe, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you" [2:183]. Ibn Shihab said: God prescribed fasting for us, and whoever wished could pay a ransom, from among those who were able to fast, whether healthy, sick, or traveling, and nothing else was required of him. Then, when God made fasting obligatory for whoever witnessed the month, the healthy person who was able to fast had the ransom removed from him, while the one who was on a journey or ill [had to make up] a number of other days. He said: The ransom that had been accepted before that remained for the elderly person who is unable to fast, and for the one who suffers from thirst or from an illness that prevents him from fasting.

2746. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: God made in the first fast a ransom of feeding a needy person. Whoever among the traveler or the resident wished to feed a needy person and break his fast could do so, and that was a concession for him. Then God revealed in the later fast: "[then] a number of other days" [2:185], and God did not mention in the later fast a ransom of feeding a needy person. The ransom was thus abrogated, and what remained in the later fast was: "God desires ease for you and does not desire hardship for you" [2:185]. This refers to breaking the fast while traveling, and He made it a number of other days.

2747. Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Wahb narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle Abd Allah ibn Wahb informed me, saying: Amr ibn al-Harith informed me, from Bukayr ibn Abd Allah, from Yazid, mawla of Salamah ibn al-Akwa', from Salamah ibn al-Akwa', that he said: "We were in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished broke his fast and paid a ransom of feeding a needy person, until this was revealed: 'So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it' [2:185]." [[The hadith: 2747 – Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Wahb, al-Misri, nephew of Abd Allah ibn Wahb, is trustworthy, one of the teachers of Muslim and Ibn Khuzaymah. Some have criticized him, but they were unfair to him, and the people of his city knew him best. Ibn Abi Hatim said: "I asked Muhammad ibn Abd al-Hakam about him, and he said: 'Trustworthy. We have seen nothing but good from him.' I asked: 'Did he hear from his paternal uncle?' He said: 'Yes, by God.'" He is biographed in al-Tahdhib and in Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/59-60.
"Bukayr ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Ashajj," of Medina, who settled in Egypt: a trustworthy Successor. Ibn Wahb said: "Whenever Malik ibn Anas mentioned Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj, he said only: 'He was one of the scholars.'" He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 1/2/113, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/403-404.
"Bukayr" is in the diminutive form. In the printed edition it appears as "Bakr" without the yaa', which is an error. There is no narration of Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani in this hadith. The hadith is that of "Bukayr ibn Abd Allah."
Yazid, mawla of Salamah ibn al-Akwa': he is Yazid ibn Abi Ubayd al-Hijazi, a trustworthy Successor. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/348-349, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/280.
Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih, after narrating this hadith: "Bukayr died before Yazid." This is correct, for Bukayr ibn Abd Allah died in the year 127, and it was said otherwise, [but] up to the year 127. As for Yazid, mawla of Salamah, he died in the year 146 or 147. Amr ibn al-Harith therefore heard this hadith from Bukayr, from Yazid, during Yazid's lifetime.
The hadith was also narrated by Muslim, 1:315, from Amr ibn Sawad al-Amiri, from Ibn Wahb, with this same isnad. Likewise al-Bayhaqi narrated it, 4:200, through the route of Bahr ibn Nasr, from Ibn Wahb.
Al-Bukhari, 8:136, Muslim, 1:315, and al-Bayhaqi, 4:200, all narrated it from the hadith of Qutaybah ibn Sa'id, from Bakr ibn Mudar, from Amr ibn al-Harith, from Bukayr.
Al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1:177-178, and added its attribution to al-Darimi, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, and others.]]

2748. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Asim al-Ahwal, from al-Sha'bi regarding His words: "And for those who are able to fast [it is] a ransom: feeding a needy person" [2:184]. He said: It was for all people. When this was revealed: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it" [2:185], they were commanded to fast and to make up the missed days, and then [it was said]: "And whoever is ill or on a journey [then a number of other days]" [2:185].

2749. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn Mushir narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim regarding His words: "And for those who are able to fast [it is] a ransom: feeding a needy person" [2:184]. He said: It was abrogated by the verse that follows it: "And that you fast is better for you, if you only knew" [2:184].

2750. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Sulayman, from Ibn Sirin, from Ubaydah: "And for those who are able to fast [it is] a ransom: feeding a needy person" [2:184]. He said: It was abrogated by the verse that follows it: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it" [2:185].

2751. It was narrated to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: al-Fadl ibn Khalid narrated to us, saying: Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from al-Dahhak regarding His words: "Fasting has been prescribed for you" [2:183], to the end of the verse. Fasting was obligatory from the night prayer (al-atamah) to its counterpart the following night. When a man prayed the night prayer, eating and intercourse became forbidden to him until the same time the following night. Then the later fast was revealed, permitting eating and intercourse throughout the night, which is His words: "And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread" [2:187], up to His words: "Then complete the fast until the night" [2:187]. He also permitted intercourse, saying: "It is made lawful for you on the night of fasting to go to your wives" [2:187]. In the first fast there was a ransom; whoever among the traveler or the resident wished to feed a needy person and break his fast could do so. God, may His remembrance be exalted, did not mention the ransom in the later fast, but said: "[then] a number of other days" [2:184]. So this later fast abrogated the ransom. [[The report: 2751 – "al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj": the printed edition has "al-Hasan" here, which is an error, as we explained in 2719.]]

* *

Others said: Rather, His words "And for those who are able to fast [it is] a ransom: feeding a needy person" [2:184] were a particular ruling for the elderly man and the elderly woman who are able to fast. They were permitted to ransom their fast by feeding a needy person and to break it. Then this was abrogated by His words: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it" [2:185]. Thus they were obliged to fast as the young man was obliged, unless they were unable to fast, in which case the ruling that applied to them before the abrogation remained in force for them at that time in its original state.
Those who said this:
2752. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Izrah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The elderly man and the elderly woman, who were able to fast, were granted a concession that they could break their fast if they wished and feed a needy person for each day. Then this was abrogated: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it, and whoever is ill or on a journey [then a number of other days]" [2:185]. The ruling remained for the elderly man and the elderly woman when they are unable to fast, and for the pregnant and the nursing woman when they fear [for themselves or the child].

2753. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, from Urwah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: "And for those who are able to fast" [2:184]. He said: The elderly man and the elderly woman. Then he mentioned a report like that of Bishr from Yazid. [[The two reports: 2752–2753 – Sa'id is Ibn Abi Urubah.
Izrah – with a fatha on the ayn and the ra, with a silent zayn between them: he is Ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Zurarah al-Khuza'i, who is trustworthy. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/1/65, and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/21-22.
In the printed edition here, and in the printed Sunan of Abu Dawud, "Urwah" appears instead of "Izrah," which is a misreading. The correction is from the manuscript of the Sunan of Shaykh Abid al-Sindi, and from the al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Bayhaqi.
The hadith was narrated by Abu Dawud, 2318 (2:266 in Awn al-Ma'bud), through the route of Ibn Abi Adi, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, with this isnad, similar in meaning.
Al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Sunan al-Kubra 4:230, through the route of Rawh ibn Ubadah, and through the route of Makki ibn Ibrahim, both from Sa'id ibn Abi Urubah, with the same isnad.
Then he narrated it through Abu Dawud's route in the Sunan, saying: "From Sa'id, [and he] mentioned it," meaning with this isnad. Had Abu Dawud's narration been through "Urwah," he would have mentioned that, and he would not have referred his isnad back to the earlier isnad, which contains "from Izrah."
Al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1:177, and added its attribution to Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim.
Al-Bukhari, 8:135, narrated something similar in meaning through the route of Amr ibn Dinar, from Ata', from Ibn Abbas. Likewise al-Nasa'i, 1:318-319, narrated it through the route of Amr ibn Dinar.]]

2754. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to me, from Qatadah, from Ikrimah, who said: The elderly man and the elderly woman had the concession to break their fast and feed [a needy person], based on His words: "And for those who are able to fast [it is] a ransom: feeding a needy person." He said: So they had the concession, which was then abrogated by this verse: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it." The concession was abrogated for the elderly man and the elderly woman when they are able to fast, and it remained for the pregnant woman and the nursing woman to break their fast and feed [a needy person].

2755. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: Hammam ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: I heard Qatadah say regarding His words: "And for those who are able to fast [it is] a ransom: feeding a needy person": there was a concession in it for the elderly man and the elderly woman who are able to fast, to feed a needy person in place of each day and to break their fast. Then this was abrogated by the verse that follows it, which says: "The month of Ramadan" [2:185], to His words: "[then] a number of other days" [2:185]. This verse abrogated it. The scholars used to hold, and to hope, that the concession remains for the elderly man and the elderly woman when they are unable to fast: they may break their fast and feed a needy person for each day. And [it remains] for the pregnant woman when she fears for what is in her womb, and for the nursing woman when she fears for her child.

2756. It was narrated to me from Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His words: "And for those who are able to fast [it is] a ransom: feeding a needy person." The elderly man and the elderly woman were able to fast the month of Ramadan, so God permitted them to break it if they wished, and [they must pay] for each day they broke it a ransom of feeding a needy person. Then God revealed after that: "The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed" [2:185], to His words: "[then] a number of other days" [2:185].

* *

Others, who read the verse as "And for those who are able to fast" [2:184], said: this was not abrogated, nor any part of it. It is a permanent ruling from the moment this verse was revealed until the Hour. They said: Its interpretation is: "And for those who are able to fast" – in the time of their youth and their adolescence, and in the time of their health and strength – when they become ill, or when they grow old and are unable to fast because of old age, [then] a ransom of feeding a needy person. [This is] not that the people had been granted a concession to break their fast, while they were still able to fast, in return for a ransom.
Those who said this:
2757. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And for those who are able to fast [it is] a ransom: feeding a needy person." He said: As for "those who are able to fast," a man was able to fast, and he had fasted before that, then an ailment, or thirst, or a prolonged illness afflicted him, or a nursing woman could not fast. Those people must feed a needy person in place of each day. If he feeds a needy person, that is better for him; and whoever undertakes to fast and fasts, that is better for him.

2758. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abdah narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Urubah, from Qatadah, from Izrah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: If a pregnant woman fears for herself, or a nursing woman fears for her child, during Ramadan, he said: they break their fast and feed a needy person in place of each day, and they do not make up the fast. [[The report: 2758 – Hannad is Ibn al-Sari, whose biography has already passed: 2058. Abdah is Ibn Sulayman al-Kilabi, whose biography has already passed: 2323. This report is similar in meaning to the two earlier reports, 2751 and 2752, through the transmission of Sa'id ibn Abi Urubah, from Qatadah, from Izrah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas. Those two are separate reports, because they are a statement from Ibn Abbas about the abrogation of the ransom and the general permissibility of breaking the fast, and their affirmation regarding the elderly man and those mentioned with him there. This one, however, is a legal opinion (fatwa) from Ibn Abbas.
Here in the printed edition "Urwah" appears instead of "Izrah," as it did in those two reports. We have restored the correct reading here as we did there.]]

2759. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abdah narrated to us, ..., from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: that he saw a female slave who had borne him a child, who was pregnant or nursing, and he said: "You are in the position of the one who is unable to fast. You must feed a needy person in place of each day, and there is no making up for you." [[The report: 2759 – This report is like the preceding one, another legal opinion from Ibn Abbas to his slave-mother, with the same meaning as the previous one. However, a gap in the isnad appears here in the printed edition, between "Abdah" and "Sa'id ibn Jubayr." We conclude that its correct form is like the earlier isnad. But we did not consider it permissible to insert it on the basis of an unreliable text, so we placed dots in place of the gap.
That this gap is genuine is supported by the fact that al-Daraqutni narrated this report in his Sunan, p. 250, through the route of Rawh, who is Ibn Ubadah: "Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Izrah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: that Ibn Abbas said to a slave-mother of his..." Then al-Daraqutni said after it: "The isnad is sound."
Al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1:179, and added its attribution to Abd ibn Humayd.]]

2760. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abdah narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Nafi', from Ali ibn Thabit, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, like the statement of Ibn Abbas regarding the pregnant and the nursing woman. [[The report: 2760 – This is a sound isnad, stopping at Ibn Umar (mawquf).
Ali ibn Thabit ibn Amr ibn Akhtab al-Basri al-Ansari: trustworthy. Ibn Abi Hatim biographed him, 3/1/177, and I did not find his biography elsewhere. The summary of what he said: he narrated from Nafi', Muhammad ibn Yazid, and Muhammad ibn Ziyad. Sa'id ibn Abi Urubah, Imran al-Qattan, Hammad ibn Salamah, and Suwayd ibn Ibrahim narrated from him. Then he narrated from Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who said: "Ali ibn Thabit ibn Abi Zayd al-Ansari: trustworthy. Sa'id ibn Abi Urubah, Hammad Zayd, his brother Izrah ibn Thabit, and his brother Muhammad ibn Thabit narrated from him." Then Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned that he asked his father "about Ali ibn Thabit, brother of Izrah and the two sons of Thabit? He said: There is no harm in him."
I found that al-Bukhari mentioned him in al-Kabir 1/1/50, and in al-Saghir, p. 171, in the biography of his brother Muhammad ibn Thabit.
His grandfather was "Amr ibn Akhtab al-Ansari," whose kunyah was Abu Zayd, and he became famous by his kunyah. Ibn Sa'd biographed him, 7/17-18, and said: "He has a mosque named after him in Basra."
The rest of the isnad, before and after Ali ibn Thabit, consists of well-known trustworthy narrators, as is evident.
Al-Tabari did not mention the wording of the report of Ibn Umar:]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 184 (part 3 of 4):

As-Suyuti mentioned it (1:179), from Nafi', who said: "One of the daughters of Ibn Umar sent to ask him about fasting Ramadan while she was pregnant. He said: She should break her fast and feed a poor person for each day." He attributed it to Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and ad-Daraqutni.

Ad-Daraqutni narrated it (p. 250) with two chains: through Hammad, from Ayyub, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar: "That his wife asked him while she was pregnant, and he said: Break your fast and feed for each day a poor person, and do not make up the days." Then he narrated it through Abu Usamah, from Ubaydullah, from Nafi', who said: "A daughter of Ibn Umar was married to a man of Quraysh, and she was pregnant, and thirst afflicted her during Ramadan, so Ibn Umar ordered her to break her fast and feed a poor person for each day."

2761- Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: It was mentioned to us that Ibn Abbas said, to a umm walad of his who was pregnant or nursing: "You are in the position of those who cannot bear it; upon you is the ransom, and there is no fasting upon you." This is when she fears for herself.

2762- Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, his statement: "And upon those who are able to fast [yutiquna] is a ransom, the feeding of a poor person." It refers to the elderly man who used to be able to fast Ramadan when he was young, but when he grew old he could not fast it, so let him give charity to one poor person for each day he broke his fast, at the time of breaking the fast and at the time of the pre-dawn meal.

2763- Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abdah narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, similarly, except that he did not say: "at the time of breaking the fast and at the time of the pre-dawn meal."

2764- Hannad narrated to us, saying: Hatim ibn Isma'il narrated to us, from Abd ar-Rahman ibn Harmalah, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, that he said concerning the words of God, may His remembrance be exalted: "A ransom, the feeding of a poor person," he said: It is the elderly person who used to fast and then grew old and became unable to do so, and it is the pregnant woman for whom fasting is not required. For each of them is the feeding of a poor person: a mudd of wheat for each day until Ramadan has passed.

* *

Others read it: "And upon those who are able to fast [yuttawwiqunahu], a ransom, the feeding of a poor person," and they said: It refers to the elderly man and the elderly woman who have grown too old for fasting, so they are charged with fasting but cannot bear it, so for them is that they may break their fast and feed a poor person in place of each day they broke. They said: The verse's ruling is established from the time it was revealed; it was not abrogated, and they rejected the view of those who said it is abrogated.

Those who said this:

2765- Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Ibn Juraij narrated to us, from Ata', from Ibn Abbas, that he used to recite it: "yuttawwiqunahu."

2766- Hannad narrated to us, saying: Ali ibn Musahhar narrated to us, from Asam, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, that he used to recite: "And upon those who are made to bear it [yuttawwiqunahu], a ransom, the feeding of a poor person." He said: "It is still in force for people today."

2767- Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, that he used to recite it: "And upon those who are made to bear it," and he said: "It is still in force for people today."

2768- Hannad narrated to us, saying: Qabisah narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, that he used to recite it: "And upon those who are made to bear it," and he would say: "It is the elderly man, who breaks his fast and feeds on his behalf."

2769- Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, saying: Ayyub narrated to us, from Ikrimah, that he said concerning this verse: "And upon those who are made to bear it" (and so he used to recite it): "It is not abrogated; the elderly man is charged to break his fast and feed a poor person in place of each day."

2770- Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he recited: "And upon those who are made to bear it."

2771- Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Imran ibn Hudayr, from Ikrimah, who said: "Those who are able [yutiquna]" means those who fast it; but "those who are made to bear it [yuttawwiqunahu]" means those who are unable to do it.

2772- al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd ar-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn Juraij informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abbad ibn Ja'far narrated to me, from Abu Amr, the client of Aishah, that Aishah used to recite: "yuttawwiqunahu."

2773- al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abd ar-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn Juraij informed us, from Ata', that he used to recite it: "yuttawwiqunahu." Ibn Juraij said: Mujahid used to recite it that way too.

2774- Humayd ibn Mas'adah narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Khalid narrated to us, from Ikrimah: "And upon those who are able [yutiquna]," he said: Ibn Abbas said: "It is the elderly man." [Note on the report: I fear that the correct reading here is "yuttawwiqunahu."]

2775- Ismail ibn Musa as-Suddi narrated to us, saying: Shurayk informed us, from Salim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: "And upon those who are made to bear it [yuttawwiqunahu]," he said: They strain to it, they force themselves to it. [Note on the report: Ismail ibn Musa as-Suddi al-Fazari; it is said that he is the grandson of the elder as-Suddi, Ismail ibn Abd ar-Rahman; he died in 245.]

2776- Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, from Muslim al-Mala'i, from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, concerning his words: "And upon those who are able to fast [yutiquna] is a ransom, the feeding of a poor person," he said: It is the elderly man who cannot bear it, so he breaks his fast and feeds a poor person for each day.

2777- Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid and Ata', from Ibn Abbas, concerning God's words: "And upon those who are able [yutiquna]," he said: "They are charged with it; a ransom, the feeding of one poor person." He said: This verse is abrogated, and no concession is granted in it except to the elderly person who cannot bear fasting, or the sick person whose sickness is known not to be cured.

2778- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Amr ibn Dinar, from Ata', from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Those who are able [yutiquna]," they force themselves to it; a ransom, the feeding of one poor person. This concession is granted only to the elderly person who cannot bear fasting, or the sick person whose sickness is known not to be cured. This is from Mujahid.

2779- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, that he used to say: It is not abrogated.

2780- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas, concerning his words: "And upon those who are able to fast [yutiquna] is a ransom, the feeding of a poor person," he says: Whoever is able to fast only with hardship, it is permitted for him to break his fast and feed a poor person for each day; and the pregnant woman, the nursing woman, the elderly man, and the one with a lasting illness.

2781- Hannad narrated to us, saying: Ubaydah narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, concerning God's words, may His remembrance be exalted: "And upon those who are able [yutiquna] is a ransom, the feeding of a poor person," he said: It is the elderly man, and the man who used to fast in his youth, but when he grew old he became unable to fast before he died; so he feeds a poor person each day. Hannad said: Ubaydah said: It was said to Mansur: "Does he feed half a sa' each day?" He said: Yes. [Note on the report: Ubaydah, with a fatha on the ain, is Ibn Humayd, with a damma on the ha, ibn Suhayb al-Hadhdha', who is trustworthy; Ibn Mu'in and others declared him trustworthy, and al-Bukhari narrated from him in the Sahih. Biographies in at-Tahdhib, as-Saghir of al-Bukhari, p. 212, Ibn Sa'd 7/2/72-73, Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/92-93, and Tarikh Baghdad 11:120-123.]

2782- Hannad narrated to us, saying: Marwan ibn Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from Uthman ibn al-Aswad, who said: I asked Mujahid about my wife, whose pregnancy coincided with the ninth month of Ramadan and with intense heat, and he ordered me that she should break her fast and feed. He said: Mujahid said: That concession also applies to the traveler and the sick, for God says: "And upon those who are able [yutiquna] is a ransom, the feeding of a poor person."

2783- Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from Asim, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The pregnant woman, the nursing woman, and the elderly man who cannot bear fasting break their fast in Ramadan and feed a poor person for each day; then he recited: "And upon those who are able [yutiquna] is a ransom, the feeding of a poor person." [Note on the report: Abu Mu'awiyah ad-Darir, Muhammad ibn Khazim at-Tamimi as-Sa'di. Ibn Sa'd said: "He was trustworthy, narrated much, was a mudallis, and was a Murji'ite. He died in 193."]

2784- Ali ibn Sa'id al-Kindi narrated to us, saying: Hafs narrated to us, from Hajjaj, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Harith, from Ali, concerning his words: "And upon those who are able [yutiquna] is a ransom, the feeding of a poor person," he said: The elderly man who cannot fast breaks his fast and feeds a poor person in place of each day. [Note on the report: In the printed edition: "Ali ibn Sa'd." Ali ibn Sa'id ibn Masruq al-Kindi Abu al-Hasan al-Kufi narrated from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, Ibn al-Mubarak and others; at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasa'i and Abu Hatim narrated from him. Abu Hatim said: Truthful; Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy. He died in 249.]

2785- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Amr ibn Dinar, from Ata', from Ibn Abbas, who said: "And upon those who are able [yutiquna] is a ransom, the feeding of a poor person," he said: They are those who force themselves to it and cannot bear it: the elderly man and the elderly woman.

2786- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from al-Hajjaj, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Harith, from Ali, who said: It is the elderly man and the elderly woman.

2787- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Imran ibn Hudayr, from Ikrimah, that he used to recite it: "And upon those who are able [yutiquna]," and so they broke their fast.

2788- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Asim, from one who narrated to him from Ibn Abbas, who said: It is affirmed for the elderly, the nursing woman, and the pregnant woman, and for those who are able [yutiquna] to fast.

2789- al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Ibn Juraij, who said: I said to Ata': What is His saying: "And upon those who are able [yutiquna]"? He said: We have been told that the elderly person, if he cannot fast, pays a ransom of a poor person for each day. I said: The elderly person who cannot fast, or one who can only do it with hardship? He said: Rather, the elderly person who cannot do it with hardship or with anything; but as for one who can do it with hardship, let him fast, and he has no excuse for leaving it.

2790- al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Abd Allah ibn Abi Yazid informed me: "And upon those who are able [yutiquna]..." the verse; it seems he meant the elderly man. Ibn Juraij said: Ibn Tawus informed me, from his father, that he used to say: It was revealed concerning the elderly person who cannot fast Ramadan, so he pays a ransom of food to a poor person for each day. I asked him: How much is his food? He said: I do not know, except that he said: the food of one day.

2791- al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from al-Hasan ibn Yahya, from ad-Dahhak, concerning His words: "A ransom, the feeding of a poor person," he said: The elderly person who cannot bear fasting breaks his fast and feeds a poor person for each day.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most probable of these interpretations of the verse is the view of the one who said: "And upon those who are able [yutiquna] is a ransom, the feeding of a poor person," is abrogated by God's words, may His remembrance be exalted: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it."

Because the "ha'" in His words "And upon those who are able [yutiquna]" refers back to "fasting," and its meaning is: "And upon those who are able to fast is a ransom, the feeding of a poor person." Since this is so, and since all the people of Islam agreed that whoever among the healthy adult men who are resident, not traveling, is able to fast the month of Ramadan, it is not permissible for him to break his fast in it or to redeem it by feeding a poor person, it is evident that the verse is abrogated.

Moreover, there are reports supporting this view which we mentioned earlier from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, Ibn Umar, and Salamah ibn al-Akwa': that after the revelation of this verse, during the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, they had the choice in fasting Ramadan between fasting and being free of the ransom, and between breaking the fast and redeeming it by feeding a poor person for each day; and that they continued doing so until the revelation: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it." Then they were bound to the obligation of fasting, and the choice and the ransom were nullified.

* *

If someone says: How can you claim a consensus among the people of Islam that whoever is able to fast it, in the condition you described, is not permitted anything but fasting it, when you know the view of the one who said that the pregnant and nursing woman, if they fear for their children, may break their fast even if they are able to fast with their bodies, together with the report narrated on this from the Messenger of God ﷺ, which:

2792- Hannad ibn as-Sarri narrated it to us, saying: Qabisah narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ayyub, from Abu Qilabah, from Anas, who said: I came to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was having his lunch, and he said: "Come, let me tell you: God has lifted from the traveler, the pregnant woman, and the nursing woman the fast and half of the prayer"? [Note on the report: Qabisah is Ibn Uqbah as-Sawa'i; his biography has passed (p. 489), and we pointed there to the discussion of his narration from Sufyan ath-Thawri, that it is not accepted; and we add here that the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from him in their Sahihs through his narration from ath-Thawri, as in the book Rijal as-Sahihayn, p. 422.

Abu Qilabah, with a kasra on the qaf and a light lam, is Abd Allah ibn Zayd al-Jarmi, with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the ra', one of the great memorizers among the Successors. His biography is in at-Tahdhib, Ibn Sa'd 7/1/133-135, Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/57-58, Rijal as-Sahihayn 251, and Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 1:88-89.

Anas, in this hadith only: he is Anas ibn Malik al-Ka'bi, from the Banu Ka'b ibn Rabi'ah ibn Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah ibn Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr ibn Hawazin. He is a Companion who has no narration from the Prophet ﷺ except this single hadith. Some who mention his lineage call him "al-Qushayri," holding that Qushayr is the son of Ka'b ibn Rabi'ah. This is what is established in some books of genealogy, such as al-Ishtiqaq of Ibn Duraid, p. 181, and Jamharat al-Ansab of Ibn Hazm, pp. 271-272, and the Hafiz followed them in at-Tahdhib. But al-Bukhari said in his biography in at-Tarikh al-Kabir 1/2/30: "Ka'b are brothers of Qushayr." And Ibn Abi Hatim said in his biography 1/2/286: "From the Banu Abd Allah ibn Ka'b, and Ka'b is the brother of Qushayr." In Abu Dawud's narration of this hadith, as will come in the takhrij if God wills: "From Anas ibn Malik, a man from the Banu Abd Allah ibn Ka'b, brothers of the Banu Qushayr."
