The Hafiz said in al-Isabah 1:73: "This is the correct view, and al-Bukhari determined it in his biography. On this basis he is Ka'bi, not Qushayri, since Qushayr is the son of Ka'b, and Ka'b had a son named Abd Allah. So he is a brother of Qushayr, not of Qushayr himself."

"Anas ibn Malik" among the narrators is five persons: Anas ibn Malik ibn an-Nadr al-Ansari, servant of the Messenger of God ﷺ, who is meant in most hadiths when the name "Anas" is mentioned absolutely; then Anas ibn Malik al-Ka'bi, who is the one here; both are Companions. Then Anas ibn Malik ibn Abi Amir al-Asbahi, father of the Imam Malik ibn Anas, who was a Successor. Then Anas ibn Malik as-Sayrafi, teacher of Khallad ibn Yahya. And Anas ibn Malik, teacher of Abu Dawud at-Tayalisi. These last two are later, narrating from the Successors. Ibn Abi Hatim wrote biographies of these five, and al-Bukhari in al-Kabir only of the first three. Ibn al-Jawzi also mentioned them all in Talqih Fuhum Ahl al-Athar, p. 320, and said concerning this "Ka'bi" and pointed to his hadith here: "This hadith was narrated by ath-Thawri, from Ayyub, from Abu Qilabah, from Anas [meaning the Ka'bi]. And with this chain from ath-Thawri there are hadiths from Anas al-Ansari."

This is correct. Therefore the use of the name "Anas" here is not acceptable from whoever used it, whether al-Tabari or one of the shaykhs of the chain, because of the confusion it causes.

The hadith was narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Kabir 1/2/30, from Qabisah, the shaykh of Hannad in this chain, and from Muhammad ibn Yusuf, both from ath-Thawri, with this text, concisely as is his custom, and he stated explicitly in the chain that it is "from Anas ibn Malik al-Ka'bi."

An-Nasa'i narrated it (1:315-316) from Umar ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, that is Ibn at-Tall, from his father, from ath-Thawri, with this text: "God has lifted from the traveler, meaning half the prayer, and the fast, and from the pregnant woman and the nursing woman."

Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad 5:29 (Halabi) from Ibn Ulayyah, from Ayyub, who said: "Abu Qilabah narrated this hadith to me, then said to me: Would you like to hear the one who narrated it to me? He said: So he pointed me to him, and I went to him, and he said: A relative of mine called Anas ibn Malik narrated to me..." and he mentioned it with a story at its beginning.

In this narration, then, there is between Abu Qilabah and Anas al-Ka'bi an unnamed man who narrated it to him from him.

Likewise al-Bukhari mentioned that there is a man between them: he narrated it after that, from Yahya ibn Musa, from Abd ar-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from Ayyub, from Abu Qilabah, "from a man of the Banu Amir: that a man called Anas narrated to him that he came to Madinah..." similarly.

I see the transmission of Qabisa and Muhammad ibn Yusuf as preferable, since it does not include the unnamed man, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Tall follows them in it. Al-Thawri is more retentive than Ma'mar and Ibn Ulayya together, and he takes precedence over anyone who differs with him in memorization and precision.

The hadith has another isnad, through a different route. Abu Hilal Muhammad ibn Sulaym al-Rasibi narrated it from Abd Allah ibn Sawada, from Anas al-Ka'bi. This is a good isnad, indeed a sound one. Abu Hilal al-Rasibi is trustworthy (thiqah), with no objection to him. Abd Allah ibn Sawada ibn Handhala al-Qushayri is also trustworthy.

Ahmad reported it in his Musnad 4: 347 (Halabi edition), from Waki' and from Affan. Uqba, his son Abd Allah, reported it from Shaybān. Ahmad also reported it in 5: 29 (Halabi edition), from Abd al-Samad. Ibn Sa'd reported it in al-Tabaqat 7/1/30, from Waki' and Affan. Abu Dawud reported it in 2408, from Shaybān ibn Farrukh. al-Tirmidhi reported it in 2: 42, from Abu Kurayb and Yusuf ibn Isa, from Waki'. Ibn Majah reported it in 1667, from Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba and Ali ibn Muhammad, from Waki'. al-Bayhaqi reported it in 4: 231, through Ubayd Allah ibn Musa and Abu Nu'aym. All of these, namely Waki', Affan, Shaybān, Abd al-Samad, Ubayd Allah ibn Musa and Abu Nu'aym, narrated it from Abu Hilal al-Rasibi, from Abd Allah ibn Sawada, from Anas al-Ka'bi, in full, as part of a story.

This isnad is connected by direct hearing (al-sama'), because Ibn Sa'd said after his narration: "Affan said throughout the whole hadith: 'He told us' (haddathana), 'He told us', to the end." This is an explicit statement of each transmitter's hearing from the one before him, up to the Companion.

al-Tirmidhi said: "The hadith of Anas ibn Malik al-Ka'bi is a good hadith (hasan). We do not know of any hadith from the Prophet ﷺ narrated by this Anas ibn Malik other than this one hadith." al-Hafiz [Ibn Hajar] in al-Tahdhib 1: 379 reported from al-Tirmidhi that he authenticated it (sahhahahu). But what is in our copies of al-Tirmidhi is only his words "a good hadith" (hadith hasan). The additional authentication is therefore to be taken from al-Hafiz's report.

[[It was said: We did not claim consensus (ijma') concerning the pregnant and the nursing woman. We claimed it only regarding the men whose description we have given. As for the pregnant and nursing woman, we know that they are not addressed by His saying: ﴿And for those who are able to do it﴾. The men are the ones alone who are meant by it, because if the women were meant by it to the exclusion of other men, it would be said: "And for those women who are able to do it, the expiation is feeding a poor person," since that is the speech of the Arabs when the discourse is addressed exclusively to women, apart from men. When it was said: "And for those who are able to do it," it was known that what is intended is the men and not the women, or men and women together. Since it is established by the consensus of all that whoever among the resident, healthy men is able to fast the month of Ramadan is not given permission to break the fast and pay expiation, the men are excluded from being meant by the verse. It is known that the women were not meant by it, for the reason we described: that when discourse about women stands alone, it says "And for those women who are able to do it," and the revelation does not use other than that.

As for the report transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ: if it is sound, its meaning is that he removed the fast from the pregnant and nursing woman for as long as they are unable to bear it, until they are able and then make up the days, just as it is removed from the traveller during his journey until he returns and makes it up. It does not mean that they are commanded to pay expiation and break the fast without obligation to make up. If the Prophet's ﷺ saying "Indeed God removed the fast from the traveller, the nursing woman and the pregnant woman" were evidence that he ﷺ meant that God, mentioned be He, removed it from them by His saying "And for those who are able to do it, the expiation is feeding a poor person," then it would follow that the traveller who breaks his fast on his journey would have no obligation to make up, and that he would owe nothing for breaking it except the expiation, since the Prophet ﷺ combined his ruling with the ruling on the pregnant and nursing woman. That is an opinion which, if anyone holds it, contradicts the apparent sense of the Book of God and what all the people of Islam have agreed upon.]]

* *

Some grammarians of Basra claimed that the meaning of His saying ﴿And for those who are able to do it﴾ is ﴿And for those who are able to [afford] the food﴾. That is contrary to the interpretation of the scholars.

* *

As for the reading of one who read: ﴿And for those who are made to bear it (yuṭawwaqūnahu)﴾, it is contrary to the codices (maṣāḥif) of the people of Islam. It is not permissible for anyone among the people of Islam to object on the basis of personal opinion to what the Muslims have transmitted as an inheritance from their Prophet ﷺ, transmitted clearly and decisively, removing any excuse. What has come as proof from the religion is the truth about which there is no doubt, that it is from God. What has been established and supported by proof as being from God cannot be objected to with opinions, conjectures, or aberrant sayings.

* *

As for the meaning of "fidya" (expiation), it is: recompense, from your saying: "I ransomed this with that" (fadaytu hadha bihadha), meaning I recompensed it with it and gave it in its place.

* *

The meaning of the speech is: And for those who are able to observe the fast, the recompense is feeding a poor person for each day of breaking the fast from the days of the fasting that was prescribed for them.

* *

As for His saying ﴿expiation: feeding a poor person﴾, the readers differ in its recitation. Some read with the annexation of "fidya" to "ṭa'ām" (food), with "ṭa'ām" in the genitive case (khafḍ). This is the reading of the majority of the readers of Medina [[In the printed edition: "maʿẓam qurrāʾ" (the majority of readers); the correct wording of al-Tabari is what is given here, as has occurred many times before and as will come shortly after, correctly. The two wordings have the same meaning in any case.]], meaning: and for those who are able to do it, that they ransom it with the feeding of a poor person.

When "fidya" was put in place of "an yafdiyahu" (that they ransom it), it was annexed to "ṭa'ām", as one says: "There is a penalty (gharama) of a dirham owed to you," meaning: it is incumbent upon me to pay you a dirham.

Others read it with tanwīn on "fidya" and the nominative on "ṭa'ām", meaning that "ṭa'ām" clarifies the meaning of the "fidya" that is obligatory upon one who breaks his obligatory fast, as one says: "A penalty is owed by me: a dirham to you," so that "the dirham" clarifies the meaning of "penalty": what is it, and what is its limit? This is the reading of the majority of the readers of Iraq.

* *

Abu Ja'far [al-Tabari] said: The better of the two readings, the most correct, is the reading of the one who reads "fidyatu ṭa'ām" with the annexation of "fidya" to "ṭa'ām", because "fidya" is the name of the action, and it is other than the "ṭa'ām" by which the fast is ransomed.

That is because "al-fidya" is a verbal noun from the speaker's saying: "I ransomed the fast of this day with the food of a poor person, I ransom it as a ransom (fidya)," just as one says: "I sat a sitting (jilsa), and I walked a walk (mishya)." "Al-fidya" is an act, and "ṭa'ām" is other than it. Since that is so, it is clear that the most correct of the two readings is the annexation of "fidya" to "ṭa'ām". The mistake of the speaker who says that leaving the annexation of "fidya" to "ṭa'ām" is more correct in meaning, because in his view "ṭa'ām" is "fidya", is clear. It is said to the speaker of that: we know that "fidya" requires a one who is ransomed, something by which he is ransomed, and a ransom. If "ṭa'ām" is the "fidya", and "the fast" is that by which it is ransomed, then where is the name of the act of the one who ransoms, which is "fidya"? This saying is an evident error, not obscure.

* *

As for "ṭa'ām", it is annexed to "miskīn" (poor person). The readers differ in reading it.

Some of them read "miskīn" in the singular, meaning: and for those who are able to do it, the expiation is feeding one poor person for each day they break the fast, as:

2793: Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Rifa'i told me, saying: Husayn al-Ju'fi told us, from Abu Amr, that he read: "fidyatun" (with indefinite nominative), "ṭa'āmu" (nominative without tanwīn), "miskīn", and he said: "for each day, a poor person." And the majority of the readers of Iraq follow this.

* *

Others read it in the plural, "miskīn" as "masākīn", "fidya ṭa'ām masākīn", meaning: and for those who are able to do it, the expiation is feeding several poor persons for the month, when the whole month is broken, as:

2794: Abu Hisham Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Rifa'i told us, from Ya'qub, from Bashshar, from Amr, from al-Hasan: "ṭa'ām masākīn", for the whole month.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The reading that is most pleasing to me among the two readings in this matter is the reading of the one who reads "ṭa'ām miskīn" in the singular, meaning: and for those who are able to do it, for each day they break the fast, the expiation is feeding one poor person. This is because in clarifying the ruling for one who breaks the fast for a single day there is a way to knowing the ruling for one who breaks the fast for the whole month, whereas in clarifying the ruling for one who breaks the fast for the whole month there is no way to clarifying the ruling for one who breaks the fast for a single day and for days that are fewer than the days of the whole month. Also, "one" (wahid) is translated for "all" (jami'), and "all" is not translated for "one". For this reason we have chosen the reading in the singular. [[The term "tarjama" means substitution (al-badal), as already passed many times. See 2: 340 and the glossary of terms.]]

* *

The scholars differed concerning the amount of food that they used to give when they broke the fast.

Some of them said: The obligation of food for a poor person for breaking the fast for a single day was half a ṣāʿ of wheat.

Some of them said: The obligation of food for a poor person for breaking the fast for a day was one mudd of wheat and of the rest of their staple foods.

Some of them said: It was half a ṣāʿ of wheat, or a ṣāʿ of dates or raisins.

Some of them said: It was what the one who breaks the fast would subsist on during the day in which he broke it.

Some of them said: It was a suḥūr and an ʿashāʾ, which would be a breaking of the fast for the poor person.

We have already mentioned some of these sayings earlier, so we disliked repeating them.

* *

The commentary on His saying, exalted be He: ﴿So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed in the interpretation of this. Some of them said, as follows:

2795: Muhammad ibn Amr told us, saying: Abu Asim told us, saying: Isa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid and Ata', from Ibn Abbas: "So whoever volunteers good," and he added another poor person's food: "it is better for him, and that you fast is better for you."

2796: al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa told us, saying: Shabl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Amr ibn Dinar, from Ata', from Ibn Abbas, the same.

2797: Hannad told us, saying: Waki' told us, from Sufyan, from Khusayf, from Mujahid concerning His saying: "So whoever volunteers good," he said: whoever feeds a poor person a ṣāʿ.

2798: al-Muthanna told me, saying: Suwayd told us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Ma'mar, from Ibn Tawus, from his father: "So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him," he said: feeding poor persons for each day, it is better for him.

2799: al-Muthanna told me, saying: Suwayd told us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Hanzala, from Tawus: "So whoever volunteers good," he said: the food of a poor person.

2800: al-Muthanna told me, saying: Suwayd told us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Hanzala, from Tawus, similarly.

2801: Muhammad ibn Bashshar told us, saying: Abd al-Rahman told us, saying: Sufyan told us, from Layth, from Tawus: "So whoever volunteers good," he said: the food of a poor person.

2802: al-Muthanna told me, saying: Hajjaj told us, saying: Hammad told us, from Layth, from Tawus, similarly.

2803: Abu Kurayb told us, saying: Amr ibn Harun told us, saying: Ibn Jurayj told us, from Ata' that he read: "fa-man tataṭawwaʿa" (with the taʾ lightened [the ṭāʾ]), "khayran", and said: he added to a poor person. [[The words in parentheses are necessary, otherwise the speech would be corrupt. The other reading of this word is "yaṭṭawwaʿ" with the yāʾ of absence (yāʾ al-ghayba), with a fatḥa on the yāʾ, the ṭāʾ doubled and given a fatḥa, the wāw doubled and given a fatḥa, and the ʿayn jussed (jazm).]]

2804: Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: Amr told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him," so if he feeds two poor persons, it is better for him.

2805: al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn Tawus informed me, from his father: "So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him," he said: whoever feeds another poor person.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: so whoever volunteers good, by fasting along with the expiation.

Those who said that:

2806: al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Salih told us, saying: al-Layth told me, saying: Yunus informed me, from Ibn Shihab: "So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him," meaning that whoever fasts along with the expiation, it is better for him.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that: so whoever volunteers good, by the poor person exceeding the amount of his food.

Those who said that:

2807: al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid said: "So whoever volunteers good," by adding food, "it is better for him."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct statement on this, in our view, is that God, mentioned be He, made it general with His saying: "So whoever volunteers good," and did not specify some meanings of good over others. Indeed, combining the fast with the expiation is volunteering good, and adding a poor person beyond the recompense of the expiation is volunteering good. It is permissible that He, mentioned be He, meant by His saying "So whoever volunteers good" whichever of these meanings the one who ransoms volunteers of his fast, and it is better for him. This is because all of that is volunteering good and supererogatory virtue.

* *

The commentary on His saying, exalted be He: ﴿And that you fast is better for you, if you knew﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, mentioned be He, "And that you fast," He means what was prescribed for you of the month of Ramadan, "is better for you" than that you break it and ransom, as:

2808: Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "And that you fast is better for you," and whoever takes upon himself the fast and fasts it, it is better for him.

2809: al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Salih told us, saying: al-Layth told me, saying: Yunus told me, from Ibn Shihab: "And that you fast is better for you," that is: fasting is better for you than the expiation.

2810: Muhammad ibn Amr told me, saying: Abu Asim told us, saying: Isa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And that you fast is better for you"... [[The report 2810: its end is missing, and I have not found it in the sources. But its correct wording is like the one before it: from breaking the fast and ransoming, as is clear.]]

* *

As for His saying, "if you knew," it means: if you know the better of the two matters for you, O you who believe, between breaking the fast and ransoming, or fasting according to what God has commanded you.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 185 (part 1 of 5):

The explanation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down as guidance for mankind and as clear proofs of guidance and the criterion﴾

Abu Ja'far said: "Al-shahr" (the month), as it is said, is originally derived from "al-shuhra" (fame). It is said of it: "Fulan has shahara his sword" (unsheathed it and brandished it at one who wishes to strike him), "yashuruhu shahran." Likewise "shahara al-shahr" (the month became visible) when its crescent appeared, and "ashharna nahnu" (we entered the month) when we entered into the month.
* *
As for "Ramadan," some scholars of the Arabic language used to claim that it was named so because of the intense heat that prevailed in it, so that the young camels (fisal) were scorched in it [[The fisal is the plural of fasil, a young camel once it has been weaned from its mother. Ramadat al-fisal means that the sand (ramda', i.e., hot sand) scorches them, so the young camels sit down because of its intense heat, and it burns their hooves and their hoofprints. "Ramidat qadamuhu min al-ramda'" means his foot was burned by the hot sand.]], just as the month in which pilgrimage is performed is called "Dhu al-Hijja," and the months in which pasture is sought are called "Rabi' al-Awwal" and "Rabi' al-Akhir."
* *
As for Mujahid, he disliked that it be said "Ramadan," and he would say: "Perhaps it is one of the names of Allah."
2811 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mujahid: that he disliked that it be said "Ramadan," and he would say: "Perhaps it is one of the names of Allah, but we say as Allah said: 'the month of Ramadan.'"
* *
I have already explained earlier that "shahr" is in the nominative case, based on His words "[fasting for] a number of days," which are "the month of Ramadan." [[See what preceded above: 415, 417.]] It is also permissible that its nominative case is in the sense of: "That is the month of Ramadan," and in the sense of: "The month of Ramadan has been prescribed for you."
Some readers have read it as "shahra Ramadan" in the accusative, in the sense of: "Fasting has been prescribed for you, that you fast the month of Ramadan." Others read it in the accusative in the sense of: "That you fast the month of Ramadan is better for you, if you know." It is also permissible to read it in the accusative as an imperative to fast it, as if it were said: "The month of Ramadan, so fast it." It is also permissible to read it in the accusative as a time adverb, as if it were said: "Fasting has been prescribed for you during the month of Ramadan."
* *
As for His words "in which the Qur'an was sent down," it is mentioned that it was sent down on the Night of Decree (laylat al-qadr) from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) to the lowest heaven, on the Night of Decree of the month of Ramadan. Then it was sent down to Muhammad ﷺ as Allah willed to send it down to him, as:
2812 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Hassan ibn Abi al-Ashras, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Qur'an was sent down all at once from the Reminder on the night of the twenty-fourth of Ramadan, and it was placed in Bayt al-'Izza. Abu Kurayb said: Abu Bakr narrated to us, and al-Suddi also said that.
2813 - Isa ibn 'Uthman narrated to me, saying: Yahya ibn 'Isa narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Hassan, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: The Qur'an was sent down in one whole piece on the Night of Decree in the month of Ramadan, and it was placed in the lowest heaven. [[The report: 2813 - in the printed edition: "Yahya 'an 'Isa," which is an error. See the commentary on report no. 300.]]
2814 - Ahmad ibn Mansur narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Raja' narrated to us, saying: 'Imran al-Qattan narrated to us, from Qatada, from Abu al-Malih, from Wathila, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The scrolls of Ibrahim were sent down on the first night of the month of Ramadan, the Torah was sent down on the sixth of Ramadan, the Gospel was sent down on the thirteenth night, and the Qur'an was sent down on the twenty-fourth of Ramadan. [[The hadith: 2814 - 'Abd Allah ibn Raja' ibn 'Amr al-Ghadani: a trustworthy narrator, one of the teachers of al-Bukhari. "Al-Ghadani" is pronounced with a dotted ghayn and a lightened dal.
'Imran al-Qattan: he is 'Imran ibn Dawar, previously mentioned at 126. His kunya is "Abu al-'Awwam."
Abu al-Malih: he is Ibn Usama al-Hudhali, a trustworthy Successor (tabi'i), from whom the authors of the six canonical collections transmitted. In the printed edition it appears as "'an Ibn Abi al-Malih"; the addition of "ibn" is an obvious error.
Wathila, with a triangular tha: he is Ibn al-Asqa', a well-known Companion. The hadith was related by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 17051 (4: 107, Halabi edition), from Abu Sa'id, mawla of the Banu Hashim, from 'Imran Abu al-'Awwam, with this chain, and it is a sound chain.
Ibn Kathir cited it at 1: 406, from the Musnad. Likewise al-Suyuti at 1: 189, and he attributed it additionally to Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman.]]
2815 - Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down." As for "in which the Qur'an was sent down," Ibn 'Abbas said: The month of Ramadan, and "the blessed night" is the Night of Decree, for the Night of Decree is the blessed night, and it is in Ramadan. The Qur'an was sent down all at once from the scriptures to the Bayt al-Ma'mur, which is "the places of the stars" in the lowest heaven, where the Qur'an descended. Then Muhammad ﷺ received it afterwards in commands and prohibitions and in wars, piece by piece. [[Rasalan rasalan: i.e., portion by portion, and group by group.]]
2816 - Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Allah sent down the Qur'an to the lowest heaven on the Night of Decree, and whenever Allah wished to reveal something from it, He revealed it, and this is His words: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [Surah al-Qadr: 1].
2817 - Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi 'Adi narrated to us, from Dawud, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, similar to it, and he added: "So its beginning and its end spanned twenty years."
2818 - Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The entire Qur'an was sent down in one piece on the Night of Decree in Ramadan, to the lowest heaven, and whenever Allah wished to bring about something on earth, He sent it down from it, until it was all collected.
2819 - Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Husayn informed us, from Hakim ibn Jubayr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Qur'an was sent down on the Night of Decree from the highest heaven to the lowest heaven all at once; then it was distributed over the years afterwards. He said: Ibn 'Abbas recited this verse: ﴿So I swear by the places of the stars﴾ [Surah al-Waqi'a: 75], and he said: "It was sent down in portions."
2820 - Ya'qub narrated to us, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, from Dawud, from al-Sha'bi, who said: It has reached us that the Qur'an was sent down in one piece to the lowest heaven.
2821 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, that Ibn Jurayj read in His words: [[Thus in the printed edition; I do not know what this is, and I fear its correct form is "Ibn Jurayj read His words..."]] "The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down," and said: Ibn 'Abbas said: The Qur'an was sent down in one piece upon Jibril on the Night of Decree, and it was not sent down from it except by command. Ibn Jurayj said: Everything that was to be sent down from the Qur'an in that year was sent down from it on the Night of Decree. So that was sent down from the seventh heaven upon Jibril in the lowest heaven, and Jibril would not convey from it to Muhammad anything except what his Lord commanded him. Similar to this are ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ and ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾ [Surah al-Dukhan: 3].
2822 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa narrated to us, from Isra'il, from al-Suddi, from Muhammad ibn Abi al-Mujalid, from Miqsam, from Ibn 'Abbas: a man said to him: "Doubt has entered my heart about His saying, 'The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down,' and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night﴾ and His saying ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾, while Allah has sent down (revelation) in Shawwal and Dhu al-Qa'da and other than them!" He said: It was sent down only in Ramadan, on the Night of Decree and on a blessed night, all at once; then it was sent down upon the places of the stars, piece by piece, in months and days.
* *
As for His words "a guidance for mankind," it means guidance for mankind to the path of truth and the straight method. [[See the explanation of "huda" previously in the language index.]]
* *
As for His words "and clear proofs," it means: and clear signs "of guidance," that is, of clarification indicating the limits of Allah, His obligations, His lawful and His unlawful. [[See the explanation of "bayyinat" previously in the language index.]]
* *
As for His words "and the criterion," it means: and the distinction between truth and falsehood, [[See the explanation of "furqan" previously, 1: 98-99.]] as:
2823 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: As for "and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion," it means clear proofs of the lawful and the unlawful.
* *
The explanation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾
Abu Ja'far said: The commentators differed regarding the meaning of "witnessing the month."

Some of them said: It is the residence of the resident in his home. They said: Whoever has the month of Ramadan arrive while he is resident in his home, it is obligatory upon him to fast the entire month, even if he later departs and travels, or remains and does not leave.

Mention of those who said this:
2824 - Muhammad ibn Humayd and Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Damghani narrated to me, both saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn Yahya, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it." He said: It is its sighting while in the home. He means: if he sees the crescent while he is resident.
2825 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Husayn informed us, from one who narrated to him, from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding His words: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it." If he witnesses it while resident, then fasting is obligatory upon him, whether he remains or travels. And if he witnesses it while on a journey, then if he wishes he may fast, and if he wishes he may break the fast.
2826 - Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, from Ayyub, from Muhammad, from 'Ubayda, concerning a man whom Ramadan overtakes and then he travels: he said: If you witnessed its beginning, fast its end. Do you not see that He says: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it"?
2827 - Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, from Hisham al-Qardusi, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: I asked 'Ubayda about a man who reached Ramadan while resident? He said: Whoever fasts the beginning of the month, let him fast its end. Do you not see that He says: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it"? [[The report: 2827 - in the printed edition: "al-Firdawsi," but the correct form is with a qaf and a dammah: Hisham ibn Hassan al-Azdi al-Qardusi, Abu 'Abd Allah al-Basri, who narrated from Humayd ibn Hilal, al-Hasan al-Basri, Muhammad, Anas, and Hafs (the sons of Sirin), and others. Among those who narrated from him were 'Ikrima ibn 'Ammar, Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, Ibn 'Ulayya, and others. He is said to be attributed to a quarter in Basra called "al-Qaradis," which is the plural of qardus, an Yemeni clan whose name the quarter took. It is also said he was a mawla of that clan. Ibn Sa'd said: He was trustworthy, God willing. He died in the year 146.]]
2828 - Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: As for "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it," whoever has Ramadan arrive upon him while he is resident in his household, let him fast it; and if he goes out during it, let him fast it, for it arrived upon him while he was in his household.
2829 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, saying: Qatada informed us, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from 'Ubayda al-Salmani, from 'Ali, as Hammad thinks, who said: Whoever reaches Ramadan while resident and does not leave, fasting becomes obligatory for him, because Allah says: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it."
2830 - Hannad ibn al-Sari narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn Muslim, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: I asked 'Ubayda al-Salmani about the words of Allah: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it." He said: Whoever is resident, let him fast it, and whoever reaches it and then travels during it, let him fast it.
2831 - Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from 'Ubayda, who said: Whoever witnesses the first of Ramadan, let him fast its last.
2832 - Hannad narrated to us, saying: 'Abda narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatada, that 'Ali used to say: If Ramadan reaches him while he is resident and then he travels, fasting is obligatory upon him.
2833 - Hannad narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahim narrated to us, from 'Ubayda al-Dabbi, from Ibrahim, who said: He used to say: If Ramadan reaches you, do not travel during it. If you have fasted a day or two in it and then travel, do not break your fast; fast it.
2834 - Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Murra, from Abu al-Bakhtari, who said: We were with 'Ubayda when he recited this verse: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it." He said: Whoever fasted any of it in the city, let him fast the rest when he leaves. He said: Ibn 'Abbas used to say: If he wishes he may fast, and if he wishes he may break the fast.
2835 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Wahhab, and Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, both saying together: Ayyub narrated to us, from Abu Yazid, from Umm Dharra, who said: I came to 'A'isha in Ramadan, and she said: "Where have you come from?" I said: "From my brother Hunayn's." She said: "What is his affair?" She said: "I bid him farewell, as he wanted to depart." She said: "Then convey my greetings to him and tell him to stay." "If Ramadan were to reach me while I was on part of the road, I would stay for his sake." [[The report: 2835 - Abu Yazid: he is the Madinan, counted among the people of Basra. He is a trustworthy Successor, whom Ibn Ma'in deemed reliable. Al-Bukhari recorded him in al-Kuna, no. 784, and said: "He heard Ibn 'Umar." See also Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/458-459. In al-Tahdhib, from al-Ajurri, from Abu Dawud: "I asked Ahmad about him, and he said: Do you ask about a man from whom Ayyub narrated?"
Umm Dharra, with a dotted dhal and a doubled ra, the freedwoman of 'A'isha: a trustworthy Successor, recorded in al-Tahdhib. Also Ibn Sa'd 8: 357, who mentions two other narrations from 'A'isha, one of which was given at length earlier in her biography 8: 46.
As for her brother "Hunayn": I have not found mention of him in any place other than this one.
The report is also mentioned by al-Suyuti at 1: 191, in similar meaning, attributing it only to 'Abd ibn Humayd. In it, "Hunayn," the brother of Umm Dharra, is not named; it only mentions that he was her brother.]]
2836 - Hannad narrated to us, saying: Ishaq ibn 'Isa narrated to us, from Aflah, from 'Abd al-Rahman, who said: Ibrahim ibn Talha came to 'A'isha to greet her. She said: "Where do you intend to go?" He said: "I intended the 'umra." She said: "You sat until the month came upon you, and then you left during it!" He said: "My baggage has already departed." She said: "Sit, until you break the fast, then depart"—meaning the month of Ramadan. [[The report: 2836 - Ishaq ibn 'Isa: he is Ibn al-Tabba' al-Baghdadi, a trustworthy narrator among those who transmitted from Malik and his generation.
Aflah: he is Ibn Humayd ibn Nafi' al-Madani, a well-known trustworthy narrator, from whom the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) transmitted.
'Abd al-Rahman: he is Ibn al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, a trustworthy imam, among the best of the Muslims. He was born during 'A'isha's lifetime.
Ibrahim ibn Talha: he is Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah al-Taymi, named here after his grandfather. He is a trustworthy Successor of high standing.
This report is also mentioned by al-Suyuti at 1: 191, attributed only to 'Abd ibn Humayd. In it: "from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim: that Ibrahim ibn Muhammad came to 'A'isha...", and it recounts something similar in meaning to what is here.]]
* *
Others said: The meaning of that is: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast what he witnesses of it."
Mention of those who said this:
2837 - Hannad ibn al-Sari narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq: that Abu Maysara went out during Ramadan, and when he reached the bridge he called for water and drank.
2838 - Hannad narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mughira, who said: Abu Maysara went out during Ramadan while traveling; he passed by the Euphrates while fasting, took a handful of it, drank, and broke his fast.
2839 - Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Murthid: that Abu Maysara traveled during Ramadan and broke his fast at the gate of the bridge. Thus Hannad said, from Murthid, but it is actually Abu Murthid.
2840 - Muhammad ibn 'Umara al-Asadi narrated to me, saying: 'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Isra'il informed us, from Abu Ishaq, from Murthid: that he went out with Abu Maysara during Ramadan, and when he reached the bridge he broke his fast. [[The two reports 2839 and 2840 are both from the narration of Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, from "Murthid," from "Abu Maysara."
Al-Tabari said regarding the first of them: "Thus Hannad said: from Murthid, but it is actually: from Abu Murthid," meaning that his teacher in the first, Hannad, erred in this. Strangely, he then narrates it in the second report after it, from another teacher, with another chain to Abu Ishaq, like the narration of Hannad which he claimed was in error!
In my view, it is Abu Ja'far, may Allah have mercy on him, who erred and missed the correct reading:
First: because two trustworthy memorizers agree, namely Sufyan al-Thawri in the first chain and Isra'il ibn Yunus ibn Abi Ishaq al-Sabi'i in the second chain, both from Abu Ishaq, that it is "from Murthid."]]

Secondly, we do not know of any transmitter whose kunya is "Abu Murthid" except "Abu Murthid al-Ghanawi Kanaz ibn al-Husayn," who was an early Companion and died in the year 12 AH. Unless al-Tabari knew of another transmitter with this kunya whose report has not reached us, and I do not think he did.

Abu Maysara, the narrator of the report in both versions, is ʿAmr ibn Sharahbil al-Hamdani al-Kufi. He was a senior Successor (tabiʿi), trustworthy (thiqah), and one of the teachers of Abu Ishaq al-Sabiʿi. He died in 63 AH, and al-Sabiʿi attended his funeral. Had Abu Ishaq wished to narrate this report from him directly, without an intermediary, nothing would have prevented him, since he was known for narrating from him. But he did not wish to commit tadlis (concealing an intermediary) in a report he had not witnessed himself, so he narrated it from the one who had witnessed it. That one is "Murthid."

My preferred view is that he is "Murthid ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Yazani," a Successor slightly older than al-Sabiʿi. Murthid died in 90 AH, while al-Sabiʿi, who was also a Successor, died in 126 AH or shortly after.

On the basis of all this, I have concluded, indeed I am certain, that Abu Jaʿfar, may God have mercy on him, is the one who erred.

2841 – Hannad and Abu Hisham narrated to us, both saying: Waki‘ narrated to us, from al-Mas‘udi, from al-Hasan ibn Sa‘d, from his father, who said: I was with ʿAli in one of his estates, three (miles) from Medina. We set out toward Medina in the month of Ramadan, ʿAli riding and I walking. He said: He fasted – Hannad said: and I broke my fast – Abu Hisham said: and he ordered me, so I broke my fast.

2842 – Hannad narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahim narrated to us, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿUtbah, from al-Hasan ibn Sa‘d, from his father, who said: I was with ʿAli ibn Abi Talib when he was returning from a land of his. He fasted, and he ordered me, so I broke my fast. He entered Medina at night; he was riding and I was walking.

2843 – Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki‘ narrated to us – and Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Ibn Mahdi narrated to us – both saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from ʿIsa ibn Abi ʿAzzah, from al-Shaʿbi: that he traveled in the month of Ramadan and broke his fast at the gate of the bridge.

2844 – Ibn Bashshar narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan said to me: "It is more beloved to me that you complete it (the fast)."

2845 – Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, from Shuʿbah, who said: I asked al-Hakam and Hammad, as I wished to travel in Ramadan, and they both said to me: "Go out." Hammad also said: Ibrahim said: "As for when it is the last ten (days), it is more beloved to me that he remain."

2846 – Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Walid narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan and Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, who both said: Whoever is reached by the fast while he is resident and in Ramadan, and then travels, may (break the fast) if he wishes.

* *

Others said: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it" means: whoever witnesses it sane, mature and legally responsible, let him fast it.

Among those who said this were Abu Hanifah and his companions. They used to say: whoever is reached by the month of Ramadan while he is healthy, sane and mature, it is obligatory upon him to fast it. If he becomes insane after it has come upon him, in the state we have described, and then regains his sanity after it has ended, he must make up the days of the month that he spent in a state of insanity, because he was among those who witnessed it, and he was among those upon whom it was obligatory.

They said: Likewise, if the month of Ramadan came upon him while he was insane, but he was of those who would have been obligated to fast had he been sane, and he recovered and was cured before the month ended, or regained his sanity a day or more before its end, he must make up the fasting of the entire month, except for the day he fasted after regaining his sanity, because he was among those who witnessed the month.

They said: If the month of Ramadan came upon him while he was insane, and he did not regain his sanity until the entire month had ended, and then he regained it, he is not required to make up anything of it, because he was not among those who witnessed it as a responsible person obligated to fast it.

Abu Jaʿfar said: This interpretation has no meaning. For if insanity removes the obligation of fasting from the one who has it, because his mind is absent for the whole month, then this should be the case for everyone who loses his mind for the entire month of fasting. Yet all have agreed that whoever loses consciousness for the entire month of fasting due to unconsciousness or *birsam* [[Birsam: an illness in which the sufferer raves. They say it is a hot swelling that afflicts the diaphragm between the liver and the intestines, and then spreads to the brain.]], and then regains it after the month has ended, must make up the entire month. No one who can be cited as an opponent of the community has disagreed with this. Since this is a consensus, it is necessary that the case of everyone who was without reason for the entire month of fasting should be the same as that of the one who is unconscious. Since this is so, it is clear that the interpretation of the verse is not the one given by those who hold this view, namely that it refers to witnessing the month or part of it while legally responsible for fasting it. Once that is refuted, the interpretation of the one who claimed that its meaning is: whoever witnesses its beginning while resident and present must fast all of it, is even more invalid and corrupt, because of the widely attested reports that the Messenger of God ﷺ went out from Medina in the month of Ramadan in the year of the Conquest, after he had fasted part of it, and he broke his fast and ordered his Companions to break theirs.

2847 – Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ traveled in Ramadan from Medina to Mecca, until when he reached ʿUsfan, he stopped there, called for a vessel, placed it on his hand so that the people could see it, and then drank it."

2848 – Ibn Humayd and Sufyan ibn Waki‘ narrated to us, both saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Tawus, from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, similarly.

2849 – Hannad narrated to us, saying: ʿUbaydah narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Tawus, from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, similarly. [[The reports 2847–2849 are three chains for one report. The first has in it "from Mujahid, from Ibn ʿAbbas," and in the other two Tawus is inserted between them. The report was also narrated by Imam Ahmad in his Musnad, in a longer form than here: 2350, from ʿUbaydah, from Mansur, through the second chain here. He also narrated it: 2251, from Husayn, from Shaybān, from Mansur. It was also narrated, in a longer form, by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), as in al-Muntaqa: 2175. It is therefore a sound report agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayhi).]]

2850 – Hannad and Abu Kurayb narrated to us, both saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: al-Zuhri narrated to me, from ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUtbah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ set out on his journey in the year of the Conquest when ten days of Ramadan had passed. The Messenger of God ﷺ fasted, and the people fasted with him, until when he reached al-Kudayd (which lies between ʿUsfan and Amaj), he broke his fast.

2851 – Hannad and Abu Kurayb narrated to us, both saying: ʿAbdah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from al-Zuhri, from ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ set out when ten – or twenty – days of Ramadan had passed, in the year of the Conquest. He fasted until, when he reached al-Kudayd, he broke his fast. [[The two reports 2850 and 2851 are two other sound chains for the preceding report, with a longer wording, and from another route, through Ibn Ishaq from al-Zuhri. It is in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham (p. 810 of the Europe edition; 4:42 of the Halabi edition) with a longer wording than here. Likewise Ahmad narrated it in the Musnad: 2392, through Ibn Ishaq. Ahmad also narrated it: 1892, from Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah, from al-Zuhri, in abridged form, and he narrated it in a longer form: 3089, from ʿAbd al-Razzaq, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhri. See also Ibn Kathir's History 4:285–287.]]

2852 – Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Salim ibn Nuh narrated to us, saying: ʿUmar ibn ʿAmir narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: We went out with the Prophet ﷺ when eighteen days of Ramadan had passed, and among us were those fasting and those breaking the fast. The one who broke his fast did not find fault with the one fasting, nor did the one fasting find fault with the one who broke his fast. [[The report 2852: Salim ibn Nuh, Abu Saʿid al-ʿAttar: trustworthy, one of Ahmad's teachers. ʿUmar ibn ʿAmir al-Sulami al-Basri al-Qadi: trustworthy and firm in hadith, as Ahmad said. The report was narrated by Muslim in his Sahih 1:308, through numerous chains, among them a chain from Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, from Salim ibn Nuh, from ʿUmar ibn ʿAmir, from Qatadah, through this same chain. He then narrated it through other chains, 1:308–309, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Saʿid. al-Suyuti (1:190–191) also attributed it to al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i.]]

* *

Since these two interpretations are invalid, for the reasons we have shown for their invalidity, it is clear that the correct interpretation is the third: "So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it," meaning all of what he witnessed while resident, "and whoever is sick or on a journey, then (let him fast) a number of other days."

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever is sick or on a journey, then (let him fast) a number of other days﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: whoever is sick or on a journey during the month and breaks his fast, then he must fast the number of days he broke, on other days than the days of the month of Ramadan.

* *

The scholars then differed about the sickness for which God permitted breaking the fast and made obligatory the making up of a number of other days.

Some said: It is the sickness for which the sufferer cannot endure standing for his prayer.

Those who said this:

2853 – Mu‘adh ibn Shu‘bah al-Basri narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Mughirah, from Ibrahim and Ismaʿil ibn Muslim, from al-Hasan, that he said: If the sick person is unable to pray standing, he breaks his fast. [[The report 2853: Muʿadh ibn Shuʿbah al-Basri, the teacher of al-Tabari: Ibn Abi Hatim included him in his biography (4/1/251), saying: "Muʿadh ibn Shuʿbah Abu Sahl al-Basri, narrated from ʿAbbad ibn al-ʿAwwam and ʿUthman ibn Mutar. Musa ibn Ishaq al-Ansari narrated from him." I have found no other biography of him. He is therefore an early teacher of al-Tabari, since he narrates from ʿAbbad ibn al-ʿAwwam, who died in 185 AH, and Sharik ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Nakhaʿi, who died in 188 AH. His student mentioned by Ibn Abi Hatim, Musa ibn Ishaq ibn Musa al-Ansari al-Khatmi, judge of Rayy, is one of the teachers of Ibn Abi Hatim, as in his biography there (4/1/135).]]

2854 – Yaʿqub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Mughirah – or ʿUbaydah – from Ibrahim, concerning the sick person who is unable to pray standing: let him break his fast. That is, in Ramadan.

2855 – Hannad narrated to us, saying: Hafs ibn Ghiyath narrated to us, from Ismaʿil, who said: I asked al-Hasan: When does the fasting person break his fast? He said: When fasting exhausts him. I said: (And when is that?) He said: When he is unable to perform the obligatory prayers as he was commanded. [[In the printed edition: "as it passed (mar)," but the correct reading seems to be what I have given.]]

* *

Others said: It is every sickness in which, for the most part, fasting increases the illness of its sufferer to an intolerable degree. [[In the printed edition: "an increase not the tolerable," which is not Arabic. The wording of al-Shafiʿi in al-Umm (1:89) is: "If the sickness of the sick person increases to a clear degree, he breaks his fast; but if the increase is tolerable, he does not break it."] This is the view of Muhammad ibn Idris al-Shafiʿi, transmitted to us from him by al-Rabiʿ.

* *

Others said: It is every sickness which is called a sickness.

Those who said this:

2856 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Khalid al-Rabiʿi narrated to us, saying: Tarif ibn Shihab al-ʿUtaridi narrated to us, that he entered upon Muhammad ibn Sirin in Ramadan while he was eating, and he did not ask him. When he had finished, he said: "My finger has been hurting." [[The report 2856: al-Hasan ibn Khalid al-Rabiʿi: Ibn Abi Hatim included him in his biography (1/2/10), saying: "al-Hasan ibn Khalid ibn Bab al-Qurayʿi. He narrated from Tarif ibn Shahal al-ʿUtaridi. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated from him." He is therefore the shaykh mentioned here, and I have found no other biography of him. The verifying scholar of the book, Shaykh ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Yahya al-Yamani, noted at the word "al-Qurayʿi" that in some manuscripts it is "al-Qarayʿi," and that it will come later in the chapter on "Khalid" as "Khalid ibn Bab al-Rabiʿi," and that "it may be that he is the father of this al-Hasan." This is a precise observation by him, may God protect him, supported by the attribution here in al-Tabari as "al-Rabiʿi." Khalid ibn Bab al-Rabiʿi is treated in al-Kabir (2/1/130–131), Ibn Abi Hatim (1/2/322), and Lisan al-Mizan (2:374). Tarif ibn Shihab al-ʿUtaridi: the printed edition gives his father's name as "Tammam," which is an error. This Tarif is Abu Sufyan al-Ashall, and he is weak. It was said that his father's name was "Saʿd," and al-Bukhari, in his biography, is the one who established his name and lineage correctly. He is treated in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir (2/2/358), Ibn Abi Hatim (2/1/492–493), and in al-Bukhari's al-Duʿafa', pp. 18–19.]]

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The correct view on this matter, in our opinion, is that the "sickness" for which God, may His remembrance be exalted, permitted breaking the fast during the month of Ramadan is that in which fasting becomes an unbearable hardship for the person. Whoever is in this state may break his fast and make up a number of other days. For when the matter reaches this point, if he is not permitted to break his fast, he has been burdened with hardship and denied ease, and that is not what God informed us He intends for His creatures in His words: "God intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship." As for the one for whom fasting is not an unbearable hardship, he is in the position of the healthy person who is able to fast, and it is obligatory for him to perform it.

* *

As for His words, "then (let him fast) a number of other days," their meaning is: a number of counted days other than these days.

As for "other" (*ukhar*), it is the plural of *ukhra*, just as they pluralize *al-kubra* as *al-kubar* and *al-qurba* as *al-qurab*. [[In the printed edition: "by their pluralizing al-kubra," which seems to be an error, and the correct reading seems to be what I have given.]]

* *

If someone says: Is not *ukhar* a description of the days?

It is said: Yes.

If he says: Is not the singular of "days" (*ayyam*) "day" (*yawm*), which is masculine?

It is said: Yes.

If he says: Then how can the singular of *ukhar* be *ukhra*, which is a description of "day," when it was not *akhar*?

It is said: Although the singular of "days" is described with *akhar*, the singular of *ukhar* is *akhar*. But "days" in the plural shifts to the feminine, so its adjectives and descriptions take the form of feminine descriptions, as one says: "The days have passed, all of them (*jumi'a*)," and one does not say "ajma'un" or "ayyam akharun."

* *

If someone says to us: God, exalted is He, said: "Whoever of you is sick or on a journey, then (let him fast) a number of other days." If, in your view, its meaning is: then he must fast a number of other days, as you have described above, then what do you say about someone who is sick or on a journey and fasts the whole month, while he is among those permitted to break the fast? Is that sufficient for him in place of fasting a number of other days, or is it not sufficient, since the obligation of fasting a number of other days remains binding upon him in its form, even if he fasts the whole month? And is it permissible for the sick or the traveler to fast the month of Ramadan, or is that forbidden to him, and it is obligatory for him to break his fast during it, until he resides and this one is cured?

It is said: The scholars have differed on all of this, and we will mention their differences and inform (the reader) of the view most correct among them, God willing.

Some said: Breaking the fast in sickness is an obligatory resolution (*'azima*) from God, not a concession (*tarkhis*).

Those who said this:

2857 – Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi ʿAdi narrated to us – and Yaʿqub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn ʿUlayyah narrated to us – both from Saʿid, from Qatadah, from Jabir ibn Zayd, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Breaking the fast on a journey is a resolution.

2858 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Wahb ibn Jarir narrated to us, saying: Shuʿbah informed us, from Yaʿla, from Yusuf ibn al-Hakam, who said: I asked Ibn ʿUmar – or it was asked of him – about fasting on a journey, and he said: "What do you think if you gave charity to a man and he returned it to you? Would you not be angry? For it is a charity from God, with which He gives to you." [[The report 2858: Shuʿbah is Ibn al-Hajjaj, the imam of the critics of narrators (jarh wa-taʿdil). In the printed edition "Saʿid" appears, which is a copyist's or typesetter's error in this chain, as will become clear from what follows. Yaʿla is Ibn ʿAta al-ʿAmiri, a well-known trustworthy narrator. Yusuf ibn al-Hakam Abu al-Hakam: a trustworthy Successor. Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy (al-Thiqat). Ibn Abi Hatim (4/2/220) included him, saying: "He narrated from Ibn ʿUmar. Yaʿla ibn ʿAta narrated from him." al-Bukhari included him in al-Kabir (4/2/376) as "Yusuf Abu al-Hakam, heard Ibn ʿUmar. Yaʿla ibn ʿAta narrated from him." Following this, in some copies of al-Kabir, appears: "This is the first, I think," meaning the one before him, Yusuf ibn Mihran. This assumption by al-Bukhari is not in its proper place, and perhaps he assumed this because it did not come to him attributed to his father, but rather under the name "Yusuf" and the kunya "Abu al-Hakam." What settles the matter and removes every doubt is that al-Dulabi narrated this report in al-Kuna wa-al-Asma' (1:154–155): "Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, saying: Shuʿbah narrated to us, from Yaʿla ibn ʿAta, who said: I heard Yusuf ibn al-Hakam Abu al-Hakam say: I heard ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar being asked about fasting on a journey..." and he mentioned something similar to what is here.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 185 (part 3 of 5):

Wahb ibn Jarir narrates from Shu'bah. Ya'la ibn 'Ata' narrates from him, and Shu'bah narrates from Ya'la. So there is no place in this isnad (chain of narration) for the name "Sa'id." This holds until the report is confirmed through Shu'bah's narration in al-Dulabi's work, as we have mentioned.

This opinion of Ibn 'Umar, and then of other Companions, applies only to the person who refuses to accept Allah's concession (rukhsah) to break the fast while traveling. Ibn Kathir said (1: 410-411): "As for the one who turns away from the Sunnah and considers breaking the fast to be disliked, it is incumbent on him to break the fast, and fasting is forbidden for him in this state, because of what came in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad and others, from Ibn 'Umar, Jabir and others: 'Whoever does not accept Allah's concession, upon him is sin like the mountains of 'Arafah.'" In this, Ibn Kathir refers to the hadith of Ibn 'Umar in the Musnad, no. 5392. See also two other hadiths of Ibn 'Umar in the Musnad, nos. 5750 and 5866.]]

2859. He related to us Nasr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Azdi, who said: He related to us al-Muharibi, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Humayd, who said: Abu Ja'far said: "My father did not fast while traveling, and he would forbid it."
[[Report 2859: Nasr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Azdi. He has passed in nos. 423 and 875. In the printed edition here, as there, it reads "al-Awdi," which is an error.]]

2860. He related to us Ibn Humayd, who said: He related to us Yahya ibn Wadih, who said: He related to us 'Ubayd, from al-Dahhak: that he disliked fasting while traveling.

* *

Those who held this view said: Whoever fasts while traveling must make up the fast when he is resident.

Mention of those who said this:

2861. He related to us Nasr ibn 'Ali al-Jahdami, who said: He related to us Muslim ibn Ibrahim, who said: He related to us Rabi'ah ibn Kulthum, from his father, from a man: that 'Umar ordered the one who fasted while traveling to repeat it.
[[Report 2861: Nasr ibn 'Ali ibn Nasr ibn 'Ali al-Jahdami: he has passed in no. 2376. In the printed edition here it reads "al-Khuth'ami," which is a clear corruption. His teacher, Muslim ibn Ibrahim al-Azdi al-Farahidi, has passed in no. 1219. The narration of Nasr from Muslim is confirmed in both their biographies.
Rabi'ah ibn Kulthum ibn Jabr al-Basri: trustworthy, though some have criticized him. He is in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Sa'd (7/2/35), al-Kabir (2/1/266), and Ibn Abi Hatim (1/2/477-478).
His father, Kulthum ibn Jabr: trustworthy, one of the junior Successors (tabi'un), but he did not meet 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. For this reason he narrates here through an unnamed man, so the isnad is weak. See the following report, no. 2866.]]

2862. He related to us Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, who said: He related to us Muhammad ibn Abi 'Adi, from Sa'id ibn 'Amr ibn Dinar, from a man of Banu Tamim, from his father, who said: 'Umar ordered a man who had fasted while traveling to repeat his fast.

2863. He related to me Ibn Humayd al-Himsi, who said: He related to us 'Ali ibn Ma'bad, from 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Amr, from 'Abd al-Karim, from 'Ata', from al-Muharrar ibn Abi Hurayrah, who said: "I was with my father on a journey in Ramadan, and I would fast while he would break the fast. My father said to me: 'Indeed, when you are resident, you must make it up.'"
[[Report 2863: al-Muharrar, with two r's, the first vowelled and doubled, is Ibn Abi Hurayrah. He is a known Successor who narrates from his father and from Ibn 'Umar. He has several hadiths from his father in the Musnad, including nos. 212 and 9562. Al-Suyuti mentioned this report in 1: 191, with similar wording, and attributed it only to 'Abd ibn Humayd. In his version the name "al-Muharrar" appears as "Muharraz" with a final z, which is an error.]]

2864. He related to us Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, who said: He related to us Sulayman ibn Dawud, who said: He related to us Shu'bah, from 'Asim, mawla (freedman) of Qurayba, who said: "I heard 'Urwah order a man who had fasted while traveling to make it up."

2865. He related to us Ibn al-Muthanna, who said: He related to us 'Abd al-Samad, who said: He related to us Shu'bah, from 'Asim, mawla of Qurayba: that a man fasted while traveling, and 'Urwah ordered him to make it up.

2866. He related to us Abu Kurayb, who said: He related to us Ibn Subayh, who said: He related to us Rabi'ah ibn Kulthum, from his father Kulthum: that some people came to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab after they had fasted Ramadan on a journey. He said to them: "By Allah, it is as if you had been fasting!" They said: "By Allah, O Commander of the Faithful, we did fast!" He said: "Did you find it too hard?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then make it up, make it up."
[[Report 2866: Its isnad is weak because it is broken (munqati'), since Kulthum ibn Jabr did not meet 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, as we explained in no. 2861.]]

* *

The reasoning of those who held this view is that Allah, dhikruhu, made obligatory, by His saying: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾, the fasting of the month of Ramadan upon whoever witnesses it while resident and not traveling. And He made for the one who is sick or on a journey the fasting of a number of other days, not the days of Ramadan, by His saying: ﴿And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾. They said: Just as it is not permissible for a resident to break the fast on the days of Ramadan and fast a number of other days in their place, because what Allah made obligatory on him by witnessing the month is to fast the month itself and not something else, so likewise it is not permissible for a traveler who did not witness the month as a resident to fast it, because what Allah made obligatory on him is a number of other days. They also argued from a report:

2867. He related this to us, Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id al-Wasiti, who said: He related to us Ya'qub ibn Muhammad al-Zuhri, who said: He related to us 'Abd Allah ibn Musa, from Usamah ibn Zayd, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who fasts while traveling is like the one who breaks the fast while resident."
[[Hadith 2867: Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'id al-Wasiti, the teacher of al-Tabari: I have found no biography of him. The name appears again later in no. 2888. But in the following isnad the name is "Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn Sa'id," with his father named "'Ubayd Allah" instead of "'Abd Allah." I give more weight to the reading in two isnads over the reading in one isnad, but this is a preliminary and unverified preference.
Ya'qub ibn Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Abd al-Malik ibn Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf al-Zuhri: disputed. The apparent judgment is that he was trustworthy, and they criticized him only for narrating from unknown men whose uprightness was not established. He is in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir (4/2/398), Ibn Abi Hatim (4/2/214-215), and Tarikh Baghdad (14: 269-271).
'Abd Allah ibn Musa ibn Ibrahim, a descendant of Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah al-Taymi: disputed. Ahmad was very weak in his assessment of him. Ibn Hibban said: "He raises what is stopped (mawquf) and gives chains to what is detached (mursal); it is not permissible to use him as evidence." In the printed edition here it reads "'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa," which is an error, since the hadith is known from the narration of "'Abd Allah ibn Musa al-Taymi," who narrates from Usamah ibn Zayd.
Usamah ibn Zayd: al-Laythi al-Madani, disputed. We preferred his trustworthiness in our commentary on the Musnad, no. 1098.
Ibn Majah narrated this hadith, no. 1666, from Ibrahim ibn al-Mundhir al-Hizami, from 'Abd Allah ibn Musa al-Taymi, with this isnad.
The hafiz al-Zayla'i (Nasb al-Raya, 2: 461-463) gave a lengthy account of its narrations. He judged that it is mawquf, being the words of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, and that its isnad is broken between Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman and his father. The hafiz judged that he did not hear anything from his father. We, in our commentary on the Musnad, no. 1660, judged that he heard this hadith from his father, since he was young when 'Abd al-Rahman died. This does not mean that he heard everything he narrates from him.
Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned in Kitab al-'Ilal, no. 694, that he asked his father about this hadith. Abu Zur'a said: "Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri, Ma'n ibn 'Isa, and Hammad ibn Khalid al-Khayyat narrated it from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Salamah, from his father, as his own statement. 'Anbasah ibn Khalid narrated it from Yunus, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Salamah, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Lahi'ah narrated it from Yunus, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Salamah, from 'A'ishah, from the Prophet (ﷺ). Baqiyyah narrated it from another, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ)." Abu Zur'a said: "The correct version is from al-Zuhri, from Abu Salamah, from his father, and it is mawquf."
Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar, in al-Talkhis (p. 195), reported that al-Daraqutni in al-'Ilal and al-Bayhaqi also judged it to be mawquf. See al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Bayhaqi (4: 244) and the response of Ibn al-Turkmani to it. The mawquf report from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf was narrated by al-Nasa'i (1: 316) through three isnads. Furthermore, al-Tabari's statement will come on p. 474 about this report and those like it, that they are "weak in their chains, and it is not permissible to use them as evidence in religion."]]

2868. He related to me Muhammad ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn Sa'id, who said: He related to us Yazid ibn 'Iyad, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who fasts while traveling is like the one who breaks the fast while resident."
[[Hadith 2868: This is another isnad for the previous hadith.
This isnad is problematic:
First, the teacher of al-Tabari is named here as "Muhammad 'Ubayd Allah ibn Sa'id," while in the previous isnad he is named "Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah."
Second, the phrase "He related to us Yazid ibn 'Iyad" is not sensible; there must be at least one narrator between them. Yazid ibn 'Iyad ibn Yazid ibn Ja'dabah al-Laythi died long ago, during the caliphate of al-Mahdi. al-Bukhari mentioned him in al-Tarikh al-Saghir (p. 172), in the section on those who died between 140 and 150 AH. It is therefore not plausible that any teacher of al-Tabari, who died in 310 AH, heard from him. I judge that between them there was "Yazid ibn Harun," for reasons we will mention, God willing.
This Yazid ibn 'Iyad is very weak. al-Bukhari said in al-Kabir (4/2/351-352) and al-Saghir: "Munkar al-hadith" (rejected in narration). Malik, Ibn Ma'in, al-Nasa'i and others accused him of lying. "Ja'dabah" is pronounced with a j, a d, and a silent 'ayn between them.
Al-Zayla'i, in Nasb al-Raya (2: 462), reported that this hadith was narrated by Ibn 'Adi in al-Kamil, from the hadith of Yazid ibn Harun: "He related to us Yazid ibn 'Iyad, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Salamah, from his father, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ)." Ibn 'Adi said: "This hadith is not raised from al-Zuhri except by Yazid ibn 'Iyad. Aqil narrated it through Salamah ibn Rawh from him, Yunus ibn Yazid narrated it through al-Qasim ibn Mabrur from him, and Usamah ibn Zayd narrated it through 'Abd Allah ibn Musa al-Taymi from him. The rest of al-Zuhri's students narrated it from him, from Abu Salamah, from his father, as his own statement."]]

* *

Others said: Permission to break the fast while traveling is a concession (rukhsah) from Allah, dhikruhu, which He granted to His servants, while the obligation is fasting. Whoever fasts fulfills the obligation, and whoever breaks the fast does so by Allah's concession to him. They said: If someone fasts while traveling, there is no making it up for him when he is resident.

Mention of those who said this:

2869. He related to us Ibn Bashshar, who said: He related to us 'Abd al-Wahhab, who said: He related to us Ayyub, who said: He related to us 'Urwah and Salim: that they were with 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz when he was governor of Medina, and they discussed fasting while traveling. Salim said: "Ibn 'Umar would not fast while traveling." 'Urwah said: "'A'ishah used to fast." Salim said: "I only learned this from Ibn 'Umar." 'Urwah said: "I only learned it from 'A'ishah." Their voices rose until 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz said: "O Allah, forgiveness! When it is ease, fast; and when it is hardship, break the fast."

2870. He related to me Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim, who said: He related to us Ibn 'Ulayyah, from Ayyub, who said: A man related to me that the question of fasting while traveling was mentioned to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Aziz, and then he mentioned something similar to the report of Ibn Bashshar.

2871. He related to me Ya'qub, who said: He related to us Ibn 'Ulayyah, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq; and Abu Kurayb related to us, who said: He related to us Ibn Idris, who said: He related to us Ibn Ishaq, from al-Zuhri, from Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab went out on some of his journeys during nights that remained of Ramadan, and he said: "Indeed the month has dwindled." (Abu Kurayb said in his report: "Or: it has passed away." Ya'qub did not doubt.) "So let us fast!" He fasted, and the people fasted with him. Then he came back once more, until when he reached al-Rawha', the crescent of the month of Ramadan appeared, and he said: "Indeed Allah has ended the journey. So let us fast, and let us not diminish our month!" He said: So he fasted, and the people fasted with him.
[[Tash'asha'a al-shahr (the month dwindled): it passed and ended, leaving only a little, from the expression "tasa'sa'a al-rajul" (the man trembled), meaning he shook from old age or senility. Tash'asha'a al-shahr means it became thin and only a little remained; it is likened to milk being mixed with water. His words "lam nathlim shahrana" come from "thalama al-inha'" or "al-sayf": to chip the rim of a vessel or the edge of a sword. That is, we did not put a flaw into our fast nor injure our month.]]

2872. He related to us Ibn Humayd, who said: He related to us al-Hakam ibn Bashir, who said: He related to me my father; and Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, who said: 'Ubayd Allah informed us, who said: Bashir ibn Salman informed us, from Khaythamah, who said: "I asked Anas ibn Malik about fasting while traveling, and he said: 'I have ordered my servant to fast, and he refused.' I said: 'Then where is this verse: ﴿And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾?' He said: 'It was revealed when we used to journey hungry and camp without being full, but today we journey full and camp full.'"
[[Report 2872: al-Hakam ibn Bashir ibn Salman: he has passed in no. 1497. His father, Bashir ibn Salman al-Nahdi: trustworthy; Ahmad and Ibn Ma'in and others declared him trustworthy. His father's name is "Salman," with a fatha on the s and a sukun on the l. In many printed references it appears as "Sulayman," which is a printing error. In al-Tahdhib and its branches it reads "al-Kindi" instead of "al-Nahdi," which is an error. The correct form is in al-Bukhari's al-Kabir (1/2/99), Ibn Abi Hatim (1/1/374), Ibn Sa'd (6: 251), and Rijal al-Sahihayn (p. 55).
Khaythamah: he is Ibn Abi Khaythamah al-Basri, a trustworthy Successor. Ibn Ma'in said: "He is nothing (laysa bi-shay')," as in Ibn Abi Hatim (1/2/394). But Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy (al-thiqat), and al-Bukhari included him in al-Kabir (2/1/197) without mentioning any criticism, and he pointed to this hadith from his narration, as is his habit in his precise references, may God bless him, saying: "Abu Nu'aym said, from Bashir ibn Salman, from Khaythamah, who said: I asked Anas ibn Malik about fasting while traveling." He neither mentioned him nor did al-Nasa'i in al-Du'afa'. This is sufficient for declaring him trustworthy and for relying on his narration, over the general criticism of Ibn Ma'in.
This report is mentioned by al-Suyuti (1: 191), who added its attribution to 'Abd ibn Humayd and al-Nasa'i. I have not found it in al-Nasa'i, and perhaps it is in al-Sunan al-Kubra.]]

2873. He related to us Hannad, who said: He related to us Waki', from Bashir ibn Salman, from Khaythamah, from Anas, similarly.

2874. He related to us Hannad and Abu al-Sa'ib, both saying: He related to us Abu Mu'awiyah, from 'Asim, from Anas: that he was asked about fasting while traveling, and he said: "Whoever breaks the fast does so by Allah's concession, and whoever fasts, fasting is better."

2875. He related to us Abu Kurayb, who said: He related to us Abu Usamah, from Ash'ath ibn 'Abd al-Malik, from Muhammad ibn 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As, who said: "Breaking the fast while traveling is a concession, and fasting is better."

2876. He related to me al-Muthanna, who said: He related to us 'Abd al-Samad, who said: He related to us Shu'bah, who said: He related to us Abu al-Fayd, who said: "'Ali was our governor in Syria, and he forbade us from fasting while traveling. So I asked Abu Qurusafah, a man among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) from Banu Layth." 'Abd al-Samad said: "I heard a man of his people say that he was Wathilah ibn al-Asqa'," and he said: "If you had fasted while traveling, you would not have had to make it up."
[[Report 2876: Abu al-Fayd: he is Musa ibn Ayyub al-Mahri al-Himsi, also called Ibn Abi Ayyub. He is a trustworthy Syrian, declared trustworthy by Ibn Ma'in and al-'Ijli. He is in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim (4/1/134).
Abu Qurusafah, with a kasrah on the q, a sukun on the r, and an unpointed sad after it: he is Wathilah ibn al-Asqa', the Companion, from Banu Layth ibn 'Abd Manat. He is called "Abu al-Asqa'," and it is said "Abu Qurusafah," as in his biography in al-Isabah, al-Tahdhib and elsewhere. This report supports this kunyah, because 'Abd al-Samad ibn 'Abd al-Warith mentions in its course that he heard a man of his people say "he is Wathilah ibn al-Asqa'."
This report, or something like it, led them into a strange error. There was another man who had companionship, named Abu Qurusafah, whose name was Jundarah ibn Khaythanah, a Companion from the Nabatean (Nabati) region. He is in al-Tahdhib (2: 119), al-Kabir (1/2/249), Ibn Abi Hatim (1/1/545), and Usd al-Ghabah (1: 307). The attention of the author of al-Tahdhib shifted, in the biography of "Abu al-Fayd Musa ibn Ayyub" (10: 337), and he mentioned that he narrates from "Abu Qurusafah Jundarah ibn Khaythanah." Then the author of Usd al-Ghabah, in the biography of this "Jundarah," mentioned that "Ibn Makula made him a Laythi, and that is nothing!!" The author of al-Tahdhib did not mention in Jundarah's biography that Abu al-Fayd narrates from him!!
In my view, it appears that when Ibn Makula said that "Abu Qurusafah" was from Banu Layth, he meant "Wathilah ibn al-Asqa'," as the narration in this report indicates. And the author of al-Tahdhib erred when he said that Abu al-Fayd narrates from "Abu Qurusafah Jundarah ibn Khaythanah," because his narration is in fact from "Abu Qurusafah Wathilah," who is undisputedly from Banu Layth.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 185 (part 4 of 5):

As for the statement of Abu al-Fayd here, "Ali was our governor in al-Sham" – I do not know what this is. What is certain is that he did not mean "Ali ibn Abi Talib," since that never happened. Perhaps there was a governor in al-Sham for them who was called "Ali." It is also possible that what is here contains a distortion, and that the correct version is "A governor in al-Sham was over us, and he forbade us..." etc.

Then I found something that supports this. In Majma' al-Zawa'id (3: 161-162), on the authority of Abu al-Fayd, who said: "Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik addressed us and said: Do not fast Ramadan while traveling; whoever fasts, let him make it up." Abu al-Fayd said: "I met Abu Qarafa Wathila ibn al-Asqa' and asked him, and he said: If you had not fasted and then fasted, you would not have made it up." Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, and its narrators are trustworthy (thiqat).

This report resembles the report of al-Tabari here, and indicates that the governor who forbade them was "Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik." So the most probable view is that the correct wording in al-Tabari's report is "A governor in al-Sham was over us," as we suspected before. The wording at the end of the hadith in the report of al-Zawa'id seems to me distorted, and the wording of Abu Ja'far is clearer and more correct than it. "Jandara" and "Khaysha" – both are with a fatha on their first and third letters and a sukun on the second.

2877 – Hannad narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, on the authority of Bistam ibn Muslim, on the authority of Ata', who said: If you fast, it suffices you, and if you break the fast, it is a concession (rukhsa).

2878 – Hannad narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, on the authority of Kahmas, who said: I asked Salim ibn Abd Allah about fasting while traveling, and he said: If you fast, it suffices you, and if you break the fast, it is a concession.

2879 – Hannad narrated to us, he said: Abd al-Rahim narrated to us, on the authority of Talha ibn Amr, on the authority of Ata', who said: Whoever fasts, it is a right that he has fulfilled; and whoever breaks the fast, it is a concession he has taken up.

2880 – Hannad narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Hammad, on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Breaking the fast while traveling is a concession, and fasting is better.
