2881 – Hannad narrated to us, he said: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, on the authority of Hajjaj, on the authority of Ata', who said: It is instruction, not obligation – meaning the words of God: "And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days" – if he wishes he fasts, and if he wishes he does not fast.

2882 – Hannad narrated to us, he said: Abu Usama narrated to us, on the authority of Hisham, on the authority of al-Hasan, concerning a man who travels in Ramadan, who said: If he wishes he fasts, and if he wishes he breaks the fast.

2883 – Humayd ibn Mas'ada narrated to us, he said: Sufyan ibn Habib narrated to us, he said: al-Awwam ibn Hawshab narrated to us, he said: I said to Mujahid: Fasting while traveling? He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to fast during it and break the fast. I said: Which of the two is more beloved to you? He said: It is only a concession, but fasting Ramadan is more beloved to me.

2884 – Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, he said: Shu'ba narrated to us, on the authority of Hammad, on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibrahim and Mujahid, that they said: Fasting while traveling – if he wishes he fasts, and if he wishes he breaks the fast, and fasting is more beloved to them.

2885 – Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, he said: Shu'ba narrated to us, on the authority of Abu Ishaq, who said: Mujahid said to me concerning fasting while traveling – meaning fasting Ramadan: "By God, neither of them is forbidden: fasting and breaking the fast. God did not intend breaking the fast except as ease for His servants."

2886 – Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, he said: Shu'ba narrated to us, on the authority of al-Ash'ath ibn Sulaym, who said: I accompanied Abu al-Aswad ibn Yazid, Amr ibn Maymun and Abu Wa'il to Mecca, and they used to fast Ramadan and other than it while traveling.

2887 – Ali ibn Hasan al-Azdi narrated to us, he said: Mu'afa ibn Imran narrated to us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Hammad, on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr: Breaking the fast while traveling is a concession, and fasting is better.

2888 – Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Sa'id al-Wasiti narrated to me, he said: Ya'qub narrated to us, he said: Salih ibn Muhammad ibn Salih narrated to us, on the authority of his father, who said: I said to al-Qasim ibn Muhammad: We travel in winter in Ramadan, and if I fast in it, it is easier for me than making it up in the heat! He said: God said: "God intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship" [2:185]; whatever is easier for you, do it.

[Note: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Sa'id, the teacher of al-Tabari, has passed in 2867, 2868. Salih ibn Muhammad ibn Salih ibn Dinar al-Tammar al-Madani: al-Bukhari mentioned him in al-Kabir 2/2/292, and did not mention any criticism of him, and noted that he narrates from his father. Ibn Abi Hatim did not record his biography, nor did al-Tahdhib nor Lisan al-Mizan, but in al-Tahdhib, in the biography of his father, it is mentioned that he narrates from him. His father Muhammad ibn Salih ibn Dinar al-Tammar: trustworthy (thiqa). Recorded in al-Tahdhib and al-Kabir 1/1/117, and a further report from him via his son Salih is narrated; and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/287.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This view is, in our opinion, more correct, because all agree that if a sick person fasted Ramadan – and he is one for whom breaking the fast is permitted due to his illness – that his fast suffices him, and there is no obligation on him to make up other days when he recovers from his illness. Thus it was known by this that the ruling for the traveler is the same as his, in that there is no making-up obligation on him if he fasts it while traveling. For what was granted to the traveler of breaking the fast and commanded with the making-up of a number of other days is like what was granted to the sick person and commanded with making-up. Then the indication of the verse is sufficient, without needing to cite another witness for its correctness. That is the saying of God the Exalted: "God intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship" [2:185]; and there is no greater hardship than requiring the one who fasted while traveling to make up a number of other days, when he has undertaken to perform his obligation in the most burdensome of states until he has made it up and performed it.

If someone of dull understanding supposes that what he fasted was not his obligatory duty, then in the saying of God the Exalted: "O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you" [2:183], "the month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed" [2:185], there is an indication that the month of Ramadan is what is prescribed for every believer to fast, whether traveling or resident, by the generality of God's address to the believers with it, in His saying: "O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you," "the month of Ramadan." And His saying: "And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days" means: whoever is sick or on a journey and breaks the fast by God's concession, then upon him is the fasting of a number of other days in place of the days he broke during his travel or illness. Then in the consistent multitude of reports from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by his saying – when he was asked about fasting while traveling: "If you wish, fast, and if you wish, break the fast" – is sufficient and adequate evidence for the correctness of what we have said on this matter, without needing anything else.

2889 – Hannad narrated to us, he said: Abd al-Rahim, Waki' and Abda narrated to us, on the authority of Hisham ibn Urwa, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Aisha: that Hamza asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about fasting while traveling – and he used to fast continually – and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: If you wish, fast, and if you wish, break the fast.

[Note: This hadith is sahih. It was narrated by Imam Ahmad and the authors of the six books, as in al-Muntaqa: 2171. This Hamza is Hamza ibn Amr al-Aslami, a well-known Companion. Recorded in al-Tahdhib, al-Bukhari's al-Kabir 2/1/43, Ibn Sa'd 4/2/45, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/212, al-Isti'ab p. 105, Usd al-Ghaba 2: 50-51, and Tarikh al-Islam of al-Dhahabi 3: 14. And it is strange after all this that Hafiz Ibn Hajar overlooked his biography in al-Isaba, while he pointed to him in the biography of "Hamza ibn Umar" with a damma on the ain and fatha on the mim. That is a biography in which some earlier scholars erred, and he clarified this error as Ibn al-Athir did! See the two chains after this. "Sarada al-sawm yasrudahu sardan": when he continues it and some of it follows another in succession.]

2890 – Abu Kurayb and Ubayd ibn Isma'il al-Habbari narrated to us, they said: Ibn Idris narrated to us, he said: Hisham ibn Urwa narrated to us, on the authority of his father, that Hamza asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he mentioned something similar.

[Note: Ubayd ibn Isma'il al-Habbari, teacher of al-Tabari: trustworthy, one of al-Bukhari's teachers. Recorded in al-Saghir p. 247, and also in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/402. Ibn Idris: is Abd Allah ibn Idris al-Awdi, passed in 438, 2030. In al-Tahdhib 7: 59, among the teachers of "Ubayd ibn Isma'il" appears "Abu Idris," which is a typographical error. This chain apparently is mursal, since Urwa ibn al-Zubayr is a Successor, as is clear. It appears that Hisham ibn Urwa or his father Urwa – one of them sometimes connected this hadith and sometimes sent it as mursal. Urwa heard it from his aunt Aisha, Mother of the Believers, as in the previous chain, and he also heard it from Abu Murawih from Hamza al-Aslami himself, as in the next chain. Malik narrated this hadith in the Muwatta, p. 295, "on the authority of Hisham ibn Urwa, on the authority of his father: that Hamza ibn Amr al-Aslami..." – narrating it as mursal, like the narration of Ibn Idris here from Hisham. Ibn Abd al-Barr said in al-Taqassi, no. 643: "Thus Yahya narrated it, not mentioning Aisha; and most narrators of the Muwatta differed with him, mentioning Aisha in it." It was narrated by al-Bukhari 4: 157 from Abd Allah ibn Yusuf from Malik – connected. And so others of the imams narrated it. The apparent view to me is that the one who sent it as mursal and connected it is Hisham or his father, and that Malik narrated it from Hisham in both forms, as indicated by the mursal narration of Abd Allah ibn Idris here from Hisham. Al-Bukhari also narrated it 4: 156, and Muslim 1: 309-310, by several chains, connected, through Hisham, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Aisha.]

2891 – Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam narrated to me, he said: Abu Zur'a Wahb Allah ibn Rashid narrated to us, he said: Hayawa ibn Shurayh informed us, he said: Abu al-Aswad informed us that he heard Urwa ibn al-Zubayr narrate on the authority of Abu Murawih, on the authority of Hamza al-Aslami, the Companion of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he said: O Messenger of God, I continually fast, so do I fast while traveling? The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: It is only a concession from God to His servants; whoever takes it, it is good and beautiful, and whoever leaves it, there is no sin upon him. Hamza used to fast perpetually, fasting while traveling and at home. Urwa ibn al-Zubayr used to fast perpetually, fasting while traveling and at home, to the extent that when he fell ill he would not break his fast. Abu Murawih used to fast perpetually, fasting while traveling and at home.

[Note: Abu Zur'a Wahb Allah ibn Rashid: passed in 2377. In the printed edition here – as there – "Abu Zur'a and Abd Allah ibn Rashid said..." appears, which is an error, as we explained earlier. Hayawa – with an unpointed ha and a waw between them with a silent ya – ibn Shurayh al-Tujibi, Abu Zur'a al-Misri: a jurist, scholar, very trustworthy. Abu al-Aswad: is "Yatim Urwa," whose name is "Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Nawfal," and he was called "Yatim Urwa" because his father had appointed him as executor. Abu Murawij al-Ghifari al-Madani: a trustworthy Successor, whom the two Shaykhs and others narrated from. The hadith was narrated by Muslim 1: 310, al-Nasa'i 1: 243, and al-Bayhaqi 4: 43, all three through Ibn Wahb, on the authority of Amr ibn al-Harith, on the authority of Abu al-Aswad, with this chain. Al-Suyuti was very brief, mentioning it at 1: 190 and attributing it to al-Daraqutni as "authenticated" only. It is in one of the Two Sahihs and one of the four Sunan. From this chain it appears that Urwa ibn al-Zubayr has two routes for this hadith: he heard it from his aunt Aisha, and he heard it in full from Abu Murawih, on the authority of Hamza al-Aslami himself, the questioner. This is not a discrepancy on Urwa's part, but a confirmation of a sound report by another like it.]

* *

In this, together with its like of reports which would make the book lengthy to cover, is the clear indication of the correctness of what we have said: that breaking the fast is a concession, not an obligation, and the clear explanation of the correctness of what we have said in the interpretation of His saying: "And whoever is sick or on a journey, then a number of other days."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says: Although the reports of what I have said are consistent, they are also consistent with His saying: "It is not righteousness to fast while traveling"?

It is said: That applies when fasting is in a situation like that in which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said that to the one he addressed.

2892 – Al-Husayn ibn Yazid al-Subay'i narrated to us, he said: Ibn Idris narrated to us, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Amr ibn al-Hasan, on the authority of Jabir: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw a man on his journey who was shaded, and a group was around him, and he said: "Who is this?" They said: "A fasting person." He said: "It is not righteousness to fast while traveling."

* *

= Abu Ja'far said: I fear that this shaykh erred, and between Ibn Idris and Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman there is Shu'ba.

[Note: al-Husayn ibn Yazid al-Subay'i, teacher of al-Tabari: thus it is recorded here. I fear that his nisba "al-Subay'i" is an inadvertent error or a mistake of the copyists. What is in this tabaqa, narrating from Abd Allah ibn Idris, is "al-Husayn ibn Yazid ibn Yahya al-Tahhan al-Ansari," who is recorded in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/67. Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Abu Zur'a narrated from him, and the Hafiz mentioned that Muslim narrated from him outside the Sahih. What supports this for me is that al-Tabari narrated another report in al-Tarikh 1: 135-136: "al-Husayn ibn Yazid al-Tahhan narrated to us, he said: Ibn Idris narrated to us..." unless this is another teacher of al-Tabari whose identity has not reached us. Al-Tabari pointed out the error of this shaykh in dropping "Shu'ba" between "Ibn Idris" and "Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman," and he was right. For Abd Allah ibn Idris did not live to narrate from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman. The takhrij of this hadith will come in the next chain.]

* *

2892m – Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, he said: Shu'ba narrated to us, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd ibn Zurara al-Ansari, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Amr ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali, on the authority of Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw a man around whom people had gathered and who was shaded, and they said: "This is a fasting man!" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "It is not righteousness that you fast while traveling."

[Note: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd ibn Zurara: a well-known trustworthy narrator, whom the authors of the six books narrated from. Some attribute him to his maternal grandfather, saying "Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn As'ad ibn Zurara." Sa'd ibn Zurara and his brother As'ad ibn Zurara are two well-known Ansari Companions, from Banu al-Najjar. In this chain in the printed edition appears "Shu'ba on the authority of Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd...", which is a clear error by the copyists, who dropped "Muhammad ibn" before "Abd al-Rahman". Muhammad ibn Amr ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib: a trustworthy Successor, whom the two Shaykhs and others narrated from. The hadith was narrated by Muslim 1: 308, through several chains, including from Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, the teacher of al-Tabari here, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Ja'far, with this chain. It was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 14242 (3: 299 Halabi), on the authority of Muhammad ibn Ja'far, with it. Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated it: 1721, on the authority of Shu'ba, with it. It was narrated by al-Bukhari 4: 161-162 (Fath), on the authority of Adam, on the authority of Shu'ba; and also in abbreviated form in al-Kabir 1/1/189-190, on the authority of Adam. Abu Nu'aym narrated it in al-Hilya 7: 159, through several chains via Shu'ba, then said: "Sahih, agreed upon. It differed concerning Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman: Sulayman narrated it in the biography of Shu'ba on the authority of Abu al-Rijal, and another narrated it in the biography of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn As'ad ibn Zurara." The Hafiz in al-Fath established that the sound version is what we mentioned. This is what is found in Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abi Dawud: 2407, and others. Al-Suyuti was very brief, for he attributed it in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 191 only to Ibn Abi Shayba, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i; whereas it is in the Two Sahihs, as you see.]

* *

Whoever has fasting reach him to the extent that the one whom the Prophet (ﷺ) addressed in that case reached – his fasting is not righteousness. For God the Exalted has forbidden everyone to expose himself to what would destroy him, while he has a path to his salvation. Righteousness is sought only through what God has urged and encouraged of deeds, not through what He has forbidden.

As for the reports narrated from him (ﷺ) in his saying: "The fasting person in travel is like the breaking-fast person at home" [see the two reports no. 2867, 2868, and the commentary on them], it is possible that it was said to one whom fasting reached to the extent that this man who was shaded reached, if that was before that. It is not permissible to attribute that saying to the Prophet (ﷺ), because the reports that came with that from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) have weak chains, and it is not permissible to argue with them in religion.

* *

If someone says: How is it conjoined to "the sick," which is a noun, with His saying "or on a journey," and "on" (ʿalā) is a particle, not a noun? [Note: "Particle" here means the preposition. The particles of attribute are the prepositions. Their explanation has passed at 1: 299, note 1.]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 185 (part 5 of 5):

It has been said: it is permissible to conjoin "ʿalā" (upon) with "al-marīḍ" (the sick person), because it carries the sense of a verb. Its interpretation is: "or on a journey," just as the Exalted has said: ﴿He calls Us for his side, or sitting, or standing﴾ [Yunus: 12], where "sitting" and "standing" are conjoined with the "lām" in "li-janbihi" (for his side), because its meaning is a verb, as if he had said: "He calls Us lying on his side, or sitting, or standing."
* *
Concerning the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: The Exalted means by this: Allah intends for you, O believers, by His permitting you, in the state of your illness and travel, to break the fast and to make up a number of other days, from the days you broke, after your residence and after your recovery from your illness, facilitation for you and ease for you, knowing the hardship of that upon you in these conditions [[In the printed edition: "bi-shiqqat dhalika ʿalaykum" (with the hardship of that upon you); the correct reading is what has been established.]]. "And He does not intend for you hardship," meaning: He does not intend for you severity and difficulty, so that He would burden you with fasting the month in these conditions, knowing the severity of that for you, and the heaviness of bearing it upon you were He to impose its fasting upon you, as:

2893. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Muʿawiyah ibn Salih related to us, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship." He said: Ease is breaking the fast on a journey; hardship is fasting on a journey.

2894. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar related to us, saying: Shuʿbah related to us, from Abu Hamzah, who said: I asked Ibn ʿAbbas about fasting on a journey, and he said: "Ease and hardship." So take the ease of Allah.

2895. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr related to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Shibl, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah: "Allah intends for you ease" — he said: it is breaking the fast on a journey, and [the making up of] a number of other days — "and He does not intend for you hardship."

2896. Bishr ibn Muʿadh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Saʿid related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship": so seek for yourselves what Allah has intended for you.

2897. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Suwayd related to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Ibn ʿUyaynah, from ʿAbd al-Karim al-Jazari, from Tawus, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Do not blame the one who fasts nor the one who breaks the fast — meaning on a journey in Ramadan — "Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship."

2898. It was reported to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, saying: al-Fudayl ibn Khalid related to us, saying: ʿUbayd ibn Sulayman related to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim regarding His words: "Allah intends for you ease" — breaking the fast on a journey — "and does not intend for you hardship," fasting on a journey.
* *
Concerning the interpretation of His words: ﴿And that you complete the period﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: The Exalted means by His words "and that you complete the period," the period of what you broke, of other days, which He obligated upon you as making up a number of other days after your recovery from illness or your return from travel, as:

2899. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr related to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding His words: "and that you complete the period," he said: the period of what the sick person and the traveler broke.

2900. Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "and that you complete the period," he said: Completing the period is that one fasts what was broken of Ramadan on a journey or due to illness [until] one completes it; when one has completed it, one has completed the period. [[The addition between the brackets is indispensable here.]]
* *
If someone says: What is the "wa" (and) in His words "and that you complete the period" conjoining it to what?

It is said: The grammarians have differed on this.

Some of them said: It conjoins with what precedes it, as if it were said: "and He intends that you complete the period and that you magnify Allah."

And some grammarians of Kufa said: This "lām" in His words "wa-litukmilū" is the "lām" of "kay" (in order that); were it dropped, it would be correct. He said: The Arabs insert it in their speech with a verb implied after it, and it is not a condition for the verb preceding it when "wa" is present. Do you not see that you say: "I came to you so that you would be kind to me," and you do not say: "I came to you and so that you would be kind to me"? But if you say it, you mean: "and so that you would be kind, I came to you." He said: This is frequent in the Qur'an, among it His words: ﴿and that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾ [al-An'am: 113], and His words: ﴿Thus We showed Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that he might be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am: 75]. Had the "wa" not been there, it would have been a condition in your saying: "We showed him the dominion of the heavens and the earth so that he would be..." When the "wa" is present, there is an implied verb after it, and "that he might be among the certain" means: "We showed him."[[This is the saying of al-Farra', and this is the text of his words in Maʿani al-Qur'an 1:113.]]
* *
Abu Jaʿfar said: This view is more correct in Arabic grammar, because His words "wa-litukmilū al-ʿiddah" do not have before them a "lām" of the same sense as the "lām" in His words "wa-litukmilū al-ʿiddah," so that it would conjoin with "wa-litukmilū al-ʿiddah" to it. And the presence of "wa" with it indicates that it is a condition for a verb after it, since if the "wa" were removed it would be a condition for the verb preceding it.
* *
Concerning the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿and that you magnify Allah for having guided you﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: The Exalted means: and that you exalt Allah by remembering Him for what He has bestowed upon you, of guidance, which He withheld from others of the people of the religions upon whom fasting the month of Ramadan was prescribed as it was prescribed upon you, so they went astray from it through Allah's leading them astray; and He has singled you out with His honor and guided you to it, and granted you success in performing what Allah prescribed upon you of its fasting, and that you thank Him for that by worshipping Him.
* *
The remembrance by which Allah urged them to magnify Him is "takbir" (proclaiming Allahu akbar) on the day of al-Fitr, according to what a group of the interpreters have taken it to mean.

Those who said so:

2901. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr related to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Dawud ibn Qays, who said: I heard Zayd ibn Aslam say: "and that you magnify Allah for having guided you" — he said: when one sees the new moon, the takbir is from the time one sees the new moon until the Imam finishes, on the road and in the mosque, except that when the Imam is present one refrains and does not proclaim takbir except with his takbir.

2902. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Suwayd related to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, saying: I heard Sufyan say: "and that you magnify Allah for having guided you" — he said: We have been informed that it is the takbir on the day of al-Fitr.

2903. Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: Ibn ʿAbbas used to say: It is incumbent upon the Muslims, when they see the new moon of Shawwal, to proclaim takbir to Allah until they finish their festival, because the Exalted has said: "and that you complete the period and that you magnify Allah for having guided you." Ibn Zayd said: It is fitting for them, when they go out to the musalla, to proclaim takbir; when they sit, they proclaim takbir; when the Imam comes, they fall silent; when the Imam proclaims takbir, they proclaim takbir; they do not proclaim takbir when the Imam comes except with his takbir, until he finishes and the prayer is concluded, and then the festival has ended. Yunus said: Ibn Wahb said: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: The consensus (jamaʿah) among us is that they go out to the musalla with takbir.
* *
Concerning the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿so that you may be thankful﴾ (185)

Abu Jaʿfar said: The Exalted means by this: that you may thank Allah for what He has bestowed upon you of guidance and success, and the facilitation of what, had He willed, would have been difficult for you.

"La'alla" (perhaps/so that) in this place has the meaning of "kay" (in order that) [[See what has preceded at 1:364, and the references in the index of Arabic linguistic topics.]], and therefore it is conjoined with it in His words: "and that you complete the period, and that you magnify Allah for having guided you, and so that you may be thankful."

**The commentary on His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And when My servants ask you, [Muhammad], concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me that they may be guided﴾ [2:186]**

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: And when your servants, O Muhammad, ask you about Me, saying, "Where am I?", then indeed I am near to them. I hear their supplication and I respond to the supplication of the one who supplicates among them.

* *

The scholars have differed regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse.

Some of them said: It was revealed concerning a questioner who asked the Prophet ﷺ, saying, "O Muhammad, is our Lord near, so that we may confide in Him, or is He far, so that we must call out to Him?" So God revealed: "And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near, I respond..." to the end of the verse.

2904. Ibn Humayd narrated to us this, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Abdah al-Sijistani, from al-Sulb ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather.

[[Hadith 2904. Jarir: he is Ibn Abd al-Hamid al-Dabbi, who has passed in 2028 and 2346. Abdah al-Sijistani: he is Abdah ibn Abi Barzah. Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned him (3/1/90) and mentioned no criticism of him. I have not found a biography of him elsewhere.

"al-Sijistani" is the correct reading, established here and in the reliable sources, as will come. In some references it appears as "al-Sakhtiyani", which is a clear printing error.

al-Sulb ibn Hakim: The Hafiz Abd al-Ghani al-Azdi al-Misri, in al-Mu'talif wal-Mukhtalif (p. 79), states that it is "Sulb", with a dotted letter yeh beneath and a damma on the sad. He described him saying: "Sulb ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather. Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated his hadith from Jarir, from Abdah ibn Abi Barzah al-Sijistani."

Likewise al-Dhahabi said in al-Mushtabih (p. 316): "Sulb ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather. He is confused with al-Salt ibn Hakim." In the margin of one of his manuscripts, quoting its margin: "al-Khatib said: it was said he is a brother of Bahz ibn Hakim, but that is not sound. He is also confused with al-Salt ibn Hakim, with a damma on the ha. It is said: al-Hakim ibn al-Salt." Likewise the Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in Tabsir al-Muntabih (a photographed manuscript in my possession), stating that "it has been said: al-Sulb ibn Hakim, mentioned earlier, is the brother of Bahz ibn Hakim, but this is not sound."

However, despite this, he mentioned him in Lisan al-Mizan (3:195) under the chapter "al-Salt", quoting al-Mizan, and mentioned this hadith for him. He mentioned al-Dhahabi's narration of it with its chain to "Muhammad ibn Humayd". Then he mentioned, also quoting al-Dhahabi, that Ibn Abi Khaythamah narrated it in a juz' of those who narrated from their fathers from their grandfathers, and that "al-Ala'i quoted it in the book al-Wushy from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad, and said: I have not seen any mention of al-Salt in the books of men's biographies." Then the Hafiz commented: "I say: al-Daraqutni mentioned him in al-Mu'talif and related the difference: is his final letter with a single dot or two? He said he is the son of Hakim ibn Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah, the brother of Bahz ibn Hakim the well-known narrator. And neither al-Salt, nor his father, nor his grandfather is mentioned in the books of transmitters, except what I mentioned of Ibn Abi Khaythamah's mention, and he added nothing to the identification beyond what is here."

This is a severe confusion on the part of al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar. Moreover, what he quoted from al-Dhahabi's Mizan al-I'tidal is not mentioned in the printed edition of it. So it appears it fell out of the sources from which the Mizan was printed.

The sounder view in my opinion is that of al-Dhahabi, Ibn Hajar, Ibn Abi Khaythamah and Abd al-Ghani al-Azdi: that it is "Sulb" with a damma on the sad and a single dot at its end. And that he, his father and his grandfather are unknown. As for Hakim ibn Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah al-Qushayri, he is a well-known Successor (tabi'i), and his father is a well-known Companion. Hakim ibn Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah's sons Bahz, Sa'id and Mihran narrated from him. So this one called "Sulb" has no connection with these.

This hadith is extremely weak, its chain collapsed in every case.

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir erred when he mentioned it (1:413-414) and made it a hadith from "Mu'awiyah ibn Haydah al-Qushayri".

al-Suyuti also mentioned it (1:194) and erred in another way: he made it "from the route of al-Salt ibn Hakim, from a man of the Ansar, from his father, from his grandfather"!! The addition "from a man of the Ansar" may be an error of the copyists rather than of al-Suyuti.]]

2905. al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ja'far ibn Sulayman informed us, from Awf, from al-Hasan, who said: The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ asked the Prophet ﷺ, "Where is our Lord?" So God, may His remembrance be exalted, revealed: "And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near; I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me," to the end of the verse.

[[Hadith 2905. Ja'far ibn Sulayman: he is al-Dab'i, with a dotted dad and a single-dotted ba. He is trustworthy; Ibn Ma'in and others declared him reliable.

Awf: he is Ibn Abi Jamilah al-A'rabi, a well-known reliable narrator from whom the authors of the six books related. A narration from him has already passed (645). He is known for narrating from al-Hasan al-Basri.

This chain is sound up to al-Hasan. But the hadith is weak, because it is mursal: al-Hasan did not link it to any of the Companions.

Abu Ja'far narrated it here through the route of Abd al-Razzaq, but I did not find it in Abd al-Razzaq's Tafsir. Perhaps it is in another place in his books.]]

* *

Others said: Rather, it was revealed in answer to a question from a people who asked the Prophet ﷺ: "At what hour do we call upon God?"

Those who said this:

2906. Sufyan ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ata', who said: When the verse was revealed, ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [40:60], they said, "At what hour?" Then it was revealed: "And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near," to His saying: "that they may be guided."

2907. Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ata' concerning His words, "I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me," they said: "If only we knew at what hour to call!" Then it was revealed: "And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near," to the end of the verse.

2908. al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ata' ibn Abi Rabah claimed that it reached him: When the verse was revealed, ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾, people said, "If only we knew at what hour we should call!" Then it was revealed: "And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me that they may be guided."

2909. Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, concerning "And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me." He said: There is no believing servant who calls upon God except that He responds to him. If what he calls for is provision for him in this world, God gives it to him; if it is not provision in this world, He stores it for him until the Day of Resurrection and wards off a harm from him by it.

2910. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Layth ibn Sa'd narrated to us, from Ibn Salih, from one who narrated to him, that it reached him that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "No one is given the supplication and then denied the response, for God says: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾."

* *

The meaning according to those who took this interpretation: "And when My servants ask you concerning Me," meaning: At what hour do they call upon Me? Indeed I am near to them at every time, I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me.

* *

Others said: Rather, it was revealed in answer to the saying of a people who, when God said to them, ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾, said: "Toward where shall we call Him?"

Those who said this:

2911. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Mujahid said: "﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾", they said, "Toward where?" Then it was revealed: ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God. Indeed God is all-Encompassing, Knowing﴾ [2:115].

* *

Others said: Rather, it was revealed in answer to people who said: "How should we call?"

Those who said this:

2912. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: It was mentioned to us that when God revealed "Call upon Me, I will respond to you", men said, "How should we call, O Prophet of God?" Then God revealed: "And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near," to His saying "they may be guided."

* *

As for His saying, "So let them respond to Me," it means: So let them respond to Me with obedience. It is said of this: "I responded to him" and "I responded him" (istajabtu lahu / istajabtuhu), meaning "I answered him", as Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi said:

And a caller called out to one who would answer generosity, but at that moment no answerer responded to him.

He means: he did not answer him.

* *

Mujahid and a group other than him said something similar to what we have said regarding this.

2913. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: al-Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Mujahid said regarding His saying, "So let them respond to Me": "So let them obey Me." He said: "The response" is obedience.

2914. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Hibban ibn Musa narrated to us, who said: I asked Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak about His saying, "So let them respond to Me," and he said: "The obedience of God."

* *

Some said: The meaning of "So let them respond to Me" is: So let them call upon Me.

Those who said this:

2915. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Mansur ibn Harun narrated to me, from Abu Raja' al-Khurasani, who said regarding "So let them respond to Me": "So let them call upon Me."

* *

As for His saying, "And let them believe in Me," it means: And let them affirm. That is: And let them believe in Me, when they respond to Me with obedience, that I am, for them, beyond their obedience to Me, the one who grants reward for it and who magnifies honour for them because of it.

* *

As for the one who interpreted "So let them respond to Me" as meaning "So let them call upon Me", he interpreted His saying "And let them believe in Me" as: And let them believe in Me that I respond to them.

Those who said this:

2916. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Mansur ibn Harun narrated to me, from Abu Raja' al-Khurasani, concerning "And let them believe in Me," he says: "That I respond to them."

* *

As for His saying, "that they may be guided," it means: So let them respond to Me with obedience, and let them believe in Me, so that they affirm, in their obedience to Me, the reward from Me for them, and that they be guided by that deed, and so be rightly guided, as:

2917. al-Muthanna narrated to me with it, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi' concerning His saying, "that they may be guided," he says: "That they may be rightly guided."

* *

If someone says to us: What is the meaning of this statement of God, may His remembrance be exalted? For you see many humans calling upon God and their supplication is not answered, and He has said, "I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me"?

It is said: There are two meanings to this:

One: that "the invocation" refers to acting upon what God has urged and commanded. The meaning of the speech would then be: "And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near to those who obey Me and act upon what I have commanded them; I respond to them with reward for their obedience to Me when they obey Me." So the meaning of "supplication" is the servant's request of his Lord and what He promised His friends for their obedience through their acting upon His obedience, and the meaning of "response" from God, which He has guaranteed to them, is the fulfilment to those who act for Him of what He promised them for what He commanded them. As it was related from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Indeed supplication is worship."

2918. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Juwaybir narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Dhar, from Yusay' al-Hadrami, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Indeed supplication is worship." Then he recited: ﴿And your Lord said: Call upon Me, I will respond to you. Indeed those who disdain My worship will enter Hell, humbled﴾ [40:60].

[[Hadith 2918. As for the hadith itself, it is a sound hadith. As for this exact chain, I do not know how it stands, given its weakness!

For Ibn Humayd, the teacher of al-Tabari, is Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Razi, whose reliability has been established previously (2028, 2253).

But it is impossible for him to say "Juwaybir narrated to us", because Ibn Humayd died in the year 248, while Juwaybir ibn Sa'id al-Azdi died about a hundred years earlier. al-Bukhari mentioned him in al-Saghir (p. 176) among those who died between the years 140 and 150. So a teacher must have fallen out between them, an error by the copyists. Moreover, this Juwaybir is very weak, as we explained at 284.

al-A'mash: he is Sulayman ibn Mihran, the well-known imam.

Dhar, with a dotted dhal and a doubled ra: he is Ibn Abd Allah al-Murhibi, with a damma on the mim, a sukun on the ra, and a kasra on the ha followed by a single-dotted ya. He is trustworthy; the authors of the six books related from him.

Yusay' (with a damma on the first ya, a sukun on the second, and an unpointed sin between them, with a fatha): he is Ibn Ma'dan al-Hadrami, in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir (4/2/425-426), and Ibn Abi Hatim (4/2/313). In the printed edition here it is written "Subay'", which is a misreading.

The hadith will come in al-Tabari at 24:51-52 (Bulaq edition) with six chains. The name "Dhar" there is written as "Zar", with a zay instead of a dhal.

It is a sound hadith. Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad (4:271, al-Halabi), from Abu Mu'awiyah, from al-A'mash, with this same chain. So it does not contain the weak "Juwaybir" mentioned here.

Ibn Kathir quoted it (7:309) from that place in the Musnad, and said: "Thus have the authors of the Sunan narrated it: al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir, all from the hadith of al-A'mash, with the same chain. al-Tirmidhi said: hasan sahih." He also said that Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Jarir narrated it from the hadith of Shu'bah, from Mansur and al-A'mash, both from Dhar, with the same chain; then he mentioned that Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim also narrated it.

It is in al-Hakim (1:490-491) with several chains, and then he said: "This hadith is sound in its chain, but they did not record it." al-Dhahabi agreed with him.

al-Suyuti mentioned it (5:355) and added its attribution to Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman.]]

* *

So he ﷺ informed that calling upon God is in fact worshipping Him and asking Him, by acting for Him and obeying Him.

Something similar to what we have said on this has been mentioned, that al-Hasan used to say:

2919. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Mansur ibn Harun narrated to me, from Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from al-Hasan, that he said regarding it: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾: "Act and rejoice, for it is a truth due from God that He will respond to those who believe and do righteous deeds, and will increase them from His bounty."

* *

The other interpretation: that its meaning is: "I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me, if you wish." In that case, although its wording is general, its meaning is particular.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 1 of 8):

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿It has been made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to go in unto your wives﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His, the Exalted's, words "It has been made lawful for you" (uhilla lakum), He means: He has released and permitted for you [[See the explanation of "halal" (lawful) earlier in this volume, 3: 300, 301.]].
* *
By His words "on the night of the fast" (laylat al-siyam), He means: during the night of the fast.
* *
As for "ar-rafath" (rafath), it is a metaphor here for sexual intercourse (al-jima'), as it is said: "huwa al-rafath wa al-rufuth" (he is rafath, and rufuth) [[See what follows on the meaning of "rafath" in this volume (2: 153–155, Bulaq edition).]].
* *
It has also been transmitted that in the reading of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) it is: "uhilla lakum laylat al-siyam al-rufuth ila nisa'ikum."
* *
The people of interpretation have said the same as what we have said concerning the interpretation of "rafath."
Mention of those who said that:
2920 – Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam al-Misri narrated to me, saying: Ayyub ibn Suwayd narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Asim, from Bakr, from Abd Allah al-Muzani, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Rafath" is intercourse, but Allah is Generous and uses euphemism.
2921 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Asim, from Bakr, from Ibn Abbas, the like of it.
2922 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Rafath" is marriage (al-nikah).
2923 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, who said: "Rafath" is approaching women (ghishyan al-nisa').
2924 – Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words "It has been made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to go in unto your wives," who said: intercourse.
2925 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.
2926 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Rafath" is marriage (al-nikah).
2927 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Kabir al-Basri narrated to us, saying: al-Dahhak ibn Uthman narrated to us, saying: I asked Salim ibn Abd Allah about His words "It has been made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, the rafath to your wives," and he said: It is intercourse.
2928 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "It has been made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, the rafath to your wives," he says: intercourse.
* *
"Rafath" in other than this context means obscenity in speech, as al-Ajjaj said:
"from idle talk and obscene speech" (ʿan al-laghā wa rafath al-takallum) [[From his Diwan, p. 59; it appears with the preceding verse in the commentary at 2: 246 (Bulaq), from a long rajaz in which he praised God and glorified Him, saying: "So praise be to God, the Most High, the Greatest... possessor of majesty and splendor, the Most Magnificent... and Knower of the manifest and the hidden... and Lord of every disbeliever and Muslim," then continued with many verses until he reached what al-Tabari recited: "And Lord of troops of pilgrims, restrained... from idle talk and obscene speech." The word asrab is the plural of sarb, meaning a herd or group of gazelles, sheep, cattle, or women, and he applied it here to pilgrims. Hajij means pilgrims. Kuzzam is the plural of kazim, meaning one who is silent, holding his tongue and humbled, from al-kazm (with two fatha), which is the outlet of breath. Al-laghā and al-laghw mean worthless talk or oath, from which no benefit or gain is obtained.
Moreover, what shows that Abu Ja'far sometimes abridged his discussion is that he did not explain the government of "rafath" by the preposition "ila" (to). Had it not been for abridgment, he would have said something on it according to his method earlier. "Rafath" is construed with "ila" because it carries the meaning of ifda' (going in unto). It is said: "afdaytu ila imra'ati" (I went in unto my wife). When he intended this meaning, he brought its particle to imply its meaning, signalling that this was what he intended by this euphemism.]]
* *
Interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this He, the Exalted, means: your women are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them.
* *
If someone says: How can your women be a garment for you, and you a garment for them, when "garment" (libas) refers only to what is worn?
It is said: There are two meanings for this:
The first: that each of them is made a garment for the other, because of their being stripped during sleep [[In the printed edition: "li-takhrujihima 'inda al-nawm" (for their coming out during sleep), which I fear is a misreading: the jim was made a kha, and the dal was joined to the ha, so the copyist thought it was a kha, due to their similarity. I did not find in the root "kh-r-j" the form "kharraja" with doubled ra' meaning stripping of garments, though they say "kharaja fulan min thiyabih" (so-and-so came out of his clothes), but its meaning does not appear here since the mention of garment is omitted from the phrase. Though I consider it distant, even if the word garment were mentioned with it. What confirms this correction for me is his saying after the following verse: "stripped in one bed."]] and their being together in one garment, and the pressing of each one's body against the other's, is like what one wears on one's body of garments. So it is said of each of them: he is a "garment" for the other, as the poet Nabigha of Banu Ja'dah said:
"When the bedfellow turns her side, they are drawn together, and she becomes a garment over him."
[[The poetry from Al-Shi'r wa al-Shu'ara', p. 255, from fine verses, and Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu Ubaydah, p. 67, and Ta'wil Mushkil al-Qur'an, p. 107, and others. Before it: "The fire lit for us a face, bright, mingled with the fa'a's brightness..." It is poetry, as you see.]]
It is narrated as "tathannat" (she bent), and so He used "garment" as a euphemism for their being together, stripped in one bed, just as "garments" is used as an euphemism for the human body, as Layla said describing camels ridden by a people:
"They pelted it with light garments, so you see for it no likeness except the startled ostrich."
[[Al-Ma'ani al-Kabir 1: 486, Ta'wil Mushkil al-Qur'an 107, and others. Their words "they pelted it with garments" — they said: meaning with light bodies (al-Ma'ani). The correct understanding is that these riders have been scorched by the desert and worn thin, so that nothing remains of them but bones with the clothes draped over them; one sees nothing but a garment flapping over every lean and thin body, and therefore the camels with their riders were likened to the startled ostrich. "Munaffar" is one that is frightened and runs off fleeing, flapping on the ground.]]
That is: they pelted it with themselves and rode it. And as the Hudhali [[He is Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali.]] said:
"He disavows the blood of the slain and its avenging, while her waist-wrap has caught the slain man's blood."
[[His Diwan, p. 26, and Al-Ma'ani al-Kabir 483, and Mushkil al-Qur'an 108, and others. From a wondrous ode of his in which he mourns his friend and intimate Nushayba ibn Mahraith, which he opened by amatory address to his beloved Umm Amr, whose name was Futayma, and before this verse he said, blaming himself for abandoning her: "Surely you, with her and the excuse, after you have persisted, and Futayma's abode has become distant, are like the woman who tended her leftover... she said: it is forbidden that her neighbour comb his hair..." and "disavows the blood of the slain..."
He says: you, in your denial of love for her after persisting in it, are like this woman who killed a slain man and seized his spoils, that is his weapon, and hid it. Al-Asma'i said regarding the report of this woman: this is a woman in whose place a man alighted, and she scrupled to anoint him or comb his hair. Then a dog came and drank from her vessel, and she washed it seven times, and that was in the man's sight, so he marvelled at her and at her piety. While he was thus, people came to her seeking a slain man with her, so she denied it and swore. Then they searched her dwelling and found the slain man and his weapon in her house.
He says: you are like this woman, denying the love of your beloved and showing that you have grown old and given up ignorance and youthfulness, yet if your heart were searched, they would see that your love for her still blazes and flares.]]
That is, "her waist-wrap" means herself. And on this basis al-Rabi' used to say:
2929 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Abu Ja'far narrated to us, from al-Rabi', regarding "They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them," he says: they are a blanket for you, and you are a blanket for them. [[Report 2929: In the printed edition "Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'id," but it has passed as number 2917, correctly as I have written it. Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd ibn Ammar ibn Sa'd al-Qaraz al-Mu'addib, narrated from his father and his paternal uncle Muhammad and his cousins, and a group of his family, and Abu al-Zinad and Safwan ibn Sulaym; and from him narrated Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and Ibrahim ibn al-Mundhir and others. Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy. Al-Bukhari said: there is scrutiny concerning him. Al-Hakim Abu Ahmad said: his hadith is not upright.]].
* *
The other meaning: that He made each of them a "garment" for the other because it is a repose for him, as the Exalted said: ﴿He made the night for you a garment﴾ [Surah al-Furqan: 47], meaning a repose in which you rest. Likewise a man's wife is his repose, to which he finds rest, as the Exalted said: ﴿And He made from it its mate that he might find repose in her﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 189]. So each of them is a "garment" for the other in the sense of his tranquillity in him. Mujahid and others used to say this.
It may be said of what covers a thing and hides it from the eyes of those looking at it: "it is his garment and his covering." So it is permissible that it was said: "They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them," meaning: each of you conceals the other, in what occurs between you of intercourse, from the eyes of all other people.
Mujahid and others used to say this:
2930 – al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them," he says: a repose for them.
2931 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them." Qatadah said: They are a repose for you, and you are a repose for them.
2932 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "They are a garment for you," he says: a repose for you, "and you are a garment for them," he says: a repose for them.
2933 – Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said regarding His words "They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them": the making love (al-muwaqa'a).
2934 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to me, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim narrated to us, from Yazid, from Amr ibn Dinar, from Ibn Abbas regarding His words "They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them," he said: They are a repose for you, and you are a repose for them.
* *
Interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves, so He accepted your repentance and pardoned you. So now, have intercourse with them and seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾

Abu Ja'far said: If someone asks us: What is this betrayal which the people were committing against themselves, from which Allah turned in acceptance and pardoned them?
It is said: Their betrayal of themselves, which Allah mentioned, concerned two things: the first, intercourse with women; the second, eating and drinking at the time when that was forbidden to them, as:
2935 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Amr ibn Murrah, who said: Ibn Abi Layla narrated to us that the man, when he broke his fast and slept, would not approach his wife, and if he slept he would not eat, until Umar ibn al-Khattab came desiring his wife, and his wife said: You had already slept! He thought she was making an excuse, so he approached her. He said: And a man of the Ansar came and wanted to eat, and they said: Shall we warm something for you?...... [[Report 2935: the place of these dots is a gap in the copies. The report of Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla was transmitted by Waki' and Abd ibn Humayd from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, and it is in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 198, with a different wording. If it were to be completed, it would read:
[We will warm something for you, will you break your fast on it?" Then his eyes overcame him and he slept. They came when he had slept, and said: Eat! He said: I had already slept! So he left the food and spent the night turning over. When he rose in the morning, he came to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned that to him. Then Umar ibn al-Khattab stood and said: O Messenger of Allah, last night I desired my wife as a man desires his wife, but she said: she had already slept! I thought she was making an excuse, so I approached her, and she informed me that she had indeed slept.]
This is another wording, but it indicates the meaning mentioned by Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, which al-Tabari relied upon. Then see the following reports 2936–2938 from Ibn Abi Layla.]] He said: Then this verse was revealed: "It has been made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to go in unto your wives" — the verse.
2936 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: Husayn ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, who said: They used to fast three days of every month. When Ramadan came they would fast, and if a man did not eat at his breaking of the fast until he slept, he would not eat until the next such time, and if he or his wife slept, it was not lawful for him to approach her until the next such time. Then a shaykh of the Ansar called Sirmah ibn Malik came and said to his household: Feed me! She said: Wait until I make something warm for you! He said: Then his eye overcame him and he slept. Then Umar came, and his wife said to him: I have slept! He did not excuse her, and thought she was making an excuse, so he approached her. Thus this one and that one spent the night turning over, back and front. So Allah revealed concerning that: "Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread at dawn," and He said: "So now, have intercourse with them," and Allah pardoned that, and it became a practice.
2937 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah narrated to us, from Amr ibn Murrah, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: They used to eat, drink, and approach women so long as they had not slept; when they slept, they left off food, drink, and approaching women. A man of the Ansar called Abu Sirmah was working on his land, and when it was time for his breaking of the fast he slept, and he woke up fasting and exhausted. When the Prophet ﷺ saw him he said: What is wrong with you, that I see you exhausted? So he informed him of what had happened to him. And a man betrayed himself regarding the matter of women, so Allah revealed: "It has been made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to go in unto your wives," to the end of the verse. [[The hadith: 2937 is part of a long hadith, some of which passed with this isnad: 2729, 2733. In the printed edition there is a distortion in the isnad here, thus: "Abd al-Rahman ibn Ubayd Allah from Utbah"! The correct form is: "Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah," who is al-Mas'udi, as we explained earlier.
We have indicated earlier that Abu Dawud narrated this lengthy hadith (507) through Yazid ibn Harun, from al-Mas'udi. But he did not mention the part here in full, rather he referred to it, citing the narration before it, saying: "Sirmah came, having worked his day," and went on with the hadith.
The hadith is extended in Musnad Ahmad 5: 246–247, through Abu al-Nadr and Yazid ibn Harun, both from al-Mas'udi, with the same chain. As we indicated in detail earlier: 2156. It contains the part here. But in it, the Ansari man is called "Sirmah," as in Abu Dawud's narration.
In the previous narration (2936) he is "Sirmah ibn Malik." In this narration here he is "Abu Sirmah."
The previous narration is mursal, and this narration is munqati', because Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla did not meet Mu'adh ibn Jabal. Further clarification about the name of this Ansari will come in the following narration: 2939.]]

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 2 of 8):**

2938. Sufyan ibn Waki' related to us, saying: My father told me, from Isra'il, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', similar to the hadith of Ibn Abi Layla, which he related through Amr ibn Murrah, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla. He said: When they fasted and one of them slept, he would not eat anything until the next day. A man of the Ansar came, having worked on his land; he was exhausted and weary, and sleep overcame him, and he woke the next morning in a state of distress. So this verse was revealed: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread [of night] at dawn﴾.

[[Hadith 2938: This is a sound isnad, were it not for the weakness of Sufyan ibn Waki', as we have said many times. However, it is established in the Tafsir of Waki', as al-Suyuti mentioned. Al-Tabari did not mention its full wording; he referred to the narrations before it. He will mention it in full after this.]]

2939. Al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Abd Allah ibn Raja' al-Basri related to us, saying: Isra'il related to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', who said: When a man among the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) was fasting and slept before breaking his fast, he would not eat until the same time the following day. Qays ibn Sirma al-Ansari was fasting, and that day he had exerted himself working on his land. When the time for breaking the fast came, he went to his wife and said: "Do you have any food?" She said: "No, but I will go and find some for you." Sleep overcame him, and when his wife returned she said: "You have slept!" By midday he had fainted. He mentioned this to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed concerning him: ﴿It is made lawful for you to go in to your wives on the night of the fast﴾, up to ﴿from the black thread﴾. They rejoiced greatly at it.

[[Hadith 2939: This is a sound isnad. Abd Allah ibn Raja' al-Ghadha'i: his reliability was established previously (2814).
The hadith is established from the hadith of Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, from al-Bara' ibn Azib al-Ansari:
Ahmad related it in al-Musnad 4: 295 (Halabi), from Aswad ibn Amir and Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri. Al-Bukhari 4: 111-112 (Fath), from Ubayd Allah ibn Musa. Abu Dawud: 2314, through Abu Ahmad. Al-Tirmidhi 4: 71-72, through Ubayd Allah ibn Musa; all of them from Isra'il, from his grandfather Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i. Al-Nasa'i 1: 305 related it through Zuhayr, from Abu Ishaq. Al-Bukhari also related it 8: 136, abridged, from Ubayd Allah ibn Musa, and with another isnad from Abu Ishaq.
Al-Suyuti mentioned it 1: 197, adding its attribution to Waki', Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nahhas in his Nasikh, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan.
The Hafiz [Ibn Hajar] extensively discussed in Fath 4: 111-112 the disagreement over the name of the Ansari and the narrations concerning it. He preferred that he was "Abu Qays Sirma ibn Abi Anas Qays ibn Malik ibn Adi..." and that the disagreement arose from this: some of them erred in his name and called him by his kunya, some attributed him to his grandfather, some inverted his lineage, and some distorted it to "Damra ibn Anas"; its correct form is "Sirma ibn Abi Anas." He did likewise in al-Isaba, at greater length, 3: 241-243, 280. "Sirma" is with a kasra on the unmarked letter (s), a silent r, and a fatha on the m.]]

2940. Al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih related to us, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, concerning the saying of Allah, may He be remembered: ﴿It is made lawful for you to go in to your wives on the night of the fast﴾. This was because the Muslims, during the month of Ramadan, when they had prayed the night prayer, were forbidden women and food until the same time the following night. Then some Muslims had intercourse with women and ate food in Ramadan after the night prayer, among them Umar ibn al-Khattab. They complained of this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so Allah revealed: ﴿Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves, so He turned to you in forgiveness and pardoned you. So now, have relations with them﴾, meaning: marry them, ﴿and eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread [of night] at dawn﴾.

[[Hadith 2940: Ibn Kathir mentioned it 1: 418-419, without takhrij. Al-Suyuti 1: 197 attributed it only to Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir.]]

2941. Al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Suwayd related to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Ibn Lahi'a, who said: Musa ibn Jubayr, a client of Banu Salima, told me that he heard Abd Allah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik narrate from his father, who said: In Ramadan, when a man fasted and then in the evening slept, food, drink and women were forbidden to him until he broke his fast the next day. Umar ibn al-Khattab returned one night from the Prophet (ﷺ), having spent the evening conversing with him. He found his wife had fallen asleep, and he desired her, but she said: "I have already slept!" He said: "You have not slept!" Then he had intercourse with her. Ka'b ibn Malik did the same. Umar went early to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him, and Allah, may He be remembered, revealed: ﴿Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves, so He turned to you in forgiveness and pardoned you. So now, have relations with them﴾... the verse.

[[Hadith 2941: Suwayd: he is Ibn Nasr ibn Suwayd al-Marwazi, and he is reliable. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib. Al-Bukhari, in al-Kabir 2/2/149, stated explicitly that he heard from Ibn al-Mubarak. He is mentioned as having died in the year 240 at the age of 91.
Ibn Lahi'a, with a fatha on the lam and a kasra on the ha: he is Abd Allah, the jurist and judge of Egypt. He is much disputed, and the verified position is that he is reliable and his hadith is sound. We have elaborated on him in the commentary on the Musnad: 87, 6613.
Musa ibn Jubayr al-Madani al-Haddha': reliable, though he errs in some of his hadith. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib and al-Kabir 4/1/281, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/139, and neither mentions any criticism of him. He is a client of "Banu Salima," with a fatha on the sin and a kasra on the lam, from the Ansar. See al-Mushtabih by al-Dhahabi, p. 270.
Abd Allah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik al-Ansari al-Salami, with a fatha on the lam, a nisba to "Banu Salima" (with a kasra): a reliable Successor (tabi'i). He was the guide of his father when he went blind. The two Shaykhs and others related from him.
The hadith was related by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 15860 (3: 460 Halabi), from Attab ibn Ziyad, from Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, with this isnad.
Ibn Kathir mentioned it 1: 420, from al-Tabari only.
Al-Suyuti mentioned it 1: 197, adding its attribution to Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim "with a hasan isnad." Its isnad was declared hasan, in my view, primarily because of Ibn Lahi'a, but in my judgment it is a sound isnad.]]

2942. Al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Al-Hajjaj related to us, saying: Hammad ibn Salama related to us, saying: Thabit related to us, that Umar ibn al-Khattab had relations with his wife one night in Ramadan, and it weighed heavily upon him. So Allah revealed: ﴿It is made lawful for you to go in to your wives on the night of the fast﴾.

[[Hadith 2942: Thabit: he is Ibn Aslam al-Bunani, with a damma on the b and a light n. He is a reliable Successor, but he narrates from junior Companions, such as Anas, Ibn al-Zubayr and Ibn Umar. He did not live to narrate from Umar ibn al-Khattab. Therefore this isnad is interrupted (munqati') and weak on that account. Al-Suyuti mentioned the hadith 1: 197, attributing it only to Ibn Jarir.]]

2943. Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father told me, saying: My paternal uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, concerning his words: ﴿It is made lawful for you to go in to your wives on the night of the fast; they are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾, up to ﴿and He pardoned you﴾. When people first embraced Islam, if one of them fasted, he would fast his day; then when evening came, he would eat food between that and the night prayer. Once the night prayer was prayed, food was forbidden to them until the evening of the following night. Umar ibn al-Khattab, while he was sleeping, was enticed by his own self and went to his wife for some need of his. When he had bathed, he began to weep and blame himself as much as you have ever seen blame. Then he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I apologize to Allah and to you for this sinful self of mine, for it adorned for me and I had relations with my wife! Do you find any concession for me, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "You were not deserving of that, O Umar!" When he reached his house, he sent for him and informed him of his excuse in a verse of the Qur'an, and Allah commanded His Messenger to place it in the middle hundred of Surat al-Baqara. So he said: ﴿It is made lawful for you to go in to your wives on the night of the fast﴾ up to ﴿Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves﴾, meaning by that what Umar ibn al-Khattab did, and Allah revealed His pardon. He said: ﴿So He turned to you in forgiveness and pardoned you. So now, have relations with them﴾ up to ﴿from the black thread﴾. Thus He made lawful for them intercourse, eating and drinking until the dawn became distinct to them.

[[Hadith 2943: This is a hadith with the chain of weak narrators (al-musalsal bil-du'afa'), which we explained in detail in (305). Al-Suyuti mentioned it 1: 197, attributing it to al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim.
We had no need to discuss it here, but we wished to introduce with it a hadith of Abu Hurayra with the same meaning. Al-Suyuti cited it 1: 197, attributing it only to al-Tabari, saying: "Ibn Jarir related from Abu Hurayra..."
Ibn Kathir mentioned it 1: 419 together with the end of its isnad, without mentioning who related it. From observing his method, it appears that he also transmitted it from al-Tabari.
We did not find it in al-Tabari, so either it fell out from the copyists or it is in another place in al-Tabari that has not reached us. We saw fit to include it for completeness and to preserve what is attributed to this great tafsir.
Ibn Kathir said: "Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah said, from Qays ibn Sa'd, from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from Abu Hurayra, concerning the saying of Allah (It is made lawful for you to go in to your wives on the night of the fast) up to His saying (Then complete the fast until the night), he said: Before this verse was revealed, the Muslims, when they had prayed the late night prayer, were forbidden food, drink and women until they broke their fast. Umar ibn al-Khattab had relations with his wife after the night prayer, and Sirma ibn Qays al-Ansari was overcome by sleep after the sunset prayer, and slept without having eaten his fill, and did not wake until the Prophet (ﷺ) had prayed the night prayer. He got up, ate and drank. When morning came he went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him of that. So Allah revealed at that time: (It is made lawful for you to go in to your wives on the night of the fast). He meant by "ar-rafath" intercourse with women. (They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them. Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves), meaning: you were having intercourse with women and eating and drinking after the night prayer. (So He turned to you in forgiveness and pardoned you. So now, have relations with them), meaning: have intercourse with them, (and seek what Allah has decreed for you), meaning: offspring, (and eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread at dawn. Then complete the fast until the night). Thus that was a pardon from Allah and mercy."
This is the wording of Ibn Kathir's narration; al-Suyuti abridged it somewhat.
This is a sound isnad from Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah to Abu Hurayra. As for what Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah transmitted, we do not know its status until we know its narrators.
Qays ibn Sa'd: he is al-Makki, Abu Abd al-Malik, and he is reliable. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/1/154, Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/99, and Ibn Sa'd 5: 355, but Ibn Sa'd mentioned that his kunya was "Abu Ubayd Allah." He said: "He succeeded Ata' ibn Abi Rabah in his gathering."
Qays's kunya in al-Bukhari is "Abu Abd Allah." The apparent position is that this is correct, because al-Dulabi mentioned him in al-Kuna 2: 59, under the heading "Abu Abd Allah."]]

2944. Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿It is made lawful for you to go in to your wives on the night of the fast﴾. He said: A man among the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) would fast during the day, and when evening came he would eat, drink and have intercourse with women. When he slept, all of that was forbidden to him until the same time the following night. Some of them deceived themselves in this matter, so Allah pardoned them and made [that] lawful for them after sleep and before it, throughout the night.

[[The addition in parentheses is indispensable; I inferred it from the report that follows it and from the context.]]

2945. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: The Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) would fast during Ramadan, and when evening came... [he then mentioned something like the hadith of Muhammad ibn Amr], and he added in it: Some of them deceived themselves, and Umar ibn al-Khattab was among those who deceived themselves. So Allah pardoned them and made that lawful for them after sleep and before it, and throughout the night.

2946. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, saying: Isma'il ibn Sharus informed me, from Ikrima, client of Ibn Abbas, that a man, whose name he mentioned [but I forgot it], from among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the Ansar, came one night while he was fasting. His wife said to him: "Do not sleep until we prepare food for you!" He slept, so she came and said: "You have slept, by Allah!" He said: "No, by Allah!" She said: "Yes, by Allah!" So he did not eat that night, and he woke up fasting and fainted. So the concession concerning him was revealed.

[[Hadith 2946: Isma'il ibn Sharus, Abu al-Miqdam al-San'ani: Ibn Hibban and Ibn Shahin mentioned him among the reliable (al-thiqat), as in Lisan al-Mizan. Ibn Sa'd mentioned him in al-Tabaqat 5: 397 and said nothing more than "he has narrated from him." Ibn Abi Hatim biographed him 1/1/177 and mentioned no criticism of him. Al-Bukhari in al-Kabir 1/1/359-360 mentioned that he narrates from Ikrima, in his own words, meaning not connected; this refers to this report, which is from Ikrima's own statement and is mursal, not traced back to any Companion. Al-Bukhari then said: "Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ma'mar: he used to yuthbij the hadith." Its editor, the scholar Shaykh Abd al-Rahman al-Yamani, transmitted from a margin of one copy of al-Tarikh al-Kabir: "that is, he does not relate it as it should be." The correct reading of this word is that it is "yuthbij," from "al-tathbij," with a thal and a jim: in the commentary on the Qamus 2: 13: "It is said: thabija al-kitab and al-kalam tathbijan: he did not clarify it. It is also said: he did not relate it as it should be. Al-Layth said: al-tathbij is confusion." This word was quoted in Lisan al-Mizan 1: 411 distorted to "yada' al-hadith" (he fabricates hadith)! This is an ugly distortion. This man was never accused of fabrication, and neither al-Bukhari nor al-Nasa'i mentioned him in al-Du'afa'.
"Sharus" is one of the rare names, and I have not found an explicit statement on its vocalization, except that it was vocalized in pen in the tafsir of Abd al-Razzaq with a fatha above the marked sin, a damma above the r, and two kasras below the unmarked s at its end. Shaykh Abd al-Rahman al-Yamani also transmitted this vocalization from one copy of al-Tarikh al-Kabir, and that a second copy in its margin is vocalized with a fatha above the sin and another above the waw, with a sukun above the r.
This hadith is mursal, as you see. It is in the tafsir of Abd al-Razzaq, p. 18. I did not find it in any other place besides these two.
We added the words [fa-nasituhu] ("so I forgot it") after the word "sammahu" from the tafsir of Abd al-Razzaq. In the printed edition it read "wa-unzilat al-rukhsa" with a waw instead of a fa'. We have kept the fa' from the tafsir of Abd al-Razzaq, since it is better here.]]

2947. Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada: ﴿Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves﴾. At the beginning of fasting they were commanded to fast three days of every month, and two rak'as in the morning and two rak'as in the evening. Then Allah made lawful for them in their fasting, during the three days and when Ramadan was first enjoined on them, eating and drinking and approaching women once they had broken their fast. Food, drink and intercourse with women were lawful for them as long as they had not slept; but if they slept, that was forbidden to them until the same time the following night. The deception of the people was that they would touch or partake of food, drink and intercourse with women after sleep, and that was the people deceiving themselves. Then Allah made lawful for them [after] that food, drink and intercourse with women until the rising of dawn.

[[Report 2947: The material within parentheses is an indispensable addition. The context of this report contains some strangeness, and I did not find it with this wording elsewhere. However, a similar report appears in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 198, which begins: "Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir related from Qatada," and it cites a report that differs entirely from it in most of its wording, though it agrees with it in some of the meaning, saying:
[This was before the fasting of Ramadan. They were commanded to fast three days of each month, one day out of every ten days. They were commanded to pray two rak'as in the morning and two rak'as in the evening. This was the beginning of prayer and fasting. They were in this fasting, and after Allah had enjoined Ramadan, when they slept they did not approach women or food until the same time the following night. Some Muslims would have intercourse with women and eat food after their sleep, and that was the deception of the people against themselves. So Allah revealed in that matter in the Qur'an: "Allah knew that you were deceiving yourselves," the verse.]]]

2948. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿It is made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to go in unto your wives﴾.
