He said: Before this verse, when one of the people fell asleep during the night, food, drink, and going in to his wife were not permitted to him until the following night. Some of the Muslims fell into this, so some of them ate or drank after their sleep, and some of them had intercourse with their wives, so God granted them this concession.

2949. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: Ramadan was prescribed for the Christians, and it was prescribed for them that they should not eat or drink after sleep, nor have intercourse with women during the month of Ramadan. Then it was prescribed for the believers as it had been prescribed for them, and the Muslims continued to act as the Christians did, until a man from the Ansar called Abu Qays ibn Sirma came. He used to work in the orchards of Medina for wages [[al-hitan is the plural of hai't, meaning an orchard of palm trees; if it has a wall around it, it is a hai't, and if it does not, it is a dahiyah, whose plural is al-dawahi.]]. He came to his family with dates, and said to his wife: "Exchange these dates for flour and make it into a porridge for me, perhaps I will eat it, for the dates have burned my insides!" She went and exchanged them for him, then she prepared it but was slow with it, so he fell asleep. She woke him, but he disliked disobeying God and His Messenger, and refused to eat, and he woke up fasting. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) saw him in the evening and said: "What is wrong with you, Abu Qays? Have you become exhausted?" [[al-tali' means one who has collapsed from fatigue, exertion, and weakness.]] So he related the story to him.

Umar ibn al-Khattab had been with a slave girl of his, along with some of the believers who had not controlled themselves. When Umar heard Abu Qays's words, he feared that something might be revealed concerning Abu Qays, so he remembered himself, stood up, and apologized to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), saying: "O Messenger of God, I seek refuge in God, I had intercourse with my slave girl, and I did not control myself last night!" When Umar spoke, those people also spoke, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You were not worthy of that, O son of al-Khattab!" So that ruling was abrogated for them, and He said: ﴿It is made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to go in unto your wives. They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them. God knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾, meaning: you were having intercourse with them in betrayal of yourselves, ﴿so He turned to you and pardoned you. So now, have relations with them and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, meaning: have intercourse with them, and he returned to Abu Qays and said: ﴿Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, [which is] the dawn﴾.

2950. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to Ata: "It is made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to go in unto your wives." He said: During Ramadan they would not touch women, nor eat or drink after they had slept, until the night of the following day. If they touched their wives before sleeping, they did not see any harm in it. A man from the Ansar had intercourse with his wife after he had slept, and said: "I have betrayed myself!" Then the Quran was revealed, and it made lawful for them the women, the food, and the drink until the white thread became distinct to them from the black thread, [which is] the dawn. He said: Mujahid said: The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) would fast during Ramadan, and when the fasting person reached the evening he would eat, drink, and have intercourse with women; but if he slept, all of that became forbidden to him until the like of it the following night. There were men among them who were betraying themselves in this, so He pardoned them and made lawful for them, after sleep and before it, during the night. So He said: ﴿It is made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to go in unto your wives﴾ ... the verse.

2951. Al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ikrimah, that he said regarding this verse: ﴿It is made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to go in unto your wives﴾, like the saying of Mujahid, and he added to it: Umar ibn al-Khattab said to his wife: "Do not sleep until I return from the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." She slept before he returned, so he said to her: "You are not asleep!" Then he had intercourse with her, until he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him, and this verse was revealed. Ikrimah said: The verse ﴿Eat and drink﴾ was revealed concerning Abu Qays ibn Sirma of the Banu al-Khazraj, who ate after sleeping.

2952. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq informed us, from Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Habban, that Sirma ibn Anas came to his family one night, and he was an old man, and he was fasting. They did not prepare food for him, so he lay down his head and dozed off. His wife brought his food and said to him: "Eat." He said: "I have already slept!" She said: "You did not sleep!" So he woke up in the morning hungry and exhausted, and God revealed: ﴿Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, [which is] the dawn﴾.

* *

As for "mubashara" (touching, intimate contact) in the speech of the Arabs, it is the meeting of skin with skin, and the "bashara" of a man is his outer skin.

* *

God, by His saying ﴿so now, have relations with them﴾, used a euphemism for intercourse. He says: So now, since I have made lawful for you the going in unto your wives, have intercourse with them during the nights of the month of Ramadan until the dawn rises, which is the distinction of the white thread from the black thread of dawn.

* *

Our statement regarding "mubashara" was also made by a group of the people of ta'wil [[Ta'wil (interpretation, the explanation of a text's meaning) is the term used by the early exegetes for explaining the Quran; the people of ta'wil are the exegetes.]].

Those who said that:

2953. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us. And Abd al-Hamid ibn Sinan narrated to us, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, from Sufyan. And Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam narrated to me, saying: Ayyub ibn Suwayd narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Asim, from Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Mubashara" is intercourse, but God is generous and uses euphemism.

2954. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Asim, from Bakr ibn Abd Allah al-Muzani, from Ibn Abbas, similarly.

2955. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muawiyah ibn Salih narrated to us, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿so now, have relations with them﴾, meaning: marry them.

2956. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Mubashara" is marriage.

2957. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to Ata regarding His saying ﴿so now, have relations with them﴾; he said: intercourse.

Every mention of "mubashara" in the Quran refers to intercourse itself. Abd Allah ibn Kathir said, like the saying of Ata, that it means food, drink, and women.

2958. Humayd ibn Mas'adah narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us. And Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Mubashara" is intercourse, but God uses euphemism for whatever He wills by whatever He wills [[The report: 2958 — in the printed edition it reads "Muhammad ibn Mas'adah," but the correct reading is what has been recorded; it appeared previously in nos. 2774 and 2883, and he is Humayd ibn Mas'adah ibn al-Mubarak al-Bahili al-Basri. Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy. He died in the year 244.]].

2959. Yaqub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Abu Bishr informed us, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, the same.

2960. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿so now, have relations with them﴾, he says: have intercourse with them.

2961. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "Mubashara" is intercourse.

2962. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ata, the same.

2963. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from al-Awza'i, who said: Abdah ibn Abi Lubabah narrated to me, saying: I heard Mujahid say: "Mubashara" in the Book of God is intercourse.

2964. Ibn al-Barqi narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Abi Salamah narrated to us, saying: al-Awza'i said: someone who heard Mujahid say narrated to us: "Mubashara" in the Book of God is intercourse.

* *

They differed regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾. Some of them said: it means offspring.

Those who said that:

2965. Abd Allah ibn Abd Allah al-Saffar al-Basri narrated to me, saying: Isma'il ibn Ziyad al-Katib narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from al-Hakam, from Mujahid: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, he said: offspring [[The report: 2965 — Abdah ibn Abd Allah ibn Abdah al-Saffar: a trustworthy transmitter among the teachers of al-Bukhari. He is one of the rare teachers from whom he narrated in his Sahih while they were still alive, for he died in the year 258, two years after al-Bukhari. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/90, and Rijal al-Sahihayn, p. 336. Isma'il ibn Ziyad al-Katib: I do not know with certainty who he is; in this biography there are several teachers in al-Tahdhib 1: 298-301, and Lisan al-Mizan 1: 405-407, but I nearly lean toward it being the one for whom Ibn Majah narrated a hadith (no. 1314) from Ibn Jurayj, under the name "Isma'il ibn Ziyad" without a title or description.]].

2966. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Sahl ibn Yusuf and Abu Dawud narrated to us, from Shu'bah, who said: I heard al-Hakam: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, he said: offspring.

2967. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Abu Tumaylah narrated to us, saying: Ubayd Allah narrated to us, from Ikrimah regarding His saying: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, he said: offspring.

2968. Ali ibn Sahl narrated to me, saying: Mu'mil narrated to us, saying: Abu Mawdud Bahr ibn Musa narrated to us, who said: I heard al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan say regarding this verse: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, he said: offspring.

2969. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, it is offspring.

2970. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to us, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to us, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, meaning: the child.

2971. Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, who said: Isa narrated to me, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, he said: offspring; if this one does not bear, then that one.

2972. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

2973. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us: Abd al-Razzaq informed us: Ma'mar informed us, from someone who heard al-Hasan regarding His saying: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, he said: it is offspring.

2974. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His saying: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, he said: what God has prescribed for you of offspring.

2975. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, he said: intercourse.

2976. It was narrated to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: al-Fadl ibn Khalid narrated to us, saying: Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim regarding His saying: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, he said: offspring [[The report: 2976 — "al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj" appears in the printed edition as "al-Hasan ibn al-Faraj," which is an error repeated many times, including in no. 2719. We see no need to repeat the note on it again.]].

* *

Some of them said: the meaning of that is the Night of Power.

Those who said that:

2977. Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i narrated to us, saying: Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to me, from Amr ibn Malik, from Abu al-Jawza', from Ibn Abbas: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, he said: the Night of Power. Abu Hisham said: Mu'adh read it this way.

2978. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Muslim ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Malik narrated to us, from Abu al-Jawza', from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, he said: the Night of Power [[The two reports: 2977–2978 — Amr ibn Malik, in both chains, is al-Nakri, with a short "n" and a sukun on the "k," a nisba to "Banu Nakrah" of Abd al-Qays. He is trustworthy. Abu al-Jawza': he is Aws ibn Abd Allah al-Rab'i, a well-known trustworthy Successor whose narrations were recorded by the two Shaykhs and by all the authors of the six books. We have explained his condition and the condition of Amr ibn Malik, who narrates from him, in the commentary on the Musnad: 2623. "al-Rab'i": with a fatha on the "r" and "b," a nisba to "Rabi'ah al-Azd," as in al-Lubab of Ibn al-Athir 1: 459.]].

Others said: rather, its meaning is: what God has made lawful for you and permitted to you.

Those who said that:

2979. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾, he says: what God has made lawful for you.

2980. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, saying: Qatadah said concerning that: seek the concession that I have prescribed for you.

* *

Some of them read it: ﴿and follow what God has prescribed for you﴾.

Those who said that:

2981. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn Uyaynah informed us, from Amr ibn Dinar, from Ata ibn Abi Rabah, who said: I said to Ibn Abbas: "How do you read this verse: ﴿wa-btaghu﴾ or ﴿wa-ttabi'u﴾?" He said: whichever of the two you wish! I said: Stick to the first reading.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct statement regarding the interpretation of that, in my view, is that it should be said: God, mentioned be His remembrance, said: ﴿and seek﴾, meaning: seek, ﴿what God has prescribed for you﴾, meaning what God Most High has decreed for you.

God, mentioned be His remembrance, means: seek what I have written for you in the Preserved Tablet [[al-Lawh al-Mahfuz: the Preserved Tablet, the heavenly record in which God has written all that is decreed.]], that it is permitted, so He permits it for you. And seeking offspring, if a man seeks it through intercourse with a woman, is among what God has written for him in the Preserved Tablet. Likewise, if he seeks the Night of Power, it is among what God has written for him. Likewise, if he seeks what God has made lawful and permitted, it is among what He has written for him in the Preserved Tablet.

The phrase ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾ may include all the meanings of goodness that are sought, but the meanings most similar to the outward sense of the verse are the statement of one who said: its meaning is: ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾ of offspring, because it follows His saying ﴿so now, have relations with them﴾, meaning: have intercourse with them. Thus, for His saying ﴿and seek what God has prescribed for you﴾ to mean: seek what God has prescribed for you in your intercourse with them of offspring and progeny, is more fitting to the verse than other interpretations for which there is no evidence of soundness from the outward sense of the revelation, nor any report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

* *

The statement regarding the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿and eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, [which is] the dawn; then complete the fast until the night﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: The people of ta'wil differed regarding the interpretation of His saying: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, [which is] the dawn﴾.

Some of them said: by His saying ﴿the white thread﴾ He means the light of day, and by His saying ﴿the black thread﴾ He means the darkness of night.

So its interpretation according to those who held this view is: eat during the night in the month of your fast, drink, and have intercourse with your wives seeking what God has prescribed for you of offspring, from the beginning of the night until the daylight appears to you by the rising of dawn out of the darkness and blackness of the night.

Those who said that:

2982. Al-Hasan ibn Arafah narrated to me, saying: Rawh ibn Ubadah narrated to us, saying: Ash'ath narrated to us, from al-Hasan regarding the saying of God, mentioned be His remembrance: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, [which is] the dawn﴾, he said: the night from the day.

2983. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, [which is] the dawn﴾, he said: until the day becomes distinct to you from the night, ﴿then complete the fast until the night﴾.

2984. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, [which is] the dawn; then complete the fast until the night﴾. He said: They are two clear signs and limits, so let not the call of a showy or weak-minded muezzin prevent you from your pre-dawn meal, for they call at a long portion of the night. And a whiteness that is sometimes seen at the pre-dawn hour, which the Arabs used to call "the false dawn," should not prevent you from your pre-dawn meal, for the true dawn is not hidden: it is a line stretching across the horizon. ﴿And eat and drink until the dawn becomes distinct to you﴾; so when you see that, then abstain [[The report: 2984 — al-Hajj'j'? al-Hujay'? (the printed text reads "al-hajī'") means a portion of the night; one says "a portion or a period of the night has passed," meaning an hour and a part of it. al-Sahar is the last third of the night, just before the dawn. al-Tariqah is a line extending across a thing, visible through a difference of color or a difference in appearance.]].

Abu Ja'far said: ... [closing] — (This is the last portion of the given text.)

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 4 of 8):

2985. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread [of dawn]" means the night from the day. So He permitted for them intercourse, eating and drinking until the morning becomes distinct to them. When the dawn became distinct, intercourse, eating and drinking were forbidden to them until they complete the fast until night. He commanded fasting from day until night, and commanded breaking the fast at night.

2986. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, and it was said to him: "Have you considered the saying of God, exalted is He: 'the white thread from the black thread of dawn'?" He said: "Indeed you are broad of nape." He said: "This is the departure of the night and the coming of the day." It was said to him: "[Is it] al-Sha'bi from 'Adi ibn Hatim?" He said: "Yes. Husayn narrated to us..." [[Hadith 2986: Husayn is Ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, the trustworthy and reliable, one of the great imams of hadith. A narration of his has passed at no. 579.
Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash greatly abridged this hadith, and omitted its isnad when he narrated it. Then he was asked about it, and clarified that he heard it from Husayn, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Adi ibn Hatim.
It will come at nos. 2987 and 2989 in abridged form, and 2988 in full, but it is established in the Two Sahihs and elsewhere, in full with a clear sound context:
Ahmad related it in al-Musnad 4: 377 (Halabi), from Hushaym: "Husayn informed us, from al-Sha'bi, 'Adi ibn Hatim informed us, he said: When this verse was revealed ('Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread'), I took two cords, one black and the other white, and placed them under my pillow. Then I kept looking at them, but the black did not become distinct to me from the white, nor the white from the black. When I awoke in the morning, I went to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and informed him of what I had done. He said: 'If your pillow were then broad! That is only the whiteness of the day from the blackness of the night.'"
'Adi's saying "When this verse was revealed" means: when it was recited to him at his conversion to Islam, because the obligation of fasting was in the early days of the Hijra, and 'Adi embraced Islam long afterwards, in the ninth or tenth year.
Al-Bukhari related it, 4: 113 (Fath), by way of Hushaym, and Muslim 1: 301 and Abu Dawud: 2349 both by way of 'Abd Allah ibn Idris, from Husayn. Al-Bukhari 8: 137 (Fath) related it in abridged form by way of Abu 'Awana, from Husayn.
Ibn Kathir mentioned it, 1: 421, from the narration of Ahmad, then said: "Both of them [al-Bukhari and Muslim] related it in the Two Sahihs by more than one route, from 'Adi." al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1: 199, and added its attribution to Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi.
His saying "broad of nape" is a metaphor for fatness and prolonged sleep, and that is evidence of heedlessness and lethargy.]].
* *
The basis for those who said this statement and interpreted the verse this way is:

2987. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Hafs ibn Ghiyath narrated to us, from Mujalid ibn Sa'id, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: I said: "O Messenger of God, [what is] the saying of God: 'And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn'?" He said: "It is the whiteness of the day and the blackness of the night." [[Hadith 2987: Mujalid ibn Sa'id: his biography has passed at no. 1614. The hadith repeats the previous one in meaning.]].

2988. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Numayr and 'Abd al-Rahim ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Mujalid ibn Sa'id, from 'Amir, from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: I came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he taught me Islam, and described to me the prayers, how to pray each prayer at its time. Then he said: "When Ramadan comes, eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn, then complete the fast until night." I did not know what that was, so I made two threads, one white and one black, and I looked at them at dawn, and I saw them as equal. So I came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, I have memorized everything you instructed me, except 'the white thread from the black thread'!" He said: "What prevented you, O son of Hatim?" And he smiled as if he knew what I had done. I said: "I twisted two threads, one white and one black, and I looked at them at night and found them equal!" So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) laughed until his molars were seen, then said: "Did I not tell you 'from the dawn'? It is only the light of the day and the darkness of the night." [[Hadith 2988: Mujalid ibn Sa'id; in the printed edition here it is erroneously given as "Mujalid 'an Sa'id". This lengthy context is mentioned by al-Suyuti, 1: 199, attributing it only to Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim.
Ahmad related it in al-Musnad 4: 377 (Halabi), from Yahya, that is al-Qattan, from Mujalid, from 'Amir, that is al-Sha'bi. But it is slightly more abridged than here.]].

2989. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Malik ibn Isma'il narrated to us, saying: Dawud and Ibn 'Ulayya together narrated to us, from Mutarrif, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Adi ibn Hatim, who said: I said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "What is 'the white thread from the black thread'? Are they two threads, white and black?" He said: "Indeed you are broad of nape if you see the two threads." Then he said: "No, but it is the blackness of the night and the whiteness of the day." [[Hadith 2989: Malik ibn Isma'il ibn Ziyad ibn Dirham, Abu Ghassan al-Nahdi: a memorizer and trustworthy. One of the teachers of al-Bukhari and other imams. Biographies in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/1/315, Ibn Sa'd 6: 282, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/206-207.
Dawud, the teacher of Malik ibn Isma'il: I was unable to identify him, as there are many named "Dawud" in this generation. In any case the hadith is sound, through the narration of Ibn 'Ulayya together with him from Mutarrif.
Mutarrif: he is Ibn Tarif al-Harithi, his biography has passed at no. 224.
The hadith is abridged, as we indicated just above. Al-Bukhari related it, 8: 137, from Qutayba ibn Sa'id, from Jarir, that is Ibn 'Abd al-Hamid al-Dabbi, from Mutarrif, with this isnad, similar to it.]].

2990. Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Rahim al-Barqi narrated to me, saying: Ibn Abi Maryam narrated to us, saying: Abu Ghassan narrated to us, saying: Abu Hazim narrated to us, from Sahl ibn Sa'd, who said: This verse was revealed: "And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread," but "of the dawn" was not yet revealed. He said: So men, when they intended to fast, would tie a black thread and a white thread to their feet, and continue eating and drinking until it became distinct to them. Then God revealed afterwards "of the dawn," and they knew that what was meant was the night and the day. [[Hadith 2990: Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Rahim al-Barqi: he is Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Rahim, passed at nos. 22 and 160.
Ibn Abi Maryam: he is Sa'id ibn al-Hakam, a well-known trustworthy narrator, whom the authors of the six books related from; passed at no. 22.
Abu Ghassan: he is Muhammad ibn Mutarrif, with the second letter (ra) pronounced with emphasis, al-Laythi al-Madani, one of the reliable scholars; the authors of the six books related from him.
Abu Hazim: he is Salama ibn Dinar al-A'raj al-Tammar, al-Madani, a trustworthy Successor; there was no one like him in his time.
The hadith was related by al-Bukhari 4: 114-115, and 8: 137, from Ibn Abi Maryam, with this isnad. Muslim 1: 301 related it from two shaykhs, from Ibn Abi Maryam.
It was also related by al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, as in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 199.]].
* *
Others said: The white thread is the light of the sun, and the black thread is the blackness of the night.

The basis for those who said that:

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 5 of 8):**

2998. Hannad ibn al-Sarri narrated to us, saying: ʿUbaydah ibn Humayd narrated to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Ibrahim al-Taymi, who said: My father travelled with Huthayfah. He said: So he (Huthayfah) travelled until, when we feared that dawn would surprise us, he said: "Is there any one of you who is eating or drinking?" I said to him: "As for one who intends to fast, no." He said: "Yes!" He said: Then he travelled until, when we were slow to pray, he dismounted and took the pre-dawn meal (saḥūr).

[Report note: This is a report traced to Huthayfah ibn al-Yaman (mawqūf, i.e., ending with a Companion), and its isnad is sound, but there are two errors in the printed edition. It will come after this, again as mawqūf, with two other isnads. Then its meaning will come as marfūʿ (traced to the Prophet), from the hadith of Huthayfah himself: 3011–3014.

Hannad ibn al-Sarri, the teacher of al-Tabari in this isnad: the printed edition has "Hisham ibn al-Sarri," which is certainly an error; there is no narrator by that name, as far as we know, and it is "Hannad." He was biographed at 2058.

ʿUbaydah (with fatḥah on the ʿayn) ibn Humayd (with ḍammah on the unpointed ḥāʾ): passed at 2781. The printed edition has "ʿUbādah ibn Humayd," which is also an error.

Ibrahim al-Taymi: he is Ibrahim ibn Yazid ibn Sharik. He and his father were trustworthy Successors (tābiʿūn), whom the authors of the six canonical books narrated from.

The apparent flaw in this isnad is a break in continuity (inqiṭāʿ), because Ibrahim al-Taymi did not meet Huthayfah and did not witness his father's journey with him. However, it became clear from the two isnads following it that he narrated this from his father, so the isnad is connected.]

2999. Hannad and Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to us, both saying: Abu Muʿawiyah narrated to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Ibrahim al-Taymi, from his father, who said: I went out with Huthayfah to al-Mada'in during Ramadan. When dawn rose, he said: "Is there any one of you who is eating or drinking?" We said: "As for a man who intends to fast, no." He said: "But I!" He said: Then we travelled until we were slow to pray. He said: "Is there any one of you who wants to take the pre-dawn meal?" We said: "As for one who intends to fast, no." He said: "But I!" Then he dismounted and took the pre-dawn meal, then prayed.

[Report note: Its isnad is sound and connected.
His saying, "But I!" is an abbreviation of his saying: "But I intend to fast." Such ellipsis is common in their speech.]

3000. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr narrated to us, saying: "I have sometimes drunk after the muezzin's saying, 'The prayer has begun,'" meaning in Ramadan. He said: I never saw anyone more inclined to do that than al-Aʿmash, and that was when he heard (the adhan). He said: Ibrahim al-Taymi narrated to us from his father, who said: We were with Huthayfah travelling by night, and he said: "Is there any one of you taking the pre-dawn meal now?" He said: Then he travelled on; then Huthayfah said: "Is there any one of you taking the pre-dawn meal now?" He said: Then he travelled until we were slow to pray. He said: So he dismounted and took the pre-dawn meal.

[Report note: This is also a sound and connected isnad.
Abu Bakr is Ibn ʿAyyash. He has passed many times, including at 2150. This isnad clearly shows his hearing from al-Aʿmash, and his seeing him do what he related of his pre-dawn meal after the adhan.
Al-Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) said in al-Fath (4: 117): "A group of the Companions held, and al-Aʿmash among the Successors held, and his companion Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash held, that it is permissible to take the pre-dawn meal until the dawn becomes clear."
He also said: "Ibn Abi Shaybah and ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated that from Huthayfah, through sound chains."
For this matter, see al-Muhalla by Ibn Hazm, in the issue at 756 (vol. 7, pp. 229–235). More takhrij will come at his marfūʿ hadith: 3011–3013, God willing.]

3001. Harun ibn Ishaq al-Hamdani narrated to us, saying: Musʿab ibn al-Miqdam narrated to us, saying: Israʾil narrated to us, saying: Abu Ishaq narrated to us, from Hubayrah, from ʿAli: that when he prayed the dawn prayer, he said: "This is when the white thread becomes distinct from the black thread of dawn."

[Report note: Harun ibn Ishaq al-Hamdani, the teacher of al-Tabari: a Kufan, a memoriser of hadith, trustworthy, one of the teachers of al-Bukhari outside the Sahih, and of al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and other imams. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Saʿd (6: 289), and Ibn Abi Hatim (4/2/87–88). He is among the teachers from whom al-Bukhari narrated while they were alive. He died in 258, two years after al-Bukhari.
Musʿab ibn al-Miqdam: his biography passed at 1291.
Hubayrah (with ḍammah on the hāʾ): he is Ibn Yarim, with fatḥah on the yāʾ and kasrah on the rāʾ, al-Shabbami, with kasrah on the shīn, a lightened bāʾ, and a mīm after the alif, a nisbah to "Shabbam." He is ʿAbd Allah ibn Asʿad ibn Jathum ibn Hashid. Ibn Saʿd said: "He was named Shabbam after a mountain of theirs."
In al-Tahdhib, al-Taqrib, and al-Khulasah it is written "al-Shaybani," which is a misreading. Hubayrah is a trustworthy Successor, some spoke against him. Only Abu Ishaq al-Sabiʿi narrated from him, and he was the maternal uncle of al-ʿAliyah, the wife of Abu Ishaq. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir (4/2/241), Ibn Saʿd (6: 118), and Ibn Abi Hatim (4/2/109–110).
This report will come with another isnad, similar in wording, at 3010.
Al-Hafiz mentioned it in al-Fath (4: 117), saying: "Ibn al-Mundhir narrated with a sound isnad, from ʿAli, that he prayed the Subh and then said: 'Now is when the white thread becomes distinct from the black thread.'" But al-Suyuti mentioned it (1: 199) with a similar wording, with the phrase "that he said when dawn rose..." and attributed it to al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir. I nearly incline to think that his saying "dawn rose" is a distortion by the copyists, because the two reports of al-Tabari here and the following one have "prayed the dawn," and what al-Hafiz quoted from Ibn al-Mundhir's narration supports this.]

3002. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Salt narrated to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Huthayfah al-ʿAttar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Bara', who said: I took the pre-dawn meal during the month of Ramadan, then I went out and came to Ibn Masʿud, and he said: "Drink!" I said: "I have already taken the pre-dawn meal!" He said: "Drink!" So we drank, then we went out while the people were in the prayer.

[Report note: This isnad is problematic, and I do not know what it is.
Ibn al-Salt: he falls between two men of this class: "Muhammad ibn al-Salt ibn al-Hajjaj al-Asadi" and "Muhammad ibn al-Salt al-Tawzi." I do not know which of them he is, or whether it is someone else.
As for Ishaq ibn Huthayfah al-ʿAttar and his father: I have not found a biography or mention of either of them in any of the references available to me. I fear there is a distortion in both of them together. If they omitted the biography of "Ishaq," it would be all the more unlikely that they omitted the biography of his father, who, on the apparent reading of this isnad, is a Successor narrating from a Companion, namely al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib. See the report after it.]

3003. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Muʿawiyah narrated to us, from al-Shaybani, from Jabalah ibn Suhaym, from ʿAmir ibn Mutar, who said: I came to ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud in his house, and he brought out some of his leftover pre-dawn meal, so we ate with him. Then the prayer was called, so we went out and prayed.

[Report note: As for this report, its isnad is sound. Al-Shaybani is Abu Ishaq Sulayman ibn Abi Sulayman, whose biography passed at 1037.
Jabalah ibn Suhaym (with ḍammah on the unpointed sīn), al-Taymi al-Shaybani: a trustworthy Successor, ascribed to "Taym ibn Shaybān," so he is "Taymi" and "Shaybani."
ʿAmir ibn Mutar al-Shaybani: a trustworthy Successor. He is biographed in Ibn Saʿd (6: 82), Ibn Abi Hatim (3/1/328), and Lisan al-Mizan (3: 225). Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Hakam ibn Bashir, who said: "Abu Mutar, from whom Jabalah ibn Suhaym narrates, is ʿAmir ibn Mutar, a Shaybani, a man of standing among the Muslims."
Ibn Hazm narrated this report in al-Muhalla (7: 233), through Ibn Abi Shaybah: "Abu Muʿawiyah narrated to us, from al-Shaybani, who is Abu Ishaq..." and mentioned it with this isnad, similar in wording.
Al-Haythami mentioned it briefly in Majmaʿ al-Zawaʾid (3: 154), in this form: "And from Mutar al-Shaybani, who said: We took the pre-dawn meal with ʿAbd Allah, then we went out and the prayer was called. Al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Kabir, and its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih." He named the Successor "Mutar al-Shaybani." In my judgment this is an error, since no narrator by that name exists. I do not know whether the error came from the narrators of al-Tabarani, from al-Haythami, or from a copyist or printer. But in my view it is an error in any case.]

3004. Khallad ibn Aslam narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn ʿAyyash narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Maʿqil, from Salim, the freedman of Abu Huthayfah, who said: I and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq were on one roof in Ramadan. I came one night and said: "Will you not eat, O Successor of the Messenger of God ﷺ?" He gestured with his hand: "Stop!" Then I came to him again and said: "Will you not eat, O Successor of the Messenger of God?" He gestured with his hand: "Stop!" Then I came to him again and said: "Will you not eat, O Successor of the Messenger of God?" He looked at the dawn, then gestured with his hand: "Stop!" Then I came to him and said: "Will you not eat, O Successor of the Messenger of God?" He said: "Bring your lunch!" He said: So I brought it to him, and he ate, then prayed two rak'ahs, then rose to the prayer.

[Report note: This isnad is weak, because it is broken (munqaṭiʿ).
Khallad ibn Aslam, Abu Bakr al-Saffar, the teacher of al-Tabari: trustworthy, one of the teachers of ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i. He died in Jumada al-Akhirah 249. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Saghir of al-Bukhari (p. 237), and Tarikh Baghdad (8: 342–343).
ʿAbd Allah ibn Maʿqil (with fatḥah on the mīm, sukūn on the unpointed ʿayn, and kasrah on the qāf), ibn Muqarrin (with ḍammah on the mīm, fatḥah on the qāf, and kasrah on the shaddah rāʾ), al-Muzani: a trustworthy Successor who narrates from his father, who was a Companion, and from ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, and others. However, he did not live to narrate from Salim, the freedman of Abu Huthayfah, because he died in 88, while Salim was killed at al-Yamamah in 12 AH during the caliphate of Abu Bakr. Therefore al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar, in al-Tahdhib, criticised what the author's source had stated, saying: "The author gave an unqualified narration from Salim, the freedman of Abu Huthayfah. The apparent reading is that it is mursal, since he was killed at al-Yamamah." This Ibn Maʿqil is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Saghir of al-Bukhari (pp. 93–94), Ibn Saʿd (6: 121–122), and al-Isabah (5: 144). In the printed edition here it is written "ʿUbayd Allah," with the diminutive, which is an error.
Salim, the freedman of Abu Huthayfah: an early Companion who died early, as we said just above. He is the one concerning whom the rule on suckling an adult was revealed. He was the freedman of Thubaytah bint Yaʿar al-Ansariyyah, the wife of Abu Huthayfah. She freed him, and he came under the patronage of Abu Huthayfah ibn ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah al-Qurashi, her husband. Ibn Saʿd said: "Salim is mentioned among the Ansar, among Banu ʿUbayd, because Thubaytah bint Yaʿar freed him, and he is mentioned among the Muhajirun, because of his attachment to Abu Huthayfah." He is biographed in al-Kabir (2/2/108), al-Saghir (pp. 21–22), Ibn Saʿd (3/1/60–62), Ibn Abi Hatim (2/1/189), and al-Isabah (3: 56–57). Ibn Abi Hatim said: "I know of no one who narrated from him." Al-Hafiz criticised this in al-Isabah, mentioning for him the narration of two marfūʿ hadiths, then he said: "Both isnads have weakness and break in continuity. So Ibn Abi Hatim's statement should be understood as meaning that nothing sound was transmitted from him." Al-Hafiz did not mention this narration of al-Tabari, which is also broken.
This report was also mentioned by al-Haythami in Majmaʿ al-Zawaʾid (4: 154), slightly abridged, and he said: "Al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Kabir, and its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih." He said this and did not point to its defect of broken continuity, unless the isnad of al-Tabarani is connected to another narrator above ʿAbd Allah ibn Maʿqil, in which case perhaps. But I do not think so.
Indeed, al-Hafiz mentioned in al-Fath (4: 117) that Ibn al-Mundhir "narrated with a sound isnad, from Salim ibn ʿUbayd al-Ashjaʿi, who had companionship (with the Prophet): that Abu Bakr said to him: 'Go out and see whether dawn has risen.' He said: I looked, then came to him and said: 'It has become white and spread.' Then he said: 'Go out and see whether it has risen.' I looked and said: 'It has spread across the horizon.' He said: 'Now let my drink reach me.'" So this Salim ibn ʿUbayd is a well-known Companion from the People of the Bench (ahl al-Suffah). The narration from him comes by another route than the narration of Salim, the freedman of Abu Huthayfah. If the isnad to him is sound, as al-Hafiz said, then it is so. Unless the mention of "Salim ibn ʿUbayd" is an error by some narrator, I have no other explanation of Ibn al-Mundhir's isnad.
Ibn Hazm narrated in al-Muhalla (6: 232) a similar meaning, with other wordings, from Abu Bakr:
Ibn Hazm said: "We narrated through the route of Maʿmar, from Aban, from Anas, from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, that he said: 'If two men look at the dawn and one of them doubts, then let them both eat until it becomes clear to them.'"
"And through the route of Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri, from Sufyan al-Thawri, from Mansur ibn al-Muʿtamir, from Hilal ibn Yasaf, from Salim ibn ʿUbayd, who said: 'Abu Bakr al-Siddiq used to say to me: "Stand between me and the dawn until I take the pre-dawn meal."'"
And through the route of Ibn Abi Shaybah, from Jarir ibn ʿAbd al-Hamid, from Mansur ibn al-Muʿtamir, from Hilal ibn Yasaf, from Salim ibn ʿUbayd al-Ashjaʿi, who said: 'Stand and shield me from the dawn, then I will eat.'"
This last wording is abridged, and from what precedes it one understands that it is also a report from Abu Bakr. Perhaps some of it was dropped by the copyists of al-Muhalla.
Then Ibn Hazm said: "This Salim ibn ʿUbayd: an Ashjaʿi from Kufa, one of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ. And this is the most sound route that could be."
I incline to think that the route of Ibn al-Mundhir, which al-Hafiz transmitted in al-Fath, is like these last two routes that Ibn Hazm transmitted, so that it is from the narration of Hilal ibn Yasaf from Salim ibn ʿUbayd. I find it very unlikely that the route of al-Tabarani, which al-Haythami mentioned, is from this direction.
Then Ibn Hazm narrated (6: 233) a similar meaning, from the narration of Abu al-Safar and from the narration of Abu Qilabah, both from Abu Bakr. These are two broken isnads, because Abu al-Safar and Abu Qilabah certainly did not meet Abu Bakr.]

3005. Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Shuʿbah narrated to us, from Mughirah, from Ibrahim, who said: "The witr is at night, and the pre-dawn meal is by day."

Something other than this has been transmitted from Ibrahim:

3006. Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, who said: "The pre-dawn meal is at night, and the witr is at night."

3007. Hakkam narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Jaʿfar, from al-Mughirah, from Ibrahim, who said: "The pre-dawn meal and the witr are between the second call (al-tathwib) and the iqamah."

3008. Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, saying: Shuʿbah narrated to us, from Shabib ibn Gharqadah, from ʿUrwah, from Hibban, who said: "We took the pre-dawn meal with ʿAli, then we went out when the prayer had been called, and we prayed."

[Report note: Shabib ibn Gharqadah al-Sulami: a trustworthy Successor, whom Ahmad, Ibn Maʿin, and others declared trustworthy. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir (2/2/232), and Ibn Abi Hatim (2/1/357).
ʿUrwah: he is Ibn Abi al-Jaʿd al-Azdi al-Bariqi, a well-known Companion. Al-Bukhari said: "Bariq is a mountain, where some of the Azd settled."
Hibban (with kasrah on the unpointed ḥāʾ and shaddah on the bāʾ): he is Ibn al-Harith, Abu ʿAqil, and he is a trustworthy Successor. Al-Bukhari biographed him in al-Kabir (2/1/77), Ibn Abi Hatim (1/2/269), and al-Dulabi in al-Kuna (2: 33).
Thus it is written in al-Tabari, from his teacher Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, in this isnad, the addition of "ʿUrwah al-Bariqi" between "Shabib" and "Hibban ibn al-Harith." The report will come after this, at 3009, from the narration of Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah, from Shabib, from Hibban, directly without an intermediary, and this is the established, preserved form from Shabib. So perhaps Ibn al-Muthanna, the teacher of al-Tabari, erred in this addition, or perhaps it was from the narration of Shabib from ʿUrwah and from Hibban, both from ʿAli, and then the isnad became confused for the copyists.
Al-Bukhari narrated this report, in the biography of Hibban in al-Tarikh al-Kabir, in brief by allusion as is his habit, in the correct form, through the route narrated here by al-Tabari:
Al-Bukhari said: "Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ghundar narrated to us, saying: Shuʿbah narrated to us, from Shabib, from Hibban: We took the pre-dawn meal with ʿAli."
Hammad, the teacher of al-Bukhari, is Muhammad ibn Bashshar al-Hafiz. Ghundar is Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar, the teacher of Ibn al-Muthanna in this isnad of al-Tabari. As you see, he narrated it directly, without an intermediary between Shabib and Hibban.
Likewise al-Bukhari narrated it through three isnads from Shabib, from Hibban. He said: "Ibn Mahbub narrated, from ʿUmar al-Abbar, from Mansur, from Shabib, from Hibban ibn al-Harith: We took the pre-dawn meal with ʿAli. Jarir said, from Mansur, from Shabib, from Abu ʿAqil. Husayn said, from Zaʾidah, from Shabib, from Tariq ibn Qurrah and Hibban ibn al-Harith, with this." In the last isnad of al-Bukhari, he added that Shabib narrated it from Tariq ibn Tariq ibn Qurrah, from ʿAli, like his narration of it from Hibban, from ʿAli. "Tariq ibn Qurrah" is a Successor, whom al-Bukhari did not biograph in al-Kabir, but Ibn Abi Hatim biographed him (2/1/486), saying: "Tariq ibn Qurrah: he narrated from ʿAli, and Shabib ibn Gharqadah narrated from him." Ibn Hibban also biographed him in al-Thiqat (p. 229).
The narration of al-Bukhari through the route of Jarir from Mansur was narrated by Ibn Hazm in detail in al-Muhalla (6: 233). He said: "And through the route of Ibn Abi Shaybah: Jarir, that is Ibn ʿAbd al-Hamid, narrated to us, from Mansur ibn al-Muʿtamir, from Shabib ibn Gharqadah, from Abu ʿAqil, who said: 'I took the pre-dawn meal with ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, then he ordered the muezzin to call the prayer.'"]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 6 of 8):

This is a set of chains that shows that the mention of "Urwa al-Bariqi" in al-Tabari's isnad here is either an error by Ibn al-Muthanna, or an addition made to the narration alongside Habban (not a narration from him), and then it was distorted by the copyists.]]

3009. Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Shabib, from Habban ibn al-Harith, who said: I passed by 'Ali while he was in the house of Abu Musa, and he was eating the pre-dawn meal (suhur). When I reached the mosque, the prayer was called [[Report 3009: Sufyan is Ibn 'Uyayna. The report repeats in meaning the report before it. Ibn Hazm also narrated it in al-Muhalla 6: 233, saying: "And from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, from Shabib ibn Gharqada, from Habban ibn al-Harith: that he ate the pre-dawn meal with 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and they both intended to fast. When he finished, he said to the muezzin: Call the prayer."]]

3010. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Safar, who said: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib prayed the dawn prayer, then said: "This is the time when the white thread becomes distinct from the black thread of dawn" [[Report 3010: Abu al-Safar, with a fatha on the fa', is Sa'id ibn Muhammad, with a dammah on the yaa' and a sukun on the ha' and a kasra on the meem. He is a reliable Successor (tabi'i) who narrated from middle-ranking Companions such as Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar. This isnad is interrupted (munqati'), because Abu al-Safar did not meet 'Ali ibn Abi Talib in a way that allows him to narrate from him. Its meaning from 'Ali has already passed, by a different connected isnad: 3001.]]

* *

The reasoning of those who held this view: the term refers only to the daytime, not to the night. They said: The beginning of the day is the rising of the sun, just as its end is the setting of the sun. They said: If its beginning were the rising of dawn, then its end would have to be the setting of twilight. They said: The consensus of the authorities that the end of the day is the setting of the sun is a clear proof that its beginning is its rising. They said: The report from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he ate the pre-dawn meal after the rising of dawn is the clearest proof for the soundness of our view.

Mention of the reports narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) on this matter:

3011. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr narrated to us, from 'Asim, from Zirr, from Hudhayfa, who said: I said: "Did you eat the pre-dawn meal with the Prophet (ﷺ)?" He said: "Yes." I said: "Was it the daytime?" He said: "If I wished, I would say it is the daytime, except that the sun had not risen" [[Hadith 3011: 'Asim is Ibn Bahdala, also known as Ibn Abi al-Najud, with a fatha on the nun, the Kufan reciter, one of the seven readers. He is reliable, and the compilers of the six books narrated from him. Zirr, with a kasra on the zay and a shadda on the ra', is Ibn Hubaysh, a reliable Successor. Mentioned at 274. Hudhayfa is Ibn al-Yaman al-'Abasi, a well-known Companion whose virtues are numerous and known.
This hadith was narrated by Ibn Majah: 1695, from 'Ali ibn Muhammad, who is al-Tanafisi, from Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, with this isnad, similar, abridged. A fuller takhrij will come for the three after it.]]

3012. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr narrated to us, saying: "'Asim did not lie about Zirr, nor did Zirr lie about Hudhayfa." He said: I said to him: "O Abu 'Abd Allah, did you eat the pre-dawn meal with the Prophet (ﷺ)?" He said: "Yes. It was the daytime, except that the sun had not risen" [[Hadith 3012: This is the previous hadith in meaning, with the same isnad. But this one is phrased in a form of emphasis, and it is authenticated; Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash intended by it to remove the suspicion of error or exaggeration in the narration.]]

3013. Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Asim, from Zirr, from Hudhayfa, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to eat the pre-dawn meal while I could see the places of the arrows. He said: I said: "After dawn?" He said: "It is the dawn, except that the sun had not risen" [[Hadith 3013: Sufyan is al-Thawri.
The hadith is in the meaning of the two before it. Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad 5: 400 (Halabi), from Waki', from Sufyan, with this isnad, similar. Likewise al-Nasa'i narrated it, 1: 303, and Ibn Hazm in al-Muhalla 6: 232, both by way of Waki'.
In Fath al-Bari 4: 117 it is narrated that Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated it "from Abu al-Ahwas, from 'Asim, from Zirr, from Hudhayfa, who said: We ate the pre-dawn meal with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); by Allah, it was the daytime, except that the sun had not risen."]]

3014. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Bashir narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Qays and Khallad al-Saffar narrated to us, from 'Asim ibn Bahdala, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, who said: I woke up one day and went out to the mosque. I said: "If only I passed by the door of Hudhayfa!" He opened for me and I entered, and there he was heating food for himself. He said: "Sit until you eat." I said: "I intend to fast." So he brought his food near, and he ate and I ate with him. Then he got up to a milch-camel (liqḥa) in the house, and began to milk from one side while I milked from the other side. He handed it to me, and I said: "Don't you see the dawn?" He said: "Drink!" So I drank. Then I came to the door of the mosque, and the prayer was called. I said to him: "Tell me of the last pre-dawn meal you ate with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said: "It was the dawn, except that the sun had not risen." [[Hadith 3014: al-Hakam ibn Bashir al-Nahdi: his biography has passed at 1497. 'Amr ibn Qays is al-Mala'i, his biography has passed at 886.
Khallad al-Saffar is Khallad ibn 'Isa al-'Abdi, also called Khallad ibn Muslim. He is reliable. He is described in al-Tahdhib, in al-Kabir 2/1/171, and in Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/367.
This hadith repeats the three before it in meaning, except that it is extended into a story. A story similar to it was narrated by Hammad ibn Salama, from 'Asim, from Zirr, from Hudhayfa:
Ahmad narrated it, 5: 396 (Halabi), from 'Affan, from Hammad ibn Salama.
Likewise al-Tahawi narrated it in Sharh Ma'ani al-Athar 1: 324, and Ibn Hazm in al-Muhalla 6: 231-232, both by way of Rawh ibn 'Ubada, from Hammad ibn Salama.
Ahmad also narrated it, 5: 405 (Halabi), by way of Shurayk ibn 'Abd Allah, who is al-Nakha'i the judge, from 'Asim, from Zirr, who said: "I said, meaning to Hudhayfa: 'O Abu 'Abd Allah, did you eat the pre-dawn meal with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'Could the man see the places of his arrows?' He said: 'Yes, it was the daytime, except that the sun had not risen.'"
Ibn Kathir mentioned 1: 422 the narration of Hammad ibn Salama from 'Asim in abridged form, and attributed it to Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, and said: "This is a hadith uniquely narrated by 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, as al-Nasa'i said." I did not find it in al-Nasa'i by way of Hammad, nor did I find al-Nasa'i's words. Perhaps it is in al-Sunan al-Kubra.
Al-Hafiz said in Fath al-Bari 4: 117, after quoting the narration of Sa'id ibn Mansur and pointing to the narration of al-Tahawi from Hudhayfa: "Ibn Abi Shayba and 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated that from Hudhayfa, by sound routes."
"Al-liqha": a she-camel recently given birth, so it is one of those that have milk.]]

3015. Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Ahwazi narrated to us, saying: Rawh ibn 'Ubada narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn 'Amr, from Abu Salama, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "If one of you hears the call while the vessel is in his hand, let him not put it down until he has fulfilled his need from it" [[Hadith 3015: This is a sound isnad.
Rawh ibn 'Ubada al-Qaysi, of the Banu Qays ibn Tha'laba: reliable. The compilers of the six books narrated from him. Ibn Ma'in and others declared him reliable. Some spoke against him without valid proof. He is described in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/1/282-283, Ibn Sa'd 7/2/50, Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/498-499, and Tarikh Baghdad 8: 401-406.
"'Ubada" is with a damma on the 'ayn and a light ta'diyf on the bā'. In the printed edition, in this isnad and the one after it, it appears as "Rawh ibn Janada," which is an error, as there is no narrator with this name.
Hammad is Ibn Salama.
Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn 'Alqama ibn Waqqas al-Laythi: reliable. The group also narrated from him.
Abu Salama is Ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf.
The hadith was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 10637 (2: 510 Halabi), from Rawh ibn 'Ubada, with this isnad and wording.
Ahmad also narrated it: 9468 (2: 423 Halabi), from Ghassan ibn al-Rabi', from Hammad ibn Salama, with this isnad. He paired with it another isnad that is mursal, from Yunus, from al-Hasan, from the Prophet (ﷺ).
Abu Dawud narrated it: 2350, from 'Abd al-A'la ibn Hammad al-Narsi, from Hammad ibn Salama, with it. Likewise al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak 1: 426, by way of 'Abd al-A'la, and al-Hakim said: "This is a sound hadith according to the condition of Muslim, though the two did not include it." al-Dhahabi agreed with him.
See our commentary on the hadith in what we wrote on the abridgement of the Sunan of al-Mundhiri: 2249 (3: 233, 234).]]

3016. Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Rawh ibn 'Ubada narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from 'Ammar ibn Abi 'Ammar, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), the like of it, and he added in it: "The muezzin used to call when the dawn had risen" [[Hadith 3016: 'Ammar ibn Abi 'Ammar, client of the Banu Hashim: a reliable Successor. Muslim included him in his Sahih.
The hadith was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 10638, from Rawh ibn 'Ubada, with this isnad, after the hadith before it, just as al-Tabari did exactly.
Ibn Hazm mentioned it in al-Muhalla 6: 232, from the narration of Hammad ibn Salama, with it, and he gave its full wording. He added at its end: "Hammad said, from Hisham ibn 'Urwa: My father used to give this ruling."]]

3017. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us = and Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Shaqiq narrated to us, saying: I heard my father say: al-Husayn ibn Waqid informed us = they both said, all together, from Abu Ghalib, from Abu Umama, who said: The prayer was called while the vessel was in the hand of 'Umar. He said: "Shall I drink it, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Yes!" So he drank it [[Hadith 3017: al-Tabari narrated it by two isnads. He narrated it from Ibn Humayd, from Yahya ibn Wadih, from al-Husayn ibn Waqid. Then he began another isnad, narrating it from Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Hasan, from his father, from al-Husayn ibn Waqid. So the two routes converge on al-Husayn ibn Waqid, from Abu Ghalib, etc.
Yahya ibn Wadih is Abu Tumayla, his biography has passed at 392.
Abu Ghalib is the companion of Abu Umama, and his name is disputed. It is said: "Hazwar", with a fatha on the ha' and the zay and a shadda on the waw, ending with a ra'. It is also said: "Sa'id ibn al-Hazwar," which is what Ibn Sa'd restricted himself to, 7/2/7. al-Bukhari, in al-Kabir 2/1/124, abbreviated it to "Hazwar." Ibn Abi Hatim gave his biography in both entries, 1/2/315-316, then 2/1/13, and in the second place he said: "Hazwar is more sound." He is reliable, though some spoke about him. al-Daraqutni declared him reliable, and al-Tirmidhi graded some of his hadiths as good and authenticated some. His biography is in al-Tahdhib 12: 197-198.
Abu Umama is al-Bahili, whose name is "Suday," with a damma on the sad and a fatha on the dal, both unpointed, and a shadda on the ya', son of 'Ajlan. He is a well-known Companion who died in the year 86 and had passed one hundred, since it is established that he was 30 or 33 years old. In Ibn Sa'd 7/2/131-132 it occurs that he died at 61 years old! That is a gross error.
This hadith has a sound isnad. I did not find it anywhere else in the tafsir of al-Tabari other than this place.]]

3018. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: Yunus narrated to us, from his father, from 'Abd Allah, who said: Bilal said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) to inform him of the prayer while he intended to fast. He called for a vessel and drank, then handed it to me and I drank, then he went out to the prayer" [[Hadith 3018: Yunus is Ibn Abi Ishaq al-Subay'i, and he is reliable. Ibn Ma'in, Ibn Sa'd and others declared him reliable. His biography is in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/408, Ibn Sa'd 6: 252, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/243-244.
'Abd Allah is Ibn Ma'qil ibn Muqarrin al-Muzani, his biography has passed at 3004.
Bilal is Ibn Rabah, the muezzin of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), one of the first Emigrants, who died in the plague of 'Amwas in the year 17 or 18. 'Abd Allah ibn Ma'qil, who died in the year 88, did not meet him. So the isnad to him is weak because it is interrupted.
The takhrij of the hadith will come in the next isnad.]]

3019. Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Tusi narrated to me, saying: 'Ubayd Allah ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Isra'il informed us, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Abd Allah ibn Ma'qil, from Bilal, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) to inform him of the dawn prayer while he intended to fast. He called for a vessel and drank, then handed it to me and I drank, then we went out to the prayer" [[Hadith 3019: Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Tusi, a teacher of al-Tabari: I do not know who he is. "'Abd Allah ibn Ma'qil," with a fatha on the meem, a sukun on the ghayn (as written in the source), and a kasra on the qaf. In the printed edition here "Mughaffal" appears, which is an error.
The hadith was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad 6: 12 (Halabi), from Yahya ibn Adam and Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri, both from Isra'il, with this isnad, similar. Then he narrated it at 6: 13, from Husayn ibn Muhammad, from Isra'il, with it. It is a weak hadith because of the break between Ibn Ma'qil ibn Muqarrin and Bilal, as we have shown.
al-Haythami mentioned it in Majma' al-Zawa'id 3: 152, from the first narration of Ahmad, and said: "Ahmad narrated it, and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir." Then he mentioned the second narration of Ahmad, then said: "Its men are the men of the sahih." He failed to note the break.
Ahmad also narrated, 6: 13, from Waki', from Ja'far ibn Burqan, from Shaddad, client of 'Iyad ibn 'Amir, from Bilal: "that he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) to inform him of the prayer, and found him eating the pre-dawn meal in the mosque of his house." al-Haythami also mentioned this from the Musnad, then said: "Shaddad, client of 'Iyad, did not meet Bilal." And that is as he said.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The more appropriate of the two interpretations of the verse is the interpretation narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "The white thread" is the whiteness of the day, and "the black thread" is the blackness of the night. This is the familiar usage in the speech of the Arabs. Abu Du'ad al-Iyadi said:

"When a dimness shone for us, and a thread of the dawn appeared, and shone" [[Al-Asma'iyyat: 28, from verses. It describes a horse he rode out on for hunting. Also in al-Lisan (khayt). In al-Asma'iyyat it reads "khayr anara," which has no meaning. Al-sudfa: the darkness of the night in the dialect of Najd, and the light in the dialect of Qays. It is also the mixing of light and darkness together, as at the time between the dawn prayer and the advanced morning (isfar). 'Umara said: darkness with light at the beginning and end of the night, between darkness and twilight, and between dawn and the prayer. Abu Du'ad meant the mixing of darkness and light. "Lāḥa": appeared and became visible from afar. "Khayṭ" (thread): here the color that extends like a thread.]]

* *

As for the reports narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he drank or ate the pre-dawn meal and then went out to the prayer, this does not negate the soundness of what we have said on this matter. For it is not objectionable that the Prophet (ﷺ) drank before dawn and then went out to the prayer, since the prayer, the dawn prayer, in his time was performed after dawn had risen and its rising had become clear, and the call to it was made before its rising.

As for the report narrated from Hudhayfa, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to eat the pre-dawn meal while I could see the places of the arrows," it was questioned in it, and he was asked: "After dawn?" He did not reply that it was after dawn, but said: "It is the dawn." This statement of his may mean: it is the dawn because of its nearness to it, even if it is not exactly it, just as the Arabs say "this is so-and-so" by way of comparison, while pointing to other than the one they named, and they say: "It is it" as a comparison of him to it. Likewise Hudhayfa's statement "it is the dawn" means: it is the dawn by comparison and by nearness to it.

* *

Ibn Zayd said regarding the meaning of "the white thread and the black thread":

3020. He narrated it to me, saying: Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, at dawn﴾. He said: "The white thread" is what comes from beneath the night, uncovering the night, and "the black" is what is above it.

* *

As for His saying "from the dawn": He, may His mention be exalted, means: until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread which is from the dawn. This does not mean the whole of dawn, but when that white thread, which comes from beneath the night with the blackness of night above it, becomes distinct to you, O believers, from the dawn, then from that moment fast, then complete your fast from that until night.

In accordance with what we have said on this matter, Ibn Zayd used to say:

3021. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: ﴿from the dawn﴾: "That white thread is from the dawn in relation to it, and it is not the whole dawn. So when this thread comes, which is its beginning, the prayer becomes permissible, and eating and drinking become forbidden to the fasting person."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: In His saying, may His mention be exalted: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, at dawn; then complete the fast until night﴾, there is clear evidence against the view of those who said: eating and drinking are permitted for one who wishes to fast until sunrise. For the white thread from the dawn becomes distinct at the start of the first appearance of dawn, and God, may His mention be exalted, has made that a limit for the one who is obligated to fast, at the time up to which He permitted eating, drinking and intimacy.

Whoever claims that he may go beyond that limit, it is said to him: "What do you say if another person permits that at forenoon or midday?"

If he says: "The one who says that opposes the community (ummah)."

It is said to him: "You also oppose what the Book of God indicates and what the community has transmitted. So what is the difference between you and him, by way of a principle (asl) or analogy (qiyas)?"

If he says: "The difference between me and him is that God commanded fasting during the day, not during the night, and the day begins at sunrise."

It is said to him: "Your opponents say the same, but for them the day begins at the break of dawn (fajr), which is the light of the sun and the beginning of its rising, not the completion of its rising. Likewise, the end of the day is the beginning of its setting, not the completion of its setting."

It is said to those who say this [the plural of "those who say" after the singular]: "If 'the day' according to you is as you have described it, namely the rising of the sun, the completion of its rising, and the passing away of all the darkness of the night and the dispersal of its blackness, then according to you 'the night' is the completion of the sun's setting, the passing away of its light, and the completion of the blackness and darkness of the night?"

If they say: "That is so!"

It is said to them: "Then it must be that the fast extends until the disappearance of the twilight (shafaq) and the passing of the sun's light and its whiteness from the horizon of the sky! If they say: 'That is so!', then they are obliged to make the fast last until the disappearance of the twilight, which is whiteness. And that doctrine, if they hold it, is refuted by the transmission of the proof, concerning which the community has agreed that it cannot involve error or inadvertence [and this suffices as a witness] to refute it." [The words between the brackets are an addition necessary for the syntax of the sentence.]

If they say: "Rather, [the night begins with] the beginning of its darkness and gloom and the sun's disappearance from our sight."

It is said to them: "Then likewise, [the day begins with] the beginning of the sun's first light and the end of the first darkness of the night."

Then the statement on this matter is reversed against him, [the author returned once more to the singular after the plural], and he is asked about the difference between the two. He will not state a position on one of them without being obliged to hold its like on the other.

* *

As for "al-fajr" (dawn), it is a verbal noun (masdar) from the saying of the speaker: "tafajjara al-ma'u yatafajjaru fajran" [the water gushed forth], when it springs forth and flows. So the one who rises with the first glimmers of the sun's light from its rising is called "fajr," because of the springing forth of its light upon them and its pouring over them, with their paths and ways, just as water gushes forth from its source. [The text as printed in the edition is this, and I could not change it, because his words indicate that he takes it as a masdar, from their saying "tafajjara" with the ta and the doubled jim. He appears to treat it as one of the masdars that came in a form other than the form of their verbs, as already mentioned above at 1:116–118. See the explanation of "al-tafajjur" previously at 2:238.]

* *

As for His saying: "Then complete the fast until the night" (2:187), He, dhikruhu, has defined the fast such that its final time is the approach of the night, just as He defined the breaking of the fast and the permission to eat, drink and have intercourse, and began the fast with the arrival of the beginning of the day and the first retreat of the end of the night. Thereby it indicates that there is no fasting at night, just as there is no breaking of the fast during the day in the days of fasting; and that the one who continues fasting without breaking (al-muwasil) is starving himself in disobedience to his Lord. As reported:

3022. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah, Waki' and Ubaydah narrated to us, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, from 'Asim ibn 'Umar, from 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When the night approaches from there and the day retreats and the sun sets, the fasting person has broken his fast." [Note on the hadith: Ubaydah is Ibn Sulayman. 'Asim is Ibn 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, a reliable Successor (tabi'i) who was born in the lifetime of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The printed edition here has "'Asim ibn 'Umar," which is an error. The hadith was also transmitted in a similar form by Ahmad in al-Musnad (192, 383), from Waki', from Hisham, with this chain; also (231) from Ibn Numayr and (338) from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, both from Hisham. Al-Bukhari transmitted it (4:171, Fath) through Ibn 'Uyaynah; Muslim (1:303) through Abu Mu'awiyah, Ibn Numayr and Abu Usamah, all three from Hisham; Abu Dawud (2351) through Ahmad ibn Hanbal from Waki', and through Musaddad from 'Abd Allah ibn Dawud, both from Hisham ibn 'Urwah.]

3023. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, saying: Abu Ishaq al-Shaybani narrated to us. And Hannad ibn al-Sari narrated to us, saying: Abu Ubaydah and Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us, from al-Shaybani. And Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to us. And Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to me, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, from al-Shaybani. All of them said in their narration, from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey and he was fasting. When the sun had set, he said to a man: 'Dismount and prepare the drink (ijdah) for me.' They said: 'If only you had waited until evening, O Messenger of God!' He said: 'Dismount and prepare it.' The man said: 'O Messenger of God, if only you had waited until evening!' He said: 'Dismount and prepare it for me.' He said: 'O Messenger of God, there is still daytime upon us!' Then the Prophet said to him a third time. So he dismounted and prepared it for him. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'When the night approaches from here'—and he struck with his hand towards the east—'the fasting person has broken his fast.'" [Note on the hadith: al-Tabari transmitted it through several chains, all of which converge on Abu Ishaq al-Shaybani. He transmitted it from Hannad ibn al-Sari, from three teachers: Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash, Abu Ubaydah and Abu Mu'awiyah; he transmitted it from Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna from Abu Mu'awiyah; and from Abu al-Sa'ib Salm ibn Janadah, from 'Abd Allah ibn Idris al-Awdi. All of them are from Abu Ishaq al-Shaybani, whose name is Sulayman ibn Abi Sulayman, from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa. Abu Ubaydah is 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Wasil al-Haddad, a reliable teacher of Ahmad, whose biography is in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Abi Hatim (3/1/24), and Tarikh Baghdad (11:3–5). In the printed edition, in this part of the chain, it reads "Abu Ubaydah and Abu Mu'awiyah, from Shayban," which is a clear error; Shayban has no connection with this chain. The correct reading is "from al-Shaybani," as we have established. The hadith was also transmitted by al-Bukhari (4:156) through Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah; (171–172) through Khalid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Wasiti; (172) through 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad al-'Abdi; and (173) through Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash. Muslim (1:303) transmitted it through Hushaym, 'Ali ibn Mushir, 'Abbad ibn al-'Awwam, 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad, Sufyan, Jarir and Shu'bah. Abu Dawud (2352) transmitted it through 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad—all of them from Abu Ishaq al-Shaybani, in a similar form. "Jadah al-sawiq fi al-laban aw al-ma'" means: he stirred it in milk or water until it mixed and became uniform. His saying "dariba bi-yadihi" means he gestured with his hand, extending it like one who strikes. "Darraba" is one of the verbs that apply to many actions except a few: one says "darraba fi al-ard" (he travelled in the land), "darraba bi-yadihi ila al-shay'" (he pointed his hand to a thing, i.e. swooped towards it), "darraba 'ala yadihi," and "darraba yadahu ila 'amal kadha" (he set his hand to such-and-such work).]

3024. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from Rufay', who said: "God prescribed the fast until night. When the night comes, you are one who has broken the fast: if you wish, eat; and if you wish, do not eat." [Note: Rufay' is Rufay' ibn Mihran Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi, who is mentioned hundreds of times by his kunya. He lived in the Jahiliyyah and embraced Islam two years after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ). He died in the year 90. Dawud is Ibn Abi Hind. See the two following chains.]

3025. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from Abu al-'Aliyah: that he was asked about continuous fasting without breaking (al-wisal) in fasting, and he said: "God made it obligatory upon this community to fast during the day. When the night comes, whoever wishes eats, and whoever wishes does not eat."

3026. Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to me, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, who said: Abu al-'Aliyah said concerning continuous fasting, he said: God said: "Then complete the fast until the night." So when the night comes, he has broken the fast; whoever wishes eats, and whoever wishes does not eat.

3027. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ibn Duqayn narrated to us, from Mis'ar, from Qatadah, who said: 'A'ishah said: "Complete the fast until the night"—meaning that she disliked continuous fasting.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: If someone asks: "What is the reasoning of the one who practises continuous fasting? You have known it [by means of] the following:"

3028. Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to you, saying: Hafs narrated to us, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr used to fast continuously for seven days; when he grew old, he made it five; when he became very old, he made it three.

3029. Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to us, saying: Hafs narrated to us, from 'Abd al-Malik, who said: Ibn Abi Ya'mur used to break his fast once a month.

3030. Ibn Abi Bakr al-Muqaddami narrated to us, saying: al-Furawi narrated to us, who said: I heard Malik say: "'Amir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr used to fast continuously on the night of the sixteenth and the night of the seventeenth of Ramadan, without breaking his fast between them. I met him and said: 'O Abu al-Harith, what do you find that strengthens you in your continuous fasting?' He said: 'Ghee, which I drink; I find that it moistens my veins. As for water, it leaves my body.'" [Note: Ibn Abi Bakr al-Muqaddami is Abu 'Uthman Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr al-Muqaddami, a teacher of al-Tabari. "al-Furawi," with a fatha on the fa and sukun on the ra, is Ishaq ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Farwah; a similar chain to Malik has already been mentioned (876). But there al-Tabari said: "Abu 'Uthman al-Muqaddami narrated to us." Here he did not mention his name or kunya, but attributed him to his grandfather.]

= And other similar cases of those who did this, whose mention would lengthen the book?

It is said: The purpose of one who did this, God willing, is to seek lightness of the body (al-khumusah) and strength for himself, not to seek righteousness before God by his action. [Al-khumusah is a verbal noun of "khamusa batnuhu khamasan" (his belly became empty), spelled with a sukun or fatha on the mim, and khamasah. The lexicographers did not mention "al-khumusah," but it is an ancient Arabic word, like their saying al-fasalah and al-fasulah, al-radalah and al-radulah, Faris between al-firasah and al-firusah, a strong man (rajul jald) between al-jaladah and al-jludah, and batal between al-batalah and al-butulah, and similar words.]

This is the counterpart of what 'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to command them, when he said: "Be rough and imitate the way of Mu'add, leap upon horses in leaps, cut the stirrups and walk barefoot." [Note: "Ikhshawshana al-rajul" means he wore rough clothing and accustomed himself to it, ate coarse food, lived a coarse life, and exaggerated in harshness. "Tama'adda al-rajul" means he imitated the harsh living of Ma'add ibn 'Adnan in hardship and abandoning luxury and the dress of the non-Arabs (al-'ajam). He means: endure the life of Ma'add in the settled and the travelling, and imitate their clothing, and leave the style of the non-Arabs. "Al-nazw" is leaping; he commands them to leap upon horses without assistance from stirrups. "Al-rukab" is the plural of rikab, which is what is in a horse's saddle into which the rider places his foot; if it is like that on a camel's saddle, it is called "al-gharz".]

He commands them in this to be hardy in their living, lest they become luxurious, incline to ease of life and tend to comfort, and then become cowardly and shrink from their enemies.

= Many people of merit have also avoided continuous fasting for those who practise it:

3032. Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq: that Ibn Abi Na'm used to fast continuously for days until he could not stand. 'Amr ibn Maymun said: "If the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) had seen this, they would have stoned him." [Note: Ibn Abi Na'm is "'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Na'm al-Bajali" of Kufa, the worshipper. Bukayr ibn 'Amir said: "If it were said to 'Abd al-Rahman, 'The Angel of Death has set out towards you wanting to take your soul!', nothing more would be in his mind than what he was already doing."
