3763 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Dharr informed us, saying: I heard Mujahid narrate, saying: Some people did not trade during the days of Hajj, so this was revealed concerning them: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord." [[In the printed edition: "So it was revealed concerning them: 'There is no blame upon you that you seek...'" and it is shown to be an error and a mistake.]]

3764 - Muhammad ibn Amarah al-Asadi narrated to me, saying: Ubayd Allah ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Abu Layla informed us, from Buraydah, concerning His saying, blessed and exalted: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord," he said: if you are in ihram, that you buy and sell.

3765 - Tulayq ibn Muhammad al-Wasiti narrated to us, saying: Asbat informed us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Amr informed us, from Abu Umamah al-Taymi, who said: I said to Ibn Umar: "We are a people who hire out (animals), so is there a Hajj for us?" He said: "Do you not circumambulate the House, and come to 'Arafat, and throw the pebbles, and shave your heads?" We said: "Yes!" He said: "A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him about what you have asked me about, and he did not know what to say to him, until Jibril (peace be upon him) descended upon him with this verse: 'There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord,' to the end of the verse. Then the Prophet ﷺ said: 'You are pilgrims.'" [[The hadith: 3765 – Tulayq ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sakan al-Wasiti, the teacher of al-Tabari: trustworthy; Ibn Hibban said in al-Thiqat: "upright in narration like the reliable ones." He is among the teachers of al-Nasa'i, Ibn Khuzaymah and others. This section concerning "Tulayq": al-Dhahabi in al-Mushtabih stated that it is with a fatha on the ta', and Hafiz Ibn Hajar followed him in Tahrir al-Mushtabih, and neither mentioned any other vocalisation. But Hafiz in al-Taqrib vocalised the first part of the name "with diminutive" by explicit statement. I incline to think it is a mistake from him, may Allah have mercy on him.
Asbat: he is Ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Khalid ibn Maysarah, a trustworthy narrator, among the teachers of Ahmad and Ibn Rahawayh and others. al-Hasan ibn Amr al-Fuqaymi (with damm on the fa') al-Tamimi al-Kufi: trustworthy, whose narrations al-Bukhari included in his Sahih. Abu Umamah al-Taymi: a trustworthy Tabi'i. We have explained his biography and its sources in the commentary on the Musnad: 6434.
The hadith was narrated by Ahmad in the Musnad: 6434 from Asbat ibn Muhammad with this chain. We have elaborated on its takhrij there. Ibn Kathir cited it at 1: 463 from the Musnad and at 464 from this place of al-Tabari, and it will come with another chain: 3789.]]

3766 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, saying: Ayyub informed us, from Ikrimah, who said: This verse used to be recited: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord in the seasons of Hajj."

3767 - Abd al-Hamid narrated to us, saying: Ishaq informed us, from Shurayk, from Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir concerning His saying: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord," he said: it is trade in buying and selling, and purchasing is not objectionable.

3768 - It was narrated to me from Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i, who said: Waki' narrated to us, from Talhah ibn Amr, from Ata', from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite it: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord in the seasons of Hajj."

3769 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Ali ibn Mushir, from Ibn Juraij, from Amr ibn Dinar, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The markets of the people in the Jahiliyyah were Ukaz and Dhu al-Majaz; when Islam came, they seemed to dislike that, until Allah, may His praise be exalted, revealed: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord."

3770 - al-Hasan ibn Arafah narrated to us, saying: Shababah ibn Sawwar narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu Umayyah, who said: I heard Ibn Umar – and he was asked about a man who performs Hajj with merchandise – so Ibn Umar recited: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord." [[The report: 3770 – Abu Umayyah: the apparent and likely view is that it is "Abu Umamah al-Taymi" mentioned in hadith 3765, and that this report is an abridgement of that hadith, but it is halted (mawquf) upon Ibn Umar.
Ibn Kathir cited it at 1: 463 from this place of al-Tabari and said: "This is mawquf, and it is strong and good."]]

3771 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us = and Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us = said: Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad informed us, from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, who said: They did not trade during the days of Hajj, so this was revealed: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord."

3772 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj informed us, from Ata', from Ibn Abbas that he recited: [[In the printed edition: "qala" (said) in place of "qara'a" (recited), which is a mistake by the copyist; see the earlier reports 3766, 3768, and the reports following this one.]] "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord in the seasons of Hajj."

3773 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: Talhah ibn Amr al-Hadrami narrated to us, from Ata', his saying: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord in the seasons of Hajj," thus did Ibn Abbas recite it.

3774 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, saying: al-Layth narrated to us, from Mujahid concerning His saying: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord," he said: trade in this world, and reward in the Hereafter.

3775 - Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to us, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning the saying of Allah, exalted is He: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord," he said: trade, which was made lawful for them in the seasons. He said: they used not to sell or buy in the Jahiliyyah at 'Arafah.

3776 - al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

3777 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah concerning His saying: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord," he said: This tribe of the Arabs would not turn aside for a lost camel or a stray animal on the night of the departure (al-nafr), and they called it "the night of the return" (laylat al-sadr), and they did not seek trade or sale in it. So Allah, exalted is He, made all that lawful for the believers, that they might turn aside to their needs and seek from the bounty of their Lord.

3778 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn Uyaynah informed us, from Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Yazid, who said: I heard Ibn al-Zubayr recite: [[In the printed edition: "I heard Ibn al-Zubayr say," and the correct reading is from the manuscript of the Tafsir of Abd al-Razzaq, p. 21.]] "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord in the seasons of Hajj." [[The report: 3778 – Al-Hafiz mentioned it in al-Fath 3: 473 and noted that Ibn Uyaynah and Ibn Juraij narrated it from Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Yazid. He did not mention who transmitted it, but from al-Tabari's narration we know that Abd al-Razzaq transmitted it from Ibn Uyaynah. It is in the Tafsir of Abd al-Razzaq p. 21, with this chain. Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Yazid al-Makki: a trustworthy Tabi'i.]]

3779 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn Uyaynah informed us, from Amr ibn Dinar, who said: Ibn Abbas said: Dhu al-Majaz and Ukaz were markets for the people in the Jahiliyyah; when Islam came, they abandoned that, until this was revealed: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord in the seasons of Hajj."

3780 - Ahmad ibn Hazim and al-Muthanna narrated to us, both saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Suqah, who said: I heard Sa'id ibn Jubayr say: Some of the pilgrims were called "al-Dajj," and they used to lodge in the left side of Mina, while the pilgrims lodged near the mosque of Mina; they did not trade, until this was revealed: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord," and they performed Hajj. [[al-Dajj: they are those who accompany the pilgrims as hired workers, muleteers, helpers and servants; it is evident that they did not perform Hajj with the people.]]

3781 - Ahmad ibn Hazim narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Dharr narrated to us, from Mujahid, who said: Some people performed Hajj but did not trade, until this was revealed: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord," so they were granted permission for trade, riding and provisions.

3782 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, concerning His saying: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord," it is trade. He said: trade during the season.

3783 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord," he said: When the people entered the state of ihram, they did not buy and sell until they had completed their Hajj, so Allah made it lawful for them.

3784 - al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad, from Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, who said: They used to avoid sales and trade during the days of the season, saying: "Days of remembrance!" So Allah revealed: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord," and they performed Hajj.

3785 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Talhah ibn Amr, from Ata', from Ibn Abbas that he used to recite it: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord in the seasons of Hajj."

3786 - al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: al-Hammani narrated to us, saying: Shurayk narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, who said: There is no harm in trade during Hajj, then he recited: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord."

3787 - It was narrated to me from Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas concerning His saying: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord," he said: This tribe of the Arabs would not turn aside for a broken-down camel, nor for a stray animal, nor wait for any need, and they called it "the night of the return," and they did not seek trade in it. So Allah made all that lawful, that they might turn aside to their needs and seek bounty from their Lord.

3788 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Mundal narrated to us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Muhajir, from Abu Salih, mawla of Umar, who said: I said to Umar: "O Commander of the Faithful, did you used to trade during Hajj?" He said: "Were their livelihoods anything but in Hajj?"

3789 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from al-Ala' ibn al-Musayyab, from a man of the Banu Taym Allah, who said: A man came to Abd Allah ibn Umar and said: "O Abu Abd al-Rahman, we are a people who hire out (animals), and they claim that there is no Hajj for us!" He said: "Do you not enter ihram as they enter ihram, circumambulate as they circumambulate, and throw as they throw?" He said: "Yes!" He said: "Then you are a pilgrim!" A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him about what you have asked about, and this verse was revealed: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord." [[The hadith: 3789 – al-Ala' ibn al-Musayyab ibn Rafi' al-Asadi: trustworthy and reliable, as Ibn Ma'in said.
The hadith was narrated by Ahmad in the Musnad: 6435, from Abd Allah ibn al-Walid al-Adani, from Sufyan al-Thawri with this chain. We said in its explanation that its chain is sahih, and that the anonymity of the man from the Banu Taym Allah does no harm, for he is known to be "Abu Umamah al-Taymi," as passed in 3765. We have elaborated its takhrij in the Musnad.]]

3790 - al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, who said: When they departed from 'Arafat, they did not trade in any commerce, nor did they turn aside for a broken-down camel or a stray animal; so Allah made that lawful, and He said: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord," to the end of the verse.

3791 - Sa'id ibn al-Rabi' al-Razi narrated to me, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Amr ibn Dinar, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Ukaz, Majannah and Dhu al-Majaz were markets in the Jahiliyyah, and they used to trade in them. When Islam came, they seemed to regard it as sinful, so they asked the Prophet ﷺ, and Allah revealed: "There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord in the seasons of Hajj." [[The hadith: 3791 – Sa'id ibn al-Rabi' al-Razi, the teacher of al-Tabari: I have not found a biography for him. He is mentioned in the indexes of Tarikh al-Tabari under this name, so the suspicion of distortion in it is removed. "Sufyan," his teacher, is Ibn Uyaynah. "Sa'id ibn al-Rabi'" may be confused with another narrator, "Sa'id ibn al-Rabi' al-Harawi al-Jarshi al-Amiri," whose biography is in al-Tahdhib, but he died early, in the year 211, before al-Tabari's birth. He is among the earliest teachers of al-Bukhari.
The hadith was narrated by al-Bukhari 4: 248, 269, and 8: 139 (Fath) through the route of Sufyan ibn Uyaynah with this chain.
He also narrated it at 3: 473–474 through the route of Ibn Juraij from Amr ibn Dinar. Ibn Kathir mentioned it at 1: 462, from the narration of al-Bukhari.
This hadith is one of the unique narrations of al-Bukhari alone, not Muslim, as al-Hafiz stated in al-Fath 3: 475. I did not find it in the Musnad of Ahmad. It is among the few sahih hadiths found in one of the two Sahihs but not in the Musnad.
A similar meaning has passed in abridged form: 3779, from the narration of Abd al-Razzaq from Ibn Uyaynah, and also passed in abridged form: 3771, 3784, from another route, the narration of Mujahid from Ibn Abbas; and 3772, 3785, from a third route, the narration of Ata' from Ibn Abbas.]]
* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿So when you pour forth from 'Arafat﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "fa-idha afadtum" (so when you pour forth), he means: when you return from where you began.

For this reason, the one who casts the arrows among the gamblers is called "mufid" (one who pours out), because he gathers the arrows and then pours them out among the players. [[al-Qidah: plural of qidh (with kasra and sukun), the arrow before it is tipped and feathered; they used to seek decisions by them in the game of maysir, and they are also called al-azlam. Al-Aysar: plural of yasr (with two fathahs), those gathered for the game from the nobles of the tribe. In the printed edition: "al-mayasirin," and the correct reading is what is given here. Al-Yasir: the one who strikes with the arrows and gambles over the camel-meat, playing with the arrows.]] And from it is the saying of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim al-Asadi: [[In the printed edition: "Ibn Abi Hazim," which is an error.]]

"I said to her: 'Return her heart to him,' so she returned it as the mani' (arrow) is returned by the mufid."
[[I did not find this verse anywhere; of the qasidah there are three verses in al-Hayawan 6: 343 of this poetry, and they are excellent verses. Al-Mani': one of the four arrows which carry neither loss nor gain in the arrows of the game, though its owner may be granted some of the camel-meat. I cannot discern the meaning of the verse until I know what precedes it, and know to what the pronouns in it refer.]]
* *

Then the grammarians (ahl al-'Arabiyya, the scholars of Arabic grammar) disagreed about "'Arafat", regarding the reason it is declined (ṣuriqat, i.e. takes tanwin, the nunation) despite being a definite proper noun, and whether it is the name of a single place or of a group of places.

Some of the Basran grammarians said: It is a name that was originally for a group, like *muslimāt* and *mu'minat*. It was given as the name of a single place, and it remained declined because it had been declined before it became the name of that place. They left it in its original state, because the *tā'* in it has become like the *yā'* and *wāw* in *muslimīn* and *muslimūn*, since it is its feminine marker, and the tanwin has become like the *nūn*. So when it was made a name, it was left in its original state, just as *al-muslimūn* is left in its state when it is made a name. [[This is the view of al-Akhfash (Lisan al-'Arab: 'rf) and Mu'jam al-Buldan ('Arafat). See Sibawayh 2: 17-18.]] He said: Some Arabs do not decline it when it is made a name, and they treat the *tā'* as the feminine *hā'* ending, but that is ugly and weak. They cited the verse of the poet: [[This is Imru' al-Qays ibn Hujr.]]

*Tanawwarathā min adhri'āt wa ahluhā*
*bi-Yathrib adnā dārihā naẓarun 'ālī*

[[Diwan: 140; Sibawayh 2: 18; al-Khizana 1: 26. It is from his famous and admired ode. The pronoun in "tanawwarathā" refers to the woman he mentions (see Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara': 68, note 3). "Tanawwara al-nār" means he looked at it from afar, so that the woman lit up for him and he saw her like a blazing fire. Adhri'āt: a town in Syria. Yathrib: the city of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which was its name in the pre-Islamic period. He says: her light appeared to him in the darkness, while he was in Syria and her people were in Medina. Then he says: the nearest one can see of it is only seen from a high place in the sky. He describes the great distance between him and her, yet she appeared to him at night from this distant place. He completes the meaning in the next verse:]]

*Naẓartu ilayhā wa-l-nujūmu ka'annahā*
*maṣābīḥu ruhbānin tashibbu li-qifāl*

[Translation: I looked at her while the stars were like the lamps of monks kindled for the one who ties (?)...]

Some do not give tanwin to *Adhru'āt*, and likewise *'Anāt*, which is a place.

Some of the Kufan grammarians said: *'Arafāt* is declined because it is in the plural form of the feminine with the *tā'*. He said: Likewise, whatever is in the plural feminine form with the *tā'*, if it is then made the name of a man, a place, a land or a woman, it is declined. He said: The Arabs hardly name anything in the plural form except as a plural, and then afterwards they make it singular.

Others among them said: *'Arafāt* is not a *ḥikāya* (quoted form), nor is it a transferred name. [[Ḥikāya: using the word in the form it had before. Its meaning will become clear in the following lines.]] Rather, the place is named, together with its surroundings, "*bi-'Arafāt*", and then the site was named by it. It is the name of the place, and its singular does not stand alone. He said: This is only permissible for places and sites, and not for other things. He said: That is why the Arabs left the *tā'* unchanged in this case, because it is a place. If it were quoted, that would not be permissible, because whoever names a man *muslimāt* or *muslimīn* does not change it in inflection from what it was originally. Therefore *'Anāt* and *Adhru'āt* differ, as they are names given by way of ḥikāya.

\* \*

Abu Ja'far said: The scholars differed about the reason for which 'Arafāt was called 'Arafāt. Some of them said: It was called that because Ibrahim, the Friend of Allah (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him), when he saw it, recognised it by its description that he had received, and said: "I have recognised it" (*'arraftu*), so it was named 'Arafāt for that reason. This view, from the one who holds it, indicates that 'Arafāt is the name of the place, and that it was named that for itself and its surroundings, as one says: a worn-out garment (*thawb akhlāq*) and a land of wide deserts (*ard sabasib*), comprising what is around it. [[See what preceded at 1: 433.]]

Mention of those who said that:

3792. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, from Asbat, from al-Suddi, who said: When Ibrahim called the people to the Hajj, they answered him with the talbiya, and whoever came to him, Allah commanded him to go out to 'Arafat, and described it to him, so he went out. When he reached the tree at the 'Aqaba, Satan confronted him to turn him back, so he threw seven pebbles at him, saying "Allahu akbar" with each pebble. He flew off and landed at the second jamra, so he blocked him again, and he threw and said "Allahu akbar". He flew off and landed at the third jamra, and he threw and said "Allahu akbar".

When he saw that he could not overcome him, and Ibrahim did not know where to go, he set off until he came to Dhu'l-Majaz. [[In the printed edition: "fa-lamma ra'a annahu la yuti'uhu, fa-lam yadri Ibrahim" — the correct reading is what I have set down from Tabari's text above, as will come in the references later.]] [[In the printed edition: "fa-anṭalaqa" — the correct reading is what I have set down.]] When he looked at him, and he did not recognise him, he passed on, and so it was named Dhu'l-Majaz. Then he set off until he arrived at 'Arafat. When he looked at it he recognised its description and said: "I have recognised it!" So it was named 'Arafat. Ibrahim stood at 'Arafat until the evening came, when he moved on to Jam', and it was named al-Muzdalifa, and he stood at Jam'. [[Report 3792 has been transmitted in full as no. 2065, with the correction mentioned there.]]

3793. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Nu'aym ibn Abi Hind, who said: When Jibril stood with Ibrahim (peace be upon them both) at 'Arafat, he said: "I have recognised it!" So it was named 'Arafat for that reason.

3794. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn Jurayj informed us, saying: Ibn al-Musayyab said: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Allah sent Jibril to Ibrahim and he performed the Hajj with him. When he came to 'Arafa he said: "I have recognised it!" He had come to it once before, and that is why it was called 'Arafa.

\* \*

Others said: Rather, it was named that after itself and other places apart from it.

Mention of those who said that:

3795. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' ibn Muslim al-Qurashi narrated to us, from Abu Tahfa, from Abu'l-Tufayl, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: 'Arafat was named that because Jibril (peace be upon him) used to say to Ibrahim: "This is the place of such-and-such, this is the place of such-and-such," and he would say: "I have recognised it!" So it was named 'Arafat for that reason. [[Report 3795: This is an problematic isnad, and I do not know its correct form. As for "Waki' ibn Muslim al-Qurashi": I have found no narrator by this name nor anything resembling it. What I almost certainly believe is that it is "Waki' ibn al-Jarrah", the well-known imam, and that the word "ibn" is a corruption of "'an". A further difficulty is that I have not found anyone named "Muslim al-Qurashi", and a third difficulty is that I do not know who this "Abu Tahfa" is.
The certainty for me is that the isnad is corrupt and not sound.]]

3796. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman, from 'Ata', who said: 'Arafa was named that because Jibril used to show Ibrahim (peace be upon them both) the rites, and he would say: "I have recognised, I have recognised!" So it was named 'Arafat.

3797. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Zakariyya, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: The base of the mountain that adjoins 'Arana and what is behind it is a station (*mawqif*), until one reaches the mountain, the Mount of 'Arafa.

Ibn Abi Najih said: 'Arafat: al-Nab'a, al-Nabi'a, and Dhat al-Nabit, and that is the saying of Allah: "When you pour forth from 'Arafat" (﴿فإذا أفضتم من عرفات﴾), and it is the middle valley.

Zakariyya said: What flows from the mountain on which the imam stands towards 'Arafa is from 'Arafa, and what is behind that mountain is not from 'Arafa.

\* \*

This report indicates that it was named that way in the manner in which one thing is named by the name of a group of different individuals.

\* \*

Abu Ja'far said: The view most correct in my opinion regarding this is that it should be said: It is a name for a single thing that was named with a plural. When it is declined, it is treated as the plural it originally was. When its declension is left out, it is treated as the name of a single well-known place, and so its declension is left out, just as the names of cities and villages that are definite are left undeclined.

\* \*

The discussion of the interpretation of the words of the Most High: ﴿فاذكروا الله عند المشعر الحرام﴾ ("So remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram").

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means: When you pour forth, returning from 'Arafa towards the place from which you began to set out to it, "so remember Allah", meaning: by prayer and supplication at al-Mash'ar al-Haram.

\* \*

We have explained before that *al-mashā'ir* are the landmarks, from the saying of the speaker: "I became aware of this matter" (*sha'artu bihadha al-amr*), meaning I knew it. So *al-mash'ar* is the marker. [[See what preceded in volume 3: 226-227 (Bulaq edition), the interpretation of "sha'a'ir".]] It is named so because prayer there, the standing, the spending of the night and supplication, are among the landmarks and obligations of the Hajj which Allah has commanded His servants to perform. And:

3798. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Zakariyya, from Ibn Abi Najih, who said: It is recommended for the pilgrim to pray in his lodging at Muzdalifa if he is able, because Allah said: "So remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and remember Him as He has guided you" (﴿واذكروه كما هداكم﴾).

\* \*

As for *al-mash'ar*: it is what lies between the two mountains of Muzdalifa, from the two narrow passages (*ma'zimayn*) of 'Arafa to Muhassar.

The two passages of 'Arafa are not part of the mash'ar. [[The ma'zam: every narrow path between two mountains. The two ma'zams of 'Arafa: the narrow pass between Jam' and 'Arafa.]]

And those who are the exegetes (*ahl al-ta'wil*) said what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

3799. Hannad ibn al-Sari narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Za'ida narrated to us, saying: Isra'il informed us, from Mughira, from Ibrahim, who said: Ibn 'Umar saw the people crowding around the small hill at Jam', and said: "O people, all of Jam' is a mash'ar."

3800. Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj informed us, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, that he was asked about the words of Allah: "So remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram," and he said: "It is the mountain and what is around it."

3801. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Za'ida narrated to us, saying: Isra'il informed us, from Hakim ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: What is between the two mountains at Jam' is a mash'ar.

3802. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Za'ida narrated to us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from al-Suddi, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the like of it.

3803. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us = and Ahmad ibn Hazim narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us = from al-Suddi, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: I asked him about al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and he said: What is between the two mountains of Muzdalifa.

3804. Al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri, from Salim, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "al-Mash'ar al-Haram" is all of Muzdalifa = Ma'mar said: Qatada also said it.

3805. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from al-Suddi, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "So remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram," he said: What is between the two mountains of Muzdalifa is al-Mash'ar al-Haram.

3806. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Za'ida narrated to us, saying: My father informed us, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Amr ibn Maymun, who said: I asked 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar about al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and he said: If you go with me, I will show it to you. So I went with him, and we stood until the imam poured forth and proceeded, and we proceeded with him, until the hands of the riders descended, and we were at the furthest of the mountains on the side of 'Arafat. He said: Where is the one who asked about al-Mash'ar al-Haram? You have entered it! I said: What have I entered? He said: All of them are mash'ars up to the farthest edge of the Haram.

3807. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Isra'il informed us = and Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us = from Abu Ishaq, from 'Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi, who said: I asked 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar about al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and he said: If you stay with me, I will leave it [to you]. So when the people poured forth from 'Arafa and the hands of the riders descended into the lowest of the mountains, he said: Where is the one who asked about al-Mash'ar al-Haram? I said: Here I am. He said: You have entered it! I said: What have I entered? He said: When the hands of the riders descended to the lowest of the mountains, that is a mash'ar all the way to Mecca.

3808. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from 'Imara ibn Zadhan, from Makhul al-Azdi, who said: I asked Ibn 'Umar on the day of 'Arafa about al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and he said: Stay with me! When it was the next day and we came to Muzdalifa, he said: Where is the one who asked about al-Mash'ar al-Haram? This is al-Mash'ar al-Haram.

3809. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Za'ida narrated to us, saying: Dawud informed us, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Mujahid said: al-Mash'ar al-Haram is all of Muzdalifa.

3810. Hannad narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Za'ida narrated to us, saying: Dawud informed us, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to 'Ata': Where is Muzdalifa? He said: When you pour forth from the two passages of 'Arafa, that is up to Muhassar. He said: The two passages, the two passages of 'Arafa, are not from Muzdalifa, but rather they are the outlets of its two sides.

He said: Stand between them if you wish, but it is more beloved to me that you stand short of Quzah. Come to us for the sake of the people's path!

3811. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Mughira, from Ibrahim, who said: Ibn 'Umar saw them crowding at Quzah and said: Why are these people crowding? Everything here is a mash'ar!

3812. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: al-Mash'ar al-Haram is all of Muzdalifa.

3813. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

3814. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: "When you pour forth from 'Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram," and that is the night of Jam'. Qatada said: Ibn 'Abbas used to say: What is between the two mountains is a mash'ar.

3815. Musa narrated to us, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: al-Mash'ar al-Haram is what is between the mountains of Muzdalifa = and it is said: it is the horn of Quzah. [[Al-qarn: the small, elongated hill cut off from the large mountain.]]

3816. I was told from 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "So remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram," and it is Muzdalifa, and it is Jam'.

\* \*

And it is mentioned from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad that:

3817. Hannad narrated to us with it, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Isra'il, from Jabir, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad, who said: I did not find anyone who could inform me about al-Mash'ar al-Haram.

3818. Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: I heard Sa'id ibn Jubayr say: al-Mash'ar al-Haram is what is between the two mountains of Muzdalifa.

3819. Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Qays narrated to us, from Hakim ibn Jubayr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: I asked Ibn 'Umar about al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and he said: I do not know. I asked Ibn 'Abbas, and he said: What is between the two mountains.

3820. Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The small hill and what is around it are mash'ars.

3821. Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from Thuwayr, who said: I stood with Mujahid at the small hill, and he said: This is al-Mash'ar al-Haram.

3822. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Hasan ibn 'Atiyya narrated to us, saying: Isra'il narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas: The small hill and what is around it are mash'ars.

\* \*

Abu Ja'far said: We have only made the first limit of the mash'ar, on the side facing Mina, the end of the valley of Muhassar on the side facing Muzdalifa, because:

3823. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Sufyan, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "All of 'Arafa is a station except 'Urana, and all of Jam' is a station except Muhassar." [[Hadith 3823: This is a mursal hadith, as Ibn Kathir said (1: 467). Malik narrated it in the Muwatta' (p. 388) that "it reached him from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)", without an isnad. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr mentioned it in al-Taqassi, no. 839, and said: "This hadith is connected through the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, through the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, and through the hadith of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib." The hadith of Jabir is narrated by Muslim (1: 348), but it has no exception for 'Urana and Muhassar. Ibn Majah (3012) narrated it from Jabir with this exception, and its isnad is very weak.
See also al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Bayhaqi (5: 115), al-Talkhis al-Habir (p. 216), and Nasb al-Raya (3: 60-62).]]

3824. Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to me, from Hajjaj, from Ibn Abi Mulayka, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, that he said: All of Muzdalifa is a station except the valley of Muhassar.

3825. Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Hajjaj, who said: Someone who heard 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr say the like of that informed me.

3826. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Sufyan, from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr said in his sermon: You should know that all of 'Arafa is a station except the bottom of 'Urana; you should know that all of Muzdalifa is a station except the bottom of Muhassar. [[Report 3826: Malik narrated it in the Muwatta' (p. 388), in similar wording, from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr.]]

\* \*

Abu Ja'far said: However, although that is so, I prefer for the pilgrim that he make his standing for the remembrance of Allah from al-Mash'ar al-Haram at Quzah and what is around it, because:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 198 (part 3 of 3):

3827 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: ʿUbaydullah ibn Musa narrated to us, from Ibrahim ibn Ismaʿil ibn Majmaʿ, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith al-Makhzumi, from Zayd ibn ʿAli, from ʿUbaydullah ibn Abi Rafiʿ, from ʿAli, who said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered the morning at Muzdalifah, he set out in the morning, stood at Quzah, and had al-Fadl ride behind him, then said: "This is the place of standing, and all of Muzdalifah is a place of standing."

3828 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Ismaʿil ibn Majmaʿ informed us, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith, from Zayd ibn ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, from ʿUbaydullah ibn Abi Rafiʿ, from Abu Rafiʿ, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, with something similar.

[[The two hadiths: 3827 and 3828. Ibrahim ibn Ismaʿil ibn Majmaʿ al-Ansari al-Madani: weak. Ibn Maʿin said: "He is nothing," and al-Bukhari said: "He frequently errs." ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿa al-Makhzumi: trustworthy, one of the people of knowledge. Zayd ibn ʿAli ibn Abi Talib: a well-known trustworthy narrator who needs no introduction. He is the one to whom the Zaydi sect of the Shiʿa are attributed, and he was a staunch opponent of the Rafida. He narrates directly from ʿUbaydullah ibn Abi Rafiʿ, but he narrated this very hadith, as will come in the takhrij, from his father Zayn al-ʿAbidin ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, from ʿUbaydullah. ʿUbaydullah ibn Abi Rafiʿ al-Madani, client of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: a trustworthy Successor. He was a scribe for ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.
This hadith is an abridged version of a longer hadith. Ibrahim ibn Ismaʿil ibn Majmaʿ made an error in it: he omitted [from his father] from the chain between Zayd ibn ʿAli and ʿUbaydullah ibn Abi Rafiʿ. He also mentioned that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "had al-Fadl ride behind him" in this hadith, whereas what happened was that he had Usamah ibn Zayd ride behind him. The riding of al-Fadl ibn ʿAbbas was in a different incident.
The hadith was narrated by Ahmad in the Musnad: 1347, from Yahya ibn Adam, from Sufyan, meaning al-Thawri, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAyyash, from Zayd ibn ʿAli, from his father, from ʿUbaydullah ibn Abi Rafiʿ, from ʿAli, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood at ʿArafah and said: "This is the place of standing, and all of ʿArafah is a place of standing," then he had Usamah ride behind him, and he was guiding his camel while people struck the camels to the right and left, and he did not turn to them. This is also abridged. Abu Dawud narrated it: 1922, from Ahmad ibn Hanbal, with this chain, and he abridged it slightly.
Ahmad also narrated it: 562, from Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri, from Sufyan, with this chain, in full. In it, after the riding of Usamah: "Then he came to Quzah, stood at Quzah, and said: 'This is the place of standing, and all of Jamʿ is a place of standing...'" to the end, in full.
ʿAbdullah ibn Ahmad narrated it in the Zawaʾid of the Musnad: 564, by way of al-Mughira ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Makhzumi, from his father, and 613, by way of Muslim ibn Khalid al-Zanji, from ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Makhzumi, with this chain, also in full.
al-Tirmidhi narrated it, 2: 100-101, in full, by way of Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri, from al-Thawri, and said: "A hasan sahih hadith. We do not know it from the hadith of ʿAli except through this route, from the hadith of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn ʿAyyash. More than one narrator has transmitted it from al-Thawri in this manner."]]

3829 - Hannad and Ahmad al-Dulabi narrated to us, both saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn al-Munkadir, from Saʿid ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Yarbuʿ, from Ibn al-Huwayrith, who said: I saw Abu Bakr standing at Quzah saying: "O people, enter the morning! O people, enter the morning!" Then he departed.

[[The report: 3829. Sufyan: this is Ibn ʿUyaynah. Ibn al-Munkadir: this is Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir al-Taymi, one of the great imams among the Successors.
Saʿid ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Yarbuʿ: the hafiz mentioned him in al-Taʿjil, p. 154, and stated that he was Makhzumi, and he pointed to this report from his narration. He said: "It occurred in others' narrations as: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Saʿid ibn Yarbuʿ." He means: in the narrations of others than al-Shafiʿi, because al-Shafiʿi narrated this report, as will come. In al-Taʿjil this entry was marked with the letter alif, which is the symbol for "Ahmad" in the Musnad. This is a typographical error; the correct reading is "faʿ", the symbol for al-Shafiʿi. ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Saʿid ibn Yarbuʿ is biographed in al-Tahdhib 6: 187, Ibn Saʿd 5: 111, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/239, but all narrations of this report have "Saʿid ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Yarbuʿ." From the two biographies that appear to me, I favour that the narrator here is not the one biographed in al-Tahdhib, and it is possible that the narrator of this report is the son of the one in al-Tahdhib. Especially since Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned him in the biography of "Ibn al-Huwayrith" as a narrator from him, even though neither he nor al-Bukhari in al-Kabir biographed "Saʿid ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Yarbuʿ."
Ibn al-Huwayrith: this is Jubayr ibn al-Huwayrith. Ibn Abi Hatim biographed him, 1/1/512, and said: "He narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. Saʿid ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Yarbuʿ narrated from him." Likewise Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr biographed him in al-Istiʿab, no. 317, then said: "There is doubt about his companionship." Ibn al-Athir biographed him in Usd al-Ghabah 1: 270, and said: "His father was killed on the day of the Conquest of Makkah, killed by ʿAli. This indicates that his son Jubayr had companionship or sight [of the Prophet]." Likewise al-Hafiz favoured his companionship in al-Isabah 1: 235 and al-Taʿjil: 66-67. All of them named his father as "al-Huwayrith," except al-Musʿab al-Zubayri in Nasab Quraysh p. 257, who named him "al-Harith," but "al-Huwayrith" is the correct form, matching what is in Ibn Hisham's Sirah p. 819 (Europe edition) and Ibn Saʿd's Tabaqat 1/2/90.
This report was narrated by al-Shafiʿi in al-Umm 2: 180, from Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah, with this chain, with an addition at the end, but in it: "from Abu al-Huwayrith." Likewise it is established in his Musnad, arranged by Shaykh ʿAbid al-Sindi 1: 256. In the printed Musnad al-Shafiʿi, in the margin of volume 6 of al-Umm, it reads: "from Jubayr ibn Huwayrith." This inconsistency indicates a distortion of the name in some copies of al-Umm and the Musnad of al-Shafiʿi, especially since al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar mentioned his name correctly in al-Taʿjil and mentioned no disagreement there, although he marked it only with al-Shafiʿi's symbol. Perhaps this error was in some copies of al-Umm and the old Musnad al-Shafiʿi, and this led al-Bayhaqi to narrate the report by a route other than al-Shafiʿi, contrary to his usual practice.
Al-Bayhaqi narrated it, 5: 125, by way of Saʿdan ibn Nasr, from Sufyan, meaning Ibn ʿUyaynah, with this chain. Ibn Hazm narrated it in al-Muhalla 3: 215-216, by way of Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, from Sufyan, with it.]]

3830 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Harun narrated to us, from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUthman, from Yusuf ibn Mahak, who said: I performed Hajj with Ibn ʿUmar. When he entered the morning at Jamʿ he prayed the dawn prayer, then set out, and we set out with him until he stood with the imam at Quzah. Then the imam departed, and he departed with the imam's departure.

* *

As for the saying of ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar when he arrived at Muzdalifah: "All of this is mashaʿir (sacred sites) leading to Makkah," its meaning is that they are landmarks of the Hajj, in each of which some of the rites of Hajj are performed, not that all of that is "the Sacred Mashʿar" such that whoever stands wherever he stands from it up to the bottom of Makkah has fulfilled his obligation of standing at the Sacred Mashʿar, which is Jamʿ.

* *

As for the saying of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad: "I did not find anyone who informs me about the Sacred Mashʿar," it is possible that he meant: I did not find anyone who informs me of its boundary, its beginning and its end, correctly and truthfully. For the limits of that, in their correctness, such that there is no addition or subtraction in them, are known only by a few people of knowledge of them. However, although the standing at its beginning and end is not without addition or subtraction except by those I have mentioned, the place where standing is needed is not hidden from anyone among the inhabitants of that region and many others. Likewise for the rest of the sites of Hajj, and the places where Allah, mighty and majestic, obligated His servants to perform rites, such as ʿArafat, Mina and the Haram.

* *

On the interpretation of the words of the Exalted: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you, though before that you were indeed among the astray﴾ (2:198).

Abu Jaʿfar said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Remember Allah, O believers, at the Sacred Mashʿar, by praising Him and thanking Him for His favours upon you. Let your remembrance of Him be through submission to His command, obedience to Him and gratitude for what He has bestowed upon you of success, in that He guided you to the sunan of Abraham His friend, after you had been in shirk, confusion and blindness from the path of truth, and after misguidance. [Let it be] like His remembrance of you with guidance, until He rescued you from the Fire through it, after you were on the brink of a pit of it, and He saved you from it. This is the meaning of His words: "as He has guided you."

* *

As for His words: "and though before that you were indeed among the astray," some of the people of Arabic grammar direct the interpretation of "in" (إن) toward the meaning of "ma" (ما), and the interpretation of the lam in "li-man" toward the meaning of "illa" (إلا). [[This is the grammatical analysis of the Kufans; see Ibn Hisham's al-Mughni 1: 191 and others.]]

So the interpretation of the speech according to this meaning is: "And you were not, before Allah guided you to what He guided you to, of the religion of His friend Abraham, which He chose for whoever He was pleased with among His creation, except among the astray."

* *

Among them are those who direct the interpretation of "in" toward "qad" (قد).

Its meaning according to the saying of the one who holds this view is: "Remember Allah, O believers, as He remembered you with guidance, and so He guided you to what He was pleased with of religions and creeds, and you had indeed been among the astray before that."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 199 (part 1 of 2):

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding the interpretation of this, and who is meant by the command to depart from where the people depart? And who are the "people" who were commanded to depart from their place of departure?

Some of them said: What is meant by His words, "Then depart," is Quraysh and those born of Quraysh, who were called al-Hums (the Hums, i.e. the strict ones) in the Jahiliyyah. They were commanded in Islam to depart from 'Arafat, which is the place from which all the other people, other than the Hums, departed. That is because Quraysh and those born of Quraysh used to say: "We do not leave the Sanctuary (al-Haram)." So they would not attend the standing of the people at 'Arafat with them, and God therefore commanded them to stand with them.

Mention of those who said this:

3831 - Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Tufawi narrated to us, saying: Hisham ibn 'Urwah narrated to us, from his father, from 'A'ishah, who said: Quraysh and those who were upon their religion – and they are the Hums – used to stand at al-Muzdalifah, saying: "We are the Servants (qatin) of God!" And whoever else there was would stand at 'Arafat. So God revealed: "Then depart from where the people depart."

[Hadith 3831: Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Tufawi, with a damma on the unpointed ta': reliable, one of the teachers of Ahmad and Ibn al-Madini and others.
This hadith is related by al-Bukhari (8:139, Fath) from Ibn al-Madini, from Muhammad ibn Khazim, from Hisham with it, somewhat more detailed. Likewise Muslim (1:348) related it from Yahya ibn Yahya, from Abu Mu'awiyah, who is Muhammad ibn Khazim, with it.
Al-qatin is the name of a group whose singular is qatin and whose plural is qitan: they are the residents of a dwelling who remain in it and do not leave it. Their saying "we are qatin of God" contains an ellipsis, meaning: the qatin of the House of God and its Sanctuary. If it is taken to mean that the qatin are the servants, then the meaning would be: the servants of God and those who attend to the affairs of His House, without need for an ellipsis. This is also a good reading.]

3832 - 'Abd al-Warith ibn 'Abd al-Samad ibn 'Abd al-Warith narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: Aban narrated to us, saying: Hisham ibn 'Urwah narrated to us, from 'Urwah: that he wrote to 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan: You wrote to me concerning the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to a man of the Ansar: "I am a Hamsi" [See the previous narrations from no. 3077 to 3087, for therein is the report of the Ansari and the statement of the Messenger of God to him.] – and I do not know whether the Prophet said it or not? Except that I heard her (i.e., 'A'ishah) relate it from him. The Hums: the creed of Quraysh – and they are polytheists – and those born of Quraysh among Khuza'ah and Bani Kinanah. They did not depart from 'Arafat; they only departed from al-Muzdalifah, which is al-Mash'ar al-Haram. The Banu 'Amir were Hums, because Quraysh had given birth to them; and it was concerning them that it was said: "Then depart from where the people depart." And all the Arabs used to depart from 'Arafat except the Hums; they would depart at dawn from al-Muzdalifah.

[Hadith 3832: Aban is Ibn Yazid al-'Attar, who is reliable; Ibn Ma'in, al-Nasa'i and others declared him reliable.
I have not found this hadith in this form elsewhere. Its meaning is established in the preceding hadith, and in another lengthy hadith related by al-Bukhari (3:411–413, Fath) through 'Ali ibn Mushir, and Muslim (348) through Abu Usamah – both from Hisham ibn 'Urwah from his father.
See also what has passed in al-Tabari: 3077–3087.
'Urwah's saying here, "but I heard her relate it": he means his aunt 'A'ishah, Mother of the Believers, and that she related this from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). This is clear from the context of the statement and from all the other reports. Perhaps he referred to them by the pronoun because both had been mentioned previously in the question of 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, to whom he is answering with this statement.]

3833 - Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Tusi narrated to me, saying: Abu Tawbah narrated to us, saying: Abu Ishaq al-Fazari narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Arabs used to stand at 'Arafat, and Quraysh used to stand short of that, at al-Muzdalifah. So God revealed: "Then depart from where the people depart," and the Prophet (ﷺ) raised the standing from the standing of the Arabs at 'Arafat.

[Hadith 3833: Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Tusi, the teacher of al-Tabari: he narrated from him in the History (1:8, 17) under the name "Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Habib"; then (1:67) under the name "Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Tusi" as here; then (1:209) under the name "Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Habib al-Tusi". It is thus established that he is the same, and he is biographied in Tahdhib and Tarikh Baghdad (5:108–109) under the name "Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Nayzak ibn Habib Abu Ja'far, known as al-Tusi". He is among the teachers of al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat. "Nayzak" is with a kasra on the nun and a fatha on the zay with a ya' between them, as vocalised in al-Taqrib and al-Khulasah.
Abu Tawbah: he is al-Rabi' ibn Nafi' al-Halabi, who settled in Tarsus; he is trustworthy, truthful, a proof, as Abu Hatim said; and he is among the teachers of him and of Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and others.
Abu Ishaq al-Fazari: he is the hafiz, the proof, Shaykh al-Islam Ibrahim ibn Muhammad ibn al-Harith ibn Asma' ibn Kharijah ibn Hisn, and he is the trustworthy, reliable Imam. His teacher Sufyan is al-Thawri.
Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah: he is Husayn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, and he is weak; Ibn Ma'in, Ibn al-Madini, Abu Hatim and others declared him weak. Perhaps he is attributed here to his grandfather, rather the original reads "ibn 'Abd Allah," and the copyists distorted it. I am certain that he is the one because he is the one who narrates from 'Ikrimah and from whom al-Thawri narrates, as in his biography in Ibn Abi Hatim (1/2/57). Furthermore, no one in this generation of narrators is named "Husayn ibn 'Ubayd Allah"; indeed, in al-Tahdhib, nor in al-Kabir, nor in Ibn Abi Hatim is there anyone claiming that. Yes, there are narrators with this name in Lisan al-Mizan, but all of them are later than this generation.
I have not found this hadith in any source other than al-Tabari, and al-Suyuti (1:227) did not attribute it to anyone else.]

3834 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from 'Abd al-Malik, from 'Ata': "Then depart from where the people depart" – from where the mass of people depart.

3835 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: al-Hakam narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Qays narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn Talhah, from Mujahid, who said: When the Day of 'Arafah comes, God descends to the lowest heaven with the angels, and says: "Come to Me, My servants, believe in My promise and affirm My messengers!" He says: "What is their reward?" It is said: "That You forgive them." That is His saying: "Then depart from where the people depart, and seek God's forgiveness; indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful."

3836 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih = and Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih = from Mujahid: "Then depart from where the people depart," he said: 'Arafah. He said: Quraysh used to say: "We are the Hums, the people of the Sanctuary; we do not leave the Sanctuary, and we depart from al-Muzdalifah." So they were commanded to proceed to 'Arafah.

3837 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: "Then depart from where the people depart." Qatadah said: Quraysh and every ally of theirs and the sons of their sisters did not depart from 'Arafat; they only departed from al-Mughammas, saying: "We are the people of God, so we do not leave His Sanctuary." So God commanded them to depart from where the people depart, from 'Arafat, and informed them that the sunnah of Abraham and Ishmael was thus: departure from 'Arafat.

3838 - Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Then depart from where the people depart," he said: The Arabs used to stand at 'Arafat, and Quraysh would consider it too great to stand with them, so Quraysh would stand at al-Muzdalifah. So God commanded them to depart with the people from 'Arafat.

3839 - It was related to me from 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning His saying: "Then depart from where the people depart," he said: Quraysh and every son of a sister and ally of theirs did not depart with the people from 'Arafat; they stood within the Sanctuary and did not leave it, saying: "We are only the people of the Sanctuary of God, so we do not leave His Sanctuary." So God commanded them to depart from where the people depart; and the sunnah of Abraham and Ishmael was departure from 'Arafat.

3840 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Najih, who said: Quraysh – I do not know whether before the Elephant or after it – innovated the matter of the Hums, an opinion they held among themselves [In the Sirah of Ibn Hisham: "an opinion they held and circulated."], saying: "We are the sons of Abraham, the people of sanctity and the custodians of the House, and the residents and inhabitants of Makkah [In the Sirah of Ibn Hisham: "and the residents of Makkah and its inhabitants."]; so no one among the Arabs has a right like ours, nor a standing like ours, and the Arabs do not recognize for anyone what they recognize for us. So do not hold anything of the Hill (al-Hill) in the same esteem as you hold the Sanctuary, for if you do that, the Arabs will make light of your sanctity [In the Sirah of Ibn Hisham: "of your sanctity."]." They said: "They have exalted from the Hill the same as they have exalted from the Sanctuary." So they abandoned standing at 'Arafat and departing from it, though they recognized and acknowledged that it is among the sites and the Hajj and the religion of Abraham, and they held that it was proper for all other people to stand there and depart from there; but they said: "We are the people of the Sanctuary, so it is not fitting for us to leave the sanctity, nor to exalt anything else as we exalt it – we, the Hums." And the Hums are the people of the Sanctuary.
Then they made for those of the Arabs who were born and who dwelt in the Hill the same as what they had by birth to them; so what is lawful for them is lawful for them, and what is forbidden to them is forbidden to them. And Kinanah and Khuza'ah had entered with them into this. Then they innovated in this matter things that had not existed, until they said: "It is not fitting for the Hums to churn butter-milk into aqit (dried curd), nor to melt ghee while they are in the state of ihram [In the Sirah of Ibn Hisham: "that they should itaqat" – to make aqit: to prepare it; aqit is something made from churned milk, boiled and left until it dries, and it is from camel's milk specifically. Salaʾ al-samn: he boiled it and treated it until its butter melted. Al-hurum (with two dammas) is the plural of haram; a man haram means muhrim (in the state of ihram).], nor to enter a house of hair, nor to seek shade except in tents of leather, for as long as they are in ihram." Then they increased this [raf'u fi dhalika: they added to it and exaggerated], saying: "It is not fitting for the people of the Hill to eat food they bring with them from the Hill into the Sanctuary when they come as pilgrims or as visitors, nor to circumambulate the House upon their first arrival except in the garments of the Hums; and if they do not find any of these, they circumambulate the House naked." So they urged the Arabs to this, and they submitted to it, and took up what they had prescribed for them in this regard [This sentence is not present in this exact wording in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham.]. And they remained upon that until God sent Muhammad (ﷺ), and God revealed – when He had perfected for him his religion and prescribed for him his Hajj [In the printed edition: "his hajj"; and in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham: "and prescribed for him the sunan of his Hajj."]: "Then depart from where the people depart, and seek God's forgiveness; indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful" – meaning Quraysh, and "the people" meaning the Arabs. So He raised them, in the sunnah of the Hajj, to 'Arafat, and to standing upon it, and to departing from it. And God removed, through Islam, the matter of the Hums – and what Quraysh had innovated from it – from the people, when God sent His Messenger.
[Report 3840: in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham (1:211–216), and the Sirah contains additions; we have noted the variations above.]

3841 - Bahr ibn Nasr narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wahb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi al-Zinad informed me, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, from 'A'ishah, who said: Quraysh used to stand at Quzah, and the people would stand at 'Arafah. She said: So God revealed: "Then depart from where the people depart."

* *

Others said: Those addressed by His words, "Then depart," are all the Muslims, and what is meant by His words, "from where the people depart," is Jam' (Muzdalifah), and by "the people" is Abraham, the Friend of the Merciful, peace be upon him.

Mention of those who said this:

3842 - It was related to me from al-Qasim ibn Sallam, who said: Harun ibn Mu'awiyah al-Fazari narrated to us, from Abu Bistam, from al-Dahhak, who said: It is Abraham. [Report: al-Qasim ibn Sallam, with the lam doubled: he is Abu 'Ubayd, the Imam and proof, author of Kitab al-Amwal and other works. Marwan ibn Mu'awiyah al-Fazari: his biography has passed (1222, 3322). In the printed edition here it reads "Harun," "Marwan"; this is an obvious error. And "Marwan al-Fazari" is among the teachers of al-Qasim ibn Sallam, as in his excellent biography in Tarikh Baghdad (12:403–406). Abu Bistam: he is Muqatil ibn Hayyan al-Nabati al-Balkhi, and he is trustworthy, as we clarified in al-Musnad (3107). Al-Dahhak: he is Ibn Muzahim al-Hilali al-Khurasani, and he is trustworthy, as we mentioned in al-Musnad (2262). This report was pointed to by Ibn Kathir (1:469), who said it was "narrated by Ibn Jarir from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim only." Al-Suyuti (1:227) made a mistake, mentioning it from the narration of al-Tabari from Ibn 'Abbas? Perhaps his mind was carried away by the frequency of al-Dahhak's narrations from Ibn 'Abbas??]

Abu Ja'far said: What we consider correct in the interpretation of this verse is that by this verse is meant Quraysh and whoever was of the Hums with them from among the rest of the Arabs, because of the consensus of the authorities among the interpreters that this is its interpretation.

Given that this is so, the interpretation of the verse is: "Whoever has made the Hajj obligatory upon himself, there shall be no obscenity, no wickedness, and no disputing during the Hajj. Then depart from where the people depart, and seek God's forgiveness; indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful. And whatever good you do, God knows it."

And this, since what we have described is its interpretation, is of the "preceded" phrase whose meaning is "delayed" and the "delayed" phrase whose meaning is "preceded," in the manner of what we previously explained in similar cases [See the index of Arabic discussions in the two preceding volumes]. Were it not for the consensus that I have described, that this is its interpretation, I would have said: the most probable of the interpretations of the verse is what al-Dahhak said, that God meant by His words, "from where the people depart," from where Abraham departed. For departure from 'Arafat is without doubt before departure from Jam', and before the obligation of remembrance at al-Mash'ar al-Haram. Since this is without doubt so, and since God, mighty and majestic, only commanded departure from the place from which the people depart, after the mention of departure from 'Arafat has concluded, and after His command to remember Him at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and then He said after that: "Then depart from where the people depart" – it was known by this that He did not command departure except from the place they had not departed from, not the place from which they had already departed; and the place from which they had departed, the time of departure from it having ended, has no justification for being told: "Depart from it."

Since there is no justification for that, and since it is impermissible that God, mighty and majestic, would command a command that has no meaning, the correctness of what he said as interpretation in this matter is evident, and the error of what opposes it – were it not for the consensus we have described and the convergence of reports with what we mentioned from those among the interpreters whose statements we have cited.

* *

If someone says to us: How can it be that this is its meaning, when "the people" is a plural and "Abraham" (peace be upon him) is singular, and God, may His remembrance be exalted, says: "Then depart from where the people depart"?

It is said: The Arabs do this often, indicating the singular by mentioning the plural. Among that is the saying of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], and the one who said that was singular, and he, according to what the reports of the historians concurred upon, was Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i [See al-Istí'ab: 301, Ibn Sa'd 2/1/42, and Tarikh al-Tabari 3:41–42; but al-Tabari did not take this approach in interpreting the verse in Al 'Imran, 4:118–121 (Bulaq)]. And from it is the saying of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteousness﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 51]; it is said: by that is meant the Prophet (ﷺ) – and the parallels of this in the speech of the Arabs are more than can be counted. [Al-Tabari will return after a few lines to mention the continuation of the interpretation of this part of the verse.]

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And seek God's forgiveness; indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ (199)

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: When you depart from 'Arafat, returning toward Mina, then remember God at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, call upon Him and worship Him there, just as He has remembered you with His guidance, so He has granted you success in what He approved for His Friend Abraham, guiding him to it from the law of His religion, after you had been astray from it.

* *

Regarding "then" (thumma) in His words, "Then depart from where the people depart," there are two possible interpretations:

One of them is what al-Dahhak said: that its meaning is: "Then depart, returning to Mina from where Abraham, my Friend, departed from al-Mash'ar al-Haram; and ask Me for forgiveness of your sins, for I am Forgiving of them, and Merciful to you." As:

Tabari's Commentary (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 2, verse 199 (part 2 of 2):

3843 - Ismail ibn Sayf al-Ajali narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Qahir ibn al-Sarri al-Sulami narrated to us, saying: Ibn Kinana, who is kunyah Abu Kinana, narrated to us, from his father, from al-Abbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I asked Allah on the Day of Arafah to forgive the sins of my Ummah, and He answered me that He had forgiven them, except for the wrongs they do to one another. I repeated the supplication that day, but I was given no answer. When it was the morning of Muzdalifah, I said: 'O Lord, You are capable of compensating this wronged person for his injustice and forgiving this wrongdoer!' He answered me that He had forgiven." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed. We said: "O Messenger of Allah, we saw you laugh on a day when you did not used to laugh!" He said: "I laughed at the enemy of Allah, Iblis, when he heard what had been said, as he began calling out 'Woe and destruction!' and putting dust on his head."

[Editorial notes on the chain: Ismail ibn Sayf al-Ajali: his identity could not be verified. Abd al-Qahir ibn al-Sarri al-Sulami al-Basri: Ibn Ma'in said "salih" and Ibn Shahin mentioned him among the trustworthy (thiqat). Ibn Kinana: this is Abd Allah ibn Kinana ibn Abbas ibn Mirdas, as clarified by the takhrij and biographical sources. He is majhul (of unknown state) per al-Taqrib and al-Khulasa. In al-Tahdhib, al-Bukhari said "his hadith is not authentic." Kinana ibn al-Abbas: al-Bukhari, in al-Kabir, and Ibn Abi Hatim mention him, transmitting from his father, and mention no criticism. Ibn Hibban included him among the trustworthy, then in al-Majruhin declared him "very munkar in hadith," while Ibn Mandah said it is said he had companionship (suhba), and al-Hafiz in al-Isaba counted him among those who had a vision (ru'ya) of the Prophet, pointing out Ibn Hibban's error. The hadith is also narrated by Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Musnad, Ibn Majah, al-Bayhaqi, and in part by Abu Dawud; al-Mundhiri quoted al-Bayhaqi's remark that it has many supporting narrations and that its truth rests on them. Al-Suyuti cited it, attributing it also to al-Tabarani, and al-Diya al-Maqdisi included it in al-Mukhtara.]

3844 - Muslim ibn Hatim al-Ansari narrated to me, saying: Bashshar ibn Bukayr al-Hanafi narrated to us, both saying: Abd al-cAziz ibn Abi Rawwad narrated to us, from Nafi, from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us in the evening of Arafah, saying: "O people, Allah has shown graciousness to you in this standing place of yours. He accepted the good-doers among you, granted the good-doer what he asked, and pardoned your wrongdoers for the sake of your good-doers, except for the wrongs among yourselves. Disperse in the name of Allah." When it was the morning of Jam', he said: "O people, Allah has shown graciousness to you in this standing place of yours. He accepted from your good-doers, pardoned your wrongdoers for your good-doers, and the wrongs among you, He has compensated for them from His own presence. Disperse in the name of Allah." His companions said: "O Messenger of Allah, yesterday you dispersed from us sorrowful and grieved, and today you dispersed from us joyful and glad!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Yesterday I asked my Lord for something He did not grant me: I asked Him for the wrongs, and He refused me. But today, Jibril came to me and said: 'Your Lord sends you greetings and says: I have guaranteed compensation for the wrongs from Myself.'"

[Editorial notes on the chain: Muslim ibn Hatim Abu Hatim al-Ansari: trustworthy (thiqa), one of the shuyukh of Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi; al-Tirmidhi and al-Tabarani declared him trustworthy. Bashshar ibn Bukayr al-Hanafi: despite extensive searching, no biography was found; he is mentioned in this chain in Abu Nu'aym's al-Hilya. Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Rawwad al-Makki: a known trustworthy narrator, noted for piety, asceticism and worship; whoever criticized him for his opinions offers no valid proof. The hadith is narrated by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya by two chains, and he said: "The wording is that of Bashshar ibn Bukayr; the hadith of Abu Hisham is abridged... a strange narration, transmitted by Abd al-Aziz from Nafi alone, not followed by others." Al-Mundhiri mentioned a similar meaning from the hadith of Ubada ibn al-Samit, saying al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Kabir with narrators relied upon in the Sahih except one unnamed man. Al-Haythami likewise mentioned it, and a similar hadith from Anas ibn Malik attributed to Abu Ya'la, in which al-Haythami said: "It contains Salih al-Murri, who is weak." Al-Suyuti also cited both without explanation of their defects.]

* *

These two reports make clear that Allah's forgiveness of the wrongs that His servants commit against one another occurs on the morning of Jam', which is the time when He, may His praise be exalted, said: "Then disperse from where the people disperse and seek forgiveness from Allah" (2:199), for your sins; indeed, He is Forgiving of them at that time, as a favour from Him to you, and Merciful to you.

* *

The other of the two, "Then disperse" (2:199), refers to dispersing from Arafah toward al-Mash'ar al-Haram. When you disperse to it from there, remember Allah there, as He has guided you.

**The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿So when you have completed your rites, then remember God as you remember your fathers, or with even more remembrance﴾**

Abu Ja'far [al-Tabari] said: By the words of His, the Exalted's, "when you have completed your rites," He means: when you have finished your pilgrimage and slaughtered your sacrifices, then remember God.[[See the explanation of "qada" (to complete, decree) in earlier volumes: 2:542–543.]]

* *

It is said of this root: "nasaka al-rajul yansuku nuskan, nusukan, nasikatan, wa-mansakan," meaning he slaughtered his sacrifice (nusk). The "mansik" is a noun, like "al-mashriq" and "al-maghrib." As for "al-nusk" in religion, it is said: "ma kana al-rajul nasikan, wa-laqad nasaka, wa-nasuka nusikan nusukan wa-nasakatan" (the man was devout, and he was pious, and became devout). That is when he became pious (taqarra'a).[[See the explanation of "nasaka" in earlier volumes: 3:75–80, and in this section, and in the sense of slaughtering. These are verbal nouns not mentioned in the lexicographical books.]] "Taqarra'a al-rajul" means he became learned in religion and devout; so he is "qari'," "mutaqarri," and "quraʾ" (with a damma on the qaf and a shadda on the ra').[[Taqarra'a al-rajul: he acquired religious understanding and practised devotion; hence he is qari', mutaqarri' and quraʾ.]]

* *

In the same sense as what we have said regarding the meaning of "al-manasik" in this passage, Mujahid said:

3845 – Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "So when you have completed your rites," he said: "the shedding of blood."[["Ihraqah" is the verbal noun of "harraqa al-dam yuhriquhu," meaning to pour out and spill it.]]

3846 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* *

As for His words: "then remember God as you remember your fathers, or with even more remembrance," the people of interpretation differed concerning the manner of "the people's remembrance of their fathers," which God commanded them to make their remembrance of Him like, as their remembrance of their fathers, or even more intense.

Some of them said: In their pre-Islamic period (Jahiliyyah, the Age of Ignorance), after finishing their pilgrimage and rites, the people would gather and boast of the glorious deeds of their fathers. So God commanded them in Islam that their remembrance should be through praise, gratitude and glorification of their Lord alone, and that they should bind themselves to remember Him frequently, in the same way they had bound themselves in the Jahiliyyah to remember their fathers.

Those who said this:

3847 – Tamim ibn al-Muntasir related to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Yusuf narrated to us, from al-Qasim ibn 'Uthman, from Anas, regarding this verse, he said: "They used to mention their fathers during the pilgrimage. One of them would say: 'My father used to feed people with food.' Another would say: 'My father used to strike with the sword!' And another would say: 'My father cut the forelocks of the Banu so-and-so!'"

3848 – Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to me, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Abd al-'Aziz, from Mujahid, who said: They used to say: "Our fathers used to slaughter camels, and do such-and-such!" Then this verse was revealed: "Remember God as you remember your fathers, or with even more remembrance."

3849 – Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Asim, from Abu Wa'il: "Then remember God as you remember your fathers, or with even more remembrance," he said: The people of the Jahiliyyah used to mention the deeds of their fathers.

3850 – Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: I heard Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash say: The people of the Jahiliyyah, when they finished the pilgrimage, would stand by the House (the Ka'bah) and mention their fathers and their days: "My father used to feed people with food! My father used to do such-and-such!" This is His saying: "Then remember God as you remember your fathers." Abu Kurayb said: I said to Yahya ibn Adam: "From whom is this?" He said: Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash narrated to us, from 'Asim, from Abu Wa'il.

3851 – Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj informed me, from one who related to him, from Mujahid, regarding His words: "Remember God as you remember your fathers," he said: When they completed their rites, they would stand at the jamrah (the stoning pillar) and mention their fathers, and mention their days in the Jahiliyyah and the deeds of their fathers. So this verse was revealed.

3852 – Ya'qub related to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from 'Abd al-Malik, from Qays, from Mujahid, regarding His words: "Then remember God as you remember your fathers," he said: When they completed their rites, they would stand at the jamrah and mention their days in the Jahiliyyah and the deeds of their fathers. He said: So this verse was revealed.

3853 – Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "So when you have completed your rites, then remember God as you remember your fathers," he said: The Arabs would boast among themselves of the deeds of their fathers on the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), when they had finished; so they were commanded to mention God instead of that.

3854 – Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

3855 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "So when you have completed your rites, then remember God as you remember your fathers." Qatadah said: The people of the Jahiliyyah, when they completed their rites at Mina, would sit in circles and mention the conduct of their fathers in the Jahiliyyah and their deeds. Their orator would give a speech and their storyteller would narrate. So God, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded the Muslims to remember God as the people of the Jahiliyyah remembered their fathers, or with even more remembrance.

3856 – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "Then remember God as you remember your fathers, or with even more remembrance," he said: When they completed their rites, they would gather and boast, and mention their fathers and their days. So they were commanded to substitute in place of that the remembrance of God, remembering Him as they remembered their fathers, or with even more remembrance.

3857 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Khusayf, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ikrimah, who both said: They used to mention the deeds of their fathers in the Jahiliyyah when they stood at 'Arafah. So this verse was revealed.

3858 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir informed me that he heard Mujahid say that on the day of sacrifice, when they slaughter. He said: "Then remember God as you remember your fathers." He said: The Arabs, on the day of sacrifice, when they finished, would boast of the deeds of their fathers, so they were commanded to remember God, the Mighty and Majestic, instead of that.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: "Remember God as children's remembrance of their fathers."

Those who said this:

3859 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from 'Uthman ibn Abi Rawwad, from 'Ata', that he said regarding this verse: "as you remember your fathers": it is the saying of the child: "O father!"
