3995 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to 'Ata': "and destroys the tillage and the progeny." He said: the tillage is the crops, and the progeny is of people and livestock. He said: he kills the progeny of people and livestock. He said: Mujahid also said: he seeks in the land the destruction of the tillage, the vegetation of the earth, and the progeny of every living creature.

3996 - Yahya ibn Abi Talib related to me, saying: Yazid informed us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak concerning His words "and destroys the tillage and the progeny," he said: the tillage is the root, and the progeny is every creature, and people among them. (His words "the tillage is the root" is a meaning rarely found in the lexicon books clearly, but it occurs there incidentally, as in the saying: "al-harth is the root of the donkey's jirdan [a plant]," which is a restriction; and this report indicates a general sense of "tillage" as: the root, which is a fine usage in the figurative language.)

3997 - Ibn 'Abd al-Rahim al-Barqi related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Abi Salamah related to us, saying: Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz was asked about "the corruption of the tillage and the progeny," and what are they: which tillage, and which progeny? Sa'id said: Makhul said: the tillage is what you cultivate; and as for the progeny, it is the progeny of everything.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Some of the readers recited "and destroys [yuhlika] the tillage and the progeny" with "yuhlika" in the nominative, meaning: "And among men is one whose speech about the life of this world pleases you, and he calls God to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents. And when he turns away he strives in the land to cause corruption therein, and God does not love corruption," so that "and he destroys" is returned to "and God calls to witness," joining it by coordination.

That reading is, in my view, not permissible, although it has a grammatical basis, because it contradicts what the consensus of the readings holds, namely the reading "wa-yuhlika" (in the accusative), and because it is in the codex and recension of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, as has been related to us: "li-yufsida fiha wa-liyuhlika al-harth wa-al-nasl" (in the printed edition: "as has been mentioned," which does not fit). That is among the strongest evidence for confirming the reading of those who read "yuhlika" in the accusative, coordinated with "li-yufsida fiha."

* *

The interpretation of the words of the Most High: ﴿And God does not love corruption (205)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be great, He means: God does not love acts of disobedience, cutting off the way, and frightening the road.

* *

"Fasad" (corruption) is a verbal noun from the speaker's saying: "fasada al-shay'u yafsudu" (the thing decayed), like their saying "dhahaba yadhhabu dhahaban" (he went). Among the Arabs are those who make the verbal noun of "fasada" to be "fusudan," and the verbal noun of "dhahaba yadhhabu" to be "dhuhuban." (See the meaning of "corruption in the land" in 1:287–290, 416, and what has preceded just before: 239. See also al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:124.)

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 206:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride takes him to sin, so Hell is sufficient for him; and wretched is the resting place﴾ (2:206).

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, exalted is His praise, He means: And when it is said to this hypocrite, whose description has been given to His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and who was told that his speech pleases him in the life of this world, "Fear Allah and be mindful of Him in your corruption on the earth of Allah, and in your striving therein through what Allah has forbidden you of His disobediences, and in your destruction of the tilth and offspring of the Muslims," he becomes arrogant, and zeal and pride seize him in what Allah has forbidden him, and he persists in his error and misguidance. Allah, exalted is His praise, says: So His punishment for his error and misguidance is sufficient for him: he is the fuel of the fire of Hell. And wretched is the resting place for its inhabitants.

* *

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning who is meant by this verse.

Some of them said: It refers to every wicked person and hypocrite.

Those who said this include:

3998 - Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Buza' narrated to me, saying: Ja'far ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: Bistam ibn Muslim narrated to us, saying: Abu Raja' al-Utaridi narrated to us, saying: I heard Ali concerning this verse, "And among the people is one whose speech pleases you in the life of this world..." to "And Allah is Kind to the servants." Ali said: "By the Lord of the Ka'bah, they fought each other."

3999 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words, "And when it is said to him, 'Fear Allah,' pride takes him to sin," to His words, "And Allah is Kind to the servants": Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, when he had prayed his voluntary prayers (al-subha) and finished, would enter his enclosure (mirbad) [[al-subha: voluntary and supererogatory prayer and the remembrance of Allah; one says, "I have finished my subha." al-mirbad: an open area behind the houses, adjoining the rooms like a courtyard in the house; it is also the place where dates are dried so that they dry out, which the people of Madinah call mirbad, and this is what is meant here.]] and send for young men who had recited the Qur'an, among them Ibn Abbas and the nephew of Uyayna, [[The nephew of Uyayna is al-Hurr ibn Qays ibn Husayn al-Fazari; it is also said al-Harith ibn Qays, and the first is more correct. al-Bukhari narrated through al-Zuhri from Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Uyayna ibn Husn came and stayed with his nephew al-Hurr ibn Qays, and he was among the group whom Umar brought close - the hadith. He is listed in al-Isabah and elsewhere.]] and they would come and recite the Qur'an and study it together, and when the midday heat came, he would leave. He said: They passed by this verse, "And when it is said to him, 'Fear Allah,' pride takes him to sin," and "And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah, and Allah is Kind to the servants." Ibn Zayd said: These are the strivers in the way of Allah. Then Ibn Abbas said to someone beside him: "Have the two men fought?" Umar heard what he said and said: "And what did you say?" He said: "Nothing, O Commander of the Faithful!" He said: "What did you say? 'Have the two men fought?'" When Ibn Abbas saw that, he said: "I see here someone who, when commanded to fear Allah, is seized by pride in sin, and I see someone who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah. This one stands and commands that one to fear Allah, and when he does not accept and is seized by pride in sin, the other says: 'And I sell myself!' and fights him, and the two men fight each other!" Umar said: "May your abilities be blessed, O Ibn Abbas." [[In the printed edition: "tiladuk" with a tā' at its beginning, which has no meaning; the correct reading is what is given here. In al-Durr al-Manthur 1:241: "lillah darruk." The Arabs say: "lillah darr fulan, wa lillah biladuh."]]

* *

Others said: Rather, it refers to al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, and we have mentioned those who said this earlier. [[See the report no. 3961.]]

* *

As for His words, "and wretched is the resting place," He means: and wretched is the bed and resting place, Hell, which Allah, exalted is His praise, promised to this hypocrite, and which he prepared for himself through his hypocrisy, his wickedness, and his rebellion against his Lord.

**Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the approval of Allah﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means: "And among the people is one who sells himself in exchange for what Allah promised to those who strive in His cause, and who has bartered his soul for it," based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties, for [the price that] they will have Paradise﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111].

* *

We have already shown that the meaning of *shara* (ﺷﺮى) is "to sell," in other places, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary. [Refer to what has passed: 2:341–343, n. 455, and the indexes of the language.]

* *

As for His saying, *ibtighā'a marḍāt Allāh* (ﺍﺑﺘﻐﺎﺀ ﻣﺮﺿﺎﺓ ﺍﻟﻠﻪ, "seeking the approval of Allah"), it means that this seller, when he sells, seeks the approval of Allah.

The accusative of *ibtighā'* (ﺍﺑﺘﻐﺎﺀ, "seeking") is governed by *yashrī* (ﻳﺸﺮﻱ, "sells"). It is as if He said: "And among the people is one who sells [himself] for the sake of seeking the approval of Allah," and then the phrase "for the sake of" (*min ajl*) was dropped and the verb took effect on the noun.

Some of the grammarians of Arabic claimed that it is in the accusative as an object of the verb, [Meaning: it is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl li-ajlihi*), and a similar case has passed: "as an explanation of the verb," 1:354, note 4.] on *yashrī*, as if He said: "for the seeking of the approval of Allah." Then, when the particle *lām* (ﻝ, "for") was removed, the verb took effect, and He said: And similar to it is *ḥadhara al-mawt* (ﺣﺬﺭ ﺍﻟﻤﻮﺕ, "fear of death") [al-Baqarah: 19]. [See the discussion of the i'rab (ﺍﻹﻋﺮﺍﺏ, grammatical case-analysis) of this word earlier, 1:354–355.] And the poet, who is Hatim, said:

*Wa-aghfiru 'awrā'a al-karīmi idikhārahu* ... *wa-u'riḍu 'an qawli al-la'īmi takarrumā*

[Diwan: 24, from fine noble verses; also Sibawayh 1:184, 464; Nawadir Abi Zayd: 110; al-Khizanah 1:491; al-'Ayni 3:75, and others. There is much variation in the transmission of this verse, and the evidence in it is the accusative of *idikhārahu* (ﺍﺩﺧﺎﺭﻩ, "his hoarding/storing") as an object of purpose.]

[He] said: When the *lām* is removed, the verb takes effect on it.

Some of them said: *Ayyumā* (ﺃﻳﻤﺎ) is a verbal noun placed in the position of a condition, [By "condition" he seems to mean, as far as I think, the sense of cause and excuse: that it is a cause, a reason, or an excuse for the occurrence of the action.] and the place of *an* (ﺃﻥ) where *bi-* (ﺑـ, "with") and *li-* (ﻟـ, "for") would be appropriate. You say: "I came to you out of fear of harm" — "for fear of harm" — and "because I feared harm." So the particle (*ṣifah*, here meaning the preposition) is not stated, so it is omitted and the verbal noun is put in its place. [He] said: If the particle were one specific letter, it would not be permissible to omit it, just as it is not permissible for someone who says "I did this for you and for so-and-so" to drop the *lām*.

* *

Then the interpreters differed about who this verse was revealed concerning, and who is meant by it. Some of them said: It was revealed concerning the Emigrants (*muhājirūn*) and the Helpers (*anṣār*), and what is meant by it is those who strive in the way of Allah.

Those who said that:

**4000** — Al-Ḥusayn ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, he said: 'Abd al-Razzāq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatādah, regarding His saying: "And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the approval of Allah," he said: "The Emigrants and the Helpers."

* *

And some of them said: It was revealed concerning certain men among the Emigrants by name.

Those who said that:

**4001** — Al-Qāsim narrated to us, he said: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, he said: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ikrimah: "And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the approval of Allah," he said: It was revealed concerning Suhayb ibn Sinān, and Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, Jundub ibn al-Sakan. The people of Abū Dharr seized Abū Dharr, but he escaped from them and came to the Prophet ﷺ. When he returned as an emigrant, they confronted him, and they were at Marr al-Ẓahrān, and he escaped again until he came to the Prophet (ﷺ). As for Suhayb, his family seized him, and he ransomed himself from them with his wealth, then he set out as an emigrant. Then Qunfudh ibn 'Umayr ibn Jud'ān caught up with him, and he gave him what remained of his wealth, and let him go.

[Report 4001: in al-Durr al-Manthūr 1:240; in the printed edition: "Munqidh ibn 'Umayr," which is an error; the correct name is Qunfudh ibn 'Umayr, whom Abū Ṭālib mentions in his well-known qaṣīdah, and Ibn Hishām mentions his lineage in his Sīrah (see 1:295, 301). Qunfudh ibn 'Umayr embraced Islam and had companionship (ṣuḥbah) with the Prophet, and 'Umar appointed him over Makkah, then dismissed him.]

**4002** — It was narrated to me on the authority of 'Ammār, he said: Ibn Abī Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabī' regarding His saying: "And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the approval of Allah," the verse. He said: A man from the people of Makkah had embraced Islam, and he wanted to go to the Prophet ﷺ and emigrate to Madinah, but they prevented him and imprisoned him. He said to them: "I will give you my house and my wealth, and whatever I possess! Let me go, and I will join this man!" But they refused. Then some of them said to them: "Take from him whatever he has and let him go!" So they did, and he gave them his house and his wealth, then he set out. Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed to the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah: "And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the approval of Allah," the verse. When he drew near to Madinah, 'Umar met him with some men, and 'Umar said to him: "Has the sale profited?" He said: "And your sale will not lose!" He said: "What is that?" He said: "Such-and-such was revealed about you."

[Report 4002: in Tafsīr al-Baghawī 1:481–482, with some difference in wording.]

* *

And others said: Rather, what is meant by it is everyone who sells himself in obedience to Allah and in striving in His way, or in enjoining what is good.

Those who said that:

**4003** — Muḥammad ibn Bashshār narrated to us, he said: Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan Abū 'Abd Allāh narrated to us, he said: Abū 'Awn narrated to us, from Muḥammad, he said: Hishām ibn 'Āmir charged the battle line until he broke through it. They said: "He threw himself into destruction!" Abū Hurayrah then said: "And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the approval of Allah."

[Report 4003: Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥasan Abū 'Abd Allāh al-Nasrī narrated from Ibn 'Awn and others; Aḥmad, al-Fallās and Bundār and others narrated from him. He was among the reliable transmitters who are counted, and he memorized from Ibn 'Awn. He died in the year 188. He is biographed in al-Tahdhīb. "Abū 'Awn" is the kunyah of Ibn 'Awn, 'Abd Allāh ibn 'Awn al-Muzanī, their mawlā. "Muḥammad" is Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn. Hishām ibn 'Āmir ibn Umayyah al-Anṣārī, whose name in the Jāhiliyyah was "Shihāb," and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ changed it. This happened in his military campaign of Kābul; see al-Iṣābah and others. His saying "threw his hand" means: he threw his hand into destruction (*al-tahlukah*), as is explained in other narrations; see what will come, report 4005, in abridged form.]

4004 — Abū Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Muṣ'ab ibn al-Miqdām narrated to us, he said: Isrā'īl narrated to us, from Ṭāriq ibn 'Abd al-Raḥmān, from Qays ibn Abī Ḥāzim, from al-Mughīrah, he said: 'Umar sent an army, and they besieged the people of a fortress. A man from Bajīlah advanced and fought, and he was killed. Most of the people spoke about him, saying: "He threw his hand into destruction!" He said: This reached 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "They lied! Does not Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, say: 'And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the approval of Allah, and Allah is Compassionate toward the servants'?"

**4005** — Ibn Bashshār narrated to us, he said: Abū Dāwūd narrated to us, he said: Hishām narrated to us, from Qatādah, he said: Hishām ibn 'Āmir charged the battle line until he split it, and Abū Hurayrah said: "And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the approval of Allah."

**4006** — Sawwār ibn 'Abd Allāh al-'Anbarī narrated to us, he said: 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī narrated to us, he said: Ḥazm ibn Abī Ḥazm narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Ḥasan recite: "And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the approval of Allah, and Allah is Compassionate toward the servants." Do you know concerning what it was revealed? It was revealed concerning a Muslim who met a disbeliever, and he said to him: "Say: there is no god but Allah!" If you say it, you will protect your blood and your property, except by their right! But he refused to say it. So the Muslim said: "By Allah, I will surely sell myself to Allah!" He advanced and fought until he was killed.

[Report 4006: "Ḥazm ibn Abī Ḥazm" al-Qaṭa'ī Abū 'Abd Allāh al-Baṣrī narrated from al-Ḥasan and others. Abū Ḥātim said: "Truthful, there is no harm in him, and he is among the reliable transmitters who remained of al-Ḥasan's companions." He died in the year 75. He is biographed in al-Tahdhīb. In the printed edition it was "Ḥizām ibn Abī Ḥizām," which is an error.]

**4007** — Aḥmad ibn Ḥāzim narrated to me, he said: Abū Nu'aym narrated to us, Ziyād ibn Abī Muslim narrated to us, from Abū al-Khalīl, he said: 'Umar heard a man recite this verse: "And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the approval of Allah." He said: 'Umar said "Innā lillāh wa-innā ilayhi rāji'ūn" (Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return), and said: "A man stood enjoining what is good and forbidding what is evil, and was killed."

[Report 4007: "Ziyād ibn Abī Muslim" Abū 'Amr al-Farrā' al-Baṣrī narrated from Ṣāliḥ Abū al-Khalīl, Abū al-'Āliyah and al-Ḥasan. He is biographed in al-Tahdhīb. "Abū al-Khalīl": Ṣāliḥ ibn Abī Maryam al-Ḍab'ī, their mawlā, a Successor (tābi'ī), biographed in al-Tahdhīb.]

* *

Abū Ja'far said: What is closer to the apparent meaning of this verse among the interpretations is what has been related from 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them, that it means enjoining what is good and forbidding what is evil.

This is because Allah, may His praise be exalted, described two groups. One of them is a hypocrite who says with his tongue what is contrary to what is in his heart, and when he is able to disobey Allah he commits it, and when he is not able he desires it, and when he is forbidden, pride seizes him in sin, for which it is indeed a sin. And the other of the two is one who sells himself, seeking the approval of Allah. So the apparent interpretation is that the group described as having sold itself to Allah and sought His approval was only selling itself to confront the wicked group, seeking the approval of Allah. This is the most prevalent and apparent interpretation of the verse.

As for what has been related about the revelation of the verse concerning the matter of Suhayb, this is not objectionable, since it is not disputed that a verse may be revealed from Allah to His Messenger ﷺ because of some cause, and that what is meant by it is everyone whom its apparent meaning encompasses.

So the correct statement on this matter is to say: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, described one who sells himself seeking His approval. So whoever sells himself in His obedience until he is killed in it, or who fights to the death even if he is not killed, [In the printed edition: "wa-istaqtala" with the conjunction "wa," which is corrupt; the correct reading is what I have recorded.] is meant by His saying: "And among the people is he who sells himself, seeking the approval of Allah" — whether that was in fighting the enemies of the Muslims, or in enjoining what is good, or forbidding what is evil.

* *

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is Compassionate toward the servants﴾ (207)**

We have already shown the meaning of *ra'fah* (ﺭﺃﻓﺔ, "compassion") in what has passed, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary here, and that it is the softness of mercy. [Refer to what has passed: 3:171, 172.]

* *

The meaning of that is: Allah is One of vast mercy toward His servant who sells himself to Him in striving against those who oppose His command among the people of polytheism and wickedness, and toward His other believing servants, in their immediate affairs and in the end of their return. So He will fulfill for them the reward for what they accomplished in His obedience in this world, and He will settle them in His Gardens for what they did in them of seeking His approval.

* *

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O you who believe, enter into peace (al-silm) completely﴾**

Abū Ja'far said: The interpreters differed about the meaning of *al-silm* (ﺍﻟﺴﻠﻢ) in this place.

Some of them said: Its meaning is: Islam.

Those who said that:

**4008** — Muḥammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abū 'Āṣim narrated to us, from 'Īsā, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid regarding the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: "Enter into *al-silm*," he said: Enter into Islam.

**4009** — al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, he said: 'Abd al-Razzāq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatādah regarding His saying: "Enter into *al-silm*," he said: Enter into Islam.

**4010** — Muḥammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my paternal uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbās: "Enter into *al-silm* completely," he said: *al-silm* is Islam.

**4011** — Mūsā ibn Hārūn narrated to me, he said: 'Amr informed us, he said: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī: "Enter into *al-silm*," meaning: in Islam.

**4012** — Abū Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Wakī' narrated to us, from al-Naḍr ibn 'Arabī, from Mujāhid: Enter into Islam.

**4013** — Yūnus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: "Enter into *al-silm*." He said: *al-silm* is Islam.

**4014** — It was narrated on the authority of al-Ḥusayn ibn Faraj, he said: I heard Abū Mu'ādh al-Faḍl ibn Khālid say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulaymān narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Ḍaḥḥāk say: "Enter into *al-silm*": in Islam.

* *

And others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: Enter into obedience.

Those who said that:

**4015** — It was narrated on the authority of 'Ammār, he said: Ibn Abī Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabī': "Enter into *al-silm*," meaning: enter into obedience.

* *

The reciters differed in the recitation of this. The majority of the reciters of the Ḥijāz recited it *"ud-khulū fī as-salm"* with a fatḥah on the sīn, and the majority of the reciters of Kūfa recited it with a kasrah on the sīn.

As for those who opened the sīn of *salm*, they directed its interpretation to making peace (*al-musālamah*), meaning: enter into reconciliation, compromise, abandoning war, and giving the poll-tax (*al-jizyah*).

As for those who recited it with a kasrah on the sīn, they differed about its interpretation.

Among them are those who direct it to Islam, meaning: enter into Islam completely. And among them are those who direct it to reconciliation, meaning: enter into reconciliation, and they cite as evidence that the sīn is pronounced with a kasrah when it means reconciliation, the verse of Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā:

*Wa-qad qultumā in nudriki as-silma wāsi'an* ... *bi-mālin wa-ma'rūfin mina al-amri naslamu*

[Diwan: 16, from his noble mu'allaqah. The pronoun in *qultumā* refers to the two who sought reconciliation, al-Ḥārith ibn 'Awf and Harim ibn Sinān, and that was during the war of 'Abs and Dhubyān. "Wāsi'an" (vast) means: the matter has settled and hearts have become at rest, so there is room for people in it which they do not have in a time of war. Al-Ḥārith and Harim had taken on the burden of guarantee with their wealth, so that people might be reconciled.]

The most correct of the interpretations of His saying "enter into *al-silm*" is the statement of the one who said: its meaning is: enter into Islam completely.

As for which of the two recitations is closer to the correct in reciting this, it is the recitation of the one who recited with a kasrah on the sīn, because when it is recited that way — though it may carry the meaning of reconciliation — the meaning of Islam and the lasting of the righteous condition is more prevalent among the Arabs than reconciliation and making peace. And the verse of the brother of Kindah is recited:

*Da'awtu 'ashīratī lil-silmi lammā* ... *ra'aytuhum tawallaw mudbirīnā*

[From verses of Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Ābis al-Kindī, and it is narrated for others. Al-Mu'talif wa-l-Mukhtalif: 9; al-Waḥshiyyāt: 75, and others. Imru' al-Qays had come to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and did not apostatize in the days of Abū Bakr, and he remained upon Islam, and he had a great and notable role in the apostasy wars. He composed the verses during the time of the apostasy. Before the verse he says: "Let me convey to Abū Bakr a message, and convey it to all the Muslims. I will never again be a neighbor to a tribe that denies what the Messenger said." "I called my tribe to *al-silm* until I saw them making war and corrupting."]

with a kasrah on the sīn, meaning: I called them to Islam when they apostatized. This was when Kindah apostatized with al-Ash'ath [He is al-Ash'ath ibn Qays al-Kindī, who came as a delegation to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the tenth year with seventy riders from Kindah, then he apostatized among those Arabs who apostatized. He fought in the apostasy until he was defeated, then he surrendered and was taken captive, and they brought him before Abū Bakr, who said to him: "What do you think I should do with you? You have done what you know." Al-Ash'ath said: "Grant me favor by freeing me from the iron and marrying me to your sister, for I have returned and embraced Islam." Abū Bakr said: "Done!" So he married him to Umm Farwah bint Abī Quḥāfah, and he remained in Madīnah until Iraq was conquered. Then he took part in the conquests until he died in the year 40, at the age of sixty-three.] after the death of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Abū 'Amr ibn al-'Alā' used to recite all the other mentions of *al-salm* in the Qur'an with a fatḥah, except this one in Sūrat al-Baqarah, for he specifically pronounced its sīn with a kasrah, directing its meaning to Islam and not to anything else.

We chose what we chose of the interpretation in His saying "enter into *al-silm*," and turned its meaning to Islam, because the verse is addressed to the believers. The address, since it is an address to the believers, can only be one of two matters:

Either it is an address to the believers in Muḥammad, who affirm him and what he brought. If that is the case, there is no sense in saying to them, being people of faith: "Enter into the reconciliation and peace of the believers," because peace and reconciliation are only commanded to one who is at war, to abandon war. As for the ally (*al-mawlā*), it is not permissible to say to him: "Make peace with so-and-so," when there is no war or enmity between them.

Or it may be an address to the believers among those before Muhammad ﷺ, the prophets who confirmed them and what they brought from God, and who denied Muhammad and his prophethood. So it was said to them: "Enter into al-salm," meaning Islam, not peace (al-sulh). This is because God, mighty and majestic, only commanded His servants to believe in Him, in His prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and in what he brought, and to what he called them, not to conciliation and reconciliation. Indeed, He forbade His Prophet ﷺ in some circumstances from calling the people of disbelief to reconciliation [[In the printed edition: "…from calling the people of disbelief to Islam," which is an undoubted error; the writer's pen slipped, placing "Islam" in place of "reconciliation." It is impossible that God would forbid His Prophet from calling anyone to Islam, and the context points to the correct reading, as you see.]], so He said: ﴿So do not weaken and call to peace while you are superior, and Allah is with you﴾ [Muhammad: 35]. He permitted him ﷺ, in some circumstances, when they called him to reconciliation, to initiate reconciliation, so His majestic praise said to him: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [al-Anfal: 61]. As for their calling to reconciliation initiated by them, it is not found in the Qur'an, so it is permissible to direct His saying "Enter into al-salm" toward that.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: If someone said to us: Which of these two groups was called to Islam entirely?
It is said: The interpretation of that has differed.
Some said: The believers in Muhammad ﷺ and what he brought were called to it.
* *
Others said: It was said: The believers in those prophets before Muhammad ﷺ, who denied Muhammad, were called to it.
* *
If someone said: What is the meaning of calling the believer in Muhammad and what he brought to Islam?
It is said: The meaning of calling him to that is the command to him to act upon all its laws and to uphold all its rulings and limits, without neglecting part of it and acting upon part. When that is its meaning, His saying "kaffah" (entirely) is an attribute of "al-salm," and its interpretation is: Enter into acting upon all the meanings of al-salm, and do not neglect anything of it, O people of faith in Muhammad and what he brought.
Ikrimah held a similar view regarding its interpretation.
4016 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ikrimah, regarding His saying: "Enter into al-salm entirely," he said: It was revealed concerning Tha'labah, Abdullah ibn Salam, Ibn Yamin, Asad and Usayd, the two sons of Ka'b, Sa'yah ibn Amr [[In the printed edition: "Shu'bah," and in al-Durr al-Manthur: "Sa'id," while in the names of the Jews: "Sa'yah" and "Sa'nah." Most of these names are among Jewish names whose verification is difficult and lengthy, due to the great divergence regarding them.]] and Qays ibn Zayd, all of them Jews, who said: O Messenger of God, Saturday is a day we used to venerate, so let us be, and we will observe it! And the Torah is the Book of God, so let us stand by it at night! So it was revealed: "O you who believe, enter into al-salm entirely, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan" [[The report: 4016 - in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 241.]]
* *
Ikrimah has thus clearly stated the meaning we have mentioned: that the interpretation is a call to the believers to reject all the notions that are not part of Islamic law, to act upon all the laws of Islam, and a prohibition against neglecting any of its limits.
* *
Others said: Rather, the group that was called to al-salm and told "enter into it" by this verse are the People of the Book, who were commanded to enter Islam.
Mention of those who said that:
4017 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Abbas said regarding His saying: "Enter into al-salm entirely," meaning the People of the Book.
4018 - It was narrated to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh al-Fadl ibn Khalid say: Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding the saying of God, mighty and majestic: "Enter into al-salm entirely," he said: meaning the People of the Book.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The correct statement in this matter, in my view, is that it should be said: God, mighty is His praise, commanded those who believe to enter into acting upon all the laws of Islam. The phrase "those who believe" may include those who confirm Muhammad ﷺ and what he brought, and those who confirm those prophets and messengers before him and what they brought. God, mighty and majestic, has called both groups to act upon the laws and limits of Islam, and to safeguard its obligations which He has enjoined, and forbade them from neglecting any part of that. So the verse is general for everyone covered by the name "faith," and there is no basis for restricting it to some over others.
Mujahid also said in accordance with the interpretation we have stated.
4019 - Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding God's saying, mighty and majestic: "Enter into al-salm entirely," he said: Enter into Islam entirely, enter into the deeds entirely.

Commentary on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He: ﴿kaaffatan﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His praise, "kaaffatan" [[In the printed edition: "jalla thana'uhu: kaaffatan" with the word "bi-qawlihi" omitted, and this is the context of the statement.]] means general, all together, as follows:

4020 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words "fi al-silm kaaffatan," he said: all together.

4021 - Musa narrated to us, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding "fi al-silm kaaffatan," he said: all together.

4022 - It was related to me from Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding "fi al-silm kaaffatan," he said: all together. = And from his father, from Qatadah, the same.

4023 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' ibn al-Jarrah narrated to us, from al-Nadr, from Mujahid, "enter into Islam all together."

4024 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn Abbas said: "kaaffatan": all together.

4025 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "kaaffatan" all together, and he recited: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36], all together.

4026 - It was related to me from al-Husayn, saying: I heard Abu Mu'adh al-Fadl ibn Khalid say: Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words "enter into the peace kaaffatan," he said: all together.

* *

Commentary on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He: ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ (2:208)

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His praise, the meaning is: Act, O believers, upon all the laws of Islam, and enter into its affirmation in word and deed, and leave off the ways and traces of Satan, not following them, for indeed he is a clear enemy to you, making his enmity manifest to you. [[See the explanation of "clear enemy" above, 3:300.]] The path of Satan that He forbade them to follow is whatever opposes the ruling and laws of Islam, and from it came the sanctification of Saturday and the rest of the customs of the other religious communities that oppose the religion of Islam.

* *

I have already explained the meaning of "khutuwat" (footsteps) with the evidence confirming its correctness earlier, so I disliked repeating it in this place. [[See what preceded, 3:301, 302.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 209:

The exegesis of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾ (2:209).

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His majesty be exalted, He means: If you err from the truth, [[See the meaning of "zall" (slip) in what has preceded, 1: 524-525.]]

and go astray from it, and oppose Islam and its laws, after My proofs have come to you and the signs of My guidance, and the soundness of the matter of Islam has become clear to you through the evidences that have removed your excuse, O believers, then know that Allah is possessed of might, and nothing prevents Him from taking vengeance upon you, and no one can repel from you His punishment for your opposing His command and disobeying Him. "Wise" means: in what He does to you of punishment for your disobedience to Him, after establishing the proof against you, and in His other affairs.

* *

Some of the exegetes have said that "the clear proofs" are Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. [[See what has preceded on the interpretation of "the clear proofs," 2: 318, 354, and then 3: 249-251.]]

This is close to what we have said in interpreting it, because Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an are among the proofs of Allah upon those addressed by these two verses. However, what we have said in interpreting it is more fitting to the truth, because Allah, may His majesty be exalted, has argued against those among the rabbis (ahbar, religious scholars) of the People of the Book who opposed Islam, citing what He covenanted with them in the Torah and the Gospel, and what He enjoined upon them through the tongues of their prophets, to adhere to it. This, and other proofs of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, are upon them, along with the proofs that bind them concerning Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an. For this reason we have chosen what we have chosen in the interpretation.

Those of the exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil, the people of interpretation) have said the same as what we have said.

* *

Mention of those who stated views on the interpretation of His words: "Then if you slip": [[See the meaning of "zall" in what has preceded, 1: 524-525.]]

4027. Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His words: "Then if you slip," he said: "Then if you go astray."

4028. Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: "Then if you slip," he said: "The slip is shirk (associating partners with Allah)."

* *

Mention of those who stated views on the interpretation of His words: "after the clear proofs have come to you": [[See what has preceded on the interpretation of "the clear proofs," 2: 318, 354, and then 3: 249-251.]]

4029. Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "after the clear proofs have come to you," he said: "after Muhammad (ﷺ) has come to you."

4030. And al-Qasim related to me, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to us, from Ibn Juraij: "Then if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you," he said: "Islam and the Qur'an."

* *

4031. It was related to me from Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "then know that Allah is Mighty, Wise," he said: "Mighty in His retribution, Wise in His command." [[See the meanings of "Mighty" ('aziz) and "Wise" (hakim) in the lexicon index.]]

**The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels?﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His majesty be exalted, He means: Do those who deny Muhammad (ﷺ) and what he brought await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels?

* *

Then the readers (qurra', i.e., the transmitters of the Qur'anic readings, qira'at) differed concerning the reading of His words, "and the angels" (wal-malā'ikah).

Some of them read: "Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels," with the nominative (raf'), conjoining "the angels" to the subject, the Name of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, with the meaning: Do they await only that Allah and the angels should come to them in canopies of clouds.

Those who said this:

4032. He related to me Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf, from Abū 'Ubayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām, who said: 'Abdullāh ibn Abī Ja'far al-Rāzī related to us, from his father, from al-Rabī' ibn Anas, from Abu al-'Aliyah, who said, concerning the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "Do they await only that Allah and the angels should come to them in canopies of clouds." He said: The angels come in canopies of clouds, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, comes as He wills.

4033. I have also related this report from 'Ammār ibn al-Ḥasan, from 'Abdullāh ibn Abī Ja'far, from his father, from al-Rabī', his saying: "Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels," to the end of the verse. Abū Ja'far al-Rāzī said: It is in some readings: "Do they await only that Allah and the angels should come to them in canopies of clouds," like His saying: ﴿And the day the sky shall be split open with clouds, and the angels will be sent down, a descent﴾ [al-Furqan: 25].

* *

Others read it: "Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels," with the genitive (khafḍ), conjoining "the angels" to "the canopies" (al-ẓulal), with the meaning: Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds and among the angels.

* *

Similarly, the readers differed in the reading of "ẓulal" (canopies). Some of them read it "fī ẓulal" (with a *ḍamma* on the *ẓā'* and a *fatḥa* on the *lām*, as in *ẓulal*), and some read it "fī ẓilāl" (in *ẓilāl*).

As for the one who reads "fī ẓulal," he takes it as the plural of *ẓullah* (canopy), and *ẓullah* has the plurals *ẓulal* and *ẓilāl*, just as *khullah* (friendship) is pluralized as *khulal* and *khilāl*, and *jullah* (large jar) as *julal* and *jalāl*.

As for the one who reads "fī ẓilāl," he takes it as the plural of *ẓullah*, as we have mentioned from their pluralization of *khullah* as *khilāl*.

It is also possible that its reader meant it as the plural of *ẓill* (shade), because *ẓullah* and *ẓill* may both be pluralized as *ẓilāl*.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct reading in this matter, in my view, is: "Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies (ẓulal) of clouds," on the basis of a report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Among the clouds are openings (ṭāqāt) through which Allah comes, surrounded." [[This will come in report no. 4038.]] By his saying "ṭāqāt" it is shown that they are *ẓulal* and not *ẓilāl*, because the singular of *ẓulal* is *ẓullah*, which is the *ṭāq* (arch/opening). And in following the script of the Mushaf. [[His saying "and in following..." is conjoined to the position of his saying "on the basis of a report from the Messenger of Allah..."]] This is likewise the obligation in every matter where the meanings are the same but the readers differ in reading, and there is no indication in one of the two readings that distinguishes it from the other except the difference in the script of the Mushaf (the codex). So the reading that should be preferred from among them is the one that agrees with the orthography of the Mushaf.

* *

As for the preferable of the two readings in "and the angels," the correct one is the nominative, conjoining it to the Name of Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, with the meaning: Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and that the angels should come to them, according to what is related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. This is because Allah, Majestic is His praise, has informed in more than one place of His Book that the angels come to them. He, Majestic is His praise, said: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angel, row upon row﴾ [al-Fajr: 22], and He said: ﴿Do they await anything but that the angels should come to them, or your Lord should come, or some of the signs of your Lord should come?﴾ [al-An'am: 158]. If someone is confused by the words of Allah, Majestic is His praise, ﴿and the angel, row upon row﴾, and supposes that its meaning contradicts the meaning of His words "Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds and the angels," because "and the angels" in this verse is in the plural while in the other it is in the singular, then that supposition is a mistake. For "the angel" (al-malak) in His words ﴿and your Lord comes, and the angel﴾ has the meaning of the collective, i.e., "the angels." The Arabs mention the singular with the meaning of the plural, so they say: "So-and-so has much dirham and dinar," meaning dirhams and dinars; and "the camel and the sheep perished," meaning the groups of camels and sheep. Likewise His words "and the angel" mean "the angels."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Then the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning His words "canopies of clouds," whether it is connected to the action of Allah, Majestic is His praise, or to the action of "the angels," and who comes in them. Some of them said: It is connected to the action of Allah, and its meaning is: Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and that the angels should come to them.

Those who said this:

4034. Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, who said: Abū 'Āṣim related to us, from 'Īsā, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, concerning the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds," he said: It is other than the clouds (sahāb); it was only for the Children of Israel in their wandering (tīh) when they wandered, and it is that in which Allah comes on the Day of Resurrection. [[See the explanation of "the clouds" (al-ghamām) in what preceded, 2:90-91, and what will come shortly: 266.]]

4035. al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā related to us, who said: 'Abd al-Razzāq informed us, who said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatādah: "Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds," he said: Allah comes to them, and the angels come to them at death.

4036. al-Qāsim related to us, who said: al-Ḥusayn related to us, who said: Ḥajjāj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: 'Ikrimah said, concerning His words "Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds": "Openings (ṭāqāt) of clouds, and the angels around Him." Ibn Jurayj said: Another said: and the angels by death.

* *

The saying of this 'Ikrimah, although it agrees with the saying of those who say that His words "in canopies of clouds" are connected to the action of the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, which we have already mentioned, nevertheless it differs from them regarding the description of the angels. For the obligatory reading, according to the interpretation of this saying of 'Ikrimah concerning "the angels," is the genitive, because he interprets the verse as: Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds and among the angels, since he claims that Allah, Exalted is He, comes in canopies of clouds with the angels around Him.

This is if he meant his saying "and the angels around Him" as referring to them being around the clouds, making the pronoun in "around Him" refer to "the clouds." But if he meant his saying "and the angels around Him" as referring to them being around the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, making the pronoun in "around Him" refer to the Lord, Majestic is He, then his saying is like the saying of the others whose sayings we have mentioned, and he does not oppose them in this.

* *

Others said: Rather, His words "in canopies of clouds" are connected to the action of "the angels," and it is the angels who come in them, whereas the Lord, Mentioned is He, comes as He wills.

Those who said this:

4037. I was told by 'Ammār ibn al-Ḥasan, who said: Ibn Abī Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabī', concerning His words "Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels," to the end of the verse, he said: That is on the Day of Resurrection; the angels come to them in canopies of clouds. He said: The angels come in canopies of clouds, and the Lord, Exalted is He, comes as He wills.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two interpretations in this matter is the interpretation of those who connect His words "in canopies of clouds" to the action of the Lord, Majestic is He, and that its meaning is: Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels should come to them. For:

4038. Muḥammad ibn Ḥumayd related to us, who said: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mukhtār related to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Zam'ah ibn Ṣāliḥ, from Salamah ibn Wahram, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbās, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Among the clouds are openings through which Allah comes, surrounded," and that is His saying: "Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels, and the matter be decided." [[The report 4038: Zam'ah ibn Ṣāliḥ al-Janadī, with a *fatḥa* on the *jīm* and the *nūn*, of Yemen: weak; Aḥmad, Ibn Ma'īn and others declared him weak. We have explained this in the commentary on the Musnad: 2061.
Salamah ibn Wahram, with a *fatḥa* on the *wāw* and a *sukūn* on the *hā'*, of Yemen: trustworthy; they spoke about him only on account of reports narrated from him by Zam'ah ibn Ṣāliḥ, and the blame in them falls on Zam'ah.
This report is weak, as you see. al-Suyūṭī mentioned it (1:241-242) and attributed it only to Ibn Jarīr and al-Daylamī.
He also cited before it something similar in meaning, as a statement of Ibn 'Abbās (mawqūf), and attributed it to 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Abū Ya'lā, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim. Perhaps the mawqūf version is closer to the truth.
See the report after it: 4039.]]

* *

As for the meaning of His words "Do they await," it means "what do they await," and we have already explained this with its reasons earlier in this book. [[It seems he means what preceded at 2:485, that interrogative particles may take the meaning of negation. I found no place other than this that points to it. See Lisān al-'Arab, entry (h-l-l).]]

* *

Then they differed concerning the manner of the coming of the Lord, Blessed and Exalted, which He mentioned in His words "Do they await only that Allah should come to them?"

Some said: There is no description of that except what He described Himself with, Mighty and Majestic, of coming, arriving and descending. It is not permissible for anyone to strain to speculate about this except by a report from Allah, Majestic is His majesty, or from a messenger sent. As for speculation about the attributes and names of Allah, it is not permissible for anyone to derive them by reasoning except by what we have mentioned.

* *

Others said: His coming, Mighty and Majestic, is similar to what is known of the coming of one who comes from one place to another and moves from one place to another.

* *

Others said: The meaning of His words "Do they await only that Allah should come to them" is: Do they await only that the command of Allah should come to them, as one says: "We feared that the Banū Umayyah would come upon us," meaning their rule.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: Do they await only that His reward, His reckoning and His punishment should come to them, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Nay, but the scheming of the night and day﴾ [Saba': 33], and as one says: "The governor cut off the thief or struck him," while in fact his assistants did the cutting.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "the clouds" (al-ghamām) earlier in this book, which suffices so that we need not repeat it, [[See what preceded at 2:90-91, and what came earlier at 263.]] because its meaning here is the same as its meaning there.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: So the meaning of the speech is: Do those who refuse to enter into submission (al-silm) entirely (kāffah) and who follow the steps of Satan (khuṭuwāt al-shayṭān) await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and then decide concerning their affair whatever He decides? [[In the printed edition: "Do they await, the refusers..." The correct reading is what I have set down.]]

4039. Abū Kurayb related to us, who said: 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad al-Muḥāribī related to us, from Ismā'īl ibn Rāfi' al-Madīnī, from Yazīd ibn Abī Ziyād, from a man of the Anṣār, from Muḥammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazī, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "You will stand in one station on the Day of Resurrection, the measure of seventy years. You will not be looked at, nor will judgment be passed between you. You will be confined, and you will weep until the tears run out, then you will weep blood, and you will weep until it reaches your chins, or it bridles you, and you will cry out. Then you will say: Who will intercede for us with our Lord so that He judges between us? They will say: Who is more worthy of this than your father Adam? Allah shaped his clay, created him with His hand, breathed into him of His spirit, and spoke to him face to face [[The word "qiblan" (with a *kasra* on the *qāf* and a *fatḥa* on the *bā'*) means face to face, openly, not from behind a veil, and without entrusting His affair or speech to any of the angels.]]. So they come to Adam and ask him that, but he refuses. Then they seek the prophets one by one, and whenever they come to a prophet he refuses. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Until they come to me. When they come to me, I will go out until I come to al-Fahṣ (the open area)." Abu Hurayrah said: O Messenger of Allah, what is al-Fahṣ? He said: "In front of the Throne." Then I will fall down in prostration, and I will not cease to be prostrate until Allah sends to me an angel who takes me by the arms and raises me, and then Allah says to me: O Muhammad! I say: Yes! And He knows best. He says: What is your matter? I say: O my Lord, You promised me intercession, so intercede for me on behalf of Your creatures, and judge among them. He says: I have interceded for you; I will come to you and judge among you. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "So I return until I stand with the people. While we are standing, we hear a violent sound from the sky, and it frightens us. The people of the lowest heaven descend with twice the number of those on earth, from the jinn and mankind, until when they approach the earth the earth is lit by their light, and they take their ranks. We say to them: Is our Lord among you? They say: No, but He is coming. Then the people of the second heaven descend with twice the number of the angels who descended, and twice the number of the jinn and mankind in it, until when they approach the earth the earth is lit by their light, and they take their ranks. We say to them: Is our Lord among you? They say: No, but He is coming. Then the people of the third heaven descend with twice the number of the angels who descended, and twice the number of those on earth from the jinn and mankind, until when they approach the earth the earth is lit by their light, and they take their ranks. We say to them: Is our Lord among you? They say: No, but He is coming. Then the people of the heavens descend in the same number, multiplied in this way, until the Almighty descends in canopies of clouds and the angels, and they have a murmur of their glorification, saying: 'Glory to the Possessor of dominion and sovereignty! Glory to the Lord of the Throne, the Possessor of majesty! Glory to the Living who does not die! Glory to the One who causes creatures to die and does not die! Most holy, most pure, Lord of the angels and the Spirit! Holy, holy! Glory to our Lord, the Most High! Glory to the Possessor of authority and greatness! Glory to Him forever and ever!' Then the Blessed and Exalted descends, carrying His Throne on that day eight, and today they are four; their feet are on the lower boundaries of the earth and the heavens, up to their hips, and the Throne is on their shoulders. Allah, Majestic is He, sets His Throne wherever He wills on the earth, then a caller calls with a call that the creatures hear, saying: O assembly of jinn and mankind, I have been silent since the day I created you until this day of yours, hearing your words and seeing your deeds, so listen to me, for it is only your pages and your deeds being read to you. Whoever finds good, let him praise Allah, and whoever finds other than that, let him blame none but himself! Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, judges among His creatures, jinn, mankind and beasts, for on that day He will indeed take retribution for the hornless from the horned." [[The report 4039: This report is weak on two grounds: because of Ismā'īl ibn Rāfi', and because of the unnamed man from the Anṣār. Moreover, this text contains strangeness (nakārah).
Ismā'īl ibn Rāfi' ibn 'Uwaymir al-Madīnī is very weak; Aḥmad, Ibn Ma'īn, Abū Ḥātim, Ibn Sa'd and others declared him weak. Ibn Ḥibbān mentioned him in al-Majrūḥīn, no. 42 (manuscript photocopy), and said: "He was a righteous man, but he would invert reports, until the majority of his narrations became the strange reports which come to mind as if he relied upon them."
Ibn Kathīr referred to this report (1:474-475) and said: "It is a well-known report, related by more than one of the authors of the Musnads and others!" I did not find it in anything before me among the sources, so I do not know how this was.
Ismā'īl ibn Rāfi' has another report, with the same meaning but much longer. Ibn Kathīr mentioned it in his Tafsīr (3:337-342) from the narration of al-Ṭabarānī in his work al-Muṭawwalāt, with its chain through Abū 'Āṣim al-Nabīl, from Ismā'īl ibn Rāfi', from Muḥammad ibn Ziyād, from Muḥammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazī, from Abu Hurayrah, raised to the Prophet. Then Ibn Kathīr said after citing it in full: "This is a well-known report, and it is very strange. Some of its parts have supporting reports in scattered traditions, and some of its wordings contain strangeness. Ismā'īl ibn Rāfi', the storyteller of the people of Madinah, alone narrated it, and he is disputed: some declared him trustworthy and some declared him weak. Several imams stated the strangeness of his reports, such as Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī, 'Amr ibn 'Alī al-Fallās; and some said of him: he is abandoned (matrūk). Ibn 'Adī said: all his reports contain problems, except that his report is written down among the weak narrators." I say [the speaker being Ibn Kathīr]: It has been disputed about its chain in many ways, and I have devoted a separate part to it. As for its context, it is very strange, and it is said that he compiled it from many reports and made them one continuous text, for which he was criticized. I heard our shaykh, the memorizer Abu al-Ḥajjāj al-Mizzī, say that he saw that al-Walīd ibn Muslim had a book which collected such supporting reports for some individual parts of this report. And Allah knows best."]]

Then Sadr al-Din ibn Abi al-Izz, the chief judge and a student of Ibn Kathir, came and referred to these two hadiths: the hadith of al-Tabari mentioned here, and the hadith of al-Tabarani. His teacher Ibn Kathir had alluded to them once in his commentary on al-Tahawiyya, pp. 171-172 in our edition, as though he considered them a single hadith. He quoted part of the lengthy hadith and then said: "It was narrated by the imams: Ibn Jarir in his tafsir, al-Tabarani, Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili, and al-Bayhaqi." His statement on this point is open to question, because the narration of al-Tabarani is found in a book other than his three Mu'jams, as Ibn Kathir reported. I also did not find it in al-Bayhaqi's Kitab al-Asma' wa al-Sifat. Further, the author of al-Zawa'id (al-Haythami) did not mention it. Had it been in one of al-Tabarani's Mu'jams or in the Musnad of Abu Ya'la al-Mawsili, as Ibn Abi al-Izz's unqualified phrasing suggests, the author of al-Zawa'id would have mentioned it, given his stated commitment in that book.
* *
Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: This report indicates the error of Qatadah's interpretation of His words "and the angels," when he said that it means the angels who come to them at death. This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) stated that they come to them after the Hour has arisen, at the standing place of reckoning, when the sky is split open. The report has been transmitted in similar terms from a group of the Companions and the Successors. We dislike lengthening the book by mentioning them and what they said about it.= It also clarifies the correctness of what we have chosen in the recitation of His words "and the angels" with the nominative case, meaning: "and the angels come to them." = It makes clear the error of the one who reads it in the genitive case, because the Prophet (ﷺ) informed us that the angels come to the people of the Resurrection at their standing place when the sky is split, before their Lord comes to them in shadows of clouds. The only exception would be if the reader of the genitive meant by His words that Almighty God intended: "unless Allah comes to them in shadows of clouds," and the angels who come to the people of the standing place when Allah comes to them in shadows of clouds are included. That would be one possible interpretation, although it is far from the view of the scholars and from the indications of the Book and the established traditions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).
* *
The interpretation of His words, exalted be He: ﴿And the matter is decided, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾ (2:210)

Abu Ja'far said: By this, Almighty God means: the judgment is concluded with justice among the creatures, [see the meaning of "qaḍā" (decided) and "qaḍāʾ" (judgment) above, 2:542-543], as we mentioned earlier from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): that the right of every oppressed person will be taken from every oppressor, even retribution for the hornless sheep from the horned ones among the animals. [See the report above, no. 4039.]

As for His words "and to Allah all matters are returned," He means: judgment among His creatures on the Day of Resurrection returns to Allah, and the ruling between them concerning their affairs that took place in the world, such as some of them wronging others, the transgressor among them overstepping the limits of Allah and opposing His command, and the doer of good among them doing good and obeying Him in what He commanded him. He will then decide between the wrongdoers and reward the people of goodness with goodness, and the people of evil according to what He sees fit. He will show favour to whoever among them was not a disbeliever, and pardon him. For this reason He, exalted be His praise, said: "and to Allah all matters are returned." Even though all the affairs of this world and the Hereafter originate from Him and return to Him, since His creatures in this world wrong one another, and some of His creatures sometimes take charge of judging between them in this world, so that some of His servants rule between them, one of them acts unjustly and another acts justly, one is correct and another errs, and the ruling can be enforced against some but not against others because of the protection of their side and their power by force. Almighty God therefore informed His servants that the return of all this is to Him at the standing place of Resurrection, where He will give each his due from the other, and repay each in full, where there is no injustice and no one can resist the enforcement of His judgment against him, where the weak and the strong, the poor and the rich are equal, where injustice vanishes and the authority of justice descends.
* *
Almighty God placed the definite article "al-" in "al-umur" (the matters) because He meant by it all matters, and did not intend some to the exclusion of others. This is like the speaker's saying: "I like honey" and "the mule is stronger than the donkey," where the definite article is used because it is not intended to refer to some particular instances rather than others, but is meant to express generality and totality.

The Interpretation of His Words, Mighty and Glorious Is He: "Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them."

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Ask, O Muhammad, the Children of Israel, those who do not await—by turning in obedience to Me and repenting to Me by acknowledging your prophethood and confirming what you have brought them from Me—except that I come to them in canopies of clouds, with My angels, so that I may decide judgment between you and those who believed in you and confirmed you, by what I have sent down to you of My Books and what I have obligated upon you and them of the laws of My religion, and between them—how many signs and proofs they were given before you, as evidence for what I had made obligatory upon them of My duties, and what I commanded them of obedience to Me, and what I sent as proofs through the hands of My prophets and messengers before you, strengthening them in their truthfulness, clearly showing that they came from Me, plainly being among My proofs for the truthfulness of My warners and messengers in what I had made obligatory upon them of believing them and believing you. But they disbelieved My proofs, denied My messengers, changed My blessings concerning them, and altered My covenant and My charge given to them.

* *

As for "clear sign" (āyah), I have already explained its interpretation earlier in our book sufficiently [[See what has passed concerning the meaning of "āyah" in 1:106, then 2:397–398, 553, then 3:184. And the meaning of "bayyinah" in 2:318, 397, then 3:249, and in this volume 4:259, 260.]]. It is here that:

4040 – Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to us, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the words of God, Mighty and Glorious: "Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them," that it refers to what God mentioned in the Qur'an and what He did not mention, and they are the Jews.

4041 – It was narrated to me by 'Ammar, he said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' concerning His words: "Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them." He says: God gave them clear signs: the staff of Moses and his hand, and He made the sea a passage for them, and drowned their enemy while they looked on, and shaded them with clouds, and sent down upon them manna and quails. These are among the signs of God that He gave to the Children of Israel, in many other signs besides them, and yet they opposed God's command, killed God's prophets and messengers, and altered His covenant and His charge to them. God said: "And whoever substitutes the blessing of God after it has come to him—indeed God is severe in punishment."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: God only informed His Prophet of these signs, commanding him to be patient with those who denied him and were arrogant toward his Lord, and informing him that this was the deed of those before them from the earlier nations toward their prophets, despite their being overwhelmed by proofs, and that those among them who are the Jews are only remnants of those whose custom was that, from among the Children of Israel whose stories were related to him. [[What is between the brackets is an addition; I fear it may be necessary for the sentence to be sound.]]

* *

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He: "And whoever substitutes the blessing of God after it has come to him—indeed God is severe in punishment" (2:211).

Abu Ja'far said: By "blessing" (ni'mah), may His praise be exalted, He means: Islam and what He has made obligatory of the laws of His religion.

By His words "whoever substitutes the blessing of God," He means: whoever changes what God has covenanted concerning His blessing, which is Islam, [[See the meaning of "tabdil" (substitution) above, 3:396.]] by deed and by entering into it, and so disbelieves in it—then He will punish him with what He has threatened as the punishment for disbelief in it, and God is severe in His punishment, painful in His torment.

* *

The interpretation of the verse, then, is: O you who believe in the Torah and confirm it, enter into Islam all together, and abandon disbelief and what Satan has called you to of his misguidance. There have come to you clear proofs from Me through Muhammad, and what I have displayed through his hands to you of proofs and lessons. So do not substitute My covenant to you concerning him, and concerning what has come to you from Me in your Book, that he is a prophet and My messenger. For whoever of you substitutes that and changes it, I will surely punish him with a painful punishment.

Similar to what we have said regarding His words, "And whoever substitutes the blessing of God after it has come to him," a group of the people of interpretation have said.

Those who said that:

4042 – Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words: "And whoever substitutes the blessing of God after it has come to him," he said: He disbelieves in it.

4043 – al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

4044 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, he said: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, he said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And whoever substitutes the blessing of God," he said: He says: whoever substitutes it for disbelief.

4045 – It was narrated to me by 'Ammar, from Ibn Abi Ja'far, from his father, from al-Rabi': "And whoever substitutes the blessing of God after it has come to him," he says: whoever disbelieves His blessing after it has come to him.

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:** ﴿The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve, and they mock those who believe; but those who fear Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, He, whose praise is majestic, means: the love of the worldly life, the hastening pleasures, has been made attractive to those who disbelieve,[[In the printed edition: "al-'ajilah fi al-dhanb" (the hastening [life] in sin), which is words without meaning. Allah called this world "al-'ajilah" (the hastening) because He hastens for those who love it whatever He wills of its adornment and pleasure, and He refers by this to His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the hastening [life], We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We please; then We have made for him Hell, which he will enter, blamed and banished﴾ [Surah al-Isra, 18].]] so they seek in it abundance and boasting, and they seek in it leadership and vanity, and they are arrogant toward following you, O Muhammad, and acknowledging what you have brought from Me, exalting themselves over those who affirmed you and followed you. And they mock those among the people of faith who followed you and affirmed you, in their abandonment of the pursuit of abundance and boasting with the worldly life and its adornment of finery and wealth, through seeking leadership and their turning toward what is with Me by renouncing the world and leaving its adornment; and those who did deeds for Me, who turned to My obedience, who renounced the pleasures and desires of the world, following you and seeking what is with Me, and out of fear of Me by performing My obligations and avoiding My disobediences, are above those who disbelieve on the Day of Resurrection, by admitting the God-fearing into Paradise and admitting those who disbelieve into the Fire.

Those who said this same interpretation as we have stated were a group of scholars.

Mention of those who said that:

4046. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, regarding His saying: "The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve": he said: The disbelievers seek the world and pursue it. "And they mock those who believe" in their pursuit of the Hereafter. Ibn Jurayj said: I think it is none other than from Ikrimah, who said: They said: "If Muhammad were a prophet as he claims, our nobles and our leaders would have followed him! By Allah, only the needy such as Ibn Mas'ud have followed him!"

4047. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, on the authority of Qatadah, regarding His saying: "And those who feared Allah are above them on the Day of Resurrection," he said: "above them" is in Paradise.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning﴾ [2:212]

Abu Ja'far said: By this He means: Allah gives those who feared Him on the Day of Resurrection from His bounties, His honors, and His abundant gifts, without any reckoning by Him against them for the honor with which He has favored them.

* *

If someone says to us: What is the praise contained in His saying "provides for whom He wills without reckoning"? It is said: The meaning of praise in it is informing that He does not fear the exhaustion of His treasuries, so that He would need to account for what goes out of them. For reckoning by the giver is only so that he may know the amount of the gift that leaves his possession to another, lest he exceed in his gifts to the point of harming himself. Our Lord, blessed and exalted, does not fear the exhaustion of His treasuries, nor any diminution of His dominion by what He gives His servants, so He does not need to account for what He gives or to count what remains. This is the meaning in His saying: "Allah provides for whom He wills without reckoning."

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 2, verse 213 (part 1 of 2)**

On the interpretation (*ta'wil*, the explanatory meaning) of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Mankind was one community, then God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners, and sent down with them the Book in truth, to judge between people concerning what they differed about.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The exegetes differed over the meaning of "*ummah*" (community) in this passage,[[See the meaning of "*ummah*" in earlier passages: 1:221; then 3:74; and Q. 100, 128; Q. 141.]] and over the "people" whom God described as "having been one community."

Some of them said: They were the people who lived between Adam and Noah, and they were ten centuries, all of them following a *shari'ah* (sacred law, way) of truth, and then they differed after that.

Mention of those who said this:

4048. Muhammad ibn Bashshar told us, saying: Abu Dawud told us, saying: Hammam ibn Munabbih told us, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Between Noah and Adam there were ten centuries, all of them upon a *shari'ah* of truth, and then they differed, so God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners. He said: Likewise it is in the reading of 'Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "Mankind was one community, then they differed."[[The report 4048 is narrated by al-Hakim in *al-Mustadrak* 2:546–547, who said: "This is a sound hadith according to the condition of al-Bukhari, though they (al-Bukhari and Muslim) did not narrate it," and al-Dhahabi agreed with him.]]

4049. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "Mankind was one community." He said: They were all upon guidance, then they differed, so God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners. The first prophet sent was Noah.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation of "*ummah*" according to this view which we have mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas is "*al-din*" (religion), as al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani said:

*I have sworn, and I have not left for your self any doubt,*
*And does one who is obedient [to God] and humbled before Him commit sin?*[[From his *Diwan* p. 40, and *Lisan al-'Arab* (*amm*), from his famous ode in which he apologized to al-Nu'man. He means: Would one who has a religion (*din*) rush into sin, when he has obeyed God and submitted to Him? So he swears to you a false oath, a perjurious oath like the one I swore, to remove from your heart the doubt about my affair.]]

He means: one who has a religion.

* * *

So the interpretation of the verse according to the meaning of these people is: "Mankind was one community gathered upon one creed and one religion, then they differed, so God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners."

* * *

The root of "*ummah*" is a group gathered upon one religion. Then the report about the "*ummah*" is given in place of the report about the "*din*," because the former points to it, as His words exalted is He say: ﴿And had God willed, He would have made you one community﴾ [Q. 5:48; Q. 16:93], meaning the people of one religion and one creed. So Ibn 'Abbas, in his interpretation of His words "Mankind was one community," meant that people were one religion until they differed.

* * *

Others said: Rather, the interpretation of that is: Adam was upon the truth, an *imam* (leader) for his descendants, and God sent the prophets among his offspring. They understood the meaning of "*ummah*" as obedience to God, calling to His monotheism, and following His command, from the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Abraham was a *ummah*, devoutly obedient to God, a *hanif*﴾ [Q. 16:120]. By His words "*ummah*" He means an *imam* in goodness who is to be followed and taken as a model.

Mention of those who said this:

4050. Muhammad ibn 'Amr told me, saying: Abu 'Asim told us, saying: 'Isa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Mankind was one community," he said: Adam.

4051. Ahmad ibn Ishaq told us, saying: Abu Ahmad told us, saying: Sufyan told us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the same.

4052. Al-Qasim told us, saying: Al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, his words: "Mankind was one community." He said: Adam. He said: Between Adam and Noah there were ten prophets, and God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners. Mujahid said: Adam was a *ummah* (community) by himself.[[In the printed edition it reads "*ummah wahidah*" (one community) in both places, which is an error; the correct reading is what I have recorded. This matches the hadith of Qass ibn Sa'idah: "He will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as a *ummah* by himself," and it is also said: "He is a *ummah* apart," as in the hadith: "Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as a *ummah* apart."]]

* * *

It is as if the one who said this view considered it permissible to name the one by the name of the group, because of the gathering of the qualities of goodness that exist in a scattered group; so they named him "*ummah*," as one says: "So-and-so is a *ummah* by himself," meaning he stands in the position of a whole community.

It is also possible that he was named thus because he was the cause of the gathering of people upon what he called them to of the qualities of goodness.[[In the printed edition it reads "cause of the gathering of the causes among people," which is a distortion. *Al-ashtat* means the scattered ones, and similarly *shatta*.]] Since Adam ﷺ was the cause of the gathering of those among his offspring who gathered upon his religion until the time of their differing,[[His words "until the time of their differing" mean: until their state became one of disagreement and dispersion.]] he was named "*ummah*" for this reason.

* * *

Others said: The meaning of this is: Mankind was one community upon one religion on the day when God brought forth the offspring of Adam from his loins and presented them to Adam.

Mention of those who said this:

4053. I was told from 'Ammar, from Ibn Abi Ja'far, from his father, from al-Rabi', his words: "Mankind was one community." And from his father, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliyah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: They were one community when they were presented to Adam; He then originated them that day upon Islam, and they acknowledged to Him their servitude, and they were one community, all of them Muslims. Then they differed after Adam.
