Ubayy used to read: "Mankind was one community, then they differed, so God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners," up to "concerning what they differed about." And God only sent the messengers and revealed the Books at the time of differing.

4054. Yunus told us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "Mankind was one community." He said: When He brought them forth from the back of Adam, they were never one community except that day. "Then God sent the prophets." He said: This was when the nations divided.

* * *

The interpretation of the verse according to this view is similar to the interpretation of the one who said, in the words of Ibn 'Abbas, that people were upon one religion between Adam and Noah; we have explained its meaning there. Only the time when people were one community differs from the time which Ibn 'Abbas specified.

* * *

Others said otherwise than all of that, saying: The meaning of His words "Mankind was one community" is upon one religion; then God sent the prophets.

Mention of those who said this:

4055. Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, saying: My father told me, saying: My paternal uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, his words: "Mankind was one community," meaning: It was one religion, then God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the interpretations of this verse is that it should be said: God, exalted is He, informed His servants that mankind was one community upon one religion and one creed. As follows:

4056. Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: "Mankind was one community," meaning: one religion upon the religion of Adam; then they differed, so God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners.

* * *

And the religion upon which they were was the religion of truth, as Ubayy ibn Ka'b said, as follows:

4057. Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi, who said: In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "They differed concerning it/him"—from Islam.[[Report 4057 will come later under number 4063, and its text here is the same as its text there, but it is a copyist's distortion, I suppose, as will be shown. In the printed edition it reads "they differed concerning it, upon Islam."]]

* * *

"So they differed in their religion,[[In the printed edition it reads "and they differed in their religion," with a waw; the correct reading is with a fa', and it is part of al-Tabari's own speech, not of the report. It follows from his earlier words: "The religion they were upon was the religion of truth... so they differed."]] then God sent, at their differing in their religion, the prophets as bearers of good news and warners, and sent down with them the Book, to judge between people concerning what they differed about," as a mercy from Him, dhikruhu (exalted is His remembrance), toward His creation, and as an excuse presented by Him to them.

It is also permissible that the time when they were one community was from the era of Adam to the era of Noah, peace be upon them both, as Ikrimah reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and as Qatadah said.

It is also permissible that it was at the time when He presented His creation to Adam. And it is also permissible that it was at another time. There is no indication from the Book of God, nor any report that establishes proof, as to which of these times it was. So it is not permissible for us to say about it anything except what God, exalted is He, said: that mankind was one community, then God sent among them the prophets and messengers when they differed. And our ignorance of the time of that does not harm us, just as knowledge of it would not benefit us, if knowing it is not an act of obedience to God.[[This is the argument of a pious, cautious, intelligent man, perceptive of the places of error in minds and of the boldness with respect to truth among the bold who rush at knowledge out of arrogance toward knowledge. If people had sense they would withhold the excess of their tongues, but they rarely do so.]]

However, whichever of these it was, the evidence of the Qur'an is clear that those whom God informed were a community "one" only upon faith and the religion of truth, not upon disbelief in God or associating others with Him. This is because God, exalted is He, said in the surah in which Yunus is mentioned: ﴿Mankind was not but one community, then they differed. And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been judged between them concerning that in which they differ﴾ [Q. 10:19]. So He threatened over the differing, not over the gathering, nor over their being one community. And if their gathering before differing had been upon disbelief, and then differing had occurred afterward, it would not have happened except by some of them moving to faith. And if that were so, the promise would be more fitting, in His wisdom, exalted is His praise, in that state than the threat, because it would be a state of some of them returning in repentance to His obedience. And it is impossible that He would threaten in a state of repentance and return, and leave that aside in a state where all gathered upon disbelief and polytheism.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: As for His words, "Then God sent the prophets as bearers of good news and warners," He means that He sent messengers to give good news to those who obey God of abundant reward and noble return. And by His words "and warners" He means those who warn those who disobey God and disbelieve in Him, of severe punishment, evil reckoning, and eternal abiding in the Fire. "And He sent down with them the Book in truth to judge between people concerning what they differed about": He means by this: that the Book, which is the Torah, judges between people concerning what those who differ differed about. So God, exalted is His praise, attributed the "judgment" to the "Book," and that it is what judges between people, not the prophets and messengers. For whoever among the prophets and messengers gave a ruling, he only judged by what the Book revealed by God, exalted is He, pointed them to. So the Book, by its indication of what its description proves to be correct, was the judge between people, even though the one who actually decides the judgment between them is other than it.

* * *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And none differed concerning it except those who were given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of mutual insolence﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His praise, "and none differed concerning it," He means: none differed concerning the Book which He sent down, which is the Torah. "Except those who were given it" means: the Jews of the Children of Israel, and they are those who were given the Torah and knowledge of it. The pronoun in "given it" refers to "the Book" which God sent down. "After clear proofs had come to them" means: after the proofs and evidences of God had come to them that the Book about which they differed, and about its rulings, is with God, and that it is the truth which they have no room to differ about, nor to act contrary to what is in it.

So He informed, dhikruhu (exalted is His remembrance), about the Jews of the Children of Israel that they opposed the Book, the Torah, and differed concerning it with knowledge on their part, deliberately opposing God regarding what they opposed Him in, of His command and the judgment of His Book.

Then He informed, exalted is His remembrance, that their deliberate commission of the sin they committed,[[In the printed edition it reads "their deliberate commission of the sin which He sent down," which is a distortion and speech without meaning.]] and their indulgence in the disobedience they indulged in by their opposition to His command, was only out of mutual insolence among them.

* * *

*Al-baghy* (insolence, transgression) is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: "So-and-so transgressed against so-and-so, *baghyan*," when he rose up against him, acted unjustly against him, and exceeded his limit. From this it is said of a wound when it festers, and of the sea when its water increases and overflows, and of a cloud when it falls on land and makes it fertile: "*baghā*." All of that has one meaning: its increase and exceeding of its limit.[[See the meaning of "*al-baghy*" in earlier passages: 1:342.]]

* * *

So the meaning of His words, exalted is His praise, "And none differed concerning it except those who were given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of mutual insolence," is of this kind. He says: The differing of these Jews from the Children of Israel concerning My Book which I sent down with My prophet was not out of ignorance of it on their part. Rather, their differing concerning it, and opposition to its judgment, after its proof had been established against them, was out of mutual insolence among them, seeking leadership of some over others, and mutual subjugation. As follows:

4058. I was told from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: Then he returned to the Children of Israel in His words, "And none differed concerning it except those who were given it," he says: except those who were given the Book and knowledge, "after clear proofs had come to them, out of mutual insolence," he says: out of insolence over the world, and seeking its kingdom, its adornment, and its finery, which of them would have kingship and dignity among people. So some of them transgressed against others, and some of them struck the necks of others.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: Then the scholars of Arabic grammar differed over the "*min*" (from) in His words, "from after clear proofs had come to them": what is its function and its meaning? And what is the coherent meaning in His words, "And none differed concerning it except those who were given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of mutual insolence"?

Some of them said: "*min*" here belongs to "those who were given the Book," and what follows it is its complement (*sila*). But he claimed that the meaning of the speech is: "And none differed concerning it except those who were given it, out of mutual insolence, after clear proofs had come to them." Some of them rejected this and said: There is no sense in what this speaker said, nor in placing "*al-baghy*" before "*min*," because when "*min*" is governed by "*al-baghy*," it is an error for it to precede it, since "*al-baghy*" is a verbal noun, and the complement of a verbal noun does not precede it. The one who rejected it claimed that "those who" is an exception, and "from after clear proofs had come to them" is an exception with another exception, and that the interpretation of the speech is: "And none differed concerning it except those who were given it—they did not differ except out of insolence, they did not differ except after clear proofs had come to them." So it repeated the speech for emphasis.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: This second view is more fitting to the interpretation of the verse, because the people did not differ except after the establishment of the proof against them and the coming of the clear proofs from God; and likewise they did not differ except out of insolence. So that is more fitting to the interpretation of the verse.

* * *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿So God guided those who believed to the truth concerning which they differed, by His permission; and God guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ (2:213)

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His praise, "So God guided," He means: God granted success to [God's] those who believed, and they are the people of faith in God and in His messenger Muhammad ﷺ, who confirmed him and what came from him as being from God, when those who were given the Book differed concerning it.

Their differing, in which God forsook them, and in which He guided those who believed in Muhammad ﷺ, and granted them success in reaching it, was concerning "*al-Jumu'ah*" (Friday). They strayed from it although it had been prescribed for them as it was prescribed for us, so they made it Saturday. Then the Prophet ﷺ said: "We are the last and the first," (or "we are the foremost") "except that they were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them, and this is the day concerning which they differed; so God guided us to it: so for the Jews is tomorrow, and for the Christians is the day after tomorrow."

4059. Muhammad ibn Humayd told us of this, saying: Salamah told us, from Ibn Ishaq, from 'Ayyash ibn Dinar al-Laythi, who said: I heard Abu Hurayrah say: Abu al-Qasim ﷺ said: [and he mentioned the hadith].[[Report 4059: Muhammad ibn Humayd al-Razi, the teacher of al-Tabari, is well known; narration from him has been mentioned many times. In the printed edition it reads here "Ahmad ibn Humayd," which is an error and a distortion.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 213 (part 2 of 2):

ʿIyad ibn Dinar al-Laithi: a trustworthy Successor (tabiʿi) who heard from Abu Hurayra. Ibn Ishaq declared him trustworthy in another report. He related it from him in the Musnad: 7481. al-Bukhari included him in al-Kabir 4/1/22, and Ibn Hibban mentioned him in Thiqat al-Tabiʿin, p. 299 (from the manuscript copy of Kitab al-Thiqat).
This is a sound, well-known, widely transmitted hadith from Abu Hurayra, authenticated through more than one channel. See the hadith that follows it.]]
4060 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from al-Aʿmash, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayra: "So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed, by His permission" [Q. 2:213]. He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We are the last (in time) and the first (in standing) on the Day of Resurrection. We are the first people to enter Paradise, except that they were given the Scripture before us and we were given it after them. Then Allah guided us to the truth concerning that over which they differed, by His permission. This is the day which Allah has guided us to, and the people follow us in it: tomorrow the Jews, and the day after tomorrow the Christians."
[[Hadith 4060: it is in the Tafsir of ʿAbd al-Razzaq, p. 23, with this same isnad. Ahmad also related it in the Musnad (7692) from ʿAbd al-Razzaq.
It was related by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others. See also the Musnad: 7213, 7308, 7393, 7395, 7693, and the takhrij indicated there in several places.]]
* *
Among what they differed over also is what Ibn Zayd said, namely:
4061 - Yunus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words: "So Allah guided those who believed" to Islam. They differed over the prayer: some prayed toward the east, and some toward Jerusalem, so He guided us to the qibla. They differed over the fast: some fasted part of the day, some part of the night, and Allah guided us to it. They differed over Friday: the Jews took Saturday and the Christians took Sunday, and Allah guided us to it. They differed over Abraham: the Jews said he was a Jew, and the Christians said he was a Christian! So Allah cleared him of that and made him a hanif, a Muslim, and "he was not of the polytheists" [Q. 3:67], meaning those among the polytheists who claimed him. [[In the printed edition: "alladhina yadʿunahu" (who claim him); the correct reading is what is recorded here.]] They differed over Jesus: the Jews made him a fabrication, and the Christians made him a god, so Allah guided us to the truth concerning him. This is what His words, majestic is His praise, refer to: "So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed, by His permission."
* *
Abu Jaʿfar said: [[In the printed edition: "qala: fa-kanat hidayat Allah jalla thanauhu..." may lead the reader to think this follows from the earlier report; it does not, but is from the words of Abu Jaʿfar, as its following context shows, and as is clear from the transmission of this earlier report in the tafsir of Ibn Kathir 1:489-490 and al-Durr al-Manthur 1:243. Therefore I separated the two statements and began this one with "Abu Jaʿfar said."]] The guidance of Allah, majestic is His praise, to those who believed in Muhammad and in what he brought, regarding what those factions of the Children of Israel who were given the Book differed over, by His permission, was that He granted them success in attaining what was the truth held by those who were before those who differed, whom Allah described in this verse, since they were one community. That was the religion of Abraham, the upright hanif, the Muslim, the friend of the Most Merciful. Thus they became a middle community, as their Lord described them, so that they would be witnesses over the people. As follows:
4062 - I was told by ʿAmmar ibn al-Hasan, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ: "So Allah guided those who believed to that over which they differed": Allah guided them at the time of difference, in that they remained upon what the messengers had brought before the difference. They adhered to sincerity to Allah alone, worshipping Him without partner, establishing prayer and giving zakat. They held to the first command, which was before the difference, and they withdrew from the difference. So they were witnesses over the people on the Day of Resurrection: witnesses over the people of Noah, the people of Hud, the people of Salih, the people of Shuʿayb, and the household of Pharaoh, that their messengers had delivered to them and that they had denied their messengers. In the recitation of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb it reads: "wa-li-yakunu shuhada ʿala al-nas" [Q. 2:143] on the Day of Resurrection, "and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path" [Q. 2:213]. Abu al-ʿAliya used to say concerning this verse: the way out of doubts, misguidance and trials.
4063 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "So Allah guided those who believed to that over which they differed," meaning: the unbelievers differed over it, and Allah guided those who believed to the truth from that. In the recitation of Ibn Masʿud it reads: "fa-hada Allah alladhina amanu li-ma ikhtalafu ʿanhu" ("over which they differed" becoming "concerning which they differed" in the sense of departing from), meaning from Islam. [[Report 4063: see the earlier report no. 4057 and the commentary on it. In the printed edition, both here and there, it reads "li-ma ikhtalafu fihi ʿala al-Islam," which is not clear in meaning; what is recorded here is the text found in al-Qurtubi 3:33 and al-Durr al-Manthur 1:243.]]
* *
Abu Jaʿfar said: As for His words "by His permission," He means, majestic is His praise, by His knowledge of what He guided them to. We have already explained the meaning of "idhn" (permission), since it means knowledge in other places, which suffices without repeating it here. [[See what has preceded, 2:449-450.]]
* *
As for His words "and Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path," He means: Allah makes firm whom He wills of His creatures and guides him to the straight way, upon the truth that has no crookedness in it, just as He guided those who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) regarding what those who were given the Book differed over out of mutual envy. He made them firm in attaining truth and correctness in it.
* *
Abu Jaʿfar said: In this verse is clear evidence for the correctness of what the people of truth (ahl al-haqq) have said: that every blessing upon the servants, in their religion or their worldly affairs, comes from Allah, majestic and mighty is He.
* *
If someone asks us: What is the meaning of His words "So Allah guided those who believed to that over which they differed"? Did He guide them to the truth, or did He guide them to the difference? If He guided them to the difference, then He misguided them! And if He guided them to the truth, then how is it said, "So Allah guided those who believed to that over which they differed"?
It is said: That is not the way you have understood it. The meaning is: Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning what was differed over in the Book of Allah, by those who were given it: some of them disbelieved by altering it, and some of them held firm to the truth and correctness in it. These are the people of the Torah who altered it. So Allah guided those who believed from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) away from what those who altered and distorted the truth had done.
* *
Abu Jaʿfar said: If what we have said is unclear to one who is heedless, and he asks: how can it be as you say, when "min" in the Book of Allah is with "al-haqq" and "li" in His words "li-ma ikhtalafu fihi," and you move the "li" to "al-haqq" and the "min" to "al-ikhtilaf" in the interpretation you give, making it inverted? It is said: such inversion is common and widespread in the speech of the Arabs, and Allah, blessed and exalted, addressed them in their own idiom. Among it is the saying of the poet: [[It is al-Nabigha al-Jaʿdi.]]
"Kanat fariduatu ma taqulu kama / kana al-zina'u fariduata al-rajmi"
("What you say was an obligation, as / adultery was an obligation of stoning"), whereas in fact stoning is the obligation for adultery. And as another said:
"Inna sirajan la-karimun mafkharuhu / tuhla bihi al-ʿaynu idha ma tajharuhu"
("Indeed a lamp, its glory is noble, / the eye is delighted by it when it is displayed"), whereas in fact it is the lamp that is delighted by the eye, not the eye by the lamp. [[The verse was referenced earlier at 3:312.]]
* *
Some have said: The meaning of His words "So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed" is that the people of the earlier Scriptures differed, so some disbelieved in part of another's Book, though all of them are from Allah, and Allah guided the people of faith in Muhammad to affirm all of them.
That is an opinion, but the first of the two opinions is more correct, because Allah only informed of their difference concerning one Book.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 214:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you? Adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken, until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the victory of Allah?" Unquestionably, the victory of Allah is near.﴾ (2:214)

Abu Ja'far said: As for His words, ﴿am hasibtum﴾ ("or do you think"), it appears that He used the interrogative *am* (or) at the beginning of a statement, with no interrogative particle preceding it, because it follows on from a preceding speech to which it is connected. [[In the printed edition: "li-masbuq kalam" ("for a preceding speech"), which is corrupt in meaning. One of the conditions for *am* in interrogation is that it be a continuation of an interrogation, because of what precedes it of speech (see what has passed, 2:493). And his saying *lisabuq* ("for a preceding") is a verbal noun that does not occur in the lexicographical works, but I have seen al-Tabari and others use it, and it will come in al-Tabari's text after 2:240, 246 (Bulaq edition).]] Had there been no preceding speech to which it is connected, and it were a beginning, it would not have occurred except with an interrogative particle; for if a speaker, beginning a statement to another, were to say, "*am 'indaka akhuka?*" ("or do you have your brother?"), he would be saying something meaningless. But if he were to say, "You are a man who is proud of his strength, or do you have your brother who helps you?", he would be correct. We have already explained some of this meaning earlier in this book, sufficiently, so there is no need to repeat it.

* *

So the meaning of the speech is: Or do you think, O believers in Allah and His messengers, that you will enter Paradise, while there has not befallen you the like of what befell those before you among the followers of the prophets and messengers of hardships, trials and tests, so that you are tried with what they were tried and tested with: ﴿al-ba'sa'*﴾ ("distress"), which is the severity of need and poverty, ﴿wa-l-darra'*﴾ ("and adversity"), which is sicknesses and afflictions [[For the meaning of "distress and adversity," see what has passed, 3:349–352.]], and you were not shaken with their shaking, meaning: there did not befall them from their enemies fear and terror, severity and hardship, until the people were slow to await the victory of Allah for them, so they said, "When will Allah give us victory?" Then Allah informed them that His victory is near, and that He will make them high over their enemy and make them prevail over it, so He fulfilled for them what He had promised them, raised their word, and extinguished the fire of the war of those who disbelieved.

* *

This verse, according to what the people of interpretation claim, was revealed on the day of the Trench (al-Khandaq), when the believers suffered what they suffered of severe exertion, of fear of the confederates (al-Ahzab), of the harm of the cold, and of the constraint of livelihood they were in on that day. Allah, mighty and majestic, says to the believers among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: ﴿O you who believe, remember the favour of Allah upon you when hosts came to you, and We sent upon them a wind and hosts you did not see﴾ up to His words: ﴿And when the eyes shifted and the hearts reached the throats, and you assumed about Allah assumptions. There the believers were tried and shaken with a severe shaking﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9–11].

Mention of those who said this verse was revealed on the day of the Confederates:

4064 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you? Adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken." He said: This was revealed on the day of the Confederates, when one of them said: "Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion" [al-Ahzab: 12].

4065 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you; adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken." He said: It was revealed on the day of the Confederates. Calamity and siege befell the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions, so they were as Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿and the hearts reached the throats﴾.

* *

As for His words, ﴿wa-lamma ya'tikum﴾ ("and while there has not yet come to you"), the majority of the grammarians interpret it to mean *wa-lam ya'tikum* ("and has not come to you"), and they claim that *ma* is a supplementary and filler particle. I have already explained the view concerning *ma*, which the grammarians call *silah* (an added particle), what its ruling is, in another place, sufficiently so that it need not be repeated. [[See what has passed, 1:405–406, then 2:230, 331. His saying *silah* means "addition," as its explanation has passed many times; look for it in the index of terms.]]

* *

As for the meaning of His words, ﴿mathalu alladhina khalaw min qablikum﴾ ("the example of those who passed away before you"), it means: the likeness of those who passed on and went before you. [[See the explanation of *khala* ("passed away") in what has passed, 3:100, 128, 129.]]

* *

I have already shown in another place that *al-mathal* ("the example") means the likeness.

* *

The people of interpretation said things similar to what we have said on this.

Mention of those who said that:

4066 – I was told by 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' concerning His words: "Or do you think that you will enter Paradise while there has not yet come to you the example of those who passed away before you? Adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken" ... [[This report is incomplete, and I have not found its completion elsewhere.]]

4067 – al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from 'Abd al-Malik ibn Jurayj, who said concerning His words: "until the Messenger and those who believed with him say": He is the best of them and the most knowing of Allah.

* *

Regarding His words, ﴿hatta yaqula al-rasul﴾ ("until the Messenger says"), there are two readings: the nominative (*raf'*) and the accusative (*nasb*). Whoever reads it in the nominative holds that, since *fa'ala* (the past tense) would be appropriate in that position, the operation of *hatta* ("until") on it is nullified, because *hatta* does not govern the past tense (*fa'ala*) but governs the present (*yaf'alu*). When a past verb precedes it and what follows it is a present verb, and that which follows it has already been done and completed, and what precedes it of the verb is not prolonged, then the eloquent form of speech in that case is the nominative in the present verb, nullifying the operation of *hatta* upon it. This is like the speaker's saying: "I went to so-and-so until I struck him" (*qumtu ila fulan hatta adribuhu*), and the nominative is the correct form for *adribuhu* if he means: "I went to him until I struck him," when the striking had occurred and was completed, and the going was not prolonged. But when the verb preceding *hatta* is in the form of *fa'ala* and prolonged in duration, and what follows it is in the form of a verb not yet completed, then the correct speech is the accusative of the present verb, with *hatta* governing it. This is like the speaker's saying: "So-and-so kept seeking you until he speaks to you" (*ma zala fulan yatlubuka hatta yukallimaka*), or "He began looking at you until he makes you firm" (*wa ja'ala yanzuru ilayka hatta yuthabbitaka*). The correct speech, which no other is correct, is the accusative with *hatta*, as the poet said: [[He is Imru' al-Qays.]]

*maṭawtu bihim ḥattā takilla maṭiyyuhum*
*wa-ḥattā al-jiyādu mā yuqdna bi-arsān*

I drove them on until their mounts were exhausted, and until the steeds were no longer led by bridles. [[His *Diwan*: 186; *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* of al-Farra' 1:133; and Sibawayh 1:417 / 2:203. The version in Sibawayh is: "*saraytu bihim*" ("I travelled with them"), and in the second place in it he transmits: "*ḥattā takilla ghazayyuhum*" ("until their raiders were exhausted").

*Matā bi-l-qawm yamṭū matwan*: he pushed them and hastened them in travel. He means: he pressed them hard and drove them in the journey until their mounts were exhausted, reaching a state of fatigue in which they no longer needed bridles to lead them, and the riders from weariness cast the bridles aside and threw them onto the horses, not caring who followed them or how they were exhausted, nor how they travelled, nor where to.]] So *takilla* is in the accusative, and the verb after *hatta* is a past verb, because what precedes it, the *matw* ("driving"), is prolonged.

Given this, the correct reading is: ﴿wa-zulzilu hatta yaqula al-rasulu﴾, with *yaqula* in the accusative, since *zilzal* ("being shaken") is a prolonged action, like *matw bi-l-ibil* ("driving the camels").

Here *zilzal* means fear of the enemy, not "the earthquake of the earth," and so it is prolonged, and the accusative in *yaqula*, although it has the meaning of *fa'ala* (the past), is more eloquent and more correct than the nominative. [[Al-Farra' has fully treated the discussion of *hatta* in *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* 1:132–138, and al-Tabari relied on him in most of what he said in this place.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 215:

The explanation of His, may His praise be exalted, words: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever good you spend is for parents and close relatives and orphans and the needy and the wayfarer. And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is knowing of it.﴾ (2:215)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Your companions ask you, O Muhammad, what they should spend of their wealth in charity, and upon whom they should spend what they spend and give in charity? So say to them: Whatever you spend of your wealth and give in charity, then spend it and give it in charity, and make it for your fathers and mothers and close relatives, and for the orphans among you, and the needy, and the wayfarer. For whatever good you do and bring about for them, indeed Allah knows it. He counts it for you until He pays you your rewards for it on the Day of Resurrection, and rewards you, for what you obeyed Him in by your good deeds, for it.

* *

The "good" that He, may His praise be exalted, mentioned in His words "Say: whatever good you spend" is the wealth about which the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked him concerning spending from it, and Allah answered them about it with what He answered them with in this verse.

* *

In His words "mādhā" there are two grammatical (i'rab) possibilities.

One of them: that "mādhā" means "what?" (ayy shay'), so it is in the accusative (naṣb) governed by "yunfiqūn" (they spend).

The meaning of the sentence then becomes: "They ask you, what do they spend?" And it is not governed by "yas'alūnaka" (they ask you). The other of the two is the nominative (raf'). For the nominative in "dhā" there are two possibilities. One is that "dhā" which is with "mā" means "alladhī" (who/which), so "mā" is in the nominative by "dhā," and "dhā" is the complement of "mā," and "yunfiqūn" is the relative clause (ṣilah) of "dhā." The Arabs do connect "dhā" and "hādhā," as the poet said: [[This is Yazid ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari.]]

"Adas! What authority does ʿAbbād have over you? You are safe, and this one you carry is free!" [[Tarikh al-Tabari 6:178; al-Aghani 17:60 (Sasi); Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:138; Khizanat al-Adab 2:216, 514; Lisan al-Arab (ʿadas), from verses in the story of Yazid ibn Mufarrigh with ʿAbbad ibn Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan. Muʿawiya had appointed him over Sijistan and Yazid ibn Mufarrigh accompanied him, but ʿAbbad was occupied with fighting the Turks and left him. This angered Ibn Mufarrigh, and he was slow to receive his reward, so he stretched his tongue at the beard of ʿAbbad, who had a large beard, and said: "Would that beards were grass, so that we might feed it to the horses of the Muslims!"

ʿAbbad understood what he wanted and demanded it from him, so he satirized him and satirized Muʿawiya by attributing Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan to Abu Sufyan. ʿUbayd Allah ibn Ziyad, the brother of ʿAbbad, seized him and tortured him in an ugly manner, then sent him to ʿAbbad. Then Muʿawiya ordered the two of them to release him. When he set off on the postal mule, he said this poem whose first line is this verse.

His word "ʿadas" is a command to the mule, until every mule came to be called "ʿadas." The poem is a good poem, so read it in the earlier references.]]

Then "tahmilīn" (you carry) is the relative clause of "hādhā."

So the explanation of the sentence then becomes: "They ask you, what is it that they spend?"

The other of the two nominative possibilities is that "mādhā" means "ayy shay'" (what thing), so "mādhā" is in the nominative, even though "yunfiqūn" falls upon it [[It has passed that "falling upon" (wuqūʿ) is the verb transitively reaching its object; consult the glossary of terms and what has passed, 2:108, 198.]], since the governing element in it, which is "yunfiqūn," cannot be placed before it, because it is not permitted to place the verb before the interrogative particle in an interrogative. As the poet said: [[This is Labid ibn Rabi'a.]]

"Do you not ask the man what he is striving for: is it a vow to be fulfilled, or error and falsehood?" [[His Diwan 2/27, poem 41; Sibawayh 1:405; Khizanat al-Adab 2:556; Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:139, and others. The evidence in it is that he put "nahb" in the nominative, and it is returned to "mā" in "mādhā." This shows that "dhā" means "alladhī," and what follows it is its relative clause, so it does not govern what comes before it. "Nahb" means a vow. He says: Is there a vow upon him in the length of his effort which he has obligated himself to? "Nahb" also means need, and it is correct in meaning in a line like this one. He says: Is it a need that cannot be avoided, which he fulfills by his striving, or are they vain wishes that they desire, which if he were free of them and abandoned them, he would lose nothing, and life would proceed for him without need for this continuous striving and prolonged scheming?]]

And as another said: [[This is Muzahim al-ʿUqayli.]]

"And they said [[This is Muzahim al-ʿUqayli]]: Recognize for her the dwellings of Mina, but not everyone who frequents Mina is one I know."
[[His Diwan 28; Sibawayh 1:36, 73, as evidence for the accusative and nominative of "kull" (every); Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:139, where he said: I have not heard anyone put "kull" in the accusative; Sharh Shawahid al-Mughni 328.

His words "tʿarrafuhā al-manāzil" with its accusative are by omitting the preposition or the adverbial, meaning: recognize your companion by the dwellings of Mina. He says: I do not know anyone who recognizes her among those who frequent Mina, so that I might ask him about her.]]

So he put "kull" in the nominative and did not make it accusative by "ʿārif" (one who knows), since the meaning of his words "and not everyone who frequents Mina is one I know" is a denial of knowing whoever frequents Mina, so it takes on the meaning of "no one." [[See more of what has passed in Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:138–140.]] This verse [was revealed], [[This addition between the brackets is necessary for the sentence to be sound.]] as is reported, before Allah made zakat on wealth obligatory.

Mention of those who said that:

4068 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: whatever good you spend is for parents and close relatives," he said: On the day this verse was revealed there was no zakat; rather it was the expenditure a man spends on his family, and the charity he gives in alms, and then zakat abrogated it.

4069 – al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Juraij said: The believers asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): where should they place their wealth? Then it was revealed: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: whatever good you spend is for parents and close relatives and orphans and the needy and the wayfarer." So that is the spending in voluntary charity, and zakat is other than all that. He said: Mujahid said: They asked and he gave them a fatwa on that: "Whatever good you spend is for parents and close relatives," and what is mentioned with them.

4070 – Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to us, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to me, saying: I heard Ibn Abi Najih on the words of Allah: "They ask you what they should spend," he said: They asked him and he gave them a fatwa on that: "for parents and close relatives" and what is mentioned with them.

4071 – Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said – and I asked him about His words: "Say: whatever good you spend is for parents and close relatives" – he said: This is from the voluntary acts; He says: they have more right to your bounty than others.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: What al-Suddi said – that on the day this verse was revealed there was no zakat, but there was spending that a man spends on his family, and charity that he gives in alms, then zakat abrogated it (naskh) – is a view that may be as he said, and may be other than it. There is no indication in the verse of the correctness of what he said, because it is possible that His words "Say: whatever good you spend is for parents and close relatives" and the rest of the verse are an exhortation from Allah, may His praise be exalted, to spend upon those whose maintenance is not obligatory, from fathers and mothers and relatives, and those named with them in this verse, and an instruction from Allah to His servants about the places of virtue in which expenditures are to be disbursed, as He said in another verse: ﴿And gives wealth, though he loves it, to relatives and orphans and the needy and the wayfarer and those who ask and for freeing captives, and establishes prayer and gives zakat﴾ (2:177). And this is the view we have stated, which is the saying of Ibn Juraij that we have related.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "miskīn" (needy) and the meaning of "ibn al-sabīl" (wayfarer) earlier, so that suffices instead of repeating it. [[See the explanation of "miskīn" in what has passed, 2:137, 293, and then 3:345; the meaning of "yatāmā" (orphans) in what has passed, 2:292, and then 3:345; and the meaning of "ibn al-sabīl" in what has passed, 3:345.]]

**The interpretation of His words, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His words, "Fighting has been prescribed for you," may His praise be exalted, He means: fighting has been made obligatory for you, namely fighting the polytheists, "and it is hateful to you."

* *

The scholars differed concerning those who were meant by the obligation of fighting.

Some of them said: By this He meant only the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, to the exclusion of others.

Those who said this:

4072 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I asked 'Ata' about "Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you." Is going out to campaign obligatory upon people because of it? He said: No! It was prescribed for those people at that time.

4073 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: 'Uthman ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Khalid narrated to us, from Husayn ibn Qays, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words, "Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you," he said: It was abrogated by ﴿They said: We hear and we obey﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 285].

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This statement has no meaning, because the abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation) of rulings comes from Allah, may He be exalted, not from the servants. And His words, "They said: We hear and we obey," are a report from Allah about His believing servants that they said it, not an abrogation of it.

4074 - Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, saying: Mu'awiya ibn 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Abu Ishaq al-Fazari narrated to us, saying: I asked al-Awza'i about the words of Allah, may He be mighty and majestic, "Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you." Is going out to campaign obligatory upon all people? He said: I do not know it so, but it is not proper for the leaders and the common people to abandon it. As for a man concerning himself alone, then no. [[The report 4074: Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Ja'far al-Saghani settled in Baghdad, was the chief of the shaykhs of Baghdad, and was one of the reliable, precise memorizers. He died in 270 AH. al-Tabari narrated from him in al-Mudhayyal (see al-Muntakhab min Dhayl al-Mudhayyal: 104). Mu'awiya ibn 'Amr ibn al-Muhallab al-Azdi, from whom al-Bukhari narrated, died in Baghdad in 215. Both are biographed in al-Tahdhib.]]

* *

Others said: It is an obligation on each individual until someone among those whose performance suffices stands up for it. Then the obligation falls from the rest of the Muslims, like the funeral prayer, washing the dead, and burying them. This is the view of the general body of Muslim scholars.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This is the correct view in our opinion, because of the consensus (ijma', the agreement of the qualified scholars) of the authorities on this, and because of the words of Allah, may He be mighty and majestic: ﴿Allah has preferred those who strive with their wealth and their lives over those who sit back by a degree. And to all Allah has promised the best﴾ [Surah al-Nisa': 95]. So He informed, may His praise be exalted, that the excellence belongs to the strivers, and that both the strivers and those who sit back have the best (reward). Had those who sit back been neglecting an obligation, they would have had the worst, not the best.

* *

Others said: It is an obligation upon the Muslims until the Hour arises.

Those who said this:

4075 - Hubaysh ibn Mubashshir narrated to us, saying: Rawh ibn 'Ubada narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Dawud ibn Abi 'Asim, who said: I said to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: I know that going out to campaign is obligatory upon people! He was silent, and I knew that if he had denied what I said, he would have explained it to me. [[The report 4075: Hubaysh ibn Mubashshir ibn Ahmad al-Tusi al-Faqih was a trustworthy man, one of the wise men of Baghdad. He died in 258, and is biographed in al-Tahdhib and Tarikh Baghdad. In the printed edition it reads "Husayn ibn Maysar," and no narrator is known by that name.]]

* *

We have already explained the meaning of His word "prescribed" sufficiently. [[See what has passed: 3:357, 364, 365.]]

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿and it is hateful to you﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: and it is one that is disliked by you (dhu karhin lakum), so the word "dhu" (possessor of) was omitted, being understood from His words "hateful to you," just as He said: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Surah Yusuf: 82].

The same as what we have said about this was transmitted from 'Ata' in its interpretation.

Those who said this:

4076 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata', concerning His words, "and it is hateful to you," he said: It was made hateful to you at that time.

* *

"Al-kurh" (with a dammah on the kaf) is what a man forces himself to do without anyone compelling him to it. "Al-kath" (with a fathah on the kaf) is what another person causes to be imposed upon him, bringing it upon him against his will. Among those reported to have said this is Mu'adh ibn Muslim.

4077 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hammad narrated to us, from Mu'adh ibn Muslim, who said: "al-kurh" is hardship, and "al-kars" is compulsion.

* *

Some of the grammarians (ahl al-'arabiyya, the scholars of the Arabic language) used to say: "al-kurh" and "al-karh" are two dialects with one meaning, like "al-ghusl" and "al-ghasl," "al-du'f" and "al-da'f," and "al-rahb" and "al-rahb." Others said: "al-kurh" with a dammah on the kaf is a noun, and "al-karh" with a fathah is a verbal noun (masdar).

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and it may be that you love a thing and it is bad for you﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Do not dislike fighting, for perhaps you dislike it while it is good for you; and do not love abandoning jihad, for perhaps you love it while it is bad for you. As:

4078 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you, and it may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and it may be that you love a thing and it is bad for you." That was because the Muslims used to dislike fighting, so He said: "It may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you" — meaning: in fighting there is booty, victory, and martyrdom for you; and in sitting back there is that you will not overcome the polytheists, you will not be martyred, and you will gain nothing.

4079 - Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Sulami narrated to me, saying: Yahya ibn Muhammad ibn Mujahid narrated to me, saying: 'Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Hashim al-Ju'fi informed me, saying: 'Amir ibn Wathila informed me, saying: Ibn 'Abbas said: I was riding behind the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "O son of 'Abbas, be content with what Allah has decreed, even if it is contrary to your desire, for it is recorded in the Book of Allah." I said: "O Messenger of Allah, where? I have read the Qur'an!" He said: "In His words: 'And it may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and it may be that you love a thing and it is bad for you, and Allah knows while you do not know.'" [[The report 4079: This is an obscure chain and the text is unusual! I have not found a biography of "Yahya ibn Muhammad ibn Mujahid," nor of "'Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Hashim," and I do not know who they are. The wording of this hadith I have not found, nor has anyone who transmits from al-Tabari reported it.]]

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah knows while you do not know﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Allah knows what is good for you and what is bad for you. So do not dislike what I have prescribed for you of fighting your enemy and battling those whom I have commanded you to fight, for I know that your fighting them is good for you in your present life and in your return, and your abandoning fighting them is bad for you, while you do not know of that what I know. Thereby He, may His remembrance be exalted, urges them to strive against His enemies and encourages them to fight those who disbelieve in Him.

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin), but turning people from the way of Allah, disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, are greater with Allah; and persecution is worse than killing﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Your companions ask you, O Muhammad, about the sacred month, which is Rajab, concerning fighting in it.

The genitive "al-qitali" (fighting) is in the case of "'an" repeated over it, and so was the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, as has been mentioned to us. And:

4080 - I was told by 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' concerning His words, "They ask you about the sacred month, fighting in it," he said: He says: They ask you about fighting in it. He said: And thus he used to recite it: "concerning fighting in it."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: "Say" O Muhammad: "Fighting in it" — meaning in the sacred month — "is great," that is, great in the sight of Allah is its being made lawful and the shedding of blood in it.

The meaning of His words, "fighting in it," is: say, fighting in it is great. He said, "Say: fighting in it is great," because the Arabs used not to strike spear-points in it, so that a man would meet the slayer of his father or brother in it and would not attack him, out of reverence for it. Mudar called it "al-Asamm" [[That is, the month of Rajab, which is "Rajab al-Asamm."]] because the sounds of weapons and their clashing are silent in it. And:

4081 - Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam al-Misri narrated to me, saying: Shu'ayb ibn al-Layth narrated to us, saying: al-Layth narrated to us, saying: al-Zubayr narrated to us, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not campaign in the sacred month unless he was attacked, or he attacked, and if that month came, he would remain until it had passed.

* *

His words, may His praise be exalted: "and turning (people) from the way of Allah." The meaning of "al-sadd" (turning away) from a thing is preventing it and warding off from it. From it is said: "So-and-so turned his face away from so-and-so," when he turned away from him and prevented him from looking at him.

* *

His words: "and disbelief in Him" — meaning: and disbelief in Allah. The "ba'" in "bihi" (in Him) refers to the name of Allah that appears in "the way of Allah." The sense of the statement is: turning (people) from the way of Allah, and disbelief in Him, and (turning them) from the Sacred Mosque, and expelling the people of the Sacred Mosque — who are its people and its custodians — is greater with Allah than fighting in the sacred month.

Thus "turning from the way of Allah" is in the nominative case by His words "is greater with Allah." His words "and expelling its people from it" are conjoined to "turning." Then He began a statement about persecution, saying: "and persecution is worse than killing," meaning: polytheism is greater and worse than killing [[See the meaning of "fitna" (persecution, trial) in what has passed: 3:565, 566, then 570, 571, and the vocabulary index in the earlier volumes.]] — meaning: the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami, whose killing you disapproved of in the sacred month.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Some of the grammarians claimed that His words, "and the Sacred Mosque," are conjoined to "fighting," and that the meaning is: They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it, and about the Sacred Mosque; so Allah, may His praise be exalted, said: "and expelling its people from it is greater with Allah" than fighting in the sacred month. [[This is the view of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:141.]]

This view, besides falling outside the sayings of the scholars, is a view with no basis. For the people were not in doubt about the grave wrong the polytheists had done to the Muslims by expelling them from their homes in Mecca, so that they would need to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the polytheists' expulsion of them from their homes, and whether that was lawful for them? Rather, no one among the Muslims claimed that against them, nor did they ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it.

Since that is so, the people did not ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ except about what they doubted regarding his ruling [[In the printed edition: "And if that is so, and the people did not ask the Messenger of Allah..." The correct reading is what I have given, otherwise the sentence is severely disrupted.]], like their doubt about the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami, for they claimed that his killer, one of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, had killed him in the sacred month, so they asked about his case, because they doubted his ruling. As for the expulsion of the polytheists of the people of Islam from the Sacred Mosque, none of them doubted that it was an injustice on their part toward them, so that they would ask about it.

There is no disagreement among all the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) that this verse was revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning the cause of the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami and his killer.

The narration from those who said this:

4082 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: al-Zuhri and Yazid ibn Ruman narrated to me, from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh in Rajab, on his return from the first Badr, and sent with him eight men from the Emigrants, none of whom were from the Helpers. He wrote him a letter and commanded him not to look into it until he had traveled two days, then to look into it and carry out what he was commanded, and not to compel any of his companions.

And the companions of 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh from the Emigrants were: from the clan of 'Abd Shams, Abu Hudhayfa [ibn 'Utba] ibn Rabi'a [[The words in parentheses are from the Life of Ibn Hisham. The text of Ibn Hisham reads: "Abu Hudhayfa ibn 'Utba ibn Rabi'a ibn 'Abd Shams — and from their allies: 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh," with the omission of "and from the Banu Umayya." I have left what is in al-Tabari as it stands, because its meaning is also sound.]] — and from the Banu Umayya — ibn 'Abd Shams; then from their allies: 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh ibn Ri'ab, who was the leader of the people; and 'Ukkasha ibn Mihsan ibn Hurthan, one of the Banu Asad ibn Khuzayma; and from the Banu Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf: 'Utba ibn Ghazwan, an ally of theirs; and from the Banu Zuhra ibn Kilab: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas; and from the Banu 'Adi ibn Ka'b: 'Amir ibn Rabi'a, an ally of theirs, and Waqid ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Manat ibn 'Urayn [[In the printed edition: "... 'Abd Allah ibn Manat ibn 'Uwaym." I have adopted what is in the text of Ibn Hisham, which agrees with what the books of biography and genealogy have agreed upon.]] ibn Tha'laba ibn Yarbu' ibn Handhala, and Khalid ibn al-Bukayr, one of the Banu Sa'd ibn Layth, an ally of theirs; and from the Banu al-Harith ibn Fihr: Suhayl ibn Bayda'.

When 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh had traveled two days, he opened the letter and looked into it, and in it was: "When you look at this letter of mine, proceed until you alight at Nakhla, between Mecca and al-Ta'if, and watch there for the Quraysh, and learn for us of their news." When 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh looked into the letter, he said: "We hear and we obey." Then he said to his companions: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ has commanded me to go to Nakhla and watch there for the Quraysh until I bring him news of them, and he has forbidden me to compel any of you. So whoever among you wishes for martyrdom and desires it, let him go forward; and whoever dislikes that, let him return. As for me, I am going forward to obey the command of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So he went forward, and his companions went with him, and none of them stayed behind. He took the route toward the Hijaz, until, when he was at a mine above al-Furu' called Buhran [[In the printed edition: "Najran," which is a clear error.]], Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and 'Utba ibn Ghazwan lost a camel they had been riding in turns, so they stayed behind to search for it, while 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh and the rest of his companions went on until they alighted at Nakhla. A caravan of the Quraysh passed by them, carrying raisins, leather, and merchandise from the goods of the Quraysh [[The "'ir" is a caravan of camels, donkeys, and mules going out for supplies, from which one trades. "Adam" is the plural of "adim," meaning tanned hide.]]. In it were 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami, 'Uthman ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughira, and his brother Nawfal ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughira, the Makhzumites, and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, a freedman of Hisham ibn al-Mughira. When the men saw them, they feared them, since they had alighted close to them. Then 'Ukkasha ibn Mihsan appeared before them, and he had shaved his head; when they saw him, they felt secure and said: "They are 'Ummar (pilgrims)! There is no harm to us from them." [[''Ummar" means those performing the 'umra. 'Umra and i'timar mean visiting the Sacred House and fulfilling its rights, in any month. It is other than the Hajj. One says of it "i'tamara," and "'amara" is not heard, but "'ammar" came as the plural of "'amir" on this triliteral form, which has been abandoned.]] The people consulted about them, and that was on the last day of Jumada [[So in the printed edition: "the last day of Jumada." In the text of Ibn Hisham and the History of al-Tabari it is "the last day of Rajab," which is the more correct of the two versions. I have not changed it, because what follows shows that the narration here is so.]]. They said: "By Allah, if you leave the people this night, they will enter the Sanctuary and shelter in it from you. And if you kill them, you will be killing them in the sacred month!" So the people hesitated and were reluctant to advance against them, then they gained courage against them, and they agreed to kill whomever they could of them and to seize what they had. Waqid ibn 'Abd Allah al-Tamimi shot 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami with an arrow and killed him. 'Uthman ibn 'Abd Allah and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan were taken captive, and Nawfal ibn 'Abd Allah escaped, and they could not catch him.

'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh and his companions came back with the caravan and the two prisoners, until they arrived before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Medina. Some of the family of 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh mentioned that 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh had said to his companions: "Indeed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is owed a fifth of what you have taken as booty."

That was before the fifth of the spoils was made obligatory. The Messenger of God ﷺ set aside a fifth of the caravan's goods for himself and divided the rest among his companions. When they came before the Messenger of God ﷺ, he said: "I did not order you to fight in the sacred month!" He held back the caravan and the two captives and refused to take anything from it. When the Messenger of God ﷺ said that, the people were dismayed and thought they had been destroyed. The Muslims rebuked them for what they had done and said to them: "You did what you were not commanded to do; you fought in the sacred month, and you were not ordered to fight!" The Quraysh said: "Muhammad and his companions have made the sacred month lawful. They shed blood in it, seized property in it, and took prisoners [in it, the men]." [[The words in parentheses are from the text of Ibn Hisham and the History of al-Tabari.]] Then some Muslims in Mecca who were disputing this said: "They only got what they got in Jumada!" [[See p. 303, note 5; the text of Ibn Hisham and al-Tabari has "in Sha'ban."]] The Jews, hoping for an omen against the Messenger of God ﷺ, said: "Amr ibn al-Hadrami was killed by Waqid ibn Abdullah!" "Amr" means "the war has been prolonged" (ʿamarat al-harb); "al-Hadrami" means "the war has been present" (ḥaḍarat al-ḥarb); "Waqid ibn Abdullah" means "the war has been kindled" (waqadat al-ḥarb). So God turned that upon them and against them.

When people talked much about this, God, mighty and majestic, sent down to His Messenger: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month﴾, that is, about fighting in it. ﴿Say: Fighting in it is grave﴾ up to His words ﴿and sedition is graver than killing﴾. That is: if you killed in the sacred month, they have barred you from the way of God, along with disbelief in Him, and from the Sacred Mosque, and expelling you from it, though you are its people and its custodians, is graver in the sight of God than the killing of those you killed among them. ﴿And sedition is graver than killing﴾: they used to tempt the Muslim away from his religion until they returned him to disbelief after his faith, and that is graver in the sight of God than killing. ﴿And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able﴾: that is, they remain upon the most vile and gravest of that, not repenting and not desisting.

When the Qur'an came down with this ruling and God relieved the Muslims of the fear and apprehension they had been in, the Messenger of God ﷺ took possession of the caravan and the two captives. [[The report 4082 is the text of Ibn Hisham's Sira from Ibn Ishaq, 2: 252–254, and al-Tabari related it in his History, 2: 262–263.]]

4083: Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: Fighting in it is grave﴾. The reason was that the Messenger of God ﷺ sent a detachment (sariyya), and they were seven men, and he appointed over them Abdullah ibn Jahsh al-Asadi. Among them were Ammar ibn Yasir, Abu Hudhayfa ibn Utba ibn Rabi'a, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Utba ibn Ghazwan al-Sulami, an ally of Banu Nawfal, Suhayl ibn Bayda, Amir ibn Fuhayra, and Waqid ibn Abdullah al-Yarbu'i, an ally of Umar ibn al-Khattab. He wrote a letter with Ibn Jahsh and ordered him not to read it until he reached Batn Malal [the words in brackets are from al-Tabari's report in his History]. When he reached Batn Malal, he opened the letter, and in it was: "Set out until you reach Batn Nakhla." [[In his History: "Batn Nakhl" in this place, and in what follows "Batn Nakhla."]] He said to his companions: "Whoever desires death, let him go on and make his will, for I will make my will and go on in obedience to the command of the Messenger of God ﷺ." He set out, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Utba ibn Ghazwan fell behind him, for they had lost a riding camel of theirs, and they went to Bahran seeking it. [[In the printed edition: "Najran," which is an error like the one that passed on p. 303; the correct reading is from the History.]] Ibn Jahsh went on to Batn Nakhla, and there he came upon al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, al-Mughira ibn Uthman, and Amr ibn al-Hadrami. They fought, and they took al-Hakam ibn Kaysan and Abdullah ibn al-Mughira as captives; al-Mughira escaped, and Amr ibn al-Hadrami was killed, killed by Waqid ibn Abdullah. That was the first spoil that the companions of Muhammad ﷺ gained.

When they returned to Medina with the two captives and the goods they had taken, the people of Mecca wished to ransom the two captives. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Let us wait and see what our two companions have done!" When Sa'd and his companion returned, the captives were ransomed. The polytheists were outraged and said: "Muhammad claims he follows the obedience of God, yet he is the first to make the sacred month lawful, and killed our companion in Rajab!" The Muslims said: "We only killed him in Jumada!" It is also said: in the first night of Rajab and the last night of Jumada. The Muslims sheathed their swords when Rajab began. So God, mighty and majestic, sent down to rebuke the people of Mecca: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: Fighting in it is grave﴾, which is not permitted; and what you did, O polytheists, is graver than killing in the sacred month, when you disbelieved in God and barred Muhammad and his companions from Him; and the expulsion of the people of the Sacred Mosque from it, when they expelled Muhammad, is graver in the sight of God than killing; and sedition, which is polytheism, is graver in the sight of God than killing in the sacred month. This is His words: ﴿And barring from the way of God, and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, are graver in the sight of God; and sedition is graver than killing﴾. [[The report 4083 was related by al-Tabari in his History, 2: 263–264.]]

4084: Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la al-San'ani told us, saying: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman al-Taymi told us, from his father, that a man told him, from Abu al-Sawwar, who related to him from Jundub ibn Abdullah, from the Messenger of God ﷺ: that he sent a group (rahṭ), and he appointed over them Abu Ubayda. When he took up to set out, he wept out of longing (ṣabāba) to the Messenger of God ﷺ. So he sent another man in his place, called Abdullah ibn Jahsh, and wrote him a letter, and ordered him not to read the letter until he reached such-and-such a place, [and the words:] "and do not compel any of your companions to go with you." When he read the letter, he said the words of submission (istirjaʿa) and said: "Hearing and obedience to the command of God and His Messenger!" He told them the news and read the letter to them. Two men returned, and the rest went on. They met Ibn al-Hadrami and killed him, and they did not know that day whether it was of Rajab or Jumada. The polytheists said to the Muslims: "You did such-and-such in the sacred month!" They came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him the story, and God, mighty and majestic, sent down: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: Fighting in it is grave, and barring from the way of God, and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, are graver in the sight of God; and sedition is graver than killing﴾ — and sedition is polytheism. Some of those who were in the detachment — I think he said — said: "By God, only one man killed him!" He said: "If it be good, then you have been entrusted; and if it be a sin, then you have done it!" [[The report 4084 was related by al-Tabari in his History, 2: 264–265; its full text will come under no. 4102.]]

4085: Muhammad ibn Amr told me, saying: Abu Asim told us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding God's words: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month, fighting in it﴾. He said: A man from Banu Tamim, whom the Prophet ﷺ sent in a detachment, passed by Ibn al-Hadrami carrying wine from al-Ta'if to Mecca, so he shot him with an arrow and killed him. There was a covenant between the Quraysh and Muhammad, and he killed him on the last day of Jumada al-Akhira and the first day of Rajab. The Quraysh said: "In the sacred month! And we have a covenant!" So God, mighty and majestic, sent down: ﴿Fighting in it is grave, and barring from the way of God and disbelief in Him﴾, and barring from the Sacred Mosque, ﴿and expelling its people from it is graver in the sight of God﴾, than the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami; and sedition, which is disbelief in God, and the worship of idols, is graver than all of this.

4086: al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri and Uthman al-Jazari, and from Muqsim, mawla of Ibn Abbas, who said: Waqid ibn Abdullah met Amr ibn al-Hadrami on the first night of Rajab, thinking it was from Jumada, and killed him; he was the first of the polytheists to be killed. The polytheists rebuked the Muslims, saying: "Do you kill in the sacred month?" So God sent down: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: Fighting in it is grave, and barring from the way of God and disbelief in Him and the Sacred Mosque﴾ — that is: and barring from the way of God and disbelief in God — ﴿and the Sacred Mosque﴾ — that is: and barring from the Sacred Mosque — ﴿and expelling its people from it is graver in the sight of God﴾, [that is:] for the killing of Amr ibn al-Hadrami — ﴿and sedition﴾, that is: the polytheism in which you are, is graver than that as well. al-Zuhri said: The Prophet ﷺ, as it has reached us, used to forbid fighting in the sacred month, and then it was made lawful [for him] afterwards. [[The report 4086 is a mursal hadith (a report whose chain omits a companion), transmitted by two chains from two of the Successors, namely al-Zuhri and Muqsim, mawla of Ibn Abbas. Ma'mar related it from al-Zuhri, and he related it from Uthman al-Jazari, from Muqsim. It is firmly established in the tafsir of Abd al-Razzaq, p. 26. We have added the waw [the conjunction] in the phrase "and from Muqsim," and the word [lahu, "for him"] at the end of the hadith in the phrase "then it was made lawful [for him] afterwards."
Uthman al-Jazari is "Uthman ibn Sajj," whose biography Ibn Abi Hatim gives at 3/1/153, and he is other than "Uthman ibn Amr ibn Sajj," whose biography Ibn Abi Hatim gives at 3/1/162. al-Hafiz al-Mizzi confused the two in al-Tahdhib, and al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar corrected him. See what we wrote on this in the commentary on the Musnad: 2562.
Muqsim, with a kasra on the m, a sukun on the q, and a fatha on the s, is Ibn Bajra, mawla of Abdullah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal. He was called "mawla of Ibn Abbas" because he was constantly attached to him. He is a trustworthy Successor.]]

4087: Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, saying: My father told me, saying: My paternal uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, his words: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: Fighting in it is grave﴾. The reason was that the polytheists barred the Messenger of God ﷺ and turned him back from the Sacred Mosque in a sacred month, and God granted His Prophet victory in a sacred month of the following year. The polytheists found fault with the Messenger of God ﷺ for fighting in a sacred month, so God, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And barring from the way of God, and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, are graver in the sight of God﴾ — than killing in it. And Muhammad sent a detachment, and they met Amr ibn al-Hadrami coming from al-Ta'if on the last night of Jumada and the first night of Rajab. The companions of Muhammad ﷺ thought that night was of Jumada, though it was the first of Rajab, and they did not realize it, and one man among them killed him. The polytheists sent to rebuke him for it, and God, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: Fighting in it is grave﴾, and something else is graver than it: ﴿barring from the way of God, and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it﴾; the expulsion of the people of the Sacred Mosque is graver than what Muhammad did, and the polytheism against God is more severe.

4088: Ahmad ibn Ishaq told us, saying: Abu Ahmad told us, saying: Sufyan told us, from Husayn, from Abu Malik, who said: When the verse was revealed: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: Fighting in it is grave﴾, up to His words ﴿and sedition is graver than killing﴾, they found it great. He said: And sedition — which is the polytheism in which you remain — is greater than what you found great.

4089: I was told on the authority of Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from Husayn, from Abu Malik al-Ghifari, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ sent Abdullah ibn Jahsh with an army, and he met some polytheists at Batn Nakhla, while the Muslims thought it was the last day of Jumada, and it was the first day of Rajab. The Muslims killed Ibn al-Hadrami. The polytheists said: "Do you not claim that you make the sacred month and the sacred land inviolable, and yet you have killed in the sacred month!" So God sent down: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: Fighting in it is grave﴾, up to His words ﴿is graver in the sight of God﴾ — than what you found great in the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami; and "sedition," in which you remain, meaning polytheism, ﴿is graver than killing﴾.

4090: I was told on the authority of Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from Qatada, who said: And he would name them [the words in the printed edition; I think the correct reading is "he would name them both"] — saying: Waqid ibn Abdullah al-Tamimi met Amr ibn al-Hadrami at Batn Nakhla and killed him.

4091: al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I asked Ata' about God's words: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month, fighting in it﴾: concerning whom was it revealed? He said: I do not know. Ibn Jurayj said: Ikrima and Mujahid said: It was concerning Amr ibn al-Hadrami. Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn Abi Husayn also informed us, from al-Zuhri, the same.

4092: al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Mujahid said: ﴿Say: Fighting in it is grave, and barring from the way of God, and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque﴾ — he said: That is: barring from the Sacred Mosque, ﴿and expelling its people from it﴾ — all of this is graver than the killing of Ibn al-Hadrami — ﴿and sedition is graver than killing﴾ — disbelief in God and the worship of idols is greater than all of this.

4093: I was told on the authority of al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh al-Fadl ibn Khalid say: Ubayd ibn Sulayman al-Bahili informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim say, concerning God's words: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: Fighting in it is grave﴾: The companions of Muhammad ﷺ had killed Ibn al-Hadrami in the sacred month, so the polytheists rebuked the Muslims for it, and God said: Fighting in the sacred month is grave, and greater than that is barring from the way of God and disbelief in Him, and expelling the people of the Sacred Mosque from the Sacred Mosque.

Abu Ja'far [al-Tabari] said: These two reports we have mentioned from Mujahid and al-Dahhak indicate the soundness of what we have said regarding the nominative case of "barring" (al-ṣadd) and "disbelief in Him," and that its nominative is "greater in the sight of God." They confirm the soundness of what we related on this from Ibn Abbas, and they show the error of one who claimed that it is in the nominative as a conjunction with "grave," and of the view of one who claimed that its meaning is: "barring from the way of God is grave," and claimed that God's words, "and expelling its people from it is greater in the sight of God," are a separate predicate, cut off from what precedes it as a new subject.

* *

4094: Yaqub ibn Ibrahim told me, saying: Hushaym told us, saying: Isma'il ibn Salim informed us, from al-Sha'bi, concerning God's words: ﴿And sedition is graver than killing﴾, he said: He means disbelief by it.

4095: Bishr ibn Mu'adh told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatada: ﴿And expelling its people from it is graver in the sight of God﴾, from that. Then He rebuked the polytheists for their deeds, their evil deeds, and said: ﴿And sedition is graver than killing﴾, that is: polytheism against God is graver than killing.

* *

It was related from Ibn Abbas in a manner like what we have said in this interpretation:

4096: Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, saying: My father told me, saying: My paternal uncle told me, saying: My father told me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: When the companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ killed Amr ibn al-Hadrami on the last night of Jumada and the first night of Rajab, the polytheists sent to the Messenger of God ﷺ rebuking him for it, and he said: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say: Fighting in it is grave﴾, and something else is graver than it: ﴿barring from the way of God, and disbelief in Him, and the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it is graver﴾ than what Muhammad ﷺ had done.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for the grammarians (ahl al-ʿarabiyya), they differed about what the nominative case of God's words ﴿and barring from the way of God﴾ is governed by.

One of the grammarians of Kufa said: In its nominative there are two possibilities. The first is that "barring" (al-ṣadd) is a conjunction (mardūd) with "grave," meaning: "Fighting in it is grave, and barring from the way of God and disbelief in Him is grave." And if you wish, you may make "barring" a predicate, meaning: "Fighting in it is grave, and barring from the way of God and disbelief in Him is grave." [[This is the view of al-Farra', as will come later in the text; see his Ma'ani al-Qur'an, 1: 141. al-Tabari refuted al-Farra's statement with wise refutation, and exposed the corruption contained in the view of one who speaks about the Qur'an without judging the rulings of God properly, so that he deems everything permissible in Arabic and grammar to be permissible to attribute to the Book of God. The refutations of al-Tabari teach a person how to adopt the character of the people of knowledge and faith: patience, pausing, endurance, and scrupulousness, lest a foot slip into the abyss of error, ignorance and bad judgment.]]

Abu Ja'far said: Al-Farra' erred in both of his interpretations. For if he reads "al-sadd" (ṣadd, "turning away") as a conjunction with "kabir" (great), the sense of the sentence becomes: "Fighting in the sacred month is a great [sin], and turning [people] from the way of God, and disbelief in God." Such an interpretation contradicts what all the people of Islam hold. For no one has claimed that God, blessed and exalted, made fighting in the sacred months disbelief in God. It is impossible to attribute to any reasonable person who understands what he says that he would say this.
