How could one of sound nature say it, when God, mighty is His praise, says immediately afterward: "and driving its people out of it is greater in the sight of God"? If the sentence were as he considered permissible in this interpretation, it would follow that driving the people of the Sacred Mosque out of the Sacred Mosque is greater in the sight of God than disbelief in Him, since He says right after it: "and driving its people out of it is greater in the sight of God." And the proof that nothing is greater in the sight of God than disbelief in Him makes plain the error of this view.

As for reading "al-sadd" as a nominative in the sense of the other reading he claimed, namely: "and turning [people] from the way of God is great," followed by "and driving its people out of it is greater in the sight of God," the meaning becomes that driving the people of the Sacred Mosque out of the Sacred Mosque is greater in the sight of God than disbelief in God and turning [people] from His way and from the Sacred Mosque. Whoever interprets it this way falls into the same error as the first speaker, by making some aspects of disbelief greater in the sight of God than disbelief itself. This error and corruption is not hidden from anyone [[al-shay' yukhayyil: it becomes confused. One says "this matter is not hidden from anyone," meaning it is not unclear to anyone; and "a thing that is mukhayyal" means a thing that is unclear.]].

* *

Some of the grammarians of Basra used to say the first view regarding the nominative "al-sadd," claiming that it is conjoined to "kabir," and making his words "and driving its people out" a nominative by way of the inceptive. We have already shown the corruption of this and the error of its interpretation.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Then the people of interpretation differed concerning His words: "They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: fighting in it is a great [matter]" — is it abrogated or is its ruling established?

Some of them said: It is abrogated by the words of God, mighty and majestic: "And fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together" [Surah al-Tawbah: 36], and by His words: "Then kill the polytheists" [Surah al-Tawbah: 5].

Those who said this:

4097 - Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: 'Ata' ibn Maysarah said: The fighting in the sacred month was made lawful in Bara'ah (Surah al-Tawbah) by His words: "So do not wrong yourselves therein, and fight the polytheists all together" [Surah al-Tawbah: 36]: He means: therein and in other than it. [[The report 4097: "'Ata' ibn Maysarah" is 'Ata' ibn Abi Muslim al-Khurasani; his father's name is said to be "'Abd Allah," and also said to be "Maysarah." He died in the year 135. See the disagreement about him and the problem regarding his case and the case of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah in the Tahdhib in his biography.]]

4098 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri, who said: The Prophet ﷺ, as it has reached us, used to forbid fighting in the sacred month, and then it was made lawful afterward. [[The report 4098: it is part of the earlier report 4086. See the commentary on it.]]

Others said: Rather, that is an established ruling: fighting in the sacred months is not lawful for anyone by this verse, because God made fighting in it a great [sin].

Those who said this:

4099 - Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, [[In the printed edition: "...from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, who said: I said to 'Ata'..." The words "from Mujahid" are an error and an added corruption, so I removed them. See the earlier report numbered 4901.]] who said: I said to 'Ata': "They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: fighting in it is a great [matter]." I said: What about them? Then is it not lawful for them to raid the polytheists in the sacred month, and then to fight them in it afterward? 'Ata' swore to me by God: It is not lawful for people to raid in the sacred month, nor to fight in it, nor is it recommended. He said: Nor do they invite [them] to Islam before being fought, nor to the jizyah; they have abandoned that.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this matter is what 'Ata' ibn Maysarah said: that the prohibition on fighting the polytheists in the sacred months is abrogated by the words of God, mighty is His praise: "Indeed, the number of months with God is twelve months in the Book of God, the day He created the heavens and the earth; of them four are sacred. That is the correct religion. So do not wrong yourselves therein, and fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together" [Surah al-Tawbah: 36].

We say this abrogates His words: "They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: fighting in it is a great [matter]," because of the widespread reports from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he raided Hawazin at Hunayn and Thaqif at al-Ta'if, and sent Abu 'Amir to Awtas to fight those polytheists there in the sacred months, and that was in Shawwal and part of Dhu al-Qa'dah, which is one of the sacred months. Thus it was known by this that if fighting in them were forbidden and a sin, he would be the furthest of people from doing it, ﷺ.

Another point: all the people knowledgeable in the biographies of the Messenger of God ﷺ agree without dispute that the Pledge of al-Ridwan concerning fighting the Quraysh took place in Dhu al-Qa'dah, and that the Prophet ﷺ only called his companions to it that day, because it reached him that 'Uthman ibn 'Affan had been killed by the polytheists when he was sent to them with the message he carried. So the Prophet ﷺ pledged that they would engage the people in battle and fight them, until 'Uthman returned with the message, and then peace was established between the Prophet ﷺ and the Quraysh, and he refrained from fighting them at that time. And that was in Dhu al-Qa'dah, which is one of the sacred months.

Since this is so, the correctness of what we have said regarding His words: "They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: fighting in it is a great [matter]," and that it is abrogated, is clear.

As for the one who supposes that the prohibition on fighting in the sacred months came after the Prophet ﷺ had made them lawful, because of his battles which we have described, he has supposed out of ignorance. For this verse, meaning His words "They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it," was revealed concerning the matter of 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh and his companions, and what happened with them and the man they killed. God revealed this verse about that at the end of Jumada al-Akhirah in the second year after the Messenger of God ﷺ came to Madinah and migrated there. The battle of Hunayn and al-Ta'if was in Shawwal of the eighth year after his coming to Madinah and migration there, and the interval between them is evident to everyone.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 217:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: The polytheists of Quraysh will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able to do so, as:

4100 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq related to me, saying: al-Zuhri and Yazid ibn Ruman related to me, from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr: "And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able," i.e.: they persist in that which is most vile and gravest, not repenting and not desisting, meaning: in seeking to tempt the Muslims away from their religion until they return them to disbelief, as they used to do with whoever among them they could reach before the Hijrah. [[The report 4100 is part of the earlier report 4082. The passage from the beginning of His words "meaning: in seeking to tempt..." is not in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham, nor in the History of al-Tabari. So it is either from the words of al-Tabari, or from the words of Ibn Humayd, or from some of the narrators of the report.]]

4101 - Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able," he said: the disbelievers of Quraysh.

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally﴾ (2:217)

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, by His words "whoever of you reverts from his religion" means: whoever of you returns from his religion, as He, may His praise be exalted, said: ﴿So they both returned, retracing their footsteps﴾ [Surat al-Kahf: 64], meaning by "returned" (fartadda): went back. From this it is said: "So-and-so reclaimed his right from so-and-so," when he took it back from him.

[[See what has preceded at 3:163, and the indexes of language in what has preceded, root r-d-d.]]

The doubling is made apparent in His words "yartadid" because the final radical of the verb is vowelled with a jazm (sukun), and when it is made quiescent, the analogy is to leave the doubling out; yet it may also be doubled and assimilated while quiescent, based on the dual and plural forms.

* *

As for His words "then dies while he is a disbeliever," he means: whoever returns from his religion, the religion of Islam, "then dies while he is a disbeliever," dies before repenting from his disbelief; these are the ones whose deeds have become worthless.

* *

By His words "whose deeds have become worthless" he means: their deeds have become void and gone. Their voiding is the loss of their reward, and the absence of recompense for them in this world and the Hereafter.

* *

As for His words "and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally," He means: those who apostatised from their religion and died in their disbelief are the people of the Fire who will be eternally abiding in it.

[[See the meaning of "companions of the Fire" in what has preceded at 2:286.]]

* *

He made them "its people" because they will not leave it; they are its residents who dwell in it, as one says: "These are the people of such-and-such a quarter," meaning its residents who dwell in it.

* *

By His words "they will abide therein eternally" he means: they will remain there lasting, without any limit or end. [[See the meaning of "khalid" (eternal) in what has preceded at 2:286–287, and the indexes of language.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 218:

The explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated and striven in the way of Allah - those expect the mercy of Allah. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, exalted is His remembrance, is meant: Indeed, those who affirmed belief in Allah, in His Messenger, and in what he brought, and by His saying "those who emigrated" are meant those who abandoned residing among the polytheists in their cities and dwelling among them in their homelands, so they moved away from them, from their neighborhood and their lands, [[The text in the printed edition was connected with what follows at the place of these dots, but it does not hold together or run consistently. So I have separated the two passages. My view is that the context and completion of the speech is: "they moved away from them, from their neighborhood and their lands, to another (place), an emigration, because of their aversion to their disbelief and their polytheism, and preference for the neighborhood of the believers among the companions of Muhammad ﷺ," and the flow of the speech indicates this.]] to another place, an emigration ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... [[The place of these dots is a lacuna beyond doubt, as if a copyist had dropped a line or two, and the beginning of the speech was, as I suppose, "Hajara al-makan yahjuruhu hajran wa hijranan wa hijratan: he disliked it and left it, leaving what he moved away from for what he moved to" - or words of this meaning.]] for what he moved to from it. The root of al-muhajara is the form "mufa'ala" from the expression "hajara al-rajul al-rajul" (when a man abandons another man) due to the enmity that exists between them; then it is used for everyone who abandons something for a matter he dislikes in it. The emigrants among the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were named "muhajirun" (emigrants) because of what we have described of their abandoning their homes and dwellings, out of their aversion to settling among the polytheists and under their authority, such that they could not feel safe from their trial with respect to themselves in their homes, to the place where they would feel safe from that.

* *

As for His saying "and strove," it means: fought and warred.

* *

The root of "mujahada" is the form "mufa'ala" from the saying of a man: "Fulan has exerted hardship upon Fulan in such-and-such" - if he distressed him and burdened him - "yajhaduhu jahdan." When the action is from two, each of whom undergoes from the other hardship and difficulty, it is said: "Fulan yujahidu Fulanan" - meaning: each of them does to his companion what exhausts him and burdens him - "so he strives against him with mujahada and jihad."

* *

As for "the way of Allah," it is His path and His religion. [[See the meaning of "the way of Allah" in what has preceded, 2: 497 / 3: 564, 583.]]

* *

So the meaning of His saying, then: "and those who emigrated and strove in the way of Allah," and those who moved away from the authority of the people of polytheism as emigrants, fearing their trial over their religions, and fought them in the religion of Allah so as to bring them into it and into what pleases Allah = "those expect the mercy of Allah," that is: they hope that Allah will have mercy on them and admit them into His Garden by the grace of His mercy toward them.

="And Allah is Forgiving," that is: He covers the sins of His servants by His pardon of them, bestowing favor upon them with mercy. [[See the meaning of "Forgiving" in what has preceded in its references in the language indexes (gh-f-r).]]

* *

It has also been mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Jahsh and his companions.

Mention of those who said that:

4102 - Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from his father, that a man narrated to him, from Abu al-Sawwar, who related from Jundub ibn Abdullah, who said: When there occurred the matter of Abdullah ibn Jahsh and his companions and the matter of Ibn al-Hadrami what occurred, some of the Muslims said: "If they did not gain in their journey - I think he said - a burden of sin, then there is no reward for them in it." So Allah revealed: "Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the way of Allah - those expect the mercy of Allah. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful." [[The report 4102 is the completion of the earlier report No. 4084, and it is in full in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 250.]]

4103 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: al-Zuhri and Yazid ibn Ruman narrated to me, from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: Allah, mighty and majestic, sent down the Qur'an with what He sent down of the command, and Allah relieved the Muslims in the matter of Abdullah ibn Jahsh and his companions - meaning: in their killing of Ibn al-Hadrami. When what Abdullah ibn Jahsh and his companions had been in when the Qur'an was revealed was lifted from them, they hoped for reward, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, do we hope that there will be for us a raid in which we are given the reward of those who strive?" So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning them: "Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the way of Allah - those expect the mercy of Allah. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."

So Allah placed them, by that, in the greatest hope. [[The report 3103 is Sirat Ibn Hisham 2: 255, and it is the completion of the earlier report 4082. In the printed edition here it read: "fawwaqahum Allah min dhalika...", and the correct reading is what I have established from Ibn Hisham.]]

4104 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: Allah praised the companions of His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with the best praise, saying: "Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated and strove in the way of Allah - those expect the mercy of Allah. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful." These are the best of this Ummah. Then Allah made them people of hope, as you hear, and indeed whoever hopes seeks, and whoever fears flees.

4105 - It was narrated to me from Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the like of it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 219 (part 1 of 4):

The explanation of the words of the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Your companions ask you, O Muhammad, about wine and drinking it.
* *
And "khamr" (wine) is every drink that covers the intellect, veiling and concealing it. It comes from the speaker's saying, "I covered the vessel (khamartu al-inā')" when I covered it, and "the man became khamir" when he entered into khamr. It is said, "He is in the khumār and ghumār of the people," meaning he has entered into the midst of the people. It is said of the hyena, "Hide yourself, O mother of ʿĀmir" (khāmirī umma ʿāmir), meaning take cover. Whatever veils the intellect of disease or intoxication, mixing with it and overwhelming it, is "khamr."

From the same root is also "khimār al-mar'a" (a woman's head-covering), because she covers her head with it. And from it is said, "He walks to you in secret (yamshī lakum al-khamar)," meaning hiding, as al-ʿAjjāj said:

In the gleaming of the eagles (standards), he does not come in secret,
He turns the earth and drives the trees before him.

[[His Dīwān: 17, from a poem in which he describes the conquests of ʿUmar ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Maʿmar al-Taymī; two of its verses have passed earlier in 2:157, and see the note there no. 2. "Lamaʿat al-rayāt": the banners fluttered. His words "yuwajjihu al-arḍ" mean Umar's army; that is, it strips the face of the earth through the severity of its trampling, its multitude and the speed of its march, comparing it to a torrent. It is said, "The rain wajjaha the earth," meaning it stripped its surface and left its mark upon it. His words "yastāq al-shajar" mean: his army is like a surging, rushing flood that strips the earth, uproots its trees and drives them along.]]
By his words "lā yaʾtī al-khamar" he means: he does not come hiding or stealthily, but openly with banners and armies. "ʿAqbān" is the plural of "ʿuqāb," which means banners.
* *
As for "al-maysir" (gambling), it is "al-mafʿil" from the speaker's saying, "This matter became easy for me (yasara lī hādhā al-amr)," when it became due to me: "he yayserū for me, yasaran and maysiran." [[I have not found this meaning in the lexicographical books, and I think it is a metaphorical usage of "al-maysir," not the original derivation of "al-maysir" from it, because the share of the gambler is due to be paid when his arrow comes out.]] And "al-yāsir" is the one who is owed, with arrows by which that is owed, or by judgment or otherwise. [[In the printed edition: "or its permitted (mubāḥ)," which has no meaning; it seems the correct reading is what I have written. And "al-fattāḥa" (with the fāʾ vowelled with a ḍamma) is judgment between two disputants who come to you for decision.]] Then the gambler was called "yāsir" and "yasar," as the poet said:

So I spent the night as if I were a cheated gambler (yasar ghabīn),
Turning, after he had been stripped, the arrows.

[[I do not know who said it. "Al-ghabīn" and "al-maghbūn" are the loser. "Ukhtulisa" (passive): that is, his wealth was taken and he lost it, so he was stripped of it, meaning robbed. "Al-mukhālaʿ" is the gambler and "al-makhlūʿ" the one whose wealth is gambled away. He says: he spent his night grieved, dejected and lowering his gaze, like a gambler who has lost everything, who began to turn the arrows in his palms, lowering his gaze, lamenting what had befallen him and what had struck him.]]
And as al-Nābigha said: [[I did not find this verse in the poetry of al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī, and I do not know whether it belongs to another of the Nawābigh or to others.]]

Or a gambler whose wealth the arrows have taken away, sorrowful, which his friends have devoured, stripped.
[[Al-wafr: abundant, wide wealth. "Asaf": extremely grieved over what he has lost; it is said: he is asaf, āsif, asfān and asīf. In the printed edition it reads "bi-ākilihi," and I preferred the reading "ta'ākalahu." "Al-ṣadīq" is singular and plural. "Mukhallaʿ": one who has gambled time after time, so his wealth perished and was spent. His words "taʾākalahu al-ṣadīq" mean they plundered it among themselves in gambling, and they were his friends; that is harder on his grief, because of the joy he sees in them and the sorrow of losing his wealth, and the baseness of his friend that grieves him.]]

By "al-yāsir" he means the gambler, and gambling is called "maysir."
* *
Mujahid used to say something similar to what we have said.

4106 – Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding His words: "They ask you about wine and gambling," he said: Gambling. "Maysir" is named so because of their saying, "Aysirū and jzurū" (Play and divide the meat), like your saying: Put down such and such.

4107 – Muhammad ibn Bashshār narrated to us, saying: Abu ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from Layth, from Mujāhid, who said: All gambling is from maysir, even the children's playing with walnuts.

4108 – Muhammad ibn Bashshār narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr, from Abu al-Aḥwaṣ, who said: ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd) said: Beware of these marked knucklebones (al-kiʿāb al-mawsūma) with which you cast divinations by throwing them, for they are from maysir. [[Al-kiʿāb and al-kaʿabāt, the plural of kaʿb and kaʿba: the dice of backgammon. His words "tazjurūnahā zajran" come from zajr, meaning urging and pushing, or from the zajr of birds, a kind of augury and soothsaying. He means what goes with them of expecting and seeking the unseen. "Al-mawsūma" is one marked with a mark that distinguishes it, a sign upon it.]]

4109 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthannā narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, saying: Shuʿba narrated to us, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr, from Abu al-Aḥwaṣ, the same.

4110 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthannā narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Nāfiʿ narrated to us, saying: Shuʿba narrated to us, from Yazīd ibn Abi Ziyād, from Abu al-Aḥwaṣ, from ʿAbd Allāh, that he said: Beware of these knucklebones with which you cast divinations, for they are from maysir.

4111 – ʿAlī ibn Saʿīd al-Kindī narrated to me, saying: ʿAlī ibn Mushir narrated to us, from ʿĀṣim, from Muhammad ibn Sīrīn, who said: Gambling is maysir.

4112 – Ibn Bashshār narrated to us, saying: Abu ʿĀmir narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from ʿĀṣim al-Aḥwal, from Muhammad ibn Sīrīn, who said: Everything that has a stake (khaṭar) – or "in a stake," Abu ʿĀmir was uncertain – is from maysir. [[Al-khaṭar: the pledge over which one stakes, and it is called "al-sabq" and "al-nadb" (both vowelled with a fatḥa), and it is the whole of what is placed in a wager; whoever wins or prevails takes it.]]

4113 – al-Walīd ibn Shujāʿ Abu Hammām narrated to us, saying: ʿAlī ibn Mushir narrated to us, from ʿĀṣim, from Muhammad ibn Sīrīn, who said: Every gambling is maysir, even playing dice while standing, shouting, and the feather a man places on his head.

4114 – Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Jarīr narrated to us, from ʿĀṣim, from Ibn Sīrīn, who said: Every game in which there is gambling, whether drinking, shouting or standing, is from maysir.

4115 – Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to us, saying: Khālid ibn al-Ḥārith narrated to us, saying: al-Ashʿath narrated to us, from al-Ḥasan, who said: Maysir is gambling.

4116 – Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to me, saying: al-Muʿtamir narrated to us, from Layth, from Ṭāwūs and ʿAṭāʾ, who both said: Every gambling is from maysir, even the children's playing with knucklebones and walnuts.

4117 – Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Ḥakkām narrated to us, from ʿAmr, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Saʿīd, who said: Maysir is gambling.

4118 – Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr informed us, from Abu al-Aḥwaṣ, from ʿUbayd Allāh, who said: Beware of these two knucklebones with which one casts divinations by throwing them, for they are from maysir. [[See the earlier note, p. 322, note 2.]]

4119 – Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to me, saying: Ibn ʿUlayya narrated to us, from Ibn Abi ʿArūba, from Qatāda, who said: As for His words "and maysir," it is gambling entirely.

4120 – Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sālim informed me, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar: that he heard ʿUmar ibn ʿUbayd Allāh say to al-Qāsim ibn Muhammad: Backgammon (nard) is maysir; what do you say about chess (shaṭranj)? Is it maysir? Al-Qāsim said: Everything that distracts from the remembrance of God and from the prayer is maysir.

4121 – ʿAlī ibn Dāwūd narrated to me, saying: Abu Ṣāliḥ narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiya narrated to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Maysir is gambling. A man in the Jahiliyya would stake his family and his wealth, and whichever of them defeated his companion took away his family and wealth. [[Al-mukhāṭara: wagering, and "qammara al-rajul ṣāḥibahu yuqammiruhu qamran" (with the mīm vowelled with a kasra) means when he played gambling with him and defeated him.]]

4122 – Mūsā ibn Hārūn narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Ḥammād narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī, who said: Maysir is gambling.

4123 – al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatāda, who said: Maysir is gambling.

4124 – al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Layth, from Mujāhid and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who both said: Maysir is gambling entirely, even the walnut children play with.

4125 – It was related to me from al-Ḥusayn, who said: I heard Abu Muʿādh al-Faḍl ibn Khālid say: I heard ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Sulaymān narrate, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, regarding his words "and maysir," that he said: Gambling.

4126 – Bishr ibn Muʿādh narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatāda, who said: Maysir is gambling.

4127 – al-Muthannā narrated to us, saying: Isḥāq narrated to us, saying: Abu Badr Shujāʿ ibn al-Walīd narrated to us, saying: Mūsā ibn ʿUqba narrated to us, from Nāfiʿ: that Ibn ʿUmar used to say: Gambling is from maysir.

4128 – al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujāhid, who said: Maysir is the arrows of the Arabs and the knucklebones of Persia. He said: Ibn Jurayj said: ʿAṭāʾ ibn Maysara claimed that maysir is gambling entirely.

4129 – Ibn al-Barqī narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr ibn Abi Salama narrated to us, from Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, who said: Makḥūl said: Maysir is gambling.

4130 – al-Ḥusayn ibn Muhammad al-Dhāriʿ narrated to us, saying: al-Faḍl ibn Sulaymān and Shujāʿ ibn al-Walīd narrated to us, from Mūsā ibn ʿUqba, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: Maysir is gambling.
* *
As for His words, "Say: In them is great sin and benefit for people," by this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Say, O Muhammad, to them: "In them," meaning in wine and gambling, "is great sin." The great sin that is in them is what has been mentioned from al-Suddī, namely:

4131 – Mūsā ibn Hārūn narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Ḥammād narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī: As for His words, "In them is great sin," the sin of wine is that a man drinks and becomes intoxicated and harms people. And the sin of gambling is that a man gambles and withholds what is due and wrongs others.

4132 – Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najīḥ, from Mujāhid: "Say: In them is great sin," he said: This was the first time wine was criticised.

4133 – ʿAlī ibn Dāwūd narrated to me, saying: Abu Ṣāliḥ narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiya ibn Ṣāliḥ narrated to me, from ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭalḥa, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His words: "Say: In them is great sin," meaning what diminishes religion in the one who drinks it.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The great sin that is most fitting for the interpretation of the great sin which God, may His praise be exalted, mentioned as being in wine and gambling: In "wine," it is what al-Suddī said: the loss of the intellect of the wine-drinker when he becomes intoxicated from drinking it, to the point that knowledge of his Lord departs from him, and that is the greatest of sins. This is the meaning of Ibn ʿAbbās's words, God willing. As for gambling, it is what occupies one with it away from the remembrance of God and from the prayer, and the arising of enmity and hatred between those who gamble with each other because of it, as our Lord, may His praise be exalted, described it by His saying: ﴿Satan only desires to cast enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of God and from the prayer﴾ [Surah al-Mā'ida: 91].
* *
As for His words, "and benefit for people," the benefits of wine were its price before it was prohibited, and the pleasure they attained by drinking it, as al-Aʿshā said in describing it:

For us, from its forenoon: foulness of soul, grief, and remembrance of cares whose effects do not cease.
And at evening: good cheer of soul, pleasure, and abundant wealth, the might of its intoxications.

[[His Dīwān: 61; al-Ashriba of Ibn Qutayba: 70. The two verses are badly corrupted in the printed edition: in the first verse "ṣaḥāhā" with an unpointed ṣād, and "mā tafuk adātuhā." In the second verse "ʿadhat nashwātuhā," and in al-Ashriba "ʿidatun," and in the Dīwān "ghadwat nashwātuhā" (with a ḍamma on the ghayn and a fatḥa on the tāʾ). The Dīwān copy is also very corrupt, so I preferred reading the word as "ʿizzatun." For al-Aʿshā says before the two verses: "By your life, wine, if you drink it, its evenings and mornings differ." Then in the second verse he explains that in "al-ḍuḥā" – which is the forenoon – it follows foulness of soul, grief and harmful cares. Then he follows that with what happens in the evening of good cheer of soul and pleasure, so there is no sense in repeating the mention of "forenoon" again; indeed, had he done so he would have contradicted his earlier verse, making wine in the forenoon or duḥā both foul to the soul and gladdening to it at the same time, and this is false. So the correct reading in my view is "ʿizzatun li-nashwātihā," as in his similar saying: "From a wine that spent the night in Babylon, pure, which leaves the youth a king, inclining, stricken." Support for this is that Ibn Qutayba placed before the preceding verses: "He said of wine that it extends hopes," then mentioned the verses; the meaning of that is that it makes him see himself as having become a mighty king who bestows abundant wealth when he is intoxicated. His words "mā tughibb adhātuhā" come from the saying "ghabba al-shayʾ," meaning it went away and was delayed. You say, "mā yughibbuka luṭfī," meaning my kindness does not stay away from you for a day, but comes to you every day, meaning consecutively.]]

As Ḥassān said:

So we drink it, and it leaves us kings and lions, whom the meeting does not repel.

[[His Dīwān: 4; al-Kāmil 1: 74, and elsewhere. "Nahnahahu ʿan al-shayʾ": to drive him back from it, restrain and prevent him. That is, we do not fear the meeting with the enemy.]]

As for the benefits of gambling, they are what they obtained from the shares of the slaughtered camel. For they used to gamble over a camel, and when one of them won against his companion, he slaughtered it, then they divided it into tenths according to the number of arrows. [[Al-anṣibāʾ: plural of naṣīb. Al-mayāsara: gambling. "Falaja" and "aflaja" (of an arrow of the gambler): won. The tenths of the camel: the shares. They used to divide it into ten parts.] And in this the poet of the Banū Thaʿlaba, al-Aʿshā, said:

And a camel of gamblers I called to generosity, and a desert's far reaches whose going astray I fear.

[[His Dīwān: 23. "Al-aysār," plural of yasar: the one who casts the arrows, and the player too, which is what is meant here. The Dīwān reads "daʿawtu li-ḥatfihā" (I called for its destruction). "Al-muqfira": the desolate wasteland. "Niyāṭ" of the wasteland: the far end of its road, as if it were joined (nīṭat) to another wasteland, hardly ever ending. This is one of fine verses in which al-Aʿshā praises his deed, saying:

And a wine of which Babylon brews, like the blood of a slaughtered beast, I stripped it of its gleam;
And a strange one that comes to kings, wise, which I said so that it would be said: who said it?!
And a camel of gamblers . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

And gambling was among them of noble conduct.]]
* *
And according to what we have said on this, the people of interpretation spoke.
Those who said so:

4134 – Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, who said: The benefits here are what they obtain from the camel.

4135 – Mūsā ibn Hārūn narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn Ḥammād narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī: As for their benefits, the benefit of wine is in its pleasure and its price, and the benefit of gambling is in what is won from gambling.

4136 – Abu Hishām al-Rifāʿī narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Zāʾida narrated to us, from Warqāʾ, from Ibn Abi Najīḥ, from Mujāhid: "Say: In them is great sin and benefit for people," he said: Their benefits before they were prohibited.

4137 – ʿAlī ibn Dāwūd narrated to us, saying: Abu Ṣāliḥ narrated to us, saying: Muʿāwiya narrated to me, from ʿAlī, from Ibn ʿAbbās: "and benefit for people," he said: meaning what they obtain of its pleasure and joy when they drink it.
* *
The readers differed in reading this:

The majority of the people of Medina and some of the Kufans and Basrans read: "Qul fīhimā ithmun kabīrun" with the bāʾ (kabīr, singular), meaning: say, in the drinking of this and the gambling of that, is a great one among sins.

And others from the two cities of Basra and Kufa read: "Qul fīhimā ithmun kathīrun" (many), meaning abundance of sins. It seems they regarded "al-ithm" as meaning "al-āthām" (sins), even though it is singular in form, so they described it by its meaning of multiplicity. [[See the meaning of "al-ithm" above, 3: 406 and following / then p. 550.]]

Abu Ja'far said: Of the two readings on this point, the one closest to the truth is the reading of whoever reads it with "ba'" (in "qul fihima ithmun kabir" is read with the consonant... ) — [translation text follows below]

Hmm, I need to correct myself: the passage as given is a Tafsir text, and I should translate it faithfully and completely without commentary. Here is the translation:

Abu Ja'far said: Of the two readings on this matter, the more correct one is the reading of the one who reads it with the letter "ba'" (as in "qul fihima ithmun kabir"), because all of them agree on His saying "wa-ithmuhuma akbaru min naf'ihima," and its reading with "ba'." In this there is clear evidence that what the first sin is described with is greatness and magnitude, not multiplicity in number. Had what was described be multiplicity, it would have been said: "wa-ithmuhuma akthar min naf'ihima" (and their sin is more numerous than their benefit).

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And their sin is greater than their benefit﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, mighty is His mention, means by this: the sin of drinking [wine] is this, and of gambling is that, is greater and more harmful to them than the benefit they obtain from them. This was so because when they became intoxicated, some of them would leap upon others and fight one another, and when they gambled, evil would arise among them because of it, and this led them to what they sinned by.

* *

This verse was revealed concerning wine before its prohibition was stated explicitly. Thus, He, mighty is His praise, attributed the sin to both of them, though the sin arises from their causes, since it results from them.

* *

A number of the people of interpretation have said: the meaning is: their sin after their prohibition is greater than their benefit before their prohibition.

Those who said this:

4138 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd told me, saying: my father told me, saying: my paternal uncle told me, saying: my father told me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: "and their sin is greater than their benefit," he said: their benefits before the prohibition, and their sin after they were prohibited.

4139 - It was related from 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far told us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "and benefits for mankind, and their sin is greater than their benefit," he makes the benefits before the prohibition and the sin after it was prohibited.

4140 - It was related from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman told me: I heard al-Dahhak say concerning His words: "and their sin is greater than their benefit," he says: their sin after the prohibition is greater than their benefit before the prohibition.

4141 - 'Ali ibn Dawud told me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih told me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, his words: "and their sin is greater than their benefit," he says: what is lost of religion and its sin is greater than what they gain in its joy when they drink it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We have chosen what we have said in this interpretation because of the consecutive and mutually corroborating reports that this verse was revealed before the prohibition of wine and gambling. It was therefore known that the sin which God mentioned in this verse and attributed to both of them refers to the sin arising from their causes, as we have described, not the sin after the prohibition.

* *

Mention of the reports indicating what we have said, that this verse was revealed before the prohibition of wine:

4142 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq told us, saying: Abu Ahmad told us, saying: Qays told us, from Salim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: When it was revealed: "They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people," some people disliked them because of His words "in them is great sin," and some drank them because of His words "and benefits for people," until it was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you say﴾ [Surah an-Nisa: 43]. He said: So they would leave it at the time of prayer and drink it at other times, until it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, wine, gambling, stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 90]. Then 'Umar said: Ruin for you! Today you have been coupled with gambling!

4143 - Muhammad ibn Ma'mar told me, saying: Abu 'Amir told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Humayd told us, from Abu Tawba al-Misri, who said: I heard 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar say: Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed three things concerning wine. The first thing revealed was: "They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin," the verse. They said: O Messenger of Allah, we benefit from it and drink it, as Allah, mighty and majestic, said in His Book! Then this verse was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾, the verse. They said: O Messenger of Allah, we will not drink it near the time of prayer. He said: Then it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, wine, gambling, stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it﴾, the verse. He said: So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Wine has been prohibited.

4144 - Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, from Yazid al-Nahwi, from 'Ikrima and al-Hasan, who both said: Allah said: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you say﴾, and "They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, and their sin is greater than their benefit." Then the verse in al-Ma'idah abrogated it, when He said: ﴿O you who believe, indeed wine and gambling...﴾, the verse.

4145 - Ibn Bashshar told us, saying: 'Abd al-Wahhab told us, saying: 'Awf told us, from Abu al-Qamus Zayd ibn 'Ali, who said: Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning wine three times. The first thing revealed, Allah said: "They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, and their sin is greater than their benefit." He said: Some Muslims drank it, whoever Allah willed among them, on that basis, until two men drank and entered prayer and began to slur speech which 'Awf did not know what it was. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning them: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you say﴾. So whoever among them drank it, drank it, and they began to avoid it at the time of prayer, until a man, according to Abu al-Qamus, drank it and began to lament the slain of Badr:

"Greet with safety, Umm 'Amr, and is there for you, after your kinsmen, any peace?"

[Editor's note: this verse is attributed to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq in this report, and 'A'isha denied it. These verses are part of verses of Abu Bakr ibn Shu'ub mixed with the poetry of Bahir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir al-Qushayri.]

"Leave me to drink in the morning, O Bakr, for I have seen death dig out Hisham..."

[Editor's note: the second and third verses are by Bahir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Qushayri lamenting Hisham ibn al-Mughira, who died before Islam; their inclusion here is a confusion in the transmission.]

He said: This reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he came in alarm, dragging his cloak from fear, until he reached him. When the man saw him, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raised something in his hand to strike him. The man said: I seek refuge in Allah from the anger of Allah and His Messenger! By Allah, I will never taste it again! So Allah revealed its prohibition: ﴿O you who believe, indeed wine, gambling, stone altars, and divining arrows are defilement...﴾ up to His words: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ Then 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: We have desisted, we have desisted!

4146 - Sufyan ibn Wakី' told us, saying: Ishaq al-Azraq told us, from Zakariyya, from Simak, from al-Sha'bi who said: Four verses were revealed concerning wine: "They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people," so they left it. Then: ﴿You take from it intoxicant and good provision﴾ [Surah an-Nahl: 67], so they drank it. Then the two verses in al-Ma'idah were revealed: ﴿Indeed, wine and gambling...﴾ up to His words: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾

4147 - Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat told us, from al-Suddi, who said: This verse was revealed: "They ask you about wine and gambling," the verse. They continued drinking it until 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf prepared food and invited people from the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), among them 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. He recited: ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾ and did not comprehend it. So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed, emphasizing regarding wine: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you say﴾. So it was permitted for them to drink from the dawn prayer until the day rose or reached midday, then they would stand for the noon prayer while sober [sahu: became sober], then they would not drink until the 'Atama prayer, which is the night prayer, then they would drink until midnight, sleep, and rise for the dawn prayer sober. They continued this until Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas prepared food and invited people from the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), among them a man from the Ansar. He roasted a camel's head for them and invited them to it. When they ate and drank wine, they became intoxicated and began talking. Sa'd said something, so the Ansari grew angry, lifted the jawbone of the camel and broke Sa'd's nose. Then Allah revealed the abrogation and prohibition of wine, saying: ﴿Indeed, wine, gambling, stone altars, and divining arrows...﴾ up to His words: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾

4148 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya told us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, and from a man, from Mujahid, concerning His words: "They ask you about wine and gambling." He said: When this verse was revealed, some people drank it and some left it, until its prohibition was revealed in Surah al-Ma'idah.

4149 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr told us, saying: Abu 'Asim told us, saying: 'Isa told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Say: In them is great sin," he said: This was the first time wine was blamed.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 219 (part 3 of 4):

4150 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding his saying: "They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefit for people." God censured them, but did not forbid them, because He intended to bring them to their term and appointed time. Then God revealed in "Surat al-Nisa'" something more severe than that: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying﴾. So they would drink it, until when the prayer time came they would abstain from it, and intoxication was forbidden to them. Then God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed in "Surat al-Ma'idah," after the Battle of the Confederates: ﴿O you who believe, indeed wine and gambling﴾ up to ﴿that you may be successful﴾. So its prohibition came in this verse, its little and its much, what intoxicates and what does not intoxicate. And the Arabs at that time had no life more pleasing to them than it. [[His saying: "ʿaysh" (life) is a fine metaphor, which the lexicon books do not restrict, and by it is meant: enjoyment and pleasure. The root meaning of "ʿaysh" is food and drink and that by which life is sustained. It was then transferred to enjoyment, and similar to it is what came in the report: "There is no life except the life of the Hereafter," so it is more fitting to interpret it as enjoyment and pleasure.]]

4151 - I was told on the authority of ʿAmmar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ, regarding his saying: "They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefit for people, and their sin is greater than their benefit." He said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: Indeed your Lord is advancing the prohibition of wine. He said: Then there was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated, until you know what you are saying﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: Indeed your Lord is advancing the prohibition of wine. He said: Then there was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, indeed wine, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are an abomination from the work of Satan, so avoid it﴾. Wine was then forbidden.

4152 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding "They ask you about wine and gambling," the whole verse: It abrogated three [[It is said "nasakht thalathan," meaning three times of abrogation, and it is permissible to say "nasakhat thalathah" as here, meaning three abrogations, since "al-naskh" is masculine.]] in "Surat al-Ma'idah," and by the prescribed punishment that the Prophet (ﷺ) set, and the Prophet's (ﷺ) striking. He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) would strike them with that as a prescribed punishment, but he would act in that by his own judgment, and it was not a named prescribed punishment, though it is a ḥadd. And he recited: ﴿Indeed wine and gambling﴾ the verse. [[That is, this verse of al-Baqarah was abrogated by the verse of al-Ma'idah in a single abrogation; then God made its punishment striking without a specified number, which was a second abrogation; then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) exercised his judgment regarding the number of strikes and their form, and his exercise of judgment was a third abrogation.]]

The statement concerning the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: The surplus﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: They ask you, O Muhammad, your companions: What is it that they should spend from their wealth, so that they may give it in charity? Say to them, O Muhammad: Spend from it the surplus (al-ʿafw).

* *

The interpreters differed regarding the meaning of "al-ʿafw" in this place.

Some of them said: Its meaning is: the excess.
Those who said that:

4153 - ʿAmr ibn ʿAli al-Bahili narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us = and Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us = from Ibn Abi Layla, from al-Hakam, from Miqsam, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: al-ʿafw is what exceeds your family's needs.

4154 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah: "Say: al-ʿafw," i.e., the surplus.

4155 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah, who said: It is the surplus.

4156 - Yaʿqub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Malik informed us, from ʿAta', regarding His saying "al-ʿafw," who said: The surplus.

4157 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: "al-ʿafw," he says: the surplus.

4158 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: al-ʿafw," he said: The people would work each day for what it required, and if that day left a surplus beyond their dependants, they would set it aside, and they would not leave their dependants hungry, but they would give it in charity to people.

4159 - ʿAmr ibn ʿAli narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, saying: Yunus narrated to us, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: "And they ask you what they should spend. Say: al-ʿafw," he said: It is the surplus, the surplus of wealth.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: what is ʿafw, that which does not appear upon the one who spends it or gives it in charity.
Those who said that:

4160 - ʿAli ibn Dawud narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: al-ʿafw," he says: What is not apparent in your wealth.

4161 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, from ʿIsa, from Ibn Juraij, from Tawus, regarding the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: al-ʿafw," he said: The small amount of everything.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: the moderate level of expenditure, what is neither extravagance nor stinginess.
Those who said that:

4162 - Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Buza' narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, from ʿAwf, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: al-ʿafw," he says: Do not strain your wealth until it is exhausted for the people.

4163 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: I asked ʿAta' about His saying: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: al-ʿafw," he said: The ʿafw in spending is that you do not strain your wealth until it is exhausted so that you must ask people.

4164 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Juraij, who said: I asked ʿAta' about His saying: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: al-ʿafw," he said: The ʿafw is what they do not exceed nor fall short in what is right. He said: Mujahid said: al-ʿafw is charity from the surplus of wealth.

4165 - ʿAmr ibn ʿAli narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Saʿid narrated to us, saying: ʿAwf narrated to us, from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: al-ʿafw," he said: It is that you do not strain your wealth.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: "Say: al-ʿafw," take from them whatever they bring you, little or much.
Those who said that:

4166 - Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: al-ʿafw," he says: Whatever they bring you, little or much, accept it from them.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: what is good of your wealth.
Those who said that:

4167 - I was told on the authority of ʿAmmar, who said: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ, regarding His saying: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: al-ʿafw," he said: He says: the good part of it; he says: your best and finest wealth.

4168 - I was told on the authority of ʿAmmar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from Qatadah, who said: He used to say: al-ʿafw is the surplus; he says: your best wealth.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: the obligatory charity.
Those who said that:

4169 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, from ʿIsa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Qays ibn Saʿd = or ʿIsa, from Qays, from Mujahid (Abu ʿAsim was uncertain) = regarding God, Mighty and Majestic's saying: "Say: al-ʿafw," he said: The obligatory charity.

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The most correct of these sayings is the saying of the one who said: The meaning of "al-ʿafw" is the surplus of a man's wealth beyond himself and his family, in their maintenance, of what they cannot do without. This is the surplus concerning which the reports from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) are widely transmitted, permitting charity from it and giving alms in the paths of righteousness. [[In the printed edition: "wa-ṣadaqatun fi wujuh al-birr" (and charity in the paths of righteousness). The correct reading is what I have established, meaning that giving charity from the ʿafw is in the paths of righteousness; as for the obligatory zakat, it has a different matter, as will come later.]]

Mention of some of the reports transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to that effect:

4170 - ʿAli ibn Muslim narrated to us, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, from Ibn ʿAjlan, from al-Maqburi, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: A man said: O Messenger of God, I have a dinar! He said: "Spend it on yourself." He said: I have another! He said: "Spend it on your family." He said: I have another! He said: Spend it on your children! He said: I have another; he said: Then you know best! [[Hadith 4170: ʿAli ibn Muslim ibn Saʿid Abu al-Hasan al-Tusi, resident of Baghdad: trustworthy; al-Bukhari in his Sahih, Ibn Maʿin, Abu Dawud and others narrated from him; his biography is in al-Tahdhib and Tarikh Baghdad 12/108-109. Abu ʿAsim: he is al-Nabil, al-Dahhak ibn Makhlad. Ibn ʿAjlan: he is Muhammad; his biography has passed: 304. al-Maqburi: he is Saʿid ibn Abi Saʿid.
The hadith was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 7413, with an addition at its beginning, from Yahya (al-Qattan), from Ibn ʿAjlan, with the same meaning. We have already indicated its takhrij there in Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Mustadrak of al-Hakim, and Ibn Hibban.
al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1/253, attributing it to these and to al-Tabari, except al-Musnad. Ibn Kathir narrated it, 1/503, from al-Tabari, then said: "Muslim narrated it in his Sahih." He was mistaken, may God have mercy on him, for the hadith is not in Sahih Muslim, with certainty, after my and my brother al-Sayyid Mahmud's lengthy searching.]]

4171 - Muhammad ibn Maʿmar al-Bahrani narrated to me, saying: Rawh ibn ʿUbadah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Juraij narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Zubayr informed me that he heard Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah say: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: When one of you is poor, let him begin with himself; if he has a surplus, let him begin with those he supports; then if he finds a surplus after that, let him give charity to others. [[Hadith 4171: Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad: 14323 (3/305, Halabi), with similar wording, along with a story at its beginning, by way of Ayyub, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir.
Muslim narrated it, 1/274, in the manner of the Musnad version, by way of al-Layth ibn Saʿd, from Abu al-Zubayr, and then by way of Ayyub, from Abu al-Zubayr.
Ibn Kathir mentioned it, 1/503, attributing it to Muslim. al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1/254, attributing it to Muslim and al-Nasa'i.]]

4172 - ʿAmr ibn ʿAli narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, from ʿAsim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatadah, from Mahmud ibn Labid, from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, who said: A man came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a gold nugget that he had found in some of the mines, and said: O Messenger of God, take this from me as charity, for by God, I have not woken up owning anything other than it! He turned away from him. Then he came to him from his right side and said to him the same, and he turned away from him. Then he said to him the same again, and he turned away from him. Then he said to him the same again, and he said: Bring it! angrily. So he took it and threw it at him with a throw that, had it struck him, would have wounded or injured him. Then he said: "One of you comes with all his wealth, giving it as charity, and sits begging people!? Charity is only from surplus wealth. [[Hadith 4172: ʿAsim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatadah: has passed at 1519. In the printed edition it reads "ʿAsim ʿan ʿUmar ibn Qatadah," which is a clear error.
The hadith was narrated by Abu Dawud: 1673, from Musa ibn Isma'il, from Hammad (Ibn Salamah), from Ibn Ishaq, with this isnad. al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak 1/413, by way of Musa ibn Isma'il, with it, and said: "This is a sahih hadith according to the condition of Muslim, though they did not narrate it." al-Dhahabi agreed.
al-Suyuti mentioned it, 1/253-254, and added its attribution to Ibn Sa'd; it is in Tabaqat Ibn Sa'd 4/2/19, by another route, from the narration of "ʿUmar ibn al-Hakam ibn Thawban," from Jabir.
"Hadhafahu bi-l-shay'" means he threw it at him. "Takaffafa al-nas" means he presented himself for people's kindness, extending his hand, so as to receive from them what they give him in charity. And his saying "ʿan ẓahr ghinan" means from a wealth by which his affairs are set right and strengthened.]]

4173 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Ibrahim al-Mukhrami, who said: I heard Abu al-Ahwas narrate, from ʿAbd Allah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: Give a small portion from the surplus, begin with those you support, and you will not be blamed for having only sufficiency. [[Hadith 4173: Ibrahim al-Mukhrami: thus it is recorded in the printed edition, and no narrator by this name is known to me. What I think likely, indeed what I nearly am certain of, is that it is a corruption of "Ibrahim al-Hajari," for the hadith is his. The writing is similar. al-Hajari is Ibrahim ibn Muslim al-ʿAbdi al-Kufi, and he is weak. He was declared weak by Ibn ʿUyaynah, al-Bukhari, Abu Zurʿah, Abu Hatim and others.
This hadith is part of a longer hadith, which al-Suyuti mentioned, 1/254, saying: "Abu Yaʿla and al-Hakim narrated it and declared it sahih, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: Hands are three: the hand of God is the highest, the hand of the giver which is next to it, and the hand of the beggar is the lowest until the Day of Resurrection. So abstain from asking and from seeking as much as you can. If you are given something good, let it be seen upon you, begin with those you support, give a small portion from the surplus, and you will not be blamed for having only sufficiency."
Al-Mundhiri likewise mentioned it in al-Targhib wa-l-Tarhib 2/10, saying: "Abu Yaʿla narrated it, and its narration is generally trustworthy. al-Hakim narrated it and declared its isnad sound."
Thus al-Suyuti and al-Mundhiri conveyed al-Hakim's authentication of it. Regarding that we have a comment: al-Mustadrak does not contain his authentication, as will come. If al-Suyuti did not quote from al-Mundhiri and follow him, then the printed copy of al-Mustadrak must have dropped the authentication they reported.
The beginning of the hadith up to his saying "and the hand of the beggar is the lowest" was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 4261, from al-Qasim ibn Malik, from al-Hajari, from Abu al-Ahwas, from ʿAbd Allah, who is Ibn Masʿud, as a marfu' report. al-Haythami in Majma' al-Zawa'id 3/97 mentioned its beginning from al-Musnad and Abu Ya'la, and the addition at its end from Abu Ya'la, and said: "Its narrators are trustworthy."
Al-Hakim's narration of it is in al-Mustadrak 1/408, by three isnads, in none of which is its wording given in full; rather, in the first he mentioned that the rest of the hadith had dropped out, and in the others he mentioned only part of the hadith, not all of it. He did not mention in it any authentication or weakening, and al-Dhahabi said nothing about that in his summary.
"Rada'a lahu min malihi yarduʿu radʿan, wa-radakha lahu radikhah": he gave him a small, little amount. "Al-kafaf" is that which restrains a person from asking people; he means: if you have no surplus wealth to spend, you will not be blamed for not giving anyone anything.]]

* *

= And other reports similar to that, which would take too long to mention in full in this book.

Since the one whom the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted his community to give in charity from their wealth, is the surplus beyond the need of the one giving charity, then the surplus of that is the "ʿafw" of a man's wealth, [[In the printed edition: "al-fadl min dhalika..." without the fa'; the fa' is necessary for the sentence to be sound.]] since "al-ʿafw," in the speech of the Arabs, regarding wealth and everything else, means increase and abundance. From this is His saying, may His praise be exalted: "until they multiplied" (ʿafaw), meaning they increased beyond what they had been in number and became numerous. [[See what he said regarding the meaning of "ʿafa" previously: 3/370.]] And from it is the saying of the poet: [[He is Labid ibn Rabi'ah.]]

But we strike the sword among us... among the fat-laden camels, the humped ones.

[[His diwan, poem 2/19; it appears again in the commentary at 9/6 (Bulaq). In the printed edition here it reads "yaʿiḍḍu al-sayfa minnā," which is an error; the correct reading is what is in the other place and the diwan. This verse is from verses in which he boasts of their hospitality to guests, especially in winter. He says when winter comes with its cold and dearth: "We do not pass beyond the barren [camels] to the young, close-to-calving ones, or the fat-bodied ones, but we strike the sword..." and "minha" refers to the camels. He says: at slaughtering we do not leave the long-necked, fat she-camels for a poor young camel or an aged one; rather we strike the sword, that is, we strike with the sword until it bites into the flesh—at the hocks of the large, heavy-humped fat ones, and these are the kawm, plural of kawma'.]]

He means by it: those with abundant fat. From this it is said to a man: "Take what is ʿafa for you from so-and-so," meaning what exceeds and is clear for you from his effort, without his exerting himself to it. [[His saying: "It was evident..." is the answer to his saying: "If the one whom the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted..." "Kāna bayyinan" here, and "adhina" here means: informed and told.]] It was evident that what God permitted in His saying, "Say: al-ʿafw," to His servants regarding expenditure, permitting them to spend it when they wish to spend it, is what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made clear to his community in his saying: "The best charity is what is spent out of sufficiency," and permitted them to it.

* *

Suppose someone says to us: "What prevents you from holding that this 'al-'afw' is the obligatory charity?" [The phrase "al-sadaqa al-mafrūḍa" means: the obligatory zakat.] It is said: We deny that because of the proof that whoever's zakat fell due on his property, and then all his property was destroyed except the amount that remained for the recipients of the charitable shares, it is incumbent upon him to hand that over to them. If the destruction of his property came after his failure to discharge the duty, then it was due to them from his property, [in the printed edition: "the duty was due to them from his property to them"; the word "fī" (in) is needed to complete and correct the meaning: "discharging the duty from his property to them." And his saying "was due to them" is a qualifier of "the duty."] And there is no doubt that this is his effort, if he hands it over to them, not his surplus. And God's naming, may His praise be great, of what He taught His servants regarding the manner of spending from their wealth as "al-'afw" (the surplus) precludes that it deserves the name "effort" in any state. Given that, the corruption of the view of those who claim that the meaning of "al-'afw" is what the owner of the wealth brings to his leader and gives him, whatever the amount of his wealth, little or much, and the view of those who claim it is the obligatory charity, is evident. Likewise, there is no basis for the view of those who say its meaning is: "what has not become apparent in your wealth" [see this view above, shortly, p. 338], because when Abu Lubaba said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Indeed, among the signs of my repentance is that I withdraw from my wealth as charity to God and His Messenger," the Prophet ﷺ said, "A third of that will suffice for you!" Similarly, it is narrated from Ka'b ibn Malik that the Prophet ﷺ said to him something similar. [The hadith of Abu Lubaba ibn al-Mundhir's repentance and his withdrawal from his wealth is in the Musnad 3:452, 502. He said: when God accepted his repentance regarding the matter of the Battle of Banu Qurayza (see Sirat Ibn Hisham 3:247, 248): "O Messenger of God, indeed among the signs of my repentance is that I abandon the house of my people, and that I withdraw from my wealth as charity to God and His Messenger." The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "A third will suffice for you."
As for the report of Ka'b ibn Malik, it is the report of the three who stayed behind (narrated by al-Bukhari in the chapter on the Battle of Banu Qurayza 6:7): when God accepted his repentance, he said: "Indeed among the signs of my repentance is that I withdraw from my wealth as charity to His Messenger!" The Prophet ﷺ said: "Keep back some of your wealth for yourself, it is better for you."] A third's share is undoubtedly clearly separate from the wealth of its owner, but in my view, as God, may His praise be great, said: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever between that as a balance﴾ [Surah al-Furqan: 67], and as God, may His praise be great, said to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿Do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched, lest you sit reproached and destitute﴾ [Surah al-Isra: 29]. That is what he ﷺ set as the limit below that, according to the amount of wealth and its capacity.

* *

Then the scholars differed regarding this verse: is it abrogated, or is its ruling binding on the servants? Some of them said: it is abrogated; the obligatory zakat abrogated it.
Mention of who said that:
4174 - Ali ibn Dawud related to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus." He said: This was before charity was made obligatory.
4175 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus." He said: No specific obligation was prescribed in it. Then He said: ﴿Take what is pardoned, enjoin what is customary, and turn away from the ignorant﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 199]. Then the obligations were revealed afterward, named.
4176 - Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi regarding His words: "They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus." This was abrogated by zakat.

* *

Others said: rather, its ruling is established and not abrogated.
Mention of who said that:
4177 - Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Qays ibn Sa'd, or Isa, from Qays, from Mujahid — Abu Asim doubted — he said: "al-'afw" is the obligatory charity.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this matter is what Ibn Abbas said, as transmitted from him by Ata, that His words "Say: the surplus" are not an imposition of an obligation that God made binding upon one's wealth; rather, it is God informing what pleases Him of expenditure and what displeases Him, in answer to the one who asked His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about what would be pleasing to Him. It is thus a discipline from God for all His creatures, in which He disciplined them regarding voluntary (non-obligatory) charities; its ruling is binding, not abrogating a ruling that preceded it with a contrary meaning, nor abrogated by a ruling that came after it. Therefore it is not fitting for the one of piety and religion to exceed, in voluntary charities, gifts, bestowals of supererogatory giving and alms, what his Prophet ﷺ disciplined them with in his saying: "When one of you has a surplus, let him begin with himself, then with his family, then with his children," and then he takes thereafter in the surplus the paths that please God and that He loves. That is the "balance" (qawam) between extravagance and stinginess, which God, may He be exalted, mentioned in His Book, God willing.

* *

It is said to the one who claims that this is abrogated: what is the evidence for its abrogation, when all agree without disagreement among them that a man may give from his wealth as charity, gift, and bequest a third? So what indicates that this is abrogated?
If he claims that by his saying "it is abrogated" he means that bringing out the surplus from wealth is not obligatory as a duty, and that if it was a duty, it has fallen away by the existence of zakat in the wealth =
= It is said to him: and what is the proof that bringing out the surplus was a duty which the obligation of zakat removed? There is no indication in the verse that this was an obligation, since there was no command from God, may He be mentioned with might, but rather in it is the indication that it is an answer to what the people asked about, as a means of making known the charities in which God is pleased?
There is no path for the claimant of that to any proof that would necessitate the soundness of what he claimed.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for the readings, they differed regarding the recitation of "al-'afw." The majority of the readers of the Hijaz, the readers of the two Sanctuaries, and the majority of the readers of Kufa recited: "Qul al-'afw" with a fatha (nasb). Some readers of Basra recited: "Qul al-'afw" with a damma (raf').

Whoever recites it with nasb makes "madha" one word and takes it as the object of "yunfiqun," as I explained earlier [see above in this part: 292, 293], and then puts "al-'afw" in the accusative accordingly. The meaning of the sentence then is: "And they ask you what thing they should spend?"

Whoever recites with raf' makes "ma" a complement of "dha" and they put "al-'afw" in the nominative. The meaning of the sentence then is: "What is it that they spend? Say: That which they spend is the surplus."

If "al-'afw" were in the accusative and then "madha" were made two words, meaning: "They ask you what they should spend? Say: they spend the surplus," and the ones who made "madha" one word with the meaning "what do they spend? Say: that which they spend" were in the nominative as a predicate [meaning: they put it in the nominative as the predicate of "alladhi yunfiqun"], it would be a correct and sound usage in Arabic.

Whichever of the two readings is recited, it is in my view correct, because their meanings are close, with each reading being widely transmitted. However, the more preferable of the two readings to me, even though the matter is so, is the reading of the one who recites it with nasb, because more of the readers recite it so, and it is better known and more widespread.

* *

The interpretation of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Thus God makes clear to you the signs, that you may reflect, in this world and the Hereafter﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may He be mentioned with might, "Thus God makes clear to you the signs," thus He makes clear — that is, as I have made clear to you My signs and proofs — and they are "His signs" — in this surah, and I made known to you in it what is in it your deliverance from My punishment, and I made clear to you My limits and obligations, and I alerted you in it to the proofs of My oneness, then to the proofs of My messenger to you, and I guided you to the manifestation of guidance. So likewise I make clear to you in the rest of My Book which I sent down to My Prophet Muhammad ﷺ My signs and proofs and clarify them for you, so that you may reflect upon My promise and My threat, My reward and My punishment, and so choose My obedience, by which you attain My reward in the Hereafter and the triumph of eternal bliss, [in the printed edition: "then exceed My obedience..." which is an error; the correct is what I have set down. One says "I chose so-and-so over so-and-so," meaning I preferred him over him. "Ikhtiyar" is followed by "ʿalā" because it includes the meaning of "faddala" (to prefer).] over the little pleasures and the slight desires, by committing My disobedience in this perishing world; whoever commits it, his return is to Me, and his destination is to what he has no power to bear of My punishment and torment.

Those of the exegetical tradition said in agreement with what we have said regarding that.

Mention of who said that:
4178 - Ali ibn Dawud related to us, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas: "Thus God makes clear to you the signs that you may reflect in this world and the Hereafter." He said: meaning in the passing away of this world and its ending, and the coming of the Hereafter and its lasting.
4179 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada regarding His words: "that you may reflect in this world and the Hereafter." He said: that you may reflect in this world and the Hereafter, so that you know the superiority of the Hereafter over this world.
4180 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said regarding His words: "Thus God makes clear to you the signs that you may reflect in this world and the Hereafter." He said: As for this world, you know that it is a house of trial and then extinction; and the Hereafter is a house of recompense and then permanence, so that you reflect and act for the lasting of the two. He said: I also heard Abu Asim mention something similar.
4181 - Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada regarding His words: "Thus God makes clear to you the signs that you may reflect in this world and the Hereafter," and that whoever reflects on both knows the superiority of one over the other, and knows that this world is a house of trial and then a house of extinction, and that the Hereafter is a house of recompense and then a house of permanence; so be among those who cut off the need of this world for the need of the Hereafter.

**The interpretation of His words, may His remembrance be exalted:** ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: "Setting things right for them is best. And if you mix your affairs with theirs, they are your brothers."﴾

The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) differed about the occasion of the revelation of this verse.

Some said: It was revealed concerning those who separated the property of the orphans who were in their care, disliking to mix with them in food or anything else, when there was revealed ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 152], and His words ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly﴾ [Surah al-Nisa': 10].

Mention of those who said this:

4182 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Adam narrated to us, from Isra'il, from Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: When there was revealed ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 152; al-Isra': 34], they separated the orphans' property. They mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and then there was revealed: "And if you mix with them, they are your brothers, and Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. And had Allah willed, He would have put you in difficulty," so they mixed with them.

4183 - Sufyan ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: When there was revealed ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best﴾ and ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly – they are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will [soon] burn in a Blaze﴾ [Surah al-Nisa': 10], whoever had an orphan in his care separated his food from their food and his drink from their drink. He would set aside some of the food, and it would be kept for him until he ate it or it spoiled.
