In Ibn Kathir, regarding this passage, it reads "Abd Allah" instead of "'Ubayd Allah," so I do not know which is correct. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan is al-Hasan al-Basri.
Ibn Kathir (1:527) transmitted this hadith from this passage and said: "This is a mursal hadith, of good quality, from al-Hasan." Perhaps he was impressed by the paronomasia and rhymed prose. As for the mursal, it is weak, because the intermediary after the Successor (tabi'i) is unknown, as is well known. Al-Suyuti also transmitted it (1:269) and did not attribute it to anyone other than al-Tabari.]]
* *
Others said: Vain oaths are those oaths that are an invocation by the one swearing against himself, such as: "If I do not do such-and-such..." or those oaths that express polytheism or disbelief.
Those who said this:
4459: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam al-Misri narrated to me, saying: Isma'il ibn Marzuq told us, from Yahya ibn Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Ajlan, from Zayd ibn Aslam, concerning God's words: "God will not call you to account for the vain (laghw) in your oaths" [2:225]. He said: It is like a man's saying: "May God blind my sight if I do not do such-and-such; may God take me out of my wealth if I do not come to you tomorrow." That is this, and God does not leave him any wealth or children. He means: If God called you to account for this, He would not leave you anything.
4460: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam narrated to us, saying: Isma'il told us, saying: Yahya ibn Ayyub narrated to me, from Amr ibn al-Harith, from Zayd ibn Aslam, similarly.
4461: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Marzuq told us, saying: Yahya ibn Ayyub narrated to me, that Zayd ibn Aslam used to say, concerning God's words: "God will not call you to account for the vain in your oaths" [2:225], the like of a man's saying: "He is an unbeliever, and he is a polytheist." He said: He is not called to account for it unless it comes from his heart.
4462: Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning God's words: "God will not call you to account for the vain in your oaths" [2:225]: The vain in this is swearing by God (the oath) which is spoken with the tongue, so He made it vain. It is when one says: "He is a disbeliever in God, and in that case he associates partners with God, and he calls upon another god alongside God." This is the vain that God mentioned in "Surat al-Baqara."
* *
Others said: The vain in oaths is that in which there is an expiation (kaffara).
Those who said this:
4463: Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih told me, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, concerning his words: "God will not call you to account for the vain in your oaths" [2:225]: This concerns a man who swears to do something harmful, then he does not do it, and sees that which is better than it, so God commands him to expiate his oath and to do what is better. [[The report 4463 is an abridgment of the earlier report no. 4404; see the note there.]]
4464: Yahya ibn Ja'far told me, saying: Yazid ibn Harun told us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak, concerning God's words: "God will not call you to account for the vain in your oaths" [2:225], he said: It is the oath that requires expiation.
* *
Others said: The vain in oaths is that in which the swearer breaks the oath forgetfully.
Those who said this:
4465: Al-Hasan ibn Yahya told me, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Hushaym informed us, saying: Mughira informed me, from Ibrahim, who said: It is the man who swears to something, then forgets it, meaning in God's words: "God will not call you to account for the vain in your oaths" [2:225].
* *
Abu Ja'far said: "Laghw" in the speech of the Arabs is every speech that is blameworthy, a worthless utterance, having no meaning, abandoned. [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "wa-fi'lan" (and an action), which is clearly a distortion; the correct reading, in my opinion, is "wa-saqtan" (and a worthless thing), which the copyist could not read and so distorted. "Al-saqt" means error, and that which you drop so you do not count it. Hajara, yahjuru, hajran: when one mixes up his speech, raves, and speaks obscenely. The speech is "mahjur" (abandoned).]] It is said of it: "Laghā fulan fi kalamihi, yalghū laghwan" (so-and-so spoke vainly in his speech) when he says something ugly in speech. From it is God's exalted saying: "And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it" [28:55], and His saying: "And when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity" [25:72]. And it is heard from the Arabs: "Laghaytu bi-ism fulan" (I was vain about the name of so-and-so), meaning I was infatuated with mentioning him in an ugly way. Whoever says "laghaytu" says "algha laghan," and this is a dialect of some Arabs. From it is the saying of the rajiz (poet of the rajaz meter): [[He is Ru'ba ibn al-Ajjaj.]]
"And the lord of herds of pilgrims, restrained from vain talk and obscene speech."
[[This rajaz was discussed earlier at 3:488-489.]]
So if "laghw" is what I have described, and the one swearing by God says: "I did not do such-and-such," when he did; or "I did do such-and-such," when he did not, connecting this to his speech by way of the tongue's rushing forward (sabuq al-lisan) without intending sin in his oath [[See the commentary on the word "sabuq" previously in this part: 287, note: 4/ and p. 427.]], but out of a habit that has become his when speech is hasty; and the one who says: "By God, this is so-and-so," while he sees him, as he said, or: "By God, this is not so-and-so!" while he sees that he is not him; and the one who says: "By God, he will certainly do such-and-such," or: "He will not do such-and-such, by God," in the way we have described, from the hastiness of speech and the tongue's rushing forward out of habit, without intentional swearing to something false; and the one who says: "He is a polytheist, or he is a Jew or a Christian, if he does not do such-and-such, or if he does such-and-such," without resolve to disbelief, or Judaism, or Christianity [[The context of these sentences marked with lines before them: "So if the laghw is what I have described, and the one swearing by God... and the one who says... and the one who says... and the one who says... all of them are speakers..."]] — all of them are speakers of abusive speech and blameworthy discourse, and swearers by their tongues of oaths in which their hearts did not intend sin. [[His words: "it was known..." is the answer to his words: "And if the laghw is what I have described, and the one swearing by God..." and his words: "laghāh" is the plural of "lāghin," like "qādin" and "qudāt."]] It was known that they are "laghāh" (vain speakers) in their oaths, and no expiation is required of them in this world, nor any punishment in the next, because God, mentioned and exalted, has informed us that He does not call His servants to account for what they have uttered vainly in their oaths, and that what He calls them to account for is what their hearts intended as sin.

Since this is so, and since it was authentically reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something other than it as better, let him do what is better and expiate his oath," he made expiation obligatory upon the swearer when he does what he swore not to do, along with the obligation to do what is better than what he swore not to do. The payment in property, or the imposition of recompense from the one who is recompensed, in place of the ones who recompense [[In the printed edition: "abdan al-jarin" and in the manuscript "abdan al-jazin," but the correct reading is what I have established, for he means by this what God prescribed in His words in Surat al-Ma'ida [5:95]:
"O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram. And whoever of you kills it intentionally, its penalty is an equivalent from the livestock..."
Al-Tabari explained the recompense there (7:28), saying: "And upon him is an expiation as a substitute." So his words here, "al-mujza," refer to the slain game whose recompense is its equivalent from livestock; and his words "min al-mujza" mean "as a substitute for it." The "abdal" here are the expiations. The "jazi" is the one who expiates for killing game with its equivalent of livestock.]] is undoubtedly a punishment, like some of the punishments that God, mentioned and exalted, has made as deterrents for His creatures for what they transgress of His limits, even though what all of them have in common is that they are purification and expiations for those punished with them for what they were punished for. [[The context of this sentence: "And since this is so, and since it was authentically reported from the Messenger of God... and the payment was in property... it is clear that..."]] It is clear that whoever makes expiation obligatory in the immediate life for what he swore by among oaths and broke, even if it is an expiation for his sin, then God has called him to account for it by imposing expiation upon him, even if the punishment He hastened for him for that removes his punishment in the next life. And since God, mentioned and exalted, has called him to account for it, it is impermissible for anyone to say, after He has called him to account for it: "It is part of the vain for which its speaker is not called to account."

Since that is impermissible, the falsity is evident of the view reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: "The laghw is swearing to disobedience," because if that were so, there would be no expiation upon the one who swears to disobey God when he breaks his oath. And in Sa'id's making expiation obligatory upon him, there is clear evidence that its bearer is called to account for it, because of what we have described: that whoever is obligated to expiate for his oath is not among those who are not called to account for it.

So if the laghw is what we have described, which God, mentioned and exalted, has informed us He does not call us to account for, and every oath that obligates its swearer, by breaking it, to expiation in this world, or whose punishment God, mentioned and exalted, has threatened for its swearer in the next, even if He has removed his expiation in this world, then it is among what the hearts of the swearers have earned, and what the people who swear have intended as sin. Everything else is "laghw," and we have explained its aspects. [[The context of this sentence: "So if the laghw is what we have described... and every oath that obligates its swearer... then it is among what the hearts have earned... so the interpretation of the speech is..."]] So the interpretation of the speech is: Do not make God, O believers, a barrier to your oaths, and a proof for yourselves in your swearing, that you should not be righteous, nor God-fearing, nor make peace between people. For God does not call you to account for what your tongues have uttered vainly of your oaths, which they have spoken of ugly and blameworthy oaths, without your intending sin, and without your intention in the resolves of your hearts being to bind the oaths you have sworn. Rather, He calls you to account for what you intended in binding oaths and obligating them upon yourselves, and you resolved to carry out what you have sworn to by intention and will. ["Carrying out what you have sworn" means persisting in it and carrying it through. He has previously stated in his speech "al-tamām 'alayhā" (completion of it), p. 441, and "tamma 'ala qawlihi" in the report 4450. But here he used "al-itmām" from "atamma 'ala al-amr," which is not in the lexicographical books, but is permissible in Arabic and sound by its analogy.] Then, at that point, you will be obligated either to expiation in this world or to punishment in the next.
* *
The interpretation of God's words: "But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned" [2:225]
Abu Ja'far said: The scholars of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed about the meaning which God, mentioned and exalted, threatened His servants with, by His words: "But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned," that He calls them to account for it, ["His servants" is the object of "God threatened..."] after the ijma' (consensus) of all of them that the meaning of His words "what your hearts have earned" is what they intended deliberately.

Some of them said: The meaning which God threatened His servants with calling them to account for is when one of them swears an oath to a lie and falsehood. [[See the explanation of "al-kasb" (earning) earlier: 2:273-274, and then 3:100, 101, 128, 129.]]
Those who said this:
4466: Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Jarir told us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, who said: If a man swears an oath while he thinks he is truthful and he is lying, he is not called to account for it. And if he swears while he knows he is lying, that is what he is called to account for.
4467: Musa ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Masruqi narrated to me, saying: Husayn al-Ju'fi told us, from Za'ida, from Mansur, who said: Ibrahim said: "But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned": It is that one swears to something while he knows that he is lying, and that is what he is called to account for.
4468: Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Hakkam told us, from Amr, from Mansur, from Ibrahim: "But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned": that you swear while you are lying.
4469: Al-Muthanna told me, [saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih told us] Mu'awiya ibn Salih told me, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas: "But He will call you to account for the oaths you have bound" [5:89]. That is the "yamin al-sabr" (oath of restraint), the false oath, by which a man swears upon injustice or severing of kinship, and for that there is no expiation except that he abandons that injustice or returns that property to its people. This is His saying, mentioned and exalted: "Indeed, those who sell the covenant of God and their oaths for a small price..." up to His saying: "And for them is a painful punishment" [3:77]. [[Report 4469: The verse at the head of this report is the verse of al-Ma'ida, and I fear that the correct reading is what is in it from the verse of al-Baqara; but the printed and manuscript editions both agree on it. Nevertheless, I prefer what I have said, because Abu Ja'far narrated in the interpretation of the verse of al-Ma'ida (7:11, Bulaq edition) from "al-Muthanna said, Abd Allah ibn Salih told us..." to the end of its chain to Ibn Abbas, then mentioned the verse of al-Ma'ida and did not bring in it the text of this report. The printed and manuscript editions omitted what I placed between the brackets, which is a repeated chain in the tafsir, the closest of which is no. 4463.
As for his words "yamin al-sabr": the better form is "yamin al-sabr" with the definite article dropped, although "al-yamin al-sabr" is permissible and good. "Yamin al-sabr" is the oath that the judge holds you to until you swear; if a person swears without being made to swear by the judge, it is not a "yamin al-sabr."]]
4470: Muhammad ibn Amr told me, saying: Abu Asim told us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned": what they bound themselves to.
4471: Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa told us, saying: Shibl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.
4472: Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Jarir told us, from Abd al-Malik, from Ata, who said: You are not called to account until you direct yourself toward the matter, [[In the printed edition: "taqsid li-amr" (aim for a matter). Al-isada: turning toward something and directing oneself to it, and from it is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit about horses: "Competing with the reins, directed forward, upon whose shoulders are the thirsty spears," meaning advancing and turned toward you.]] then swear to it by God, the One besides whom there is no god, and your oath binds upon it.
* *
= Abu Ja'far said: The necessary implication of this interpretation is that God's words, mentioned and exalted, "But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned," refer to the Hereafter, where He punishes with whatever punishments He wills. And that the expiation is only obligatory upon the swearer in oaths that are vain. Likewise it was reported from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, that he did not consider expiation obligatory except in oaths that are vain; but as for what the hearts have earned and bound themselves to sin with, he did not consider expiation obligatory in it. We have already mentioned the reports from them to that effect earlier. [[See the earlier report no. 4404.]]

Since this is their interpretation of the verse, then it follows on their view that the meaning of the verse in Surat al-Ma'ida [5:89] is: "God will not call you to account for the vain in your oaths; its expiation is feeding ten needy persons from the average of what you feed your families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave. Whoever does not find [the means] shall fast three days. That is the expiation for your oaths when you swear. But He will call you to account for the oaths you have bound, so guard your oaths." [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "But He will call you to account for what you have bound, and guard" (wa-ihfazu). I have added the word that the copyist omitted from the verse. Al-Tabari means that God's words "But He will call you to account for the oaths you have bound" are a fronted element meant to be delayed, and therefore he cited the verse in its text except this clause, moving it to its place according to the meaning of their interpretation.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 225 (part 4 of 4):

In line with what we have mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas regarding this matter, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, and other groups besides them used to say, and we have already mentioned the reports from them on this earlier. [[These are the earlier narrations from: 4436.
Here ends an old division of the copy from which our manuscript was transcribed, and there came in it the following text.
"Followed by: And others said: the meaning which God promised His servants as a reckoning is...
And may God bless Muhammad the Prophet and his family abundantly.
* *
On the original from which it was copied:
I have read it in full by listening from its beginning, by my reading before the Judge Abu al-Hasan al-Khasibi, from Abu Muhammad al-Farghani, from Abu Ja'far al-Tabari - and my brother 'Ali, may God preserve him, and Muhammad ibn 'Ali alla... and Nasr ibn al-Husayn al-Tabari and Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn 'Isa al-Sa'di - in Sha'ban in the year 408 (AH)."]]
* *
[[Its beginning in the manuscript:
"In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
My Lord, make it easy."]] And others said: the meaning which God, exalted is He, promised His servants as a reckoning by this verse, [[In the printed edition: "the reckoning for it by this verse," and what is in the manuscript is better.]] is the oath of one who swears to something false which he knows to be false. In this, according to them, God made expiation obligatory, but not for the idle oath (laghw) which one swears while he is mistaken in his oath, thinking that what he swore to is as he swore, and it is not so.
Mention of who said that:
4473 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned," meaning: for what your hearts intended, and what you intended in it of sin, for this you bear the expiation.
4473 (repeated) - I was told by 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the same exactly.
* *
It seems that the proponents of this view directed the interpretation of God's reckoning His servant for what his heart has earned of false oaths to mean that it is a reckoning from Him by obligating him to expiation for it. Other groups besides those who said the saying similar to Qatadah's held that expiation is obligatory on one who swears a false oath, among them 'Ata' and al-Hakam.
4474 - Abu Kurayb and Ya'qub narrated to us, both saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj informed us, from 'Ata' and al-Hakam, that both used to say of one who swears falsely, intentionally: he must make expiation.
* *
Others said: rather, that has two meanings: one of them is a reckoning for the servant in the life of this world by God obligating him to expiation for it, and the other is a reckoning in the Hereafter unless He pardons.
Mention of who said that:
4475 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned": as for "what your hearts have earned," it is what your hearts have resolved upon. A man swears an oath knowing it is false, intending to settle his matter. The oaths are three: "laghw," "'amd" (deliberate), and "ghamus" (the perjurious oath). A man swears an oath while he intends to do something, then he sees something better than that; this is the oath which God, mentioned is He, said: "But He will call you to account for what you have resolved upon with oaths." This one has expiation.
* *
It seems that the proponent of this view directed the interpretation of His saying "But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned" to other than what he directed the interpretation of His saying "But He will call you to account for what you have resolved upon with oaths." He made "for what your hearts have earned" refer to the perjurious oaths which one swears knowing that he is in his oath an evildoer, and "for what you have resolved upon with oaths" refer to the oath in which one begins to break or fulfill, while at the time of swearing it he is resolved to fulfill it.
* *
Others said: rather, that is: holding belief in associating partners with God and disbelief.
Mention of who said that:
4476 - Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam narrated to me, saying: Isma'il ibn Marzuq narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Ayyub narrated to me, from Muhammad - meaning Ibn 'Ajlan -: that Zayd ibn Aslam used to say concerning God, mentioned is He, "But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned," like a man's saying: "He is a disbeliever, he is a polytheist." He said: God does not call him to account until that is from his heart. [[The report: 4476 is the earlier report no. 4461.]]
4477 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His saying: "God will not call you to account for the idle oaths in your oaths," he said: the idle oath in this is swearing by God with what is only on the tongue, so he made it idle, which is that he says: "He is a disbeliever in God, and then he associates partners with God, and he calls upon a god along with God." This is the idle oath which God, mentioned is He, said in Surat al-Baqarah: "But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned." He said: for what was in your hearts as truth, He calls you to account for it. If there was not truth in your heart, He does not call you to account for it, even if you sinned. [[The report: 4477 is the completion of the earlier report no. 4462.]]
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this matter is to say: God, mentioned is He, warned His servants that He would call them to account for what their hearts have earned of oaths. What their hearts earn of oaths is what they intended and resolved upon, with knowledge and awareness of what they intend and desire. This occurs in two ways:
One of them: by way of resolving upon that which, by the resolve of the one resolved, makes him sinful at the time of his resolve, and by his doing it he deserves reckoning from God for it. This is like one who swears about a thing he did not do that he did it, and about a thing he did that he did not do, intending a false statement [[In the manuscript "asl al-kadhib" is an error by a copyist who did not read the original well; in the printed edition: "al-qil al-kadhib," and the good correct reading is what I have established.]], and mentioning that he did what he swore he did not do, or that he did not do what he swore he did. Such a swearer - if he is among the people of faith in God and His Messenger - is subject to God's will on the Day of Resurrection: if He wills, He calls him to account in the Hereafter, and if He wills, He pardons him by His grace. There is no expiation for him in it in this world, because these are not oaths in which one breaks. Expiation is obligatory only in oaths by breaking them. The false swearer in his oath, his oath is not one in which breaking is initiated, so expiation is not required in it. [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "and expiation is obligatory" but the manuscript has placed a sign between the two words thus "~", which indicates the later word precedes the earlier.]]
The other way: by way of resolving upon establishing the binding of an oath at the time of his resolve to that. This is not something for which its owner is called to account until he breaks it after swearing. If he breaks it after swearing, he is called to account for what his heart had earned - of swearing by God upon sin and falsehood - in this world, through the expiation which God made as expiation for his sin.
* *
Commentary on God's saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God is Forgiving, Forbearing﴾ (225)
Abu Ja'far said: Thereby God, mentioned is He, means: "And God is Forgiving" to His servants regarding what they uttered idly of their oaths, which God, mentioned is He, informed that He does not call them to account for, and if He willed He would call them to account for them, and would not have called them to account for it, so they expiate it in the immediate life of this world by expiating it; and if He willed, He would call them to account in the later Hereafter by punishment for it, but He conceals it for them, and overlooks for them by His pardon of punishment in it, and other of their sins; "Forbearing" in His leaving hastening punishment upon the people of His disobedience for their sins.

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿For those who swear off their wives, a waiting period of four months﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His words, "For those who swear off" (yu'lūna), He, exalted is His remembrance, means: for those who swear an oath. The "oath" (al-alya) is the swearing, as related:

4478 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Maslama ibn 'Alqama narrated to us, saying: Dawud ibn Abi Hind narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, concerning His words "For those who swear off," that they swear.

* *

It is said: "Fulan swore off (ā-la yu'līy), īlā' and alya," as the poet said:

*"We have sufficed against him who hid himself in the dust, and we have broken the oath of those of us who swore."*
[I have not found this verse, nor identified its speaker. In the manuscript and the printed edition it reads "min turab," but the meaning requires what I have written.]

It is also said: "ulwa and ulwa," as the rajiz (poet of the rajaz meter) said:

*"O ulwa, what is ulwa, what is my ulwa?"*
[I have not found this rajaz. In the printed edition it reads "ma alwā," and the correct reading is from the manuscript.]

It has also been related from them that they say "ilwa" with a kasra on the alif.

* *

"Al-tarabbus" means: waiting and pausing.

* *

The meaning of the speech is: for those who swear off, that they abstain from their wives, a waiting period of four months. The phrase "that they abstain" is omitted, being sufficiently indicated by what appears in the speech.

* *

The people of interpretation differed concerning the nature of the oath by which a man becomes one who swears off (mūlin, a muli) from his wife.

Some of them said: The oath by which a man becomes a muli from his wife is that he swears, in a state of anger and by way of harm (ḍirār), that he will not have intercourse with her in her vagina. As for whoever swears not by way of harm and not in anger, he is not a muli concerning her.

Those who said this:

4479 – Hannad ibn al-Sari narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Simak, from Harith ibn 'Umayra, from Umm 'Atiyya, who said: Jubayr said: "Nurse my nephew along with your son!" She said: "I cannot nurse two!" So he swore that he would not approach her until she weaned him. When she had weaned him, he passed by a gathering, and the people said to him: "How well you have nourished him!" Jubayr said: "I had sworn that I would not approach her until she weaned him!" The people said to him: "This is īlā'!" So he came to 'Ali and asked for a ruling, and he said: "If you did this in anger, your wife is not lawful to you; otherwise, she is your wife."
[The reports 4479–4485: The report of Simak is mentioned by al-Bukhari in al-Kabir (4/1/12): "Atiyya ibn Jubayr al-'Anazi, related by Shu'ba from Simak. Sufyan said from Simak from Abu 'Atiyya ibn Jubayr. Abu al-Ahwas said from Harith ibn 'Umayra from Umm 'Atiyya: that Jubayr swore and came to 'Ali." In al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil (1/2/262): "Harith ibn 'Umayra narrated from Umm 'Atiyya; Simak ibn Harb narrated from him in Abu al-Ahwas's report from Simak from him. Ibrahim ibn Tahman narrated from Simak from Harith from 'Atiyya ibn Jubayr from his father, who said: I said to 'Ali, I heard my father say so." Ibn Abi Hatim also mentioned him (3/1381–1382): "'Atiyya ibn Jubayr al-'Anazi," and the narrators differed about him from Simak ibn Harb. Shu'ba said from Simak from 'Atiyya ibn Jubayr, who said: I said to 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him). Abu al-Ahwas narrated from Simak from Harith ibn 'Umayr from 'Atiyya from 'Ali. Hammad ibn Salama narrated from Simak from Umm 'Atiyya from 'Ali. Sufyan al-Thawri narrated from Simak from Abu 'Atiyya ibn Jubayr from 'Ali: "I heard my father say part of that, and part of it from me."
Al-Bayhaqi related it in al-Sunan (7: 381–382) by way of Dawud ibn Abi Hind from Simak from a man of Banu 'Ijl, from Abu 'Atiyya, that he married his brother's wife while she was nursing his nephew. He related it also by way of 'Ubayd Allah ibn Mu'adh, from his father, from Shu'ba, from Simak, from 'Atiyya ibn Jubayr, who said: My mother was nursing a boy…]

4480 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Simak, that he heard 'Atiyya ibn Jubayr say: The mother of a boy related to me died, and the wife of my father was nursing him. He swore that he would not approach her until she weaned him. When four months had passed, it was said to him: "She has become irrevocably separated from you!" (I think, Abu Ja'far was uncertain, he said this). So he came to 'Ali asking for a ruling, and he said: "If you said that in anger, you have no wife; otherwise, she is your wife."

4481 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Dawud narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, saying: Simak informed me, saying: I heard 'Atiyya ibn Jubayr mention something similar, from 'Ali.

4482 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn 'Abd al-Majid narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from Simak, from a man of Banu 'Ijl, from Abu 'Atiyya: that his brother died and left a young son, so Abu 'Atiyya said to his wife: "Nurse him!" She said: "I fear that you will cause harm to both of them through ghīl" [Aghālat al-mar'a waladaha and aghāla fulān waladahu mean: he had intercourse with his mother while she was nursing him. "Al-ghīl" is the name of that milk, which they used to say, when the child drank it, made him waste away and fall ill. The act is called "al-ghīla" (with a kasra on the ghayn). In the Sunan of al-Bayhaqi: "I fear that you will ghtāluhu," a derivation from it, which is not found in the lexicography books.], so he swore that he would not approach her until she weaned them both, and she did so until she had weaned them both. Then the nephew of Abu 'Atiyya went out to the gathering, and they said: "How well Abu 'Atiyya has nourished his nephew!" He said: "No! Umm 'Atiyya claimed that I would cause harm through ghīl, so I swore that I would not approach her until she weaned them." They said to him: "Your wife has become forbidden to you!" So I mentioned that to 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), and 'Ali said: "You only intended good, and īlā' is only in anger."
[In the printed edition it reads "ghudhi," but the manuscript is better. The phrase "la-husn ma ghadhā" is originally "husun" in the form of a verb (fa'ala), moved to the sense of praise: the sīn was lightened and quiescent, and its vowel transferred to the ḥā'. Suhm ibn Hanzala al-Ghanawi said: "The people did not prevent me from what I wanted, nor from giving them what they wanted, husn dhā adaban." It is thus like "ni'ma and bi'sa."]

4483 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from Simak, from Abu 'Atiyya: that his brother died – and he mentioned something similar.

4484 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: Dawud ibn Abi Hind informed us, from Simak ibn Harb: that a man's brother died, so he said to his wife: "Nurse my nephew!" She said: "I fear that he will have intercourse with me!" So he swore that he would not touch her until she weaned him. He abstained from her, until, when she had weaned him, he took the boy out to his people, and they said: "You have indeed nourished him well!" He told them his situation, and they mentioned his wife. He said: So he went to 'Ali and made him swear by Allah: "What did you intend by that?" – meaning īlā'. He said: So he returned her to him.

4485 – 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: [This is so in the manuscript and printed edition. I think the correct reading is "Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la al-San'ani," the teacher of al-Tabari; I have not found "'Ali ibn 'Abd al-A'la" among his teachers. See what follows at no. 4669.] al-Muharibi narrated to us, from Ash'ath ibn Sawwar, from Simak, from 'Atiyya ibn Abi 'Atiyya, who said: A brother of mine died and left an orphan, a suckling child, and I was a poor man who had nothing with which to hire a wet nurse for him. My wife said to me – and she had a son by me whom she was nursing: "If you spare me yourself, I will spare you both!" I said: "How can I spare you myself?" She said: "Do not approach me." I said: "By Allah, I will not approach you until you wean them both." He said: She weaned them both, and they went out to the people, and they said: "We see that you have only done well in caring for them!" He said: So I related the story to them, and they said: "We see that you have only sworn īlā' against her, and she is separated from you!" He said: So I came to 'Ali and related the story to him, and he said: "Īlā' is only what is intended as īlā'."

4486 – Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Bakr al-Barsani narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, from Jabir ibn Zayd, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: There is no īlā' except in anger.

4487 – Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: There is no īlā' except in anger.

4488 – Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, from Abu Fazara, from Yazid ibn al-Asamm, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: There is no īlā' except in anger.
[The report 4488: "'Abd al-Rahman" is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi. "Abu Wakī'" is al-Jarrah ibn Malih al-Ru'asi. Abu Dawud said: trustworthy. Al-Nasa'i said: there is no harm in him. Al-Daraqutni was asked about him and said: "He is nothing; he makes many errors." It was asked: "Is he to be taken into account?" He said: "No." In the manuscript and printed edition it reads "Ibn Wakī'," which is an error. See al-Muhalla of Ibn Hazm (10: 45). "Abu Fazara" is Rashid ibn Kaysan al-'Absi. Ibn Ma'in said: trustworthy. Ibn Hibban said: upright in narration when the narrators above and below him are trustworthy. He has one hadith in Muslim.]

4489 – Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from Simak ibn Harb, from Abu 'Atiyya, from 'Ali, who said: There is no īlā' except in anger.
[The report 4489 is an abridgement of no. 4482 by another chain. See the earlier comment on the report no. 4479.]

4490 – Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada, that 'Ali said: If a man says to his wife while she is nursing, "By Allah, I will not approach you until you wean my son," intending the welfare of his son, he said: There is no īlā' upon him.

4491 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Mansur al-Sulami narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Muslim al-Ta'ifi, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: A man came to 'Ali and said: "I said to my wife: I will not approach her for two years." He said: "You have sworn īlā' against her." He said: "I only said it because she is nursing!" He said: "Then no."

4492 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from Simak ibn Harb, from Abu 'Atiyya, from 'Ali, that he used to say: Īlā' is only what occurs in anger, when a man says: "By Allah, I will not approach you! By Allah, I will not touch you!" As for what occurs in the reform of the matter of nursing or other things, it is not īlā', and she does not become separated from him by it.
[The report 4492 is another chain for the hadith of Abu 'Atiyya mentioned earlier at no. 4482. See the comment on the report no. 4479.]

4493 – Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman – meaning Ibn Mahdi – narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, from Hafs, from al-Hasan: that he was asked about it, and he said: "No, by Allah, it is not īlā'."

4494 – Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn Mansur narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata', who said: If a man swears because of nursing, it is not īlā'.

4495 – Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: al-Layth told me, saying: Yunus told me, saying: I asked Ibn Shihab about a man who says: "By Allah, I will not approach my wife until she weans my child!" He said: "I do not know īlā' to occur except by swearing by Allah, in what a man intends to harm his wife by, by abstaining from her. And we do not know the obligation of īlā' except upon those. So do you not see that this one who swore to abstain from his wife until she weans his child swore only for a matter in which he seeks good? So we do not see that what is incumbent upon this one is what is incumbent upon the muli who swears in anger."

* *

Others said: It is the same: if a man swears concerning his wife that he will not have intercourse with her in her vagina, whether his oath was in anger or not in anger, all of it is īlā'.

Those who said this:

4496 – Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mughira, from Ibrahim – concerning a man who said to his wife: "If I have intercourse with you until you wean your child, you are divorced," and he left her for four months. He said: It is īlā'.

4497 – Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la informed us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Abu Ma'shar, from al-Nakha'i, who said: Anything that comes between him and having intercourse with her, and he leaves her until four months pass, then it falls upon him.

4498 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Hibban ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Awana informed us, from al-Mughira, from al-Qa'qa', who said: I asked al-Hasan about a man whose wife was nursing a boy, and he swore that he would not have intercourse with her until she weaned her child. He said: "I do not see this as anger, and īlā' is only in anger." He said: Ibn Sirin said: "I do not know what this is that they narrate! God only said: 'For those who swear off their wives' until '…indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.' When four months have passed, let him propose to her if he desires her."
[The report 4498 is by Hibban ibn Musa ibn Sawwar al-Sulami, Abu Muhammad al-Marwazi. He narrated from Ibn al-Mubarak, Abu Hamza al-Sukkari and others; from him al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat; he died in the year 233. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib. In the manuscript and printed edition it reads "Hassan ibn Musa," which has been corrected in no. 2914 and will be correct in no. 4528. "Abu 'Awana" is al-Wadda' ibn 'Abd Allah al-Yashkuri, trustworthy. Ibn al-Mubarak was asked: "Who is the most narrating (or the most sound) of people from al-Mughira?" He said: "Abu 'Awana." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib.]

4499 – Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim – concerning a man who swore that he would not speak to his wife – he said: "They used to regard īlā' as occurring in intercourse."

4500 – Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, who said: Every oath that prevents intercourse until four months pass, it is īlā'.

4501 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: I heard Isma'il and Ash'ath, from al-Sha'bi, the like of it.

4502 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mughira, from Ibrahim and al-Sha'bi, who both said: Every oath that prevents intercourse is īlā'.

* *

Others said: Every oath that a man swears in order to distress his wife is īlā' on his part concerning her, whether it is over intercourse or other things, whether he swears in contentment or in displeasure.

Those who said this:

4503 – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Khusayf, from al-Sha'bi, who said: Every oath that comes between a man and his wife is īlā', if he says: "By Allah, I will make you angry! By Allah, I will distress you! By Allah, I will strike you!" and things like this.

4504 – Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam narrated to me, saying: My father and Shu'ayb narrated to me, from al-Layth, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b al-'Amiri: that a man of his family said to his wife: "If I speak to you for a year, you are divorced." He consulted al-Qasim and Salim, and they said: "If he speaks to her before a year, she is divorced; and if he does not speak to her, she is divorced when four months pass."

4505 – Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, saying: I heard Hammad say: I asked Ibrahim: "Is īlā': that he swears not to have intercourse with her, nor speak to her, nor join his head to hers, or that he will make her angry, or that he will deprive her, or that he will distress her?" He said: "Yes."

4506 – Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, saying: I asked al-Hakam about a man who said to his wife: "By Allah, I will make you angry!" and he left her for four months. He said: "It is īlā'."

4507 – Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Wahb ibn Jarir narrated to us, saying: I heard Shu'ba say: I asked al-Hakam, and he mentioned the like of it.

4508 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: al-Layth told me, saying: Yunus narrated to us, saying: Ibn Shihab said: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab told me [in the printed edition: "Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab told me that he said: if he swears…"; the correct reading from the manuscript omits "qāla"]: that if a man swears that he will not speak to his wife for a day or a month, he said: "We see that this is īlā'." And he said: "Unless he swore that he would not speak to her, but he would touch her; then we do not see that this is īlā'." And al-fay' (return) is that he returns to his wife and speaks to her or touches her. Whoever does that before the four months pass has returned. And whoever returns after four months while she is in her 'idda, he has returned and retains his wife, except that one divorce has passed for her.
[In the printed edition: "al-arba'a al-ashhur," but the manuscript has a correct and acceptable Arabic form.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The reasoning of those who said, "The ila' (oath of abstention from intercourse) applies only in anger and harm," is that God, may His remembrance be exalted, made the fixed term set for ila' a way out for the woman from the husband's 'adl (the husband's harming his wife by withholding good treatment, so that he neither treats her as a husband should nor lets her manage her own affairs) and his injury to her, in what is due to her from him of good companionship and fair treatment. If the man is not withholding her or harming her by his oath and his vow to abstain from intercourse with her, but is rather seeking her contentment and meeting her need through it, then by that oath he is not a mu'li (one who takes an oath of abstention), because there is no meaning there of harm and bad treatment reaching the woman from her husband, so that the term set for the mu'li would be a way out for her from it. [[In the printed edition: "yalhaq al-mar'a" (the printed text reads "yalhiq al-mar'a"), and the correct reading from the manuscript is as given here.]] [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "alladhi ja'ala al-mawla" (the term that was set for the mawla), but the context requires what is established here. The pronoun in "minhu" refers to "la ma'na hunalika".]]

* *

As for the reasoning of those who said, "The ila' in a state of anger and in a state of contentment is the same," it is the generality of the verse: God, may His remembrance be exalted, did not single out some of His words, "for those who take an oath of abstention from their wives is a waiting period of four months," from others, but made it general to every mu'li and every one who swears. So everyone who swears about his wife that he will not approach her for a period longer than the term God has set for her waiting period is, according to some, a mu'li from his wife. According to others, he is a mu'li even if the period of his oath is the term God has set for his waiting period.

* *

As for the reasoning of those who held the view of al-Sha'bi, al-Qasim and Salim: God, may His remembrance be exalted, made the term He fixed for the mu'li a way out for the woman from her husband's bad treatment and his injury to her. Swearing that he will not have intercourse with her or approach her is no more deserving of being among the meanings of bad treatment and harm than swearing that he will not speak to her, or that he will hurt or anger her, because all of that is harm to her and bad treatment of her.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the interpretations we have mentioned is the view of the one who said: Every oath that prevents the one who swears from intercourse for longer than the period God has set as the waiting period for the mu'li, whether said in anger or in contentment. That is for the reason we mentioned earlier to the proponents of that view.

We have already set out the corruption of the view of those who oppose it in our book Kitab al-Latif (the title of an earlier work by al-Tabari) sufficiently, so we dislike repeating it in this place.

* *

On the interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿And if they return, then indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, God, may His remembrance be exalted, means: If they return to abandoning what they swore they would do to them, namely abstaining from intercourse with them, so they have intercourse with them and break their oaths, then ﴿indeed God is Forgiving﴾ for the lie they told in their oaths that they would not come to them and then came to them, and for what passed from them to them, by swearing to what it was not theirs to swear to, and then swearing to it, ﴿Merciful﴾ toward them and toward other of His believing servants. [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "wa bima salafa minhum" (and for what passed from them), but the context requires what is established here.]]

* *

The root of "fay'" (return) is returning from one state to another. From it is His, may His remembrance be exalted, words: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them﴾ up to His words ﴿until it returns to the command of God﴾ [Surat al-Hujurat: 9], meaning: until it returns to the command of God. From it is also the poet's saying: [[He is Suhaym, slave of the Banu al-Hasahas.]]

*So she returned without fulfilling the purpose for which she had come, and of a person's needs there is that which is not fulfilled.*

[[His Diwan: 19; Hamasat Ibn al-Shajari: 160, and elsewhere from his splendid, wondrous qasida, one line of which has passed earlier (1:106, 447). The pronoun in "fa'at" refers to his beloved whom he mentioned and what was between him and her. The version of al-Tabari and Ibn al-Shajari is more pleasing to me than the version of the Diwan: "wa lam taqdi alladhi huwa ahluhu" (and she did not fulfill that which was her concern). He says: she returned to her people having lost what she had intended to do; his love and his passion made her forget what she had resolved and intended. So he consoles her by saying that a person may seek to accomplish something while God wills other than it, and then he does not achieve it.]]

It is said from it: "Fa'a fulan yufi'u fay'atan," like "al-jai'a" and "fay'," and "al-fay'a" is the single occurrence. [[He means that it is the form for a single occurrence, though it is used in the place of the verbal noun, like "al-rajfa" and "al-rahma". The noun derived from it is "al-fay'a" and "al-jia'a" (with the fa' and jim vowelled with kasra).]] As for shade, it is said: "faa'a al-zillu yafi'u fayu'an wa fay'an." It may also be said "fayu'an" in the first sense as well, [[Most lexicons make "fayu'" a verbal noun in the first meaning and do not make it a verbal noun in the meaning of shade. What al-Tabari said is good and sound.]] because "fay'" in all things means return.

* *

Those who interpreted the Qur'an said the same as what we have said on this, except that they differed concerning what makes the mu'li one who has returned (fa'in).

Some of them said: He is not a fa'in except by intercourse.

Those who said that:

4509 — Ali ibn Sahl al-Ramli narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Layla, from al-Hakam, from Miqsam, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The fay' is intercourse."

4510 — Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Ziyad ibn Abi al-Ja'd, from al-Hakam, from Miqsam, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The fay' is intercourse." [[The report 4510: Yazid ibn Ziyad ibn Abi al-Ja'd al-Ashja'i al-Ghatafani, a client of theirs. He narrated from al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba, 'Asim al-Jahdari, his paternal uncle 'Ubayd ibn Abi al-Ja'd, and his brother Salama ibn Ziyad, and others. From him narrated Waki', Ibn Numayr, Abu Nu'aym and others. Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy (al-Thiqat). In the printed edition it was "Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad 'an Abi al-Ja'd," and the correct reading is from the manuscript.]]

4511 — Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from al-Hakam, from Miqsam, from Ibn 'Abbas, the like of it.

4512 — Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from a companion of his, from al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba, from Miqsam, from Ibn 'Abbas, the like of it.

4513 — Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Husayn, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq, who said: "The fay' is intercourse."

4514 — Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi 'Adi narrated to us, from Shu'ba, from Husayn, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq, the like of it.

4515 — 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Bayan narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yazid informed us, from Isma'il, who said: "'Amir did not consider the fay' to be anything but intercourse."

4516 — Tamim ibn al-Muntasir narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Harun informed us, saying: Isma'il informed us, from 'Amir, the like of it.

4517 — Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from 'Ali ibn Badhayma, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "The fay' is intercourse."

4518 — Abu 'Abd Allah al-Nash'i narrated to us, saying: Ishaq al-Azraq narrated to us, from Sufyan, from 'Ali ibn Badhayma, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the like of it. [[The report 4518: "Abu 'Abd Allah al-Nash'i" is Muhammad ibn Harb ibn Harman al-Nash'i, also called al-Nashastaji, Abu 'Abd Allah al-Wasiti. He narrated from Isma'il ibn 'Ulayya, Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Wasiti, Ishaq ibn Yusuf al-Azraq and others. He died in the year 255. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib.]]

4519 — al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "The fay' is intercourse; he has no excuse unless he has intercourse, even if he is in prison or on a journey" — Sa'id being the speaker.

4520 — Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to me, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he said: "He has no excuse until he has intercourse."

4521 — al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Hammad and Iyas, from al-Sha'bi — one of them said: from Masruq — and he said: "The fay' is intercourse"; and the other said, from al-Sha'bi: "The fay' is intercourse."

4522 — Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, concerning a man who took an oath of abstention from his wife and then was prevented by illness, who said: "He has no excuse until he has intercourse."

4523 — Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to me, from Qatada, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, concerning a man who takes an oath of abstention from his wife before he consummates the marriage or after he has consummated it, and then an obstacle befalls him that restrains him, or he does not find what would bring him to her: that when four months have passed, she is more entitled to herself.

4524 — Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from al-Hakam and al-Sha'bi, who said: "If a man takes an oath of abstention from his wife and then wishes to return, there is no return except by intercourse."

* *

Others said: "The fay'" is returning by the tongue or the heart in a state of excuse, and outside a state of excuse, it is intercourse.

Those who said that:

4525 — Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, from al-Hasan and 'Ikrima, that they both said: "If he has an excuse and calls witnesses, that is his" — meaning concerning a man who took an oath of abstention from his wife, and then was prevented by illness or a road, and called witnesses to his returning to his wife.

4526 — Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la informed us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from a companion of his, from al-Hakam, who said: "Al-Nakha'i and I discussed that, and al-Nakha'i said: 'If he has an excuse and calls witnesses, then he has returned.' And I said: 'He has no excuse until he has intercourse.' So we went to Abu Wa'il, and he said: 'I hope that if he has an excuse and calls witnesses, it is permitted.'" [[The report 4526: "Abu Wa'il" is Shaqiq ibn Salama al-Asadi al-Kufi. He reached the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) but did not see him. He narrated from Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Mu'adh and others among the Companions and the Successors. Al-A'mash said: Abu Wa'il said to me: "O Sulayman, if you had seen me when we were fleeing from Khalid ibn al-Walid, and I fell from the camel and my neck nearly broke! If I had died that day, it would have been the Fire!" He said: I was eleven years old that day. He died after al-Jamajim in the year 83. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib.]]

4527 — al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, from al-Hasan, who said: "If he takes an oath of abstention, then becomes ill or is imprisoned or travels, and then returns, he has an excuse not to have intercourse." He said: "I heard al-Zuhri say the same."

4528 — al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Habban ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, saying: Abu 'Awana informed us, from Mughira, from Ibrahim — concerning a woman in postnatal bleeding whose husband takes an oath of abstention from her — who said: "This is about a man of the Muharib tribe, about whom the companions of 'Abd Allah were asked, and they said: 'If he is unable, he should expiate his oath and call witnesses to the return.'" [[The report 4528: See "Habban ibn Musa" in the earlier report no. 4498. His saying "this is about the Muharib" means the tribe of Muharib, among whom was Abu al-Sha'tha' al-Muharibi, "Sulaym ibn Aswad ibn Handhala al-Muharibi," who will appear in the following reports, especially report no. 4535, where the one who took the oath of ila' is mentioned.]]

4529 — Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from Abu al-Sha'tha', who said: "A guest came to him, and he took an oath of abstention from his wife, and she gave birth and bled. He wished to return, but he could not approach her because of her postnatal bleeding. So he went to 'Alqama and told him about that. He said: 'Have you not returned in your heart and become content?' He said: 'Yes!' He said: 'Then you have returned! She is your wife!'" [[Nufisat al-mar'a (passive voice) and nafisat (with fatha then kasra) nafsan (with two fathas) and nifasan: she gave birth. Its root is "al-nafs" (with fatha then sukun), which is blood; it was so named because of the blood that accompanies the child and follows it.]]

4530 — al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim: that a man took an oath of abstention from his wife, and she gave birth before four months had passed. He wished to return but could not because of the blood, until four months had passed. So he asked 'Alqama ibn Qays about it, and he said: "Have you not returned to her in your soul?" He said: "Yes!" He said: "Then she is your wife."

4531 — 'Imran ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Warith narrated to us, saying: 'Amir informed us, from al-Hasan, who said: "If a man takes an oath of abstention from his wife and then is unable to approach her because of an excuse, he should call witnesses that he has returned, and she is his wife."

4532 — 'Imran narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Warith narrated to us, saying: 'Amir narrated to us, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, from 'Alqama, the like of it.

4538 — Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mughira, from Hammad, who said: "If a man takes an oath of abstention from his wife and then returns, let him call witnesses to his return. If he calls witnesses while not knowing that this does not suffice in place of having intercourse with her, and four months pass before he has intercourse with her, then she is his wife. But if he knows that there is no return except by intercourse in this matter, and he returns and calls witnesses to his return, but does not have intercourse with her until four months have passed, then she has separated from him."

4539 — al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: al-Layth narrated to me, saying: Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Shihab said: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab narrated to me: that if a man takes an oath of abstention from his wife, he said: "If he is ill and cannot touch her, or he is traveling and detained, then when he returns and expiates his oath, and calls witnesses to his return before four months pass, we see nothing but that it is right for him to keep his wife, and nothing of her divorce is lost." He said: And Ibn Shihab said, concerning a man who takes an oath of abstention from his wife, and there remains for her from him only one divorce, and he wishes to return at the end of that period while he is ill or traveling, or she is ill or menstruating, or absent so that he cannot reach her, until four months have passed: is there any allowance in any of that, that he may expiate his oath though he cannot have intercourse with his wife? * *

Others said: "The fay'" is returning by the tongue in every state.

Those who said that:

4541 — Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: al-Dahhak ibn Makhlad narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur and Hammad, from Ibrahim, who said: "The fay' is that he returns with his tongue."

Ahmad said: "Trustworthy, trustworthy." Abu Hatim said: "He is one of the earliest companions of al-Hasan." Al-Daraqutni said: "He has few narrations." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 226 (part 3 of 3):

4544 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Ayyub, from Abu Qilabah, who said: "If he returns (fa'a) in his heart, it suffices him; he says: 'He has returned.'"

4545 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, saying: Shuʿbah narrated to us, from Ismaʿil ibn Rajaʾ, who said: They mentioned the oath of abstention (iyla') in the presence of Ibrahim, and he said: "What do you think if his member does not become erect? When he calls witnesses (to his return), then she is his wife."

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The scholars differed in their interpretation of "al-fayʾ" (the return) in proportion to their differing on the meaning of the oath that constitutes "iyla'" (abstention by oath).

Whoever holds that a man does not become one who has sworn abstention (muwlin) from his wife in the sense mentioned by God in His Book unless he swears not to have intercourse with her, takes the return to be a return to doing what he swore not to do, namely intercourse, in the vagina, when he is able and it is possible for him; and when he is not able and it is not possible, then (the return is) the forming of the intention to do it when he is able and it is possible, and the declaring of what he intends with his tongue so that the Muslims may know it, according to the view of the one who says so.

* *

As for the view of the one who holds that the return is intercourse and nothing else, he does not regard an impediment as an excuse for him, and does not regard any way out of his oath for him other than returning to what he swore to abandon, which is intercourse.

* *

As for the one who holds that he may be one who has sworn abstention from her by swearing to abandon speaking to her, or that he will harm or anger her, or other similar oaths, then the return, in his view, is a return to abandoning what he swore to do, which harms her, by resolving to give it up, and declaring that with his tongue, in every situation in which he resolves to return.

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The most correct of these statements in our view is the statement of the one who said: "The return is intercourse," because a man is not, in our view, one who has sworn abstention from his wife except by swearing to abandon intercourse with her for the period we mentioned, for the reasons we described earlier. Since that is the abstention, the return that nullifies its ruling must necessarily be only that which is contrary to what the one who swore abstention swore to abandon. For when He made its ruling, if he does not return to what he swore to abandon, the ruling that God made clear for them in His Book, the return to that is known to be doing what he swore to abandon, if he is able to, and that is intercourse. However, if he is prevented from the return, which is intercourse, by an excuse, it is not permissible that he be one who has truly abandoned intercourse with her, because a person is only one who abandons something when he has a way to both doing it and abandoning it. As for one who has no way to do a thing, he is not one who abandons it.

Since that is so, forming the resolve in his heart to have intercourse with her suffices him in the state of excuse, until he finds a way to have intercourse with her. If he declares that with his tongue and calls witnesses against himself in that state to repentance and return, it is more pleasing to me.

* *

The commentary on God's words: ﴿So indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ (2:226)

The scholars of interpretation differed regarding its meaning.

Some of them said: the meaning of that is: "Indeed God is Forgiving" to you for what you committed by returning to them, from breaking the oath you swore by God not to approach them, "Merciful" to you in lightening for you the expiation (kaffarah) of your oaths which you swore upon them and then broke.

Those who said that:

4546 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan: "So if they return, then indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful," he said: "There is no expiation upon him."

4547 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, who said: If he returns, there is no expiation upon him.

4548 - Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Hibban ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, saying: Abu ʿAwanah narrated to us, from Mughirah, from Ibrahim, who said: They used to hold, regarding the saying of God: "So if they return, then indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful," that its expiation is his return. [Report 4548: "Hibban ibn Musa" occurred in this chain before as number 4528, and see also number 4498 and its commentary. In the printed edition and the manuscript here it was "Hammad ibn Musa," which is an error and distortion. See what follows at number 4549.]

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: This interpretation that we have mentioned is the one necessary according to the view of the one who claims that every one who breaks an oath is sinful in remaining upon it (ḥaraj: sinful), so there is no expiation upon him for breaking it, and its expiation is the breaking of it. [Ḥaraj: sinful. We have already mentioned the statement of the lexicographers on this word in volume 2, p. 423, note 1, and then in this volume 4, p. 224, note 1.]

* *

As for the view of the one who made it obligatory upon the one who breaks any oath he swears by, [expiation], whether the breaking was pious or not, then its interpretation is: "Indeed God is Forgiving" to those who abstain from their wives regarding what they broke of their abstention, so if they return and expiate their oaths, by what God obligated upon those who break their oaths of expiation, "Merciful" to them, by His dropping punishment from them in this world and the next for that, by covering it for them through what He imposed on them of recompense and expiation, and by what He granted them of the respite of four months, so He did not give the wife from whom her husband abstained in that period what He gave her after the four months. As follows:

4549 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Hibban narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, saying: Yahya ibn Bishr narrated to us, that he heard ʿIkrimah say: "For those who abstain from their wives is a waiting of four months. So if they return, then indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful. And if they resolve on divorce..." He said: "And that is God's mercy! He gave him authority over her during the four months, except with an excuse, because God said: ﴿And those from whom you fear disobedience, admonish them and forsake them in the beds﴾ [Surah al-Nisa': 34]."

[Report 4549: See the comment on the earlier report 4548. Yahya ibn Bishr al-Khurasani Abu Wahb narrated from ʿIkrimah, and Ibn al-Mubarak narrated from him. Ibn al-Mubarak said: "If Yahya ibn Bishr narrates to you from someone, do not mind if you did not hear it from him." He is biographed in al-Kabir 4/2/263 and al-Jarh wa'l-Ta'dil 4/12/13. He occurred earlier in al-Tabari's chain as numbers 3619, 3652 and will come at number 4749.]

* *

Mention of some who said: if the one who returned from abstention, then upon him is expiation.

4550 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: "For those who abstain from their wives is a waiting of four months," which is the man who swears to his wife by God that he will not marry her, then waits four months. If he does marry her, he expiates his oath by feeding ten needy persons, or clothing them, or freeing a slave; and whoever cannot find (the means), then fasting three days.

4551 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: al-Layth narrated to me, saying: Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Shihab narrated to me, from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, with something similar.

4552 - Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Hibban ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, saying: Hammad ibn Salamah informed us, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, who said: If he abstained and then had intercourse with her before the four months, he expiates his oath.

4553 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Hibban narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, saying: Abu ʿAwanah informed us, from Mughirah, from Ibrahim, regarding the woman in postnatal bleeding from whom her husband abstained, he said: "This concerns one who is at war (muharib). The companions of ʿAbd Allah were asked about it, and they said: If he is unable, he expiates his oath and calls witnesses to the return." [Report 4553: See the earlier report 4528, and the reports that follow it and the commentary on them.]

4554 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: If he returns to her, he expiates his oath, and she is his wife.

4555 - It was narrated to me from ʿAmmar, from Ibn Abi Jaʿfar, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ, the like of it.

4556 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: ʿUthham narrated to us, from al-Aʿmash, from Ibrahim regarding abstention, he said: He is made to stop before the four months pass; if he takes her back, then she is his wife, and upon him is an oath, which he expiates when he breaks it.

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: This second interpretation is the correct one in our view, for the reasons we have already set out in our book "Kitab al-Ayman" (The Book of Oaths), that breaking an oath necessitates expiation for every oath whose breaking begins after swearing, whether the oath concerned disobedience or obedience.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 2, Verse 227 (Part 1 of 3)**

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if they resolve on divorce, then indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ (2:227)**

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the meaning of the words of Allah, may His remembrance be exalted: "And if they resolve on divorce."

Some of them said: The meaning of that is: For those who swear off (yu'lun, sing. al-mawla, one who takes an oath of abstention from his wives, known as ila') that they will abstain from their wives, there is a waiting period of four months. If they return (fa'a), that is, if they return to what Allah has made obligatory for them in terms of good companionship (al-'ishra bil-ma'ruf) during the four months that Allah has appointed for them as a period of waiting away from them and from intercourse with them, and their companionship with them during that time is in accordance with what is obligatory, then "indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful" to them. But if they do not return to them (wa-in tarakū al-fay' ilayhinna) during the four months in which Allah has appointed the waiting period for them, until they expire, then their wives whom they swore off are divorced by the passing of those (four months).¹ The passing of them, according to those who say this, is the indication of the husband's resolve to divorce the wife whom he swore off.

¹ *The pronoun in His words "bi-muddiyihinna" refers to the four months.*

* *

Then those who held this interpretation differed among themselves about the divorce that falls upon her with the passing of the four months.

Some of them said: It is an irrevocable single divorce (taṭlīqa bā'in).

Those who said this have reported:

4557 – Abu Hisham narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Bishr narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatada, from Khilas or al-Hasan, from Ali, who said: "When four months have passed, it is an irrevocable divorce."

*Report 4557:* Abu Hisham is Muhammad ibn Yazid ibn Muhammad ibn Kathir al-'Ajli, Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i, judge of Baghdad; they speak about him. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib. Muhammad ibn Bishr ibn al-Farafisa ibn al-Mukhtar al-'Abdi narrated from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Umar al-'Umari, and Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arūba. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib. "Khilas," with a kasra on the kha and a light lam, is Khilas ibn 'Amr al-Hajari al-Basri. He narrated from Ali, 'Ammar ibn Yasir, 'A'isha, Abu Hurayra, Ibn 'Abbas and others. Qatada and 'Awf al-A'rabi and Dawud ibn Abi Hind narrated from him. He is trustworthy (thiqa). He is biographed in al-Tahdhib.

Qatada said: "The saying of Ali and 'Abd Allah is more pleasing to me regarding ila'."

*Report 4558:* The statements of the Companions and the Successors regarding ila' can be found in full in Nasb al-Raya (3:241–243), al-Muhalla by Ibn Hazm (10:42–49), Sunan al-Bayhaqi (7:376–382), Fath al-Bari (9:375–379), Ibn Kathir, and al-Durr al-Manthur in the tafsir of this verse. No one has fully mentioned these reports as Abu Ja'far, may Allah have mercy on him, did.

4560 – Ibn Abi al-Shawarib narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Ma'mar narrated to us, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from Abu Salama: that 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and Zayd ibn Thabit used to say: "When the four months have passed, it is one irrevocable divorce."

He died in the year 150. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib. "'Abd al-A'la ibn Maymun" heard from his father, 'Ikrima and 'Ata', and Ja'far ibn Burqan heard from him. He is biographed in al-Jarh wal-Ta'dil 3/1/27.

⁶ *Iltanafa al-amr ita'nafan and istanafahu means he took its beginning, started it, or began it anew. It derives from "al-anf" (with a fatha and then a sukun), and the anf of everything is its beginning.*
