Hizqil called out to them and said: [[In the manuscript: "fa-nadahu" (he called to him), with a letter ṭa' written above the hā'; in al-Durr al-Manthur (1:311): "fa-nada Hizqil" (Hizqil called out); in the printed edition: "fa-nadahum," which I have adopted as in Tarikh al-Tabari (1:237).]] "O bones, Allah commands you to come together!" So the bones of each person came together. [[After this, in al-Durr al-Manthur (1:311): [Then he said: "O bones, Allah commands you to let sinew and tendon grow," and they bound together and were strengthened with sinew and tendon.] In Tarikh al-Tabari: "O decayed bones."]] Then Hizqil called out a second time and said: "O bones, Allah commands you to clothe yourselves in flesh," and they were clothed in flesh, and after flesh, skin, and they became bodies. Then Hizqil called out a third time and said: "O spirits, Allah commands you to return to your bodies!" [[In the printed edition: "ila ajsadik" (to your bodies); I have adopted the reading of the manuscript, Tarikh al-Tabari, and al-Durr al-Manthur.]] They rose by Allah's permission and cried "Allahu Akbar" in one single cry. [[Report 5598: Muhammad ibn Sahl ibn Askar al-Tamimi, Abu Bakr al-Najjari, the memorizer and traveler, was described by al-Nasa'i and Ibn Adi as "trustworthy," settled in Baghdad and died there in 251 AH; his biography is in al-Tahdhib. Isma'il ibn Abd al-Karim ibn Ma'qil ibn Munabbih al-San'ani narrated from his paternal cousin Ibrahim ibn Aqil and his paternal uncle Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil. Ahmad ibn Hanbal narrated from him. al-Nasa'i said: "There is nothing wrong with him," and Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy. He died in Yemen in 210 AH; his biography is in al-Tahdhib. The report was narrated by al-Tabari with this chain in al-Tarikh (1:237) and in al-Durr al-Manthur (1:311).]]

5599 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying: "Have you not seen those who left their homes, and they were thousands?" He said: a great number who left fleeing from jihad in the way of Allah. Allah caused them to die, then brought them back to life and commanded them to fight their enemy. That is His saying: "And fight in the way of Allah, and know that Allah is Hearing, Knowing."

5600 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from Anbasa, from Ash'ath ibn Aslam al-Basri, who said: While Umar was praying, with two Jews behind him—and when Umar wanted to bow he would spread his arms away from his sides [[Kharā al-rajul fi sujudihi: he spread apart, separating his upper arms from his sides. In a hadith: that the Prophet ﷺ, when he prostrated, would spread his arms.]]—one of them said to his companion: "Is he the one?" When Umar turned from his prayer, he said: "What do you think of one of you saying to the other: 'Is he the one?'" [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "ra'ayta" without the interrogative hamza; the correct form is from al-Tabari and al-Durr al-Manthur. The Arab usage "ara'ayta kadha" means asking for information, i.e., "tell me about such-and-such."]] They said: "We find him in our book: [[In the printed edition and Tarikh al-Tabari: "inna najid fi kitabina"; in the manuscript and al-Durr: "najiduhu," which I have adopted. In Tarikh al-Tabari, after "ya'tي ma a'ta Hizqil" (gives what Hizqil was given). "Al-qarn" (with fatha and sukun): a fortress; also a solitary hill; qarn al-jabal: its summit.]] 'A horn of iron, who will be given what Hizqil was given, who 'revived the dead by Allah's permission.'" Umar said: "We do not find in the Book of Allah 'Hizqil' or 'revived the dead by Allah's permission' except for Jesus." They said: "Do you not find in the Book of Allah: 'And messengers We have not related to you'"—[[In the printed edition: "rusulan lam yaqsusuhum" without the waw and with a yā' in "yaqsusuhum"; in the manuscript the same, except the yā' is unpointed. I have adopted the text of the verse as it appears in Tarikh al-Tabari.]] [Surah al-Nisa': 164]—Umar said: "Yes!" They said: "As for the bringing to life of the dead, we will inform you: the Children of Israel were struck by a plague, and some of them left until, when they were at the edge of a mile, Allah caused them to die. They built a wall around them, until, when their bones had decayed, Allah sent Hizqil, and he stood over them and said: 'What Allah wills,'" [[In the printed edition: "faqama 'alayhim ma sha'a Allah," and the correct reading is from the references and the manuscript.]] so Allah raised them for him. Then Allah revealed concerning this: "Have you not seen those who left their homes, and they were thousands?" to the end of the verse. [[Report 5600: al-Tabari narrated it in his Tarikh (1:238), and al-Suyuti recorded it in al-Durr al-Manthur (1:311). In the printed edition, the manuscript and al-Durr: "Ash'ath ibn Aslam al-Basri"; in al-Tarikh: "Ash'ath 'an Salim al-Nasri," and "Ash'ath ibn Aslam al-'Ijli al-Basri thumma al-Rab'i," who narrated from his father that he saw Abu Musa al-Ash'ari; Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah narrated from him. His biography is in Ibn Abi Hatim (1/1/269). As for "Salim al-Nasri," he is Salim ibn Abd Allah al-Nasri, known as "Salim Sablan," whose biography is in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim (2/1/184); he narrated from Uthman, Aisha, Abu Sa'id, and Abu Hurayra; Sa'id al-Maqburi, Bukayr ibn Abd Allah and others narrated from him. I think what is in al-Tarikh is closer to the correct version.]]

5601 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from Anbasa, from al-Hajjaj ibn Artat, who said: They were four thousand.

5602 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi regarding: "Have you not seen those who left their homes, and they were thousands," to His saying: "then He brought them to life." He said: There was a village called Dawardan, before Wasit, [[In the manuscript: "Dar Wardan," with an extra rā'; the correct form is in Tarikh al-Tabari, al-Durr al-Manthur, and Mu'jam al-Buldan. It is in the eastern part of Wasit, a farsakh away from it.]] in which the plague struck. Most of its people fled and settled in a district of it, so those who remained in the village perished, while the others were spared. Not many of them died. [[In al-Tarikh: "fa-lam yamut minhum kathir" (not many of them died).]] When the plague lifted, they returned safe. Those who had remained said: "These companions of ours were more prudent than we were! If we had done as they did, we would have survived! If the plague strikes again, we will go out with them!" So it struck the next year, and they fled—they were some thirty-odd thousand—until they settled in that place, which was a wide valley. [[Al-afyah and al-fayyah: wide, spread out in its regions; it is said "rawdah fayha'" (a fragrant meadow), from this.]] A king from the bottom of the valley and another from its top called out to them: "Die!" They died. When they had perished and their bodies had decayed, a prophet called Hizqil passed by them. When he saw them, he stopped over them and began to reflect upon them, twisting his jaw and fingers. [[In the printed edition: "yalwi shadqayhi" (twisting his two jaws); I have adopted the text of the manuscript and Tarikh al-Tabari. Lawa shadqahu: he tilted it in wonder at what he saw and witnessed.]] Allah revealed to him: "O Hizqil, do you want Me to show you how I will bring them to life?" He said—and his reflection was only that he was amazed at Allah's power over them—"Yes!" It was said to him: "Call out!" He called: "O bones, Allah commands you to come together!" and the bones began to fly toward one another until they became bodies made of bones. Then Allah revealed to him: "Call out: 'O bones, Allah commands you to be clothed in flesh.'" So they were clothed in flesh and blood, and in the garments in which they had died, which were still upon them. Then he was told: "Call out!" He called: "O bodies, Allah commands you to rise!" and they rose.

5603 – Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, saying: Mansur ibn al-Mu'tamir alleged, from Mujahid, that when they were brought to life they said: "Glory be to You, our Lord, and praise be to You; there is no god but You," and they returned to their people alive, knowing that they had been dead, with the mark of death upon their faces. [[Al-sahnah (with fatha and sukun): condition, color, state; the surface of the face and its appearance.]] They did not put on a garment without it becoming greasy like a shroud, [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "illa 'ada kafanan dasiman" (except it became a greasy shroud); in Tarikh it is vocalized with a damma on the dal and sukun on the sin, which is an error, since this is the plural of adsam and dasim, and this is not the place for a plural. The phrase "kafanan dasiman mithl al-kafan" is not Arabic usage, so I omitted it and adopted what is in Tarikh. As for the other report in al-Durr al-Manthur, it is: "illa 'ada kafanan dasiman," without "mithl al-kafan." Either this or that is correct.]] "and dasam" means the fat and marrow of meat; and a person "dasam" a garment or "adsam" it when the garment is soiled and dirty, clinging with the residue of meat and fat. The shrouds of the dead are greasy, because of what flows from their bodies after they have decayed and their bodies have rotted. Until they died at their appointed times that had been written for them. [[Reports 5602 and 5603: in Tarikh al-Tabari (1:237, 238) and al-Durr al-Manthur (1:310), not in this wording.]]

5604 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Awsaja narrated to us, from Ata al-Khurasani: "Have you not seen those who left their homes, and they were thousands?" He said: They were three thousand or more.

5605 – al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Abbas said: They were forty thousand and eight thousand, [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "aw thamaniyat alaf" (or eight thousand), which is not consistent; the correct reading is in al-Durr al-Manthur (1:311).]] they were enclosed by pens, and their bodies had become fragrant and foul. Indeed, that smell is still found today in that tribe of Jews. They were thousands who fled from jihad in the way of Allah, so Allah caused them to die, then brought them back to life, and commanded them to fight. That is His saying: "And fight in the way of Allah," the verse. [[Al-haza'ir: plural of hazirah, what surrounds a thing, made of reeds or wood to protect against cold, wind, and enemies; "hazzara hazirah": he made it. Al-hazr: confinement and prevention. "Arwaha" and "arah" (for water, meat, and other things): their smell changed and became foul.]]

5606 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, from Wahb ibn Munabbih that Kalib ibn Yuqanna, when Allah took him after Yusha', [[In Tarikh: "Yufanna" with a fa'.]] left behind among them—meaning among the Children of Israel—Hizqil ibn Buzi, [[In Tarikh: "Buzi" with a dhal.]] who was the son of the old woman. He was named "the son of the old woman" because she had asked Allah for a child when she was old and barren, and He granted her one, which is why he was called "the son of the old woman." He is the one who prayed for the people whom Allah mentioned in the Book for Muhammad ﷺ, as we have been informed: "Have you not seen those who left their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death? Then Allah said to them, 'Die,' then He brought them to life. Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks." [[Report 5606: in Tarikh al-Tabari (1:237, then 238, abridged) and al-Durr al-Manthur (1:311).]]

5607 – Ibn Humayd narrated to me, saying: Salama narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, saying: It has reached me that among their accounts is that they left fleeing some of the plagues—of pestilence, or of a sickness that afflicted people—fearing death, and they were thousands. Until, when they alighted in a high place of the lands, Allah said to them: "Die," and they all died. The people of that land went out and enclosed a pen around them to keep out the beasts, then left them in it, because they were too many to be buried. Then ages and eras passed over them, until they became decayed bones. Hizqil ibn Buzi passed by them, stopped over them, marveled at their situation, and compassion entered him. [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "wa-dakhalahu rahmah," which I have adopted as in Tarikh al-Tabari.]] He was asked: "Would you like Allah to bring them to life?" He said: "Yes!" It was said to him: "Call out to them, say: 'O decayed bones that have rotted and decayed, let each bone return to its owner.'" He called out to them with this, and he looked at the bones leaping, each taking hold of the other. Then it was said to him: "Say: 'O flesh, sinew, and skin, clothe the bones by the permission of your Lord.'" He said: He looked at them, with sinew seizing the bones, then flesh, skin, and hair, until they were formed into shapes without spirits in them. Then he prayed for them to live, and something from the sky overtook him, distressing him until he fainted from it. [[In the manuscript: "fa-taghsahu min al-sama' karbuh" (unpointed). In the printed edition: "fa-taghsahum min al-sama' kadiyyah," which is meaningless; what I have written is the text of al-Tabari's Tarikh. Karabahu al-amr: it overtook him, pressed hard on him, and took hold of his breath, so he is "maku' al-nafs" (distressed in spirit).]] Then he regained consciousness while the people sat saying: "Glory be to Allah, glory be to Allah," for Allah had brought them to life. [[Report 5607: in Tarikh al-Tabari (1:238).]]

* *

Others said: the meaning of His saying "and they were thousands" is: "and they were in agreement" (mu'talifun). [[That is, it is the plural of "ilf" (with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the lam). Ibn Sida said regarding "aluf": "In my view it is the plural of 'alif,' like shahid and shuhud." See the rest of the books of tafsir.]]

Those who said this:

[5608] Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd, concerning the words of Allah: "Have you not considered those who went out from their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death? Then Allah said to them, 'Die,' and then He gave them life" — he said: It was a town in which the plague descended. A group of them went out, and a group remained. The plague struck the group that remained, while those who went out were not afflicted by anything. [In the printed edition: "did not afflict them," but I have kept what is in the manuscript.] Then it lifted. Then it descended the following year, so a group larger than the first one went out, and the plague became severe among the group that remained. When the third year came, it descended, and they all went out, leaving their homes. Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, said: "Have you not considered those who went out from their homes, and they were thousands" — it was not a faction that drove them out, as one goes out for war and fighting, their hearts being united; rather they went out fleeing. When they were in the place to which they went seeking life, Allah said to them: "Die," in the place where they had gone seeking life there. So they died. Then Allah gave them life: "Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind are not grateful." He said: A man passed by them while they were bones shining (lit. glistening), so he stopped to look, and said: "How will Allah give life to these after their death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years. [Report 5608: al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 311, abridged. It will come abridged as no. 5905.]

* *

Mention of reports from those who said: the departure of these people from their homes was fleeing from the plague.

[5609] Amr ibn Ali narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Adi narrated to us, from al-Ash'ath, from al-Hasan, concerning His words: "Have you not considered those who went out from their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death?" He said: They went out fleeing from the plague, and Allah made them die before their appointed times, then He gave them life until their appointed times.

[5610] al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Hasan, concerning His words: "Have you not considered those who went out from their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death?" He said: They fled from the plague, so Allah said to them: "Die!" Then He gave them life so that they might complete the remainder of their appointed terms.

[5611] Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Amr ibn Dinar, concerning the words of Allah, may His remembrance be exalted: "Have you not considered those who went out from their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death?" He said: The plague struck their town, so some people went out and some remained. Those who remained in the town died, and the others survived. Then the plague struck their second town, so some people went out and some remained, and more of those who went out than of those who remained. Allah saved those who went out, and those who remained perished. When it was the third time, they all went out except a few, so Allah made them die, along with their animals. Then He gave them life, and they returned to their lands [and had forgotten their town, and whom they had left behind]. They multiplied there, until one would say to another: "Who are you?" [In the manuscript: "they returned to their lands, and had forgotten their town and whom they had left behind, and multiplied there, one saying to another," with a blank space in the text; the printed edition omitted this blank, making the sentence "they returned to their lands and multiplied there, until one says to another," adding "until." I preferred to infer the meaning and kept what is in the manuscript, and I think the blank was filled as shown. I have not found this report elsewhere.]

[5612] al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, who said: I heard Amr ibn Dinar say: The plague struck their town — then he mentioned something similar to the report of Muhammad ibn Amr, from Abu Asim.

[5613] Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada: "Have you not considered those who went out from their homes, and they were thousands" — the verse. Allah detested them for their fleeing from death, so Allah caused them to die as punishment, then raised them to the remainder of their appointed terms so that they might complete them. Had the appointed terms of that people come, they would not have been raised after their death.

[5614] Reported from Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Husayn, from Hilal ibn Yasaf, concerning His words, may He be exalted: "Have you not considered those who went out" — the verse. He said: These people were from the Children of Israel. [In the printed edition: "These people were from the Children of Israel, when the plague struck among them"; in the manuscript: "These were a people from the Children of Israel, when it struck..." The copyist struck the alif of "qawman" and made it "qawm," so it is clear that "kana" is an addition by the copyist, as it appears correctly in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 311.] Whenever the plague struck among them, their wealthy and their nobles went out, and their poor and lowly remained. He said: Death became severe among those who remained, and those who went out were saved. Those who went out said: "If we had remained as these did, we would have perished as they perished!" And those who remained said: "If we had departed as these departed, we would have been saved as they were saved!" So they all departed together in one year: their wealthy, their nobles, their poor, and their lowly. Then Allah sent death upon them, and they became bones glistening. He said: The people of the towns came and gathered them in one place. A prophet passed by them and said: "O Lord, if You willed, You would have given life to these, so that they might populate Your lands and worship You!" He said: "Or would it be dearer to you that I do it?" He said: "Yes!" He said: "Then say: such and such," so he spoke it, and he looked at the bones, and a bone would move out from beside the bone that was not its own to the bone that was its own. Then he spoke what he was commanded, and the bones were clothed with flesh. Then he was commanded with another matter and spoke it, and they were sitting up, glorifying and magnifying God. Then it was said to them: "And fight in the way of Allah, and know that Allah is Hearing, Knowing."

[5615] Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Sa'id ibn Abi Ayyub informed me, from Hammad ibn Uthman, from al-Hasan, that he said concerning those whom Allah caused to die and then gave life: they were a people who fled from the plague, so Allah made them die as punishment and detestation, then gave them life for their appointed terms. [Report 5615: "Hammad ibn Uthman," who narrated from Abd al-Aziz al-A'ma from Anas. Sa'id ibn Abi Ayyub narrated from him, and he narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri. Ibn Abi Hatim said: "I asked my father about Hammad ibn Uthman, and he said: he is unknown." Al-Bukhari recorded his biography in al-Kabir 2/1/20, and Ibn Abi Hatim in 1/2/144.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two views regarding the interpretation of His words "and they were thousands" is the view of the one who said: "By 'thousands' is meant the great number," rather than the view of the one who said: "By it is meant unity," in the sense of the unity of their hearts, and that they went out from their homes without any division or enmity among them, but out of flight — either from jihad or from the plague. This is because the consensus of authority holds that this is the interpretation of the verse, and the isolated view is not to be set against what has been widely transmitted from the Companions and the Successors.

* *

The most correct of the opinions regarding the number of the people whose departure from their homes Allah described is the view of the one who set their number at more than ten thousand, rather than the one who set it at four thousand, three thousand, or eight thousand. This is because Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, informed us that they were "thousands," and fewer than ten thousand are not called "thousands." One says "they are thousands" when they are three thousand or more, up to ten thousand. It is not permissible to say: "They are five thousands" or "ten thousands."

The plural of the small number is formed on the pattern "af'al," and it is not formed on "af'ul," like the rest of the small plurals whose second radical is a sukun after the alif at its beginning [In the manuscript: "and on the rest of the like of the small plural," the correct reading being that of the printed edition]. The custom of the Arabs, for every letter that begins a word, whether ya, waw, or alif, is to form the small plural on "af'al," as they pluralized "al-waqt" as "awqat" and "al-yawm" as "ayyam," and "al-yusr" as "aysar," because of the waw and ya at the beginning of those words. It is occasionally formed on "af'ul," but the eloquent usage is what we have mentioned, and among it is the words of the poet: [The poet is Bukayr, the deaf one of the Banu al-Harith ibn Abbad.]

They were three thousands and a battalion, two thousand non-Arab (a'jam) of the Banu al-Fidam.

[Note: al-Naqa'id 645; Tarikh al-Tabari 2: 155; al-Aghani 20: 139; Lisan (alf), and others. This verse is one of his poems on the day of Dhu Qar, the day on which the Arabs gained revenge over the Persians and defeated Khosrow Abarwiz ibn Hormuz. The battle of Dhu Qar took place a few months after the battle of Badr, and when news of it reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: "This is a day on which the Arabs gained justice from the non-Arabs, and by me they were helped." On this day the Banu Shayban were people of valor and steadfastness, and al-A'sha and Bukayr al-Asamm praised them.

Al-Tabari here narrated "they were three thousands," but the transmission in all the sources is:
"Arabs, three thousands..."
This is because Khosrow appointed al-Nu'man ibn Zur'a over Taghlib and al-Namir, appointed Khalid ibn Yazid al-Bahrani over Qudaa and Iyad, and appointed Iyas ibn Qabisa over all the Arabs, with his two battalions, al-Shahba' and al-Dawsar, so the Arabs were three thousand. He also appointed Hamarz al-Tustari over a thousand of the cavalry, and appointed al-Khanabzin over a thousand, so the non-Arabs were two thousand (al-Aghani 20/134). This is the correction of the agreed-upon transmission and its explanation. The beginning of these verses is:
If you are a pourer of the wine to its people, then give drink to the vineyard of the Banu Hammam,
and Abu Rabi'a and Muhlim all of them, who preceded with the goal of the most glorious days,
they struck the sons of the free on the day they met them with the Mashrafi swords upon the resting place of skulls,
Arabs, three thousands... [remaining verse lines omitted in the source]

By his words "Banu al-Fidam," he means the Persians, because the Magians had a custom of their religion that when they drank, they tied a cloth over their mouths like a veil, so that group among them was called the Banu al-Fidam.]

* *

As for His words "fearing death," it means that they went out from fear of death, fleeing from it. [See what preceded in volume 1: 354, 355 regarding the interpretation of "hadhar al-mawt" and its grammatical analysis.] As:

[5616] Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words "fearing death": fleeing from their enemy, until they tasted the death from which they fled. Then He commanded them, and they returned, and He commanded them to fight in the way of Allah. They were the ones who said to their prophet: "Send us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah" [Surah al-Baqarah: 246].

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, urged His servants by this verse to persevere in jihad in His way and to be patient in fighting the enemies of His religion. He encouraged them by informing them and reminding them that causing death and giving life are in His hand and to Him, not to His creatures; and that fleeing from fighting, escaping jihad, and meeting the enemy, and retreating into fortresses or hiding in houses and dwellings, saves no one from His decree when it descends upon his courtyard, and does not avert the causes of his death when it alights at his abode [in the manuscript and printed edition: "bi-uqubatihi" (punishment), but in the manuscript it is undotted; the "uqwa" of a house is its courtyard and what is near it. One says: "he alighted at its uqwa," and "the horses alighted at the uqwa of the enemy"], just as it did not benefit those fleeing from the plague, whose state Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, described in His words: "Have you not considered those who went out from their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death" — their fleeing from their homelands and their moving from their dwellings to the place to which they hoped for safety by going there, and to the refuge hoped for salvation from death, until the command of Allah came upon them and He left them all lifeless, fallen, and dead upon the earth; and those who engaged the distress of the pestilence and mixed themselves with the great affliction were saved from what befell them.

* *

Concerning the interpretation of His words: "Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks."

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may He be exalted, He means: indeed Allah is possessed of bounty and grace toward His creation, by making clear to them the path of guidance and warning them of the paths of destruction, and other of His blessings which He bestows upon them in their world and their religion, their souls and their wealth — as He gave life to those who went out from their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death, after causing them to die, and made them an example and admonition for His creation, a lesson by which they may take heed, and so that they might know that all matters are in His hand, and submit to His decree, and direct all desire and all fear to Him. [In the printed edition: "that they submit... and direct," and in the manuscript: "that they submit... and direct."]

Then He, may His remembrance be exalted, informed that most of those servants upon whom He bestows His great blessings and favors with His immense graces disbelieve in Him, direct desire and fear to other than Him, and take a god besides Him, out of ingratitude for His blessings, the least of which requires from them gratitude that weighs heavily and praise that burdens. So He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: "But most people do not give thanks," meaning: they do not thank My blessing which I bestowed upon them, and My grace which I bestowed upon them, by worshipping other than Me, and directing their desire and fear to those besides Me who possess no harm or benefit for them, and possess no death, life, or resurrection.

[At this point a part of the old division ends. The manuscript then has after it the following: "And may Allah bless our master Muhammad the Prophet and his family, and greet them abundantly." Then the next division begins with the following: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. My Lord, help."]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 244:

The explanation of His words: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah, and know that Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: "And fight" — O believers — "in the way of Allah," meaning: in His religion, which He has guided you to [see what has preceded in the explanation of "the way of Allah" in 3:583, 3:592, and the references there], not in obedience to Satan — against the enemies of your religion [the word "enemies" is the object of "fight," and the context is: "Fight, O believers... the enemies of your religion"], those who bar others from the way of your Lord. Do not hold back from fighting them when you meet them, and do not be cowardly in warring against them, [in the manuscript it reads "wa la tahummu 'an qitalihi 'inda liqa'ihim, wa la tahibbu 'an harbihim," without dots, with the singular pronoun "qitalihi." The editors of the printed edition corrected it, not reading it well, and made it "wa la tajbunu 'an liqa'ihim, wa la taq'udu 'an harbihim," changing, altering, dropping, and doing as they pleased!! And His saying "wa la tahtammu 'an qitalihim" comes from their saying: "ihtamaytu min kadha" and "tahammaytu" — when one guards against something and abstains from it. "Min" and "'an" in this place are equivalent.] for your lives and deaths are in My hand. Let none of you be prevented from meeting them and fighting them by fear of death and dread of destruction for himself through fighting them, which would lead him to flee from them and run away from them, so that you are humiliated; and the death you feared will come to you in the refuge you have sought, [wa'ala ila al-makan ya'ilu, wa'ulan wa wu'ulan wa wa'lan: he sought refuge in it seeking deliverance. Al-mau'il: the place of refuge.] just as it came to those who went out from their homes fleeing death, whose story I have related to you, and their fleeing from it did not save them from its descending upon them when My command came to them and My decree befell them; nor did it harm those who stayed behind them what they had not feared, since their appointed times had repelled them and I had turned them away from their souls. [al-hawba': the soul, or the courage of the heart.] So fight in the way of Allah against those whom I have commanded you to fight, of My enemies and the enemies of My religion, for whoever among you is kept alive, I will keep him alive, and whoever among you is killed, his killing was by My decree.

Then He, may His remembrance be exalted, said to them: And know, O believers, that your Lord is "Hearing" of the words of those among your hypocrites who say about those of you who were killed in My way: "If they had obeyed us and sat in their homes, they would not have been killed," "Knowing" of what their breasts conceal of hypocrisy, disbelief, and scant gratitude for My favor upon them, [in the printed edition: "what their breasts hide," and I have restored what is in the manuscript. "Ajanna al-shay'": he concealed, hid, and kept it secret.] and My blessings upon them in their own selves and their families, and of other matters of theirs and of My servants.

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says to His believing servants: So thank Me by your obedience in what I have commanded you regarding jihad against your enemy in My way, and other than that of My command and prohibition, since these people have disbelieved My blessings. And know that Allah is Hearing of their speech, and Knowing of them and of others, and of what they are upon, remaining in faith and disbelief, obedience and disobedience, encompassing all of that, until I recompense each one for his deed: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: There is no basis for the view of those who claim that His saying "And fight in the way of Allah" is a command from Allah to those who went out from their homes, being thousands, to fight, after He had given them life. For His saying "And fight in the way of Allah" cannot be free — if the matter were as they interpreted — of one of three possibilities:

- Either it is coordinated with His saying "Then Allah said to them: Die," and that is impossible, for He would have caused them to die and then commanded them, while they were dead, to fight in His way.

- Or it is coordinated with His saying "then He gave them life," and that too is meaningless. For His saying "And fight in the way of Allah" is a command from Allah to fight, while His saying "then He gave them life" is a report of an action that has already passed. It is not eloquent to coordinate a future-tense command with a past report, were both of them reports, because their meanings differ. How then would a command be coordinated with a past report?

- Or its meaning is: "Then He gave them life and said to them: Fight in the way of Allah," and "the saying" was dropped, as He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: ﴿When the criminals hang their heads before their Lord: "Our Lord, we have seen and heard"﴾ [Surah as-Sajdah: 12], meaning: they say, "Our Lord, we have seen and heard." And this too is permissible only in a place where the apparent sense of the speech indicates its need for it, and the hearer understands that the speech is intended even though it is not mentioned. As for places where there is no indication that the speech needs it, there is no basis for the claim of one who asserts that it is intended there.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 245 (part 1 of 2)**

*On the interpretation of His words: ﴿Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him manifold?﴾*

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: Who is it that spends in the way of God, thereby aiding one who is weakened [[To say "a man is mudaʻaf" means his mount has become weak; he aids him by replacing it with another mount.]], or strengthens one in poverty who wishes to fight in the way of God, and gives to one of them who is needy? That is the goodly loan which a servant lends to his Lord.

God, may His remembrance be exalted, called it "a loan" (qard) because the meaning of "qard" (loan) is that a man gives another person his property as a possession, so that the other repays its like when he is asked for it. Since one who gives to the needy in the way of God gives them what he gives only seeking what God has promised him of abundant reward with Him on the Day of Resurrection, He called it "a loan," since the meaning of "qard" in the language of the Arabs is what we have described.

He, may His remembrance be exalted, called it "goodly" (hasan) because the giver gives that out of the recommendation of God to him and His urging him to it, seeking reward. It is obedience to God and disobedience to the devils. [[In the printed edition it reads "and disobedience to the devils," while in the manuscript it reads "and to the sultan," which is a copyist's error.]] This is not because God has any need of any of His creatures, but it is like the saying of the Arabs: "I have for you a loan of sincerity (qard sidq) and a loan of evil (qard sawʼ)," concerning a matter that brings a man joy or grief [[In the printed edition: "a matter that comes to the man…" and in the manuscript: "yaʼti fihi al-rajul," without dots. Abu Hayyan, in his tafsir (2:248), transmits this statement from al-Akhfash, and its text is: "for a matter whose joy or grief comes," but I have deduced the reading as I have set it down; everything that preceded is a distortion.]], as the poet said [[He is Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt.]]:

*Every man will be recompensed for his loan, good or evil, and indebted to what he has done.* [[His Diwan: 63; and al-Lisan (q-r-d). Its wording is: "or indebted, like what he did," and in the Diwan: "like what he did."]]

* * *

So the "loan" (qard) of a man is what has preceded of his good deeds or his evil ones. This verse is a parallel to the verse in which God, may His remembrance be exalted, said: [[In the printed edition: "God said in it, may His remembrance be exalted," and I have kept what is in the manuscript.]] ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is like a grain that sprouts seven ears; in every ear is a hundred grains, and God multiplies for whom He wills, and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 261].

* * *

In accordance with what we have said regarding this, Ibn Zayd used to say:

**5617** — Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words, "Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan," he said: This is in the way of God; "so that He may multiply it for him manifold," he said: For one, seven hundred times.

**5618** — al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʻAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʻmar informed us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: When the verse was revealed, "Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him manifold," Ibn al-Dahdah came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Prophet of God, do I not see our Lord asking us for a loan from what He has given us for ourselves? I have two plots of land: one in the upper part (al-ʻaliyah) and the other in the lower part (al-safiliyah), and I have decided that the better of the two shall be a charity! He said: The Prophet ﷺ used to say: "How many a bunch of dates, hanging low, is there for Ibn al-Dahdah in Paradise!" [[The hadith 5618: This is a mursal hadith, so its isnad is weak, because Zayd ibn Aslam is a Successor (tabiʻi), and he did not mention who narrated it to him from the Companions.
The hadith is established in the tafsir of ʻAbd al-Razzaq, p. 31 (photographed manuscript), from Maʻmar, with the same.
It is in al-Suyuti 1:312, and he did not attribute it to anyone other than ʻAbd al-Razzaq and al-Tabari.
Ibn Kathir (1:594) mentioned that Ibn Mardawayh narrated something like the following hadith, 5620, "from the hadith of ʻAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, from ʻUmar, marfuʻan, similar to it."
ʻAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam is very weak, as we have shown in 185, so there is no value in this narration.
Another mursal hadith with the same meaning will come after this, then 5620, from the hadith of Ibn Masʻud. We will defer clarifying the origin of the story until we speak of it there.
As for the wording "Ibn al-Dahdah" and "li-Ibn al-Dahdah": this is what is established in the tafsir of ʻAbd al-Razzaq, and it is what we have set down here. In the manuscript, in both places, it reads "al-Dahdahah," and in the printed edition "Abu al-Dahdah" and "li-Abi al-Dahdah." What is in the tafsir of ʻAbd al-Razzaq is more likely, because it is the original from which al-Tabari narrated.
As for the wording "innama aʻtana li-anfusina" ("what He has given us for ourselves"): it is what is established in ʻAbd al-Razzaq, and it is better. In the printed edition it was "mimma" instead of "innama."
"Al-ʻadhq" (with a fatha on the ʻayn and then sukun) is the palm tree; as for "al-ʻidhq" with a kasra on the ʻayn, it is the spathe (ʻarjun) of the palm tree. And "al-mudhallal" (with the first lam fatha and shadda): the one whose clusters have been lowered until its fruit is easy to pick, because it is near the one who plucks it.]]

**5619** — Bishr ibn Muʻadh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʻid narrated to us, from Qatadah: that a man in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, when he heard this verse, said: "I will lend to God!" So he went to the best orchard he had and gave it in charity. He said: Qatadah also said: "Your Lord asks you for a loan, as you hear, and He is the Protector, the Praiseworthy, and He asks His servants for a loan." [[The hadith 5619: This is also mursal, so its isnad is weak, and its end is a statement of Qatadah (mawquf). Al-Suyuti mentioned it (1:312), attributing it to ʻAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir only, and did not mention Qatadah's statement at its end.
In the manuscript: "wa yuʻsir ʻibadah" ("and makes His servants poor"), thus without dots and without vowels; I have left what is in the printed edition as it is, since it fits the sense. The report is in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:321, but it omitted this last sentence attributed to Qatadah.]]

**5620** — Muhammad ibn Muʻawiyah al-Anmati al-Nisaburi narrated to us, saying: Khalaf ibn Khalifah narrated to us, from Humayd al-Aʻraj, from ʻAbd Allah ibn al-Harith, from ʻAbd Allah ibn Masʻud, who said: When the verse "Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan" was revealed, Abu al-Dahdah said: O Messenger of God, does God really want a loan from us?! He said: Yes, O Abu al-Dahdah! He said: Your hand! He said: [[In the printed edition: "He said: Your hand, before," and in the manuscript: "yadaka qila," then he placed an alif above the yaʼ after the qaf, as if he intended to make it "qal," as I have set it down and preferred it, based on the text of Majmaʻ al-Zawaʼid 9:324: "He said: Show us your hand. He said: So he gave him his hand."]]

So he gave him his hand. He said: "I have indeed lent my Lord my orchard, an orchard in which there are six hundred palm trees." Then he went, walking, until he came to the orchard, and Umm al-Dahdah was in it with her children. He called out to her: "O Umm al-Dahdah!" She said: "Here I am!" He said: "Come out! I have lent my Lord an orchard in which there are six hundred palm trees." [[The hadith 5620: This is a very weak isnad.
Muhammad ibn Muʻawiyah ibn Yazid al-Anmati, the teacher of al-Tabari: trustworthy, his biography is in al-Tahdhib and Tarikh Baghdad 3:274–275.
Khalaf ibn Khalifah ibn Saʻid al-Ashjaʻi: trustworthy, he changed (his memory) in the last part of his life, died about the year 181 at the age of 101, and we have discussed his biography at length in the Musnad: 5885.
Humayd al-Aʻraj al-Kufi al-Qassas: he is Humayd ibn ʻAli, as al-Bukhari affirmed in al-Kabir 1/2/351, and in al-Duʻafa, p. 9. It is said: "Humayd ibn ʻAta'," and this is what Ibn Abi Hatim affirmed (1/2/226–227) and Ibn Hibban in Kitab al-Majruhin, no. 265. He is very weak. Al-Bukhari said: "munkar al-hadith" (his hadith is rejected). Abu Hatim said: "weak in hadith, rejected in hadith; he adhered to ʻAbd Allah ibn al-Harith from Ibn Masʻud, and nothing is known from ʻAbd Allah ibn al-Harith from Ibn Masʻud!" Ibn Hibban said: "He narrates from ʻAbd Allah ibn al-Harith from Ibn Masʻud—a copy that seems fabricated. His report is not used as evidence when he is alone."
ʻAbd Allah ibn al-Harith al-Zubaydi al-Najrani al-Mukatteb: trustworthy. The statement of Abu Hatim, that nothing is known of him from Ibn Masʻud, was mentioned earlier in the biography of the one who narrates from him. So the fault in this narration lies with Humayd al-Aʻraj.
This hadith was also narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim, from al-Hasan ibn ʻArafah, from Khalaf ibn Khalifah, with this isnad, as Ibn Kathir (1:593–594) transmitted from him.
Al-Suyuti mentioned it (1:312), and added its attribution to Saʻid ibn Mansur, Ibn Saʻd, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, al-Tabarani, and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʻab al-Iman.
Al-Haythami mentioned it in Majmaʻ al-Zawaʼid 6:320, in similar wording, and said: "al-Bazzar narrated it, and its narrators are trustworthy." Then he mentioned it again, 9:324, with another wording similar to it, and said: "Abu Yaʻla and al-Tabarani narrated it, and its narrators are trustworthy. The narrators of Abu Yaʻla are the narrators of the Sahih."
Thus al-Haythami said in both places. I do not have an isnad among the isnads to which he attributed it, nor among the books that al-Suyuti mentioned, except Ibn Saʻd, and I did not find it there, because the printed edition of Tabaqat Ibn Saʻd omits much of the book, as is well known.
The story of Abu al-Dahdah has another authentic origin, from the hadith of Anas, narrated by Ahmad in the Musnad: 12509 (3:146, Halabi), with a sound isnad: "From Anas: that a man said: O Messenger of God, indeed for so-and-so there is a palm tree, and I maintain my orchard by it. So command him to give it to me, so that I may maintain my orchard by it. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: Give it to him in exchange for a palm tree in Paradise. He refused. Then Abu al-Dahdah came to him and said: Sell me your palm tree for my orchard! He did so. Then he came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: O Messenger of God, I have bought the palm tree for my orchard. He said: Then make it for him; you have given it to him. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: How many a bunch of dates has been hung up for Abu al-Dahdah in Paradise! He said it several times. He said: Then he came to his wife and said: O Umm al-Dahdah, come out of the orchard, for I have sold it for a palm tree in Paradise. She said: The sale has profited, or a word similar to it."
This hadith of Anas is in Majmaʻ al-Zawaʼid 9:323–324. He said: "Ahmad and al-Tabarani narrated it, and its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih." There occurred in the printed edition of Majmaʻ al-Zawaʼid a omission of about a line in the middle of the hadith, which is corrected from this place.
It has a second authentic origin. Muslim narrated in his Sahih 1:264, from Jabir ibn Samurah, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ prayed over Ibn al-Dahdah, then a bare-backed horse was brought, and a man tied it and mounted it, and it began to prance with him, and we followed it running behind it. He said: A man of the people said: The Prophet ﷺ said: How many a bunch of dates, hanging or suspended, is there in Paradise for Ibn al-Dahdah." "Or he said, according to Shuʻbah: for Abu al-Dahdah."
As for "Abu al-Dahdah": he is Thabit ibn al-Dahdah, or Ibn al-Dahdahah. He is called "Abu al-Dahdah" or "Abu al-Dahdahah." He is biographied in al-Isabah 1:199. Then he was biographied in al-Kuna 7:57–58, and the disagreement was mentioned as to whether he is one person or two. Then he claimed that the truth is that the second is other than the first! He relied for this on a hadith he quoted from a narration of Abu Nuʻaym, which is weak, and that in its isnad there is a man "weak in hadith"!! So the argument based on it falls without doubt.
The *haʼit* (wall): a palm orchard that has a wall surrounding it. If there is no wall around it, it is a "dahiyah" (open land).]]

* * *

As for His words, "so that He may multiply it for him manifold": it is a promise from God, may His remembrance be exalted, to one who lends to Him and spends his wealth in the way of God, of multiplying the reward for his loan and his expenditure beyond any limit or end, as:

**5621** — Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: ʻAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan, so that He may multiply it for him manifold," he said: No one knows what this multiplication is.

And:

**5622** — al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Ibn ʻUyaynah, from a companion of his who mentioned from some scholars, who said: God has given you the world as a loan, and has asked you for it as a loan. So if you give it to Him willingly, with your souls content, He will multiply for you [the reward] between one good deed and ten, and to seven hundred, and to more than that. But if He takes it from you while you are unwilling, and you are patient and do good, there will be for you blessings and mercy, and He will make guidance obligatory for you. [[He means the saying of God, may He be exalted, in [Surah al-Baqarah: 156–157]: ﴿Those who, when a calamity afflicts them, say: Indeed we belong to God, and indeed to Him we return. Those—upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and those are the guided ones﴾.]]

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The readers (qurra') have differed concerning the recitation of His words: ﴿fa-yudaʻifahu﴾ with the alif and with a raising (of the verb), in the sense that: "Who is it that lends to God a goodly loan, so that He multiplies it for him"—taking "yudaʻifu" as coordinated with "yuqriḍu" (lends).

* * *

Others recited it with the same meaning: ﴿fa-yuḍaʻifahu﴾, except that they recited it with a shadda on the ʻayn and without the alif.

* * *

Others recited: ﴿fa-yudaʻifahu lahu﴾ with the alif affirmed in "yudaʻifu" and with the verb in the accusative (naṣb), in the sense of a question. It is as if they interpreted the speech as: "Who is the one who lends to God a goodly loan, so that He multiplies it for him?" They made His words "fa-yuḍaʻifahu" a response to the interrogative, and made "Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan" a noun, since "alladhi" and its complement (ṣilah) are in the position of "ʻAmr" and "Zayd." It is as if they directed the interpretation of the speech toward the saying of the speaker: "Who is your brother, so that you honor him?" For the more eloquent form, in responding to an interrogative with the fa', when there is no preceding future verb to be coordinated with it, is the accusative.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The recitation most correct in our view is the recitation of one who recites ﴿fa-yudaʻifahu lahu﴾ with the alif affirmed and "yudaʻifu" in the raised form. Because in His words "Who is it that will lend to God a goodly loan" there is the meaning of a condition (jaza'). When a condition has the fa' in its response, the response is not with the fa' in the raised form. Therefore the raising in "yuḍaʻifu" is more correct in our view than the accusative. We chose the alif in "yudaʻifu" over its deletion and the shadda on the ʻayn, because that is the more eloquent of the two dialects and the more common on the tongues of the Arabs.

* * *

*On the interpretation of His words: ﴿And God withholds and extends﴾*

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: that He is the one in whose hand is the withholding and extending of the provision of His servants, not any other whom the people of polytheism claimed to be gods, and took as lords besides Him, worshipping them. This is like the report transmitted from the Messenger of God ﷺ, which:

**5623** — We were told this by Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna and Muhammad ibn Bashshar, both saying: Hajjaj narrated to us; and ʻAbd al-Malik ibn Muhammad al-Raqqashi narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj and Abu Rabiʻah narrated to us, both saying: Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Thabit, Humayd, and Qatadah, from Anas, who said: Prices rose in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ. They said: O Messenger of God, prices have risen, so set prices for us! The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Indeed God is the Withholder, the Extender, the Provider, and I hope to meet God while no one seeks redress from me for an injustice in person or property." [[The hadith 5623: ʻAbd al-Malik ibn Muhammad al-Raqqashi Abu Qilabah, the teacher of al-Tabari: his biography has passed at 4331.
Hajjaj is Ibn al-Minhal al-Anmati.
Abu Rabiʻah: he is Zayd ibn ʻAwf al-Qatʻi, and his nickname is "Fahd." People spoke much about him for hadiths he narrated from Hammad ibn Salamah. As for al-Bukhari, he said in al-Kabir 2/1/369: "They were silent about his confusion." He is also biographied in Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/570–571, and Lisan al-Mizan.
Be that as it may, he did not narrate this hadith alone, so his weakness, if he was weak, does not affect it.
The hadith is sound with this isnad, through Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal, and from the other transmissions that we will mention.
Ahmad narrated it in the Musnad: 12618 (3:156, Halabi), from Surayj and Yunus ibn Muhammad, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Qatadah and Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas.
He also narrated it: 14102 (3:286, Halabi), from ʻAffan, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Qatadah, Thabit, and Humayd, from Anas.
Al-Tirmidhi (2:271–272) and Ibn Majah: 2200—both from the route of Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal with this isnad. Al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a good sound hadith."
Abu Dawud narrated it: 3451, from the route of ʻAffan, from Hammad, with the same.
Al-Suyuti mentioned it (1:313) and added its attribution to al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan.]]

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: By this—may God bless him and grant him peace—he means: that high and low prices, abundance and constriction, are in the hand of God, not of anyone else. Likewise His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, "And God withholds and extends," by "withholds" He means He straitens the provision of whom He wills of His creatures by withholding it, and by "extends" He means He widens it by extending provision to whom He wills among them.

And He, may His remembrance be exalted, intended by that saying to urge His believing servants, whom He has granted abundance of His bounty and whose provision He has widened, to strengthen those among them who are in straitened circumstances with their wealth, to aid them by spending on them, and to equip them (ḥumūlah) to rise up and fight His enemy, the polytheists, in His cause. [[al-ḥumūlah (with a fatḥah on the ḥā’): everything on which people are carried, such as camels, donkeys and others. Al-ḥumūlah (with a ḍammah on the ḥā’): loads and burdens. I fear that the correct wording in the original is "bi-l-infāq ʿalayhi wa-ʿalā ḥamalatihi" ("by spending on him and on his mounts"), and his saying "ʿalā al-nuhūḍ" ("to rise up") is linked to his saying "wa-maʿūnatihi" ("and aiding him").]] So He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: Whoever sets forth for himself a treasure with Me by giving to the weak among the believers and the needy among them what they can use to aid themselves in fighting in My cause, I will multiply for him from My reward many times over what he gave and strengthened them with? For indeed I — O you who are made wealthy — [[In the printed edition: "fa-innī anā al-mūsiʿ alladhī qabaḍt" ("For I am the Wealthy One who withheld"), which is a statement that is never correct; the right reading is what is in the manuscript. And "al-mūsiʿ" means the rich one whose wealth has increased, from their saying "awsaʿa al-rajul" ("the man became possessed of abundance"), meaning he became one of plenty and wealth, and his wealth increased. God, exalted is He, said: "The wealthy man according to his means, and the straitened man according to his means" (Q. 2:236). See what preceded on the explanation of "al-wasʿ" in this part, page 45. The context of the phrase is "fa-innī … alladhī qabaḍt" (For I … who withheld).]] who withholds provision from the one whom I have commissioned to aid and give to him, so that I may test him with patience in what I have tested him with — and who extends to you what I have extended, in order to test you by your deeds in what I have extended to you, so I may see how you obey Me in it. Then I will recompense each of you according to the measure of your obedience to Me regarding what I tested you with and examined you by, of wealth and poverty, abundance and constraint, when you return to Me in your Hereafter and your going back to Me in your final return.

* *

Those whose sayings on this reached us among the people of ta’wīl (interpretation) said something similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

5624 – Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: "Who is it that will lend to God a good loan" (Q. 2:245), the verse: He knew that among those who fight in His cause there are those who do not find strength, and among those who do not fight in His cause there are those who find wealth. So He urged these people, saying: "Who is it that will lend to God a good loan, so that He may multiply it for him many times over? God withholds and extends" (Q. 2:245). He said: He extends for you, while you are heavy about going out and do not desire it; and He withholds from this one, while he is glad of heart to go out and it is light for him. So strengthen them with what is in your hand, and there will be a share for you in that.

* *

Commentary on His saying: "And to Him you will be returned" (Q. 2:245)

Abū Jaʿfar said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, means by that: To God is your return, O people. So fear God regarding your souls, that you neglect His obligations and transgress His limits, and that whoever among you is given extension of provision act with it in a way other than what his Lord has permitted him to act with it; and that whoever among you is straitened — when He has withheld his provision — bring his straitened state to disobedience and to transgressing what He has forbidden him, so that he thereby deserves, when he comes to his Creator, what he has no power to bear of His painful punishment. [[In the printed edition: "fa-yastawjib bi-dhālika minhu bi-maṣīrihi…" (so he deserves thereby from Him by his coming…), which is a statement severely corrupt. In the manuscript: "ʿanhu maṣīruhu" (his coming to Him), and it is evident that the unpointed "h" in "ʿanhu" is the "d" of "ʿind" (with Him).]]

* *

Qatada used to interpret His saying: "And to Him you will be returned" as: And to the dust you will be returned. [[In the manuscript: "wa-ilā al-thawāb" (and to the reward), and "min al-thawāb…" (from the reward…), which is evidently corrupt; but it is evidence of the great inattention of the copyist at this place in the book, as you have seen of its misreadings and distortions in the earlier places of this commentary.]]

5625 – Bishr ibn Muʿādh narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatāda: "And to Him you will be returned": from dust He created them, and to dust they will return. [[In the manuscript: "wa-ilā al-thawāb" (and to the reward), and "min al-thawāb…" (from the reward…), which is evidently corrupt; but it is evidence of the great inattention of the copyist at this place in the book, as you have seen of its misreadings and distortions in the earlier places of this commentary.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 246 (part 1 of 3):

The explanation of His saying: ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah"?﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His saying, "Have you not considered," He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: Have you not considered, O Muhammad, with your heart, [[See the meaning of "have you not considered" and "seeing" in what has passed: p. 266, and the references in the footnote.]] so that you know by My report to you, O Muhammad, "the chiefs" — meaning the notables, nobles and leaders of the Children of Israel — "after Moses," meaning: after Moses had been taken and had died, "when they said to a prophet of theirs, 'Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah.'"

It has been reported to me that the prophet who said this to them was Shamwil [[I will mention in the following notes what came in the genealogy of these names, in the form they take in the book of the people that is before us, from the Early Chronicles, in chapter six. "Shamwil" there is "Samuel."]] son of Bali [[Bali is not mentioned in the genealogy of Shamwil in the book of the people; rather, among them he is "Samuel son of Elqanah."]] son of Alqamah [[(Elqanah)]] son of Yarham [[(Yeroham). In the printed edition it reads "Barham," an error; in the manuscript it is undotted, while in Tarikh al-Tabari 1:242 it has the dotted ḥāʼ.]] son of Ilihu [[(Elihu or Eliel). It is apparent that it is "Ilihu."]] son of Tahu son of Suf [[(Tuh). In the printed edition: "Yahu Suq," which is an error; in the manuscript "Bahu Suf," undotted. Both have dropped "son of" between the words. The correct form is from Tarikh al-Tabari. "Tuh" is mentioned in the book of the people, in the First Book of Samuel, chapter one, in the form "Tuhu."]] son of Alqamah son of Mahith [[(Mahath).]] son of Amusa [[(Amasai). The genealogy in the book of the people after this is: "Amasai son of Elqanah son of Yoel son of Azariah son of Zephaniah son of Tahath son of Assir son of Abiasaph." Some of it is not mentioned in the genealogy transmitted by al-Tabari, and what he transmitted afterwards has inversions and displacements, as you see.]] son of Azariah son of Zephaniah [[(Zephaniah). In the printed and manuscript editions: "Safiyyah."]] son of Alqamah son of Abi Yasaf [[(Abiasaph). In the printed edition: "Abi Yasq"; in the manuscript: "Abi Yasf."]] son of Qarun [[(Korah).]] son of Yasehar [[(Izhar).]] son of Qahath [[(Kohath).]] son of Lawi son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim.

5626 — Ibn Humayd narrated this to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "from Abu Ishaq," which is an error; it is a chain that recurs in al-Tabari from "Muhammad ibn Ishaq," the author of the Sirah.]] from Wahb ibn Munabbih.

5627 — And also al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Karim narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil told me that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: "He is Shamwil, he is Shamwil" — and he did not attribute him as Ibn Ishaq did. [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "as Ishaq attributed him," which is an obvious error; see the earlier note.]]

* * *

Al-Suddi said: Rather, his name was Shim'un (Simeon). He said: He was named "Shim'un" because his mother asked Allah to grant her a boy, and Allah answered her prayer and granted her one, and she bore a boy and named him "Shim'un," saying: "Allah has heard my supplication."

5628 — [Bi-dhalika] Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi. [[What is between the brackets is an addition required by the context, as in the chain of the report that preceded.]]

* * *

So "Shim'un" is, according to al-Suddi, of the pattern "fa'ul," from her saying: "He has heard [sami'a] Allah's supplication [du'a'ahā]." [[In the printed edition: "from her saying, 'heard,'" omitting "innahu," and I have restored what is in the manuscript.]]

* * *

5629 — al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: "Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs..." — he said: "Shamu'il." [[In the printed edition: "Shim'un," which is an error beyond doubt; the correct form is what is in the manuscript and in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:315.]]

* * *

Others said: Rather, the one whom their people among the Children of Israel asked to appoint for them a king to fight in the way of Allah was Yusha' (Joshua) [[(Yashu').]] son of Nun son of Afra'thim [[(Ephraim). In the printed edition: "Afra'thim"; the correct form is what I have recorded from the History 1:225. In the manuscript it is undotted.]] son of Yusuf son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim.

5630 — al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated this to me, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "And their prophet said to them" — he said: Their prophet after Moses was Yusha' ibn Nun. He said: And he was one of the two men upon whom Allah bestowed His favor. [[He means those mentioned in His saying, may He be exalted, in [Surat al-Ma'idah: 23]: "Two men of those who feared (Allah) and whom Allah had favored said..." — the verse.]]

* * *

As for His saying: "Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah," the people of interpretation differed concerning the cause that led the chiefs of the Children of Israel to ask their prophet for this.

Some of them said: The cause of their request was what follows:

5631 — Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated this to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: After Moses, Yusha' ibn Nun succeeded among the Children of Israel, establishing the Torah and the command of Allah until Allah took him. Then Kalib ibn Yafuna [[(Yafnah). In the printed edition: "Yuqna"; the correct form is from the manuscript and the History 1:238.]] succeeded them, establishing the Torah and the command of Allah until Allah, may He be exalted, took him. Then Hizqil [[(Hezekiel), in the book of the people.]] ibn Buzi succeeded among them, and he was the son of the old woman. Then Allah took Hizqil, and the calamities grew great among the Children of Israel, and they forgot what Allah's covenant to them had been, until they set up idols and worshipped them apart from Allah. So Allah sent to them Ilyas [[(Elijah). This is "Elijah the Tishbite," mentioned in First Kings, chapter 17.]] ibn Nasa [[I did not find the genealogy of "Elijah," and his saying "Nasa" I did not find. In the manuscript it is "Sa," undotted and unclear; in the History of al-Tabari 1:239 it is "Ilyas ibn Yasin."]] ibn Finhas [[(Phinehas).]] ibn al-'Izar [[(Eleazar).]] ibn Harun ibn 'Imran as a prophet. The prophets among the Children of Israel after Moses were sent to them only to renew what they had forgotten of the Torah. Ilyas was with a king of the kings of the Children of Israel called Ahab, [[(Ahab). In First Kings, chapters 16 and 17. In the printed edition, the History, and the manuscript it is "Ahab," with the ḥāʼ unpointed.]] who used to listen to him and believe him. Ilyas would manage his affairs for him. All the rest of the Children of Israel had taken an idol to worship apart from Allah, and Ilyas began calling them to Allah, but they would not listen to him at all, except what came from that king. The kingdoms were scattered in Syria, each king having a region of it that he consumed. [[(Ya'kuluhā), meaning he prevails over it and its revenue and tribute become his. In the hadith of 'Amr ibn 'Anbasah: "the eaten of Himyar is from its eaters" — the eaten (al-ma'kul) is the subject population, and the eaters (al-akilun) are the kings. They call the lords of the tribes who take the quarter (al-mirba') and other things "al-akal." And in the hadith: "I have been commanded (to go to) a town that devours the towns," meaning Medina: its people, by Islam, prevail over the other towns.]] Then that king, with whom Ilyas was and who managed his affairs and regarded him as guided among his companions, said to him one day: "O Ilyas, by Allah, I do not see that what you call the people to is anything but falsehood! By Allah, I do not see So-and-so and So-and-so" — and he counted kings among the kings of the Children of Israel — "who have worshipped idols apart from Allah, except in the same way as we are, eating, drinking and enjoying ease as rulers. [[In the printed edition: "mālikīn"; in the manuscript: "mulkiyyīn"; I have kept what is in the History of al-Tabari.]] Does what you claim is false diminish their worldly affairs [— their matter which you claim is false]? [[The addition between the brackets is from the History of al-Tabari, and the speech is not sound without it.]] And we do not see that we have any superiority over them." And they claim — [[In the printed edition: "wa-yazʻumūna," and I have kept what is in the manuscript and the History.]] — and Allah knows best — that Ilyas invoked "Inna lillah" (sought refuge), his hair and skin stood up, then he rejected him and departed from him. That king then did what his companions did: he worshipped idols and did as they did. [[Up to this point al-Tabari narrated it with this chain in his History 1:239; the next part is in 1:240, and other narrations separate them.]] Then after him Allah appointed among them al-Yasa' (Elisha), [[(Elisha), in the book of the people.]] and there happened among them what Allah willed; then Allah took him to Himself. And successors came after him, and their sins grew great. They had the Ark, which they inherited from one another, generation after generation; in it is tranquility (sakinah) and a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind. They did not meet an enemy but that they would bring forward the Ark and advance with it before them, [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "wa-kānū...," and I have kept what is in the History, which is better.]] and Allah would defeat that enemy. [[After this in the History is the following text: "And the sakinah — as Ibn Ishaq reported from Wahb ibn Munabbih, from some people of Israel — was the head of a dead cat; when it cried out inside the Ark with the cry of a cat, they were certain of victory, and the conquest came to them."]] Then there succeeded among them a king called Iyla', [[(Eli). In the book of the people, and in the History of al-Tabari "Ayla'" [Ilaf]. The more probable is that what is in the printed edition and the manuscript is correct, due to its closeness to the form "Eli," although al-Tabari mentioned in his History 1:243 "Ayla" [Eyla]. Eli was one of the great priests of the Children of Israel, and he judged for them forty years. The account of Eli's death at the seizure of the Ark is mentioned in the book of the people, First Samuel, chapter four.]] and Allah had blessed them in their mountain, Iliya, which no enemy could enter against them, and they needed nothing else with it. One of them, so they say, would gather the earth on a rock, then scatter the seed in it, and Allah would bring out for him what he and his family would eat for a year. And one of them would have an olive tree, from which he would press what he and his family would eat for a year. When their calamities grew great and they abandoned the covenant of Allah to them, an enemy attacked them, and they went out to it, bringing out the Ark with them as they used to bring it out, and they advanced with it, and they were fought against until it was seized from before them. Their king Iyla' came and was informed that the Ark had been taken and seized, so his neck bent, and he died of grief over it. So their affair became confused among them, [[In the History of al-Tabari: "fa-marija amruhum baynahum." To be confused (maraja al-amr) means to be mixed up, to be perplexed and disturbed in strife.]] and their enemy trampled them, until some of their sons and women were struck down. [[Up to this point, al-Tabari's History 1:240–241 has been completed.]] Among them was a prophet whom Allah had sent to them, but they would not accept anything from him; he was called "Shamwil" [[(Samuel), in the book of the people.]], and he is the one Allah mentioned to His Prophet Muhammad: "Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, 'Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah'" — to His saying: "And we have been expelled from our homes and our children" — Allah says: "And when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except a few of them" — to His saying: "Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers."

= Ibn Ishaq said: Their account, as some of the people of knowledge narrated to me from Wahb ibn Munabbih, is that when the affliction came upon them and their lands were trampled, they spoke to their prophet Shamwil ibn Bali, saying: "Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah." The foundation of the Children of Israel was the gathering around kings, and the obedience of the kings to their prophets. The king would lead the armies, and the prophet would manage his affairs and bring him news from his Lord. When they did this, their affair was set right; when their kings became arrogant and abandoned the command of their prophets, their affair was corrupted. Thus, when the kings followed the community into misguidance, they abandoned the command of the messengers: one group they called liars and would not accept anything from, and another group they killed. That affliction continued upon them until they said to him: "Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah." He said to them: "There is in you no fulfillment, no truthfulness, and no desire for jihad." They said: "We used to dread jihad and shun it, because we were protected in our lands, and no one trampled them, so no enemy prevailed over us in them. But now that this has come, jihad is necessary, so that we may obey our Lord by fighting our enemy, and protect their sons, our women and our offspring."

5632 — I was told by 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His saying: "Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel," to "And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers." Al-Rabi' said: It was mentioned to us — and Allah knows best — that when Moses was near death, he appointed his youth Yusha' ibn Nun over the Children of Israel, and Yusha' ibn Nun led them with the Book of Allah, the Torah, and the sunnah of their prophet Moses. Then Yusha' ibn Nun died, and appointed another over them, who led them with the Book of Allah and the sunnah of their prophet Moses, may peace be upon him. Then he appointed another, who led them in the manner of his two companions. Then he appointed another, and they recognized some of his conduct and rejected some. Then he appointed another, and they rejected most of his conduct. Then he appointed another, and they rejected all of his conduct. Then the Children of Israel came to one of their prophets when they were harmed in their persons and their wealth, and they said to him: "Ask your Lord to prescribe fighting for us!" That prophet said to them: "Would you perhaps, if fighting is prescribed for you, not fight?" — to His saying: "And Allah gives His kingdom to whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing and Knowing."

5633 — al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, regarding His saying: "Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs: Appoint for us a king" — he said: Ibn 'Abbas said: This was when the Torah was lifted up and the people of faith were taken out, and the tyrants had driven them out from their homes and their children. [[(Istukhrija), with the passive form: it was taken to mean being driven out of their lands. This word is not mentioned by the lexicographers; it is an Arabic word that has become arcane.]]

5634 — I was told by al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say, regarding His saying: "When they said to a prophet of theirs: Appoint for us a king" — he said: This was when the Torah was lifted up and the people of faith were taken out.

* * *

Others said: The cause of their request to their prophet for that was what follows:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 246 (part 2 of 3):

5635 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Musa, when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Appoint for us a king that we may fight in the cause of Allah"﴾. He said: The Children of Israel used to fight the Amalekites, and the king of the Amalekites was Jalut [(Jaliyat) in the book of the people]. They prevailed over the Children of Israel, imposed the jizyah upon them, and took their Torah. The Children of Israel would ask Allah to send them a prophet to fight alongside. The tribe of prophethood had been destroyed, and none of them remained except a pregnant woman. They seized her and imprisoned her in a house, fearing that she would give birth to a girl whom they would exchange for a boy, given the Children of Israel's desire for her offspring. So the woman began to supplicate Allah to grant her a boy, and she gave birth to a boy and named him Shim'un [in the History of al-Tabari, after his saying "Shim'un," it reads: "She said: Allah has heard my supplication". See the report earlier, no. 5628, and what precedes and follows it]. The boy grew up, and she sent him to learn the Torah in Bayt al-Maqdis [in the printed edition: "she sent him to learn", and I have confirmed what is in the manuscript and the History], and a shaykh from among their scholars took charge of him and adopted him. When the boy reached the age at which Allah would send him as a prophet, Gabriel came to him while the boy was sleeping beside the shaykh, and no one was trusted with him except the shaykh [in the printed edition: "la ya'tamin" (not trusted), and in the Egyptian print of the History: "la yaitaman," while the European edition and the manuscript read: "la yatamman." Amanahu, amanahu and i'tamanahu and itamanahu (with the taa doubled) are equivalent; see the commentary of the author of Lisan on the view of one who said the latter is rare]. He called him in the dialect of the shaykh: "O Shamwal!" [al-lahn: language and dialect. In the History: "Shamwil," and the apparent meaning of this report indicates that "Shim'un" is "Shamwil" and that the two are dialects with one meaning. See the earlier reports 5626–5629 and the comments on them]. The boy rose in alarm to the shaykh and said: "Father, did you call me?" The shaykh disliked to say "No" lest the boy be frightened, so he said: "My son, return and sleep!" He returned and slept. Then he called him a second time, and the boy came again and said: "Did you call me?" He said: "Return and sleep; if I call you a third time, do not answer me!" When it was the third time, Gabriel appeared to him and said: "Go to your people and convey to them the message of your Lord, for Allah has sent you among them as a prophet."
