I have adopted what is in the manuscript.]] It is possible that this remnant is the staff, the broken Tablets, the Torah, or some of them, the two sandals, the garments, and jihad in the way of God, and it is possible that it is some of that. That is a matter whose knowledge cannot be attained by deduction or by linguistic means, and its knowledge cannot be reached except by a report that makes knowledge necessary. There is no report among the people of Islam about this with the description we have mentioned. Since that is so, it is not permissible here to declare one opinion correct and to weaken another, since what we have said is permissible.

* *

The discussion of the interpretation of His words: ﴿The angels will carry it﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: The people of interpretation differed about the manner in which the angels carried that chest.

Some of them said: The meaning is that it is carried between the heavens and the earth until they set it down among them.

Mention of those who said this:

5701. al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Ḥajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The angels brought the chest, carrying it between heaven and earth while they looked at it, until they set it down before Talut."

5702. Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: When he (i.e., the Prophet, to the Children of Israel) said to them: ﴿And God gives His kingdom to whom He wills﴾, they said: "How can we know that God has indeed granted him this? It is only your own desire in this!" He said: "If you have indeed denied me and accused me, then the sign of his kingship is: ﴿That there will come to you the chest, in it is tranquility from your Lord﴾," to the end of the verse. He said: So the angels descended with the chest by day, while they looked at it openly, until they set it down among them. They acknowledged it without being pleased, and went out angry. And he recited until he reached: ﴿And God is with the patient﴾.

5703. Mūsa told me, saying: ʿAmr told us, saying: Asbāṭ told us, from al-Suddi, who said: When their prophet said to them: ﴿Indeed God has chosen him over you and has increased him in knowledge and physical stature﴾, they said: "If you are truthful, then bring us a sign that this is a king!" He said: ﴿Indeed the sign of his kingship is that there will come to you the chest, in it is tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind, carried by the angels.﴾ The chest and what was in it arrived at the house of Talut in the morning, and they believed in the prophethood of Shamʿun (Simeon) and submitted to the kingship of Talut.

5704. al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥya told us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatada, concerning His words: ﴿The angels carry it﴾: he said: "They carry it until they set it down in the house of Talut."

* *

Others said: The meaning is that the angels drive the animals that carry it.

Mention of those who said this:

5705. al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥya told us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from some of his shaykhs, who said: "The angels carried it on a cart, pulled by a cow."

5706. al-Ḥasan told us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: ʿAbd al-Ṣamad ibn Maʿqil informed us, that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: "Four angels were assigned to the two cows that moved with the chest, driving them. The two cows moved with them at a rapid pace, until when they reached the edge of al-Quds (the Holy Land), they went away."

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The most correct of the two views is the saying of the one who said: "The angels carried the chest until they set it down for them in the house of Talut, standing among the Children of Israel." [[In the printed edition: "ḥattā waḍaʿathu fī dār Ṭālūt," omitting "lahā" (i.e., for the Children of Israel). In the printed edition also: "fī dār Ṭālūt bayn aẓhur Banī Isrāʾīl," omitting "qāʾiman." In the manuscript this word was: "mā bayn aẓhur li-Banī Isrāʾīl," and I read it as "qāʾiman."]] That is because God, exalted is His mention, said: "The angels carry it," and He did not say: "The angels bring it." And what the cows dragged on carts, even if the angels were driving them, they did not carry it, because "carrying" in its known sense is the carrier's direct bearing of what he carries himself. As for what is carried by something else, although it is permissible in the language to say "he carried it" meaning he helped the one carrying, and although its carrying was because of its cause, it does not follow the way of what one directly carries with his own body, in the common usage of people. Directing the interpretation of the Qur'an toward the more prevalent of the languages is better than directing it toward the more unusual, so long as there is a way to that. [[In the printed edition: "awlā min tawjīhihi ilā an lā yakūn al-ashhar…", which is a mixture of confused words. In the manuscript: "ilā ilā an lā yalr," with the second "ilā" struck through. The correct reading is what I have read, and similar words have occurred many times in Tabari's discourse.]]

* *

The discussion of the interpretation of His words: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers﴾ (2:248)

Abu Jaʿfar said: God, exalted is His mention, means by this that His Prophet Ashmuwil (Samuel) said to the Children of Israel: "Indeed, in your coming of the chest, in it is tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind, carried by the angels: ﴿a sign for you﴾," meaning: a mark and an indication for you, O people, of my truthfulness in what I have told you: that God has sent you Talut as king, if you had indeed denied me regarding what I told you of God's making him king over you, and had accused me in my report to you of that: ﴿if you are believers﴾, meaning: if you are those who confirm me when the sign you asked me for comes, confirming my truthfulness regarding what I told you about the matter of Talut and his kingship. [[See the explanation of "faith" in the sense of "affirmation" in what preceded in the earlier parts. See the indexes for the language.]]

* *

We have only said this is its meaning because these people had disbelieved in God by denying their prophet and rejecting his saying: ﴿Indeed God has sent Talut to you as king﴾, by their saying: ﴿How can he have kingship over us when we are more entitled to kingship than him?﴾, and by their asking him for a sign of his truthfulness. Since that was disbelief on their part, [[In the printed edition: "fa-in kāna dhālika minhum," and the correct reading is what is in the manuscript.]] it is not permissible to say to them, while they are disbelievers: "For you, in the coming of the chest, is a sign if you are among the people of faith in God and His Messenger," when they were not among the people of faith in God or His Messenger. Rather, the matter in this is as we have described its meaning: they asked for a sign for the truthfulness of his report to them, so that they would acknowledge his truthfulness. So he said to them: in the coming of the chest, as he described it to them, is a sign for you if, at its coming in that way, you are confirming me in what I said to you and told you.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 249 (part 1 of 2):

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿When Talut set out with the troops, he said, "Indeed, Allah is going to test you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who takes a handful with his hand." But they drank from it, except for a few of them.﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: In this report from Allah, exalted is He, something has been omitted, and the indication of what was mentioned has made its mention unnecessary. The meaning of the speech is: "Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers." Then the ark came to them, in which was tranquility from their Lord and a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun had left, carried by the angels. At that, they affirmed their prophet, acknowledged that Allah had sent Talut as king over them, and submitted to him in this. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿When Talut set out with the troops.﴾ He would not have set out with them except after their approval of him and their acceptance of his kingship, because he was not one who could compel them to do so, so that it might be supposed that he drove them to it by force.

* *

As for His saying "fassala" (set out), it means: he departed with the troops and moved on with them.

* *

The root of "al-fasl" is cutting off. It is said of it: "The man separated (fassala) from such-and-such a place," meaning he cut off from it, passing beyond it, departing for another place; he "yafsilu fusulan." And "fassala al-'azm wa al-qawl min ghayrih" (he separated the bone and the speech from other than it), meaning he cut it and made it clear; and "fassala al-sabiyy fisalan" (he weaned the child), meaning he cut him off from milk [[See the explanation of "al-fisal" earlier in this part: 67.]]. And "qawl fasl" means a decisive speech that distinguishes truth from falsehood and cannot be turned back.

* *

It was said: Talut set out with the troops that day from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and they were eighty thousand fighters. None of the Bani Isra'il stayed behind from departing with him except one who was ill because of his illness, or an elder because of his old age, or one excused who had no ability to rise up and go with him.

Those who said this:

5707. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: A certain one of the people of knowledge narrated to me, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: Talut set out with them when they had gathered around him, and none stayed behind from him except an elder with an illness, or a blind man excused, or a man in a holding who had to remain there. [[The report 5707: "istawsaqu lahu" means they gathered to him in obedience and submitted. "Al-darir" is the man weakened by illness, whom the sickness has harmed. (See what has passed on p. 231 and at the end of report 5659, with the commentary on it.)]]

5708. Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: When the ark came to them, they believed in the prophethood of Shamun (Samuel) and submitted to Talut's kingship, and they set out with him, and they were eighty thousand. [[The report 5708: it is in the History 1:243, from a long report, most of which has passed earlier.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: When Talut set out with them in the manner we have described, he said: "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river." That is, indeed Allah is testing you with a river, to know how obedient you are to Him.

* *

We have already shown that the meaning of "al-ibtila'" (testing) is examination, earlier, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary [[See what has passed: 2:49; 3:7, 220.]].

And Qatadah used to say in accordance with what we have said on this:

5709. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning the words of Allah, exalted is He: "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river." He said: Allah tests His creation with whatever He wills, in order to know who among them obeys Him and who disobeys.

* *

It was also said: Talut said "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river" because they complained to Talut about the scarcity of water between them and their enemy, and asked him to supplicate to Allah that He cause a river to flow between them and their enemy. Then Talut said to them at that time what is reported as his words: "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river."

Those who said this:

5710. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: A certain one of the people of knowledge narrated to me, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: When Talut set out with the troops, they said: "The waters will not carry us. So supplicate to Allah for us that He cause a river to flow for us!" Talut said to them: "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river," the verse.

* *

As for "the river" about which Talut informed them that Allah was testing them with it, it was said: It is a river between the Jordan and Palestine.

Those who said this:

5711. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said concerning "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river": al-Rabi' said: It was mentioned to us, and Allah knows best, that it is a river between the Jordan and Palestine.

5712. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river." He said: It was mentioned to us that it is a river between the Jordan and Palestine.

5713. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river." He said: It is a river between the Jordan and Palestine.

5714. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn Abbas: When Talut set out with the troops, going to fight Jalut, Talut said to the Bani Isra'il: "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river." He said: A river between Palestine and the Jordan, its water sweet and good.

Others said: Rather, it is the river of Palestine.

Those who said this:

5715. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river." The river by which the Bani Isra'il were tested is the river of Palestine.

5716. Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river." It is the river of Palestine.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who takes a handful with his hand; but they drank from it, except for a few of them.﴾ This is a report from Allah, exalted is His mention, about what Talut said to his troops, when they complained to him of thirst. He informed them that Allah was testing them with a river, then he made them know that the testing which he had told them of from Allah through that river was that whoever drinks from its water is not of him, meaning: he is not of the people of his guardianship and obedience, nor of the believers in Allah and in meeting Him. The evidence that this is so is the saying of Allah, exalted is His mention: ﴿Then when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him﴾. So He excluded from the believers those who had not crossed the river. Then He specified the believers in Allah and in His meeting when they drew near to Jalut and his troops by His saying: ﴿Those who were certain that they would meet Allah said: "How many a small company has overcome a large company by the permission of Allah!"﴾ And He informed them that whoever does not taste it, meaning: whoever does not taste the water of that river. The "ha'" in His saying "fa-man shariba minhu" and in His saying "wa-man lam yat'amhu" refers back to "the river," and the meaning is its water. The word "water" was omitted only because the hearer understands it from the mention of the river: the intended meaning is the water that is in it.

* *

The meaning of His saying "lam yat'amhu" is: he did not taste it. That is: whoever does not taste the water of that river is of me, meaning: he is of the people of my guardianship and obedience, and of the believers in Allah and in His meeting. Then He made an exception from "man" in His saying "wa-man lam yat'amhu" for those who take a handful with their hands. So He said: whoever does not taste the water of that river, except one who takes a handful with his hand, he is of me.

* *

Then the readers differed on the recitation of His saying "illa man ightarafa ghurfatan biyadihi" (except one who takes a handful with his hand).

The common readers of Medina and Basra recited it as "ghurfatan" with a fatha on the "gh" of "ghurfah," meaning a single handful, from your saying: "I took a handful (ightarafat ghurfatan)." "Al-ghurfah" with a fatha here is the very act of "al-ightiraf" (scooping), and it is the verbal noun (masdar) [[The "act" means the verbal noun, as has passed just above on p. 330, note 1, and as the following sentences will state explicitly until the end of the discussion.]].

Others recited it with a damma, meaning the water that gathers in the palm of the one who scoops. So "ghurfah" with a damma is the noun, and "ghurfah" with a fatha is the verbal noun.

* *

The more preferable of the two recitations to me is the damma on the "gh" in "ghurfah," meaning: except one who scoops a palmful of water. This is because the form "ghurfah" with a fatha differs from the verbal noun of "ightaraf," since the verbal noun of "ightaraf" is "ightirafah," while "ghurfah" is the verbal noun of "ghirafa." Since "ghurfah" with a fatha differs from the verbal noun of "ightaraf," the "ghurfah" that means the noun, as we have described, is closer to the meaning than the "ghurfah" that means the act. [[This is a fine distinction which one rarely finds in the books of lexicography. See the Lisan al-'Arab, root (gh-r-f), and what al-Kisa'i and others said on this.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We have been told that most of them drank from that water, so whoever drank from it became thirsty, and whoever scooped a handful was refreshed.

Those who said this:

5717. Bishr narrated to me, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who takes a handful with his hand; but they drank from it, except for a few of them." He said: The people drank according to the measure of their certainty. As for the disbelievers, they kept drinking but were not satisfied; as for the believers, a man would take a handful with his hand, and it would suffice him and satisfy him.

5718. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah: "Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who takes a handful with his hand." He said: The disbelievers used to drink and were not satisfied, while the Muslims used to scoop a handful and it sufficed them.

5719. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who takes a handful with his hand; but they drank from it, except for a few of them." He meant the believers among them. The people were numerous, and they drank from it, except for a few of them, meaning the believers among them. Each of them would take a handful, and it would suffice him and satisfy him.

5720. Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: When the ark and what was in it came to the house of Talut, they believed in the prophethood of Shamun and submitted to the kingship of Talut, and they set out with him, and they were eighty thousand. Jalut was among the greatest of men and the most fierce in might; he would go forward before the troops, and his companions would not gather to him until he routed whomever he met. When they set out, Talut said to them: "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me." So they drank from it out of awe of Jalut. Four thousand of them crossed over with him, and seventy-six thousand returned. Whoever drank from it became thirsty, and whoever did not drink from it except for a handful was refreshed. [[Report 5720: this is part of the report in the History 1:242–243. Al-Tabari divided it in this commentary in many places, which we have indicated: numbers 5635, 5638, 5679, 5690, 5708.]]

5721. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: Allah placed upon the tongue of Talut, when he set out with the troops, and he said: "None shall accompany me except one who has an intention for jihad." So no believer stayed behind from him, and no hypocrite followed him. ... They returned as disbelievers, because of their lies in their saying when they said: "We will not touch this water, a handful or anything else." [[In the manuscript: "wa-lam tatba'uhu munafiq, raja'u kuffaran, fa-lamma ra'a qillatahum qalu: lan namussu hadha al-ma'" — both phrasings do not work in either case. I believe a line or part of a line has fallen from the copyist, whose meaning is that some of those who went out with him returned as disbelievers because of their lies in that saying. What makes me favor this is that he says afterward, "He said: And the remainder took the handful," which is evidence that he had earlier mentioned those who drank from the river. In the printed edition: "wa-la ghayrihā," and I have kept the manuscript's wording, which is correct.]] For he had said to them: "Indeed Allah is testing you with a river," the verse, and they said: "We will not touch from this a handful or anything other than a handful." [[In the printed edition: "lan namussu min hadha" with an added "min," and I have kept the manuscript's wording.]] He said: The remainder took a handful and drank from it until it sufficed them, and some was left over. [[In the printed edition: "fa-shariba minha," and I have kept the manuscript's wording.]] He said: Those who did not take a handful were stronger than those who took it.

5722. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Abbas said concerning His saying: "Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who takes a handful with his hand": each person drank according to the measure of what was in his heart. Whoever scooped a handful and obeyed, was refreshed for his obedience. [[In the printed edition: "rawiya bi-ta'atihi," and what I have written is closer to the manuscript and to what is correct.]] And whoever drank and drank more, disobeyed and was not refreshed for his disobedience.

5723. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, in a report he mentioned, from a certain one of the people of knowledge, from Wahb ibn Munabbih concerning His saying: "Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who takes a handful with his hand." Allah, exalted is His mention, says: "But they drank from it, except for a few of them." And he said, according to what they claim: whoever persisted in drinking from what he was forbidden did not become refreshed, while whoever did not taste it except as he was commanded, a handful with his hand, it sufficed him and was enough for him.

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him, they said: "We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, exalted is His mention, "Then when he crossed it," He means: when Talut crossed the river. The "ha'" in "jawazahu" refers back to "the river," and "huwa" is a pronoun for Talut's name. His saying "wa-alladhina amanu ma'ahu" means: and those who believed crossed the river with him, and they said: "We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops."

* *

Then they differed concerning the number of those who crossed the river with him that day, and those among them who said: "We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops."

Some of them said: Their number was the number of the people of Badr: three hundred and some odd men (thalathumi'ah rajul wa-bid'a 'ashara rajulan).

Those who said this:

5724. Harun ibn Ishaq al-Hamdani narrated to us, saying: Musab ibn al-Miqdam narrated to us; and Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us; both of them said: Israil narrated to us, saying: Abu Ishaq narrated to us, from al-Bara' ibn Azib, who said: We used to speak of the number of the companions of Badr being equal to the number of the companions of Talut who crossed the river with him, and no one crossed with him except a believer: three hundred and some odd men. [[The report 5724: this is a report from al-Bara' ibn Azib concerning the number of the people of Badr. Al-Tabari narrated it by six chains, all of them from Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, from al-Bara' ibn Azib.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 249 (part 2 of 2):

Ahmad narrated it in the Musnad 4: 290 (Halabi edition), from Waki', from his father (that is, al-Jarrah ibn Mulayh), and from Sufyan (that is, al-Thawri), and Isra'il. All three narrated from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara'.

Al-Bukhari narrated it in his Sahih 8: 228, through the chain of Zuhayr, through the chain of Isra'il, and through the chain of al-Thawri. All three narrated from Abu Ishaq, with the same wording.

Ibn Kathir mentioned it 1: 603, drawing on the narrations of al-Tabari, with the isnads abridged. Then he mentioned that al-Bukhari narrated it.

Al-Suyuti mentioned it 1: 318 and added its attribution to Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Dala'il. But he forgot to attribute it to Ahmad.

[[ 

5725 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Bakr narrated to us, saying: Abu Ishaq narrated to us, from al-Bara', who said: "We used to speak of the companions of Badr on the day of Badr as being equal in number to the companions of Talut: three hundred and thirteen men, those who crossed the river."

[[The hadith 5725: Abu Bakr, the transmitter from Abu Ishaq, is Ibn Ayyash.

My brother, Mahmud Muhammad Shakir, mentioned that he found in the manuscript, at the end of this hadith, after his saying "those who crossed the river," a very strange word, which is "fasakata" (then he was silent), clearly written. I have not found it elsewhere, and I could not determine what it is. It was deleted in the printed edition.

I say: I too have not found this word, and I could not determine what it is. For this reason we have deleted it from this printed edition of ours, while noting that, in fulfilment of scholarly trust.]]

5726 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu Amir narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', who said: "We used to speak of the companions of the Prophet ﷺ as being on the day of Badr three hundred and some ten men, equal in number to the companions of Talut who crossed with him, and none crossed with him except a believer."

[[The hadith 5726: Abu Amir is al-Aqadi, Abd al-Malik ibn Amr.]]

5727 - Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', with a similar report.

[[The hadith 5727: The father of Waki' is al-Jarrah ibn Mulayh ibn Adi al-Ru'asi. He is trustworthy, but he was criticised without proof, as we explained in the commentary on the Musnad, in the hadith 650. Waki's narration from his father of this hadith is one of the narrations of the Musnad that we pointed to in the previous hadith, 5724.]]

5728 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammil narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', who said: "We used to speak of the companions of the Prophet ﷺ as being on the day of Badr equal in number to the companions of Talut on the day they crossed the river, and none who crossed with him except a Muslim."

[[The hadith 5728: Mu'ammil is Ibn Isma'il al-Adawi. Sufyan, in this and the preceding one, is al-Thawri.]]

5729 - Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Mis'ar narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from al-Bara', the like of it.

[[The hadith 5729: Abu Ahmad is al-Zubayri, Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr al-Asadi. Mis'ar is Ibn Kidam; his biography has passed at 1974.]]

5730 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of God ﷺ said to his companions on the day of Badr: 'You are equal in number to the companions of Talut on the day he met [the enemy].' And the companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ on the day of Badr were three hundred and some ten men."

5731 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: "God tested those who believed at the river, and they were three hundred, a little more than ten and less than twenty. Then Dawud ﷺ came and completed the number with him."

* *

Others said: Rather, four thousand crossed the river with him, and only the people of faith were separated from the people of disbelief and hypocrisy when they met Jalut.

Mention of those who said this:

5732 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: "Four thousand of the Children of Israel crossed the river with Talut. When he and those who believed with him crossed it, and they looked at Jalut, they turned back as well, saying: 'We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops.' Then three thousand, six hundred and some eighty turned back from him as well, and there remained three hundred and some ten, the number of the people of Badr."

[[The report 5732: This is part of the long report which he narrated in the History 1: 242–243, and which he divided in the Tafsir, as we pointed out in the note on report 5720. Abu Ja'far's version here reads "and there remained three hundred and some ten," while in the History it reads "and nineteen."]]

5733 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ibn Abbas said: "When he and those who believed with him crossed it, those who had drunk said: 'We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops.'"

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two views on this matter is what has been transmitted from Ibn Abbas and said by al-Suddi, namely that the one who crossed the river with Talut was the believer who had not drunk from the river except a handful, and the disbeliever who had drunk much of it. Then the distinction between them took place afterward by seeing Jalut and meeting him, and the people of polytheism and hypocrisy withdrew from him, [[In the printed edition: "wankhadhala 'anhu" with a dhal, which is an error that does not fit here; the correct form is in the manuscript. Inkhazala 'anhu means he separated and stood alone; in another report: "Abd Allah ibn Ubayy inkhazala from that place," meaning he went off alone and returned with his people.]] and they are those who said: "We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops." And those of insight went on by God's command with their insight, and they are the people of steadfastness in faith, and they said: "How many a small company has overcome a great company by God's permission, and God is with the patient."

* *

If one who is heedless should think that it is not possible that only the people of faith who remained steadfast with him in their faith crossed the river with Talut, and those who had drunk no more than a handful, because God, may His remembrance be exalted, said: "When he and those who believed with him crossed it," so it was known that none crossed with him except the people of faith, as the report from al-Bara' ibn Azib transmits it, and because if the people of disbelief had crossed the river as the people of faith did, God would not have singled out the people of faith for mention in that [[Context: "If one who is heedless should think ... then the matter in that is contrary to what he thought."]], then the matter in that is contrary to what he thought. For it is not improbable that both groups, I mean the group of faith and the group of disbelief, crossed the river, and God informed His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about the believers by the crossing, because they were among those who crossed it with their king, and He left out mention of the people of disbelief, even though they had crossed the river along with the believers.

What indicates the soundness of what we have said on this is the saying of God, may His remembrance be exalted: "When he and those who believed with him crossed it, they said: We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops. Those who expected that they would meet God said: How many a small company has overcome a great company by God's permission." God, may His remembrance be exalted, made it necessary that "those who expected that they would meet God" are those who said, at the crossing of the river: "How many a small company has overcome a great company by God's permission," and not others who did not expect that they would meet God. And that "those who did not expect that they would meet God" are those who said: "We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops." It is not permissible to ascribe faith to one who denied that he would meet God, or who doubted it. [[This is a clear proof, passed earlier, containing such insight, understanding, and precision as deserves to be pondered.]]

* *

Discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops. Those who thought that they would meet God said: How many a small company has overcome a great company by God's permission. And God is with the patient.﴾ (2:249)

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation (ta'wil) differed about the matter of these two groups, I mean those who said "We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops," and those who said "How many a small company has overcome a great company by God's permission," as to who they were.

Some of them said: The group who said "We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops" were people of disbelief in God and hypocrisy, and they were not among those who witnessed the fighting against Jalut and his troops, because they turned away from Talut and from those who remained steadfast with him in fighting the enemy of God, Jalut, and those with him. They were the ones who disobeyed God's command by drinking from the river.

Mention of those who said this:

5734 - Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, the like of that.

* *

This is the saying of Ibn Abbas, and we have already mentioned the report on that from him above. [[See the report number 5722.]]

* *

5735 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij: "Those who thought that they would meet God," those who took a handful and obeyed, those who went on with Talut, the believers, and those who doubted sat down.

* *

Others said: Both groups were people of faith, and none of them had drunk from the water except a handful. Rather, they were all people of obedience, but some of them were more certain in conviction than others. They are the ones whom God informed about, that they said: "How many a small company has overcome a great company by God's permission." And the others were weaker in conviction, and they are the ones who said: "We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops."

Mention of those who said this:

5736 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "When he and those who believed with him crossed it, they said: We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops. Those who thought that they would meet God said: How many a small company has overcome a great company by God's permission, and God is with the patient." And the believers were, some of them, much better and more resolute than others, while they were all believers.

[[What is between the brackets ["wa-Allah"] is an addition from the manuscript.]]

5737 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: "How many a small company has overcome a great company by God's permission," that the Prophet said to his companions on the day of Badr: "You are equal in number to the companions of Talut: three hundred." Qatadah said: "And with the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Badr were three hundred and some ten."

5738 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "Those who did not take a handful are stronger than those who took it, and they are the ones who said: 'How many a small company has overcome a great company by God's permission, and God is with the patient.'"

* *

On the view transmitted from al-Bara' ibn Azib, that only the number of the companions of Badr crossed the river with Talut, it is necessary that both groups whom God described with what He described them, their state is as Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said of them.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two views on the interpretation of the verse is what Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, and Ibn Juraij said, and we have already mentioned the proof for that earlier, just before.

* *

As for the interpretation of His saying, "Those who thought that they would meet God," it means: those who knew and were certain that they would meet God. [[See the discussion of His saying "would meet God" earlier, at 2: 20–22 and 4: 419.]]

5739 - Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, concerning "Those who thought that they would meet God," that they were certain.

* *

So the meaning of the speech is: Those who were certain of the return and believed in the going back to God said, to those who said "We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops": "How many a small company," meaning by "how many" a great number, "has overcome a great company by God's permission," meaning: by God's decree and destiny. [[See the explanation of "permission" earlier at 2: 449–450 and 4: 287, 371.]] "And God is with the patient," that is: with those who restrain themselves for His pleasure and obedience. [[See the meaning of "patience" earlier at 2: 11, 124 and 3: 214, 349, and the indices of language.]]

* *

We have already come to the explanation of the senses of "thinking" (zann), and that one of its meanings is certain knowledge, with what indicates the soundness of that earlier, so we disliked repeating it. [[See what passed: 2: 17–20, then 265.]]

* *

As for "fi'ah" (company), they are the group of people, with no singular from its own form, and it is like "rahṭ" (band) and "nafar" (party). Its plural is "fi'at," and "fi'un" in the nominative, and "fi'in" in the accusative and genitive, with its nun vowelled with a fatha in every case. And "fi'in" in the nominative, with the case-ending on its nun in the nominative and the yā' dropped, and in the accusative "fi'ina," and in the genitive "fi'in," so the case-ending falls in the genitive and accusative on its nun. In all of this the yā' remains in its state. If it is made a construct, one says: "ha'ulaa'i fi'inka" [[In the printed edition: "fi'nak," which is an error.]], with the nun retained and the tanwin dropped, as the speakers whose dialect is "hadhihi sinin" (these are years), in the plural of "sanah" (year), say "hadhihi sininuka," retaining the nun, giving it case-endings, and dropping the tanwin from it for the construct. And so the rule is for every defective noun such as "mi'ah" (hundred), "thubah," "qillah," and "izzah." As for those whose defect is at their beginning, their plural is with the taa', like "iddah, iddat" and "silah, silat."

* *

As for His saying, "And God is with the patient," it means: God helps the patient in holy fighting for His cause and in other kinds of His obedience, and gives them victory and triumph over His enemies who turn people from His path and oppose the course of His religion.

* *

Likewise it is said of anyone who helps a man against another: "He is with him," meaning he is with him by aiding and supporting him. [[See the explanation of "with" earlier at 3: 214.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 250:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they came out before Jalut and his hosts, they said: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His saying, exalted is His remembrance, "And when they came out before Jalut and his hosts," He means: when Talut and his hosts came out before Jalut and his hosts.

* *

The meaning of His saying "they came out" (barazu) is that they went out onto the open ground (al-biraz) from the earth, which is what is raised and level. For this reason, the man relieving himself is said to "tabarraza" (went out into the open), because people in ancient times, in the Jahiliyyah, used to relieve their needs in the open ground. This is like what is said: "taghawwata" (went to relieve himself), because they used to relieve their needs in the "ghaʼit" (low, sunken ground) of the earth, which is the depressed part of it, so it was said of the man: "taghawwata," meaning he went to the ghaʼit of the earth.

* *

As for His saying, "Our Lord, pour upon us patience," it means that Talut and his companions said: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience," meaning: send down upon us patience.

* *

As for His saying, "and make firm our feet," it means: strengthen our hearts for fighting them, so that our feet may be firm and we do not flee from them. "And help us against the disbelieving people," who disbelieved in You, denied You as God, worshipped other than You, and took idols as lords.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 251 (part 1 of 4):

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they routed them by the permission of Allah, and Dawud killed Jalut﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "So they routed them" [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "By His saying, exalted is He His remembrance, 'so Talut routed...' ", but the context requires adding "they routed them" from the text of the verse.]] — exalted is His remembrance — Talut and his troops routed the companions of Jalut, and Dawud killed Jalut.

In this statement something has been omitted, leaving it out being sufficient because of what is evident from it. The meaning of the speech is: "And when they went out to face Jalut and his troops, they said: 'Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make our feet firm, and help us against the disbelieving people.'" So their Lord answered them, pouring His patience upon them, making their feet firm, and helping them against the disbelieving people — "So they routed them by the permission of Allah." But the omission of this was because of the indication of His saying "So they routed them by the permission of Allah," that Allah had answered the supplication they had made to Him.

* *

The meaning of His saying "So they routed them by the permission of Allah" is: they routed them by the decree of Allah and His destiny. [[See the meaning of "permission" previously, briefly: 352, note 3. Refer there. As for His saying "fallalūhum" (they routed them), it is from the saying of people: "fallaltu al-jaysh falla," meaning I defeated and broke the army. In the manuscript and printed edition it reads "qatalūhum" (they killed them), from killing, and this is an error with no good in it, for defeat is breaking, not killing. And "hazamahu" means he broke him, not killed him.]] It is said from it: "The people routed the army, a rout (hazīma) and a hazīmā." [[ "Hazīmā" with a kasra on the ha, and a doubled kasra-marked zay, and a fatha-marked mim for the maqsura alif.]]

* *

"And Dawud killed Jalut." This Dawud is Dawud son of Ishay, [[(Jesse) in the books of the people, (1 Samuel: Chapter 17).]] the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ). The cause of his killing him, as:

5740 — al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Bakkar ibn 'Abd Allah informed us, saying: I heard Wahb ibn Munabbih relate: When Talut went out — or he said: when he emerged — against Jalut, Jalut said: "Send out to me whoever will fight me; if he kills me, then my kingdom is yours, and if I kill him, then your kingdom is mine!" Dawud was brought to Talut, and he made a covenant with him that if he killed him he would marry him to his daughter, [[qadāhu 'ala kadhā: he reconciled with him upon it, from qadā' (decision and judgment), and similar to it is what came in the Treaty of Hudaybiyya: "This is what Muhammad made peace upon."]] and that he would make him judge over his wealth. Talut dressed him in armour, but Dawud disliked to fight him with a weapon, [[The word "bi-silāh" (with a weapon) is absent from the printed and manuscript texts, and it is indispensable; I added it from the text of the report in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 318–319.]] and said: "Indeed Allah has not helped me against him, the weapon will not avail!" So he went out to him with a sling and a pouch containing stones, and then faced him. Jalut said to him: "You are fighting me?!" Dawud said: "Yes!" He said: "Woe to you! You have come out only as one goes out to a dog with a sling and stones!" [[In the manuscript: "Amma rahb illa kama takhruj," and in the printed edition: "Imma takhruj ilayya illa kama yakhruj," and what is in al-Durr al-Manthur is closer to the manuscript, with the copyist's transcription particularly at this point.]] "I will surely scatter your flesh, [[In the manuscript: "la-ardanna lahmaka," and it seems that what is in the printed edition is correct, and so it is in al-Durr al-Manthur.]] and I will surely feed it today to the birds and the beasts!" Dawud said to him: "Rather, you are the enemy of Allah, worse than a dog!" Then Dawud took a stone and slung it, and it struck him between his eyes until it penetrated his brain, [[In the printed edition and al-Durr al-Manthur: "it struck between his eyes and penetrated," and I have kept what is in the manuscript.]] so Jalut fell and those with him fled, and Dawud cut off his head. When they returned to Talut, the people claimed the killing of Jalut; some of them brought the sword, and something of his weapons or his body, but Dawud had hidden his head. Talut said: "Whoever brings his head is the one who killed him!" So Dawud brought it, and then said to Talut: "Give me what you promised me!" Talut regretted what he had stipulated for him, and said: "Indeed the daughters of kings must have a dowry, and you are a bold and courageous man, so bring her dowry: three hundred foreskins of our enemies." [[al-ghulfa, al-gharla and al-qulfa (with the first letter vowelled with a damma and the second sukun) is the covering that is cut away by circumcision from the private part of a man.]] He was hoping by that that Dawud would be killed. Dawud raided and took captive three hundred of them, cut off their foreskins, and brought them. Talut had no choice but to marry him to her, but then remorse overtook him. He wanted to kill Dawud, until Dawud fled from him to the mountain, and Talut rose against him and besieged him. When one night sleep overpowered Talut and his guards, Dawud came down to them, took Talut's ewer from which he used to drink and perform ablution, cut some hairs from his beard and some of the fringe of his garments, [[The hem of a garment (hudb al-thawb wa-hadabatuhu): its edge on the side of its fringe.]] then Dawud returned to his place and called out to him: "Your guards and you have slept. Had I wished to kill you last night I would have done so; this is your ewer, some of your beard hair and the fringe of your garments!" And he sent [it] back to him. [[What is between the parentheses is an addition required by the context.]] Talut realised that had he wished he would have killed him, so that inclined him toward him and he gave him security, and pledged to him by Allah that he would not see any harm from him. Then he departed. Later, at the end of Talut's affair, he began secretly plotting to kill him. Talut never fought an enemy without being routed, until he died. — Bakkar said: Wahb was asked while I was listening: "Was Talut one to whom revelation came?" He said: "Revelation did not come to him, but there was with him a prophet called Ushmuwil to whom revelation came, and he is the one who made Talut king."

5741 — Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, saying: Dawud the Prophet had four brothers, with whom was their father, an old man. Their father remained behind, and Dawud remained behind with him from among his brothers, tending his father's sheep for him, and he was the youngest of them. His four brothers went out with Talut, and his father called him when the people had drawn close and some of them had approached others.

= Ibn Ishaq said: Dawud, as some people of knowledge told me from Wahb ibn Munabbih, was a short, blue-eyed man, [[His saying "azraq" means blue-eyed, and the Arabs used to consider blue eyes ominous. (See al-Hayawan 5: 330–333.)]] with little hair on his head, and he was pure and clean of heart. [[This paragraph of the report was transmitted by Abu Ja'far in his History 1: 247.]] His father said to him: "My son, we have prepared food for your brothers, for them to be strengthened against their enemy; take it out to them, and when you hand it to them, come back to me quickly!" He said: "I will do so." He went out and took what he had carried for his brothers, with his pouch in which he carried stones and his sling with which he used to throw at his sheep. When he departed from his father and passed by a stone, it said: "O Dawud! Take me and place me in your pouch, and with me you will kill Jalut, for I am the stone of Ya'qub!" He took it and placed it in his pouch and walked on. While he was walking he passed another stone, which said: "O Dawud! Take me and place me in your pouch, and with me you will kill Jalut, for I am the stone of Ishaq!" He took it and placed it in his pouch, then went on. While he was walking he passed another stone, which said: "O Dawud! Take me and place me in your pouch, and with me you will kill Jalut, for I am the stone of Ibrahim!" He took it and placed it in his pouch. Then he went on with what he had until he reached the people, and gave his brothers what had been sent with him. He heard in the camp the people discussing Jalut and his great standing among them, [[In the manuscript: "sami'a dawhars al-nas bi-dhikr Jalut," and I could not make out what that was, nor what it means, so I left what is in the printed edition as it is, for its meaning is close and sound.]] and the people's awe of him, and what they magnified of his affair, [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "wa-mimma yu'azzimun," and what I have adopted fits the context. The manuscript is very rich in distortion and corruption here, as you see.]] so he said to them: "By Allah, you magnify the affair of this enemy greatly, but I do not know what it is! By Allah, if I saw him I would kill him! Bring me before the king." So Talut was brought before him, and he said: "O king, I see you magnify the affair of this enemy! By Allah, if I saw him I would kill him!" He said: "My son! What strength do you have for that? [[In the printed edition: "fa-atni ma 'indaka min al-quwwa," which is weak speech. The correct reading is from the manuscript, which the printer or copyist did not read well. Compare what will come in the report, 5742, and his saying "My son," and his question "Have you sensed in yourself anything," p.]] And what have you tested in yourself? [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "wa-mimma jarrabta," and the context requires what I have adopted.]] He said: "The lion used to attack a sheep of mine, and I would overtake it, seize it by its head, break its jaws off it, and take the sheep from its mouth. [[al-lahyan are the two bones in which the teeth are set, the two walls of the mouth; the singular is "lahan" (with fatha then sukun).]] So call for a coat of mail for me, so I may put it on." A coat of mail was brought and cast on his neck, and it filled the eye of Talut and his soul and those present of the Children of Israel. [[In the printed edition: "wa-mathala fiha fa-mala'a 'ayn Talut," and in the manuscript: "wa-sal fiha mal 'ayn Talut," unpointed and unclear. I have adopted "mathal" from the printed edition, as it is probably close to correct. In the printed edition: "wa-man hadar," and I have adopted the manuscript reading.]] Talut said: "By Allah, perhaps Allah will destroy him by it!" In the morning they returned to Jalut, and when the people met, Dawud said: "Show me Jalut!" He was shown him upon a horse wearing his armour. When he saw him, the three stones began leaping in his pouch, one saying: "Take me!", another saying: "Take me!", another saying: "Take me!" He took one of them and placed it in his sling, then whirled it with it and released it, and it struck Jalut between his eyes and split his skull, [[Damaghahu damghan: he wounded him so that the wound reached the brain. This wound is called "al-damigha".]] and he fell from his mount, and he killed him. Then his army was routed, and the people said: "Dawud has killed Jalut!" Talut was deposed, and the people turned to Dawud in his place, until no mention of Talut was heard any more — except that the People of the Book claim that when he saw the Children of Israel turning away from him to Dawud, he resolved to assassinate Dawud and sought to kill him, but Allah turned that away from him and from Dawud, and he recognised his error and sought repentance from it to Allah.

* *

There is also related from Wahb ibn Munabbih, concerning the affair of Talut and Dawud, a statement contrary to the two reports we mentioned before, which is:

5742 — It was narrated to me by al-Muthanna, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Karim narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil narrated to me that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: When the Children of Israel handed over the kingship to Talut, a prophet of the Children of Israel received a revelation: [[In the manuscript: "awha ila bani bani Isra'il," and in the printed edition: "awha ila nabi Bani Isra'il," and I have adopted what is in Tabari's History.]] that he should tell Talut to raid the people of Madyan, and leave none alive in it but kill them, for I will make him victorious over them. So he went out with the people until he came to Madyan, and killed all who were in it except their king, whom he took captive, and he drove their livestock. Then Allah revealed to Ushmuwil: "Are you not amazed at Talut, when I commanded him with My command, yet he was deficient in it, [[In the printed edition: "fa-ikhtan fihi," from treachery; in the manuscript: "fa-ikhtar fihi," from choosing, meaning he chose what he wished from it and did not carry it out fully as it was. I have adopted what is in the History. "Ikhtall" from "khalal," which is corruption and weakness in an affair, and failing to firm it up and secure it. One says "akhal bil-amr," meaning he did not fulfil it; and "akhal bi-makanihi," meaning he was absent from it and abandoned it. So the meaning of "akhtalla fihi" is that he became weak in it and introduced a flaw into it. I have not found its text in the lexicon books, but its formation is Arabic.]]

This, and in the manuscript and the printed edition it reads: "when I commanded him, so he [fought]" (إذ أمرته فاختان), with "بأمري" omitted. I have restored it from the History.]] So he brought their king as a captive and drove their livestock! Go to him and say: "I will surely strip the kingship from his house, and it will never return to him until the Day of Resurrection, for I only honour those who obey me, and I humiliate whoever holds My command cheap." So he met him and said to him: [[In the printed edition and the manuscript, "له" (to him) is omitted; I have restored it from the History.]] "What have you done?! Why did you bring their king as a captive, and why did you drive their livestock?" He said: "I only drove the livestock to offer them up." [[I.e., to make them an offering to God, sacrificing them as an offering.]] Samuel said to him: "God has indeed stripped the kingship from your house, and it will never return to it until the Day of Resurrection!" God then revealed to Samuel: "Set out to Ishai, and he will present his sons to you. Anoint with the holy oil the one I command you to anoint, and he will be king over the Children of Israel." So he set out until he came to Ishai and said: "Present your sons to me!" Ishai called his eldest son, and a tall, handsome man came forward. When Samuel looked at him he was impressed and said: "Praise be to God, indeed God is All-Seeing of His servants!" God revealed to him: "Your eyes see only what is apparent, but I look into what is in the hearts. It is not this one!" He said: "It is not this one." [[The words "He said: 'It is not this one'" are missing from the manuscript and the printed edition; I have restored them from the History.]] "Present another to me." So he presented six, and each time he said: "It is not this one." He said: "Do you have any other sons besides these?" He said: "Yes! I have a ruddy youth, [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "a son was born to me ..."; I have restored what is in the History. The word "amghar" here is not in the manuscript or the printed edition; I have restored it from the History. The amghar is one whose face has redness and whiteness. In the book of that people (1 Samuel, chapter 16) he is described as fair-haired.]] who is a shepherd of the sheep." He said: "Send for him." When David came, a ruddy youth arrived. He anointed him with the holy oil and said to his father: "Keep this secret, for if Saul were to learn of it, he would kill him." Goliath set out with his people towards the Children of Israel and encamped, and Saul marched with the Children of Israel and encamped, and they prepared for battle. Goliath sent to Saul: "Why should my people and your people be killed?" [[In the printed edition: "Why do you kill my people and I kill your people"; I have restored what is in the manuscript and the History.]] "Come out to me, or send out to me whomever you wish. If you kill me, the kingship will be mine, and if I kill you, the kingship will be yours." Saul sent a herald into his army: "Who will come out against Goliath? If he kills him, then the king will marry him to his daughter and make him a partner in his kingdom." [[At this point the report that al-Tabari transmitted in his History, 1: 247–248, of this narration ends.]] Jesse sent David to his brothers. [[Al-Tabari said: "He is Ayshi" (أيشى), but the scholar of hadith said: "Ishi" (إشى).]] [[This interposed sentence is present in the manuscript and was omitted from the printed edition.]] They were in the army, and he said: "Go and provision your brothers, [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "fa-radd" (so return to) your brothers; this is not correct. The correct reading is that he sent him with provisions to his brothers, as already mentioned earlier, and the proper wording is probably "fa-zawwid" (provision them) or "bi-zad ikhwatika" (with provisions for your brothers).]] and tell me the news of the people, what they have done." He came to his brothers and heard a voice: "The king says: Who will come out against Goliath! If he kills him, the king will marry him to his daughter." David said to his brothers: "Is there none among you who will come out against Goliath, kill him, and marry the king's daughter?" They said: "You are a foolish youth! Who can withstand Goliath, for he is one of the remnants of the giants!!" When he saw they were not eager for this, he said: "I will go and kill him!" They rebuked him and were angry with him. When they became heedless of him, he went off until he came to the herald and said: "I will come out against Goliath!" So he was taken to the king, who said to him: "No one answered me except a youth of the Children of Israel, this one!" He said: "My son, will you come out against Goliath and fight him?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Have you sensed anything in yourself?" He said: "Yes. I was a shepherd of the sheep, and a lion attacked me, so I seized it by its jaws and tore them apart." He called for a bow and a full set of equipment; he put it on and mounted the horse, then rode a short distance from them, then turned his horse and returned to the king. The king and those around him said: "The youth has lost his nerve!" He came and stood before the king, who said: "What is your matter?" David said: "If God does not kill him for me, this horse and this weapon will not kill him! So let me fight as I wish." He said: "Yes, my son." David took his satchel, slung it over himself, put stones into it, and took his sling with which he used to tend the flock, [[So it is in the manuscript and the printed edition; it would be more appropriate to say "yarmi bihi" (he hurled with it).]] then set off towards Goliath. When he drew near to his army, he said: "Where is Goliath, that he may come out to me?" So he came out to him on a horse fully armed. When Goliath saw him he said: "Do you come out to me?!" He said: "Yes." He said: "You bring me a sling and stones, as one brings to a dog!" He said: "That is so." He said: "Without doubt, I will divide your flesh among the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth!" David said: "Rather, may God divide your flesh!" David placed a stone in his sling, whirled it, and let it fly towards Goliath. It struck the nose-guard of the helmet that was on Goliath, penetrating until it reached his brain, and he fell from his horse. David went to him and cut off his head with his sword, then came back carrying it in his satchel, dragging his spoils behind him, until he threw it before Saul, and they rejoiced with great joy. Saul departed, and when he was inside the city, the people were mentioning David, and he felt resentment within himself. [["He felt resentment within himself": that is, he was angry, but did not show his anger, and he envied him for what the people were saying about him.]] Then David came to him and said: "Give me my wife!" He said: "Do you want the king's daughter without a dowry?" David said: "You did not stipulate a dowry for me, and I have nothing!!" He said: "I will not burden you with anything beyond your ability. You are a bold man, and in these mountains of ours there are the Jarajima, who plunder people, [[The Jarajima are the Nabataeans of Syria. Ihtarabahu: he robbed him and looted him. He says: they are brigands who seize people's property and plunder them.]] and they are uncircumcised. So if you kill two hundred of them, bring me their foreskins." [[Ghulf (with a dammah and then a sukun) is the plural of aghlaf, meaning one who is uncircumcised. As for "bring me their foreskins" (fa-utni bi-ghulfihim), it is the plural of ghulfah (with a dammah and then a sukun), which is the skin on which circumcision is performed.]] Every time he killed one of them, he strung his foreskin on a thread, until he had strung two hundred foreskins. Then he brought them to Saul and threw them before him. [[In the manuscript: "two hundred foreskins to Saul," with a blank space between them; I have left what is in the printed edition as it stands, since it is a passable context. However, the printed edition had: "Then he brought them to Saul and threw to him," so I have made it as you see.]] He said: "Hand over my wife to me, for I have brought what you stipulated." So he married him to his daughter, [[In the manuscript: "qad ... wa-akthar al-nas" (already ... and most of the people), with a blank after "qad"; I have left what is in the printed edition as it stands, since it fits the context.]] and most people mentioned David, and this increased their amazement at him. [[It seems in the manuscript it reads: "wa-ra'awhu 'inda al-nas 'ajaban" (and they saw him as a marvel among the people), but I could not verify it, so I have left what is in the printed edition as it is, since its meaning is close.]] Saul said to his son: "You must kill David!" He said: "Glory be to God, he is not deserving of that from you!" He said: "You are a foolish youth! I see that he will surely drive you and your family out of the kingship!" When his son heard this from his father, he went to his sister and said to her: "I fear that your father will kill your husband David, so tell him to take his precaution and hide himself from him." His wife told him this, and he hid himself. In the morning, Saul sent someone to summon David, and his wife had arranged on his bed something in the likeness of a sleeper, with his blanket. When Saul's messenger came, he said: "Where is David? Let him answer the king!" She said to them: "He spent the night ill, and now he is asleep; you can see him on the bed." They returned to Saul and told him this. He waited an hour, then sent again, and she said: "He is asleep and has not yet awoken." They returned to the king, who said: "Bring him to me even if he is asleep!" They came to the bed and found no one on it. They went to the king and told him, so he sent for his daughter and said: "What led you to lie?" She said: "He ordered me to do so, and I feared that if I did not carry out his order, he would kill me!" David had fled into the mountain until Saul was killed, and David ruled after him.

5743 – Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: Saul was the commander of the army. Abu David sent David with something to his brothers, and David said to Saul: "What will I receive if I kill Goliath?" He said: "You will receive a third of my kingdom, and I will marry you to my daughter." [[In the printed edition: "a third of my wealth," but in the manuscript: "a third of my kingship (mullî)"; I judged it to be "mulki" (my kingship), because of what will come in the reports Nos. 5744 and 5747.]] So he took his satchel and put three hard stones (marw) in it, [[Marw is the plural of marwah, and al-marw are white, shining stones from which fire can be produced; marw is the hardest of stones.]] then he named those stones: "Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." Then he put his hand in and said: "In the name of my God and the God of my fathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob!" He brought out "Abraham," placed it in his sling, and it pierced thirty-three eggshell-like coverings of the head, and killed thirty thousand behind him.

5744 – Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: On that day, the father of David crossed the river with Saul, along with those who crossed, together with thirteen of his sons, and David was the youngest of his sons. One day he came to him and said: "Father, I do not throw my sling at anything without knocking it down!" He said: "Good news, my son! For God has placed your provision in your sling." Then he came to him again and said: "Father, I entered among the mountains and found a lion lying down, so I mounted it and seized it by its ears, and it did not frighten me!" [[To frighten (hāja) something (yahīju): to disturb it and make it flee. It means: it did not drive me away from my place there.]] He said: "Good news, my son! For this is a good thing God has given you." Then he came to him another day and said: "Father, I walk among the mountains and glorify God, and no mountain remains without glorifying God along with me!" He said: "Good news, my son! For this is a good thing God has bestowed on you." David was a shepherd, and his father used to come after him, bringing food to him and his brothers. [[In the History of al-Tabari: "yatī abāhu wa-ilā ikhwatihi" (he comes to his father and to his brothers), but the correct reading is what is in the commentary.]] The Prophet [[The words "The Prophet ... " to the end of the sentence give the impression that it is cut off, but it is not so; al-Tabari, as is his custom, divides the report and distributes it among various places in his commentary. This report here is the completion of the earlier reports: 5720 and 5732, as we pointed out in the note there, and as we will point out again later. The Prophet is Shamun (Simeon), as passed in those reports.]] [peace be upon him] came with a horn containing oil, [[See the explanation of "qarn" (horn) above: 307, note 1.]] and a coat of mail of iron [[In the printed edition: "a garment of iron" (wa-thawb min hadid), and similarly in al-Durr al-Manthur, which is an error. In the manuscript in all the following places, in al-Tabari's History, and in al-Baghawi's commentary it reads: "tannur min hadid" (an oven of iron). The tannur is a type of stove, which is not suitable here. As for "sannur" (with a fatha on the sin, the nun, and a shaddah on the waw), it is a leather garment made of hide (the tanned skin) worn in battle like a coat of mail. This is supported by what was narrated just above, p. 358, that David was brought a coat of mail and it was thrown over his neck, and by what will come in Nos. 5746 and 5747.]] and sent it to Saul, saying: "The one among you who will kill Goliath, this horn will be placed on his head, and it will boil until it is anointed with it, not running down over his face, and it will be on his head like a crown, and he will enter this sannur and fill it." [[In the printed edition: "wa-thawb min hadid" (and a garment of iron), and it is an error; in the manuscript, in all the following places, in al-Tabari's History and in al-Baghawi's commentary: "tannur min hadid" (an oven of iron). The tannur is a type of stove, which is not suitable here. As for "sannur" (with a fatha on the sin, the nun, and a shaddah on the waw), it is a leather garment made of hide (the tanned skin) worn in battle like a coat of mail. This is supported by what was narrated just above, p. 358, that David was brought a coat of mail and it was thrown over his neck, and by what will come in Nos. 5746 and 5747.]] Saul summoned the Children of Israel and tested them with it, but none of them fit it. [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "fa-jarrabahum fa-lam yuwāfiquhu" (he tested them, and it did not fit him), with "bihi" (with it) omitted; I have restored it from the History.]] When they had finished, Saul said to David's father: "Do you have any son left who has not attended us?" He said: "Yes! My son David remains, and he brings us food." [[In the printed edition: "bi-ta'āmina" (our food); I have restored what is in the manuscript and the History.]] When David came to him, he passed three stones on the road, which spoke to him and said: "Take us, David, and with us you will kill Goliath!" He said: he took them and placed them in his satchel. Saul had said: "Whoever kills Goliath, I will marry him to my daughter, and I will make his ring part of my kingdom." When David came, they placed the horn on his head, and it boiled until it was anointed with it, and he put on the sannur and filled it. [[He was a sickly man, and pale-faced: a sickly man (rajul musqam), and a sickly woman (imra'ah musqam) likewise, meaning one who is often ill and hardly recovers. Musfar comes from the expression "is-far lawnuhu" (his colour turned yellow), which is due to sickness and weakness.]] No one could put it on except that he was shaken by it. When David put it on, the garment tightened around him until it split. [[It is said: "tanaqqadat al-ghurfah" (the room split) and other things: they cracked, and a sound was heard, which is the noise of breaking and cracking.
In the printed edition it reads "yanqud" with a lower dot (yā' tahtiyya), but the correct form, from the manuscript and the History, is with the letter as in the manuscript.]] Then he walked towards Goliath. [[Goliath was among the largest and strongest of men.]] When Goliath looked at David, terror of him was cast into his heart, and he said: "Youth! Go back, for I have mercy on you and do not want to kill you!" David said: "No, rather I will kill you!" He took out the stones and put them into the sling, and each time he raised a stone he named it. [[I added "minha" (from them) from the History.]] He said: "This is in the name of my father Abraham, the second in the name of my father Isaac, and the third in the name of my father Israel." Then he whirled the sling, and the stones became one stone; then he released it and it struck between Goliath's eyes, and I pierced his head and killed him. [[In the printed edition: "fa-naqaba ra'sahu fa-qatalahu" (he pierced his head and killed him); the correct form is from the History and, with some error, from the manuscript.]] Then it continued to kill every person it hit, passing through him, until no one remained alive from it. They were routed then, and David killed Goliath, and Saul returned. Saul married David to his daughter and made his ring part of his kingdom. The people turned towards David and loved him. When Saul saw this, he resented it and envied him, and wanted to kill him. David learned that he intended this, so he laid a skin of wine in his bed. [[To cover (sajā) something or a dead person: to cover it and spread a cloth over it. The zaq (with a kasrah on the zay) is a goatskin flayed from one leg, and from its head and neck, then treated until it becomes a water-skin; they most often used it for wine.]] Saul entered David's sleeping place, while David had fled, and struck the skin a blow that split it, so the wine poured out of it, and a drop of wine fell into his mouth. He said: "May God have mercy on David! How much he drank of wine!!" Then David came to him on the following night in his house while he was asleep, and placed two arrows at his head, at his feet, and on his right and left, two arrows each, [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "sahmayn" (two arrows) only once; I have restored what is in the History, which is correct. The words "then he went down" (thumma nazal) afterwards are an addition from the History, not in the manuscript or the printed edition.]] then he went down. When Saul awoke, he saw the arrows and recognised them, and said: "May God have mercy on David! He is better than me: I had him in my power and killed him, but he had me in his power and spared me!" Then he rode one day and found him walking in the wilderness, while Saul was on a horse. Saul said: "Today I will kill David!" [[When David was alarmed, he could not be overtaken.]] So Saul spurred his horse after him, and David was frightened and ran, and he entered a cave. [[Ishtadda: he ran swiftly. Al-shadd: swift running.]] God revealed to the spider, and it spun a web over him. When Saul reached the cave, he looked at the spider's web and said: "If he had entered here, he would have torn the spider's web!!" It seemed to him [[The phrase "khayyala ilayhi" (it seemed to him) means that doubt entered his mind about the matter, because it was unclear to him. I did not find this expression verbatim in the lexicons, but it is sound Arabic, from the expression "akhāla al-shay'" (the thing became confused).]] so he left him alone. [[The report 5744 is the completion of the earlier reports which I pointed out in the note on the two reports 5720 and 5732, as I pointed out above in the nearby notes. It is in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 319 and in al-Baghawi's commentary (in the margin of Ibn Kathir) 1: 604–608, with different wording, though close to it.]]

5745. Related to me from Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: It was mentioned to us that when Dawud (David) came to them, he had with him a pouch (makhla) containing three stones. Jalut (Goliath) came forward against them and called out: "Is there no man to come out against a man?" Talut (Saul) said: "Who will come out against him? Or shall I come out against him?" Dawud stood up and said: "I will!" Talut had him put on his coat of mail, and [Dawud] began to see that it rose and lifted him up. [[Shakhasa yashkhusu shukhusan: rose up and became high.]] Talut was amazed at this, so he put on him all his equipment. Dawud threw at them one of those stones, and it struck among the people. Then he threw a second stone and it struck among them. Then he threw the third and killed Jalut. God gave him kingship and wisdom and taught him of what He willed, and he became their leader, and they gave him their obedience.

5746. Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd related to me concerning the words of God, may He be remembered: ﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel?﴾ And he recited until he reached: ﴿Then when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them. And God is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾ He said: God revealed to their prophet: "Among the sons of so-and-so there is a man by whom God will kill Jalut. His sign is this horn: when you place it on his head, water will flow [from it]." So [the prophet] came to him and said: "God has revealed to me that among your sons there is a man [[In the printed edition: 'that among the sons of so-and-so...' again; the correct reading is from the manuscript and the History.]] by whom God will kill Jalut!" He said: "Yes, O Prophet of God!" He said: So he brought out to him twelve men like pillars, [[Sawari is the plural of sariya: a pillar, of stone or baked brick. A hadith says that he forbade joining the pillars, which are the pillars of the mosque, during congregational prayer, because it breaks the row.]] and among them was a man outstanding over them. [[Bara'a yabra'u fa-huwa bari': he became complete in every excellence and beauty, and surpassed his companions in knowledge and other things. It is said: a bariah woman, meaning one surpassing in beauty and intellect. Every person who rises above and excels is bari' and fari'. In the History, "bari'" appears without "alayhim", and both are the same; a description of him as "al-Jasim" will come shortly, and the two have close meanings.]] He began to present them to the horn, but it showed nothing, so he would say to that tall man: "Go back!" and he would send him back. God revealed to him: "We do not take men according to their appearance, but We take them according to the soundness of their hearts." He said: "O Lord, he claims that he has no son other than him!" He said: "He lied!" [The prophet] said: "My Lord has indeed called you a liar, and says that you have another son besides them!" He said: "He has spoken truly, O Prophet of God. [[In the printed edition: "Sadaqa" without "qad"; it is in the manuscript and the History.]] I have a short son whom I was ashamed for people to see, so I put him with the sheep!" He said: "Where is he?" He said: "In the ravine of such-and-such, on the mountain of such-and-such." So [the prophet] went out to him and found that the valley had flooded between him and the spot to which he used to bring his flock back [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "between him and that which he used to bring back...": the correct reading is from the History. Arahha ghanamahu and ablahu yurihuha irahatan: he returned it to its pen where it would shelter at night. Al-mariah (with a damma on the m): the shelter of camels and sheep.
