It is from ar-rawah, which is traveling in the evening.]] He said: He found him carrying two goats, crossing with them and not wading through the flood. [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "carrying two goats, crossing with them, and not wading", with "two goats" and the second [word] omitted, and the printed edition dropped the first "al-sayl". I have kept what is in the History, which is correct. It is said: "jaza al-makan wa-ajazahu" with the same meaning. In the hadith of the Sirat: "I and my community will be the first to cross over it" with a damma on the ya'.]] When he saw him, he said: "This is he, without doubt! This one has mercy on animals, so he is even more merciful to people!" He said: So he placed the horn on his head and it poured forth water. [[At this point what al-Tabari transmitted in his History from this lengthy report ends. 1:247.]] Then [the prophet] said to him: "Nephew, have you seen anything here that amazes you?" [[A'jabahu al-amr ya'jibuhu: he drew out his wonder at it, as he saw it as a marvellous matter.]] He said: "Yes, when I glorify God, the mountains glorify Him with me; and when a leopard or a wolf or a beast of prey comes and takes a sheep, I stand up to it and open its jaws to get it back, and it does not frighten me!" He said: And he found with him his pouch. [[In the printed edition, "qal" [he said] was dropped between the two statements; it is indispensable, because the report is not continuous, as you will see in what follows: "He said: He passed by..." meaning Dawud. The sifn (with a damma and sukun) is the shepherd's bag, in which his food, provisions and whatever else he needs are kept.]] He said: He passed by three stones which were pushing against one another, [[In the printed edition: "ya'thiru ba'duha 'ala ba'd", which is meaningless. In the manuscript it is "yantari" without dots, and this is the correct reading. Intazā Fulan 'ala Fulan and tanaza 'alayhi: to rush against someone with evil and to leap at each other; from an-nazw, which is leaping.]] each one of them saying: "I am the one who will be taken!" And this one says: "No! It is me that he will take!" And the other says the same. He said: So he took them all and threw them into his pouch. When he came with the Prophet ﷺ and they went out, their prophet said to them: "God has indeed sent Talut as king," so there was [the story] of their prophet and their story, as God mentioned in His Book, and he recited until he reached: ﴿And God is with the patient.﴾ He said: Their affair became united, and they were all together, and he recited: ﴿And help us against the disbelieving people.﴾ [[At this point ends a part of the old division from which our copy was taken, and in it is the following text: "Followed by: And Jalut came out on a piebald steed, in his hand a bow and arrow. And God bless Muhammad the Prophet and his family, abundantly." Then after that: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Compassionate. O Lord, make it easy."]] Jalut came out on a piebald steed, [[In the printed edition: "qaws wa-nushshab" (a bow and arrows); I have kept what is in the manuscript.]] in his hand a bow and arrows, and he said: "Who will come out? Send out your leader to me!" He said: Talut was terrified by him. He said: He turned to his companions and said: "Who is the man who will spare me Jalut today?" Dawud said: "I will." He said: "Come!" He said: So [Talut] removed a coat of mail of his and put it on him. He said: And God breathed of His spirit into him until He filled him. He said: Then [Jalut] shot an arrow, and it landed in the coat of mail. He said: Dawud broke it, and it did him no harm, three times. Then he said to him: "Take now!" Dawud said: "O God, make them one stone!" He said: And he named one Ibrahim, another Ishaq, and another Ya'qub. He said: So he gathered them all together, and they became one stone. He said: He took them and took a sling, and he whirled it to throw it. [Jalut] said: "Will you throw at me as a beast of prey or a wolf throws? Throw at me with the bow!" He said: "I will not throw at you today except with this!" [Jalut] said the same thing to him again, and he said: "Yes! And you are less to me than a wolf!" So he whirled it, and in it was the command of God and the authority of God. He said: Then he released it, sent forth. He said: It came as a shadow and struck between his eyes until it came out of the back of his head. [[Azalla al-shay' yazillu: it came near and approached. In the hadith of Malik: "When he approached, arriving, a grief came over me."]] Then [the stone] killed from his companions behind him so many and so many, and God routed them.

5747. Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: When they crossed that [river]—meaning the river about which God said, relating the words of Talut to his soldiers: ﴿Indeed God will test you with a river﴾—and Jalut came, and fighting him was difficult for Talut, Talut said to the people: "If Jalut is killed, I will give whoever kills him half of my kingdom, and I will share with him everything I own!" So God sent Dawud—and Dawud at that time was a shepherd of sheep on the mountain, and nine brothers of Dawud had gone out to fight with Talut, and they were more robust than him [[In the printed edition: "anad minhu". It shows no meaning. In the manuscript it is "anad" without dots, and I read it so as from "al-badad", which is the breadth between the shoulders, the bulk of the frame, and the wide separation between the limbs. This is the description of his brothers as mentioned in earlier reports. This is according to them saying in the description: "a man abad, and a woman bada'".]] and richer than him, [[In the printed edition: "a'tā minhu" (more hostile than him); in the manuscript: "a'nā minhu", and the correct reading seems to be what I have given.]] and more known among the people than him, and more honoured with Talut than him. They went out to fight, leaving him with their sheep. Dawud said, when God cast into his soul what He cast and honoured him: "Today I will entrust my Lord with my sheep, and I will go to the people, and I will look at what has reached me of the king's words concerning the one who kills Jalut!" So Dawud came to his brothers, and they blamed him when he came to them. They said: "Why have you come?" He said: "To kill Jalut, for God is able that I should kill him." [[Qadir from their saying: "qadara Allah al-shay'" and "qaddarahu": He decreed it, ordained it.]] So they mocked him. [[Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid said: Abu Dawud had sent something to his brothers with Dawud, so he took a pouch and put three mirwas in it, then named them "Ibrahim", "Ishaq", and "Ya'qub". Ibn Jurayj said: They said: He was weak and of poor condition, so he passed by three stones, and they said to him: "Take us, O Dawud, and fight Jalut with us!" So Dawud took them and put them in his pouch. When he put them in, he heard one of them say to its companion: "I am the stone of Harun, by which such-and-such a king was killed." The second said: "I am the stone of Musa, by which such-and-such a king was killed." The third said: "I am the stone of Dawud, by which Jalut will be killed!" The two stones said: "O stone of Dawud, we are helpers for you!" So they became one stone. And the stone said: "O Dawud, throw me, for I will seek help from the wind"—and his helmet, as they say, and God knows best, contained six hundred pounds—"and I will fall on Jalut's head and kill him!" Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid said: He named one Ibrahim, another Ishaq, and the other Ya'qub, and said: "In the name of my God and the God of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub!" And he put them in his sling. [[What is between the two lines is a parenthetical statement inserted within the stone's speech. The pronoun in "baydatihi" refers to Jalut.]]—Ibn Jurayj said: So he set off until he reached Talut and said: "You have made for whoever kills Jalut half of your kingdom and half of everything you own! Is that binding on you if I kill him?" He said: "Yes!" The people were mocking Dawud, and the brothers of Dawud were more severe against him than that. [[Qawl: "anta"... Talut did not appoint anyone who claimed he would kill Jalut without putting on him a coat of mail that he had with him; then if he was not capable of it, he would take it off him. [[Al-qadr (with fatha and fatha or sukun): the measure, meaning according to his measure and his size.]] It was a full coat of mail of Talut's armour, so he put it on Dawud, and when he saw it fitted him, he ordered him to advance. Dawud advanced and stood in a position where no one could stand, wearing the coat of mail. Jalut said to him: "Woe to you! Who are you? I pity you! Let another of these kings come forward against me! You are a weak, pitiful human being! Go back!" Dawud said: "I am the one who will kill you by God's leave, and I will not turn back until I kill you!" When Dawud refused anything but fighting him, Jalut advanced toward him to take him with his hand, confident of overpowering him. Dawud took the stone out of the pouch, called upon his Lord, and threw it at him with the stone. The wind knocked his helmet off his head, and the stone fell on Jalut's head until it entered his inside and killed him. [[Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid said: When Jalut was struck by the stone, it broke through thirty-three helmets from his head, and it killed thirty thousand behind him. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And Dawud killed Jalut.﴾ Dawud then said to Talut: "Fulfil for me what you promised." [[In the printed edition: "Wa-fa bima ja'alta" (and fulfil what you promised); in the manuscript: "wa-li bima ja'alta" (and to me what you promised). The correct reading is what I have given. "Fa" is the imperative of their saying: "wafā lahu bi-l-shay' yafī": he fulfilled to him with the thing. It is an imperative of one letter.]] But Talut refused to give him that. So Dawud departed and settled in a city of the cities of the Children of Israel until Talut died. When Talut died, the Children of Israel turned to Dawud, came to him, and made him king, and gave him the treasuries of Talut, and said: "No one kills Jalut except a prophet!" God said: ﴿And Dawud killed Jalut, and God gave him the kingship and wisdom and taught him of what He willed.﴾

* *

Discussion of the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And God gave him the kingship and wisdom and taught him of what He willed.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may He be remembered, He means: God gave Dawud the kingship and wisdom and taught him of what He willed. The pronoun in His words "wa-atahu Allah" refers to Dawud. "Al-mulk" is the authority, and "al-hikmah" is prophethood. [[See the explanation of "al-mulk" in what has preceded: 1:148–150; 2:488; and this: 311, 312, 314.]] [[See the explanation of "al-hikmah" in what has preceded: 3:87, 88, 211; and this: 16, 17.]] And His words "wa-allamahu mimma yasha'" mean: He taught him the craft of making coats of mail and measuring in the weaving, as God, may He be remembered, said: ﴿And We taught him the making of armour for you, to protect you from your violence.﴾ [Surah al-Anbiya: 80.]

* *

It has been said that the meaning of His words: "And God gave him the kingship and wisdom" is that God gave Dawud the kingdom of Talut and the prophethood of Samuel.

Mention of those who said this:

5748. Musa related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, who said: Dawud was made king after he had killed Talut, and God made him a prophet, and this is His words: "And God gave him the kingship and wisdom." He said: The wisdom is prophethood; He gave him the prophethood of Shamun and the kingship of Talut.

* *

Discussion of the interpretation of His words: ﴿And were it not that God repels some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted, but God is full of bounty toward the worlds (251).﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may He be remembered, He means: Were it not that God repels some people—those who are people of obedience to Him and faith in Him—from others, who are people of disobedience to God and association with Him—just as He repelled from those who stayed behind Talut on the day of Jalut, from among the people of disbelief in God and disobedience to Him—and He had given them what they had asked their Lord from the outset, namely the sending of a king over them so that they might fight with him in His way—by means of those who fought with him from among the people of faith in God, certainty and patience, [namely] Jalut and his soldiers. [[The structure of this sentence: "as He repelled from those who stayed behind Jalut ... by means of those who fought with him ... Jalut and his soldiers," in the manner of Abu Ja'far in long consecutive passages.]] "The earth would have been corrupted," meaning: its people would have perished by God's punishment upon them, and the earth would thereby have been corrupted. [[See the meaning of "corruption" in what has preceded: 1:287, 416; 4:239, 243, 244.]] But God is full of favour upon His creation and of graciousness toward them, by repelling with the righteous among His creatures the wicked, with the obedient the disobedient among them, and with the believer the disbeliever.

* *

This verse is a declaration from God, may He be remembered, to the hypocrites who were in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, who stayed behind from his battles and from fighting with him because of the doubt in their souls and the sickness of their hearts, and to the polytheists and disbelievers among them. It informs them that the punishment for their disbelief and hypocrisy is delayed only by the faith of the believers in Him and His Messenger—those who are people of insight and resolve in God's affair, and possessors of certainty that God will fulfil His promise to them in fighting His enemies and the enemies of His Messenger, [granting them] victory in this world and success in His gardens in the next. [[In the printed edition: "in the Hereafter"; in the manuscript: "fi al-akhar". Had he intended it that way he would have said: "from victory in the present life, and success in His gardens in the Hereafter." But I find it a corruption of what I have given.]]

* *

Ahl al-ta'wil (the people of interpretation) have said in accordance with what we have said concerning this.

Mention of those who said that:

5749. Muhammad ibn Umar related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning God's words: "And were it not that God repels some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted." He says: And were it not that God repels by the righteous from the wicked, and by the remnant of the descendants of people, some of them from others, "the earth would have been corrupted" by the destruction of its people. [[In the printed edition: "bi-l-bar" with the printed text "bi-l-bar" or "al-bar"; I have kept what is in the manuscript.]]

5750. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And were it not that God repels the people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted." He says: And were it not for God's repelling by the righteous from the wicked, and by the remnant of the descendants of people, some of them from others [[In the manuscript and in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:320: "akhlaq al-nas", and "al-akhlaf" is the plural of khalaf, meaning those who succeeded the righteous, from among the people of righteousness, piety and God-fearing.]], [the earth] would have perished through its people.

5751. Ibn Waki' related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Handhala, from Abu Muslim, who said: I heard 'Ali say: "Were it not for a remnant of the Muslims among you, you would have perished."

5752. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' concerning His words: "And were it not that God repels some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted," he says: Whoever is on the earth would have perished.

Abu Humayd al-Himsi Ahmad ibn al-Mughira narrated to me, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Hafs ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Suqa, from Wabra ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, God repels calamity from a hundred households of the neighbours of a righteous believer because of him." Then Ibn Umar recited: ﴿And had God not repelled some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted﴾.

[[The hadith: 5753. Ahmad ibn al-Mughira, Abu Humayd al-Himsi, Tabari's teacher: he is Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Mughira ibn Sayyar, cited here by his grandfather's name. He is reliable (thiqa). Al-Nasa'i narrated from him and declared him reliable. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded him at 1/1/72 under the name "Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Sayyar" and said: "He wrote from him, and he is truthful and reliable."
Yahya ibn Sa'id: al-Attar al-Ansari, Abu Zakariyya, al-Shami al-Himsi. Ibn Ma'in and others declared him weak. Abu Dawud said: "jaiz al-hadith" (acceptable in narration). Muhammad ibn Musaffa al-Himsi, the hafiz, said: "Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Attar narrated to us, and he is reliable." So his fellow townsman and student declares him reliable, and it is presumed that he knows him better than others. Al-Bukhari mentioned him in al-Kabir 4/2/277 without mentioning any criticism. Ibn Hibban, in al-Majruhin, was extremely rash without proof, saying: "He was among those who narrated fabrications from reliable narrators and problematic reports from trustworthy ones. It is not permissible to argue with him in any way, nor to narrate from him except for consideration by specialists."
Hafs ibn Sulayman: al-Asadi al-Bazzaz al-Kufi al-Qari, the transmitter of the well-known "reading of Hafs," by which people recite in Egypt and elsewhere. He is very weak and abandoned in narration, despite his eminence in recitation. I have explained his weakness in detail in my commentary on the Musnad: 1267.
Muhammad ibn Suqa (with a damma on the unpointed sin): al-Ghanawi al-Kufi al-Abid: reliable, and agreed upon.
Wabra ibn Abd al-Rahman: a known reliable Successor (tabi'i), from whom the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others narrated.
Ibn Kathir mentioned the hadith at 1: 606-607 from this passage and said: "This isnad is weak, for this Yahya ibn Sa'id is al-Attar al-Himsi, who is very weak."
Al-Dhahabi also mentioned it in al-Mizan, under the biography of "Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Attar," 3: 290, from this Yahya with this isnad.]]

Ahmad Abu Humayd al-Himsi narrated to me, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Uthman ibn Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, God reforms through the righteousness of a Muslim man his children, his grandchildren, the people of his household and the households around him, and they remain under God's protection as long as he is among them."

[[The hadith: 5754. Uthman ibn Abd al-Rahman: thus in Ibn Kathir's transmission of it from this passage. It may be "Uthman ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Umar ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas al-Madani," who belongs to the same generation, but he is not mentioned among the teachers of Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Attar, nor among those who narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir. I have not found, among those biographers of the name "Uthman ibn Abd al-Rahman" whom I have seen, anyone through whom the isnad can be made consistent other than him.
This Waqqasi (i.e., Uthman ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Waqqasi): very weak. Ibn Ma'in accused him of lying. Abu Hatim said: "Abandoned in narration, lost in narration, a liar." Al-Bukhari said in al-Du'afa' (p. 25): "They abandoned him."
In my view, the more likely conclusion is that the name of this narrator is distorted in the copies of Tabari. I almost conclude that the correct reading is "Anbasa ibn Abd al-Rahman," for he is the one who narrates from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, and Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Attar narrates from him.
This may be supported by the fact that the copyist of the manuscript wrote this name without an alif after the mim, in the old style of the scribes, as "Uthman." But it appears that he wrote it hesitantly, from a copy whose writing was unclear, because he stretched the end of the word, writing the nun extended so that it looked like a sin, and then the name became confusing to him, so he made the extended letter into a nun. Changing the two letters before it is easy: one points the nun with three dots, making it a thelth (ث), and then turns the ba' so that it becomes a mim. The name thus moves from "Anbasa" to "Uthman."
Whichever the narrator here is, "Uthman" or "Anbasa," the hadith has a feeble and collapsed isnad with no standing.
As for "Anbasa ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Anbasa ibn Sa'id ibn al-As": very weak. Abu Hatim said: "He is abandoned in narration; he used to fabricate hadith." The name of his grandfather is also "Anbasa" like his own. In the Tahdhib it is wrongly written as "Uyayna," which is a typographical error.
Ibn Kathir mentioned the hadith at 1: 607 and said: "This too is strange and weak, for the same reason mentioned earlier!" He means the weakness of "Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Attar." We have already shown in the previous hadith that he is not weak.
Al-Suyuti mentioned it at 1: 320, and attributed it to Tabari "with a weak isnad." Then he attributed it to no one other than Tabari.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We have already shown the meaning of His saying "the worlds" (al-'alamin) and cited the narration concerning it. [[See what has passed: 1: 143-146 / 2: 23-26.]]

* *

As for the recitations (qira'at, the variant modes of reciting the Qur'an), they differ concerning the recitation of His saying: "And had God not repelled some people by means of others."

A group of reciters recited it as ﴿ولولا دفعُ الله﴾, in the form of the verbal noun (masdar), from the saying of the speaker: "God repelled from His creation, so He repels repulsion (daf'an)." They argued for their choice of this by saying that God, may His mention be exalted, is the One who alone repels from His creation, and no one contends with Him to overpower Him.

* *

Another group of reciters recited it as ﴿ولولا دِفَاعُ الله الناسَ﴾ [[In the printed edition: "another group of reciters," and I have kept what is in the manuscript.]], also in the form of the verbal noun, from the saying of the speaker: "God contended against His creation, so He contends (yudafi'u) with contention (mudafa'a) and defence (difa'an)." They argued for their choice of this by saying that many of His creatures oppose the people of God's religion and His guardianship and the believers in Him. By their fighting them and opposing them, they contend with God through their conjectures [[In the printed edition: "by their falsehood," and I have kept what is in the manuscript.]] and overpower Him through their ignorance, while God contends with them on behalf of His allies, the people of His obedience and faith in Him.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The view I hold on this matter is that both are recitations that the reciters have recited and that the community as a whole has transmitted, and that there is no contradiction of meaning in recitation by either of the two readings. For whoever defends something against another defends it with some means of defence. [[In the printed edition: "his contender is a defender of it," but in the manuscript the phrase is "his contention on it is not a defender," which is unclear; the correct reading is what I have given. This is because God defended the unbelievers from what was guaranteed to the believers of victory, by means of some people. So it is established that Tabari's expression requires that the word be "with something."]] And when the one repelled is prevented from being repelled, he is a defender for his contender. There is no doubt that Jalut and his soldiers, in fighting Talut and his soldiers, were attempting to overpower the party of God and His army, and in their attempt there was an attempt to overpower God and to contend against Him concerning what He had guaranteed them of victory. This is the meaning of "God's contending" concerning those whom God defended through those among His allies who fought Jalut and his soldiers. It is clear, then, that the recitation of whoever recites ﴿وَلَوْلا دَفْعُ اللَّهِ النَّاسَ بَعْضَهُمْ بِبَعْضٍ﴾ and the recitation of whoever recites ﴿ولولا دفاع الله الناس بعضهم ببعض﴾ are equivalent in interpretation and meaning. [[In the printed edition: "so it is clear," and the correct reading is from the manuscript.]]

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These are the verses of Allah which We recite to you in truth, and indeed you are among the messengers﴾ (2:252).

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "These are the verses of Allah" [[See the use of "dhalika" and "tilka" meaning "this" and "these" in what has passed: 1:225-227 / 3:335.]], exalted is His remembrance, He means: these are the verses in which Allah has related the account of those who went out from their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death, and the account of the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, who asked their prophet to send them Talut as king, and what follows of the verses up to His saying, "And Allah is Bountiful to the worlds."

By His saying, "the verses of Allah," He means His proofs, His signs, and His evidences. [[See the explanation of "al-ayah" in what has passed: 1:106, then this part: 337, and the references in the note there.]]

* *

Allah, exalted is His remembrance, says: So these proofs which I have informed you of, O Muhammad, and made you know of, are: My power to cause to die those who fled from death in a single moment, though they were thousands, and My giving them life after that; and My making Talut ruler over the Children of Israel, after he had been a water-carrier or a tanner, not of the people of the house of kingship; and My taking that kingship away from him because of his disobedience to My command, and My transferring his kingship to Dawud because of his obedience to Me; and My granting victory to the companions of Talut, despite their small number and weakness of strength, over Jalut and his soldiers, despite their great number and severity of might. [[In the printed edition: "proofs against those who denied," and I have retained what is in the manuscript. The context: "So these proofs ... are My proofs."]] These are My proofs against those who denied My blessing, opposed My command, and disbelieved in My messenger from among the People of the Two Books, the Torah and the Gospel, who know what I have related to you of the hidden reports, which they know to be from Me.

You did not fabricate them or invent them yourself, O Muhammad, because you are unlettered, and you are not one who has read the books, so that their affair would be confused for them, and they would claim that you read that and learned it from some of their scriptures. Rather, they are My proofs against them, which I recite to you, O Muhammad, in certain truth, just as it was, without any addition to it, without any distortion, and without any alteration of anything from what it was. "And indeed you," O Muhammad, "are among the messengers," meaning: you are truly a messenger who follows obedience to Me and prefers My pleasure over your own desire. So in this matter, the path of those messengers before you who stood firm in My command and preferred My pleasure over their own desires, whom the desires and the worldly greed did not alter, is your path, just as Talut's desire altered him, and his preference for his kingship over what I have with the people of My guardianship. But you prefer My command, as the messengers before you preferred it.

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those messengers — some of them We preferred over others. Among them are those to whom Allah spoke, and some of them He raised in rank.﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His words, "Those," exalted is His remembrance, He means the messengers whose stories Allah related in this surah, such as Musa ibn 'Imran, Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Shamwil, Dawud, and all others whose accounts are mentioned in this surah. He, exalted is His remembrance, says: These are My messengers, some of whom I preferred over others. I spoke to some of them, and the one to whom He spoke among them was Musa (ﷺ). And He raised some of them in rank above others through honour and elevated status, as follows:

5755 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the words of Allah, exalted is His remembrance: ﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others﴾. He said: He says: Among them is one to whom Allah spoke, and He raised some of them above others in rank. He means: Allah spoke to Musa, and sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to mankind entirely.

5756 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

* *

Among what indicates the correctness of what we have said on this matter:

5757 - The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I have been given five things that no one before me was given: I was sent to the red and the black (people); I was supported with awe, so that the enemy is struck with fear of me at a distance of a month's journey; the earth was made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification; spoils of war were made lawful for me, though they were not lawful for anyone before me; and it was said to me: Ask, and you will be given. So I kept my request as an intercession for my community, and it will reach those among you, if Allah wills, who do not associate anything with Allah."

[[The report: 5757 — he related it without a chain of narration, and its wording varies. It is from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas in the Musnad, no. 2742, and the Musnad 5: 145, 147, 148, 161, 162 (Halabi edition), and al-Mustadrak 2: 424. Muslim narrated it without this wording, 5: 3, and al-Bukhari (al-Fath 1: 369, 444) in other places. It is a sound hadith.]]

* *

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave 'Isa, son of Maryam, the clear proofs, and We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His remembrance, "And We gave 'Isa, son of Maryam, the clear proofs," He means: We gave 'Isa, son of Maryam, the proofs and evidences of his prophethood, such as healing the blind and the leper, reviving the dead, and similar things, along with the Gospel that I sent down to him, in which I clarified what I had obligated upon him.[[In the printed and manuscript editions: "He, exalted is His remembrance, means by that," which is not correct.]][[See the explanation of "clear proofs" (al-bayyinat) above, 2: 328 / 4: 271, and the references there; and see the index of language.]]

* *

By His words, exalted is His remembrance, "And We strengthened him," He means: We supported him and helped him,[[See the explanation of "ayyada" above, 2: 319, 320.]] "with the Holy Spirit," meaning the Spirit of Allah, who is Jibril. We have already mentioned the disagreement of the scholars concerning the meaning of "the Holy Spirit," and what is most correct of the statements on this matter earlier, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it in this place.[[See what has preceded, 2: 320–323.]]

* *

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if Allah had willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: By this, exalted is His remembrance, He means: And if Allah had willed, ﴿those who came after them would not have fought﴾[[In the printed edition, the verse is completed as: "after the clear proofs came to them." I have kept what is in the manuscript.]] — meaning after the messengers whom He described as having preferred some over others and raised some in rank, and after 'Isa son of Maryam. Signs had come to them with what is a deterrent for whomever Allah guides and grants success.

* *

By His words, "after the clear proofs had come to them," He means: after there had come to them signs from Allah that made the truth clear to them and displayed the path for them.

* *

It has been said that the "ha'" and the "mim" in His words, "after them," refer to Musa and 'Isa. Those who said this:

5758 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada: ﴿And if Allah had willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them﴾, he said: means: after Musa and 'Isa.

5759 - It was reported to me from 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', his words: ﴿And if Allah had willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them﴾, he said: means: after Musa and 'Isa.

* *

**The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿But they differed, so among them were those who believed and among them were those who disbelieved. And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought one another; but Allah does what He wills﴾ (2:253)**

Abu Ja'far said: By this, exalted is His remembrance, He means: But these people who came after the messengers differed, because Allah, exalted is His remembrance, did not will that they not fight one another. So they fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them from their Lord forbidding fighting and disagreement, and after the proof had been established against them regarding the oneness of Allah, the prophethood of His messengers, and the revelation of His Book. Thus some of them disbelieved in Allah and His signs, and some of them believed in that. So He, exalted is His remembrance, informed that they committed what they committed of disbelief and disobedience, after knowing that the proof had been established against them that they were in error, deliberately choosing disbelief in Allah and His signs.[[In the manuscript: "they committed what was sent down of disbelief," which is an obvious error from the scribe's great haste, as is clearly seen from the change in his handwriting at this point as well.]]

Then He, exalted is His remembrance, said to His servants: ﴿And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought﴾, meaning: And if Allah had willed to restrain them — by His protection and His granting of success to them — from disobeying Him, they would not have fought, and they would not have fought or differed. ﴿But Allah does what He wills﴾, by granting success to this one to obey Him and believe in Him, so he believes in Him and obeys Him, and by forsaking that one, so he disbelieves in Him and disobeys Him.

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 2, Verse 254:

On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, spend from what We have provided you, before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession. And the disbelievers—they are the wrongdoers.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: O you who believe, spend in the way of Allah from what We have provided you of your wealth, and give charity from it, and render from it the rights which We have made obligatory upon you. Thus Ibn Juraij used to say, as has reached us from him:

5760 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, regarding His words: "O you who believe, spend from what We have provided you" — he said: from the zakat and voluntary charity.

* *

"Before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession" — he says: Store up for yourselves with Allah in your worldly life from your wealth, by spending from it in the way of Allah, giving charity to the needy and the poor, and paying what Allah has made obligatory upon you concerning it. And purchase with it what is with Him, what He has prepared for His friends of honour, by sending that forward for yourselves while you still have the means to purchase it, through what He has urged you to and commanded you with regarding spending from your wealth. "Before there comes a Day in which there is no trade" — meaning: before the coming of a Day in which there is no trade. He says: On it you will not be able to purchase what you were able to purchase in the world—by spending from your wealth which He has provided you, by what He commanded you or urged you to, while you were capable—because it is a Day of recompense, reward and punishment, not a day of action, earning, obedience and disobedience. So there will be no way for you then to purchase the dwellings of the people of honour by spending, or by acting in obedience to Allah, [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "فيكون لهم إلى ابتياع ..." and the correct reading in this context is "لكم"; the word "سبيل" is the subject of "كان" in "فيكون لكم إلى ابتياع ..."]].

Then His remembrance, may He be exalted, informed them that this Day comes after the cessation of the action by which the pleasure of Allah is attained or the arrival at His honour through spending of wealth [[ Irtifa' al-'amal: its ending and passing away. It is said: "irtafa'a al-khisam baynahuma" and "irtafa'a al-khilaf", meaning it ended and passed away, so that nothing remained for them to disagree over or dispute. It is a metaphorical use of "irtafa'a al-shay'" meaning "it rose". This meaning is not specified by the lexicons, but it is correct Arabic and occurs frequently in the books of scholars. It has preceded in the words of Abu Ja'far, and I explained it, though I do not know its location at present.]], since there is no wealth there by which that could be attained. It is a day on which no friendship is beneficial as it was in the world, for a man's friend in the world would benefit him by supporting him against whoever sought to harm him or wished him evil, and by aiding him in that. So He, may His remembrance be exalted, also removed from them that hope, for on the Day of Resurrection no one supports another against Allah. Rather, ﴿the close friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾, as Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, said [[This is the verse of Surah al-Zukhruf: 67.]]. He also informed them that on that Day, along with their lack of means to purchase what they could have purchased in the world by spending of their wealth and working with their bodies, and their lack of supporters among friends and helpers among brothers [[Al-nusara' is the plural of nasir. Al-khullan is the plural of khalil. Al-zuhara' is the plural of zahir: one who aids you, strengthens your back and supports you.]], there is no intercessor for them who will intercede with Allah as was the case for them in the world. For some of them would intercede in the world for others by kinship, neighbourliness, friendship and other such causes, but all of that is nullified on that Day, as Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, reported of the words of His enemies among the people of Hell in the Hereafter when they are there: ﴿So we have no intercessors, nor a sincere friend﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 100-101].

* *

The wording of this verse is general in respect of intercession, but what is meant by it is specific. Its meaning is: "Before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession" for the people of disbelief in Allah, because the people of Allah's guardianship and faith intercede for one another. We have demonstrated the soundness of this with what suffices without repeating it in this place [[See what preceded at 2:23, 33.]].

* *

Qatadah used to say concerning this:

5761 - Bishr narrated to us with it, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words: "O you who believe, spend from what We have provided you, before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor friendship, nor intercession": Allah knew that there were people who loved one another in the world and interceded for one another, but on the Day of Resurrection there is no friendship except the friendship of the righteous.

* *

As for His words: "And the disbelievers—they are the wrongdoers," He, may His remembrance be exalted, means by this: those who deny Allah and reject Him and His messengers "are the wrongdoers"—meaning: they are the ones who place their denial in other than its place, who do what is not theirs to do, and who say what is not theirs to say.

* *

We have already shown the meaning of "wrongdoing" with its evidences previously, sufficiently so as not to repeat it [[See the meaning of "disbelief" in the language indexes of what preceded, and the meaning of "wrongdoing" at 1:523, 524, and in the language indexes.]].

* *

Abu Ja'far said: In His words, may His remembrance be exalted, in this place: "And the disbelievers—they are the wrongdoers," there is clear evidence for the soundness of what we have said, and that His words "nor friendship, nor intercession" are intended to refer to the people of disbelief. Therefore He followed that with: "And the disbelievers—they are the wrongdoers." This indicates that the meaning is: We deprived the disbelievers of support from friends and intercession from allies and relatives, and in doing so We were not wronging them, since that was a recompense from Us for their disbelief in Allah in the world. Rather, the disbelievers are the ones who wrong themselves by the deeds they committed which made punishment from their Lord obligatory for them.

* *

If someone says: How is the threat directed at the disbelievers when the verse opens with mention of the people of faith?

It is said to him: The verse was preceded by mention of two categories of people: one of disbelief and the other of faith, which is His words: "But they differed, so among them were those who believed and among them were those who disbelieved." Then Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, followed the two categories with what He mentioned to them, urging the people of faith in Him to what brings them closer to Him, namely spending in His obedience and in fighting His enemies from among the people of disbelief in Him, before the coming of the Day whose description He gave. He informed about the state of His enemies, the people of disbelief in Him, since fighting the people of disbelief in Him is disobedience to Him, and their spending is in obstructing His way. So He, may His remembrance be exalted, said: O you who believe, spend, you, from what We have provided you in My obedience, while those who disbelieve in Me spend in My disobedience, before there comes a Day in which the disbelievers will be unable to purchase what they neglected to purchase in their worldly life, and on which there will be no friend to aid them against Me, nor intercessor to intercede for them with Me so that his intercession saves them from My punishment. This on that Day is My doing to them as a recompense for their disbelief, and they are the ones who wrong themselves apart from Me, since I am not unjust to My servants. And:

5762 - Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahim narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Abi Salamah narrated to me, saying: I heard 'Umar ibn Sulayman narrate from 'Ata' ibn Dinar that he said: Praise be to Allah who said: "And the disbelievers—they are the wrongdoers," and did not say: "The wrongdoers are the disbelievers."

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: We have already explained the interpretation (*ta'wil*) of His saying "Allah" [[See the explanation of "Allah" above, 1:122–126.]].

* *

As for the interpretation of His saying "there is no god but Him": its meaning is a prohibition against worshipping anything other than God, the Living, the Self-Subsisting, whose attributes are those with which He, may His remembrance be exalted, described Himself in this verse. He says: "Allah," to whom the worship of creation is due, "the Living, the Self-Subsisting," there is no god besides Him and no one is worshipped besides Him. That is, do not worship anything other than the Living, the Self-Subsisting, whom neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes, and who has the attributes described in this verse. [[In the printed edition: "do not worship anything besides Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting." The correct reading is from the manuscript.]]

* *

This verse is a declaration from God, may His remembrance be exalted, to the believers in Him and His Messenger, concerning what was brought by the disputants over the clear proofs [[In the printed edition: "the disputants over the clear proofs," with an added "in," which is an error that corrupts the sense. The correct text is that of the manuscript. "The clear proofs" (*al-bayyināt*) is the subject of "brought," and "the disputants" (*al-mukhtalifīn*) is its object. The clause between the two dashes is parenthetical, and his saying below, "and they differed about it, so they fought over it," is coordinated with his saying "concerning what was brought..."]] after the messengers, whom God informed us He preferred over one another. They differed about it and fought over it: some disbelieved in it, and some believed in it. So praise belongs to God who guided us to affirm it and granted us success in acknowledging it.

* *

As for His saying "the Living": it means the One who possesses everlasting life and a subsistence that has no beginning limited by a bound and no end limited by a term. [[In the printed edition: "has no beginning limited by a bound" with the letter ya, as a verb, and then the following phrase is "and no end which is extended," producing a strange verb that does not exist in Arabic. In the manuscript the word is "bi-ḥadd" without dots, and its correct reading has the preposition bāʾ at the beginning. There is also "bi-amad" as I have written it. The *amad* is the limit that one reaches. He says: it has no beginning with a bound from which it starts, and no end with a term at which it arrives.]] Everything other than Him, though it is living, has a beginning that is bounded and an end that is extended, and it ends when its term ends and expires when its limit is reached.

[[In the printed edition: "and an end which is pulled," which again alters the manuscript and produces a word that Arabic derivation does not permit and that is never used in speech. In the manuscript it is "mamdūd," as I have fixed it. It derives from their saying "mudda lahu fī kadhā," meaning it was made long for him in such-and-such. It is better to say it derives from *al-madd*, which is a span of time.

They used *mādadtu al-qawm* from *al-mudda* (term): "I set a term for the people that they would reach." In a hadith: "Woe to Quraysh! War has destroyed them. What would it harm them if we made a truce with them for a term?" That is, we would set a term for them, which is the duration of the truce.

Ibn Ḥajar said in his introduction to *al-Fatḥ* (p. 182): "His saying (*fī al-mudda allatī fīhā Abā Sufyān*): that is, a term of peace was set between him and him. From this is (*in shāʾū mādadtuhum*). It is a form of *fāʿala* from *al-madd*. There is no doubt that the triliteral form is permissible, so that it may be said *madda lahu muddatan*, meaning he set for him a term at whose end it stops." I seem to have read this in some books of biography, and I hope to find it and fix it, God willing. So the meaning of his saying "an end that is extended and ends with the ending of its term" is: an end for which a term has been set, which ends when its goal ends.]]

* *

Those who held this view among the people of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wīl*) include a group.

Those who said that:

**5763** – I was told, from ʿAmmār ibn al-Ḥasan, who said: Ibn Abī Jaʿfar related to us, from his father, from al-Rabīʿ, concerning His saying "the Living": He is living and does not die.

**5764** – Al-Muthannā related to me, who said: Isḥāq related to us, who said: Ibn Abī Jaʿfar related to us, from his father, from al-Rabīʿ, the same.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The people of inquiry (*ahl al-baḥth*) have differed concerning the interpretation of this. [[This is the first time al-Ṭabarī uses the expression "*ahl al-baḥth*," by which he means the people of theological speculation (*al-mutakallimūn*).]]

Some of them said: God named Himself "living" only because He directs affairs to their proper courses and decrees things in their measures, so He is living through His management, not through a life.

Others said: Rather, He is living with a life that is an attribute of His.

And others said: Rather, it is one of the names by which He is named, so we say it in submission to His command. [[In the printed edition: "fa-qulnāhu," which is also correct in the manuscript.]]

* *

As for His saying "the Self-Subsisting" (*al-qayyūm*): it is *fayʿūl* from *al-qiyām* (standing), and its original form was *qayyuwum*. The *waw* that was the middle radical of the verb was preceded by a silent *yāʾ*, so the two were merged and became a doubled *yāʾ*.

The Arabs do the same with every *waw* that was the middle radical of the verb and was preceded by a silent *yāʾ*. The meaning of His saying "the Self-Subsisting" is: the One who stands over the provision for what He created and preserves it, as Umayya said:

*Lam takhluq al-samāʾ wa-l-nujūm*
*wa-l-shamsu maʿahā qamarun yaʿūm* [[Divan: 57; al-Qurṭubī 3:271; Abū Ḥayyān's *Tafsīr* 2:277. In the printed edition and al-Qurṭubī: "*qamarun yaqūm*," which has no meaning. The correct reading is in the manuscript and in Abū Ḥayyān. *ʿāmat al-nujūm taʿūm ʿawman*: they swam, like their saying "the stars glided in the sphere, gliding in gliding" (*sabbaḥat al-nujūm fī al-falak tasbaḥ sabḥan*).]]
*qaddarahu al-muhayminu al-qayyūm*
*wa-l-jisra wa-l-jannatu wa-l-jaḥīm* [[In all the references: "wa-l-ḥashr" (and the gathering), which is an error and a corruption that I have no doubt about. In the manuscript it is "wa-l-ḥasr" without dots, and its correct reading is "al-jisr" as I have written it. In al-Bukhārī's hadith: "then the bridge (*al-jisr*) is brought," and Ibn Ḥajar said: that is the *ṣirāṭ*, which is like a bridge between Paradise and the Fire over which the believers pass. It is not mentioned under its entry in the lexicons, so it should be noted there, for this is the source of the corruption of this word. In some references: "wa-l-jannati wa-l-naʿīm" (and Paradise and bliss), but what is in al-Ṭabarī is the correct one. This is in addition to the fact that Umayya's poetry is numerous and confused.]]
*illā li-amrin shaʾnuhu ʿaẓīm*

(Translation of the lines: The sky and the stars were not created, nor the sun with the moon swimming beside it; He decreed them, the Guardian, the Self-Subsisting, and the bridge, Paradise and Hell, except for a matter whose affair is great.)

* *

Those who held the same view as what we have said include the people of interpretation.

Those who said that:

**5765** – Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, who said: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, who said: ʿĪsā related to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, concerning God's saying "the Self-Subsisting": he said: the One who stands over everything.

**5766** – Al-Muthannā related to me, who said: Isḥāq related to us, from Ibn Abī Jaʿfar, from his father, from al-Rabīʿ: "the Self-Subsisting": the guardian of everything; He protects it, provides for it, and preserves it.

**5767** – Mūsā related to me, who said: ʿAmr related to us, who said: Asbāṭ related to us, from al-Suddī: "the Self-Subsisting": He is the Standing One.

**5768** – Al-Muthannā related to me, who said: Isḥāq related to us, who said: Abū Zuhayr related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: "the Living, the Self-Subsisting": he said: the Standing, the Ever-Enduring.

* *

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: God, may His remembrance be exalted, means by His saying "neither drowsiness overtakes Him" that drowsiness does not seize Him so that He dozes, nor does sleep come upon Him so that He becomes heavy with sleep.

* *

*Al-wasn* (drowsiness) is the thickening of sleep. [[*Al-khuthūra* is the opposite of thinness. It is said: "the milk, honey, or such was *khathara*," when it became thick and congealed. Its figurative use is the saying "so-and-so is *khāthir al-nafs*," meaning his soul is heavy, not pleasant or active, and has become languid in lethargy. Al-Ṭabarī used it skillfully, giving sleep a *khuthūra*, which is the intensity of languor, as if its thinness had gone and it had become heavy and thick. I have not found this expression before him.]] From it is the saying of ʿAdī ibn al-Riqāʿ:

*Wasnānu aqṣadahu al-nuʿāsu fa-rannaqat*
*fī ʿaynihi sinatun wa-laysa bi-nāʾimi* [[From some of his verses in *al-Shiʿr wa-l-shuʿarāʾ*: 602; *al-Aghānī* 9:311; *Majāz al-Qurʾān* 1:78; *al-Lisān* (w-s-n) (r-n-q). In all of these there are many references. Before the verse, in mentioning his beloved "Umm al-Qāsim," he says:*
*wa-ka-annahā wasṭa al-nisāʾi aʿārahā*
*ʿaynayhi aḥwara min jāʾidhi Jāsimi* [[*Al-jāʾidh* are wild cow antelopes, which have beautiful eyes. Jāsim is a place where wild cow antelopes abound. "*Aqṣadahu al-nuʿās*" means drowsiness killed him and caused him to die. It is said: "a snake bit him and he was killed," that is, killed on the spot, at once. *Rannaqat* means it mixed into his eye. Its origin is from *tarnīq al-māʾ*, which is making water turbid with mud until the mud overcomes the water. It is also good to say it is from *tarnīq al-ṭāʾir bi-janāḥayhi*, which is the bird's fluttering when it beats its wings in the air and stays in place without flying away. This figurative sense is more pleasing to me in poetry.]]

Among the proofs of what we have said, that it is the thickening of sleep in the eye of a person, is the saying of al-Aʿshā, Maymūn ibn Qays:

*Taʿāṭā al-ḍajīʿa idhā aqbalat*
*baʿīda al-nuʿāsi wa-qabla al-wasan* [[His *Divan*: 15. It follows the verse that preceded it, 1:345–346, in describing women he enjoyed:*
*idhā hunna nāzalna aqrānahunna*
*wa-kāna al-maṣāʿu bi-mā fī al-jawni* [[In all these verses, see the reference as earlier.]]
*Taʿāṭā al-ḍajīʿ* ...
*ṣarīfiyyatan ṭayyiban ṭaʿmuhā*
*lahā zabadun bayna kawbin wa-dinn*

Its wording *taʿāṭā* is from the saying about a woman: "she gives her lover her saliva," that is, she offers him from her saliva before her. His saying *aqbalat*, in my view, means: she was accommodating, obliging, and submissive, from *al-qabūl*, which is acceptance. The lexicographers did not mention this, but it is good in Arabic, similar to their saying *asmaḥat* (she became accommodating), from *al-samāḥ*, when she became easy and submitted and agreed with what her companion asked. That is what seems good to me. It is not from *al-iqbāl* (turning toward something), but from *al-qabūl*. In one narration, instead of this, it is "*idhā sāmahā*," and the *Divan*'s narration is: "*baʿīda al-raqādi wa-ʿinda al-wasan*."

*Ṣarīfiyya* is good wine; he called it *ṣarīfiyya* because it had been taken from the jar at that hour, like the *ṣarīf* milk, which is the milk that flows from the udder hot when it is milked. In the *Dīwān*: "*ṣalīfiyya*" with *lām*, but the correct form is with *rāʾ*. He says: when she submits to her companion after her sleep is far off, or before her drowsiness, she gives him pure wine from her saliva that foams with froth between the cup and the jar, and no time has passed upon it so that it spoils. He says: her saliva is wine, in her wakefulness before drowsiness, which is the beginning of the languor of the soul and the change of temperament, and after her blame, when human mouths have changed and their odors have become repugnant. It removes from her the defect in both states, and that rarely happens among women or others.]]

And another said [[This is also al-Aʿshā.]]:

*Bākarathā al-aghrābu fī sinati al-nawmi*
*fa-tajrī khilāla shawki al-sayyāl* [[His *Divan*: 5; *al-Lisān* (gh-r-b). From a magnificent *qaṣīda*, in which he came to mention his beloved. Before it he says:*
*wa-ka-anna al-khamra al-ʿatīqa min al-Isfanṭi*
*mamzūjatan bi-māʾin zulālin*
*bākarathā al-aghrāb* ...
*Al-Isfanṭ* is the best and most expensive kind of wine. *Bākarathā*: at the beginning of the day, hastening to her. *Al-aghrāb* is the plural of *gharb* (with a fatḥa and sukūn), which is the cup. *Al-sayyāl* is a tree with slender branches, having white thorns whose roots are like the molars of virgins, and women's teeth are compared to them. He says: when she sleeps, the good taste of her mouth does not change, but it is as if the wine flows between her molars, with a fragrant scent. As for his saying *bākarathā al-aghrāb*, it is like his saying in the earlier poem that it is *ṣarīfiyya*, meaning it was taken from its jar at its hour. He says: the cups were filled with it in the morning, meaning the cups hastened to it from its jar, and that is better for it.

This is so. The explanation of the *Dīwān* has: "*al-aghrāb*: the edge of the teeth and their whiteness," and he lengthened in its explanation, but I do not accept it. What I have explained is found in *al-Lisān*, and it is more deeply rooted in poetry and in understanding it.]] meaning at the time of its stirring from sleep and the drowsiness of sleep in its eye. From this one says: "*wasana fulānun fa-huwa yūsinu wasanan wa-sinatan wa-huwa wasnān*," when he is like this.

* *

Those who held the same view as what we have said among the people of interpretation include:

**5769** – Al-Muthannā related to me, who said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣāliḥ related to us, who said: Muʿāwiya ibn Ṣāliḥ related to me, from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His saying, exalted is He: "neither drowsiness (*sina*) overtakes Him." He said: *al-sina* is drowsiness, and *al-nawm* is sleep. [[That is, sleep is well-known, and drowsiness is other than sleep. See the following report, 5772 and what comes after it.]]

**5770** – Muḥammad ibn Saʿd related to me, who said: My father related to me, who said: My paternal uncle related to me, who said: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās: "neither drowsiness overtakes Him" — drowsiness is slumber.

**5771** – Al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā related to us, who said: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, who said: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatāda and al-Ḥasan, concerning His saying "neither drowsiness overtakes Him": both said: a nap.

**5772** – Al-Muthannā related to me, who said: ʿAmr ibn ʿAwn related to us, who said: Hushaym informed us, from Juwaybir, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, concerning His saying "neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him": he said: *al-sina* is the *wasna*, which is less than sleep, and *al-nawm* is deep slumber.

**5773** – Al-Muthannā related to me, who said: Isḥāq related to us, who said: Abū Zuhayr related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: "neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him": *al-sina* is drowsiness, and *al-nawm* is deep slumber.

**5774** – Yaḥyā ibn Abī Ṭālib related to me, who said: Yazīd informed us, who said: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, the same.

**5775** – Mūsā related to me, who said: ʿAmr related to us, who said: Asbāṭ related to us, from al-Suddī: "neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him." As for *sina*, it is the breeze of sleep that seizes the face, so that a person dozes. [[In the manuscript "rīḥ" is without dots. Here *al-rīḥ* means dominance and strength, as in the poetry of al-Aʿshā, or Sulaymān ibn al-Sulaka:*
*a-tanẓurāni qalīlan rayatha ghaflatihim*
*aw-taʿdawāni fa-inna al-rīḥa lil-ʿādī*
*that is, dominance. It may also be read as "al-ranaḥ" (with a fatḥa on the rāʾ and sukūn on the nūn), which is dizziness. From it: "tarannaḥa min al-sukr" when he swayed from drunkenness, and "ranaḥa bihi" (in the passive, with the nūn doubled) when he was made to turn about as one who has fainted, or when weakness has seized his bones from a blow, fright, or drunkenness.]]

**5776** – I was told, from ʿAmmār, who said: Ibn Abī Jaʿfar related to us, from his father, from al-Rabīʿ: "neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him": *al-sina* is the one who is drowsy, between sleeping and waking.

**5777** – ʿAbbās ibn Abī Ṭālib related to me, who said: Munjāb ibn al-Ḥārith related to us, who said: ʿAlī ibn Mushir related to us, from Ismāʿīl, from Yaḥyā ibn Rāfiʿ: "neither drowsiness overtakes Him": he said: drowsiness. [[The report 5777: "ʿAbbās ibn Abī Ṭālib" is ʿAbbās ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubriqān, whose biography has passed under no. 880. "Munjāb ibn al-Ḥārith," whose biography has passed under nos. 322–328. "ʿAlī ibn Mushir al-Qurashī," the Kufan, the *ḥāfiẓ*. He related from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd al-Anṣārī, Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, and Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid. He was trustworthy and died in 189 AH. His biography is in *al-Tahdhīb*. "Ismāʿīl" is Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid al-Aḥmasī. He related from his father, Abū Juḥayfa, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Awfā, ʿAmr ibn Ḥurayth, and Abū Kāhil, who were Companions, and from Zayd ibn Wahb, al-Shaʿbī, and others of the senior Successors. He was trustworthy and firm, and died in 146 AH. His biography is in *al-Tahdhīb*. "Yaḥyā ibn Rāfiʿ" is Abū ʿĪsā al-Thaqafī. He related from ʿUthmān and Abū Hurayra, and Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid related from him. His biography is in *al-Kabīr* 4/2/273 and Ibn Abī Ḥātim 4/2/143.]]

**5778** – Yūnus related to me, who said: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said concerning His saying "neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him": "the drowsy one" is the one who rises from sleep without understanding, to the point that he may take up a sword against his own family.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: God, may His remembrance be exalted, meant by His saying "neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him" that calamities do not befall Him and afflictions do not reach Him. That is because *al-sina* and *al-nawm* are two states that cover the understanding of one who has understanding and remove those who are afflicted with them from the condition they were in before they afflicted them.

* *

So the interpretation of the speech, given that the matter is as we have described: "Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living" who does not die, "the Self-Subsisting" over everything that is below Him through provision, sustenance, management, and direction from one state to another, "neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him," nothing that alters others alters Him, nor does what removes Him from what He has never ceased to be remove Him; the changing of conditions and the alternation of nights and days do not affect Him. Rather, He is the Ever-Enduring in one state, and the Self-Subsisting over all creation. If He slept, He would be overcome and subdued, because sleep overcomes the sleeper and dominates him. If He became drowsy, the heavens, the earth, and all that is in them would be crushed, because the standing of all of that is by His management and power, while sleep preoccupies the Manager from managing, and drowsiness prevents the Decreer from decreeing by its drowsiness. [[In the printed edition: "*yumāniʿ*" with the letter yāʾ at its beginning, which is an error with no benefit. He mistook the reading of the manuscript because the fatḥa on the mīm joined to its beginning.]] As:

٥٧٧٩ - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Aban informed me,[[In the printed and manuscript editions it reads "wa-akhbarani al-Hakam" (with a waw). The correct reading seems to be without the waw: "akhbarana Ma'mar qal, akhbarani al-Hakam ibn Aban", as I have written it, since Ma'mar narrates from al-Hakam ibn Aban. See his biography in al-Tahdhib, and as it appears in Ibn Kathir 2:11, which is correct. The author (Mahmud Shakir) commented: "This is one of the reports of the Children of Israel, and it is known that Musa (peace be upon him) would not be unaware of such a matter concerning Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; He is exalted above it." Ibn Kathir was right, for the People of the Book attribute to the prophets of Allah things that would have been better for them to leave alone.]] from Ikrimah, the freedman of Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾: that Musa asked the angels, "Does Allah sleep?" So Allah revealed to the angels and commanded them to keep him awake for three nights, not letting him sleep. They did so. Then they gave him two flasks and told him to hold them, then they left him and warned him not to break them. He said: So he began to doze while they were in his hands, one in each hand. He said: He kept dozing and waking, dozing and waking, until he fell into a deep sleep, and he struck one against the other and broke them. Ma'mar said: It is only a parable that Allah struck: He says, "Likewise the heavens and the earth are in His hands."

٥٧٨٠ - Ishaq ibn Abi Isra'il narrated to us, saying: Hisham ibn Yusuf narrated to us, from Umayyah ibn Shibl, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from Ikrimah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) telling on the pulpit about Musa (ﷺ). He said: "It occurred to the mind of Musa: Does Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, sleep? So Allah sent to him an angel who kept him awake three nights. Then He gave him two flasks, a flask in each hand, and commanded him to guard them. He said: So he began to sleep, and his hands almost met, then he would wake and hold one away from the other. Then he slept a sleep, and his hands struck together and the two flasks broke." He said: "Allah struck a parable for him: that if Allah were to sleep, the heavens and the earth would not be held firm."

[[Report 5780: Ishaq ibn Abi Isra'il, whose name is Ibrahim ibn Kama Mujra, Abu Ya'qub al-Marwazi, a resident of Baghdad. Al-Bukhari narrated from him in al-Adab al-Mufrad, and Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and others. Ibn Ma'in said: "He is one of the trustworthy Muslims. * *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His remembrance be exalted, "To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth," He means that He is the owner of all of that, without partner or equal, and the creator of all of it, apart from every deity and object of worship.[[See what preceded in the tafsir of "To Him belongs...", 2:537.]]

He means by this that worship is not fitting for anything other than Him, because a possession is only at the disposal of its owner, and it has no service to render to anyone other than by his command. He says: All that is in the heavens and the earth is My possession and My creation, so none of My creatures should be worshipped besides Me, while I am its owner, because it is not fitting for a servant to worship other than his owner, nor to obey anyone but his master.

* *

As for His words, "Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?", He means: Who is it that can intercede for His servants if He wishes to punish them, unless He releases him and gives him permission to intercede for them?[[See the meaning of "shafa'a" (intercession) in what preceded, 2:31-33, and what preceded shortly: 382-384. And the meaning of "idhn" (permission) in what preceded, 2:449, 450; then 4:286, 370; then this one, 352, 355.]] He, may His remembrance be exalted, said this because the polytheists said: "We only worship these idols so that they bring us near to Allah in nearness!"[[This is the interpretation of the verse in Surat al-Zumar: 3.]] So Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, said to them: To Me belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, together with the heavens and the earth, as a kingdom, so worship is not fitting for other than Me. So do not worship the idols that you claim will bring you near to Me in nearness, for they will not benefit you with Me nor avail you anything. No one will intercede with Me for anyone except by My releasing him and permitting the intercession for the one for whom it is made, from among My messengers, My friends and the people of My obedience.

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not encompass anything of His knowledge except what He wills﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means that He is the One who encompasses everything that has been and everything that is to be, in knowledge, and nothing of it is hidden from Him.

* *

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said that:

٥٧٨١ - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from al-Hakam: "He knows what is before them": the world; "and what is behind them": the hereafter.

٥٧٨٢ - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "He knows what is before them": what has passed of the world; "and what is behind them": of the hereafter.

٥٧٨٣ - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said concerning His words "He knows what is before them": what has passed in front of them of the world; "and what is behind them": what will come after them of the world and the hereafter.

٥٧٨٤ - Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "He knows what is before them," he said: As for "what is before them," it is the world; "and what is behind them," it is the hereafter.[[The addition in the brackets is necessary.]]

* *

As for His words, "and they do not encompass anything of His knowledge except what He wills," He means, may His remembrance be exalted: He is the Knowing One to whom nothing is hidden, encompassing all of that, singled out for it apart from all others beside Him. No one other than Him knows anything except what He wills to make known to him, so He wills and makes it known. He means by this that worship is not fitting for one who is ignorant of things; how then can one worship what understands nothing at all, such as an idol or a statue? He says: Devote worship to the One who encompasses all things in knowledge, who knows them and from whom nothing small or great is hidden.[[In the printed edition: "akhlisu" (devote); I have written what is in the manuscript, which is correct.]]

* *

The people of interpretation said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said that:

٥٧٨٦ - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "and they do not encompass anything of His knowledge," he says: they do not know anything of His knowledge, "except what He wills," that He makes them know.[[Omitted from the numbering: 5785, through oversight.]]

* *

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation differed about the meaning of "al-Kursi" that Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, mentioned in this verse as having extended over the heavens and the earth.

Some of them said: It is the knowledge of Allah, may His remembrance be exalted.

Those who said that:

٥٧٨٧ - Abu Kurayb and Salm ibn Janadah narrated to us, both saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, from Mutarrif, from Ja'far ibn Abi al-Mughirah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: "His Kursi extended" he said: His Kursi is His knowledge.

٥٧٨٨ - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Mutarrif informed us, from Ja'far ibn Abi al-Mughirah, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, the same; and he added to it: Do you not see His words, "and its preservation does not weary Him"?

* *

Others said: "Al-Kursi" is the place of the two feet.

Those who said that:

٥٧٨٩ - Ali ibn Muslim al-Tusi narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Samad ibn Abd al-Warith narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Jahadah narrated to me, from Salamah ibn Kuhayl, from Amarah ibn Umayr, from Abu Musa, who said: The Kursi is the place of the two feet, and it has a creaking like the creaking of a saddle.[[Report 5789: Ali ibn Muslim ibn Sa'id al-Tusi, a resident of Baghdad. Al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from him. Trustworthy. He died in 253. Biographed in al-Tahdhib. And "Amarah ibn Umayr al-Taymi" saw Abd Allah ibn Amr, and narrated from al-Aswad ibn Yazid al-Nakha'i, al-Harith ibn Suwayd al-Taymi, and Ibrahim ibn Abi Musa al-Ash'ari. He did not meet Abu Musa. The hadith is munqati' (disconnected). Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:327, attributing it to Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat.
Al-Ati'tt (creaking): the sound of a saddle and of new cord, and the sound of a door; it is a stretched, coarse sound, not like a screech but rougher.]]

٥٧٩٠ - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth," for the heavens and the earth are within the Kursi, and the Kursi is before the Throne, and it is the place of His two feet.

٥٧٩١ - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Zuhayr narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak concerning His words "His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth," he said: His Kursi is that which is placed beneath the Throne, upon which kings place their feet.

٥٧٩٢ - Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ammar al-Duhni, from Muslim al-Batin, who said: The Kursi is the place of the two feet.[[Report 5792: Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir 2:13 by way of Sufyan, from Ammar al-Duhni, from Muslim al-Batin, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, and attributed it to Waki' in his tafsir. Al-Hakim narrated the same in al-Mustadrak 2:282, as mawquf on Ibn Abbas, and said: "Sahih according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs, though they did not narrate it." Al-Dhahabi agreed with him. Ibn Kathir said: "Ibn Mardawayh narrated it by way of al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr al-Fazari al-Kufi, who is matruk (abandoned), from al-Suddi, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, as marfu', and this too is not sound." See Majma' al-Zawa'id 6:323 and Fath al-Bari 8:149.]]

٥٧٩٣ - al-Rabi' narrated to me, saying: Ammar narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth," he said: When it was revealed, "His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth," the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: O Messenger of Allah, this Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth; what then of the Throne? So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ up to His words: ﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate﴾ [al-Zumar: 67].[[Report 5793: It does not occur in the tafsir of this verse in Surat al-Zumar.]]

٥٧٩٤ - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words "His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth," Ibn Zayd said: My father narrated to me, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The seven heavens within the Kursi are nothing but seven dirhams thrown into a shield." He said: And Abu Dhar said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The Kursi in relation to the Throne is nothing but a ring of iron thrown in the middle of a desert wasteland."[[Report 5794: The report of Abu Dhar, cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:328, attributing it to Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azamah, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat. Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir 2:13 and gave the wording and chain of Ibn Mardawayh, by way of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Tamimi, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Thaqafi, from Abu Idris al-Khawlani, from Abu Dhar.]]

* *

Others said: The Kursi is the Throne itself.

Those who said that:

٥٧٩٥ - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Zuhayr narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: al-Hasan used to say: The Kursi is the Throne.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Each of these opinions has a valid line of reasoning and a school of thought, but the one most deserving to be the interpretation of the verse is what has come from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is what follows:

٥٧٩٦ - Abd Allah ibn Abi Ziyad al-Qatawani narrated to me, saying: Ubayd Allah ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Israil informed us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abd Allah ibn Khalifah, who said: A woman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Ask Allah to admit me to Paradise!" So he exalted the Lord, may His remembrance be exalted, then said: "Indeed His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth, and He sits upon it, and there remains of it the measure of four fingers"; then he gestured with his fingers, gathering them, "and it has a creaking like the creaking of a new saddle when it is ridden, because of its weight."[[Report 5796: "Abd Allah ibn Abi Ziyad al-Qatawani" is "Abd Allah ibn al-Hakam ibn Abi Ziyadah," whose biography was given under number 2247. "Ubayd Allah ibn Musa ibn Abi al-Mukhtar, whose name was Badhdham, al-Absi, their freedman": al-Bukhari narrated from him, and he and the rest narrated through Ahmad ibn Abi Suraj al-Razi, Ahmad ibn Ishaq al-Bukhari, Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd Allah ibn al-Hakam al-Qatawani and others. Trustworthy, truthful, good in hadith, a master of the Qur'an and the foremost of Israil's students. Biographed in al-Tahdhib.
"Abd Allah ibn Khalifah al-Hamdani al-Kufi" narrated from Umar and Jabir; Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i narrated from him. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat. Biographed in al-Tahdhib. Thus al-Tabari narrated this report as mawquf. Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir 2:13 by way of Israil, from Abu Ishaq, from Abd Allah ibn Khalifah, from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him).
Ibn Kathir said: "Al-Hafiz al-Bazzar narrated it in his famous Musnad, and Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Jarir in their two tafsirs, and al-Tabarani, and Ibn Abi Asim in his two books of the Sunnah, and al-Hafiz al-Diya in his book al-Mukhtar, from the hadith of Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, from Abd Allah ibn Khalifah, and it is not that well known. Regarding his hearing from Umar there is doubt. Some narrate it from him as mawquf from Umar (I say: as al-Tabari narrated it here), some narrate it from Umar as mursal, and some add a strange addition to its text (I say: this is the addition of al-Tabari in this hadith), and some omit it. More strange than this is the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im concerning the description of the Throne, as Abu Dawud narrated it in his Kitab al-Sunnah from his Sunan (no. 4726). And Allah knows best."
Qal bi-yadihi: he gestured with it; see what preceded of al-Tabari's tafsir on that in 2:546-548.]]

٥٧٩٧ - Abd Allah ibn Abi Ziyad narrated to me, saying: Yahya ibn Abi Bakr narrated to us, from Israil, from Abu Ishaq, from Abd Allah ibn Khalifah, from Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), similarly.
