٥٧٩٨ - Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Israil narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abd Allah ibn Khalifah, who said: A woman came, and he mentioned something similar.[[Reports 5797 and 5798: "Yahya ibn Abi Bakir," whose name is Nasr al-Asadi, Abu Zakariyya al-Kirmani by origin, resided in Baghdad, narrated from Ibn Uthman, Ibrahim ibn Tahman, Israil and Za'idah.
Al-Sittah narrated from him, along with Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim al-Dawraqi, Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ahmad ibn Abi Khalaf, and others. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat. He died in 208 or 209. Biographed in al-Tahdhib. In the printed edition it read "Yahya ibn Abi Bakr," which is an error.
These two reports are two other chains for the earlier report number 5796; see the commentary on them.]]

* *

It is fitting here to note that the strongest evidence for the correctness of this reading is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, namely the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, transmitted by Ja'far ibn Abi al-Mughirah from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from him, that he said: "It is His knowledge." [[It is a wonder that Abu Ja'far contradicts himself at this point! For he began by saying that the reading most fitting for the interpretation of the verse is what has come in the report from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in the hadith describing the Kursi, and then he returned at this point saying: "As for what the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates as its soundness, it is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas that it is the knowledge of Allah, glorified is He." So it is either this or that, and it is impossible that the best interpretation of the meaning of "al-Kursi" should be what came in the first hadith, and that its meaning should also be "knowledge," as he claims the apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates. How can two meanings differing in description and essence be combined in one interpretation?! And if the report of Ja'far ibn Abi al-Mughirah from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas has a sound chain, then the other report transmitted by Muslim al-Batin from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas has a sound chain meeting the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), as al-Hakim said, and as in Majma' al-Zawa'id 6:323: "Narrated by al-Tabarani, and its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih," as I explained in the commentary on the report 5792. Whatever is said about them, neither of them will be preferred over the other except by a preponderating factor that must be accepted. As for Abu Mansur al-Azhari, he said when mentioning the Kursi: "The sound report from Ibn 'Abbas is what 'Ammar al-Dhuhni transmitted from Muslim al-Batin from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: 'The Kursi is the place of the two feet, and as for the Throne, no one can estimate its measure.' He said: This is a report on whose soundness the people of knowledge are agreed. He said: Whoever reports from him that the Kursi is knowledge, has nullified it," and this is the saying of the people of truth, if Allah wills.]]

Al-Tabari sought to argue further that the Kursi is "knowledge," by the words of the Exalted: "Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge." Why then did he not make "al-Kursi" to be "mercy," since both are in one verse? And why did he not make it so, given the words of the Exalted in Surah al-A'raf 156: "He said: My punishment I afflict with whom I will, and My mercy encompasses all things"? Deriving the meaning of al-Kursi from this verse, as al-Tabari did, is very weak, and one who is as cautious, subtle and precise as he is would be above it.

As for what he cited after this of evidences for the meaning of "al-Kursi," most of it does not stand on anything, and some of its interpretation is objectionable, as I will show later, if Allah wills. He considered it as evidence and proof that it did not come in the Qur'an in any place other than this one with the meaning they stated, and that it came in another verse with what is established in sound language as the meaning of "al-Kursi," namely the words of the Exalted in "Surah Sad": "And We did try Solomon, and We placed upon his throne (kursiyyihi) a body, then he repented." Written by Mahmud Muhammad Shakir.

This is because of the indication of the words of the Exalted, "and its preserving does not burden Him," that this is so. He informs that the preserving of what He knows and encompasses of what is in the heavens and the earth does not burden Him. Likewise He informs about His angels that they said in their supplication: ﴿Our Lord, You encompass everything in mercy and knowledge﴾ [Ghafir: 7], so He, exalted is His remembrance, informs that His knowledge encompasses everything; likewise His words: "His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The origin of "al-Kursi" is knowledge. [[I fear the correct reading is: "The origin of al-Kurs: knowledge" (with a fatha on the kaf and a sukun on the ra'), from what Ibn al-A'rabi transmitted from their saying: "karasa al-rajul" (with a fatha then a kasra), when his knowledge crowded upon his heart. Abu Ja'far's making this the origin is a wonder of wonders! For the linguistic root testifies against it, and this explanation of Ibn al-A'rabi is also a witness against it. The root (k-r-s) originally refers to the accumulation of a thing, its compacting and gathering of some of it upon some. His subsequent saying: "and from it is said of a page, karrasa," and the better is to say: it is from the gathering of its sheets one upon another, or the joining of some of them to others.]] From it, a written sheet containing knowledge is called a "karraasa," and from it is the saying of the rajaz-poet describing a hunter:

Until when he gathered it and became compact *

[[I did not find the rajaz, and his saying "ihtazahaa" means he gathered it and drew it to himself. I do not know to what the pronoun returns: to the hunter or to his dog? The use of this rajaz as evidence that he means by "tukarras" knowledge has no proof for it, unless we find the rest of the poem, and no one among the lexicographers mentioned it.]]

meaning knowledge. From it the scholars are called "al-karasi," because they are the ones relied upon, as one says "awtad al-ard" (the pegs of the earth). By this he means that they are the scholars by whom the earth is set right. [[This explanation is taken from the saying of Qutrub, as will come, that they are the scholars; but the root of the language indicates that the origin of this is the firm thing that is relied upon, like the chair (kursi) on which one sits, and calling scholars by this is pure metaphor.]] From it is the saying of the poet: [[I do not know who said it.]]

Around them are fair-faced men and a band... *
chairs of the affairs when they befall

[[I did not find the verse, except among those who quoted from al-Tabari. In Asas al-Balagha (k-r-s), he recited it after his saying: "The scholars are called al-karasi, from Qutrub," and he recited the verse. I did not find anyone who mentioned that among the trustworthy lexicographers.]]

He means by this scholars of the events of affairs and their calamities. The Arabs call the origin of everything "al-kirs," and it is said from it: "So-and-so is noble of kirs," meaning noble of origin. Al-'Ajjaj said:

Indeed the Holy One, master of the holy, knows *
that Abu al-'Abbas is more entitled to the soul
to the mine of the noble kingdom, its kirs *

[[His Diwan: 78, and Lisan (q-d-s) (k-r-s). "Al-quds" is Allah, glorified is He, the Pure, free from defects and imperfections. And "al-qudus" and its master: its Lord. The explanation of the meaning of "al-Qudus" and "al-Quds" has passed in this tafsir, 1:475, 476 / 2:322, 323. "Abu al-'Abbas" is Abu al-'Abbas al-Saffah, the Abbasid caliph. The author of Lisan narrated "al-qadim al-kirs" (the ancient of origin), and "al-ma'dan" (with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the dal): the place of everything and its firm origin, and from it: "mine of gold and silver," which is the place where gold and silver grow, then they are extracted from it, and it is called in our time "al-manjam" (the mine). He says: Abu al-'Abbas is more entitled to the caliphate, of firm origin and noble.]]

He means by this: noble of origin. And it is narrated:

in the mine of glory, the noble kirs *

* *

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And its preserving does not burden Him, and He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾ (255)

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His remembrance, "and its preserving does not burden Him," He means: it does not weigh on Him nor burden Him.

* *

It is said from it: "This matter has wearied me, so it wearies me, weariness and ya'dad (weariness)," [[His saying "iyaadan" is a verbal noun I did not find in the books of language; al-Tabari has provided it to us.]] and it is said: "What wearies you is mine to be weary of," meaning: what burdens you is mine to be burdened by.

* *

Those of the people of interpretation have said things similar to what we have said on this.

Those who said that:

5799 - Al-Muthanna ibn Ibrahim narrated to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas: "And its preserving does not burden Him," he says: does not weigh on Him.

5800 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "And its preserving does not burden Him," he said: its preserving does not weigh on Him.

5801 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words: "And its preserving does not burden Him," does not weigh on Him, does not exhaust Him, its preserving.

5802 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Hasan and Qatadah regarding His words: "And its preserving does not burden Him," he said: nothing weighs on Him.

5803 - Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Buza' narrated to me, saying: Yusuf ibn Khalid al-Samti narrated to us, saying: Nafi' ibn Malik narrated to us, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words: "And its preserving does not burden Him," he said: its preserving does not weigh on Him.

5804 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Za'ida narrated to us= and Yahya ibn Abi Talib narrated to us, saying: Yazid informed us= both said together: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak: "And its preserving does not burden Him," he said: does not weigh on Him.

5805 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, from 'Ubayd, from al-Dahhak, the like of it.

5806 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: I heard him, meaning Khallad, say: I heard Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Madini say regarding this verse: "And its preserving does not burden Him," he said: does not become heavy upon Him. [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "yukthir 'alayhi" (multiply upon Him), and the correct is what I have established: "kabura 'alayhi," meaning it was heavy upon him.]]

5807 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa ibn Maymun, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding the saying of Allah: "And its preserving does not burden Him," he said: it does not distress Him. [[Karathahu al-amr yakruthuhu: the matter became severe upon him and reached him with hardship.]]

5808 - Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And its preserving does not burden Him," he said: does not weigh on Him.

5809 - It was narrated to me from 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His words: "And its preserving does not burden Him," he says: its preserving does not weigh on Him.

5810 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "And its preserving does not burden Him," he said: its preserving does not become difficult for Him.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The "hu" (him), the "mim" and the "alif" in His words "hifzhuhuma" (their preserving) refer to "the heavens and the earth." So the meaning of the speech is: His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth, and the preserving of the heavens and the earth does not weigh on Him.

* *

As for the interpretation of His words "and He is the Most High," it means: and Allah is the Most High.

* *

"Al-Ali" is the form "fa'il" from your saying "'alla ya'lu 'uluwwan" (he rose), when he rose, "so he is 'al' and 'ali'," and "al-'Ali" is the one possessing elevation and height above His creation by His power.

* *

Likewise His words "al-'Azim": the one possessing greatness, before whom everything is beneath, so there is nothing greater than Him. As:

5811 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Al-'Azim," the one who is perfect in His greatness.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The people of inquiry differed concerning the meaning of His words: [[See what passed concerning the mention of "ahl al-bahth" (the people of inquiry) shortly before: 387, note 2.]]

"And He is the Most High."

Some of them said: By that is meant: He is the Most High above peers and likenesses, [[In the manuscript: "al-nazr" without a ya. "Al-nazr" (with a kasra then a sukun) is like "al-nazir" (peer), as in "nidd" and "nadid". It is possible that "al-nazr" (with two dammas) is the plural of "nazir," and they break the adjective "fa'il" into "fa'l" with two dammas, making it like the noun "fa'il," as they said for "jadid, judud" and "nadhir, nudhr." As for "al-nazaʾir," the plural of "nazir," it is irregular in its pattern.]] and they denied that the meaning of this is: "He is the Most High in place." They said: It is not permissible that a place should be empty of Him, and there is no sense in describing Him with elevation of place, because that would describe Him as being in one place rather than another.

Others said: The meaning is: He is the Most High over His creation by the elevation of His place above the places of His creation, because He, exalted is His remembrance, is above all His creation and His creation is beneath Him, as He described Himself as being upon the Throne, so He is elevated above them by that.

Likewise they differed concerning the meaning of His words "al-'Azim."

Some of them said: The meaning of "al-'Azim" in this place is: the one who is magnified, the form "maf'al" being turned into "fa'il," as it is said of aged wine, "khamr 'atiq" (ancient wine), as the poet said: [[He is al-A'sha.]]

As if the ancient wine of... *
... mixed with cool water

[[His Diwan: 5; this verse has passed in our note just before: 390, note 3. "Al-zulal": clear, sweet, cold water, pleasant to the throat.]]

And it is actually "mu'taqa" (aged). They said: So His saying "al-'Azim" means: the one who is magnified, whom His creation magnify, fear and revere. They said: The saying of the speaker "He is great" can only bear one of two meanings: one of them is what we described, that He is magnified; the other is that He is great in extent and weight. They said: And in prolonging the discourse on the view that the meaning is that He is great in extent and weight, is the soundness of what we have said.

* *

Others said: Rather, the interpretation of His words "al-'Azim" is that He has a greatness which is an attribute of His.

And they said: We do not describe His greatness with a modality, but we ascribe that to Him from the standpoint of affirmation, [[Affirmation: affirming the attributes of Allah, glorified is He, as He described Himself, without interpretation, in contrast to the Mu'tazilah and others. See what passed 1:189, note 1.]]

and we negate of Him that it be in the sense of resembling the greatness known among created beings, because that would be likening Him to His creation, and He is not so. These people rejected what the people of the view we previously mentioned said, and they said: If the meaning of that were that He is "magnified," it would necessarily follow that He was not great before He created creation, and that this meaning would be nullified at the annihilation of creation, because there would be no one to magnify Him in those states.

* *

Others said: Rather His saying that He is "al-'Azim" is a description by which He describes Himself with greatness. They said: Everything beneath Him of His creation is in the sense of smallness, because of their smallness before His greatness.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 256 (part 1 of 2):

On the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become clearly distinct from error﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The people of ta'wil (interpretation) differed regarding the meaning of this.

Some of them said: This verse was revealed concerning a group of the Ansar, or a man among them, who had children whom they had made Jews or Christians. When God brought Islam, they wanted to compel them to accept it, so God forbade them from this, until they themselves would choose to enter Islam.

Mention of those who said this:

5812. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi 'Adi narrated to us, from Shu'bah, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: A woman would be one whose children did not survive (muqlat), so she would vow that if a child of hers lived, she would make him a Jew. When the Banu al-Nadir were expelled, there were among them sons of the Ansar, and they said: "We will not leave our sons!" So God, may He be exalted, revealed: "There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become clearly distinct from error."

[The two reports 5812 and 5813 are in Ibn Kathir 2:15 and al-Durr al-Manthur 1:329. Ibn Kathir said: "Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i both narrated it from Bundar, and from other routes from Shu'bah similarly. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih narrated it from the hadith of Shu'bah." See also al-Sunan al-Kubra of al-Bayhaqi 9:186, and Sunan Abi Dawud 3:78-79, no. 2682. In the printed and manuscript copies, number 5813 reads "Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, from Sa'id," which is an error; the correct reading is "Shu'bah." The words "He said: whoever wished to stay, stayed, and whoever wished to leave, left" are from the speech of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, as in the Sunan of al-Bayhaqi. The hadith there is traced back to Ibn 'Abbas, which is correct, but I have left what is in al-Tabari as it stands.
The word muqlat (with a dammah on the mim) and muqlat (with a kasrah on the mim) refer to a woman whose children do not survive. The term also appears as muqlat meaning a woman who has only one child. However, the first meaning is what is intended in this report.]

5814. Humayd ibn Mas'adah narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us. And Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us, from Dawud, from 'Amir, who said: A woman among the Ansar would be one whose children did not survive, so she would vow that if her child lived, she would place him with the People of the Book in their religion. Then Islam came, and groups of the sons of the Ansar were upon their religion. They said: "We only placed them upon their religion, and we see that their religion is better than ours!" And now that God has brought Islam, let us compel them! So it was revealed: "There is no compulsion in religion." The outcome was a distinction between those who chose Judaism and those who chose Islam: whoever joined them chose Judaism, and whoever remained chose Islam. The wording of the hadith is that of Humayd.

5815. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard Dawud, from 'Amir, with a similar meaning, except that he said: "The distinction between them was the expulsion by the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of the Banu al-Nadir. Those among them who were Jews and had not become Muslim went with them, and those who had become Muslim remained."

5816. Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Dawud narrated to us, from 'Amir, similarly, except that he said: "The expulsion of al-Nadir was to Khaybar. Whoever chose Islam remained, and whoever disliked it went to Khaybar."

[Reports 5814-5816 are different wordings of a single hadith. See 1:329. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated it. See also reports 5823 and 5824 below.]

5817. Ibn Humayd narrated to me, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad al-Harashi, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from 'Ikrimah, or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his words: "There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become clearly distinct from error." He said: It was revealed concerning a man of the Ansar from the Banu Salim ibn 'Awf called al-Husayn, who had two Christian sons, while he himself was a Muslim. He said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I not compel them, since they refuse anything but Christianity?" So God revealed this about him.

[Report 5817. See Ibn Hajar's discussion in identifying the Companion in "Husayn al-Ansari, unnamed," and then in the chapter on kunyas, "Abu al-Husayn al-Ansari al-Salimi," where both contain a good investigation. See Ibn Kathir's tafsir 2:15 and al-Durr al-Manthur 1:329. See also the following report, number 5819.]

5818. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Awanah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, who said: I asked Sa'id ibn Jubayr about His words: "There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become clearly distinct from error." He said: This was revealed concerning the Ansar. I said: "Specifically?" He said: "Specifically!" He said: In the Jahiliyyah, a woman would vow that if she gave birth to a son, she would make him a Jew, seeking by this that he would live long. He said: Then Islam came, and some of them were among them. When the al-Nadir were expelled, they said: "O Messenger of God, our sons and brothers are among them." He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) remained silent about them, and God, may He be exalted, revealed: "There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become clearly distinct from error." He said: Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Your companions have been given a choice. If they choose you, they are of you, and if they choose them, they are of them." He said: So they expelled them along with them.

[Report 5818 is in al-Bayhaqi's al-Sunan al-Kubra 9:186, through the route of Sa'id ibn Mansur from Abu 'Awanah. It is also mentioned by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:329, who adds its attribution to "Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir," and it includes an addition: "In the Jahiliyyah, when a woman was nazur (having few children) and muqlat, she would vow that if she gave birth to a son, she would make him a Jew," and the rest of the report is the same. In al-Bayhaqi and al-Durr al-Manthur it is written muqlah with a closing ta' marbutah, which is an error. Nazirah (with a fathah and a kasrah) and nazur are words for a woman with few children.]

5819. Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding His words: "There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become clearly distinct from error," up to "there is no breaking of it." He said: It was revealed concerning a man of the Ansar called Abu al-Husayn. He had two sons, and merchants came from Syria to Medina carrying olive oil. When they had sold their goods and wanted to return, the two sons of Abu al-Husayn came to them, and the merchants invited them to Christianity, so they became Christians and went back to Syria with them. Their father came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "My sons have become Christians and left. Shall I pursue them?" He said: "There is no compulsion in religion." [In the printed edition, the verse is completed as "the right path has become clearly distinct from error," which is not in the manuscript or al-Durr al-Manthur.]

No command to fight the People of the Book had been given that day. He said: "May God remove them far away! They are the first to have disbelieved!" Abu al-Husayn resented the Prophet (ﷺ) because he did not send for them, so God revealed: "But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what is disputed between them, then find within themselves no discomfort at what you have decided, and submit in full submission" [Surah al-Nisa' 4:65]. Then indeed "There is no compulsion in religion" was abrogated (naskh), and the command to fight the People of the Book was given in Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah).

[Report 5819. It is in al-Durr al-Manthur 1:329, which attributes it additionally to Abu Dawud in his book on abrogation (Nasikh) and to Ibn al-Mundhir. Ibn Kathir also points to it in his tafsir 2:15. Abu Ja'far did not mention this report in the tafsir of the verse of Surah al-Nisa', nor did he make it an opinion apart from the opinions he mentioned. This is evidence of his abridgment of this tafsir, as they narrated from him.]

5820. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding God's words: "There is no compulsion in religion." He said: It concerned the Jews, the Banu al-Nadir. They had nursed men of the Aws. When the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered their expulsion, their sons from the Aws said: "We will surely go with them, and we will adopt their religion!" But their families prevented them and compelled them to Islam, and this verse was revealed concerning them.

[In the printed edition: "It concerned the Jews, Jews who nursed..." and in the manuscript: "the Jews were Jews who nursed," both of which are errors. In al-Durr al-Manthur 1:329: "al-Nadir had nursed." I think the phrase "Banu al-Nadir" was dropped by a copyist, or the correct reading is as in report 5822: "al-Nadir were Jews..."]

5821. Ibn WakI' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan. And Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, both from Sufyan, from Khusayf, from Mujahid: "There is no compulsion in religion." He said: Some men of the Ansar were nursed among the Banu Qurayzah, and they wanted to compel them to Islam, so this was revealed: "There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become clearly distinct from error."

5822. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: al-Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Mujahid said: "The al-Nadir were Jews, and they nursed [children]," then he mentioned something similar to the hadith of Muhammad ibn 'Amr, from Abu 'Asim. Ibn Jurayj said: 'Abd al-Karim informed me, from Mujahid, that the sons of the Aws had adopted their religion; they had embraced the religion of al-Nadir.

[In the manuscript: "the sons of the Aws had adopted their religion." I fear that what is in the printed edition is more correct.]

5823. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from al-Sha'bi, that a woman among the Ansar would vow that if her child lived, she would make him one of the People of the Book. When Islam came, the Ansar said: "O Messenger of God, shall we not compel our children who are among the Jews to Islam? We only made them part of it, and we see that Judaism is the best of religions?" So when God brought Islam—

[In the printed edition: "When Islam came," and in the manuscript: "When he came," and the correct reading is what I have set down.]

shall we not compel them to Islam? So God, may He be exalted, revealed: "There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become clearly distinct from error."

5824. It was narrated to me from 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Dawud, from al-Sha'bi, the like of it, and he added: He said: The distinction between those among them who chose Judaism and those who chose Islam was the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir. Whoever went out with the Banu al-Nadir was of them, and whoever left them chose Islam.

[Reports 5823 and 5824. See the earlier reports 5814-5816.]

5825. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: "There is no compulsion in religion," up to His words: "the firmest handhold": He said: It is abrogated (mansukh).

5826. Sa'id ibn al-Rabi' al-Razi narrated to me, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, and Wa'il, from al-Hasan: that some men of the Ansar had been nursed among the Banu al-Nadir. When they were expelled, their families wanted to bring them back to their religion, so this was revealed: "There is no compulsion in religion."

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: the People of the Book are not compelled to adopt a religion when they offer the jizyah (poll tax), but they are left upon their religion. They said: The verse concerns a specific category of unbelievers, and nothing of it has been abrogated.

Mention of those who said this:

5827. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding "There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become clearly distinct from error." He said: This tribe of the Arabs was compelled to it, because they were an unlettered people who had no book they knew, so nothing was accepted from them except Islam. The People of the Book are not compelled to it when they acknowledge the jizyah or the kharaj, and they are not turned away from their religion, so they are left alone.

[In the manuscript: "fa-khuliya 'anhum" (so they were left alone). The two are the same.]

5828. Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Sulayman narrated to us, saying: Abu Hilal narrated to us, saying: Qatadah narrated to us regarding His words: "There is no compulsion in religion." He said: It refers to this tribe of the Arabs; they were compelled to the religion. Nothing was accepted from them except death or Islam. But the People of the Book had the jizyah accepted from them, and they were not killed.

5829. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Bashir narrated to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Qays narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak regarding His words: "There is no compulsion in religion." He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was commanded to fight the idolaters of the Arabian Peninsula, and nothing was accepted from them except "There is no god but God" or the sword. Then he was commanded regarding others than them to accept the jizyah from them, so he said: "There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become clearly distinct from error."

5830. al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "There is no compulsion in religion." He said: The Arabs had no religion, so they were compelled to a religion by the sword. He said: The Jews, Christians and Magians are not compelled when they pay the jizyah.

5831. al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ibn 'Uyaynah informed us, from Ibn Abi Najih, who said: I heard Mujahid say to a Christian slave of his: "O Jarir, become Muslim!" Then he said: This is how they used to be addressed.

5832. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "There is no compulsion in religion; the right path has become clearly distinct from error." He said: That was when people entered Islam, and the People of the Book gave the jizyah.

* *

Others said: This verse is abrogated, and it was revealed only before fighting was enjoined.

Mention of those who said this:

5833. Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ya'qub ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Zuhri informed me, saying: I asked Zayd ibn Aslam about the words of God, may He be exalted: "There is no compulsion in religion." He said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was in Mecca for ten years, not compelling anyone in religion. Then the idolaters refused anything but fighting them, so he asked God's permission to fight them, and He permitted him.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these opinions is the view of the one who said: this verse was revealed concerning a specific category of people. He said: By His words, may He be exalted, "There is no compulsion in religion," He means the People of the Two Books (Jews and Christians), the Magians, and everyone whose remaining upon their religion, which opposes the religion of truth, is permitted when the jizyah is taken from them. And they deny that any part of it has been abrogated.

We said this is the most correct of these opinions, because of what we have demonstrated in our book Kitab al-Latif min al-Bayan 'an Usul al-Ahkam: that an abrogating text does not abrogate unless it negates the ruling of the abrogated text, so the two cannot coexist. As for what has an apparently general form of command and prohibition but a specific inner meaning, it is not abrogating or abrogated [see what he said earlier on the conditions of abrogation, 3:358, 563].

Since this is so, and since it was not impossible to say that there is no compulsion for anyone from whom the jizyah is taken in religion, and since there was no evidence in the verse that its interpretation is otherwise, and since the Muslims had all transmitted from their Prophet (ﷺ) that he compelled some people to Islam, and he refused to accept anything from them but Islam, and he ruled that they be killed if they refused it, as with the worshippers of idols among the idolaters of the Arabs, and as with the apostate from the religion of truth to unbelief, and those like them; and that he left others uncompelled to Islam by accepting the jizyah from them and letting them remain upon their false religion, as with the People of the Two Books and those like them; it became clear that the meaning of His words, "There is no compulsion in religion," is only: there is no compulsion in religion for anyone from whom it is permitted to accept the jizyah, by his paying the jizyah and his acceptance of the rule of Islam.

There is no sense in the view of the one who claims that the verse is abrogated in its ruling by the permission to fight.

* *

If someone says: What do you say about what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, and from those from whom it is narrated, that it was revealed concerning some of the Ansar who wanted to compel their children to Islam?

Abu Ja'far said: We say that this report's soundness is not disputed. However, a verse may be revealed about a particular matter, while its ruling is general to everything that resembles the meaning for which it was revealed. Those about whom this verse was revealed, as Ibn Abbas and others mentioned, were a people who followed the religion of the People of the Torah (Ahl al-Tawrah) before Islam was firmly established for them. So God, may His remembrance be exalted, forbade compelling them to embrace Islam, and He revealed, in forbidding that, a verse whose ruling encompasses everyone who was in a similar situation, who held to one of the religions from whose adherents the jizya (poll tax, a tax paid by non-Muslim subjects under Muslim rule) may be accepted and who were allowed to remain upon them, in the manner we have described.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of His words, "There is no compulsion in religion," is: no one is to be compelled into the religion of Islam. [["عليه"، أي على الإسلام. — "upon it", that is, upon Islam.] The definite article "al" was added to "din" (religion) to specify the religion that God intended by His words "there is no compulsion in it," and that this religion is Islam.

It is also possible that the article was added as a substitute (ʿaqīb) for the implied pronoun "hu" in "al-din," [["عقيبا" أي بدلا وخلفا منه... — "ʿaqīban" means a replacement and substitute for it; its root is ʿaqīb, meaning whatever follows and replaces something. ʿAqībuka is the one who alternates with you in work: he works once and you work once.] so that the meaning of the statement becomes: "He is the Most High, the Mighty; there is no compulsion in His religion; right guidance has become distinct from error." This interpretation seems to me closer to the meaning of the verse.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for His words, "right guidance has become distinct," it is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker, "rashadtu, fa-ana arshadu rushdan, wa-rashadan, wa-rishadan," which is used when one hits upon the truth and what is correct. [[انظر ما سلف في معنى "رشد" ٣: ٤٨٤، ٤٨٥. — See what has preceded regarding the meaning of "rashad," 3:484–485.]]

* *

As for "al-ghayy" (error), it is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker, "Fulan has erred (ghawā), so he errs (yaghwā) ghayyan and ghiwāyah." Some Arabs say, "Fulan ghawā yaghwā." The reading of the reciters is God's words, "Your companion has not gone astray (ḍalla) nor erred (ghawā)" [Surah al-Najm: 2], with a fatḥah (on the first letter), and this is the more eloquent of the two dialects. It means that when one transgresses the truth and goes beyond it, he has strayed.

* *

So the meaning of the statement is: the truth has become clear from falsehood, and the path of the seeker of truth and rectitude has become evident to him, distinguishing him from misguidance and error. Therefore, do not compel anyone from among the People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitābayn), [and from among those whom I have permitted you to take the jizya from,] [[أي، فلا تكرهوا من أهل الكتاب ... أحدا على دينكم ... والزيادة مما يقتضيه السياق. — That is: do not compel any of the People of the Book... anyone to your religion. The addition is required by the context.]] [anyone] to your religion, the religion of truth. For whoever turns away from right guidance after it has become clear to him, his affair is with his Lord, and He is the one who will punish him in the Hereafter.

* *

The commentary on His words: "Whoever disbelieves in Ṭāghūt and believes in God"

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wīl) differed regarding the meaning of "Ṭāghūt" (a false object of worship that transgresses against God).

Some of them said: it is Satan.

Those who said this:

5834 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Ḥassān ibn Fā'id al-ʿAbsī, who said: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb said: "Ṭāghūt is Satan." [[الأثر: ٥٨٣٤ -"حسان بن فائد العبسي"... — Report 5834: Ḥassān ibn Fā'id al-ʿAbsī. Abu Ishaq al-Sabiʿī narrated from him. Abu Ḥātim said he was a shaykh; al-Bukhārī counted him among the Kufans; Ibn Ḥibbān mentioned him among the reliable Successors. He is biographed in al-Tahdhīb, al-Kabīr, and Ibn Abi Ḥātim. In the printed edition it was "al-ʿAnsī," and the correct reading is from the manuscript. Ibn Kathīr quoted this report in full in his tafsir.]]

5835 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Ibn Abī ʿAdī narrated to me, from Shuʿbah, from Abu Ishaq, from Ḥassān ibn Fā'id, from ʿUmar, the like of it.

5836 - Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Malik informed us, from someone who narrated to him, from Mujāhid, who said: "Ṭāghūt is Satan."

5837 - Yaʿqūb narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Zakariyyā informed us, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: "Ṭāghūt is Satan."

5838 - al-Muthannā narrated to us, saying: Isḥāq narrated to us, saying: Abu Zuhayr narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, regarding His words, "whoever disbelieves in Ṭāghūt," he said: "Satan."

5839 - Bishr ibn Muʿādh narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah: "Ṭāghūt is Satan."

5840 - Mūsā narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī, regarding His words, "whoever disbelieves in Ṭāghūt," [he said: it is] "with Satan."

* *

Others said: Ṭāghūt is the sorcerer.

Those who said this:

5841 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthannā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Aʿlā narrated to us, saying: Dāwūd narrated to us, from Abu al-ʿĀliyah, that he said: "Ṭāghūt is the sorcerer."

* *

This narration of ʿAbd al-Aʿlā has been contradicted, and I will mention the disagreement afterward. [[في لأثر الآتي رقم: ٥٨٤٤. — In the following report, number 5844.]]

* *

5842 - Muhammad ibn Bashshār narrated to us, saying: Ḥumayd ibn Mas'adah narrated to us, saying: ʿAwf narrated to us, from Muḥammad, who said: "Ṭāghūt is the sorcerer." [[الأثر: ٥٨٤٢ - حماد بن مسعدة... — Report 5842: Ḥammād ibn Mas'adah, whose biography was given under number 3056. In the printed edition it was "Ḥumayd ibn Mas'adah," which is an error here; the correct form is from the manuscript. "Ḥumayd ibn Mas'adah" is the shaykh of al-Ṭabarī, whose biography was given under report 196.]]

* *

Others said: rather, "Ṭāghūt" is the soothsayer (kāhin).

Those who said this:

5843 - Ibn Bashshār narrated to me, saying: Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, saying: Shuʿbah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said: "Ṭāghūt is the soothsayer." [[الأثر: ٥٨٤٣ - ... والصواب "شعبة"... — Report 5843: The printed edition and manuscript both read "Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us," but the correct reading is "Shuʿbah"; compare the same chain in report 5813 and the note on it.]]

5844 - Ibn al-Muthannā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Wahhāb narrated to us, saying: Dāwūd narrated to us, from Rafīʿ, who said: "Ṭāghūt is the soothsayer." [[الأثر ٥٨٤٤ - رفيع، هو أبو العالية الرياحي... — Report 5844: Rafīʿ is Abu al-ʿĀliyah al-Riyāḥī, whose biography has been given many times earlier.]]

5845 - al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding "whoever disbelieves in Ṭāghūt," he said: "They are soothsayers upon whom devils descend, casting [things] upon their tongues and hearts." [Also] Abu al-Zubayr informed me, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, that he heard him say, when he was asked about the ṭawāghīt to which they used to bring their disputes: "In Juhaynah there was one, in Aslam there was one, and in every tribe there was one; they were soothsayers upon whom the devil descended."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view I hold regarding "Ṭāghūt" is that it is everyone who exceeds the bounds against God and is worshipped instead of Him, whether by compulsion over those who worship him, or by obedience of those who worship him to him, and whether that object of worship was a human being, or a devil, or an idol, or a statue, or whatever kind of thing it may be.

* *

I hold that the root of "Ṭāghūt" is "Ṭaghwūt," from the saying of the speaker, "Fulan ṭaghā yaṭghū," when he exceeds his measure and transgresses his limit. It is like "jabarūt" from "tajabbur" (tyranny), and "khalabūt" from "khalab" [[في المطبوعة والمخطوطة "الحلبوت من الحلب" بالحاء المهملة، والصواب ما أثبت. ... — In the printed edition and manuscript it reads "ḥalbūt from ḥalab" with an unpointed ḥāʾ; the correct form is as given. It is said: "a man khalabūt and a woman khalabūt," meaning one who deceives and lies. Poetry on this: "You ruled, and when you ruled you deceived, and the worst of rulers is the treacherous khalabūt." ] (deception), and similar nouns that come in the form "fa'lūt" with the addition of the waw and the taʾ. Then its final radical, meaning the final letter of "ṭaghwūt," was moved, so that it was given a middle position, and its middle was moved to the place of its final letter, as it is said: "jadhaba" and "jabadha," "jādhib" and "jābidh," "ṣāʿiqah" and "ṣāqiʿah," and other nouns that follow this pattern.

* *

So the meaning of the statement is: whoever denies the lordship of every object of worship apart from God, and disbelieves in it, [and believes in God,] [[ويؤمن بالله، يقول: ويصدق بالله أنه إلهه وربه ومعبوده — He says: and affirms in God that He is his God, his Lord, and his object of worship. [Editor's note: look up the meaning of "faith" in the language indices earlier.]]] [then he has grasped the most firm handhold.] He says: then he has held fast to the most secure thing one can hold to in seeking deliverance for himself from God's punishment and retribution, as:

5846 - Aḥmad ibn Saʿīd ibn Yaʿqūb al-Kindī narrated to me, saying: Baqiyyah ibn al-Walīd narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abī Maryam narrated to us, from Ḥumayd ibn ʿUqbah, from Abu al-Dardāʾ: that he visited a sick neighbor of his and found him in the marketplace, gurgling [in his throat], not understanding what he meant.

He asked them: "Does he want to speak?" They said: "Yes, he wants to say: 'I believe in God and disbelieve in Ṭāghūt.'" Abu al-Dardāʾ said: "And how do you know that?" They said: "He kept repeating it until his tongue was broken, so we know he only wanted to speak it." Abu al-Dardāʾ said: "Your companion has succeeded! Indeed God says: 'Whoever disbelieves in Ṭāghūt and believes in God has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, which has no breaking, and God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.'" [[الأثر: ٥٨٤٦ - "أحمد بن سعيد بن يعقوب الكندي"... — Report 5846: Aḥmad ibn Saʿīd ibn Yaʿqūb al-Kindī, Abu al-ʿAbbās, narrated from Baqiyyah ibn al-Walīd and ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd al-Ḥimṣī; al-Nasāʾī narrated from him. Ibn Ḥibbān mentioned him among the reliable narrators. He is biographed in al-Tahdhīb and Ibn Abī Ḥātim. Ḥumayd ibn ʿUqbah is Ḥumayd ibn ʿUqbah ibn Rūmān ibn Zurārah al-Qurashī, said to be al-Filasṭīnī. He heard Ibn ʿUmar and Abu al-Dardāʾ, and Ibn Abī Maryam and al-Walīd ibn Sulaymān ibn Abī al-Sāʾib narrated from him. Aḥmad said: "Abu al-Ghayrah narrated to us: I asked Abu Bakr, 'Ḥumayd ibn ʿUqbah, I think he is an elder, and you narrate from him from Abu al-Dardāʾ?' He said: 'He told me that everything he narrated to me from Abu al-Dardāʾ, he heard from Abu al-Dardāʾ.'" He is biographed in al-Kabīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and Taʿjīl al-Manfaʿah.
It is said: "Fulan is in the sūq, and in al-sayāq," meaning in the death-throes at the moment of death, as if his soul is being driven out of his body. "He is driving his soul, and driving with his soul," meaning he is struggling with the agony of death and its throes. It is said: "Fulan gharghara, yughargharu," meaning he gave up his soul at death. And al-ghargharah is the soul's rattling in the throat, and usually with it there is a sound, like the gurgling of water in the throat. His words, "until his tongue was broken," mean that he was unable to speak. Everyone who is unable to do something has been "broken" from it. This is here a fine expression depicting what happens to the tongue of the dying person.]]

* *

At this point ends a section of the old division from which our copy was taken, in which there is the following text:

"Followed by the discussion on His words: 'then he has held fast to the most secure handhold.'
And may God bless our master Muhammad, the Prophet, and his family, abundantly."

Then the next section begins:

"In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate,
O Lord, make it easy." [[الجزء بعده — the section after it.]]

* *

The commentary on His words: ﴿Then he has held fast to the most secure handhold﴾

Abu Ja'far said: "Al-ʿurwah" (handhold) here is a metaphor for the faith to which the believer clings. He likened his attachment and grip upon it to one who holds fast to the handle (ʿurwah) of a thing that has a handle by which to hold it, since every thing with a handle is grasped by whoever wants it through its handle.

God, may His remembrance be exalted, described the faith by which the one who disbelieves in Ṭāghūt and believes in God holds fast as being among the most secure handles of things, by His words "al-wuthqā" (most secure).

* *

"Al-wuthqā" is "fuʿlā" from "al-wuthāqah" (security, firmness). For the masculine one says "huwa al-awthaq" (he is the most secure), and for the feminine "hiya al-wuthqā," just as one says "fulan al-afḍal" (so-and-so is the most excellent), and "fulānah al-fuḍlā" (so-and-so, feminine, is the most excellent).

* *

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wīl) said something close to what we have said on this.

Those who said this:

5847 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿĀṣim narrated to us, from ʿĪsā, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid regarding His words "by the most secure handhold," he said: "Faith."

5848 - al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Abu Ḥudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, the like of it.

5849 - Mūsā narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī, who said: "The most secure handhold" is Islam.

5850 - Aḥmad ibn Isḥāq narrated to us, saying: Abu Aḥmad narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from Abu al-Sawdāʾ, from Jaʿfar, meaning Ibn Abī al-Mughīrah, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, regarding His words "then he has held fast to the most secure handhold," he said: "There is no god but God." [[الأثر: ٥٨٥٠، ٥٨٥١ - "أبو السوداء"... — Reports 5850 and 5851: Abu al-Sawdāʾ is ʿAmr ibn ʿImrān al-Nahdī, who narrated from al-Musayyib ibn ʿAbd Khayr, Abu Mijlaz, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Bāsiṭ, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim; Ḥafṣ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Sūqah and the two Sufyāns narrated from him. He is reliable, and biographed in al-Tahdhīb.]]

5851 - Ibn Bashshār narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from Abu al-Sawdāʾ al-Nahdī, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, the like of it.

5852 - al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Isḥāq narrated to us, saying: Abu Zuhayr narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: "Then he has held fast to the most secure handhold," the like of it.

* *

The commentary on His words: ﴿There is no breaking of it﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words "there is no breaking of it" God, may His remembrance be exalted, means: there is no snapping of it. The "hā'" and the "alif" in His words "lahā" (of it) refer to "al-ʿurwah" (the handhold).

* *

The meaning of the statement is: whoever disbelieves in Ṭāghūt and believes in God has held fast, in obedience to God, to something he does not fear will fail him when he holds it, nor that God will forsake him when he is in need of Him in the terrors of the Hereafter, like one who holds to the firmest of the handles of things whose handles one does not fear will break. [[في المطبوعة والمخطوطة: "كالتمسك بالوثيق"... — In the printed edition and manuscript: "like the grasp of the firm"; the correct reading required by the context is as given.]]

* *

The root of "al-faṣm" is breaking, and from it is the saying of al-A'shā of the Banū Thaʿlabah:

"Her smile reveals teeth well-spaced, neither irregular nor broken."
[[ديوانه: ٢ من قصيدة... — His Dīwān: 2, from a poem of al-Aʿshā's finest poetry. Preceding it are lines completing its meaning:
"Do you abandon a lady, or do you visit her, or is the rope with her, loose and severed?
Or is right guidance more fitting? For a man whose knowledge will benefit him, if he knows.
Like a guide whom you may find a man, having become clear, then stopped when he advanced.
He disobeyed those who pitied him, following his error, and every sincere advisor is accused by him.
That was only youth, and only the punishment of a man who has sinned.
And a glance of the eye at an unguarded moment, at the place where the companions dwelt in the desert of Zamm.
And her smile..........
So she departed, and in her breast was a crack, like the crack of glass that does not mend."
His words "wa-mubsimahā" (and her smile) are in the accusative as a conjunction with what precedes, and it is a noun of place/manner, meaning her smiling. "Al-shatīt" is the scattered, widely spaced one, meaning: her teeth are well-spaced, not overlapping in their roots. "Al-akas" comes from "al-kasas" (with two fatḥahs), meaning that the upper palate is shorter than the lower, so the two upper incisors are behind the lower ones inside the mouth. It is a defect in the front teeth. The version in the Dīwān reads "munqaṣim," which is the better meaning. It is said: the thing breaks apart without becoming separated. As for "al-qaṣm," it is breaking into a complete separation. But al-Ṭabarī cited it for "al-faṣm" with the "fā'." Both are defects.
The line was distorted in the printed edition: "... ʿan sanab al-nabāt ghayr kasr," and the correct reading is in the manuscript, but it is undotted, so it was misread.]]

* *

The people of interpretation said something close to what we have said on this.

Those who said this:

5853 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿĀṣim narrated to us, from ʿĪsā, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid regarding His words "there is no breaking of it," he said: "God does not change what is with a people until they change what is in themselves."

5854 - al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Abu Ḥudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, the like of it.

5855 - Mūsā ibn Hārūn narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī: "There is no breaking of it," he said: "There is no severance of it."

* *

The commentary on His words: ﴿And God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing (256)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: God, may His remembrance be exalted, means: "And God is All-Hearing" of the faith of the believer in God alone, who disbelieves in Ṭāghūt, at his affirmation of God's oneness and his disavowal of the rivals and idols that are worshipped instead of God. "All-Knowing" of what his heart has resolved upon regarding the tawḥīd (affirmation of God's oneness) of God and the sincere devotion of His lordship, and of what his inner self has embraced of disavowal of the gods, idols, and Ṭāghūts, and of other things that the soul of every one of His creatures conceals. No secret is hidden from Him and no matter is concealed from Him, until He recompenses each one on the Day of Resurrection for what his tongue spoke and his soul harbored: if it was good, then good; and if it was evil, then evil.

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the false deities (ṭāghūt); they bring them out of light into darkness.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "Allah is the Protector of those who believe," may His remembrance be exalted, He means: their helper and supporter; He takes them under His care with His aid and success [see his explanation of "al-walī" (protector) earlier: 2:488, 489 / then: 563, 564]. "He brings them out of darkness" means: [see the discussion of "al-ẓulumāt" (darknesses) earlier: 1:338].

He brings them out of the darknesses of disbelief into the light of faith. By "darknesses" in this place He means disbelief. Darkness was made a parable for disbelief because darkness prevents the eyes from perceiving and distinguishing things, and likewise disbelief prevents the eyes of the hearts from perceiving the realities of faith and knowing its soundness and the soundness of its causes. So He, may His remembrance be exalted, informs His servants that He is the Protector of the believers, and the One who makes the realities of faith, its paths, its laws and its proofs visible to them, and their Guide, thus granting them success in His proofs, which remove doubts from them, by uncovering from them the motives of disbelief and the veils that darken [from] the eyes of the hearts. [The addition between the brackets is indispensable and is not in the printed edition nor in the manuscript.]

Then He, may His remembrance be exalted, informs about those who disbelieve in Him, saying: "And those who disbelieve," meaning those who deny His oneness, "their protectors," meaning their helpers and supporters who take them as allies, "are the false deities (ṭāghūt)," meaning the rivals and idols they worship besides Allah, "they bring them out of light into darkness," meaning by "light" faith, in the manner we have explained, "into darkness," and by "darkness" the darknesses of disbelief and its doubts, which stand between the eyes of the hearts and the sight of the radiance of faith and the realities of its proofs and paths.

* *

The people of interpretation have said in accordance with what we have said:

Those who said this:

5856 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light," he said: from misguidance into guidance. "And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the ṭāghūt," i.e., the Satan; "they bring them out of light into darkness," he said: from guidance into misguidance.

5857 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Zuhayr narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak: "Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light," the darknesses: disbelief, and the light: faith. "And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the ṭāghūt; they bring them out of light into darkness," they bring them out of faith into disbelief. [In the manuscript: "from the darknesses into disbelief," which is a very clear error.]

5858 – It was related to me from ʿAmmar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His exalted saying: "Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light," he said: from disbelief into faith. "And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the ṭāghūt; they bring them out of light into darkness," he said: from faith into disbelief.

5859 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from ʿAbdah ibn Abi Lubabah, from Mujahid or Muqsim, concerning God's saying: "Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the ṭāghūt; they bring them out of light into darkness," he said: There was a people who believed in Jesus and a people who disbelieved in him. When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), those who had disbelieved in Jesus believed in him, and those who had believed in Jesus disbelieved in him — i.e., He brings out those who disbelieved in Jesus into faith in Muhammad (ﷺ) [in the printed edition: "i.e., He brings out those who believed..." which is not correct; in the manuscript: "When Allah sent Muhammad, those who disbelieved in Jesus believed in him, and those who believed in Jesus disbelieved in him, into faith in Muhammad..." with a omission by the copyist due to haste: "i.e., He brings out those who disbelieved in Jesus", which I have restored from the context of the discourse, from the report that follows, despite its error in it, and from al-Durr al-Manthur 1:230; see the note on the following report]. "And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the ṭāghūt," who believed in Jesus and disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ), he said: "they bring them out of light into darkness." [The report 5859: ʿAbdah ibn Abi Lubabah al-Asadi, who narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, Abu Wa'il, Mujahid and others of the trustworthy scholars of Kufa; he is biographied in al-Tahdhib. In the printed edition and manuscript in this place it reads "ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Lubabah," which is an error; the correct form will come in the following report.]

5860 – Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard Mansur, from a man, from ʿAbdah ibn Abi Lubabah, say concerning this verse: "Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light," up to "those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever," he said: They are those who had believed in Jesus son of Mary; when Muhammad (ﷺ) came to them they disbelieved in him, and this verse was revealed concerning them. [In the printed edition and manuscript: "when Muhammad (ﷺ) came to them, they believed in him," which is the copyist's hasty error; the correct reading is what I have given, and see al-Durr al-Manthur 1:230, where the correct form is found, and which is also indicated by the context of al-Tabari's discussion that follows.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This statement we have mentioned from Mujahid and ʿAbdah ibn Abi Lubabah indicates that the verse's meaning is specific, and that, since the matter is as we have described, it was revealed concerning those Christians who disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ), and concerning those idol-worshippers who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ) and who had not acknowledged the prophethood of Jesus, and the other communities whose people denied Jesus.

* *

If someone says: Were the Christians upon the truth before Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent, so that they disbelieved in him?

It is said: Whoever among them was upon the religion of Jesus son of Mary (ﷺ) was upon the truth, and it is them whom Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, meant by His saying: ﴿O you who believe, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa: 136].

* *

If someone says: Is it possible that His saying: "And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the ṭāghūt; they bring you out of light into darkness," refers to other than those whom Mujahid and ʿAbdah mentioned — that they meant by it believers in Jesus — or to people other than apostates from Islam? [In the printed edition and manuscript: "apostasy and Islam," which is an improper conjunction here, since he means those who apostatized from Islam.]

It is said: Yes, it is possible that the meaning is: "And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the ṭāghūt; they hinder them from faith and lead them astray, so that they disbelieve," so their misleading them until they disbelieve is a bringing them out of faith, meaning their turning them away from it and depriving them of its good, even if they had not been in it before, like the saying of a man: "My father expelled me from his inheritance," when someone else possessed that inheritance during his lifetime and deprived him of his share of it; the man never possessed that inheritance so as to be expelled from it, but when he was deprived, and what would have been his was withheld from him had he not been deprived, it was said: "He expelled him from it." And like the saying of one who says: "So-and-so informed me from his battalion," meaning he did not count me among its people, and I was never in it before that. So likewise His saying: "They bring them out of light into darkness" may possibly mean their bringing them out of faith into disbelief in this sense, [in the printed edition: "yahtamil" with a yā' at its beginning; I have kept what is in the manuscript,] although what Mujahid and others said is closer to the interpretation of the verse. [In the printed edition and manuscript alike: "Mujahid and others," which is an error; see the earlier note: p. 427, note 1.]

* *

If someone says to us: How did He say, "And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the ṭāghūt; they bring them out of light," joining the predicate of "ṭāghūt" with "they bring them out," while "ṭāghūt" is singular?

It is said: "Ṭāghūt" is a noun used for both the collective and the singular, and it may be pluralized as "ṭawāghīt." When its singular and plural are rendered with one form, it is like their saying: "a just man (rajul ʿadl) and just people (qawm ʿadl)," and "a fiṭr man and fiṭr people" [i.e., a man who breaks his fast, and people who break their fast], and similar nouns that come in the singular form, whose singular and plural are alike, just as al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas said:

"So we said: Submit, for we are your brothers, and the breasts have been cleansed of grudges."

[Sirah Ibn Hisham 4:95, al-Lisan (akhā), Majaz al-Quran 1:79, from a long qasidah of his on the day of Hunayn, concerning the defeat of Hawazin, mentioning Qarib ibn al-Aswad and his flight from his father's tribe, and Dhu al-Khimar and his people's imprisoning him for death; after the verse: "As if the people, when they came to us, out of enmity after peace, were blind."

He addresses Hawazin ibn Mansur ibn ʿIkrimah, the brothers of Sulaym ibn Mansur, who are the people of al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami. This verse is taken by them as evidence for pluralizing "akh" (brother) with the suffix of waw and nun, like ʿAqil ibn ʿUlfah al-Muri's saying: "The Banu Fazarah were the worst of uncles... and I was to them like the best of the Banu al-Akhyan." So his saying "akhūkum" means "ikhwatukum" (your brothers). This is another aspect other than that for which the verse is cited; and the evidence for al-Tabari's statement is what came in the report: "You are the father and we are the son." Al-Ihn is the plural of ihnah, meaning deep-seated hatred.]

* *

Interpretation of His saying: ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever﴾ [2:257]

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: those who disbelieve are "the companions of the Fire," the people of the Fire who will abide therein — meaning in the fire of Hell — and not others from among the people of faith, for an endless duration, forever. [See the interpretation of "companions of the Fire" and "abiding" earlier: 2:286, 287 / 4:317.]

* *

Interpretation of His saying: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham concerning his Lord, because Allah had given him kingship?﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham concerning his Lord," may His remembrance be exalted, He means: Have you not considered, O Muhammad, with your heart [see the discussion of "seeing" earlier: 3:75–79 / 3:160 / and this part: 266, 291].

"The one who argued with Abraham," meaning the one who disputed with "Abraham," meaning Abraham, the prophet of Allah (ﷺ) [see the meaning of "ḥājja" earlier: 3:121–200], "concerning his Lord, because Allah had given him kingship" — meaning: he argued and disputed with him about his Lord because Allah had given him the kingdom.

* *

This is a marvelling from Allah, may His remembrance be exalted, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), concerning the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord. That is why "ilā" was introduced in His saying "Have you not considered the one who argued," and the Arabs likewise do this when they wish to express wonder at a man in some of his deeds they disapprove of, saying: "Do you see this?!" meaning: Have you seen the like of this, or like this?! [See the meanings of the Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:170.]

* *

It is said: "The one who argued with Abraham concerning his Lord" was a tyrant in Babylon called Nimrod ibn Kanʿan ibn Kush ibn Sam ibn Nuh. It is also said: he is Nimrod ibn Falikh ibn ʿAbir ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshadh ibn Sam ibn Nuh.

Those who said this:

5861 – Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, from ʿIsa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding God's saying: "Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham concerning his Lord, since Allah had given him kingship?" He said: He is Nimrod ibn Kanʿan.

5862 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Huthayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

5863 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nuʿaym narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Layth, from Mujahid, the like of it.

5864 – Ibn Wakiʿ narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from al-Nadr ibn ʿArabi, from Mujahid, the like of it. [Report 5864: al-Nadr ibn ʿArabi al-Bahili, whose biography has passed at 1307. In the printed edition and manuscript it reads "ibn ʿAdi," which is an error.]

5865 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham concerning his Lord," he said: We used to relate that he was a king called Nimrud, and he was the first king to tyrannize on earth, and he was the owner of the tower in Babylon.

5866 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, who said: His name was Nimrud; he was the first king to tyrannize on earth, and he argued with Abraham concerning his Lord.

5867 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' concerning His saying: "Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham concerning his Lord, since Allah had given him kingship?" He said: It was mentioned to us that the one who argued with Abraham concerning his Lord was a king called Nimrud, the first tyrant to tyrannize on earth, and he was the owner of the tower in Babylon.

5868 – Musa narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: He is Nimrud ibn Kanʿan.

5869 – Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said: He is Nimrud.

5870 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, the like of it.

5871 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, saying: Zayd ibn Aslam informed me, the like of it.

5872 – al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Kathir informed me that he heard Mujahid say: He is Nimrud. Ibn Jurayj said: He is Nimrud, and it is said he was the first king on earth.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 258:

The interpretation of His saying, ﴿When Abraham said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." He said, "I give life and cause death." Abraham said, "Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." So the one who disbelieved was confounded. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ (2:258)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His mention be exalted, He means: Have you not seen, O Muhammad, the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord when Abraham said to him, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death"? That is, my Lord is He in whose hand is life and death; He gives life to whom He wills and causes death to whomever He wills after giving life. He said, "I do that: I give life and cause death. I spare the one whom I intended to kill, so I do not kill him, and that is my giving him life," and in the speech of the Arabs this is called "giving life," as He, may His mention be exalted, said: ﴿And whoever gives life to one, it is as if he had given life to all mankind﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 32]. "And I kill another, and that is my causing him to die." Abraham (ﷺ) said: Indeed Allah, who is my Lord, brings the sun from its east, so bring it, if you are truthful that you are a god, from its west! Allah, may His mention be exalted, said: "So the one who disbelieved was confounded," meaning he was cut off and his argument was refuted.

* *

It is said of it: "Bahata yabhutu bahtan" (he was confounded). It has been related from some Arabs that they use "bahata" with this meaning. It is said: "Bahata al-rajul" (the man was confounded) when you falsely accuse him of something: "bahtan, wa-buhtanan, wa-bahatah." [The noun "bahatah" I have not found in the lexicon books, but it is sound by analogy.]

* *

It has been related that some reciters read: "fa-buhita alladhi kafara" (so Abraham confounded the one who disbelieved), meaning: so Abraham confounded the one who disbelieved.

* *

The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) said in accordance with what we have said.

Those who said that:

5873 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying, "When Abraham said, 'My Lord is He who gives life and causes death,' he said, 'I give life and cause death.'" It was mentioned to us that he summoned two men, killed one and spared the other, and said: "I give life to this one! I spare whom I wish and kill whom I wish!" At that, Abraham said, "Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west," "so the one who disbelieved was confounded, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."

5874 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "I give life and cause death": I kill whom I wish and spare whom I wish; I leave him alive and do not kill him. And he said: The kings of the earth, east and west, were four men: two believers and two disbelievers. The two believers: Sulayman ibn Dawud and Dhu'l-Qarnayn; the two disbelievers: Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar) and Nimrod ibn Kan'an. None other than these ruled them.

5875 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Zayd ibn Aslam: The first tyrant on earth was Nimrud. [In the history (of al-Tabari): "Nimrud" with an unpointed dal; in the manuscript likewise, though it does not dot the dotted letters. Both are permissible: with the unpointed dal and with the dotted dhal.] People would go out and procure food from him, and Abraham went out to procure food along with those who procured it. Whenever people passed by him, he said: "Who is your lord?" They said: "You!" Until Abraham passed, and he said: "Who is your lord?" He said: "Who gives life and causes death?" He said: "I give life and cause death!" Abraham said: "Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west!" "So the one who disbelieved was confounded." He said: So he sent him back without food. Abraham returned to his family [In the manuscript and the printed edition: "ʿala ahlihi," and what is better is what is in the history of al-Tabari, which is what I have adopted]. 

He passed by a reddish sand dune and said: "Shall I not take from this and bring it to my family, so that their hearts will be content when I tell them!" He took from it and came to his family. He said: He set down his goods and slept. His wife got up to his goods, opened them, and behold, the finest food anyone had ever seen. She prepared it for him and brought it to him. Now he had left his family with no food among them. He said: "Where is this from?" She said: "From the food you brought!" He knew that Allah had provided for him, and he praised Allah. Then Allah sent to the tyrant an angel: "Believe in me and I will leave you in your kingdom!" He said: "And is there a lord other than me?!" The angel came to him a second time and said the same, and he refused. Then he came to him a third time, and he refused. The angel said to him: "Gather your hosts for three days!" The tyrant gathered his hosts. Allah commanded the angel, and he opened upon him a gate of gnats, so the sun rose but they could not see it because of their multitude. Allah sent them against them, and they ate their flesh and drank their blood, leaving nothing but bones, while the king remained as he was, untouched by any of it. Then Allah sent a gnat against him, which entered his nostril, and he remained for four hundred years being struck on the head with hammers, and the most merciful of people toward him was the one who clasped his hands and struck his head with them. He had been a tyrant for four hundred years, so Allah tormented him for four hundred years as his kingdom had been, and Allah caused him to die. [In the printed edition: "then Allah caused him to die," and what is in the manuscript and history is adopted.] He is the one who built a tower toward heaven, and Allah came upon their building from the foundations, and he is the one of whom Allah said: ﴿So Allah came upon their building from the foundations﴾ [An-Nahl: 26]. [In the manuscript: "fa-ati Allah bunyanahu min al-qawa'id," then he wished to correct it, and repeated it as it was, without striking out the first.]

5876 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam informed me, regarding Allah's saying, "Have you not seen the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord," he said: He was Nimrud, who was in Mosul, and people came to him. When they entered upon him, he said: "Who is your lord?" They said: "You!" He said: "Feed them [amiruhum]." [In the printed edition: "mirūhum," and what is in the manuscript is adopted; both are correct. Mara yamiru and amara: to bring them provisions (mirah, the imported food); and mara al-qawm and amarahum also: to give them provisions.] When Abraham entered, with a camel, going out to procure for his son, he displayed them all, and he said: "Who is your lord?" They said: "You!" He said: "Feed them!" [In the printed edition: "mirūhum," and what is in the manuscript is adopted.] Until Abraham displayed them twice, and he said: "Who is your lord?" He said: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death!" He said: "I give life and cause death; if I wish I will kill you and cause you to die, and if I wish I will spare you." Abraham said: "Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west!" "So the one who disbelieved was confounded, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people." He said: "Remove this man from me and do not sell him anything!" So all the people went out, having procured their food, and Abraham's two sacks were shaking [al-juwaliq (with a damma or kasra or fatha on the lam) is a kind of container, plural juwaliq and juwaliqat, which we now call "shawal"; and "istafqa al-shay'" means it moved about, here from their emptiness]. When he looked at the dark mountains of his family, he said: "My two sons Isma'il and Ishaq will grieve me! If only I filled these two sacks with this valley and took them, the eyes of my child would be comforted, until night when I would pour it out!" He filled them, sewed them up, and brought them. The children ran to them joyfully, and he laid his head in Sarah's lap for a while. Then she said: "What keeps me sitting? Abraham has come weary and exhausted [lughb: he has become utterly worn out, from al-lughub; they mostly say lagh'ib, while "lughb" is rare in their speech, and here it is an echo]. If only you would get up and prepare food for him until he rises!" He said: She took a cushion and placed it in his place, and slipped away little by little lest she wake him. She came to one of the two sacks and opened it, and behold, there was flour of pure white (hawari: the finest, purest white flour, of the highest quality; al-naqa: the wheat from which the flour has run). She took some of it, kneaded it, and baked it. When she came to wake Abraham, she brought it and placed it before him. He said: "What is this, O Sarah?" She said: "From your sack! You have come, and we have nothing little or much." He went to look at the other sack, and behold, it was the same, and he knew whence that came.

5877 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: When Abraham said to him, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death," he said, "I give life and cause death," and he summoned two men, spared one, and killed the other. He said: "I give life and cause death." He said: "That is, I spare whom I wish."
