Abraham said: "Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west," "so the one who disbelieved was confounded, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people."

5878 - Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: When Abraham came out of the fire, they brought him in to the king, who had never entered upon him or spoken with him before, and he said to him: "Who is your lord?" He said: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." Nimrud said: "I give life and cause death! I put four men in a house, where they are neither fed nor given drink, until they perish of hunger; I feed two and give them drink, and they live, and I leave two and they die." Abraham knew that he had the power, through his authority and kingship, to do that. Abraham said to him: "Indeed my Lord is He who brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west!" "So the one who disbelieved was confounded," and he said: "This man is insane! Do you not see that from his madness he dared against your gods and broke them, and that the fire did not consume him?" He feared being exposed among his people, meaning Nimrud, and that is the saying of Allah, may His mention be exalted: ﴿And that was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people﴾ [Al-An'am: 83]. He claimed to be a lord, and he commanded that Abraham be taken out.

5879 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Kathir informed me that he heard Mujahid say: [Nimrod] said: "I give life and cause death: I give life by not killing, and I cause death to whom I kill." Ibn Jurayj said: He had two men brought, killed one and spared the other, and said: "I give life and cause death." He said: "I kill, and cause to die whom I kill, and give life," meaning: "I spare," so I do not kill.

5880 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, saying: It was mentioned to us, and Allah knows best, that Nimrod said to Abraham, among what he said: "Have you seen this god of yours that you worship and call others to worship, and what is the power by which you exalt him over others?" Abraham said to him: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." Nimrod said: "I give life and cause death!" Abraham said to him: "How do you give life and cause death?" He said: "I take two men who have deserved death by my judgment, I kill one and I cause him to die, and I pardon the other and leave him, and I have given him life!" Abraham then said: "Indeed Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west, if you know that it is as you say!" So Nimrod was confounded at that, and did not return any answer to him, and he knew that he could not manage that. His saying, may His mention be exalted, "So the one who disbelieved was confounded," means the proof fell upon him, that is, Nimrod.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: His saying, "And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people," means: Allah does not guide the people of disbelief to a proof by which they can refute the proof of the people of truth in argument and dispute, because the proofs of the people of falsehood are refuted.

* *

We have explained that the meaning of "zulm" (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its place, and the disbeliever who denies what he denies has placed his denial in other than its place, so by that act he is a wrongdoer to himself.

* *

Ibn Ishaq said in accordance with what we have said.

5881 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me: "And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people," that is: He does not guide them in argument during disputation, because of the misguidance they are upon.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 1 of 6):

The discussion of the words of Allah: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, "Or like the one who passed by a town," may He be exalted and remembered, Allah means a case similar to the one He referred to with His words, "Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord," as a matter of wonder at it for Muhammad (ﷺ).
* *
His words, "Or like the one who passed by a town," are coordinated with His words, "Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord." The phrase "Or like the one" is coordinated with "the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord," even though their wordings differ, because their meanings are similar. The words, "Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord," mean: Have you, O Muhammad, seen anyone like the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord? Then He coordinated it with "Or like the one who passed by a town," because it is characteristic of the Arabs to coordinate a statement with a similar meaning that has preceded it, even if its wording differs.
* *
Some of the grammarians of Basra claimed that the "kaf" (like) in His words, "Or like the one who passed by a town," is superfluous, and that the meaning is: Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham, or the one who passed by a town?
* *
We have already explained earlier that it is impermissible for there to be in the Book of Allah anything without meaning, which makes it unnecessary to repeat that here. [[See what has passed: 1: 439-441 / 2: 331, 400.]]
* *
The people of interpretation differed concerning "the one who passed by a town which was fallen upon its roofs."
Some of them said: He was Uzair (Ezra).
Those who said this:
5882 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Nahiyah ibn Ka'b: "Or like the one who passed by a town fallen upon its roofs," he said: Uzair. [[The report 5882: "Najiyah ibn Ka'b al-Asadi" narrated from Ali, Ammar ibn Yasir, and Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, Abu Hassan al-A'raj, and Yunus ibn Abi Ishaq narrated from him. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/107, and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/486.]]
5883 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: Abu Khuzaymah narrated to us, saying: I heard Sulayman ibn Buraydah on His words, "Or like the one who passed by a town," he said: He was Uzair.
5884 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "Or like the one who passed by a town which was fallen upon its roofs," he said: It was mentioned to us that he was Uzair.
5885 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah [the like of it]. [[The addition between the brackets is indispensable.]]
5886 - It was narrated to me from Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, on His words, "Or like the one who passed by a town," he said: al-Rabi' said: It was mentioned to us, and Allah knows best, that the one who came upon the town was Uzair.
5887 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Ikrimah: "Or like the one who passed by a town which was fallen upon its roofs," he said: Uzair.
5888 - Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Or like the one who passed by a town," he said: Uzair.
5889 - It was narrated to me from al-Husayn, saying: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say on His words, "Or like the one who passed by a town which was fallen upon its roofs," that he was Uzair.
5890 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Salm al-Khawwas said to us: Ibn Abbas used to say: He was Uzair. [[The report 5890: "Yunus" is Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la, whose biography has been given many times. "Salm al-Khawwas" is Salm ibn Maymun al-Khawwas al-Razi al-Zahid, one of the great Sufis. He buried his books, and he used to narrate from memory and would err. Ibn Hibban said: He was among the great worshippers of the people of Syria, overcome by righteousness, until he neglected memorizing and mastering hadith, so he is not used as proof. He is biographed in Lisan al-Mizan and in al-Jarh 2/1/267. In the printed edition it read "Salim al-Khawwas," which is an error; the correct reading is from the manuscript.]]
* *
Others said: He was Urmiya ibn Halqiya, [[In the people's book (Scripture) it is Irmiya. The printed edition had the same, but I have kept what is in the manuscript, since it was followed throughout what comes after, and it was written thus in other books. See the "Book of Jeremiah" in their scripture.]] and Muhammad ibn Ishaq claimed that Urmiya was al-Khidr.
5891 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us with that, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: The name of al-Khidr, as Wahb ibn Munabbih used to claim from the Children of Israel, is Urmiya ibn Halqiya, and he was from the lineage of Harun ibn Imran. [[This opinion was refuted and rejected by al-Tabari in his History 1: 194, and what precedes it.]]
Those who said this:
5892 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil narrated to us that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say on His words, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?", that Urmiya, when Bayt al-Maqdis was destroyed and the books were burned, stood in a side of the mountain and said: "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" [[The report 5892 is part of the earlier report no. 5661.]]
5893 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from one who is not accused, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: He was Urmiya.
5894 - Muhammad ibn Asker narrated to me, saying: Isma'il ibn Abd al-Karim narrated to us, saying: I heard Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, the like of it.
5895 - Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa ibn Maymun, from Qays ibn Sa'd, from Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr, concerning the words of Allah, "Or like the one who passed by a town which was fallen upon its roofs," he said: He was a prophet and his name was Urmiya.
5896 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Qays ibn Sa'd, from Abdullah ibn Ubayd, the like of it.
5897 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Bakr ibn [Mudar] informed me, saying: They say, and Allah knows best, that he was Urmiya. [[The report 5897: in the printed and manuscript editions there is a blank in place of what is between the brackets; I have added it from the preceding chains. The biography of "Bakr ibn Mudar al-Misri" has passed under no. 2031, and see this chain in what follows, nos. 5929-5949.]]
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these sayings is to say: Allah, may He be exalted and remembered, marvelled at His Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the one who said, upon seeing a town fallen upon its roofs, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?", although he knew that He had begun its creation from nothing. His knowledge of His power to originate it did not satisfy him, until he said: How will Allah bring it to life after its death! We have no clarification, from any route that could validly provide clarification, of the name of the one who said that. It is permissible that he was Uzair, and it is permissible that he was Urmiya, and we have no need to know his name, since the purpose of the verse was not to inform the creation of the name of the speaker. Rather, its purpose is to inform those who deny Allah's power to revive His creatures after their death and to restore them after their annihilation, and that He is the one in whose hand is life and death, from among the Quraysh and all the other Arabs who denied that, and to establish the proof against those among the Jews of the Children of Israel who lived around the emigration place of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), by informing His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) of what removes their doubt about his prophethood and cuts off their excuse regarding his mission. For these reports which He revealed to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) in His Book were among the reports that Muhammad (ﷺ) and his people did not know, and knowledge of them was only with the People of the Book; Muhammad (ﷺ) and his people were not among them, but rather he was unlettered (ummi) and his people were unlettered, [[By the ummi is meant one who has no book. See the explanation of "ummi" above: 2: 257-259.]] so it was known to the People of the Book among the Jews who lived around his place of emigration that Muhammad (ﷺ) knew that only by revelation from Allah to him. Had the purpose of that report been to name the speaker of that statement, the evidence would have been set up for it clearly, cutting off excuse and removing doubt; but the aim was to censure his saying, so may He be exalted and remembered made that clear to His creatures.
* *
The people of interpretation differed concerning the "town" which the speaker passed by, saying: "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?"
Some of them said: It is Bayt al-Maqdis.
Those who said this:
5898 - Muhammad ibn Sahl ibn Asker and Muhammad ibn Abd al-Malik narrated to me, both saying: Isma'il ibn Abd al-Karim narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil narrated to me that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: When Urmiya saw the destruction of Bayt al-Maqdis like a great mountain, he said: "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?"
5899 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil informed us that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: It is Bayt al-Maqdis.
5900 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from one who is not accused, that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say that.
5901 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, who said: It was mentioned to us that it is Bayt al-Maqdis, which Uzair passed by after Bukhtnassar the Babylonian had destroyed it.
5902 - It was narrated to me from al-Husayn, saying: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say on His words, "Or like the one who passed by a town which was fallen upon its roofs," that he passed by the holy land.
5903 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Ikrimah, concerning His words, "Or like the one who passed by a town," he said: The town is Bayt al-Maqdis, which Uzair passed by after Bukhtnassar had ruined it. [[In the printed edition it is "Bakhtnassar" as one word, as likewise in the History and elsewhere; but the manuscript in this place and everything following it writes it as two separated words, so I have kept it as it is, which is also correct.]]
5904 - It was narrated to us from Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning "Or like the one who passed by a town," he said: The town is Bayt al-Maqdis, which Uzair passed by after Bukhtnassar had ruined it.
* *
Others said: Rather, it is the town in which Allah had destroyed those who left their homes, being thousands, fearing death, and Allah said to them: Die.
Those who said this:
5905 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning the words of Allah, may He be exalted and remembered: ﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes while they were thousands﴾, he said: It was a town in which the plague had descended. Then he related their story, which we have mentioned in its place from him, until he reached ﴿So Allah said to them: Die﴾, in the place to which they had gone seeking life, so they died, then Allah revived them, ﴿Indeed Allah is bountiful to mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 243]. He said: A man passed by it while it was bones scattered, so he stood looking and said: "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him," up to His words "he has not changed." [[The report 5905 is part of report 5608.]]
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The correct statement about this is like the statement about the name of the speaker: "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" Both are the same and do not differ.
* *
The discussion of the words of Allah: ﴿and it was fallen upon its roofs﴾
Abu Ja'far said: By His words, "and it was fallen," may He be exalted and remembered, means: it was empty of its people and inhabitants.
* *
From this is said: "The house became empty, it empties, emptiness and vacancy (khuwiyyan)", and it may be said of a town: "it became empty (khawiyat)", and the first is more eloquent and more chaste. As for a woman who is in postpartum bleeding (nufasa), it is said: "she became empty, she empties, emptiness (khawan)" with shortened form, and it may also be said of her: "she became empty, she empties," as it is said of a house. Likewise: "the belly became empty, it empties, with intense emptiness", [[In the printed edition it is "khawa'an shadidan"; the correct form is from the manuscript. It is also said with the form "khawa'" with a long vowel, but the shortened form is more elevated.]] and if one said of the belly what is said of the house, and of the house what is said of the belly, it would be correct, but what I have mentioned is the more eloquent.
* *
As for "al-urush" (roofs), they are structures and houses; its singular is "arsh," and the plural of its paucity is "a'rush." [[So it came in the manuscript and the printed edition: "a'rush," whereas the lexicographers stated "a'rash," and both are plurals of paucity; I have not seen them mention "a'rush," but it is the analogical pattern, since "fa'l" (with fatha then sukun) mostly takes "af'ul" (with damma on the 'ayn) in its paucity plural, like fals and aflus, unless it is hollow, waw or ya, in which case the usual paucity plural is "af'al," like thawb and athwab, and bayt and abyat. From this it becomes clear that al-Tabari's text is correct and follows the analogy of the language, and that its plural "a'rash" is an exception to its pattern.]]
Every building is an "arsh." It is said: "so-and-so roofed (arsha) a house, he roofs and roofs, roofing (arshan)," [[In the printed edition: "arsha fulan wa-yu'rishu wa-ya'rushu wa-'arasha 'arishan," which does not stand; it intended to correct what was in the manuscript and spoiled it, not reading it well. In the manuscript: "arsha fulan idha yu'rishu wa-ya'rushu 'arshan," but he first wrote "ta'arusha" without dots, then put the letter 'ayn at the start of the word "ya'ri," and when the corrector saw "idha" in the text he deleted it and altered the rest, without doing it well.]] and from it is the saying of Allah, may He be exalted and remembered: ﴿and what they were building (ya'rishun)﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 137], meaning: they were building. From it comes "the arish of Mecca," meaning its tents and structures. [[In the lexicon: "al-urush: the houses of Mecca." In the hadith of Ibn Umar: "that he used to cut off the talbiyah when he looked at the urush of Mecca." Ibn al-Athir said: "the houses of Mecca, because they were palm-branches set up and shaded over," and they said: they are the houses of its needy people.]]
* *
In accordance with what we have said on this, the people of interpretation said likewise.
Those who said this:
5906 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, who said: Ibn Juraij said: Ibn Abbas said: "Khawiyah" means ruin. Ibn Juraij said: It reached us that Uzair went out and stood at Bayt al-Maqdis, which Bukhtnassar had ruined, and he stood and said: "After what you had of holiness, fighters, and wealth, what you had!" So he grieved. [[See the earlier note on p. 443, no. 1. In the printed edition it is "min al-Maqdis," which is a plain error; al-Quds means purity, sanctification and blessing.]]
5907 - It was narrated to me from al-Husayn, saying: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say on His words, "and it was fallen upon its roofs": it is ruin.
5908 - It was narrated to us from Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: Uzair passed by it after Bukhtnassar had ruined it.
5909 - Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "and it was fallen upon its roofs," he says: fallen upon its ceilings.
* *
The discussion of the words of Allah: ﴿He said: How will Allah bring this to life after its death? So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years﴾
Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of that, as has been related to us: [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "and the meaning of that, as I have mentioned, is that..." which does not stand; the correct context is what I have given.]]
That its speaker, when he passed by Bayt al-Maqdis, or by the place which Allah mentioned he passed by, in ruin after having known it populated, said: How will Allah bring this to life after its ruin? [[In the printed edition it cites the verse text "after its death," and I have kept what is in the manuscript, which is correct, to serve as an explanation of his saying "after its death," as the context indicates. See the explanation of "death" meaning the ruin of the land and the decay of its building, above: 3: 274.]]
Some of them said: [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "Some of them said," which seems connected to what precedes; if that were so, the rest of the speech would be corrupted and disordered, and al-Tabari would have needed to mention the sayings of others afterward, but he did not do so. The correct reading, which the context requires, both before correction and in what follows, requires what I have given.]] His saying of that was doubt about Allah's power to revive him.
So Allah showed him His power over that, making an example of it in himself, then showed him the place whose rebuilding and revival he had denied His power over: He revived what he had seen before its ruin, and rebuilt what had been before its ruin. [[His saying "revived what he saw ..." and "rebuilt what had been ..." is the comparative form "af'al" of "life" and "building," and they are not verbs; that is, better in life, and more populated in building.]]
* *

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 2 of 6):

It was the case that the one who said this, as has been reported to us, had known the place populous with its people and inhabitants. Then he saw it empty upon its roofs, its people perished, and they scattered by killing and captivity, so that no one remained in that place, and their homes and dwellings were ruined, and nothing remained but the traces. When he saw it thus, after the state in which he had known it, he said: "In what manner will God bring this to life after its ruin, so that He restores it?" [[See the explanation of "anna" (how/whence) in what has passed, 4: 413-416, and in this part, 5: 312.]] This was a expression of disbelief, as some of the people of ta'wil (interpretation, here meaning the exegetes) have said. So God showed him the manner of its revival by means of what He struck in his own self, and in his water-skin and in his food. [[In the printed edition: "wa-fima kana min sharabihi wa-ta'amihi" (and in what was of his drink and food), the editor did not read the manuscript well, misreading it. In the manuscript: "wa-fima kana min ida' wa-bihi wa-ta'amihi," and the correct form of this corrupted sentence is what I have established. The "idawa" (with a kasra on the hamza) is a small vessel of leather made for water, its plural being "adawa" with a fatha on the waw. I added "fi" between "wa" and "ta'amihi" because the context requires it.]] Then He made him know His power over that and over other things, by showing him, with his own eyes, the revival of what had seemed to him a marvel regarding God's power to revive. So when he saw that, he said: "I know that God is capable of all things." [[Qur'an 2:259.]]

* *

And the reason for his saying that was as follows:

5910 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, who said: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from one not suspected, from Wahb ibn Munabbih al-Yamani, that he used to say: God said to Armiya when He sent him as a prophet to the Children of Israel: [[See what has passed on p. 440, where it is written "Awrmiya," and it is here as I have established. What follows a few lines later will be compared with what has passed.]] "O Armiya, before I created you I chose you, and before I formed you in the womb of your mother I sanctified you, [[In the history of al-Tabari: "in the belly of your mother," the same.]] and before I brought you out of her belly I purified you, and before you reached striving I made you a prophet, [[In the printed edition: "naba'tuka," and I have established what is in the manuscript and the history. It is better to leave out the hamza in it, and to understand it as from the word "nabi" (prophet), and "nabba'a" meaning he made him a prophet or he considered him a prophet. And "tanabba'a al-kadhdhab" means he claimed prophethood.]] and before you reached maturity I chose you, [[In the history: "ikhtabartuka" (I tested you), and what is in the tafsir is the good and correct reading. A difference in some wording will come later which I will not specify until I find it suitable for determination.]] and for a great matter I selected you." Then God, may His remembrance be exalted, sent Irmiya to the king of the Children of Israel to guide and direct him, and to bring him righteousness from God in what lay between him and Him. He said: Then the troubles grew among the Children of Israel, and they committed sins, and made lawful what was forbidden, and forgot what God had done for them and how He had saved them from their enemy Sanharib (Sennacherib). So God revealed to Awrmiya: [[I have established what is in the manuscript at this place; see the previous note no. 1.]] "Go to your people, the Children of Israel, and recount to them what I command you, and remind them of My blessing upon them, and make known to them their transgressions." = Then he mentioned what God sent Armiya with to his people, the Children of Israel. [[What is between the two lines is the speech of Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari), for he cut off the flow of the report and moved to what he intended. What follows begins in his history, vol. 1: 287.]] He said: Then God revealed to Armiya: "I am going to destroy the Children of Israel by Yafith" — and Yafith is the people of Babylon, and they are of the offspring of Yafith ibn Nuh — and when Armiya heard the revelation of his Lord, he cried out and wept and tore his garments, and threw ashes upon his head, and said: "Cursed be the day on which I was born, and the day on which the Torah was taught to me, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "luqiyat al-Tawrat" (the Torah was met with), and I added "fihi" (in it) from the history, and it is better. In the history: "luqqint" from the verb of instruction, and what is in the printed edition and the manuscript is very correct. "Laqiya al-shay' yalqahu" (with the shadda on the qaf and the passive form) means he was taught it, and was alerted to it, and was instructed in it. The two are the same in meaning. Thus it came in the Book of God: "And none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune." (Qur'an 41:35)]] and the worst of my days is the day I was born in, so I was only kept back as the last of the prophets for what is worse for me! [[In the manuscript: "illa lima huwa ashirru 'alayya," and there is no harm in it.]] If He had intended good for me, He would not have made me the last of the prophets among the Children of Israel! Because of me they will be struck with misery and destruction!" Then when God heard the humble supplication of al-Khadir (Armiya) and his weeping and how he spoke, [["Al-Khadir" is "Armiya" himself, according to what Wahb ibn Munabbih, the transmitter of this report, claimed, as has passed from him in no. 5891.]] He called out to him: "Armiya! Is what I revealed to you hard upon you?" He said: "Yes, my Lord, let me die before I see among the Children of Israel what does not gladden me." [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "ahlikni fi bani Isra'il," with "qabla an arwa" (before I see) dropped, and I have established its correct form from the history.]] God said: "By My mighty might, I will not destroy Jerusalem and the Children of Israel until the matter comes from you in that." Armiya was then delighted at what his Lord had said to him, and his soul was content, and he said: "No, by Him who sent Moses and his prophets with the truth, I will never command my Lord to destroy the Children of Israel!" [["La amiru rabbi" (I do not command my Lord) means: I do not ask Him for that, nor do I call upon Him. It is a metaphorical use of the word "amr" (command), good and eloquent Arabic, and you rarely find it in books of lexicography, and rarely find evidence for it. For when one supplicates, he says "Lord, destroy them," and that is a supplication, and every supplication implies this action of command, but it is not a command to God, exalted is God above that greatly. This metaphor in negation is better than in affirmation. See what will come in the report on p. 450, and note: k 4.]] Then he went to the king of the Children of Israel and informed him of what God had revealed to him, and he rejoiced and was glad and said: "If our Lord punishes us, it is for many sins which we have sent ahead for ourselves, and if He pardons us, it is by His power."

= Then they remained after this revelation for three years, not increasing except in disobedience, and they persisted in evil, [[In the history: "wa-tamadayya fi al-sharr" (and they both persisted in evil), which is better.]] and that was when their destruction drew near, so revelation became scarce, until they did not remember the Hereafter, [[In the printed edition: "hatta lam yakunu" — and I have established what is in the manuscript and the history, and it is correct Arabic.]] and He withdrew from them when the world and its affairs distracted them. Then their king said: "O Children of Israel, desist from what you are upon before a violent punishment from God strikes you, and before there are sent against you kings who have no mercy for you. Your Lord is near to repentance, extending His hands with good, merciful to whoever turns to Him!" [[In the history: "wa-qila an yab'ath Allah 'alaykum qawman la rahmata lahum bikum" (and before God sends against you a people who have no mercy for you).]] But they refused to turn away from anything of what they were upon. [["Naza'a 'an al-shay' yanza'u nuza'an" means he refrained and desisted.]] And God cast into the heart of Bakht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar), son of Nabuzaradhan [son of Sanharib, son of Daryas, son of Nimrod, son of Falagh, son of Abir = and Nimrod was the king of Abraham (ﷺ), who argued with him about his Lord] = [[In the printed edition: "Bakhtnassar ibn Na'un ibn Zadhan," and the correct form is from the manuscript and the history. This addition between the parentheses was not in the manuscript, but I added it from the history, because the discourse needs it later when mentioning Sanharib, and that he was the grandfather of Bakht Nassar. His saying "ibn Nabuzaradhan" is in the book of the people (ibn Nabu Bulasar). As for "Nabuzaradhan," it is mentioned among them that he was the commander of a garrison called "Bani Khadh Nasir," and that was Bakht Nassar. This genealogy has been related by al-Tabari before this place in his history, 1: 283, with some difference.]] that he should march to Jerusalem and do there what his grandfather Sanharib had wanted to do. So he set out with six hundred thousand banners, intending the people of Jerusalem. When he departed marching, news reached the king of the Children of Israel that Bakht Nassar had come with his armies, intending you. So the king sent for Armiya, and he came, and the king said: "O Armiya, where is what you told us, that our Lord had revealed to you that He would not destroy the people of Jerusalem until the matter came from you in that?" [[Al-amr (the matter) means the supplication and the request. See the earlier note on p. 449, note 4.]]

[[In the printed edition: "wa-qad tamaththal" with the waw, and I have established what is in the manuscript and the history, and it is very good.]] Armiya said to the king: "My Lord does not break His promise, and I am confident in Him."

= When the term drew near and the end of their kingdom approached, and God resolved to destroy them, God sent an angel from Him and said to him: "Go to Armiya and ask him for a legal opinion," and He instructed him concerning what he should ask about.
The king came to Armiya, and an angel had appeared to him in the form of a man from the Children of Israel, [[In the printed edition: "rajul..." with "ana" omitted, and I have established what is in the manuscript and the history.]] and Armiya said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "A man from the Children of Israel, asking you for a ruling about some of my affairs." So he permitted him, and the angel said: "O prophet of God, I came to you asking for a ruling concerning the people of my kin. I have joined their ties of kinship with what God commanded me, I have done nothing to them but good, and I have not withheld honour from them; so will my honouring them only increase their anger toward me? Give me a ruling concerning them, O prophet of God." He said to him: "Be good in what is between you and God, join what God has commanded you to join, and rejoice in good." So the angel departed from him. Then he remained for some days, and came again to him in the form of that man who had come before, and sat before him. Armiya said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "I am the man who came to you concerning my family!" [[In the history alone: "I came to you asking about the matter of my family."]] The prophet of God said to him: "Have their characters not yet become pure for you, and have you not seen from them what you love?" He said: "O prophet of God, by Him who sent you with the truth, I know of no honour that one of the people brings to his kin except that I have brought it to them, and more than that!" The prophet said: "Return to your family and be good to them, and I ask God, who sets right His righteous servants, to set right your relations, and to unite you upon His pleasure, and to keep you from His wrath!" Then the king rose from him and remained for some days, and Bakht Nassar and his armies had settled around Jerusalem, more numerous than locusts. [[In the printed edition: "bi-junudihi" (with his armies), while in the manuscript it is "junudihi" without the waw. I have established what is in the history, where there is also "bi-akthara min al-jarad" (more than locusts).]] The Children of Israel were struck with great terror, and that weighed heavily on the king of the Children of Israel, so he called Armiya and said: "O prophet of God, where is what God promised you?" He said: "I am confident in my Lord."

= Then the king came to Armiya while he was sitting on the wall of Jerusalem, laughing and rejoicing in the victory of his Lord that had been promised to him. He sat before him, and Armiya said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "I am the one who asked you for a ruling concerning my family twice." [[In the history: "I came to you concerning the matter of my family..."]] The prophet said to him: "Has the time not yet come for them to awaken from what they are in?" The king said: "O prophet of God, every harm that came to me from them before today, I bore patiently, and I knew that what was in them was in my wrath. But when I came to them today, I saw them doing a deed that does not please God and that God does not love." The prophet said: "What deed did you see them doing?" He said: "O prophet of God, I saw them engaged in a great deed of God's wrath. If they had been upon what they were upon before today, my anger would not have been so severe against them. I would have been patient with them and hoped for them, but today I was angry for God's sake and for yours. So I came to inform you of their news, and I ask you by God, who sent you with the truth, only that you pray to your Lord to destroy them." [[In the printed edition alone: "alladhi ba'athaka" without "huwa."]] Armiya said: "O Possessor of the heavens and the earth, [[In the printed edition alone: "ya malik al-samawat."]] if they are upon truth and righteousness, then preserve them, and if they are upon Your wrath and a deed You do not approve, then destroy them!" When the word had come forth from the mouth of Armiya, God sent a thunderbolt from heaven upon Jerusalem, and the place of the offering caught fire, and it was swallowed up by seven of its gates. When Armiya saw that, he cried out and tore his garments and threw ashes upon his head, and said: "O King of the heavens, O most merciful of the merciful, where is your promise which you promised me?" Then it was called out: "Armiya, it has only befallen them what has befallen them because of your fatwa which you gave to Our messenger," and the prophet was certain that it was his own fatwa which he had given three times, and that he was the messenger of his Lord, and Armiya flew away until he mingled with the wild beasts.

= Bakht Nassar and his armies entered Jerusalem, and he trod upon Syria, and he killed the Children of Israel until he annihilated them, and he laid Jerusalem waste. Then he ordered his soldiers that each man fill his shield with earth and then cast it into Jerusalem, so they cast the earth into it until they filled it. Then he returned to the land of Babylon, taking with him the captives of the Children of Israel, and he ordered them to gather everyone who was in Jerusalem, all of them, so there gathered before him every young and old of the Children of Israel. He chose from them seventy thousand boys; [[In the printed edition: "ninety thousand boys." In the manuscript: "seventy boys," dropping "thousand." In the history: "he chose from them one hundred thousand boys," but after that he returned and related what will come: "and he took the seventy thousand boys," so I fear the reading in the history is an error, and the correct reading is "he chose from them seventy thousand boys out of one hundred thousand boys."]] and when the spoils of his army came out, and he wanted to distribute them among them, the kings who were with him said to him: "O king, all our spoils are yours, but distribute among us these boys whom you have chosen from the Children of Israel!" So he did, and each one of them received four youths, and among those youths were Daniel, Azariah, Mishael and Hananiah. [["Azriya," "Mishaeel," and "Hannaniya" — thus their names are written in the Book of Daniel, chapter one. In the printed edition it was "Misayil," and I have established what is in the manuscript and the history. In the history after this place there is an enumeration of these youths from the tribes of the Children of Israel.]] Bakht Nassar divided them into three groups: a third he kept in Syria, a third he took captive, and a third he killed. He took the vessels of Jerusalem until he brought them to Babylon, [[In the printed edition alone: "bi-asbiyat Bayt al-Maqdis" (with the wares of Jerusalem), which is an error with no meaning here.]] and the seventy thousand boys until he brought them to Babylon, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "the ninety thousand." This contradicts what has passed in the report in the manuscript, as we mentioned in note 1, and I have established what is in the history.]] So this was the first calamity by which God, may His remembrance be exalted, reminded the Children of Israel of their transgressions and their wrongdoing. [[In the printed edition alone: "al-waqi'a al-ula allati dhakara Allah," and then follows in the manuscript and the printed edition "... ta'ala dhikruhu nabi Allah bi-ihdathihim..." and the correct reading is from the history.]]

When Bukht Nasr turned back toward Babil with the captives of the Children of Israel, Armiya (Jeremiah) came upon a donkey of his, with a jug of grape juice in a *zukra* and a basket of figs. [[The *zukra* (with a damma on the z and sukun on the k) is a small leather container in which drink is kept. In the History (Tarikh) it is written as *rakwa*, but the correct reading is that of the Tafsir, for the *rakwa* (with a kasra and sukun) is a small leather vessel from which water is drunk. It is like a cup, not like a waterskin.]] until he reached Iliya. When he stood over it and saw the ruin that was in it, doubt entered him, and he said: "How will God bring this to life after its death?" So God caused him to die for a hundred years, along with his donkey, his juice and his basket of figs, which were with him where God made him die, and He made his donkey die with him. [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "and his donkey died with him." I have adopted what is in the History.]] God then blinded the eyes against him, so no one saw him. Then God raised him up and said to him: "How long have you remained?" He said: "I remained a day or part of a day." He said: "Rather, you remained a hundred years. Look at your food and your drink, which has not spoiled," meaning, has not changed, "and look at your donkey, and We will make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh." He looked at his donkey, and its bones were joining one to another. [[In the printed edition alone: "its bones join one to another." I have adopted what is in the manuscript and the History, and what comes later under no. 5933. In the History it reads "yatasil" as in the printed text. As for his saying "yatasil," its root is the form "yifta'il" from "wasala." The original of the verb is "irtasal, yartasil, fahuwa mutarsil." But the dialect of the Hijaz and especially the Quraysh is that this waw and its like are not assimilated, while others assimilate it and say "ittasal, yattasil, fahuwa muttasil." From "wafaqa" they say "ittafaq, yattafiq, fahuwa muttafiq," and similar forms. Al-Shafi'i in his Risala followed this usage. See paragraphs 95, 569, 574, 662, 1275, 1333, and my brother al-Sayyid Ahmad's comment on paragraph 95. In a hadith: "The name of his arrow, peace be upon him, was al-Mutasilah," so called as an omen of its reaching the enemy. See the comment on the report no. 5933 below.]] Its bones had died with him, along with the sinews and tendons. Then how flesh was clothed upon them until they were complete. [[In the printed edition: "then how He clothed..." and it comes later under no. 5933 as I have set it, and it is the correct reading.]] Then the spirit entered it, and it stood and brayed. He looked at his juice and his figs, and they were in the same state as when he had put them down, unchanged. When he witnessed of God's power what he witnessed, he said: ﴿I know that God is over all things competent﴾. Then God let Armiya live on after that, and he is the one who is seen in the wastelands and the lands.

5911 – Muhammad ibn 'Askar and Ibn Zanjawayh related to me, both saying: Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Karim related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil related to me that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: God revealed to Armiya while he was in the land of Egypt: "Go to the land of Iliya, for this is not a land of permanent residence for you." So he mounted his donkey, and when he was part way along the road, with a basket of grapes and figs, and he had with him a new waterskin which he filled with water. When there appeared to him the shape of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and what surrounded it of villages and mosques, and he looked at a ruin that cannot be described, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "and he looked at a ruin." The correct reading omits this waw, see the following note.]] and saw the demolition of Bayt al-Maqdis like a great mountain, he said: [[In the printed edition: "and he saw the demolition..." while the manuscript has: "The sense of the context requires the reading of the manuscript, and the omission of the waw from 'wa-nazara' as already mentioned in the note before it."]] "How will God bring this to life after its death?" He journeyed until he reached a dwelling place among its ruins, tied his donkey with a new rope, hung up his waterskin, and God cast sleep upon him. When he slept, God took his soul for a hundred years. When seventy years of the hundred had passed, God sent an angel to a great king of the Persian kings called Yusk. [[I do not know the correctness of this name, and I have not found it in any other book.]] He said: "God commands you to set out with your people and rebuild Bayt al-Maqdis and Iliya and its land, until it returns to being more prosperous than it ever was." The king said: "Give me three days until I prepare for this work and what is needed for the performance of the work." So he gave him three days, and he appointed three hundred *qahramans*, and gave each *qahraman* a thousand workers and what was needed as tools of the work. [[The *qahraman*: one of the king's trustees and intimates, like the treasurer and the agent who guards what is under his hand and manages a man's affairs.]] His *qahramans* set out for it with three hundred thousand workers. When they began the work, God returned the spirit of life to the eye of Armiya, while the rest of his body was dead. [[In the printed edition: "and the rest of his body dead," and the correct reading is what is in the manuscript at this place, and in what follows in the manuscript and the printed text under no. 5938. The word "rest" here means what remained after the return of his head to life. It is a permissible Arabic figure of speech. See the comment on no. 5938 below.]] He looked at Iliya and the villages around it, and the mosques, rivers, and tilled fields working, building and renewing, [[Thus in the printed edition and the manuscript: "wa-l-hurut." I fear the correct reading may be "wa-l-harrathun," the plural of *harith*, the one who ploughs the land.]] until it became as it had been. After thirty years, completing the hundred, the spirit was returned to him. He looked at his food and his drink, which had not spoiled, and he looked at his donkey standing in the same condition as the day he tied it, having neither eaten nor drunk, and he looked at the halter on the donkey's neck, unchanged, new. [[The *rumma* (with a damma or kasra on the r and a doubled m): a piece of rope with which a captive is shackled, or which is placed on a camel's neck. The lexicographers say it is the worn-out piece. But here he has used it without this description, indeed describing it as a new halter, which is good and unobjectionable.]] A hundred years of wind, a hundred years of cold, and a hundred years of heat had passed over it, and it had not changed or deteriorated at all. [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "lam tantaqis" with the unpointed sad, which is an error. The correct reading is what I have set. "Intaqada" the rope and other things: when its strands are untwisted, its fibres are destroyed and it decays. As for his saying "shay'an," it means "a little," nor much, and it is a good expression in Arabic.]] Armiya's body had wasted away through decay, and God made new flesh grow on him, and his bones were raised while he watched. God said to him: ﴿Look at your food and your drink, which has not spoiled, and look at your donkey, and We will make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We raise them, then clothe them with flesh﴾. When it became clear to him, he said: ﴿I know that God is over all things competent﴾. [[Report 5911: "Muhammad ibn 'Askar" is Muhammad ibn Sahl ibn 'Askar al-Bukhari, whose biography was given under no. 5598. "Ibn Zanjawayh" refers to two men: Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Malik ibn Zanjawayh al-Baghdadi, from whom the four (authors of the Sunan) related, along with 'Abdullah ibn Ahmad and others. He died in the year 258. He is trustworthy but makes many errors. The other is Humayd ibn Makhlad ibn Qutayba al-Azdi, from whom Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Abu Zur'a, Abu Hatim and others related. He was of good jurisprudence, wrote and travelled, and was a leading figure in knowledge. Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said: "There has not come to us from the youths of Khurasan the like of Ibn Zanjawayh and Ibn Shabawayh." His death is disputed between the years 247 and 251. I think this is the teacher of al-Tabari, and perhaps what follows will indicate his identity, God willing.]]

5912 – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: 'Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil informed us that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say, concerning His words: ﴿How will God bring this to life after its death?﴾: when Bayt al-Maqdis was laid waste and the books were burned, Armiya stood in a side of the mountain and said: ﴿How will God bring this to life after its death?﴾, ﴿So God caused him to die for a hundred years﴾. Then God returned to life some of the Children of Israel, at the end of seventy years from the time He caused him to die, and they built it up for thirty years, completing the hundred. When the hundred was over, God returned his spirit, and it had been rebuilt in its former state. He began to look at the bones, how they were joining one to another, [[To join (iltam) a thing: "yaltaim," and "altam" (with the hamza eased) means when one part is brought together with another and gathered.]] then he looked at the bones, how they were clothed with sinew and flesh. When this became clear to him, he said: ﴿I know that God is over all things competent﴾. Then God, exalted be His remembrance, said: ﴿Look at your food and your drink, which has not spoiled﴾. He said: His food was figs in a basket, and a jug with water. [[Report 5912: it has passed truncated under no. 5661, and see the comment on it there. The *mikhtal* (with a kasra on the m): the basket in which dates or grapes or other things are placed.]]

5913 – Musa related to me, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town which was fallen on its roofs﴾. That was because 'Uzayr passed coming from Syria on a donkey of his, with grape juice, grapes and figs. When he passed by the town and saw it, he stood over it and turned his hand over and said: "How will God bring this to life after its death?" =Not as a denial on his part, nor a doubt=. So God caused him to die and made his donkey die, and they both perished, and a hundred years passed over them. Then God revived 'Uzayr and said to him: "How long have you remained?" He said: "I remained a day or part of a day!" It was said to him: "Rather, you remained a hundred years! So look at your food of figs and grapes, and your drink of juice =﴿which has not spoiled﴾, and so on."

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿Then He raised him; He said: How long have you remained? He said: I have remained a day or part of a day. He said: Rather, you have remained a hundred years﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His words, exalted be His remembrance: ﴿Then He raised him﴾, He means: He brought him back to life after his death.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "ba'th" (raising) earlier. [[See what has passed: 2:84, 85.]]

* *

As for the meaning of His words ﴿How long have you remained?﴾: "kam" in the speech of the Arabs is an interrogative asking about the amount of a number. [[See what has passed concerning the meaning of "kam" in this part, 5:352.]] In this place it is in the accusative case, governed by "labithta" (you remained), and its interpretation is: God said to him: What is the measure of the time you remained dead before I raised you from your death alive? The one raised after his death said: I remained dead until You raised me alive, a day or part of a day.

* *

It is mentioned that the one raised was Armiya, or 'Uzayr, or whoever was meant by God in this report.

* *

He only said: ﴿I remained a day or part of a day﴾ because God, exalted be His remembrance, had taken his soul at the beginning of the day, and then returned his soul at the end of the day after the hundred years, and he was asked: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ He said: I remained a day; he thought the sun had set. So for him that was a day, since it is mentioned that he had his soul taken at the beginning of the day, and he was asked about the length of his stay dead at the end of the day, and he thought the sun had set, so he said: ﴿I remained a day﴾. Then he saw a remnant of the sun still left unset, so he said: ﴿or part of a day﴾, meaning: "Rather, part of a day," as God, exalted be His remembrance, said: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand, or they increase﴾ [al-Saffat: 147], meaning: "Rather, they increase." [[See what has passed on "aw" meaning "bal" (rather) 2:235-237.]] So his saying: ﴿or part of a day﴾ was a retraction by him of his saying: ﴿I remained a day﴾.

* *

A group of the people of interpretation said in agreement with what we have said on this matter.

Those who said that:

5914 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, concerning His words: ﴿Then He raised him; He said: How long have you remained? He said: I have remained a day or part of a day﴾: he said: It was related to us that he died at mid-morning, then He raised him before the sun set, and he said: ﴿I have remained a day﴾. Then he turned and saw a remnant of the sun, and he said: ﴿or part of a day﴾. Then He said: ﴿Rather, you have remained a hundred years﴾.

5915 – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada: ﴿How will God bring this to life after its death?﴾ He said: He passed by a town and was amazed, and said: ﴿How will God bring this to life after its death?﴾ So God caused him to die at the beginning of the day, and he remained a hundred years, then He raised him at the end of the day, and said: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ He said: ﴿I have remained a day or part of a day﴾. He said: ﴿Rather, you have remained a hundred years﴾.

5916 – It was related to me from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, who said: al-Rabi' said: God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him, and said: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ He said: ﴿I have remained a day or part of a day﴾. He said: ﴿Rather, you have remained a hundred years﴾.

5917 – Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, who said: Ibn Jurayj said: When he stood over Bayt al-Maqdis, which Bukht Nasr had laid waste, he said: ﴿How will God bring this to life after its death?﴾! How will He restore it as it was? So God caused him to die. He said: It was related to us that he died at mid-morning, and was raised before sunset after a hundred years, and He said: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ He said: ﴿A day﴾. When he saw the sun, he said: ﴿or part of a day﴾.

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿So look at your food and your drink, which has not spoiled﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted be His remembrance: ﴿So look at your food and your drink, which has not spoiled﴾, He means: the years which passed over it did not change it.

* *

His food, as some of them mentioned, was a basket of figs and grapes, and his drink a jug of water.

Some others said: Rather, his food was a basket of grapes and a basket of figs, and his drink a *ziqq* of juice. [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "*zaqq*" in the nominative; the accusative is better.]]

Others said: Rather, his food was a basket of figs, and his drink a jar of wine, or a *zukra* of wine. [[The *zukra* (with a damma on the z and sukun on the k): a small leather waterskin in which drink or vinegar is kept.]]

We have already mentioned earlier what some of them said on this, [[meaning the reports which passed concerning the story of "the one who passed by the town."]] and we will mention what it contains in what is to come, God willing.

* *

As for His words ﴿which has not spoiled﴾, there are two readings:

One of them: "lam yatassan" (without the final *ha'*) when connected, and with it when stopping. Whoever reads it this way makes the *ha'* in "yatassanhu" a superfluous addition, [["Silah" means an addition and superfluity, in the sense of being nullified. See what has passed: 1:190, 405, and comment 4/406, comment 2 thumma: 548.]] like His saying: ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90], and makes the verb "tafa''altu" from it: "tasannaytu tasanniyan," and he justifies this by saying that "sanah" (year) has the plural "sanawat," so the form "tafa''altu" is sound. [[In the printed edition: "according to its method," while the manuscript reads "'ala sihha" (according to soundness). Since it was not dotted in the manuscript, the printer did what he wished! In the Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' and in Lisan al-'Arab it is "'ala sihha," so I have adopted it from them.]]

Whoever says in "sanah": "sanina," then it is permissible on this basis, though rare, that "tasannaytu" is "tafa''altu," the nun being changed to a *ya'* since the nuns multiplied, as they say: "tazanniytu," whose origin is "al-zann" (suspicion). Some have said it is derived from His words: ﴿of black mud altered﴾ [al-Hijr: 26, 28, 33], meaning changed. That too, if it is so, is also something whose nun was changed to a *ya'*. [[This whole passage is verbatim from al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:172-173 and Lisan (sanah), with slight variation in some wording.]]

This is the reading of most of the readers of Kufa.

* *

The other of them: affirming the *ha'* both when connected and when stopping. Whoever reads it this way makes the *ha'* in "yatassanhu" the final radical of the verb, makes it jussive governed by "lam," and makes the verb from it "tasannahta," and the imperfect "atassanhu tassanuhan." [[Here he means by "fa'ala" and "yaf'alu" the past and present, which is not the earlier "tafa''altu" that we corrected as in p. 460, note 3.]] He says in the diminutive of "sanah": "sunayhah" and "sunayyah," and "asnaytu 'inda al-qawm" and "asnahtu 'indahum," when you stay a year. [[In the printed edition there is omission, addition and alteration. It had: "He said in the diminutive of sanah: sunayha, and from it: asnahtu 'inda al-qawm wa-tasannahtu 'indahum," and I have restored what is in the manuscript, which is also correct, though the confusion may have arisen from the mention of "sunayya" and "asnayta." But it is permissible that the speaker of this statement holds both to be allowed, which is why I have set it as in the manuscript, and it is not to be changed except by proof. The words of al-Tabari will come shortly: "that this is a sound way in both cases."]]

This is the common recitation of the people of Medina and the Hijaz.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: In my view, the correct recitation in this matter is to affirm the "hā'" (the final *hā'*) both in continuous recitation and at pause, because it is written in the codex of the Muslims, and affirming it has a sound basis in both cases.

The meaning of His saying ﴿it has not changed﴾ is that the years have not passed over it so that it alters, according to the dialect of one who said "asnahat ʿindakum asnih" (I have stayed with you a year), meaning, when he remains for a year. As the poet said: [[Suwayd ibn al-Samit al-Ansari, though it is said to be Uhayha ibn al-Jullah.]]

*"It is neither a barren one nor a rujabiyya,
but ʿarāyā in the years of calamities."*

[[Al-Farra', Maʿani al-Qur'an 1:173; al-Amali 1:21; Samt al-La'ali: 361; Tahdhib al-Alfaz: 520; al-Lisan (ʿ-r-y, q-r-h, s-n-h, kh-w-r, r-j-b); and al-Isaba in his biography. The lines are from verses he composed concerning a debt he had incurred and was asked to repay, so he paid it off from his people's wealth and was ashamed before them. The order of the verses, as I surmise, is:

"I have become estranged from my people, as though
I had brought upon them one of the disgraces through debt:
I borrow, and my debt to them is not a burden,
but to the sturdy, enduring, long-lived palms.
Upon every productive one, whose trunks seem
daubed with pitch or with the mud of a water-drawer.
It is neither a barren one nor a rujabiyya,
but ʿarāyā in the years of calamities.
I borrow against its fruits and its roots,
for a near master or a distant one."

*Dāna yadīnu*: he borrowed money. *Al-shumm*: the tall ones. *Al-jilad*: those very patient of thirst, heat and cold, meaning the palm trees. *Al-qarāwiḥ*, plural of *qarūḥ*: the palm whose heart has been cleared and which has grown tall, which is best for it. *Al-khawwār*: the one heavy with fruit. He describes its trunks as daubed with pitch or mud, because when they are so treated they are stronger and more noble. *Al-māʾiḥ*: one who draws water from a well, that is, one who irrigates. *Al-sanhāʾ*: one that bore fruit one year and did not bear the next, which is a defect in palms. *Qawluhu "rujabiyya"* (with the *rāʾ* vowelled and the *jīm* doubled and fatha, or fatha without doubling): both are rare derivations from *al-rujba* (with a damma and a sukun): when a noble palm is feared to fall because of its height and heavy fruit, a support is built beneath it, with which it is propped up, that is, "its support." This happens when it reaches weakness, but he honours it thereby. *ʿArāyā*, plural of *ʿarīyya*: the palm whose fruit is given away in its year, which he does out of generosity. *Al-jawāʾiḥ*: the barren, hard years that sweep away wealth.

He says to his people: "I have come to borrow from you, on the condition that I repay from my palms and my property. So why this alarm? Do you fear that my debt will be a burden you must pay? Here are my palms, and I describe to you their quality and generosity, which you know better than I do."]]

He thus made the *hā'* in *al-sanah* (the year) original, and this is the eloquent dialect.

* *

It is not permissible to delete a letter from the Book of God, whether at pause or in continuous recitation, when its affirmation has a well-known basis in their speech.

If someone objects that in the codex, letters have been added which are superfluous for the intention of pause, and that the proper practice in recitation is to omit them, as in His saying ﴿So follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90], and His saying ﴿Would that I had not been given my account﴾ [al-Haqqah: 25], then these are cases where there is no doubt that they are superfluous and were added for the intention of pause. But what may be an original, non-superfluous letter of the word is not permissible to treat as superfluous and extra (*ṣilāt*, filler elements), since it is affirmed in the codex of the Muslims. [[See the meaning of "ṣila" above, p. 460, note 2.]]

Moreover, even if that letter is superfluous in those cases where there is no doubt it is superfluous [[In the printed edition: "wa-in kāna zāʾidan", and the correct reading is that of the manuscript.]], the Arabs do connect speech to a superfluous element and pronounce it as they do in a state of pause, so that their connecting it and stopping at it are the same. This practice of theirs is evidence for the soundness of the recitation of those who recite all of these with the *hā'* affirmed in both continuous recitation and pause. Yet even so, His saying ﴿has not changed﴾ has a ruling distinct from the ruling of those words whose *hā'* is superfluous beyond any doubt. [[In the printed edition: "mā kāna hāʾuhu zāʾidan lā shakk fī ziyādatihi fīhi", in the masculine, which is quite correct, but I do not know why it was altered from the manuscript text.]]

* *

What shows the soundness of what we have said, that the *hā'* in *yatasannahu* belongs to the dialect of the one who said "qad asnahat" and "al-musānaha", is what follows:

5918: I have related this on the authority of al-Qasim ibn Sallam, who said: Ibn Mahdi related to us, on the authority of Abu al-Jarrah, on the authority of Sulayman ibn ʿUmayr, who said: Hani, the client of ʿUthman, related to me, saying: I was the messenger between ʿUthman and Zayd ibn Thabit. Zayd said: "Ask him about His saying *lam yatasann*, or *lam yatasannahu*." ʿUthman said: "Put a *hā'* in it."

5919: I have related this on the authority of al-Qasim, and Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-ʿAttar related to us on the authority of al-Qasim, and Ahmad and al-ʿAttar related to us, all on the authority of al-Qasim, who said: Ibn Mahdi related to us on the authority of Ibn al-Mubarak, who said: Abu Wa'il, a shaykh from the people of Yemen, related to me on the authority of Hani al-Barbari, who said: I was with ʿUthman while they were reviewing the codices. He sent me with a shoulder of mutton to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, on which was written: *lam yatasann* and *fa-amhili al-kafirin* [al-Tariq: 17] and *la tabdila lil-khalq* [al-Rum: 30].

He said: He called for an inkpot and erased one of the two *lāms*, and wrote ﴿There is no change in the creation of God﴾, and he erased *fa-amhil* and wrote ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers﴾, and he wrote ﴿it has not changed﴾, adding the *hā'* to it. [[The report 5918: Hani is Hani al-Barbari, client of ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, whose biography is in al-Kabir 4/2/229 and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/2/100. Sulayman ibn ʿUmayr, who narrated from Hani, client of ʿUthman, and from whom ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak narrated, is in al-Kabir 2/2/30 and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/133. As for "Abu al-Jarrah", I have not identified him. See the following report, for I fear that the isnads of the two have become confused, since Ibn al-Mubarak is the one who narrates from Sulayman ibn ʿUmayr. See also al-Durr al-Manthur 1:323.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: If that were from *yatasanna* or *yatasannan*, Ubayy would not have added a *hā'* for which there is no place in it, nor would ʿUthman have ordered its addition.

It has been related from Zayd ibn Thabit on this matter something similar to what was related from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wil*) differed concerning the interpretation of His saying ﴿has not changed﴾.

Some of them said the same as what we have said, that its meaning is: it has not changed.

Those who said this:

5920: Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, on the authority of one not suspected, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih: ﴿has not changed﴾, it did not change.

5921: Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Saʿid related to us, on the authority of Qatadah, concerning His saying ﴿has not changed﴾: it did not change.

5922: al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, on the authority of Qatadah, similarly.

5923: Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: ʿAmr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, on the authority of al-Suddi: ﴿Look at your food and your drink, which has not changed﴾, meaning: "Look at your food," of figs and grapes, "and your drink," of juice, "has not changed," meaning: it has not changed so that the figs and grapes became sour, nor did the juice ferment; they remained sweet as they were. That was because he came travelling from Syria on his donkey, with juice, grapes and figs. God caused him to die, and caused his donkey to die, and a hundred years passed over them. [[Report 5923 is the continuation of the earlier report no. 5913.]]

5924: I have related on the authority of al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Muʿadh say: ʿUbayd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say concerning His saying ﴿Look at your food and your drink, which has not changed﴾: it did not change, though a hundred years had passed over it.

5925: al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq informed us, saying: Abu Zuhayr related to us, on the authority of Juwaybir, on the authority of al-Dahhak, similarly.

5926: al-Muthanna related to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah related to us, saying: Muʿawiya related to me, on the authority of ʿAli, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying ﴿has not changed﴾: it did not change.

5927: Sufyan related to us, saying: My father related to us, on the authority of al-Nadr, on the authority of ʿIkrimah: ﴿has not changed﴾: it did not change.

5928: Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: ﴿has not changed﴾: it did not change over a hundred years.

5929: Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Bakr ibn Mudar informed me, saying: They claim in some books that Jeremiah was in Ilya when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it, and he left it for Egypt and stayed there. God revealed to him that he should go out from it to Jerusalem. He came to it and found it in ruins. He looked at it and said: "How will God bring this to life after its death?" So God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him up, and his donkey was alive, standing at its tether, and his food was a basket of grapes and a basket of figs, which had not changed from their state. [[*Al-rubat*: what something is tied to; here he means the place where it was tied, the hitching post. *Al-sall* and *al-salla* are the same: the basket in which bread and other things are carried. It is said that *sall* is the plural of *salla*, which is among the rare plurals, for it is a made thing, not a created one, and there is no feminine marker distinguishing its singular, like *ʿinab* and *ʿinaba*, *burr* and *burra*.]]

Yunus said: Salam al-Khawwas told us: his food and drink were a basket of grapes, a basket of figs, and a skin of juice. [[In the printed edition: "Salim al-Khawwas", which is an error. The correct form is from the manuscript: Salm ibn Maymun al-Khawwas, whose biography passed at no. 5890.]]

* *

Others said: the meaning of that is: it did not become putrid.

Those who said this:

5930: Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim related to us, on the authority of ʿIsa, on the authority of Ibn Abi Najih, on the authority of Mujahid, concerning His saying ﴿has not changed﴾: it did not become putrid.

5931: al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Najih, on the authority of Mujahid, similarly.

5932: al-Qasim related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, who said: Mujahid said concerning His saying ﴿Your food﴾: a basket of figs; ﴿and your drink﴾: a jar of wine; ﴿has not changed﴾, that is, it did not become putrid.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: I think that Mujahid and al-Rabiʿ and those who said what they said [[Al-Tabari did not mention a report from al-Rabiʿ earlier, so I fear that his report may have dropped out from the copyist's text. The saying of al-Rabiʿ in the interpretation of part of this verse has passed earlier with its isnad at no. 5916.]] saw that His saying ﴿has not changed﴾ comes from the saying of God, exalted is He, ﴿from black, moulded clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 26, 28, 33], meaning, the one whose smell has changed by putridity, from the speaker's expression "tasannana" (it became putrid). But I have already shown the evidence earlier that this is not so. [[See what passed earlier, p. 460.]]

If someone supposes that it is from *al-asan* (putrid odour) in the speaker's saying "asina hadha al-ma'u yaʾsanu asanan" (this water became putrid), as God, exalted is He, said ﴿in it are rivers of water unchanged [ghayr āsin]﴾ [Muhammad: 15], then if it were so, the sentence would have been: "Look at your food and your drink, which has not become putrid (*lam yata'assan*)," and it would not have been "yatasannahu".

* *

[If it is said:] [[What is between the brackets is an addition necessary for the sentence to be correct.]] It is from that, except that its *hamza* has been dropped.

It is replied: Even if its *hamza* were dropped, it is not permissible to double its *nūn*, for the *nūn* is not doubled, whereas in *yatasannahu* it is doubled. If the form from *yata'assan* were pronounced with the *hamza* dropped, it would be said *yatassan*, with its *nūn* lightened, without a *hā'* added to it. In this there is clear evidence that it is not permissible that it be from *al-asan*.

* *

On the interpretation of His saying ﴿And look at your donkey﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation differed concerning the interpretation of His saying ﴿And look at your donkey﴾.

Some of them said: the meaning is: look at My giving life to your donkey, and at its bones, how I raise them and then clothe them with flesh.

Then those who interpreted this differed concerning this interpretation.

Some of them said: God, exalted is He, said this to him after He had brought him back to life as a well-formed creature, and then wished to give life to his donkey, as an instruction from Him, exalted is He, about how He would bring to life the town which he saw lying in ruins upon its roofs, so he said: ﴿How will God bring this to life after its death?﴾, expressing astonishment at God's giving life to it.

Those who said this:

5933: Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of one not suspected, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: God raised him and said: ﴿How long have you remained?﴾ He said: ﴿I have remained a day or part of a day﴾, up to His saying ﴿then We clothe them with flesh﴾. He said: Then he looked at his donkey, which was joining part to part, with its sinews and veins; it had died together with him. Then flesh clothed it until it was complete, and then the spirit flowed into it, and it stood up braying. He looked at his juice and his figs, and they were in the state in which he had left them, unchanged. When he beheld the power of God that he beheld, he said: ﴿I know that God is powerful over everything﴾. [[Report 5933 is the end of the earlier report no. 5910.]]

5934: Musa related to me, saying: ʿAmr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, on the authority of al-Suddi: Then God brought ʿUzayr to life, and said: "How long have you remained?" He said: "I have remained a day or part of a day." He said: "Rather, you have remained a hundred years! Look at your food and your drink, which has not changed, and look at your donkey, which has perished and whose bones have decayed, and look at its bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh."

Then God sent a wind, which brought the bones of the donkey from every plain and mountain, which the birds and beasts had carried off. They gathered together, and he assembled them, part joined to part, while he looked on, until it became a donkey of bones with no flesh and no blood. Then God clothed the bones with flesh and blood, and it stood up as a donkey of flesh and blood, but with no spirit in it. Then an angel came walking until he took hold of the donkey's nostril, and he blew into it, so the donkey brayed, and he said: ﴿I know that God is powerful over everything﴾.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: So the sense of the words, according to the interpretation of the one who holds this view, is: look at Our bringing your donkey to life, and at its bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh, and so that We may make you a sign for the people. In His saying ﴿And look at your donkey﴾ there is then something omitted from the speech, which is understood from its outward meaning, and the definite article in His saying ﴿And look at the bones﴾ replaces the intended *hā'*, for the meaning is: "look at its bones", meaning: the bones of the donkey.

* *

Others among them said: Rather, God, exalted is He, said this to him after He had breathed the spirit into his eye. [[In the printed edition: "fī ʿaynihi" in the singular; I have kept the manuscript reading.]] They said: it was the first of his organs into which God breathed the spirit, and that was after He had made him a well-formed creature, and before He brought his donkey to life.

Those who said this:

5935: Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim related to us, saying: ʿIsa related to us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Najih, on the authority of Mujahid, who said: He was a man from the Children of Israel, into whose eyes the spirit was breathed, so he looked at all his creation when God brought him to life, and at his donkey when God brought it to life. [[In the printed edition: "fa-nazara", and in the manuscript: "fa-nazara" written without dots, and the correct reading is as I have read it for you.]]

5936: al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Najih, on the authority of Mujahid, similarly.

5937: al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, who said: He began with his eyes, and breathed the spirit into them; then with his bones, raising them; then he joined one to another; then he clothed them with sinews, then veins, then flesh. Then he looked at his donkey, and his donkey had decayed, and its bones had whitened in the place where he had tied it. He was called: "O bones, come together, for God will send down a spirit upon you," and each bone hastened to its fellow, and the bones joined, then the sinews, then the veins, then the flesh, then the skin, then the hair. The donkey had been young, and God brought it back as a grown animal that had grown shrivelled, [[*Al-jadhaʿ* (with two fathas): the young of animals and others. *Tashannana* (of skin or a waterskin): when it dries and shrivels from age or from old age.]] and nothing was left of it but the skin, from the length of time. His food had been a basket of grapes, and his drink a jar of wine. Ibn Jurayj said, from Mujahid: He breathed the spirit into his eyes, then he looked with them at all his creation when God raised it, and at his donkey when God brought it to life.

* *

وقال آخرون: بل جعل الله الروح في رأسه وبصره، وجسدُه ميتٌ، [[في المطبوعة والمخطوطة: "وجسده ميتا"، وهو خطأ، ويدل على صواب ما أثبت، الآثار التالية.]] . فرأى حماره قائمًا كهيئته يوم ربطه، وطعامه وشرابه كهيئته يوم حَلَّ البقعة. ثم قال الله له: انظر إلى عظام نفسك كيف ننشزها.

ذكر من قال ذلك:

٥٩٣٨ - حدثني محمد بن سهل بن عسكر، قال: حدثنا إسماعيل بن عبد الكريم، قال: حدثني عبد الصمد بن معقل أنه سمع وهب بن منبه يقول: ردَّ الله روح الحياة في عين أرْميا وآخرُ جسده ميت، [[يعني بقوله: "وآخر جسده ميت"، أي سائره وباقيه، وقد جاءت هذه الكلمة هنا على الصواب في المطبوعة والمخطوطة، وقد مضت في المطبوعة في الأثر رقم: ٥٩١١، محرفة، فهذا دليل آخر على صواب قراءتنا للنص.]] . فنظر إلى طعامه وشرابه لم يتسنَّه، ونظر إلى حماره واقفًا كهيئته يوم ربطه، لم يطعم ولم يشرب، ونظر إلى الرُّمة في عنق الحمار لم تتغير، جديدةً. [[الأثر: ٥٩٣٨ -انظر الأثر السالف رقم: ٥٩١١، والتعليق عليه.]] .

٥٩٤٠ - حدثت عن الحسين، قال: [[في المطبوعة والمخطوطة: "الحسن"، وهو خطأ، بل هو"الحسين بن الفرج"، وهو إسناد دائر في التفسير، أقربه رقم: ٥٩٢٤.]] . سمعت أبا معاذ، قال: حدثنا عبيد بن سليمان، قال: سمعت الضحاك يقول في قوله: ﴿فأماته الله مائة عام ثم بعثه﴾ ، فنظر إلى حماره قائمًا قد مكث مائة عام، وإلى طعامه لم يتغير قد أتى عليه مائة عام، ﴿وانظر إلى العظام كيف نُنشرها ثم نكسوها لحمًا﴾ فكان أول شيء أحيا الله منه رأسَه، فجعل ينظر إلى سائر خلقه يُخلق.
