٥٩٤١ - حدثني المثنى، قال: حدثنا إسحاق، قال: حدثنا أبو زهير، عن جويبر، عن الضحاك في قوله: ﴿فأماته الله مائة عام ثم بعثه﴾ فنظر إلى حماره قائمًا، وإلى طعامه وشرابه لم يتغير، فكان أول شيء خلق منه رأسه، فجعل ينظر إلى كل شيء منه يوصل بعضه إلى بعض. فلما تبيَّن له، قال: ﴿أعلم أنَّ الله على كل شيء قدير﴾ .

٥٩٤٢ - حدثنا بشر بن معاذ، قال: حدثنا يزيد، قال: حدثنا سعيد، عن قتادة، قال: ذُكر لنا أنه أول ما خلق الله منه رأسَه، ثم ركبت فيه عيناه، ثم قيل له: انظر! فجعل ينظر، فجعلت عظامه تَواصَلُ بعضها إلى بعض، وبِعَيْن نبيّ الله عليه السلام كان ذلك، فقال: ﴿أعلم أن الله على كل شيء قدير﴾ .

٥٩٤٣ - حدثت عن عمار، قال: حدثنا ابن أبي جعفر، عن أبيه، عن الربيع: ﴿وانظر إلى طعامك وشرابك لم يتسنَّه وانظر إلى حمارك﴾ وكان حماره عنده كما هو = ﴿ولنجعلك آيه للناس﴾ ، وانظر إلى العظام كيف ننشزها) . قال الربيع: ذكر لنا والله أعلم أنه أول ما خلق منه عيناه، ثم قيل انظر! فجعل ينظر إلى العظام يَتواصل بعضها إلى بعض، وذلك بعينيه، فقال: [[في المخطوطة والمطبوعة: "فقيل: أعلم ... "، وهو سبق قلم من الناسخ.]] . ﴿أعلم أن الله على كل شيء قدير﴾ .

٤٦٤٤ - حدثني يونس، قال: أخبرنا ابن وهب، قال: أخبرنا ابن زيد قال قوله: ﴿وانظر إلى طعامك وشرابك لم يتسنَّه وانظر إلى حمارك﴾ واقفًا عليك منذ مائة سنة = ﴿ولنجعلك آية للناس وانظر إلى العظام﴾ يقول: وانظر إلى عظامك كيف نحييها حين سألتنا:"كيف نحيي هذه"؟ [[في المطبوعة: "كيف نحيى هذه الأرض بعد موتها"، وليس ذلك في المخطوطة، بل الذي أثبت، وهما سواء.]] . قال: فجعل الله الروح في بصره وفي لسانه، ثم قال: ادع الآن بلسانك الذي جعل الله فيه الروح، وانظر ببصرك. قال: فكان ينظر إلى الجمجمة. قال: فنادى: ليلحق كل عظم بأليفه. قال: فجاء كل عظم إلى صاحبه، حتى اتصلت وهو يراها، حتى أن الكِسْرة من العظم لتأتي إلى الموضع الذي انكسرت منه، فتلصَقُ به حتى وصل إلى جمجمته، وهو يرى ذلك. فلما اتصلت شدها بالعصب والعروق، وأجرى عليها اللحم والجلد، ثم نفخ فيها الروح، ثم قال: ﴿انظر إلى العظام كيف ننشرها ثم نكسوها لحمًا﴾ فلما تبين له ذلك، ﴿قال أعلم أن الله على شيء قدير﴾ . قال: ثم أمر فنادى تلك العظام التي قال: ﴿أنَّى يُحيي هذه الله بعد موتها﴾ كما نادى عظام نفسه، ثم أحياها الله كما أحياهُ.

٥٩٤٥ - حدثني يونس، قال: أخبرنا ابن وهب، قال: أخبرني بكر بن مضر، قال: يزعمون في بعض الكتب أن الله أمات أرميا مائة عام، ثم بعثه، [[في المطبوعة: "أرميا"، وأثبت ما في المخطوطة، وقد سلف مثل ذلك مرارا، حتى في الأثر الواحد، انظر ما سلف -ص: ٤٤٨ تعليق: ١.]] فإذا حمارُه حيٌّ قائمٌ على رباطه. قال: وردَّ الله إليه بصره، وجعل الروح فيه قبل أن يبعث بثلاثين سنة، ثم نظر إلى بيت المقدس وكيف عمر وما حوله. قال: فيقولون والله أعلم: إنه الذي قال الله تعالى ذكره: ﴿أوْ كالذي مرّ على قرية وهي خاوية ... ﴾ ، الآية. [[عند هذا الموضع، انتهى جزء من التقسيم القديم الذي نقلت منه نسختنا، وفيها ما نصه:
" يتلوهُ: ومعنى الآية على تأويل هؤلاء:
وانظر إلى حمارك ولنجعلك آية للناس.
* *
وصلى الله على سيدنا محمد النبيّ وآله وصحبه وسلم كثيرًا"
ثم يبدأ بعده بما نصه:
" بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
رب يسر يا كريم".]] .

* *

ومعنى الآية على تأويل هؤلاء: وانظر إلى حمارك، ولنجعلك آية للناس، وانظر إلى عظامك كيف ننشزها بعد بلاها، ثم نكسوها لحمًا، فنحييها بحياتك، فتعلم كيف يحيي الله القرى وأهلها بعد مماتها.

* *

قال أبو جعفر: وأولى الأقوال في هذه الآية بالصواب قولُ من قال: إن الله تعالى ذكره بعث قائل: ﴿أنَّى يحيي هذه الله بعد موتها﴾ من مماته، ثم أراه نظير ما استنكر من إحياء الله القرية التي مرّ بها بعد مماتها عيانًا من نفسه وطعامه وحماره. فحمل تعالى ذكره ما أراه من إحيائه نفسه وحماره مثلا لما استنكر من إحيائه أهل القرية التي مرّ بها خاويةً على عروشها، وجعل ما أراه من العِبرة في طعامه وشرابه، عبرة له وحجة عليه في كيفية إحيائه منازل القرية وجِنانها. وذلك هو معنى قول مجاهد الذي ذكرناه قبل.

وإنما قلنا: ذلك أولى بتأويل الآية، لأنّ قوله: ﴿وانظر إلى العظام﴾ إنما هو بمعنى: وانظر إلى العظام التي تراها ببصرك كيف ننشزُها، ثم نكسوها لحمًا.

وقد كان حماره أدركه من البلى = في قول أهل التأويل جميعًا = نظيرُ الذي لحق عظامَ من خوطب بهذا الخطاب، فلم يمكن صرف معنى قوله: ﴿وانظر إلى العظام﴾ إلى أنه أمرٌ له بالنظر إلى عظام الحمار دون عظام المأمور بالنظر إليها، ولا إلى أنه أمر له بالنطر إلى عظام نفسه دون عظام الحمار. وإذْ كان ذلك كذلك، وكان البلى قد لحق عظامه وعظام حماره، كان الأولى بالتأويل أن يكون الأمرُ بالنظر إلى كل ما أدركه طرفه مما قد كان البلى لحقه، لأن الله تعالى ذكره جعل جميع ذلك عليه حجة وله عبرةً وعظةً.

* *

القول في تأويل قوله: ﴿وَلِنَجْعَلَكَ آيَةً لِلنَّاسِ﴾

قال أبو جعفر: يعني تعالى ذكره بذلك: ﴿ولنجعلك آيه للناس﴾ أمتناك مائة عام ثم بعثناك.

وإنما أدخلت"الواو" مع اللام التي في قوله: ﴿ولنجعلك آيه للناس﴾ وهو بمعنى"كي"، لأن في دخولها في كي وأخواتها دِلالة على أنها شرطٌ لفعلٍ بعدها، بمعنى: ولنجعلك كذا وكذا فعلنا ذلك. [[انظر معاني القرآن ١: ١٧٣.]] . ولو لم تكن قبل"اللام" أعني"لام" كي"واو"، كانت"اللام" شرطًا للفعل الذي قبلها، وكان يكون معناه: وانظر إلى حمارك، لنجعلك آية للناس.

* *

وإنما عنى بقوله: ﴿ولنجعلك آية﴾ ، ولنجعلك حجة على من جهل قدرتي، وشكَّ في عظمتي، [[انظر معنى"آية" فيما سلف في هذا الجزء ٥: ٣٧٧، والتعليق: ٢، ومراجعه هناك.]] . وأنا القادر على فعل ما أشاء من إماتة وإحياء، وإنشاء، وإنعام وإذلال، وإقتار وإغناء، بيدي ذلك كلُّه، لا يملكه أحد دوني، ولا يقدر عليه غيري.

* *

وكان بعض أهل التأويل يقول: كان آية للناس، بأنه جاء بعد مائة عام إلى ولده وولد ولده، شابًّا وهم شيوخ.

ذكر من قال ذلك:

٥٩٤٦ - حدثني المثنى، قال: أخبرنا إسحاق، قال: حدثنا قبيصة بن عقبة، عن سفيان، قال: سمعت الأعمش يقول: ﴿ولنجعلك آيه للناس﴾ قال: جاء شابًّا وولده شيوخ.

* *

وقال آخرون: معنى ذلك أنه جاء وقد هلك من يعرفه، فكان آية لمن قدِم عليه من قومه.

ذكر من قال ذلك:

٥٩٤٧ - حدثني موسى، قال، حدثنا عمرو، قال: حدثنا أسباط، عن السدي، قال: رجع إلى أهله، فوجد داره قد بيعت وبُنيت، وهلك من كان يعرفه، فقال: اخرجوا من داري! قالوا: ومن أنت؟ قال: أنا عزير! قالوا: أليس قد هلك عزيرٌ منذ كذا وكذا!! قال: فإن عزيرًا أنا هو، كان من حالي وكان! فلما عرفوا ذلك، خرجوا له من الدار ودفعوها إليه.

* *

قال أبو جعفر: والذي هو أولى بتأويل الآية من القول، أن يقال: أن الله تعالى ذكره، أخبر أنه حمل الذي وصف صفته في هذه الآية حُجة للناس، فكان ذلك حُجة على من عرفه من ولده وقوْمه ممن علم موته، وإحياءَ الله إياه بعد مماته، وعلى من بُعث إليه منهم.

* *

القول في تأويل قوله تعالى: ﴿وَانْظُرْ إِلَى الْعِظَامِ كَيْفَ نُنْشِزُهَا﴾

قال أبو جعفر: دللنا فيما مضى قبلُ على أنّ العظام التي أمِر بالنظر إليها، هي عظام نفسه وحماره، وذكرنا اختلاف المختلفين في تأويل ذلك، وما يعني كل قائل بما قاله في ذلك بما أغنى عن إعادته.

* *

وأما قوله: ﴿كيف ننشزُها﴾ فإن القرأة اختلفت في قراءته.

فقرأ بعضهم: ﴿وَانْظُرْ إِلَى الْعِظَامِ كَيْفَ نُنْشِزُهَا﴾ بضم النون وبالزاي، وذلك قراءة عامة قرأة الكوفيين، بمعنى: وانظر كيف نركّب بعضها على بعض، وننقل ذلك إلى مواضع من الجسم.

* *

وأصل"النشوز": الارتفاع، [[جاء في المطبوعة والمخطوطة "وأصل النشز": الارتفاع"، وأنا أرى صوابه: "النشوز"، لأنه هو المصدر، ولا مصدر لهذا الفعل غيره في رواية أهل اللغة، ومحال أن يدع الطبري المعروف إلى المجهول. والمخطوطة في هذا الوضع سيئة جدا، كثيرة التصحيف والإهمال، وبحضه لم أشر إليه لشدة وضوحه، وفساد خط كاتبه وإهماله، كما ترى في التعليق التالي.]] . ومنه قيل:"قد نشز الغلام"، إذا ارتفع طوله وشبَّ، ومنه"نشوز المرأة" على زوجها. [[في المخطوطة: "وفيه نشور المرأة على وجهها"، وهذا دليل على شدة إهماله.]] . ومن ذلك قيل للمكان المرتفع من الأرض:"نَشَز ونَشْز ونشاز"، [[في المخطوطة: "نشر ونشره ونشاره"، وهو خطأ كله، والصواب ما أثبت.]] . فإذا أردت أنك رفعته، قلت:"أنشزته إنشازًا"، و"نشز هو"، إذا ارتفع.

* *

فمعنى قوله: ﴿وانظر إلى العظام كيف ننشزها﴾ في قراءة من قرأ ذلك بالزاي: كيف نرفعُها من أماكنها من الأرض فنردُّها إلى أماكنها من الجسد. [[في المخطوطة: "فبرزها إلى أماكنها"، وهو فاسد. وفي المطبوعة: " الجسم"، ورددته إلى المخطوطة.]] .

* *

وممن تأول ذلك هذا التأويل جماعة من أهل التأويل.

ذكر من قال ذلك:

٥٩٤٨ - حدثني المثنى، قال: حدثنا عبد الله بن صالح، قال: حدثني معاوية، عن علي، عن ابن عباس في قوله: ﴿كيف ننشزها﴾ كيف نُخرجها.

٥٩٤٩ - حدثني موسى، قال: حدثنا عمرو، قال: حدثنا أسباط، عن السدي: ﴿كيف ننشزها﴾ قال: نحرِّكها.

* *

وقرأ ذلك آخرون:"وَانْظُرْ إِلَى الْعِظَامِ كَيْفَ نُنْشِرُهَا" بضم النون. قالوا: من قول القائل،"أنشرَ الله الموتى فهو يُنشِرهم إنشارًا"، وذلك قراءة عامة قرأة أهل المدينة، بمعنى: وانظر إلى العظام كيف نحييها، ثم نكسوها لحمًا.

ذكر من قال ذلك:

٥٩٥٠ - حدثني محمد بن عمرو، قال: حدثنا أبو عاصم، قال: حدثنا عيسى، عن ابن أبي نجيح، عن مجاهد:"كيف نُنشِرها" قال: انظر إليها حين يحييها الله. [[في المخطوطة والمطبوعة: "نظر إليها"، والصواب ما أثبت.]] .

٥٩٥١ - حدثنا المثنى قال: حدثنا أبو حذيفة، قال: حدثنا شبل، عن ابن أبي نجيح، عن مجاهد، مثله.

٥٩٥٢ - حدثنا بشر، قال: حدثنا يزيد، قال: حدثنا سعيد، عن قتادة مثله.

٥٩٥٣ - حدثنا يونس، قال: أخبرنا ابن وهب، قال: قال ابن زيد في قوله:"وانظر إلى العظام كيف نُنشرُها" قال: كيف نحييها.

* *

واحتج بعض قرَأة ذلك بالراء وضم نون أوله، بقوله: ﴿ثُمَّ إِذَا شَاءَ أَنْشَرَهُ﴾ [عبس: ٢٢] ، فرأى أنّ من الصواب إلحاق قوله:"وانظر إلى العظام كيف ننشرها" به. [[هو ابن عباس، فيما روى الفراء في معاني القرآن ١: ١٧٣.]] .

* *

وقرأ ذلك بعضهم:"وَانْظُرْ إِلَى الْعِظَامِ كَيْفَ نَنْشُرُهَا"، بفتح النون من أوله وبالراء. كأنّه وجّه ذلك إلى مثل معنى: نَشْرِ الشيء وطيِّه. [[هو الحسن، فيما روى الفراء في معاني القرآن ١: ١٧٣.]] . وذلك قراءة غير محمودة، لأن العرب لا تقول: نشر الموتى، وإنما تقول:"أنشر الله الموتى"، فنشروا هم" بمعنى: أحياهم فحيُوا هم. ويدل على ذلك قوله: ﴿ثُمَّ إِذَا شَاءَ أَنْشَرَهُ﴾ وقوله: ﴿أَمِ اتَّخَذُوا آلِهَةً مِنَ الأرْضِ هُمْ يُنْشِرُونَ﴾ [الأنبياء: ٢١] ؛ [[سقت الآية بتمامها، وفي المطبوعة والمخطوطة: "آلهة من الأرض هم ينشرون".]] .. وعلى أنه إذا أريد به حَيِي، الميت وعاش بعد مماته، قيل:"نَشَر"، ومنه قول أعشى بني ثعلبة: [[في المطبوعة والمخطوطة بإسقاط: "ومنه"، وهو غير مستقيم.]] .

حَتَّى يَقُولَ النَّاسَ مِمَّا رَأَوْا: ... يَا عَجَبًا لِلْمَيِّتِ النَّاشِرِ [[ديوانه: ١٠٥، وسيأتي في التفسير ١٩: ١٤ / ٢٥: ٣٢ / ٣٠: ٣٦ (بولاق) وهو في أكثر الكتب، وقد مضى بيتان منها في ١: ٤٧٤، تعليق: ٢ /٣: ١٣١. وقبله يذكر صاحبته، فأجاد وأبدع: عَهْدِي بِهَا فِي الحَيِّ قَدْ سُرْبِلَتْ ... هَيْفَاءَ مِثْلَ المُهْرَةِ الضَّامِرِ
قَدْ نَهَدَ الثَّدْيُ عَلَى نَحْرِهَا ... فِي مُشْرِقٍ ذِي صَبَحٍ نَاثِرِ
لَوْ أَسْنَدَتْ مَيْتًا إلَى نَحْرِهَا ... عَاشَ، وَلَمْ يُنْقَلْ إِلى قَابِرِ
حتَّى يَقُولَ الناسُ. . . ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
الصبح (بفتحتين) بريق اللون والحلى والسلاح، تراه مشربًا كالجمر يتلألأ. ونائر: نير. يقال: "نار الشيء فهو نير ونائر" و"أنار فهو منير".]] وروي سماعًا من العرب:"كان به جَرَبٌ فنَشَر"، إذا عاد وَحَيِيَ. [[انظر معاني القرآن للفراء ١: ٣٠.]] .

Abu Ja'far said: My view on this is that the meaning of "al-inshaz" and the meaning of "al-inshar" are close to each other, because the meaning of "al-inshaz" is assembling, restoring, and returning the bones to their places (rad al-'izam ila al-'izam), and the meaning of "al-inshar" is returning life to the bones. [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "... wa radd al-'izam min al-'izam, wa i'adatuha la shakk ..." and this is a statement that does not stand at all; the copy at this point is corrupted to an extreme degree, and the copyist was very negligent and prone to omissions, as was noted in previous annotations. Therefore I have endeavoured to correct this and what follows until its meaning and wording are sound.]] And their restoration, there is no doubt, is returning them to their places and positions in the body after they had separated from them. Although the two differ in wording, they are close in meaning. The Ummah has transmitted both readings in a manner that removes all excuse and establishes proof, so whichever of the two a reader recites is correct, since their meanings are harmonious [[In the manuscript: "la n'imad wa ma'nuha", the correct reading being that of the printed edition. His words "li-inqiyad ma'naihima" mean: for the soundness and evenness of their two meanings and their running together on a single course that does not differ, as one leads the other. See what has passed, 4:105, note 1, in his words "qada qawluhu" and the explanation of their saying "hadha la yastaqim 'ala qawd kalamika".]]. And no proof obliges the judgment of the correctness of one over the other. [[In the printed edition: "li-ihdahuma min al-qada'" with an added "min"; in the manuscript "li-ahadihima min al-qada'" with an added and erroneous word; the correct reading is what is given here.]]
* *
If someone supposes that "al-inshar", since it means giving life, is the more correct, because the one commanded to look at the bones while they are being raised (yunshar) was commanded to do so in order to see with his own eyes what he denied when he said: ﴿How will God give life to this after its death?﴾ — [then he has erred]. [[I added what is between the brackets, because the context requires it. There is no sense in seeking to correct this sentence by linking his words "fa-inna ihya' al-'izam..." as an answer to his words "fa-in zanna zan..."]]. For the giving of life to the bones in this place is undoubtedly intended as returning them to their places in the body of the one being observed, and he is brought to life [[yuhya: passive voice, from "ihya'"]], for the restoration of the spirit that had left him at death. [[In the printed edition and manuscript: "la i'adat al-ruh ...", which is a plain error, as shown by the context that follows. For it means that "giving life to the bones" is composed of two things: returning the bones to their places, and restoring the spirit to them. You will see this in his argument later.]] What shows this is His saying: ﴿Then We clothe them with flesh.﴾ And there is no doubt that the spirit was breathed into the bones that were raised (unshizat) only after they were clothed with flesh. [[In the printed edition and manuscript: "al-'izam allati unshirat" with the letter ra', which is an error; the correct form is with the letter zay, meaning they were assembled and returned to their places.]]
Since that is so, [[In the printed edition and manuscript: "wa-idha kana dhalika kadhalika", the correct reading being "idh".]] and since the meaning of "inshaz" is the assembling of the bones and returning them to their places in the body, and that is the meaning of "inshar" [[His words "and that is the meaning of inshar": and the meaning of inshar is also the returning of the bones to their places in the body for the restoration of the spirit that had left them at death, as has just passed.]], and since it is known that the two meanings are equal, and that they agree in meaning rather than differ, this is a clarification of the soundness of what we have said about it.
* *
As for the third reading, reciting it is not permissible in my view, namely the reading of one who reads "kayfa nanshuruha" with a fatha on the nun and with the ra', because it is anomalous against the reading of the Muslims and departs from the sound, eloquent speech of the Arabs.
* *
The discussion on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Then We clothe them with flesh﴾
Abu Ja'far said: The Exalted means by His saying: [[In the printed edition and manuscript: "bi-dhalika" in place of "bi-qawlihi", which does not stand.]] ﴿Then We clothe them﴾, that is, the bones, ﴿with flesh﴾, and the "ha'" in His saying ﴿Then We clothe them with flesh﴾ refers to the bones.
* *
The meaning of "nakswuha": We dress them and cover them with it, as a man's body is covered by the garment he wears. The Arabs do likewise, making everything that covers something and conceals it a garment (libas) and a clothing (kiswa) for it. [[See what has passed on the meaning of "libas" and "kiswa", 3:489-492, and this part: 44.]] From it is the saying of al-Nabigha al-Ja'di: [[This verse is attributed to Labid ibn Rabi'a al-'Amiri and to Qurdah ibn Nafatha al-Salalong. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said in al-Isti'ab (228): "Most of the scholars of reports say that Labid did not compose poetry since he embraced Islam. Some of them said: he did not say anything in Islam except his saying: ..." and he mentioned the verse, then said: it has been said that this verse belongs to Qurdah ibn Nafatha al-Salali, and that is more correct in my view. Then he returned at p. 536 and mentioned Qurdah ibn Nafatha al-Salali, saying: he was a poet who came to the Messenger of God ﷺ among the Banu Salul, and he appointed him over them after he and they had embraced Islam, so he composed: ... The verse has been attributed to Labid. Abu 'Ubayda said: Labid did not say anything else in Islam. Abu al-Faraj mentioned this in his Aghani 14:94 and others. See Mu'jam al-shu'ara': 338, 339; al-Shi'r wa al-shu'ara': 232; al-Mu'ammarin 66; and Diwan Labid, al-Ziyadat: 56. And there are many others.]]
"So praise be to God, that my term did not come upon me until I was clothed in a garment of Islam."
[[See the previous annotation. This verse is established in al-Nabigha's qasida (in his Diwan: 86), in his satire against Ibn al-Hay, whose mother was al-Hayya and whose name was Siwar ibn Awfa al-Qushayri, who had satirized al-Ja'di and abused his maternal uncles from the Azd, who were neighbours in Isfahan, and so he composed his qasida on that, which begins: "If you see the shades of the days have withdrawn from me, and I have lifted a train that was dragging..."]]
So he made Islam, since it covered what was upon him and concealed and removed it, a clothing for him and a garment.
* *
The discussion on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿So when it became clear to him, he said: I know that God is capable of all things﴾ (2:259)
Abu Ja'far said: The Exalted means by His saying: ﴿So when it became clear to him﴾, so when it became clear to him by direct sight what he had considered improbable of God's power and majesty before seeing it [[See the meaning of "bayn" in the word indexes of the earlier parts.]]. ﴿He said: I know﴾ now, after the witnessing, the clarification and the explanation [[In the printed edition: "ba'd al-mu'ayana wa-l-ittidah bihi wa-l-bayan", which is corrupt and defective; the correct reading is from the manuscript.]]. ﴿That God is capable of all things﴾.
* *
Then the readers differed on the recitation of His saying: ﴿He said: I know that God﴾.
Some read it "qala i'lam" [as an imperative], on the meaning of a command, with joining the alif of "i'lam" and vowelling the mim with a jazm. This is the common reading of the reciters of Kufa. They mention that in the reading of 'Abd Allah it is "qila i'lam" in the form of a command from God, who gives life after his death, so he was commanded to look at what God gives life to after its death. Likewise it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas.
5954 - Ahmad ibn Yusuf al-Taghlabi related to me, saying: al-Qasim ibn Sallam related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Harun, who said: in the reading of 'Abd Allah it is "qila i'lam anna Allah," in the form of a command. [[The report 5954: Ahmad ibn Yusuf al-Taghlabi, the Ahwal, the companion of Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam, is known by that. He narrated from Sulayman ibn Harb, Muslim ibn Ibrahim, Rawh ibn Zayd, Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam and others. Related from him Abu 'Abd Allah Niftaway the grammarian, Muhammad ibn Makhlad, Abu 'Amr ibn al-Simmak, Makram ibn Ahmad and others. 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad said: "thiqa." He died in 272. His companionship with Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam shows me that he is the one meant in the earlier report no. 5919; see the note on it. In the printed edition and manuscript: "al-Tha'labi", which is an error.]]
5955 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, I suppose — Abu Ja'far al-Tabari doubted — I heard Ibn 'Abbas reading: "fa-lamma tabayyana lahu qala i'lam," and he said: that was only said to him.
5956 - It was reported to me from 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: It was mentioned to us, and God knows best, that it was said to him: "Look!", so he began to look at the bones, how some of them joined to others, with his own eyes. Then it was said: "Know that God is capable of all things."
* *
Abu Ja'far said: According to this view, the interpretation is: When it became clear to him of the affair of God and His power, God said to him: Know now that God is capable of all things. If an interpreter turns His saying "qala i'lam" — though he reads it as an imperative — to mean that it comes from the one about whom this verse recounts his story, it is a sound reading, and it would be like one who says: "Know that such-and-such has happened," in the form of a command from him to another, while he means himself.
* *
Others read it: ﴿He said: I know﴾, as a report about himself by the speaker, with a hamza on the alif of "a'lam" and a rafa' on the mim, meaning: when it became clear to him from God's power and great dominion by his witnessing what he witnessed, the one who had become clear said: I know now that God is capable of all things.
This is the reading of the common reciters of Medina, and of some reciters of Iraq, and with this reading a group of the interpreters have interpreted it.
Those who said that:
5957 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from one not accused, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: When he witnessed what he witnessed of God's power, he said: ﴿I know that God is capable of all things.﴾
5958 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: 'Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil informed us that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: ﴿So when it became clear to him he said: I know that God is capable of all things.﴾
5959 - Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, who said: by the eye of the Prophet of God ﷺ [[In the printed edition: "yu'na nabi Allah 'alayhi al-salam"; in the manuscript it is garbled and undotted, so its reading was not well made. That is: the raising of the bones was by the eye of the Prophet, seeing it directly; a similar thing has passed just above in no. 5942.]], meaning the raising of the bones, he said: ﴿I know that God is capable of all things.﴾
5960 - Musa related to me, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, who said: 'Uzayr said at that moment — meaning at witnessing God's revival of his donkey — ﴿I know that God is capable of all things.﴾
5961 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Abu Zuhayr related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: He began to look at every part of him, how one part joined another, ﴿so when it became clear to him he said: I know that God is capable of all things.﴾
5962 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said the like.
* *
The more correct of the two readings in this matter is the reading of the one who reads "i'lam" with a joined alif and a jazm on the mim, as a command from God, the Exalted, to the one whom He had revived after his death, commanding him to know that God — who showed him with his own eyes what He showed him of His great power and dominion, by reviving him and his donkey after a hundred years of death, and by their being restored to their condition on the day their spirits were taken, and by His preserving for him his food and drink for a hundred years until He returned it to him as it was on the day he placed it, unchanged [[In the printed edition and manuscript: "wa-hafiza 'alayhi ta'amahu ...", which is a disorder in the speech; the correct reading is what is given here. His words "wa-hifzihi" are in the genitive, conjoined to "min ihya'ihi iyyahu wa-himarahu ...".]] — is capable of all things likewise. [[His words "'ala kulli shay' qadir kadhalika" are attached to "bi-an ya'lama anna Allah ... 'ala kulli shay' qadir", and what lies between them is a description of God, so that it separates the name "inna" from its predicate.]]
We chose this reading and judged it correct over others because what precedes it is a command from God, the Exalted, spoken to the one God revived after his death, and an address to him, namely His saying: ﴿Look at your food and drink, that it has not spoiled; and look at your donkey ... and look at the bones, how We raise them﴾. So when it became clear to him this as an answer to his request to his Lord: ﴿How will God give life to this after its death?﴾, God said to him: "Know that God" — who did these things as you saw — is capable of other things beyond them, as He is capable of what you saw and its like. [[The structure of this sentence is like the previous one in the earlier annotation: "know that God ... is capable of other things."]] As the Exalted said to His friend Ibrahim ﷺ, after answering his request in His saying: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ — ﴿And know that God is Mighty, Wise﴾. [[This is the next verse of "Surat al-Baqara".]] He commanded Ibrahim to know, after showing him how He gives life to the dead, that He is Mighty and Wise. Likewise He commanded the one who asked, saying: ﴿How will God give life to this after its death?﴾, after showing him how He gives life to it, to know that God is capable of all things. [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "wa-kadhalika amara alladhi sa'ala ..." with the waw; the correct reading is with the fa'.
See also what al-Farra' said in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:173-174.]]

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 260 (part 1 of 4)**

On the interpretation of His words, ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest."﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, He means: "Have you not considered when Abraham said, 'My Lord, show me'?" The reason it is appropriate to link His words ﴿And when Abraham said﴾ to His words ﴿or like the one who passed by a town﴾, and to His words ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord﴾, is that His words ﴿Have you not considered﴾ do not mean "Have you not seen with your eyes," but rather "Have you not considered with your heart," meaning "Have you not known, so that you remember?" [[See the meaning of "seeing" earlier in this volume, 5: 429, and the note on it, no. 2.]] Thus, although its wording is that of "seeing," it is sometimes linked to what agrees with its wording and sometimes to what agrees with its meaning in speech.

* *

The people of interpretation differed about the cause of Abraham's request of his Lord that He show him how He gives life to the dead. Some of them said: His request of his Lord was because he saw an animal that had been torn apart by beasts of prey and birds, so he asked his Lord to show him the manner of its revival, despite its flesh being scattered in the bellies of the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth, so that he might see that with his own eyes, and thereby his certainty would increase, beyond his knowledge of it by report. So God showed him that as an example of what He had informed him He had commanded.

Mention of those who said this:

5963 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead."﴾: It was mentioned to us that the Friend of God, Abraham (ﷺ), passed by an animal that was divided among the beasts and the predators, and he said, ﴿"My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest."﴾

5964 – al-Hasan narrated to us, from someone, saying: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.﴾: He said: Abraham passed by the dead carcass of an animal that had decayed, and had been divided among the winds and the beasts of prey, so he stood looking, and said: "Glory be to God! How will God give life to this?" – and he knew that God was able to do that. That is His words ﴿"My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead."﴾ [[In the manuscript: "fa-qaddama yanzuru" (he advanced, looking); the correct reading is what is in the printed edition.]]

5965 – al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Juraij said: It reached me that Abraham, while he was walking along the road, came upon the carcass of a donkey, upon which were beasts of prey and birds, having torn its flesh apart [[Tamazza'a al-qawm al-shay': the people divided the thing among themselves and separated it; from al-tamzi', which is cutting up and scattering.]], and its bones remained. When the beasts of prey left, and the birds flew off to the mountains and hills, he stopped and wondered, [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "fa-waqafa" with the fa'; the better reading is to omit it.]] then said: "My Lord, I know that You will gather it from the bellies of these beasts and birds! My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead!" He said: "Have you not believed?" He said: "Yes! But the report is not like seeing with one's own eyes."

5966 – Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: Abraham passed by a fish, half of it on land and half of it in the sea. What was in the sea was eaten by the creatures of the sea, and what was on land was eaten by the beasts of prey and the creatures of the land. The wicked one [[al-Khabith: meaning Iblis, may God curse him.]] said to him: "O Abraham, when will God gather this from the bellies of these?" He said: "O Lord, show me how You give life to the dead!" He said: "Have you not believed?" He said: "Yes! But so that my heart may be at rest!"

* *

Others said: Rather, the cause of his request of his Lord was the debate and argument that took place between him and Nimrod about that.

Mention of those who said this:

5967 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, saying: When what took place between Abraham and his people occurred, as God recounted in "Surat al-Anbiya'," Nimrod said to Abraham, as they claim: "Tell me about this god of yours which you worship and call others to worship, and which you mention in terms of a power by which you exalt him over others – what is it?" Abraham said to him: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death!" Nimrod said: "I give life and cause death!" Abraham said to him: "How do you give life and cause death?" = Then he mentioned what God related of his argument with him = He said: Then Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest." = without any doubt about God, may His remembrance be exalted, or about His power; rather, he loved to know that and his heart yearned for it, so he said "so that my heart may be at rest," meaning: what his heart yearned for, once he knew it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: These two views – the first and this last – are close in meaning, in that Abraham's request of his Lord to show him how He gives life to the dead was so that he might see with his own eyes what he already knew by report.

* *

Others said: Rather, his request of his Lord was at the glad tidings that came to him from God, that He had taken him as a friend (khalil). So he asked his Lord to show him quickly a sign of that, so that his heart might be at rest that He had chosen him for Himself as a friend, and that this would confirm the certainty he already had.

Mention of those who said this:

5968 – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: When God took Abraham as a friend, the Angel of Death asked his Lord for permission to give Abraham the glad tidings of that, and He permitted him. So he came to Abraham while he was not in the house, and entered his dwelling. [[Abraham was the most jealous of people; if he went out, he would lock the door.]] When he returned and found a man in his house, he leapt at him to seize him, [[In the printed edition: "fa-lamma ja'a wajada fi darihi rajulan, fa-tha'a ilayhi li-ya'khudhahu qala"; I have kept what is in the manuscript.]] and said: "Who gave you permission to enter my house?" The Angel of Death said: "The Lord of this house gave me permission." Abraham said: "You have spoken the truth!" and he knew that he was the Angel of Death. He said: "Who are you?" He said: "I am the Angel of Death. I have come to give you the glad tidings that God has taken you as a friend!" So he praised God and said: "O Angel of Death, show me the form in which you seize the breaths of the disbelievers." He said: "O Abraham, you cannot bear that." He said: "Yes." He said: "Then turn away!" So Abraham turned away, then looked at him, and there he was: a black man whose head reached the sky, with flames of fire coming out of his mouth, and there was not a single hair on his body except in the form of a black man from whose mouth and ear-openings came flames of fire. Abraham fainted. Then he came to, and the Angel of Death had changed back into his first form, so he said: "O Angel of Death, if the disbeliever meets nothing at death of affliction and grief except your form, it would suffice him. Now show me how you seize the breaths of the believers." He said: "Turn away!" So Abraham turned away, then looked, and there he was: a young man, the most handsome of people in face and the most fragrant in scent, [[Min al-'Arabi al-mu'arraq: a usage in which the pronoun referring to a collective is made masculine singular, as in the report, and as in the report of 'Ammar ibn Yasir (Ibn Sa'd 3/1/183): "'Ammar ibn Yasir was among the tallest of people in silence and the least in speech," and as in the hadith: "The best of women are the righteous of Quraysh, the most tender toward a child in its youth, and the most protective of a husband's property," and as in the verse of Dhu al-Rummah: "Mayya is the most beautiful of the two creatures in neck, and in the nape of the neck, and in the nape."]] in white garments. He said: "O Angel of Death, if the believer had nothing from his Lord of the coolness of the eye and honor except your form, it would suffice him."

The Angel of Death departed, and Abraham stood calling upon his Lord, saying: "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead, so that I may know that I am Your friend!" He said: "Have you not believed that I am your friend?" = meaning: "Do you not affirm it?" = He said: "Yes! But so that my heart may be at rest through Your friendship." [[Al-khullah (with the kh vowelled and the l doubled), al-khalalah (with the kh vowelled either way), al-khululah and al-khalalah (with the kh vowelled): friendship.]]

5969 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Thabit narrated to us, from his father, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding His words ﴿but so that my heart may be at rest﴾: "Through friendship." [[The report 5969: "Amr ibn Thabit ibn Hurmuz al-Bakri," also called Amr ibn Abi al-Miqdam. He narrated from his father, Abu Ishaq al-Sabi'i, al-A'mash and others. Narrated from him Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, Sahl ibn Hammad, Yahya ibn Adam and others. Ibn al-Mubarak said: "Do not narrate from Amr ibn Thabit, for he used to revile the early generations." Abu Zur'a, Ibn Ma'in and al-Bukhari declared him weak. Abu Dawud said in his Sunan: "A wicked Rafidi, and a bad man." He died in the year 172. Biographed in al-Tahdhib. As for his father: Thabit ibn Hurmuz, Abu al-Miqdam. He narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others. Narrated from him his son, al-Thawri, Shu'ba and others. He was an elderly shaykh, a follower of the Sunnah. Biographed in al-Tahdhib.]]

* *

Others said: He said that to his Lord because he doubted God's power to give life to the dead.

Mention of those who said this:

5970 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ayyub, regarding His words ﴿but so that my heart may be at rest﴾: He said: Ibn Abbas said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more hopeful to me than this one." [[The report 5970: Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 335, attributing it to Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir. His words "arja" are the superlative of "al-raja'," which is hope, the opposite of despair.]]

5971 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, saying: I heard Zayd ibn Ali narrate from a man, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: Abd Allah ibn Abbas and Abd Allah ibn Amr arranged to meet. He said: We were at that time young men, and one of them said to his companion: "Which verse in the Book of God is most hopeful for this community?" Abd Allah ibn Amr said: ﴿Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves..."﴾ [[I added at the beginning of the verse "Say" according to the way of recitation.]] [al-Zumar: 53], until he finished the verse. Ibn Abbas said: "As for you, if you are saying that it is, then the one more hopeful for this community than it is the words of Abraham (ﷺ): ﴿"My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest."﴾" [[The report 5971: Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 1: 335, attributing it to Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Jarir; al-Hakim said: "He authenticated it." It is in al-Mustadrak with a different wording, 1: 60, through "Bishr ibn Hujr al-Sami, narrated to us, Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salama, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, who said: Ibn Abbas and Ibn Amr met, and Ibn Abbas said to him..." Then he said: "Sound according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs, though they did not record it." al-Dhahabi criticized him, saying: "In it there is a break in the chain." It seems that the reason for the break is that Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salama did not meet Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, for the latter died in the year 130.

This: and the meaning of his words "as for you, if you are saying that it is": in the sentence there are omissions in accordance with the Arabic practice of abbreviation, and its meaning is: "As for you, if you are saying that, it is among the most hopeful verses, and more hopeful than it is the words of Abraham."

The omission of the predicate of "inna" is common in Arabic. Among that is what came in a hadith of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The emigrants said: 'O Messenger of God, the Ansar have preferred themselves over us; they gave us refuge, and they did this and that for us.' He said: 'Do you not recognize that for them?' They said: 'Yes!' He said: 'Then that is...'" So his words "then that is" mean: "Then that is a reward from you to them," i.e., your recognition of their deeds and their kindness, as a reward to them. Abu 'Ubayd said: "This is an abbreviation of the speech of the Arabs, in which one suffices with the pronoun, because the speaker's intention is known." See Amali Ibn al-Shajari 1: 322, and others.]]

5972 – al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: I asked Ata' ibn Abi Rabah about His words ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest."﴾ He said: Some of what enters the hearts of people entered the heart of Abraham, so he said: ﴿"My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes,"﴾ He said: ﴿"Take four birds"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260], so that He might show him.

5973 – Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Aban al-Misri narrated to me, and they both said: Sa'id ibn Taleed narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Bakr ibn Mudar narrated to me, from Amr ibn al-Harith, from Yunus ibn Yazid, from Ibn Shihab, who said: Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib informed me, from Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham, when he said, 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said, 'Have you not believed?' He said, 'Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest.'" [[The report 5973: "Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Aban al-Misri": I have not found a biography of him in the books available to me. "Sa'id ibn Taleed" is Sa'id ibn Isa ibn Taleed al-Ru'ayni, ascribed to his grandfather. al-Bukhari narrated from him, and al-Nasa'i narrated from him through Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Hakam al-Misri. He was a trustworthy and firm transmitter of hadith.

And Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim ibn Khalid al-Utaqi al-Misri: he narrated from Malik, hadith and legal questions, and from Bakr ibn Mudar, and Nafi' ibn Abi Nu'aym al-Qari. Ibn Yunus said: "Ahmad ibn Shu'ayb al-Nasawi mentioned him while we were with him, Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, and he praised him highly and at length." Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat and said: "He was a good and virtuous man, among those who studied law under Malik, built upon his principles, defended them, and supported those who adopted them." Biographed in al-Tahdhib. And "Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Ya'qub al-Ansari al-Misri": he narrated from his father, Salim ibn Abi al-Nadr, al-Zuhri, Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Ansari, Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, and Yunus ibn Yazid al-Aylini, who was of his generation. Narrated from him Mujahid ibn Jabr and Salih ibn Kaysan, who were older than him, and Qatada and Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj, who were among his teachers, and Rushdin ibn Sa'd, Bakr ibn Mudar, and others. He was trustworthy. Abu Hatim said: "He was the most retentive of memory of the people of his time, with no equal in memory." Sa'id ibn Ufayr said: "He was the most eloquent of people and the most narrating." Biographed in al-Tahdhib. See the rest of its takhrij in the following report.]]

5974 – Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Yunus informed me, from Ibn Shihab and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, from Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: and he mentioned something similar. [[The report 5974: This hadith was narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih, saying: "Ahmad ibn Salih narrated to us, Ibn Wahb narrated to me," like the chain of al-Tabari. And with a similar wording in the earlier chain. See al-Fath 8: 150, 151. The Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) also discussed it fully in al-Fath, in the commentary on the "Book of the Traditions of the Prophets" in al-Bukhari (al-Fath 6: 293, 294), and he pointed to the earlier chain of Ibn Jarir. See the Hafiz's remarks on its chain.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most preferred of these views for the interpretation of the verse is what is authentically transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he said, namely his words: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham. He said: 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead?' He said: 'Have you not believed?'" = and that his request of his Lord, to show him the giving of life to the dead, was due to a passing impulse from Satan that arose in his heart, like what we mentioned earlier from Ibn Zayd: [[Meaning report no. 5966; what al-Tabari said is, in my estimation, part of the report.]] that when Abraham saw the fish, half of which was on land and half in the sea, and the creatures of the land, the creatures of the sea, and the birds of the air had all been feeding upon it, Satan cast into his soul and he said: "When will God gather this from the bellies of these?" So Abraham then asked his Lord to show him how He gives life to the dead, so that he might witness it with his own eyes, and so that Satan would no longer be able to cast into his heart what had been cast into it when he saw what he saw of that. So his Lord said to him: ﴿"Have you not believed?"﴾ meaning: "Have you not affirmed, O Abraham, that I am capable of that?" He said: "Yes, O Lord! But I asked You to show me that so that my heart may be at rest, and so that Satan cannot cast into my heart what he did when I saw this fish."

5975 – Yunus narrated to me this, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, from Ibn Zayd. [[The report 5975: It is part of the report I indicated, no. 5966.]]

* *

The meaning of His words ﴿so that my heart may be at rest﴾ is: so that it may settle and be calmed by the certainty that it attains.

* *

This interpretation that we have stated is the interpretation of those who directed the meaning of His words ﴿so that my heart may be at rest﴾ to mean: that it may increase in faith, or to mean: that it may attain certainty. [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "li-yuwaffiq" in these three places; this is an error with no meaning, and the correct reading is what I have given, from Tafsir al-Qurtubi 3: 300.]]

Mention of those who said that: "so that he may attain certainty," or "so that he may increase in certainty or faith." [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "li-yuwaffiq" in these three places; this is an error with no meaning, and the correct reading is what I have given, from Tafsir al-Qurtubi 3: 300.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 260 (part 2 of 4):

5976 - Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Abu Nu'aym related to us, from Sufyan, from Qays ibn Muslim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "that my heart may be at rest" – he said: that I may be certain. [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "liyuwaffiq" in these three places, which is an error with no meaning; the correct reading is what is established here, from Tafsir al-Qurtubi 3: 300.]].

5977 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us. And Ahmad ibn Ishaq related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Abu al-Haytham, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "that my heart may be at rest" – he said: that my certainty may increase.

5978 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Abu Zuhayr related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak: "but that my heart may be at rest" – he says: that it may increase in certainty.

5979 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "but that my heart may be at rest" – he said: The Prophet of Allah Ibrahim desired that he might increase in certainty above his certainty.

5980 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar said, and Qatadah said: that it may increase in certainty.

5981 - Related to us from Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "but that my heart may be at rest" – he said: Ibrahim desired that he might increase in certainty.

5982 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Kathir al-Basri related to us, saying: Isra'il related to us, saying: Abu al-Haytham related to us, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "that my heart may be at rest" – he said: that my certainty may increase.

5983 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: al-Fadl ibn Dukayn related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Abu al-Haytham, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "but that my heart may be at rest" – he said: that it may increase in certainty.

5984 - Salih ibn Misma'r related to us, saying: Zayd ibn al-Hubab related to us, saying: Khalaf ibn Khalifa related to us, saying: Layth ibn Abi Sulaym related to us, from Mujahid and Ibrahim concerning His saying: "that my heart may be at rest" – he said: That I may increase in faith alongside my faith.

5985 - Salih related to us, saying: Zayd related to us, saying: Ziyad informed us, from Abd Allah al-Amiri, saying: Layth related to us, from Abu al-Haytham, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning the saying of Allah: "that my heart may be at rest" – he said: That I may increase in faith alongside my faith.
* *
We have already mentioned earlier the statement of the one who said: the meaning of His saying "that my heart may be at rest" is: that I am your intimate friend. [[The reports nos. 5968, 5969.]].
* *
Others said: the meaning of His saying "that my heart may be at rest" is: so that I may know that You answer me when I call upon You, and give me when I ask You.
Mention of those who said that:
5986 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas concerning His saying: "that my heart may be at rest" – he said: I know that You answer me when I call upon You, and give me when I ask You.
* *
As for the interpretation of His saying: "He said: Do you not believe?" – it means: Do you not confirm (believe)? [[See the lexical indexes earlier regarding "al-iman" in the sense of "al-tasdiq" (affirmation).]] As:
5987 - Musa related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi.
5988 - And Ahmad ibn Ishaq related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Qays ibn Muslim, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: "Do you not believe?" – he said: Do you not have certainty that I am your intimate friend?
5989 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His saying: "Do you not believe?" – he said: Do you not have certainty?
* *
The discussion on the interpretation of His saying: "He said: Take four birds of the birds"
Abu Ja'far said: Thereby He, exalted is His mention, means: Allah said to him: "Take four of the birds." He mentioned that the four birds are: the rooster, the peacock, the crow, and the dove.
Mention of those who said that:
5990 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to me, from some people of knowledge: that the People of the Earlier Scripture mention that he took a peacock, a rooster, a crow, and a dove.
5991 - Al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: The four birds: the rooster, the peacock, the crow, and the dove.
5992 - Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me: "He said: Take four of the birds." Ibn Jurayj said: They claim it was a rooster, a crow, a peacock, and a dove.
5993 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "He said: Take four of the birds." He said: So he took a peacock, a dove, a crow, and a rooster, their species and colours differing.
* *
The discussion on the interpretation of His saying: "Then cut them to you" (fasurhunna ilayk)
Abu Ja'far said: The readers differed in reading this. The majority of readers of Medina, the Hijaz and Basra read: "fasurhunna ilayk" with a damma on the sad, from the speaker's saying: "sirtu ila hadha al-amr" [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "sirtu hadha al-amr" omitting "ila", and the correct reading is what is established here.]] – when one inclines toward it: "asur suwaran", and it is said: "inni ilaykum la-asur," meaning: longing, inclining. And from it is the poet's saying: [[Its speaker is unknown; al-Farra' recited it.]]
Allah knows that we, in our glancing back, on the day of parting, toward our beloveds are inclined (suwar).
It is the plural of "asyar, saw'a, suwar, like aswad and sawda'." And from it is al-Tirimmah's saying:
Chaste women, except that, or that desire inclines them, and desire is a striking affliction for lovers.
By his saying "aw an yuswiruha hawan" he means: that it inclines them.
* *
So the meaning of His saying: "fasurhunna ilayk" is: gather them to you and turn them towards you, as one says: "surw wajhaka ilayya," i.e., turn your face toward me. Whoever directs His saying "fasurhunna ilayk" to this interpretation, there is in the speech for him an omitted element, omitted because the apparent meaning indicates it. Its meaning then for him is: He said: "Take four of the birds and incline them to you," then cut them, "then place upon every mountain a portion of them."
* *
It may also be that the meaning of that, when read so with a damma on the "sad," is: cut them, as Tawba ibn al-Humayyir said:
When I pulled the rope, its ropes creaked with the tips of wood, strong in their knots.
So it brought the means close to me until I reached it, with my rising, and my climbing nearly cut it.
[[These two verses are from a long poem I have in the poetry of Tawba ibn al-Humayyir. The first verse here should be placed later, because the meaning does not hold on Abu Ja'far's transmission; its order in the transmission of his poetry, with a difference in the transmission: "fa-nadaytu Layla, wal-humulu ka-annaha..." ...]]
Meaning: he cuts them. If that is the interpretation of "fasurhunna," then there is in the speech an inversion, and its meaning is: "Take four of the birds to you and cut them," with "to you" connected to "take."
* *
A group of the people of Kufa read: "fasirhunna ilayk" with a kasra, meaning: cut them.
Some grammarians of Kufa asserted that they do not know "fasurhunna" nor "fasirhunna" in the sense of cutting in the speech of the Arabs – and that they do not know the kasra or damma of the "sad" in that except with one meaning, = and that both are dialects with the meaning of "inclining" = and that the kasra of the "sad" is a dialect of Hudhayl and Sulaym; and they recited for a man of Sulaym: [[I do not know its speaker.]]
And a hair-strand that makes the neck incline, and a dark, fine, rare one, upon the necks like the hanging clusters of grapevines.
[[Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 174. Lisan (sayr): "al-far'" is hair that is complete and abundant; "hahf" is black, fine, abundant, rare; "al-layt" is the hollow of the neck; the two layts. "Qinwan" is plural of "qinw" (with kasra then sukun), the cluster of dates and what is in it of fresh dates. "Al-dawalih" is plural of "dalih": heavy with load here. Its original sense is what walks; one says a camel is "dalih" when it walks with its heavy load without a spreading gait. Likewise a cloud is "dalih," heavy and slow in its passage. It is a good, sound metaphor.]]
By his saying "yasir," he means: incline. And that the people of this dialect say: "sarah yasiruhu sayran," and "sir wajhaka ilayya," i.e., incline it, as you say: "surhu." [[See what preceded in Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 174.]]
* *
Some grammarians of Kufa claimed that there is no known direction for His saying "fasurhunna" nor for the reading of one who read "fasirhunna" with damma and kasra of the "sad," in the meaning of cutting, except that it is "fasir hunna ilayk" in the reading of one who read it with a kasra on the "sad," from the inverted form, in which the "lam" of the verb was placed in the position of its "ayn," and its "ayn" in the position of its "lam," so it is from "sara yasri sarywan" – for the Arabs say: "bata yasri fi hawdihi" when he drew water, then cut and drew water. [[This is a good explanation, not found in the lexicon books.]] And from that is the poet's saying: [[I did not know its speaker.]]
She cut a glance which, had it met the middle of an armored man, who went forth while the vessels of the belly gushed blood...
"Sarat," she cut a glance; and from it is another's saying: [[I did not know the speaker of either.]]
They say: Syria kills its people, so who for me, if I do not come to it, with immortality? My fathers became Bedouin; would that they had cut for them from death, if they had not gone, and my grandfathers!?
[[Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 174; Mu'jam ma-Musta'jam: 773; Lisan (ariba), (sham). "Ta'arraba" means they dwelt in the desert and did not attend the towns. He says my fathers and grandfathers settled the desert, dwelt there, and did not attend the towns, so that was no deliverance for them from deaths. His saying "wa-jududi" is conjoined to "aba'i." The verse's version in Lisan is better: "ta'arraba aba'i, fahalla sarahum / min al-mawti ramla 'Aliji wa-Zarud." These are two known places in the land of the Arabs.]] He means: cut them, then its "ya'" which was the "lam" of the verb was moved and made the "ayn" of the verb, and its "ayn" was changed and made its "lam," so it was said: "sar yasir," as it was said: "'athi ya'tha 'athan," then its "lam" was changed and made its "ayn," so it was said: "'aha ya'idhu." [[See what preceded of that at 2: 123, 124.]]
* *
As for the grammarians of Basra, they said: "fasurhunna ilayk," whether read with a damma on the "sad" or with a kasra, has the same meaning in this place: cutting. They said: They are two dialects: one is "sara yasur," and the other "sara yasir," and they cited as evidence the verse of Tawba ibn al-Humayyir mentioned before, and the verse of al-Mu'alla ibn Jammal al-Abdi [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "ibn Hammad," which is an error, as all the references agree that it is "ibn Jamal" with a jim or "Bani Hammal" with a ha. It is attributed to Aws ibn Hajar al-Tamimi, and to another other than him who is also called Aws ibn Hajar, as you see in the references mentioned after.]]:
And there came a choice flock of smooth-flanked, pure ewes, whose kids a black, marked he-goat separates.
[[Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubayda 1: 81; Amali al-Qali 2: 52; al-Tanbih: 93; Simt al-Lali: 685, 686; then in Lisan al-Arab (zi'ab), (sawr), (dahs), (khala'), (sawa'), (anaq), (zanam). The verse is attributed to Aws ibn Hajar in this form: "yaswa' anuqaha ahwa zanim / lahu zi'ab kama sakhiba al-gharim," which is a composite verse. The correct version in the lexicon entry (zanam): "wa-jaat khul'atun dahsun safaya / yasuru anuqaha ahwa zanim / yufarriqu baynaha sadi'un rabahu / lahu za'bun kama sakhiba al-gharim."]] meaning: he separates its kids and cuts them. And with the verse of al-Khansa':
"Lazallat al-shumm minha wa-hiya tansar..."
[[Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubayda 1: 81 and its references there. The verse is not in her Diwan.]]
By "al-shumm" she means the mountains, that they split and separate. And with the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 260 (part 3 of 4):

فَانْصَرْنَ مِنْ فَزَعٍ وَسَدَّ فُرُوجَهُ ... غُبْرٌ ضَوَارٍ: وَافِيَانِ وَأَجْدَعُ [[Diwanuhu: 12. Al-Mufaddaliyyat: 873. Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu ʿUbayda: 81. Al-Adddad of al-Asmaʿi and Ibn al-Sikkit: 33, 187. This narration, which Abu ʿUbayda, al-Asmaʿi, Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Tabari transmit as "fa-nasrun" ("so they turned away"), is a strange reading, and within the context of the poem it is even stranger. I reject its meaning, and I find that it disrupts the verse. The context is a description of a wild bull, a bull whose prime has passed, which the dogs of the hunters have continually terrified until they struck fear into its heart. When morning comes, fear enters it lest a hunter ambush it with his dogs. It keeps casting its eye into the hidden corners of the land and then falls silent to listen, so that its hearing confirms what it sees. At that moment it stands in the sun, warming itself from the dew of the night. Then Abu Dhu'ayb says: "Then it began to turn its back, and there appeared to it / the first of the pursuing hounds, close and being held back." He means: the vanguard of the dogs appeared to it, having drawn near to it, while the hunter restrained them until he released them all upon it. "It was startled by a fright, and the dogs closed its paths: / grey fierce ones, two complete ones and a cropped-eared one." He means: the fear agitated it, so it ran a fierce run while the dogs were behind it and around it, having cut off its escape route. It is also transmitted as "fa-nasaʿa min faza" ("it fled from fright"), meaning it went off in one direction. "Al-ghubr al-dawari" are the hunter's dogs. "Minha wafiyan" refers to two dogs whose ears were intact. "Al-ajda'" is one whose ear is cut off, either as a mark on it or from long practice in hunting bulls, which gored it with their horns until its ears were severed.]]

They said: the saying of the speaker "ṣurtu al-shay'" has two meanings: I inclined it, and I cut it. They also related by transmission: "ṣurnā bihi al-ḥukm", meaning: we decided the judgment by it.

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: This view that we have mentioned from the Basrans, namely that the vowelling of the "ṣād" in His saying ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾ (with a ḍamma or a kasra) is the same in meaning, that both are dialectal variants with the meaning here of "cut them up", and that the phrase "ilayka" (to you) is placed before "fa-ṣurhunna" because it is connected to His saying "fa-khudh" (take), is closer to the truth than the view of those Kufan grammarians whom we cited, who denied that cutting has an intelligible sense in this context except by way of the inversion I mentioned. [[The wording: "... is closer to the truth ... because of the consensus of all the people of ta'wil ..."]] The consensus of the people of ta'wil is that the meaning of His saying ﴿fa-ṣurhunna﴾ does not depart from one of two meanings: either "cut them up", or "gather them to you", whether read with a kasra or a ḍamma. Their unanimous agreement on this, without any of them distinguishing between the meanings of the two readings, I mean the kasra and the ḍamma, provides clear evidence for the soundness of the view of the Basran grammarians whom we cited, and for the error of the view of the Kufan grammarians. For if they had interpreted His saying ﴿fa-ṣurhunna﴾ to mean "cut them up", on the basis that the original form was "fa-ॐāṣirhunna" [i.e. fa-āṣirhunna], and then it was altered to "fa-ṣirhunna" with a kasra, by the transposition of the "ya" (of the root ṣ-y-r) and the moving of the "ra" into the place of the "ya", then, without doubt, given their knowledge of their language and their understanding of its speech, they would have distinguished between the meaning when it is read with a kasra on the "ṣād" and its meaning when read with a ḍamma, since it would not be permissible for one who altered "fa-āṣirhunna" to "fa-ṣirhunna" to read it "fa-ṣurhunna" with a ḍamma on the "ṣād". Yet they, despite their differing readings, interpreted it as one meaning in one of the two senses we mentioned. In that is the clearest evidence of the error of the one who said that when it is read with a kasra on the "ṣād", interpreted as "cutting", it is an inversion of "ṣaray yaṣrā" into "ṣāra yaṣīru" [i.e. the root ṣ-r-y/ṣ-w-r], and the ignorance of one who claimed that the speech of the Arabs does not know "ṣāra yaṣūru" and "ṣāra yaṣīru" in the sense of "cut".

* *

Mention of those present with us regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fa-ṣurhunna﴾, that it means: "then cut them up".

5994 – Sulayman ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbar related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Salt related to us, saying: Abu Kudayna related to us, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbas: concerning ﴿fa-ṣurhunna﴾ he said: "It is Nabataean (nabaṭiyya), so split them up." [[The report 5994: "Sulayman ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbar ibn Zurayq al-Khayyat." Ibn Abi Hatim said: my father was asked about him and said: "truthful"; I heard Hajjaj ibn al-Shaʿir praising him exceedingly and mentioning him with goodness. He is biographied in al-Tahdhib and Tarikh Baghdad 9:52. "Muhammad ibn al-Salt ibn al-Hajjaj al-Asadi" passed as no. 3002. "Abu Kudayna" is Yahya ibn al-Muhallab al-Bajali, who passed as no. 4193 without a biography. Ibn Maʿin, Abu Dawud and al-Nasaʾi said: "reliable". He is biographied in al-Tahdhib.]]

5995 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar related to us, saying: Shuʿba related to us, from Abu Jamra, from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said concerning this verse ﴿fa-khudh arbaʿatan mina al-ṭayr fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾ [take four of the birds and cut them up to you]: "It is only a parable." He said: "Cut them up, then place them in the quarters of the world, a quarter here and a quarter there, then call them and they will come to you running." [[The report 5995: "Abu Jamra" is Nasr ibn ʿImran ibn ʿIsam al-Dabbaʿi. He related from his father, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar and others. Shuʿba, Ibrahim ibn Tahman, his son ʿAlqama and others related from him. He is biographied in al-Tahdhib. He passed without a biography as no. 3250, and the letter "ra" of his name ("Jamra") dropped out in print. In the printed and manuscript editions it is "Abu Hamza", which is an error.]]

5996 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Muʿawiya related to me, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn ʿAbbas: concerning ﴿fa-ṣurhunna﴾ he said: "Cut them up."

5997 – Yaʿqub related to me, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Husayn informed us, from Abu Malik concerning His saying ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾: he says, "Cut them up."

5998 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn ʿAwn related to us, saying: Hushaym informed us, from Husayn, from Abu Malik, the same.

5999 – Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Yaman related to us, from Ashʿath, from Jaʿfar, from Saʿid: concerning ﴿fa-ṣurhunna﴾ he said: "The wing of this one is at the head of that one, and the head of that one is at the wing of this one."

6000 – Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla related to us, saying: al-Muʿtamir ibn Sulayman related to us, from his father, who said: Abu ʿAmr claimed, from ʿIkrima concerning His saying ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾: "ʿIkrima said in Nabataean: cut them up."

6001 – Ahmad ibn Ishaq related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad related to us, saying: Israʾil related to us, from Yahya, from Mujahid: ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾ he said: "Cut them up."

6002 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Huzayfa related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾: "Pluck them by their feathers, and tear their flesh to pieces," [[This wording appears in both places, in the manuscript and the printed edition, except that in the printed edition it reads "intafhunna" with dots, while in the manuscript it reads "isfhunna" without dots. I think it should be read: "ashbiʿhunna, rishahunna wa-luhumahunna tamziqan" ("satisfy them, their feathers and their flesh with tearing"), or a letter close in meaning to this.]] then mix their flesh with their feathers.

6003 – Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim related to us, from ʿIsa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾ he said: "Pluck them by their feathers, and tear their flesh to pieces." [[This wording appears in both places, in the manuscript and the printed edition, except that in the printed edition it reads "intafhunna" with dots, while in the manuscript it reads "isfhunna" without dots. I think it should be read: "ashbiʿhunna, rishahunna wa-luhumahunna tamziqan", or a letter close in meaning to this.]]

6004 – Bishr ibn Muʿadh related to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ related to us, saying: Saʿid related to us, from Qatada: ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾: the Prophet of God (peace be upon him) was commanded to take four of the birds and slaughter them, then mix together their flesh, their feathers and their blood.

6005 – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatada concerning His saying ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾: he said: "Tear them apart." He said: "He was commanded to mix the bloods with the bloods and the feathers with the feathers, then place upon every mountain a portion of them."

6006 – Related to me, on the authority of al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Muʿadh say: ʿUbayd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak (on ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾) say: "Split them," and it is in Nabataean "ṣarrā", which means splitting.

6007 – Musa related to me, saying: ʿAmr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾ he says: "Cut them up."

6008 – From ʿAmmar related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar related to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ concerning His saying ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾: he says: "Cut them up to you and tear them into pieces."

6009 – Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, from Ibn Ishaq: ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾, that is, "cut them up," and it is "al-ṣawr" in the speech of the Arabs. [[Al-ṣawr: the term denotes cutting or splitting something into parts.]]

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: From what we have mentioned of the views of those whose reports we have transmitted, concerning His saying ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾ as meaning "then cut them up to you", there is clear evidence for the soundness of what we have said regarding this, and the invalidity of the view of those who disagree with us.

Since this is so, it is equally valid whether the reciter reads it with a ḍamma on the "ṣād", "fa-ṣurhunna" ilayka, or with a kasra, "fa-ṣirhunna", since they are two well-known dialects with one meaning. [[In the printed edition: "an kānat al-lughatān maʿrūfatayn", which does not correctly read the manuscript, owing to the scribe's haste in what he wrote and his neglect.]] However, although that is so, the one I prefer to recite is "fa-ṣurhunna ilayka" with a ḍamma on the "ṣād", because it is the higher and more common of the two dialects, and the more widely used among the Arabs.

* *

[As for the view of those who interpreted His saying ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾ as meaning "gather them, turn them towards you, and bring them together", it is a view held by a small group of the people of ta'wil.] [[What is placed between these brackets is an addition I have deduced from the context of the tafsir. It is his refutation of the first view, which passed on pages 469, lines 3 to 7, and he did not return to mention it again. In the printed edition, in its place, it reads: "And according to a small group of the people of ta'wil it means: 'make firm'" (awthaq). This is a modification by an early copyist or the printer. The manuscript, however, has its text connected with what precedes and follows: "and most of them in the Arab tribes among the people of ta'wil are a small group: mention of those who said this." What I have deduced is, God willing, closer to the context of the tafsir. This is another proof of the copyist's great negligence in many places due to his haste and lack of care.]]

Mention of those who said this:

6010 – Muhammad ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾: "ṣurhunna" means: "make them firm (awthiqhunna)."

6011 – Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I asked ʿAṭāʾ about His saying ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾, and he said: "Gather them to you."

6012 – Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: ﴿fa-ṣurhunna ilayka﴾: "Gather them."

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Then place upon every mountain a portion of them, then call them, and they will come to you running﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: The people of ta'wil differed regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿thumma ijʿal ʿala kulli jabalin minhunna juzʾan﴾ [then place upon every mountain a portion of them].

Some of them said: it means: upon every quarter of the world, a portion of them.

Mention of those who said this:

6013 – Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar related to us, saying: Shuʿba related to us, from Abu Jamra, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿thumma ijʿal ʿala kulli jabalin minhunna juzʾan﴾ he said: "Place them in the quarters of the world: a quarter here, a quarter here, a quarter here, and a quarter here, then call them, and they will come to you running." [[In the printed and manuscript editions it reads "ʿan Abi Hamza", which is an error. See the preceding comment on report 5995.]]

6014 – Muhammad ibn Saʿd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas: ﴿thumma ijʿal ʿala kulli jabalin minhunna juzʾan﴾ he said: "When he had tied them up, he slaughtered them, then placed upon every mountain a portion of them."

6015 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Saʿid related to us, from Qatada, who said: The Prophet of God was commanded to take four birds and slaughter them, then mix together their flesh, feathers and blood, then divide them among four mountains. It has been related to us that he sprinkled [shakala] upon their wings, [[I have not understood the meaning of "shakala ʿala ajniḥatihinna" (sprinkled upon their wings). Perhaps there is a corruption in it that I have not discerned, or perhaps it means that he scattered the feathers of their wings. I have not found this report in any other place.]] and held their heads in his hand. The bone went to the bone, the feather to the feather, and the morsel to the morsel, and that was by the eye of the friend of God, Abraham (peace be upon him). Then he called them, and they came to him running on their feet, each bird flying to its head. [[In the printed and manuscript editions it reads: "wa-yulqi kulla ṭayrin bi-raʾsihi", and the correct reading is with "ilā" added.]] This is a parable which God gave to Abraham, meaning: just as He raised these birds from these four mountains, so God will raise people on the Day of Resurrection from the quarters and regions of the earth.

6016 – Related to me, on the authority of ʿAmmar, who said: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar related to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ, who said: He slaughtered them, then cut them up, then mixed together their flesh and feathers, then divided them into four portions, placing upon every mountain a portion of them. The bone went to the bone, the feather to the feather, and the morsel to the morsel, and that was by the eye of the friend of God, Abraham. Then he called them and they came to him running; that is, they ran on their feet. This is a parable which God showed Abraham, meaning: just as I raised these birds from these four mountains, so God will raise people on the Day of Resurrection from the quarters and regions of the earth.

6017 – Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq related to us, from some people of knowledge, that the People of the Book relate that he took the four birds, then cut each bird into four parts, then went to four mountains and placed upon each mountain a quarter of each bird. Upon each mountain there was a quarter of a peacock, a quarter of a rooster, a quarter of a crow and a quarter of a dove. Then he called them and said: "Come, by God's permission, as you were." Each quarter leapt to its companion until they were gathered together, and each bird was as it had been before he cut it. Then they came to him running, as God said. It was said: "O Abraham, thus does God gather His servants and revive the dead for resurrection, from the east and west of the earth, and its north and south!" So God showed him the reviving of the dead by His power, until he knew that, meaning what Nimrod had said of falsehood and vanity. [[In the printed edition: "bi-ghayr mā qāla Namrūd" (other than what Nimrod said), and in the manuscript: "bi-ʿayr mā qāla", unpointed; the correct reading is what I have given. This is an explanation of the reference in His saying "until he knew that".]]

6018 – Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: ﴿thumma ijʿal ʿala kulli jabalin minhunna juzʾan﴾: "He took a peacock, a dove, a crow and a rooster, then said: 'Separate them. Place the head of each one with the breast [jawshawsh] of another, the wing of another, and the leg of another with it.'" [[Al-jawshawsh: the breast. It is said: "a portion of the night has passed" (madā jawshawsh min al-layl), meaning a part of it has gone, by metaphorical extension from this.]] So he cut them and separated them into quarters upon the mountains, then called them, and they came to him all together. God said: "As you called them and they came to you, so, having revived these and gathered them after this, likewise I will gather these also," meaning the dead.

* *

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: "then place upon every mountain of the mountains" which the birds and the beasts of prey that were eating the flesh of the animal Abraham had seen dead had reached. Abraham, on seeing it, asked that God show him how He would revive it and the rest of the dead besides it. They said: there were seven mountains.

Mention of those who said this:

6019 – Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: When Abraham said what he said upon seeing the animal from which the birds and beasts of prey had scattered as he drew near to it, and he asked his Lord what he asked, [God said:] ﴿fa-khudh arbaʿatan mina al-ṭayr﴾ [take four of the birds]. Ibn Jurayj said: So he slaughtered them, then mixed together their blood, feathers and flesh, then placed upon every mountain a portion of them, wherever he had seen the birds and beasts of prey go. He said: So he made them seven portions and held their heads with him, then called them by God's permission, and he watched every drop of blood fly to the other drop, every feather fly to the other feather, and every morsel and every bone fly, some of it to other parts, from the tops of the mountains, until each corpse met the other in the sky. Then they came running until each reached its head.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 2, verse 260 (part 4 of 4):

6020 - Musa related to me, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, who said: ﴿Take four birds and make them incline toward you﴾, then place on seven mountains a portion of them on each mountain, then call them and they will come to you running! So Ibrahim took four birds and cut them into pieces, and did not place a piece of one bird with its companion. Then he placed the head of this one with the leg of that one, and the breast of this one with the wing of that one, and divided them among seven mountains. Then he called them, and each piece flew to its companion, and then they all came to him.

* *

Others said: Rather, God commanded him to place that on every mountain.

Mention of those who said that:

6021 - Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: ﴿Then place on every mountain a portion of them﴾, he said: Then scatter them over every mountain, then call them and they will come to you running; and thus God gives life to the dead.

6022 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Huthayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: Then make them into parts on every mountain, then call them and they will come to you running; thus God gives life to the dead. It is a parable which God struck for Ibrahim.

6023 - Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to us, saying: Ibn Jurayj said, Mujahid said: ﴿Then place on every mountain a portion of them﴾, then scatter them as parts over every mountain = then ﴿call them﴾, come by God's permission. Thus God gives life to the dead. It is a parable which God struck for Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

6024 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to me, saying: Abu Zuhayr related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: He commanded him to vary their legs, heads and wings, then place on every mountain a portion of them.

6025 - I was told on the authority of al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say, concerning His saying: ﴿Then place on every mountain a portion of them﴾, so Ibrahim varied their legs and wings.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct interpretation of the verse is what Mujahid said, namely that God, may His remembrance be exalted, commanded Ibrahim to scatter the four birds' parts, after cutting them up, over all the mountains which Ibrahim could reach at the time God charged him with scattering them and dispersing their parts upon them. For God, may His remembrance be exalted, said to him: ﴿Then place on every mountain a portion of them﴾, and "kull" (every) is a particle that indicates encompassing what it is attached to; its form is singular but its meaning is plural. [[See what preceded regarding the meaning of "kull", 3:195.]].

If that is so, then the mountains on which God commanded Ibrahim to place the parts of the four birds cannot be outside one of two meanings: either they are some of them, or all of them.
